_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game, and considering the game description, especially the emphasis on character development, I ended up being very disappointed and unsatisfied.  TLDR:  While you could get the game on sale for less that 5 USD (DO NOT SPEND MORE THAN THIS!, I got it for $3.74), do you really want to spend your TIME on a poor experience?  Much of the negative reviews are accurate.  The game is downright clunky, and feels unfinished.  There is a lack of rebinding for all keys.  Putting parry on the same key as shoot just ends up messing up parry, which resulted in my VERY rarely using it.  I mostly used it just in testing, concluding it not to be worth the effort.Stealth in this game is very strange.  You get no feed back as to how stealthy you are being at any time.  You just try sneaking up to enemies and try to one hit kill them.  You will actually probably spend most of the game playing this way.  Sneak, hit with the biggest baddest weapon you have, kill that enemy, and those around him don't get aggroed at all.  So you just rinse and repeat.  Most poorly thought out stealth system EVER.Enemies can charge you in this game.  After they miss you, because of course you will dodge, the enemy will not stop, or hit a wall, etc... No, they will abrupt bounce off an imaginary wall and make a beeline right at you.  It is the most annoying janky mechanic for rushing I have every encountered.  This happens for one boss encounter too where he throws two weapons at you.  Yea, dodging those were SO much fun. :/  What were they thinking?!Most enemies just attack left or right, probably due to the severe lack of animations for up or down movement for enemies.  No way they would get diagonal animations haha, yea, right.  Only the main character has animations for 8 cardinal directions, BUT not for attack.  Oh, you will attack in the correct direction, but it just won't look like it, hahaha.  This results in some very gimmicky type of methods for killing enemies.  A good rule-of-thumb is to attack enemies from the top or bottom.  The bigger they are the easier it is to hit them without them being able to hit you, as their hit box is their entire size, and maybe a bit more.  Oh, and you can attack through walls or obstacle  with ease.There are a fair amount of weapons, but you will only use a few.  If you can figure out what enemies are weak to one of the 5? "elements" in the game, some of the elemental weapons, fully upgrade with the same element, can one shot some of the elite enemies.  This takes some trial and error because there is virtually no feedback from the game other than trying to guess at how much the health bar went down for each weapon element.  No numbers pop up or log.  You just have to guess.  So you will just be using a few elemental weapons and a couple hard hitting weapons.  Fast attack weapons are not very useful as you won't be able to get in more than a couple shots, and a harder hitting weapon will attack just fast enough for you to get a good hit in and then dodge away.Oh, did I forget to mention you can shoot in the game?  This is also pretty janky, but can be quite effective, and the game AI doesn't handle it very well.  Ammo mostly plentiful.  So if you want the game to be even more boring, you can shoot most things to death from a distance.I am probably missing some more things, with the game mechanics, but you get the idea.As for the story, meh.  I really was hoping for some twist or something that gave it more depth.  You could have just replaced everything with Satan and his demon followers, and it would have fit perfectly into the story.  It is just not a very compelling story.  Also, the art direction is very uninspired.  Just blood and gore everywhere for everything in some shape or form.  Just so boring.Summary:  Everything about the game is meh, and results in a poor experience.  If I could, and would refund the $3.74, but I can't get my time back.  I feel like I should be payed for playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay Morbid: The Seven Acolytes its a weird game, its like a mix of metroidvania and dark souls..The good:The game itself has some diverse mobs and maps which also are quite beautiful so that's always a +, you also have a rune mechanic which boosts your weapon dps, blessings(aka lvl's.), its not hard to finish it if you just follow the path ahead of you.,the insanity mechanic is nice but its very niche with no major penalty if you reach zero, the worse thing that can happen is enemy can respawn as a ghost and you  can just kill it again so no biggie, i think that's about it.The bad:Uh.. where do i start.. okay so first this game has the weirdest chest mechanic i ever saw.. if you open(break) a chest and you rest at a shrine(bonfire) the chests which had weapons or consumables drop again.. which can led to a infinite farm method for some consumables which it's super stupid.,the map system is eh.. bad most of the time i had to make a map in my own head to know where i was because you can only check a map at a shrine(bonfire) and from there you have to deduct where your position is on the map.. and now for the last part,The ugly:Okay here i have some more complains that made me think less of the game, so here i start.First off.. the bosses are mediocre at best, from all the bosses in the game only 2~3 made me actually think how should i approach the fight, the others were just move away 2m and use strong attack, run again away 2m and use strong attack then rinse and repeat until the boss is dead., the mobs also work the same way.. some of them were more unique but other than that it was niche, they do look good tho but that alone cant carry them., the weapons are also mediocre, you don't have a category from weapons besides their attack speed.. which makes them either fast-normal-slow-super slow in attacks(the highest was 140 base attack speed vs i think.. 65?~) no move set for weapons just basic light/heavy attack(i found 2~3 weapons that had so to say a boss attack instead of heavy attack but that's about it).,the xp in this game is badly done since you get no penalty towards xp even if you die and you don't lose any items or anything so you could just throw your body at the enemy until you succeed if that tickles your fancy., story wise.. im gonna be honest i had no idea what the game is about.. something about some slayer race that got wiped out and you are the only one left so you have to kill the gods to redeem yourself or something..very meh, the worst part was the fact that when you take any type of dmg may it be a 1 dot from a bleed/poison you will not attack, so if you wanted to attack somebody and was winding up a strong attack and you got hit well you have to redo it again, so you lost your stamina for the attack and the strong attack as well, there is no poise for the enemy so they can always attack you if you dmg them. :)This is one of those moments where i wish steam had a neutral vote option instead of yes/no but i did enjoy my time in this game so i will give it a thumbs up, should you play this game? sure.. was fun.

_childDocuments_.review: + Simple, yet satisfying combat+ Very cool level up mechanic+ Nice enemy and boss variety+ Excellent graphics- Frustrating map design- Frequent gameplay annoyances- Very limited settingsSouls-like games are very hit-or-miss – it’s kinda hard to replicate what made the Souls series work so well. Yet every once in a while, we get an indie studio that tries to do just that – and some can get pretty close. Morbid is the latest to try to break into the genre, this time from an isometric viewpoint.Morbid: The Seven Acolytes is a solid take on the Souls-like genre. It’s got some incredibly fun combat, a very cool level up mechanic in place of the traditional skill-based one, nice enemy and boss variety, and some excellent graphics rounding it all out. It isn’t without its issues – mainly with regards to its map design and frequent gameplay annoyances – but it is definitely worth a look for fans of the genre – it’s one of the better ones to have come out this year.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Long story short, this game has some interesting foundation, but fails to build upon it and forms a lackluster experience that just fizzles out way too fast.As you can probably see from the screenshots, the game looks great. And it looks great in game too. The aesthetic is interesting. But, like I always say, after initial wow moment you start looking through the prettiness, and start looking at what's beneath. There, you find that it's a relatively competent soulslike hack and slash. The moves feel good, combat feels satisfying... so it should be good, right? And yet, it's just... not. Maybe it's because the enemy AI is incredibly easy to outmaneuver, even if the constant threat of getting killed in just a few hits is keeping things at least somewhat fresh. The enemy design is, in one word, annoying. Not talking about their visual design - it's all a little too samey and gory, but that's beside the point - I'm talking about their combat behaviour. You have your regular dudes who approach you and slash you until you die, you have larger dudes who approach you and stab you slowly until you die -  those are serviceable but uninspired, they walk right into your attacks. But then there are enemies which spawn smaller flying enemies that are hard to hit. It's just an annoyance. Then, there are some ranged enemies who sometimes attack you on sight, sometimes... not. And even then, dodging their attacks is not fun, even if they're not immediately dangerous. Not sure why, is it the bullet pattern, speed?Then there's the world. The lore is, well, dare I say gorecore? You know what I mean. Crapsack world possessed by fleshy monstrosities. Literally everything sucks, there is no hope. And it's done in such a way that it seems that even if you do manage to succeed, everything is too messed up to even attempt any reconstruction. But even such worlds manage to be interesting. This one? I don't know. Lots of lore dumps, not enough of actual feeling for how everything is. This also means that the levels are just not very interesting. Infested wasteland beach, infested village, infested docks, infested cave. Locations are just more of the same. Games which require repetition due to difficulty must have good, detailed environment design to make the progression easier to track, and also to reward the player with interesting places and vistas. Here it's easy to just get lost, since everything looks the same. The sameyness is so strong, it becomes almost immediately obvious that the levels will just be a slog - and indeed, the game delivers on that promise.There are also some minor issues which lessen the experience even further. For example, weapon chests respawn, so you can get infinite copies of one weapon. That lessens the worth of the find. I haven't found a way to stash, or even unequip items that are in your shortcuts, and the game doesn't send stuff that you can't carry to your stash. Flesh walls which normally you destroy by destroying their 'kernel' regrow every time you rest or leave the screen, and then explode the moment you approach (since they should be already dead in the first place).So... yeah. It's a rather flawed piece. I can't really think of anything redeeming about it, apart maybe from the fact that the pixel art clearly took a lot of time to craft. Dev(s), if you're reading this, apologies for such a scathing critique. I hope you can learn from this and make better games in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Morbid: The Seven Acolytes. I was genuinely impressed by the mechanics of this game. Yeah, it's a bit something to get used to using the usual souls formula with stamina based attack system, but the actual gem in this game was the parry system. If you could learn all the different parry timings of the enemies, you'd have a great time clearing out every single last group of enemies. As you progress through the story, you'd start to learn which enemies are genuinely a decent enemy which you don't mind wailing on, and then you get the tiny spores and the ghost skulls that just...infuriate me to no end. I like them big swords so I have to start planning my attack so far ahead like I'm busy investing in Bitcoin and if I get hit once, it cancels my attack. This game has a great variety of weapons to use, with a new system which is called the Sanity. The less you have of this, the more damage and XP you earn, however, the drawback is that you'll more often than not have to face the enemy you just killed again as it revives as an apparition. The levels were beautiful, the music made the whole ambience and filled up the world with a sense of mystery and dread. There were a level or two that I really didn't enjoy because it was difficult to understand where to go because of the colors and the top down view.Because this game is a 2D souls-like game, it will suffer from the obvious thing: Hitboxes that don't really coincide with the position of the character. What I mean with this is that you can really exploit it where you stand diagonally from enemies and you'll be able to hit them. This also works against you and if you don't utilize your roll/dodge, you'll die more often than not. But, this is a part of the game so I think that's why it personally didn't bother me. I know it would probably bother some other people though.Fun game that took me around 12 hours to complete and get 100%, but I'm not the best in these types of games, even though I thoroughly enjoy them. I think if you are a fan of any souls-like games and you have a love for pixelated graphix, then this is a game for you. With the generous content, levels, weapons, ranged weapons, a parry system that I personally find very precise and I loved it, it really is worth it for the price, sale or no. Highly recommend.It's Morbin time - Some cringy singer that can't act.

_childDocuments_.review: It's way too slow and clunky even for a souls like. The enemy AI is obnoxiously bad, and they did a terrible job with the top down aspect of it. I find the polish to be severely lacking, the maps are nonsensical, they're like somebody put art over a voronoi pattern. _childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD.....+ Excellent graphics and music + Frequent new weapons and items to discover + No bugs or unfairness in combat + You can “break” the combat with certain items, which feels great + Frequent save points and no need for grinding + Sanity mechanic is interesting, though I wish it had more impact on the game + Level design is well made, though sometimes finding the next area can provide challenges THE BAD......- The game offers various battle mechanics, but melee combat is the only viable playstyle - The weapons could have more difference in their playstyles - The early game is dull due to too slow stamina recovery - The early game bosses and enemies are boring due to having no relevant variety in their attacks - For some reason most of the “blessings” (skills) are only left for the last 1-2 hours, and on the other hand you only get your first blessing 1-2 hours in. I see no reason why access to all blessings is not offered earlier on. - A bit pricey for the amount of content it offersCONCLUSION......The game hurts itself by limiting the early game with limited stamina and skills, since the most fun comes with them unlocked. The melee combat also seriously lacks in depth - especially in the early game. You will have most fun with the game in the later half, when you can run through it spamming roll and smashing enemies with few hits while enjoying the awesome graphics and music. In short, the game makes a fine dark themed hack-and-slash, once you get through the early hours, and you recognize that head-on melee combat is the only proper way to play the game.7 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: after reading the developer's comment and reading the subsequent link I've decided I'm going to finish the game and replace my review upon completion. it is very easy to forget not all developers are big companies with a dozen people. This feels a lot like someone's "first game", it feels largely incomplete and many of the design choices don't make any sense. Disclaimer: I've played 7 hours and probably won't play much more if any at all. The story: feels generic and uninspired - I can't really say much more than that without ruining anything. but you could literally play "generic action RPG madlibs" and probably get it mostly right. MechanicsHit Box Detection: is wildly inaccurate. I'm behind an enemy they swing left and I get hit? Or i'm facing an enemy swing my sword and somehow magically miss? Weapon Rune System: you can put runes on your weapons, no way to know how many runes you have on your weapon or how many slots it even has without having it selected. Then when you have it selected you don't have a way of identifying what runes are actually installed, Hope you don't forget! The rune removal tool is a consumable (takes up inventory space) so there is a limited number to how many you can have in your inventory. The rune removal tool also destroys the runes so there is no reusing them. maybe you can get a better way of removing them later on? that would make sense but I don't think i'm going to play enough to find out. Weapon buffs: most weapon buffs are self explanatory. however there were a few that I could not figure out, there was no explanation for, and after testing I still had no idea what it did. Namely bleeding and "sanity loss" did not appear to do anything to the enemies. and there was no way in game of finding out at least as far as I could tell. repetitive combat: combat literally boiled down to, get behind enemy, power attack, dodge, repeat. poor/no controller support: When i plug a controller in (because the keyboard controls are awful) i have no way of accessing the inventory. So i had to boot up DS4 windows in order to use my controller. Inventory: limited space inventory (diablo 2 style) with a limited "stash". what is the point of having a limited inventory AND a limited stash? limited inventory i get, but having a finite amount of space in the stash makes little sense to me. Flawed upgrades: you get 3 upgrades after beating your first boss. More Health, More healing from healing item, and faster stamina recovery. The faster stamina recovery is misleading. the stamina bar refills a lot faster, but the cool down from attack to the start of refill does not change at all. So you can attack, dodge, run and be out of stamina because the recharge has not kicked in yet. then when it finally does kick in, lighting fast. If you've mad it this far thank you for reading. I really wanted to like this game. But i just couldn't get behind it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a perfect example why you cant really make a decent balanced soulsborne by a small indie studio.By a glance the game offers a bunch of different mechanics, that kinda mix bloodborne and sekiro ideas, but most of them are unrewarding or completely pointless:- shooting does little damage and you have too little ammo to bother- an entire trigger button is dedicated to stealth, but additional stealth damage isnt that great to spend time on sneaking on enemies.- parrying/blocking and close combat in general is badly telegraphed, ill timed and overall horribly implemented and unrewarding. Your best bet is not to engage in melee, but dodge and reenter combat.- bad attack telegraphing makes dodging possible, but unreliable.- after first attack most enemies immediatly counterattack, but because melee combat isnt worth the effort, fast melee attacks are almost useless.- weapons movesets are short and dont differ much, so you're basically stuck with a very few possible attacks overall.All of the above leaves you with clubbing oncoming enemies with timed heavy attacks on the verge of your range, rolling back and repeating, which gets quite tedious after a short while. Most enemies have a one or two possible attack moves. Bosses have a little variation in their attacks, but still mostly you get every enemy by the same strategy.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel really bad giving this a negative review, but hear me out.I’ve been playing hack n slashly / melee combat kinda games since the 16 bit days.  Secret of Mana, Illusion of Gaia, Terranigma, various Ys games, various Zeldas, all the Darksiders, all the Devil May Crys, all the Soulsborne except Demon Souls, Noih, Bastion, Hyper Light Drifter… you get the idea.  This kinda Sh1t is my bread and butter.Seven Acolytes ticked all the boxes for me, an isometric Bloodborne meets Bastion with great music and amazing pixel art.  I even picked it up on launch day.  But after even a few minutes, I knew that this was not a title that I could enjoy playing because the enemies don’t stagger or have their animation interrupted when they take damage, or if they do, the stagger animation is so miniscule I couldn’t notice it.  So every time I hit an enemy, I would either have to parry immediately and thus break my combo or (more often then not) I would get hit because the enemy would strike while I was still in my combat animation and we’d do this weird, overlapping hit dance which boiled down to a war of attrition. Or we’d no this other weird dance where I was having to dodge/parry between every hit and there was no rhythm or flow to anything.   That is, when the enemies where actually attacking in my direction. I understand that this is by design, but this was in no way for me fun and I knew that I would not enjoy this. Hitting an enemy once, rolling a way, hitting them once again, then rolling away again, is not fun for me. I’m an old hand at these sorts of games I can tell quite early on the difference between what for me will be difficult mechanics that I’ll get the hang of or mechanics that I will not enjoy, and sadly this was the latter.I’m definitely not saying that this is a bad game, but it definitely was not for me.  Again, I feel bad giving this a negative review as clearly the devs put a lot of love and effort into it.  If you don't mind that enemies don't stagger you may absolutely love this - i couldn't enjoy it. FYI, if you are looking for an indie Bloodborne, I suggest you look out Lucah: Born of A Dream.  It may have a very weird aesthetic and art style, but that game absolutely nails isometric Souls/Bloodborne combat.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but I begrudgingly started dragging my feet to try and finish the game and still quitting when I got to the final boss. It has a Bloodborne like mechanic with the main weapon and then a gun secondary to fight enemies. It was interesting starting out but then got really monotonous and boring about halfway through the game. There were a lot of negatives with this game largely with fighting mechanics, weapons/upgrades, map, and enemy/boss design. Most of the enemy or boss encounters are dodge-hit-dodge-hit-dodge-hit which gets old fast. Halfway through the game, the enemy and bosses start becoming huge damage sponges. If I didn't have any gun ammo, it would take 10+ minutes just to get the bosses health down to kill it. When I was at the final boss, I slipped up on my 2nd or 3rd attempt almost killing it and then later after more attempts ran out of gun ammo. Didn't feel like doing it after that and I'm not sure if there is even a place to farm gun ammo. Along with the enemy & boss issues, the run-back to a boss or area was very frustrating in some parts of the game. The weapons and upgrades are very limited. You will find there is only a limited number of weapons worth using and you end up using only them 3/4 of the game. There are other weapons later on but the stats are useless on them which is annoying. The weapon upgrades consist of rune slots which can be fire, electric dmg, poison, life steal etc. but majority of the time, you only need fire dmg or  attack speed. All the other ones are gimmicky.  There are quests that give you more weapons/items but most of the time these items are useless. Another issue with that made the game frustrating was the map. You have no idea where you are at as your character is never shown on the map and you only discover other layouts when you find a new shrine to rest at. I would find myself wasting time going into dead ends and having to fight through the same or more enemies as I have no idea where I'm at. Overall, it's right on the line of being mediocre. Only a few bosses and enemies were interesting to fight against. Would not recommend purchasing unless on a large sale. 4/10

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The game isn't fun to play on the most fundamental level. It's rare that I quit a game this early on, but there's just nothing appealing about how this one plays.- Can't rebind gamepad controls- Only 8 directional movement despite having to use the stick for it- You can't instantly stop your movement when letting go of the stick, your character will have to slow down gradually and it feels awkward enough to bother me despite the game not focusing on movement at all- Extremely slow attack animations, slow enough that I would actively avoid attacking things I didn't have to because I knew it would slow down my progress through the level by half. This goes beyond soulslike conventions- Attacks don't have animations matching the direction you're attacking in - you're always swinging to the side even if you're attacking upwards- There are stealth mechanics to slow the game down even more- Not even an hour of playtime and I already collected like 20 different runes that can only be used once to permanently upgrade weapon statistics- The parry doesn't stagger enemies, so you can't take advantage of the extra counter attack damage... especially since you don't seem to actually get that damage boost in the first place for some reason- Weak audio design and repetitive soundtrack- Bad AI - enemies mostly swing in the wrong direction and behave erratically- Bland level design with awkwardly placed invisible barriers. You can't even jump down slight elevation changes, something A Link to the Past figured out back on the SNES.

_childDocuments_.review: To talk about a souls-like, I find the most useful thing to do is look at what's different from dark souls. Loadouts: You can hold two combos of one melee weapon and one range weapon and switch between the two with a button. There are no shields, only parrying. There is no armor, only health. There is no poise, everything staggers you. This means swarms of gnats remain dangerous until the very end.Ranged weapons: guns felt negligible for the entirety of the game. They don't do anywhere near melee damage, have severely limited ammunition, and you would have to use one of your three consumable slots as a reload button.  Stealth: I actually came back to add this after writing everything else- I forgot it was in the game until I saw one of the other reviews mention it. Don't worry about this. You don't have to do it, even if you aren't stealthed enemies won't notice you if you're not in the direction their sprite is facing, and even if you run up to something's front you can usually get a heavy melee attack off before they react.Leveling: There is no money in this game, and so nothing to drop on death to pick up later and no stores. Instead, you get exp on kill and one token per level. Tokens can be spent (with increasing cost per upgrade) to enhance one thing at a time. max health, estus restored per charge, stamina bar, etc. You are limited in the number of aspects you can have enhanced at a time, two to start with one extra per boss cleared. Well, I say that, but you actually have nothing until you kill the first boss. Also, you have to find in the world access to investing in new stats.Weapon upgrades: You can't directly make an object deal more damage, no greatsword plus three. Instead, each item has differing numbers of augment slots, into which you can put elemental damage, health/sanity on kill (flies and traps don't count), or attack speed. I understand the enemies have different resistances, but I never cared to think about it. My first elemental weapon said it did substantially more damage than the greatsword I was swinging, but failed to kill enemies I was oneshotting with the 'weaker' weapon, so the game taught me early that the only stat that really matters is physical damage. Maybe if anything gave me real trouble I'd use a consumeable to put an element on my weapon, but the only trouble I actually found myself in was occasionally needing a faster weapon, not a better damage type. Sanity: this is the vertical bar in the trailers. Sanity, when full, reduces the damage you deal and take. This is terrible. Do not keep sanity full. It's actually somewhat difficult to keep sanity empty, since it regenerates at a point per second if it's low to take away the damage bonus. The damage bonus is substantial. With an upgraded health bar and restoration (the most accessible upgrades), the extra damage taken is negligible. There are two other downsides to low sanity. An obnoxious pulsing filter over the screen to remind you your sanity is low, and you frequently have to kill normal enemies twice. When an enemy dies and you have low sanity, a ghost copy of them will rise from their body. It either has slightly more health than the original, or different resistances, I didn't check.The solution I found to this, and what other reviews refer to as clunky combat, was to use the biggest, heaviest weapon I could find. The range usually means you can hit through walls, through corners, and from positions they just can't hit you from. Keeping low sanity means big heavy weapons tend to kill in one hit. Doubling the enemies doesn't mean anything if you kill both in one hit before they can react.For what it's worth, I enjoyed my time listening to a podcast (sorry to the sound team and anybody who wants to know in the reviews) and giving a parade of nonthreatening enemies the old unga-bunga for a few hours. I have seven hours in game, I beat it, and I feel like I found every shiny thing, so I'd say the game has five to ten hours of content, without counting NG+. I didn't read any of the lore, so I can't comment on it, but I didn't have to and that's on brand. I'm feeling a strong 6/10, no regrets playing it through. I personally wouldn't buy it full price or tell anybody this is a must play. Just give it a shot if you got it from humble bundle or gamepass or something, see if it's for you, and remember to try the Leg.

_childDocuments_.review: It's passable, but in my opinion definitely not worth the full asking price. At the same price point, you could get much more polished and/or expansive isometric games (Hades, Hyper Light Drifter, Grim Dawn) or Metroidvanias with some similarities (Hollow Knight, Blasphemous, Dead Cells, Rogue Legacy 2).Delving deeper, the only thing I feel this game nailed is the atmosphere. I'm a sucker for dark fantasy, and Morbid's world is cool. The sprites and environments look nice, and they did a pretty good job with the world building, but the actual game part of the game is where it falls flat.The combat seemed deliberately designed to be slow and deliberate at first, backed up by some of the dev posts in the forum; your combos are super slow, you get staggered by any damage you take, and enemies don't get staggered by your attacks, but you have a dodge roll and a parry that both give you i-frames. You then learn that you can stagger enemies with perfect parries that allows for a powerful counterattack. As soon as you realize that last fact and start using it, the combat becomes trivialized.You deal puny damage with normal attacks on big enemies and bosses, but learn the perfect parry timing on an attack, and you can down even bosses in a handful of hits. You either do this, or get frustrated spending a ton of time slapping them with what feels like wet noodles while they two or three-shot you. There are a good number of weapons with different reach, attack speeds, elements and some drain effects. Sadly, the optimal, least frustrating, way to play defeats the purpose of having anything other than damage stats. Everything boils down to what weapon hits hardest in a single hit.There are also a bunch of different usable items that you find a literal ton of, but the only ones I ever felt the need to use were the basic health/sanity recovery ones. You are also capped at holding 10 of any one item at a time, so all of the excess that you're guaranteed to find just go to waste. To pile onto this, a lot of the non-respawning loot drops in the world happen to be common usables instead of meaningful loot.All said, a real disappointing gameplay experience given how good the aesthetic and world are.TL;DR If you've got the money and haven't played all of the games I mentioned up top, I highly recommend you check those out before dropping it on this.

_childDocuments_.review: Morbid: The Seven Acolytes is a flawed but still pretty good souls like action game, now then story. The land of Moana is in turmoil, once a great and prosperous kingdom now turned into ruin by evil deities known as the Gahars and there seven acolytes. The Gahars and seven acolytes have twisted the land and the people making horrible monsters and abominations as they rule the land with an iron fist. But there are warriors who desire these evil deities banishment, known as the Strivers they have dedicated their lives in destroying the acolytes for the death of the acolytes means the banishment of the Grisha for they cannot exist in our world without their acolyte tethers, unfortunately there's only one striver left in the Kingdom a lone girl whose fate and hope of an entire land rests on her shoulders.So then the likes, the story is really good like any Souls game the story is told through item and note descriptions, it's quite well written and paints quite a gruesome and tragic picture sort of like bloodborne and like bloodborne the story also takes some good inspiration from Lovecraft with its gods and even certain enemy types, if you're a fan of Lovecraft and read his work you'll definitely get some of the references. The RPG Maker style graphics is really good; it’s pretty well detailed with a great use of colors especially the color red. And each environment is quite pretty to look at, a lot like bloodborne, but also a lot like some Game Boy Advanced games like classic Legend of Zelda.The levels are very good and pretty diverse with each level having a good bloodborne type of feel to it, from a desolate Shore to Gothic City even Haunted Woods and each one has its own unique design that makes you want to explore and discover all its secrets, all wrapped up in this sort of 2D Style that makes you think of classic handheld Legend of Zelda games.The enemies and bosses are really good each one with its own gruesome and horrifying design and unique powers and the enemies as you advance through gets tougher and tougher which helps you keep you on your toes. The bosses are very good as each one has their own unique and gruesome designs; probably the two best bosses with gruesome designs are Lady Tristana, Mother Grief and Bile Toad Putrus, the Spawn Of Disgust.The gameplay was good if you played games like bloodborne or a classic handheld Zelda game then you've played this kind of game before, but there are tough enemies and bosses that keep you on your toes, an expansive world that you must explore in order to find weapons or items to help you progress, there's also these blessings that give your character certain abilities like to run longer, hit harder and ruins that gives a weapon different attributes like fire damage attributes, you also have to balance your sanity like if you have no sanity you can hit harder and gain more XP, but at the cost of having your character fight more monsters. The weapons themselves each have their own unique look, you have your standard axes and swords and firearms, but other weapons have certain abilities like fire and Ice damage or this blood mace that allows you to summon a bunch of spikes from the ground to do more damage. The music is very good with plenty of great tracks that just fit with this type of game probably my favorite soundtrack is during the boss fight with Maestro Bibe, The Anxious Prodigy, as you are fighting his servants he's playing on his piano.There's also some nice side quests to do which was good as not only will you get some good rewards, you also can unlock a new blessing slot which allows you to use another blessing. Also I really like the descriptions for everything, you see when you defeat an enemy or boss or pick up an item or weapon you get a description like with any Souls like game, which was very good as it helped with giving you more insight into the world and telling you that Moana  might have been screwed up before the Gahars and their seven acolytes took over.So then the dislikes, to start there is no in-game map technically, what I mean by that is there is a map but it's only accessible at save points which was really annoying especially in certain areas like this expansive forest. I also would have liked a counter to show me how many times I died because of the death achievement, also for some reason I couldn't find one particular item in the game the one that is after limbs no matter how hard I looked. There is also no merchant which would have made getting that last item a lot easier and there are some little bugs in the game, but nothing that a quick restart of the game can't fix.Alright with that said, Morbid: The Seven Acolytes is a flawed but still pretty good souls like action game, with a really good story, really good RPG Maker style graphics and really good enemies and bosses. So I recommend this game if you like Bloodborne or souls like games then you may like this game, it just requires a big patience. I also heard of the sequel coming and I'm definitely looking forward to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Strange design decisions, particularly having a parry system that doesn't disrupt enemy poise, and instead allows for enemies to very quickly continue and sometimes rapidly attack. The only reward you get for perfect parries are higher damage but if the enemy can very quickly attack you before countering finishes then it doesn't seem much of an award. There is a really difficult timing to be had for an extremely perfect parry but doesn't seem worth investing the time into practising. As a result you are left with the simple tactic of attack, dodge, attack dodge, recharge stamina, repeat.The map and travel system is difficult to adapt to I would say, probably because we have been spoiled by modern games' map systems telling us exactly where we are and where to go. This game gives you a static map with no indication as to where you are on it. It does highlight the rest points but doesn't tell you which one you are at which I think would be beneficial. This coincides with the fact you can only use the map at rest points so you have to rely on remembering roughly where you are and where you need to go, which as I write this, is kind of a nice due to my point of being spoiled. I think one thing that could have been nice is an adjustment to the quest system. I had one outstanding quest, and I had no ideas who to return to to complete it. Maybe something like an icon one each map if there were any quests to complete to tell me at least which map to return to.There were a couple of enemies which I think were ridiculously designed. Both in the latter stages of the game where on would repeatedly spawn ethereal enemies - it got to the point where my screen was just covered in them and it was nigh impossible to get to the centre and attack the enemy. Another one where it shot a ball of blood that would chase you, and the only thing you could do is block it for it to form a puddle of damaging blood in front of you. The ball pretty much chased me half way across the map (might be a slight exaggeration). There was another enemy I just did not know how to damage - I used melee and firearms and nothing seemed to work?It definitely took me a while to get used to the game. Honestly I hated it at the start and nearly uninstalled it but something possessed me to power through it and give it a chance. _childDocuments_.review: This is another one of those flawed gems that's not really getting a fair analysis by critics. I think a lot of people that bought this were looking for a fast paced button masher and that's not what it is.Morbid feels like a much older ARPG albeit with modern console-style controls. The pacing of the gameplay is very slow and deliberate. There are mechanics that will punish you for making bad choices with how you configure your loot. The world is semi-open and many of the bosses do not have a set order in which they need to be killed.There are plenty of weapons to find with different attack patterns as well as other attributes such as reach. These weapons also come with a set number of rune slots. Runes add elemental damage (Fire/Frost/Electrical/Poison/Bleed) or enhance the weapon in other ways, such as adding attack speed or life leech. Enemies seem to be resistant or perhaps even outright immune to certain types of damage, while vulnerable to others. Figuring this out on a per-enemy basis is mostly a matter of common sense. For example, if an enemy is raining fireballs down on you there is a good chance it is resistant to fire damage.Like many games that draw upon the works of H.P. Lovecraft for inspiration there is a sanity mechanic. Sanity is represented by a blue bar. Certain enemies have attacks that drain sanity quickly. High sanity reduces damage dealt and damage taken, while low sanity does the opposite, and very low sanity allows a chance for slain enemies to respawn as apparitions, meaning they effectively have to be killed twice. The intent of this mechanic seems to be for players to allow sanity to drop low enough that your character's damage is enhanced, but not so low that apparitions begin to spawn. Managing sanity is optional for the most part as there are plenty of items that restore it, so it is easy to keep the bar nearly full if you don't mind taking the loss to your damage.Leveling up does occur although it will not impact your character until you find your first blessing. Blessings are Morbid's stand-in for Dark Souls' attributes with the caveat that they must be found in the game world in the form of statues before you can put points into them. While this is a unique idea, and the developer did a good job of ensuring that the most important blessings are found early on in the game, it does lead to the problem of finding that one type of blessing you were really looking forward to getting so late that it just doesn't impact the majority of your playthrough. Want to put points into a blessing that lets you attack faster with your melee weapons? You won't be doing so until about 75% of the way through the campaign, assuming that you actually find the statue.  * * The game is full of unique weapons each with their own accompanying lore to read similar to Dark Souls. Unfortunately you'll have to figure out which one's you like and ditch the rest as you go. Your inventory is a grid with limited space akin to the Diablo games, and two-thirds of this grid will quickly get filled up with consumables and runes. This leaves only enough room to keep three or four spare weapons at most. The smallest weapons take only one inventory square but these are not common. The majority of the weapons you'll find take at least two squares, and there are some that fill a whopping six. Thankfully equipping weapons prevents them from using precious inventory space.The way healing works is very similar to the Dark Souls franchise. You have healing stones that get restored for free by meditating at a shrine, which doubles as a checkpoint. Meditating however also respawns all enemies in the game world, except for bosses. The potency of your healing stones can be upgraded by funneling skill points into the corresponding blessing, and the total number you have is upgraded by looting items deliberately placed at certain locations in the game world. There are other consumables as well, which heal over time instead of providing health instantaneously. These heal over time consumables can be grinded to stacks of 10, but once you use them, they're gone, until you find more.There are ranged weapons too, which seem to be intended for additional utility rather than being relied on completely. Much akin to the healing stones described previously, their ammunition is also restored for free by meditating at shrines, but can also be refilled with consumable ammunition packs found in the game world as random loot. Ranged weapons come in the form of muskets, crossbows, and shotguns. I found muskets to be the only truly useful ranged weapon type, as their shots pierce through rows of enemies. Runes can also be added to ranged weapons.Overall the game is not very difficult if you choose your weapons wisely and use the rune system to your advantage. It does however need to be played like a Souls game, with your attacks being selected deliberately, and your dodge-roll's immune frames used to your advantage to avoid the attacks of your enemies.Morbid's art style is fantastically disgusting which should appeal to fans of this type of game. Its sound effects are also good, being somewhat reminiscent of early ARPGs such as Diablo. Unfortunately outside of a nice end-credits theme and some good tracks for the bosses, Morbid's music is largely ambient, repetitive and forgettable. Turning the music off may be the best option, although I wish there was an option to leave boss music on. It is however worth noting that you effectively get Morbid's soundtrack for free with your purchase, as each piece of music is stored in the game's root folder as an OGG file.I give the game a tentative thumbs-up. It's a slow-paced methodical romp through a vile world that mixes Lovecraftian horror and Steampunk fantasy elements. If that's your thing, then give the game a chance, but be aware that it does have a few shortcomings.(Took ~9 hours to complete with relatively thorough exploration).* NG+ and Stash features were added by the developer in post-release patches.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was very fun, and an isometric souls-like was very interesting to play. The level design is engaging and each area feels unique as well as enjoyable to explore. The enemies are varied and have several attacks in their arsenal. Bosses were all well designed from both an aesthetic viewpoint as well as balance wise. Nice amount of weapons in the game and the addition of ranged weapons is fun. Leveling up has it's own unique method of making your character stronger via blessings and overall the mechanics are straightforward and easy to understand. The lore is engaging and fun to read and the menagerie is awesome. My only complaint is that I feel the developers were afraid or maybe too cautious with sanity damage(not enough enemies dealing sanity damage and not in enough quantity) and that in general the enemies did too little damage. Even bosses were underwhelming when they hit you. That tied in with the generous amount of consumables that are littered all over the place, as well as re-spawn-able chests to stack up on certain items for free in certain areas made the game a little too easy. Oh and one more thing the inventory system sucks lol. Not enough room, no chest or hub to put your extra items or weapons which causes you to have to leave stuff behind. They give you just about every weapon you find in the game towards the end in case you want to use it again but you have to navigate an entire area to find chests to break and see which weapon is in what chest because you won't remember most likely which weapon is where. Also there are mobs in the way. It's pretty silly and is a rather bad way to deal with not allowing your players to keep the weapons they find throughout the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals are great, definitely the best part about the game. Music is good, too, and adds a lot of atmosphere to the game. Unfortunately, 6 hours in and it's never been fun.The fight mechanics are just terrible. Nearly every movement action is tied to stamina. Running, dodging, swinging weapons, and blocking uses stamina. There are guns that don't use stamina, but they need ammo and there isn't much of it. If you're out of stamina you literally cannot do anything but try to walk away from a fight. It's also inconsistent when it recovers. There's a small pause before stamina starts rebuilding. Sometimes that pause is short, other times it takes a long time. That inconsistency breaks any sense of timing since you can't rely on it.Nearly every melee weapon feels heavy and slow, and every enemy can break your attacks mid-swing... yet you can't break an enemy's attack the same way. Guns are fast and don't use stamina, but they're not all that useful because of the limited ammo available. There's a parry system, and a "perfect parry" is supposed to allow your follow-up attack to be more powerful, but I've never once been able to use it.Using items, healing, and switching weapon sets makes your character stop moving for a moment, leaving you vulnerable. Nearly every item is either weak or comes with a con of some sort.Fighting anything has been a chore and absolutely not fun at all. There's never a feeling of accomplishment other than just getting a fight over with. There have been so many fights where I've died to absolutely stupid things caused by the poor fight mechanics. Every fight is attack once or twice, dodge or run to evade, repeat and hope I don't get hit.I wish I could recommend the game, I just can't justify the time wasted on repetitive, unfair fights. It's just not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Eh, give it a pass. Combat feels really slow, damage between different weapons types feels completely random with a faster-animation fist weapon dealing significantly more damage per hit than slow heavy blades. Stats are just icons that take a bit to figure out and are listed really unintuitively. I'm not sure if half the damage types are even effective, fire and poison seemed to deal a lot of extra damage on most enemies, while ice or lightning Level design is maze-y and bland, no map unless you're at a shrine but it's hard to pick out landmarks when half of them are "house with fence" when the entire forest is dotted with "house with fence". Half the time you're just wandering around hoping you find the flesh-tumor you need to hit to make invincible fungus get out of your path, which sometimes is halfway across the map. Just have to hope the tumor you hit killed the line of fungus you remember and not some other one you didn't find yet. Also, it's damn near impossible to figure out if terrain is walkable or not, half your time is spent rubbing your face along nooks and crannies until you realize that trees in the foreground somehow block your movement behind them.Enemies are super simple as well, but sometimes attacks happen faster than you can react to them. The parry mechanic is super easy to forget about, and cheap damage can come out of nowhere. Bosses also have a disgusting amount of health, to the point where the fights drag out for way too long as you just hit them two or three times, roll away, and wait to it again. _childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for 2D Dark Spuls, or you want a lightweight souls-esque game to take on the go, search no farther. Morbid is a great take on the genre.It's hard to make a good "souls" game. There are a lot of facets you really have to nail in order for it to be fun and rewarding. Morbid is a little rough around the edges, but overall they got a lot of stuff totally right.The good: Asthetic and music are well done and cohesive. Combat is weighty and VERY souls-like. Managing stamina, dodging, parrying, choosing the right angle of attack or right weapon for an encounter, it is souls to the core and very well executed. Weapon variety is also quite good. Different weapons have different attack speeds, ranges, and elemental damages. Different weapons (even if they are in the same class) genuinely feel different to use. Bosses are well done and there is a decent bit of variety in attack styles. Boss quantity is also good, with a few bosses per map stage. Speaking of maps, they are confusing at first but once you spend some time there you learn the area and don't really get lost. Again, very souls-like. I also like how upgrades are hotswappable but also upgradeable. You can change around builds on the fly but have to be careful about which upgrades you sink xp into based on how you want to play. The neutral: It is easier than most souls games I've played. The rarest achievement is for dying 100 times. I had to go grind out 30 deaths or so after completing all the other achievements. Story, quests, and world are just average. Not bad, but there isn't a ton of lore unless you want to go read in your little in-game wiki a lot. XP gain also seemed rather low to me. There are 15ish "blessings" (upgrades) you can acquire in game, equipping up to 7 of them at a time. Each blessing takes 15 XP levels to max rank. At the time I 100%'d the game I was level 58, and I had spent some time grinding for XP and fully upgraded the blessing that boosts your XP gain. Long story short, you won't be able to upgrade your blessings much over the course of a game. Last thing: there really aren't many numbers in game for things like blessings and buffs. Eg, if I equip the blessing to boost xp acquisition, is it going to boost it 2% or 20%? The game doesn't say. This is cool from a lore/realism standpoint but annoying when you are trying to decide what to slot into a build and you really don't know quantitatively what anything does.The not-so-good: limited inventory space, limited overflow inventory space, only being able to carry 10 of each consumable item, not being able to split stacks of items to store some in the stash, elemental damage types with no clear distinction between them or when one is more effective than the other, having limited numbers of runes (weapon upgrades) that are PERMENANTLY DELETED when you remove them from a weapon, and basically the entirety of the upgrade and inventory systems. They are passable and don't get in the way of the gameplay too much but are not well done.Bottom line: the gameplay is what matters in a souls game and they nailed it. Most everything else (except the style) is pretty average

_childDocuments_.review: Morbid: The Seven Acolytes is a top-down, pixel art soulslike, or perhaps a "souls-lite", that I had never heard of prior to receiving a key for it from a friend. Curious, I gave it a try. I found it surprisingly enjoyable given my mixed experience with the genre overall and certain technical shortcomings with this game in particular.Though I enjoyed parts of Dark Souls 3, Elden Ring and in particular Bloodborne, certain aspects of souls-style gameplay has always rubbed me the wrong way. The relentless difficulty, opaque stat interactons, lack of navigation aids, and in particular the forced PvP invasions... souls games are not exactly welcoming to new or casual players. I've had a better time in games that borrow elements from the series then the series itself: Blasphemous, Darksiders 3 and now Morbid are examples of such. Thankfully Morbid is a strictly solo experience and therefore has no invasion mechanic, which already makes it hugely more enjoyable to play as a whole. And though there's no real-time map, there are at least static maps with landmarks you can view at Shrines, the game's bonfire analogues. Morbid is set in the benighted realm of Mornia, lorded over by dark gods called the Gahar, born of human consciousness. You take the role of the last surviving Striver of the Order of Dibrom. With your island headquarters destroyed and your Order all but wiped out, it falls to you to face the Gahars' champions, the titular Seven Acolytes, and redeem your fallen home. Standing in your path are masses of mutated and murderous minions and a handful of minibosses, but there are a few friendly NPCs, some of which offer sidequests. Aesthetically, mechanically and thematically, Morbid owes a lot to Bloodborne and its cosmic horror inspirations in turn- blood, guts, depressive NPCs and body horror abound. There's even a sanity meter, although this is a more minor mechanic then other games that have it. Your sanity level apparently has an effect on you damage, XP gain and number of "Specters" encountered, though I never noticed much of a difference.There is no blocking in Morbid, but you can parry, and you can also use a firearm or crossbow, ammo for which is refilled when you meditate at a Shrine. If your parry is well-timed you can perfect-parry, stun your enemy and counter-attack them for greatly increased damage. Enemies in Morbid can kill you extremely quickly, per genre standard. The combat plays out in one of three ways: You get dead, you dodge and slash enemies until they die, or if you're good, you execute some perfect parries. Most enemy melee attacks can be parried, including that of the bosses, but the timing is tight and different for each enemy. While there are a variety of weapons to use, I find its best to use a weapon with long range and good damage such as the Grim Reaver greatsword, and getting in a sneak charge attack before you're noticed. On that note, you can sneak around if you want, and this is in fact highly effective compared to other games in the genre- while crouched, you are virtually invisible to the AI and can walk right past most enemies at will. Unlike most games in the genre, there are no actual "souls" or any currency or shops at all. Enemies grant traditional RPG experience on death and there is actually no penalty for dying- which is good, because its going to happen fairly often. After defeating the first Acolyte, you gain the ability to spend XP at Shrines to purchase upgrades for your blessings: various passive buffs that provide permanent boosts so long as they are equipped. You start with two blessing slots and earn an additional slot per Acolyte defeated.Enemies drop both the typical soulslike consumables and also runes that can be slotted into your gear for passive buffs, Diablo-style, which also no doubt inspired the grid-based inventory system. This is important for getting the most out of your weapons. However, your inventory and stash will fill up with items and weapons fairly quickly. you can only carry 10 of any consumable at one time, and there is no ability to split stacks of items- an odd omission in this day and age. Still, drops are rather plentiful compared to other souls games and you typically won't be hurting for items. Aside from viewing the map and spending XP, you can meditate at a Shrine to recover your health, ammo and reset the area- where in Dark Souls this happens automatically when interacting with a bonfire, in Morbid you choose when this occurs. You can also view lore entries about weapons, enemies, the world areas and the like, use an equipment stash, and use fast travel, which works a bit oddly here. You can fast travel FROM any Shrine, but not TO them- instead, you can only fast travel to specified locations, typically area entrances. I found this a rather odd choice.Morbid is also on the whole shorter then other games the genre, though I'd hardly count that against it. It does not overstay its welcome and though some fights are irritating, there's nothing even approaching the cheapness of say, the fight with Malenia in Elden Ring.If you are looking for a slightly more accessible souls-like experience, Morbid's bite-sized approach and grim charm might appeal to you. I certainly had more fun with it then I thought I would.

_childDocuments_.review: Great bosses, good music, overall fun game since we are all waiting on that Bloodborne PC port. Gameplay is fun and actually simple. Dodge, attack, occasionally shoot. At least we have maps, although you will most likely get lost constantly before finding them and I think this was by design.A big issue here are the weapons. Most are simple and almost completely the same. The stats don't really tell the player much allowing you to experiment with runes a bit. Runes are little accessories you equip to weapons instead of upgrading them at a blacksmith. There is a red sword that is just better than the rest but it loses you sanity. You can get around this with Sanity Drain runes. Most weapons are either useless or very good.Keep in mind you also don't level the character themselves, until you beat the first acolyte. _childDocuments_.review: Just off the top, I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys isometric hack n slash games, or soulsborne games with a mild-to-medium challenge. Some stuff about me, that'll let you know if my opinion is useful to you: I've played pretty much every Souls-style game I can get my hands on multiple times; I'm a big fan of the genre. I beat this particular game in just under 7 hours, collecting all the items, completing all sidequests, and beating all bosses. The game DOES have a New Game + option, which may add variety to those who want more, but I haven't engaged with it yet.So, as to the game, at it's simplest, Morbid is an Isometric Soulslike:It has a dark and mysterious story about a seemingly doomed world told primarily through NPC dialogue and item descriptions. It has a dodge rollIt has parry mechanicsIt has a Melee + Gun loadout a-la Bloodborne.It has a leveling system that encourages you to build your character a variety of waysIn fact, there are many many more things that are identifiably "Souls" in its DNA, but there's more to it as well. The relatively short runtime could be a blessing for some people, especially those that don't have a considerable amount of time to invest in a larger game. The pixel art-style is excellent, with dozens of evocative enemies culminating in some truly excellent boss designs. The Weapon system encourages the player to swap to new weapons frequently, as opposed to getting used to a single weapon early and upgrading it until the end.Indeed, the game is much more encouraging than your standard Souls-Like, seeing no need to take the player's resources upon death, or requiring the player to invest said resources in anything other than their own growth. There were a couple enemy types and mechanical elements I feel like would have been served by seeing more play in the game, but their limited use makes sense with a 7 hour runtime. Similarly, some areas feel like they're just reaching their potential as you reach their end. It's also a little bit odd how many NPCs populate the world, given that only a small number of them serve any purpose. The areas themselves, while beautiful, are sometimes difficult to navigate due to somewhat unclear walls and passages. This is especially true in the areas with a lot of greenery. By the end of a couple zones, you'll not feel particularly confident that you actually know how to get from point A to point B again if you'd need to. That said, each boss is a delightfully curated experience, with unique mechanics and a clear identity; each has an obvious road to success that are easily identified, while still allowing players to tackle the encounter in multiple ways. A couple of the bosses in particular were an absolute delight from their introduction all through to their conclusions. It is important to note, if you're a fan of this genre and consider yourself reasonably skilled, you will not have a difficult time with most of the encounters here. The game provides more than enough of an ability to heal and maneuver that you will rarely be more than moderately challenged. What this means is that there is little reason to "Get Good" at Morbid, but at the same time there is almost 0 time wasted on runbacks, repeated deaths, or learning mechanics. Ultimately, Morbid is a gorgeously gory game, filled to the brim with monsters, weapons, and the melancholic woe one comes to expect from the genre, while providing a more accessible formula and play-time that leaves us with a fun and intriguing game that can be beaten in a day or two.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really high quality 2D souls-like game, which takes influence from Bloodborne and HP Lovecraft.The combat, RPG elements, art, music, exploration, lore, world-building and combat are on point. It's a joy to explore this blood-soaked, surreal world of fishmen and blobby creatures. The level of challenge is really enjoyable; it starts off fairly easy but towards the mid-end game you'll really need to carefully hone your build, your perks and your weapon upgrades to take down the late-game bosses. Lots of strange NPCs to meet, beautiful environments to explore, packed with secrets and mysteries.It's rare to experience such a successful 2D souls-like, especially when it's coming from a small dev team. The only comparisons I can think of are DarkMaus and Below. The game has a little bit of jank, which is to be expected, but overall it's a triumph. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Morbid: The Seven Acolytes is an entertaining isometric Souls-like game where you play as the last surviving Striver of Dibrom on her journey to defeat the Seven Acolytes. When I first reviewed this game after beating it a while after the launch, I had fun with it but couldn't give a recommendation due to many of its shortcomings, now that the game has had several major updates (update 5 being the latest as of writing this) I decided to revisit it and see what has been changed.Visuals and audio create a dark and sometimes even slightly foreboding atmosphere as you travel through the dilapidated areas that are littered with the horrors that now plague the lands. Enemy designs range from mundane to eldritch horrors and surprisingly often delve in to the realm of body horror while the overall tone of the lore is clearly inspired by Lovecraft.Combat, boss mechanics and balancing still have many of the original shortcomings. While combat itself is mechanically entertaining and hitboxes have been improved a decent amount from the launch, enemy AI and their attack patterns still struggle a lot when it comes to vertical movement which still largely trivializes majority of the encounters in the game as players tend to have advantage when it comes to attack reach vertically.Replayability of the game has been improved a bit by introducing a new game plus option, but the lack of weapon variety (both melee and ranged) as well as limited customization in form of assigning runes (+attack speed, +fire dmg etc.) to your weapons and choosing which blessings - permanent buffs such as increased health bar, take less damage etc. - to use and level up does not really support multiple playthroughs as there simply isn't enough variety in the way the game plays out regardless of your weapon choice.Morbid is a relatively short experience, my first playthrough of the game took roughly 7 hours out of which about an hour or more was spent wandering around trying to figure out where I needed to go next. Fortunately updates have addressed this issue to some degree, as you can now access a map from shrines that allows you to see a rough layout of the area as well its connection points to other maps which helps a lot as some of the areas are still a little too maze like. That being said I think the updates have addressed many of the issues I had with the game originally, added some additional QoL features/tweaks and while there are still some shortcomings as well as the overall experience being on the easy side - the game itself is in a solid place now and I would recommend it - but would definitely also recommend checking out the demo first, after all that is the fastest way to see if the game is something you would like.

_childDocuments_.review: We need a "so-so" option for reviews sometimes.  I was sold this on a "It feels like a 2d Bloodborne!" comment from someone a while back.  Sadly, this game only has two things in common with Bloodborne - you have a gun, and the story is eldritch horror.  That is not enough to say "2d Bloodborne"  Combat is VERY much more Souls than Borne (there's at least one review complaining that combat isn't fast enough.  He's/she's right.) - you block with your weapon and dodgeroll.  There's no gun-parry nor visceral, and the dodgeroll is definitely more Souls speed than Borne speed.  The big problem there is - at least on keyboard controls - block and shoot are the same button.  Did I say "block"?  I'm sorry, that's wrong.  It's a parry.  That's it.  The animation is a block, but it's a parry.   Not a very effective one too - the game says "attack after parry for massive damage", but I just cannot get that to trigger.  Assuming the parry even registers - which it feels like it doesn't half the time (then again, I can't get the parry timing in DS2 down so that may just be me). Also, I still can't figure out how to use the seven skill points I already have.  Still, a fun little game so far.  If you're looking for a 2d Bloodborne, this ain't it.  But if you're looking for a 2d eldritch souls-like, you may want to give this one a try.

Everyone else: take a close look, before you decide to buy it.I don't enjoy games where you run into a much too many enemies / combats every other step you take.Plus, it's a hard enough game, if you are not a "soulslike" veteran.In the end, that makes a game that is no fun to play, for me.I really think, the direction video game development has been going quite a while now - with almost any game being "roguelike/roguelite" or "soulslike" - just sucks. _childDocuments_.review: This game may be a little expensive considering it's length. But for the quality of the gameplay it's worth it.BOSSESAll of the bosses were unique. Some more difficult than others. But all very doable. Only 2 of the 10 I beat on first try.Rest usually regard 3-5+ tries. And even at the end when I was facing 3 bosses in a fairly short time span it didn't feel overwhelming.MAPSAnd each map always introduced a few new enemy types. Some of which were very surprising or difficult. Each of them had a unique and pleasing aesthetic. On one hand they felt a little difficult to navigate due to the 2D nature and things blending in. But on the other that challenge to navigate and find all the secrets on the map was rewarding.BALANCE/PROGRESSIONI felt they did a fairly good job of balancing the game. Even with the best weapons towards the end of the game, you still couldn't take any bosses or enemies for granted. The Blessings system was a neat way of introducing "stats" in a way where you could equip and upgrade them as you pleased via skill points from leveling up. Plus the Rune system for weapons was a nice touch. I didn't realize how this system worked early on. But once I did I always had my weapons kitted out with runes.CONCLUSIONOnly complaints for me were some very minor bugs pertaining to ranged attacks sometimes getting stuck and the hit detection being finicky on occasion. Overall a very good game with no breaking bugs as far as I my experience went. Would recommend to any games that enjoy the ARPG and Soulslike genres.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% completion in ten hours with a controller. Fun enough to finish, not to ever play it again.The art and setting are certainly the best part of the game. Enemy variety and appearances are very nice, and none of the bosses (the titular seven, plus a few extras) felt like filler. Other than that, it of course takes heavy inspiration from Dark Souls. Work from checkpoints through chaff to get to bosses, and earn experience and consumables on the way while wielding a variety of weapons. But it's simpler, with parrying but no blocking, no punishment on death, no real NPC interactions, and no rekindling of the not-bonfires.I found the game rarely challenged me, and when it did stacking consumables obliterated all before me. Progression is tied to boss kills as well as general XP gain and you likely won't be near max by the end of the game without heavy grinding. The experience is enjoyable, but if you're looking for a challenge you'll probably need some self-imposed limits or slog through a few new game + levels.The game prominently features a sanity meter. I still have no idea how exactly this works, beyond making you deal less damage when you are more sane and spawning enemies when you're insane. Enemies generally lower it, but raising it to max in the lategame is trivial, however this feels like you're spending resources to nerf yourself.$25 feels stiff. Currently it's available in the Humble Monthly bundle for $12 with several other games. I'd recommend getting it there. Otherwise, wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I've not played any Dark Souls games, but I know the general mechanics and higher difficulty associated with the series. So when given the chance to play Morbid: The Seven Acolytes (MSA), I was trepidatious yet also excited to challenge myself. Expecting to fail frequently, I actually only died against regular enemies a handful of times. For those who'd be wary of a game that might be too difficult, MSA isn't a brutally hard choice.As you explore and fight ghastly monsters, you'll gain weapons, and runes that can be equipped onto them. In addition, there's shrines where you can refill your hearts, which is MSA's version of the bonfires. Refilling your health does respawn all enemies though. For quite a while, it won't seem like there's a purpose in killing enemies, because there doesn't seem to be any way to use your level-ups. What you'll discover after killing the first boss are blessings, which is where you invest those level-ups, for things such as a larger health bar. Another important bar is the one for sanity. It tends to hover around 30% full, steadily decreasing even when not hit by psychic attacks, so you'll occasionally have to replenish it with items. If it drops too low, the edges of the screen flash purple, and enemies you kill will sometimes spawn spectral versions of themselves. They can be defeated, but it's an extra hazard to contend with. The controls take some time to get used to, but I found they worked well enough with my controller. Even though there's a parry system in the game, which I think was supposed to be used often, I pretty much never touched it. Something to be aware of is that if you bring up your inventory, it doesn't pause the action.Of the little that I'm shown of this world, I'd have to say things are royally screwed. With the people worshiping wicked gods, it's soiled the entire land. It's not safe to wander out into once settled areas, with the docks devoid of fish, replaced by sailors mutated into fish men. You get some dialogue intermittently from NPCs and as you kill acolytes, but most of the game's lore is contained in shorter blurbs you have to read at shrines. If you take the time to read them, it holds interesting information about what's going on. However, having to read the game's plot points this way isn't the most effective means to convey a story. MSA takes an overhead view, and is made up of 2D images, which makes good use of dark colors and palettes. The developers managed to avoid making environments that look bland or washed out, despite the colors they used. Some environments don't look particularly terrifying or grisly, as they resemble what cities or darker forests would look like. However, with the abundance of blood and parasites littering these areas, and how you'll never know when a tougher enemy might show up as you explore, you'll often feel on edge. Whenever you see the disturbing, twisted monsters thought up for this title, it'll really cement how messed up this world has become.When listening to the background music in the different areas, it doesn't suit the dark visuals and atmosphere very well. I enjoy simple melodies and tunes that aren't overly dramatic or intense, but the songs are too slow and at ease to be dreadful. It's not quite calm enough to be soothing music, but it doesn't resonate and create an effect that MSA could otherwise capitalize on. The sound effects of attacks and item effects all suited the game appropriately, so I don't have any complaints with that.🌟 Though I didn't level up the range of blessings enough to try different playstyles, I do think the variety of effects would support different ways of how you fight enemies. For instance, increasing your stealth and sneak attack damage, could make for an interesting assassin build.🌟 The monsters have interesting designs, and in some cases, origins. Most of them are pretty easy to bamboozle, but they still look monstrous. ❌ Your inventory only has 44 slots, with weapons taking up more space relative to how cumbersome the weapon would be. This means you carry only a few of the game's many weapons, dumping the rest like rubbish.❌ I'm not sure if there are more strategic ways to fight certain bosses and enemies or not. When fighting the 3rd boss, I felt like I won simply because I had enough health and resources to tank it.❌ Since I wasn't spending much time repeatedly killing enemies to level up my blessings, most of them were very low level. 🔍 Combat emphasizes distancing and timing. You'll want to get in the habit of hitting the enemy once and immediately dodge-rolling away. It's often a good idea to put distance in-between you and the enemy if your stamina is low or they're attacking, repeating as often as necessary.🔍 It's helpful to save your ammo for elite enemies and boss battles. Since you can fire it without a stamina cost, it's a good way to get chip damage in as your stamina refills.🔍 Your sanity bar will steadily decrease, so get used to that. In some situations, it's to your advantage to let it idle near empty, instead of refilling it immediately.I'm glad that MSA wasn't as difficult or riddled with cheap traps and deaths as I anticipated. There were some situations that raised my ire, but when I sought out the path of least resistance and tried another approach, I was able to make it work. Since you unlock more slots for blessings by beating acolytes, there's a system in place to prevent you from becoming too OP, while also having a couple of skills to invest into if you're getting stuck.  There are strange combinations of positives and negatives in MSA, as I think the visuals are great, while the music short changes the atmosphere. The lore is engaging, but it's not delivered very well. I like the hit and run style of the combat, though I don't think it cohered into the complex system it strove for. Overall though, I enjoyed MSA, and would recommend it for those who enjoy tough, but mostly fair games.

_childDocuments_.review: 2d dark souls, but not good.The game looks great, but the gameplay is very dull and uninteresting.Lack of a minimap paired with extremely large and "samey" looking areas makes it impossible to really get a sense of where you are in the world. The only maps you are given can only be used at save points, and even then they dont really help much.The enemy AI is extremely predictable and easy, both regular enemies and bosses"exploration" gets old fast, not only because everything looks the same, but because after finding your 20th rune and 50th piece of food you stop really caring or looking forward to finding things.
