_childDocuments_.review: Remothered: Broken Porcelain is a flawed, but still very solid and good horror, adventure game and a good sequel/prequel to Remothered: Tormented Fathers. Okay the story.Celeste Felton the adoptive daughter of the Felton's, years ago she had disappeared presumed kidnapped and she never returned home, that is what the general public believe. But in secret Celeste Felton had returned home to her family, where did she go? What happened to her well? Well we soon find out what happened to the young teenager and what she went through as we go through the past as well as the future seeing what happened after the events of the first game with Rosemary Reed, all this being told by the mysterious old woman madam Svenska.Now let’s talk about the likes, the story is really good it can be a bit confusing at first as it jumps around, but as it keeps going it starts to click, I think the story jumping around from different perspectives and not being in order is to represent fragmented memories the first game and this game has heavy themes of memory manipulation and forgetting. But like I said if you continue seeing the story play out it soon starts to click and in the story there were plenty of touching moments in it especially at the end this story almost made me cry it's that good.The graphics/levels are both very good; the graphics are pretty detailed with plenty of nice colors and pretty detailed backgrounds. The game itself takes place in the Ashman inn and it's a pretty interesting level/world as we explore it seeing the different parts of the hotel. I think the basement level was probably the best, it was not just a creepy basement, but also had a good mad scientist laboratory feel to it.The gameplay is basically the same as it was in tormented fathers IE running, hiding and avoiding the stalkers, but you also get a chance to fight back especially in later stages when you get a weapon to use against two of the stalkers which I really liked that. The atmosphere in the game is good and can be pretty spooky for first time players especially when you get into the basement level.Like the first game the music in this game is very good with plenty of nice tracks to listen too, the voice acting in the game is okay there are some voices that work but some are questionable especially for Celeste. The characters in the game are good I especially loved Lindsay she was probably my favorite character she was adorable, pretty funny and sweet.The stalkers in the game we're pretty good each one with their own unique look and weapon, my favorite has to be Porcelain he just has this great intimidating look to him and it gives off this great Jason Voorhees vibe.This game has boss fights where you have to fight the stalker, it was a mixed bag others were good others not so much. This game also has an upgrade system and I found it pretty interesting as you can upgrade your skills making the game a lot easier. Finally the absolute best in the game were all the notes and collectibles you can get, like I said in all my other reviews that have notes and collectibles those things can do wonders in helping in improve the game’s world and expand it. And these notes and collectibles are no different. Now let’s talk about the dislikes, the game does have some bugs in it, from what I read the game when it first launched had a lot of bugs and it was practically unplayable that's why I waited for so long to play the game until it was patched. But sadly the game still has some bugs in it.There are two that can be game breaking like in the west wing of the Inn where I was blocking a stalker from entering a door and after the stalker left for some reason I couldn't open that door no matter what I did.All so when I was running from a stalker I had to climb up to a window, I didn't climb up to the window and in fact just lost the stalker and when I went back to climb up the window it wouldn't like me do that, but those were fixed after restarting. There was all so little bug where I couldn't open the face in the first level but that was fixed when I use my keyboard, and some of those bugs can be quite frustrating when you're trying to get all the achievements for the game. And speaking of achievements some of them are a real pain in the ass to get, the absolute worst achievements are the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the bloodbath achievements; they were just so hard, annoying and unfun to get.As I mentioned in the likes the voice acting was okay but there were definitely some weird moments in it like Celeste she has a British accent which I found it extremely weird and kind of off-putting I mean she's born in Italy, now I'm not saying that she should have an Italian accent I'm just saying it's strange that she has a British accent with no explanation to it. Then there is old Stefano Ashmann at first his voice sounded good, old and kind of frail sounding. But as later in the game it sounds a lot different more pathetic and kind of like he has something in his mouth, I don't know maybe it was intentional it just sounded off putting to me.Later in one cutscene for some reason Lindsay who had an American accent in one scene develops a British accent but then she goes back to sounding American again like what happened did the voice actress get sick and they couldn't get her so they had to improvise? Finally sometimes when the character speaks it sounds like it's being recorded in a booth, I don't know it's those weird touches that just kind of pulled me out of the experience a little bit.As I have said this game has boss fights in it and it was a mixed bag, the two most annoying boss fights was the one with Stefano Ashmann and the second time you battle Porcelain they were both pretty annoying. And lastly as I said the story is really good, but I have to admit there were some parts that just felt kind of dumb like the whole telepathy/mind over matter thing, it just felt a little too out there.All right now that that's all said and done with Remothered: Broken Porcelain is a flawed, but still very solid and good horror, adventure game and a good sequel/prequel to Remothered: Tormented Fathers. With a really good story, very good graphics/levels and pretty good stalkers. So despite the game's flaws and shortcomings I do recommend this game if you like the first one then you're probably going to like this one, I do recommend playing the first game and reading the comic Remothered Lambs to the slaughter before playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more frustrating than fun, not because it's particularly difficult but because it feels extremely unpolished. I think the graphics are the best part, as if the developers put most of their time into making a game that looks pretty with no substance.The AI is annoying, beelining for your position when they had no reason to; sometimes the prompt to stealth attack them just wouldn't show up despite hovering behind them for a good while. On the otherhand, the AI can be extremely exploitable; both of these extremes make for an experience that is simply underwhelming and not gratifying. The items aren't well explained and the "inventory" system is extremely clunky, which is made worse when being chased.I haven't played any other game in the series, but the writing in this one is kind of all over the place. It's a lot like the game: mostly boring with some things intended for shock value just sprinkled in willy-nilly. The audio quality too is totally wacky; characters in the same room will sound distant then super close depending on the camera angle.I really wanted to like this game; I received it from a Humble Choice and after getting Song of Horror from a different month, I was hoping Remothered would be an old school Resident Evil style horror game. But it's just too dang frustrating most of the time and flat boring the rest.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★★★★★★ + ★★★★★★★★ 18/10+) Intensely dramatic story.+) Great environment designs.+) Distinguishable graphics.+) Well planned mapping.+) Keenly thought-out checkpoints.+) Artistic music and ambience is excellent.+) Highly optimized control. (Especially door opening)+) Crouch-sprinting has been implemented. One might think this will make things easy but the way game is played is quite different from previous series, so this element was actually helpful. Very, in fact.+) Collectible items are added and they are also currency for upgrades. The upgrades aren't necessary but helpful.+) That said, yes, upgrade system has been implemented. You might say it's little off place for the genre, but it serves as a subtle contribution.🌀 Story of previous series felt very much forced. But when you play this prequel it makes all sense. Yes, there are still "as-is elements" but I find that part also interesting in this case, so no complaints from me. Most importantly, the story is very touching and immensely dramatic. I dropped tears HARD at the end. I believe this game has the most emotional story of all horror games, nay, of all games. Which is why I selected this game as one of my seven main horror games. Considering how fun the core gameplay is, it is only natural.

Even with the route with Andrea and just looping her with the TV and her office, it's such a tedious process. Visually, the game is amazing. Everything in this game screams "The Shining" so hard. And the last and the biggest positive of the game is the main character. _childDocuments_.review: Remothered: Broken Porcelain : By Triple F"Remothered: Broken Porcelain" is a survival horror game developed by Stormind Games and published by Modus Games, serving as both a sequel and prequel to "Remothered: Tormented Fathers." Set in the eerie Ashmann Inn, the game follows Jennifer, a troubled young girl with a mysterious past, as she uncovers the secrets lurking within the inn’s haunted walls. While "Broken Porcelain" ambitiously aims to blend horror storytelling with stealth-based gameplay, the final product falls short of expectations, hindered by technical issues, narrative inconsistencies, and clunky mechanics. Nonetheless, it remains an intriguing experience for those who appreciate psychological horror and character-driven stories.The story of "Broken Porcelain" is intricate, weaving together timelines and characters to create a multi-layered narrative that delves into themes of trauma, obsession, and revenge. The game attempts to build on the mysteries introduced in "Tormented Fathers," offering new insights into the sinister figures involved in the events of the Ashmann Inn. While Jennifer’s journey reveals some compelling moments of horror and suspense, the story struggles with pacing and coherence. Flashbacks and surreal sequences, though atmospherically intriguing, often feel disjointed, leaving players piecing together events in a way that can feel more confusing than mysterious. The game’s ambition is evident, but it occasionally feels weighed down by overly complex storytelling.Gameplay in "Broken Porcelain" combines exploration, stealth, and puzzle-solving, with an emphasis on evading hostile enemies rather than direct combat. Players must navigate the Ashmann Inn carefully, as Jennifer lacks any substantial means of defense; instead, she relies on tools like throwable items and distractions to evade enemies. The stealth mechanics are tense, especially in dimly lit areas where enemies lurk around every corner, creating a constant sense of vulnerability. However, the controls are somewhat unresponsive, and inconsistent AI behavior can make encounters feel unfair or frustrating. While the core stealth mechanics hold potential, they’re often undercut by clunky interactions that detract from the tension the game seeks to build.The puzzles scattered throughout "Broken Porcelain" add a layer of engagement and challenge, requiring players to search for clues, manipulate objects, and combine items to progress. These puzzles range from simple object retrievals to more complex environmental challenges that often contribute to the game’s atmosphere of unease. However, the puzzles sometimes suffer from a lack of clarity, leaving players struggling to understand their objectives. While the sense of discovery can be rewarding, the game could benefit from more intuitive design to reduce frustration and maintain immersion. Still, the puzzles play a significant role in adding depth to the gameplay experience.Visually speaking, "Remothered: Broken Porcelain" captures the horror aesthetic effectively, with dimly lit corridors, shadowy figures, and unsettling decor that create a foreboding atmosphere within the Ashmann Inn. The art direction emphasizes an eerie, abandoned feel, with detailed textures and subtle visual cues that help build the game’s unsettling ambiance. Character models are crafted with attention to detail, though some animations appear stiff or outdated, which occasionally breaks immersion. Sound design, however, is a major strength, with haunting ambient effects and tense musical cues that heighten suspense and keep players on edge. The voice acting is strong, especially for Jennifer and the main antagonists, adding to the game’s narrative weight.One of the game’s most significant issues is its technical performance. Upon launch, "Broken Porcelain" faced numerous bugs and glitches, ranging from frame rate drops and stuttering to clipping and AI malfunctions that impacted gameplay. Although patches have since addressed some of these issues, the game’s technical stability still feels inconsistent. These problems not only hinder player immersion but also amplify frustration during crucial stealth moments. For a game heavily reliant on atmosphere and tension, such disruptions significantly impact the overall experience, making it difficult for players to stay fully engaged with the horror elements.Despite its flaws, "Remothered: Broken Porcelain" offers an interesting narrative and an atmospheric setting that may appeal to fans of psychological horror. Its themes of trauma and revenge give the story a dark emotional edge, and the protagonist’s vulnerability enhances the game’s horror factor. However, the ambitious narrative and complex themes might feel overwhelming or disjointed for players seeking a straightforward horror experience. While it doesn’t fully meet its potential, the game remains a unique entry in the horror genre, particularly for those who enjoy character-driven stories with a psychological twist.On a final note, "Remothered: Broken Porcelain" is an ambitious yet flawed horror experience that shines in its story and atmosphere but struggles with gameplay execution and technical stability. The game’s eerie setting, unsettling story, and strong sound design create an experience that can be compelling for horror enthusiasts, even though it’s marred by control issues and performance hiccups. For players who can look past these limitations, "Broken Porcelain" delivers a haunting, albeit imperfect, journey into the psychological horrors of the Ashmann Inn. While it may not fully satisfy fans of polished horror titles, it offers a distinctive and memorable experience for those willing to brave its challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommend, and strictly for the story and atmosphere, not the gameplay.tl;dr: One of the most intriguing and heartbreaking plots I've ever encountered in a video game. I find the core gameplay rough, but I don't like stealth horror, so take that with a grain of salt. I highly recommend the story if you like psychological and/or survival horror plots. If nothing else, maybe just find a movie-fied let's play of the cutscenes and such, because the atmosphere is brilliant when the gameplay works.The long version: I haven't (and can't currently) played the first Remothered, but this is one of my favorite stories ever told in a videogame. It's pretty damn convoluted in the middle, but gets cleared up ENOUGH by the end. But every element-the atmospheric choices, the VO, the music-helps to serve the tense and tragic atmosphere of the scenario. If you like RE plots but want something sliiiightly more believable (once all is explained) and focused more on interpersonal dynamics than just running through corridors and shootan monsters, I'd imagine you'll dig this. That being said, I don't like stealth horror games. Like at all. I find them unfun and the monsters stop being scary after about five minutes. Remothered: Broken Porcelain is maybe my favorite stealth horror yet, but I still wouldn't say I liked the gameplay. Using distraction items is kinda awkward, enemies take a long time to wander off, and there are various corners of the maps where the camera doesn't wanna cooperate. I still found these enemies scarier than most Clock Tower-esque stalkers, but that's not a high bar. Regardless, I almost called it off at about the two hour mark, but I REALLY wanted to see where the story was going, so I pushed through. The most fun I had with this game was in the latter half, where it diverges from the stealth gameplay more often. Even then, R:BP strikes me as, shall we say, Kojima-inspired in that there are tons of cutscenes and not that much gameplay, all told. It's more like an interactive movie with stealth horror elements.I'm not sure if I loved the story so much BECAUSE of the gameplay experiences i went through, but I suspect the cutscenes and just a bit of the gameplay would easily make for a good movie. Hell, even the run time wouldn't be too crazy, since I cleared the whole game in five and a half hours. So yeah, if you don't wanna deal with the gameplay, I still recommend watching the movieBut also, fair warnings all around: I'm 90% sure this franchise is dead in the water. The devs are on to other IPs and the lead writer has abandoned the planned third game in the trilogy. That being said, this game stands alone incredibly well. The ending was so flawless that I assumed the series was meant to end with this one-or at least go in a completely different direction.

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't even consider trying this game until you've played the first one. It's entirely a story-focused experience that has LOTs of elaborate, intricate, and oftentimes frankly convoluted plots points. Before purchasing the game I think that's THE most important thing to keep in mind.That said, I think the game does a good job with closure to the story and continuity with the previous title. This doesn't feel like one of those situations where they retroactively made up a bunch of plot points to force a sequel/prequel to work with the previous title. The story is clearly deliberate and carefully planned out from the very beginning.Gameplay-wise it honestly isn't much of anything special. It's pretty engaging and most of the animations are very nicely done, but it feels immersive and story driven, nothing more and nothing less. Sometimes it's a little fumbly, and the AI isn't very good. Extremely basic behavior, no memory of player's actions/locations at all after breaking line of sight. Just very straight forward behavior. Disappointingly, this simplicity is paired with lopsided difficulty at times. You'd think a simple AI would be easier to wrangle into a consistent margin of difficulty but evidently that wasn't the case.Bugs were relatively minimal but a lot of transitions when interacting with hostiles (or vice versa) felt extremely strange with weird jump cuts and sometimes the AI even forgetting where I was immediately after, when I'm left right behind them at the end of a jumpy animation. Little things like that maybe 3-5 times throughout the course of the entire game.Art-wise this game looks top notch. Environments are consistently remarkable, graphics are good, characters are detailed, most animations feel solid. Music was repetitive at times (looking at you, high pitched whistle in the main menu) but it was good.Overall, I think this game has a lot holding it back but I recommend the game specifically for those interested in playing BOTH games. Do not deprive yourself the necessary context to understand the story. It's the primary content to the game. The story felt like I was watching a cult classic mystery horror TV show or something. Constant twists and turns, a couple really solid characters, and a pretty cohesive plot in the grand scheme of things.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this review by being upfront with the fact that I haven't played Remothered: Tormented Fathers, I received this game in a humble bundle and decided to give it a try and thankfully this game provides a recap of the previous game. Sadly that recap is the only concise bit of storytelling you will get from this game. I understand that Chris Darril has a vision for this series especially since from what I read he planned on making a trilogy from this IP but after playing Broken Porcelain I honestly don't know how a trilogy would be possible since the story now feel closed and shut. But lets talk about the "story" if you can understand it and again in all honesty after I finished the game I read the wiki synopsis to better understand which is already troubling. The fact that I had to rely on an external source to better understand a congested story that feels like its riding an express flight to the conclusion just screams bad story telling but the fact that the RECAP for the previous game does a better job at explaining things just further boggles my mind. Story aside the gameplay? Jesus Christ HOW DO YOU RUIN BASIC GAMEPLAY!? Objectives sometimes never make sense, features are introduced only to be used once or twice, the gameplay loop of being chased is clunky and more frustrating than scary especially since hiding NEVER works, and the idea of upgrading your character is a throwaway idea that I rarely used. Pair these issues with an incredibly short play time and you literally have a game that YouTubers would play for some quick views and honestly its insulting. I'm not sure if there was studio interference or a lack of time but this game just feels bad. There's some moments where I actually enjoyed the chemistry between two of the characters but beside that everything isn't "half-baked" its just raw.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game and enjoyed the experience. I think it was a good sequel for the first version and it answers your questions from the story of the first game well and reveals the story to you.The story of the game was wider and more detailed this time, from the cutscenes of the game to the clues and documents found in the game that reveal the story and many of the mysteries of the game well to you, but For me, the story of the game was a bit confusing and disjointed.The gameplay was a good improvement over the first version, and this time, in addition to defense, you can attack the enemy at a suitable time and defeat the enemy. In addition, you have a special ability and a skill tree that you can play by improving your skills make it easier.The graphics and design of the models and environments are very good and they have good details, the lighting and visual effects are also well done.The music and sound of the game are just as good as the first version and are fully compatible with the game environment and atmosphere.With all the improvements this game had over the first version, it had a weaker experience for me. After all the updates provided for the game, the game still has technical problems. The game was not as scary as the first version and it was scary for me just before facing the enemies, but these did not make me give up the experience of this game and curiosity and want to leave the game story half-finished.Score 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to recommend this but ultimately I do if you enjoyed the first one. It dose a good job of wrapping up the plot from the original and dose a lot to make it a squeal that isn't just an expansion of the first one by taking the game play in new direction. I can see what they were going for it just wasn't as exciting or effective as the first game. You are able to fight back a bit more in this game and it weakened a lot of the tension the first game had and it felt more frustrating then fun. I waited a bit for patches as I heard the game was nearly unplayable at launch I ran into no technical problems that hurt anything (two times it looked like some animations didn't work right but other then that it was solid and I wouldn't have mentioned anything in my review but I heard horror stories with this game at launch that scared me away) I do think the story is better as it ends and wraps things up nicely. Don't try to play this before the first one despite it technically being a prequel not only dose it spoil stuff this game will be impossible to follow.  It follows 3 timelines and is somewhat convoluted as a story about mind controlled moths can be however if you pay attention it is an interesting horror story about 2 horrific families and is worth digging into.One final note this game is significantly less graphic imo then the previous entry. It's not a problem and  most likely because several of the characters are significantly younger. Just letting people know if the previous game turned you off because of it or were worried it escalated if you can handle the previous game you will be fine for this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially bought this and the first game [on ps4] because people said it was a lot like Clock Tower, and I love me some Clock Tower... but, this game is somewhat uncomfortable to listen to.Angry Violins smother out any other sound so it make listening for Stalkers difficult and the reticle is almost non-existent for opening doors or picking up items so there's lots of time wasted when trying to open up all the things.Also the bugs. Prompts for survival will also sometimes come in late and it will take the Protag to get hit a few times or even death for the prompts to "magically spawn" into steps to progress.The camera that focuses the Player's POV will also clip onto walls and through furniture and walls without actually focus on nothing so the "clue" is often missed.Minorly, subtitles will not match with the voice lines, showcasing lines that have been cut from the dub.Back to being uncomfortable to listen to, I can handle a lot of vulgar and hateful things if it's to prove a point to establish an antagonist. name: Total War: WARHAMMER III
detailed_description: Immortal Empires is Now Available to all Total War: WARHAMMER III Players Immortal Empires is the culmination of the entire Total War: WARHAMMER series. Combining the campaign maps, races, and factions from all three games* into a single, epic sandbox campaign. It’s the most complete and definitive Warhammer strategy experience ever conceived! Immortal Empires is Out Now *All owners of Total War: WARHAMMER III can now access the Immortal Empires Campaign. However, there are several races available in Immortal Empires that are unlocked if you own Total War: WARHAMMER, Total War: WARHAMMER II or DLC across the entire trilogy. Join Our Discord Server
about_the_game: The last roar of a dying god ruptures the boundary between worlds, opening a portal to the Realm of Chaos. From this maelstrom, the four Ruinous Powers – Khorne, Nurgle, Tzeentch and Slaanesh – emerge, spreading darkness and despair. The stern warriors of Kislev and the vast empire of Grand Cathay stand at the threshold, as a vengeful Daemon Prince vows to destroy those who corrupted him. The coming conflict will engulf all. Will you conquer your daemons? Or command them? With seven unique races and hundreds of units under your command, raise an army and dominate in epic real-time battles across a world of breathtaking scale and spectacle. In the most ambitious and groundbreaking Total War title to date, dive into a captivating narrative that will take you to the mind-bending Realm of Chaos and back again. Forge your empire in a strategy sandbox that ensures no two campaigns are ever the same. Play as 10 Legendary Lords! Will you side with the Chaos Gods and take one of their Daemonic Champions, play as an ancient transforming Dragon from Grand Cathay, defend the frozen nation of Kislev with the Ice Queen or play the ultimate villain as the Daemon Prince? Customise the Daemon Prince to your own unique design with a huge suite of body parts and powers, creating billions of potential combinations to suit your own playstyle. Multiplayer is now bigger than ever. With the vast 8-player Realm of Chaos multiplayer campaign, the intense 1 v 1 Domination mode, the story-driven multiplayer campaigns built around Kislev and Grand Cathay and ranked & custom battles, there’s no shortage of ways to cause chaos with friends.
short_description: The cataclysmic conclusion to the Total War: WARHAMMER trilogy is here. Rally your forces and step into the Realm of Chaos, a dimension of mind-bending horror where the very fate of the world will be decided. Will you conquer your Daemons… or command them?

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, and I wish I could recommend it, but the state of development has been far short of what one would expect from a company of this size.Updates are slow to roll out, and each one represents a step forward followed by a tumble down the steps. To be fair, some bugs are expected when discussing a project of this size, but this isn't a matter of a few avoidable inconsistencies. This is a constant rotation of features not working and game pieces missing. Strategy games lose their appeal when they don't have all the pieces in the box.Maybe one day Creative Assembly will put together a team large enough to not only expand content, but curate and maintain this game in the way that it needs. If that day comes then I will change this review with glee. But until that day comes, I'll have to advise that you pass on this, as it does not work as intended.

_childDocuments_.review: I just can't understand what CA's greenskin programmers are thinking. What a siege town needs is better pathfinding AI, proper arrow tower construction, and fewer bugs to enhance the experience, so just cutting it out would be a bit of a no-brainer. There's no argument that siege warfare should be in towns. If siege warfare doesn't have a good experience, it should be improved and done well rather than deleted. The fact that Warhammer II does not have normal siege warfare was criticized, but Warhammer III showed a hint of improvement, and then it was deleted directly, which is really incomprehensible.

_childDocuments_.review: The culmination of the series. Is the game perfect? No, far from it. But there's nothing here that can't be fixed by patches and expansions. The foundations are as solid as a WH Total War game can be, with the most experimental factions to date, with interesting rosters, map decisions, and pretty different playstyles. Forget doing more or less the same thing successfully whether it's with Lizardmen or Empire - you need quite different approaches to each faction, and their battles play out differently as well. The issues will be fixed sooner or later, but as of now, the game is extremely fun already.

_childDocuments_.review: Between Warhammer 1-3, I have thousands of hours and believe this is arguable one of the best fantasy strategy games. The diversity of fantasy races is large. Each faction also adds enough uniqueness that there is a great deal of replay value. If you enjoy strategy games, this should be in your library.Please note that there is a lot of DLC and most can be bought on sale (which occur very often and I would highly suggest waiting for a sale, they happen almost every other month). Also, the base games count as expansions for warhammer 3 and offer access to 4 races each. Also, getting the most recent DLC would grant access to base-level content from previous DLC for the same race. For instance, Champions of Chaos will provide content from older Warriors of Chaos DLC or the new Thrones of Decay will grant access to content from Warhammer 1 (dwarfs and empire).Post-Thrones of Decay DLC, CA has shown a commitment to updating the core campaign experience and deliver better customer value. There have finally been patches to core gameplay issues such as AI pathing and responsiveness that has made battles much more enjoyable again. There is a plan to move to smaller DLC packs going forward. As long as these smaller packs include reworks and campaign balancing, I recommend playing Warhammer 3. If CA goes back to their greedy, anti-customer practices pre-Thrones of Decay, I will be sure to change my review. For now, it appears CA is back to its Warhammer 2 glory days where making great content and keeping the game patched and fresh.

_childDocuments_.review: Although some issues remain, Creative Assembly have demonstrated their commitment to maintain and improve this game in the long-term, so I'm reversing my negative rating to a positive one.The DLC Roadmap is a little slow compared to TW:WH II, but nobody can deny that Immortal Empires is an incredible achievement, and one of the greatest gaming experiences money can buy.UPDATED IN MARCH 2024 - ORIGINAL NEGATIVE REVIEW FROM AUGUST 2023 BELOWWhile I've had many enjoyable hours with this game, I cannot recommend it in its current state. After the incredible ride we had with TW:WH II, with frequent updates, great quality DLC, with a bunch of free content to top it off, the support for this game is astonishingly lacklustre in comparison.My main complaint is the long list of known bugs and quality-of-life issues still present in the game 18 months after it's initial release. It feels as though the development team are more focused on driving up DLC sales than actually fixing the base game - and often new DLC has introduced even more bugs into the game.To note a small number of issues at the time of writing this review, the following examples make certain lords and factions virtually unplayable as some of their core mechanics are broken:- Wood Elves, introduced in the Realm of the Wood Elves DLC (£14.99), cannot acquire Ariel, their unique hero introduced in the Twisted and the Twilight DLC (£7.99) who is linked to the main questline for the Wood Elf faction. If you acquire her through confederation, rather than through the bugged quest, all five of her unique items vanish and cannot be obtained in any way. - Lizardmen - Oxylotl, introduced in the Silence and the Fury DLC (£7.99), cannot reliably use his teleportation feature. As a lord, his unique faction mechanic is entirely dependent on his army being able to quickly zip across the map to complete quests. If he doesn't complete them in time, his faction usually suffers some significant debuffs. The issue is that about 10% of the time, his teleportation mechanic simply doesn't work, resulting in an automatic failure of said quests. - Lizardmen - Nakai, introduced in the Hunter and the Beast DLC (£7.99), cannot recruit his signature units, the kroxigors.- Bretonnia, a faction introduced through free updates to TW:WH and TW:WH II, cannot progress their troths for Damsel heroes in TW:WH III.Just those examples account for almost £40 worth of broken content (almost enough to buy a separate full price AAA game).If things improve, I'll happily return and change my rating, but for now it remains negative. It is so disappointing to see Creative Assembly go the way of Bethesda, by addressing bugs with the whole "Oh, ignore that, let the modders fix it. Anyway, how much are we charging for the next DLC?" type attitude.P.S. Please do something to improve the Daemons of Chaos faction on Immortal Empires. So much effort was put into his unique equipment mechanic that it seems every other aspect of this faction has been neglected to the point where the flagship faction for the release of TW:WH III, that is the main feature on the game's cover, is probably the weakest and most hated faction in the whole game.

_childDocuments_.review: After updating to GeForce driver 511.79 and playing around with the benchmark I've found a nice compromise of graphics and performance. Screen Space Shadows, SSAO and shadow detail and turning down fog were the big bang-for-your-buck changes. It's still relatively heavy performance wise compared to TW3K, but there's a lot more going on too, I guess. I'm sure they'll keep working on it. Performance in battle and loading/turn times haven't been an issue at all and generally seem as good or better than what I had in TWW2. Once you get past performance it's really good Warhams with lots of cool factions - it's great! The new minor settlement battles are just what I wanted. Looking forward to many, many years of support and a burgeoning mod community.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War: Warhammer III is a game that has its fair share of bugs, but it is also perhaps the only series out there currently that tackles battlefield meta strategy in an appealing manner.Rather than you micromanaging engagements of maybe 5-20 individual units as you would in most traditional strategy games. Total War has you oversee anywhere from hundreds to thousands of units at once. And your duty is to orchestrate the movements of these armies like a force of nature manipulating the flow of the ocean's currents. Have your foot soldiers hold the line while your cavalry attempt to flank and smack into the rear of the enemy.Create elaborate formations to allow your ranged units to more easily shoot the enemy.Mix in your monsters with your canon fodder units to bolster their effectiveness.These slower-paced aspects of combat are massively appealing to people like me who don't really enjoy the fast-paced click-y nature of most strategy games. Technically it's a RTWP (Real-time-with-pause) game, but some people prefer to play with this off. For someone like me who likes to relax as I consider my next move, this is massively appealing.There is also a fairly simple 4X layer attached to the game as well which is just as important as the individual battles. Because it's simple, it's easy to get used to even if you don't care much for grand strategy.As for the matter of content...The Warhammer sub-series of Total War games has adopted a unique DLC model that isn't really seen elsewhere. Basically, everything purchased in the older games carries forward into the newer games, so you only need to buy things once.While a cool idea in theory, this has had the unfortunate snowballing effect of the game effectively costing multiple hundreds of dollars to get the full package by the time this game hit the scene.The "good" news is that generally you don't -need- to buy everything if you're not inclined to. Content will still appear in the game whether you own it or not, and the only difference is if you are able to directly access it yourself (i.e., the Vampire Coast will still be present on the map no matter what).Because of this, if for example you do not like playing as the High Elves or or Dark Elves, the "Queen and the Crone" DLC pack has literally no value to you, as it only adds content for those two factions.All in all, I think it's definitely worth getting. Don't be put off too hard by the price. Buy the base game and just pick up stuff that interests you as you go along. Particularly now since you can purchase the DLC a-la-carte and no longer have to purchase WH1/WH2 as a prerequisite, it's easier than ever.

It is actually IMO one of the best RTS /grand strategy games ever made. This is game is a different story and its honestly the final straw for me after watching ive loved for years get destroyed.I can now honestly say i hate total war. The Developers have absolutely gouged us for years but keep fans coming back because there is no other game quite like Total War. It is admittedly a great game design that no one else seems to be able to get quite right but i simply can no longer get past the business behind it.  Practices like paying for gore in a game built around warfare (especially Warhammer like WTF?!) , and releasing factions as overpriced DLC are but a few of the offenses made to fans. It should be inexcusable.  I could even forgive that if the newer games were good or offered anything new.   In my 2 hours of play time i barely even had the willpower to play past the tutorial due to crashes , poor optimization, and honestly just general boredom. There is absolutely nothing new about this game beyond cosmetics that this game brings to the series. _childDocuments_.review: Total War: Warhammer 3 is the third installment in a series, that prior to release had demonstrated that Creative Assembly's production teams had worked hard over the previous years to refine and improve the fantasy franchise. At some time between TWW2 and TWW3 something changed. Despite already having experience meshing W1 into W2, the W3 release was a bit of a clusterf*ck. The issues at launch were myriad, but the community waited for the patches to be sorted out. They kept on waiting. At the time of writing this review we are about one and a half years post initial release and there are still rampant issues and glitches, and many of these problems are issues unique to the third game. Further DLC that has been released seems to only exacerbate this. And now, just prior to the Shadows of Change DLC release we are seeing massive price hikes with seemingly reduced content and support for the game that is virtually nonexistent. To top it all off, the community receives a message from the Chief Product Officer that effectively threatened to kill CA's own cash-cow franchise Three Kingdoms-style if the fanbase doesn't buy the DLC.What the hell, CA. This game series had so much potential, and now because you think you can, you're going to grab the money and pull a "Game of Thrones" season 8 on us? Please understand, stripping your support teams from your flagship product to reallocate resources and funding elsewhere is not the community's fault. Whatever finance bro you hired to manage the allocation of you assets needs to be given a pink slip. I can't recommend this game due to these issues. I'll change my recommendation and update this review if CA makes a noticeable shift in their attitude towards their customers, but honestly I'm not holding my breath.

_childDocuments_.review: Greetings from an old Warhammer fan. This is gonna be a bit of a harsh review of the current product, I promise I'll keep it short and to the point.I'll begin with the most relevant. This game is NOT worth your money. Highly consider your interest in this game before investing. Factions are designed to be hindered until you pay for the DLC to get them proper rosters of units to fight with. Moving past the obvious balancing bias, why are we charging 25 dollars for 3 new faction lords and a new hero? We just paid 25 dollars for an entire new faction, an entire new roster, new buildings new heroes new spells.. Correct me if i'm wrong but as far as I can tell we're only getting 4 new units? What? 10 dollar DLC for 25 is absurd. _childDocuments_.review: Its effectively more of the same. That fact may well be enough to put you off, as their monetisation practices are a little shady. Also, the four chaos factions are quite diverse, but they do have a lot of overlap in places and of course, the demons of chaos faction is a combination of all four, so calling it eight factions at launch (including the day 1 DLC ogre kingdoms) may be a bit of an exaggeration.I think there is plenty to like here for people who like campaign mechanics or are interested in the new factions (I just couldn't resist playing as chaos). The new multiplayer campaign stuff sounds cool but I've not had a chance to try it out yet, and I don't really do multiplayer battles so I can't speak to that. I myself haven't had major bugs or issues like that, its much more stable for me than the other games were when I first tried them, and they have a lot of nice QoL improvements as this is effectively a continuation of 2. Load times are improved, the AI aren't overly annoying with hero actions or continuous attempts at diplomacy. This content here could easily be a hundred hours, but as ever total war die hards will have the same issues with warhammer 3 that they had with 1 and 2. For me, its worth the price of admission but I didn't pay extra for the day 1 dlc.TL;DR If you have content for 2 that you haven't completed yet, play that and wait for a sale for this unless you really need to try the new factions and campaign mechanics. If you are a long time total war player who longs for the days of medieval 2, Warhammer 3 will not be any more satisfying than warhammer 2 was

_childDocuments_.review: I am a Total War noob who has some experience playing RTS games such as Age of Empires, Black & White 1&2, and LOTR: Battle for middle earth 2. I had my first experience with the 2nd installment of the warhammer series and while I thought the units looked incredible and watching them fight was super cool, I was totally scared off and overwhelmed by the intricate systems such as diplomacy, building and resource management to name a few. It had me running scared, and thought these games just weren't for me. After re-watching the lotr and hobbit movies I had an itch for some high fantasy, political intrigue, and massive battles, so I decided to give this one a try since the base game is available on GamePass. Thanks to the new tutorial in warhammer 3 I was able to baby step my way into being comfortable with the major systems at play and felt the tutorial did a great job of still offering a compelling experience while drip feeding you these systems at times when they are relevant, giving you a fuller understanding of how they impact your game as a result. At the time of writing this review I have 128 hours played which is more than any other game in my steam library currently, and this my most recently purchased game. All of this is to say, I'm really glad that I gave this series another shot and stuck through the tutorial. I would currently rate this among my favorite games at the moment and would recommend to anyone who like myself, would watch the battle of the five armies and think, "I want to play a game where I can do that!", and doesn't mind taking the time to learn a new game. It can be a bit intimidating at a glance but if you complete the tutorial and really buy into that part of the process you will have experienced a kick ass part of the story that gets you excited to jump in and a good working knowledge of how to play many of the factions. I say many and not all because there are a decent number of legendary lords or even complete factions that have totally unique mechanics and would not recommend them until you have a decent grasp of the basics. A few beginner friendly factions that I would recommend are Kislev, Grand Cathay, Bretonia, Green Skins, and the High Elves. There are many others that are great for beginners but these are the only I have tried and have a decent amount of reliance on the mechanics taught in the tutorial. Another thing of note is the multiplayer, its a ton of fun and would highly recommend it! I've played with two other people so far, but I believe you can have up to 8 people simultaneously and I'd love to give it a shot.Summary: Great game with tons of content and replayability that is deeply rewarding to learn and is now easier than ever to pick up thanks to the great tutorial. If you don't choose a beginner friendly faction to start you may just get overwhelmed and put off from the game.

_childDocuments_.review: The pros slightly outweigh the cons. I play on legendary, so keep that in mind.PROS:-Excellent prologue-Cool story-Cool maps-Astounding animations-Some truly epic battles that even occur organically sometimes-Asymmetrical gameplay-Realms of Chaos maps and mechanics-Diplomacy is much improvedMeh:-Settlement, siege battles and set piece battles are much more interesting than in WH2, but still rather meh-There is some blurriness to the visuals, but it reminds me of an impressionist painting, so I'm not that bothered-Somewhat frequent stuttering on campaign map; during end-turns it's a roll of the dice if deselecting fast forward will be registeredCONS:-Autoresolve does not save you any time; rather it punishes you with a devastating and unreasonable result that can have long-term consequences, even when anyone in a coma could win the battle handily; on my system, this means around 2 minutes to load in, around 5 minutes to fight, and around 2 minutes to load back into the campaign, meaning that per battle I am losing around 9 minutes of my life that I can never get back. PLEASE fix this-To compensate for an inept AI, CA's solution for providing a challenge is to make your enemies collectively at least 15x stronger than you. No really, I did the math.      -I'm not sure when, but all of my immediate rivals stopped warring with each other and became defensive allies almost instantaneously with me as their sole focus, even though some of them were beating me in the race for the forge (meaning that they weren't prioritizing winning the game by going after their new allies, but instead were prioritizing making my experience miserable)     -At one point, I had 30 settlements and was able to field 3 good armies, but all five of my immediate (allied) strategic threats had around 10 settlements and were able to consistently have 3 good armies at any one time EACH -> 15x my strength at least. This means WAVES of cheating AI that makes for a depressing grind that I have to wade through before I can have fun progressing the storyOverall: pros slightly outweigh some MAJOR cons that can and should be fixed. Also, modding is on the horizon, and that can't come soon enough . I'm also looking forward to Immortal Empires. My advice: approach with caution. A casual experience might well be enjoyable, but if you're looking for a challenge that isn't utterly contrived... look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War Warhammer 3 has the potential to be one of the greatest strategy games of all time. As such, it pains me to say that it has utterly failed to live up to its potential up to this point. I can't understand what CA was thinking releasing this game in the state it did, and I can't figure out why they only update the game whenever a DLC comes out. While Champions of Chaos and Forge of the Chaos Dwarfs were excellent DLCs in their own right, CA can't expect players to fork over $25 every few months in order for the game to receive the updates it so desperately needs. While Shadows of Change looks to be adding very interesting content, it doesn't make sense for it to be priced the same as a race pack. Until CA can get its act together, I wouldn't recommend supporting them. Instead of working on other games, they should consolidate their resources and finish their most ambitious game to date. I suppose time will tell how this game turns out, but at the moment, its future doesn't seem very bright.

_childDocuments_.review: Total War Warhammer III is in an interesting position. As the capstone in a massive hit trilogy of games, a certain expectation is placed upon this game even before people try it. It's supposed to be the culmination of years of hard work and attention to detail that not many games would aspire to match.Warhammer III has a chance to live up to those expectations in the future. The main campaign mode currently on offer is being steadily improved by the team at CA, while we all await the big release of Immortal Empires. There are still some things that Warhammer II does better currently, such as variety (with all DLC's considered, it's no wonder), UI, and even unit responsiveness. Many of these issues are probably going to be worked on in the coming months. UI will get a much needed color swap option with the release of IE.A direct "Yes I recommend this game" is not the answer. I would say if you own the first two games, 3 will be worth it when IE is released. If this is your first foray into the incredible world of TW:WH games, it's a hard decision. You won't have access to IE without the other two games, which would ironically give you Mortal Empires, the previous combined map. More value is arguably within the first two games. I recommend trying 1 and 2 first, and if you like how ME plays WH3 will definitely be worth it at that point.My overall rating of WH3 as of writing: 8.5 / 10Edit: Since the release of Immortal Empires, the game is in a much better state, properly focused on the fun mechanics that made its predecessor so great. AI still behaves in peculiar ways, and some systems are broken, but what the third game currently lacks in polish is made up for in spades by sheer scope and ambition. The vast Warhammer Fantasy world is replete with details, and almost every major faction is represented here. If you enjoy Warhammer Fantasy, Immortal Empires delivers.Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Total War: Warhammer III is an absolute gem in the strategy game genre. This captivating title seamlessly blends turn-based strategy and real-time tactical battles, immersing players in a dark and enthralling world. What makes it truly outstanding is the vibrant modding community, which adds a new layer of excitement and customization to the game.With Total War: Warhammer III, you're not just limited to the base game. The modding community offers an array of modifications that can transform your experience, providing new units, visuals, campaigns, and more. The possibilities are virtually endless, ensuring that every playthrough feels fresh and exciting. Accessing and installing mods through the Steam Workshop is straightforward, and the active community ensures compatibility with updates.Even without mods, the game itself delivers a fantastic strategic experience. The campaign's depth and the intense real-time battles are a joy to delve into. The variety of playable factions, each with its distinct mechanics and playstyles, ensures countless hours of engaging gameplay. Visually, the game is stunning, with detailed units and sprawling battlefields that come to life. The epic orchestral score further enhances the immersive experience.In summary, Total War: Warhammer III is a strategy masterpiece that gets even better with mods. The game's strategic depth and breathtaking battles alone make it worth playing, but the ability to customize and enhance your experience takes it to a whole new level.

_childDocuments_.review: I have loved the Total War games since Rome 1. I've also gotten a lot of enjoyment out of this series. However it's become quite obvious that CA has no interest in putting adequate time or money in to QA or bug fixing. There are paid DLC bugs that have gone unfixed for months despite modders discovering simple database entry fixes. Headlining patch features don't work despite the fact that a single gameplay test would be enough to find out it isn't working. Each patch seems to introduce new game-breaking bugs, like ranged units running in to melee. Some broken features continue to be broken after receiving one or more fixes. There are loads of broken database entries that have been identified by the community but continue to go unfixed. When I go back and play other Total War games it becomes obvious how unresponsive units are to orders in WH3.And in the middle of this environment, CA tries to institute a 150% price hike on new DLC which seems half-baked and reeks of "minimum viable product." It would be one thing if this price hike either came alongside1) the announcement of a custodian team that would be dedicated to cleaning up bugs and broken features, OR2) the DLC was so massive that it fundamentally reshaped the game (ex; the Fall of the Samurai expansion for Shogun 2)But neither of those things happened. CA is essentially asking for expansion-level prices for non-expansion DLC content, while not seriously re-investing that money in to the game. I do not wish continue to financially support a game that seems to receive inadequate support from the company. Nor can I recommend that anybody else purchase it when it is in this state.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface my review with this: I believe that Total War Warhammer 3 is fun.Let me follow that up with this before the rabid community of this game burns me at the stake:The game is in no way shape or form perfect. It has some glaring flaws that do impede upon the greatness that the game could be. However, I feel that a lot of people are hyperbolizing just how overwhelming these flaws are. Is the UI rough?Yes, red on red on red was a dumb choice and I feel like CA should roll back to Warhammer 2's color scheme for UI or at the very least adjust them to something else.Are the Chaos Realms bad?I can't say for certain because I personally really enjoy them. They give me the option to hunt down the other legendary lords in the game before they can grab souls or allow them to get the soul while I destroy their homeland. I feel that most people who dislike them simply don't like hunting other lords down which is understandable. The realms force a player to alter the way they play in a way that may be against what they're used to which is poor game design. I just happen to like that form of play. I do wish that I could send lords other than my legendary lord through the rifts if only simply to teleport though.The unit responsiveness is bad?This problem I can completely agree with. The way units act in this game is very peculiar and quite often ends in units taking more damage than they should. Ranged units not firing when they have sightlines to their targets. Cavalry turning around to re-engage with an enemy because one unit is trapped in the fray (which has always been a problem with these games). Cathay's formation attack ability ending up with their units being less effective at fighting than they would be without it being on.Overall, this game has problems, but I personally can overlook them because I think this is the most fun I've had playing a TWW game. The outpost system is fantastic. Having other faction's units in your army comps opens so many doors for strategy and fun. Being able to see what a friendly AI faction is doing with its lords is such a massive boon to AI/Player relations. The new factions are almost all interesting and fun to play as (Just not a huge fan of Kislev personally, sorry). The Chaos Rifts themselves are fantastic because they allow you a timed option to hop around and target factions that you need to kill in exchange for your land getting tainted with usually enemy corruption and always hostile armies.In conclusion, I can see why people are frustrated with CA's recently released roadmap, but again I think people are being overly hostile about it like they usually are online. I enjoy this game for what it is and have had a blast playing it. If you can look past some issues (most of which will likely be fixed in the coming months to year (or fixed with mods that are already out)) then I do recommend this game. Otherwise, I would wait until the end of the year and see what the state of the game is then.

That's unacceptable.Game is gorgeous, needs some work.  Delay again next time, some of us won't pitchfork you I swear.Update after two minor patches and several weeks/30+ hours of playtime:  Not much performance improvement at all, I stand by my original statement that they should have delayed it another few months and either optimized more or worked out DLSS.  Over 80% of the campaign map is 50ish fps on a 90 - it's insane.  It isn't a smooth 50 either, it's 42,51,44,65,43 if you scroll around. Pros:- Many civs to play (of course they will release many more for $$$ DLC)- New map and new units, including Eastern styles.- More players for multiplayer, however.. this feature doesn't really matter in its current state.Cons:- Forced mini game in the main campaign, that you cannot ignore or you will lose, time wasted.- Lots of stutters for some people playing online.- Very boring campaign. - Very short campaign.- Some civs are very weak and underwhelming, not very enjoyable to play, some are overpowered.- The siege battles, almost become a "Tower defense" build more towers, keep casting magic.. win?- Feels rushed and yet again that we need to be the testers for another CA game.Now there are other pros and cons, but in the end this review most likely will change once Mortal Empires content is added and other things are fixed, overall I enjoy playing co-op with friends on these type of games, but this one just isn't fun at all, you get burnt out very quickly because like I stated you have to play the mini-game if you do not, the AI will which they will win and your time is wasted. That also doesn't fix much it only removes one major annoyance and opens another. I would not recommend picking this game up in its current state, we know they won't have a big discount but I am sure you can read all the other players reviews and witness things for yourself now days, I would avoid this game until they add Mortal Empires and fix many other issues with the game, making it more enjoyable for all players. _childDocuments_.review: Total War: Warhammer 3 is a visually stunning game that delivers intense and impactful battles. Players have a plethora of leaders to choose from, making for excellent replay value, especially with the Immortal Empires mode. The game's strengths lie in its graphics and immersive battles, but there are a few areas that could use improvement.The Realm of Chaos campaign can feel tedious with its portal system. The game could also benefit from more in-depth diplomacy and money management options. The siege system feels outdated and could use a revamp; it feels less tedious to defend on an open field than in high walls.Despite its flaws, Total War: Warhammer 3 is a must-try for strategy game enthusiasts who enjoy epic battles. Its great graphics, impactful battles, and many leaders make for a memorable gaming experience, especially with the Immortal Empires mode. However, those looking for more depth in diplomacy and siege gameplay may want to approach the game with more caution. Overall, Total War: Warhammer 3 is an excellent game with plenty of enjoyable gameplay, even if it has some shortcomings.

The new campaign sucks and forces you into playing a very specific way, completely the opposite of what total war players expect and want. The new UI is ugly. The features they added either don't work, like saving formations and unit groupings, or are tedious and should never have been added. Seiges are less fun with all the goofy little buildable things popping up, and they are far more frequent than in the last game. AI is worse than before, with units struggling to navigate the new settlement maps. On the campaign, the AI gangs up on the player despite having better things to do, yet is too cowardly to attack. So expect a ton of enemy armies dancing around your territory not engaging you while you're forced to deal with the new campaign mechanics instead of conquering territory. The new units are cool, but the faction tech trees and what not are terribly balanced and bugged. The developers regressed with their balancing, so there are now a ton of useless paths to spend points on, instead of everything feeling equally valuable. I would rather play the new factions in the old engine.

_childDocuments_.review: The Ultimate Victory end game scenarios are broken garbage. Who came up with this trash?I have had games where I was friends with Dwarves for the entire game, we propped each other up against the already EXTREMELY UNBALANCED Chaos factions. Got each other through the worst of it. End game scenario pops up with Dwarven Grudge book BS, spawns a dozen full dwarf armies in my lands (I have 3 armies) and all dwarfs are immediately at war with me. How is this fun? How is this fair? Why are pre-established factions spawning units out of thin air? This amount of units would bankrupt any faction at this time in the game within 2 turns, yet they don't go bankrupt. So that to me immediately suggests that these factions are no longer bound by the rules of the game that everyone else is playing by. So its no surprise when they clean sweep every faction that is limited by things like currency, army limit, etc.Its not even fun, I have tried multiple times to fight through these and achieve the "Ultimate Victory Condition" its just not worth the headache.

_childDocuments_.review: I wrote my initial negative feedback when I had 100 hours on it. Now that I have nearly 400 and additional 100$ spent on DLCs, I enjoyed some parts, but... I'm also a person who enjoyed other TW titles (1 or 2K+ hours) and played WH3 on the hardest difficulties.-The game is designed as a cash-cow. You won't even get a chance to experience a faction fully unless you own all the DLCs within it, since you will miss out on units and crucial faction mechanics. With free factions you must buy a DLC with one lord in order to fully experience it, or even buy a DLC with a faction and then another one or two just to unlock the additional lords in order to gain access to all the faction units and mechanics. Also the lords that are paid obviously have the most interesting campaigns, the free ones are usually very mediocre.-The price is ridiculous. WH1, WH2, WH3 are required and prepare another 100$ at least for DLCs. I don't mind spending money that much, but some of you might do, I still think it's a bit over the board. As mentioned above, you are forced to buy them with some (majority) factions, if you want the full experience. 25$ for DLC to unlock 1 faction, then 15$ DLC to unlock 2 lords in order to get a full experience of that faction. You might even end up not enjoying the faction after trying it out for 1-2 hours and say hello to 25$ wasted (will happen quite often), or you buy the lords that you won't play just to unlock the units for the one that you want to play. Now you just realize, that you could have bought a fully fledged new game for that price. Also count with a lot of money wasted on things you won't enjoy - spent a lot of hours of my playtime this way (trying to find something enjoyable where I wasted my money).-The campaigns are - go capture (X amount) of settlements and make sure you own these cities within them. Game won. Wait. You have end game crisis scenario where a couple of enemy units spawn, that you might as well just auto resolve. You should get to the part where you're able to auto-resolve majority of your fights and just conquer anything you want (steamroll is the professional gaming term) around turn 30-60 even on the hardest difficulties. The campaign just loses meaning around that time. The end game crisis is around 4-6 hours after your campaign victory conditions are met, if you want to spend more time on just auto resolving everything.-This title is far from strategic and is very arcady. If you're looking for a strategically challenging game (even on hardest difficulties), look for other TW titles ( 2 DLCs = another game or even 2 in the case of older ones which are great). The fights are having way too many mechanics to abuse them. Some lords being able to nearly take out the whole force of their own, mages wiping huge part of their army before they can even reach yours (at that point the battle is won), and the whole way the fights are fought is in the way of put this certain mystical creature vs this instead of trying come up with strategical positioning and maneuvering of how to win the fights. Some people might enjoy it. Some fights can be challenging, just want to highlight the arcady part.-The AI is dumb. Doesn't matter what the difficulty is. If the enemy has reinforcing army, they will just stand still and let you crush 1/2 of their army before they arrive. You can blob up big chunk of their army and just destroy it with artillery and a couple of spells. Many other things to mention, but I think this should be enough to understand it.-The campaigns with the story (not the sandbox version).-Some factions are fun to play (for me it's Tomb Kings - DLC) and some lords have great campaigns (Alarielle, Sniktch - both DLCs) with interesting mechanics.-It has high replayability, new factions, new lords, you just have to buy them.-Exploring new faction is amazing, if like it (happened to me with Tomb Kings), but you might as well not like it (Chaos Dwarfs for me - 25$ DLC).-The fights even if they're not so realistic and kinda arcady, can sometimes be great fun. I just started to like it more and more the longer I played the game.If you like fantasy and strategy, this game is a great combination of it and you will for sure love it. You can easily spend a lot of hours on this game. Be prepared to have a couple of 100s of $ ready to spend on it. If you want a great strategic challenge, maybe to train your thinking, go for other titles. Always keep in mind that before buying this game in order to get the full experience and explore it fully, you can buy multiple other games for the price of this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Thrones of decay was a banger. Really pleased with their current attitude and where theyre going if this is the quality theyre gonna put out!----------------------------------------------------------------------------This game is great and starting in 2024 the company has worked to make it right from the previous dlc disaster. But it cannot be ignored that there are an egregious amount of bugs with the base game for the amount of changes coming from patches in a 6 month patch cycle. _childDocuments_.review: I think the game's in much better state that when it first dropped, and definitely among my favourite TW titles of all time now. Its great as well that CA have lowered the bar of entry for new players by opening up Immortal Empires to those who don't own the first two games, more players means more content for everyone.There are a few negatives. The Realms of Chaos campaign provides a great intro to the faction mechanics of each of the game 3 races, but the mid-to-end game is very repetitive, which is a shame as it does at times feel like the most polished and balanced of the campaigns on offer. Immortal Empires has its limitations in terms of balance, AI behaviour and the like.THE POSITIVES: Immortal Empires, while clearly still developing, is fantastic. There are so many varied factions and lords to chose from its hard to see how anyone could tire of the game, especially with more to come in future content patches. The map is vast, even on Long Campaign completion half of it might still be under fog of war. Things like the ally outpost system allowing you to recruit other races' units adds to that replayability still further. I would love more narrative elements, more quests, and some reworks for certain older factions, but i'm sure that will all come in time. And to be honest even if it didn't I would still consider IE the quintessential TW:WH experience. Despite all I said about Realms of Chaos above, I still think the campaign has a place as a faction tutorial. The first 20 or so turns deliver tutorial quests and a good feel for how the factions work, and I have dipped back into it several times to test out the new factions in a more 'on the rails' experience than IE offers. I wouldnt really recommend anyone playing ROC campaign to completion more than once (well, twice because the Warriors of Chaos campaign runs a little differently) but i think it remains a great tool for learning about the factions.Quality of Life was a big thing that saw improvement on game 2. I don't know how we coped without Quick Deal Diplomacy, a combined item, ancillary and skill point UI, and im not even joking. Hours of time saved from clicking between characters and factions on the diplomacy screen. I know i'm probably forgetting some other great ones but let the lesson be that great and positive changes were made.The new factions are a mixed bag, but as a long time Dawi player it may put my name in the Book forever to admit that Cathay have become my favourite faction by far. Some people may call me mad; to those people, i say...Sky Junks. Overall, would heartily recommend to new players, and to older WH players who may have held off from getting it after seeing the issues with the launch. Its not perfect by any means, but playing it now I no longer feel drawn back to play Warhammer 2, and i am confident that it will only get better and better with time!

_childDocuments_.review: It was supposed to be the best game in the trilogy. Sadly, CA took a wrong direction with this game, we had several delays during the game's cycle, we have bugs that are not fixed, and now it looks like they want to hurry up and end this game earlier than predicted.During WH1, we got 5 DLC's out of which 2 were Race packs, during the games lifecycle of 1 and a half year. During WH2, we got a DLC mostly every 3-4 months with more units, new mechanics for each lord and several other FLC's that accompanied that DLC, and all of this, while keeping the same price as WH1.Now with WH3, the game got 1 and a half years since its release, and what we got is the following:CoC DLC which gives 4 new LL for the Warriors of Chaos race( NONE of them with new mechanics), the characters were suited more to the monogod races instead, ONLY 1 NEW UNIT (Chaos Warshrine) and alot of reskins. Priced at 16€ which is a 60% increase to a standard DLC pack from WH1 or 2 (those are priced at 10€)Chaos Dwarfs racepack: Priced at 25€, this DLC adds the newest race at the time of writing this review; the Chaos Dwarfs. Unit wise, it offers similar content as older races. However' the race comes with just 3 LL and 1 LH, while the racepacks from WH2 came with 4 LL and 1 aditional LL as a FLC. So we basically get 3 LL lords in WH3, vs potentially 5 LL in WH2, and the 40% LL reduction comes with a 31% price increase! (19€ for TK and Vcoast racepacks vs 25€ CD)And finally, the newest DLC: Shadows of Change. The newest tactic issued by CA: make the LP's across 3 races instead of 2. While it seems logical to do so, judging the magnitude of the game, one would expect also the increase in content, right? Well, not CA!. So what we get out of this Lord Pack? 3 new LL, 1 LH and 1 aditional LH as a FLC. These LL are accompanied by 3-4 new units each for a total of somewhere between 10-12 new units spread across 3 races! By comparison, during the 2 race LP's we got in the last 2 games, we had an average of 5-6 new units/ race. So this means a 40%-50% content drop for a staggering price of 25€! Basically, CA values this DLC the same as the Chaos Dwarfs racepack and skyrockets the price by 150% compared to previous lord packs.With the new policy, with 2 DLC's you get for WH3, you pay almost the entire price of a polished, just released AAA game in the form of Baldur's Gate 3. You do the math and see if it's worth it. The board at CA crossed the line.

_childDocuments_.review: Get this,  I played as Balthasar Gelt.   Turn 30,  I get offered a Confederation with Averland that only has one town with 3 buildings in it,  the capital building,  at level 2,  a building to make cavalry units and an economic building pulling in 250 gold per turn.   I'm pulling in 330 gold a turn,  I have 3 towns and a fort in my own lands.  I'm doing well,  growth is slow but strong and steady.  I'm stabilized and on the way up.  I accept this Confederation offer with Averland because it's only got one city,  it's capital and one army and suddenly my cash stockpile turns from +330 gold to -3300 gold and the reason I'm given when I mouse over it is ARMY UPKEEP.   So I figured,  OH,  okay,  this must be the UPKEEP of AVERLAND's ARMY,  They must have more than one army,  but oh no this was not the case,  Averland has one army near their capital and after I disband more than half of it leaving 4 units and a leader in the face of a very possible VAMPIRE INVASION from the east,  I'm still -2,380 gold in the red.   Then the Sylvan's declare war on me, after wiping out a dwarf faction I was trading with and had a non-aggression pact.   I've got one full army lead by Balthasar Gelt,  I have one other army garrisoning one village with only 3 units and a leader and I have another in my 3rd town with only 5 units.  If I disbanded every unit and hero I had I would still be -200 gold in the red.   All of these factors are educating me that the economy in this  game is TOTAL TRASH.     I wouldn't take this game for free.   I prefer a modded Warhammer 2 with all of the DLC I've already purchased years ago.  it's a better game in every way.  Even without the 'new factions'.Install the SFO: Grimhammer II mod in Warhammer II and there is no comparison,  the mod surpasses the original game, improving it immensely. It's an incredibly well done mod.

_childDocuments_.review: Creative Assembly promised, and they delivered.Sega once again releases a quality gaming experience that reminds me we live in a world where Microsoft stole their market share and lowered the average for everyone.Gameplay wise, this title has all you can expect from a new Total War iteration.Interesting and dynamic factions, realistic cavalry that's mostly ineffective against any form of pointy stick or projectiles, as they should, otherwise you'd still see them on battlefields today. (Crécy, Aljubarrota, Agincourt) Stop complaining about cavalry being weak; just ask the English why they spammed arrows and not horsies.The campaign would benefit from some pacing tweaks as the main story forces you to dart for the objectives, not giving you the time to enjoy your PWNG over everyone else. You have to keep an eye on rifts inside your territories as they'll spawn chaos armies every 15 turns or so in the beginning, and then more frequently after turn 50. So the larger your territory, the less you'll be enjoying yourself, as the loop will just have you force-marching your troops to swat chaos armies that'll in turn create unrest and rebellion. We get it, it's the end times. It's not balanced... unless you choose to only have as much territory as you can defend every turn.Now, Creative Assembly listen here; this review might change in the future depending on how mod support is implemented, and that includes at the level of the map editor.I find it worrying that *non-commercial* projects based around popular IPs that receive more love from the fans than from the faceless corporations that own them are, able to be taken down. We know there's pressure to restrict the modding abilities of players going forward, but I would remind you that longevity in a Total War game, is often tied to modding. It is in your best interest to support modders.The hype and Hopium for the new Mortal Empires map is, justifiably, tied to my positive review, too. I'm not tottally unbiased.
