_childDocuments_.review: The game that I expected Sludge Life to be differs greatly compared to the experience I came away with. Even if you’re tempted to generically classify the game as a collect-a-thon or a mini-open-world, Sludge Life ends up presenting itself as much more. Sludge Life seems to avoid any explicitly game-like objectives. Hunting around for tags is mainly used as an extrinsic push to lead you to areas you’ve yet to explore. The most interesting stuff you find tends to have no numerical in-game value associated with it. The game even touches on unexpected topics with a satirical yet serious tone. Sludge Life is way more interesting than you’d expect for a game that has contextual auto-peeing.I've begun to truly appreciate games that have little to no distance between the 'play' button and actual gameplay. From the beginning of Sludge Life, you essentially have free reign over the whole island. The only thing separating you from your ambitions is distance (and maybe two helpful items). You are tossed into the game with no other premise than to follow your instincts, find new places/items/characters to interact with and do some tagging along the way. Basically, everything is ‘optional’, but you still want to run around and see it all. Movement is simple yet quick with a generous mantle that often saves you from the vertical consequences of messy jumps. Getting around is enjoyable enough to rouse the movement-shooter enthusiast part of me that gets hungry for more mobility mechanics whenever it catches the scent of intrinsically rewarding traversal.The islands you hop between include plenty of passive stories that draw connections to other places, people, brands, and events. Places and things that characters mention usually physically exist within the islands and coming across them brings you deeper into the narrative of the spaces that you’ve explored. The many political undertones that make the Sludge feel grounded and lived-in further enhance the believability of what once seemed to be no more than an odd parkouring indie game. Most of the people here have a tangible role in this gloomy, gross, and isolated labor society.The laptop pause menu is a fantastic example of Sludge Life’s creative use of diegetic elements. The laptop’s retro interface makes it stylistically appealing and consistent with the technology found elsewhere in the game’s world. It’s intuitive to use, as it should be if it were someone’s real personal computer. Furthermore, the various features of the laptop reveal details about the norms of this society as well as the personality of Ghost themself. Another clever way in which the laptop is used is to keep gameplay information off your main screen. There is no HUD or ‘tag counter’ to clutter your screen and break the illusion that Sludge Life so creatively casts.While the warped/hard-edged pixel filter is a large part of Sludge Life’s signature presentation, the visuals became very nauseating very early on. Thankfully, the game allows you to turn off and alter a variety of settings (including the main filter). There’s also the option to add a much-needed reticle to the center of the screen. After spending a bit of time taking in the uncanny default visual effects, I thoroughly recommend diving into the settings and customizing the game to fit your needs.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, get ready for a sentimental one with a few spoilers.Sludge Life pulled me in with its attractive art style just from the steam page. It was on sale at the time for like.... idk, 2 dollars, and so I picked it up. I didn't expect the game that I got.Opening up sludge life, you're greeted with a nasty desktop that has some warpy effects as you move the mouse around. It sets the tone with the almost blurred VHS filter that I don't quite have the words for. Entering the game, you literally just throw your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ computer at the wall and see a dirty, messy room of a storage container that functions as an  tutorial to the movement the game. Floaty, but on point and satisfying, Sludge Life plays almost like a greatly simplified, streamlined Mirror's Edge. No running on walls or any of the complex maneuvers, but the running, vaulting, etc mechanics are just plain addictive and it makes you wish the map was  bigger once you finish the game.Onto actually playing, though. The gritty, nasty visual effects blend right into the tone of the game, with choppy lettering reminiscent of subtitles from the 80s-early 2000s. It really brings you back to a place that, for people who have at least grown up within the past 20 years, feels almost nostalgic, lost, and homey at the same time. The dialogue is brilliant, comedic, and precisely in tone; One can go from hearing someone talk about how some lady with a scar on her eye stole their washing machine, to hearing someone muse about life and their purpose here, to finding the girl who stole the washing machine and having a nice conversation with her. The people feel like real people, stuck in this sludge of a dump. The way people are either apathetic, philosophical, absurd, or whimsical feels organic and real, the way that one would feel just talking to people they know. Playing through the game, I got a real feeling of understanding for these people, and a connection between my own sludge life and theirs. This game feels like rock bottom, like everyone knows that there's nowhere further down than here.This game reached me at a very apt time in my life. I won't go into detail, but it's had me feeling a lot of the same ways that this game feels. Lost, wanting for an escape, and just wanting to find your place in all of it. It's helped me kind of redirect my gaze towards it all in at least a small way, and it's helped.The gameplay tasks of tagging spots is also very neat, and the game gives you plenty of tools to both easily achieve your goals and have a lot of fun doing it. There are multiple spots in which you've got to be a little crafty or clever to get to it, such as a hidden item needing a vent that i eventually found before immediately talking to the person who gives the player a clue about the vent. It was a fun moment.There's a camera (that has a different file directory than your regular screenshots) that can be used to both seek out tags and take pictures of them, or really anything else you might want. In short, Sludge Life is a beautiful game that has a lot to say about the world, but doesn't have to directly say much to get to the point. The world feels both lived in and stagnate, like everyone there is alive but have simply given up. Everyone is on strike, so not even the CLOPS (police) will try to do anything about you unless you walk right up to them, in which they'll smack you and usually have a pretty funny line to boot. Almost makes you  to get hit. I still haven't found everything in the game, with about 2 achievements left to get, but from the first night i played sludge life I knew that it would be a very special game for me. I've heard that there's a second one out, and I cannot wait to play it once i get the money. Until then, I recommend you play this game at least a little high if you smoke, as it really helps the atmosphere eek into your bones i feel, but it's not necessary to enjoy the experience. I hope this review helps. "Hey, Two Eyes. Tell me what this SMACK smells like."

_childDocuments_.review: I initially played through the entirety of Sludge Life on Nintendo Switch, but I decided to play through the game again on Steam, now that I own a Steam Deck. I already loved Sludge Life, but after revisiting it, I can comfortably say it is my favorite game published by Devolver Digital (not counting Sludge Life 2, I haven't beaten it yet, but I will likely find it to be an improvement), and among my favorite indie games of all time. Sludge Life boasts a unique gameplay premise with tight controls that revolves around tagging as many walls with your graffiti as possible by using first-person parkour mechanics. The more walls you tag with your artwork, the more rep you gain, which allows you to collaborate with some of the local taggers and create impressive artwork together. The world isn't too big, but it's compact, with a lot to explore and details to uncover. Sludge Life is all about the little details— between the cigarette butts and drawings littered on the floor of the playable character's home, to hidden switches in the offices of CEOs, there's a lot to appreciate. Sludge Life is also endlessly entertaining with its wonderfully useless gameplay mechanics, such as a dedicated fart button, urinating when standing near open toilets, and being able to smoke the cigarettes that you find around the area. Sludge Life's soundtrack, although of very good quality, feels somewhat same-y, with a lot of songs sounding kind of similar to each other. Regardless, the music of Sludge Life is very enjoyable. The visual design and audio design are Sludge Life's crown jewels. The visual presentation is unique and mesmerizing, coupled with impressive and colorful punk artwork shown in the game's graffiti, which has served as a big inspiration to my own artwork. Similarly, the sound is a feat of its own. Every little sound is accounted for. I recommend playing Sludge Life with a good pair of headphones for a better impression of this. Sludge Life is a loving and hilarious tribute to graffiti and hip-hop culture that is well worth your time and money, especially if you are looking for something unique and artsy to dive into. It's a short burst of pure genius that I can confidently STRONGLY recommend to anyone who takes video games seriously as an artform.

The game has meme potential, but I feel pretentious trying to enjoy it on my own. Certainly an interesting game if you can pick it up in a bundle or on sale.

Not long into the game you steal some diamonds (there's even an achievement for it) but those are never used for anything, referred to, found missing by the owner etc. You just... Steal diamonds. There's no point or consequences to anything in this game.A few NPC interactions made me chuckle but it's all one-liners. There are no "characters" per se, or quests, or interactions between different NPCs, or anything. They're just there, they tell you something of little value and that's it. _childDocuments_.review: Essentially everything I would want in a weird, psychedelic exploration based walking sim.It's bizarre, has fun mechanics that stop it from becoming boring and tedious and almost every area has something completely unique and interesting to look at or interact with. It also has a great sense of humour but also some interesting ideas on society that luckily don't encroach on being preachy or annoying. Just enough to make you think, then move on to taking a photo of a cat with two buttholes.In addition to this I really loved some of the mechanics that were unnecessarily fun to use. I'm a sucker for items in games that make you feel like you're really interacting with them. For example the laptop having it's own desktop and app, the camera functioning as a guide but also allowing you to take pictures, which was honestly a wonderful addition considering how strange the world is. There is no reason to take photos other than for yourself, yet I took over 100. The apps all feel unique and semi realistic and interactable objects and people in the world make it feel just that bit more real rather than an empty wasteland to wander around in.The feel of the game was the most important to me since it could have been a boring walking sim but it luckily succeeded massively in that department. A few negatives purely for fair criticism.Firstly and mainly, the performance is horrible. The graphics are quite simplistic (but fitting for the theme) yet it would have consistent frame drops and chug horribly. This is the second time that a game from this developer (Heavy Bullets is the other game) has performed terribly with zero reason due to low graphical intensity. Not only that but both of these games are within a category of around 3-4 games that I have never been able to find the cause of the issue and never truly fixed. Some advice for anyone having the same issue of huge frame drops, turn off vsync and crank the FPS limiter to the max amount, this caused the frame drops to not stop, but only drop to a much higher level, calming the hitching. This is also proof that it isn't my hardware struggling to run the game since it ran better at a much higher frame rate which disguised the hitching.Secondly it's short. Personally I thought it was short and sweet and the world is interesting enough to explore due to your own curiosity.The issue comes in when I say that I got this game for free (I believe it was free due to a promotion of the sequel that is soon to release).This game usually retails at $15. I don't think there is anywhere near enough content for that cost. Personally I would say it should be around $7/£5.I was able to complete this game to %100 in 4 hours and as stated before I was taking photos and exploring for the fun of it. Without me entertaining myself I could have completed the game, secrets and all within 2.5 hours. There is a reason this game can bee speedrun to 100% in less than 25 minutes.The thing is whether this is an issue to you. Since I got this game for free I had absolutely no issue with the short length and enjoyed every second. If I paid $15 for it and completed it just after the refund period ended I would feel like I had been scammed.Little issue, the climbing can be frustrating. Luckily there isn't a huge punishment for failing to climb something but it is worth mentioning.I would also like to mention that one of the other games from this same developer, High Hell also had near identical issues to this game. Incredibly short, performance issues and crashing, frustrating movement. Although I do like Sludge Life it is worrying that the issues that plague this developers games haven't been rectified as new games are released, Heavy Bullets was released in 2014 and the performance issues are identical in this game. I will have to try Disc Room and see how that holds up.Enough complaining because I do actually like this game a lot. It's rare to find a game where exploring is so satisfying and captivating and the world is so unique and insane that it can surprise you everytime you go somewhere new. Although the issues I have talked about might seem major, they really aren't to me. I just felt obligated to mention them since Steam reviews don't care for fair and informative reviews and I want people to understand the game fully before paying for it.Overall it is nice to see the developers of this game find a genre that allows players to fully experience the weird world that they wanted to create. This game feels right. It allows the player to interact with the strange universe that was present in High Hell without the restrictions of a level based shooter all while fully fleshing out the world and leaving the player with a fully realised experience of weirdness and intrigue.Is it worth the asking price? No.Is it worth the short amount of your time it takes up. Absolutely.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much. This has to be the most aesthetically pleasing game I've ever played. The artstyle is so unique and makes everything looks so cool to the point I found looking at random kitchens, dumpsters and toilets to be entertaining. The worldbuilding is great too as the random bits and pieces of information you get on whats going connect with each other. The open world is so well crafted too. The surface area of the map is really small and everything is really close by but the world still feels like it has way more too explore than most AAA games. Not a single corner of this game feels ignored. I haven't had so much fun exploring a video game map since I was 10 playing splitscreen Lego Marvel with my little brother. This game made me feel like how it felt to play video games as a child again 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game during the free-to-keep promo and had a bit of fun exploring the strange island of Sludge Life for an hour... but I wouldn't recommend paying full price, or really any price, for this game. The gameplay mostly consists of walking around the island and occasionally interacting with certain objects or spray painting the environment in predetermined areas, plus listening to NPCs - and the unique art direction and funny interactions (press 'F' to fart) had me consistently engaged for the game's hour-long length.However, the conversations with NPCs are very short. The platforming is sometimes wonky. And, most importantly, there are many areas where almost nothing can be interacted with, leaving the visually impressive map devoid of genuinely interesting gameplay. Plus, there are multiple endings to Sludge Life, but none of them are actually communicated to the player properly - you just have to wander around and find them on your own. If this game was longer, with far more available interactions around the island, I would probably be able to recommend buying it. But I can't recommend paying $15 for an hour of walking around, smoking and looking at graffiti.The store page for the upcoming sequel says that Sludge Life 2 will be "twice as dense" as the original - I hope they deliver, because the actual content of Sludge Life is wayyy too spread out. Had I bought this game for full price, I would have been sorely disappointed, and I would only recommend trying out Sludge Life if it goes free-to-keep again in the future. 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: is quite a challenge to accurately classify, because it dabbles in so many things at the same time. Foremost, it's a first person adventure, complete with traversal tools and quirky NPCs to interrogate. There is literally no height you can't reach or room you can't access. As you progress, you'll then discover an assortment of collectibles, ranging from objects you can pocket to locations you can tag. While not specifically a puzzle game, trying to reach certain places, open certain doors, or perform certain to-do tasks require lateral thinking. Shoot hoops, smoke cigs, fly high with shrooms, fiddle with apps on your virtual laptop.Interspersed within your exploration are a colorful cast of characters. There are no fetch quests or dialogue options, and none say more than a few repeating sets of lines, but that's fine: They provide hints, humor, or socio-economic commentary that feels uncomfortably familiar even today. As you raise your street cred you'll find fellow taggers stop giving you the cold shoulder and unlock special collaborative murals. Spread your art across the island to... well, win nothing really, but unlock a special trippy ending if you know where to go.The real highlight for me was the puzzles. SLUDGE doesn't look like it has any business being a puzzle game, but it has its fair share of surprises. Discovery is its primary objective, and to list them all would ruin the fun, but here's a couple roundabout examples: A fully fleshed out strategic minigame you can play on your laptop, entirely optional. A deadly laser grid blocking your path. A graffiti spot you can't reach on a satellite dish. A door that slams shut as soon as you get close to it. Changing your dietary preferences(?)For all its strengths, SLUDGE has a couple of demerits. It lacks a clearly defined plot, and its endings don't really provide any closure. Its inclusion of drugs has gotten the game an unfortunate ban in Australia (the C key is literally dedicated to using cigarettes). It's short, and it lacks replayability after you've uncovered every secret, unless you're a speedrunner.The game's longevity will depend largely on how much you're willing to invest in it. It's possible to reach its good ending in as little as 5 minutes, provided you know exactly what to do. Experienced blind, it's about a 1-2 hour dive, and then maybe another 1-2 hours for secrets and TO-DO tasks (aka achievements). Given this, I find it tough to recommend at full price. Wait for a sale, or if you see this in time, add it now and keep it forever before 3/30/23 - presumably a limited time promo for its upcoming sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a game where from the beginning we basically don't know what's going on. We are thrown on some island with many different locations, and our goal.... is basically its absence. We explore the island, put up our author tags, eat snails and meet various strange people living on the island.The first thing that strikes the eye after unpacking the game is the bizarre, but having a certain charm, graphics. In this game, well-detailed character models or buildings don't matter, because everything is kept in VHS style, something like that. Also the sound design is really good.It is worth noting that the game has a lot of elements that make it not aimed at children. Smoking cigarettes, eating magic mushrooms or peeing from the tower balcony are some of the elements that can be encountered during the gameplay.The game has three different endings, but we don't have to play three times. We will unlock all the endings during one playthrough of the game. In fact, we can reach the endings quite quickly even by accident.Sludge Life is a very interesting title. Although it can be said to be an island walking simulator, each NPC encountered or tag placed made me enjoy traversing more areas of the city. The price seems to be a little too high for the short gameplay time, but at one time it was given away for free, and promotions of this game occur quite often.

_childDocuments_.review: Graffiti Town. A bit of a note before we begin. I've played this game before as I've owned this on Epic Game Store and 100% twice before and I haven't fully replayed it once it came to steam, hence the low hour count.Story:You play as Ghost. A graffiti tagger who decides that it's time to be the best tagger in town and so you decide to traverse the corporate town owned by GLUG and tag it in your own unique style. There's really not much a story in Sludge Life. There's tons of dialogue as pretty much every citizen of the town will talk to you and have multiple things to say, but it's more of a relaxing exploration game with some visual storytelling. The dialogue here is weird and funny and really matches the weird tone of the game. Graphics:When I first saw the developers game High Hell, I fell in love with the art style. Grimy nature, saturated colors and just a weird style really was satisfying to look at. Then Sludge Life came along and when I first saw it in action it felt like a great continuation of the style. The corporate town is visually very pleasing to explore and is actually designed in a way where every bit is packed with detail. It's mostly consumed by filth and grime, but there's more cozy corners like an apartment complex with people just hanging out, a basketball court and of course the highlight of the game which is the graffiti which just looks absolutely awesome. Audio:The soundtrack of Sludge Life is a very experimental techno feeling one and I genuinely like it's weirdness. Everything about it just fits it's weird tone and whenever you come across people just sitting back and listening to these tunes, it's just a fun little addition.There's also a bunch of other really satisfying audio designs like the spraying or that little jingle that says Ghost whenever you tag a spot, it's really cool stuff. The way the audio is designed is great and it definitely feels like a lot of care was put into making it feel like it matches the world.Gameplay:Sludge Life is a very simple exploration game where your only real goal is to tag spots across the town. You walk around and will hear a spray can shake which indicates that you can tag that particular spot, but some places will require an unorthodox way of getting to them.I genuinely loved my time with Sludge Life, playing this game is a very relaxing experience and something about it just mellows me out, however I do have to admit that there's some issues with the core experience, but I really want to begin with the positives.The exploring part is genuinely a ton of fun. You can find a lot of weird stuff and you being nosy is both rewarded and penalized (don't worry, it's sort of a joke). Around the world you can find items that can help you traverse the world faster or even find computer programs including a pretty addictive mini game called Crypt Keeper. The traversal is probably the games biggest problem. The movement feels a bit too slippery as jumping, getting up the ledges and just getting up high buildings requires a bit of practice. There's really not much indication what kind of distance you have to jump to grab a ledge and sometimes you won't grab it even though you're supposed to which will require you to find a different way up (don't worry though usually there's a few different ways to get to the same spot). which could get annoying when the one you want to do isn't really possible. At first I hated it, but after I got the hang of it I genuinely had a blast using it, but it's still could have been so much better. There's also not much to do in the game, once you mop up all the tags, there's some fun side activities you can tend to (doing the 100% isn't difficult and won't take longer than a 3 hours at most) and I definitely wanted to get that 100% when I finished the main quest, but once you reach the end, there's really not much reason to go back to it.Verdict:Sludge Life is such a unique and fun game, which you can just sit back, relax and tag some spots, while exploring a bizarre world that is just fun to explore. While there are some issues with the movement, it did not detract from my enjoyment of the game and I have no trouble recommending this. Bring on Sludge Life 2.Final Rating:8.5/10Pros:+ Gameplay feels fun and relaxing+ Exploring the world is a ton of fun+ Great art style+ Really good audio design Cons:- Movement feels a bit janky- Short If you liked this review please consider joining  and

Multiple endingsSince I got it for free, I'm very impressed. I wouldn't pay full price though.Maybe £6.00 or something but that's just me. I've added the next game to my wishlist though based on the short fun I've had with this. Fairly easy achievements but some of them were annoying. You have to do a couple in one sitting/session. They reset if you exit the game. One of them is to eat 20 slugs - not too bad if you use a guide I guess. Theone that's annoying is a mini game you unlock by finding it as a collectable in the world. You have to defeat the last boss which is very RNG based, or inother words, you have to get lucky and hope he's not surrounded by baddies or it's basically impossible and you have to do the 20 whole levels all over again. _childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a first-person exploration game with platforming elements. It’s a strange and trippy experience, but surprisingly fun.There’s not much of a story. You play as Ghost, an aspiring graffiti tagger, who wakes up in a small shipping container (which acts as your base/home). After a short tutorial, you’re free to explore a small open world—a polluted island filled with shipping containers and various industrial buildings, surrounded by sludge. The vibe is bizarre, with characters dressed in “gangsta-style” attire, plus some odd hybrid or animal-like characters. Nearly everyone you meet is rude or weird.Tagging is one of the core mechanics of the game, with 100 preset locations to vandalize. Figuring out how to reach these hard-to-access spots is part of the fun, as many are in tricky, high-up places. The game has three different endings, though only one involves tagging all 100 spots.While exploring, you can interact with various items—eating shrooms and slugs, drinking soda (or maybe alcohol?), and smoking cigarettes. As you progress, you’ll find helpful tools like a glider and a teleportation device, which make getting around the island easier. The controls are generally okay but can feel imprecise at times.The UI is designed like a computer desktop where you can install apps, complete with annoying pop-ups. There’s even a surprisingly fun mini-game included. I noticed after two hours that I hadn’t unlocked any achievements, but once I checked the to-do list on the computer, they began unlocking. The list acts as a helpful guide, providing direction with goals and challenges since the game lacks a structured story or quests.While the game’s strange music and art style didn’t fully appeal to me, they fit well with the overall atmosphere. There’s also a default VHS-style graphic setting, which adds a grainy, distorted look/filter. I preferred turning it off for a cleaner appearance.It’s a short game, but since it was given away for free in March 2023, I can't really complain.
_childDocuments_.name: SLUDGE LIFE

_childDocuments_.review: I think my attempt at writing a review of Sludge Life will be a failed one. If nothing else, this is a game unlike any other I've played, and it defies description at every turn. Not quite a walking sim, not quite a sandbox, with minimal gameplay or story to speak of, Sludge Life follows the player character Ghost, a tagger on a mission to graffiti all of an island for reasons unknown. The game lasts all of two hours, which are spent tagging walls, urinating in random places, and eating as many banana slugs as you can find while you explore a small open world filled with many characters, all of whom offer very few, but very unique lines of dialogue. The game features minor parkour, but the controls feel almost as irreverent as the game itself, with slippery movement that gives the impression that Ghost doesn't quite understand how their own body works. The game has a bright and colorful palette, with clashing tones and a low-key soundtrack that make Sludge Life feel like it was put together by someone on copious amounts of drugs after they strolled through a garbage plant. For all of its short runtime, Sludge Life offers an overwhelming, indescribable, and all-around absurd experience that I believe is worth trying at least once. I don't think this game is good or bad - it completely and utterly denies being classified in such an objective manner. However, I appreciated it enough to give Sludge Life a 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: SLUDGE LIFE

_childDocuments_.review: The presentation of the game is top-notch. One of my personal favorite presentations of any game probably, incorporating a mix of a colorful palette with well-done 3D assets. It just looks fantastic. The music is also great even if it doesn't feature too much throughout your playthrough.The game can be beaten in 4 hours, which is perfect because I feel that the simplistic gameplay would get tiring if it goes any longer. It's essentially a collect-a-thon where you try to tag up designated tagging spots within a tiny but reasonably filled map. Movement is just WASD and jump, so traversing the map can get kinda dull until you get some gadgets. The main draw of the game for me and what kept me playing is just seeing all the wacky stuff and quirky people you'd encounter as you try to collect everything.I enjoyed my time with the game. There's a Sludge Life 2 that I haven't played yet and I would love to see how that game fleshes out the mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a great open world collectathon, getting tags and gliding around the highly expansive world is an overjoy to play in. For starters, the aesthetic is gorgeous. The mix with pixel walls and 3d buildings fit the mold for the game’s experience and attitude. There are also so many places to go, like Gen Pop or any of the stackers. There are also a lot of funny details in the backgrounds, like the massive baby near Gen Pop, or the chef that cut his hand open at the Glug Tower. Overall, the aesthetic of this game is one of the best I've seen in a video game. Gameplay however, isn’t as great as the inventive backgrounds. The whole point of the game is to spray paint your logo on every surface, along with many other things. At first, this is very fun and finding new sprays can be rewarding. But when you have got to the last few sprays, not using the vandal's eyes, it could be very tiresome and boring. Don’t get me wrong, there is a lot more than sprays in Sludge Life. You can find all of the items, smoke some ciggys you find around, and play other games in the control panel found around the world. Sadly, the game is very short, around two hours to get one ending and four to 100% the game. But in conclusion, Sludge Life is an atmospheric collectathon, with a beautiful world, and lots of things to do, however it does it in a short time frame.

_childDocuments_.review: definitely get this game if the atmosphere captured in the screenshots even mildly piques your interest because the game does an even better job of immersing you into that world through its engrossing LSD fever dream art style dizzied by the VHS-quality HHBF distorted positional in-world music crackling out of boomboxes cleverly placed all over a no-loading-screen open world as you parkour your way to leave your Ghost logo on a crazy overhang that makes other taggers think "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Ghost, you animal!". I really want to thank the devs for doing great job filling up the world and making it interesting. There's a whole culture of taggers in the midst of a workplace strike in a city flooded with sludge. You meet other taggers who when you get to their location you'll find them with their own theme song and tags which you'll also see around the city.In terms of vibe, it atmospherically feels like Happy's Humble Burger Farm with that hazy VHS style filter and location dynamic music. There are no boundaries, so you can go wherever you want to get those walls tagged and those toilets urinated. Yes, urinated. This game captures the early-to-mid 2000s South Park and Postal feel and humor. There's good worldbuilding in it too, lots of stories, events, and culture that you don't really find out much about but which you keep getting glimpses into by talking to other people you meet.In terms of gameplay, it's a parkour platformer that feels slippery when going up a ledge. The game won me over moreso because of the atmosphere and the visuals than the game mechanics, and that's not something that's easy for a dev to do without turning it into a walking simulator. But again, the focus is definitely on the art, the culture of Sludge City, and the source of fresh green eye-cucumbers for the CEO.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge, a word that resonates with a sense of stagnation, filth, and decay. Its very utterance conjures images of a viscous, dark substance oozing through the crevices of our society, polluting our minds and suffocating our progress. Whether it be in the physical or metaphorical sense, sludge represents the obstacles that hinder our growth and hinder the development of a better world.In the realm of environmental concerns, sludge takes on a tangible form. It is the muck and mire that accumulates in our rivers and streams, the remnants of our industrial endeavors. It is the result of heedless consumption, where waste is irresponsibly discarded and left to fester. The sludge not only threatens the delicate balance of aquatic ecosystems but also seeps into the groundwater, poisoning the very source of life. It serves as a reminder of our shortsightedness and the consequences of our actions.Metaphorically, sludge permeates through various aspects of our lives. It represents the mental and emotional baggage that weighs us down, inhibiting our ability to progress and thrive. Sludge can be found in the form of societal norms and prejudices that hinder progress and limit the potential of individuals. It can be seen in the bureaucratic red tape that stifles innovation and hampers the implementation of necessary reforms. Sludge is the complacency and inertia that prevent us from addressing pressing issues, leaving us stuck in a perpetual cycle of inaction.Sludge can also be found in our personal lives. It is the clutter that accumulates in our homes, filling our spaces with unnecessary objects and stifling our sense of tranquility. It is the toxic relationships that drain our energy and leave us feeling trapped. Sludge is the self-doubt and negative thoughts that hold us back from pursuing our dreams and reaching our full potential. It is the fear and uncertainty that paralyze us, preventing us from taking risks and embracing change.The effects of sludge are far-reaching and pervasive. They can be seen in the deterioration of our physical and mental well-being, the degradation of our environment, and the stagnation of our collective progress. However, it is essential to recognize that sludge is not an insurmountable obstacle. Just as sludge accumulates gradually over time, it can also be slowly eradicated through conscious effort and collective action.To combat environmental sludge, we must adopt sustainable practices and advocate for responsible waste management. We must invest in renewable energy sources and reduce our reliance on fossil fuels. Additionally, we must hold corporations accountable for their actions and push for stricter regulations to prevent further environmental degradation.Addressing societal and personal sludge requires introspection and a willingness to challenge the status quo. It necessitates dismantling oppressive systems and embracing diversity and inclusivity. It demands fostering a culture of innovation and empowering individuals to overcome self-doubt and pursue their aspirations. It requires creating support systems that encourage personal growth and wellbeing.In conclusion, sludge represents the obstacles that impede progress and hinder our ability to create a better world. Whether it manifests in the physical form of environmental pollution or the metaphorical form of societal and personal barriers, sludge reminds us of the consequences of our actions and the urgent need for change. By recognizing the existence of sludge and taking proactive steps to eliminate it, we can pave the way for a brighter and more promising future.

_childDocuments_.review: To the guy who sent the clown award: Thanks! But your wife's boyfriend still owes me $20- If you tend to gravitate towards visually impressive games that sell themselves on eye candy and impressive visuals, you'll wind up bouncing right off of Sludge Life. It's purposefully grimy and smoggy, likely to reflect the anti-capitalist counterculture bent of the narrative- When I say "smog", I mean "LA in the 90s" levels of smog. The concept of draw distance will become a distant memory after you load into the hazy open world of Sludge Life. It's like a flashback to Silent Hill fog- In addition to the omnipresent cloud of industrial fumes, there's an aggressive VHS-style overlay that adds yet another bit of visual distortion to the experience. In principle, I understand that the intent in most games like this is to make them feel more "retro", but I don't know how much scan lines actually make me feel nostalgic. I'll chalk it up to "artistic choice", but honestly, the game could have done without them- The music is perfectly inline with the visuals. doseone's alternative hip-hop stylings capably underpin the parkour action with synthesizers and Reagan-era samples. The artistic unity of the audio and visuals is impressive and probably the game's greatest strength- If you didn't expect a game like this to have much of a story, congratulations, because you're absolutely correct. You play as Ghost, a tagger (graffiti artist) in Ciggy City, a town that's more or less entirely run by the Glug Corporation. In addition to manufacturing all of the products available for purchase in town, Glug and its many subsidiaries also appear to control the police, schools, and all other services. The company's quest for profit has left Ciggy City a wasteland, with the ocean already flooding the entirety of the town while many of its citizens and workers are left to populate stacked shipping containers, tents, building crevices and other ad hoc living situations- As Ghost, you have no real stated objective. The main thing you're left to do is explore the town and plop graffiti on designated tag spots- The vibes are as chill as can be. There are no stakes. Dying has no consequences. The music is relaxing. There's plenty of humor- On that last point, Sludge Life employs an unfortunate amount of "lel randem" comedy, but without the level of try-hard spark that leads to a lot of inward cringing and eye rolling. Instead, it's a bit more carefree and lackadaisical its approach. If you can envision a game where all the dialogue is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Sludge Life would be that. When it lands, it can be pretty humorous, at least- To sum it all up, there's some interesting world building going on here, but without much to do within the world, it feels like a waste of potential- Due to the heavy emphasis on vertical exploration, parkour is the predominant gameplay mechanic you'll be experiencing. It feels like a lot of notes were taken from first-person "schmoovement" games like Lovely Planet, Cyber Hook, or SEUM, then subequently crumpled up and thrown in the trash. Without any pressing need to move quickly, the speed and free flowing aspects of those games are binned. What you're left with is sort of a mess- You can't see your feet, so you'll fall off narrow platforms and girders constantly if you try to go to fast. Jumping feels awkward owing to the first-person perspective, and how close you need to be to a ledge to mantle up it is something that I failed to get a feel for even by the end of my playthrough. Some walls are climbable through repeatedly jumping at them, but it's not clear which ones qualify. Altogether, the platforming feels janky and frustrating. The engine feels like is constantly at odds with the mechanics that were programmed into it- Unlike most platformers that have the sprint controls bound to a left stick click, that action merely makes you fart in Sludge Life. While funny, it doesn't actually boost your movement speed at all- The items you find do offer some respite from the horrible platforming. The Glider can help you soar from rooftop to (slightly lower) rooftop, and the Warper allows you to set a custom teleport point. About to attempt a tricky jump or need to cross a narrow platform? The warper can quickly return you to the start so you can try again after you almost inevitably fall to your death. You'll also come across warp stations that can help you quickly navigate between the small open world's major areas- Finding these items and warp points is helpful, but your main goal is to tag billboards, buildings, statues, and other surfaces you'll stumble across. The Camera item can help you spot these tag spots in the early game, but you'll later find another item, the Vandal Eyes (ha), which can provide additional guidance. You may also notice "Blue Caps", hallucinogenic mushrooms that allow you to leave your body and fly around for a short period of time before you rubberband back to your body and vomit all over what's directly in front of you. These are pretty helpful for scoping out hard-to-reach tag locations- Some graffiti you'll be making are collabs with other taggers scattered around the city. You'll have to up your cred by tagging a set number of locations before working with them, though- There are also apps that you can find for your laptop (menu screen), but these primarily seem to help with tracking achievements- From what I understand, there are three different endings: A "good" one, a "bad" one, and a "weird" one. The weird ending requires tagging all the locations, which I did not do, so I can't speak to it; however, it's safe to say that in a game like this, the good and bad endings are fairly weird too- I don't know that I'll replay it. I'm not sure I even want to go back and finish up the achievements. The gameplay just isn't fun enough to motivate any sort of revisit- Well, it's yet another game with really good audiovisual presentation and worldbuilding but with dogwater gameplay. Your enjoyment is wholly dependent on how much you value you assign to its strengths. As an exploration-focused platformer, I wouldn't recommend it, but as a piece of interactive art, it's at least interesting- I played through the whole thing on the Steam Deck, but I think I'd suggest playing with a mouse/keyboard setup. It ran very well and without bugs, but the frustrating platforming would have been less so with WASD controls instead of the analogue stick. If you like the music and artstyle, maybe throw it on your wishlist and wait for a steep discount. If you're looking for meaningful exploration or fun parkour, though, you're bound to wind up a little disappointed. I found the world interesting enough that I'll be checking out the rest of the series down the road, but more out of curiosity than enthusiasm

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game for free. Initially, I liked the vibe of the game, the odd characters you meet and the weird world Sludge Life is set in, but the vibe fades very quickly. The game apparently has endings, but try as I might, I did not find a way to end the game. Some objects you find and can use in the game don't seem to have a deeper meaning and it seems the main goal is to tag every spot - which is fun at first, but that too gets annoying really quickly. The biggest problem is the games lack of movement options. No double jump, no running and while you can heave yourself up ledges, it only seems to work half the time. You get a glider eventually, but it is very awkward to use and not very useful.As a game to just explore and spend a weird hour or two in, I think Sludge Life is fine (and it has a cool soundtrack), but the goal isn't very clear-cut, movement is a pain, there are a few hidden or locked areas I have no idea how to get into (with no hints) and the aesthetic of the game, it being a weird sewery dump, is only interesting for a short time. It also emphasizes how "random" it is all the time, as nothing seems to really have a point to it. That's charming in games like Crypt Worlds, but not here. Nothing you do really has a point to it, and I know that is the vibe the game is going for, but it is also kind of a waste of the thematic and aesthetic. There COULD be something cool going on here, but playing the game is like, well, like trudging through sludge. Fitting.Getting all achievements would also be a pain as some of them seem really annoying (like eating all sludges in one session). Maybe these things will be improved in a sequel, because I feel like this game could have been interesting, if it was fleshed out a bit more. And for what it is, 14.99 is way too high of a price if you decide to buy it - that is almost Highway Robbery for how little there is to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a game made by a Drug User. You can tell the developer is a Drug User from scintillating NPC dialogue such as "I'm so high right now," unintelligible hipster gibberish, or horrible communist nonsense (but I repeat myself.) Unlike other Drug Users, Terri Vellmann got off his ass and made a game and, true to his political priors, loves handing it out for free, which is how this review appears before you today. _childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a casual exploration game set on a very quirky and vibrant island. Although there is no linear story, you find purpose in finding vandalism spots and getting to know the interesting residents and the island. To me, Sludge Life is an art game and a comfort game. As someone who is absolutely terrible at platformers and parkouring, I found many spots difficult to reach. However, my skill issue did not keep me from enjoying the game as there is so much to explore. The camera feature is my favorite part of the game and makes me want to come back every once in a while just to go on a digital photo walk. The mini games are pretty fun too. I really enjoy the dungeon crawler. Like some other reviews suggest, I would suggest adjusting certain settings (like mouse sens) to enjoy the game, as it can be nauseating especially the first time you play it. If you are attracted to the visual style, then you should play this game for sure. The music is also great and also very enjoyable to listen to outside the game.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is a super weird game. I can see how some people might like this game and some might not, but I thought it was a blast. About 3-ish hours in I found the way 'out,' but I know I'm going to be going back to try to hit all the tag points and stuff like that. It's just plain FUN to play, even if it feels like you're mostly just goofing off.So what's the point? I have no idea. I guess you're some kind of graffiti artist living in this world of sludge owned by some greedy evil corporation. The ground is sludge, everything is haphazardly thrown together, everyone is grumbly and grumpy, and the entire place is cluttered beyond belief. You walk around. You talk to people. You find secret entrances, climb things, meet strange people, find bizarre things you weren't expecting, and paint your graffiti everywhere. Eventually you find an escape pod and take off, and credits roll.Now, you may be thinking to yourself, "That doesn't sound like a normal game where there's a point or a goal. It sounds like you're just wandering around doing random stuff." And.. you know.. that's pretty much the case. Had I consulted a walkthrough guide, I probably could've beat this game in no time. But the world was just FUN to interact with, so I had no desire at all to consult a guide. I had a lot more fun just wandering around, exploring, finding. Yes, this is one of those worlds where you actually WANT to probe every little corner to find what may be hiding - whether giant turds, cats with two buttholes, enormous sleeping babies, bored employees or anything else. You'll be heading into a room expecting more garbage and disarray, and all of a sudden, think, "WHAT!? What is THAT!?"I seriously enjoyed the careless, mindless gameplay. When you finish using an item, you casually toss it onto the ground. It's always THERE for you to use, somehow.. but for example, you finish using the camera, so you just toss it aside. That's the tone of the entire game - very little in the way of consequences (besides dying if you plummet from an enormous height), very little that's serious, and very little "need" to make any progress if you don't want. (And you know what I mean, where some games you feel compelled to continue ever onward.. In this game you're literally just kinda bumming around doing stuff.)You can pee, fart, spit, jump, crouch, climb, fall, glide, teleport, all kinds of random stuff.I really don't know what else to say about this game. If you're expecting an intense experience, or a very clear and engaging story, or well-defined goals, or anything like that, this isn't that. Mainly just explore, have fun, do stuff, find secrets, and find your way out. That's about it.That being said I had a great time. The characters are unforgettable. The atmosphere is gritty and gross. It's the VIBE you play this game for.Graphics fit the theme and are pretty decent. I've read about some people getting motion sickness from this game, but that didn't happen for me - I was fine in this case. Sound effects fit the theme.. I loved the music, though. It's just bizarre-sounding hip hop and weird stuff. The controls were easy to use and didn't feel unfair, and I never got 'stuck' anywhere. Overall great.Worth full price? Hmmm, that's a bit of a question. For $15, I think it's going to depend on how much you like games like this that are more about open-ended exploration, goofing around, and more about the vibe than the actual game. I can tell you that I bought it for THREE bucks, so it might be worth it to wishlist and wait for a sale. At three bucks it's a dead steal for pretty much anyone. So if you want right into this world right away, it might be worth full price, but if you're not sure, just take note that I got it for 80% off and maybe sit on it.End of the day, I'm glad I pulled the trigger on this weird little title. It made me actually laugh, which is not usually the case for 'funny' games. And, works PERFECTLY on Steam Deck, so heck yeah.I say go for it if you can get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Bizzare and stylish, yet somberly grounded parkour/collectathon game.Sludge Life oozes a certain type of vibe. The "kids fresh out of high-school goofing around behind a gas station, smoking cigarettes and talking about nothing in particular, trying to not let the overwhelming hopelessness sink in, because they know that staying in their hometown just means having no perspectives for the future" kinda vibe. It's heavy and soul-crushing. So how do you combat these feelings? Sludge Life's answer is: creative expression through street art, friendly competition and human connections.Okay, that was kinda depressing, but it's a video game, right? So what's the gameplay? Well, it's mostly a platformer with some parkour elements, gadgets to unlock and secrets to look for. Leave your street tag all around the town and create unique street art by comboing with your fellow street artists. It's not that complicated and it doesn't need to be. The movement feels fine and I didn't encounter any massive bugs or glitches.Sludge Life high point is definitely it's aesthetic. The graffiti are genuinely amazing pieces of art and I believe real-life artist were involved. The soundtrack is fitting and works well with everything else. The town you're  exploring is full of surprises and what the cool kids call enviromental storytelling. You're gonna find some unique characters and whacky stuff happening just around the corner. While the subject matter is essentially about being stuck in a dead-end town with no perspectives, while giant corporations kill the world for more profit, it's not a terribly depressing game in tone. I feel like the sparks of hope found throughout Sludge Life are there for a reason.Overall, I think you're gonna enjoy this game whether you like the movement based gameplay or just simply vibe with the style you see in the trailer. Oh yeah, there's this weird screen filter that's on by default and it was giving me a headache if I tried to play with it on. Thankfully, it can be turned off. Just a headsup.

_childDocuments_.review: It's so relaxing, not just in a gameplay way, but in a weird cultural way.  This is utopia, not the clean 1950s space program utopia, but it's a DIY slacker utopia where everyone just hangs out, ignores their job responsibilities, and listens to beats.  Goals are simple - climb stuff and tag stuff.  You'll think you get the whole dynamic within a few minutes and then come back a week later and realize there's another place to climb or another way to sneak through a window and get some puzzle-solving endorphins without even realizing you were solving one.  Because there's always another place to check out anyway.  Graphically & sonically, it's super stylized, but doesn't feel lazy - everything works smoothly and looks great.  The soundtrack by Doseone is cool too and adds to the low-pressure feeling.If you've ever been frustrated because you just wanted to wander and climb everything in some other game, but it locked you into a particular story or gameplay mechanic, this is the game for you.  Overall a great end of the day wandering experience.Editing after playing more to say that it's really well-designed (and relaxing) that you can play this game and make progress without realizing that there even is progress to be made.  As you achieve more things, it starts to feel more like an adventure game, there are even a couple legit puzzles to solve.  But that's not a complaint, I think all Myst-like games need this much jumping.  I got the Good Ending but felt sad about it so I'm sticking around till I get the Weird Ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish I found this sooner as I discovered Sludge Life through the next fest demo of Sludge Life 2. After playing the demo of SL2 I dove right into this one and had a blast! Tore through the whole thing in one sitting which isn't to hard, but I did a whole 100% complete run. The main reason I did it one sitting, it was very captivating in the sense of old school 90s video game stylings with a modern feel. It heavily reminded me of playing Normality. You have a sense of what you can do, but what you should be doing just naturally happens as you explore and talk to people. The game world has its own things going on and it's not until later after you progress do people start acknowledging you, not everyone does which I find to be a good thing, not everyone needs to know who the "main character" is.Playing the game is satisfying all the way around, jumping and scrabbling on things is endless fun. I even noticed a small detail with the edge grabbing that is perfect; (might be hard to explain) If you jump towards a ledge and are still going up the edge grab will happen, if you try to jump from a distance and you're going to fast downward by the time you get close to the edge the grab won't happen. It sounds in text form not fun, but it's so well implemented that in game it works great.Every time you tag is a delight, that tag sound is pure excitement.The music is really good and the game underplays the music a LOT. It keeps the music to boomboxes around the game world so it's not always playing. I grabbed the album from Bandcamp and there are a lot of bangers on there that I don't think even show up in the game itself, do yourself a favor and check out the soundtrack.My final thoughts: I love the pure gameplay that's in here, the world is what it is and spends zero time trying to explain it to you, I love that. The dark comedy and weird stuff going on just delights me to no end.It feels refreshingly different with it's own sense of self, if anything it brings back stuff from 90s video games that I feel we've lost overall and I'm so happy it's here.It's just fun, pure distilled fun.Extra: You can turn off the VHS filter, it might not be for everyone, I went back and forth on it but finally just left it on.There are settings that make little sense when you first start playing, mess with them after you've played a bit and they should click.The camera is a lot of fun and I used it to recall locations of banana slugs when going for that 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: A great yet quirky game. I never expected to actually, to put it plainly,  this game. The whole grunge/trashy oil rig aesthetic really got to me. The story, while not explicitly the main focus is still a welcome presence in the background.The characters are actually quite humorous, with their dialogues being the actual way the player can get the background of the character we play as and the whole vibe of the area in general.Spray paint tagging is not a concept that I am well aware of, but the designs of the tags used in game are quite fancy and cool. The music is especially important that actually sets the tone for the entire game. the rapper known as 'Big Mud' has quite a few good songs in the game.Gameplay wise, the way this game sets particular 'objectives' is quite unconventional. You can go the whole game without even understanding what you are meant to do. There will be hints in the dialogues and the world around you, but there isn't a defined quest menu where you can see what you have to do (except there actually is, but you have to go to an end game area to find this list and install it as an 'app' on your in-game laptop). This was really nice, as there really isn't any hand holding done by the game and the player is actually quite free to do as they wish. The gadgets that are received to complete said objectives are also quite unique and nice - there is a glider, a camera, a teleporter and a tag spotter... which is actually just someone's eyes in a small jar.Unfortunately, as is with many games published by Devolver Digital, they are too short. The same problem does persist in this game, but it is entirely worth the time spent to play.8.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: SludgeLife is a game that defies traditional conventions and captivates players with its unique and unapologetic approach. As an avid gamer, I have fallen head over heels for this gritty masterpiece, and I can't help but express my sheer admiration for the experience it offers.One of the aspects that makes SludgeLife so remarkable is its immersive and atmospheric world. The game transports you to an industrial wasteland, where dilapidated structures and polluted environments create a sense of desolation. Yet, within this bleak setting, a peculiar charm emerges. The graffiti-covered walls, neon signs flickering amidst the gloom, and the hauntingly beautiful soundtrack combine to create an unmistakable ambiance. SludgeLife effortlessly infuses grime and chaos with an artful touch, making every corner of its world feel like a canvas waiting to be explored.The freedom to roam and explore is another aspect that truly sets SludgeLife apart. The game offers a refreshing departure from linear narratives, encouraging players to chart their own course through its intricate web of secrets and surprises. Whether I was scaling towering structures, tagging graffiti in hidden spots, or discovering hidden collectibles, the feeling of discovery and adventure never waned. SludgeLife rewards curiosity, allowing me to stumble upon unexpected encounters and mind-bending visuals that left me in awe.What truly sealed the deal for me was SludgeLife's offbeat sense of humor. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, delivering a healthy dose of satire and wit that had me grinning from ear to ear. From quirky characters spouting absurd lines to tongue-in-cheek references scattered throughout, SludgeLife kept me engaged with its infectious charm. It's a testament to the game's ability to blend dark themes with lightheartedness, creating an experience that feels refreshingly different from anything I've played before.Moreover, SludgeLife's art style deserves special mention. The deliberately low-fi visuals, filled with vibrant colors and pixelated textures, accentuate the grungy aesthetic of the game. It's a deliberate departure from hyper-realistic graphics, and it works wonders in creating a world that feels simultaneously retro and contemporary. The visuals are both rough and beautiful, capturing the essence of the environment perfectly and enhancing the overall experience.Finally, it's worth mentioning the game's excellent soundtrack, which adds yet another layer of immersion. The combination of electronic beats, ambient tunes, and lo-fi melodies creates an atmospheric backdrop that further engulfs you in SludgeLife's world. Each track felt meticulously crafted, amplifying the emotions and enhancing the gameplay experience.In conclusion, SludgeLife is an exceptional game that embraces its own unique brand of grime and elevates it to a work of art. With its immersive world, open-ended exploration, offbeat humor, distinct art style, and captivating soundtrack, it's no wonder why I've fallen head over heels for it. SludgeLife defies expectations and provides an unforgettable journey through an industrial wasteland where beauty can be found even in the most unexpected places. If you're looking for an unconventional and unforgettable gaming experience, SludgeLife is an absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is an absurdist 3D platformer based around spray painting (tagging) various walls across a fictional shipyard. Reading other reviews, the game’s humour and stylistic content seems to have polarised reviewers who struggle to explain in words the game’s aesthetic beyond “grungy”. However, I feel Sludge Life’s awkward, surrealist humour stems directly from shows like The Eric Andre Show, Adult Swim and, taking it even further back, BBC’s The Mighty Boosh.Reviewers have struggled to categorise Sludge Life into a specific genre, with labels such as “walking simulator”, “open-world adventure” and “3D platformer” being handed around slightly hesitantly. For the most part, you’ll be trying to reach high ledges, jumping across shipping containers, gliding, jumping and crawling through vents and other tight spaces. And honestly, it’s pretty fun if a little clunky and lacking in depth. There’s a real satisfaction of ticking off your in-game to-do list that I feel will really resonate with late 20s home owners.Set in an abstract patch of the sea, players explore a shipyard complete with disgruntled striking employees, an anxiously leaking oil rig, dilapidated apartment block, laboratory, radio tower and sports centre. The game’s pull is in its deliberate lacks of cohesion and its illogical situations. For example, knocking door-to-door on the apartment block led to me discovering:🟢 A news agency run entirely by pigeons🟢 A sleeping baby the size of a lorry🟢 A group of students high on shrooms hypnotised by a TV show presented by an oscillating slugLater, I met a depressed self-depreciating bird sitting atop a stack of near unclimbable shipping containers who told me “Sometimes I just sit here and doubt myself”. It’s the type of humour designed to be made into viral content, YouTube shorts and reaction GIFs, but isn’t quite bottom of the barrel humour either. While it’s not laugh out loud humour, Sludge Life did elicit lots of big smile across its succinct 2.5 hour runtime.I had a really fun time with Sludge Life, and it became the perfect remedy for a long day of work. It doesn’t require too much thought, but is smart enough to hold your attention. It’s a short game, and it’s full £12.99 is certainly too steep, but it felt satisfyingly manageable and a welcome distraction from the real world.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a unique and immersive first-person exploration game that takes you on a journey through a surreal, grungy world filled with unexpected surprises and strange encounters. As you explore the decaying urban environment, you'll encounter bizarre characters, hidden secrets, and a whole lot of sludge.One of the most striking things about Sludge Life is its art style. The game features a minimalist, almost abstract aesthetic that manages to convey a great deal of mood and atmosphere with very little detail. The world is dark, gritty, and full of decay, but there's also a strange kind of beauty to it all. The visuals are accompanied by a fantastic soundtrack that perfectly captures the game's strange, surreal vibe.Gameplay-wise, Sludge Life is a mix of exploration, platforming, and puzzle-solving. As you make your way through the world, you'll need to use your wits and reflexes to overcome obstacles and uncover hidden areas. The game also features a number of optional tasks and missions, which can help you unlock new abilities and items.One of the things that sets Sludge Life apart from other games in its genre is its sense of humor. The game is full of strange, absurdist humor that will have you laughing out loud at times. From the characters you meet to the strange objects you collect, everything in Sludge Life feels like it was designed with a twisted sense of humor in mind.Overall, Sludge Life is an excellent game that's well worth your time if you're a fan of exploration games, platformers, or just weird and surreal experiences. The game's unique visuals, fantastic soundtrack, and bizarre sense of humor all come together to create something truly memorable.(I recommend for people who are bored)

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life is a very strange game. It looks, sounds, and plays like a drug trip. That is both its most interesting element and cumbersome downside, it is brutally weird, to the point where its hard to tell whether there's any nuance or if its simply one crude joke. However I do like that part of it, it is uniquely charming and presents an interesting world for you to explore. The visuals are well done, and the music is surprisingly good, the only problem I have is the lackluster feeling controls. Movement is sluggish with unsatisfying jumps and a clamber that refuses to work half the time. Outside of all that this is a pretty well made indie with a good amount of stuff to do, just enough to not overstay its welcome. The concept of making tags is fun and gives a nice incentive to explore and find weird and wacky stuff along the way. As for the price I received this when it was given away for free so from my perspective its not really worth the full $15, partially cause of its brevity, but mainly because of its very love it or hate it style. I'd probably wait for a sale down to $10 before I fully recommend it, and make sure its for you. I liked it a surprising amount and it was definitely enough content to where I was satisfied completely.3/5

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge life is a short and sweet game about exploring a nasty little town and finding spots to tag. Each item assists in finding tagging spots, or increasing your mobility, and have to be used in interesting ways to get to certain secret locations. I would compare it to "A Short Hike", ABZU, Journey and Valley  for being a simple game with satisfying movement.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fun. The vibes and atmosphere is top notch and so is the music. _childDocuments_.review: Sludge Life does so much strange things with complete confidence. It's an exploration platformer with a unique art direction. Basically, you play as a character named Ghost and roam a polluted island and spray graffiti on given locations, and talk to the weird inhabitants.With a cell-shaded look and sharp pixelated borders stills from the game looks like art someone has made with MS paint in the 90s. It also makes the think of Pushwagner a bit.The sound design is very "in your face" and well made with a few exceptions, such as the jumping sound which becomes annoying after a while.Overall the game is very fun and does not overstay its welcome. I do have a few gripes with the movement though. Everything is presented in a way that encourages speed and sloppiness, therefore the controls must be extremely snappy and precise. right now you feel that Ghost doesn't do what I tell him. He stops too late and he fumbles when he climbs on a beam. This really takes away from the experience and feels like an artificial difficulty. It's not fun to climb the same stuff many times because the character doesn't do what I want.I hear they are working on a sequel and I hope they iron out the movement and maybe add some more parkour-like movement to enhance the fluidity of the game. I will get the sequel as long as it's not too pricey.

_childDocuments_.review: WOW. This is good. Let me tell you that I got this game when it was free on steam (I think it was free on epic games too at one point?) just so I would have it in my library, on the off chance that I wanted to play it later and wouldn't have to buy it. I had no actual plans on playing it. Curiosity got the better of me, and I decided to play it, see what it was all about. The screenshots looked cool.I had no idea it was exactly what I was craving from a game.You play as Ghost, one of the graffiti artist from around this place. You have no idea what you look like, but you can only imagine you are some kind of goop or semi-solid creature (Your crouching is very, VERY low. Chin-touching-the-ground-level low).You go around, traversing this world, looking for tagging spots, and tagging them. Getting to the often-inconveniently-placed tagging spots is the fun part. Parkour mechanics are simple, but you need none more, they're exactly what you need.Along your adventure, you will meet other taggers (and ex-taggers). Once you tag enough locations yourself, you will unlock collab-murals with one of the taggers you will meet.You will also obtain items, which will help you find tagging locations and also reach them. The camera works just like binoculars, it helps you see tagging locations from longer ranges (tagging icon only appears when you are close to the location). The vandal eyes work like a compass, guiding you to the exact location of the nearest tagging spot.The glider helps you... glide.The warper teleports you to the anchored location.Let's dumb it down to some pros and cons:Pros:- great atmosphere- great concept- great execution- some lore- traversing the city is fun, so is platforming- 3 endings- multiple achievements- collect-'em-all style mechanics for tags, slugs, apps and items- decently big world- unique graphics and art style- some secrets- cool music- smart puzzles- you can get high from shrooms, smoke and drink sodaCons:- pretty boring NPC dialogue, semi-con- VHS filter on by default. I thought it was forced at first, but it was annoying. Turns out you can disable it, so also only a semi-con- limited replayability- some puzzles may be annoying. You might get stuck. I had to do some googlingTHING YOU SHOULD KNOW BEFORE PLAYING (I have not seen anyone mention this):Endings do not reset your progress. Only if you wipe it. (Make sure to agree to trying to recover it in the bad ending. It will go back to normal)Overall: 9/10. Initial playthrough is amazing. Replaying might be boring.

_childDocuments_.review: Sludge life is a short little sandbox game that can be best described as a "Delinquent Simulator". You're incentivized to go out and spread your brand onto the city by tagging various spots with your name and character (the "Ghost").Despite your character being (allegedly) underaged, and fully capable of committing underaged-substance-use crimes, This game is not for kids- even though the swearing in this world is very-unlike real life's swear words.The worldbuilding is spot on. This clearly gives me a "Splatoon's-crunked-up-ghettopunk-neighbor" vibe in terms of atmosphere. Your home is a shipping container, the place is owned by a megacorp dealing with a strike and an incompetant CEO who's holed up in the corporate penthouse. Most of the populace has stopped giving a damn, the security guards are violent douchebags,  drunks are everywhere, half the people are mutated, and Taggers like you are the only ones gutsy-enough to stick it to the man.The flaws of this game? Well, first off, due to the premise of this game being an exploration game and delinquent sim, there isn't a terrible amount of combat, that's not a big deal. The one problem I have with exploring things, is that despite most of the game being relatively simple to figure out, there are a few puzzles in the game which require unusually-interactice solutions in order to progress.Also, the air physics in this game are janky in a rather unpleasant way, not as bad as some games but here it's a bit "bitter tasting" so to speak.Also, the collect-a-thon sh*t has never really set well with me, and this game has quite a bit of it. This game normally retails for $15. I generally can deal with short length if the game offsets it with replayability, or being lower-priced. Sadly, this game lacks in the replayability department, but since I got it for free, it counts. I don't think I would've bought this game for full price though.

_childDocuments_.review: A very cute little open-world exploration game with light platforming and puzzle solving. You take on the role of Ghost, a green goblin-esque fellow, who has made it his mission to tag all the good spots with their distinct graffiti in his city, which is a depressing mix of gray concrete, an oil platform and an industrial-chemical wasteland in the middle of a polluted ocean full of sludge. Over the course of the game you will figure out a path and climb to hard to reach spots to cover in your art and talk to some weird NPCs in this tiny but completely open world.  There are no enemies to speak of, the only way to "fail" is by falling from a high place and breaking every bone in your body.The main appeals of this game are mostly it's aethetic, which stands unabashedly on its own two urban graffiti-style legs and the fun exploration through a combination of platforming and puzzle solving, which rewards you with collectibles, items that make platforming easier or open new paths and of course a way to get too the credits. It's not just about collectibles though, you will also have some amusing moments by talking to eccentric NPCs, whos' dialog ranges from just funny too stories about drug abuse and the misery of living in this dystopic world, where greedy corporations have polluted the earth. It's sort of like a cyberpunkish story, but replace the cybernetics with graffity and cartoonish characters. The world of sludge is not just random dialog with no connection, it does have a small but funny background plot about a beloved mascot and a protest as you explore and fits the punk vibes, but I will leave it to you to discover. And of course you will encounter just some out of place weird, sometimes even dark but funny things in this world, it treats your eyes with a lot of diverse stuff within its small contrainsts and never feels lame or predictable.But when I talk about this game's open world being tiny, I really mean tiny. Completing the game while tagging all of the 100 spots will probably take you 2 to 3 hours at most and you will rapidly run out of interesting areas to explore as you finish them one by one until only the hunt for achievements is left. The game's platforming can also be frustrating at times. I often found myself accidentially vaulting over an object I just wanted to climb on, plunging to my death as my character just fall down on the other side. What surfaces are climbable can also be a bit unclear at times.All in all, I had a very pleasant afternoon exploring the small but colorful world of Sludge Life and if you enjoy games with a unique design, weird things to discover and some light puzzle-platformer gameplay, then the couple of bucks this game costs will be worth it.
