_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend it enough - atmospheric, free roaming, and loaded with life. The music of this game, unlike High Hell, basically carries you through the world of the game on a cloud.I think one of the best aspects of Vellman's games is that they're so incredibly loaded with a sense of the character themselves - in High Hell, it was seeing yourself in the mirrors, burning money, vandalizing things as part of your objectives, and rescuing animals.Here, the little touches are what make the entire game have a soul. I've never gone out and tagged IRL but this makes me wish I did, and you feel like you're the character. You're walking around smoking, drinking energy drinks, getting high and hanging out on top of high buildings, breaking into stuff, causing shenanigans, talking to friends, getting accosted by weirdoes, and just living life.The collect-a-thon mechanics are only one aspect of the game, because it's really just a vehicle to make you experience the world that Vellmann and Doseone have made. It feels unmistakably cool. There's a whole lotta games that wish they were this game, and not very many that actually are. The things that make this game are the extremely precise sense of humor and worldview in a fantastical environment that feels incredibly relatable, and all of the visual gags that don't try to force themselves on you. There's a very strong sense of play, and the open-ended nature of the gameplay makes it extremely rewarding to find these things yourselves.Also, god, wear headphones for this. You absolutely need to experience this with bass blasting. It has such a huge impact on it.It's a blessing that it's so easy to play through in a sitting, and that's been part of why I revisit it.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever played a game that could be succinctly described as “Beautifully Ugly”? Sludge Life stands up to that description very much so. Its artstyle stands out from most games that come out these days, it’s the reason I bought it while browsing Steam using the Discovery Queue. The cartoon cel shaded art style caught my eye and rose to the top of all the white noise that is new releases on Steam. I am pretty picky when it comes to games, for example I used to only buy games when they were on sale. What I buy however, has been consistently influenced by visuals. There are other factors, of course, but a game with great art direction can really compel me to want to play it. The subtle VHS-like vignette adds a lot to the aesthetic, and the loud cartoon colors contrast greatly with the sludgy wasteland the game takes place in. The whole of Sludge Island where the game is set feels convincingly lived in, with people looking bored working at their jobs, sleeping midday because of the few prospects they have in life, Or just winning a bet super hard by spinning on their head for eternity. The main gameplay loop involves spraying graffiti in predetermined spots throughout Sludge Island as all the authority figures called “Clops” are either striking or busy. A veritable dream for an up and coming tag artist. You play as Ghost, one such tag artist and your goal is to earn the respect of the Islands five other prolific taggers by hitting as many spots with your sludgy green ghost blob logo as you can. There are also tons of other shenanigans to get yourself into like smoking, drinking, talking, farting, and finding lost snakes. I spent maybe half my time playing Sludge Life, finding graffiti spots and the other half goofing off, finding people to talk to, and laughing my ass off. Make no mistake, Sludge Life is a Funny game, not “funny” like it's trying too hard or is really cringeworthy. Sludge Life has great comedic writing and some of the dialogue is ridiculously hilarious. My only gripe is that it's too difficult to find the other graffiti artists. Once you impress them, by hitting milestones of spots tagged, some of them give you tools that make it much more fun to explore and keep you on track. While I had enough tags to have impressed two of them, I found three graffiti artists, all of which were not the ones I had impressed. And while I did find them eventually, I wish there was an easier way to track them down. I loved my time with Sludge Life, unfortunately that wasn’t a lot of time. The final time I recorded was just under two and a half hours until I found one of the game's three endings. I’ve definitely taken issue with games being too short before and Sludge Life is asking for fifteen dollars for, what most will play, a three hour game. Not a great ratio, sure, but despite that I think the game more than deserves a buy.

As stated above (in a new move I'll be trying in my reviews) I was able to 100% complete this game in just three and a half hours according to Steam. I could see ten dollars being reasonable, but hey, I'm not a game developer, so I don't really understand how to price a game in a manner in which they could still turn a profit.I personally don't regret spending the money. I feel this is something I can come back every now and then and play all over again. To me, this is a game I think I'd have fun memorizing. However, I know not everyone will think the way I do. a lot of people might not want to replay the game, memorize it, speedrun it, etcetera, and that same demographic would probably be better off spending money elsewhere on something longer and more expansive, say a rogue-like, or even Mirror's Edge.Rest assured, though, if you decide to purchase, you get a great little walking/parkour simulator with fun characters and art style, and the pleasure of listening to Big Mud's raps. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game feels like a mash-up of  and  by way of . In my first two hours of play, I smoked a cigarette (a "ciggy"), took a photo of a dizzy pigeon, got bit by a snake, smacked by a  "clop", found a  baby, chatted with a half-insect kid whose mom is a Certified Public Accountant, talked to a guy about a literal s**t he took (and left in the toilet), then I climbed a tower, found a bird person chilling on a couch up top, and then I  backflipped off of the damn thing- falling to my death.And I respawned in a hospital bed, and now I'm in debt! You'll know quickly if this is your kind of jam or not. I bought into the vibe and aesthetic IMMEDIATELY. I loved this. One of the first games I actually intentionally lowered the resolution on. Visually, everything is line-traced, like a cartoon, and it comes through a lot better in 1280 x 720 than it does in 4K. I'm giddy to play more, and had to force myself to stop so I could savor the experience of finding more and more weird stuff in this delightfully gross world. Unless you're speeding through this, looking for objective based gameplay, there's no way you're gonna see everything Sludge Life has to offer in under two hours. But it's not the kind of game that gives you rigid, structured, goals and compels you to do them either. At the same time, I feel like it's reductive to call it a walking simulator. It's more like a "do whatever you want and explore to your heart's content" kind of game. Which is rad. If you ever found yourself playing a game with a cool world that you low key wish you could explore, but the gameplay is linear enough to prevent that- this game is for you. Provided you vibe with the toilet humor and low-fi aesthetic. Be a punk, screw the clops, go throw up some tags and backflip off a building. :)

detailed_description: JOIN THE DISCORD JOIN THE NEWSLETTER About the Game The cosmos is calling. Take the helm of an interstellar expedition of discovery spanning the vast and vibrant infinity of space. The definitive Out There: Oceans of Time experience is available now, with the new Redshift Update. New Oxygen management system on Rocky Planets Expeditions New class skills New Consumable Items New maps for all expedition types New way to explore maps (Tunnels, Ancient Portals, and Unstable Structures) Overall difficulty balancing The successor to the award-winning Out There, Oceans of Time blends resource management and interactive fiction for a space survival epic where death is one wrong decision away. As Commander Nyx, explore a vast galaxy that is different every time you play, as you search for the Archon; a cosmic villain set on dominating the civilisations of the galaxy. Encounter other strange lifeforms and learn to communicate, trade, and conduct diplomacy as you build a coalition of allies in your mission to find the Archon. Recruit new members from the alien races you cross paths with, and build a team capable of traversing the cosmos. Manage your crew, your ship and its systems; the mission’s success is down to your decisions as Commander. Experience a deep, branching narrative written by FibreTigre, dialogue by Christos Gage ( Daredevil (Netflix, 2015), Spider-Man (Insomniac, Sony, 2018)) and beautiful interactive cutscenes illustrated by renowned artist Benjamin Carré ( Transformers: Age of Extinction, Alone in the Dark ). Out There: Oceans of Time is developed by Mi-Clos Studio, the creators of Out There and Sigma Theory. FEATURES Navigate an expansive cosmos that is different every time you play. about_the_game: The cosmos is calling. Take the helm of an interstellar expedition of discovery spanning the vast and vibrant infinity of space. The definitive Out There: Oceans of Time experience is available now, with the new Redshift Update. New Oxygen management system on Rocky Planets Expeditions New class skills New Consumable Items New maps for all expedition types New way to explore maps (Tunnels, Ancient Portals, and Unstable Structures) Overall difficulty balancing The successor to the award-winning Out There, Oceans of Time blends resource management and interactive fiction for a space survival epic where death is one wrong decision away. As Commander Nyx, explore a vast galaxy that is different every time you play, as you search for the Archon; a cosmic villain set on dominating the civilisations of the galaxy. Encounter other strange lifeforms and learn to communicate, trade, and conduct diplomacy as you build a coalition of allies in your mission to find the Archon. Recruit new members from the alien races you cross paths with, and build a team capable of traversing the cosmos. Manage your crew, your ship and its systems; the mission’s success is down to your decisions as Commander. Experience a deep, branching narrative written by FibreTigre, dialogue by Christos Gage ( Daredevil (Netflix, 2015), Spider-Man (Insomniac, Sony, 2018)) and beautiful interactive cutscenes illustrated by renowned artist Benjamin Carré ( Transformers: Age of Extinction, Alone in the Dark ). Out There: Oceans of Time is developed by Mi-Clos Studio, the creators of Out There and Sigma Theory. FEATURES Navigate an expansive cosmos that is different every time you play. Explore unexplored terrain and collect resources for your ship, and the next leg of your journey. Recruit from a diverse range of Alien lifeforms, and build a team capable of surviving the furthest reaches of the cosmos. An epic space-saga penned by FibreTigre, with dialogue from Christos Gage.
short_description: Out There: Oceans of Time is a space exploration game that puts you at the helm of an interstellar mission of discovery spanning a vast and vibrant cosmos.

_childDocuments_.review: so i played the beta or demo or whatever it was and they had a mechanic where by exploration was risky and challenging because you would run out of "energy" while exploring, this was over tuned in the beta and made the game very punishing/un-fun. they have decided to remove the "energy for exploration" mechanic entirely. which aside from removing an aspect of what made the process tense and risk/reward it has also left the game feeling hollow as a significant part of the character abilities and items are based around making the process of exploration more efficient which felt rewarding when it mattered but just pointless now that they don't? the strange thing is that lets say they changed the mechanic to something as simple as running out of energy results in your ship collecting you automatically (i.e you can no longer explore, this could mean you fail the main objective of said exploration) then it would by all accounts make the game design around this process of rewarding players with better exploration character buffs/items still valid. if i had to guess i would say they backed out of their original vision for the game in wake of many complaints about a system that needed work rather than removing.  which is a shame. Trouble is the game-play loop of exploring and levelling up crew really dose feel gutted without that distinct need for a challenge to overcome. right now exploration is really more of a click and point adventure rather than the tense decision making process it used to be.  then again if i had publishers/players protesting about a core mechanic then i too would feel very tempted to just remove it for the initial sales. hopefully they will add this component back in as an "option" sort of the difference between story mode and normal for those of us that like are rouge-likes punishing.

_childDocuments_.review: short version: original OT's resource grinding is a bad centerpiece for a longer roguelike space exploration/adventure game. long version: it pains me to not be able to recommend this. I love the original game (65 hrs on it & more to come) & waited patiently for this, but I don't think what they did here works. what makes me play the original is that's it's short, unforgiving, mysterious, and to the point (get home) and I love the art style & music. this game is easier, has expanded gameplay mechanics which are.. ok, neither good or bad, but make things take longer. since the game takes longer, it's more frustrating when bad luck wipes you out (although there are save points now in white dwarf systems). things I like: the music's great, being able to finally take hydrogen out of the scoop & put it directly into the engine is great, and the greenhouse mechanics are kind of cool. things I don't like: dropping the original's comic book style, the morale system is an unnecessary chore because the characters are void of personality, the character writing is really bad (apparently this game's dialog was written by a professional screenwriter, but you wouldn't know it), the character models are fugly, the planet models don't look near as cool or varied as they did in OT, planetary exploration is repetitive, the labyrinthine star path you have to follow feels arbitrary, the story is generic space opera stuff...  but the core of this is still a resource grinding game so there's little narrative depth (not w/these characters, anyway) or a conflict (since combat isn't a feature). the original game is about getting home & grinding resources because you HAVE to, this game is about saving humanity (or something) & exploring, but with no straightforward objective & expecting you to enjoy grinding resources & taking care of your unlikable crew for the fun of it. I don't know who this is going to appeal to. I think the hardcore fans of Out There are going to be disappointed at the generic new look & all the shoehorned-in time wasting mechanics. And I think anyone new to it looking for a space roguelike are going to find it strangely lacking in depth for an asking price of >20$. Pick it up on sale, I guess. that's all I've got.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, it's been noisy on our spaceship as of late. You hear that? That’s the sound of wasted potential, bouncing nervously wall to wall, echoing across the barren room, a sign that reads “gameplay” above its door. In the room across it – the one where the sign says “narrative” – you’ll find its occupant, the know-how necessary to translate all those great ideas the developers have had into a solidified narrative, completely checked out; its absence seemingly overlooked during development. They both came down to the same conclusion: that bigger isn’t always better, especially when the biggest chunks are missing.  is the sequel to , a 2015 space-exploration, resource-management roguelike which I haven’t had the pleasure of playing. Taking a quick gander at its store page, however, reveals a game that seems to be beloved by many. So why does this new game, one that’s supposedly taking everything from the old one and turning it up to eleven, have a much more mixed reception? Now, I don’t have the necessary experience to compare the two, but with how barebones and bloated of a game  is, it seems that too much time has been spent inflating and less so innovating as much as necessary to support this different, seemingly more narrative-driven approach.And that breaks my heart a little; I’m a narrative-loving kind of guy, but I think I’ll pass on going down this particular wormhole. It all creates this sinking feeling in my gut that slowly expands as the playtime counter on Steam goes up. Eventually, the intrigue wears off, and the understanding for what the developers were going for, but failed to do, evaporates. I become uncanny, and all that’s left are feelings of disappointment. Alas, for where I was promised considerable depth, I only found a puddle’s worth. The story begins with our two main characters, Captain Nyx and Officer Sergei, escorting a dangerous wolf-like creature known as The Archon to a space prison of sorts. It doesn’t take long for things to go awry, The Archon to escape, and our two characters to end up in a century-long cryostasis slumber as their escape pods limp away to the nearest habitable planet. While the setup seems as cliché as can be, there are glimpses that what’s underneath could be more inventive. Unfortunately, it doesn’t get much better. It’s all ideas and barely any refinement. Throwing things at the wall, seeing what sticks, then just leaving it there, hanging. What the universe that these characters inhabit is like, what The Archon’s grand plans are, and how have the past one hundred years affected it all are things merely mentioned in passing, or not at all. There’s no cohesive world to explore, no compelling mystery to uncover, no expansive lore to get lost in. It’s exposition dump after exposition dump, with some meagre attempts at characterisation thrown in. Some branching moments in the story try their best at tempting a replay out, in the hopes of there being a sudden realization that makes everything worthwhile, but the ordeal as a whole is so unrefined that I’m hard pressed for motivation to go looking for what I’ve missed.The gameplay is divided into two sections: interstellar travel and expeditions. You’ll be spending most of your time aboard your ship, flying from star system to star system, the goal being reaching the next objective. Along the way, you’ll be tending to its parts and crew by managing four bars: fuel, oxygen, hull, and morale. Should any one of these fall to zero, it’ll mean a game over in the vast majority of cases, at which point you’ll be sent back to your last manual save. Manual saves can only be performed at specific space stations, but these aren’t as rare as you might think, and should you quit out, you’ll be able to resume from the very spot you did so at, provided you haven’t died. Still, permanently losing progress in a narrative-inclined roguelite is a pet peeve of mine, so keeping these bars filled is non-negotiable. To stave off death, you’ll be visiting planets. As each planet is of a specific type, so are the resources you need spread out among them. For example, Hydrogen and Helium – both used for refuelling – can only be found by sending a probe to a gas giant, while you’ll have to land on a rocky planet and drill out Iron to repair your hull. Everything your ship does corresponds to a module or technology aboard, and they’ll wear off the more you use them, eventually needing to be repaired. Add in the fact that each ship – as you have the option of swapping between ‘em should you find one abandoned, adrift in space – has different stats that govern how efficient it’ll be when it comes to depleting these bars and you’ve got a decent foundation to add more gameplay elements onto. But, there aren’t any. What you do an hour in is the same thing you do after ten, albeit more efficiently. I don’t know where this “steep learning curve” other reviews are talking about comes from, as I’ve only died twice – both times to running out of fuel – near the beginning of the game. After that, for the next eight hours or so, I’ve never come close to it. It’s an easy system to learn from and figure out. Once you do, the game has no curveballs to throw your way to shake things up. Sure, a text-based event will sometimes pop up, urging you to decide on how to resolve it. However, most decisions will inform you in advance of their outcomes, so you can just steer clear of what isn’t in your favour. A decent number of events also have the option to be ignored, so it’s almost a non-feature at that point.  Planetary expeditions are similar in that regard. You can find them after scanning certain planets for anomalies, then landing and deploying your team to complete a specific objective and maybe pick up some resources along the way. They’re explored by moving across a hexagonal grid while avoiding tiles with hazards on them. These hazards can inflict a negative effect on one of your crew members, which can eventually lead to death. However, there’s almost always an alternate route to find as long as you’re the least bit patient, and even then, the chance of getting inflicted is only 25%, with possibilities to lower it further, making the tiles rarely a considerable threat. Nyx, Sergei, and any other crew members you recruit later in the game (though none other than the first two are actual characters) differ by abilities and classes, though these are negligible mostly. They’ll sometimes provide a nice benefit, but never will they pull an expedition from certain doom. They’ll be most important during text-based encounters, similar to those in space, that occur on certain tiles.  Each class has a limited number of action points, consumed when picking an option exclusive to that class during the encounters. Theoretically, you could find yourself in a bad spot, with no points to pick the winning option, but as each event informs you which class you’ll need to get the best outcome before you even find it, let alone step on its tile, you’re free to ignore any that might pose a risk to your party; a realization that turns expeditions into an assembly line of clicking around for as many resources as you can find. I’ve explored the stars and found… very little of note.  might be the next great space RPG, but only with substantial additions and reiterations to its gameplay and narrative. As it is? A bit intriguing, but hardly recommendable.

_childDocuments_.review: What an unbearably frustrating game Out there: Oceans of time truly is. Don't get me wrong, it's not the game per se, what is an issue is the ludicrous save game function. I can't imagine that it would have been too much of an effort to ask the devs to be able to create multiple save points, but not so with Out there: Oceans of time.Firstly, whoever came up with the idea of creating in-game save points at certain locations like white dwarf stars for example needs to seriously give their heads and wobble because the save game function in Out there: Oceans of time is flawed beyond credibility. Game number 1) game started up fine and as it was the first play, I decided to take the path of the tutorial. This in itself was not too bad a thing briefly went about explaining the game mechanics.Game number 2)  was going to be my first proper try. I gleaned information off the Internet to help steer me in the direction of the playable game and everything was going fine, right up until hour 15 when I found myself restarting the game after a break, only to find that the game save had become corrupted and the first 15 hours went down the drain so to speak. I was not to be daunted by this error situation; thinking that the problem was one of those "bad luck moments" however, I was about to be proven savagely wrong.Game number 3)  by this time I'd grown accustomed to the mechanics of the game and felt comfortable with all the keys and settings et cetera, so I set about my third attempt at a viable game but sadly, this too was doomed to failure, only this time I manage to clock up 21 hours of actual and actual playtime I once again visited the ludicrous in-game save point and save the game. I went out for a couple of hours to see a friend, when I got back I booted the game up only to be presented with an exclamation mark inside a red triangle informing me of an incompatible save. So 21 hours of my life wasted because someone in the devs can't be bothered to make the save game work. Had I known about this game's issues, I simply wouldn't have bought it as it is now. Needless to say, I am not going to be playing this game again and my advice to you is simple: do NOT waste your money on a game that lets you down so easily.I wish this had happened to me within the refund period on steam because if it did, I would be £20 better off.  Needless to say, I feel let down and disappointed and in light of that comment.If the Devs read this, firstly, shame on you for releasing a "Pig in a poke" and I challenge to correct my errors, lest it be the last you'll ever see of me.FIX IT.... I DARE YOU.Yours extremely disappointedWulfrune

_childDocuments_.review: I don't want to give that game a negative review but... I got to say, the biggest new feature, the away missions and the related new moral resource kills it for me. That despite I really liked the predecessor and had this one on my wish list for a long time,  me. These forced away missions turn a relaxing casual game into a pointless grind fest.  The game got quite an update regarding the visuals and story animations. Also there are multiple languages included right from start, although the game contains a lot of text! I also found no bugs yet except for quite huge frame drop  when you do away missions and don't use a good graphics card. The problem are the away missions themselves. You now have new resource called "morale", that goes down whenever you jump between star systems. You can only increase it by completing away missions and visit villages while doing so. That means, you are more or less forced to do these missions. On the other hand you can't do them whenever you like because there is a cooldown of two jumps per crew member. So you not only have to do them but also in a certain interval! Before you can start such a missions, you have to compelete a mini game that gets quickly annoying. The missions then turned out to be very time consuming for usually little rewards. In the first "Out There" game, you landed on a planed, talked to some aliens and maybe drilled for resources. Quick and simple. Now you walk arround like 20-30 minutes on a single planet, mostly because you can only move like 4-5 tiles per turn, no auto-walk possible to already explored areas. You also have to do some micro management and evade dangerous tiles by walking longer ways arround. That has probably to do with the system they had in place during development, where you could only stay on a planet for a certain time so you had to choose whether to take the risk or not. Either way, I can't get into these missions, they just take too long for too little reward and also get boring quickly. There should be a an option to auto-resolve these, like it is with any other event in the game. Probably to somewhat offset the annoyance that away missions are, you can now save manually in some star systems. I actually had no problem to lose in the old game without being able to load some save. But there are run took also only like 2-4 hours, if it went really good, so if you bascially complete the game, in average it was more like 30 minutes to an hour if you screw up. Here most of my playtime are away missions with very little overall progress.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm completely fine with the monotonous gameplay because it evokes the same feeling I would expect when travelling through space. It's fine to not have too much action at once, and I think this game is an upgrade over the original where objectives are much more clear and the paths to them are more defined. What does not pass the bar for me is the amount of gamebreaking bugs there are in a game like this. Objectives in this game are broken to the point where you will lose a significant portion of your save data, and literally be unable to progress in the game. There are no backup saves, or ways to revert saves to help fix these issues when they arise, and the devs are terrible at responding to bugs and feedback. Their discord does not work to submit bug reports and the discussion thread is rarely looked at. I would not recommend this game on the basis of how unplayable it actually is, not because of the gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: If this was under 10 dollars, I would recommend it as a decent time waster. Right now though I can't recommend it. I liked the visuals and sounds. The concept looks interesting: Explore a universe, explore planets, harvest materials to survive and build things, find new ships and new party members. Sadly, the exploration is pretty much pointless since there is nothing unique to discover. Harvesting materials is either busywork so you can keep travelling or to build modules that only make travelling more efficient, which is moot since there is hardly any point to exploring. Exploring planets with your party is also repetitive since there is nothing really unique to discover. No cool items to find nor lore or secrets. You can discover new ships, which sounds great, but their only difference is the looks and how much space they have. The point to having more space is just to make things less tedious which feels unrewarding.The game play loop is basically repetitive maintenance to get materials and fuel so you can get to the next place so you can get materials and fuel etc.So, how is the story then? The premise is interesting, but the execution is extremely shallow. The characters act and talk like they are 12 years old and although the story introduces some cool concepts the way it unfolds feels immature and like I said: Shallow. There are multiple endings it seems, but the one I got felt very unrewarding without any choice in how it turns out (The judge ending) and I did not feel like doing the busywork to get the other ending(s)Final verdict: If you can get this game for a big discount and want something mindless to just keep clicking through then it's decent. For it's full price or until they release an expansion which greatly expands the game play I would say to skip this.Alternatives for this game would be games like Diluvion, Rebel Galaxy or Between the Stars.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't in good conscience recommend this. Maybe in a few months (or years, at this rate) when the big issues are ironed out, things will be better, but considering that this game was meant to release a year ago, it should be incredible by now. Good:-The ability to drag resources directly into the fuel, oxygen, or hull is the best quality of life improvement from the original game I could have asked for. -The increased interaction with other life is very enjoyable. The trading system is awesome (if a bit overpowered), and I like building a massive crew. Bad: -Expeditions suck, for many reasons, and other people have explained the main failures better than I can. Some of the less game-ruining ones, however, I'd like to discuss. For one, the mini-game to find anomalies is incredibly tedious, and adds nothing. Sweeping a planet for the 20th time isn't fun, it's just a waste of time. Also, what's the point of multiple anomalies per planet if you can only actually visit one? From a gameplay perspective, having to choose is interesting, but there is no in-game explanation for it, which just makes it frustrating.-It's easy. From someone who beat Omega Edition multiple times, it's *mind numbingly* easy. I understand that the difficulty was the biggest criticism of the first game, but a hard mode would be nice. Specifically, the fuel costs are nearly negligible, expeditions have basically no downsides, there are too many slots, and there is no longer any incentive to min-max. Out There Omega was, at its core, an inventory management game; this game has somehow managed to trivialize that aspect of it. Bugs: -Wormhole generators aren't very useful, entirely due to their map. You have almost no frame of reference: your goal pointers go away, your trail is gone, and it changes the way you've angled the camera. This cost me a game.-Sometimes, when you've finished an expedition or looked at an abandoned ship, the game thinks your cargo hold is open when it isn't. Clicking the button to close it does nothing, and exiting to the main menu and coming back is the only solution. -Expeditions cause ridiculously low frame-rates. The graphics option in the settings does nothing to alleviate this.-If you fly away from a planet you have discovered an anomaly on, but haven't visited, the anomaly disappears.I desperately wanted to like this game, and I honestly feel robbed. I expected much better considering the original Out There's quality.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a neat game, and better than the original Out There (in my opinion).  However, it's INCREDIBLY limited and doesn't let you do things in any logical manner.  The first example, when you get the opportunity to create bunks for your crew, you are FORCED to discard or destroy something (if, like me, your ship is full) to make the component.  And, if you were trying to make room, it FORCES you to put it where you made room.  No, you can't move components around, you have to disassemble them and you lose resources in the process.  And you can't stop the tutorial from forcing you to do it RIGHT NOW.  And it does this EVERY TIME you get a required component.  Sure, it's an OCD thing, but if you're not going to make the game user friendly, it's not worth a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: i really tried to like this game so lets go with the positives: the graphics are great. music is atmospheric and fitting. but thats about it. gameplay is like this:go to planet>collect resources>go to next planet>collect resources>go to next planet>start expedition>collect resources> and so on. there is NOTHING else! no space battles, no nice conversations (hello star control!), nothing! the story makes no sense at all, and frankly i dont even get it. cubes that created the world and then decided to destroy it?!? weird babys in tubes?!? bird-gods that eat suns?!?its sad i have to give a negative review on it because this game could be great, but how it is now it isnt.

_childDocuments_.review: Not really much play here.  The seems to be a lot going on with all the ship components and resources, but you get basically everything in the first 5 hours.  And since you have access to it all there really was no replayability desire.  Endgame is a boring chore as you are just jumping as fast as you can to get to the story points, there are no threats or progress at this stage.  Character progression is nonexistent as you complete the game with characters at level 2, with none of their skills or classes were necessary or added anything to gameplay.  Effort was put in to make this a "non combat" game, but in doing so conflict was removed.  This makes the gmae unchallenging and dull, and there is not enough "chrome" to bring it to the level of a visual novel.Suggestions;Don't force the "roguelike" this game would play just as well in a set universe (like a starflight type game)If it's a set universe you will be able to add more set challenges, with multiple quest lines occurring simultaneously  This would give you time as your game mechanic for conflict if you really need to keep guns off the ships.  Perhaps helping the different races might lead to different endings and replayability?  Time as a factor would make lots of those character abilities do something, if you had limited time on an expedition then maybe the skill that lets you move more hexes would have meaning, but now where there is no time limit what does it matter?More than anything the game feels like a shell for a space MMOrpg, thouvgh I doubt the developers are that ambitious.Bottom line right now, just no good.It's pales in comparison to FTL (2012)It's got less gameplay and story than Starflight (1986)It can't even compare favorably to the original space roguelike on the old apple][ computer "Sundog" (1984)Sorry, Out There:  Oceans of Time 2/10

_childDocuments_.review: A daring attempt to expand on Out There: Omega Edition, but sadly lost focus and fell flat.New ship management gameplay can be fun; ship navigation feels largely the same as OTOE; UI is streamlined with hotkeys, can have softlocks occasionally though but nothing can't be fixed with good old alt+f4, remember to save often.Unfortunately the core feature of OTOE: survival, is not here in OTOOT. Staying alive is so utterly trivial you have to actively sabotage your run to be in real danger of an early game over. Another core feature of OTOE, learning alien language is also getting sidelined here. Choosing the right response will only slightly alter the inventory of alien vendor and recruit roster. Hell, you can safely ignore the shopping system entirely, since resource is hardly a problem.And lastly, to me the real crime is the writing in this game. In OTOE the random events that happen when you jump to a new star did a good job setting the atmosphere of the game -- the dread in face of the unknown, the wonder of the universe, the helplessness of flinging oneself into the void using utterly inexplicable alien technology, the struggle to tread the fine line between functional and lunatic and functional lunatic, and mixed with a healthy does of body horror. But all this, is absent in OTOOT. The random encounters become few and far between, and what left of them reads as bland as the instructions printed on the back of your instant noodle package. The new protagonist, Cpt. Nyx and her sidekick are not that likable, and the main plot is... whatever. The canon ending also somewhat undermined the plot of OTOE, Oh and there's one steam achievement,  , which is broken at the time of writing of this review. And the community manager over at the official discord confirmed there's no planned fix in sight, making it impossible to 100% this game. If you are into that kind of thing, avoid this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's OG Out There but 'bigger and better'. I can't really explain it any better.I can however list a few issues:- Very rare UI bugs (none are critical, you just have to restart the game if it happens).- Early game expeditions should be much more punishing RNG-wise, right now it's actually harder to do late-game ones (and please don't bring back expedition timer).- There's something wrong with expedition rendering/generation stuff - depending on the location it can bring even the mightiest CPUs/GPUs down to it's knees.QoL suggestions:- Hotkeys for space views (planet/system/galaxy)- Allow skipping all cinematics/animations (ie end of expedition)- Perhaps 1 spare space in drill/post-expedition screen to allow moving stuff around when you're fullBalance suggestions:- Nerf early game Archon ship - it's way too good, especially morale/comfort - you don't  have to replace it until you get Nyx's ship- I think it's worth specializing ships, that is locking some slots to be cargo/tech/module, otherwise it's not really worth swapping themP.S.:To all the people comparing the game's writing to Mass Effect - have you actually played ME lately? Because if you did you'd remember how weak ME writing is. This game is ME-ish at best, but condensed as necessary to fit the game loop. It is ME in 10 lines of dialogue it requires to progress the story. If you somehow think otherwise I'm going to disappoint you - you're delusional. ME has always been and always will be your average overarching space opera, which actually reminds of Kojima's MGS writing. And just to be clear - I've played ME & MGS on both consoles & PC multiple times (mostly on consoles).Overall, it's a great successor to OG Out There barring some bugs & a few balancing issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of the original. Sadly my first impressions of this sequel were not great. Initially I was put off by the poor quality of the animations in the cutscenes; having a quality on par a bad mobile MMO. And the writing in the intro/tutorial is pretty bad too, not to mention it's all there just to set up one of the worst possible plots. None of what unfolds gives you any reason to care about any of the characters, let alone anthing that happens with regards to the plot.As for the game mechanics. Surface exploration felt underwhelming to play, though it looks good. As for the core gameplay, I feel like this incarnation suffers from the same problems as the original, where there's an optimal depth to plumb for fuel, and an optimal depth to mine. At least the previous mobile game had the decency to keep the probe slider at your preferred setting. This game is worse by virtue of resetting the probe slider to a default value and making you have to specifically dial in the value on the probe slider each and every time.At this juncture my journey abruptly ended. Was playing the game via cloud gaming service 'geforce now'. 40 minutes in to the game and geforce had some problems and had to close. When I logged back in to geforce all those 40 minutes of progress were lost. Nor did I feel like I really achieved any interesting gameplay during those 40 minutes. I don't mind games being difficult, but 40 minutes is a long time to spend retreading the exact same ground because the developers can't be bothered to figure out how to do saves properly. A hard game can be fun, especially when the difficulty is well defined within the context of the game world. There's no reason this should stop the game from being robust in the face of the real world.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fine little space explorations and survival game. The survival mechanics come in two flavours: (1) Managing ship resources (fuel, hull repair elements, O2, morale) and (2) away missions on planets where your away party has some abilities and an item to help manage the dangers, perform actions, and O2 supply if relevant. The away missions happen on a tile grid.There is no combat.This game has no voice over. However, dialog cut scenes are short, have just a few lines of dialog per character, and progress is at the speed of the player. There is no choice during these dialog cut scenes, just pace management so you can read your speed (again, short sentences).The graphics are appropriate for this kind of game. The developers failed to use standard library and resolution & scaling approaches to support a variety of screen dimensions. This may make the game hard to read or play for some players.There is no wide-screen/ultrawide screen support.There are black bars instead.The left and right "screen" limits are narrow, making certain side-scrolling mechanics effectively broken (there are two fun operators, > and <, which would have meant it was not broken if they were used with the x-axis cursor position).The game is short. For me full completion was 17 hours. I took my time.On a $/hour entertainment scale, this game is poor.However, the game mechanics are limited and the length is very appropriate for the game. I was ready for it to be done. So it's just about the price.All in all, a decent game with a few flaws that don't get in the way of enjoying the campaign and the mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall good game.Story: "Out There" haha geddit? This is my biggest gripe with the game because it feels like the biggest missed opportunity. Characters and their motivations are mostly esoteric, and most character interactions are over and done with in less than a minute. It feels very roguelike, which I suppose it is, but it's also frustrating because it feels like an RPG storyline compressed into like 500 lines of dialogue. As the most egregious example, at the end of the game (obviously SPOILERS) I am allowed to ask one question. I get THREE CHOICES and when I pick "yo who made this weird ♥♥♥♥ the whole game is sorta based around" I get, not in so many words, "the developers, moron."Bruh.Meanwhile I'm surrounded by better questions, in my opinion, like "What the everliving ♥♥♥♥ happened around Earth!?" The funniest ♥♥♥♥ is there's a character in my crew for most of the game who definitely knows, but I can't ask them.BRUH.The game handwaves all of this sort of questioning I imagine my crew would be desperately interested in with, basically, "it is beyond your understanding." The worst kind of cop-out. I get that sometimes answering the questions makes a setting boring and the interest is in unanswered questions, but usually this is done by having people who have answers be all dead, or utterly insane, or out of reach. Out There has them join your ♥♥♥♥♥♥' crew, say "beyond ur understanding lol" then like, I dunno, travel with you for weeks or months or years and just sorta awkwardly stare at you in the hallway on your way to the mess. It is very frustrating.At one point literally billions of people die and the dialogue around that is like, two paragraphs worth.Gameplay:Gameplay overall is good. You are constantly juggling resources and there are a lot of resources to juggle. Fuel, oxygen, hull, and morale will end your game. Space is gargantuan and basically bereft of space travelling life in the OT universe. If your fuel runs out nobody is gonna come by, ask for some Galactic Standard Credits TM, and fill you up. You just float alone in the void and eventually die.Speaking of "credits" there's no such thing. In space everything is done in barter, which makes sense when you're interacting with planets that as far as I can tell run the gamut from "megalopolises that haven't seen a ship in years" to "tiny tribal villages." This makes storage an incredibly important resource because aside from a few infinitely-storable trade goods (think art and things) you need to both have stuff to sell and the space to accept the stuff you want.On top of managing your storage space you're also constantly eyeing new blueprints, rare resources to build those blueprints, and then when you finally get everything you want you find a ship with 10 extra slots and now you have to do the whole thing over again. It keeps everything from getting boring.There are flaws here too though. Your performance and resistance cap out at 10. Nothing tells you this, so I kept trying to pump up one or both before I realized I'd wasted a ton of time and effort on more-or-less literally nothing. Certain technologies, placed next to each other, have synergies. But nothing tells you what has synergies, or what those synergies do. You just have to guess, which is infuriating for some of the higher-end technologies. Often this is pretty easy to guess; engine related things should be put next to the engine for example. But whether or not something works out is kind of a crapshoot. Drill upgrade next to the drill? No synergy. Telescope upgrade next to the telescope? Synergy.Graphics/Sound: Middle of the road honestly. Nothing awed me. Nothing made me think "this is garbage." I was just like "yes this is a game and these are sci-fi sounds." Definitely wouldn't spring for the soundtrack.Overall: Like I said at the top, overall good game. It's fun. It's absorbing. The plot is good enough/interesting enough for me to care about it, which means it isn't terrible it just isn't good either. Same can be said about the graphics. If it's worth 20 bucks for you to ♥♥♥♥ around in space for 10-20 hours, buy it. Otherwise, don't.

_childDocuments_.review: Phew, I'm giving this the thumbs up - It IS the Out There that we know, love and remember but it just takes a bit a of digging to get there....First, the downers:-the game is not as slick and stylish as the original. There is more graphical horsepower on display here, but somehow the simplicity of the original game's animation and the paired down character images were (for me) more mystical and evocative of a surreal sci-fi mood. The 3D rendered characters don't do it for me - bring back the lush portaiture artwork we have previously seen in Out There Chronicles and Sigma theory. - the music and sounds are just dull in comparison to the thumping swagger of the originals. Seriously could they not just release a modded version with all the original music and sound effects? I miss it...- the gameplay is a bit fiddly at first, but thats OK because it leads to the uppers...which are The Uppers - Yep, this game does capture the free roaming spirit of the original game but you have to stick with it to find that out. There are the same quixotic and risk/reward scenarios to encounter and a rich vein of sci-fi lore to explore. - It took me a while to get used to the additional crew and exploration mechanics, but now I'm there and they add a new dimension to the game whilst all the old anxieties around oxygen, fuel and hull are there. This game doesn't have the elegant, simplicity of the original game, nor the artistic and musical flair, but for all that this is still an authentic Out There experience. The feeling is closer to that of an expansive table top game, with varied and satisfying universe to explore. Worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to spend fuel to travel out of a system and back to a system so that I can "rest" before I can go on another expedition... Which will likely strand me... The game isn't so intriguing that I care to tolerate that mechanic. If I'm landed on a planet then why can't I just rest without spending fuel or oxygen? The answer is because there is no "resource" to spend that makes sense, so they make you arbitrarily spend fuel and oxygen and hull points to regenerate characters and prevent you from doing too many expeditions back-to-back... This killed any semblance of immersion I had.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game and would be back for another run through soon.  The early game is a bit challenging because of the number of slots available on your starter ship, but that kept it exciting and it is very satisfying when you get a nicer ship with more space to work with.   Starting about mid-game,  this becomes more of a relaxed jaunt through space, just enjoying the spacy ambiance.  It is simple and relaxing with gameplay being straightforward.  It is a nice way unwind.I only ran into only one bug on my first playthrough, and it was with the autosave system.  But the developers are very active on discord and are planning to address this in the next patch.  They even sent me a fixed up save file.  It is good to see more games in the space exploration genre and I wholeheartedly support indie developers in this space, which is my favorite genre of games to play.  There is no space combat in this game, so the focus is purely exploration with a little bit of resource management and survival.    I think there is a solid foundation here that the devs could potentially build upon. More depth and meaning to that exploration game loop (without necessarily tying it to a storyline) would be very welcome for example.  Overall, I would recommend this to someone wanting to spend a few hours in a casual space-themed game.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sucked in. I came across an anomaly shortly after finding a new ship that put me off course. I was on the brink of being out of fuel when I happened upon the husk of the ship I stripped. It still had fuel but I couldn't transfer it. I had to rebuild enough systems to make it a tanker and scout nearby systems without a telescope for gas giants to scoop. Took a while just getting enough gas to move the tanker around. Then I had to backtrack to where I left my ship. Doing all this without running out of O2 was hairy, but pulling it off made me a fan!
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: I have been so excited about this game for a while now! I played the older version a lot and was super excited for an updated version of that. I personally don't agree with the negative reviews that this game has received. Compared to the older version of this game, this is fantastic. There is so much more to do and explore. It is more challenging without sacrificing the core concept of the previous game. I would recommend this game without a doubt and am willing to play through a new game while it is getting spruced up. Thank you for creating this game and expanding on an already fabulous game.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Buggy, wait for a few patches!- A last-minute change before release (no more time limit on away missions) made many abilities and items literally useless.- Two crashes to desktop in 4 hours (but barely any progress lost, thankfully).- After bartering, I lost all items I offered, but gained none of the things I bartered for.- Many of the choose-your-own-adventure prompts make no sense for your crew, or the environment.- Typos, and some strange writing that seems to generally be not native English.- Other players in the forums have reported other bugs I haven't seen.The game has nice graphics and music, and these issues are fixable. If you are interested, make sure to check recent patch notes before you buy. I will probably come back and play more after some patches.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, the game does not anticipate (very well) possible actions of the players. It is not always "intelligent".  Unless you do some actions in precisely the correct order devised by the game developers, even though a different order is possible, the user will be forced to take actions that are stupid.  Or, go back and reload from an earlier point in the game.  Frustrating! I got so tick-off that I uninstalled the game!
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Out There's game play loops do not scale well to the extents of Oceans of Time. While Omega was perfect in this regard, Oceans of Time tries to spread the game play too thin. Too bad as it looked promising (and still can be fixed). Music is great. Graphics are mediocre but functional. The UI looks good but it has some quirks. Did not encounter any bugs during my sessions.I will give this game the benefit of the doubt and give a thumbs up since I like the developer and hope that they will continue improving this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: It is a survival game, in space. It can be very hard to start, resource use, blueprint availability, what abandoned ship you find all lead into a different experience. The game is not short, taking me some 11 hours. However I also had a ship that was optimised with nearly all blueprints and 90+ bar oxygen use, if you want to play my way it will take you longer. Tip - when your ship is high level - jump black holes everywhere you will save an unholy amount of time. If you understand the vastness of space, a journey of seemingly insignificant people doing great things and take pride in knowing that you resource managed your way out of a nightmare then you will enjoy this game. If you have played Out There the original then you will enjoy this just as much.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: When I saw the title, I was hoping it would be like the original, but with time travel. Instead, it's like the original with some additional surface exploration elements that felt more tedious than interesting. I know I didn't play it long, but I didn't much care for being unable to turn off the planet-to-planet travel animations (only the system-to-system ones) and the somewhat misleading title.Between the two, I prefer the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Glitchy to the point of unplayability in my case. The devs are admirably doing their best to address the issues most players seem to be having though. I adored the first game, both Chronicles' chapters, and eagerly awaited the release of this one, but I'm left disappointed by the terribly written dialogue and the direction they chose to take the gameplay itself in.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Pros : Spacescapes are awesome, ship detail is incredible, fluidity of play is good, quite a lot of space to explore.Cons : a bug or two trying to heal and the game didn't update the animation, wasn't sure if a heal happened, spent a few extra action points (totally fixable, I'm sure), would love a big more "side-track" quests - you have free roam, but the number of plot-quests are limited, perhaps this is on purpose to allow for future updates or DLC's. Your 3 ship attributes really tether you to short trips to keep your stocks up (fuel/oxy/hull) and morale takes a hit pretty quickly on a multi-jump push. It's better than it was before in the beta, but could use a little more optimization. Would love a bit more autonomy to make multi-dozen jump moves (perhaps future quests would force you traverse the tendrils of the galaxy or bisect it more than 20-50 hops).Suggestions : More ship selection - I'd love to see a ship even larger than the Vanguard (50-75 slot Starship of some sort). This would give you capabilities to keep the ship upkeep and fuel reserves well in balance with a long cross-galaxy traverse. Also, finding other humans would be kinda nice - you get the impression that Nyx and Sergei are impersonal officers unable to draft their own kind :p I still absolutely recommend this to others - there's so much potential for add-ons, DLC's or even mods with the traverse-able galaxy as large as this.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first Out There, and this one is even better. Better graphics, more things to do, and the added Expeditions mechanic really gives the game more weight as well. Definitely worth the price. No performance issues, running at a buttery smooth 144fps, at least for me, I read a review of someone not getting great FPS but the lowest mine has dropped is 90fps, with graphics on the highest setting, and it's only happened briefly. Jumps right back to 144. A must have if you think space is cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: With many of the other reviews I do have some minor issues.i think the game needs to have some difficulty sliders to either make it more story or having more difficulty parameters. Graphically it's pretty and should run fine on low end systems, the exploration is fun, however again nerds some tweaks.Music is nice, I'm no connoisseur on game music however it's pleasant to listen to.I would like to see some more RPG aspects, and perhaps side missions while flying around.Think I'd probably have been better released as early access so Devs could improve upon feedback, that said the Devs are active and I imagine are working on issues.Sadly now having gotten to the end of the game. I've had to retract my recommendation. The game has the potential for a lot more content, and sadly falls pretty short; especially for the asking price which by no means is a lot however you'd kinda expect a bit more.What really made irked me was having discovered something in a nebula (end story stuff) the bloody tooltips just stayed on the screen. Completely covering up half if the game's interface (ok not half but a few buttons when your refining / drilling.)I dont know if the devs ran out of money.. I'd personally love to play it again, if they have a chance to address some of the issues raised (mostly by others already)I'm happy to say good by to my money, i've had 2 nights of entertainment and it's actually one of the few of many games that i have actually finished.. so that's a plus i guess.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: i buy it for myself and for  a friend. i loved this game in android and played many times. it was omega version and i thinked  its the same style just in pc. but sadly  this desktop version of game is far from mobile one. added weird dialogue scenes.  added 3d expedition s.. all features like this is an big extra but this extra is slammed main features o game. this game in android was a survival fantasy that basedon resource planning strategy and i loved this but now there is lot of additions that taked game from there and put in some kind of rpg with lot of dialogues.this game is not bad. but its taste far from orginal android version. so if you want that old taste like me, i not recommend this game. but in other situations this game not bad and you will like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels a little too unpolished for the price. The gameplay is slow, what I've seen of the writing is bland and the UI is clunkyMy biggest issue is that you spend a lot of you time on the system/galaxy map that have some of the most boring grafics in the game. Other parts have decent grafics, but I feel like the part of the game I spend the most time in recieved the least effort.If the game was cheaper I might have given it more of a chance, but it didn't catch me in the first hour so I would rather return in...
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the story line of this game. The mechanics were simple and streamlined. I wasn't bogged down by the need to do repetitive tasks over and over again just to earn xp. To help put it into perspective, my crew had a max level of 3, so visiting planets and doing missions was more or less optional. I am not saying that there are not some tasks that require repeating (ie fueling up, repairs, oxygen), but they do not seem so overbearing that it feels like a grind. I was able to finish a version of the story line in about 6hrs and I am excited to play again to unlock/complete alternative story line endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Rough. Very rough. It plays like a game from early 2000s. The ship inventory is hilariously small. No voice acting. No update in over 250days, dispite the fact that there's clearly still stuff that needs to be fixed and improved in the game... so if the devs don't even support the game, then why should you?
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Almost an hour into the game I encountered a game breaking bug. It caused me to force quit the game and now i'm just disappointed and don't even know if my progress was saved. I posted this in discussions. What I did get to experience looked like it was heading in the right direction. I'm debating on refunding until this is fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a neat story/narrative on a grand, epic scale w. some interesting twists/turns.Very tough on the RNG-end of rogue-games.But once you figured out the system behind the RNG, it's not that tough any longer.It can become quite grindy, but once you find the capital ship, it's rather breezy but repetitive though.Omega is your friend and your Gollum-precious - hoard it well!Maybe, just maybe, there'll be one day a first-person perspective type of this game/story......that'd be really grand!
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game but it has issues.It took around 8 hours to beat tracking down all the main quests.  There were mini-games that were there for no purpose or to make things complicated for no good reason.  For example: scanning for anomalies has no fail.  You just scan until you find them.  It ends up being a needless waste of time.  It was much easier than the original.     Issues:- I think the ending was incorrect given the quests that were completed (cubes not dealt with). - Resources bought in villages would often disappear.- Being unable to skip/hasten the expedition summary is annoying.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: so as a heads up to those with powerful GPUs this game will overwork them for no reason, I recommend lowering the voltage so that the game cannot do that. as for the game itself. I have played the original out there and this one seems just as great only with some exploration feature. seems like its going to be fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Had to build a Plant building on my ship. Supposedly received the materials to do so did not. So game progress was stuck at the build screen since i didn't have the materials to build the item. Also not entertaining quite boring actually. Exploration is just clicking decision making while exploring seems bland and non consequential. Hazards feel like they have a much higher than 25% chance of triggering.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review: Incompatible save, 2 incompatible save, 3 incompatible save.  The save files corrupt constantly. You can go into the game, play a loaded game, save it. Use that same game then next time it's corrupted.  The game doesn't have as many of the random fun elements of out there omega and obvious lack of creativity when compared to the original.  The random events are more often than not just negative. The sense of wonder isn't there like the first, fancy visuals aren't needed or 3d models.   Good writing is required. I wanted to support the company, but stick to the original on your phone.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

_childDocuments_.review:
The successor to the award-winning Out There, Oceans of Time blends roguelike, resource management and interactive fiction for a space survival epic where death is one wrong decision away.

As Commander Nyx, explore a vast galaxy that is different every time you play, as you search for the Archon; a cosmic villain set on dominating the civilisations of the galaxy.

Encounter other strange lifeforms and learn to communicate, trade, and conduct diplomacy as you build a coalition of allies in your mission to find the Archon.

Recruit new members from the alien races you cross paths with, and build a team capable of traversing the cosmos. Manage your crew, your ship and its systems; the mission's success is down to your decisions as Commander.
_childDocuments_.name: Out There: Oceans of Time

name: Hades
detailed_description: ALSO FROM SUPERGIANT GAMES The god-like rogue-like returns! About the Game Hades is a god-like rogue-like dungeon crawler that combines the best aspects of Supergiant's critically acclaimed titles, including the fast-paced action of Bastion , the rich atmosphere and depth of Transistor , and the character-driven storytelling of Pyre . BATTLE OUT OF HELL As the immortal Prince of the Underworld, you'll wield the powers and mythic weapons of Olympus to break free from the clutches of the god of the dead himself, while growing stronger and unraveling more of the story with each unique escape attempt. UNLEASH THE FURY OF OLYMPUS The Olympians have your back! Meet Zeus, Athena, Poseidon, and many more, and choose from their dozens of powerful Boons that enhance your abilities. There are thousands of viable character builds to discover as you go. BEFRIEND GODS, GHOSTS, AND MONSTERS A fully-voiced cast of colorful, larger-than-life characters is waiting to meet you! Grow your relationships with them, and experience thousands of unique story events as you learn about what's really at stake for this big, dysfunctional family. BUILT FOR REPLAYABILITY New surprises await each time you delve into the ever-shifting Underworld, whose guardian bosses will remember you. Use the powerful Mirror of Night to grow permanently stronger, and give yourself a leg up the next time you run away from home. NOTHING IS IMPOSSIBLE Permanent upgrades mean you don't have to be a god yourself to experience the exciting combat and gripping story. Though, if you happen to be one, crank up the challenge and get ready for some white-knuckle action that will put your well-practiced skills to the test. SIGNATURE SUPERGIANT STYLE The rich, atmospheric presentation and unique melding of gameplay and narrative that's been core to Supergiant's games is here in full force: spectacular hand-painted environments and a blood-pumping original score bring the Underworld to life.
