_childDocuments_.review: If you don't like reading novels, here's the gist: Hades is a wonderful game and a mediocre roguelite. If you're here for a visual novel or a Supergiant game, go ahead. If you want to play a good roguelite, look elsewhere.---    Hades is very interesting; it’s made me rethink the way that I measure out the quality of games. It’s made me think about what a “good game” truly is. It’s made it much easier for me to examine and understand why I hate dating simulators and visual novels.     This insight isn’t because it’s a 10/10 masterpiece - I’d say it’s a solid 7/10. Maybe a 6/10 when I see the same room layout for the third time that day, or the blandness of all the weapons starts to make combat run together into a mush. It instantly drops to a 3/10 if my hammers (little upgrades that the game is very stingy with) give me boring options. Roguelites (and roguelikes even more so - more on that later) heavily depend on gameplay variance, and Hades very often struggles with this. There is a good reason, though: Hades is a Supergiant game before it’s a roguelite. This isn’t what I was promised, but it’s what I should have expected.    I haven’t played any other Supergiant games, but I’ve heard plenty of people talk about them. Story, characters, art, atmosphere, and sound. These are the most important parts of a Supergiant game, and Hades has it in spades. It has a lot more, even: the similarities between Thagreus’ and Hades’ voice patterns; the ways that Elysium slowly introduces you to the mechanics of the bossfight before you actually fight them; the furies changing up just as you get used to fighting Meg; Hermes’s keepsake; the voice acting; the character design...I could go on.    All this to say that Hades is a supremely crafted game, and every second of care - every drop of passion - is magnified in its presentation. It’s a middling roguelite, though.     Over my time playing through this game, I’ve noticed that there are two qualities that a roguelite/like needs to be a good game. It’s a bit convoluted, but it’s the best way I can think of to clearly explain what’s wrong with Hades: inter- and intra-run variance. “Intra” refers to games changing up gameplay mid-run, while “inter” refers to changes between each run. Both of these are necessary to make a good “roguey” game that doesn’t end up feeling like Malt-O-Meal in your brain. Usually, roguelites will focus on inter-run variance, while roguelikes will focus on intra-run variance. Hades follows this rule in an interesting (but ultimately ineffective) way.     While most roguelites have you collecting power-ups between runs, driving you to move forward through a feeling of getting stronger and improving via gameplay, Hades’s primary motivator is story. Your relationship to the various characters throughout the world can be advanced in a visual novel-style progression of “giving them a universal love currency.” You can only give one love potion to each character (that may or may not show up in the hub) per run. As you progress in the game, the story of each character slowly unfolds, masterfully giving you a glimpse of not just the characters you talk to, but the world that the game takes place in. I’d actually like it if the other driving forces of variance weren’t utterly bland.There are six different weapons, each with four different variants (aspects). This should (in theory) provide 24 different ways to play. In practice, most of the weapons feel like aspects of some common-ancestor blunt object, and the aspects themselves feel like banal power-ups. Power-ups have their own issues, though. First, there are the hammers: the only source of meaningful intra-run variance. They’re heavily RNG gated - and even then, they only spice up the gameplay on occasion. Often, they’ll simply boost your numbers or give you something boring like being able to attack repeatedly with a button held down. Then there are the boons: the “real” power-ups. They almost never meaningfully change the way you play the game (and even then, when they do change up gameplay, they often serve to make it more boring, such as Ares’s “Doom” mechanic), and on most occasions act as increases to numbers accompanied by fancy graphics.That’s not even the real issue with combat, though: the real issue is that weapon progression is paced awfully. The process of farming up the item required to unlock the different aspects of each weapon (Titan Blood) is like pulling teeth. This would be fine if each weapon had enough depth to warrant waiting that long to unlock new abilities, but they’re mind-numbingly flat. The optimal techniques and strategies for each weapon will usually reveal themselves by the third area of your first run with the weapon or the first area of your second run. There are two possible reasons that titan blood is as scarce as it is; to pad out play time, or to scale with the progression of players who aren’t as good at the game. With the quality and forethought on display for the rest of the game, I’m more inclined to assume the latter. As I said before, Hades isn’t a bad game - it’s just a mediocre roguelite. The story is swiftly losing my interest, and a dull curiosity (along with a feeling of “maybe it gets better soon and I can write a better review!”) is currently the only thing keeping the game installed on my computer.Perhaps there is a fantastic and intricate roguelite buried under another 30 hours of trudging, but the opportunity cost is too high for me to care. Like "The Witcher 3", his game isn’t made for me, despite being masterfully crafted. As of writing, the top review on Steam starts: “I thought I didn't like Rougelike's before Hades... This game has completely changed my opinion on the genre.”

_childDocuments_.review: I got Hades as a gift because I was hogging Steam Shared library, not for the early access hype. I enjoy the game, it's a fun action rouge-like with stellar art direction. I am a fan of SuperGiant's other titles, Pyre, Transistor and Bastion. I admire that the developer carried over mechanics from former games into Hades, such as backstabbing from Transistor, trinkets from Pyre, and replaying the music tracks in the palace, which was inspired by Bastion. I do feel like more could have been done to give Hades extra points. I feel like this was a missed opportunity in Hades. In Bastion, you would get familiar with the range of weapons in the game by playing the puzzle levels that reward you a first, second, and last place reward, first place being the best. In Hades, you whack a skeleton that doesn't fight back. It teaches you the controls, but I can do that by simply looking at the controls menu in the game. I'd much rather train on an obstacle course to understand the nuances of the game, like cornering moves and wall slamming.  I was disappointed with this level because the challenge is always to clear the enemies without getting hit. I would like it more if there was more variety to this challenge, like with the Chaos boons that give a penalty to using moves. Why not make a challenge to backstab all enemies? Why not make a challenge to never use a cast? Why not make a dash limit? Make a set of challenges opposed to doing the default one. Rouge-likes are all about select variety in outcomes. I'm often puzzled how the Olympians can all just "forgive and forget" after the rooms where you pick one boon over another. You're in for a treat no matter what if you choose this room. I'd like it better if there was an rng chance for them to resent not being picked and take away a boon of theirs to spite Zagreus for it. There's more risk versus reward for the player to consider always grabbing the most boons by Elysium. Oh and I don't like the romance bits of Hades. They felt shoehorned in.  It kind of makes me uncomfortable that Aphrodite is unclothed too, I would prefer if you can choose a skin that has clothes on. I don't mind her being flirtatious because she's the goddess of love, but draw clothes.Hades is a thrilling game, so I do recommend it. Just give your hands a break if you play with Malphon.

_childDocuments_.review: Huh, that's probably one of the few times when I write review of the game before I complete it. But, well, I'm not planning to do so anyway. Hades is a well-crafted rogue-like which is about escaping the underworld. Combat works very well, there are different weapons and different "variations" (called aspects in game) of them. If you are new to rogue-likes or just want some casual 15-20 hrs experience, than this is a good pick for you.My main problem with this game is that it rewards successful escape attempts mostly with storyline progression, not the difficulty changes, like TBoI: Rebirth does, for instance: there are no "extra floors" (idk, route going sideways, alternative versions of floors or whatever), completely new bosses or anything like that (well, at least to the point after finishing the main story there was none). Variety also isn't entirely here: we have roughly 10 enemy types tops per floor making it up to 30 - not very great for a game you want to replay for hundreds of hours. Bosses variation is even worse with ~3 variations in the first floor (not counting "aided versions" as extra ones since movesets are almost exactly the same - it's not a new bossfight). Boons are numerically have high variety (roughtly 200, I believe) but you get them in such abundance that you are likely to see ~80-90% of them in your options after 15-20 hours of you gameplay. So, well, not that great. So, most of these issues seem to be fixable with a bunch of dlc's with extra content, however, at current state, I do not see any actual reason, expect "completitionism" to play this game after you finish the main story and maybe grind for epilogue. Due to the issues I mentioned, my experience was somewhat like this (each number indicate # of escape attempt):1) Die at the end of tartarus2) Finish tartarus, die to hydra3) Kill hydra, die in the middle of elysium4-6) Die some more at elysium7) Reach hades, die to him in the first phase8-10) Some more unsuccessful runs11) Reach hades phase 2, die because of having no idea what was happening12) Kill hades12-24) Successful runs with 1 random death to hades 2nd phase25) End.So basically, once I reached the hades, game stopped from becoming actually harder in any noticeable way. I was basically replaying almost exactly the same game for over 10 times with only difference being that my character becomes stronger with further investments and I become more accustomed to enemies' patterns. So, I don't really see how this game is a goty material, but, well, it is an alright game after all.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades ReviewThe first time I beat the final boss in Hades, I felt an enormous sense of relief. I'd been fighting to see this ending for hours (months, technically, if you count my time in early access), and in roguelikes, it feels better than usual to see an ending. But while I was definitely a little too proud of putting together a set of abilities and perks that shredded the boss after they wrecked me just a few tries ago, that wasn't why I felt tears welling up. I'd gotten so caught up in the story of my character, Zagreus, and the heroes, villains, and gods that had helped him get here that I was elated to have finally gotten him to the end of his journey. What sets Hades apart isn't just that it's a great roguelike with the kind of repeatable depth that makes it engrossing to play for hours, but also how it uses its structure to tell an ongoing story about family, secrets, and resolution.That Hades' narrative is so entwined with its combat is nothing new for the developers at Supergiant Games, who've established themselves as masters of putting your actions in sync with the stories they tell. In a roguelike such as Hades, it means playing as Zagreus, a god of rebirth. Tired of living under his father Hades' thumb and seeking answers about where he comes from, he sets out to escape to the world of the living, battling various undead monsters, living creatures, and mythological figures on his way out.Your godliness justifies the endless runs through the depths of the underworld, since dying and coming back to life is par for the course in Greek myth. One of the best parts of Hades, in fact, is returning to the House of Hades time and again after you die. It's not just a pit stop on the way to the next run--it's the centerpiece Hades hinges on. There, figures such as Achilles, Hypnos, and Nyx console you after your deaths, praise you for making progress, and confide in you about one another. You chat with them, undertake side quests, and exchange gifts to deepen your relationships. Eventually, they become vital allies on your quest, even if they're not in the thick of combat with you.These interactions, as much as the precise combat, are the reason I kept coming back to Hades; while I was skeptical about how the roguelike structure would meld with Supergiant Games' focus on characters and stories, they've written and voiced reams of dialogue and lore, and almost all of it is delivered with vigor and is intriguing enough to pore over between your treks through hell.When you finally decide to take another stab at escaping, runs are broken up into a few different worlds, each made up of several randomly ordered chambers. Hades' combat builds on Bastion's tight, isometric fights and infuses them with the endlessly repeatable appeal of random buffs, modifiers, random enemy layouts, currencies, and progression that slowly turn the seemingly impossible task of reaching the surface into something manageable.Combat is quick and reactive, letting you chain attacks into dashes, dashes into special moves, and so on as you learn how to whittle enemy shields, avoid traps, and work over bosses. Each of the six weapons you can equip pushes you to play differently, and weapon-specific modifiers nudge you towards using different parts of your toolset; you might be comfortable poking enemies from afar with the Varatha spear, for example, but with a boon from Daedalus that triples the damage of your dash attack, you're going to want to close the distance and juke constantly. That, and how buffs interact in myriad surprising and effective ways, means I'm still not tired of making these runs, dozens of hours later. In more crowded fights, the Switch's smaller screen makes text and combat readability an issue, as these chambers are large enough to lose details (and runs). Other than that, though, combat is an outstanding mix of random variables and consistent action.

_childDocuments_.review: SuperGiant Games made the decision to engage in epic game store exclusivity.After watching the no-clip documentary about this game, it's clear that having a high review percentage on store reviews (primarily the ones hosted on Steam) matters to developers. Hosting a game exclusively on a store that does not allow users to leave feedback on their experience for other customers to review is fundamentally anti-consumer. It only benefits one party, the developers. SuperGiant gave their reasons and to be fair, they were pretty rational. Among other reasons, I can understand wanting to avoid negative reviews that are based on a deliberately incomplete, early access game. Avoiding the need to translate the game to multiple different languages for the steam release was also something I had not considered. At the end of the day, SuperGiant can rationalise it all they want but this will always be a mark against them.That being said, the game itself is fantastic. I thoroughly enjoyed the art, the soundtrack, the voice acting and the combat. One aspect that really impressed me was the sheer among of unique dialogue that's present in the game. Even when I was actively looking for it, repeating events only began to happen around 25-30 runs in. It felt like every time I returned from a run there was more new plot/character development to explore. Finally, the last thing I want to highlight is how well SuperGiant naturally represented minority communities in the game. I grow tired of how often minority groups are retconned to the detriment of the story or at worst, included at their expense. This really was a refreshing breath of fresh air. Writers, take notes please. If I am being pedantic, the mechanism to unlock the hidden weapon aspects isn't designed well. You have to exhaust the entire story dialogue pool of an NPC to access the necessary hidden weapon aspects dialogue. The problem is every time I would try to cycle this person's dialogue by doing a run I would just progress the story further, meaning I would have to do even more runs to get the dialogue option I need to unlock the hidden aspects. This problem would be solved if I could just talk the NPC about the hidden aspects whenever I want if I meet the unlock requirements.I have other small problems with the game (I would have liked if boon dialogue ran in the background while you looked at your choices rather than being completely front loaded) but as a whole it's a great experience and I'm looking forward to their next game. Well done SuperGiant.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is an amazing roguelike RPG, and a testament to good game design. Its engaging, has a great story you tease out over multiple runs, great gameplay that doesn’t punish you unnecessarily and an amazing soundtrack and vocals. I can’t recommend this game enough, if you haven’t played it you should. You play as Prince Zagreus, son of the god Hades who is desperate to escape his father Hades, and his infernal realm. After the gods of Mt Olympus become aware of your existence they make contact with you, and offer boons in order to help you in your efforts to escape. Each run has different gods contact you and bestow different blessings, and slowly introduces a wider range of side characters you can interact with and explore their stories as you get closer to the surface and escaping. After my first escape (after many failed attempts) I thought it was a great story, only to find out that it’s really only the beginning of the story and as you complete more runs and converse with the NPC’s you expose all the secrets that gods have been keeping and start escaping to help avert a war between the entire pantheon.  Most of the creature and locations lore entries are expanded by visiting or encountering them enough times, however NPC’s need gifts after a set amount of visits.The gameplay while not being unique, is extremely rewarding. Essentially you start off in Hades palace where all the dead arrive, where you can converse with NPC’s (which moves their stories forward one conversation at a time), get scolded from Hades for being useless, trade items for rewards, spend money to upgrade the Palace and edit the weapons, perks and difficulty of the next escape attempt before setting off.While every escape attempt is different, the premise is the same, with you having the clear 3 layers of the underworld and the temple of Styx you have to trek through, defeat their guardians and inhabitants who are being ordered by Hades to stop you. It’s a neat idea that by “killing” the inhabitants you are meting out the punishment they deserve, and that by stopping you they are ensuring the security of the realm (no dead souls have ever escaped), or in the Satyrs case killing the heathens who defile the temple of Styx and don’t venerate the gods.   Everything useful to you during a run is lost upon escaping (or death), and it becomes a balancing act of deciding picking boons that help you in the current escape attempt, or items (gems, darkness, gifts) that will be used for future upgrades or conversations with the NPC’s and various gods. Replayability is very high and hasn’t just been tacked on as an afterthought as the whole story revolves around completing multiple escapes. The game actively encourages you to increase the difficulty (after a successful escape attempt) by limiting the items required for permanent weapon upgrades and different weapon aspects (each weapon has multiple forms that all change how they function) to only be awarded by each boss once at each difficulty level. When making runs harder you have full control over what setting you increase (it could be extra enemies, standard enemies have abilities, harder bosses, you lose boons as you progress ect), and you eventually get to a point where you need to have multiple of these selected. The game also keeps a record of the highest difficulty you have escaped with for each weapon, and the fastest attempt for those who limit to compete.Each of the god’s boons can affect your primary moves in different ways (dash’s, attacks, magic casts, dodges and summons), and have different effects depending on which other boons are selected or what weapon is being used. Each of the boons have different tiers and levels, with a higher tier boon having better effects (say increase in damage %) over a lower but higher level boon. The Gods (while sounding friendly) are jealous and can offer to replace an existing rival’s boon with a higher tier one, or very rarely combine boons together so you get unique abilities that combine the best of both gods.For a game that’s essentially a display on family dysfunction the graphics are crisp and colourful in a way that cel shading exploits. Each arena has an abundance of hues that help define each layer of the underworld, with Tartarus having a darker dungeon setting, Asphodel being the traditional hell of bubbling lava and Elysium having softer blues and greens where the righteous live in dead. As the relationships expand you can tweak the house with different upgradesCharacters and enemies are all animated extremely well (enemies have tells to advise you of their attacks), and secrets are hidden in plain sight in the fishing games. The UI is minimalist so it doesn’t interfere with the action happening on screen, and each character really stands out. Traps aren’t hidden, though will catch you unaware if you don’t pay attention and the action can be quite hectic. The De-motivationals that usually play at the start of each run are hilarious (basically Hades musings on how you will fail, or why everything sucks).The vocals and music are amazing. They absolutely nailed the soundtrack for the game, with plenty of string and percussion tracks that align with the action happening on screen, with the more sombre music or tracks with vocals playing in resting areas or after certain events. The vocals are also amazing, with the dialogue between Hades & Zagreus being a standout. Hades put-downs are quite humorous to listen to (of you, when you change items around the palace and when he’s berating having useless minions or those in his court who displease him).Getting 100% achievements will take multiple runs through the game due to the random nature of stage rewards and conversations, but is highly worth it and nothing too strenuous, though time consumingFor more reviews please visit

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is a great roguelike where you play Hades' son and try to escape hell, fighting a bunch of different ennemies & mythical bosses Positive points : - The story is great , it is one of the game that made me stop again to read dialogues in video games , they are well written , very entertaining & needed in order to understand some quests - The gameplay feels great , it is not too hard to first pick up but it is still hard enough that you will probably need a couple of upgrades before completing your first run- The post first run (Called pact of punishments) allows you to play with a bunch of modifications to the gameplay in order to make the run harder to complete and get more rewards , pretty much like every roguelike , here it is done in a good way , nothing very innovative but a lot of options & it is well done- The upgrade system of the character is very well thought in my opinion as well as the trinket system allowing for very different way of playing the game...Negative points :- ...That being said, some builds are clearly stronger than others & you will probably tend to favour one or two path builds when you get into higher heats (Heats being the difficulty that you assign to the run with the pact of punishments) - The environments are really repetitive , despite being well designed after 60hours of play I felt like a mouse in a cage to be honest- Finishing the game on highest heats is not really rewarded by the game- Some of the weapons variations (called aspects) feel borderline unplayable compared to their counterparts- Some of the unlocks are pretty shady and will probably make you refer to youtube tutorials to know how to unlock stuffSo is Hades worth your money ? Definitely ! It is a great game that will keep you entertained for hours (finished the 100% after 60hours but I've rushed it and stopped more than necessary on guides which I don't recommend if you really want to enjoy everything the game has to offer)One of my favourites roguelike ever and I do hope that a DLC or a sequel will come at one point to let us explore more of this beautiful world

_childDocuments_.review: Hades was released as an Early Access title in 2018 and has come a long way to winning accolades after its 1.0 Release. Hades is a dungeon crawler rogue-lite, where we play as Zagreus, the Prince of the Underworld based on Greek mythology. Hades became very popular not just for its gameplay loop, but also for the Narrative/Story elements in the game. No other roguelikes/rogue-lites have told a story before, infused with its gameplay elements and that is what stands out in Hades compared to all the other games in the genre.You will experience the connections between Greek Gods and their thoughts. It's a surreal experience that Hades provides and sets a very high bar for future games of the genre to break through and so far none has excelled Hades, either in the gameplay loop or the narrative.The game is worth the full price for the experience it provides, but as I'm a patient gamer myself, I would recommend getting it on sale to have an amazing and unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I escaped. And now it's time to escape.Hades is a beautiful game with an intriguing narrative. The latter of which is more often than not left out of the rogue like/lite equation. Sometimes entirely. So it was greatly appreciated. The folks at Supergiant know how to deliver an atmosphere, that's for certain. But it gets the actual key ingredient of a good like/lite right as well; progression balance. I always felt like I was accomplishing something, unlocking something, or just plain getting better each time I played a loop of Hades. This pleased me greatly and often led to the "one more try.." situations.It does perhaps suffer from too many layers inside and outside of the gameplay. Don't get me wrong, I'd always rather have too much than too little. And I will put the huge caveat here that I play games without spoilers. A game like this is primed for me to completely miss the "meta" or whatever you want to call it. But you inevitably have to leave some avenues untouched until game+. A lot. Most. The overwhelming majority even! There's more than one weapon you can use, each with their own learning curves. I never left the default sword because learning another would be a break in my progression momentum. There's a handful of different currencies to collect and spend, but I likely missed that "game meta" on some of them and never accrued remotely enough. And so I didn't expand on the game areas they bought. There's a gift/friend system for all the characters you interact with, but they're all deep and have seemingly particular requirements to complete that are guesswork. With so many characters/Gods to choose it was a roll of the dice which to commit to. I ultimately only completed one of those. That's just a few examples of the layers. I'm barely past the tip of the iceberg and then game+ opens another whole can of worms with run/loop modifiers/challenges. I was drowned in unlockables and knew I never would, nor would want to, "100%" this game.But that's subjective. It's rad as heck all that is there for the people who want it. Whether they're the true champions or the weirdos that follow scripts of how to play games. There is oodles and oodles of dopamine accomplishment hits to be had and then another pile more. I just felt the strong parts of the game, specifically the story, couldn't keep pace with all those branching tunnels there were to explore. Then the gameplay is competent and fun enough to wield, but it can't do the same heavy lifting as other games in the genre. I won't call it a weakness, but the gameplay is shallow enough to notice. I'm nearing the end of my journey. I most definitely have to "escape" a few more times. I most definitely want to finish exploring a couple those 'tunnels' I started down. But will I even touch half of all of what Hades has? Nope. Which again, is awesome in its own right. I just can't do the 100's of hours with it like I have with others because the depth isn't in the gameplay, but elsewhere. I will unfortunately have to escape the game itself soon.Absolutely recommend the game wholeheartedly. Great fun. Whether you beat it once or dozens of times, you'll always be rewarded with something. All the praise is well deserved.It's a darn near perfect game on Steam Deck!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm in total awe of how polished, impulsive and deep this game is. It's like a neverending christmas. At first I thought it' just another roguelike action game, but after a few attempts and some dialogue within the house of Hades, I was quickly sucked in. Combat feels pretty ordinary at first. You swing this big sword and dash around in similar looking chambers spawning various creatures of the Underworld, pick up some powerups and eventually die. Then you do it all over again. And again, and again, and again.. you get the idea. Sounds kinda boring and repetitive? I thought so too after the first few hours but had I quit there, I would've missed one the best action games I have played in a very long time, perhaps ever.Slowly you become more familiar with all the boons, powerups, enemies and unlock new weapons, skills, trinkets... Doing the same thing repeatedly suddenly becomes a strength as you discover new ways to build your character for each run. And how character building works is simple yet effective and surprisingly deep. Pick a weapon, a trinket and after first few boons you can have a completely different gameplay experience. And most of them work without ruining the balance. There are no clear OP builds that see you wreck the game at exit attempt 15. It's still a very skill-heavy game and requires precision and patience to finally succeed. Some builds are obviously stronger than others but it also comes down to personal preferance and playstyle. Trial by error is part of the fun.The game is so much more than the sum of it's parts that it's difficult to thoroughly explain. It's like some magical onion with infinate layers that once peeled, give all new kinds of flavors. And not just any flavors, but flavors that play together with existing ones in surprising and great-tasting manner. It's amazing. Best twenty euros spent.

_childDocuments_.review: John F. Kennedy, the 35th president of the United States, was assassinated on Friday, November 22, 1963, at 12:30 p.m. CST in Dallas, Texas, while riding in a presidential motorcade through Dealey Plaza. Kennedy was in the vehicle with his wife, Jacqueline, Texas Governor John Connally, and Connally's wife, Nellie, when he was fatally shot from the nearby Texas School Book Depository by Lee Harvey Oswald, a former US Marine. Governor Connally was seriously wounded in the attack. The motorcade rushed to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where Kennedy was pronounced dead about 30 minutes after the shooting; Connally recovered.About 70 minutes after Kennedy and Connally were shot, Oswald was arrested by the Dallas Police Department and charged under Texas state law with the murders of Kennedy and of J. D. Tippit, a Dallas police officer. At 11:21 a.m. on November 24, 1963, as live television cameras covered Oswald being moved through the basement of Dallas Police Headquarters, he was fatally shot by Dallas nightclub operator Jack Ruby. Like Kennedy, Oswald was also taken to Parkland Memorial Hospital, where he soon died. Ruby was convicted of Oswald's murder, though it was later overturned on appeal, and Ruby died in prison in 1967 while awaiting a new trial.After a 10-month investigation, the Warren Commission concluded that Oswald assassinated Kennedy, that Oswald had acted entirely alone, and that Ruby had acted alone in killing Oswald. Kennedy was the eighth and most recent US president to die in office, and the fourth (following Lincoln, Garfield, and McKinley) to be assassinated. Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson automatically became president upon Kennedy's death.In its 1979 report, the United States House Select Committee on Assassinations (HSCA) agreed with the Warren Commission that Oswald's three rifle shots caused the injuries that Kennedy and Connally sustained. After analysis of a dictabelt audio recording the HSCA concluded that Kennedy was likely "assassinated as a result of a conspiracy". The committee could not identify a second gunman or group involved in the possible conspiracy, although the HSCA concluded that analysis pointed to the existence of an additional gunshot and "a high probability that two gunmen fired at [the] President".The U.S. Justice Department concluded active investigations and stated "that no persuasive evidence can be identified to support the theory of a conspiracy" in the assassination. However, Kennedy's assassination is still the subject of widespread debate and has spawned numerous conspiracy theories and alternative scenarios. Polls conducted from 1966 to 2004 found that up to 80 percent of Americans suspected that there was a plot or cover-up. The assassination was the first of four major assassinations of the 1960s in the United States, coming two years before the assassination of Malcolm X in 1965, and five years before the assassinations of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy in 1968.

_childDocuments_.review: style, present in previous releases like  and , shines brightly in , too. A key part of that style is a rich plot with well-written, well-realized, well-acted characters. Impressively, the game’s identity manages to stand out despite being rooted in the extremely familiar world of Greek mythology.You play as Zagreus, hunky prince of the underworld and sulking son of Lord Hades himself. Each run represents an attempt to escape from the underworld to the mortal world on the surface, away from your wrathful father and back towards your unknown mother. Along the way you encounter your highfalutin Greek god relatives, from Artemis to Zeus, eager to help you come home to Olympus. Each death sends you back beneath Tartarus to the bloody pool in the House of Hades, where you interact with fellow dark residents to further the plot or just pet your three-headed dog Cerberus. structures its entire plot around the fact that you’ll die and play again many times. Even after you beat the game once you won’t entirely know what’s going on. To experience this story, you need to do a lot of fighting. Fortunately, ’ combat matches its narrative when it comes to gripping you and never letting go. masterfully nails its minute-to-minute mechanics alongside the larger character and story progression. - Gorgeous art and lush music- Rich characters and emotional storytelling- Great voice acting- The story and characters are fascinating- Addictive weapon and ability combinations- Roguelite structure is inherently repetitiveDISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT | AMAZING |

_childDocuments_.review: I have never played any of the games made by Supergiant Games before, so I was completely unbiased and even hesitant when I bought this game, but I can say it without exaggeration that Hades is as close to perfection as possible (obviously there are no such things as perfect games or anything but come on) and it truly deserves all the praise it got.It is a masterfully crafted action roguelike, with fast paced action, blood pumping soundtrack, beautiful visuals and a surprisingly and I mean SURPRISINGLY deep story. The storytelling is really something else in this game (for a roguelike) and it's managed in a very clever way. Between the escape attempts (and during them) you can socialize with the characters in the House of Hades which serves as sort of a main hub. The story unfolds bit by bit as you get to know the gods and other characters and forge stronger bonds with them and it goes on and on and on and on and on and on and when you think you completed the game IT KEEPS GOING FOR ♥♥♥♥♥ SAKE. And thank the gods that it does, because all of the characters are funny and likeable, the dialogues are witty and well-written and you just keep wanting more.The gameplay itself is action-packed, very fun and extremely varied. There are so much variables; 6 different weapons, 4 aspects/weapon, hundreds of boons/skills, different keepsakes, modifiers and so on. I've played over 90 hours so far and never had the same run twice.Everything just feels perfectly in it's place, and the complete experience is very smooth, enjoyable and entertaining. I raise my virtual hat to Supergiant Games for creating this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Should you buy this game? Yes! Oh, you want more? Keep reading...GAMEPLAYIt's pretty. It's intense. It's just plain fun! It's basically an isometric roguelike. Think diablo, but, you know... roguelike... You fight your way out of Hades which is a series of floors to clear of enemies. After you clear a room you receive either an upgrade (Boon) which provides a random upgrade (ex. Attack damage, Special damage, etc) of random potency (from common to legendary), or you receive some permanent currency. You play with one of six different weapons, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.Oh and when you die (and you will...), you lose everything (except your permanent currencies and your weapon's permanent upgrades). You die a metric f*@kton in this game, so you'd expect it to be quite tedious, however that's not the case here: You see, the story progression is linked to reaching certain points in your run, talking to NPC's you come across, killing certain bosses and of course - returning to base (aka dying). So, in a way, you look forward to dying again and again and again. It's quite genius actually. Also, the dungeon chambers are randomised so you won't have the same run twice ever. STORYFirst thing's first: I was astonished at the quality of the dialog in this game... it's seriously brilliant. Witty, emotional, and virtually 100% cringe-free. Truly a novelty in this day and age where any old Stephenie Meyer can just spit up some hogwash and call it good dialog.The characters are very interesting. You meet basically all of the Olympian gods, as well as legendary figures such as Achilles, Orpheus and Eurydice, the furies, and Cerberus, each who has a distinct personality and sense of humour. And you can forge a bond with almost all the NPC's in the game.EVERYTHING ELSEMusic is pretty awesome, think ancient greek music meets metal. Sound design is ok I guess. Graphics are good, very pretty game. Kinda shellshady though, but hey some people may like that.LASTLY......I would not recommend you play this game for hours back-to-back. This game is meant to be played in intervals. Play for an hour or two then take a break and come back when you're refreshed. If you play this game for hours on end, you're gonna get pretty frustrated and burn out quickly. Just enjoy the ride and savour the experience.(...but if you're anything like me then you're probably gonna play it for hours on end anyway lol~)

_childDocuments_.review: I have a hard time staying interested in rogue-like games, so I was always a little hesitant to try this game.  But with its full release this past week, I decided to give it a try, and what a great decision that was.  Mechanically, it's great.  Combat feels fluid and I feel right at home whether I'm aiming ranged attacks, dashing around the battlefield performing quick strikes, or making slow methodical attacks at specific weak points.  There's also enough that carries over from each run to make you still feel your progressing, and you get to make meaningful choices that will make every run feel varied while simultaneously not feeling completely random, as other rogue-likes tend to seem.  Finally, let's not forget the substantial replay value, with large, end-game goals to keep your attention!The story is captivating and there's tons of dialogue.  The narrative element is what really makes this game shine beyond all others.  For those of you who, like me, have a passion for Greek Mythology-- this is a game you will love.  The storied characters and locations you know and admire are here, and you get to have a say and participate in those settings.  Of course, I can't mention those things without praising the stellar art and sound design. Half the fun of this game was meeting all the characters so I could see their gorgeous vignettes.  The music is stellar and atmospheric, and the sounds of your weapons feel visceral and keep your attention.In short, Supergiant have exceeded all my expectations with this title.  This is easily my new favorite game of all time, and that is not something I say lightly.  If you're on the fence, I encourage you to pull the trigger and buy this game, especially if its on sale.  It's an experience you don't want to miss out on.10/10 Supergiant, excellent job!

Each run through the game is different, with randomly generated levels and enemy encounters that keep things fresh and exciting. The game also features an engaging story that unfolds as you progress, with memorable characters and interactions that make you feel invested in Zagreus' journey.The game's presentation is also top-notch, with gorgeous hand-drawn graphics and a fantastic soundtrack that perfectly complements the action on-screen. The voice acting is also superb, with talented actors bringing the game's characters to life and adding to the overall immersion of the game.Overall, Hades is a must-play game for anyone who enjoys action-packed rogue-like games. _childDocuments_.review: A fantastic action-adventure game with rogue-like elements and a fantastic use of Classical mythology. Everything about it is marvelous - the art, the voice work, the music, the mechanics, the plot, the characters, etc. Highly addictive and highly enjoyable satire.EDIT: The lone obstacle to enjoyment is the Orpheus/Eurydice dyad. I can appreciate the decision to make Orpheus look like the love-child of Neil Gaiman's Morpheus/Dream and Steve Buscemi. I can appreciate the decision to make Eurydice embittered by his failure and determined to never forgive him. But making Orpheus a whiny sniveling drip while Eurydice is sassy & tough & the REAL talent behind Orpheus's legend... Ugh. The game does an amazing job making ancient legendary figures "relatable" for modern players, but the whole Orpheus/Eurydice bit felt like something a first-year Creative Writing student minoring in Gender Studies would think groundbreaking & subversive while the rest of us roll our eyes at the tiresome cliches. At least the game does a better job with its modernized version of Achilles & Patroclus...

_childDocuments_.review: Classic Supergiant style in a tidy roguelike. The game's well-paced so you don't really get burnt out before unlocking the next thing. The boss fights are fun and pretty difficult, and it feels rewarding once you get good enough to get through the game pretty consistently. The game looks and sounds great, and the voice acting is superb. Each character has a VA attached to them and they feel alive thanks to their performances. There's also so many of them too! I'm 70+ runs into the game and I'm still getting all-new voice lines from characters. Pretty insane.Each run feels different and will absolutely be that way- you can customize SO many things about each run you go on. You have various upgrades for yourself and your weapons. There's also tons of things to unlock in the game, from story progress to upgrades to simple cosmetic choices in the main hub.The enemies and bosses are also pretty well-designed. They take a bit of getting used to but they all have good tells so you can learn and adapt to them. Eventually, you get good enough that you'll succeed no matter your upgrades, and you'll know your enemies inside out. However, that isn't to say the game will get easy. The game on its own provides a good difficulty to start, and once you unlock the Pact of Punishment well, that's where the real punishment starts.It can be played casually and just focus on the story or you can up the difficulty by taking on the Pact of Punishment for some pretty brutal runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is an exceptional roguelike dungeon crawler developed and published by Supergiant Games, the creators behind critically acclaimed titles like Bastion and Transistor. Released in 2020, "Hades" combines fast-paced, skill-based action with a richly detailed story set in the underworld of Greek mythology. Players control Zagreus, the son of Hades, on his quest to escape from the underworld and reach Mount Olympus, with each escape attempt offering a unique combination of challenges and rewards.What sets Hades apart from other games in the roguelike genre is its masterful blend of gameplay, narrative, and character development. The combat is fluid and satisfying, with various weapons and abilities that can be combined in myriad ways to suit different play styles. The game's difficulty is well-balanced, challenging players without feeling unfair, and the progression system ensures that every run, successful or not, contributes to unlocking new aspects of the story and character interactions.The narrative and character work in Hades are exceptional, with a cast of well-realized Greek mythology characters who have their personalities, motivations, and stories to tell. The voice acting and writing are top-notch, adding depth to the world and delighting every interaction. The game also explores themes of family, rebellion, and seeking one's path in life, making the story resonate on a personal level for many players.Hades is stunning visually, with a distinct art style that brings its characters and environments to life. The soundtrack is equally impressive, featuring energetic and atmospheric tracks that perfectly complement the action and exploration.In conclusion, Hades is a masterpiece of game design. It offers a compelling mix of challenging gameplay, engaging storytelling, and deep character development. Its ability to keep players returning for "just one more run" is a testament to its quality and addictiveness. Whether you're a fan of roguelikes or just love a well-told story, Hades is a game that shouldn't be missed.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Supergiant is no amateur game studio. They have produced some fantastic titles that have firmly rooted themselves as must-play narratives and showcase a masterclass of sound design. Beautiful artwork, beautiful soundtrack, beautiful narrative. They innovate and do not stick to a formula, bouncing between play styles like nobody's business. Hades is their attempt at a roguelike.And they smashed it out of the park.Hades is--by far--their most gorgeous, most gripping, and satisfying game to date. The art is jaw dropping, the voice acting is smoother than silk and richer than cream. The soundtrack is not only something to write home about, but it's adaptive and will flow in and out no matter what pace you play.The gameplay is slick, diverse, and worryingly addicting. The characters are lovable and unique, and each run is a one-of-a-kind experience, only to be further infused with the addition of the "New-game-plus" Pact of Punishment.The story, too, will hold your attention. The character dynamics are wonderfully written and are entirely up to you to choose. Their are many, many side-quests and storylets, and all of them ring true that rich lore Supergiant is known for.Oh, and this is all just early access.They don't even leave me room to complain. They are so, so very involved with the community. Every bug, every hiccup, poor design choices or gameplay features, they listen to the community. Hotfix after hotfix, update after update, they even go as far to list what features were chosen by the community in the changelog.I cannot sing enough praises about this game, and I am eagerly looking forward to it's official release.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

Basically all the things Supergiant excel at; they did it well with Bastion and Transistor (then I skipped Pyre) and then they dialed it to 11 with this absolute gem of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's got:-Really interesting story and re-imagining of Greek Gods tied to the roguelike mechanics (dying over and over, randomly changing layout/items etc).-Full voice acting, and this isn't baby's first voice acting playset oooh no, there are several thousand lines of dialogue, 3000 added in the latest update before the game left early access. Also Thanatos(Death) because Zagreus is just that hot. That last sentence is a pun because Zagreus' feet are on fire.-Cerberus is a very good boy. _childDocuments_.review: 155 hours and 49/49 achievements at the time of writing this review, 0 minutes played for the last couple of weeks, if not months. despite having an insane amounts of dialouge, incredible gameplay and diversity in weapons and weapon variations, lots of boons and conditions to play around with, after i 100%ed the game i feel empty.personal fastest run is slightly above 12 minutes and i feel like this is where the game suffers once you've finished the endgame. in other roguelikes you can push runs to be hours long with infinite amounts of loops in a run, whereas in hades runs will eventually end. the stronger you are, the shorter the run. logical, yes, but it also means you dont get to appreciate or enjoy your strong build enough. i want runs where i push the boundaries of the game while enemies keep getting stronger, i want runs where i can truly feel like a god amongst these dumb chain hand goons.eventho i adore this game and will definitely recommend it to everyone, i think what it needs is more options for infinitely looping runs. let me break the game, that's what's so fun about roguelikes. 10/10, faultless in each aspect, absolute masterpiece.just give me longer runs without me having to intentionally pick weaker boons and i'll give it an 11/10

_childDocuments_.review: Super Giant games always have incredible artistry. The visuals are fantastic, the writing is fantastic, the score is fantastic, the voice acting is fantastic. Super Giant games have always been ok in the gameplay department. Bastion was simple but effective, Transistor was very easily broken, Pyre was a Visual Novel with occasion bouts of simple gameplay. The problem with Hades is that it leans into the gameplay, hard, and has some of the worst gameplay Super Giant has created thus far. Retreading the same few areas over and over quickly becomes a chore, after two run the first two levels become a solved game and Hades forces you to replay them over and over to get new content. Weapon balancing is all over the place with some being completely worthless and others allowing you to effortlessly walk through the game with 0 damage. Bosses are pose 0 threat, have inflated health pools, and must be fought over and over again. When an enemy is between you and a wall it's a guaranteed kill, but the game still makes you mash attack 10 times before they die. By the end you're picking buffs not based on fun builds or becoming more powerful but more for what will waste the least amount of your time. This game has incredible talent behind it, but unlike other Super Giant games it does not respect your time. The game is a gorgeous slog, and without some major reworking I could not possibly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I think the insane rating that this game has (around 220k reviews with 98% positive??? at the time of writing) is completely justified. _childDocuments_.review: Amazing combat, great dialogue with a witty take on Greek mythology. Each weapon offers a unique way to play the game. All the upgrades you can find and different combinations of "boons" of the gods make the gameplay feel fresh and exciting every time you try to escape the underworld. Definitely a game to check out if you like quick and precise combat. Or if you're just a sucker for good voice acting (this game nails every single character).PS. if you are one for the story, and the story alone (which in this game is GREAT) there is an option to go "god mode" which lets you play through the game without much difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: I say this as the highest compliment to Supergiant Games: Hades has ruined roguelites for me. The genre is probably my favourite of all and I have been a fan of SSG's catalogue ever since the release of Bastion so I expected good things. After playing it for a while, I realized it was even better than I could've hoped. It has everything you want in a roguelite - you always want to go back for one more run, it's buttery-smooth, responsive, and just plain fun. The polish and subtle details in this game astound me and even after completing it I would still stumble across new voice lines from the colourful cast of characters. That brings me to my next point which is the story and characters. Incredibly charming and vivid, the dialogue and voice acting in this game is phenomenal (which, frankly, is unheard for this genre). The soundtrack is second-to-none and if you're like me you'll often be tempted to just stop what you're doing and listen to your surroundings (Looking at you, Eurydice). If you're a fan of roguelites do yourself a favour and buy this immediately as you're doing yourself a disservice if you don't. And if you aren't a fan of the genre... well, you probably will be by the time you've made it through this game. It's just that good. GOTY 2020.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is flawless in every shape and form. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, don't get me wrong. However, this game almost won game of the year and all these other awards that I feel are undeserved. If I could compare it to my two other favorite roguelikes, Gungeon and Isaac, I would say it ranks slightly lower for one purpose only: replayability. Hades has a great soundtrack, story, design, artsyle, everything. For those reasons it beats the other two. BUT, and this is a very large but, I cannot replay Hades as I would the other two, and it just comes down to variety. Isaac and Gungeon each at least have 6 characters, Isaac has about 12 if I remember correctly. This is more than or equal to Hades already. Hades has I believe 8 gods, each with 10-20 upgrades/items, which comes out to a max of 160. It's not bad, but it's not nearly good enough. This coupled with the lack of exploration choices, floor types, enemy types, and boss fights makes Hades markedly below the other two and others in the genre in general. If you want to dump hours into a roguelike, this will work, but there are better options. If you simply want a few dozen hours of great fun and story telling, this is a great game for you. It was much easier to beat than Isaac or Gungeon, which each took me up to 100 hours or more, while Hades I had beat on my 8th run, which was maybe 15-20 hours. It is more accessible to the average gamer, but to a roguelike fan like myself I think you may find it will fall short.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun at first but game design in my opinion, horrible.The game is designed for many, many playthroughs of the same level but with different builds / weapons etc. If you enjoy customization, experimentation, interaction of these different builds then you will love this game. Also, if you like immersing yourself in the dialogue that is dispersed between every run, you may also enjoy this game. But, if you like actual gameplay, I do not recommend this game. You beat the game once...and mechanically speaking, you're just going through the same motions over and over and over. Definition of a roguelike/roguelite I know...but the game is just too easy and to actually be required to simply beat the game over and over - not even required to do it on higher difficulty or weapon. Other roguelikes/roguelites just you beat the game once and generally unlock a harder path that needs to be beaten or it's just beaten.Sure, there are additional difficulty modifiers through heat, but the only mechanical changes are giving elites special abilities and harder version of bosses (not that much harder) and none of this is required. I got nothing for beating the game on Extreme measures 4. To actually beat the game, you just need to beat the same last boss 10 different times. Then there's the epilogue that I don't even. I've beaten the game like 40 times now and no end in sight with almost every dialogue exhausted.The only reason I spent so many hours on this game is because of completion OCD and I practically fall asleep playing this game (literally) and have to stop playing the game for the day and play it another day.The bosses are very easy. Once you're more familiar with the game, have maxed your upgrade tree, you can literally face tank and button mass every boss fight without consequence. I started doing this to save myself time on every run. There was one time I was doing 1000 dmg every 0.5 seconds with a bow. Combined with some damage reduction boons, I stood in front of all the bosses and took the hits and button mashed. I was able to do this with many other weapons as well. Skillful game. Fast speedruns of the game just require a lot of good luck so you can one shot everything and face tank the boss to kill him in literal 10 seconds.I invested a lot of hours into the game, but I really can't say I've been enjoying the last 30-40 hours.By design this game will attract a lot of people due to some artificial progression built into the game. Very grindy by nature, but done better than Dead Cells. If you didn't like Dead Cells because of how grindy it was, you may still like this game.Overall, I don't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to throw in the towel on this one. _childDocuments_.review: I really shouldn't have listened to the judgment of “famous internet people” who shall go unnamed here, but here we are and I wish to put my thought into written form.There is nothing negative that I can say about the game’s core design, art, story or other aspects. All are at least decent if not well above average for a video game, especially coming from an indie studio. Art and Story. Perhaps the most stellar of all is the art style and the spin on old Greek mythology surrounding Hades. The art style also bleeds into the visuals and the graphics did not strain the eyes.Combat. The weapons are distinct and facilitate different styles of combat, the Daedalus hammers further increase this diversity. Adding boons to this creates interesting and diverse ways to dish out damaged to the enemies. Foes are rather basic mechanically, but varied and numerous enough to create very challenging scenarios. Very challenging indeed, which is precisely why this immense diversity of ways to build up Zagreus ultimately means nothing if you are not a good player as you’ll have to narrow down your choices to essentials to stay alive. Grab Athena’s dash, grab Hermes’s +1 dash, then grab boons and the Daedalus upgrade with the biggest damage multipliers. Take the spiked collar keepsake, grab as many centaur hearts as you can. Furthermore, with most weapons the best strategy is taking potshots and staying mobile (bow, rail) or dash-strike while dashing like a madman (the rest), the latter of which begins to physically hurt by the time you reach a boss, at least in my experience.Economy. Hades has a deceptively deep grind, especially considering there are few reliable ways to get any resource outside of the limited bounties. You might wonder, why didn’t you just use God Mode? Well, I did, but began using it a tad too late, after the 50th failed attempt or so. And even then, 20% damage reduction with 2% increments for each death meant next to nothing. By stroke of luck and very good hammer upgrades and boons, I escaped once, but never escaped again. The very fact that you need to escape numerous times to fully enjoy the story (and grind economy) is also disappointing and ultimately lead to this negative review. Much like the ridiculous economy, you also have to grind for your easy mode. Wonderful.Were the runs shorter, if the enemies beyond Tartarus has less health or if the combat didn’t put such an enormous strain on my fingers, perhaps I might have recommended Hades to others. If you don’t do well in this kind of game, stay away, save yourself the torment. I was fooled, you don’t have to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Supergiant has done a great job as always with regards to... well, everything? The characters are fantastic (and wow, the voice acting!), the art is magnificent and inspired, and the music is wonderful even if you listen to it outside the context of the game. I stood in Eurydice's chamber for /way/ too long listening to her sing. I haven't played a whole lot of other roguelikes, I'll admit that. But I think something about the fact that when you die -- it's not a hard, total reset. And it doesn't feel like one, either. RoR2 and BoI both kick you back out to the starting page when you do die, which does make sense for them as games, too. But the endless way that you just... you die, and you come out of the pool, and you start over again. I've definitely played way more attempts than I've meant to just because of the flow of it. It never feels like starting over.I'm looking forward to beating this. I'm delighted that there's an option to make it easier in order to make the story accessible to people that aren't great at these kinds of games, too. Usually my option is just to read a wiki synopsis or something, and you lose out on so much that way. But I think I'm going to keep plugging away at this until I'm able to beat it on my own... It's too mesmerizing to put away for long.

_childDocuments_.review: Not only is it the best dungeon crawler out there, it is one of the best games I've ever played. Restarting every time you die may seem frustrating, but on the way you learn how to master different weapons, figure out how different upgrades work, and have a blast destroying everything in your way. There are  endless things to upgrade and max out in this game so I see myself playing this for a while. Truly a masterpiece in terms of gameplay, characters, and art.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Safe to say I completely love this game. A huge nod to Supergiant games for their efforts here. I'm not hugely experienced with Roguelites but I feel this one really is special. The lore and mythology, the combat and the gameplay loop, the character interactions and story - all these things came together so seamlessly for one of the most immersive experiences i've had. The voice acting and sheer level of wit/personality in the dialogue is outstanding, the story was heartwarming yet still filled with trials and tribulations, and the sound design and music added so much atmosphere and memorable moments, more than I can really count honestly. Visually for a 2D game, it's so detailed, vibrant and full of charm as a Supergiant game often is. Just have to add - Zagreus is one of the best leads in a game that I can possibly think of.The combat/gameplay loop was really really addicting to me. I can see it not being for everyone but if you get through some runs of this game, you will not regret it as it gets better and better. It's meant to kick your ass early as a roguelite often does, but the rate of build up/rewards you get as you go along feels very good and there are many, many ways to play even in the similar confines of the games areas. As someone who loves ARPG's and theory, this game was perfect for experimenting with things and finding out what works and what doesn't.Do try this game sometime, it's not a full price game and it really is a true gem. I may be overselling it but it's not often I feel this much excitement or passion about a game.

_childDocuments_.review: You see, I am 29 years old guy, losing my passion in gaming. Every games feels so stale, pointless and boring. Send help.Jokes aside, this is one of the best rogue-lites/roguelikes I've ever played next to Enter the Gungeon, Risk of Rain 1 and 2, Heat Signature, and Slay the Spire. _childDocuments_.review: Got this game for my birthday.Frankly, had I known exactly how good this game was when a friend suggested I add it to my wishlist? I would've not waited and simply bought it outright by myself.The game is absolutely addicting. And it gives that super satisfying sense of accomplishment, even though you get killed and have to start over. Simply the fact that you found a means to progress further than you could prior thanks to your vigilant interest in the story and gameplay, is nothing short of delightful.The humor, the quippy conversations and the slightly comical graphics style, all meshes together super well; none of it feels forced, or out of place, or irritating. The game as a whole feels 'right'. It's hard to describe, and at first, I was skeptical, cause it tosses you right into the action without giving you a proper introduction as to what's going on. The beautiful part of that? Is that the game transitions fluidly from the sudden grating action, to a smooth and relaxed introduction to what's going on. It's truly a well put together game and I cannot wait to see what it'll look like when full release comes around.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even like roguelike usually and this game is addictive AF, it tests your reflex and split second decision making, as well as your mastery of the game's wide and complex weapon and skill (boons) system, where there is a multitude of build combinations that keeps the game fresh even after 60+ runs for me, and I don't expect that to change any time soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: Hades is one of the most brilliant games I've ever played, it takes elements from many other popular games and makes them it's own by refining and iterating on these ideas.This is the first roguelike to genuinely incorporate all of it's mechanics into it's story, even your deaths, usually ignored by most games, are mentioned and a part of the narrative, there are many characters you'll meet and start to care about as you delve into it, the visual style is impeccable, the gameplay is fast and responsive, and the weapons you'll unlock very varied, changing the experience significantly every time, aided by the god's boons which allow you many different builds for your runs, you'll take a very long time to even learn the available variations.This is Supergiant's very best, and it might be my game of the year (well, if Cyberpunk manages to disappoint that is), can't recommend enough.

_childDocuments_.review: For someone who has never played any rogue like games before, and grew up playing mainly shooters and sports games. Hades is the perfect breathe of fresh air. Even after beating the game i found myself drawn back wanting and craving to continue more runs. With so many different weapons, and variants hades sinks you in a hole of everlasting weapon, and boon combinations to perfectly suit your play style, and try new things. The lore and dialogue are beyond amazing I’m 70+ hours in and have never gotten the same dialogue.  The sound track is “chef kiss” making every boss fight feel intense. you will fall in love with all the characters and there backstories. This game truly holds a special place in my heart and I’m so excited they announced a sequel. I think rogue-like and rogue-lites are my new favourite genre of games. For anyone who is hesitant it’s worth every dollar and the challenge of dying and relearning the boss patterns is rewarding when you finally finish your first run.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot of fun, but like all Supergiant Games, there's a lot of style and very little substance. It's clear all the effort when into the clear and vibrant art, the great music and sound effects, and the excessive voice acting. Those things alone don't necessarily make the game worth playing though. The combat is fun and the enemy and boss variety is OK at best. The meta upgrade systems give a decent reason to push yourself along. However, the large emphasis on story is where this game kind of falters for me. There is a large amount of unique exposition for pretty much every flow chart of scenarios, but all of it is fluff and amounts to nothing. I've long since started skipping dialogue despite it still having unique voice lines I haven't heard before because it's always meaningless drawn out statements that answer no questions.There are very few biomes, weapons, and upgrades. Once you've played the game for a few hours you've likely seen everything the game has to offer. The maps themselves have little variety in the way of special rooms and it's very easy after a while to always be able to get to the last boss. If you compare the game to other roguelikes, there is actually very little variety here. I was hoping this would be improved with 1.0, but from what I've seen the game is pretty much the same as early access as far as I can tell so far.Despite all of this I would still recommend the game. The combination of all the systems, though low in variety, still make for a solid experience overall. It captures that "one more run" feel well, but know that while your upgrades maybe different, pretty much everything you run into is kind of deterministic. Run variety will solely be based on your build choices and the map will extremely rarely throw something at you that you haven't seen before. If this game had maybe double its current biomes, trinkets, upgrades, weapons, and had more special room encounters it would probably be the best action roguelike out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Hades

_childDocuments_.review: I generally have a hard time to get into Roguelikes, where you repeatedly start over from the beginning, but this game both has the narrative drive and gameplay reinforce one another, simply addicting.This game will easily sit among my favourites for a long time forward, as even if you complete it, the fast paced combat and variety is engaging as .Cheers to the eternal escape of the underworld!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played. The gameplay itself is great -- refreshing among roguelikes, not too repetitive, and with a decent variety of enemies and playstyles with ever-changing strategies with good Boons to choose from.But the main selling point is the game's story: Every single character goes through their own development, and every single character's arc is complete, understandable and fun to go through. Losing runs is never tiresome since even when we lose, the story progresses and Zagreus gets a little bit closer to everyone in the Underworld *and* to the Olympian gods.The OST is amazing, from the normal sound effects of attacks, traps, weapons, enemies and bosses to the songs -- and the songs are perfect and tied to the characters. Following Orpheus and Eurydice's story and getting to see how they are emotionally from the songs they sing, both alone and together, is a whole experience on its own.I'm not sure if there is a perfect game in the world, but Hades is as close as it gets.

_childDocuments_.review: Unbelievable.  This is the best realization of the roguelike formula so far. They've taken the tonnage of lessons from all the games that paved the way and just created the ultimate iteration.The balance between the tension of losing a within a run and permanent progression. The mix of single use, single run, and cross-run currencies. The pace of gameplay and cadence of upgrades. The resource bonus for using a different weapon than the previous run. It's all just tuned stunningly well. Everything that clearly worked well in precursor games is kept or expanded upon, while weaker areas of contention are mercilessly cut. And this is all done even with the confidence to comment on it in-universe, like when your character muses that he wishes he has a health flask, or a boss taunts you for arriving already at low health. It's as close to perfect as the genre can get.Then, on top of nailing all of these design elements that would make it a good game no matter what its skin, they wring every last absolute drop out of the Greek pantheon theme and setting. Characters with recognizable personalities are everywhere. The boons offered by the gods are all thematically strong, and just by seeing which gods you are coming across you start to understand what kind of run you can put together on sight. There is even, against all odds, a compelling story, in a genre that basically laughs at the idea of attempting a narrative.Damn well better end up on some GOTY lists is what I'm saying.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only play for three hours and it's already a blast.I would recommend that you go into the game as blind as possible and enjoy discovering all the intricacies it has to offer by yourself.Draped in a pastiche of Greek mythology, it's a nuanced and interesting take on dungeon-crawling fun. I've been consistently impressed by how creative and engaging the game is with so little playtime.I especially love the dynamic you get to have with the Gods of Olympus. As you adventure, you have the ability to communicate with them and channel their strength as your own, enhancing your abilities or replacing previous blessings from other Gods over the course of any one run through the underworld.This culminates in an engaging upgrade system that is equal parts 'finding yourself trapped fighting a horde of skeletons summoned by Ares for accepting a blessing from Athena over him' and 'wishing Poseidon was your gay uncle in real life'.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was highly recommended by friends, and it simply hasn't been a fun experience getting this game working properly or playing it.  Since i'm quite obviously in the extremely small group of dissenting opinions, I felt I'd describe why and try to be informative about it.  I don't know if this game was originally a console title, but my technical issues seem to be typical of console ports.  Even ignoring these technical headaches, I have to recommend avoiding this title - and now I better explain why.Several people I know really like this game.  I thought I would too, and had it on my wishlist for quite a while before getting it so there was some real anticipation built up to play it.  The game has some technical issues that need working out, but outside of that display settings problem none of them are really deal breakers.  Ultimately, the game suffers from a variety of gameplay and design issues that range from annoying to game-ending to baffling.  The end result is that I feel other games are worth my time more than Hades, but I also understand that's a personal opinion from my own experience and no one else's.  Thanks for the games Supergiant, seriously - at least Bastion and Hades, because I have friends who really like them and enjoy them for all they're worth.  On the other hand, this is two in a row that haven't appealed to me and I don't know if they ever will.  Even if I'm failing to find the fun in your games, I'm honestly OK with that given the popularity they enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Hades has to be one of the most refined rogue-lites so far.Everything about this game is good. During the first escape attempt, I already knew I was playing a game that was special. Hades is a game that makes you want to play it again and again -- something that can't be said for a lot of the games in this genre.There's a lot of content. Until about 100 hours in I received several new, voiced dialogues (by amazing voice actors) every run, a lot of it advancing the plot or developing the characters in a meaningful way. The difficulty curve is just right. The game gets progressively easier the more you play, but you never feel artifically held back. If you want to challenge yourself, you can increase the difficulty or do speedruns.To not appear as a total shill for Supergiant Games, I'll say that I wish there were more unlockable levels, enemies and bosses. There could also be more viable boon and keepsake combinations to work with. After 100 hours it feels like I've exhausted most of the options.Hades is easily the game of the year for me. It's well worth the price and everyone I've recommended it to have loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, but after a while it started to feel like a chore for me.The idea is that you play as the son of Hades trying to escape the underworld with the help of the rest of the gods and characters from greek mithology.It's a good roguelite, and it's beautifully written, and as a game is also really fun; also the way it tells its story is brilliant, by adding context through conversations you have before bosses or when earning upgrades from gods, etc. Is a really clever game that has a lot of heart, but it also became a bit of a slog for me after a while.Just the process of figthing the same enemies and bosses after a while just couldn't be varied enough because of the conversations present in the game, for me to just want to keep playing it, furthest I got was the final boss which I tried to beat a couple of times, only to then fail, and afterwards all my motivation to keep playing the game was lost.I just didn't want to play for the 48 time against the same bosses, enemies, etc.But it's a really good game either way, so I'm recommending it because of this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily the best action-roguelike I've played. The progression from run to run, slowly getting stonger and learning how to manipulate your runs is done extremely well. Not to mention the incredible voice lines and the character development of the various underworld individuals.
