_childDocuments_.review: Beyond a Steel Sky is a fantastic adventure game. I played the original many years ago - I think you can play it for free nowadays with ScummVM - and it was a landmark in excellent sci-fi storytelling in games. I don't remember too many of the details any more, but the good news is you don't really need to know all that much to get up to speed with this one. The protagonist lives in the outback in a post-apocalyptic future. In the first game, with the help of a robot he built in a junkyard, he defeated an out-of-control techno-organic virus that was taking over a city. At the opening of this game his quiet life in the bush is disrupted and he finds himself heading back to the city to figure out what's happened since he left.One of the best things about Beneath a Steel Sky - and something that is continued in Beyond a Steel Sky - is its sense of humor. Unlike the Sierra or LucasArts games of old, or the modern adventures that try to recreate those ones, it doesn't try to turn everything into a gag. The situations are grim and the characters take their predicament seriously... but they're never so joyless that they would leave a good pun unsaid. The light comedy sprinkled here and there helps to make the game feel less oppressive than its crapsack world otherwise would, and the occasional references to relics of our time never feel like pandering. It's an absolute masterclass in how to tell a story with some easter eggs and levity without drowning it in cringey fanservice.The controls are in the Telltale/Life is Strange style, which work okay in almost all situations, except for a handful of infuriating timed segments where you need to click in exactly a specific location to do something, and if you miss, then the thing you're trying to click moves away and you need to start all over again. Bigger hotspots would've gone a long way. But aside from that, it's pretty much perfect. The puzzles are all fairly solvable, although i admit i did look at a walkthrough once or twice. The story is linear, and there aren't really any red herrings or side conversations unrelated to the plot. But the game is still over 10 hours long, and it's gripping pretty much all the way through. In short, this is just a great game. Great sci-fi. Great adventure. Get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautifully done, classic point and click adventure. You have free motion within the 3D environment but the game follows the standard of clicking on items and choosing actions. Revolution has streamlined the interface to limit actions to only those appropriate and they made inventory easy to access when it is usable.The artwork is engaging and reminded me of the later Broken Sword games (with more detail and higher resolution). The characters were interesting and likable. The voice acting is professional and I enjoyed the various accents. There is a lot of dialog to move through and (in most cases) dialog topics 'gray out' once they are exhausted.  I usually skip through dialog and speed read the subtitles but, in this game, I found myself slowing down to enjoy the audio portion of the game.Although Beyond a Steel Sky is a standalone game, I would strongly encourage you to play through the free Beneath a Steel Sky first to have full context. I found the older game a bit tedious and used a walk-through in some areas to avoid hours of 'try this, try that.' What was really interesting was to see the differences and similarities in how the city, characters, and LINC sections compare between old and new.Be advised, this is a long and somewhat complicated game with a lot of areas to explore and objects to examine. There is a very cool hacking feature that adds to the complexity. I often found myself wondering how someone would figure out some of the hacking scenarios without any assistance. Note that a hint feature is provided.The game automatically saves at regular intervals and also provides multiple slots for explicit saves. If you are a 100% achievement hunter, be prepared to play through twice since the first decision point for an alternate ending appears early in the game.I highly recommend Beyond a Steel Sky to anyone who enjoys a narrative adventure. It includes all the elements that I appreciate in this type of game - a charming and brave protagonist, a story that makes sense, a heroic quest, and (as an added bonus), some deep thoughts about the nature of humanity!One added note - the game includes a large number of cut scenes (some long and some short) which need to be watched. Thus, this is not a game to play in a hurry.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Starts off very promising, like really really promising and makes an impression that you're about to play through an amazing adventure game with some solid puzzles, fun dialogue and a mystery to unravel. Graphics were also quite well done and controls worked very well.Sad to say that at some point, this all changed for the worse. For me, it was the part where you had to fetch a poem to get the invitation for the aspiration gala. At that point I was about 8 hours into the game. All that charm the game worked so hard to built up disappears in the next hour or two.Why? Cause of the puzzles they force you to do. Hacking billboard to billboard, floating around as Joey, using logic by moving a square around, it all just feels 'off'. And 'off' is definitely what you want to turn the game to at this point. It also doesn't help that the dialogue becomes less tolerable, gone are the witty cute comments but hello annoying oneliners intented to be funny but god Joey do you really really need to shut the ♥♥♥♥ up already. The story tries to save it all in the end but it's not strong enough to carry this mess to the finish, it gets an 'okay' but that's it.So why recommend? Like I said, the first 8 hours are very very good.It's the last 4 that were utter ♥♥♥♥ so I'll give the game an 6/10 to keep it fair.Barely recommendable, get it on sale to temper your disappointments (or maybe I'm being too harsh?).
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: I know some people were critical of Beyond a Steel Sky, so held off a little before buying and playing.Having played the original, and now played the sequel, I can say... It's a good game. It's well worth playing.The graphics are beautiful, the voice acting is stellar, and there's an interface element that works really well.Why were people disappointed, imho? Well, perhaps that's a question answered better by directly comparing it to the original: I would especially praise the graphics, the fun "hacking" part of gameplay, the voice acting, and the witty dialogues. I liked the touch of having unvoiced ambient dialogue show up if two characters were within "earshot", too.I would especially criticise the same things I like to some extent - it's really irritating trying to use inventory items on someone who is constantly walking away. There are other issues at times with the controls, too, though mistakes are pretty easy to correct. In dangerous situations, you tend to get a bit of time or it will just reset if you fail. A lot of the puzzles revolve around this hacking feature, with some amusing consequences and attention to detail. But this may seem repetitive or not totally obvious to some players. Trying to get everything you want to hack at once activated can seem tricky at times.I had one crash, when another character asks you to sit down to proceed, and I instead said I was ready verbally, without sitting down. That's probably what caused it. But the autosave feature is pretty robust so I just had to redo things within that room.And now the plot and story aspects... The world-building elements are great. It feels like good attention to detail, and really is all brought to life with great voice acting. The characters themselves largely fall into established archetypes, but that works here.A major female character is unfortunately underdeveloped. Her motivations and history are barely explained, if at all. It's a shame and a missed opportunity. This stands out, because she's perhaps the only character who otherwise feels very real and human, without leaning on a stereotype, in the game.There are a couple of plot holes. An obvious one for me (absolute spoiler) That said, the plot does make enough sense, the goals are pretty clear, and it's a very enjoyable game. I especially liked how clear my objectives always were without even looking, and liked that things were pretty linear in that respect. Not so overwhelming. That Joey also keeps you on track is also pretty nice, and there's an in-game hint system if you get stuck.I'd recommend it. I'd give it somewhere around a 7.5/10. I'm not going to be thinking about the implications of it and raving about it to friends new to adventure games, perhaps, but I'd definitely recommend it as a smooth, fun game with a long play time that doesn't get boring. I'd recommend it to adventure game fans without a second thought.

At its heart it is a traditional adventure game which takes what is best about old school adventure games such as story, exploration and puzzles and adds them to Beyond in a way that modernises the adventure game genre and ensure that this game can be enjoyed equally by old school adventure game fans and newcomers alike.Full review here:

_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game after about 11 hours of absolute delight. What can I say? It's been a great journey. I was scared about the gameplay, instead it was so much fun. Innovative, while keeping a familiar environment for traditional P&C lovers. You have an inventory, but you don't get to use it a lot. When you use it, though, is never for abstruse puzzles. They're always logical. And talking about logic, the real innovation of the game is the scanner, which allows you to hack the various machines and automatons you encounter. Some of the puzzles were tough, but NEVER illogical, and most importantly fun to solve.Graphics is great and very clever. With clever I mean it's a particular kind of 3D that - I think - will still be nice in 5/6 years from now (because of the comic book style, the lines, the smoothness of the animations). This is something Revolution is really good at, because that's the same thing they were able to achieve with Broken Sword 3 (which is still cool). While I'm a fan of 2D adventure games, I think this look would be good even for a new Broken Sword title, or whatever the team will decide to develop next.Music was fantastic, I've heard some John Williams' vibes all over it (with a personal touch, of course). The first time you get to enter Union City, the music is just majestic, it's definitely a OST I'd like to buy and listen while working.Last but not least, the story: wow. I won't talk too much about it, because I want to avoid spoilers as much as I can, but I can say that the story is the perfect conclusion to the events started with the first BASS. You can still play this "sequel" without having played the first one, but I suggest you to grab a FREE copy of it on GOG and play it first. Special mention to the characters, especially Foster and Joey, who are brilliant both visually and vocally. I loved the actor who played Foster, very versatile (but I'll still be here hoping for Italian voice overs, sooner or later. Let me dream!).My conclusion is that every adventure game lover out there should play this game. Revolution is still making fantastic games, teaching us all important lessons when it comes to game design, plot, characters and so on.Be vigilant!
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: This game is caught between being a sequel to 1994's Beneath A Steel Sky, and also being a remake of 1994's Beneath A Steel Sky. A goal of Beyond A Steel Sky was to be enjoyed by people who never heard of the first game, which causes problems in writing continuity. The game must explain things to the player that Robert Foster, the main character, should already know, and does so in such painfully excruciating detail that I wish there was less dialogue.The game has times when it feels rough, which hopefully will continue to be patched, or learned from in future projects from the studio. Puzzles are mixed in complexity, but some do not allow for slight variation in coming to the answer, forcing one way to solve the puzzle.Hacking presents a clean interface, but does not allow for freedom in how something can be hacked, as you are restricted to moving specific shaped commands, and most options are locked to avoid obviously messing up how an object is programmed. It is really cool to be able to hack multiple objects at once, but that loses its appeal when a lot of puzzles require hacking to move forward.Beyond A Steel Sky hurts the integrity of the themes and concepts of Beneath A Steel Sky by repeating them on a surface level. This could have simply been a remake of Beneath A Steel Sky to build a foundation for creating a fresh sequel.Highly recommend playing Beneath A Steel Sky, as it has been freely available for over 15 years.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. I am new to this series, but I am a big fan of scifi and story driven games. Unfortunately this game doesn't really pay off. To be transparent, I had a bug where i had to replay the entire first 2 hours of the game to resolve it. That puts a bad taste in your mouth.The puzzles are either SUPER easy or arbitrary and confusing. The devs have created an interesting hacking system, but you never feel clever using it. It never pays off. Everything you do seems random, rather than clever. The hint system tells you how to technically progress rather than gives you story-based hints.As the story progresses, it is incredibly predictable and none of your learned skills ever pay off. There are no branching story arcs that I could see, and I never really felt any ownership of the final outcome. This game seems like it could have been good with some additional dev work/budget but it never really comes together.By the end of this game, I could not be bothered to care about  the outcome. I had no connection to the characters or their world. I usually love games like this, and I feel this seriously missed the mark.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't play Beneath a Steel Sky when it first came out.  But, I played it when GOG added it for free, so quite a long time ago still.  I don't remember it perfectly, but I don't really think this game makes sense as sequel.  The plot is too similar to the first game, more like a remake, while the timeline seems all janked up.  I wonder if this game started out as a spiritual successor and then was turned into a sequel part way through.I'll explain.  You explicitly play the same character as the first game, and he looks no older than in that game and yet 2 regime changes have happened in the city since game 1 and everybody living in the city can't seem to remember it any other way.  At one point you discover a zip code from the era when you were first in the city and only a couple of people are even able to recognize it as that.  Later you meet you a guy who regards your robot companion from the first game as a god and the events of the first game as myth, and yet when you talk to him you are offended to be thought of as around his age rather than around his daughter's age.  It's really weird.  Then let's mention the myth of your previous visit to the city.  In it, the story goes that you left your robot companion as king of the city when you left (I think the author of the first game must have been a Wizard of Oz fan).   He ruled the city benevolently for what seems like generations bringing them into a new age of prosperty and happiness and then left the city to strike out into the desert leaving behind a board of wellmeaning civil servants to rule in his place.  (all of this while your character doesn't age at all, again)  Well, in the current game, you visit a museum where you can see 3D recreation of memorable objects from the first game  (a fun idea).  In this museum is the chip board of your robot.  (He didn't leave into the desert at all!)  In the museum the chip board has been hooked up to a speaker and can talk to people but the security guard has removed power from the machine because the robot was too rude.  Well, already this doesn't make much sense, how can people believe that the robot left to the desert if they can directly talk to him?  Maybe they don't really believe it is him but just a recreation?  But then after you manage to steal the chipboard, the city news feed announces that some one has stolen their savior from the museum!  So, they do believe that that was really Joey?  How did this script get approved?Well, the story isn't everything in a game, even if it's so front and center as it is in this one.  But at least for the portion of the game I played, the puzzles aren't great either.  most of them involve this game's version of hacking which is to open up a screen where you connect to all the wifi devices in the area and move hightlighted subroutines between them.  But this is really frustratingly implemented.  The range of your hacking device is very limited and much of the game time is spent positioning yourself just so and waiting until all the robots moving around that you need to interact with all happen to be in range of your device at the same time.  The worst example of this is when I quit playing the game.  You have to annoy this poet guy out of a coffee shop so you can interact with his kindle-like device.  To do this you have to put the most annoying, loud, blaring music through the coffee shop's loud speaker so that he is so annoyed he has to leave.  They have the total cacophony of the awful music, him complaining, security guard robot sounding their sirens while you work on the actual hacking stuff and then thing you need are all moving around so you can never get just what you need on your hacking device, and there's some trial and error here too because you have to figure things out.  Like in any adventure game, ideas that you think will work don't work and only what the designers have thought up will actually matter.  It was so obnoxious and frustrating that finally I had to tear off my headset and calm down.In addition to that there are some bugs.  Sometimes (often) you move up to people and the trigger to talk to them doesn't appear.  Sometimes I have to run back and forth to the person and all around them until I'm able to get to talk to them.  Ugh.So, I didn't finish the game.  Maybe the puzzles farther in are brilliant and make you feel clever for solving them.  Maybe the plot and even the timeline somehow finally make sense in the end.  But it's just too annoying for me to find out.

The first happened when the girl was walking over to her workbench. The pathing broke and she was uninteractable. _childDocuments_.review: Technically, the game could have used a last brush of polish. It begins with a cutscene where the lettering flickers back and forth. That's not a great problem, but it is indicative for the rest of the game: NPCs walk into you while you talk, the camera angles while talking are weird. Sometimes the camera clips into geometry. Most of that isn't too terrible. Once after a cutscene, I couldn't move or interact and has to reload a recent autosave. And even when in range of something interactable, sometimes clicking won't bring up a menu.Gameplay wise, I'm not impressed. The beginning gave me high hopes. You are gathering things, trading, luring birds. As soon as that part is over, you barely use your inventory again. Now and then the crowbar comes in handy, but you carry the same four items the entire game. Instead of stealing everything that isn't nailed down, we hack our way through the city.There are lots of devices that can be hacked, and some logic blocks can be moved from device to device. Mostly, you invert logic to open doors... Some of these puzzles aren't bad, but mostly the problem is, that it is monotonous. One puzzle is , because it changes logic in devices in a way you haven't encountered and is hard to notice... As a filler, there is a towers-of-hanoi and some cube-turning puzzles in there.Story wise... It's terrible, or I don't understand some things.We left Joey - our friend - to rule the city, but when we , we do not talk at all about the intervening time? If it's just a copy of him, we don't even ask him what he might have done? People treat him like a savior, but that goes by uncommented.The whole reason for coming to the city is finding the missing kids. The Utopia/Distopia isn't greatly explored. In the first game, there was a progression from the tops of the towers to the lower tiers of the city. Here, we see only very few self-contained set-pieces and interact very little with people from different social status. The whole ending sequence feels overwritten and under explained.If you have played the first game and thirst for more from the same universe, this game is just okay. As a stand-alone adventure game, it's not interesting and gets tedious half-way through.

_childDocuments_.review: A game that continuously winks at - and stays true to - its predecessor. In my opinion, this is what a modern point-and-click adventure should be like. Not with overly complicated puzzles that nobody has time for in today's world, but story-driven, and with an ingenious internal hint system, so you don't have to look up walkthroughs if you're ever stuck. I've been playing Revolution's adventure games since the nineties, so thanks Charles Cecil and your team, for immersing me in this world for 10 hours once again. Two thumbs up!

_childDocuments_.review: Not really an adventure game. Some okay puzzles but often just extremely obvious tasks to tick off step-by-step. _childDocuments_.review: Beyond a Steel Sky is a Point-Click adventure game that takes place in what seems to be another universe akin to Treasure Island or Broken Sword, that I somehow NEVER heard of before. Graphically, this game I can compare to Tales from the Borderlands or even Borderlands (first comparison for the sake of similar game types). You take control of Robert Foster, some dude who lives in the wastelands called The Gap in this heavily distopian universe, until a Stalker comes out from the sea and kidnaps one of the children in poor Rob's village. He goes in a grand quest to discover who is behind this infant-kidnapping schemes. I'll not talk about mechanics because you know how that goes when you talk about point-and-click games (if you couldn't get the hint, there are NO GAMEPLAY MECHANICS to even speak of)... So the narrative is what we're concerned about here... and this one isn't so good either. Hear me out on this one; if you haven't played the first game (Beyond a Steel Sky, it's like an MS-DOS game or something) you'd be very VERY confused. Hopefully the game is free on Steam, and I made the grave mistake of not playing it first before playing this one, as this is basically a sequel (again, I blame the devs for not naming this game BASS2 or something). Overall, it's safe to say that I got very confused at the very first few chapters of the game... Like how the heck does your main character know most, if not all, of the citizens in Union City? Who the F is this Joey everyone keeps talking about? I AM CONFUSION. However, when you stick with it and learn about the few bits of lore you need to understand the plot, you become absolutely hooked to this game. I technically finished it in one seating, with the help of internet guides of course (lol, point-and-click games am I right?).And although I was on the verge of cringing really hard by the end, I enjoyed this experience. What I didn't enjoy, however, is how every other character's facial expressions were so detailed and Robert would always have this blank, lame look on his face, like he'd just realized he'd left a pizza in the oven for a whole day... But I guess this lame main character was countered by the ability to change clothes once you unlock them through the apartment's wardrobe (kinda lol). This game is , flat main character, good storytelling but confusing plot... Oh and the child abduction thingy is never explained so, that's another lame thing about the game. However, the scenery was nice, and the dystopian cyberpunk feel is amazing! If anything, play it for the nonchalant dark humor, and get some robots to steal their masters' poetry and claim it as their own (lol).

_childDocuments_.review: Wow so glad that after all this time they've worked hard on producing a good game. Something that nods to the past but yet something that uses new technology to enhance the game. I started playing the iOS version and loved it so bought it as soon as it launched. _childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of Revolution but after playing this game for 10 hours I ran into a game breaking bug that will require me to replay about 2 hours of gameplay. And the bug is extremely obvious and i can think of 3 ways of fixing it without reworking the puzzle mechanics.There's a puzzle in the Piazza area requiring moving hacking assets around the map. Any amateur designer would flag this as a high risk puzzle for game breaking. So either have an autosave when the zone loads that doesn't get overwritten, enable the reset from the hacking menu (it's disabled for me only in this area), or have the area reset when you leave it. None of that is present here and I'm not going to replay a huge section of the game.  I verified the solution via several walkthroughs and I can't continue it. Revolution does not provide technical support in this case and there isn't a patch.Price is too high for a game with obvious scripting bugs. Would recommend the game in several months if this is fixed + price reduction.

_childDocuments_.review: I disagree that you need to have played and be nostalgic about the first game in order to appreciate this game. I've never played the first one and I love this game. Good graphics, lots of things to do and figure out and places to go. Some interesting scifi themes. You get points that move you up in society, and have to deal with pros and cons of conforming to the rules to get more points. Some of the puzzles are really hard, but it's very satisfying if you figure out the answer without help from the internet. There are some strange surreal bits that I won't spoil. I'm Australian so I appreciated the Australian accents, don't hear that much in video games. Some parts were slow or a bit repetitive but overall I recommend this game for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, great sequel to the classic Beneath a Steel Sky.  Revolution Software does it again.  Robert Foster chases a kid who has been abducted back into Union city where he takes the identity of a man named Graham.  With the reluctant help of Graham's wife, a small underground movement of people, and of course his pal Joey, Foster finds out that the culprit is none other than.  Well you have to play the game.The graphics are cartoonish, on purpose.  Yet still very beautiful.  The puzzles are the norm for a point and click adventure game despite the 3d world. And if the puzzles are too hard, there is a built in hint system.  As for bugs, well once I had to restart the game because I couldn't talk to a kid named Ember.  But thanks to frequent autosaves I lost less than a minute of game time.  And it only happened once.  I am actually looking forward to playing it again in a few weeks.  This time I can correct a few mistakes, it seems that the relationship between some characters can change if you play your cards right.  So it does have some replay ability.  However for the most part it is a linear story. So I highly recommend it and hope you have as much fun as I did.To be honest, I have never written such a glowing review before.  I almost sound like a fanboy.

_childDocuments_.review: I imagine my opinions below have already appeared more than a few times in the hundreds of previous reviews. However, I want to continue supporting the game by leaving this positive review.I really enjoyed this game. I continued thinking about it after I'd finished, pondering on the experience. If you've played through Beneath a Steel Sky, I especially recommend Beyond, it's a great sequel. If you've never played Beneath a Steel Sky, or it's been years since you've played it, I suggest that you play through it before playing Beyond. While this game does a decent job of catching you up, I think worthwhile aspects of the story will have more impact if you have the previous game fresh in your mind.I won't go over the game's premise, as the store page does the job. As for the genre, it's definitely an adventure game, but more in the traditional point 'n click sense (although I played with a controller), versus the modern platform adventure game. The atmosphere and puzzle design are definitely the focus.As for the visuals, sound, and voice-acting, I enjoyed them all the way through. The voice-acting in particular is a treat for those that heard the voices in the first game. Regarding the visuals though, I want to see this game in HDR! Even without HDR though, I was a fan of the visual style well before the credits rolled.I hope this game is not the end of the Steel Sky universe. Regardless, a big thank you to the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: You know how modern remakes of cartoons basically butcher the shows we loved as kids? Yeah. That. You can debate me on if Beyond a Steel Sky (BASS2) is a cynical cash grab made by talentless hacks cashing in on the goodwill and nostalgia of Beneath a Steel Sky (BASS1) while carving up its premise and setting in a savage butchery of its material for parts, or a loving attempt to bring the series back from the dead with good will, good intentions, and a respectful follow on of the original story set in a carefully reimagined world using modern technology to improve on the foundations left behind…What you can’t debate me on, is if it’s good. But I’ll get to that. BASS2 takes up a decade after BASS. We once again find ourselves as Robert Foster, the apocalypse survivor, handyman, and all round nice guy as he has continued wandering ‘The Gap’ (a space between cities where life is considered to be brutal, uncivilised, and short. Despite all evidence.) He is preparing to move on again when the child of a family he’s been staying with is attacked and kidnapped by mysterious forces. Rob takes this personally and sets out to rescue the boy in an ‘ask everybody about everything’, rub things on other things, but mostly move words around, point and click adventure.  Right. Sleeves up folks, ‘cause I have a LIST. This is a clear and unequivocal no from me. Which is heart-breaking as BASS1 is one of the greatest point and clicks out there. This as its legacy is indescribably tragic. This game is bad. I cannot see a single reason you’d want to pick it up. If you’re an old fan, this isn’t the sequel you want. If you’re a newcomer the deeper story isn’t going to make a lick of sense and it’ll just be sci-fi setting 6 with plot line 3b and a badly written example of that… If you want puzzles and mechanics these ones aren’t good at that. BASS2 has nothing for anyone.And finally, the closing whimper of the ‘ideological boss battle’ at the finale really is the congealed blood clot posing as a cherry on this rotting ill-defined refuse pile pretending to be a cake. They couldn’t even let us pick moments from the game we’d witnessed, or give us a chance to fix the directive. As I sit here shaking my head ready to have finished on that note it occurs to me. If I were a cynical man, I’d say this was a concerted effort to bring down and unmake everything that made BASS1 great. Tarnish its image and end it by tearing down everything we built. What an ignoble end and tragic fate to a childhood classic. Revolution, you can do better than this. You  have done better than this.  with reviews by genre.

_childDocuments_.review: At some point in the game, Foster makes a comment like, "Sure, new is nice, but you just can't beat the original." In this case, I couldn't agree more with this sentiment. I'd recommend it to newcomers but there is nothing particularly interesting about the gameplay or story. Everything goes exactly as you would expect. I feel like you see less of Union City than in the first game. They literally copy/paste one segment of the original, beat for beat. I wasn't such a big fan of Beneath a Steel Sky either, but I thought that, after a 25 year gap, perhaps the sequel had a good reason to exist. I was sorely mistaken. The original has much more character.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Broken Sword series and the original BASS game (or all of Revolution's games), I was a bit hesitant to see what BASS 2 would bring. Overall, I thought the story line was thought out and consistent with the original. There are homages to the original if you have played, but if haven't played BASS it is not too hard to follow (though I do recommend playing the original first -- sadly it isn't available on steam...maybe in the future? It is available elsewhere though). The graphics project the right feel for this game. I actually felt they were a beefed up version of the original. If you are looking for those really crisp graphics you see elsewhere these days, this might not be the game for you. These graphics are more comic book  feel (not shocking given Gibbons involvement) and they set the mood for the game -- gritty and offbeat. I know some people aren't fans, but I enjoyed them. I also enjoyed the soundtrack/music. It didn't overpower the scenes and it added to the world of Union City.There are some mildly annoying bugs that will hopefully be worked out. My favorite was the character that appeared to be standing on her desk rather than beside it. Other than that there are a few glitches/bugs sometimes it can trip up the game, but if you restart it from a manual or auto save point it seems to realign itself. I enjoyed the game. Obviously, it will never be the original BASS, but I think it adds to the Foster's story and I enjoyed returning to Union City. Looking forward to Revolution's next game as always.

_childDocuments_.review: just got a big update, and many of the technical issues that plagued my experience have reportedly been remedied. As such, I have changed the review to positive, and updated its contents. is a direct sequel to the 1994 point-and-click , and continues the story of Robert Foster and .  features enjoyable gameplay and likeable characters, but suffers from a few rather bland plot points, and lacks some polish. gameplay is reminiscent of classic point-and-click titles; it couples a relatively modern third-person perspective, free camera and WASD controls with point-and-click interaction. Upon coming to and highlighting an object, players have the option to interact with it, use an inventory item, or inspect it, causing Foster to comment. Movement and camera control feel pretty good.Much of one’s progression through the game involves solving various puzzles using the environment and inventory items. For example, finding a firecracker to scare away some birds in order to access the door they were blocking. A hint system is present if players get stuck.Adding another dimension to the puzzle solving is the new hacking system; Foster can now interact with various electronic devices via his hacking tool. For instance, if a door won’t open because Foster isn’t allowed in, he can switch the door’s programming so that it opens when approached by someone who  authorised.I liked the hacking system quite a lot, I only wish I got the chance to use it more often and in more ways. is presented as a series of small levels that players will visit multiple times throughout the game. These are filled with NPCs who move around and interact in an attempt to make the world feel alive, and the game does a decent job of accomplishing this. Some areas from the first game are revisited, offering a little slice of nostalgia for fans. Ambient dialogue is silent, which feels a bit jarring, as all other encounters are fully voiced.  ditches much of its predecessor’s grungy, industrial aesthetic in favour of a clean, sci-fi look. It all looks quite nice, with nicely modelled sci-fi vehicles, buildings and holograms, but as someone who’s seen a lot of this kind of thing before, it felt quite generic. Later in the game, however, Foster returns to the high up industrial area of the city, and it looks great. The orange-tinted skyline and sound of wind rushing past sets a fantastic scene, and will undoubtedly bring nostalgia to bear in those who played the first game.Like its predecessor,  features a serious tone, but offsets it with humorous dialogue and character moments. Foster visits  once again; a place he once saved with his robot buddy Joey, whom he left behind to run the city and improve the lives of its citizens. This time, he’s on the trail of a child kidnapped from his village.  is now a utopian place where every human need is attended to, but at the cost of its citizens’ freedom of both body and thought, not to mention the unseen moral and physical costs of maintaining such a place. Various nods to the previous game are present.  features a dialogue wheel similar to  or , which allows players to choose responses to give and questions to ask in conversations. This doesn’t see much use in story-heavy encounters, however, as Foster has his own personality and will converse automatically.  also features a number of quite amusing personalities, and most character interactions are interesting, entertaining, or both. It does feature a generic moustache-twirler antagonist though, unfortunately.Sadly, when using the dialogue wheel, conversation can feel disjointed; some options will cause an NPC to speak as if they’d forgotten what you’d just told them, or vice-versa. Likewise, in scripted dialogue encounters, Foster sometimes mentions things that he and the player are aware of, but the person he’s speaking to shouldn’t be, yet they just continue as if they know exactly what he’s talking about.The weakest point of the story is its ending, and emphasis placed on characters in it. The game overstays its welcome by continuing after what feels like an (albeit somewhat inconclusive) ending to present a final sequence that’s out of place with the rest of the game. This sequence delves into the moral and philosophical failings of the utopian , but the delivery is so blunt and on the nose that I found it hard to enjoy or even take seriously, especially when coupled with the bizarre manner in which it’s presented. The emotional value of this sequence also hinges almost entirely on the player having experienced the previous game, and even then, falls a bit flat. first released on mobile, and as one would expect, its graphics are a bit dated, though still quite nice.There are a few nice views to be had, and the high-quality comic book style cutscenes in the beginning of the game are a nice throwback to the previous entry. features pleasant music, particularly the main-menu track, though for the most part it’s relatively unremarkable. I did notice one track that sounded reminiscent of the style used in the previous game, however, so that was nice. Sound effects are good, with some nice ambient sounds like vehicles flying overhead and the wind rushing past when up on a tall building.Using the specs listed above, I got a consistent 60fps on the highest settings, with very rare dips into the 40’s.Shadow quality has a large effect on GPU usage; having shadows on “epic” caused my GPU to run up to 95% load. All other graphics settings had minimal impact, even on their highest options.NPCs can occasionally have trouble pathfinding around the player or each other, and can get stuck. The game still lacks some polish, but I'm confident it will continue to be improved. is an enjoyable game with solid gameplay that offers something a little different, as well as a line-up of likeable characters and good humour, though a couple of plot points did fall a bit flat.

_childDocuments_.review: An avid fan of the original, having first played it on the Amiga where it came on FIFTEEN disks, I was excited by the prospect of a sequel.I was a bit unhappy at the move to third person, especially as I've played many point n click adventure games, including recent ones such as those by Wadjeteye (which include an incredibly good cyberpunk point n click), but I reserved my judgement.Unfortunately, this game lets down the original in almost every way. I'll break it into bulletpoints:- The original game was a point n click adventure game. This tries to be similar. However in the original, there were all kinds of things you could interact with. The premise was generally, that you had a problem to solve, and you explored the world looking for ideas and clues that would help you solve it. Various characters would help or offer advice, but you'd always be pulled in looking for something that would address a problem. However, in this game it's the opposite. You generally walk into a room, find three or four interactable items, without any idea of what you're really doing or looking for. You end up hunting the puzzle itself, then figuring out how these four items help to solve it. Pretty much every room is self-contained, so you don't need to travel around the world looking for things, you just need to figure out how to make the few things you have fix the problem.- Often you don't know what you're doing. Many times I was just wandering around trying to figure out what to do, when I'd talk to someone and there would be a dialogue choice that made no sense, as if I'd missed some critical part of the story. I had to piece it together myself sometimes, it was bizarre.- The puzzles were either painfully obvious, or ludicrously fiddly/bizarre. It's good that the game has a hint system, although for some reason it makes you wait a minute between hints - you've generally done the first three hints so you have to wait around for it to tell you there's something somewhere you can interact with that you missed. It doesn't always make sense. One puzzle near the end had no explanation and even the solution didn't make any sense to me.- The dialogue, is not great. With the exception of Joey, who appears to retain the humour of the original, the rest of the characters are plain and uninteresting. They don't feel like they have lives, they just exist solely to speak about whatever it is you need to ask them about.- There are lots of bugs/graphical glitches. Occasionally I had to reload the game to fix a stuck item.- Lots of stuff was unexplained throughout the story, or just made no logical sense. I won't post any spoilers, but people's motives were unexplained, why people didn't do certain things was unexplained, various characters' motivations were unexplained.- The story itself was pretty weak, and the conclusion wasn't really satisfying or logical.- It lost the 'noir' factor of the first game. It seemed a bit to happy, even when bad things happened.- There weren't really any good plot twists, the 'reveals' were so obvious as to barely elicit more than a shrug.The good parts are, some of the voice acting was very good, it was interesting to see/hear some of the characters from the first game, and Joey was pretty amusing.I think making the game more sinister (even the villain just felt like a comic relief character), fixing the storyline, and improving the puzzles would have made this game much better.I can barely recommend it to even diehard fans of the original, as I hope that one day there will be another successor and we can forget this one existed.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure what to say about this game. I don't have the nostalgy glasses, and remember the previous game as visually interesting but rather rough and with a lot of rubber chicken in terms of gameplay. Loved the environment and the art, that was what I came for  and got it, but I missed a more refined product.Cutscenes are sometimes terribly edited. Animations aren't always ok. Sometimes a character gets trapped in a jerky loop between both characters talking, or the camera directly focus on a wall. There were a lot of unpolished details, but my main problem was the writing. The story is functional but it wasn't great. Joey Bender routine was ok, Robert  Foster is a very dated character and dialogues weren't as sharp as they thought. Even the final revelation was written in a very basic way while pretending to be deep. Characters felt underdeveloped: a squaredjaw hero, a basic baddie with moustache, a bad woman (somehow developing Songbird character was considered a hidden sidequest (?)), a funny 90's buddy and a vaguely romantic interest. The gameplay had serious issues in how the information was released, you could talk about things that still didn't know, and solve puzzles that you didn't even know what for they were. This is a basic for narrative games design and it happens a ton of times. Less number of dialogue options but more developed dialogue and in correct order could have been a better option.Let's go with the good part, the art is wonderful, it makes the game look better than it is. The environments are cool, you can see that there are some limitations in budget or time, but everything looks impressive. Most of puzzles are ok, and the hacking puzzles are a very good concept. Some of them are very funny. With a little more of love dedicated to this system it could have been so fun in terms of experimentation, but there are some ocasional troubles (I got trapped in the cafeteria room trying things, the distance you can detect a machine is pure nonsense). This kind of puzzle has a lot of potential and with time and creativity some classic puzzles can be made in other games, in this it was fun but not glorious. Loved the hint system too, in terms of accesibliy it should be included in every modern adventure game. Music was good, maybe too epic for the story. I recommend the game? I don't know. The pace wasn't great, didn't feel like a real story most of the time and characters felt plain. I've struggled to keep on going sometimes. It didn't feel organic at all. Somehow everything was so promising of a very big thing and at the end it didn't deliver much. A better writing with twists and well acted cutscenes with good characters is something that could have improved the story a lot, But woah, what a cool place to live that city. Really loved the Metropolis sets and enjoyed this one a lot. But other than that I can say that the game isn't bad, just ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: It really pains me that I cannot recommend this game, because Beneath a steel sky was one of the standout games of my youth.The original managed to be funny and yet convey a feeling of dread at the same time. You were having amusing conversations with interesting characters, yet you really felt that something more sinister was going on and that you didn't belong.Not in this sequel, the characters are bland, not only in the conversations you have with them, but the facial animation is so extremely poor, that I swear the old pixel game managed to show more emotion than the blank stare the people in this game constantly have. Never do you have the feeling that you are in danger and near the end, the story gets so dumb that I stopped caring anyway.The hacking mechanic that is introduced is fun at first but gets tedious quickly as you just have to figure out where to stand to link up the right objects. I was baffled at the simplicity of the final "puzzle", which reminded me of toys that a toddler would have and the difficulty level was on that level. Not a very good choice for ending your game.The city is actually quite nice. It does look like an idyllic version of the bleak, industrial city it was in the first game. But it never feels alive, because the people living there never feel real. I'm tempted to talk about some specific moments in the game that were particularly badly done, but I don't want to spoil anything.If, like me, you're a big fan of the original, maybe get this one with a huge discount, just for 'member berries. If not, let this one pass you by.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond a Steel Sky is like a warm hug from an old friend. It's got all the things you loved about classic point-and-click adventure games, but with a fresh coat of paint and a whole lot of heart. The story is funny, the characters are quirky, and the puzzles are just challenging enough to keep you engaged without making you want to pull your hair out. If you're looking for a charming and nostalgic adventure, this title is definitely worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Thoroughly enjoyed this adventure - was a fun romp through a sci-fi dystopian universe - presumably in outback Australia with all the accentsSome of the voice acting was a bit janky, but the main characters were great. The writing was engaging, you can really talk to characters a lot to learn about the world, and it was genuinely funny (and bittersweet at the end!)The puzzles were very light, but clever with a neat hacking mechanic I haven't seen anywhere else. Overall, heartily recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Still a bit rough around edges here and there, but nothing that can't be sorted out.The story is great and has the same sort of witty cynicism found in the original. The graphics are pretty and the soundtrack is actually really good if you stop to listen to it. The puzzles aren't that difficult, but are enjoyable to solve nonetheless.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: We're back on track again, friends. This also applies to my beloved Revolution Software, who have not delighted us with games for a long time, and Robert Foster, who is returning to Union City almost 30 years later. How many things have happened in our lives during this time, and his wrinkles have not even increased, and he looks much better and more beautiful than in the 1994 game. This time, in the city of the future, where people lead an ideal existence, he is led by the search for missing children, stolen by huge machines and brought here. Here he will discover that the bright future turned out to be not so ideal, will meet new and old friends, and will experience real adventures. It should be said right away that the main character here is an incredibly straightforward and simple person, which is what captivates. In our age of postmodernism and the deliberate complication of everything that the hands of creators can reach, sometimes you want to feel in the shoes of a simple hero, like Indiana Jones or George Stobbart, who simply fights for good, using ingenuity and inner strength for this. Someone may say that he is too old-fashioned, but I liked this tradition very much. Other characters are also spelled out well, the story lacks an adventurous spirit of adventure, and tragic moments, and of jokes, where can we go without them.The visual picture, although it gravitates towards the comic style, looks quite stylish, the city of the future really looks great. There are many puzzles, most of them are complex, but if the riddle is stumped, then you can always use the flexible hint system. I liked the non-standard approach to riddles, even if there is one claim. Boxes and laser beams would seem to have something in common. Fans of games from Revolution Software will immediately understand what's the matter, each of these things has become a fundamental puzzle in their various games. And a lot of people didn't like it... And here we again have a puzzle that will be repeated many times - manipulating electronic circuits, and if at first it looks very fun, then at some point it even starts to be a little annoying. Yes, in the end they very coolly implemented this idea right in the battle, but this does not negate the fact that this puzzle during the game is too much. The creators make it possible to learn a lot of interesting facts about the life of the city, adding a huge number of dialogue options, reference museum materials, which allows the player to irrevocably plunge into the atmosphere of the future."Beyond a Steel Sky" is another testament to the never-fading skill of the veterans of the genre, presenting us with a completely classic adventure from the inside, but with the knowledge that in 2020 something modern must also be offered. Witty, elegant, and with great attention to detail, the game unfolds for the player in a great and exciting adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sad that I can't recommend this game. I have played all of Revolution's games and this is the first I didn't enjoy. Nonetheless, I finished it in the hope that the narrative might give some additional rewards... Nope.Beneath a Steel Sky is a classic of early point and click gaming, and genuinely too me months to complete in the days before online walkthroughs were everywhere. While the sense of humour wasn't quite as pitch perfect as Broken Sword, the world building was great.So how do you go about making a sequel 25 years later? Well, surely the first thing you wouldn't do is fill it with content that would be completely incomprehensible without playing a game that came out on floppy disks. I must have played the game through 3 or 4 times and there are screens burned into my consciousness, but hey, it's been a long time. I don't know who that woman is, why do you think I would? She's bothering me.The game is OK, although it feels a lot easier than the original. I had to avail myself of the hint system 5 times in my 13 hours, otherwise things were a bit too obvious. There's one mechanism that is a kind of innovation, but I found that playing with it, rather than logically solving the puzzle, was often enough.Speaking of which, the puzzles.... When I was a kid my aunt would give me cheap little puzzles for Christmas. They were fine for an 8-year-old, but now many of them appear on the internet all the time. And yet... they appear in this game. Is this a game for 8-year-olds? I just don't get it.The climax of the game reaches for some kind of philosophical enquiry (combined with terrible - as in terribly easy - puzzles), and again, I was disappointed.Who is going to play this game? If it's people who were playing adventure games in the mid-90s then this game is way too easy. If it's younger people who are new to adventure games, then why create a sequel to a really old game?I'm confused.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Beneath a Steel Sky, diving into its sequel felt like a reunion with an old friend. The game seamlessly blends nostalgia with innovation, offering familiar characters and settings alongside fresh storytelling and gameplay mechanics. Visually pleasing and filled with rich detail, the game's world drew me in from the start. The narrative, filled with intrigue and mystery, kept me hooked until the very end. This is more than just a sequel; it's a love letter to fans of the original and a testament to the enduring appeal of the adventure genre. Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the series, this is a journey worth taking.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone do yourself a favour and play Beneath A Steel Sky directly before this, then imagine if you'd played it in the 90s being able to step back into that world decades later to this level. Awesome. Great setting and story, acting, nostalgia nods, pacing and a built-in hints system? Solid A. Now get back to making me more Broken Sword please xx
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the original game, I think this is well worth playing. It's an excellent continuation!-The story is good. It's fun to return to Union City and see how it has changed over time. If you haven't played the original I think you'll find it to be a fun and interesting setting.-The art is well made. It does a Telltale-like visual style combined with obvious comic book influences. -Gameplay is pretty simple and the puzzles are generally not that hard to figure out. It doesn't have the issue that some adventure games have of weird, bizarre solutions to things. And the hacking mechanic is pretty fun. I really enjoyed running around wreaking havoc with my hacker device.If you didn't play the original - which a lot of people these days probably haven't - then don't worry. The important parts of the plot of the first game are summarised in the intro to this and any other necessary stuff explained through, but you don't need to have played the first one at all. For those who did there's some fun little references sprinkled throughout the game. IF YOU:-Like Telltale-style adventure games, or-Played Beneath A Steel SkyTHEN GET THIS!
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: Don't buy this game in it's current state, it is a buggy mess. Crashes to desktop quite a bit until i set it to full screen, borderless windows causes it to crash. Even with full screen it crashes, but much less. The saves are annoying as it autosaves over previous saves and when you run into bugs preventing you from advancing, there are no saves for you to go back to, making it so you have to start over. There are so many bugs that prevent advancement into the story that it is just an exercise in futility.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond a Steel Sky

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give this a mostly-thumbs-up, the game sure has it's ups and downs.Kinda feels like this 100% rides on the nostalgia on Beneath the Steel Sky, for a sequel it's not entirely wrong, but... I'm not entirely sure how a newcomer would perceive the game.Most puzzles are good, but occasionally I feel like the logic just wasn't sound, . Also some of the hacked electronics do not function as you'd expect. Maybe there's too much freedom and the devs did not expect all the combinations that could be done? dunno. Also, some parts require finding a specific spot to stand so the player character has range to hack multiple devices at once. I get the idea, but in practice it's just wandering the level until you find the spot. Not really fun exercise.Other than puzzles, the game had it's fair share of jank. Occasionally I had to hammer WASD-keys repeatedly to get Foster moving, usually after dialogue/cutscenes, but sometimes after just interacting with an item in the world. Most cutscenes/dialogue parts the image was framed so that the chest of the npc was center frame... why? At first I thought this was an issue with FOV, but even after setting everything on default, the issue persisted. Maybe the game isn't intended to be played on 16:9 screen? Who knows. Not game breaking, but just annoying.All in all, kinda feels like a 6/10 nostalgia bait, to be brutally honest. The game still offers more pros than cons, but still I'm left with a meh/kinda-ok feeling about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the game, the storytelling, the artwork and the concept are great.There are a couple of issues that I think need mentioning: As of now (19.07.2020) , there are a couple of Bugs in the game possibly preventing your advance. save regularly on manual slots, to not loos too much time. This can be very annoying if you are not sure if there is a bug or you just don't manage to understand the puzzle right.The playtime is a bit short in my book, I probably used about 7h for a full run-trough with the backtracking i deeded to do from bugs this made a bit over 9h in total. Given the price at release I think that's borderline expensive, but not out of the realm of other AAA games produced today unfortunately.I would have liked to have some side content. The world would support lots and lots of it, but its probably out of the game to stay true to the original adventure feeling.And lastly, i thing its a bit on the easy side for an adventure, but that will hugely scale with your personal experience with that type of game.Nonetheless, I think it is a great game! I would suggest to by it at a later point when its somewhere below 20$ equivalent to stay in line for the amount of content, but I was ok to shell over the additional money to support the studio and the continuation of this type of game personally,
