name: DOOM 64
detailed_description: Originally released on Nintendo 64 in 1997, DOOM 64 is an action first-person shooter and a direct sequel to the events of DOOM II. In celebration of DOOM’s 25th anniversary, an enhanced version of DOOM 64 was released on PC and consoles in 2020 and can now be played here. Story Years have passed since you stopped Hell’s invasion of Earth. Quarantined for humanity’s safety, the UAC research facilities on Mars were abandoned and forgotten...until now. A signal from a degraded satellite suggests a single entity remains, and it has the power to resurrect the demons. As the only surviving marine who fought Hell’s forces, you are sent on a lone crusade to hunt down the Mother of Demons and stop a renewed demonic invasion. Features Released in 2020 to celebrate DOOM’s 25th anniversary, this enhanced version makes it even easier for players to enjoy the original game on modern platforms. Features include: Upgraded visuals Improved mouse and keyboard controls Gamepad/controller support Widescreen resolution support Native 60 FPS support More than 30 action-packed levels Additional “Lost Levels” continuing the story

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely my favorite of the old Doom games. The most visually interesting title with a gritty feel to the graphics, a deep color rich environment with actual lighting (no more fullbright), good sound, good animation. interesting level design, and gameplay has been tightened up and smoothed out. I think some people didn't like this one because it was too much of a departure visually from Doom 2 but honestly how many times can you remake the same game and keep it engaging? The only thing this doesn't do better than the other ones is music.I would recommend playing this one if you want that old school gaming experience without being  old and clunky.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people dismiss DOOM 64 as a spin-off, since it was always assumed to be a DOOM port for the Nintendo 64. However, id Software actually developed an entirely new DOOM game from the ground up. It's the direct sequel to DOOM II. (While DOOM 64 is technically the 3rd game, it's not really comparable to DOOM 3 as the games are completely different experiences)Everything has changed:The only thing that hasn't changed is the gameplay, which is still the tried and true run-and-gun experience DOOM is known for. In the earlier levels, the maps and lighting could be better, but the second half of the campaign makes up for it, especially in Hell. The level design also includes much more puzzles this time around, the majority of which are solved by hitting switches around the map. While I normally dislike backtracking in DOOM, it's tolerable here because they spawn new enemies along the way to help you know where to go and keep things interesting. I think DOOM 64 is a much friendlier game for those who aren't used to Classic DOOM, as it's the final (official) iteration of the Classic DOOM experience.If you've played the original DOOM games and haven't tried out DOOM 64, you're really missing out. It's the literal DOOM 3, don't sleep on it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a classic. Puzzles to get through, steps to retrace, spawning hordes and weapon drops to help against those hordes. I didn't end up playing DOOM 64 when it was new... but playing it now both takes me back and entertains new fancies. *I* am glad it popped up on Steam.

_childDocuments_.review: When reviewing a game like this you have to take in the time period, and the games that came out around that time. While Doom 64 holds up in its own right, it lacks a lot compared to modern FPS games, and even comparatively to other FPS games around this time. There is no vertical/diagonal aiming. To sprint you press the spacebar. There is no jumping. Doors don’t look like doors, and aren’t always obvious to the player. You have codes for levels that you’d have to enter to play that level (there are thankfully also saves, but they don’t show your time, so it’s hard to tell which one is the newest). Enemies are 2D while the environment is 3D; all of these things are odd and outdated, but I don’t think they detract as much as you’d think they would. It’s still Doom at the end of the day, and Doom is all about shooting and gore. In the same year, 1997, ‘GoldenEye 007’ came out, a game that had directional shooting, 3D enemies, 3D weapons, and was just in general leaps and bounds above Doom 64, on the same console. A year later, 1998, Half-Life came out, a game that defined what a campaign shooter would look like for the future to come. Half-Life had puzzles, voiced scenes, jumping, 3D everything, a showcase of many different environments, amazing graphics for its time, physics, platforming, seamless levels, and much more… Half-Life really puts a damper on a lot of games around its time period, and even after, so it’s a rough comparison, but one that gives ‘Doom 64’ no excuse for the supposed limitations. Now what does the game do well? Doom 64 has a surprisingly long campaign, with a decent amount of variety while maintaining the theme. It has a wide array of weapons, and a lot of varying puzzles. The game is dense in scope, and while it’s not crazy hard, I’d imagine on the hardest difficulty I’d quickly change my mind. Despite these positives, each positive comes with its own caveat. Its long campaign gets tiring and repetitive - this is doubled down by the fact that each mission itself isn’t that long, but most of your time spent is backtracking, making what is meant to be a fast paced shooter a headache at times. You have a lot of weapons, but because of the lack of directional aiming, weapon weight/drag/inertia, recoil, and other modern FPS mechanics, most weapons differ mainly in damage, with some differing in AOE. While it’s still good in its own right, it feels very dated, giving me mixed feelings. Is the game still enjoyable? Sure. Would I rather be playing a lot of other games? Yes.

_childDocuments_.review: is an odd one. It was originally made by Midway for the Nintendo 64, and it's a darker, more atmospheric take in the series before DOOM 3 was actually a thing while having the fast paced action DOOM is known for. It has been forgotten for a while... up until now thanks to the release of DOOM ETERNAL. is your typical DOOM in terms of gameplay. You start out with your pistol and fists, you find more weapons as you play through the levels, you kill demons, you find key keycards, you can find secrets, it's nothing you're not used to if you played the first two. What is new however are the looks and sound. Midway went with a more unsettling look to the enemies, and the soundtrack is no heavy metal anymore. They went with a style that makes you feel alone, that you need to survive, and it works while maintaining what makes DOOM great. In general, the game looks decent for the time and hardware it was on, and it looks much better in the rerelease.The level design are also very DOOM, but they're also my biggest problem with game. Don't get me wrong, they're fun to explore, but many times I found myself getting confused/lost on what to do. The traps can also be a bit frustrating to deal with your first time, especially where at times they feel like they come out of nowhere without any hint (one section in Level 2 where you need to stand in yellow lights so you don't get crushed, for example). Again, the levels are still fun to play through, but the trial and error can be an issue.This port's optimization is absolutely fantastic. Sure, this is an old game, but I'm able to play this game at "1366x768 60Hz" resolution at 60FPS with very little problems on this old Windows 7 laptop. There's also many graphics options, like enabling Anti-Aliasing, V-Sync, and a filter to make the N64 graphics less pixelated. The game's also in widescreen, you can set the brightness, and the shimmering the N64 version had is gone. It controls well with the mouse and keyboard, and you can rebind any key to your liking. The scrolling is a bit weird, but it works and you can get used to it. This is a really solid game. It's still DOOM, and while the level design can be poor, it's still a great way to spend your time. As for the port, it's the best way to experience this game. For 5 dollars, that's a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a stellar game, there's no doubt. But I couldn't put my finger on why I was finding it such a slog to get through until my most recent replay, and it's because it has such a dark atmosphere. It's a game of muted colours, shadowed hallways, and incredibly creepy ambient music. It's a potent mix that creates a deeply oppressive vibe, but it strips a lot of the raw fun that typified Doom 1 and 2. It's surprising that such a quiet and unsettling game was released solely on the N64 - a console known more for the light-hearted tone of its games more than anything else. But if you're looking for blistering speeds and raw energy, then that's where this game stands apart. For some that may be a good thing - it allies itself in that sense with Doom 3, a game I love. But I do find that, with the simpler visuals and gameplay, there is slightly more room for boredom to set in. You're not ripping through levels to empowering tunes, you're skulking through levels with an overwhelming sense of...well...doom. And the greys and browns that permeate the hallways lend their colour to the mood of the game, in sense. Doom 64 is very well made, but it's a marathon rather than a sprint.

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings on this one as a Doom vet and boomer shooter vet. The gunplay is the Doom you remember with some visual improvements, the port is great because it's Nightdive, and it's a decently long campaign.It's also cryptic as hell in a way that people expect old Doom to be but it usually isn't (most of the puzzles in this game are you pressing a switch and then having to guess what just happened, some other puzzles are genuinely worse). The highest difficulty turns the game into a slog, because it replaces a lot of fodder enemies with Knights and Barons, who aren't very threatening if you can strafe and who tank a ton of abuse, meaning that some levels can basically turn into holding down fire with the super shotgun and occasionally stepping left and right. And the final boss is a level of genuinely punishing that borders on unfair if you haven't powerd up the Unmaker enough to trivialize it.If you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love Doom and boomshoots and are starting to scrape the bottom of the barrel, then this is probably more worth your time than most. If you're new to Doom, this is a bad starting point. If you're new to boomshoots, this is a bad starting point. If you're even just kind of on the fence about boomshoots or classic Doom, absolutely avoid this in favor of 1, 2, and Final Doom.Strong candidate for a neutral rating, but I'll give it a thumbs-up for the absolutely fantastic port work.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from someone who never played the N64 Version, I thought this was great. Kind of like a late 90's remaster of original D00M...except with brand new maps, and redesigned enemies and weapons (special shout-out to the pistol which handles a lot better than classic D00M). Or perhaps, original D00M with a QUAKE influence. Forget mouse-look, forget reloading, ducking for cover, jumping or DLC...this is how we used to play FPS's: just keep firing until you run out of ammo.Only draw back was sitting through all the developer screens at the beginning. Bethesda, id, Nightdive, Kex, McDonald's, Coca-Cola etc etc. Put them all on the same screen and I'll appreciate them just as much!

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible way to cap off the classic DOOM trilogy. I find it very odd, however, that it was originally exclusive to the Nintendo 64, but that does not get in the way of the game's replayability, enjoyability, and success as a whole. I thoroughly enjoyed it; so much so that I ended up getting all of the achievements, which was not necessarily a cakewalk, but just like the game itself, was very much enjoyable and worth it. _childDocuments_.review: One of the most underrated  games, filled to the brim with content that isn't in the other classic titles. Some of the maps feature incredibly obtuse excuses for puzzles that might cause you to look up a guide in frustration, but fans of the series should still find a lot to love about this underdog entry.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall it's an alright Doom. Level design is pretty good, though it relies a lot on backtracking. The atmosphere is a lot darker and creepier than typical Doom fare, and this is reflected in gameplay with an emphasis on puzzle-based levels, and how much damage enemies can dish out, forcing the player to take corners slowly, and even listen for specific demon noises (though sometimes they'll wait until the player is in the middle of the room before surrounding them with multiple pain elementals or some other nonsense). While I do like the darker aesthetic, there are some levels or encounters that are strictly action based, similar to earlier Dooms, but the music never reflects this. Every single track in the game, save for the title screen and ending screen, is dark and ambient, usually not much more than sustained string notes.I feel like I should also mention the Lost Levels campaign, which is exclusive to this port. Overall, they just feel like more Doom 64 levels, which isn't necessarily a bad thing.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played doom 64 (since I never owned an n64), but I've gotta say, that this game looks very nice on PC. Even though I've never played doom 64, it looks like Bethesda has faithfully remade the game and updated the control scheme in comparison to either: "The Ultimate Doom" or "Doom II" on steam where you can only look around using the arrow keys or awkwardly using the mouse.This game is similar to those games and for the new experience (for me) of one of the classic doom games, I would recommend this game. Especially at $1, but even full price may be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 3 and this are the only enjoyable titles in the Doom franchise.Wanting to make a comparison this is much better than Doom 1 and 2 thanks to the plumbeous,superfine,very suitable soundtrack and the pitch dark ambientations.In some aspects it's below Doom 3 (lack of cutscenes), in some it's better(level design).Obviously i do not even compare this game to Doom 2016 and Eternal because they are unsuccessful attempts that do well only in terms of graphics,failing totally in atmosphere,for me the most important aspect in a game,and it doesn't come from my heart to consider them even games, but abortions.The DLC "Lost levels" add nothing to the experience.A valuable and bewitching jewel of other times7.6/10But the Original Doom 64 for PC is better than this version,which is too polished in graphic for my taste and which I do not recommend

_childDocuments_.review: It's Doom 64; not much needs to be said, this is just really well remastered and constantly on sale. If you're a new fan to retro FPS games and missed out back on the Nintendo 64, do yourself a favor and pick this up. Always a fun experience; the atmosphere is wonderful and there are times where the level design is ahead of it's time. Rip it, tear it, burn it!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about Doom 64? It was the first FPS I played as a kid. The dark atmosphere and the ambient soundtrack in combination with the sound effects really sell you on the feeling of being alone and distraught. Some may miss the Revenants and Archviles, but they make up for it with a much more threatening Pain Elemental and more aggressive Lost Souls. This game was a perfect way to wrap up the Classic Doom series and now it bridges to the new Doom games. The game is simple, fun and doesn't get in your way while you're playing. Just be prepared to get lost because most of these maps are far more complex than what you'd see in Doom & Doom II.PS: This port is essentially Doom 64 EX under a different renderer. Good job on getting Kaiser and co. to do the ports Bethesda.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I only played the first DOOM a bit at a friend's house when it was released.  This ported N64 version is such a good trip down memory lane.  Oldskool gaming with  smooth game play and many confusing moments. The levels are small, but have really a  great maze like feel. There are a  lot of hidden rooms  to be found and a massive amount of demons to be slaim. I am now at  chapter 11, and it really gets spicy. Loving it!  There is no auto save, so be sure to also save when starting a new chapter. You can quicksave (f6)  whenever you want, which I like.   Not being able to aim up or down and the inability to jump takes some getting used to.  And graphics wise...well it is exactly what you can expect from a 1997 game.  Because of the ported version to modern pc hardware, it plays like a charm.  Definitely worth the 5 eur I spent on it!  And it looks like the game is far from over yet, so  I stop writing, so I can slay more demons!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 essentially functions the same as Doom 1/2, but as it was made later the game is noticeably updated. The graphics are a little more complex, sounds are a little more complex and the maps are bigger. The art style is odd for the game and is definitely one of the worse ones for the franchise, and while the gameplay is still pretty good the maps aren't perfect. Often on maps there are buttons that create bridges or open doors, but with where the button is placed you have no idea what it actually does until you happen to come across the new structure/opening it created. The progression map to map doesn't often make sense either but that doesn't matter much for an old Doom game.The main thing that separates this game from the others is the soundtrack. Instead of the upbeat metal-inspired songs of Doom 1/2 the soundtrack is full of creepy ambient sounds. I guess it makes sense for what is essentially the prequel to Doom 3 to have a creepy feeling but it makes the rest of the game feel off since it's still fast-paced. Still an okay game.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say? The game still holds up after all these years. Can't speak for younger players\those newer to the franchise, but this old game still keeps you on your toes at max difficulty and is a great piece of nostalgia for Doom vets.3 good things:1. Choosing super creepy ambiance over the traditional MIDI metal was a nice touch (reminds me of Doom 3 if it were made in '97).2. Level design\layout is really good for the time period and feels appropriate for the combat scenario. The levels don't get boring\repetitive in my opinion.3. The Unmaker and the ability to upgrade it was a nice touch and like Doom (2016) makes secret hunting especially worthwhile.3 bad things (I really struggled here):1. I've always had mixed opinions about some of the secrets in the Doom games which you'd spend ages trying to figure out (I know it's optional). I'm all for a clever scavenger hunt, but when it involves being at the right place\time when you destroy a final barrel, it's super easy to miss\never figure out without a guide and I don't get much satisfaction out of it. More frustrating than anything.2. I think it's great that we got a proper PC port, but they kind of goofed some of the weapon keybinds IMO, such as the Super Shotgun & regular shotgun being tied to the same key. I definitely got used to it (since ammo conservation often doesn't necessitate using the SSG for every enemy so I can switch back and forth) but seems like a quick fix.3. It'd have been nice if they'd added a Mission Select setup similar to Doom 2016 where I can go revisit\replay old levels with my existing loadout from the latest point in the campaign, right from the main menu. It'd help in the case of missing a Demon Key for instance. You can "warp to level," but it's not the same IMO.All in all - solid Doom game that I'm glad to have finally played. Don't how I missed out on this in the old 64 days. 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: The game might be old and late to PC, but it's still a damn good Doom game. The game is a whole lot easier than classic Doom, but none the less, you'll find yourself in some tricky spots, especially if you don't get the upgrades for the Unmaker.64 definitely gives a good sense of horror from the 90's also giving a bit of an idea where the inspiration for Doom 3 came from. dim lights, sudden demon teleports, very eerie music with plenty of opportunities to make you feel on edge. It might not be scary in modern standards, but the game is still creepy none the less, but in my opinion loads of fun to play and I'm happy I finally got to play and enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly did not think this would be nowhere near as good as Ultimate DOOM or DOOM 2 but surprisingly it's just as good or in some cases even better. It does have it's flaws though. Also this originally being a cartrage game means that the enemies are a lot more limited compared to the PC versions of DOOM. However Those two things aside this game is a gem as both level design and enemy placement are top notch and almost every map is fun to play with only a handful being bad (dark citadel, unholy temple, and dark entries are the worst)

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty neat art style, plus good, wholesome, classic-DooM violence.The music is a lot more creepy and ambient than in the other games. Think less MIDI dad-rock and more like the original Quake soundtrack.The level design has a lot of mazes and key-hunting like any other classic DooM game, but now there's a bit of room-over-room trickery with the engine. If you don't like running around labyrinths full of monsters while humping the walls looking for a secret door, this game might not be for you.One complaint I do have is that the level design can be somewhat unclear and confusing at times. This is to be expected with the other games, but this one has a nasty habit of doing things like requiring you to run to a specific spot in a room to open a door or lower an elevator without clearly indicating that you need to do that. You may also run into a lot of situations where you need to shoot a button to progress, but other buttons with identical textures can't be activated by shooting them. These sorts of things would be fine if they were part of revealing a secret, but many instances of this are required to beat a given level.tl;dr - If you like the other classic Doom games, this game is probably for you. You don't even need to grow a third arm just to use the N64 controller to play it!

It's much more of a puzzle game then fps.Sure the graphics are blocky and the monsters are clunky, but its hella fun!  I honestly did not expect to like this game as much as I do.I let my 14 year old kid play it...he likes it too.  Yes...buy this game..its cheap and well worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: imagine you're playing Doom 64, but you can actually see what the ♥♥♥♥ you're doing and don't need to use a aborted boomerang to play it.As usual with Nightdive, they've done an excellent job porting this two-and-a-half decade old game to modern systems with modern controls and video options. Technically, it runs flawlessly (as it should) and contains a wealth of visual upgrades such as antialiasing and higher resolutions. Control-wise, WASD keyboard and mouse is the standard here (although some default keybindings are weird: spacebar to sprint?!), as well as gamepad support. Not only that, but a secret episode of 6 extra levels has been included. It's not on the same level as the phenomenal Shadow Man Remastered, also ported by Nightdive Studios, which is probably the greatest remaster ever made, but there has been a huge effort put into this very polished release. As usual, the original feel of the game is preserved immaculately, but made far more accessible (read: not stuck on a long defunct console selling for $50 AUD minimum). The default pricing of $7.55 AUD is actually a bit of a lowball in my opinion. I'd happily pay $20 AUD for this.Onto the game itself, which was developed by Midway under supervision from id Software in 1997, as a Nintendo 64 exclusive. At the time it was praised for its atmosphere and gameplay but faulted for its lack of innovation and multiplayer; its contemporaries like Quake 2 and the Turok series were seen as more technologically advanced, with 3D models for enemies instead of sprites, more complex level geometry and more platforming abilities such as swimming. The lack of multiplayer was particularly odd, especially for Doom, the originator of the deathmatch, on a console swimming in splitscreen shooters. Goldeneye 64 released a year prior and is still remembered today for its 4-player action. I personally never had any interest in the game, having been far too young to buy it on release and never owning a 64, and with 64 emulation being very poor up until recently.In terms of gameplay, it's Doom to a T. Armed to the teeth with a wide variety of firearms, all returning from previous games in the series, you play through a linear set of levels, some hidden, dispatching hordes of a variety of distinct monsters. These monsters also return from previous entries, with some absences due to limited cartridge space, and some new additions that are mostly palette swaps, but which are nonetheless welcome. You'll find secret areas, dodge environmental traps such as crushers, push switches to reveal new pathways, and collect coloured card keys. Apart from some slightly more sophisticated level alteration, such as activating a large weight which breaks through the floor, it's the same old Doom.Really where it differentiates itself from its predecessors is the atmosphere, which will be familiar to those who have played Williams Entertainment's port of Doom for the PlayStation. Sound effects are entirely different, or reused in different ways, some better, others less so. Monsters have had their stats altered slightly, and their sprites are all entirely new, created from CG models. And of course the levels themselves are different, despite retaining the same themes and characteristics; you've still got tech bases and hellish temples, laid out in Doom's trademark abstract style. Coloured lighting returns from the PlayStation version, providing a distinct visual difference from its predecessors. The largest departure is the music, composed by Aubrey Hodges (also the composer of the PlayStation version). Here, other than the introduction cinematic and level end screens, the themes are entirely atmospheric and industrial, rather than the classic techno-metal we've come to expect from Bobby Prince. This is a double-edged sword for me. It succeeds brilliantly at providing an extremely tense and foreboding atmosphere, and combined with the new lighting which is overall far more moody and dark, immerses you in these grotesque environments. However, the original Doom and Doom II were also able to achieve this feeling when necessary, while still providing far more melodic, memorable and frankly far superior tracks. Listen to Bobby Prince's "Sinister" from Doom's Halls of the Damned (E2M6) level for example:  I understand music is especially subjective, so your mileage may vary, but I won't remember any of these tracks the moment I finish the game.Overall, it's more classic Doom, presented in a unique and sometimes fascinating way, finally freed of its exclusivity and available on modern platforms. As someone who has wanted an official* way to play this for a long time, I'm very happy with this release. It won't supersede Doom II: Hell on Earth as the pinnacle of the classic games for me, but it's an engaging and satisfying experience nonetheless.*I do not want to discount the amazing fan efforts that went into recreating and reverse engineering Doom 64 before this port was available. As usual, Doom fans are amazing and provided custom map sets and even whole recreations of Doom 64 far before its official re-release. In particular, Sam Villareal's Doom 64 TC and later Doom 64 EX were instrumental in contributing to the renewed interest in this game and I doubt this would even exist without his ingenuity and passion.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: underrated as hell, doom 64 was the last of the "classic"  styled doom games for a while and it went out with a unique entry. doom 64 is strange, its horror focus is bewildering at first but grows on you over time with a amazing art style and atmosphere that is perfectly invoked by the soundtrack. Unlike doom 3 however, which also tried for a more horror tone, doom 64 doesn't abandon or soften the iconic combat loop the franchise is know for. With tons of great levels packed to the bone with great traps and frantic monster battles, doom 64 still feels like doom, just a more surrealist variation on the series. It of course features the iconic Unmaker, a cut weapon from the original doom, a demon based laser rifle that has the unique distinction of being up gradable by finding 3 secret keys, in 3 secret levels. It can be a pain and confusing at points to acquire them, the gun more than makes up for it by becoming comically  overpowered. though it may have the occasional confusing and frustrating level, doom 64's pros majorly outweigh its cons and even handles elements from previous games better, doom 64 is a lost gem that is slowly getting the status it deserves as the bold, weird, and wonderful game that it is  8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is a first-person science-fiction horror-themed shooter game developed by Midway Games for an enhanced version of the id-Tech 1 Engine, and re-released by Nightdive Studios via the Kex Engine. Taking place after the events of DOOM II, the player takes control of the battle-weary Doom Marine as he returns to the setting of the first game to exterminate a mysterious entity reviving previously slain demons.In a number of ways, the original DOOM was embedded deeper into the world of 90’s home computer gaming more than any other market. It was, at the time of its release, the most exacting 3D world in the entire gaming industry at large, when accounting for speed and screen-size. For a while, home consoles just couldn’t quite compete, despite a handful of earnest attempts. A wave of home console ports of DOOM populated the mid-to-late 90’s, with technical visionary and id Software co-founder John Carmack himself behind the wheel of at least one of them. Most of them couldn’t even light a candle to the original. Perhaps the greatest of these initial adaptations, however, was Midway Games’ remix and restoration of the previously id-helmed Atari Jaguar port for the technologically superior Sony Playstation. Featuring both DOOM and DOOM II in a single package, new audio-reverberation, an all-new score of CD-quality music, colored lighting, new sound effects, and a handful of totally original levels, the Playstation’s initial DOOM outing is a memorable one, and a profound enough update for the other John of id, John Romero, to call it the “best DOOM yet," at the time of its release. Even the Playstation’s DOOM, though, with all of its special effects, failed to live up to the PC original in a number of ways. It was missing entire swaths of the campaigns, most of the story intermission screens, and much of the more computationally impressive geometry originally found in the majority of its levels had to be sanded down.It wasn’t until two years later, in 1997, that home console players saw a DOOM release that was, for the most part, an unmitigated parallel and expansion of the experience that gaming PC owners had been enjoying for four years, with the Nintendo 64 release of DOOM 64. Unlike the Playstation version of DOOM, though, DOOM 64 is an entirely new campaign of exclusively original levels. It has its own storyline and its own artstyle, and its designers were free to alter various aspects of the game’s mechanics to suit its target platform better. Like the Playstation’s DOOM, it kept all of the eye-catching special effects that had made that port so appealing, and seized on them to create set-pieces and environments that would have been impossible in the 1993 home computer release of DOOM. The architecture and geometry of this new DOOM defer to a consistent artistic vision, one which takes full advantage of colored lights and radial fog to evoke a murky, lived in feeling, echoing the effect that the dynamic, diminished lighting of the original games used to have, but with a bolder, more extant visual maturity.Beyond just the visuals, DOOM 64 offers the most balanced combat experience in any of these classic-style DOOM games. Despite its smaller monster pool, every single encounter feels well choreographed. The Doom Marine feels both heavier and nimbler under the joystick than he did on a keyboard, and the ferocity with which the game pits intersecting arrays of moving projectiles at him makes the added precision necessary and satisfying. This heavier movement and the somewhat truncated monster variety marry to form a mobile and surprisingly sadistic campaign. But much of this sadism comes not from the snarling hoards, but from the riddling, vexing level design. Tricks and traps abound, alongside arcane puzzles whose solutions are obscured by dimly arbitrated movement and opaque sequences of switch-presses. The stop-and-go pace that classic DOOM has always had has never been as staccato as it is here, but the gripping, dreary musical accompaniment and dreamily austere visuals match the carnage with the confusion with ease.It's no exaggeration to say this is the first time a DOOM game has cared so consistently about presentation and mood. I recall an uncommonly effective series of events in DOOM 1's third episode, “Inferno”, when the player peers through a series of slits in the wall overlooking a courtyard of tortured souls nailed to crosses. As they step forward to survey this view, an ambush of battle-hungry foes springs out from behind them. It's a mean and nightmarish kind of trick, and every single level of DOOM 64 evokes the same philosophy as that moment. Creepy environmental set-dressing, playful psychological trickery and atmospheric mood-building all wrap around the core of DOOM’s gameplay. Future evolutions of the DOOM IP would take these same emotions and principles and use new advances in game design and technology to evoke them in new ways, from DOOM 3 onward to DOOM Eternal. DOOM 64 was the first to do so, using admittedly similar technology and game design to create an expertly massaged experience with more a refined focus towards particular reactions.The narrative, too, feels more directed and considered than those of the previous DOOM releases. From the haunting sound of babies’ cries underscoring the main menu, to the Doom Marine’s plaguing nightmares, referenced in the game's manual, every aspect of the presentation deals with themes of cycles and rebirth. The initial setup of the levels reinforce this, with the Doom Marine literally being made to walk the halls he's already thoroughly conquered, while “the familiarity of the situation” is commented on directly in one of the games’ text screens. Even the demons themselves, already returning foes of a kind, are said to be reconstructed tissue taken from the fallen carcasses that littered past killing-fields. Ultimately, the Marine's descent becomes an ascent and he himself is reborn by the end of the game. The character arc within this game mirrors that of the player themselves across the entire DOOM franchise, and framing it as a sequel is another instance of rebirth.Despite taking place after DOOM II, DOOM 64 isn't exactly a sequel to DOOM II. It's more like DOOM told through the lens of Quake's moody dreamscapes than a properly forward-moving evolution of DOOM II’s design. It's a surprising and cerebral adventure designed to thrill and dull the player into a uniquely jittery fugue state which can only really be understood through experiencing it. It pulls the player into a meditative zone, reactive and yet still thinking critically. Like Quake, it positions the player as someone somewhere between Daedalus and Theseus—both the master of the maze and the victim of its bloodthirsty secrets. In another sense, it transforms the player into the Minotaur, tumbling through underground shadows, hunting for the sounds of nearby intruders, and tapping loose bricks to reveal hidden passageways, until eventually comes the Cyberdemon, like a real minotaur, and the vicious spell is reset.By its climax, the campaign does what no title in this franchise had done before, and sends the player off with a satisfying and deeply foreshadowed confrontation, one whose setup had been deeply woven into the entire campaign before it. It feels, in this way, like the entire game is the culmination of DOOM’s impact up to that point, a refinement and enhancement of the tones, textures and impressions that DOOM had carved out for itself. It was also kind of the last calling card for this brand of software-rendered first-person action, which the industry, with Quake, had largely begun to age past. With that new age came new priorities. Future installments in the franchise would pull from the varying expressions of DOOM’s legacy, in their own ways. But none of them would ever truly marry horror with triumph as maliciously or as gorgeously as Midway Game’s DOOM 64.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly wish I could like Doom 64 but something about this game takes all the fun and drains it away as you spend so much time back tracking and trying to find out where you need to go. I also had to play this game in window mode to avoid feeling sick from the movement. I wasn't a fan of keyboard and mouse so I did use a gamepad and it worked fine. No crashes or any issues like that thankfully.Overall, just not my thing even though I love Doom.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I'm reviewing a 25 year old game.If you like the classic early '90s Dooms like I do, this is more of that albeit without the fun thrash metal soundtrack (this soundtrack definitely veers more towards the "horror" side of Doom) and some lesser quality animations for the shotguns. The gameplay and gore is here though and it's definitely worth $5 and even more so for the $1 I got it for on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: An underrated gem!  Picked up as part of the Doom bundle and it is worth even the nominal part of the price that it cost.  I think with the sale discount and bundle discount, this game's share of the price came to only a dollar and some change.  I have this game on an old N64 and this version plays better.  They really cleaned up the graphics, which is nice for such an older Doom Game.  Works great with my Logitech controller for PC, but I'm sure mouse and other controllers work fine as well.  Only downside is no story, not even limited attempt.  I'm a few levels in and I don't understand the scenarios as being anything other than 'kill the monsters' which is fine for Doom.  Same guns as Doom franchise, but at this point there are no gun mods available, they added that for later games.  So in short, it is not Eternal/2016 but is fun solid gameplay and comparable to older Dooms.8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Nightdive, please add mouselook as an option.  Overall, if you're a fan of Doom 64 on the n64, you're going to like this port.  The textures look great, the polygon edges look great, movement and input looks great, and it doesn't take long to get over the missing mouselook feature.  Also, the lost levels were actually some of my favorite levels.  The switches and keys and monster spawning gets repetitive, but the level layout and design is some of the best in Doom 64 in my opinion.  Definitely worth $5.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly think this game doesn't get enough recognition as a DOOM game. Everybody be praising the classic DOOM 1 and 2 and as much as I respect classic games, it was nice to have a change in the atmosphere of the DOOM series. We all know and love the loud music that played while we were slaying demons by the tens, but in DOOM 64, that all changes. You are walking around in quiet hallways and lonely rooms, encountering only a few demons at a time, until you really start to get far in the game. And in the soundtrack, you can't hear very much except for the faint sounds of babies crying and such. The boss battle is either impossible or super easy, depending on my experience, but everyone else seems to have a much more realistic time trying to defeat it. All in all, you should definitely buy this game, especially for the base price it's at right now. If you can get it on discount, which I did at 90% off, you can even buy this game for 49 cents!!!

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 features the same objectives that have defined the series, and mostly the same awesome weapons. You have to go through dozens of levels, finding keys, shooting demons, pressing switches, and finding hidden weapons. Doom 64 is a memorable game that one can look fondly at years later. It's a great addition to the Doom series, however, don't expect modern controls or visual improvements. It's the same game with the same quirks as the original N64 version.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This game never fails to amuse me even playing it time and time again, either the original system, Doom64 EX or even this.This game was made for the PC, the old n64 controller was terrible and made it very difficult. But EX rolled around, a faithful recreation of the game, felt and played much like it. Even the old Hectic cheese remained the same. But it didnt have what 64 did, the engine. Amazing on what it did, but the 64 had a few actions that EX couldnt.I played on Watch Me Die! Difficulty, the big thing that comes with this is much harder mob masses. And 3 Cyberdemons prior to final level.... And Pain Elementals, like Doom 2.... CAN KISS MY ASS.The Lost Levels, the 2nd campaign was difficult in the right ways. First 2 levels aren't shy about the ammo, but after that it's lax, but then the mob encounters actually needing to use strategy instead of lul'zing around.I highly recommend this game. Both for fun, and competitive running. And if enough of the masses figure out, even creating usermade levels for it too. ;D
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid port of an often overlooked classic. But overall, it's a good time for people who like older shooter games. It also looks a bit nicer running on PC and all.

_childDocuments_.review: This game delivers. I never got a chance to play it on the N64 and I heard this game was always the basterd child of the DOOM series. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is so good and if it was released on PC back in the day it probably would have gotten the attention it deserves. _childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I was a day one owner of the Nintendo 64, and a huge Doom fan. But I don't think I realized back then that this version of Doom was unique. I must have assumed it was just the original game ported to N64.  Anyway, after all these decades, I played this game for the first time on Steam. It's a great addition to the Doom franchise. I can't believe I almost missed out on it. I also would have expected this to be a watered down version made for a younger audience, but no, this is more brutal and difficult than the original. It also has an eerie soundtrack that can be quite unnerving at times. Playing with Mouse/Keyboard is almost cheating as I'm sure this was way more challenging on the N64 controller, but I had a blast going through this game. To get 100% achievements you will almost certainly need to get some online help to find all the secrets, as they are hidden better in this game than any other Id Software title. It must have taken years to find them all back in the day.Tech-wise since I never played the original, I had to find some YouTube footage to compare. As expected this port is fantastic. It preserves the look and feel of the original, but adds support for modern hardware with high frame rates and high resolution and widescreen support. I give this an A+ and super glad it showed up on Steam and that I didn't skip it again.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to play Doom Eternal but I thought I'd wait until the price comes down a little, in the meantime I decided to try Doom 64, a game I never had a chance to play before and never bothered to find out how to play or emulate. This game is awesome, just a solid old school shooter with a creepy environment, music and a true 'Doom' feeling. I really enjoyed playing throughout the whole campaign, I even feel like this is right there on the same level as Doom 1 and 2, this could even become my new favorite. There's one thing that I didn't like at first and that was the fact that the game relies a lot on pressing switches that open doors or areas on the map that keep you coming back and forth all over the map, however this is a feature that I felt made this game unique and just appreciated the map design. I recommend this game to anybody who's looking for a solid old school FPS.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: You'd be surprised how well this game has aged even without mods. The only thing lacking is the oomph in the weapons. These classic fps games have immersion levels at 100%. Not in a way that is "realistic" - but in a way that you feel you just got put in a world and you have to figure out a way to solve things. You don't get that feeling with modern games with "triggers", but oh well, at least we have nice graphics.Doom is a mindless shooter, some idiots say. The same idiots who never played the game and watched a gameplay clip where you see a nameless guy shooting demons. What they don't see is the maze-puzzle-like level design which you cannot beat unless you actually use your brain to memorize segments and have above average navigational skills - something lacking in current gen video games. Not to mention how the combat has a strategic element to it as well.Great game.  Def worth a buy. Recommend using a controller on this game. IF you don't have a controller, use only keyboard - just like classic Doom games  were designed for (unless you mod it). Because Doom 64 was developed for the Nintendo 64 console - which didn't even have a decent analog stick. So playing with the mouse n kb even on the highest difficulty is too easy and breaks the balance. And not being able to look up or down while using a mouse feels extremely weird too, so I recommend playing the game the way it was intended to be.As for the port, it's awesome. Unlocked framerates, FOV slider, ultrawide  - it's awesome. I hope they do the same with classic Doom 1 and 2.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this on the old Nintendo 64 in the past, as well as the modified version called "Brutal DOOM 64" which I downloaded for free from another website where you can download Brutal DOOM games from. However this edition on Steam gives you easier controls, especially the most convenient key bindings for satisfying gameplay, I didn't realize first when re-visiting the dark atmospheric world of DOOM 64 thanks to the dark and creepy soundtrack composed by Aubrey Hodges, how much this PC experience drew me in. This edition of DOOM 64 has the gameplay from the original N64 exclusive release as well as the lost levels I think, once you complete the game or maybe it's available once you start a new game? Anyways, It's a blast to play. I would definitely recommend to not just hardcore Doom fans, but anyone who likes retro shooters. I do like the 1993 Doom and Doom II also but Doom 64 is definitely alot of fun and it's only sad that this particular game did not receive a sequel after its 1997 release on the Nintendo 64.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Good atmosphere, with the moody lighting and ambient music. The sprites look wack compared to Classic Doom, but the game itself is a fun romp, with the improvements in the engine allowing for more creative level design. The Lost Levels is fine, with one later stage taking forever to clear, but it's a trade-off for probably one of the better final levels in the official releases.5/5.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Now. this game is the ONLY DOOM game (thusfar) to make me use a walkthrough, and it was on the FIRST map, sure this could be boiled down to a me problem, but still. anyways, the graphics look nice-ish, the enemies look pretty cool. but the thing that i HATE most about this game is there's no DOOM guy face in the HUD. its still alright tho. 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Listen up, maggots. DOOM 64 has arrived on PC, and let me tell you, it's a bloodbath. You wanna know what's awesome about this game? EVERYTHING. The weapons, the enemies, the levels – it's all pure carnage, and I love it.Now, let's talk about the weapons. You got your classic favorites like the shotgun and chaingun, but there are some new toys to play with too. The plasma rifle will melt your enemies' faces off, and the Unmaker is like a Swiss Army knife of demonic destruction. And don't even get me started on the BFG 9000. That thing is like a nuclear bomb in a gun, and it's my personal favorite.Speaking of enemies, DOOM 64 doesn't disappoint. You got your usual suspects – imps, demons, and whatnot – but there are some new faces too. The nightmare imps are a real pain in the ass, and the motherdemon will make you regret ever stepping foot in hell. But no matter how tough the enemies are, I've got a solution: just rip and tear until it's done.The levels in DOOM 64 are dark, moody, and just plain badass. There's a real sense of atmosphere that sets this game apart from the rest of the DOOM series. And let's not forget the music – it's like a heavy metal concert in hell, and I'm the headliner.Now, some of you might say that DOOM 64 is too hard, too brutal, too unforgiving. Well, let me tell you something, weaklings: that's the whole point. This game isn't for the faint of heart. It's for those of us who like to get our hands dirty – and covered in demon blood.In conclusion, DOOM 64 on PC is a must-play for anyone who loves fast-paced, gory action. It's like a symphony of violence, and I'm the conductor. So strap on your armor, grab your weapons, and get ready to show these demons who's boss. It's time to rip and tear, until it is done.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: After a full playthrough of this game, here is my verdict.Awesome installation of the DOOM series. Everything feels satisfying. The guns, the pickups, killing enemies. Not exactly like the first 2 DOOMs, but still acceptable.The atmosphere is great. The music creates an incredibly unsettling feel the entire time, and while a lot of players are bummed about the lack of badass guitar riffs, I think it fits perfectly.Now, my complaint. Remember how I said that this game is satisfying, well this part isn't. I got real tired of the whole "oh, press this button to open a door, then strafe to the opposite side of the map in order to go through said door!" It got INCREDIBLY mind-numbing very fast, and ruined a lot of my enjoyment. Even the original DOOM's puzzles were less bs.I digress, the rest of this game makes up for this flaw. While I prefer DOOM 1 and 2 better than this, this is still an experience worth trying. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is my second favorite Doom game in the series and I love (almost) everything about it. From the more grim/Gothic artstyle, to the ambiance, enemy design, and I liked the Unmaker (and the "what the #### is this" joke is kinda cute, had the game had more jokes it perhaps could've been more like Postal 1?) and the level design is great (mostly the og levels, the new "lost" levels are.... just rehashes of the already existing ones but it's fine), just wish opening the map would show how many kills, secrets and pick-ups we've got. It's not a flawless game (damn you Lost Souls and Pain Elementals) but it's worth it, especially since Doom 64 did manage to capture almost everything that ID wanted the original Doom to be.Edit: Finally got 64(.1) hours on this game, my opinion hasn't really changed all that much.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun! Despite the game's age, the soundscape alone still makes some of the later levels really feel like you're in hell (you can hear the souls of the damned scream in agony). It's a simple game that isn't very long if you just want to go through the main 28 levels, so it is easy to just pick it up and play through it. The achievements will get you to play all the main and secret levels on the highest difficulty + the exclusive new levels, so I am taking a stab at earning those right now.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: If, like me, you still enjoy the old Doom games (or the remastered versions at least), then this is a very good continuation of that formula.The new modernised controls are excellent. Just like 'DOOM Classic Complete' on PS3, this game lets you use the left stick for movement and strafing and the right stick for turning. Both are fully analogue inputs so you can adjust your movement speed, strafing speed and turning speed in real-time (I don't know how much of this was included in the original). You can also use the left trigger to interact so you don't have to move your thumbs off the sticks.The updated graphics look really good on my 1920x1080 monitor, while still retaining the retro style of the original. It's not 'true HD' but it looks like it's been upscaled to some degree.Nightdive Studios always do fantastic work when updating '90s games, and this is another example of that.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Despite its flaws, this game is a masterpiece.Pros:- Fully remastered N64 title- An absolute blast to play!- A classic Doom title, one that longtime fans and newcomers to the series should experience- Tough but extremely rewardingCons:- Level design sucks; may cause frustration- It takes FOREVER to get through the publisher/dev logos upon booting up the game- Tough but extremely rewarding
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: LOOK UP A GUIDE BEFORE PLAYING THIS GAME.I like this game, and I really wish I loved it, but it has some serious flaws. On the bright side, the visuals, sound design, and gameplay are great! UNFORTUNATELY the game is let down by terrible puzzle design and a final boss that docks a whole point off the rest of the game. Imagine a Marauder from DOOM Eternal but faster, MUCH stronger, and has a ludicrous damage output thanks to multiple simultaneous rapid-fire high damage homing attacks. You're supposed to access three secret levels to acquire weapon upgrades and special keys needed to make the final level 90% easier so you can save all your resources for the boss. Of course the game NEVER EXPLAINS THIS TO YOU, YOU JUST HAVE TO KNOW. If you don't go out of your way to do this, the final level consists of a tidal wave of demons (actually a pretty fun, lengthy battle- a worthy finale) followed by the aforementioned boss fight, by which point you will almost certainly have little to no health and ammo, and will be reduced to dust by the boss' attacks in no joke about four seconds. Good game, could've been great if the devs hadn't decided to just troll the players but I guess 90s gaming was developed by sociopaths.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: After years of waiting we've finally received an official port of Doom 64!  Ever since I played this game on my N64 back in 2015 I knew I wanted it on PC.  This game is an absolutely phenomenal throwback to the style of FPS titles that were prevalent in the mid-90s.  The port of the game was handled very well as the developers did not tamper with the game's original rendition.  Obvious care was put into providing the best possible experience by including an absolutely flawless controller support.  This allows for the game to be played the way it was meant to be back in '97.  Boasting unique graphics and possessing a wonderfully ambient atmosphere, Doom 64 has stood the test of time.  I would highly recommend it to both Doom fans and retro gamers alike.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A criminally underrated Doom game, the atmosphere and music are amazing, gameplay is the most varied in comparison to DOOM II, while it´s tone is more like Quake than Doom with the monster designs and castles and weapon designs, it´s still a great Doom game and this is definitely the way you want to play Doom 64 because this game hasn´t aged well with that weird N64 control scheme.9/10 - COD is temporary but DOOM is Eternal.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I really really tried to enjoy this game, however, I got completely disappointed from it. Technically speaking it's not a bad game, but as a DOOM game is really mediocre in many ways (Personally) Let me explain this in a small summarise of everything. The whole ambience tries to give you a scary setting, but I honestly don't know how's that supposed to happen when at the same time gives you like 7 different weapons and you're essentially a unstoppable force. The music is almost gone for somehow? one of the most iconic things related to doom are its soundtracks, most of them violent and catchy, but here's just weird noises at the background (yes i know, there's plenty of them at the original ones, but it's just a part of the soundtrack, and not the whole of it) Considering this was released after and not before QUAKE, in terms of graphics is really disappointing (I'm aware that making anything work on a Nintendo 64 is no joke, and that's exactly my point, why?) the levels felt way too compressed, the enemies' sprites are way less menacing than before, and many animations were cut (even the super shotgun one is missing) and the levels are unnecessarily frustrating, in the first 2 games, the traps were supposed to be used to challenge those who wanted to look out for secrets, and here, they're literally everywhere, most of them unskippable, and at the other hand, most of the levels are just running mindlessly from point A to point B hoping to find what's the button doing when you press it. I really tried, but I didn't liked this one.

_childDocuments_.review: People keep saying it's some sort of "forgotten cult classics" and stuff.You know - maybe there are reasons it is "forgotten". Don't get me wrong - it's still DooM and more DooM is always welcome. There are certain problems with 64 though. Pretty serious problems.Do you remember monsters from classic? Pixelated they were nonetheless hellishly elegant both in looks and animations. There was weight in all of their movements. Why-oh-why did they changed the design for 64? Say what you want - the game is ugly. Fight me on that, I dare you. The engine was upgraded, yes. Now it can do 3D bridges and colored lights. Skyboxes were redone. And with all these possibilities for God only knows why, 64 is dark, brown and look more like Quake 1 in terms of both color and level design. And not in a good way.Same goes to gameplay. 64 has some built-in scripting system that allows more tricks (yes and traps too). This is good, right? Well, yes. At the same time everything became slower. And I can't say it's a complement. They nerfed the BFG! Can you imagine that?As for the music and level design... Well, there are some undoubtedly cool moments in levels. Overall it's mostly "castles in water full of hellknights". Music... Someone on youtube commented one of the tracks for then upcoming Eternal as "It's just noise". 64's OST is noise. Literally. One could say it's atmospheric ambient. Yeah, on a technical level... Sort of. You know what? Quake 1 did the same trick and did it so much better.Why recommend then? There's a certain charm in 64. It's ugly, slow, basically has no music, castle themed but still charming for some reason. It's "forgotten classic" not because of the platfrom it was released on back in the days or unfitting name. It has problems. It's still DooM. And it would take extreme effort to really break the DooM formula.

_childDocuments_.review: So, Doom 64. To be honest, I'd probably give this a neutral review if I could, but between positive and negative, I’m leaning more towards negative. So why is that?Well, to start with the positives, it’s nice to see the ID tech 1 engine in its final form, with lots of fancy features that we didn’t see in the original DOOM games. It’s also nice that we got one last hurrah of classic-style DOOM before we moved on to DOOM 3. It’s also incredible that we’re finally able to play a DOOM game on PC that was until now (fan mods aside) locked to the Nintendo 64. Personally, I was very excited to learn that DOOM 64 wasn’t a simply yet another port of DOOM as the name might suggest, but a whole, brand-new DOOM game! But as to the game itself… There’s a lot I didn’t like about it. To start with what I see as the game’s biggest issue, the complete shift in focus as to how the levels are designed compared to the original DOOM games. A lot has been said about DOOM 64’s focus on puzzles and traps compared to the original, but in reality, 95% of these “puzzles” all involve hitting switches. Enter a new room but can’t see how this new room helps you progress in the level? Surprise! There’s a hidden switch you need to press! Most likely, on one of the many pillars in the room! But by far, the worst of these switch “puzzles” are the ones that involve hitting a switch which opens up a room God knows where, because it’s usually on the other side of the map and you can’t see or hear where this door is. So, your only choice is to hit the switch, then wander aimlessly around the level until you stumble upon an area that looks new. The game uses this “puzzle” CONSTANTLY, often multiple times in the same level. It creates a lot of backtracking, and it feels like blatant padding. People often complain about classic DOOM's levels being too maze-like, but the amount of wandering around and backtracking in DOOM 64 ends up creating similar levels of annoyance. Similarly, are the switch puzzles that also involve timing, where the door will close again if too much time has passed. While the original DOOM games used this type of switch puzzle too, it was only ever for secret areas, as opposed to DOOM 64 which uses them as part of progressing the level.As to the infamous traps, to be honest, they feel cheap at the best of times. You’d expect them to be punishment for failing or maybe getting greedy, but in many cases, you’re required to trigger them in order to progress the level. And a lot of them involve simply confining the player then spamming them with projectiles until a timer runs out. How much damage you wind up taking being a total roll of the dice. They are sorta neat, in that we never really saw anything like this in the original DOOM, but overall, they’re more annoying than anything else.Another big change that I’m not a fan of is a reduced focus on combat. There are now far fewer enemies compared to the hordes of demons in the original, with a much significantly larger percent of the level is now spent on wandering around. There’s only one point in the game that I can recall anything close to the scale that was in the original DOOM, and that’s literally in the last level just before the final boss battle.In terms of design and gameplay, I swear it looks like the DOOM 64 devs chose to focus on the weakest part of the original DOOM. That is, wandering around an empty level with no enemies to kill because you can’t find the thing you need to open the next part of the level. Another big change that I’m not a fan of is the presentation. Yes, the game is more technically-impressive compared to the original DOOM, but a lot of the design choices are a backwards step. While the modelling and detail on DOOM 64’s weapon sprites do look nice, (most of the time, an improvement over original DOOM’s weapon sprites), the animations and sounds make DOOM 64’s arsenal feel weak and puny compared to the originals. For example, original DOOM’s shotgun didn’t feel powerful just because it did a lot of damage, but because the animations and sounds sold its power. The firing animation showed it kicking like a mule, accompanied by a mighty “BOOM!” and crisp “KA-CHUCK!” as Doomguy pumped it. The animation depicting this action, of course, shows Doomguy fiercely slamming the pump back because this is a beast of a weapon that needs to be wrangled like a wild stallion! DOOM 64’s shotgun by comparison barely moves when it’s fired and pumped, and the sound it produces is more of a sad muffled fart than an explosion. It still takes down enemies just as well as the original, but it doesn’t “feel” powerful like the original shotgun. Pretty much all of DOOM 64’s weapons suffer from this issue, which makes me wonder if this truly was what the designers intended, or if it might have been a limitation imposed by the Nintendo 64. Weak muffled audio is definitely a common problem with the N64 at least. And speaking of the audio, it’s not great here either. While some of the sound effects are the same as the original DOOM, the ones they used for the replacements aren’t really improvements. For example, the health pickup is that generic sci-fi “VWOOM” sound effect that was used EVERYWHERE in movies and games from the late 90s. And while I respect their decision to use ambient music in service to enhancing DOOM 64’s dark atmosphere, it’s a tough act to follow considering how great original DOOM’s music was!But back to the new replacement sound effects, the new monster sounds are rather samey. It’s not like in the original DOOM where each monster (well, save for processed soldiers and shotgun guys) had their own, very distinctive sound associated with them that let the player know exactly who was around and what they’re currently doing. Also, for some baffling reason, they did reuse the “monster spotted player” effect from original DOOM, but it’s now used for “monster idling”. Not only does this make no sense (the monster stands around constantly roaring) but it’s needlessly confusing for players of the original DOOM.And on the topic of monsters, the new CGI sprites really don’t look great, with them often looking like they’re made from clay. Which is rather ironic, since a number of the monster sprites in original DOOM were digitized photos of actual clay models. The animation also looks stiff, and the monsters don't move very much. Which is again, ironic, since a number of original DOOM’s monster sprites were based on clay models. In conclusion, while DOOM 64 is based on classic DOOM’s DNA, which should make it an awesome game, the changes they decided to make hurt the game more than they improve it. And I don’t think that’s simply me as a “boomer shooter” pish-poshing because they changed stuff from how it was in classic DOOM. As I said at the beginning of my review, these changes feel like they were made by focusing on the weaker aspects of classic DOOM, which is the exact wrong way to go about improving on a game. Maybe if you’ve never played any of the original DOOM games and you were unaware of these differences, your experience with DOOM 64 might not be tarnished. I’ve heard the game is popular with people who never played any of the original games. If that’s you, by all means! Try the game out, you might love it! But fans of the original DOOM probably won’t be head-over-heels for DOOM 64. It’s worth playing for one final serving of a game that’s pretty similar to classic DOOM (I finished the game after all) but overall, I felt the game was a disappointment, that was far more steps backwards than it was forwards.

_childDocuments_.review: Few franchises can boast Doom’s staying power, at least on PC. You’ve got your  (1993) and , both of which feel fun and fresh to play even today. On the other hand,  (2016) and  did for boomer shooters what  and  did for first-person horror walking simulators back in the day – meaning, everyone’s doing it now! Honestly, it seems like in whichever generation a couple of Doom games crop up, they can’t help but be massively influential and universally praised.Sure, there was a lull in there that lasted for, what, a decade? A bit more? But even , as polarizing as it was to cause it, was regarded as a success by critics and, if anything, a decent survival-horror experience by fans. Its departure from the fast, run-and-gun style of gameplay that boomer shooters are known for – and even more so in recent years – was disappointing to many, but honestly? I feel like Id Software did the right thing by not continuing down that road; not until they were prepared for some more innovation, at least.  Released back in 1997 and developed by the now-defunct Midway Games,  wasn’t just a port of the smash hit to Nintendo’s console, but somewhat of a re-imagining as well. Most notable – and this is what you’ll frequently see the game praised for – is the oppressive and claustrophobic atmosphere. No, you aren’t blasting demons with heavy metal music playing in the background. Instead, you’ve got an assortment of ambient tracks, made up of spooky-sounding strings, ominous chanting, and crying babies. Yes, really. Paired with a grittier take on  classic visuals, and gloomy lighting, it allows for the shooter to be played from an entirely different perspective where, in addition to running and gunning, you’ll be carefully crawling through maze-like levels, unnerved to your limits, checking every corner for enemies, where an Imp or a Hell Knight might be lying in wait.It’s amazing how big of a shift in perspective can be achieved with a different soundtrack and some tweaks to what are, essentially, the same assets from the previous titles in the franchise. Some of the enemies and weapons have gotten their sound effects reworked as well, with the new ones being a lot more appropriate. The Chaingun sounds beefy as all living hell, while the Imps no longer screech like a pissed-off donkey.-  😱So, with it being a re-imagining, you won’t be playing through the original lineup of  levels. Instead, you’re offered 31 completely new ones (not counting those unlocked through in-game secrets), taking you through both the heavily industrialized sci-fi bases as well as the labyrinthine depths of Hell. The enemy roster includes most of the enemies from the previous two games (as well as a few surprises that I won’t spoil) while excluding a couple from the second one. In all other things, it’s classic Doom to a fault.When  at its best, you’ll be inching through Hell’s hallways, taking in the ambiance and carefully listening for where danger might lurk; checking corners and bracing yourself every time you open a door. Or, in those areas that are a bit more open (and aren’t under-represented in the game by any means), you’ll be running around, performing the necessary ‘dance’ needed to best each enemy, dodging out of their attacks and swiftly cycling through your arsenal, picking the appropriate weapon from moment to moment as the ever-changing tides of battle force you to mix things up. Need to deal with a bunch of shotgun-wielding zombies before closing in? Gun ‘em down from afar with your Chaingun. Got a couple of hard hitters, like the Mancubus, thrown in there as well? Quickly get your rocket launcher out and blow ‘em up before they can do the same to you. Did a swarm of Lost Souls just spawn in behind you? Swap to your BFG and obliterate them with a single click. This is Doom as you and I know it and love it, even with the movement being somewhat clunky and getting you occasionally stuck on things.The problem is - we’ve been playing Doom for years. We aren’t some kid in the ‘90s who never got a chance to experience it previously because it was not released on their console of choice. We’ve already played the best it has to offer, and I don’t think a change in perspective, a new weapon, and a bunch of fresh, but mostly unremarkable maps are enough to not make  a bit redundant. Add on to that the fact of there being no modding support, and you’ve got yourself the most dated, albeit most faithful to the original experience, game in the series.  There are other things that frustrate me, but these might be either unreasonable to hold against a game this old or too much dependent upon personal preference; like the way sprites turn with the camera. What I wouldn’t give for some voxels, as it’d save me from having to look at Imp ass every time a dead one enters my field of view. Or how there’s no way to zoom out on the map, making it useless for finding your way around unless you just want to consult it regarding your immediate surroundings. Sure, you don’t need it to find your way around, but my guess is that I’d have saved plenty of time hunting for door switches if it was actually usable. And don’t get me started on some of the traps there are that can cause nearly unavoidable, cheap deaths. Pfft! Oh, and the Lost Soul? It’s not okay. It attacks too fast and the time of its pre-attack phase is like half a frame! We can’t keep pretending that it’s this one enemy that’s just annoying to deal with, but still cute in a certain ‘love to hate it’ kind of way. It is not okay!!! And the fact that it can deal damage even when it’s above you, where you can’t hit it, because each entity’s hitbox extends infinitely upwards? Ugh!  I felt like I was done by level 17, which is a bit more than halfway through a game that took me almost 20 hours to beat on the second-highest difficulty, ‘I Own Doom’ (because I do, it says so in my library). The repetitiveness of fighting the same enemies over and over while not changing up the level design philosophy that much had gotten to me. After all, I can’t hunt around forever for door switches, keys, and the doors those switches opened. It should also be kept in mind that it’s possible to mod the entirety of  into , with all the other quality-of-life benefits modding can provide, such as vertical mouse look (and voxels). So, maybe, unless you’re looking for a curated, “true-to-the-nineties” experience, or just want to showcase some achievements on your profile, then sit this one out? If you just want to play a classic Doom game, or just want more classic Doom, you can get that elsewhere.  I get that muddies my recommendation a little bit – but It’s still a recommendation, more so for the qualities  inherits from the previous Doom titles and then the way it applies its own charms to them, than those charms alone.

_childDocuments_.review: Better than Doom 3 which is for orange boomers. Doom 64 is pretty much what happens when you get ID Software, Nintendo, and a team of basically DOOM and Quake nerds in the same room in 1997, while telling them "hey we're totally not just going to market this ♥♥♥♥ as a port but please make a totally original, official sequel to DOOM 2 and DOOM 1 exclusively for this...*unveils monstrosity* thing."Doom 64 introduced a variety of mechanics, ideas, and enemies to the series that were used later on in both the new reboots of the series.
