_childDocuments_.review: Back in 1997, DOOM 64 was surrounded by 2 blockbusters: Quake which was already rocking, and GoldenEye 007 which was a few months away. What exacerbated the competition more, was its repression due to N64's unpopularity and insubstantial capabilities; back then, this made people not batting an eye on the new sequel of DOOM—there is a reason for calling this game the DOOM game you've never played. As a matter of fact, it is the only DOOM game that was not developed by ID Software but was made under their supervision by Midway Studios. Nearly 23 years later, Nightdive Studios bought this relic into life for DOOM fans to rip and tear in HD.As a DOOM game, it stays loyal to the tradition by including a plot to fill the space. The entire story is presented through cool text on different slides between some levels after completing them; the game doesn't go far from the classic narration of stories in video games. In short, there are no twists or anything interesting that can capture the player's attentiveness. Anyway, who cares! It's a DOOM game, where your shotgun is the story and its bullets are the twists.Armed with a ruinous armament, all the player has to do is kill everything first and kill everything later. The customary is well-preserved in DOOM 64 by having the same mechanics as the originals. In terms of brutality, it stands on a higher stage compared to its predecessors. The Unmaker is a new weapon in DOOM 64 that fires laser beams and shares ammo with the BFG9000 and the Plasma Rifle. The weapon has 3 artifacts that the player can collect to unlock its full potential. Piece of advice, be sure to know the exact levels that have the artifacts, as if you miss an artifact, you have to go back to that level where you missed it to collect it and move on from that particular level again.The main theme of DOOM 64 levels lean toward being dark, atmospheric, and grim. It blindly follows the same route as the originals in terms of level design; in contrast, they only differ in the main theme. Low resources in the game are well-utilized by dispensing brilliant map designs in addition to adding distinguishing combos of strategically allocated enemies with bosses to plummet the boredom factor. There isn't a genuine level select option in the menu, but there is a hidden level called Hectic; after completing this level the proper way, a new option will unlock in the main menu of the game called the Features Menu. This option unlocks all the levels of the game, all maps, all weapons/ammo, and all cheats.The preponderance of replayability in DOOM 64 is in digging secrets, playing hidden maps, and finding Easter Eggs. In the re-release, Nightdive Studios included a set of missions called The Lost Levels; these levels act as a link between DOOM 64 and DOOM 2016. Including a multiplayer mode or any other new mode could've remarkably pumped up the replay value, especially that this is a repackage. An option of showcasing the player's progress within the game instead of the temporary one we get after completing a level would've been great. Lastly, I don't see any excuse for the limited save slots.True-hearted fans of DOOM 64 did their best through modding and emulating to bring it under the radar; their remarkable effort was enough for it to run on other platforms but was inadequate in optimizing it. Thanks to Nightdive Studios, DOOM 64 runs on modern hardware in HD like a cutting knife in a block of butter. A vital handicap in the original release is the dim lighting; the player can hardly see anything in certain areas of the game. In the re-release, the illumination is improved; however, the player may need to crank up the brightness in some parts of the game.I like the nostalgic control scheme of FPS classics, despite it being weird. For those who aren't familiar with this style, in brief, the vertical movement of the weapon is restrained, and the player must rely on the protagonist's movements to have the enemies in range. By words, this sounds arduous, but in action, it's a lot better. I can assuredly say that the controls are very fluid and perfectly abolish most of the drawbacks of the aforementioned control style. Sadly, navigation can get a bit irritating in tight situations, especially while doing timed, pitch-perfect platforming. I find the key-bindings option in the menu vexatious; the reason for this is the unification of gamepad and keyboard controls in the same menu.Due to N64 hardware limitations, the turning wheel got stuck in terms of visual aggrandizement. this lead to the diminution of DOOM 64 among the ambitious titles in that time. The irony is that nowadays, this serves the game quite well in terms of triggering a wistful smile by presenting retro graphics through HD display. The visual style in DOOM 64 sway away from being DOOM to being Quake; it has the foundation of DOOM and the tone of Quake—this may upset some fans. Fortunately, its gory and dark visuals serve its atmospheric setting.The sound design in DOOM 64 doesn't differ a lot from its predecessors but with minor enhancements like hearing empty shells hitting the ground after firing the shotgun despite the missing animations of reloading the super shotgun and cocking the ordinary one. Also, new enemies come with their unique sounds. To match the creepy environment and increase the bone-chilling factor, DOOM 64 soundtrack took a different path from the heavy metal style to a more ambient approach.The re-release of DOOM 64 is set to be a sterling example of experiencing the past in HD. After being free from the chains holding it in the Nintendo's exclusivity, it's a decent opportunity to have the complete collection and the total experience of the DOOM universe. Sadly, some aging wrinkles of DOOM 64 were hard to patch by Nightdive Studios. In summation, they did a splendid job!

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 on the N64 was a game that I couldn't really get into. The galaga shaped controller really made it difficult to enjoy even simple movement puzzles, and the visuals on the system, though for the time definitely nice, didn't sit well with me. I passed Doom 64 to the side for a long time, opting to play Doom 1 and 2 through mods and what not instead.Now that Doom 64 has been properly, OFFICIALLY, ported to the PC, and I finally put in the effort to play this game and beat it, I can easily say that Doom 64 is now one of my favorite Doom games. This, this game right here, is the true Doom 3, which is funny considering that it was originally made by Midway but whatever.Using the right settings, Doom 64 can look quite crisp (though it does make enemies look a little weird up close). The guns are meaty and pack a punch; you can feel the kick of the super shotgun. The music, though I would have preferred it to be the over the top head banging metal Doom is known for, is a welcome addition to the game and lends Doom 64 a different feel than Doom 1 and 2.Also, I cannot wait for mods to appear so that all the missing monsters may return; like a mod that differentiates the Zombiemen from the Shotgunners would be fantastic, because base Doom 64 does not show the difference (due to the hardware limitations of the N64 of course).If you like Doom, get Doom 64 (you probably already do since you pre-ordered Doom Eternal ;D ). If you like old-school FPS games, get Doom 64. If you own Doom 64 and have not played Doom 64 because you're too busy playing Doom Eternal...

The sprite work holds up relatively well despite its age, and because of that aforementioned age, you can run this game on a walnut strapped to a 9V battery.This game also marks the first of only two appearances of the Unmaker(Unmaykr in DE), a weapon that leaves you asking a most preposterous but frightening question: Why did Satan need a gun?

_childDocuments_.review: Why are so many people praising this as a wonderful port?  20 minutes in and I'm still on the first level because I just can not seem to get key binds to remap correctly.  Not to mention the key map menu intermittently flashes between keyboard and game-pad binds (annoying at best). The worst part, the game doesn't show updated binds most of the time.  So if you want to open doors with spacebar, and the game originally uses E, you remap it to spacebar and the game still reads E as the mapping, even though spacebar is now the key bind.  Then, after 2 or 3 minutes of gameplay, it "remembers" the original bind and your back in the menu remapping to spacebar, again.Also has sprint always been this sluggish in Doom 64?  I originally played cartridge Doom 64, and re-played on an emulator back in 2012-ish, and I don't remember sprint being this slow, or taking as much time to reach max velocity.  Could just be my memory failing me though.I really do hope these issues get addressed as I love this game a lot, and had hopes that this re-release might bring some attention to the heavily under rated gem that is Doom 64.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't care what Hugo Martin says, Doom 64 is the worst classic Doom game.Let's start with level design. Pathfinding has always been a part of Doom's level design. Even in Doom 1 & 2, sometimes you'd come across a locked door and need to find the key, sometimes there were multiple pathways available to you, etc. In Doom 64, that's every level, all the time, and to a degree that Doom 1 & 2 never hit. At least once per level I'll find a random switch, press it, hear the door opening noise from somewhere in the level, and now I need to go find which inconspicuous section of wall was actually the door that just opened up. Sometimes doors or keys won't open up / appear until you've stepped into a certain area of the map, and of course no indication is given for this, sometimes you just return to a previous area and see that it's changed. There's a lot of running around like a chicken with its head cut off trying to find the way forward / trying to find what just changed when you hit that switch / etc. This experience isn't helped by the new musical style. The soundtrack is all "atmospheric" ambient tracks, which expose the pathfinding and backtracking for the tedious busywork it really is. In Doom 1 & 2, at least you got to jam out to some copyright-infringing MIDI metal while you hunted for keys and secret switches.Let's talk about encounter design next. Doom 1 & 2 are essentially first-person bullet hell games. Lots of enemies on screen throwing lots of projectiles at you. Doom 64 can't do that, thanks to the memory limitations of the N64. The number of enemies that can be loaded in at any one time is much lower than Doom 1 & 2. The designers have tried to compensate by frequently using more difficult enemies - you'll see a lot more Barons, Mancubi, Arachnotrons, etc. than you ever did in Doom 1 & 2 - but because you move so fast, those encounters aren't actually challenging. It's really not hard to circle strafe around a group of Barons and dodge all their projectiles. The encounters are punishing, because those projectiles hurt a lot, but they're not hard. The other way the designers have tried to compensate is by upping the number of ambushes. Like pathfinding, ambushes have always played a part in classic Doom, but, like pathfinding, here it's cranked up to an annoying degree. Walk into a room and suddenly 10 Lost Souls spawn in. Open a door and there are three shotgun guys on the other side who immediately blast you. Even if it kills you, it's only artificially difficult - once you reload the game, the ambush loses all challenge, because the only challenge came from the surprise, which is now gone.The result is a game that's mind-numbingly dull 90% of the time thanks to the low enemy numbers and excessive backtracking. I have a number of problems with the things that Doom 2 adds to Doom 1, but it's still fundamentally more of the same. Same engine, same assets, same design team behind it. It made me rage in places, but I played all the way to the end. Doom 64 is the first classic Doom game that I actively don't want to play. Playing it is just a drag; I'm bored out of my mind 90% of the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Contrary to popular belief Doom 64 isn't an N64 port of the original Doom, this game is actually a full on sequel, taking place directly after the events of Doom 2 with a completely new campaign, so in a way Doom 64 is the true Doom 3. Doom 64 feels a lot like Doom 2, but with a complete graphics overhaul. Instead of the bright colorful look Doom 2 had, they went for more of a dark and gritty look, in some ways the game resembles Quake more than it does Doom to be honest. Gameplay is nearly identical to Doom 2 however but there is a new weapon added to the mix, an alternative to the BFG called the "Unmaker", and it's pretty fun to use.The soundtrack and general atmosphere is completely different too, there's no actual music within levels anymore, instead you'll be hearing creepy ambient tracks as you walk down dimly lit corridors, Doom 64 has an atmosphere that feels like something out of a horror game, and I kinda dig it. If you like Doom 2 chances are you'll like Doom 64 as well, there's also a brand new episode added in with this version of the game and I think it's worth picking up for that alone.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: While there are some shortcomings that most likely come about from the restrictions of the N64 the game was designed for, Nightdive has performed art by creating such a fantastic port for DOOM 64.The level design compared to the previous DOOM installments is, overall, a great improvement, in part from experience and also from the advancements to the engine allowing for greater verticality and more dynamic environmental effects. The lighting and aesthetics of the game are impeccable and make the game really stand out for an N64 game. Dark, gothic, with a wide colour palette helps keep things feeling fresh, even when the same assets are reused. Shoutout to Aubrey Hodges for the one of the creepiest game OSTs I've heard in my entire life. Really damn good.Buy this game full price or on sale. Either way, experiencing the game is worth whatever cost you pay.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like other DOOM games then this is definitely more of it. Its got a lot of levels and all the classic enemies and weapons you'd expect as well as secrets and all that. Pretty good but it does have some issues.First of all even on easy difficulty the enemies do a lot of damage and some are bullet sponges which can be annoying. The super shotgun doesn't have a reload animation so that sucks. The delay between shots with the shotguns is way too much. Weapon switching is too slow. Lost Souls and Pain Elementals attack way too frequently. When walking down stairs you can't stop half way you just slide all the way down which is annoying. Some parts of levels feel like the devs made them like that to troll you, such as a lava pit that is impossible to get out of without restarting the level. Trying to rebind controls seems a bit glitchy. You lose all your weapons when you die so if you aren't saving you're not gonna have a good time. Sometimes when you shoot it does more damage and other times it doesn't do enough which is odd. The final boss is ridiculously unbalanced and is basically impossible to defeat if you don't use the BFG. The biggest issue with the game of course is that there is no freelook which is a pain because it means if you want to hit enemies who are above or below you then you have to hope that the game tracks them and aims at them accordingly which is only half of the time, the game can't even detect enemies who are too far away so you have to make sure you're close enough.Aside from all that though its pretty good if you like the old games. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Some call it "the real Doom 3" since its a whole new set of totally original levels and visuals designed by Midway. The addition of colored lighting and fog, along with the moody atmospheric soundtrack by Aubrey Hodges, makes for a more "horror" themed experience. As far as the level design goes, there are an abundance of almost unfair traps and they spare no time in ramping up the difficulty quickly. You'll be facing the toughest monsters just a few levels in. For Doom veterans, its a welcome challenge!

_childDocuments_.review: I have no nostalgia for DOOM 64 and apart from watching some speedruns, i have no firsthand experience in the classic DOOM games. My review will be focused on if DOOM 64 is worth playing today for people who are completely new to the series. And my short answer is absolutely yes.While the DOOM series is kind of misrepresented as a mindless shooter on the internet, the thought provoking level designs that need thinking to progress makes me think quite the opposite for the series. DOOM 64 is a perfect example of show, don't tell. It never directly tells you what you have to do but levels hide clever indicators that guide you towards the right path. This results in a lot of "Eureka" moments that makes the player feel smart.There are 28 levels with varying degrees of quality. Some make total sense and feel fun to play while the others are literal mazes that are complete nightmares to navigate. Gameplay is as expected super solid. You can't look up and down which might seem like a problem for some but you get used to it very quickly. It also doesn't ammo starve you as much as the newer games which i actually think is the better approach depending on the difficulty. Apart from that i must mention the difficulty apart from the last boss was perfect. To expand the topic, the last boss is completely garbage. This would be the biggest con of DOOM 64. It's a sudden massive spike in difficulty and straight up an unfair fight. For the performance and the look of the game, i think the enhanced version does a great job at making it look and play modern. All in all, DOOM 64 is a solid retro shooter that every fan of the genre must at least give a shot. Though don't forget to take some breaks in between every couple of levels since the game can be a bit fatiguing.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is my favorite old school Doom game. The atmosphere, level design, and gunplay are some of the best in the series. Also, since this is a good port, you don't have to bother with trying to set up a source version. Even though Doom 64 is a really good game, it still falls short in some areas. For instance, Doom 64 has the least amount of enemy interactions out of all of the old school Doom games. Due to this, the pacing is much slower than in Doom l and ll. Also, the lack of enemies makes Doom 64 pretty easy on the hardest difficulty. However, considering the N64 lacked power and dual analog sticks, I'm not sure if these can even be classified as problems. Overall, I had a fantastic time with Doom 64. If you want a slower-paced Doom game, this is a great buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played doom64 when it was first released, and like many others I assumed it was just a slightly updated port of the original doom. Atmosphere is great, graphics are still good enough for those of us who still like old school FPS, and the level design early on at least is surprisingly good. In some ways the combination of horror atmosphere, run and gun old school game-play and levels which feel intricate but are designed to be surprisingly intuitive really remind me of Dusk. Can definitely recommend at under £5.

_childDocuments_.review: W3D & Doom started the whole FPS craze.FPP - First Person PerspectiveFPS - First Person ShooterDoom clone - term that was used from '92 to '96 (release of Quake) that means the same as FPS, just doom was so groundbreaking that every other fps game was compared to it.All of FPS are FPP, but not all FPP are FPS.The alternative being third-person perspective -- or TPP -- which, technically speaking, should include any game where you're looking at the character you're controlling from the outside, but which, in practice, is usually used to describe games with an over-the-shoulder "follow cam" (as opposed to "isometric", top-down, side-view, and probably others).The FPS term wasn't widely used before release of Quake, before that they were all called "Doom Clones" or FPP. Doom was actually the first game that brought recognition to the FPS genre as something distinct (even though there are games that fit FPS description and predate doom about 19 years, Id themselves released at least 3 FPS games before doom - Hovertank 3D, Catacomb 3-D and Wolfenstein 3D)So if you want to be specific use FPS, if for example you want to talk about System Shock or Deus Ex use FPP as they're mix of FPS and RPG. And all games that came after doom and before quake can be called doom clones (heretic, hexen, duke nukem 3d, shadow warrior e.t.c.)There's also a subgenre of FPP that contains vehicular combat (i.e. descent series) that some consider to be FPS and some do not so in this case it's safer to use FPP.

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD:The shooty-shooty-bang-bangGreat level designSometimes downright creepy musicGreat weaponsTHE BAD:"New" weapons and monsters are 99% re-skinsStory, as ever in old-skool DOOM, is non-existent and you get nowt but a single screen for your troubles upon completionTHE UGLY:Well...it's not a bad looking game as such, with somewhat crisper and more detailed sprites than the previous games. This is a pretty bare-bones port, which is reflected in the lower price.OVERALL:I had a lot of fun with this. _childDocuments_.review: This is a cool game. It's Doom, after all. I love the atmosphere and unsettling sound design. Features includes cheap/annoying enemy placement, confusing level layouts, lots of running around as you try to solve obtuse puzzles, WAY too many beefy enemies in tiny spaces, and more. There is a noticeable decrease in quality compared to the original campaign. I hate to say "they don't make 'em like they used to," but level design was pretty dope back in the day. I suppose it was somewhat worth it for the tiny bit of lore at the end.Anyway, the majority of the game is a blast, and you should definitely play it if you're a Doom fan. _childDocuments_.review: Doom's cybernetic heart beats with a rythm of science fiction. Future soldiers, high-tech weaponary and isolated installations on a far-flung world. It's blend that provides the key aesthetic for Doom: a fusion of metallic sci-fi with fleshy hellspawn. The satanic influences originate from Id's D&D sessions, where at the climax of the lengthy campaign the entire planet was overrun with demons. No longer constrained by the grid-based stone walls of Wolfenstein, Id's imagination could run riot: an indulgence of pure twisted fantasy. A departure from a loose historical basis: from 'heil Нitler' to 'hail Satan' Id have never been particularly afraid of controversial subjects. Still, the devil has all the best tunes - and a game like Doom needed a killer soundtrack. Id didn't have to look too far for inspiration: the tunes playing on their office stereo would provide ample material. Tracks evocative of Metallica, Slayer, Pantera, Judas Priest. True, they were lo-fi MIDI renditions but from first level to the last, Doom is chock full of trash riffs. Every inch the compelling experience: the world was ill prepared for a game like Doom. An amalgam of pop culture, it borrowed heavily from its era - but paid back the debt with interest. From influenced to influential and an impact that resonates today. A new genre forged, and gameplay choreography re-rehearsed countless times. Doom's success, invited others to follow in its footsteps. And why not? It's only natural. There is magic in Doom's heart. It's primitve, still raw and the essence of action beats throughout its chambers. Two decades later and it still kicks arse.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DooM 64 is one of the few games in the N64's library that didn't age like milk just five years after the console and it's horrific trident-o-torture controller were put six feet under. And that's probably because DooM 64 was really out of season back in 1997. 3D shooters like Quake, Goldeneye, Turok and Descent had already hit the market, and the faux-3D Build Engine games like Duke Nukem, Shadow Warrior and BLOOD did a lot in order to make it's worlds as fleshed and "3D"-feeling as they could. But here comes DooM 64, with all the abstract levels and lack of vertical aiming one would expect from a pure DooM game, which in '97 had gone out of fashion. Thus, the game received pretty average reviews upon release, with folks praising the atmosphere, but criticizing the dated design.I've been a DooM fan probably longer than folks who say "DooM Slayer" instead of "Doomguy" have been alive, with the first game I remember playing was my dad's burned copy of Ultimate DooM for Windows 95. I even got the Collector's Edition of DooM 3 for my 7th birthday (yeah, my folks kinda didn't give a ♥♥♥♥), which came bundled with Ultimate DooM and DooM 2. However, DooM 64 really just kinda slipped my grasp until I retroactively started collecting 5th gen systems and their games. While the Saturn's 2D and first party offerings alongside Playstations cavalcade of RPG and survival horror bangers have held up well (reminder, I played these with no prior nostalgia), I found the N64's library kinda anemic, and stuff that was praised to range from middling to downright cumbersome.Yet DooM 64 was different. Much like the 2D games on the Saturn (that almost never made it to the west), DooM 64 used it's rather humble gameplay and visual style to make something really tight, atmospheric and visually interesting. While the game had to be played using the N64's god awful controller, it didn't feels as awkward to use thanks to the relatively simple gameplay. ♥♥♥♥ just kinda worked in DooM 64's favor in a way that it hasn't for it's more "graphically impressive" contemporaries. I played DooM 64 EX a bit later down the line, and it's kinda everything one would have wanted from an unofficial source port of the game by included QoL like mouse and keyboard support, higher resolutions and even mouse look (if you care for that sorta thing). For a while, it was probably the best way to play DooM 64 on more modern systems. But here comes Nightdive, remastering the game and dropping it on basically every modern platform alongside DooM Eternal. And like most Nightdive remasters, it's really good, especially on the Switch with it's gyro support.Basically, what I'm saying is, this game is really good, and if you like classic DooM, you'll probably really enjoy this moodier take on the game. It's a bit more focused on puzzels, probably to a fault, but the overall gameplay, level design and V I B E S more than make up for that.So play it...
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: PROS - Great set pieces with a big focus on colored lighting. Very dynamic and original map layouts with more vertical spaces, something that sticks out from most shooters now. Great atmosphere. No heavy metal, just moody dread synths. Really changes it up from the classics.Every gun feels good and meaty-sounding.There's this fun way to play with Auto-run where you're essentially E-braking by pulling the left trigger, much like ADS but great for run-and-gunning for quick stops for better accuracy- something i'd love to see in modern shooters.CONS - A lot of locked doors with goodies behind make you spam every wall to find the secret door, makes you want more grounded exploration. You almost need a map, which ruins the pacing for such a run and gun action game.40% fun bob-and-weave gun-play 60% where the hell do I go? A switch you press opens a hidden door you didn't see across the level. I'm thankful ID understood the faults in this design and made their game more about action and less about exploration.Game is dated for sure but it's a super classic. If you don't mind having to resort to a few walk-throughs for certain levels, it's really nice to be able to step back in time to a game like this right off the cuff of Eternal. Level design is top notch and you can tell it was the template for the latest Doom.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I passed on this with my N64 because I was a hardcore Doom PC player, and I saw the pictures and wrote it off as a weird port of the game I loved so much. That was apparently a mistake. I am so glad that I am playing this finally, and sorry that I dismissed it back in the day. I don't know how this handled on the 64, but I am playing it with my gamepad just fine. If you loved the original Doom, don't pass on 64  like I did. It is just more of what you loved about the original with a slightly different look.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It brings me great joy to see Kaiser's work on full display here. Not only did he create the DOOM 64 EX engine to allow us to enjoy this incredible game on PC with modern hardware, but he also showcases his WAD-making talents by making excellent maps that take full use of DOOM 64's unique mechanics and style with the awesome additional episode included in this release.If you're a fan of classic DOOM and haven't given this game a shot, then you really have been missing out.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 has the same gameplay like the previous original Doom games with the only difference that it comes with more puzzles and many times you'll catch yourself wondering what to do or where to go. It requires more thinking, focus and memory for the map than the previous games where you just run around shooting monsters or pressing door switches, and many times it gets confusing because of its level design structure.My personal negatives were that the music is not that good (in fact at all) compared to the previous games and that the final boss battle is straight out stupid. The boss is a bullet sponge no matter which powerful weapon you use (even the bfg gun). The only way to beat it (atleast for me) was to hide behind a door button and just spray whatever clip I had left on her. The rockets the boss aims at you are unavoidable unless you find a trick like I did and kind of break the game. It's the worst boss battle I ever played in any game because it's so unbalanced. All in all, the game is okay but I think it could've been a little better. I recommend it for the experience but it's nowhere epic like the first two Doom games were. Especially the soundtracks. You won't find epic thrilling music here. Which is a shame because the soundtracks in the first Doom games were what made the games so unforgetable, so epic and simple timeless. Random tip: Watch out for the traps in some maps. I'd recommend saving at every new level (especially if you play this for the first time) because sometimes the traps are unavoidable and you end up getting stuck there.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It's the hidden gem of the Doom Franchise, practically.It keeps the fast-paced rythm of the series but in a different key, levels are much more eerie and with a darker vibe.There's new weapons, new enemies to keep the series fresh, and clever level design.Visuals used to be impressive in those days, and the soundtrack is in line with the high standards set by the previous games.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Once I saw this game on the store page I got it and started it straight away! Reminds me of the good old days with my tiny but hugely fun Nintendo 64 collection - Zelda, Shadowman, Banjo, Mario and Goldeneye and Perfect Dark. Conker was fun too but I never could get the last grab on that alien at the end there so I won't mention that game. Oh.It plays much like other early titles in the series - run around with an arsenal of guns and survive through the levels. The notable failing (perhaps the only one) is not being able to look up or down like you can in the Quake titles. The art is much more enjoyable than the pixel graphic DooM I or II, but it would have been nice if the weapons got a higher resolution with the PC port. There is a good range of levels and environments - a few are sensational - and I rarely encountered any bugs. The only one I recall was a texture bug with one of the moving water tiles, perhaps this is why there's an epileptic warning in the title sequence.DooM 64 really has some great levels, I can even remember the names, as I named some of the ambient soundtracks after them in my music library: Dark Entries, with the booby-trapped entry hall that launches an almost unending barrage of homing missiles at you; Watch Your Step, where almost everything you pickup or walk on spawns daemons; Pitfalls, with it's eerie chasm-echoes, wind-like ambience that goes so well with the giant pitfalls in the main area of the map.Part of what makes you want to find all the secrets is the new weapon, the Unmaker. This beastly laser isn't too hard to get, but it really shines when you power it up with the 3 pentagram artefacts. One is obtained on each of the 3 secret levels, but they may take a little more effort to get. But once you get them, they make the final boss a joke even on the hardest difficulty: I just run up to the thing and shove the Unmaker down its throat to keep it stunlocked as the gun is basically fully automatic and triple-shot at maximum power.You may have to look up a code to input if you want to enter the Fun levels for achievement purposes, but all in all it's a great port - the sort of game you wish all ports could turn out as good as.So if you never played it, or if you did and want to again, I highly recommend DooM 64. Comes with Lost Levels, a few fun levels (code needed) and a super secret easter egg level after destroying all barrels in level 1, if only briefly!(I left the game paused a few times, so I have finished all achieves in less time than it says I played)
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the Best Classic Doom game in the franchise right there with the first game in my opinion!Amazing atmosphere, great controls, everything about this game is incredible even if it kicks my ass a bunch of times. i can only do nothing but Praise Nightdive's work on this port. an Absolute must buy for Classic FPS and Doom fansgo get it! it's only 5 bucks you cowards!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I gave the game a 'thumbs up' but only because it doesn't deserve a thumbs down.DOOM 64 isn't a terrible game, even when it was originally out on the Nintendo 64 console.  It's really just a prettier version of the original DOOM/DOOM II games, but it's not a groundbreaking game.  It gets boring pretty quickly, actually.Even back when the N64 was big, there were better FPS games to play outside of DOOM 64, namely GoldenEye, Perfect Dark, Quake II, or even Duke Nukem 64.If you're a DOOM purist or REALLY enjoyed playing the orignal DOOM games, you won't be disappointed with this.  I'm told there's even a BrutalDOOM mod for DOOM 64, which I haven't admittedly tried for DOOM 64 (only the original DOOM), but am pretty sure is pretty cool too.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: + Fun levels+ Lots of secrets+ Cool demon gun+ Lost Souls die in 1 shotgun blast- Really dark and muted, more Quake than Doom. I prefer Doom 1 and 2's style, but..+ ..there are now some sliders to make the game more/less dark- Caco is no longer cute- Animations suckMidway did a good job with Id's baby, and Nightdive did a great port. _childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: My personal favorite of the classic Doom games. It's a lot darker in tone and atmosphere, a lot more challenging than vanilla Doom aside from the Plutonia Experiment. It might feel less diverse, but the enemy roster is well used all throughout and the levels themselves are quite distinct from the rest of Doom.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is the real Doom 3. I do mean that. It's dark, disturbing, and horrifying in the best possible way.The graphics are a gigantic upgrade, looking far better than ever before in the classic doom series. All of the characters look far more fleshy, if that's the word to use.The music, however, is the greatest part. The composer, Aubrey Hodges, is an absolute genious, combining industrial sounds with disturbing violins and other classical instruments.The gameplay is mostly unchanged, save for a new weapon which can be upgraded. Sadly, some monsters, such as the Archvile, Spiderdemon, SS soldier, Chaingunner, revenant, and Icon of sin are left out. We do, however, have a new final boss and an upgraded imp.Overall, fantastic entry in the doom series.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid port that allowed me to discover the excellent game that is Doom 64.I'm really impressed with Midway's adaptation of this classic doom. Even if it has certain flaws and it's hard to put it on the same level as more recent retro fps, Doom 64 possesses a strange charm carried by its dark and disturbing visual ambience accompanied by a sublime atmospheric soundtrack, undoubtedly one of the best in the series.For me, the only real flaw in this game was the excessive use of switches to open doors at the other end of the map, with no indication of where to go. Apart from the feeling of sometimes wasting time in labyrinthine levels, it was a real pleasure to discover this game. A must-have for all fans of the doom saga.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is my favorite "classic" Doom game. The slower, more considered pace, the emphasis on atmosphere, and the dark ambient soundtrack are all great design choices, and a welcome update to the Doom/Doom II formula. I think Doom 64's design anticipated the direction Doom 3 would take, but without departing as much from the series' core concepts up to that point. I enjoyed playing this on the couch with a controller rather than with keyboard/mouse, and it felt like the best way to experience this game; I don't think I could say that for any other game in the series.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: More of a puzzle-oriented take on "DOOM" than its earlier installments, there's still plenty of mowing down demons to keep one's bloodlust satisfied. Gun switching is easy, traps littered throughout levels can catch you by surprise (those fireballs certainly come to mind), and Aubrey Hodges's soundtrack with its ambient noise and discordant, non-directional sensibility makes the atmosphere delightfully unsettling and foreboding. It's a far scarier experience than most other "DOOM" games I've played, especially with solid headphones.The big change from the original console version for the N64 (aside from some new levels and achievements) is the ability to save anywhere, which makes later levels far more manageable. As such, the exercise of actually getting through the game is more user-friendly.Aside from some poorly-implemented platforming, the only other notable negative is that the puzzles, while not "hard" in the sense of having the pieces in front of you and being difficult to figure out, are a bit aggravating. Most of the later levels will usually have one moment of not quite knowing where to go or what to do, and not in a way that feels appropriately challenging for a game like this. It's never enough to make you feel "lost," but you may find yourself smacking your head for not realizing you didn't see this one thing or do this one action."DOOM 64" is nevertheless a very fun game, one that satisfies the craving for early "DOOM" gameplay while also offering something intriguing enough on its own to justify giving it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Looks and runs great, rendering with Vulcan. 1920x1080 144hz There are annoying and unskippable intro videos. You can remove them.Find Doom 64 in your library list. Right-click and hover over the "Manage" tab, it should expand. Click "Browse local files" to open the game files. There will be a folder named "movies". You can delete the entire folder, or go inside and delete the videos you want.

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Leagues better than the N64 console version, the general graphics and brightness tweaks are very welcome additions, the gameplay is an all-time classic in the genre and the dichotomy of the colorful visuals and dark atmosphere is what makes this version of the game special.666/10, finally get to enjoy this game without squinting my eyes at the screen.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good game. I know you are skeptical because it is not familiar looking and not the same as Doom 1, 2 and the rest, but it has the same soul and game play, and feels like a good doom game, and is in ways better. The atmosphere is better, for example. It has a darker tone of despair. There is nothing in this game that is worse than the other Doom games, The guns are fantastic and sound great and feel and play great. This is an extremely underrated game that you will absolutely enjoy. Some of the puzzles are also really good and a bit more in depth than the other classic games.Bethassda is a wretched horrible company and you have to wait for their stupid rotating box logo to spin as it takes its time to connect to the internet when you press the Start button.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the best and worst thing about Doom 64 is that it's just more of the same. Alongside Doom and Doom II, this is just more levels with the same gameplay. But if it ain't broke, don't fix it. After you play those two classics, there's no reason not to check this one out too. It has slightly better graphics, but not by much, more detailed sprites mostly, other things like the weapons actually look a bit worse at times. Levels are somewhat more straightforward but do include some new wacky mechanics too. The aesthetics are darker and grittier and the banging metal soundtrack is replaced with chilling ambiance. Beyond that, it's the pinnacle of oldschool boomer shooter goodness as we all know and love it.I'm pretty hyped for when they finally release Dooms 4 through 63, can't wait. It is rather odd though that after all that, we are still just collecting keycards and navigating mazes. Hey, props to id for sticking to their guns I guess.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I'd played DOOM and DOOM 2 more times than I could count and on more platforms than I can remember since I was a kid and I decided, upon revisting them for nostalgia's sake, that I'd finally give this game a shot. It is undeniably rough. I don't think coming right off of playing 1 and 2 back to back did it any favours because it really emphasised the differences when compared to the originals but it's still a mostly fun game. The final boss felt a little cheap and I didn't enjoy it as much as the end to the other games but overall it was decent. Definitely one I'd say is worth playing at leas once if you've experienced everything else the series has to offer (suffice to say it's orders of magnitude better than Doom 3 which was, and remains, an absolute bin fire of a game) but it's not one I think I'd ever go back to now that I've beaten it.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Far more fun than I expected. It starts out slow, but give it time. The ambiance builds nicely. The soundtrack really sells the unsettling dread vibe. The level design gets a little backtracky, and the puzzles a little obscure at times, but it is a fantastic Doom game, and an even more fantastic classic shooter. I just wish it had multiplayer.9/10 Will play again multiple times8/10 I recommend to the right friends
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A little story first - some 6-8 years ago (don't remember exactly, sorry) I was playing the WAD "After the Apocalypse" (I think it was called like this?..) by SGTMarkIV. The map was good, but what blew me completely out was the music - atmospheric dark ambient which I didn't hear in any game before.This exact music was the first thing which led me to the reveal that consoles had wildly different versions of the game, namely PSX ones. Later on, when I played "Hell on Earth Starter Pack", I discovered more of the music. The one at MAP28 also blew me away after some time adjusting to it. One more search - and the grail has been found - the music belonged to some game called Doom 64, which I didn't know that it existed.Getting Doom64Ex up some months later was a hassle, but the price was worth it - because later I discovered a hidden underrated gem of N64 exclusives (then). The graphics looked very good (and they still do), the guns were much more powerful feeling than the original Doom 1-2 ones, the atmosphere with oppressive ambient of Aubrey Hodges and truly marvelous level design which pushed idTech 1 to its limits was just a cherry on the top. But it required a ROM of the game and it had some limitations (30 FPS for instance). Still, it was a great experience.While pre-ordering Doom Eternal back when it was still in development, I saw that Doom 64 is also getting re-released alongside it. I was actually pumped for that - way more than I should have been. And believe me, Doom 64 running on a new engine is now the definitive way to experience this underrated classic which it always has been. New "Lost Levels" campaign is also high-quality - it's a shame that it is way too short but it is worth it.So, to sum it up - this is a truly worthy Doom game which still stays true to the formula. Sound design might be offputting to some (I've seen comments talking about "monsters and music sound boring"), but give it a try - and you'll love it (or not). Doom 64 is also quite cheap here, so it's basically a gorgeous steal asking for itself.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is... well, basically it's just more DOOM. And it's hard to go wrong with that. However, the monsters have gotten cosmetic makeovers and the atmosphere overall is much more on the creepy side than the original two titles, from level design to music to everything else. No more banging melodies by Bobby Prince, with background music being minimalistic and ambient instead. It's hit or miss, but for me it was different and interesting, and it fit the overall tone of the game quite well.At it's pricepoint, I highly recommend DOOM 64 for any fans of the originals or old-school FPS titles in general. When the main complaint online appears to be the lack of option to enable jumping and vertical aiming in a DOOM game, you just know that there are no real problems to speak of with this port.A couple of pointers, though. Save a lot and often. This game will break your heart by slapping you with a falling floor trap right in front of a level end switch. And you will not be able to get up. Similar stuff happened on a few levels. Don't be the guy forced to pistol start a late game level or load up a few levels earlier.Also, Pain Elementals and Lost Souls are your new priorities. The Mother Demon has not fed them since the first slaughter, it appears. By the time you grunt from pain and turn 180 degrees to see what hit you, the Lost Soul has already had second or even third servings of your sorry ass. There's little to no pause in their attacks. And when you get a swarm.. you get the drift. Damn ravenous bastards.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who discovered Doom 64 in the retro second-hand games section of Gamestation in the mid 2000s, I was one of the few who got to appreciate a game that few people knew existed.Doom 64 feels a little slower than the previous Doom games. In some ways, I'd say it has a far more refined, yet oppressive atmosphere. The gameplay of Doom is there, but the maps are a bit smaller in scale, with the developers having to put more thought into constructing each encounter.I grew up on Doom and although the classic Doom games will always tickle the nostalgia bone, Doom 64 balances trying new things, while maintaining the feel of an authentic Doom game.This version gets everything right and I cant recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: While I really REALLY like Doom 64 this simply aint how it was intended to play. This game is all about mood and atmosphere and that kind of goes out of the window when playing on PC. Your not suppose to play it like classic Doom, your suppose to move slower and be "weaker" for lack of better word. Playing this on an old tube TV with the Nintendo 64 just feels and also looks better if you have good TV and a stereo system. But I guess this is good for those who never tried it or simply don't have their old N64 anyone and want to relive some of the nostalgia it just is not exactly how it is suppose to. The horror is only 50% there when on PC.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: So this was originally on the Nintendo 64, eh? Curious how well the hyper fast combat of oldschool DOOM translated to that console with the kind esoteric controller it has (still love that system regardless).Glad this game got a proper official port onto PC. Before people had to resort to N64 ROMhacks if they wanted to play it with a keyboard and mouse. Of course I didn't touch the original console version nor the ROMhacks, so my only impression of DOOM 64 is through this PC port. Gameplay wise it doesn't spew as many demons at you as DOOM and DOOM 2, which I think was due to the memory limit of the original console it ran on. Still felt fun despite that, and the difficulty felt right all the way through (Always play on Ultra-Violence). Enemy variety and behaviour is pretty much the same as previous classic DOOMs, but the Revenant, Cacodemon, and Archvile aren't present. There's the Specter version of the Imp though.What makes this version of DOOM unique in comparison to other versions of DOOM is not only the unique artstyle, soundscape, and level design, but also an original unlockable weapon called the Unmakyr (Replaces the BFG and makes an reappearance in DOOM Eternal) and a final boss named the Mother Demon. The Unmakyr can be upgraded throughout the game by finding Demon Keys hidden in various levels, eventually turning into a souped-up plasma gun. The Demon Keys also act as locks for the final boss level, making the fight slightly easier to get through, which I find to be lovely incentive to explore each level for secrets.Really enjoyed the unique artstyle and sound design of DOOM 64. It helped to make this game feel distinct from the other DOOMs. Level design is similar to DOOM and DOOM 2 in which everything could be made in its engine, but DOOM 64 made interesting use of enemy layout and rising and falling platforms not seen in the OGs. Gets my respect for that.Had a blast playing all 39 levels this re-release had to offer. Played it blind the first time without finding any Demon Keys, so the final boss was quite a pain to beat alongside the horde of demons that spawned alongside it. Had to look up a walkthrough to find them on my 2nd playthrough as well as the secret levels. So if you're looking to scratch that classic DOOM itch with new visuals and levels; this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a unique take on Doom in terms of the looks, mainly the same gameplay as Doom 2 except for the slower movement and lack of a few enemy types. It's now also the canonical sequel to Doom 2 and prequel to Doom 2016 in the "Doom Timeline"(TM) as well, so that's kinda neat, seeing as it wasn't even developed by ID Software itself. 9/10 - It's Doom, of course it's good

_childDocuments_.review: Animated infernal backgrounds, deep and crisp sound effects, nightmarish monsters, hugely complex and interactive maps and a kickass bizarre soundtrack, this gets to be the definitive old school Doom version of all. If it were (officially) ported 20 years earlier it might've gotten a bit more well deserved attention, but free unofficial ports did a great job too not so long ago before this one. However, with few bonus maps added, enhanced texture support and native widescreen compatibility thrown into the mix, it seems like a must for fans of Doom or any old school shooter, thus we get a port well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this back in 97 I never thought I would be finished with this title honestly. Though not the Doom guy (or Doom slayer) we all know this unknown marine has a hell of a time fighting I think are the best demons in all of Doom history. IMO. I was terrified at a young age seeing how monstrous that Cyberdemon was, now I was laughing as I ended one after the other. I hope anyone who grew up with the N64 version like I did take time and enjoy going through each of the 30 plus levels again and conquer Watch Me Die! like I did. Doom 64 is a great experience!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I can't get Jim Sterling's "It's time to ♥♥♥♥ on Bethesda"-intro (which has a catchy music along a point) out my mind while writing this. Did somebody send a company-wide memo urging everybody to ♥♥♥♥ something up, no matter what? Bethesda finally has a game (mostly) without live service crap neither bugged to hell (no pun intended), but still can't stop being Bethesda. I am not even complaining about what feels like an hour of intro videos (which can be skipped with a bit of effort). Neither about News/Bethesda club on the main menu, which is already stretching it. But the Bethesda icon as a loading cursor in the otherwise old-school menu, coupled with the jarring Bethesda icon appearing amid the game when saving is too much. This is a classic! Everybody knows Doom is now owned by Bethesda and everybody is grateful for Doom 64 officially on PC. You don't need to shove yours into everyone's face!Speaking of being grateful, yes I am. With that whole "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on Bethesda" out of the way, damn is this game good!On the surface, it looks like Doom 1 & 2, but it's in fact a precursor to Doom 3. Meaning less open arenas, less enemy count overall (but unlike Doom 3, you keep your fast walking speed), more emphasis on the atmosphere. The dark, moody atmosphere coupled with the eery soundscape in place of rocking music creates a sense of horror crawling under your skin and staying there. Look, I get how the precursors were scary when playing them as a kid, but when viewed through the same lens as Doom 64 now, those are about as much horror as Resident Evil 6 is an action : superficially yes, but let's be real.Feel free to call me contrarian, but I prefer this one to Doom 3. I also prefer Doom 3 BFG over the original release as I'm into shooting games for mostly shooting and not flashlight management. Doom 64, more so than Doom 3 BFG, is thick on horror atmosphere but doesn't put it into the place of action. Similar to Doom 3 though, the game has ways to surprise you, to make you feel that sense of doom. The level & encounter design nudges you against rushing into rooms headfirst, there's less stuff to kill overall but more really unpleasant situations to get into, you're dealing with all this in the action manner of it's precursors making Doom 64 the go-to action horror game. Please don't get me wrong, Doom 3 is a good game and I'm replaying it on my Switch, not regretting having bought it twice for a single moment. In fact, it's corridors (contrary to arenas in the rest of the Doom series) are a good fit for the limp analog stick FPS gameplay experience.I rarely talk about visuals in my reviews and this is a port of a decades-old game, but the visual style is ageless. In fact, I prefer well-crafted sprites over common high-poly-no-artistry visuals any day of the week. Speaking of technicalities, it has mouselook, and mouselook is enabled by default. Speaking design, the supershotgun is delicious.All in all, worth a purchase. A fantastic game I finally get to enjoy with proper KBM controls. Yes, source ports have been in existence for dunno how long, but legally obtaining the game content hasn't been exactly feasible all those years and I salute Bethesda for releasing an official port of that gem!PS: Doom Eternal (and Doom '16) canonize Doom 64, in case you still need a reason to play it. Just sayin'...

_childDocuments_.review: The level design in this game is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ past level 5. The combat isn't engaging, it's infuriating. You'll walk over the same spot you just passed and out of nowhere it will spawn 10 Barons of Hell and 6 Hell Knights and expect you to kill all of them without running out of ammo or dying. And that's just level 8! In level 9, they spawn you in between 4 Mancubi that are all shooting at you at different times, so you can hardly dodge them without luck, and even after you kill them, it spawns Hell Knights, Barons, Cacodemons, and Pain Elementals everywhere around you. You get one Soul Sphere, one Mega Armor, and one Invulnerability, along with some other minor pickups. That's it. The invulnerability just barely lasts long enough to kill the Barons with a rocket launcher or chainsaw, and you still have the Cacodemons, Mancubi, and Pain Elementals to deal with, not to mention the 30+ Lost Souls that have just been spawned by said Pain Elementals. It's a cluster♥♥♥♥, and that's putting it lightly. There's hardly any thought put into the combat, they just throw a handful of random enemies at you in some random formation and expect you to kill them. That's all it is. There is no effort put into the difficulty, strategy, or puzzles.It's fun for a 20 minute pass-time, but nothing more. Don't pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: An overall good game that is unfortunately held back by antiquated design.If you've played and liked the classic Doom games from the 90's, chances are very good that you will enjoy this, as it's almost identical to those games, which is both to its benefit and detriment sometimes. The only thing that really separates this game from others in the series is its sound design. Doom 64 goes for more of a subtle and unnerving series of sounds that one can't even really call music most of the time. It actually does a better job on the horror soundtrack side of things than Doom 3.Also, Doom 3 largely did away with mowing down hordes of demons for more corridor shooting, and Doom 64 certainly has its fair share of both, there will still be occasional moments of outright desperation when fending off the demons of Hell.The biggest problems in this game mostly just stem from being a product of its time: The lack of an autosave triggering at the start of every level, forcing you to restart with all your weapons, ammo, extra health and armor all taken away means that you'll have to create saves constantly. But more than that, you'll have to quicksave several times too as, while they aren't frequent enough to be a core gameplay problem, there are still multiple instances where you can fall into a pit with absolutely no way out and just slowly die, with the absolute worst offenses coming when the game decides to literally collapse the ground out beneath you without any warning whatsoever. (Though again, to be clear, this only has happened to me in game 2 times, and even when exploring some other pits to see if there was a way out, oftentimes there was)Another mark against the design came in the form of a pit that didn't have a lift, but instead had "stairs" on one of the walls that were like 1 pixel wide, looked like shadows, had never been featured in any other map prior to that point (or after for that matter), and didn't even work the first time I tried them and just assumed I was on the wrong track.An easily rectified stumbling block came when I was asked to get a yellow key out of a cage that was connected to two switches when no combination of actions could grant access. There was a third switch OUTSIDE the room, but not only does it not look like a switch, it doesn't even make any SOUND when pressed so the player is given no indication whatsoever that it has a mechanical function within the game.The game also feels too easy, probably because the only really threatening enemies are, surprisingly, the Lost Souls and Pain Elementals. Just about every enemy can be dispatched with the Super Shotgun, and if you save at the start of every level and reload so that you keep all your items then most of the time killing demons becomes super easy, barely an inconvenience. So I'd recommend challenging yourself by letting your character die and restarting every level with just the pistol if you feel the game is too easy or just want to experience the game in a different way. However, again, it would be nice if the player could simply choose from 3 modes: 1 where the game plays normally with death being penalized harshly, a 2nd where the game autosaves at the start of every level and reverts back to that save after death, and a 3rd where the player is automatically stripped of all their gear after every level for more of a challenge.Keeping an eye and ear out is also important, as there are times when things trigger based on where the player is standing, or sometimes switches are connected to things that are much further away. Sometimes SHOOTING switches is required if you want to trigger them. Again, they're some of those old design choices made in an attempt to keep the gameplay varied, but don't get extensively tutorialized and/or widely featured in the levels.On the technical side of things, I've been getting screen tearing and I think the game crashed once, but aside from that have had no problems.Not being able to skip the opening logos for the companies is a minor irritant, and I always feel dirty when "Bethesda" appears on the screen, but overall, the game's a good time. Probably best played in shorter bursts rather than marathoned so that one doesn't get too fatigued by combat. And hey, if the more horror-style sound design isn't your thing, you can always just go into the options to turn off the music, and play some metal and/or classic Doom tracks in the background while you play!

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a classic Nintendo 64 game that was never “officially” ported to PC (and other consoles) until now. Doom 64 is a follow up to Doom 2. It keeps the same classic Doom gameplay and it brings about some enhancements. Doom 64 has a completely new look and new graphics. It has much more of a creepy, horror look and feel to it. With regards to the music, they went a completely different direction with Doom 64. The previous Doom games (The Ultimate Doom, Doom 2, and Final Doom) had music that was upbeat and good. Doom 64’s music is completely different. The music in Doom 64 is just creepy ambiance music and sounds that are intended to add to the horror of the game. It does fit with the creepy look and feel of the game. Although some players may miss the upbeat music of the previous Doom games. One thing about this official port that some players may not like is that this port does not have mouselook (the player can’t look up or down). The developer said that the reason for this is because in the original Nintendo 64 game, the player couldn’t look up or down. And they wanted this official port to be as faithful to the original Nintendo 64 game as possible. This port has graphical enhancements, sound enhancements, and a higher framerate than the original Nintendo 64 game had. Also, this port comes with a brand new campaign with brand new levels (in addition to the main campaign). So you get the original levels and some new levels too. This official port of Doom 64 is probably the most faithful port of the original Nintendo 64 game that there ever will be. If you played Doom 64 on an actual Nintendo 64 console back in the day, and you want to play it again on PC, I definitely recommend this official port. Yes, there are other ports and mods of Doom 64 available for PC. And they’re good too. I would say that if you’re looking for the port that is the most faithful to the original Nintendo 64 game, I’d go with this one. Doom 64 is a good game and I definitely recommend it

_childDocuments_.review: Great little horror shooter, amazing how the ambient soundtrack transforms the experience from regular DooM completely. Just pick "Watch Me Die", you'll be fine.Movement feels weirdly floaty and pickup hitboxes feel a tad smaller than the sprites, but you'll get used to this.Unlike regular DooM I rarely felt the need to run, walk speed is fast enough to traverse the small levels and dodge projectiles.No need to run, this is a THINKING MAN'S shooter.That is also implied by the level design and puzzles that range from intuitive to baffling and feedback-lacking to what feels, to my spodbrain at least, a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. (Final Outpost)I'd probably criticize some of the more weirdly hidden secrets / secret levels too, if I could find them.Very good spooky time for a fiver.EDIT: The later hell levels do turn into some proper DooM slugfest at times, and while some of them have their own problems (hope you like baronspam in a tight corridor), it's mostly good stuff.So if you were disappointed by the scale of early-level battles, just be patient.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I recently just got Doom 64, I do recommend it. Graphically, it's an interesting take on what came before and it does retain the classic Doom style in some ways. One thing to note if you're interested in playing it is that the system requirements are not entirely indicative of what's needed to play it, as you can play it with less that 8GB and it's only 90-ish megabytes to install. Since it's a recent port, it has features that make it run quite well on modern systems and the controls can be configured easily.EDIT: I finally started playing it seriously for the first time this week on Bring It On!, and it's just as good as any other of the old school Doom games but with moody lighting and music. The levels looked and felt good to play, except for a few confusing ones that came up here and there. Most of the gameplay from classic Doom is still there while still feeling like a different experience due to the lighting and the mostly new (new for 1997) textures and objects, etc. If you're not familiar with Doom 64, there are Demon Keys hidden in some levels that you definitely should find to power up the "demon deleter" or the "Unmaker" (Unmakyr, if you're familiar with Doom Eternal). This makes the end boss, the Mother Demon much easier. Though you can use the BFG as always if you didn't find the keys, it does enough damage to work. There was also a new episode made for the port by Kaiser, who at one point created an unofficial port of Doom 64 and developed the KEX engine framework that eventually led to this official port. "The Lost Levels" feel like they belong in Doom 64 and play just as well as the main campaign does, but you are required to find the Demon Keys in the final level in order to fight the Sister Resurrector. So you will have the fully-powered Unmaker to fight her with, and you can take out everything else in the level beforehand to make the boss fight less hectic. I have yet to try these out, but there are community-made expansions you can find for a fresh experience. The Unmaking is one of these, being a 40-map megawad. And there's Doom 64 Reloaded as well.But I'd say Doom 64 is well worth the price and more, and it's part of the canonical Doom timeline these days. (Doom, Doom 2, Doom 64, Doom 2016, and Doom Eternal are all canon)

_childDocuments_.review: I got this alongside Doom Eternal and you know what. I went into this expecting to hate it, since its N64 Doom. _childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is arguably the most atmospheric and genuinely creepy version of DOOM-- the stellar ambience & killer sound design earned it the nickname MOOD 64 back in the day. This port has the original campaigns in all their sprite-based glory and it runs extremely well, no frame dips or stuttering and there's no input lag at all. There's also a "lost" episode in addition to the originals and they are no joke on the highest difficulty setting so if you're looking to revisit a classic or try it out for the first time you should still find some novelty. In terms of difficulty: this is about on par with later DOOM II levels, though a big part of that is the more advanced scripting used-- there are some unconventional puzzles / mechanics that were never seen in the originals. On the highest default difficulty the challenge really ramps up after only a few levels and a big part of that is the sheer volume of hard mobs the game throws at you. There are quite a few tough maps in the original campaign but the lost levels are often significantly harder in general (the very first level is a good primer-- the whole campaign is roughly as tough), think Thy Flesh Consumed on UV but thankfully the pacing rarely gets quite as hectic-- this isn't Plutonia level hard but it's definitely not always easy.My only real complaint is that having some cut content re-added / finished (the Revenant, Archvile and heavy weapons guy were all scrapped in the original release because of space limitations on the Nintendo 64 cartridges) would have been perfect and really enhanced the original version. That and having some quality of life changes you come to expect on PC like mouse free-look would have been nice. That being said, this is the definitive official release and DOOM64 never looked or played better.It's not quite as refined as some modded projects but hey, it's an official port and is a perfect lead-in for DOOM 2016 / Eternal. It's also pretty cheap and legitimately gets you the WAD file if you want to look at some of the excellent PC DOOM64 mod projects.Solid 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially slightly disappointed in this port, but I still think it's a great way to play one of the best Doom games. The removal of true-mouse aiming from Kaiser's previous Doom 64 EX port, as well as a few other QoL features like crosshairs and visible item/enemy/secret count is unfortunate, but I get why that decision would be made. In exchange, I now have an official way to play the game with mouse aiming that doesn't jitter (I had issues with EX, even after installing the Win10 mouse fix). I'll take it. As for the new levels, they are excellent. Sufficiently difficult with some quality art design and great understanding of the specifics of what makes Doom 64's monsters and weapons so fun to mess with. The last level in particular is great fun, a sort of mashing of the final two levels of Doom 64 together, with a outer ring just filled with high level enemies and cyberdemons, with a mad dash to find all the demon keys among the chaos. The final boss is lame, especially since there's no way to not have a fully upgraded Unmaker by the time you fight it, but it's a much better final level than the main campaign itself. Even if this didn't come with Doom Eternal, I would have happily bought it on it's own. Great game, one every single Doom fan should play, and a port worthy of it.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat mechanics in *Doom 64* feel outdated and clunky, lacking the precision and fluidity that modern players have come to expect. The controls are unwieldy, often making encounters with demons feel more like an exercise in frustration than an adrenaline-fueled battle. Many players have noted the sluggish movement and awkward weapon switching, which can turn a simple firefight into a chaotic mess of missed shots and unnecessary deaths. Instead of the tight, intuitive layouts that made previous *Doom* titles so engaging, *Doom 64* offers sprawling, confusing maps filled with convoluted mazes and obscure keys. You’ll spend more time running in circles trying to figure out where to go next than actually fighting monsters. It feels less like a challenge and more like a punishment for daring to explore. I can only imagine how many players have thrown their controllers in frustration after getting lost in these poorly designed levels. Rather than posing a genuine threat, foes often behave like mindless drones, charging at you with little strategy. The once-feared cacodemons and imps lose their terrifying edge, becoming laughable caricatures of their former selves. The difficulty curve swings wildly, with some encounters feeling far too easy while others seem arbitrarily punishing. Players have reported moments where it feels like the game is rigged against you, leaving you wondering if it’s a design choice or just poor execution. The shotgun, a staple of the series, sounds and feels weak, lacking the visceral punch that should accompany such an iconic weapon. When you blast an enemy at close range, you expect an explosive impact, not a feeble pop. Instead of exhilaration, you’re left with disappointment. If you dare to criticize this game, be prepared for a barrage of clown awards from the most fragile FPS fanboys you’ve ever encountered. It’s as if they’ve made it their life mission to defend this title, treating any critique as a personal affront. The irony is astounding—these individuals who preach about “free speech” and “different opinions” are the first to silence anyone who dares to challenge their nostalgia. labeled everything from “casual” to “fake gamer” for merely pointing out the glaring flaws in a game they hold dear. The level of denial and entitlement within this community is truly remarkable. They seem so trapped in their nostalgia that they can’t fathom that maybe—just maybe—*Doom 64* isn’t the masterpiece they remember. It feels like the developers relied on the *Doom* name to carry the game, rather than focusing on innovation or improvement. For a franchise that has consistently pushed boundaries, it’s disappointing to see a title that feels like it’s dragging its feet while the rest of the industry has sprinted ahead. It’s sad that many fans are stuck in the ‘90s, clinging to outdated mechanics and a flawed game, rather than embracing the evolution of gaming. If you’re looking for an FPS that actually holds up to modern standards, look elsewhere. This game is not only a frustrating experience but also comes with a fanbase so thin-skinned it could make a tissue factory jealous. I’ve heard it all before, and it only strengthens my belief that *Doom 64* is best left in the dusty archives of gaming history. Enjoy your nostalgia, but don’t pretend it’s more than what it is: a mediocre title that should have remained a forgotten relic of the ’90s.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve never played Doom 64 before and despite hearing that it was not just a port of the original Doom or it’s sequels or expansions, I never really cared to play it either. Partially because I was never as big into id software FPS titles. Partially because, well, it’s Doom again, even if the levels are new, right? And that’s where I was somewhat wrong as Doom 64 feels different. So I’m really glad that it got officially ported to newer systems and PC.Despite being a yet another adaptation of the Doom engine and the gameplay you usually associate with the classic Doom, Doom 64 has a distinctly more horror look and feel to it. The lighting is far more dramatic than in the classic PC Doom titles, with some rooms being completely pitch black until you flip some switch, use of harsh contrasts, lots of coloured lighting that actually still looks good and not flat and simplistic as you’d expect from an FPS on an engine this old. At the same time, the game never really suffers from this darker more horror inducing design the same way Doom 3 suffered. It’s still classic Doom as you remember it and it flows fantastically fun.Another absolute standout of this game is the soundtrack. And I implore you to listen to it. Unlike the original PC soundtrack that was all metal-inspired midi files, Doom 64, just like the Playstation ports of Doom (same composer), have a very dark moody ambient soundtrack. It is insanely creepy and good and fits the game really well. From harsh distorted metallic noises to warbled voice lines and baby crying over haunting ambience – this soundtrack has it all. The game wouldn’t be as good without it.But the game itself – yeah, it’s just lots of good classic Doom levels. With this new remastered port adding several new levels in its new little campaign on top. Most of the levels are genuinely good, in my personal opinion topping some of the levels from the old officially released expansions that often relied too much on utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ trickery and insanely high and often unfair difficulty. And even some of the more bs levels in the game, available via passwords or after beating an honestly bs level, are in reality fun to play. Dumb but fun. While the main levels are almost consistently good with only a few ones that have really obscure ways of progression.This is somewhat unexpected, but after finishing Doom 64 I feel like it might actually be my favorite classic Doom. Maybe it’s the darker mood of the game, maybe it’s the speed of super shotgun (it’s faster than in the PC games), maybe it’s something else, but I really loved playing Doom 64 in this new updated release. If you like Doom, definitely give this one a go.
