_childDocuments_.review: This port is just utter garbage.👎 High input latency. That alone makes it outright unplayable on my PC (and no, a Ryzen+RTX notebook is not too underpowered to play a 25 years old N64 game smoothly).👎 A series of annoying intro movies that don't skip by pressing any key or button. I know about "-skipmovies" or deleting the movie files but that's undocumented behavior. By default it's hostile towards the gamer.👎 YOU CAN'T UNBIND KEYS/BUTTONS! Sure, you can assign a new action to a key or button in the options but the existing one will not be cleared, meaning more and more actions will be stacked onto a single key.Prepare to edit "Saved Games\Nightdive Studios\DOOM 64\kexengine.cfg" in a text editor by hand like a cave man.👎 In-game localized keyboard layouts are respected, in the menus they are not. Don't even bother trying to figure out the difference beween US layout and your localized one because of the unbinding problem. Edit kexengine.cfg.👎 No modern texture filtering techniques, not even optionally. The original graphics were made with the N64's native resolution and CRT TVs in mind where the screen itself does interpolation work just through the way CRTs work. Low-res sprites and textures with bilinear filtering aged like fresh milk in the sun when viewing them on modern PC screens at HD resolutions.Luckily there is least an option to turn texture filtering off for a sharper, pixelated look that works way better with modern screens. I know modern texture filtering would be "not authentic to the original" but that argument can go were the sun doesn't shine. Intro movies, , etc. are "not authentic to the original" either and those made it in!👎 No way to use one of the many community-made source ports like GZDoom with this game to remedy the negatives stated above (at least at time of writing).Absolution and Brutal Doom 64 are mods for Doom 2, not for this. So yeah, if you want a better way to play Doom 64 on your PC, buy Doom 2 and follow one of the many guides how to replace this port with GZDoom + Doom 2 + Absolution or Brutal Doom 64 (I prefer the latter).The heartbreaking part about the port is that the game itself is amazing but the Bethesda/Nightdive release is not the way to experience it.Just don't buy this individually. If you got it as part of a bundle, follow a guide to replace this game with Brutal Doom 64 v2.5. At least you get Steam Overlay and playtime tracking.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're coming straight from DOOM or DOOM 2 like me, the first thing you'll notice is how different the control scheme is. Running is bound to the Space Bar and the only interact key is E. The second thing you'll notice is that the keybind menu is completely ******* useless. Maybe it's some bug or i'm too stupid to understand it, but it's not worth rebinding your controls. Even if you could I can't really recommend it, DOOM 64 isn't in the same engine as DOOM 1 and 2, so learning some new muscle memory is for the best. The third thing I noticed was that this game is real 3D (I'm saying "I" instead of "you" because i genuinely was too distracted by the keybind menu). For the first time, DOOM supports true 3D with room-over-room capabilities. Since DOOM 64 was originally for the Nintendo 64 (duh) the game was made without the use of the original DOOM engine, and you can quickly tell. Getting Gud at DOOM 1 and 2 meant mastery of the DOOM engine: knowing how to leap the furthest from a ledge, figuring out how to abuse the 2.5D nature of the game, the vertically infinite missile splash, etc. You see, DOOM 1 and 2 arn't true 3D, so the quick movement of the og DOOM games can be credited to the fact that you are only gliding through a 2D plane. In DOOM 64 this is no longer the case. In this engine you can only move around when your feet are planted. In a game with no jump button this isn't really an issue, but you can fall down stairs because of it. Seriously, if you approach a staircase too fast or at a bad angle you lose control of your movement as you bounce down each step. This never annoyed me because I think it rewards precise movement but I think it's a good example of how utilizing quirks in a game's engine can improve gameplay. When it comes to difficulty it has its spikes, no DOOM game doesn't, but for the most part it's easier than DOOM 2 but harder than DOOM 1, total sweetspot. DOOM 64 also puts more focus on puzzle solving than it's combat. Not to say that 64's combat isn't up to par, but the devs really put the true 3D engine to use when it comes to each level and it's secrets. Nightdive Studios absolutely nailed it with this game, I really thought that Id Software made this until I had to look it up because this game deserves the title of DOOM 3 way more than that other game does.  If anything I hope this stops being seen as a port or a spinoff DOOM game because it can sit comfortably next to its predecessors. 8/10, PLEASE FIND THE DEMON KEYS DON'T MAKE MY MISTAKE.edit: put -skipmovies in your launch options to remove the long, obnoxious, and unskippable animations when you start the game.

It runs at 4K60 with SMAA enabled on budget hardware at release (tested on a 1050 Ti). It retains everything from the original while adding improved gamepad controls, higher resolutions/framerates, and an entire new episode to play through.Fans of the franchise, pick this up. Anybody looking for an expertly crafted classic FPS experience, pick this up. It holds up, and this port does the original justice. _childDocuments_.review: Level design brought to you by who I can only assume is the most annoying person on earth. Doom 64's level design is unremittingly snide and obnoxious, whether it's hiding the way up out of a pit via a near invisible staircase, enough monster closets to staff every haunted house attraction in the western hemisphere, or a perverse lust in allowing you to take damage from some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doming you in the back of the head every five microseconds.Much can be said about Doom 64's adherence to its core aesthetic, virtually everything drips atmosphere and the soundtrack drones in the background, a relentless throb of despair and anxiety; but this aesthetic is handily countered by the fact that some mischievous imp freshly loosed from the Build Engine Committee on Making Levels Annoying circle of hell makes the experience feel like someone is perpetually mocking you every step of the way.Don't get me wrong, Doom 64 isn't particularly hard, every monster has a tad bit too much HP and there's a preponderance of claustrophobic corridors that demands the most pedestrian of left-right strafing skills, but none of this makes the game particularly difficult - as far as the Doom series is concerned, it's a bit between Doom I and II in difficulty. It is instead, however, as I said before, an incredibly annoying game to play purely because the level design has little regard for appropriate pacing or any design philosophy that doesn't hyper-fixate on tricks and traps. Virtually everything here is recursive in some way, a switch opens a door or path you better remember from before, keys are hidden in roundabout layouts that demand a Copernican sense of direction, almost every new path you open releases a fresh case of freeze-dried monster closet that's ostensibly there to lead you in the right direction but instead just allows the monsters to wander aimlessly, completely negating any sort of organic attempt to pull you towards your goal.This isn't like Doom I or II where the tricks and traps were thrown in occasionally to spice things up and the rest of the design relied on levels that mostly expanded outwards, versus the absurdly dense designs of Doom 64's. These things wind in on themselves like a pair of tangled headphones. It's not unusual to grab a key then cross over to the opposite side of a map, grab that key, cross over to the opposite side of the map, all the while unlocking parts of the levels via switches which inevitably don't give the clearest feedback for what has just been uncovered. This all occurs so often within a single level that unless you're keeping rapt attention, it's astonishingly easy to lose the thread - let alone coming back to a save after a day of not playing. There's not much interesting added to the arsenal here either, most of the weapons feel like inferior versions of their PC brethren, with not nearly as much kick or juicy feedback. The most compelling contribution is the Unmaker, which can be upgraded by finding artifacts across the level, but you'll already be having a hard enough time just routing out of these ennui inducing labyrinths, forget trying to find some squirrely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in a game with mazes that would make Daedalus kark himself in frustration.All the enemies are additionally uglier, less creative versions of their progenitors, and the new inclusions (of which there are few) are utterly uninspired.This game may have been somewhat compelling for its atmosphere and relatively "creative" (in a tortured, twisted way) level design back in the 90s, especially on consoles where the standards for shooters were significantly lower, but these days it's nothing more than an aggravating curiosity - big skip on Dookie 64 in my honest opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: My personal favorite of the 2.5d Doom games. I played it with Doom 64 EX a while back, so this wasn't my first time playing through the bulk of the game. Nightdive did a good job for the most part, though this port lacks some of the "modernization" options from D64EX (no vertical mouselook, jumping, or crouching). I miss the vertical mouselook from D64EX, but this port gives you a really good FOV slider. Overall, it's a very faithful port to the original gameThe combat is generally the same as it is in Doom 1 & 2. Several enemies have been cut (chaingunners, revenants, archviles, and spider masterminds) and a new weapon has been added (the unmaker). The only new enemies are the final boss and nightmare imps, but some enemies and weapons have seen redesigns. Pain elementals in particular are nastier in this game than any other game in the series. The BFG sees its weakest iteration in the series here, as it lacks most of the power it used to have. The new weapon, the unmaker, becomes ludicrously overpowered if you get all three of the demon keys. It is capable of melting cyberdemons in seconds, so it's worth trying to find all of the keys.This game greatly deviates from the first two games in regard to atmosphere and music. Levels tend to be darker and more purple or red. Colors in general are darker, and enemies have spookier designs than before.  The music is less rock and more ambient horror. The music is slow, drones a lot, and is filled with bizarre sound effects. I think it works quite well with the new designs and color palette.This game's level design is generally solid, but it has some shortcomings. It uses a lot of traps and switch puzzles, with the latter of which getting annoying after a while. There is one trap early on in the game where you fall into a pit and a small army of spectres spawn in around you. It's a really effective, terrifying trap and an excellent use of spectres. Unfortunately, the bulk of this game's traps consist of spawning hell knights behind you or unexpectedly dropping you into an inescapable pit. Some of this game's puzzles are rather unintuitive, particularly in the secret levels. In the first of the three secret levels, you need to get a keycard by interacting with a random panel on a wall with nothing distinguishing it. There's also the problem that door sounds don't travel very far, so you may not even know what a button did until you explore the whole level.This version of the game has a bonus campaign added to it, though it's a bit less than two hours long. It's more of the same with no particular increase or decrease in quality over the levels from the original game. They're consistent and enjoyable, though the first level is pretty difficult. You don't get the unmaker until the very end (unless it's in a secret I missed), but the game gives you so much ammo for it that you can just melt your way through the last few enemies in the campaign.Overall, it's pretty good. It's an underappreciated entry in the series. Source port is good and the new levels are excellent (aside from the final boss being really anti-climatic, just like in the base game). Heck, it works better than Doom 64 EX, which sometimes softlocks on map 20. Get it if you like OG Doom.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a shame that even back in the 90’s, DOOM 64 was already late to the party, because this is probably one of the best DOOM games ever released. I don’t know if it’s because I had really low expectations or if the revamped version from Bethesda did a great job, but going through the same old formula felt strangely refreshing with DOOM 64.A well-respected gaming website gave this game a score of 4.8 out of 10, which might had been a fair rating for the original Nintendo 64, but it doesn’t do justice to this refreshed version from Bethesda. DOOM 64 looks just like any old DOOM game, but with Quake’s gameplay. It immediately rang a bell when I got the super shotgun and started killing the hellish monstrosities like I used to do in Quake. It didn’t feel like the classic double-barrelled shotgun from DOOM II, but it was quite amusing nonetheless.One thing I wouldn’t miss from DOOM 64 are the “puzzles”, though. The eighth level in particular has a gotcha to obtain a certain yellow key that wasn’t fun at all to go through. Perhaps the devs tried to bring a bit more variety to the gameplay, but DOOM is fundamentally all about mowing down hordes of hellish spawns and that’s what the audience expects, anyway.Putting that unfortunate design choice aside, the action in DOOM 64 is appropriate and it is definitely worth to try out if you’ve played the original MS-DOS titles but didn’t have a Nintendo 64 to try this exclusive at the time. It is a strange time travel in the game’s saga, because while it is still a DOOM game, it plays quite differently from the first titles. I would say that it feels like an intermediate between DOOM II and DOOM 3, where the action feels like the former but there’s a grim aspect that somewhat resembles the latter. But don’t worry: you won’t need to decide whether to use a flashlight or a gun. :)

You'll most probably like this then, guaranteed.And just play on the hardest difficulty, or else it will be TOO easy, trust me.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is the great "forgotten" Doom game that some, myself included,  would argue to be the true Doom 3 over the 2004 main series entry. Somehow retaining both the older Doom game's fast and frantic action and also combining it with Quake's far more morbid atmosphere resulting in arguably a far more unnerving experience than Doom 3's attempts at horror. While it is fantastic that the game is finally unshackled from the ancient N64 hardware this port does have elements that leaves a lot to be desired.Doom 64 is canonically the third Doom game, taking place after the events of Doom II where Doomguy, being the only experienced marine to survive both the initial Mars moon invasions as well as the aftermath on Earth, is sent to a remote UAC base that has once more began to spew forth demons into the universe. Amusingly with the newer Doom game's releases focusing on the Doom Slayer this lost chapter of the Doom saga is now canonically placed seeing the main character here continuing on to become the main character for the later games. Where this leaves Doom 3 is anyone's guess, but the story of Doom 64 joins the dots to show how Doomguy ended up in hell to fight the demons for all time.Story aside (who cares about Doom lore?) the game is tonally a far darker game than its prior outings, both visually and audibly with a stronger lighting system and a step away from Bobby Prince's old midi scores. Simply adding coloured lighting to Doom as well as a stronger contrast between bright spots and the shadowy expanses covering most of the levels changes the old goofy adventure against the camel sampled imps to squinting into the darkness to see if there is an odd sprite moving about. Further to this is the darker, more ambient score by Aubrey Hodges, pulling away the old heavy metal midi and revealing a darker, more industrial backing. More than anything the horror comes from this element and its constant creep in tone slowly becomes the primary unnerving element. Where I initially found it cheesy in the opening levels, by the later hell missions it was so heavily engulfing that during my first playthrough I had to stop on occasion just to take a break from how suffocating the atmosphere was.Further highlighting the atmosphere is the level design. Doom has always had fantastic levels and Doom 64 is no exception. While none of the original designers were working on it, a lot of the moments scream of pure, dickish intent like the finest moments of Romero's works. Sometimes it is a little bit much as on a couple of maps there are fast firing, homing missile traps at locations that is little fun to contend with, but as a whole its suitably fiendish without going too far. Atmosphere wise however it is an interesting prospect in comparison to similar titles of the time. While Doom has always leaned far harder on the abstract designs, more about the flow and feel of a game than if it had any practical purpose, Doom 64 feels like an odd blend of both the abstract and real, where tech bases have desk terminals and some things that could be perceived as industrial equipment it equally has moments where you would think "what is this supposed to be?" This was in a post Duke Nukem world where other contemporary tiles tended to have real world logic applied far more than the typical iD fare and so Doom 64 ran the risk of seeming dated. Despite this the majority of Doom 64 takes place in hell alowing for a far more abstract feel to work well and expand on the ideas already implemented in the older games of the series. In comparison Doom II's unholy cathedral can vaguely be seen as a cathedral of some form, but that would require a good degree of imagination to pull off. The hell levels in Doom 64 with the true 3d environments seem to have various forms of coherent themes that have areas that have a vague semblance to human society, but are all slightly off in ways to make them uncanny. A large temple may contain a library, a torture chamber or various armoires and bastions for defence, only to be located next to a maze of corridors that seem illogical or various pits filled with flesh and bone for inexplicable reasons. The structure being formed by an eldritch logic that is just beyond the grasp of your own thinking and confounding the player, further enhancing the already thick and moody atmosphere by the visuals and sound.Aside from the aesthetic values, Doom 64 plays like the previous entries in the series. Fast moving, high action and requiring little in terms of wit or intellect to get through. You are still a dude with a shotgun murdering thousands of demons over and over  level after level with little in the way of plot, which can easily be ignored if you wish, bogging things down. Despite all the superb "show dont tell" world building the game has, if you did not like the prior games this will be equally stupid. Conversely if you liked the first two entries, Doom 64 is easily an equal to those.CONTINUED IN COMMENTS: Port quality.

_childDocuments_.review: REVIEW #73DOOM 64----------I love me a good, old-school DOOM game, and with time, DOOM 64 has become my favorite out of the handful of 90s-era releases from the series. The higher quality presentation of graphics and sound, the colored lighting, the new level scripting system, and the moody background ambiances are an incremental but definite step forward from the original two MS-DOS games. This new PC re-release of this D64, originally a Nintendo 64 exclusive, not only brings all of those improvements back with password-less saves, higher resolution and keyboard/mouse, but it also features an episode full of lost levels and password-less saves.Add the fact that DOOM 64 on its own is a really fun game on its own (despite a couple of levels that make the game feel a little stale and a new enemy art design that may not be as appealing as the original to some old-school DOOM players), and you've got an excellent title that any fan of the series (or any 90s-era FPS, for that matter) should consider. I love this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 was my introduction to the Doom franchise as a little kid. I would watch my dad play it on our N64, marveling at the graphics, the sound design, the weapons, and the eerie atmosphere. Playing with the N64 controller was unwieldy, so my dad never got very far into the game but my imagination would run wild with what the game had in store for players who managed to delve deeper into Hell.Fast forward 20 something years later and this remaster hits stores. I had played Doom64EX, which required an actual Doom64 ROM in order to work, and was a bit of a pain in the ass, but I was still enamored with the game. Coming back to it all these years later, and it still hits the same way it did when I was a kid. It feels so good to play; the weapons are punchy and have added effects that weren't in the original Dooms (such as the chaingun shaking the screen while you fire it), the levels are great with some challenging secrets to uncover, some of which utilize the new (for the time) scripting, enemies are beautifully designed, and the atmosphere is second to none in the Doom franchise. If you're a Doom vet, you might get a decent challenge out of it. Or you might find it a bit too easy. Either way, though, this is a must play. More Doom is always a good thing.

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64-----------------------------------DOOM 64 is one of the more interesting entries in the DOOM franchise. As with other Nintendo 64 titles, DOOM 64 is not a direct port of the original DOOM PC game to the console, but rather its own self-contained story complete with all-new levels, secrets, and assets. At first glance, it is pretty easy to ascertain that DOOM 64 borrows from classic DOOM only its engine, archetypes, and story points. Every monster has an all-new sprite, sound effects, and, in some cases, all-new variants, such as the nightmare Imp. Each weapon has similar changes as that of the monsters, with notable changes being the dual-bladed chainsaw and the addition of the BFG-like weapon, the Unmaker. DOOM 64 also added another layer to its secret levels by hiding demon runes in each secret level (barring Hectic) that incrementally upgraded the Unmaker. You can complete these secret levels without even collecting or realizing that these demon runes exist. Trust me, they're worth finding especially if you're playing on Watch Me Die! The ambiance of the game is a far cry from the heavy metal mayhem of the original DOOM, opting for a more atmospheric and horror-themed soundtrack and darker, more foreboding lighting and level design. It is a nice change that helps set DOOM 64 apart as a unique entry in the franchise. It is a PC port of a 90's console game, so that is something to take into consideration; if you don't like the feel of those classic DOOM engine FPS games, then DOOM 64 won't change your mind. QUALITY OF LIFE/MODERNIZATION:-----------------------------------As with many of Nightdive's remasters of classic FPS games, they've included a handful of quality of life changes and modern accessibility features that further expands the accessibility of DOOM 64 to a modern audience that doesn't know much about or is not interested in learning about source ports or dealing with emulation issues. Native widescreen support and 60-FPS, controller/gamepad support, addition of the "Lost Levels," and improved mouse and keyboard controls are just a handful of the advertised quality of life upgrades and features.Overall: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The real Doom 3, and an underrated classic that stands as the perfected form of the classic Doom formula. Doom 64 flew under a lot of folks' radars back in the day due to its console exclusivity and title leading many to believe it was simply an N64 port of the 1993 original. It is, in fact, an entirely new Doom campaign that takes the series in a darker and bolder direction. Gameplay is still the same as before, but levels are toned down in size compared to Doom II and some of the more overpowered enemies from that game are gone (don't let the door hit you on the way out, Archvile). As a tradeoff, the gameplay loop is a bit more varied. Key-hunting is still here, as always, but there's an increased emphasis on puzzle-solving that makes finding these keys a much more involved and rewarding endeavor. The puzzles aren't too complicated and don't outstay their welcome, so the game stays well-paced from beginning to end. There's even an optional sidequest involving the acquisition of three hidden artifacts that can increase the power of the game's new weapon, the Unmaker.More prominently, Doom 64 features a newer art style, colorfully moody lighting and an ambient soundtrack from Aubrey Hodges, who also composed the music for the PlayStation and Saturn ports of Doom prior to this game. The presentation gives Doom 64 a very tense and oppressive atmosphere, and while it never goes into full-on survival horror, I still very much enjoyed playing it in the dark with the sound up.Night Dive's port of the game is by far the definitive version. Samuel "Kaiser" Villarreal (who also worked on the unofficial PC port, Doom 64 EX) did some incredible work here, and the game runs flawlessly. It's a very vanilla experience that lacks the modern conveniences of EX, but playing classic Doom with mouselook and jumping is sacrilege anyway. If you're on the fence, though, this version features some additional "Lost Levels" that were cut from the original game, and the mouse movement feels a lot better compared to EX for some reason. All in all, the paltry $5 asking price for this official port of Doom 64 is extremely hard to pass up. Can't recommend highly enough.

The answer is a resounding: HELL YEAH!But first - the bad parts:- Intro:When you start it up there's just 45 (!) seconds of videos which you cannot skip. And that is before the actual intro which is 55 seconds that you can luckily skip. So, if I wanna play just for a short period of 10 minutes or so this wastes basically 10% of my time.EDIT: You can just kill the video folder which reduces the loading by a whooping 40 seconds down to 5!- :The very first thing I see after the intro is an error from . I haven't asked the game anything besides starting it and it already has a connection issue. I didn't even tell it to connect! What the hell?- Key bindings:I played like and hour or so and wondered why I was moving so slow when I considered myself running. Turns out - I wasn't running! To run you need to press space bar (instead of shift) and to use you press E (instead of shift). So - not even does it seem there's no way to easily get the original layout back, I also cannot change it to shift for running! And to top it of - the menu is so confusing because the display constantly toggles between current keyboard and current controller bindings, so it's extra hard to read what your keys are right now.EDIT: After starting it again a couple of times it finally seems to work. In case it doesn't for you - you can also manually set "speed" to lshift in the config file for the game.- Sometimes an enemy standing on a lower level can block you going down even if you cannot see. So I end up in situations where I keep getting damaged and there's an invisible wall that keeps me from moving. I guess this is intentional but it's annoying af.On to - the good parts:In the end all these are minor flaws. The game itself runs smoothly and looks fantastic. With all the lighting and atmospheric tunes in the background this really feels like and entirely different Doom. Back in the days of the N64 I - as many others - discarded this game as just a bad Doom clone, but boy was I wrong. _childDocuments_.review: About friggin time!If you're curious about the base game and have never played it before, this is the TRUE sequel to DOOM II. It picks up right where that one left off, and the game has redesigned enemies and whatnot. The atmosphere is by far the best in the entire series with a much more evil and sinister feeling throughout (I was terrified of this game as a kid, but never with the other original dooms), the levels are mixed more with a hybrid of medieval gothic and hellish theme, the music is more dark ambient than 80s metal, and the level design is more puzzle based than previous games but thankfully without being too frustrating. If you get stuck, you will usually be able to find your way after searching for a couple of minutes, it's not too bad honestly like you would expect. Along with the original Doom (yes over Doom II), I personally think that this is actually the best game in the series. As for THIS port itself; absolutely amazing stuff, just as expected from my bois at nightdive, the kings of boomer shooter remasters. This is nearly a flawless port, capturing all of the magic of the original while adding some new essential features. 60fps (as opposed to the 30 or so of the original), higher resolutions, smoother textures, controller support, an entirely new and exclusive episode, manual/quicksaves, as well as the original password system if you want to play the game how it was back in the day, and a plethora of others. I think the only things that I don't like about this port is that you have to be connected to the internet to play (I'm assuming, since it always connects when you start up the game), as well as the fact that you can't skip the company intro logos even if you've already seen it. It takes up 30 seconds of your time every single time you want to start up the game which is rather excessive imo. And lastly, I really wish there was the option to play coop or deathmatch in here with some deathmatch exclusive maps and steam workshop so others can make maps and keep the longevity of the game going. We'll see in the future.As it stands now, this is a DAMN good port, and one that is definitely worth MORE than the asking 5$ price. STOP SLACKING AND BUY IT!!!!

Yeah, it sucked back then too, but it was kinda cool lookin'.+ EVERYTHING is SUPER deadly, both your arsenal and the enemies.+ The level design is mind-boggling at times, and downright clever at other times, but LOTS of fun any which way. But be warned; there's LOTS of traps...Some really dirty tricks, too; perfect for a relaxing Halloween night.+ Awesome, haunting music that is actually genuinely scary at times.+ An AMAZING final boss fight.+ 'bout 10 hours of action-packed gameplay. (That extra hour or so was probably just from me being confused by some of the puzzles. And I don't even mind admitting that.)+ VERY clever level design.+ Hey, did I mention how clever the level design is? Seriously, love it.CONS:- The Pain Elementals spawn twice as many lost souls per "attack", which is a PAIN. And a bit of a problem... (See below.)- The lost souls are FAR more aggressive. Which is to say, they may be fragile, but they'll kill you as easily as a hell baron will if you aren't careful. They deal lots more damage, and attack in a very rabid pattern that punishes you for moving. Which is kinda lame, albeit that it 'does' make you appreciate the times when there 'is' music playing...Also, the music is more to the tune of the Playstation version of DOOM 1, rather than the old-school rock you'd expect from the regular versions of DOOM and DOOM II. - There's so very few secrets in this one for some reason. _childDocuments_.review: I rate Doom 64 3.5/5. Pretty good.  This creepy game (with really creepy ambient “music”) is even better on PC than it was on the Nintendo 64.This is a very good port of the version of Doom which was released on the Nintendo 64 gaming console. While its environments are not nearly as big and the enemies are not nearly as numerous as those in the first Doom or in Doom 2, this is still a fairly nice and creepy retro game with pretty good level design. PC gamers interested in every Doom game which has come out should definitely play this through at least once. While it is a fairly short game (it took me only 8 hours to play through), at only 5 USD it is well worth the price and can often be gotten on sale for even less.+Great use of what were evidently extremely limited Nintendo 64 hardware resources. Good level/puzzle design. Still feels like a classic Doom game.+As in prior Doom games, there are several difficulty levels.+Fairly responsive controls which can be rebound to any keys.+The light levels seemed just fine on a modern 1080p computer monitor. Did not seem too bright or too dark to me, but stayed true to exactly how I remember it looking on the Nintendo 64 (except now the game has even better resolution).+Nice lighting effects.+I didn’t notice any bugs or errors. The game ran perfectly for me.+/-This game has some extremely, unbelievably creepy ambient “music” but it isn’t really fun to listen to like the first two Doom game’s soundtracks could be.+/-The sound effects work well, with every single sound having a particular meaning but the sounds are of fairly low quality and tend to sound a bit muddy.+/-Doom 64’s levels are usually smaller than those found in the first Doom and Doom 2 and usually have fewer enemies as well. There’s not as many different types of enemies as in Doom 2 either (except Doom 64 has a unique boss monster). This was all probably due to the severe technical limitations of the Nintendo 64 game console for which Doom 64 was designed. However, the levels are still well made.+/-Rather than focusing on being as action-oriented as Doom or Doom 2, this game focusses on being creepy and often succeeds (thanks in large part to the amazingly creepy ambient music). Doom 64 also has some rudimentary colored lighting effects which the first Doom games did not have (they hadn’t been invented yet when those games were first released). The result is an odd, creepy game with some interesting lighting which retains the classic Doom retro gameplay style.+/-The new weapon, the “Unmaker” seems almost too powerful even in its default, non-upgraded state. Once you get it, the plasma gun and the BFG 9000 (which you get almost immediately beforehand) become almost totally obsolete and so go mostly unused for most of the game since they all use the same type of ammo. There’s also almost never enough enemies around to justify the large ammo costs of firing the BFG 9000.-This is a fairly short game, taking about 8 hours if played through casually.-No alternate endings (other than dying). The game’s ending is also nonsensical. Your character chooses to remain in Hell?! WHAT. What is your character, some sort of militaristic reincarnation of Jesus with guns?!-The first two Doom games had a cooperative mode so you could play it with others (in addition to a player versus player mode) but Doom 64 apparently does not. The absence of this seems odd.-As in Doom 1 and Doom 2, this game has a few secret alternate levels to find and explore but I think actually doing so would be fairly tedious (I found one). I wish all the secret levels were also accessible from a menu after the game is beaten on any difficulty level but they’re not. Game developers shouldn’t hide their hard work.-Why are the minimum system requirements so high?! There is no way the now very, very old Nintendo 64 had the equivalent of 8 GB of RAM or a GTX 660 yet this port claims to require something equivalent to this. Doom 64’s graphics are actually a few steps below those of the PC version of Quake 2 (an even earlier game) and yet the system requirements for Doom 64 are greater. This game’s requirements should be far more flexible so as to work on a far greater variety of machines. It should be possible for the same, fairly low-end game to be set to different preset speeds so it can work with radically different processor clock speeds.

_childDocuments_.review: Whenever I talk about Doom 64, people always say, "Oh, that was a port of Doom to the Nintendo 64, right?"Nope. It isn't. This is an entirely new game, and one you should really check out if you're a fan of oldschool Doom.Some fans call this the "Real Doom 3", and for good reason. While it plays like Doom, and while it has (mostly) all the same enemies and weapons you'd find in your usual Doom games -- Imps, barons, cyberdemons, you know, the whole crew -- the tone of the game has taken a heavy Gothic horror slant to it. Everything's darker and moodier. Monster sprites are more realistic and grotesque. Sound effects are all new; some, like the Star-Trek-sounding doors and the "whoosh" sound of a monster's thrown projectile, are seriously unforgettable. Music is all ambient and horror-esque (one track famously features a sample of a baby crying). There's a new weapon that hasn't made it into any other Doom game, and a pretty awesome sidequest related to it -- if you find three secret levels and find the secret items hidden within them, the gun becomes so powerful that you basically get to skip the final boss fight altogether.Level design is a bit different here. Unlike classic Doom, Doom 64's map scripts can spawn monsters wherever they want at any time. This makes monster ambushes much more frightening, as you would walk into the middle of a room only to have monsters appear all around you, or turn a corner to suddenly find that monsters have repopulated a room you thought you'd already cleared out. Some maps use this to create battle-arena rooms with multiple waves of enemies. Maps can also trigger stuff when certain enemies are killed, so you might be locked in those battle-arena rooms until everything's dead. The scripts make it seem as though the floors and walls themselves are possessed by demons who just want to toy with you at every turn.Monster properties have all been reworked, too. Mancubus fireballs now travel annoyingly slow, making them oddly more dangerous. Arachnatrons fire a double-stream of plasma which moves surprisingly fast and can snipe you from across the level. Lost Souls are far more aggressive. Pain Elementals shoot two Lost Souls at once, making them one of the biggest threats in the game. And the Cyberdemon not only shoots some seriously fast-moving missiles, but he fires them at a downward slant so you have to dodge the splash damage when they hit the floor. Personally, I loved all of the monster changes; it's been a long time since Doom monsters have made me feel afraid and uncomfortable to fight them up close!My criticisms of this port are:* Every time you boot up the game, you have to sit through about 8 logo / credits screens before you even get to the title screen. This takes almost a full minute. I wish I were joking.* The game's sprites look like blurry garbage unless you go into the graphics settings and turn off "filtering" which is on by default for some unfathomable reason. * There are more than a few "where the hell do I go now??" levels. * Three or four of the levels will probably drop you into an inescapable acid pit with no reason or warning. Even for oldschool standards, that's a pretty low blow.* If you want to see the fully-powered lasergun, you'll absolutely need a FAQ to find the second demon key level. While I mostly was impressed with the cleverness of the hidden secrets, this one's just unforgivably obtuse. Ditto if you want to find the level "Hectic" (which also unlocks cheat codes and five bonus levels when beaten)Doom 64 is a tragically overlooked cult classic in every sense of the word, not having gotten an official re-release until now. While it's true that a few fan-made mods have already brought the game to PC with varying levels of quality, Doom 64 as a commercial product is finally free of its decades-long shackles to the N64 cartridge, and maybe it'll finally get the widespread appreciation it deserves alongside the rest of the classic Doom campaigns like TNT and Plutonia. Plus, alongside the release of Doom Eternal, they've even added a short new campaign with a half-dozen maps that supposedly tie the story in with Doom 2016 in some way. (Most of the new maps are combat-heavy and feel like scrapped deathmatch maps, which isn't a bad thing.)Oh yeah, and it's on Nintendo Switch too, if you're into that!8 / 10! (Achievement hunters: 100% requires you to beat nearly all of the game on the hardest difficulty. Heavily depending on how skilled you are at classic Doom, how much you like to save-scum, and how much you'd want to check a FAQ, this could take you 12-20 hours.)

_childDocuments_.review: To many people back in the day, DOOM 64 might have sounded like nothing but a Nintendo 64 port of DOOM, judging by the title. They were wrong, since this is a completely new game! Initially, it was going to be called "DOOM: The Absolution" according to reports, but the stupid naming convention Nintendo imposed wouldn't allow it. Without taking any merit whatsoever from the masterpiece that is DOOM 3, this feels much closer to a third installment of the series, since it's more technically advanced than the previous DOOM titles and expands on them, as a true sequel would.This DOOM title differs quite a bit from the previous games, due to cartridge limitations. It plays out similarly to DOOM II, but a few demons were cut, like the Arch-vile or the Revenant, weapons were reworked, controls were altered to fit the monstrous N64 controller and less demons will overwhelm the player simultaneously. Nightmare difficulty was planned, but "Watch me Die!" ended up being the hardest one here, being similar to Ultra-Violence instead. We now play it with keyboard and mouse which makes it a walk in the park, since it was balanced towards N64 controller players, where movements and aim couldn't be as precise. It can still challenge the player of course, but for experienced DOOM players however, this will be a breeze. Maybe as hard as DOOM, but significantly easier than DOOM II.The heart pumping Metal covers with MIDI tracks were replaced by atmospheric and eerie soundscapes, and everything is darker this time around, both in tone and literal lighting. The vibe leans more towards Quake than DOOM. It's funny how the edgiest and creepiest DOOM came out on a Nintendo console of all places! Maybe this direction was influenced by console limitations, who knows? Regardless, it's highly appreciated.This is an enhanced version made by Nightdive Studios, with many tweaks to make the game playable on PC. There's a new map pack, "The Lost Levels", whose sole purpose is to link old school DOOM events all the way to DOOM 64 directly to DOOM (2016) and DOOM Eternal lore! This makes DOOM 64 a solid entry in the series' lore, rather than a separate universe like DOOM 3, which is a whole other can of worms. There's also achievements, where this guide will come in handy:

_childDocuments_.review: This is onses where, even though it's a really good game and I really like it, I have to go thumbs down because of significant technical issues/glitches with the game that result in less than an expected/hoped for gaming experience.If you're too young to remember the cartridge game days, this version of Doom was originally released on the Nintendo 64 console in 1997 and features different levels than in the PC versions. It has been optimized for newer PCs as well. Originally the only way to get this was to have pre-ordered Doom Eternal but now it's available as a standalone game.This updated version certainly looks better on PC than the N64 original did, on higher-end PCs the game looks really good in HD and generally manages to maintain a very smooth frame rate, although sometimes it sometimes gets a bit choppy at moments. If you've played the old Doom PC games, you'll recognize the various sound effects and voices as they're the same here. Considering how the old N64 controllers were, this version's controls are much easier to work with and ports well to dual-stick gamepads. While the familiar gameplay is the same with some tricky puzzles to figure out, there are a few problems both getting there and during play-when I first got this game it wouldn't even start due to apparent graphics driver/setup issues (it makes you use Vulkan, not DX or OpenGL), but after a couple weeks and a GPU driver update or two (using a GTX 1660 Ti GPU) the game suddenly started working. There are fixes mentioned in the forums but none of them seemed to work. However, it is a little unstable at times and has unexpectedly crashed on me a couple of times as of this review. At least the best thing about the game is the price-if it's regular price it's onlt $5 but when on sale you can get it for as little as $1.50 so you're not losing much. Also, one last buyer beware if you're thinking LAN party: There is no multiplayer here. It's single player only.It's still a fun Doom game and a good bargain bin find, but it's all about whether or not it will work for you, and it's pretty much a toss-up. Wait for a sale when you can get it for under $2 before thinking about picking it up, just prepare to be patient and frustrated in the event it doesn't start up as hoped for and throws crazy error screens at you. That's why I do not recommend the game even though it's great and worth playing, but what good is a game when there's no guarantee you can even get in and play?)Footnote: The game tries to make you sign up for or log in with a Bethesda account when you first start up the game. This is NOT REQUIRED to play the game)

_childDocuments_.review: I love Doom. I always planned on picking up Doom 64's unofficial PC ports (not sure if they are still out there on the internet) as I've played Doom 1 and 2 to death. I am sort of mixed on the game. The limitations of the N64 are very apparent. Limited frames of animation for your weapons and the enemies is very disappointing. The redesigns for the enemies work really well and are explained in the game. The music is often praised for its direction towards horror, but honestly in my opinion it's very weak. Doom is not a horror game, I would rather listen to heavy metal riffs than atmospheric moans and groans. You won't even notice the music once the action picks up and it's probably the weakest aspect of the game.The gameplay is a continuation of the classic Doom games. You will kill plenty of demons, hit switches and collect keys. I beat the game on the 3rd difficulty, it was a comfortable challenge, but I don't think the game is too difficult overall more so that there are some maps with huge difficulty spikes.There are new features such as scripted events and traps. The scripted events are more than just monster spawns, there are times where the levels shift and move. There should have been more of these as they are infrequent. I can do without the traps. Some of the traps are literally beginner traps that add nothing but frustration. You won't know the ground will collapse and send you into a pit of lava unless you already played it. I would not have had the patience to get through some of the levels without the ability to save. Some of the puzzles can be a bit obtuse and frustrating if you aren't paying close attention. One particular map had you hit the correct switch based off where the mega-sphere you see first appears. I don't really understand how you were supposed to figure that out as it changes every time. The weapons also have received some changes. The chain gun has a faster rate of fire and ammo is plenty, still a great weapon for staggering and taking out large amounts of the fodder enemies. The rocket launcher has given "unnecessary recoil" causing you to step back and also has a slightly longer delay for firing (could be wrong though). The plasma rifle I hardly used because the unmaker is far more powerful. The BFG no can cause splash damage to you and feel very ineffective, I seldom used it. The pistol, shotgun and super shotgun are pretty much the same.This release includes the "lost episodes" which from a story perspective makes very little sense. It's supposed to tie the story to Doom 2016 however I think the vanilla ending is better. The levels are much more difficult than the vanilla game. It gives you a real fight with the Mother demob.If you like Doom 1 and 2 go ahead and grab it, just don't expect "Doom 3" instead expect a classic Doom game if it was made by someone else.

_childDocuments_.review: I realize this game was the gateway for a lot of people into the series, as even years after the PC release, that version was still not accessible to everyone. Because of this, it holds a lot of nostalgia for those people. But, if you were fortunate enough to experience the original, this is just an inferior experience.I find the level design to be one of the most disappointing changes in the game. The original Doom levels I feel had a good stream of fire fights with occasional puzzle solving. This dynamic feels switched in Doom 64, with fights being a minor distraction between puzzle solving. And that puzzle solving isn't fun. It's mostly a process of flipping a switch then going through the level and figuring out what it did. Granted, there was a bit of this in the original level design, but there's a lot more in Doom 64, and it gets old really fast. Levels are also a lot tighter and that doesn't work well for a game like Doom.In terms of graphics, I can take or leave the redone sprites. I still prefer the original game's, but if they weren't going to do a straight port I can understand the decision. However, the textures are just bland and ugly. And some levels make use of this yellow light which gives them a urine colored tint.If you're curious to discover the game because you missed it on the N64, at least wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Being the huge hipster I am, when Doom Eternal was announced alongside Doom 64 coming to PC and consoles, I have to admit I was more excited for an official PC release by the legends at Nightdive than I was for the new game. I had played a fair bit before on an unofficial PC port and enjoyed it, but this timeI absolutely loved it.++Visually the game is stunning. Yes, this Nintendo 64 exclusive FPS from 1997 not even running on a fully 3D engine is stunning. The art-style and character designs are brilliant and the colour palette gives the game a feel of its own.++Doom's timeless, nigh unmatched FPS combat is retained fully, but with enough slight changes to make it feel like its own thing.++I'm all about atmosphere, and Doom 64 is one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played. Seriously. There were times where I felt like I was in a dreamscape version of hell thanks to the superb visuals, music and level design++This port contains new levels. They're not all that memorable, but ♥♥♥♥ it, it's more Doom 64 which is awesome, and they totally didn't need to do it but they did which is also awesome.++Top-tier level design+Very well lengthed+The game sounds really good. It barely even sounds all that low quality.+Has just about all the graphical, audio and controls options you'd want, including texture filtering and individual controller button binds+Weapons have a lot of weight and impact to them now+The infamous soundtrack is much more ambience than it is music and it is suitably creepy+Lots of secret levels and hidden goodies. The secret levels are actually unique in this because of how much they effect the actual game in ways I won't spoil but is widely discussed anyway.+-There's no vertical aim setting. This may sound awful to anyone who's never played an FPS without vertical aim but TRUST ME. You WILL get used to it very quickly and will realise it's not all that bad. It would've been nice if they could've added it as an option but there's only so much they can do with the original engine and unfortunately this is something that simply cannot be fixed.-N/A--N/ASound: 8.5/10Graphics: 9.5/10Gameplay: 9.5/10Content/Replayability: 5/10Overall: 9.5/10There's nothing really I can complain about here. Doom 64 is a hell of a game and the fact that it was an N64 exclusive has absolutely not affect on its quality. This is a true classic.

_childDocuments_.review: After Doom released in 1993, every FPS game in the mid 90s tried to mimic it. Including it's sequel Doom 2. In fact the Doom IP was so popular, ID software allowed a game consisting of fan made Doom maps called Final Doom to be sold at Retail. (no this game was not a legit sequel to Doom 2). But in spite of this, after a couple years of Doom clones dominating the PC market, ID software released a game called Quake in 1996 and it changed everything despite having lots of parallels to Doom. Thanks to the game's Full 3D models and ground breaking online multiplayer mode, the old Doom gameplay became dated by comparison. However, in 1997 Williams software were given the green light to make their own original Doom game on consoles after the positive reception the Playstation version of Doom received from both fans and the original designer of Doom, John Ramero. This game would go on to become Doom 64. When Doom 64 came out in the spring of 1997 for the Nintendo 64, the  game completely under performed with low sales and lukewarm reviews. Due to being given an miss leading name, being released on a console known for full 3D games, being an M rated title with Satanic imagery on a system marketed towards kids, and the fact that the Doom franchise was just all around declining in popularity due to newer FPS titles like Quake, Goldeneye, and Turrok utilizing cutting edge technology. But in the early 2010s, that started to change. When younger generations started to develop an interest in the Doom series, they did research on Doom 64 thanks to the power of the internet, and discovered that this game was the actual sequel to Doom 2 as apposed ID's 2004 series reboot that was inappropriately named Doom 3. From there on out, this game got gradually more popular to the point where PC mods got released to loads of acclaim. And now we have reached a point where we can now play this game publicly and in a way that it was meant to be played. On a PC with a mouse and Keyboard. So how does the actual sequel to Doom 2 hold up now that's its being sold publicly? Lets see for our selves. Now I wont do a pros and cons segment here, because this is one of those rare games where what you like or don't like about it depends on what your personal tastes are. But What I will say is an objective positive of the game is that it plays exactly the same as the previous games... except that the mouse controls are vastly superior to Doom 1 and 2. And I found myself pulling off maneuvers that I could never pulled off in those games or this game's console version that matter. so it wins in the controls department. When it comes to the more subjective stuff I noticed that the level design is a lot more cryptic and puzzle oriented then the first two games, while it took me some time to adjust to this I eventually adapted to this no problem. Some may take a little longer then me, but I recommend to those people to give it a chance since it helps the game feel more uniqe unlike Doom 2 which played it too safe at times. It should also be mentioned that this game has a lot more secret levels then usual, in fact some of  them have these secret optional keys that power up the newest gun in this game, The Un-Maker, which will make the final boss easier the more you collect (think of them like the four sage temples from Zelda: Breath of the Wild). Hint: you'll need at least two of them to make  the final level a smooth fun ride. But the biggest difference between this game and the first two is the visuals and music. This game goes for  a more atmospheric and fear inducing tone, unlike Doom 1 and 2 which go for a more bright and colorful "YEAH, I'm gonna kill them all and love it" type of tone. The lighting is more realistic and dark, the music now goes for moody ambiance like the Quake 1 music by Trent Raznor as opposed to Doom 1 &2's music which mimics AC/DC, Alice in Chains, and Judas Priest, and the sprite models have been given complete re-designs. Most of which I'll admit look a lot more intimidating and 3 dimensional to the point where the old sprites  look more cartoony by comparison (except for the Mankibusses, and a couple of your guns). In fact  this was the only game I have ever played that managed to scare me through visuals and sound alone. Lastly, I should mention that while I do understand why some people didn't like this tone shift when it came to the PS1 version of Doom 1 & 2 due to the fact that the port was trying to take games that where designed with a different tone in mind and change the feel completely. However, This Game I feel is the right type of game to do something like this to. Mainly due to being an actual sequel That IS designed with this tone in mind, as well as the fact that one of the criticisms of Doom 2 is that it played things too similarly to the first game. So in a way, taking an approach like this is actually what the doctor ordered when it comes to making a sequel that raises the stakes. Overall, I can see why some people will see this as either the best or the worst of the original era Doom games. This games addresses the "playing it too safe" problem Doom 2 had to a T. And is once again one of those games where what you like or don't like about it depends on your personal tastes. As for me, I think all of these changes are for the best and are a welcome addition to this series. And for me, out of all the Doom sequels I have played, This is the best one. If your one of those people that have played this game and cant get into it due to the different tone and level design.I recommend that you keep giving it a shot, I promise that you'll eventually get into it. And If you grew up playing the original N64 version, get it anyway. There's lots of new additions for old players too. And the fact that the system requirements are not very high makes the reason to buy this all the more stronger. I give this game a 9.5 out of 10This is the perfect follow up to Doom 2 and I give it the title of being the REAL Doom 3. Going from Doom to  Doom 2 to This, makes for the perfect FPS trilogy in my eyes.

_childDocuments_.review: I never played this on the N64, but I've played every Doom game on PC. This a review for people who are only interested in this as a PC game, compared to all the others.Good:- Decent number of levels, secret levels, and enemies.- Decent level lengths and designs. - Classic arsenal of weapons, plus a new super weapon. - An actual brand new final boss (other than the Cyberdemon or Spider Mastermind), unlike the annoyance that was the Icon of Sin in Doom II.- Same enemy roster roll-call upon beating the game, just as fun this time as when beating Doom II.- Puzzles, but nothing as obscure or annoying as in Hexen- Quick-saves, quick-loads, and level select.- Extra levels apart from the main campaign.- Multiple difficulties.Bad:- No music, just ambient sounds (listed as bad, but for me, it suited the game fine).- You can zoom out of the mini-map, but the default is way too zoomed in. Also, the zoom setting isn't saved between levels, meaning you start each level having to zoom out your mini-map again. - 3 hidden "keys" to power up your new super weapon (new to the series anyway). Good idea, but the intricacies and non-direct means of acquiring them are far too obscure for the average gamer to attain them without referring to a guide. Also, dying not only removes any collected weapons, but the keys you've acquired too. No means of reacquring them without reverting to a save file. - Fewer enemies than in Doom II. - Fewer unique art assets than in Doom and Doom II. - Weapon switching takes far too long, even when using the number keys. - Ammo, for most of the levels, on the second-highest difficulty anyway, is far too plentiful. - Some very cheap "traps" with no escape, such as pits with no way out, ceiling crushers with no means to avoid them, items you cannot acquire lest you wish to die under said trap, etc. - Text messages fade out, slowly. If you want to read the map name on the mini-map, you will probably have to wait a few seconds while "quicksave" disappears. Verdict: Most of my gripes could be shrugged aside based on the fact this was made as an N64 title. But therein lies my biggest fault with this game. It is at once too easy, as well as too hard. No small feat to accomplish. On PC, combat is more or less what any fan of the Doom series would expect. The hardest parts stemming from puzzles and acquiring items with either obsessive-compulsive disorder, or through the use of an online guide (though granted, those "keys" are optional). But here's where I'm at a loss. The N64 didn't provide number keys to switch to a weapon with a single key press. Nor did it provide quick-saving (that I'm aware of). Because the game does get harder in later levels (first 8 levels are a breeze, they do ramp up significantly later on though), and because of the way that certain paths can lead to a cheap death with no means to escape, anticipate, or avoid without trial and error, I'm convinced that this game would have been too challenging for most as a console experience. On PC played today, it is still fun, but I personally don't find it nearly as engaging as Doom or Doom II. There was a charm to the original sprites, graphics, and music that this game lacks. Perhaps because of its console roots, many of the levels could be confused with one another, due to the graphics not being different enough. I will grant that after level 8, things start to change up a bit both graphically and in difficulty. Conclusion: If you've played all the others and never played Doom 64, you may as well pick it up for the price is reasonable for about a 7-8 hour experience. Don't expect to want to play it again anytime soon though.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a little reluctant to try this but I'm glad I did. This is one of the most fluid and fun FPS games I've ever played. Even if I died (and I did a lot), I NEVER got truly frustrated, and instead felt encouraged to plan my attacks and git gud (hint: save often). I also enjoy the element of horror added to the game: Aubrey Hodges' score delivers an eerie, uncomfortable ambience while you search the labyrinthine tunnels of Hell and run into enemies. If you're looking for a great classic FPS you can't really go wrong with this game. It holds up VERY well despite being a 1990's game, with fair and balanced gameplay, an awesome array of weapons, creative enemies, and full of secrets to explore. And it's super cheap, too!

_childDocuments_.review: Finally an official port for this often-overlooked Nintendo 64-exclusive entry in the Doom series!PROS:+ The Lost Levels, a brand-new mapset designed specifically for this release+ Striking gothic reimagining of Doom II visuals, arsenal and bestiary+ The Unmaker, a memorable addition to the Doom arsenal+ Darker, grittier, scarier atmosphere reminiscent of Quake+ Aubrey Hodges' excellent sound design+ Easily the most faithful port CONS:- Some occasionally nasty difficulty spikes due to cramped level design and cheap traps- Thefully-powered Unmaker, so overpowered it makes even the BFG obsolete- Not the best port, due to a lack of modern options (including mouse look)- Slower pace than Classic Doom due to original console-friendly design- No attempt to integrate the Fun Levels into the main map rotation- Missing the Outcast Levels and Redemption Denied mapsets- No attempt to recreate the missing Doom II monsters- Bethesda preventing further patches and support- The absurdly ugly Pain Elemental redesign
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 has always been one of my favourite doom games. Even back when i used to play Brutal Doom 64 I still loved the game. The level design has held up extremely well, better than Ultimate Doom and Doom 2 in my opinion. As for this port, it's easily the best one out of the bunch. Brutal Doom 64 changed far too much and is incredibly unbalanced on high difficulties, Doom 64 Retribution was very inaccurate, and Doom 64 EX was good, but was based on an old sourceport and had a few issues. This port cleans up these issues and overall improves the experience. The mouse aiming is silky smooth and this port is incredibly optimized, I have a toaster of a pc and I ran it at 1080p and I never once had a single hitch during my playtime. As for the new content, the Lost Levels are a great inclusion, they're challenging and have even better level design than the original Doom 64. Nightdive have done an extraordinary job with this port, and I definitely am excited to see what they do next.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:+Great level design; hard to get lost, easy to get a feeling of when traps will appear.+Amazing soundtrack; Gives Doom 64 a haunting mood compared to 1 and 2 (which may not be what want in a Doom game).+Gameplay controls are easy to pickup and play.+The graphics are great and I love the redesigned enemies.The meh:~There are a few glitches in this game that may pop up.  There are three that I've encountered: 1) Get soft locked inside a puzzle room because the teleport wouldn't open, 2) missing textures, 3) enemies getting stuck inside moving platforms.(I'm not counting this as a negative because of how rare this glitches are).~Normal difficulty is too easy and even the hardest difficulty isn't very hard (I did die plenty however).  This probably because it's originally a console shooter.The bad:-It is hard to know either an object is interactable or not, for example: there was a light source that acted as a button that I need to press in order to get a door key.This is rare so consider it a minor negative.-Shotgun and super shotgun take up the same weapon slot.  Same goes for fist and chainsaw.  This is only mildly irritating.I was going to mark the final boss as a negative but after a second playthrough on hardest difficulty it's not all that tough to strafe and avoid its projectiles using buildings.  I would rank this higher than Doom 2 and personally maybe even Doom 1 (but I would have to do a second playthrough of that game before I can say that with confidence).Yes, I recommend this game or as a gift to any FPS fans.  You will get your money's worth.(Also the Bethesda account creation is skippable, in case you're wondering).

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is a perfect example of how well a game can age provided that it is given proper controls, a high resolution, and a high framerate. I love this game so much, as it is my favorite classic DOOM game. (DOOM 2016 is my personal favorite so far, as I haven't played DOOM Eternal yet.) The game's atmosphere was incredible to me, and I loved the levels as well, which has caused me to replay them quick a lot.DOOM 64 has great level design, atmosphere, combat, and music, but people should know what they are getting into before trying it out. This game has levels that are a bit more puzzle-based than the previous DOOM games, and the music isn't upbeat metal music, but more atmospheric and unnerving music. Nevertheless, the fast-paced gameplay from the previous games is retained, along with the weapons. You will be greatly rewarded in this game for being thorough and discovering secrets.I should mention that out of all the classic DOOM games to purchase from Steam, DOOM 64 works the best right out of the box. Be sure to adjust the video settings so they work properly. For some reason, the VSync is a bit wonky with this game, so you might need to go to your graphics card control panel and adjust the VSync settings to be forced on for all games. I tried having VSync on in-game, but there was still screen tearing for me until I forced VSync to be on for all games. This game easily scores a 10/10 for me! Play this game if you are a DOOM fan, FPS fan, Horror fan, retro fan, or just want a good throwback that works well with modern PCs.

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry, I don't think this is a good game. Chances are you already know if you like it or not, but to me it feels like a Doom knock-off rather than a Doom game. I was 16 when this game originally came out in 97 and I didn't own an N64 because I already had a computer I played Doom games on. And believe me, I played the HELL out of Doom and Doom 2 on that thing. Played over dial-up, made maps, the whole thing. I don't even think I knew about Doom 64 until the 2010s. It seems to be a favorite among people of a certain age, maybe who were younger than me when it came out, I dunno. Maybe it's a nostalgia thing for them, maybe they had an N64 but no PC on which to play Doom and Doom 2? I dunno. All I can say is I just don't enjoy this game (yes I'm aware Steam doesn't show me having played it long, but I've played ports of it before). I know that the game is considered to be a sequel to Doom 2 or something, but I don't see why they threw out all the original Doom art. I'm sure they could have gotten the original sprites and textures and maybe even the engine from id, after-all they were already licensing the Doom name, so why not? I know a lot of this is just subjective, but I feel like the sprites in this game just look cheap (even with texture filtering off). There's something about the way they are pre-lit, the scaling and the color palette that I just find unpleasing. The animation speed and number of frames in the animations is off too. Watching an enemy I just killed slowly collapse to the floor in what seems to be too few animation frames is jarring and ugly. The wall textures are dull compared to the original Doom games and the lighting is bland and at times even harsh. I'm aware the game has colored lighting which is technically more advanced tech than Doom and Doom 2 but I don't really care. There's an overall lack of atmosphere to the game. The level layout feels really uninteresting compared to the brilliant maps that the older games were known for. Nothing about the weapons feels satisfying, the shotgun barely moves in your hand when you fire it, the sounds of weapons are underwhelming. The sprite scaling of the enemies is off, the zombies feel like they are 8 feet tall. I just don't get why they did this this way.I'm aware that this port on Steam isn't the greatest, but don't make the mistake of thinking I'm giving this game a bad review because of that. I'm not. I straight up just don't think it's a good game. If you do, good for you, enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Like so many Doom titles, this one is pretty misleading. As I explained in my review of , this is not the 64th part of the nameless and silent Space Marine but, be careful, here it comes:Strictly speaking, the game is actually the third part, as it was developed for the Nintendo 64 by Midway Games in coordination with id Software, which was re-released by Bugthesda in March 2020, and the story takes place after Doom 2.So Doom 64 is actually the third part which would then make Doom 3 the fourth part, which isn't right either because Doom 3 is actually a reboot, which is what Doom (2016) also is and ok, let's just leave that alone...The game proved at the time that Doom can also flop, as it only caused many people to shrug their shoulders because the screenshots made people think that it was another version of Doom (1993), which included everything from a calculator to a toaster has been ported to pretty much everything. For others, the game with the “old-fashioned” 2-D enemies and the “retro game play” was simply too outdated.It wasn't until a few years later that an, albeit rather small, fan community built up around the game, which is probably due to Doom 64 EX, which was a very popular fan port of the game for the PC.The game was remastered by Nightdive Studios, who had made a name for themselves with remastered games like Forsaken, Blood: Fresh Supply or Turok and had done a good job of porting. The game runs on the Kex Engine with a stable refresh rate, although there are no other notable innovations and you can expect the same “mushy textures” and pixelated 2D sprites as in the original.Thanks to the higher resolutions, the image still looks pleasantly sharp and clean and you can adjust the optics a little better using an FOV slider, edge smoothing, V-Snyc and two brightness controls. In addition, the game now offers free key assignment and the ability to save freely, including quicksave and quickload. The classic level selection via code is still possible and so the porting plays cleanly and in my opinion is quite successful.Nothing has changed in terms of content and all the levels that existed in the original are there. But there is a small additional point that should not be ignored. There is a new chapter at the end that is supposed to build a kind of bridge to the new Doom offshoots with new levels and more story snippets.Doom 64 is a direct sequel to Doom 2 from 1994 and brings back the Marine, who once again has to shoot his way through a demon-infested station on Mars.So it plays just like the first two parts where you can't look up or down or jump. So you rush through the more than 30 levels at high speed, collect key cards, discover secrets and work your way to the exit where you slaughter tons of demons., if you're one of them too.The typical weapons are also back in this game and there is also a new energy weapon, the Unmaykr, which is also making its return in Doom Eternal.Sure, the game is about “old-fashioned” action, but that’s exactly why it’s so much fun.The fights and the stupid opponents aren't really the challenge in the old games. Rather, as in the first two parts, the challenge is to explore the labyrinth-like environment and not get lost. The levels here are quite small, but they are neatly nested and full of switches, teleporters, elevators and doors. Even if you have a good sense of direction, getting lost isn't difficult. If you press a switch, a passage opens somewhere, a platform goes down or a key card appears somewhere, where you can often only guess where exactly it was. It's certainly a bit out of date today, but in the 90s such level design was common practice, which you certainly can't blame the game for.Graphically, the game is still reminiscent of its two predecessors, but the engine did a lot more back then and Doom 64 offered a much better lighting model so that the environment was immersed in more colorful light. In addition, all 2-D enemies were replaced with more detailed ones and a texture filter smoothed the pixelated wall textures.The look and feel of the original Doom were omnipresent, which is why some Doom fans consider the game to be the “real Doom 3”.Doom 3 was just a complete reboot that had a completely different focus with tons of jump scares and dark levels.But that's another story that I'll tell you another time.✔ classic “good old” gameplay✔ technically perfect game✔ Graphics options and free key assignment✔ new chapter with new levels✔ free saving✔ old cheat codes still work✔ great soundtrack✔ many levels of difficulty✘ confusing level design✘ Hardly any graphical changes/improvements✘ no multiplayer mode✘ Played through quite quicklyRevised and reposted: November 26, 2023

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is an absolute must play for DOOM and Retro Shooter fans alike! It is the most dark and gothic of the classic games and certainly hits hard in the atmosphere department with its amazing soundtrack comprised by Aubrey Hodges (He also did the soundtrack for DOOM PS1, Final DOOM PS1, Quake 64, and Quake II 64). The games levels are all excellent and filled to the brim with demons to slaughter and secrets to find. Most of the demon roster returns from DOOM II/Final Doom (excluding the Revenant and Arch-Ville) and all have had a make over for this iteration which helps make this one stand out a bit more when put next to it's predecessors. _childDocuments_.review: Not bad as a freebie for pre-ordering Eternal. However, I'm not sure if I'd suggest purchasing this Doom title on its own. Optimistically stepping into my first-ish classic Doom experience, I was disappointed to find that playtime boiled down to a lot of key hunting. Firefights exist as trickles of demons between every other room. With D64's reduced enemy density, the experience averages out to meandering through a hall of mirrors. It can be difficult to tell a wall apart from a locked/unlocked door or discern between a button and an inert computer screen. Buttons in one room may activate an inconspicuous item around another corner, only supplying a faint audio queue to hint at the new location. I know there's more to the series, so hopefully future time with spent Doom 1 & 2 will better showcase that legacy.

_childDocuments_.review: As the 3rd installment of Doom, Doom 64 attempts to resurrect an aging and outdated engine for one final romp. Unfortunately, the "technical advancements" lag behind other ID titles of the time (Quake was close to a year earlier) and do little make this tile stand out from it's franchise predecessors. The colored lighting feature is nothing more than a cheap hack. Monster turn purple or orange abruptly when they step into the light map; it looks terribly unnatural and the game would actually be better without it. The addition of echo to the sound effects in enclosed spaces is way over-done and sounds genuinely horrible.,, again, less would be more. The additional mapping capabilities are underwhelming or perhaps underutilized, as the maps are not as clever and the ambiance is not as immersive as Doom and Doom II. While the game does pick up some after the 10th level or so, it is a weak sequel.
