_childDocuments_.review: Reliving Hellish Nightmares: Review of "DOOM 64"Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)"DOOM 64" resurrects the classic first-person shooter experience from the depths of gaming history, offering players a nostalgic trip to the days of demon-slaying and pulse-pounding action. Developed by Midway Games and released in 1997 for the Nintendo 64, this entry in the DOOM franchise carves its own dark path with an eerie atmosphere, intense battles, and a sense of old-school charm that holds up surprisingly well today.Set as a standalone sequel to the original DOOM games, "DOOM 64" places players in the worn boots of the DOOM Marine as they journey to eliminate the remaining forces of hellish entities. The storyline is sparse but effective, serving as a backdrop for the frenzied action that defines the game.The gameplay in "DOOM 64" sticks to the classic formula that made the series famous: fast-paced shooting, non-stop movement, and a wide arsenal of weapons. The controls and level design feel remarkably polished, offering a fluid and visceral experience that transports players back to the early days of FPS gaming. The game's combat sequences remain thrilling, with each enemy encounter a test of reflexes and strategy.Visually, "DOOM 64" features an eerie and atmospheric design that sets it apart from its predecessors. The dark and ominous environments, along with the gloomy lighting, contribute to a haunting ambience that heightens the sense of dread. The game's graphics, while limited by the hardware of its time, hold up surprisingly well and still manage to convey a sense of tension and foreboding.The audio design also plays a crucial role in the experience. The menacing sound effects and eerie music enhance the overall atmosphere, creating an auditory backdrop that adds to the tension and immersion.One of the game's standout features is its unique enemies and level design. "DOOM 64" introduces new demons and challenges that set it apart from its predecessors. The levels are meticulously designed, offering a mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and frenetic combat that keeps players engaged throughout their journey.However, "DOOM 64" is not without its limitations. The game's controls and movement might feel somewhat archaic to modern gamers accustomed to more refined mechanics. Additionally, while the classic gameplay and atmosphere hold up well, some players might find the absence of modern features and conveniences a bit jarring.In conclusion, "DOOM 64" is a testament to the enduring appeal of classic FPS gameplay. Its atmospheric design, intense battles, and nostalgic charm make it a must-play for fans of the DOOM series and retro gaming enthusiasts alike. While the game's age is evident in certain aspects, its ability to deliver heart-pounding action and create an unsettling atmosphere remains a testament to its enduring impact. If you're ready to revisit the roots of the FPS genre and face the horrors of hell once again, "DOOM 64" offers a thrilling journey back to the dawn of demon-slaying mayhem.

_childDocuments_.review: I will separate two thing in my review: the game, and the port.Is the game worth playing if you're a classic Doom fan?Depends. There's still running and gunning, but the game is moody, slower. There's no metal to make you feel pumped, just unnerving ambient. Monsters are in this late 90's brownish palette, looking creepier, but less distinct than in classic Doom. But once you get familiar with the game, it's very satisfying. The weapons have a great feel, even if they're crippled by very limited animation. Their sounds are eargasmic. (Well, all sounds in this game are good). The combat is challenging but very satisfying- for most of the game, especially closer to the end, I would often find myself in disbelief that I managed to survive some more intense parts. Things can get really crazy sometimes and it feels great. Plus, the game's story makes it a great coda for the classic Doom- many people call it a "real Doom 3" and I really get why.ATTENTION- if you suffer from migraine seizures or are sensetive to strobe lights- DO NOT PICK UP THE FIRST SOUL SPHERE IN MAP04. The strobe that turns on when you do is like the early 2010's "YOU DESERVE SEIZURES FOR YOUR POST" troll gifs. Since it's pretty early in the game, when classic Doom fans would still not get used to how different it is, I know more than one person who abandoned the game after that. Frankly, this is a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game design, making the game punish the player with hard enemies is cool, making the game punish the player (or around a dozen % suffering from said problems) with seizures or debiliating headache is just dumb. I wish they could give an option to disable it instead of seizure warning screen that adds few seconds to your loading time, each time you launch the game.And what about the port?I've never played the original, but I've played Doom Ex, which was flawless. This port is based on it. I personally hate filtering and resizing because it just looks blurry to me, thankfully you can disable it. I wish I could disable mouse in menus as well, it can get really frustrating to operate this weird scrolling. Other thing that is a minus for me, compared to Doom Ex, it misses some features but adds useless stuff like  login (it does absolutely nothing, I think you get some Doom Eternal cosmetics if you do it but otherwise it's just logging in, taking some time to do so every time, for no profit for player whatsoever). Still, since Doom Ex creator did get money for it, plus he made some maps (that I wasn't able to reach yet) I'm happy to pay those few dollars for his works, and for the work of the original Doom 64 creators. Plus, since WAD files have somewhat recognizable data, I hope this port will make the game modable, while preserving its original feel.So, tl;dr: buy this if you like Doom lore and shooting at stuff, don't buy it if you don't like late 90's gritty aesthetics and unnerving ambient, and whatever you do, don't pick up the soulsphere on the map 04.

_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game overall and a fun version of DOOM - assuming you like circle-strafing wave after wave (after wave) of Barons. It's like the level designers couldn't remember how to place any of the other enemy types. BUT, word of warning: I've played Ultimate DOOM and DOOM II through to completion on Ultra Violence with no guide and using no save states - one 'life' for each level. Where if you die, you go back to the start and try again, and about three-quarters through DOOM 64 even I gave up on that and had to make the occasional checkpoint. Not because the combat or combat traps are hard (the part that *should* be challenging) but because of the designers' annoying penchant for disgusting, cheap traps that were never part of DOOM. Dart traps, lava pits that are inescapable should you fall into them (sacrilege) and ridiculous 'gun emplacements' in walls that spew rockets out when you can't even work out where they're coming from or what triggers them. These things may only be in a handful of levels, but they still rankle because they're not DOOM. Then there's the beyond silly last boss with skies full of Vore style homing rockets and Diablo fire stomps that launch you into the air. WTF. Yeah, those Midway guys should have just made DOOM II with new visuals and levels and left it at that! On the same note, I never fired the useless 'Unmaker' once after first trying it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a great side-game to the main series. Although the enemies look a bit different, the game has entirely new SFX and musical style, it's still very much Doom. The level design isn't quite as strong in general as Doom and Doom 2 as there's several levels that can get confusing and frustrating quickly. However the campaign has a lot of great ones as well, with 25 main levels and 3 "fun levels" and 3 secret levels, there's plenty of content. This version also has an extra 6 "lost" levels that bridge the stories of Doom 64 and Doom 2016, plus another "fun" level.This game has all of the enemies from Doom and Doom II except the Revenant, Archvile and Spider Mastermind. it does, however have a couple new enemies, the Nightmare Imp and the Mother Demon, as well as the Pain Elemental acting slightly differently. The weapons are the same but with the addtion of the Unmaker, though some function differently. The super shotgun seems to do more damage, the plasma rifle fires slower but hits harder per shot. But in general if you know how Doom weapons work then they work mostly the same. The Unmaker is a special laser weapon you find somewhat early on that shares ammo with the plasma rifle and BFG. It starts out somewhat weak but as you find upgrades for it throughout the game, it quickly becomes completely overpowered and surpasses even the BFG in firepower.If you're a fan of the oldschool Doom games then I highly recommend you give this a shot. I missed out originally because I never owned an N64 growing up but I was certainly not disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games I never got to play back in the day and to be honest I forgot it even existed. I did however spend a fair amount playing the classic Doom games, which to this day are still extremely fun to play. Luckily, Doom 64 is no different.Obviously this game was developed for the Nintendo 64 so graphically it got an upgrade over the classic PC Doom games. The gameplay is the same aswell as the creatures and guns are (mostly) the same. There isn't really much to say about this game. If you like the originals , you will like Doom 64.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: I got this as part of the Eternal pre-order.It's a fun game. Remember you can save anywhere at any time! Being an older game, it'll attempt to autoaim along the vertical line.The original campaign ramps up fairly slowly, hitting its first difficulty spike on Level06, and again on Level09. It was originally designed for a controller, but it will still become engaging and challenging enough.The Lost Levels are definitely meant to be played after the original campaign. Their difficulty curve is a little less forgiving, being fairly strict with ammo and demon distribution.Technical issues abound if you don't run this on Win10! I did get it running on Win07 before, and my method for that was to click on the .exe in the install location, and then go download the missing .dll it said was missing to the install location.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely classic Doom but it feels like they improved a ton of things from the older games and managed to make a pretty satisfying 4 Hour experience. Although Nightdive was WAY too faithful with the port, leading to problems that will hurt the game's playability and longevity in the future for new generations of FPS players coming back to it.+One of the biggest improvements from the original N64 game is that the game had some of the most abysmal visibility issues on original hardware. The game was so pitch black and you couldn't see anything you might as well have had your eyes closed. It forced players to turn up the brightness on their TV to an absurd and inappropriate level. Now, the brightness has definitely been fixed. The game is finally visible and it's just dark enough so that it doesn't become a problem when looking at the screen and searching for enemies. This is by far the best part of the port.+The guns in 64 are much better mainly because they sound meatier and the impact of things like the shotgun and pistol are quite impressive. The game has the typical Doom Arsenal alongside a new weapon that shoots beams out of it. If you go through the secret levels you can upgrade it apparently, but I didn't know that until it was too late. Still, the weapons are a big step up from Ultimate Doom and Doom II, which is great because you want to see the game improve over every entry.+The atmosphere is also one of the biggest step ups from Ultimate Doom and Doom II. The game lacks the MIDI music and goes for more of a terrifying soundscape. In fact, I was so tense at points I literally jumped out of my seat when enemies attacked me from behind. Trust me, I pretty much screamed and almost fell out of my seat when that happened a couple times. Although, Doom is, and never will be a horror game. But this is the closest I think any of the original games aside from Doom 3 that is easily comparable to what we might call 'Horror'. It's really freaky.+There are some puzzles that can be a bit weird, but I figured all the cryptic ones out (The Yellow Key Jail) on my first try pretty much by accident. Some of the other puzzles involve hitting a combination of switches to unlock doors with the three keys you have gotten in the last chunk of the game and I felt so smart for figuring that out. The game feels rewarding for having you figure out these puzzles and it's never to the point where you have to look up a walkthrough.*In terms of the difficulty, I played on Normal Difficulty (Bring It On) and the game is mostly easy until the latter half of the game, mostly the final few levels. Although I don't think the game is really that difficult to begin with. The final boss provided a strong fight with hordes of enemies spawning. If you got stuff from the secret levels you can stop that from happening but I didn't know that. Thankfully, going right up into their faces with the rockets with the invincibility the game nicely gives you alongside the mega sphere helps a lot. The final boss took a couple tries but I do think it's doable. Just have to diagonal run from it's projectiles or hide behind some of the switches with your BFG or Rocket Launcher. If you run out, the double shotgun usually does the trick to finish it off. I'm pretty competent at FPS Games and have played so many this almost felt like a breeze. I would suggest if you're a veteran player to play on a harder difficulty (maybe not the hardest though).-A couple of problems though. One is that Nightdive was too faithful and decided not to add any QOL features like a level select or proper auto save at the beginning of each level. Instead you have this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ password system that should have been thrown out for how archaic it is. I don't know nothing about porting games or game development but I don't get why Nightdive doesn't just rearrange the code or program new things into it for these features considering the fact that they're essentially making a new version of the game for newer consoles and PC. It can be frustrating when you get cocky and don't think you need to save, then fall into a death trap and have to restart from a couple levels back because the game doesn't properly auto save your game. This drives me nuts in so many of these FPS Ports and Remasters from the 90's. Although that's just me talking out of my ass and having wishful thinking.-There's also a couple of VERY obnoxious visual effects in this game. Stuff like flashing lights and blinding brightness when you pick up power ups are very annoying and hurt my eyes when playing. BE AWARE if you have epilepsy, though these are mostly rare occasions when this happens.-Final Thoughts-Doom 64 is worth playing and it's dirt cheap. It's basically pennies when it goes on sale, but that asking price of CDN $6.49 is absolutely worth biting the bullet for. I wouldn't suggest this as your first FPS game if you're new to the genre, I would recommend something more along the lines of Modern Warfare 2007, Halo: Combat Evolved, Half-Life 2, or Doom 2016 (on an easier difficulty of course for all of them) if you want to get into this genre. Doom 64 has some stuff that is archaic and dated and some of the levels have big annoyances in them and the amount of Lost Souls was absurd and irritating, but the game itself for anyone who has played a decent amount of games in the genre, veterans wanting to pick up something that will reflect their tastes or people wanting to revisit it will want to get this. It's really good altogether.

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 is amazing! It does so many awesome things, and it honestly might be the best classic DOOM game! The soundtrack to this game is so much different compared to DOOM and DOOM II. While the previous installments had a kick ass metal soundtrack, DOOM 64 goes for a much more atmospheric and tense soundtrack, with many ambient tracks that often have very disturbing sounds. The level design is just as great as the originals, although sometimes a bit hectic. All of the enemies have been redesigned and look pretty fantastic! The weapons have also had an aesthetic overhaul and look great as well! And while on the topic of weapons, a new one has been introduced, The Unmaker! This new gun shoots out laser bolts for a rather high damage output! And if you can find the three Demon Keys hidden in secret levels, you can upgrade this unholy firepower to become even more devastating! DOOM 64 is an amazing game that any DOOM fan should play!

_childDocuments_.review: I love the DooM series, but I honestly can't recommend this entry. Outside of the bad ass intro war scene, the awesome ambient music, the brutal double chainsaw....this game is disappointing in almost every important way.Game play wise, you will be backtracking, switch hunting and figuring out what the button you just pressed did. You will be trying to figure out how to get to the next door MORE than actual combat. Almost every button you press will need you to search the whole level to see what changed to progress. Traps are cruel and unforgiving, and not devious and fun like the classic games, since the classic games still gave you a chance to survive. Not this game. You will be constantly quicksaving and quickloading, floors dropping from under you into lava, and spawning in a baron 2 feet away from you in a small room. MANY times enemies will spawn right in front of you in a boring fade-in effect, without any really interesting encounters or compositions of enemies. Your worst enemy is the lost soul, who moves the fastest in the game, and will attack you VERY quickly, melting your health in a blink of an eye. They arent fun to fight against due to their attack rate and movement speed.The new weapon, the unmaker, looks and sounds boring and uninspired. Ill admit I never bothered finding the secret emblems to power this weapon, so I never had it powered up. The game REQUIRES you to find secrets to power this weapon, and finding secrets werent fun at all. The final boss was completely boring and frustrating due to her homing rockets being almost the same speed as your run. The final bosses' design was uninspired as well, she just looked like a brown HR Giger alien.Monster designs are pretty decent, with the Pinky being the best looking remade monster, looking more beefier and demonic. The humans are boring and stiff looking, while the imps are alien looking, and the cyberdemon manages to look less intimidating than the classic design. All monsters retain very choppy animation and somehow look more stiff and uninspired compared to classic doom sprites.Running around these levels were boring and I just wanted to finish the game because it came with eternal. Play it, beat it once, uninstall it.4/10

_childDocuments_.review: Do not let the different platform of provenience fool you, this is actually a proper DooM game...a bit different from the classic ones on PC but a proper DooM game.The game itself is articulated on 28 (?) levels (the ? is intended because there are several secret levels) and the plethora of enemies is more or less the classical one but with some peculiar graphical differences.The Revnant, for example, is missing but you will get the Nightmare IMP.As for the weapons, like the cube in DooM 3, you will get an interesting one that will unleash its true power with all the 3 relics.The gameplay is the usual, run, kill, find the red key, open the door with the red key, dammit I need the blue key now, run, kill, kill some more, run again, find the blue key, run back, kill some more spawned enemies, open the door with the blue key....oh hell now i need the yellow key....At the end of every level you will get a password to use in the menu, this password will actually teleport you to that level...a great thing if you want to play some parts of the game to get the achivements.Plus, if you beat a particular secret level you will get a menu where you can select the level you want and all the weapons you want (there is even the possibility to enable the cheats but this will prevent you from getting the achivements)The difficulty goes form a casual gamer to a more experienced one.Personally for me playing it on the Deck was a blast. The game runned smoothly and with the analogs you could easily strafe right and left to avoid the enemies attack.One thing that I really find annoying is the music...forget the classical metal/rock midi ones, in this one it will be some kind of dark chant that, yeah sure is great as ambient, but after a while you will get annoyed from it expecially if you are playing with a headset or earbugs.And really?...less than the 17% of you guys got the BFG?....geez kids play the damn game!

_childDocuments_.review: I've only got an hour in this game, but I've played Doom 64 before. On both the N64 and Doom 64 EX on GZDoom. Sure that's an option, but this is honestly a fair price for a really good port of the game.If downloading a sourceport doesn't appeal, this is a good option. It runs good, plays well, and is true to the original experience. BUT HOLD YOUR HUGE GUTS ONE MOMENT THERE, BUCKAROO.You have to understand that Doom 64 is a different experience compared to Dooms 1 & 2. There's no thrash metal riffs with accompanying visuals. It finds itself in between the classic Dooms and Doom 3 in terms of gameplay. The aesthetic style even takes some cues from Quake. It's much more dour and forlorn than Doom and plays quite a bit slower than those. However, this was by design. Remember, this was a Doom experience crafted for the controller. You know, that awful thing that Nintendo passed off as a controller for the N64? This was crafted to make most of analog stick input and, frankly, they succeeded. This is still a quality doom experience. If that sounds good to you, then this would be a definitely good pick up for its price.

_childDocuments_.review: The remaster of DOOM 64 is a fantastic reimagining of the classic 1997 first-person shooter. As a fan of the original game, I was thrilled to see that the remaster not only preserved the feel of the original game but also added some new features and enhancements.One of the standout features of the remaster is the updated graphics. The game's visuals have been given a major overhaul, with improved textures, lighting, and character models. Despite the updated graphics, the game still manages to retain the classic look and feel of the original game, and the new enhancements only serve to make the game even more immersive.Another great addition to the remaster is the inclusion of new levels. The original DOOM 64 had some of the best levels in the entire franchise, and the remaster takes things even further with new levels that are just as well-designed and challenging as the original ones. These new levels provide a fresh challenge for players who are already familiar with the game and make the remaster even more enjoyable for new players.The remaster also includes a range of quality-of-life improvements that make the game even more accessible and enjoyable to play. For example, players can now save their progress at any time, which makes it easier to pick up and play the game on the go. The game also includes new controls that are optimized for modern controllers, which makes the game even more intuitive and easy to play.Overall, the remaster of DOOM 64 is a fantastic update to an already classic game. With updated graphics, new levels, and quality-of-life improvements, the game manages to feel both fresh and familiar at the same time. If you're a fan of first-person shooters or the DOOM franchise, this game is definitely worth checking out.

Especially with the new "Lost Levels" campaign (I've beaten it on "Watch me die!" and it tore me a new one). The community is even giving their attention & TLC to DOOM 64 by breeding more life into a game that was unfortunately limited because of the N64's cartridge space. _childDocuments_.review: This is a solid port of an often overlooked treasure from DOOM's legacy. A different, but not entirely unfitting, take on the classic DOOM formula, 64 is a much more tense and atmospheric horror shooter than its predecessors, with an outstanding ambient soundtrack by Aubrey Hodges. In addition to the main 32 level campaign, this port, adds a brand new episode with even more new levels, which I found thoroughly enjoyable to play through.I've found very little off or questionable about this port from my boys at Nightdive, aside from a couple of very minor quirks. The default brightness was a tad high for me and messed with the original's moody darkness, but thankfully turning the overall brightness setting down all the way seems to get it about on-par with the original. And I find the time between booting the game up and being able to actually start playing to be just a tad too long, thanks largely to the lengthy company intros (which are thankfully skippable by just deleting the files from the directory) and the wait time for the game to check its connection to Bethesda's servers (thankfully, actually using a Bethesda account appears to be completely optional). Otherwise the port seems to be everything I could have hoped for! The controls seem well-adapted for keyboard and mouse, and are completely rebindable (even if the menu is a bit annoying about how it shows alternate inputs, by just shuffling between them). There's a decent handful of video customization options for enabling texture filtering and anti-aliasing, and increasing the FOV. And the mad lads, for no real reason other than posterity, have left the original game's password save system intact, despite adding proper save games. Completely unnecessary, and entirely appreciated for the novelty!The performance seems rock-solid, for me, and seems to be pretty well-optimized. Those minimum system requirements are  inflated. I have no trouble keeping a steady 60 at 1680x1050, on an old Core 2 Duo with 3 gb of RAM and a Radeon HD 7800. Your old toasters should have no trouble here!It might be tempting to let this release be overshadowed by Bethesda's criminal decision of locking it to Eternal's release date, but for real don't sleep on DOOM 64 - you'd be missing out! It's a solid port of an excellent game!

_childDocuments_.review: A great game that deserves to sit among the pantheon of both fantastic Doom games and FPS games in general. The overall feel of Doom 64 is a little slower and more intense than Doom or Doom II. It retains the tense quick paced high damage carnage you expect with some tricks never seen in previous iterations. As for major differences, the weapons and monsters all have new sprites. They feel a little more "real" while not deviating too far from the established style of Doom. This game has a much improved lighting system that, along with the sound, has been treated well by the remaster. Overall it's fun and impressive for a port of an N64 title. It may actually hold up better than Doom & Doom II, and certainly better than Plutonia and TNT. It's cheap and a great time. Buy it and remember to RIP AND TEAR!

_childDocuments_.review: Finally it is available for PC! Back then I wished this came out for the PC when it was fresh and new, because for me this is the true DOOM 3 by id! _childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 is a very different but an original take on Classic Doom.  The maps are totally different from the PC-version and the overall visual style is more sinister. I couldn't stand Doom 64 back in the late 90's because of the different sounds and the ambient music, but later on I had a chance to experience the game again in the early 2000's, and I managed to look under the surface of the game.Then I realized what I had missed back in the late 90's. Doom 64 is a very solid Doom game, I've come to realize that the different sounds and the ambient music I used to hate so much decades ago are the very reason behind the unique feeling and the style of this game. Doom 64 also feels and plays very much like the other Classic Doom games, despite looking quite different from its predecessors. And yeah, I've grown to like the music and the sounds quite a lot over the years.Never judge a book by it's cover. Lesson learned.

_childDocuments_.review: Really glad Doom 64 is getting some long deserved love now.  It's Doom, but spooky.  Great level design (aside from a few questionable puzzles), STELLAR atmosphere and music, fun combat, and an aesthetic that still holds up, especially in its use of moody colored lighting.The port itself is great, and is more about bringing the original game up to par in areas like resolution, frame rate, FOV, etc than it is about adding modern effects or modifying the gameplay.  There's no bloom or fancy new lightmaps, because Doom 64 didn't have those.  There's no vertical look because Doom 64 didn't have it.  Weapon sprites will always be unfiltered because that's how they were on the N64.  It's quite playable by modern standards but keeps the original experience as intact as possible, which I really appreciate.This is a no brainer if you're a fan of the original Doom games, or really if you're just a fan of "boomer shooters" in general and appreciate a moodier creepier take on that style.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll break this into two parts: 1. the port and 2. the game.As to 1: the port is great. Before Bethesda packaged this as a pre-order bonus for Doom Eternal, we had Doom64Exe, which was also great. There are a few texture glitches in the user uploaded source port that are not present here, or at least I didn't encounter them. We also get a few nice perks, including steam achievements and better controller support. Both Exe and this Bethesda port feature widescreen format and unlocked frame rates, neither of which are present on the original N64. Of course, the game still looks best the way it was intended: on an N64 cart through a CRT. As to 2: the game is good but not perfect. If you're like me, you might've thought Doom 64 was an N64 port of the original Doom. In fact, it is a totally unique game, designed by Midway Studios of all people. Officially, the game succeeds Doom II. However, there are a few notable steps back. The most obvious is the player animations have been pared down, likely due to cart limitations at the time. So, reloading is purely aural. Another is the removal of nearly half the cast of enemies, and most the new additions being mere re-skins of other enemies, again likely due to cart limitations. Thankfully, a majority of the non-returning enemies are Doom II's most annoying. Confusingly, they kept Pain Elementals, and somehow made them even an even greater nuisance. Overall, this is classic Doom: bloody, frenetic, kickass. In my opinion, it doesn't quite reach the levels of Ultimate Doom, but it certainly exceeds Doom II in terms of substantive gameplay scenarios. The levels are still quite open-ended, as in Ultimate Doom, but not as obscure as in Doom II. You shouldn't need a guide to experience most of what Doom 64 has to offer. In particular, the strength of this game is its atmospheric lighting, abstract level designs, and pacing. You will either love or hate the new enemy models, which were first 3D rendered before being turned into sprites. I love them. Where this game is at its worst is when it retains the ball-busting design philosophy of Doom II. Thankfully, much of the "unfair" levels have been relegated to secret areas. In a lot of ways, this feels like a true "Doom 3" insofar as it elaborates and expands the design space of classic Doom without abandoning the core tenets of early id game-making.

_childDocuments_.review: does a great job at delivering , while also offering some QoL additions and a new episode, however to me, personally, this port would benefit drastically from a headbob slider or an option to disable it -  (compared to the original 2 classic DOOM games) legit give me  to the point where I don't even want to play the Nightdive port.If you experience something similar, If not, I recommend it regardless because it is in every way superior to this port, offering more options, more variety of foes to fight, much, much better movement, better visuals, more fluid gameplay flow and some more content and levels to enjoy.DOOM 64 (CE), as a game, is simply incredible.I shouldn't have slept on it for as long as I did, as I believe it is on par with the first and second DOOM game in terms of quality, design and enjoyment. The redesigns of the monsters and arsenal work exceptionally well in the dark, moody hallways of this game, which are lit with colorful ambiance and neon lights which resonate an atmosphere that is unique, thrilling, creepy yet incredibly cozy and just overall a highlight of this game - along with its chilling soundtrack that is just as great as Quake's OST in terms of both approach and execution.The gameplay flows along the levels which are memorable and engaging (especially the secret levels and what they have to offer to the player), the combat encounters are thoughtful and work well within the areas they are confined in, and the difficulty and tension escalates steadily and in a manner that pushes the player forward, rather than stuns them in any capacity. Every level in this game was enjoyable for me even the first time, which is not necessarily something that would be the case in either prior DOOM game.Overall, DOOM 64 is amazing and is a worthy installment that is unique in its own ways, which all only benefit its own identity and make it a confident piece of the DOOM franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique take on the classic DOOM formula, leaning heavily into the atmosphere and horror DOOM3 tried to capture. The Aubrey Hodges soundtrack adds so much to the mood of the game, and the colored lighting and mapwork are extremely well done, adding to the demonic setting the game conveys. Maps are mostly well done, though throughout the game and especially at the later half there are some frustrating puzzles and I had lots of points where I just didn't know what to do to continue a level. Art design is good as well, with enemy sprites looking less exaggerated and more fear-inducing. I absolutely think any DOOM fan should at least play this, as it has a very distinct style that none of the other games really capture, besides Quake 1 and 2. The Lost Levels are great as well, they serve as a good companion piece to DOOM Eternal if you plan to play that.

_childDocuments_.review: A different flavor of DoomIf you've played classic Doom 1 or 2, you'll have a reasonable idea of what to expect in general, so I'll focus on the differences. The remaster means that you get somewhat higher resolution graphics, a bunch of save slots, and better default keys, though it's still very much like the DOS games. The monsters and weapons mostly behave like what you'd expect, though there are a handful of new ones.Graphically, the monsters are if anything higher resolution, with an art style that skews more towards aliens than pure horror. Level design also emphasizes the sci-fi aspects, and does a lot with interesting lights, and rather more saturated colors. A Marathon comparison (or once you get out of the tech base, Heretic/Hexen) is somewhat tempting.Sound effects are mostly better, especially the weapons (though ambient monster sounds less so). The almost Quake-like ambient music definitely sets a different mood from the metal themes of the DOS versions, though perhaps clashes with the scenery.Level designs have lots of neat features in terms of interactions, scripted events, secrets, use of movement. etc, though are comparatively short and usually cramped. The former is presumably from N64 hardware limitations, but is in practice not really a drawback. They're still fun levels. The latter does restrict things quite a bit, limiting your ability to dodge and use cover until things open up in the later levels.In conclusion: if you want more Doom, this is a good choice.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of the iconic Doom series, I was thrilled to find  this hidden gem from the franchise. Having spent countless hours battling demons on Doom 1, 2 and 3 over the years, I eagerly dove into this reimaged edition, and I can confidently say that it exceeded all of my expectations.From the moment I launched the game, I was greeted with nostalgia-inducing visuals that seamlessly blended the classic atmosphere of the original with modern graphical enhancements. The dark and foreboding corridors of each level were brought to life in stunning detail, immersing me in a world teeming with danger and mystery.But it wasn't just the visuals that impressed me; the gameplay itself felt as smooth and satisfying as ever. The tight controls and fast-paced action that have defined the Doom series were present in full force, delivering adrenaline-fueled combat encounters that kept me on the edge of my seat. Whether I was mowing down hordes of demons with my trusty shotgun or navigating treacherous traps, every moment felt like a thrill ride.Of course, no Doom game would be complete without its signature arsenal of weapons, and Doom 64 PC Edition does not disappoint in this regard. From the iconic Super Shotgun to the devastating BFG 9000, each weapon felt powerful and distinct, giving me plenty of options for dispatching my demonic foes in creative ways.But perhaps the most impressive aspect of Doom 64 PC Edition is its level design. Each stage is expertly crafted, offering a perfect balance of exploration, puzzle-solving, and intense combat encounters. From sprawling industrial complexes to hellish infernos, every location felt unique and memorable, ensuring that I was always eager to see what the next level had in store.Overall, Doom 64 PC Edition is a masterful return to form for the classic franchise. With its gorgeous visuals, exhilarating gameplay, and expertly designed levels, it's a must-play for fans of the series old and new alike. Whether you're a veteran demon slayer or a newcomer looking to experience the roots of one of gaming's most beloved franchises, this game is sure to satisfy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the third and last entry in the classic Doom series, Doom 64 is less known as its predecessors but it's not because it's not a good game on the opposite it's great. The gameplay is everything that made Doom so much fun, it's the satisfying fast-paced run and gun dance to slaughter hordes of demons. Its level design has improved as progression is generally smoother and less confusing. The caveat is there are now traps added into the mix, it's an interesting extra challenge in rooms with demons but in other cases there are few spots where it made traversal slightly annoying. The enemy variety is greater than Doom but lesser than Doom II which isn't necessarily bad as it may still have Pain Elementals it doesn't have Arch-viles which makes me happy. The next and most obvious change is visuals more precisely animated textures and lighting which both infuse some more life into the levels. A fair warning about something regarding lights, a section where you can get a supercharge powerup before a corridor with an alarm will make it flash red to the point of almost giving me a headache but I immediately rushed to the exit which I strongly recommend as this will disable the alarm and let you safely return to explore it. Lastly It's important to talk about the music, it's drastically different but it's great at setting a dark and ominous atmosphere however I do miss the blood-pumping metal of the previous games. Overall it's a great game that I strongly recommend for anyone fan of retro shooters or the classic Doom games.

_childDocuments_.review: took me by surprise. Growing up I never owned a Nintendo 64 (I was a PlayStation kid), so for years I operated under the belief that no such conversion of id’s classic first-person shooter had made its way onto Nintendo’s console. By the time I learned of its existence, my interest was best described as “indifferent”. I just casually assumed it was  all over again, not caring to dig any deeper into Midway Games’ title.What a putz.  is no mere remake of the original game, but a sequel to the events of . And, curiously enough, a more compelling and interesting game than id’s own , which followed some years later. You may boo and jeer me all you wish, but it’s true.For starters it’s a far creepier game than , creating a pervasive sense of quiet unease without ever laying it on too thick (there’s no ludicrous villainous laughter or any comical jump scares, for instance).We start our war against Hell’s relentless evil in a sealed UAC base, long since left dormant. Here the game echoes with traces of  dread and isolation, its horror far more acute than the original games. But then I never considered those games horror per se, and now, having played the entire series, I feel like only  and  can lay claim to being proper horrors titles.That’s not to say  is some kind of survival horror, though. It’s as action-packed and brutal as you’d expect from a  game, with a host of ghastly demons intent on pulverising you with balls of flames and sizzling orbs of energy. Unfortunately they’re not nearly as confounding as the game’s plethora of repetitive puzzles.Whilst I loved the bizarre and unsettling architecture of the world – especially Hell itself, with its great walls of fire and crackling violet thunderstorms raging above desolate sierras – they aren’t easy to navigate. You’re going to need to find keys to progress, but that involves pressing buttons to open doors and clear obstacles. The problem? It’s often a mystery as to where these doors are, meaning you’ll spend a lot of time racing around the map looking for whichever door has opened. It’s an in inelegant and frustrating piece of design.But beyond that you have a thoroughly enjoyable  game, brimming with atmosphere and the kind of gory, white-knuckle combat you’ve come to expect from the series. Sure, it was a little outdated even for the time, relying on the tried-and-true  formula, but I see little point in marking it down for that.It’s , and that formula was more than good – it was revolutionary. Kudos to Nightdive Studios for bringing it to PC, enabling players who missed out the first time to play it anew.

_childDocuments_.review: First time I played this game was via a sourceport as a mod for DOOM II. And frankly, I don't see any reason to play this new version over that one. The sourceport version provided infinite possibilities for configuration and had awesome extra content. It also ran smoothly with zero issues.This version, on the other hand, is very limited in configuration, has unskippable intro videos, shoves  in your face and doesn't even allow a three-dimensional free look. Which, yeah, I get it, this is essentially a 2D game, and the original never had it. But the original, as well as Doom 1 and 2 were developed for controller and keyboard controls respectively. When playing with a mouse, it feels pretty weird not to be able to move your camera up and down. Besides, that feature just makes it easier to enjoy and admire the beauty of the environments. Why not add it as an option at least?To make things worse, this version has weird performance issues on Linux that are linked to input, apparently. Other users reported that they had to use a controller or remap the bindings, but I don't wanna do either of those things. And why should I, when there's a perfectly functioning sourceport version of this, which is free (if you own DOOM II)?Bottom line is, just play the sourceport version.Tbf though, if you wanna play with a controller, I guess this version lets you do that. But if you're gonna do that, why not just emulate the original N64 version? I guess, it is more convenient to just have this game in Steam with a one-click install, but that's the only advantage this version has.As for the game itself, it is fine. A lot of people say it's better than the first two, but I don't think so. Sure, it's more atmospheric and all, but it's also much slower with many puzzles and whatnot. And I don't think this kind of gameplay fits well with the mechanics of what was a fun run&gun shooter.

_childDocuments_.review: A more fitting successor to Doom II than the slow, horror FPS Doom 3. Doom 64 has the fast gameplay of the first two games, with arguably more obscure key-hunting sequences. Enemy and weapon sprites are given a new coat of fresh paint. Level design can be occasionally frustrating, but the atmosphere is an achievement given the time this game was released. Maps are somewhat colorful yet unsettling due to the oppressive soundscape. Doom 64's OST is similar to Trent Reznor's OST for Quake, using things like droning sounds and  baby cries to create an unnerving feeling. Worth a playthrough for fans of retro FPS.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a major problem with setting up keyboard mappings. Specifically, if you change a key to a different function, it does not replace the previously set function. Rather it creates a second function for that key. For instance, if a given key is set to move forward, and you remap that key so that it's strafing left instead, pressing that key causes the player to move diagonally (forward left). There is no obvious way I can tell to eliminate the original settings.As result, the game in unplayable when trying to use my normal keyboard/mouse setup. The game seems cool, but there's enjoyment to be had from my perspective.EDIT: Now that Chosen "SCIM" 41 has given me the solution to the issue, the game is playable and enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Doom 64 had the unfortunate luck of being released in 1997. Beginning development in 1994, it was originally planned as an N64 launch title. It was delayed to allot time for map redesigns, which brought it to a 1997 release. That same year saw the release of: Turok; Goldeneye, Blood, and Shadow Warrior. Duke 3D and Quake already had a year on the market. 	I'm name-dropping a lot of games to elucidate the fact that D64 was outdated even by 1997 standards. All of the games I mentioned had a mixture of:	You can still find some old 1997 Gamespot and IGN reviews for this game online. Both of which give the same verdict: yet another Doom game that still plays like Doom from 1993. While Duke3D and Blood had visually distinct areas and set pieces (subways, strip clubs, haunted mansions), D64's maps all blend together because they reuse the same "non descript space station" textures. Which was ok in 1993, but outdated in '97. Crazy how fast the genre developed back then.	Because of this, D64 was overlooked and forgotten. It played it too safe. Which shows you that a game review is a matter of perspective. Doom 64 was definitely an outdated game even in 1997. It was also a well designed Doom game in the vein of the older entries. And in 2021 it's that quality that shines more than the former because it's no longer 1997. The difference between 1997 and 1994 in 2021 is negligible, even if there were games on the market that had more advanced features.	So this release (first PC release) is giving the game a new shot at a larger audience. What Doom64 excels at is its attempt at a horror atmosphere. The levels are dimly lit in parts, and overall darker than before. It's a middle ground between the horror theme Doom 3 attempted, and classical Doom. You get your ambient soundtrack, but you retain the fast movespeed, enemy count, and backtracking map design. I found it substantially more enjoyable than D3.	Atmosphere aside, everything else is standard Doom fare. D64 plays it extremely safe and does little beyond giving us more levels. When a franchise plays it too safe the only remedy for that is either an evolving storyline, increasing quantity (more weapons, levels, etc), or a prolonged wait time between titles to prevent fatigue. We don't have a yearly console Doom port anymore, so D64 is able to shine more on its good qualities nowadays: good map design. 	It's a competent Doom game, and for better or worse there's not much to say beyond that.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't have an N64 growing up, and my friends who did, did not have this. I can't tell how close this is to the original, but this plays just like vanilla DOOM.The overall tone is darker and moodier. This is partially due to the low lighting and use of different colored lighting, but also thanks to the soundtrack provided by Aubrey Hodges. Where Bobby Prince Jr. provided thrash and metal-inspired tracks that gave DOOM a blistering pace, the soundtrack here makes you watch your back and fear what's around the corner. The engine used here can also do things that the original DOOM engine could not, such as arrow traps and a key that can randomize its position on the map.Due to time and storage constraints, the full bestiary is not available. Still, the devs made the most of what they had, and you will still deal with some relatively challenging situations, so you won't be bored.There are many that say that this was the "true" DOOM 3: Given that the gameplay is mostly the same and follows Doomguy from the first 2 games, I'd say they're right. With DOOM Eternal, it makes even further sense.If you are a fan of DOOM and played the original games, this is a perfectly good port.

_childDocuments_.review: (PLAYED THIS BEFORE ON BRUTAL DOOM, I HAVE NEVER OWNED AN NINTENDO 64)Before I start this review I just want to say I played this in a modded version of DOOM titled "BRUTAL DOOM 64", But now the real deal is here, so lets review it.DOOM 64 is a 1997 FPS-Horror that is developed by ID Software. It is a direct sequel to DOOM II: Hell On Earth. DOOM 64 changes the DOOM franchise drasticly and by this I mean it changed its direction. While keeping the classic firearms you get, the whole action and brutality that makes you feel like a god gets taken away and this time you get left with this eerie suspense and horror-setting. The monsters has had an update in terms of designs as you can tell by the screenshots above if your new to 64 or have played it on Nintendo 64. They are now more.. scary looking the what they used to be, they are also a bit geared and beefed up since the last games. But anyways am going to go through the pros and cons of the gamePROS:- Updated designs during its time of weapons, monsters and level designs to be more "HD"- Horror-atomsphere- Eerie and suspense, there's no action-beatup themes, its just very like something you hear out of Silent Hill, its like the music is like something is around every corner.- The gun sounds are statsfying- New enemies (Nightmare Imp, Mother Demon)- There is some great action moments, like the boss fights is just what you need for a classic- This game isn't a game like the previous dooms where you can just rush it, my personal view, to flee the atomsphere and tension, it is "take your time" sort of game.Cons (Not a lot)- How 64 ties into its plot is very confusing, DOOM 64 is pretty much DOOM 3. (I thought DOOM 64 was a complete reimagine of DOOM 1 in a more horror-setting)Thats all I can say about DOOM 64, I've played this many times when I played the modded version and I was very impressed with it, the horror-suspense is what.. kept me playing it. I do like the updated sprite models, they are more unnerving espeically the cacodemon. but I can give nothing but praise to this game.Thankyou ever so much Bethesda/ID for remastering and re-releasing a classic for everyone to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: It's classic DOOM with an atmospheric horror twist. And honestly? I think it's up there with DOOM 1 and 2. I really love tonal switch up from blasting demons away to heavy metal, to trying to survive the horrors of hell. The gothic imagery is superb and the ambient, distorted soundtrack creates such an unsettling atmosphere. It's such a great tone for DOOM that I honestly don't know which I like more. Both are great.Gameplay is just as good as ever. Great weapon variety and the guns feel and sound so impactful. The new weapon; The Unmaker is absolutely devastating and with the Demon Key upgrades, it even makes the BFG seem underpowered. I also prefer a lot of the weapon designs in this game. Level design is mostly great. It feels more like DOOM 1 with it's endless corridors and tight spaces. But it also has DOOM 2's more open levels thrown in for good measure. One annoyance I did have was trying to find where to go. DOOM's levels have always been labyrinthine-y. But 64 has too many switch scattered about that aren't too clear on what they open. There's also traps which, unless you have the power of foresight. Will end up getting you in rather cheap ways. Enemy placement for the most part is fine. A few cheeky Hell Knights behind a door, but I've come to expect that from DOOM. I feel they do overdo it a bit with Hell Knights and Barons. It's like one of the most common enemy in the game and you get sick of fighting them in small spaces. The maps visually have this really nice progression in theme as you go through the game. It starts with the classic sci-fi Phobos base levels from DOOM 1 but goes more gothic and disturbing as you enter hell. As mentioned before, the game has some really amazing gothic imagery. DOOM has always had gargoyle faces on the walls, but 64 takes those few gargoyles and really goes in on that horror aesthetic. Coupled with the soundtrack creates such a creepy atmosphere. Enemies designs is just as good as DOOM 1/2's. The sprite work is incredibly done, with each enemy being very distinct from each other. Making it easier to track with enemy to priorities in fights. This to me is essential in a DOOM game and 64 does a great job. The designs themselves is honestly personal preference. They more or less follow the original designs but with some changes. Overall, I prefer 64's Imps, Pinkies and Cyber-Demon (Which is basically the same sprite but higher res) But a lot of the charm and character of a lot of Demons are lost to fit with the horror theme. Cacodemon and the Pain Elemental just don't do anything for me. A few enemies were changed for 64. There's a new Imp called a Nightmare Imp. Which is basically a more powerful Imp with some added Spectre in there. Mancubus now fire rockets instead of flameballs. And the Pain Elemental got the biggest (and most annoying) redesign by far. They don't resemble the DOOM 2 version at all and instead fire 2 Lost Souls at once. Lost Souls are also way more deadly, as they charge quicker and end up constantly hit you if you're not paying attention. Aside from that, every enemy more or less is the same. Also Chain Gunners, Arch-viles and the Spider Mastermind have been cut from the game. (And nothing of value was lost)TL;DR DOOM went through a goth phase and it was actually really, really good. If you like DOOM 1 and 2. There's no reason not to pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played through the first two Doom games in the last 30 years more times than is healthy - this thing doesn't deserve to be called Doom. There are switches that open random doors or activate lifts so you'll always run around and look what exactly changed; it's even worse if they're timed. The map design also seems uncharacteristic for a Doom game; ok, 1 and 2 also had mazes where you could get lost and crushers, that...well, crush you, but this thing is on a totally new level...maybe that's a console or just Nintendo 64 thing? No idea, never owned any. Then the strobe light effects were also annoying as hell...i could go on and on.Overall the gameplay felt more like a chore and i finished it just for the sake of completing the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the entire series of the Doom games, I just had to buy myself a copy of DOOM 64 for myself! DOOM 64 is a fun but addictive game to play but unlike The Ultimate Doom and Doom II: Hell on Earth, I found DOOM 64 to be a little darker environmentally but still enjoyable. _childDocuments_.review: It's a great underrated game in the Classic Doom series that has a whole lot of originality going for it. Playing this game feels like an actual descent into Hell. The soundtrack makes you constantly feel uneasy, and each level is jam packed with demonic imagery. The level design is much better than Doom 2's and in some cases the original game, however some of the puzzles and switch-activated doors can be a bit cryptic and annoying. The new Lost Levels campaign is short but sweet and presents a good challenge, but if you're hoping for a huge tie-in with Eternal you'll be disappointed - check it out only if you love classic Doom and want to experience some new Doom 64 content.

_childDocuments_.review: Never played through Doom 64 before and it's a pretty good game.Game plays like you'd expect. Levels are mostly well designed. Probably the biggest annoyance is that there is one level where you can fall down into a pit and it looks like there is no way out of it. There's actually a very, very small straircase along the side that barely has any depth to it which you can't visibly see unless you know to look for it.There're some differences in some of the monsters. Imps fireballs move much slower, Lost Souls are much more aggressive and threatening and Pain Elementals are capable of spawning multiple Lost Souls at once.On the downside, there are a couple monsters removed from the game. No Heavy Weapons Guy, Archvile or Spider Masterminds. There are only two new creatures. The Nightmare Imps which are just Imps but harder to see, move quicker, and their fireballs move faster. The other new creature is the final boss who is a bit annoying as she fires out 4 auto-seeking fireballs in a wide spread that are fast moving and it's nigh impossible to successfully dodge more than 2 of them.Monster in-fighting is inconsistent, like there're different rules for it on different levels. Some monsters won't fight a monster of a differing type even if they're being hit by it's projectile and taking damage from it. I've also had levels where I know there was a previous level where I got 2 differing monsters to in-fight before, but now they won't do it on this level. Can be a bit frustrating if you're trying to have some fun with the mechanic.This game also has a stuttering issue for whatever reason. It's not a massive problem, but every 10 minutes or so you can expect the game to stutter 3 times in a row for half a second to a full second each time. On very rare occasion, it will do multiple stutters back to back or within a short time frame. It's not enough to be game breaking, but the game is still playing while you're stuttering, so if you're in a fight while it's happening it could result in you dying. Especially if it happens while fighting a CyberDemon.Doom 64 is an old school shooter that's better than most modern shooters.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much worth it, it's a solid Doom game.The levels are very well made, hard to get lost, the texture work is a step up from the first two games, they provide a great atmosphere with the new lightning effects added.The combat is pretty much the same as the first two, quite a bit more slow paced, but still challenging and fun.This time we do not have music, but ambient sounds, similar to Quake, which I think complements the overall aesthetic this game has.I think this is a better way to enter the older Doom franchise than Doom and Doom 2. Also is really cheap for what it offers.

_childDocuments_.review: HI THERE, DOOM NOSTALGICS!Well, first of all, my review on this game may be suspicious, as I’ve been a fan of the Doom Franchise since the first one, and Doom 64 was also my first game on this wonderful console. _childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly frustrating.It wants you to create a Bethesda account before it lets you reach the menu. You'd be forgiven for thinking that clicking "cancel" would cancel the launching of the game, but you can play it without a Bethesda account, as the cancel button just gets rid of the pointless login screen and takes you to the menu. The tickbox for getting spammed with Bethesda news is another sour point - why would I recommend  a game that wants to push advertising? The mouse interface on the menu is a bit broken, as you have to use the scrollwheel to reach certain options. The intro video feels ameteur. Nothing about the game gives me a positive sense of value for money.The charm of Doom was lost, as I don't recognize the levels, which feel modular and lack character in 3D. I got stuck in the corridors trying to find all the switches. Within seconds of starting I was surprised to find out I was supposed to hurl myself down an elevator shaft - wasn't this game supposed to be about survival? Enemies are either weak and alone, or you just encounter clumps of bullet sponges through endless keycard mazes. The level design is basic, and has noob traps like buttons that hurt you (and ceilings that crush you for no reason). On the second level there's a weird combination of button and key that I had to strafe-run to reach in time - how would a new player have known that? How does it make sense? Some doors and elevators just look like walls.I wonder if the 94% positive rating is based on nostalgia. I liked the original Doom, but this one has little to no merit. If you liked Doom and wanted more (and already played Quake) then LucasArts Outlaws would be a classy alternative. The Half-Life series and Halo trilogy had far better campaigns than this as you could see the way forward. I don't think the console era is an excuse for how poor the gameplay is, as Goldeneye offered fair longevity without being pointlessly difficult. The playerbase is anti-social, which is weird for a singleplay game, as asking for help when getting stuck leads to all sorts of nonsense like being given false advice or insulted (or just told to use noclip). Having to frequently turn to a YouTube playthrough ruins what little sense of immersion is offered, but the game doesn't flow when you're stuck without the help.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, let me say: I love the cool character sprites, the level design, the lighting, the creepy atmosphere, the sound design, the eerie music tracks, and the gameplay, of course. It's all SO good that I personally like Doom 64 a bit better than the classic Doom 1 and 2.Now, the first time I experienced Doom 64 wasn't on the Nintendo 64 - it was through the unofficial Doom 64 Retribution mod for GZDoom, which was probably the best way to experience the game back in 2018.In 2020, Bethesda finally released their official port of Doom 64. In 2024 I finally decided to play the official port and re-experience the game. So far I've beaten the main campaign, the new Lost Levels campaign, and the Cat and Mouse fun level, and I must say... It has the same satisfying gameplay I remember, and all the other elements that make it so awesome. Although, there are a few improvements that could be made, such as:- Adding more customization options- Giving people the ability to select a stage without having to beat Hectic, just like in Doom + Doom 2- Adding officially approved mods and level packs periodically, as they do with the enhanced versions of Quake and Doom + Doom 2- Online multiplayerThat said, if you are a Doom fan, and/or you like First Person Shooters, I definitely recommend you get this official port of Doom 64, even at full price!Additionally, as of 2024, there is an even better way to play Doom 64, which does require buying this version of the game:  This mod offers a lot more customization options, and a bunch of extra content not available in the official port.If you don't care about Steam achievements, you can buy this version, then download and set up Doom CE, and play Doom 64 exclusively there. _childDocuments_.review: This game is practically what Doom 3 could have been. It has the gameplay like the classics but it adds new graphics that makes it more scary. So it has horror and and pretty much more demon slaying goodness. The reason why it has "64" because it originally was for Nintendo 64, until after Doom Eternal release, they re release Doom 64 and added the lost levels which extended the story what has happen to Doom Guy (Keep noted that Doom 3 is a total reboot, while Doom 2016 and Doom Eternal has connections with this story).This game follows after Doom 2, story wise. If you want, you can also get Doom 1 and 2 since they also updated them to make modern controls possible without the use of DOS. In case anyone wanna pick up the story, even though it doesnt show it clear as day but if you look it up you'll gather the pieces on whats going on. Since gameplay wise, it just takes you right in and you just have to make your way through the levels.Also, if you want to play the Lost levels, you must beat the main story in Doom 64. Doing so, when you play new game you are given a choice either play the main story or lost levels. While the lost levels dont have much levels comparing to the main story, its still nice to add new stuff in the game.One last thing to mention also, gameplay behaves just like Doom 1 and 2. So in case anyone doesnt know how Classic Doom works, you cant look up and down, and you have to rely on auto aim to hit your enemies (just aim at them even if they are above or below you and it'll automatically shoot up or down as long as you can see them).Very worth playing honestly, get it.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly kind of think this game is the best of the classics (This game is the real Doom 3). Owing to the N64's limitations, the game is lacking some things from Doom 2, namely a few enemy variants and weapon animations, but the game makes good use of its relatively small (Less than Doom 2, more than 1) enemy variety and the level design, in my opinion, is consistently good and fun, something that I can't say in good conscience about the latter parts of Doom 2. The game runs extremely smooth (with the exception of two weapons that have animations which seem to be stuck at a lower framerate, but ultimately has no bearing on gameplay) and you can actually see what's going on since the brightness has been reworked a bit. It's more classic Doom, with sprite work and ambience that isn't really available in the games that preceeded it. The new levels that were added in this version are actually well designed and really fun as well.Do be advised that if you're accustomed to the additional features from Doom 64 EX, this version is pretty barebones in terms of gameplay options. However, with some finagling, you can make the WAD functional with EX, if you so choose. Complaints? I guess the baron's blood could've been changed to red. The unmaker and chainsaw have strangely choppy animations compared to every other weapon. The ability to freelook and remove autoaim would've been neat (with disabled achievements since it can affect progression on, like, 2 levels). But overall, I can't come up with any notable complaints that actually have significant bearing on my experience.I highly recommend this game on the grounds that the base game is great and you can legally own the WAD for use with other versions. It's great to see this once hidden gem finally receive the recognition it deserves. Just play it!

_childDocuments_.review: A Good solid port that I can say would even work on a potato! (my iGPU a Intel HD4600 could play this no sweat)I really liked the fact the game actually offers you 3 API's to pick between: Vulken, DX11 and OpenGL Now about the game itself, Its the often forgotten yet really solid entry in the franchise and the 1st time they really started to go for the more horror and atmospheric experience which was then continued with Doom 3 and RoE before going back to the more as I describe heavy metal feeling (which im down for as well lol)I do find this one a bit more on the easy side but has its gotcha! moments too, Players on the younger side that grew up on more modern shooters may have less fun with this given these days you get your hand held more in where your supposed to go and this game will not tell you where you are supposed to be going or what you are supposed to be doing. It also still has (and as I recall the last Doom to have) the keycard system that was big in the 90's I would still recommend checking it out however as the 1st time to officially play it since the original N64 release, for nostalgia nuts or people who enjoy older styles of games. This should be on your list to buy and play especially at the very reasonable price point it gives you! Also for those who have Doom Eternal, this game can unlock some items in that game via your Bethesda account!

This was always a really good game, and the port has improved it.Upsides:-Plays just like the original Doom games.-Lighting has been increased. The N64 was almost unplayably dark in some areas.-Added a few new levels and story cards to add a little bit of lore tying previous Doom games to the new iteration.YMMV:-No mouselook. This wasn't in the original and it isn't here.-The hidden weapon still makes the game facerollingly easy if you put the time into unlocking it.Downsides:-I had one achievement (for fully-unlocking the hidden weapon) fail to give me credit *shrug*
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Great classic Doom game, very faithful to the original and only has the essential upgrades (144fps, high resolutions).Don't forget to add -skipmovies to the launch options,to get those demon keys and to save after every level.Also never shoot pain elementals with the rocket launcher, not a good idea.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: Likely the most underrated and obscure entry in the doom series prior to this long overdue port. When I first heard about Doom 64 way back when, I assumed it was just a port of the original Doom for the Nintendo 64 and skipped it altogether. I was absolutely wrong. While it definitely shares the gameplay style of Doom and Doom II, it has its own original story and tries to introduce a little tinge of horror with some well executed moody lighting and a suitably haunting ambient soundtrack. It also sports new sounds and an all new visual style, featuring updated sprites for all the classic enemies and weapons along side some original creations.Doom 64 is a pretty respectable length, clocking in at 32 levels if you include the secret ones. I believe this edition also includes some extra "lost" levels as well which is a nice touch. The story of the game is a direct sequel to the events of Doom II, and if you played and paid attention to the background lore of Doom 2016 actually kind of explains the predicament the doom marine finds himself in at the beginning of that game. If you enjoy the gameplay of the other classic doom games I would highly recommend this entry as well, you should feel right at home.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: While I found this one slightly less replayable, this is a fantasic game, which takes a wholey new direction for the franchise (well, not wholey new, Doom on PS1 had kinda delved into this game's brand of atmosphere, but still). What's more, this game's level design is easily the most consistently high quality of the classic Doom games.For me, this is the real Doom 3.Also, fantastic job by the ever-brilliant Nightdive Studios porting it to PC and fixing this game's jarring lighting issues on the N64.(Formerly:great nightdive port of an amazing game. best classic doom game, don't @ me)

_childDocuments_.review: Refunded Doom Eternal so i have to wait until that goes trough before i can rebuy this one.I only played a bit of it, but this game was really great. I especially loved the level design of the second level.The two cons of this game for me are the mouse aim not having a free aim option and the music not fitting fast paced combat. One can be fixed trough source ports although they currently don't support the wad.I also checked out Brutal Doom 64, this has even nicer atmospheres, allows for music replacements and has free aim. But i noticed important differences in the levels making it less fun to play than the original version you get with this. (Specially there is an item pickup on the second level that causes all the doors to open with pinkies, with barrels in the middle. I loved this as it put me on my toe's but did not feel unfair. In the free remakes this doesn't happen and you get the powerup free).So is it worth the money? I'd say so. Is Doom 64 EX better in terms of features? I'd say so, but that one does require a wad and the N64 rom. Using my tool availible at  you can patch the wad from this release to be compatible with Doom 64 EX. Including the new levels.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOM 64

_childDocuments_.review: A totally underrated and genuinely spooky entry into the franchise. The dark hallways and ambient, foreboding soundtrack that gives off an almost Silent Hill-esque atmosphere, mixed with the ever classic fast twitch Doom gameplay style makes this a one of a kind entry in this kind of genre. The new, PC exclusive add-on pack isn't bad either, but don't expect any new groundbreaking tricks, as it's more or less just an excuse to tie the classic series in with the newer game's canon.Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This port is alright. Bit janky here and there compared to EX (hell, it IS based off of EX after all, just more limited) but solid overall. I'd say unless you really care about achievements, just stick to Doom 64 EX instead or play Doom 64 Retribution if you really don't care about a true vanilla experience. Lost Levels will more than likely get ported over anyways.Speaking of the lost levels, most of them suck as in it really feels like you have to go out of your way to find secrets if you don't wanna feel like you're underpowered or lacking in ammo. The only level in lost levels I found myself enjoying was the final level.

_childDocuments_.review: When Doom was initially released, it significantly influenced the entire FPS genre of that time. Over the years, various enhancements were implemented, and subsequently, a version for the N64 was introduced. The rationale behind this decision was quite apparent considering the remarkable success of games like Goldeneye and Turok. Consequently, it seemed only natural for Doom to seize a share of the spotlightTo be honest, despite owning an N64, I regrettably never had the opportunity to experience this game on the console itself. Nevertheless, when I came across the opportunity to purchase and play it on Steam, I seized it without any hesitationNow, if I were to draw a comparison between this release and its classic counterpart, what discernible dissimilarities would manifest? In terms of aesthetics, this rendition exudes a darker atmosphere, infusing an exhilarating element into the formula. From an action standpoint, this port proves to be quite commendable, as the developers successfully adapted the gameplay to the keyboard-mouse combination, a fundamental requirement in modern-day FPS games. Regarding the sound effects and soundtrack, they aptly fulfill their intended purposeA substantial array of maps awaits, providing ample content to captivate players for several hours. Furthermore, the inclusion of puzzles adds a welcome dose of diversity to the overall experience. Acquiring all the achievements may pose a moderate challenge, but with patience and perseverance, it is indeed achievableIn conclusion, for enthusiasts of the franchise, venturing into this rendition is undoubtedly recommended

_childDocuments_.review: I finally played and completed Doom 64 while waiting for the next Doom game. Many people claim this game is a masterpiece, but is it really?Doom 64 combines elements from Doom 1, 2, and 3. Although it's a sequel to Doom 2 and a prequel to Doom 2016, it doesn't include all the enemies from its predecessor. However, it does feature all the weapons plus one additional one that also appears in Doom Eternal (that by the way, I never needed to use).Did I enjoy this game? Not really. Some levels were enjoyable, but others were a nightmare to complete, often giving me a headache. The abundance of ammo and the ease of enemy encounters, at least on normal difficulty, made the game too easy. Despite this, I did enjoy the cyberdemon fights and the final boss battle.I found myself using the double barrel shotgun 90% of the time without ever running out of ammo. In case of low ammo, I was switching to the minigun and quickly replenish my shotgun ammo in less than 5 minutes. The double barrel shotgun was surprisingly strong even at long distances, further reducing the game's challenge.I really enjoyed the "Lost Levels" though, six additional maps unlocked after beating the main game. Each level takes around 10 minutes to complete and features plenty of enemies. However, the final boss of this episode (which is the same of the main game) was poorly designed for the map, as its "rockets" failed to spawn properly.The lack of music and dark environments reminded me of Doom 3, though thankfully, the game allows you to increase the brightness.While the enemies have new animations and sprites, the removal of the double barrel shotgun's animation, my personal favorite, is disappointing. On the other side, the weapons have satisfying sounds.In conclusion, I don't plan to replay Doom 64 unless I'm doing a marathon of all Doom games or trying the "Brutal Doom 64" mod. The game lacks memorable music, enemy encounters, has too much ammo, and features boring maps. I can only recommend it to classic Doom fans.
