_childDocuments_.review: Let me start with the statement: I do not hate this game. In fact, I found it pretty entertaining. But mostly it is this weird thing I can barely comprehend. A bizarre anomaly in the structure of Doom reality. Like when you go to your girlfriend's parents for a christmas dinner and suddenly you are introduced to her crazy uncle who smokes two man size bags of weed and talks to a tree. It's interesting, but in the end you are left with just one question:Why? Why does this game exist and what was the thought process behind designing it? Why do developers make some decisions in that way, but not another?So, firstly let's skip some boring parts. This is a port of an N64 game from 1997. Porting was done by Nightdive using their KEX engine. It run flawlessly. I never experienced crashes, in very few instances there were frame drops. It has proper FOV adjustment — which could be a numerical number instead of a slider, but oh well, at least we have it. Despite being a console port mouse and keyboard controls are fine, never have an issue with it, however the mouse is little floaty, despite turning off v-sync, but it's not a deal breaker, you can easily adapt to it. So yeah, in this department all is fine.Idea behind the game is simple. You are a Doom marine, you kill demons. But instead of just porting the game from the PC, Midway — developer of this game, it wasn't made by ID software — decided to change everything. Levels, graphics, monsters, guns. The graphics were especially very improved. So is it a port or new game? Who knows, who cares, I have two barrels of super shotgun pointed in the nearest imp, I don’t have time to think about this.So yeah, now for meat and potatoes. I have several issues with this game.Firstly, D64 made the same mistakes that Doom3 did. It's trying to be something different than everyone expected. It's trying to be a horror game, but unlike D3, due to hardware and software limitations, and also incorrect design premise, fails completely. Hardware was n64 and lack of it computing power, which contributed to limited design capabilities; software was using ID1 engine to create unsettling atmosphere — engine to primitive to do a horror stuff; premise — well, you cannot expect from me to be scared when I have 100 rockets and bunch of shotgun shells in my inventory. And I am not saying it's a bad choice, it's just bizarre and in my opinion, not working properly. Because to achieve this feeling many aspects of core Doom gameplay was nerfed. Monsters are slower, there are fewer of them, Doomguy also moves slower, even when you are running. Enemy projectiles are so slow that it's almost laughable — I can stand and just see how imps fireball slowly… gently… flying towards me, like a butterfly. In another case I can easily dodge three hellknight while sipping tea, and they cannot hurt me. OG doom was never too hard — compared to, for example, Blood — but in this case I can count on one hand times when I died, and It was my first even playthrough in this game. You cannot scare me, devs, when I'm this unstoppable force of nature, spreading death everywhere I look. Especially when you throw at me pixelated, cartoonish monsters. Second, overall design. The strongest part of this game. Mostly. Graphics are improved, better resolution, better textures, more detailed. But it's on engine from 1993, developed on a console in 1997. Besides, even if I can see improvement, I also feel that all this is done mostly to levels, and it was achieved with a lot of sacrifice. Yeah, textures are better, there are a lot of clever tricks with lighting too, but thanks to this different aspect of the game suffers. Yeah, levels are prettier, but they are also much simpler than in OG games. It's just corridors, big square arenas, more corridors, stairs. Not much of different level geometry, not much of level complexity. When I stand before the door it is going to lead me to another corridor, and then to another big arena, and then another room, and then another corridor….. At some point game started to be more like arena shooters (Painkiller, Serious Sam) — you go to the room, monster jumps you, you kill them, then AND ONLY THEN switch appears, you pressed it, more monsters spawn (with no visual que, they just appears from thin air, thank God there is sound of it), after killing them doors opens, you proceed to next room where all this circus is repeated…   Thirdly, enemies. Another case of bizarre decisions. They have better sprites, but also they are more blurred compared to pixelated ones from Doom 1 and 2. And due to n64 limitations there are fewer of them. There are no Chain Gunners in D64, no Revenants, no Archvilles, not even a Spider Mastermind. The core monsters of Doom are gone. Some of you will cherish this, but they were always crucial in proper Doom experience, and a smaller roster of monsters made the game simpler, less engaging and easier. After the third room with only hellknights in a row I was starting to yawn — speaking of with. Game overused the poor knight to the point I started to feel sorry for those guys.And little more about monsters: There is no different model for shotgunner and pistol zombie. Why? Especially when you have two different types of imps, one normal, and one semitransparent and with faster projectiles? Design of enemies is hit or miss. Some are more unsettling, like pinky or pain elemental, some are just bland, like imps (just and alien with no mouths), some are ok, like zombie mans or Cyberdemon, or spiders, some just derpy — Hellknights/Barons, Cacodemons (cute tiny hands this one have, so precious!). I also liked the invisibility effect on specters — in more dark areas they really can jump on you when you are not prepared.  Next, weapons. And another: why? All previous arsenal is here. But again, in some instances devs cuts corners. There is no reloading animations when using shotgun and super shotgun. WHY? IT IS SO ICONIC PART OF DOOM, THAT RELOADING OF SUPER SHOTGUN, DON'T TAKE IT AWAY, PLEASE! Chaingun is much, much better in this game, same I can say with chainsaw — now it just melts every enemy. No pinky is a problem now, bwahahaha! Rocket launchers now have knockback. Again — why? As for Plasma and BFG — introducing the last weapon made them obsolete. No kidding, in the entire game there was one moment when I used the BFG. Because Unmaker exists, and you can grab one before Plasma and BFG. And this thing, even not upgraded, is OP. Too much OP I think. Only with one rune it literally melts everything, even Barons. With two no Cyberdemon was even a threat. It breaks a balance, monsters was not design to counter this kind of weapon. Thanks to Unmaker, the rest of the difficulty is thrown out of the window. Devs try to mitigate it by throwing less energy packs, but if you conserve ammo for stronger enemies only, you will be swimming in it.What else? There is no music. Only ambience. There are no cool midi metal riffs, no combat songs, only humming in the background. They probably did this to make the atmosphere more unsettling, but again, it's not working for me. I prefer shredding demons with a cool soundtrack. So, time for closure. It's a decent game. But mediocre Doom. More misses than hits. Changing pace and atmosphere was a bad decision. Doom is not a horror game, it's not working here nor in Doom3. And I think most people look at this game through the lens of nostalgia. “It was a cool game, because it was on n64, and it was a cool console when I was kiddo!” they say. Well, im scrub slav from central Europe who never owned a n64 or psx, or nes, or even a PS2 so maybe im less biased than you guys. Or I'm just rambling after too many shoots of Jack Daniels…

_childDocuments_.review: DOOM 64 takes you back to the hellish roots of the franchise, cranking up the intensity with unforgiving action and dark, atmospheric levels that feel like a fever dream straight from the depths of hell. This isn’t your average demon-slaying romp—this is DOOM on hard mode, where the shadows seem alive, and every corner could be your last.The graphics may scream "retro," but the vibe is timeless—blood, guts, and pure adrenaline. The music? Just as aggressive, driving you to blast through hordes of demons with ruthless efficiency. And speaking of demons, they’re nastier than ever. Every time you hear the guttural roar of an Imp or the stomp of a Hell Knight, your trigger finger gets itchy, and your heart races. There’s something about DOOM 64’s claustrophobic level design that makes each battle feel like a fight for your life.Weapons feel as satisfying as ever—whether you're mowing down demons with the classic shotgun or going full carnage with the BFG, every kill feels gloriously brutal. But don’t get cocky—this game will punish you if you let your guard down. The difficulty ramps up fast, and with its eerie lighting and labyrinthine levels, it keeps you on edge the entire time.In short, DOOM 64 is a love letter to old-school FPS fans, dripping in nostalgia but with enough edge to make even modern players sweat. It’s not just a game, it’s a demonic gauntlet—one that’ll leave you breathless and craving more carnage. If you’re ready to embrace the chaos, grab your shotgun and dive headfirst into the inferno.

name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist
detailed_description: The Choices You Make, Make You. Growing up in humanity’s first extrasolar space colony means navigating a new world full of wonder, danger, and beauty. Explore the wilderness, study, fall in love, discover strange creatures, and deal with the consequences of your actions. Your choices will directly affect the lives of your friends and the fate of the colony. What kind of world will you help make? Will you survive to enjoy it? Why do you remember doing this before? Growing Up on an Alien Planet You have your whole life ahead of you. Will you spend it studying in school, or diving into the intriguing flora and fauna of this new world? Will you introduce space-age technology, or live in harmony with nature? Will you battle massive beasts, or nurture future generations? Realized in brilliant watercolor, the world of Vertumna is yours to explore. Your Pasts and Your Futures Matter Everything you learn and experience will make you and your colony stronger. You will thrive and you will make mistakes. These formative moments - your memories, decisions, and friendships - become collectible cards you carry with you. Each season brings new obstacles on Vertumna. The battle cards you earn from your experiences give you new options for overcoming these challenges, whether that is navigating relationships, learning new skills, exploring the planet, or staying alive. Every decision counts, during this life and the next. How Many Lives Will YOU Live? The cosmos is full of incredible mysteries, and your ability to remember your past lives is one of them. There are dozens of different endings to your story. How many lives will it take to save both your colony and the planet? Are you ready to wake up again? Features: Use memories of past lives to explore 800+ story events. Discover more than 250 battle cards as you grow up on an alien planet. Play your best hand in challenge encounters to ace your math test or escape from a wild snapbladder. Make friends, fight with your parents, go on dates, fall in love, and save the colony. 29 wildly different endings based on the choices you make each month. Pick from 25 colony jobs, like goofing off as a depot clerk, or surveying the valley. Grow into 15 skills, including bravery, toughness, organization, and empathy. Get to know 10 dateable characters, including dog-boys, aliens, hot politicians and stone cold killers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely in my top 10 games of all time.The game's main function is the fact that you relive your live over and over. Without spoilers, I can can say it is done really well. With spoilers  The card game part isn't anything special. It's not especially difficult, my first playthrough I didn't lose a single card game challenge. The special part is the deck-building part. You have little control over what exactly goes into your deck, but they are determined by the memories you make and how you go about challenges. The art in the game is amazing. The character's portraits and sprites change as the years go bye. In some events the game gets rid of all the text and just displays a fullscreen image for several seconds for important events. The cards are all unique and distinguishable.The characters are all enjoyable and fun to get to know. At first glance, it seems like the characters each have one defining trait that makes up their character, something that often happens in other games. However, this game has probably the most in-depth and dynamic characters I've seen in a while. Characters change over the years, depending on what happens in the colony, who dies, and how you interact with them. They each have multiple endings to their own story, and will come upon some of them even without your help. Some of the romanceable characters will start dating throughout the story if you don't woo them first.All in all, the best life-sim game I've ever played, not a bad card game, amazing dating sim, and an emotional roller coaster.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - Yes.  Absolutely Yes.  If you enjoy narrative-driven games and a replay cycle then you can and should enjoy this without issue.=====I did not know this game existed until I heard about it from a friend earlier this week.  They absolutely gushed about it and how amazing it was and all the cool things it did.  So on a whim I said "sure I'll give this a try."  That was two days ago and this has been the only thing I've been able to think about.I'll keep the synopsis brief because, as a narrative game, telling too much of the story is a spoiler: you're a kid born on a colony ship who crash-lands on your new homeworld and you have to survive, work hard, and grow up while going through the trials and tribulations that are common with striking into a new frontier.  You'll make memories, you'll suffer losses, but if you keep at it you'll make it to adulthood in one piece.  Hopefully.Speaking of memories, one of the core mechanics of this game is cards: this is as much a deckbuilding game as much as a visual novel and you get more cards by completing events that happen organically through the game: based on skill, relationships, jobs, and story events.  Some, like your youngest memories "giggling" and "crawling" can even be upgraded to be more powerful.  But the game doesn't punish you for not having a perfect deck: you can stress your way to victory or settle for a partial reward--not everything has to be completed perfectly.  If you LOVE card challenges you can add more difficulties, if you HATE card challenges you can even disable the whole system and leave it to some amount of chance.The other major mechanics are time and stress: the planet you live on has thirteen months per year and you spend 10 years living (ideally), doing one job per month to grow yourself as you see fit.  But you can't keep doing that job ad infinitum, you have to break and relax every once in a while to not burn out.  This puts time limits on certain events despite looking like you have all the time in the world, and when it comes due you better be ready to move on.Mechanics aside, the narrative is as much about your Friends' stories as much as your own and they are incredibly well-written.  Your peers grow up with you and you contribute to their lives as much as they contribute to yours.  You can even end up dating one or more of them, as per visual novel fare, though there are consequences for the story depending on how you progress.The game does have some uncomfortable subjects, some more intense than others, but the devs put a great deal of forethought into warning players and provided a list of everything that comes up that could be troubling, to the point that they also include specific spoilers.  It might be a bit much, but it's a good consideration on the part of the devs.The only real problem I have with the game is how it isn't quite clear how to complete certain events in the game and how opaque some of the things are.  The silver lining is that the devs intentionally built this game around a replay mechanic that flags things you've seen and done in prior playthroughs so you can make new outcomes that weren't originally available.There's plenty more to unpack, but I leave that for you to discover.  The bottom line is that I haven't seen a game this well-made in a long time, and I will now be following the devs to see what else they do.  I wholeheartedly recommend this to everyone, especially when it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A newage teen drama with an interesting cast of characters, an exotic setting with well thought-out lore and plenty of high-stakes decisions for the player to make. There's romance, tension, and intrigue to be found in the crumbling space colony you try to build and even worse, not everyone will survive. Since the game is fully released and there likely won't be any major patches, I would lower my expectations when trying to find closure.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a fascinating story.  I love the combination of card game with visual novel sort of storytelling.  The concept of the time loop allowing you to fix mistakes based on previous playthroughs is immensely satisfying.  And the fact that the game tells you in the spoilers section whether or not someone can be saved preventing you from overinvesting time into trying to save someone who can't be.  That being said it is also nice that just cause someone can be saved either in your first playthrough or with additional knowledge going into others doesn't mean it is going to be easy.  I also liked that given the game ends when you are 20, some of your romances fizzle out by the time of the epilogue.  Too often in these types of games you get "and they lived happily ever after", or worse it goes super bleak like "unfortunately they died shortly after" never any thing like "as time grew on you drifted apart" as is one of the potential romance endings in this game.  I love this, cause while I'm all for escapism, how often does a relationship started by teenagers actually last?That being said, it is worth noting this game is NOT for the faint of heart.  Game doesn't hesitate to pointlessly kill a prepubescent child within the first hour or so of the game.  Keyword is pointlessly, they strive to make great efforts to show that while any death, especially one of a child, is impactful it isn't always due to something like space vikings or whatever, it can literally be something like a toy short circuiting.  Thankfully that death can be undone as quickly as literally loading a prior save after it has happened, but it shows you that they aren't going to pull any punches.My only real complaint about the game is there is a lot of soapboxing during certain parts of the game.  While most things in it give you options some things are just presented as out and out wrong (without showing why, or in some cases literally showing the exact opposite leaving you confused as to the author's intent).  For example, the game goes to great lengths to show Capitalism as a negative force, and yet you still get "money" in the form of Kudos and there is a character who flat out says it doesn't make sense to give the same amout to someone who did nothing while someone else did all the work.The game also punishes you for staying neutral on too many things.  You more or less are forced to pick a side if you want a decent ending.  You leveled up your combat abilities as your focus because you liked the bonus it provided? Well I hope you weren't planning on talking anything out with the natives because if so you just earned yourself an everyone dies ending... This isn't necessarily a con as again you made that decision and you decided too late that it was a bad one.  Point is, that's another theme in this game is stick to your guns, and in some cases that is very much literal.TL;DR Game has its flaws no doubt, but it is definitely extremely enjoyable despite these.  Also similar to a rogue like game, a single playthrough isn't even a fraction of the full game.  I played through several times and still haven't seen all the endings.  Another nice caveat is the game remembers what youve encountered in other playthroughs even if you don't and is somewhat forgiving in that respect.  I appreciated the story, the inclusiveness, and the thought provoking side of the fact that almost no character is universally good or evil.  I also loved the fact you could save people you failed to in a prior playthrough, few things are as satisfying.9/10 GG

_childDocuments_.review: – Unique and interesting characters– Sometimes heartbreaking, beautiful story– Visual novel + RPG + deck builder gameplay– The most complex narrative-based game I’ve played with so many outcomes– Tons of replay value– So much gorgeous artwork– Overall a lovely game & a lovely story!This game is wonderful. I’m feeling a lot of feelings now that I’ve finished.Gameplay is relatively simple, in that all you have to do is talk to characters, make choices, choose an activity to do each month, and play some card games. But I’ve never played a narrative-based game this complex!It’s part visual novel, part RPG, part deck builder. There is a linear story, but it doesn’t work by having a storyline that branches every so often. There are 12 skill/personality stats, stress level, rebellion level, some hidden story stats, colony food, colony defense, and a bunch of relationships. All these things are constantly affecting or being affected by your choices. Some are easy to adjust (like getting a skill by going to class), some less so (like figuring out ways to build colony defense). There are also seemingly simple choices that can affect things in ways you won’t even realize at the time. Doing certain activities a lot or at the right times can also trigger events. But the real complexity comes from how all of these things work together. It’s really cool.This game also has soooooooooo much replay value and rewards you for replaying. There are so many characters to get to know, things to learn about the world, little events to see, and endings. And so many ways relationships and other things can differ within the endings. Special endings too. And the premise involves the player living many lives and having memories of past lives, so there are certain things you can only do once your character has certain memories.There reached a point in my first playthrough when I stopped having to really think about the decisions I was making and just sort of became my character. The way you’re with them from age 10 to 20, you really get to develop them and watch them grow, and I was surprised at how I found myself going with the flow and exploring life with them.And all the other characters! I loved getting to know them more and more in each playthrough. They’re imperfect, and I love them. They do sort of have one main defining characteristic, which can make them seem a bit flat at first, but most of them had more depth and I felt for them more once I got to know them. And they have cute or interesting or complicated relationships with each other, not just you. I very badly want an actual novel about them. Especially Dys 🥺❤️ So lonely and distanced from everyone, but also so passionate. And ok, sorta Vace too, because yes, he’s awful, but I love characters who actually admit to being wrong and try to be better (and his rudeness cracked me up sometimes).Now, the dating element. You can stick to friendship and the game is no less rich for it. You can even flirt without getting locked in, and you won’t be punished for flirting with everyone. If you accidentally end up dating someone or change your mind, you can break up, no hard feelings. (It is a little weird to break up and have the character be like, “Ok!” like they didn’t even care in the first place, but whatever.) If you are going to date though, don’t expect a dating sim because there’s no guaranteed HEA. There are 10 options (4 guys, 4 girls, 1 nonbinary person, and 1 alien who uses he/him pronouns but I’m not entirely sure he has a gender), plus an 11th you can get just in the epilogue. But… Some characters are not into committed exclusive relationships. Some end up dating other people if you take too long or don’t make the right choices. Some feel very strongly about having or not having kids. Some relationships don’t last in the epilogue, or something complicates them. There are some things I don’t love about this aspect (namely how awful the game makes you feel if you try to get with either of the two characters who are clearly supposed to be with each other), but it makes all the characters feel like they are their own people, rather than just existing to date the player.The story is interesting, but it’s also heartbreaking the first time. At least it was for me. But it does get better. Some of the bad things are preventable, you just have to figure out how. There’s a thought-provoking element to it all as well. Not just the obvious things in the story, like whether humans should colonize a new planet, but also things like how much of what happens in the lives of others is your responsibility?There’s a lot of cool lore and whatnot to discover too. Fascinating alien lifeforms and the history of the planet.– Gorgeous artwork, and so much of it. Backgrounds. Characters, including at various ages for many of them. Unlockable CGs throughout the game as you get to know different characters. Alien lifeforms. Art for each of the 29 endings. Art on all of the many cards you get. The graphics when you walk around and explore are cute too.– The music was unobtrusive and pleasant. Which I think is good for a game you’re going to play so many hours of.– The game lets you choose what pronouns and gendered words are used for the player character, with full customization. You can also choose appearance between masculine, feminine, and androgynous (it seems the only difference is hair length, and maybe a slight difference in outfit, but there’s a lot of art in the game, so that’s understandable). And you can change any of these things at  during the game.– Lots of diversity among both dateable and background characters! Canonically not-straight characters and relationships (and you can date characters of any gender regardless of your gender). Also characters who are trans, nonbinary, demisexual, polyamorous, POC, neurodivergent, and physically disabled. If you want to know more specifically (I don’t consider these spoilers, but some may prefer learning these things as they get to know the characters): *SPOILER*  *END SPOILER*– You can have pets! And they make an adorable little squeaky sound when you click on them.– You can have an unlimited number of saves, which is super helpful for planning ahead and doing strategic playthroughs when you’ve seen a lot already and just want to get the different careers and endings. Also if you just want to come back and look at the outcome of a different dialogue or small choice. The auto saves are great if you mess up a choice.Overall, it’s a beautiful game and a beautiful story. When you’re just about finished playing, I suggest doing one final “perfect” playthrough, whatever that means to you. I’m so glad I did. Just knowing all the outcomes separately didn’t have the same effect. I didn’t realize seeing it all together would touch me so much, but it really did!*Review can also be found on my blog (link in profile).*(May not include everything)– Can use mouse, keyboard (including one handed with either hand), combo of both, or controller.– Can change keys used.– Can turn off screen shake.– Can make menus bigger.– Trigger/content warnings available.– Can turn card-based games off (though it may cause you to lose some, I’m not sure how it works).– No TTS, not accessible for blind players or screen readers.

_childDocuments_.review: A bittersweet game no matter which angle you look at it with. The story, especially when completed on subsequent timelines, is heart-wrenching. I say this to give kudos; however, the satisfaction of managing to accomplish a near-perfect ending felt disproportionate to the amount of labor required to get there. Your time is so limited, and I constantly felt stretched too thin when meticulously trying to meet all the prerequisites for certain events and outcomes. I recommend experiencing 2-3 playthroughs, though I personally can't see myself completing a 4th.

_childDocuments_.review: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is a really interesting game to play that starts to fall off after your first playthrough. I’m recommending the game because it’s a compelling story that I thoroughly enjoyed playing for my first playthrough (which took ~12 hours), but it isn’t without its limitations.Pros:Cons:Ultimately, this game seems like a game with high replayability, but the more I played it the less I enjoyed it. My first playthrough was a blast, my second playthrough was interesting, and I won’t be playing a third playthrough. I still recommend I Was A Teenage Exocolonist because it’s a well made game that’s fun for a while, but I don’t expect to play this game any more.

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I try to 100% a game before leaving a review, but that would take a lot of time and I've got some big feelings.This is hands-down the best visual novel I've ever experienced. It's clear that a lot of thought and care went into the story. It is uniquely re-playable, where most visual novels I've experienced encourage skipping and save manipulation, this game answers the question or replay ability such that my second play through didn't feel like a chore.The characters are well written. Across two playthroughs I've initially loved and then disliked some, while growing to appreciate others I initially disliked. It was easy to put myself in the perspective of the main character and a lot of the narrative twists and turns gave me legit feelings. This is more of a game than most visual novels. Mechanically, the story moves along through the player choosing different skill challenges based on memories you've collected while playing. Essentially it's a deck builder that has you puzzling out the optimum play with rules reminiscent of poker; 3 suites and wilds, building straits and flushes. The difficulty of this challenge is pretty low, but I played the more challenging version on my second play through and found myself needing to use pickups to succeed in challenges frequently, even having to give up on some of them. If this aspect of the game play sounds boring to you, you can actually just turn it off as well. I made sure every member of my household got a copy, and one of my partners has been extremely excited about the story and how our playthroughs differ. I honestly can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: absolutely stunning. genuinely, if people don't start looking at this game as a real best of 2022 contender, i might just get into utopia's blep tea contraband and start losing my mind. sometimes relaxing, sometimes surprising, sometimes viscerally tragic, and always true to itself, i was a teenage exocolonist deserves every bit of praise it's gotten and all the love it's yet to receive. every moment of this game was so incredibly and uniquely delightful in a way i haven't experienced in gaming before-- i've just finished my first playthrough, and i find myself oddly drawn to tears by it. very few stories i've read, let alone games i've played, come at their premise with such an amount of care: not just effort, but detail, and affection for it. there is so much love, here. the take on the nature of humanity that this story takes is heart-wrenchingly gorgeous, painful, joyful, hilarious, campy and fun and strange. it's an odd little thing, and unabashedly so. exactly as it should be. raising sol felt like raising my younger self, and even if you think you won't find anything here for you-- underneath and interwoven with the technicolor world and the fun mechanics and the politics and the most lovingly human (and sometimes nonhuman) characters i've ever seen-- this a story about growing up. as a narrative experience, it rivals (and then handily surpasses) any big studio game i have ever played, and does so with ease. i think where the story of iwatec succeeds, most of all, is in its discussion of loss. the human experience is full of it, in big and little ways. you're in a timeloop, so sometimes, naturally, you can stop the bad thing from happening. sometimes you can't. sometimes the best parts of iwatec are losing, terribly, inevitably, and piecing sol back together again after. a wonderful tale on what it means to be human. i don't think i know the answer, yet, but i'm about to wake up again and find out.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: Very enjoyable! Might be a little niche, but I like that niche so I'm having a great time.Mild criticism: The story sometimes feels almost at odds with the art style (things get pretty dark!) and on my first run I was a little shocked by it. By the second run I was expecting it, so it didn't get me, but seriously: mind the content warnings! Some story beats are either seriously on-the-nose or feel a little over-the-top (although... still not as wild as things get in the real world, so), and there are a few points where people incorrectly act like I have or haven't done something, but I feel like that's sort of inevitable in such an expansively-branching story and it's not enough to reduce my enjoyment. I kind of wish there were more gifts to give to my friends :/Praise: I like the in-depth pronoun and title customization options (which are entirely optional) and generally enjoy the writing and story as well. It hits me hard in the emotions, all over the spectrum, and really makes me care about these characters and this colony. The only thing I was leery about going into it was the card/deck-building part since I've never been into that, but it's honestly very intuitive and includes options to both make it harder and to just skip it entirely. I also like that there's a certain amount of failure that's normal and expected, and the difficulty of the card challenges really feels like it tracks perfectly to your focus in a particular field. If I focus on mental stats, then physical challenges are harder but not impossible and mental challenges are usually a breeze.Overall, deeply enjoyable!

_childDocuments_.review: A queer-friendly, idealistic sci-fi masterpiece (with romance!!) in a carefully crafted pastel world, with stellar art and fantastic characters, in which you're a kid of whatever gender you prefer, growing up in a brand-new planetary colony full of people trying to make an actual egalitarian utopia, and struggling to survive when things keep going wrong.What more could I have asked for? I'm in love with this game. I started out enjoying it from the beginning, and it just kept growing and growing on me even more with every new scene. The writing is wonderful, the story very clever and cohesive, and the art is just gorgeous. I feel so engaged with all of the characters, who are all endearing in their own ways (well... almost all of them) and are delightfully complex (I love Dys, Sym and Marz, they are amazing). I absolutely love the exoplanet colony survival set-up of the story, and the narrative, community-as-family theme of the plot adds a really fresh and heart-warming touch that has been far too rare in the sci-fi genre.And romance! As you grow up throughout the game, you can romance your increasingly gorgeous friends of various genders, with even some polyamory arrangements possible. The game doesn't feature anything very explicit though there are implied sexual encounters that you can choose to engage in with your potential paramours when you're older, which are brief and tasteful. And I saw a bit of a booty, once.And uh, yeah, there's even a sexy dog-boy, and a pretty alien. The card game mechanic is fun, but I ended up turning it off after my second playthrough. My first playthrough I played on hard mode, and ended up failing most of the late-game challenges, but in regular mode I didn't have too much trouble (though that was my second playthrough).If this sounds good to you at all, get this game, you won't regret it. The narrative can change vastly with every playthrough, and it's packed full of satisfying, exciting, meaningful content and fun. It took me about 16 hours to beat on my first playthrough, but I also took my sweet time. I got the best ending on my third playthough (it was wonderful, by the way) and I still want to play to try and see different things and outcomes, and romance different characters!

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't know what to expect when I started playing this, but wow - this was so much better than I could've imagined. The narrative felt (for the most part) very reactive, which stood out against any other minor flaws the game might have had. Because of this, the role-playing part of this RPG was so rewarding and engaging. I crafted a character in my mind, and when I clearly wanted my character to be acting a certain way, the game read my mind and always had a narrative path ready for me to go down. The story was (to me) very touching, and I loved that they didn't shy away from the bad and the ugly of what this world would be like while still maintaining some of that childlike joy. I genuinely teared up at multiple parts, and was giddily grinning at others.A few major mechanics of the game had to grow on me, especially the deck-building, but I really felt like I got sucked into the game almost immediately. The attention to detail, the gorgeous illustration and art style, the careful balancing of difficulty as the years progress - a lot of passion and care clearly went into making a game, and it shows.My only real issue with the game is that after the careful hours I spent crafting my first run through, and finally getting the hang of the deck-building challenge mechanic, the ending of the game felt very rushed and anticlimactic. It wrapped up the loose ends, but I did feel like for my story's ending, there should've been more urgency and stress in the final moments.It's a game that practically is begging to be replayed at least a few times to unlock different ending, but more important, different stories throughout the 10 years the narrative spans. I can't wait to dive back in!!

_childDocuments_.review: For those who enjoy a good visual novel style game with interesting characters, choices, story and a very unique artstyle that doesnt require you to be a pro gamer this game is definitely for you. (Be warned this game isnt all sunshine and rainbows despite its bright colors, Serious themes are there)So what exactly is the game about? Well you are a 10 year old on a colony ship that fled earth (that is now a horrible place) seeking a better life on a world through a wormhole. After landing on the world you as a child must navigate through 9 years of life as you and your people try to settle on this new beautiful world. Along the way you could decide to try to befriend the other kids who all have their own story as they grow up. How does this game play? You as a character can move around the "camp" choosing what activity to involve yourself this month, you can also interact with the other kids giving them a gift each season and doing their events. Each activity gives you points in certain skill areas (12 in total, 4 for social, 4 for Mental, 4 for Physical). Each skill has 3 thresholds that will give you perks once you pass that amount and some decisions are gated behind having a certain amount of a certain skill. Some activities even gain you frienship with certain characters. How are activities or such done? Well its a very simple card game that you can take your time with, the game gives you a number to reach and randomly pulls out a certain amount of cards from your pool. Each card is eitherr red, blue, yellow or pink which counts as all 3 colors (so it is affect by all the positives but also the negatives) each card has a number and some have special effects depending on the card. With the cards you are given you must reach the score given by aligning the cards hoewever you want along the limited solts given. Their number is added to your count, pairing up cards of the same color, value or doing a scaling left to right (so 1 2 3, 6 7 8 etc) earns you extra points. The scaling must be a minimum of 3 cards long to take effect (so just a 1 2 doesnt work). Sometimes you are faced with "challenges" which have a much higher score to reach but 3 rounds to get there although the first round allows only 3 cards at a time and each round unlocking an additional slot (so round one is 3, then 4 then 5). Beating the score by a wide margin and getting good scores earns you extra skill points so take your time to think about it (no timer). So dont forget to trim your deck from time to time so you dont have the risk of the game pulling out low value cards or cards of all 3 colors at the same time as sometimes the hand you have literally makes the challenge impossible. (But collectibles can help)New cards are earned as you do events and such as the cards represent your "memories", they arent literal cards your character has.Each time you complete one activity the game advances by one month and each year is composed of 13 months with a total of 5 seasons with three months each except for one who lasts only one month. The seasons are important for the birthday of the other kids and what kind of collectibles you can find. (Some events only happen at a certain year at a certain season)As you do activities and some events your character will accumulate stress once it reaches 100 you are forced to do a rest for a month or reduce stress through an event. Kudos is your money you can use to buy stuff later and rebellion represents how rebellious you are towards authority, it mostly is there to affect the endings in a minor way and some event gating.For the other kids your age, each will hang around the "camp" and you can freely interact with them, some decisions and gifts earn you their friendship with each having a unique card associated to them that you will unlock once you reach their first friendship threshold and the following 2 thresholds upgrade the card further through an event. (Characters with a speech bubble above them means they have an event to fire off if you interact with them) The upgrade events are gated behind the three stages of life you and the kids will have (Kid,Teenager, young adult) so dont be surprised if you focused one character but arent immediately getting all the upgrades.This game has a LOT of writing that i honestly recommend you read as not only is the writing very well done but also because you might skip over important information regarding the "quests" of the game. Yes this game has sort of "quests" where an event is affecting the overarching colony and you need to actually read what the other characters say and remember it as there is no "quest log" like other games. Skip at your own peril as the correct actions will give you a little note above the dialogue or the dialogue itself will tell you what to do and when.One last interesting aspect of the game is their incorporation of your previous playthroughs in your new ones. I wont tell you why exactly but your character can somewhat remember things you have done in your past "lives". In terms of gameplay this translates to your character being able to either "skip" a high skill check or doing a job several times at the right moment or even maybe stop an oncoming tragedy (signified by a purple swirly next to the choice). This is how you earn your best possible ending as your first playthrough will have events you simply cannot prevent as your character is unaware of it happening etc. (The game will also keep the birthdays and likes and dislikes of each kid once you discovered it in their profile)At the beginning of year 20 your game ends and depending on what you have done and what jobs you did the most you will get one of 29 possible endings (some occur before year 20), you then get an epilogue of your life and the friends you make along the way.So what are my thoughts on the game as someone who has gone 100% completetion on it? I loved this game whole heartedly,how in gods name i missed this for a year i have no idea. The characters have a "character stereotype" as their base but they become so much more as the game progresses, each one is an interesting person worth exploring (Anemone best girl ill die on this hill). The game has a unique artstyle that reminds me of comic books with the planet and environnement having vibrant and beautiful colors but doesnt shy away from how deadly things can be in the wild. The music is top tier especially the epilogue music being one of the few game songs that makes me feel genuine heartache. (Recommend listening to it fully at least once).The game offers you great freedom in what you do while not stressing you too much about time allowing to think your choices out as long as you like.The story itself might not be the most revolutionnary one out there but its still a very good one thats very well written and supported by a great cast of characters.The replayability of the game is also very high as each path you walk in your playthrough is extra baggage in your next one that can help you solve problems much faster giving you more time to focus on other parts of the story.As an indie game yes there are parts of the game that might feel a little less "cooked" that the rest but to be honest its far from game ruining. This is a beautiful game lovingly crafted by a small indie team that deserve a lot of praise for putting together this amazing game. Yes the price is a bit on the high side but if you enjoy this type of game you can sink a great amount of time into as you explore things it is well worth your money. If its too much then simply wait for a sale but this game has earned itself a place dear in my heart that few other games have.So yes i strongly recommend this game and yes Anemone best girl fight me.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard for me to believe I'm leaving a negative review for a game that's so beloved by everyone, so maybe it's just me, but in the end I gave up on the story toward the very end of my first play through of "I was a Teenage Exocolonist".The main issue was that as much as the choices you make are supposed to determine your experience, I was constantly left with the feeling that my choices didn't matter at all. Some examples:-It's clear a loved one is dying of exposure to the environment? Doesn't matter if I spent loads of time with them and constantly yelled at them to stay inside: since I didn't specialize in biology and found a cure, their death seems to have been inevitable.-There's a character I really wanted to romance? I couldn't just come out and say I was into them, I had to grind their favor over the years AND carry out a whole sequence of actions in a precise order and literally fight a rival for them because I couldn't just come out and start dating them earlier so they got engaged with someone else (I literally had to look up a guide for how to do all this and it was ridiculously complex).-Wanted to get to know a wide variety of characters? Most of the characters' real development is blocked behind a grind of tasks, and you're limited to how much time you have at your disposal so I couldn't develop various relationships in parallel with different characters and most stayed as casual acquaintances which isn't at all interesting.-Similarly, the whole experience of character development was almost purely stressful, in that I always felt like I wasn't using my time well. If you want to be even slightly rounded out as a character you will fall short in the most important challenges and tests. In other words, if you're not completely dedicated to, say, combat skill or intelligence, you'll fail the really critical related challenge that is necessary to make a real difference to the story in the late game. But, like relationship building, you barely have the time to focus on any one thing, so it just feels like you're constantly falling short.The story is interesting (if kind of forced and difficult to really influence as stated above), the art is very pretty and the deck building aspect of the game is well done, at the right level of casual. Overall though, for the reasons mentioned above it was not as enjoyable as I hoped or expected.I'm not a regular player of visual novels, so maybe this was a me problem, but unfortunately I cannot personally recommend this game given my experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing to know about this game is that you  save scum. The game wants you to do it and frankly you are missing out if you don't. There are game mechanics crafted around it, if you play all or most of your play-through 'straight' then you will have to replay the game to experience it. This game is comprised of three parts, visual novel/story choices, deck builder, and time management. All three are handled well here, and intermix. The story is handled really well and your choices definitely matter. One of the pitfalls games often do with "choices matter" is that they allow your actions to open up new paths, but they don't make your choices restrict others. I'm glad to say Exocolonist has the brass to do both. Characters will leave or enter the story due to your choices, not only that but you can only get certain choices depending on how you spend your time. A player that spends a lot of days studying versus one that spends a lot of time in combat training will simply not have the options of the other. You get micro choices in the moment with dialogue and actions, while you also make macro decisions over the years as you craft your character into what you want them to be. The deckbuilder fits right into this as your decisions on how you use your time changes what cards are in your deck, and succeeding or failing a game will have narrative impact. Making game mechanics intermingle so naturally is no easy feat, and its great that this is all on top of an engaging and interactive story. This game is a fair bit better than it has any right to be.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance simple choice-consequence relation sim with a card mini-game sprinkled over. But the more you play it, the more you understand that there is so much more in it. So many complex details, so many complex choices that lead to sometimes catastrophic consequences. One thing though for some people - do understand that this game does really dive deeply into such topic as puberty, growing up in community where people live in total peace with LGBT, veganism, vegetarianism and genetic enhancements. And game makes Main Character, you obviously, take some hard choices sometimes as if to follow or not some of these paths as in choosing being true to your pacifist nature, being vegetarian or even having one or multiple relations with people of your/other or androgynous genders. But worry not, all these choices are yours to take and only yours. There are also endings for both people, who don't want to "hug Nature" and "be one with Nature". Another warning that should probably exist about this game is that you need to be aware of many 18+ themes in it - death of main characters, sexual innuendos, very graphic and detailed descriptions of some gross or horrific processes, animal cruelty/human cruelty and etc. Please, check CONTENT WARNING section before playing.And the art, it is just incredibly beautiful. Have to really say kudos to the designers of levels, characters and aliens. The music is also very good. Yeah, it does get repetitive at some point, but even then you may not notice it while playing as the music is not annoying or pushing on you, it is just a relaxing background.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beutiful. The art style drew me in, the game play and story kept me playing, and not only here, I also bought the game for my Switch to be able to play it on vacation. The replay value is immense and the stories of all the characters are touching and well written... and if something goes wrong and one of them dies, it's a real sting in my heart.I recommend this title to anyone liking visual novel style games, some slight management tasks, and matching up of characters.The 'battles', or rather challenges, are done by an easy to learn card game mechanic that lets you customize your deck over the course of you growing up.If there's something I don't like that much it's that it seems to be each character has a defacto epilogue that doesn't really change much. _childDocuments_.review: I would absolutely, wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of visual novels/Persona-style experiences. The story (which I won't be spoiling here) is deeply immersive and allows you to get invested much more than most games I've ever played. The characters are written so realistically and so well that I legitimately began to feel the same way about them as I do my actual friends.    It also gets bonus points for being inclusive and actually getting representation right. There are multiple non-white characters who are allowed to have personalities beyond being non-white as well as some major characters being LGBT+ who are actual people with flaws and strengths and three dimensionality which are both things I've seen disturbingly little of in media.   The art of this game is absolutely GORGEOUS to look at. The specific moments you can get highlighting the designs of each of the characters as well as the artwork are truly astounding and I could look at this game for days and still be able to find new details in the backgrounds or character designs, which are so full of personality and life that you can get a great sense of who each character is just by looking at them. Honestly, my only issue with the game is that the UI covers the artwork too quickly when you first see them and I wish that it would hold on them a little longer. This is rectified however, by the gallery menu, where you can look at the artworks you've unlocked without a block of blue showing up and covering half of it within five seconds.   The music in this game is phenomenal, it adds just the right amount of wonder and curiosity at the right moments and can make some instances feel truly magical. There was only one song I didn't like in the moment but that just because the audio mixing wasn't done right and it was far too loud for the tender moment it was placed in. The main menu theme is the highlight for me.   I also have to appreciate the fact that this is a "choices matter" game where your choices ACTUALLY MATTER. The things you do and don't do in the game have far-reaching consequences. Big events can    happen or be prevented depending on if you collected x amount of items while outside the colony or if you have enough friendship with one of the other colonists or picked one dialog option over another. If you don't have enough of one stat, you can't help one of your friends with a task and get a better ending.    The game overall juggles a number of ideas which, under different developers, might have fallen apart and crushed them. But Northway Games was able to hold it together in order to create what is, so far, my choice for best game of 2022. Outside of the singular grievance outlined in the section about the art, I genuinely cannot think of any area this game let me down in and as such, I would give this game a 10/10 and I can't wait to see what Northway makes next.   With all that being said, you should absolutely check out the content warnings (another very unique and much appreciated thing this game does) before you play the game, to ensure you can actually enjoy the experience. _childDocuments_.review: A very good role-playing game where you play a child (who grows into a teenager) in a new colony on an alien planet. Lots of characters to meet, skills to specialise in, jobs to do and paths to choose. Text heavy but all the text is well written and the overall story has some twists and turns that keep you engaged. Usually in these sorts of games there's at least 1 bad mechanic but everything here works, the exploration is decent, the card mechanics are good, the dialog choices make sense. More than anything I was compelled to keep playing to the end to try my best to get a happy(ish) ending for my character and her partner. Lots of replay value too (no spoilers!). Feels finished and like a complete video game. If any of that sounds good, buy it!

_childDocuments_.review: Have you enjoyed stories about  a crew of abuse survivors at the bottom of the ocean trying to work at an energy plant or a group of genetically modified astronauts drifting towards some highly intelligent and conscious-less danger which will leave no one intact? Well then, how about growing up  stranded in a small colony on an unfamiliar and unfriendly planet with nowhere to go? Knowing you've been failed in many ways by those, who brought you there, yet trying to squeeze any opportunity to make things  for you and those who've been there together with you. This is a dark, claustrophobic and terrifying story carefully wrapped into a teenage visual novel drama with all the love, fondness and attention to littlest details. And speaking of teenage drama, this game also gets it surprisingly brilliant, making one feel an entire spectrum of human emotion and crying the eyes out of compassion. Whatever you're looking for: either a (somewhat) heartwarming story of growing up on another planet with romance, taming unicorns and stuff, or a grim dystopia that will break your heart, you'll find every aspect executed masterfully and with great care.Another little soothing thing for this old lady's heart is accurate and down to earth autistic representation, that feels real compared to a bioengineered superhero like Siri.Cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is interesting because you can complete a life cycle in about 1 day of game play. The challenge is trying to save everyone you are supposed to save (and want to save) while still ensuring the colony is safe and thriving. There are a lot of different paths you can take, and each one emphasizes the value of a different aspect of life. Do you want to be creative, or tough? Have high reasoning skills or be good with animals? These values aren't always opposed to each other, but you do have to come to terms with the fact that you can't do EVERYTHING (at least not in one lifetime!) And of course, any review would be incomplete if it didn't discuss the fantastic representations of gender, sex, relationships, and family within this game. I saw someone comment that it was a WOKE game and I hope to god that Steam considers making WOKE a tag so that I can easily find more games that show such wide and beautiful acceptance of what it means to be human.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic and engaging card/visual novel combination. The basic gameplay loop is to create a deck of "memory" cards. Remove older, less potent, memories, and seek newer, more effective, ones. With dating-sim/relationship aspects and time management it *feels* like a Persona game with different gameplay loop elements. If you like chill deck-builders, puzzle games, Persona-type visual novels, dating sims with puzzle elements, or just interesting stories, go for it!Edit: I am modifying this review to respond to the number of negative reviews complaining about the "Depressing" ending and first year. I would like to respond to that: Yeah, *chances are* you won't do the right things and get a depressing ending your first time  (I started a new game on my Switch - yes, I own this on two systems - and accidentally got almost a perfect playthrough  just by switching up my playstyle ). That's on purpose: That's the second act setback. The entire point of the game is to SPUR YOU ON because your first playthrough will probably be very depressing - if not, then just accept the ending and move on.That's just part of storytelling: The point of this game is experiencing  Just make your choices and move on. Choice paralysis doesn't have to be a thing because there is always another playthrough .

_childDocuments_.review: With how excited I was after playing the demo, I'm happy to say that Exocolonist has lived up to and exceeded my every expectation and then some. The writing is stellar, the art is beautiful, the music (and silence!) are brilliant, the characters are complex, the story is compelling, the challenges are satisfying, and it's all so incredibly well paced.So many games have systems that fight with themselves, but it's a rare game indeed where every element is seamlessly interwoven into every other. Exocolonist pulls off this feat beautifully. Your every choice and action, how you plan ahead and spend your time, affects your relationships and skill progression and accumulated memories, which themselves help you overcome challenges and lead the story in different directions and open up an incredibly varied array of events.Your memories are a central theme too, with your character's experiences embodied as the very cards you use to overcome challenges, but also echoing across lifetimes. Just as you and your real-life human memories as a player lead you to want to try different things in another playthrough, your memories within the game from other lifetimes also provide new choices it would never have occurred to you to make through prophetic dreams, letting you take different actions without having spoiled them for you the first time through.And even the fact of your character having these dreams is woven into the story so well, from how your character feels about them to how others react to your actions. In other words, far from just an incentive to play again, the game feels like a whole meta-experience that spans multiple lifetimes. I've seen games try to pull off this kind of depth with parallel worlds or time travel shenanigans, but never have I seen a game succeed at it so spectacularly well! I love it.All the systems feel smoothly integrated like this. The in-game currency of Kudos reflects your standing with the other characters and the community, but also allows you to nanoprint gear which helps with challenges, or gifts to give to friends, or to change your deck in subtle ways. The card game looks simplistic in screenshots but feels so satisfying to play and never seems to become dull - even on easier challenges, there's always a motivation to try your best, whether it's to earn a bonus skill point or just an extra kudos for getting the best hand you can with what you were dealt. If it's too easy, you can set it to be harder, and if it's too hard, you can push through at the cost of stressing yourself out. And how you feel day to day, whether it's heroic or popular or depressed or stressed out all affects how effective you are at different things, which feeds back into the planning.Your level of stress limits how hard you can work and how much you can explore, encouraging you to take breaks which keeps the pacing nice and smooth. But the in-game breaks are themselves a pleasure. They don't just relieve stress, they result in all manner of interactions with other characters, bonding with your pets, unexpectedly learning new things and gaining skills, not to mention leaving you feeling amazing afterwards which makes you even more effective when you get back to it. And all this is tied back into the story and relationships too. The only regret is that you can't literally learn everything and spend time with everyone (at least within one lifetime!).And unlike many games with a diverse and varied cast like this, the characters all seem to have a lot of depth, especially as you all start to get older. I was certainly more attracted to 2 or 3 of them, but even those I was annoyed with initially grew on me, or I wanted to get to know them because of another character's interactions with them, or to nudge them into being a better person, or just to see what their deal is. So many games are filled with stereotypes or tropes or simplistic morality, but Exocolonist really takes it deep and gradually seeing more and more of this nuanced complexity really makes learning about the world and the characters a wonderful experience.The satisfaction of exploring really sparked my imagination too. In the demo, the area outside the colony that you can explore is certainly enjoyable but somewhat modest in size, but the moment I made it to a wider region I was amazed at how expansive it was and at all the different wildlife and encounters I came across. Not only was the scenery gorgeous and the music really enchanting, but it left me filled with curiosity each time I came across something. (And even here the things you find tie back into the other systems when you get back to the colony!) I'm barely into the first larger area and already the bestiary is many fold longer, and I even got to name a new species myself! It really feels like exploring an original new world with its own unique and complex and varied ecosystem.I'm truly enjoying this game and feel so eager to share it with others and to play more over the coming weeks and months. If you're at all on the fence about it, I highly recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: French existentialist Simone de Beauvoir argues in her 1947 book  that  that the personality and the core beliefs of each human individual is defined through their environment and their actions, and that the challenges that allow those personality-shaping events are the ones that truly test the scope of the limits between their limitations and potential, their past against their future, the comfort of familiarity against the fear of the unknown."I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" is a quiet meditation on this and other questions asked by de Beauvoir and her fellow existentialists, packaged stealthily in the wrappings of a Solarpunk-themed dating game.  Beneath the cotton candy colored environment of Vertumna and the egregiously tumblr-era character designs lies , one that manages to succeed at the challenge of remaining both replayable and emotionally impactful.  IWATE introduces the concepts of string theory, mortality, identity, collectivism, and on and on and on as each character you meet lives, grows, dies, lives again, and becomes a different person entirely.When asked about the passing of her lover, the famed philosopher Jean Paul Sartre, de Beauvoir simply said   Vertumna asks you to spend ten years with it before it lets you go, and readily welcomes you back again for the next loop of a cycle that continues on into infinity.  But each of those cycles of ten years creates a unique you, and the life you live with its people is truly splendid.ps: rex is best boy, even with the dumb tattoo, fight me.

_childDocuments_.review: even if you don't like visual novels, i highly recommend you give this one a chance. its a fantastic game with wonderful engaging writing, genuinely likeable characters that are drastically more than just their 'cliche' or 'genre' (ex: the adventurous tomboyish girl, the quiet emo boy, etc etc etc) and who act real and feel like genuine people with many layers, even the side characters. the story itself is incredibly engaging and something that keeps you coming back, and the card mechanic will if the story winds up not. the entire game feels real while also fiction, exploring characters and giving dynamic options with enough mechanics but wiggle room and options to make it much more engaging than just a visual novel, and the story and characters making it much more fun than the sum of its parts with the card mechanic and stat building. everyone is so likeable, even the ones that are on the meaner or more annoying end. less in the way you can't despise them, but more in the way they're so well written they mesh really well with the world and you understand why they do the things they do. the soundtrack is also a hit which is VERY good since i was a little worried that it would be grating after playing so long since its definitely a more long-term game (15+ hours i'd wager) but it genuinely doesn't get old as long as your in the game. its also very inclusive and diverse, regarding both lgbtq+ options (changing pronouns, changing gender presentation, etc) AND just people themselves! people of color (with skintone range! and hairstyles! its not just a desaturated pale brown with straight hair for everyone!), plus sized, people with tattoos, people with different body types who actually look like their body-types (ex: fat characters actually look fat instead of just being bigger, athletic characters look athletic without looking like a bodybuilder, etc etc etc), people with piercings, people with scars (and not the anime styled ones implying they're a villain!), people with facial hair or body-hair, etc etc etc, INCLUDING DISABLED FOLKS!! both for accessibility AND representation! the main character's mother uses a mobility aide!!!!!!! GENUINELY, from the bottom of my heart, if you have the money, i highly recommend it!! even if you watch a playthrough for it and Then decide (since things vary WILDLY playthrough to playthrough) its worth the money! and if you don't like it, you can refund it, and move along. its worth at least a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: Over the years I've played plenty of narrative games where choices matter, but few have made me feel as many things as this one did. Simply hearing the music makes me tear up a little, remembering the sheer emotions this game evokes. My first play through ended horrifically. I cried  throughout. But I was also very aware I had messed up somewhere. Rather than putting the game down, I immediately jumped into a second playthrough to fix my mistakes. Turns out I had missed a massive chunk of lore the first time round due to bad decisions. It was a pleasant surprise to find more new things each time. In all it took three playthroughs before I was really happy with the ending and four completed routes before I felt like I had properly gotten to know the world and the characters in it. But I'm still not quite finished. There's a lot of replay value in this game, and really it's designed to be played more than once to get the full experience. Replaying isn't difficult as the writing and story make you want to find out more. The characters are memorable, and as much as I may have wanted to fix everyone's problems, ultimately the game treats these characters as independent people. I'm glad the game didn't let me fix every problem at once, because it made the characters and world feel much more real and that my decision to help or not did actually matter. But you also aren't a white knight destined to save everyone.The card game is fun with difficulty levels to suit each player, but it can also be turned off if it's getting too repetitive. The art and progression of characters as they age is also beautifully done. Overall I really do feel like this game hits all the right boxes for players who are interested in a game with good lore, nice mechanics, and a little bit of strategy. I've recommended it to just about all my friends who play narrative driven games. It's not hard to see why when I'm about to start a fifth playthrough, a few months later now that I'm starting to forget some details, to try and fix one more problem I missed before. 10/10 Buy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: About ten or so years ago, there was a dearth of stat-based, build-your-own adventure RPGs to supplement visual novel style play. A spiritual evolution of them, this game is probably the most aesthetically pleasing, varied, and rewarding of them, though it does keep a good amount of occasionally frustrating progress road blocks that can wreck a playthrough (If you wannabe a certain character's lover, you gotta' make like the Spice Girls and get with their friend). You play a child who grows up on an alien planet with a colony of humans trying to survive, and choosing to live how you see fit. While the character has one unified art style and only changes later in life, you can present and be called by binary and non-binary options (And if you want to be as anatomically impaired as a Ken Doll, go for it!). Your can give your path whatever head start you would like (Though super strength helps the other categories more than you'd think. A variety of other fields and paths require a minimum of physical abilities, and giving a double to stat boosts in that category minimizes the effort required to meet those standards). Your progress involves building stats and gathering cards from various life experiences . I'm not normally a card system person because random draws will punch you in the gut every chance it can, but it's poker style, which allows a lot of flexibility and ability to punch above your weight in meeting certain scores.To put this upfront, you will not be able to do everything you want the first playthrough. It is designed to be played multiple times, and the first time can be a melancholy experience. Every time you reach certain breakthroughs, you can far more easily access them on the next round and focus on something else. Or you can make people think you're crazy. The story is flexible, and learning new parts can even change it, depending on what you do with it. Like the older games, there can be hard roadblocks that require guides or ignoring most other things to get through them, but the game mostly gives you reasonable hints on what to do and where to go, and many times, the way through is trying something you haven't tried before.While its ilk leaned more heavily on the VN experience, this has a more varied experience. You can freely wander the colony, and eventually, explore the alien world if you so choose. The presentation is more of an illustrated storybook, and everything looks and moves very nicely. The game is accompanied by a pulsing and appropriately electric score. If I do have one quibble, there are certain cutscenes that would be nice to skip on session after the first run. The characters hit that sweet spot of sharing certain universal qualities that you can connect their types, but are individual enough to stand on their own. They are of various walks of life, sexualities, and attitudes, and exploring their complexities is fun, and helps inform the story. While some guides indicated that the fate of characters you have a relationship with will stay 99% the same on various endings, I have found much more variety depending on how everything else shakes out. Some characters are more flexible than others, however.Overall, it's an extremely successful game that's kind of a roguelite interactive novel. I'm not normally a fan of going through the same experience over and over, but I've gone through five full runs, and I'm trying to hammer out time for another, so......... I'd call that pretty good.

_childDocuments_.review: This has become one of my favourite games and I really recommend it. There is a lot of depth to the story, how you handle your relationships with others on the colony, the environment and politics. Even with the simple skills, cards and gifts system, how you choose to spend your time dramatically shapes the world around you. I also like the option of being able to read through my choices and get into the story or if I've seen it before or just want to chill was some music, I can scroll through the dialogue quickly and just concentrate on collecting and the card game. This game handles sex and gender so well, the non-binary options are so fluid and the ability to romance whoever is amazing.My only criticisms would be, making it easier to skip dialogue outside of clicking though each statement and more of a variation in gifts you can buy outside of cake, I can't imagine my friends appreciating my giving them random sticks and eggs I find on the ground, year after year. However, my biggest issue with the game is race. The two most sexualized characters, who have the most revealing clothing in the game are the darker skinned ones. Rex, is super openly sexual and also animalized like a dog, and Marz is at the start of the game is a materialistic, self-absorbed, overweight bully at the start of the game and by the end keeps most of her negative characteristics, but has this glow up where she just has the most revealing outfits. It wouldn't be that bad if other characters had this treatment, the only other character that reads as Black is Rhett the head of security, and he plays into a more positive trope, but at some point his physique despite his age is brought up. There's also Tangent and Dys, Asian coded twins, Tangent being into STEM and Dys being a socially awkward loner. It's just more racial tropes the game seems to gave fallen into despite handling gender and sexuality so beautifully.I still love this game and play it all the time and would highly recommend it to others. However, Marz's portrayal did give me really terrible callbacks to how people perceived me when I was a kid, and plays on my concerns on how people might see me as an adult. I bring this up, so others know what to expect when getting into this game, and that developers can be aware of how these subtle stereotypes can be repeated even with well intended storytelling.
