_childDocuments_.review: I'll probably edit this review once I dive deeper into the game on subsequent playthroughs as that seems to be a major component of the experience, but I just had to make a review after my first playthrough. I finished this game about 3 days ago and can't get it out of my mind. I found this game by chance in 2022 during a Steam promotion for indie games while looking for a visual novel with romance/dating sim elements and ended up playing the demo. I'm forever grateful I stumbled on this game on that day. The characters and worldbuilding are just very well handled. Very few games actually take a serious approach to tackling a subject like someone growing up and experiencing adolescence over the course of years while also exploring their relationships with others and their environment. Actually writing compelling stories with the various potential friends/love interests is just astonishing to me. The handling of this kind of cast while also clearly establishing the passage of time and how their environment impacts them is just top-notch. You can tell the writers had tons of fun writing about all the various lore, fauna, etc. because they truly gave this entire world so much life. Even some background characters with minimal screen time became memorable parts of the experience and still stick with me. I have to applaud the devs for also being willing to tackle various tough topics both on large and smaller scales from stuff like different aspects of politics to things like domestic abuse. I can understand some being mixed on certain handlings of these things, but I appreciate there was a serious attempt to tackle these topics or issues with complete sincerity. I also have to appreciate the deck-building aspect which is one of the primary gameplay focuses outside the general visual novel/adventure game-esque segments. The deck-building I just adore because it's truly a case of being somewhat easy to learn, but hard to master and depending on how you play and choices you make, this can be either pretty good or bad. I also loved that the cards in the deck are based on memories from the main character's experiences. It was a great way of tying into core themes of the game itself while also talking about a broader subject regarding how experiences can help us overcome certain obstacles, but also letting go of certain memories can open opportunities for greater ones. Very few games make me emotional, but when I completed my first playthrough, I got very emotional. This game just presents itself so well that I couldn't help but seriously care about the characters and seeing how my choices impacted their lives really felt meaningful. Even 72+ hours after beating the game, I can't wait to dive back in and explore more aspects of these characters and this world I missed the first time while also learning from my first playthrough, just like the main character. This game truly feels one-of-a-kind as very few if any games have the same core components and execute it this well. This is one of the few cases where I would be completely open to the devs taking the core systems of this game and using them to make another game while maybe putting a twist on or re-contextualizing certain gameplay elements in a different kind of setting. This developer has earned my respect and adoration for the rest of my life.Small note: The soundtrack selection is stellar. "The Child You Were" by Frances Aravel is by far my favorite and a clear standout track. Such a great song choice for this game. Tying in the themes of that song into this game gives it a somber brilliance which really helped give the finality of a playthrough some emotional weight.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was entertaining and alienating at the same time/space. You start playing as a 10-year old survivor of a colonial space-ship crash.  You get knocked out before the ship crashes, so while you're knocked out for several days, the adult castaways set up the essentials of your "exocolony" community. You play in cycles of months within seasons within 13-month years and success/fail progress is determined by a random card game, though you can disable that and opt out of a hard mode. Part of the gameplay premise is to reincarnate at the beginning of the game after a playthrough, perhaps changing strategy with the benefit of dream-like memory scraps from previous lives. This  part of the game's design plus the beautiful graphics is what intrigued me at first, but after my first play-through I don't feel like playing it again. I thought it would be science fiction but it's more of a fantasy game set it outer space. The colony is run by technocrats and there isn't any voting age achievement because there's no voting, your politics are limited to trying to influence the technocrats by one conversation each. You have 2 biological parents which seem not to be necessarily the norm, and they tell you at age 10 you should go figure things out by yourself so if you want, school's out FOREVER. There are visual-novel type conversations possible but sometimes your friends just keep saying the same thing over and over again so I started skipping them, likewise doing harvest-moon type gifts seemed to make no difference. There are some monsters and like a fantasy game they live outside the walls and invade once a year except your card game might beat them. The colonists deal with food shortages but everything else seems to be provided by uber-nanoprinting.  Children have the futuristic equivalent of a cell phone grafted into their palm at age 3 (they don't glow red at age 30 though) and that's the closest the game comes to having any religion. There is vague history about an ecological catastrophe on their motherplanet but other than one Star Trek pun about doctors there is no sense of history, or how the space ship was provided. Perhaps some guy built it in his barn on Krypton. During my first play-through, I managed to install the woman that does my nails as a new government, it was like having Gilligan's Island run by Ginger instead of the Professor. Everybody looked marvelous.

_childDocuments_.review: A remarkably rich setting and cast of characters make this game stand out among the crowded space of visual novels. It also has a truly  array of possible endings; I think it's based on which skills you get or which activities you do most often? (So far I got "Novelist" and "Athlete".)The unique card mechanics feel strange at first, and perhaps even too simple; but as the game progresses, their subtle strategy becomes clearer. Accomplishing important tasks, especially  often gives you very powerful cards that tilt the rest of the game. The  provide an interesting way to make the game more replayable while enriching the story. The way that you can accumulate information across playthroughs, but otherwise have to start over from scratch, gives it a bit of a roguelite feel. With the skill-building system, there is a subtle dance between trying to stay well-rounded and specializing in what you're good at that I still haven't mastered after two full playthroughs (though I definitely did better the second time than the first). Hint: Staying well-rounded early on will keep your options open, but you definitely want to max out at least one skill by the end. It isn't flawless, though. The difficulty is inconsistent; some tasks seem trivially easy and others virtually impossible. (The ability to adjust the difficulty helps with this, but also feels a bit like cheating.) Despite the large, rich cast of characters, you can't really do much with most of them on any given run, because you can't greatly improve their opinions of you without giving them gifts that are often quite scarce. The political messages of the game are also a bit heavy-handed (I screenshotted one of the worst examples).But the game's greatest flaw is its opacity: the options available to you are often limited in ways you aren't even told about. On my first playthrough, I missed a lot of the most useful skill-building activities because I simply didn't know they were an option; you have to unlock them through conversations and other activities. And I finished my second playthrough still not understanding how to increase the "security rating" of the colony. Still, despite its rough edges, "I Was A Teenage Exocolonist" provides a deep, immersive, and replayable experience in a rich, vibrant sci-fi world. If you have any proclivity for science fiction visual novels, you'll probably like it.

_childDocuments_.review: "I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" is an entry in the somewhat niche genre of LifeSim games set on a distant alien world.For those unfamiliar, a LifeSim game is one in which you control a character over a period of their life (often during adolescence to young adulthood). Time passes in chunks (sometimes fixed, sometimes variable) during which you choose how the character spends their time or reacts to certain events. These choices feed back into your character in the form of stats and branching narratives that enable or disable future choices. At the end, the culmination of choices usually results in an epilogue that reflects what kind of choices you made during the time you controlled the character and how they play out years or even decades into the future. The genre encourages replayability because you can't take every choice at every branch and some choices ripple through years of a character's life, so trivial attempts to save/reload doesn't let you see everything.LifeSims are somewhat of a novelty as games because they struggle to find legs on their own. You might see them as a secondary mechanic in another game (like in the Persona series), but there are some entries that stand just on the appeal of the branching paths (Long Live the Queen). Usually a "pure" LifeSim game has simple pass/fail checks on narrative branches to lock out choices you don't have the skills for."I Was a Teenage Exocolonist" daringly attempts to lead with the LifeSim mechanic as the main hook, supplementing it a deckbuilding mechanic where most challenges see you drawing a hand of cards and attempting to assemble the highest scoring combination of 5 cards from the ones drawn. From an initial deck of cards, new memories are added when you build relationships with characters, overcome obstacles, or face adversity, tying your success in the challenges back to what you have done throughout the story. Score is calculated based on the face value of the card (usually 1-8 but some even higher), plus combo points for sets of matching colors, numbers, or sequences. Many cards also have additional effects that modify either themself or other cards. Didn't get quite the hand you needed? Collectibles can be spent to change the cards or just draw more in hopes of a better outcome. Taken in a whole, the challenge resolution mechanic is a surprisingly robust and engaging system and tying it to the narrative element helps the two create a feedback loop.Once you complete your play through of the game (probably 15 hours for your first one), you have a chance to start over, knowing more about how the game works and ready to try something different. But not only do you know more, your character also remembers some things from the other life. They are haunted by memories of alternate futures, and having been there you now open up chances to alter the story further by acting on information that wasn't available the first time you encountered a situation. Can you find a path through the keeps everyone alive and happy? Is that even the best outcome? Join us on Vertumna and find out.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally prone to hyperbole, but I Was a Teenage Exocolonist genuinely is a modern classic. The quality of the writing, the complexity of the characters, the emotional investment, and the amazing replayability make this game stand out.Currently Exocolonist has nowhere near the profile or credit it deserves, and I would encourage anyone on the fence about whether this is likely to be their thing to give it a go. Please.Exocolonist is very much its own game, however it straddles a space somewhere between visual novel (VN), RPG and princess builders (such as Long Live the Queen and Volcano Princess).The risk of dropping a term like “visual novel” about a game such as this is that it risks creating the impression of click and read. I hate click and read, and most VNs leave me cold. I therefore use the term advisedly because it’s not like that at all. What the game is, instead, is heavily story driven with more reading than most people are likely used to.In Exocolonist you play as the main protagonist arriving on a new colony world. Your primary interactions are with other colony ship children who age together with you across seasons and years until you are 20 years old, at which point the game ends.Gameplay involves walking around different, smallish, maps interacting with other characters, building up skills and relationships, and revealing factoids about the other children, the new world you have colonised, and ultimately the adult world going on around you and their politics.Most events and interactions trigger stat increases across 12 broad categories. What areas you focus on can dramatically alter the events that you trigger and the skill checks you are able to pass across your journey.All main characters are potentially romanceable, although mostly in a pragmatic way – which is to say, most romance chains stay effectively platonic and the characters you romance maintain their own autonomy and quirks. The relationship outro also inevitably peters off into melancholy – for example distant characters stay distant, they drift away emotionally or get absorbed in their work, etc. Kind of like real life.Or you can completely skip all romance chains and focus on saving your colony from collapse, or investigating this strange new planet you have found yourself living on, or on a career, or (eventually) playing politics with the adults.It’s all very adult, and realistic, and emotionally impactful, but may feel a touch unsatisfying if your main goal in computer gaming is pure escapism.Other than walking around maps, training up stats, triggering events, and interacting with other characters the other main element of gamification here is the card system.As you experience the world you are rewarded with cards as a proxy for life’s experiences – such as [played] “Hide and Seek with Nougat”, “Harvesting Mushwood” and [learned] “Dys's Secret”. The cards have one of three different colors, corresponding to broad stat building themes, and a number. Later events as you age inevitably reward cards with higher values. To pass a skill check you need to arrange your cards into straights and runs.The card system was more than complex enough for me as it gives a wonderful sense of agency, without being overly onerous or punishing. The tests are inevitably a reasonably straightforward exercise in pair matching and light mental arithmetic.Finally, I absolutely despise replaying most games - one run though of a game is inevitably enough. Except in this case, where I have completed three full runs and started a fourth. (A full run takes around 7 hours.)Exocolonist has a wonderful ability to encourage replayability. In part, this is because it is so content-dense that it is literally impossible to experience more than a fraction of what the game has to offer on a single playthough. The game also, very smartly, acknowledges the conceit with references to past (and future) lives and an end of game admonishment to “do better next time”.There is, indeed, a lot of incentive to do better next time, in part because bad things happen in the game to nice people, and across multiple replays you can find ways to save them and to improve the colony's chances of success.Taking certain routes through the story can also unlock additional story lines and options in future playthroughs.If you haven’t worked this out already, I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Can be a tad grindy, as often management games like these are, but well worth your time. From the ability to create a character of many combinations of sex and gender, the choices with actual stakes in the story's progression, and an interesting take on the evolution of human culture and interaction, the game creates a story that is your own. It would be nice to customize your race but given the art requirements as characters are drawn sprites and not textured 3d models, I can understand why you have a fixed character.The card battling mini-game adds some variety to break up the story and conversations with NPCs but performing them over and over again starts getting a little long in the tooth, especially in the exploration portions outside the settlement. It would also be nice to be able to purchase the little items you can scavenge to use as gifts for the colonists as if you don't have enough bravery to go out exploring you're rather limited in obtaining them. It is also difficult to get rid of low end cards, so late game when you need to hit 100+ points in a challenge you'll still see 0 and 1 point cards in your draw.Part of the game is obviously trial and error as there is a New Game+ option. I'm looking forward to seeing a new story but at the same time I'm not excited about doing all the card battles again. There's an option to have it autoplay but challenges are resolved with a modified coin flip in that mode while I can play the battles to a win nearly every time. The story, art, both character and card, and creativity on display are all great. If you're a fan of management games, trainer games, or visual novels, you'll probably dig it. It's got the trappings of a cozy life sim but there are some really traumatic events so make sure to read the content warnings as while there's no visible gore, your choices will impact people in your colony in emotionally rough ways. I'm not ashamed to admit that I was rather upset several times during my first play through ( in a good way ). Music is mostly good, with some of the tracks feeling rather nice but a few I found to be a bit out of place. Thankfully there's a way to skip tracks you don't like.The card mini-game CAN get a little tedious but it's not a deal breaker by any stretch. Dunno if it'll scratch the itch for a hardcore deck building game fan but definitely would sate a casual's lust for card battles.Buy the game, give the dev some money. They earned it. You can tell the game is a labor of love. I'd love to see another installment and catch up with the descendants of my little colony.PS - Doggo himbo is the best boi. Give him all the hugs.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, and if you got to the point of reading reviews for it, you should probably play it. The graphic style is beautiful, the sci-fi is hard, and there is lots of replayability. The core card mechanic is okay, but once you get the hang of it, it gets trivial (at least on Normal). I played through the Exocolonist two times, one blind and one with a guide, and I enjoyed both playthroughs.There is one caveat that some of you might need to be aware of. The target audience of this game is clearly US, young, and at least somewhat woke.The characters and narrative are largely built around gender, professional and personal identity. History of the world has overpopulation and climate crises as its central issues. You might be a conservative person from another part of the world, as I am, and find some of the game naive or too in-the-face (fitting, really, for a game called 'I Was a Teenage Exocolonist'). Still, the game isn't propaganda, it's speculative sci-fi written from a particular worldview. If you can suspend your disbelief a bit, there is much fun to be had here for the price.

_childDocuments_.review: It's...okay. This is one of those times I wish Steam had a 'neutral' review option, because ultimately I'm conflicted on the game.There's a lot of effort put into the art style and general depiction of an alien planet, most of which land excellently. The core gameplay is decent as an idea, but ultimately ends up being tedious especially given the game wants you to replay it multiple times. And a major part of the problem is that it doesn't really engage very well with the whole groundhog day loop situation. There are some parts where you have influence over what's going to happen next, but it feels a bit too restrained. For a game that wants you to believe your choices matter and what you know from loop to loop matters, it ends up falling flat compared to other time travel or time loop fiction.It's a game with a lot of charm, a great art style and then a bunch of good ideas. But a lot of the good ideas end up badly executed and pull down the game as a whole. If they had focused around three or four core conceits and then really refined those to a sheen, I think the game would've been a classic. As is, my current opinion of the game falls on the side of 'A bit disappointing'. That said, I'll be keeping a lookout for their next game, whenever that might be.

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. There is a good variety of characters and types of romances. I found my favorite romances to be very endearing and spicy at times. I have played it through multiple times, note that itself is also a game mechanic and you remember your past lives, and I have enjoyed them all. The core of the game is managing your relationships with your fellow exocolonists as well as choosing some skills you would like to focus on learning and maxing out. Then there is also dealing with the struggles of the planet itself and the alien races there. It's a story driven, dating sim, and management type of game. As you gain skills, encounter events, and evolve your relationships you will get more and more cards. Some folks here don't seem to like this system. I enjoyed it alot but after around 3 playthroughs it can get tedious, however you can simply turn the card system off in favor of a coin flip system. _childDocuments_.review: So my playtime in this game should speak for itself, really, but if you want more details, read on!I'm not sure what I was expecting with this game, but what I got was part visual novel, part card puzzle, and a whole lot of fun. You play through your characters life from age ten to age twenty, in a colony on an alien planet. You choose which skills you want to invest in, and the activities you want to do, and these will open up the many different careers you can have and the multiple endings. If you want to get everything I highly recommend looking up a guide as some can be tricky and others you just kind of fall into which was pretty fun. The characters really sell this game, every one is fleshed out and feels real, you fall in love with them and watch them grow up and go through so many different life events.  You can romance any of the kids/teenagers with a few secret ones stashed in there if you look. My favourites are probably Cal, Rex, and Vace. But my besties are always Marz and Tammy, and if you play it you'll soon see why. The world and the idea behind the colony is really cool and very well done. You're viewing this all as a kid at first, but as you get older you get more say and eventually you can decided the fate of the colony and how you want things to shape up. You definitely get a lot of choice here, and it really helps sell this. The card games aren't tricky, you're just adding cards together to get to a number, and all the cards are memories you have experienced. The artwork is on another level - it's just so beautifully drawn and it really feels like a real world with the effort they've put into absolutely everything. There's a gallery so you can collect images and endings and look at them whenever you want and see the beautiful artwork again and again. Nothing ever feels samey it always feels interesting and different each time you play. And the soundtrack is phenomenal - just the perfect music for anything you could be doing. I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of dating sims, choose your own adventure novels, or even a sci-fi fan, it really does have something for anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, will ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ *destroy* you.Words cannot even begin to describe the pure emotional rollercoaster that is this game. I honestly cannot even stress that you *need* to buy this game. I haven't even beaten my *first* playthrough yet because this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me up so bad.This game is about growing up. Outside of your first class that you have to take, your parents tell you that at 10 years old, your life is in your hands. School is technically optional, but as long as you _contribute_ to the colony in some capacity, they will support you. This game takes place over 10 years, which is then broken into 13 months. Each time you do an "Activity" you effectively spend the month doing that and hanging with friends.And Time is both your greatest asset and weakness. As a year can disappear in the literal blink of eye, and the world will move on without you.This game is a CRPG, but its also a "dating" sim, and your choices matter. Who you end up spending time with will determine how your character develops in the game. I decided I wanted to play as a shy kid/teen, and largely neglected the needs of the colony. In doing so, I ended up getting certain character's killed because I didn't care or pay attention to what my people needed.And when you find out that your actions got someone killed...This game doesn't gut punch you. It _uppercuts you_ into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ *Stratsophere* and rips your heart out. And because of this, I ended up being truly alone by my 17th birthday, and was legitimately feeling sick to my stomach over the choices I made to the point where I said to myself "I *need* to fix this." And this game makes you *care* about each and every one of the characters either consciously, or subconsciously.This brings me to the next part of this "Game" where your character has Object Permanence. Basically, your character retains knowledge of previous saved game states. These come in the forms of "Dreams" or "Nightmares." Which acts as a "reset" button functionally. This means that *some* of the deaths in this game *Could* be avoided. Or prevented entirely. And lemme tell you when you *Save* someone that you previously got killed, you will be sobbing tears of joy. Literally. When I saved certain characters I balled just as hard as I did when I saw them expire.And that brings us to, well *You.* It's *Your* life after all. For starters, this game offers you the choice of being whoever you want to be. You can pick which gender you want your character to be, or rather their appearance, between Male, Female, or Non-binary. You can also customize your character's pronouns. Whether you want He/Him, She/Her, or They/Them. And there is a *lot* of variety available. Basically for custom pronouns the game gives you every instance in which your pronouns will/could become relevant, and you may type in what you want the respective reply to be. I personally chose She/They as my character's pronouns just to see, and while *subsequent* playthroughs can make this a bit tedious, considering your choosing every instance in which you can be referred to, its not really *that* big of an issue.On top of that, the game has fairly good reprisentation all across the board. You have men, women, Non-binary, and trans characters that exist in the game, and every single character has their own pronouns that they are referrerd to as. This makes it easier because most of these characters *do* look rather androgynous, but in an attractive, and good way. Which, frankly speaking, had my bisexual panic going off all the time. Speaking of which, you can also engage in any relationship (once your 16/17), of any kind. You can be polyamorous, monogamous, or have open relationships with certain characters.All this to say, this game *will* make you cry. It can get...very dark at times, and though it might be a "T" rated game, it is one of the few that really pushes the envelope to a borderline M from such a cute, charming, innocent looking title. So, while it might be tempting to name your character "Trickydick69" with "Zoogle/Zayhos" pronouns, it does require a certain degree of seriousness. But you do you.If your a dollar/hr kind of gamer, then buy this game. Your average playthrough will be close to 20 hours by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to admit, I picked this game up originally kind of on a whim. I needed something new to stream, and I thought, well the artwork looks cool if nothing else.And now... Well maybe two, first if you like story driven games, you like the feel of the design, and you can handle potentially difficult content, pick this game up. I appreciated the content warnings on the title screen, which manage to be both a warning, without spoiling anything, so definitely take a look, to keep yourself safe when playing. Give yourself that first time experience, make those mistakes, suffer the consequences, and learn from them for next time. This isn't a game you "win", or play perfectly. _childDocuments_.review: I was a Teenage Exocolonist is a pretty decent narrative RPG with card-based battles. The game starts you out as a little kid born on a colony ship that has you eventually end up in a wormhole and crash on a nearby planet. It is then up to you to determine the choices that this planet & colony will navigate over the next 10 years of your life, ultimately ending at your 20th birthday. This game has 29 endings based on who you interact with over the course of the game such as who you level up with to become best friends or who you fall in love with. It also has choices that determine the end of the game based on what skills you specialize in whether it's medical, combat, engineering or others.My first play through of this game I ended up making a guy character and I heavily invested into the engineering skill eventually becoming a master in robotics & created a robot companion that follows me around. I then eventually got into a solid friendship with the loner Dys and eventually started dating his Sister Tanget. Which had me working together with her in later years. She eventually got so skilled in engineering that she developed a chemical bomb and one of the leaders of the colony convinced her to use it outside, which started a long term plague and killed all wildlife resetting the planet's ecosystem. However on my second playthrough, I made a female character & I ended up focusing entirely on combat & didn't focus on education at all. I even chose every rebellious option and when it came to the card battling system, I preferred to battle every monster that would attack the colony. In which I was able to prevent a bunch of characters deaths by being strong enough to defend against the monster attacks. I eventually befriended another athlete called Nem and we heavily played sportsball together in the colony when we were not fighting monsters. In which when I got to my 20th birthday, I ended up ending the game as a professional sportsball player and later a super supportive friend for Nem, who was going through domestic abuse. In which I become her guardian.With that being said, If your looking for a narrative heavy RPG about growing up as a kid or teenager while navigating relationships within a colony on a new planet, then this is your game. There's a lot replayability here within the game for multiple playthroughs. The game also allows you to be able to romance anyone and allows you to represent your sexuality in anyway you desire, which is great because it really allows you to have a more personable experience.In terms of the card battling system, the way that it's presented it's simple to understand and also simple to learn and even twink if you want it to be a harder difficulty. The way it works in terms of moving the story forward or simply introducing a new event or a choice makes sense when it comes to the battle system. The music for the game is also top notch and very enjoyable. Overall, I give the game a solid 7.5/10. I appreciate the narrative the developer is trying to tell within this game and I enjoy the relationship building and choices that are presented here.My only con with this game is I don't think this game is worth the full price of $25 unless your extremely into narrative RPG life sims. While I did have fun with this game, I only did two playthroughs in roughly 6 hours and that was enough of the game for me. Therefore if your like me and not really a huge fan of these games, I would only buy this on a major sale or wait for it to be heavily discounted. Once again I like the game, It's just the fact that playthroughs can go so fast in a short amount of hours. That you really have to be the kind of player who wants to explore every relationship dynamic to really feel like you got your money's worth. I think if your able to get this game at $10-$15, it's more justifiable,  Regardless, I recommend this game. Tons of people to friend or date. If I do another playthrough, I will probably try to romance the dog boy.

_childDocuments_.review: This has been one of the more engaging stories I've played. The plot strings are intriguing and interesting and placed to tug my curiosity along to the point that I KNOW I'm going to play through again, and the mechanic that encourages additional playthrough has already gotten me thinking about what I would do differently on the next game but not regretting what I chose now in any fashion. The choices feel realistic for what my character can do, and anything I can't is filed away in my thoughts for the next time around.Edited to add that, they are very straightforward and open about the content warnings. The emotional impact of this game can be pretty intense, especially if you had a rougher childhood. There's a big button in the menu, and when you start it even emphasizes that they have it. If you have trouble with unhappy situations or endings (and it doesn't encourage you to go back and start a new game to try to fix it, which is one of the big themes of the entire storyline) then this may not be a game for you. New playthroughs have new options, which is one of the things that's drawing ME back to play again once I finish my current play.As for the technicals, I've not had any bugs of any sort to cause crashes. The game runs beautifully, and is beautiful on it's own. The artwork is wonderful and sets the tone, the character designs are impressive in the depth of representation and presentation. I was pleasantly surprised at the constant use of 'they', and everything is just so equal in terms of representation! And it's presented as if it's a normal thing, which it is, but still noteworthy in this particular day and age. I really appreciate the fact that I get the name of the song thats playing and who wrote it when I bring up the main menu, and that the artist names are presented in a way that I can actually see them! Its just...overall such a good setup, I'm hard pressed to think of anything really negative to say! If you're not a fan of card style puzzles, they have a way to not worry about it. If you are, they have a way to make it really challenging!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really amazing game, it came totally out of nowhere for me and hit me right in the gut. Beautiful visuals, a lovely soundtrack and a wonderful cast of characters, all backed up by some pretty solid game design. The card game used to resolve conflicts is fun and well thought out, and it even adds a feature that basically needs to be in all Life Sims from now on: when you solve a particular problem in one playthrough, you can solve it on subsequent playthroughs without having the stats you needed the first time. For example, if you spend a run being a xenobiologist and invent a new crop or cure an alien plague, you can get that same bonus in later playthroughs despite being specced as a soldier or politician. It's a VERY smart way to implement metaprogression that frees the player to really explore the game's branching paths instead of having to memorize when certain stats are needed ("I need [number][stat] on [day] to avoid eating the poison chocolates and dying like an idiot" to borrow an example from the lovely Long Live  The Queen). If you're like me and this wasn't anywhere on your radar, I'd strongly urge you to give it a try!

Also, your dad gives you tons of hugs and emotional support no matter how poorly life treats him and the colony. 10/10, protect him at all costs OR ELSESome shortcomings that I can think of (this is honestly just nitpicking)- I personally think the game's name is... well, fitting, but to me it's just a tad too reminiscent of overly descriptive and absurd isekai titles.- The "overworld" art direction might put off some people. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, there is not much for me to say that hasn’t already been said by other players in their own reviews. Also, if I wrote everything I had to say this would be an entire essay and I am unfortunately limited by the word count lol.The art is beautiful, both with the characters as well as out in the world when you get to move around, everything is top notch. Lots of pink and purples, but hey this is an alien planet, there is no better reason to go wild with the colors and designs!Music is great, it really feels otherworldly while having a kind of nostalgic feel to it that fits the sci-fi setting as well as the atmosphere they wanted the game to have.The story is straight forward, you live in a colony recently arrived on an alien planet trying to survive, but that is by design since the real magic happens with -how- you play. This game is a true and proper RPG, every choice you make matters and there is no true ending: there are good, bad, bittersweet, better than others, etc. and it is up to you which one you like best, what you would change, etc.The paths are never obvious, the game won’t tell you which choice is better or where you should head up next, it is all on you. The characters, oh the characters, I could write an essay for each character on just how great they are. Obviously everyone has their favorites and I personally have a soft spot for the twins. Every character here feels real and organic. They feel real, they have their own stories, they go through their own struggles and decisions, they have their strengths, weaknesses and best of all: they grow as they age. I don’t mean just design, I mean personality. They never stay with just a default personality the entire game, they learn and become wiser, their view changer either a little or completely because of their own experiences;some have to do with the player choices, but most do not, this is their life and you are not the center of it, you are part of it. The mean bully with an ego will not stay the same when they grow, the little cinnamon roll who wants everything to be nice and happy and is overall weak will show their strength just lies elsewhere (btw *chef’s kiss* with how they showed this), if  two characters dislike each other they might not stay disliking each other the entire game, same with if they like each other. Life is messy and gives you lessons which change your views and behavior, this game does a great job on showing this. These are your friends and they grow with you.Another thing I liked was the way friendships work. In many games I have played that have a friendship pointer if you want the character to be your friend or more you have to agree with everything they do or how they view the world, not here. These characters have their views but they also recognize that you have your own, even if you might not agree with each other chances are your points won’t go down, you’ll just get a response that says “I disagree with you and here is why… but I can see why you don’t see it like that”. It is a detail that I really like and it just adds more layers to the characters, your relationships romantic or not, feel -real-What I'm trying to say in very little words (which is hard): This is an amazing game and worth every penny

_childDocuments_.review: This game pulled me into the world better than anything I have ever played. It is a fantastic journey that covers all aspects of the emotional range. The replay of the game is less satisfying than it could be which is in part down to how niche it can be to change major events. I understand the idea that somethings just aren't meant to be but it is upsetting if that happens to be the route you wanted but another route that somebody else might have enjoyed can work out perfectly.  My last point is more because I am addicted to the game than it was needed but I do wish there was more. I feel like the final stage of the game is less expanded and a bit more rushed than the earlier years due to the overwhelming amount of thing that can be tied up during this time compared to the earlier years.Right now I have had my mini vent about how this game is only 95% as good as it could be let me talk about why this game is a masterpiece. This game builds on the concept that bad events are gripping and that, because it is a game, the story does not need to end well all the time. This is not a new idea but when combined with its mature handling of sensitive, relatable and current topics, it allows for a world that you could see existing in the not so distant future even though it is set on another planet! It also goes without saying that the music and artwork are fantastic or the world really would not work as well as it does. The characters created are all unique and have really well developed personalities (well outside of repeat events like birthday gift giving which I feel like could be improved by having a new response each year). They also feel like a community that is developing together which you do have an effect on (again on the second play through this feels a little less true). At its core the game is a visual novel but the game play side makes it feel like a game as well which is hard to do without taking away from the speed at which the story develops. Not once did I feel like a year went by faster or slower than the others and the game always found a way to make that year interesting and memorable. I also didn't realise how hard it was to not be a murder when your life is at risk until I realised I was doing it. Last but not least the card game aspect is nice as it is complex enough to be interesting but easy enough to pickup that I don't actively want to turn it off or just fail (this was still true on the replay for me until I was basically just too strong for anything to be hard).So to sum it up buy this game if you want a great story, if you feel that the 8-10 hours you will get on the one run is not worth the price and you don't want to see how the game works behind the scenes (which you really will on a second play trough) then wait for a sale. Do not buy it if you want to have a happy escapism experience. If you want to get truly lost an in alternate reality then buy it. This game is in my top 10 of all time. Thank you Northway Games!

_childDocuments_.review: The game shines when it comes to the creatures and and world building of the alien planet. The card puzzles were also fun and helped make leveling up more interesting. The art style is beautiful. However, the writing of the game and the story feels like it was made by people who spend a lot of time on tumblr and twitter. There's a lot of focus on how bad we are (or were as this game is not on Earth). The way you buy upgrades still felt like capitalism despite the game preaching against it. And despite our racist colonialist past being brought up, the colonists refuse to admit it counts with them too. I was disappointed with how it felt like trendy topics were brought up for brownie points with their audience, but those topics weren't truly challenged, including the morality of colonizing a new planet and the violence that comes with it. The characters felt bland. It felt like the focus was on creating an identity and sexuality catch 'em all rather than an engaging relationship system. The relationships and romance system felt shallow and for some characters they already have a built in partner. Being with them means breaking up their happy relationship. I think a more robust relationship system would have fixed this and given us more time to explore the characters and bond with them.Basically the areas that felt like sci-fi and the future shone, but everything else fell short. This is 2024 masquerading as the future while it explores trendy online discourse.If I sound salty it's because I expected to love this game but it left me disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist explores a decade of the lives of the first generation of children not born on Earth. While the genre of life sim games where you go about your life month to month raising personal stats and strengthening bonds is nothing new, I'm enraptured with the depth Exocolonist has to its systems and ideas. Sometimes it feels like choices are very telegraphed in games like this, that paths are direct linear routes without much leeway or wiggle room. Exocolonist can unfold into over 30 different endings, not even accounting for the different ways certain smaller storylines can end within a larger ending. It's easy to miss things, easy to have a bad outcome, but this a game that encourages you to carry on and, eventually, overcome. As the early game hints, there's more to this game than just a singular playthrough. This is a game really doesn't fully begin until you've beaten it that first time. From there it can unfold in various other ways as you try and grow and improve on what came before. The first thing I wanted to do when I saw the credits was start playing again right away, and that's exactly what the game wanted from me to. I can already see how much play time one can get out of Exocolonist just halfway through my second playthrough. While many things will obviously stay the same many more can change, either completely on purposely or entirely on accident. It's rare that I feel a game actually accurately represents just how much your choices matter in a game, but if anything Exocolonist undersells just how much agency you have in shaping things. The writing is interesting, which is of course integral in a game so heavy on the plot. Each of the characters you grow up with are quite interesting with personalities that shift and develop over the years. While some moments certainly feel tropey or even a bit on the nose, there's a sincerity to the writing in Exocolonist that cuts through any of those unsubtle moments. It helps that this is a game starring children growing into adults, you can't really blame a writer for making the puberty arc full of high strung emotions or for having the 14 year old kid with bright hair love the anime OVAs they found on the ship's medialogs. Moments of intensity or high emotion in the story work and land and I found myself generally invested throughout the length of my first playthrough and even more so starting my second. In particular if you are someone with an interest in exobiology, or generally enjoy the idea of fictional ecosystems and how humans might interact with them, this game is ripe with rather fleshed out worldbuilding and has a solid base on ecological concepts. While I don't think that Exocolonist is a game for everyone, I feel like it's an extremely easy sell to anyone remotely interested in what it has to offer. It also certainly helps that the game is abundantly queer friendly with perhaps the most robust custom pronoun/gendered terms options I've seen in a game. Generally a lot of games that veer into "dating sim" territories feel somewhat trashy if not outright exploitative. Exocolonist takes great lengths to avoid this while also adding nuance to its romance systems. I can't think of another dating sim where characters will start getting together on their own if you don't put yourself in the running for their hearts. Overall, this is one of those long rambling reviews where if you've actually made it to the end, we both know you're probably either bored at work, or are about to go buy this game. Either way: have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: The game has great art, an interesting story, and well fleshed out characters (love 'em or hate 'em.)  I was pretty emotionally impacted by certain story events that came up in my play though.The game play is pretty easy, it's a mix of time management to raise stats and meet certain thresholds for different story events, and also a simple mini-game where you use the "memories" (cards) you collect throughout the story to make Poker-esque hands.  You can focus on Strength, Intelligence, or Social/Emotional Intelligence and each has different cards and abilities as well as different story lines you can follow.The game is meant to be replayed or even save-scummed, with that being mechanically part of the game as well as plot.  (I've gotten 2 endings so far in about 30 hours of play.)Exocolonist is very LGBTQ+ focused, which could turn some people off but is an even bigger draw to those whom it will connect to since we're lacking a lot of great media for that audience.I'd give the game an 8.5/10 overall, could be a 9/10 but I found some of the grind tedious and annoying to have to re-cover ground I've already taken.  Still, 100% worth the buy.

_childDocuments_.review: As other reviews have stated, do NOT wait for a sale. The devs deserve every penny they get for this game. You'll live a teenage life one month at a time starting from age 10, where every event is handled in the form of a quirky poker game, and your core memories are the cards. You have a bunch of skills that you can raise by playing this game of poker, and a ton of paths to take. Junction points, Life or death. Do you become an upstanding citizen of your colony, persuasive enough to take over as Governor, or do you live a life of danger, putting yourself on the frontlines. _childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about this game, especially during the early hours. However, it really, and I mean REALLY, screws the pooch when it comes to the ending and the whole "meta" business.IWaTE is essentially the Princess Maker. Every month you have to choose an activity and then test your stats against various challenges and story events that arise throughout your daily life. There's one important twist though - it's all a time loop, so some of your actions in previous playthroughs have an effect on your subsequent attempts at getting a better ending.Okay, sounds cool enough. BUT:1) Pretty much every challenge is tied to a "fun" little card mini game that repeats itself for hundreds (probably thousands) times per playthrough. Sure, you can opt into the "resolve card battles with RNG" option, but it's highly suboptimal, and the time wasted on this minigame quickly begins to add up.2) Building good relationships with characters requires a grind of Stardew Valley proportions, as you need to constantly run back and forth between people and spam them with gifts while keeping track of their birthdays.3) If you neglect your relationship with some characters and don't bother doing certain activities until late into the game, the narrative logic will break and start referring to the events that were resolved years ago or treat your MC like they are still twelve years old (when you were actually supposed to experience the aforementioned events).Getting the "golden" ending, which is the only one with any sort of closure or effort put into it, requires beating the game half a dozen times, but after completing IWaTE just once and reading a couple guides, I couldn't be bothered to go through all that grind and padding all over again.It's truly mind-boggling how the devs managed to botch a fairly interesting concept this much. Therefore, can't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: no spoilers as alwaysI initially was a lil turned off by the art style, but had to try for the queer rep & cause so many folks seem to love this game, & I'm so glad I did! I actually warmed up to the art style quite quickly~ the environment BGs in particular are so pretty!I thoroughly enjoyed the extensive options for pronouns & other social terms/titles, & how such a wide variety of different kinds of queerness were woven into the characters & their relationships so naturally (whether gender, sexuality, romance, relationship style, family structures etc). I really loved the characters, they all felt real & had interesting arcs, which u really need to do multiple playthroughs to experience, it's designed really well for replayability! I really appreciated that following the kids from age 10-20 was well handled, with everything feeling v age-appropriate.while it maintains a fairly light & sweet not-too-deep vibe, it definitely doesn't shy away from darker things like death, grief, illness, mental health, trauma, tragedy...I loved the way relationships between the characters & ur player work!! all the characters maintain their agency & stay true to their desires & needs, even when they change- it doesn't stoop to that gamified/coercive/transactional entitlement zone that games too often do. i do have a few critiques, like how even though there are some open relationship & polyamory options (which is wonderful!), they are still based in a hierarchical relationship escalator ideal (ie: open relationship is less serious/commited than an exclusive "romantic" relationship) & most options are actually quite mononormative, but overall I was quite impressed!the gameplay is very straightforward & simple, & I found the whole combo of everything to be quite engaging and enjoyable! I may utilize the dice rolls in place of the card game on further playthroughs (which I for sure will do!), a cool option if u wanna focus on story.that being said, the story is alright? it's nothing groundbreaking that's for sure, it's definitely more focused on the characters, but I felt like it didn't really need to be anything more than it was.it does touch a bit on the complications of what it means to colonize a planet, & I was sort-of satisfied by the level of critique in my playthrough, though I think it could have easily been focused on more, & I wonder how different playthroughs will affect what I think. I did appreciate that it wasn't heavy-handed & focused more on giving space for u to think on things. however, keep in mind that there is a wiiild amount of different possibilities & variations on how each playthrough might unfold, so I'll see how further playthroughs inform my perspective~overall, a breezy & cozy game with a simple & enjoyable gameplay loop, adorable characters & a satisfyingly huge amount of choice & variation in how the story could unfold!

_childDocuments_.review: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist illustrates how well can RPGs and visual novels blend together, especially when written with care and finesse. It is spectacular in its variety, scope and re-playability potential—a merit Northway Games intentionally built upon. In other words, there are hundreds and hundreds of choices. No playthrough is ever the same.What I appreciated the most is that there is humanity within the characters. They evolve due to their occupation, your influence, global events or simply because they are growing up. Everyone has their good and bad moments, style, unique worldviews, insecurities and wishes—all of which is depicted in a colourful narrative rife with choices. It is thus very easy to become completely immersed and emotionally invested during a playthrough.I love to come back to this game. It is one of the best and most wholesome ones I have played.

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for a well made, story based game and this game didn't disappoint. It's not easy to critique it, it's really solid in pretty much every aspect. The writing is very good, the artwork is fantastic, the soundtrack is solid. The gameplay, whilst not very important for the genre, is good enough.I think it's a little bit too easy to min max the stats, as the skill checks towards the mid-late game get somewhat effortless. The card mingame gets too samey after a while too. Lastly, the soundtrack gets too samey as well after a while, I really think it could use some more songs to spice up some scenes. The characters are somewhat static, as they don't care whether you're the governor or if you're 150 iq scientist. Such personality traits being adopted by the player rarely affect dialogue. Other than that, I think the game nails everything.If you're wondering if this game is too gay or leftist or whatever, don't be. I feared the same thing. The game doesn't push its ideology on you, really. Most of the characters are presented equally, and every ideology can be adopted by the player in equal viability.  If you wanna be a militarist, go for it. If you wanna be a hippie, go for it. Both are viable. 8.4/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the writing in the game, and my first playthrough felt really good. The overall plot is interesting and you get drawn into the world pretty easily.the problems start coming with subsequent playthroughs. This might just be that my first playthrough was actually quite successful, in terms of the worst possible outcomes to the best. Spoilers aheadThe core gimmick here is that you're stuck in a sort of time loop, and memories from your previous playthroughs give you new options and make it easier to get a good outcome in the game. Ultimately these changes are actually fairly minor in terms of the main plot, mostly serving to make things you could have achieved in your first run through other means easier.Pretty quickly, especially if you made an effort to befriend everyone in the colony, you'll reach a point where there's not much else to see in the game, and you'll reach that point long before you unlock the different endings. Some of the 'hidden' parts of the game aren't nearly as well hidden as they seem to think they are. Combined with the gameplay consisting of a card minigame and clicking through menus to train your stats, new playthroughs take a long time for very little new content.This kills a lot of the replay value, which is ironic for a game with a core premise involving a time loop. It's still worth playing, I got around 20 hours from two playthroughs (steam playtime is including leaving the game open for a few hours) but I'm already feeling like I've scooped out most of the content the game has to offer having only achieved three endings (I reloaded after the 'hidden' one to get an actual ending on my first playthrough).

The card game is quick and I enjoy it; usually being able to win without too much effort.  The gameplay loop - walk around a bit, have an interaction, do a puzzle - was addictive to me.Probably my biggest complaint is that the endings for the game are all independently qualified for. I received some ending segments that gave conflicting information and could have easily linked to each other.  However there are A TON of variations and I only ran into this on maybe my 4th or 5th playthrough.  That said this game was fun enough to keep me playing through 5 times and beyond.  There's a lot to love even in a single playthrough, but my favorite part of the game was exploring the different possibilities across runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Ridiculously engaging VN! While it can be considered a dating sim, I think it does plot and friendships better. (More later.) Plot is amazing, characters are (mostly) likable and have growth! Epilogues are very detailed, the best in any game I've seen! Love the main gameplay draw, that you remember your past lives and can influence events in your next playthrough! Many different activities with unique scenes that help subsequent playthroughs feel fresh! You can have pets (and interact with them-not just eye candy!) Graphics are pretty, and I like that the seasons are part of the plot too, also not just eye candy! Card battles help add some variety.My main complaint is that some of the things you need to do (either for friendships or dating) can feel uncomfortable. There are a few characters that you need to break up to be able to date. There are a few characters that will break up with you in the epilogue no matter what. Hence why I'm hesitant to like this game as a dating sim. There's a character that starts off pretty toxic, and while there is growth if the friendship is high enough, to get that friendship up you have to pick options with violence towards creatures. In this same vein: there's a character that will always die, and for a game that's main draw is replaying to save characters, this feels bad.A smaller complaint, but it can feel repetitive/grindy on subsequent playthroughs. It does a good job of having enough content/adding content, but a lot of big character/plot scenes will repeat. I still recommend this VN and had a great time! I spent 64 hours on two playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: In this text based game you play as one of many children growing up on an alien planet, Earth's first space colony. The story follows the protagonist from age 10 to age 20 as you struggle to grow up, but also to survive. During each month you get to choose an activity to do and gain corresponding stats that unlock different dialogue choices. You can build your relations with the characters you grow up with and learn more about them by hanging out with them or giving them gifts. There are also card game challenges in which you use cards representing your memories to succeed in certain tasks.This game is masterfully written. Your choices truly impact the story and world around you, including your choice to ignore something. There is so much lore and things to learn, not just about this unexplored planet, but also the group you came there with and what led you to leave earth. The many paths you can take will twist and turn and intersect in different ways and the game is designed for you to replay it and explore! During your playthrough you can notice how the writing changes to reflect your character's growing worldview and vocabulary. The game explores the whimsy of childhood but also pretty quickly tackles heavy themes and have many gut wrenching moments as well as thoughtful scenes and messages. The characters are complex, multifaceted people that will grow alongside you and have their own arcs, even if you don't interact with them, making the world feel alive. You can eventually choose to romance characters but its worth noting that this is  a dating game. The relationships can be messy and lead to breakups depending on the character and your choices. Characters that are not dated can end up together or your actions can lead to another couple breaking up. But the relationships can of course also be incredibly sweet and heartwarming, its all a part of life! The presentation is absolutely gorgeous. The music, the character art and the backgrounds are all stunning, words can't give them justice. All characters are well designed and expressive and the fully illustrated scenes are always a treat. The UI is nice and simple with an in universe reason to exist and you can change its transparency and size according to your needs. The artwork on the cards is pretty as well but can feel a little out of place sometimes since they where all made by different guest artists but that doesn't subtract from the overall feel of the watercolor style and synthetic tunes.Character diversity is not a problem and the game is very inclusive. There is a broad range of people with different ethnicites, body types, mobility, gender and preferences, It never feels 'forced' or tokenized, everyone is just allowed to be their own people. You can choose, change and customize your gendered language at any time if you so wish, independent of appearance. Polyamory is possible with certain characters and you can date all the characters regardless of gender.The game is also well optimized with many options to increase performance. Even though its already pretty light since its a text based game, its nice to see! I played this on a laptop at times and it ran smooth there as well aside from some minor problems with the cloud sync. I Was A Teenage Exocolonist is a beautiful and heavy story game with card based mini-challenges, deep lore, well developed characters, inclusivity and a lovely soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game with gorgeous art, an interesting and diverse cast of characters, and a solid premise.I'm usually not a fan of time-management games, I get anxious about mis-managing my time early on leading to a bad end later, but Exocolonist's core concept and semi-rogue-lite setup means that that isn't really an issue, allowing you to explore all the way through the consequences of your choices.And you'll want to see those consequences. While you're usually more averting disasters than redirecting the entire path of the colony, getting to know different characters and learn different knowledge and skills about the world is engrossing thanks to the solid worldbuilding and strong character writing.All-in-all strongly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I was a QA tester on this game and have put hundreds of hours into it across multiple platforms. I was not asked to write this review and there was no expectation I would. I just genuinely adore this game.I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is a rare type of game that presents a narrative of both breadth and depth  and then allows players to explore that narrative through repeated groundhog's day scenario replays. There are over 600,000 words in the Exocolonist script, but you will only encounter maybe 1/8th of that script or so in any one playthrough. You control Sol (who you can name whatever you'd like), a man, woman, or non-binary character who grows from age 10 to age 20 over the course of the 10 years that a single playthrough of Exocolonist entails.You will decide what Sol does every single month during this 10 year period, including where they work, who they hang out with, and defining your version of Sol's opinions and beliefs through hundreds upon hundreds of dialogue choices. The game combines a Princess Maker style character progression system with a very compelling and emotional choice-rich narrative and card battles using cards which represent the many memories and choices your Sol has made. All of this together creates a surprisingly reactive system that encourages you to roleplay as a different Sol each time you replay. Through narrative choice you will be able to define everything from who Sol is attracted to and where they work down to the very granular level, such as whether or not Sol eats meat, what they think about the way the colony is run and which factions within the colony's web of characters Sol supports.And that's only the start! There are 10 dateable characters, each with their own story arcs that can end in any number of ways, and a vast array of secondary characters with their own arcs and often surprising backstories, many of which hold a further level of depth to them if you really go digging into everything this game has to offer. I could go on and on about the incredible aesthetic of the art in this game (I love Exo's future clothes!) and how fun it is to watch these characters grow physically alongside their narrative arcs, or gush about the emotional and stylish synth soundtrack, or Vertumna's incredibly vibrant ecosystem, but instead I want to talk about another reason why Exocolonist is always going to have a special place in my heart:Most sci fi depictions nowadays are bleak. Dystopias have become the norm in our cultural representations of the future, and for good reason, as our present day reality is itself quite the dystopia. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist does not follow this recent tradition. And that's not to say Exo's vision of the future is at all naive or happy go lucky, either. Instead it does something far greater and gives you a rich and conflicted future in which characters are free to express themselves and to live comfortably in that expression, but there are still those who would like to take away that freedom out of fear, malice, or misguided attempts to help others. Exocolonist's future is beautiful and scary and awe-inspiring and most important to me, it gives me hope. It thoughtfully presents a future different from those I've encountered before and then fills in that world with an incredible level of care and detail so that you can live in this world for as many groundhogs as you'd like.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a reluctant yes for me. I did enjoy it, but ultimately I think the game lets its efforts to be progressive get in the way of making all of its characters feel alive, and its efforts at being inclusive are not entirely successful.I don't have a problem with progressive stories, settings, or messages in games. But what bothers me is when that comes at the expense of making less progressive characters believable. For example, about halfway through the game, a new character about your age is introduced. His name is Vace, he's meant to be a foil for the more touchy-feely colonists you grew up with, and he's a colossal stereotype. He's very into the military, he's self-centered to the point of parody, he's a  and his genetic augmentation--I promise I'm not joking about this--is that he  Similarly, Tammy is (I believe) the only female character who comes within spitting distance of doing the whole homemaker thing, and she's portrayed as an enormous idiot--literally good for nothing except cooking, cleaning, and being motherly. The efforts at being inclusive are a problem for the story in another way. There are two gender-nonconforming characters (a trans girl, who you grow up with, and a nonbinary person, who arrives later), and they're both portrayed as flagrantly mentally ill. The trans character , the NB character self-describes as extremely weird, and they're both autistic-coded (the NB character moreso than the trans character). Consider also that in the same event the NB character arrives in, another character arrives--a literal furry. There is a real sense that there's a "freaks and geeks" contingent and a "normal" contingent of characters, which is not how a genuinely inclusive game works. I don't think this was out of any malice. It seems to have been born of a genuine desire to be inclusive. But it just doesn't work very well. It really is a good game, and obviously a lot of love went into it. I like it despite its flaws, which is what makes the flaws so frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game yesterday, and in the meantime it has swallowed 19 hours of my life.The story and characters are excellent and very compelling. The stakes are high, and the game pulls no punches, with consequences that made me cry and yearn to start over. The gameplay difficulty is on the low side but is enough to keep you engaged. The thing that will make the most difference to the outcomes of the story are going to be your decisions, however, not your skill.Which is perhaps a good thing, since the game also heavily encourages replaying through various mechanisms. One is the aforementioned high-stakes outcomes based on your decisions. Without spoiling exactly what it is, there is a second mechanic that weaves the excuse to replay through the story itself.In summary, you will fall in love with these characters and watch as circumstance tears them apart, then you'll do whatever you can to create a brighter future for them.

_childDocuments_.review: A game filled with an incredibly diverse cast of characters, mature and heartbreaking stories, and breathtaking art. I typically tend to find coming-of-age stories featuring young protagonists rote and uninteresting, but this one is truly something special. I found myself repeating this game obsessively trying to find all of its secrets and lore. You can really feel the love and dedication the dev team had towards this. _childDocuments_.review: Turns out this game was 22% of my total steam game-play for the year of 2023. The first most obvious charm of IWTE is the art and music. I loved the music on the soundtrack; it intertwines with the gorgeous and colorful art throughout every scene. It's very unique.Secondly, the game-play is quite smooth and easy access for all types of players. There's options to view possible triggers, as well as changing how your game actually works. You can turn off the card game and focus on the story, and you're able to skip through dialogue you've already seen. These features make it more re-playable than it already is, especially for people who might be achievement mining. People have different playing styles and levels, and this was definitely taken into mind.Thirdly, the characters and relationships! IWTE truly dives into the nuances of relationships, particularly the emotional and peculiar ones of teenagers. I love the fact that you can see other characters interact and see the depth to each personality. My only real qualms with the game have to do with some of the endings and the way they interact. I won't dive into the depths of it, but sometimes the endings feel unfinished when you understand the connections in the game. One catastrophic thing happens in one ending that can be ignored completely in another if you meet certain requirements. TLDR; Love this game after buying it out of pure curiosity. Very unique gameplay that make it replayable. Lovely to listen to and look at. Considering the team was not big at all, it's a seriously impressive game. Thank you for making this game. And if you're reading this review to see if you should get it: I think you should.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game to others, but I hold a bitter attitude toward it personally. I genuinely tried my best to love this game. With pleasing aesthetics, intriguing stories, and a creative and attractive description of the future, the game had every advantage to be my Game of 2022.At that time, I was set back by a series of events and saw only the darkest days. Instead of attracting me with its imaginary future, it impressed me with its optimistic perspectives on the future. I was used to coming across one and other pieces of sci-fi where there were cool androids and social Darwinist structures. The logic just began with "We had a tough planet to deal with and "rebellious" people to control, so we certainly required blood and iron," which were not necessarily metaphors. And I just kept thinking, "Oh, here definitely goes a potential tragedy, and they will turn back to cruel futures soon." Still, the tiny colony exhibited its resilience and people stepped forward again from the past. They changed and grew, but not in the way those false prophets claimed, in which only the ruthless opportunists survived.I honestly didn't know what to feel about that. Everything in this game seemed way too gentle for me.  Though it was indifferent to say so, I just felt every event the game designed to make me sympathize with the characters was not really traumatizing enough. The characters in the game had complex backgrounds and met with challenging events, but they were all masters in dealing with pressure and never lacked support from others. I should admit I even felt a bit jealous about that. Their past was more temporary than an ever-bleeding wound, and none of the effects seemed permanent. Those events were also less devastating than I supposed. Other characters were also resilient and had their way of dealing with their problems. No one was really helpless here.The game is a masterpiece, but I can't feel the sense there personally. Nothing really tricky means the good ending isn't impressive enough. I'll recommend it anyway because I think these disadvantages are mainly personal, but I do have a conflict in my mind here.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the storytelling behind Exo is competent and the gameplay enjoyable, the metagame is not for me. I enjoy playing games because I can win/get a good score with an understanding of the game and how it plays. Having to undergo multiple failures in order to get optimum outcomes is not what I come to games for. This game, for all that it clearly positions itself as accessible and progressive, demands to be played in a certain way for its artistic vision. Well, if I wanted to endure bleak outcomes in the hope of getting it right next time I'd just pay attention to my real life. Having to battle an inscrutably literal zero-sum game meta-system was only possible with guides diluted whatever joy the game brought and I still flubbed it. Had I known what this game required of me, I would not have purchased it. It's right for some, but not for meEdit: upon further playing to try and get some better outcomes for my peace of mind, I have discovered that no matter what you do Dys will commit suicide in ending cards and the narrative clearly approves of his decision. Had I known that,  as a person who has lost many people to suicide and is still struggling with active suicidality, I find this abhorrent. I know that the creators may not have thought about Dys's narrative arc in this fashion, but the way the ending cards are set up now it's pretty clear cut. From his name, to his backstory, to his obsession with death, culminating in rejecting his human life including a romanced Sol and reconciled Tangent right down to the injection of ambiguity with an animal observing the colony, everything about Dys's arc that remains constant throughout the meta-game indicates narrative approval of this fate. I sincerely hope the creators change this because it punched me in the gut when I realized I couldn't save Dys, obviously because I was projecting about myself. That really sucked.
