_childDocuments_.review: It's a frustrating game that actively undermines the potential of the concept it is based on. The different lives you experience over and over again are supposed to play out differently as the player, and the main character, retain memories of past lives. The groundhog-day concept is difficult to pull off in visual novels, but Teenage Exocolonist fails to deliver on that front, as an observant reader will understand all hidden mechanics during the second playthrough - and as the illusion falls apart, all that's left is a major grind to unlock various combos of endings. Of which most are completely dull and merely reflect "who you spend most time with" and "what was your most frequent profession". And it's only the late endgame when the results of your choices make any meaningful difference on the story, as it's very much on rails for the overall 90% of time. Beyond the identical story across most of the in-game events, all that's left is a numbers game on where you put most of your points towards. The card game mechanic (which is more of a dynamic puzzle than a deckbuilder), although relatively unique and fairly complex despite such simple rules, failed to amuse me enough to get through all the rehashed content more than twice - and yes, I did get to some of the "best" endings in that time.Peculiarly, the game boasts LGBT-friendly features, and is widely acclaimed for featuring custom pronouns and independent gender and appearance sliders for your character - not toggles, each is a continuous spectrum that allows you to make the main character e.g. exactly 35% male, if you want; changeable at literally any time during the game. Very inclusive and welcoming! But it's just a farce, both sliders secretly snap to just three values, and their position literally never affects anything story-wise; to the ridiculous point where other character's sexual preferences follow whatever the player character looks like and considers themselves at the moment. I can't decide if that's an amusing reflection of a gender-inclusive utopia, or an insulting afterthought on the studio's part merely to appeal to queer audiences and capitalize on their enthusiasm.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a delightful act of storytelling that takes you through a tale that is an emotional roller coaster in the best possible way. There is cast of complex characters that you will come to know and care for, and the card-game challenge mechanic is fresh and zippy (you can also choose to minimize it, or increase the difficulty, depending on your preferences). However, do not be fooled by the pastel colour pallet and soft music- this game does not pull punches. Your choices, even ones you don't think are important, have consequences. Sometimes those consequences are lethal, and not to you. I urge you to not save-scum during your first playthrough. Feel the sting of regret, the tug of loss, and the joy of sudden discovery. It will make subsequent playthroughs (and you will want to do more than one) so much more satisfying. For all its potential grief, however, the game is ultimately about hope. About who humans are at our core, and that we can choose to be better than our circumstances. That we *have* to, if we're going to survive. Even thrive.

_childDocuments_.review: Five hours in and I'm hooked. That's enough for now, but it was a fun and thoughtful time. I appreciate the speculative-fiction side of the story. While I highly doubt we'll ever reach other solar systems, such stories are rich ground for considering how we might grow up more here on Earth.20241011 After detoxing from videogames, I don't recommend any games anymore. I do recommend collective action towards improving public welfare, rather than trying to amass as much as we can individually. Perhaps IWaTE is a gateway to new understanding for you, in which case consider launching from there into reading related books and finding people with whom you can learn and grow.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly its rather depressing how little attention this game's gotten, cause it knows what it wants to be, and it does it amazingly. A VN that is charming, depressing, tense, sometimes all of the above.You control a 10 year old child that is on board a colony ship to colonize an alien planet. You start off with a great deal of freedom to build this character too, picking from their childhood friends, starting stats, sex/gender (there's an entire drop down list of pronoun stuff you can mess with to customize how people refer to you). After landing, you've got 10 years to increase stats, build relationships, and try to keep the fragile little colony from dying to the hostile planet. Where the game shines is the freedom to build your character as you want, while still making it feel like you can actually something even if their stats suggest they may not be able to. The main gameplay loop involves picking a task for each month, then you play a brief card game with an ever expanding deck of cards, which are earned by exploring and interacting with others. You have to make a hand high enough to equal or exceed the target score to get the best result in an event. Sometimes all that does is give you a skill point, other times it determines whether you succeed or fail, based on the context. If that sounds boring to you or you just want to play the story without messing with it, the game gives you the option to shut it off, or make it harder. I personally like the game, as each game takes maybe 30 seconds to a minute to finished based on how quickly you can process the cards you got, so it doesn't interrupt gameplay to an annoying degree.As for the story, its great too. It really feels like you are a child on a hostile planet, learning about it as you grow up. How you interact with the planet and the colony changes the outcome, including whether several characters live or die to see the end of the game. There are also enough events that occur throughout the game that it doesn't get stale. Just when you feel like you're getting the hang of things or the colony is about to become problem free, another issue arises. The game does deal with some dark themes, but the devs have a list of such events that you can look at before playing if you think it may be an issue to you. Basically the devs have really gone out of their way to make this game as inclusive as possible, which is a nice gesture on top of the games quality. One run of the game will take you about 11-12 hours roughly, each year takes maybe an hour to do. I won't spoil anything, but the game does have a system in place that allows you to get a bit more out of future runs each time you finish a game, which makes it all the more worthwhile to get to the end. If you like VNs, stat raising games, and/or a good story, pick the game up and give it a try. You won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A fabulous game, in every sense of the word.At its core, I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is a very solid life sim/visual novel with an (entirely optional) deckbuilding mechanic used to resolve challenges. Combined with the excellent writing, it's already an exemplary addition to the genre. Where the game pushes the boundaries of its genre into the sublime is through its "Groundhog Day" (or more accurately Groundhog Decade) central conceit. This takes the way most players play this sort of game - consulting walkthroughs or wikis on your second (or greater) playthrough to get the events/endings you want and avoid the ones you don't - and turns it into a game mechanic. The game remembers previous playthroughs and lets you use knowledge from those past lives to steer the fiction. Frankly, it's genius.The game isn't perfect. If anything, I wish the devs had leaned even harder into the Groundhog Day mechanic, since there are some situations your character will face that feel like they should be influenced by past lives, and I would have been happier if past lives also affected a character's starting stats and/or deck. Many mechanical rewards arrive so late in the game that they feel pointless. Very rarely, events will happen that don't make a ton of sense due to when they can happen in a character arc or the overall story. But these are minor things compared to the triumph this game turned out to be, and given the sheer depth and scope of content written into the game it's inevitable a few mix-ups would slip through the cracks.It's a real gem in the genre, and I look forward to seeing what the studio comes up with next.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, without a doubt, one of the best written story-forward games I've ever played. Each character is charming, each interaction is immensely entertaining. It's so easy to fall in love with. So easy to let it break your heart. Rigorous deckbuilder it is not, however, so don't expect the gameplay to be especially challenging. The real meat of the game came from long conversations with my friend over the motivations of our character under the weight of the many plot threads they found themself wound up in. Moments as simple as a character offering us a kiss became 40 minute long debates about our character's sense of self worth once placed into the context of the rest of their circumstances. There's a fantastic beating heart to this game; a loving philosophy. I never quite understood the hype around games like Undertale and people's feelings for it. I think this game brought me a little closer to that. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is tragically obscure. We've been proselytising the game to anyone who will listen. Hopefully, if you play it, you will, too. There's a real magic here.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played Volcano Princess, the concept of a life-sim over developmental years may be familiar to you. Except in this game, you are the princess (or prince) and the world is much more foreign and dangerous. If you're the kind of person to replay things over and over there's a lot of variations in how things happen to explore, but even if you aren't there's still a good 15-20 hours of gametime and what's here is really quality. Expect to go in, make mistakes, be surprised, and learn how to make the best of things.The music is good, not industry-leading but solid and thematic in a way that sets the mood well when it needs to. A solid soundtrack can often make or break a game so it's good to see this one holds up.Visually, the game stands out. In a game like this where everything has a sort of illustrated or drawn quality to it, as opposed to more modern 3D rendering, art direction and talent is make-or-break, and it makes. Each environment has a distinct look and atmosphere that easily sticks in your memory, the characters are both recognizable and interesting, and the alien fauna don't disappoint either.  The card-style challenge gameplay is as thought-provoking as you need it to be; there are settings to disable it entirely, as well as to crank things up to even harder requirements. I played on normal and eventually wound up eventually gearing out of having to work much to succeed at anything, which was fine by me as it takes some work to get there and even without failed checks there's a lot of time management to demand your attention. The writing is better than I expected. You need strong characters and narrative in a game like this and it delivers. The world had way more cool things to explore and learn about than I expected 'some exoplanet' to have, which pays dividends throughout pretty much the entire game. By necessity of how quickly time flies by, and how optional many character interactions are, the other people in the story get their development and key moments in a somewhat brief manner, but I think it's handled well. It's left up to the player to extrapolate the rest of the shared time their character spends with others from the brief windows that stand out as lasting memories.

_childDocuments_.review: I may not be a 'teenage' player anymore, but god do I love this game!First Off, the graphics are phenomenal. All of the character and environment art are gorgeous, and the world building is just so well put together and thought out. Not to mention, the characters are 3 dimensional! Although they all have different augments, that is not their whole personality. A lot of media where characters have 'quirks' or 'powers', it gets very cliche and stereotypical. In this game all of the characters are very fleshed out!A feature that I really love is that there is save/load options. This game is incredibly based on the choices you make and you get the "best ending" there are a lot of requirements you have to reach. Being able to go back and change things or start from a certain point in so useful if you're trying to get a lot of different endings.The only feature that may sway people away is the card game mechanic. But, as someone who was wary of that at first, it is actually one of my favorite parts of the game! You gain cards based on memories and decisions that you make that effect your character. The card mechanic is fairly easy to figure out and understand, and there's also an option to turn it off if that's not for you! Overall, I think this game is gorgeous and underrated. It has definitely become one of my most cherished games I've ever played.Tang my beloved <3

_childDocuments_.review: So a friend mentioned in passing about this game, they didn't own it nor did they know much about it but I looked into it and watched some of the gameplay videos on the store page and was interested. Though, I was struggling with the 20+ gbp price tag. Roll around September First 2022. Said friend gifts me the game, I knew I had to play it and play it I did. 6 hours of gameplay. 6 hours of one playthrough of a fantastic, changing story that gave me laughs, smiles, joy swiftly followed by gutpunches, heartbreak and genuinely pain. I'm an emotional person and I feel this may be best experienced if you are one too. It's worth the asking price. It's effectively a story book in which you make choices with an optional card game, which I personally played. I romanced Anemone, I became Military Hero, I made friends, lost one early and so young. (Triggering themes will be present, as someone with depression, it didn't trigger me but if you're more sensitive or are currently struggling, maybe skip for now.) I died in my early thirties, after my partner, with two children. I sobbed through the ending cutscene, it wasn't quite the Cyberpunk ending cutscenes but it was ♥♥♥♥♥♥ close. I highly recommend I Was a Teenage Exocolonist and I look forward to my next playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Your relationships with the characters are very controversial and there is nothing you can do about. You will be forced to steer away from monogomy just to be with the character you wanted your MC chooses. It's honestly demotivating to play another play through because you don't really have full control of how the story goes even with the mods that make it easier. The problem is not the game, but the writing, the STORY. The main character has got to be the most UNFORTUNATE character that I have ever seen in all of main characters. Even with all the synchronicities, no matter how many reincarnations you take, you will always be alone in the end. I already got the "best ending", but I don't think I feel satisfied with how the story went with the characters alone. The catastrophes and corruption, I get all that. The devs are trying to make it somewhat "relatable" to real life which I don't hate but there are just some situations that does not happen to everyone and it's just hyperbolic. Pretty one everyone in this game will leave or even cheat on you in the end, which will a sour taste in your mouth. It's just not worth it.If you like childhood memories and wholesome moments, then try it. Though prepare to get bombarded with controversial relationships when you decide to form your social life for the main character. To be honest, it's best to let him/her/them be alone until the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting visual novel with a unique take on the raising sim genre. You play as Solanaceae, Solana, Solane, or whatever you choose to call the player character. You can also choose to be male, female, or nonbinary. The game centers around a card game that can determine whether you pass certain skill checks, but I just skip it. Thanks for making that a choice, I find the card game boring. You, your family, and your childhood friends, among many others, are colonizing a foreign planet, which as it turns out, is pretty complicated! You can use the colony's resources to increase your stats, or go exploring the planet which also grants stat increases (you can explore outside the colony once you're old enough - unless of course you sneak out). That's all I'll tell you without spoiling anything. This game has a lot of ups and downs, but overall I felt that a lot of love was put into it. I enjoyed it!The good: The story and character designs are very interesting, it doesn't gloss past the dangers of space and colonizing foreign planets, polyamorous romance options, branching story paths, many different endings you can get, plenty of characters to make friends with/romance (don't always expect a happily ever after though), I'm glad for the content warnings since this game's story can get brutal at points, the game encourages multiple playthroughs through its storyline which makes it very replayableThe bad: I felt like the futuristic aspect kind of got hammered into your face at some points, the card game isn't very fun or interesting (though it can be skipped completely), why does everyone have ridiculous names like 'halitosis'? sorry but that was funny lol the teacher's name literally means bad breath

_childDocuments_.review: ✔️ Very nice story with colorful and interesting characters.✔️ Pretty artwork and music.✔️ Original and fun simple but efficient card-based gameplay.✔️ Quite a few possible choices with various outcomes.💭 The fact the game has been designed with multiple playthroughs in mind makes the first one a bit... weird? It's probably just due to what we are used to in the video games and media in general, but something about it bothers me a bit. _childDocuments_.review: So, I had been browsing through Steam for a game to play after finishing another one and stumbled upon this. At first I thought it looked like it was a cute little game to spend my time with. Little did I know that I would end up going on an emotional journey. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is an amazing game where you essentially go on a journey of 10 years (maybe less if you do things different). In that journey you'll lose people, or you just might save them, you'll also make friends, or even fall in love. This game is a wonderful coming of age story about how you must fight your place in a world where it seems like it doesn't want you there. By the end of my first journey, because yes this game is all about the succeeding playthroughs, I was extremely attached to everyone I befriended and was super emotional by the end that I couldn't help but play another run. So, if you're looking for a game where it draws you into the story and you really feel a part of it? Well, this is your game.

I NEEDED to redo every play through so I could save as many as possible on the next time, or maybe the time after at that, or please please the time after that. I WANTED to play the damn card game, again and again. How could you make me contradict myself so willingly, developers?Teenage Exocolonist is just great. All the game systems are amazing, meaning they are so intuitive you don't even notice they're there. The story work is top tier. Everything ties into everything else in a way that keeps you perpetually moving forward. You can just enjoy your play. . .and cry your eyes out when your best friend decides to give up humanity and download his consciousness into an alien computer, effectively killing the person you've come to love and depend on, but not  killing him so there's no mourning, no closure, just an empty hole - but that's what he says wants so cool I guess. . .Anyway. _childDocuments_.review: I've completed several playthroughs of Exocolonist and it continues to demand my attention and my heart. The game itself is a mishmash of raising sims like Princess Maker and Long Live the Queen, with RPG-like stat checks and some exploration mechanics, as well as deck-building. The card mechanics are intuitive, and there's a hard mode for people who enjoy pain. The setting is unique and thought-provoking and addresses many hypothetical challenges of space colonization. There are clear environmentalist and anti-capitalist leanings in the overall plot, but the player is free to disagree with these precepts and can even express ideological differences within the plot (there's a lot of endings and choices to make!). Players are given significant choices and impact on the plot as well as character development, both of the main character and their fellow colonists. Art and music are consistently excellent. The alien designs are particularly fun and often walk the line between grotesque and adorable.Probably the most interesting aspect of the game is how it changes on replay -- in short, the main character is able to somewhat remember the results of past playthroughs, and this impacts the choices available to them throughout the game. This creates a sort of meta-plot that normally exists solely in the mind of the player after a half-dozen or so runs -- we know what works, what doesn't, what's coming...and may or may not have the skills and knowledge needed to stop it (this time). In comparison to other raising sims, Exocolonist does have a few quality of life changes and some shifts to the usual formula. The gender sliders let you customize your MC's gender identity completely (gender is solely aesthetic throughout the game as far as I can tell!). The aforementioned "visions" that push you one way or the other also help players remember what's coming next rather than having to use a guide. Romances are a bit atypical -- most romanceable characters have a default love interest that they will gravitate toward unless the MC makes some effort to intervene. This doesn't result in cheating, but rather represents character dynamics. Your love interests are complex in that they'll move on if you don't express interest in them consistently and make sure to build the relationship.All in all, if you enjoy self-aware raising sim-like games, and solarpunk sci-fi, you'll probably love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If I were to ever make a game, this is the kind of game I'd hope to make.The world is thought out and complex in a way that makes it easy to imagine yourself in it. I felt like I really was exploring an alien planet and discovering it and learning to understand it along with the characters. It's beautiful and exciting and scary and that's what exploring and discovery is all about.The characters are well written, acting their age and feeling shaped by their environment and growing in ways that are understandable but not stale. Their arcs as well are interesting to watch take shape, especially as you find ways to influence them. I genuinely felt attached, which is a rare for me.The story unfolds in interesting ways and I find I learn more the more I play which shapes my perspective of the characters and events, though I have a preferred outcome every time I play. It's compelling and, while it can be harsh, it never feels cruel. I always feel as if the events unfolding make sense rather than a direct punishment of my actions or inaction.The art and music is really enjoyable and, though I prefer a unified and consistent art style, it never bothered me when there were inconsistencies.The game play is fun and challenging at times, I like the card game mechanic, though sometimes I found it repetitive and tedious once I'd leveled up past a certain point or replayed the game. I thought choosing to skip the card challenges would mean I just automatically "won" them so I could focus on completing the story, but that is not in fact what happens. I found not actively playing the card game challenges left me very under leveled which made the game even harder rather than easier.Overall, well worth the time and money I've sunk into it.

_childDocuments_.review: A thoroughly enjoyable time with this game. There's enough variation and changes between lives that I was quite happy to jump straight into a second life straight away. I'm not enough of a completionist though to chase all the endings. It's likely a nice one to jump back into after some time away though.I love that it is memories that form the basis of the deck building, even to the point where I would refuse to remove a useless 0 or 1 point card just because the memory it represented was important to me.Stopping at 20 years old is simultaneously too long and too short, so well played on the design there. Too long because I'm so eager to get to those later years when I have everything available to me, and I'm not just a 'kid' to be ignored. My GOTY for 2022 thus far.It is engaging, immersive, beautifully written with incredible visuals, and the world-building is just outstanding. Nothing exists without a reason, from the people to the world and its flora and fauna, and every action (or inaction) has consequences. _childDocuments_.review: Deep story, world, science and characters that keep me coming back for more, with gameplay that ties very nicely in with the story. I love how character choices impact your deck, because eventually it means you will naturally stray more toward certain choices due to your previous choices, thus going along with the character's wishes.... Or, as in my first playthrough, do a complete and uncharacteristic flip midthrough when a new character arrives that you desperately want to impress. It absolutely ruined my deck but it was still a fun little treat because the personality flip I made very clearly showed in the gameplay.The worldbuilding feels very thorough and gives great depth to the game, no matter which personality/character traits you end up focusing on. I also like how the time twist ties into the overarching mystery and that I can bring some previous choices with me into the next playthroughs, makes every time I start a new game feel a little more interesting because I know certain things might happen differently this time around due to my and the character's knowledge from past playthroughs. Only thing I could possibly wish for would be a more varied and complex deckbuilding system, because after a few playthroughs it tends to get quite repetitive. It helps that I can skip the deck gameplay part entirely if I want to, but I don't really want to either since it means I get less rewards. But alas, this is a very minor complaint in the grand scheme of things!HIGHLY recommend this game, it will stay with me for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall quite an enjoyable experience. The art style and music are both very, very lovely. Perhaps my favorite part of the game. Sometimes I would just pause in the middle of an event to appreciate the beautiful art work of the landscape. Gameplay-wise, the mechanics are quite simple and relatively easy to grasp. I enjoyed the card game system for about a couple of hours, but its relative lack of complexity made it become more of a chore once I hit ~10 hours. Still, I'm quite amazed by the variety of events throughout, and there are many delightful characterization and lore details scattered in them, which I always enjoy a great deal.Story-wise, the writing quality does fluctuate a bit. In general, I found the story and characters to be quite charming, and the game does capture some of the early-teen/teenager struggles and turmoil rather well. Yet after finishing the game, I do feel a bit unsatisfied in that there's definitely untapped potential for both the characters and the story left unexplored, and consequently the narrative came off as a bit flat when I reach the ending. To me, the writing quality starts to take an obvious dip once the Heliopause lands. I understand that an expanded cast requires more time and efforts to craft well, but personally I would much prefer a smaller cast with more depth than a bigger cast with more breath--but that's just my personal preference.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked IwaTE quite a lot, but I think if I was attracted to men, I'd like it even more.  The fact is that artistically, all the men grow up to be extraordinarily attractive, and the women are mostly androgynous.Also worth noting: this game allows for complete pronoun customization (and independent of late teen masculine or feminine appearance), doesn't appear to have any kind of gender restriction on romances, and features non-binary characters, so if you find any of that problematic, and you probably will not enjoy this game.  Or maybe it would expand your horizons?  That'd be nice.The basic gameplay is what you'd expect from a life/dating sim: manage your time, raising a skill bar and improving your relationships with various people, with a fairly simplistic deckbuilding aspect: it's essentially "get the best poker hand" with a semi-customized deck.  It's marginally more complicated than that, but the bonuses for straights and flushes and x of a kind are where you get most of your points.  Once you select your task for a month, get some story, then play your cards.  You get perks for every 33 in a stat that either improves your card gameplay or unlocks new activities around the colony to raise related stats and improve your relationship with different colonists.The story is where IwaTE really shines; there are a TON of mysteries and stuff going on - you start off as a kid and the adults definitely don't tell you everything!  It's a gritty, tough exocolonist life; people you know WILL die (certainly one death is mandatory until a second playthrough).  I only managed to head off one impending disaster on my first playthrough, but was hit with so many other bad things.  I still grew up to become the chief engineer for the colony and felt pretty good about it, but it's still interesting to consider all the paths not taken; I'm sure there's a true end somewhere if you can save everybody if you can solve the food crisis or cure disease or improve colony defenses enough (but actually all of the above, plus a lot of other stuff!).Unlike many visual novels, though, rather than having a lot of very, very short "bad end" stubby branches to the storyline, something bad happens, but the colony just continues - a lot of time with fewer colonists or bleaker prospects ahead.  I really like this approach, and it feels like what I choose matters, instead of just populating a gallery with grim deaths and then immediately rolling them back, the colony feels like a real place, that keeps moving forward even as things get bad and worse instead of shunting you down a "correct" path after every mistake.  Some of the second playthrough choices already seem to allow you to go down a true bad end, too, so if you like schadenfreude, there's a place for you here too.  I definitely already had some plans for my second playthrough when I finished my first, but number three is going to be quite miserable for my colonists, I think.  Also, the idea that I'm considering a third playthrough after having just starting my second one, in spite of not having three partners I'm interested in should tell you just how much I like this game.Anyway, thumbs up for everybody, because it's a genuinely good story with an excellent approach to the visual novel space and simple but fun gameplay, but thumb way up if you're attracted to men, because that's definitely what the artist liked.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this? God, absolutely, I've already recommended it times to literally anyone who bothers listening to me about video games. Don't pay attention to my hours played, it is very low compared to the adoration I have for this game. Very, very low. I really need to play it more.Lets get down to this. Firstly, I love the art style, the art style was the main pull for me. While I'm willing to play a game with the appearance of something pulled out of the depths of the nineties, I have a soft spot for games with beautiful art styles. This is no exception. The art, all throughout, is aesthetically pleasing. But, no, the art style isn't the main selling point, there's so much meat to this game.You're met with a pronoun system when you're making your MC. Of course, you can go with set pronouns of she/her, he/him, and they/them, but no, they didn't stop there. What did those absolute madlads do? . I didn't use it, I was fine with using commonly used pronouns, I'm one of them they/them folks myself, but it made me incredibly happy to see the detail put into the pronoun ability.The characters are all lovable in their own ways and I got way too attached. Look, I'm a sucker for character diversity, from appearance to personality, and I Was A Teenage Exocolonist has a lot that I could ask for. I didn't expect the dogboy, but I'm not complaining, he was so adorable and then he got hot. Incredibly hot. That can be said about literally almost all of our peers in the game, though, like, oh my god?Anyway, away from my thirsting, even the non-romanceable characters are wonderful. From the start, my buried daddy issues hit me like a truck, and if that wasn't enough, my mommy issues came to light and hit me like a train. The mom and dad of this game are phenomenal and I would literally die for them. Even the non-important characters were memorable and I adore all of them. As somebody who is picky about character design, all of the character's designs are phenomenal and I want to shake hands with the artists and designers, and perhaps give them all forehead kisses because the artwork and the design are so wonderful. The story is good and compelling, this is coming from somebody who actively skips the story of any game they play. Yes, my girlfriend is occasionally distressed by it, particularly when I skip any Elder Scrolls plot, the amount of psychic damage that woman has taken from my antics should really be reimbursed. I lack the attention span for any complex story, I am maybe three-years-old at best, BUT this game managed to get my two-year-old brain to sit down and listen.Look, you've probably seen the screenshots. I sure hope you've seen the screenshots, what are you doing in the reviews if not? Weirdo. But, look, this game is primarily a written story, and I get that some people have the reading comprehension of a toddler, so if this isn't your cup of tea, it isn't. But, if you can at least TOLERATE games with a ton of reading, then I recommend you try.I won't say much on the story, I want you to explore that on your own, but let me tell you, you will NOT regret it. I'll let you hit me if you do regret it, but, like, I guarantee it's great.So, as said, it's primarily a written story. But! But!! But!!! Not all the time. That's what got me. I was like "♥♥♥♥♥ what?" when I first started playing. So, yeah, there's combat, you can fight things, but it's a card-based game fighting system. You have to get your card number higher than the goal, and it's pretty easy for  me. But, you can explore around, which is cool. The characters look super cute in the moving around style. I'll go talk to an adult Cal and he's, like, super cute in the art style, then I get hit in the face with how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hot he is when his actual picture comes up. Like, hot damn, none of these characters need to be that-Okay, I'm thirsting again, sorry.Anyway, you play a kid from 10-years-old to 20-years-old, and let me tell you, when my character went through puberty, I got some war flashbacks. You really start getting attached to your character and your peers, you also can go to school to level up your stats. Each of your stats is better for specific things, and there's a bunch of different endings. Also, you can romance your besties. Lets talk about that.The romances feel kind of... eh? The characters feel fleshed out, they have their own motivations, but the romance I went through felt a bit dull. I romanced Dys, our typical emo adventuring boy (not really, he's got more depth and I love him), and I sort of regret not dating the alien because APPARENTLY Dys accepts a polyamorous relationship with him. I am still upset about this turn of events because I have two hands and they're meant for my cute emo boyfriend and his hot alien boyfriend.But, anyway, the romances themselves were... I don't know? The build up was phenomenal, though, but... Thinking about it, that's okay. The romance doesn't need to be a big thing, especially when the build up was so good. Speaking from experience, when you've been best friends for a while, the transition from platonic to romantic doesn't feel big and extraordinary, and that's what I love about romancing the characters of I Was A Teenage Exocolonist.In a lot of media, the build up is intense, and the romance is full of passion, but in reality, that doesn't happen as often as it does in media. But from my own experiences, when you're already so close to someone, not much changes when you take the leap into a romantic relationship. I can't truly complain about the romances of IWATE because they felt realistic, and I'm just not too used to that in media.Look me in the eyes and ask me that again. Actually, please don't, eye contact makes me uncomfortable.$25 isn't bad for this game, actually, that's pretty low for this game. It has a ton of replayability, and the characters you get close to begin appearing on the menu screen. This game has parents who love you, a compelling storyline, memorable characters, and a horny dogboy that I can hug for friendship points.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. The setting and cast of characters are refreshingly spun vibrant takes on classic tropes. Well-written dialogue, plenty of different paths and hidden twists to experience. Good for replay for a story-focused game. The amount of choices has been really engaging and immersive, and Your choices help shape everything from who your character is to your friend's lives and the fate of your colony.My only criticism is that there is a lot of allure to try so many new activities, but spreading out your progress between your skills too terribly much is discouraged as it might limit you later. There are 12 skills (4, physical, 4 mental, 4 social), which is otherwise really cool, but often you will encounter an event/dialogue option with a skill score requirement. I suggest saving your game often, as your decisions, big and small, will sometimes matter a lot, and there are bonuses to be earned for making the right calls in events and in challenges. Challenges take the form of a fun card game in which you use your characters memories as cards, with opportunities to collect different memory cards throughout your story based on your decisions. Memory cards can be cut from your memory deck through forgetting them during certain activities, so your character ends up forgetting a lot of their earlier memories  as most of us do.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had my eye on this game for the past few months, after a friend mentioned the demo and the general plot, and when I tell you this game was well worth the wait: it was.The art style and music composition are stunning, the world-building is immersive and carefully crafted (I admire anybody who can come up with whole new planets and xenofauna and so on; that takes some serious talent), and the storyline itself is just... Amazing. Your choices have serious weight to them, and I was pleasantly surprised with how much my "routine" around the colony had to evolve in order to respond to the narrative. Each character feels real; they have their morals and their interests, and they either stick to them or evolve with the surrounding environment.I also, as a nonbinary person, really enjoyed how the character creation and subsequent dialog adapted to the chosen expression of the player. Being able to completely choose my pronoun sets (aside from the he - they - she slider) and titles was an incredible option as is, but the game went above and beyond in not only introducing other gender diverse characters, but handling topics that are often "binary limited" in a way that gives the player proper fluidity in their expression.Overall, Northway Games did phenomenal with this game, and I really do hope more people give it a chance. I certainly know I will be replaying this game a few times to explore different story lines and outcomes.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR in case you don't want to watch the video:1. The art is some of the best I've seen - its not fully animated, but every character has variety of facial expressions based on their reaction and disposition toward you.2. The deckbuilding elements - while not the key focus - is well polished and actually fun and challenging at times. Your cards are created from the 'memories' you get as you grow up through your teenage years, and they consist of the social skills, mental skills, and physical skills that you get along the way, ether alone, or with your friends.3. You only have 10 years to experience (10-20 years old), and your actions can easily breeze through the seasons, so spend your time wisely!4. At the end of the day, the story is the real deal here - you can choose to play a 'story mode' which skips the card battles if you choose to. But be warned, your story and dialogue choices still matter greatly! Every new play through will be different - more plays means more options thanks past memories, and sometimes this can completely alter the course of the game and its characters!5. There's no voice acting and lots of reading I would HIGHLY RECOMMEND this to players who enjoy a great storytelling experience, and don't mind lots of reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Alrighty, my first ever review for a game and this one absolutely deserves it. Side comment before I ramble, I will absolutely recommend this game to anyone who loves games with multiple endings, games that acknowledge our current world and our future, strategic card games (which can usually be completed or altogether turned off if not!), and/or games where you can quickly get attached to characters.I LOVE games that are heavy in story and allow for variety in character, and this game checks those boxes and more. There's lovable characters, characters that are easy to hate, relatable characters, cool alien life that you can keep as pets, an amazing art style, a thrilling story, and the sci-fi exocolonist life you can dream of. Some aspects of this game are very full of care, and I heavily recommend reading the content warnings before playing. The story is crafted so beautifully to incorporate some harsher topics relevant to the story, and less-plot-relevant things can be missed if you feel a bit of ick reading about them. Each character is unique in their own ways, and each one will shape your views of the world you're playing in (and maybe the real world too!) It's also pretty long compared to other games of the same type, in my opinion. Which I think makes it better! It gives you more time to explore the world and the personalities of the people in it.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit hesitant to jump into this game as it looked kind of "cheap" for lack of a better term. But damn am I glad I jumped in. 10 mins in the "cheap" look had turned to charming and it just works wonderfully with the whole feel of the game.I think i'm a little over halfway into the game and the story is great, I want to just keep playing to see where it goes. The progression (for both your character and just game mechanics) system also helps to give you that one more turn feel as well. The card game aspect of this reminds me a lot of Pazaak from Knights of the Old Republic (Basically futuristic Blackjack) which i've been looking for in a game for the last 20 years. Not engaging enough to be its own game, but perfect as a side/mini-game in a bigger game. I love it, but I can see people thinking its too simple.Overall this game is great, but with warning flags if your not a fan of reading  dialogue (Tho it is great dialogue) or playing a simple card game to abstract challenges. (Tho it is a fun game) If neither of those two things scare you away give this game a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: As one might guess by the time spent on the game so far, I consider it a deeply enjoyable experience. Or, many experiences- since that's sort of the crux of I Was A Teenage Exocolonist: playing it multiple times to achieve new options, better stats, more friends- and many timelines can lead to The Perfect Ending... or a tragedy. It's all up to you to figure it all out, at your own pace. I love the cast, even the ones I don't like on a moral level have a degree of appeal in where they fit into the overall experience- the designs are colorful, interesting, diverse in culture and identity and goals. In short, I highly recommend it to any scifi fan who likes visual novels- and Especially ones who wish visual novels had more interactivity.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. The art direction is brilliant, the story is very engaging and each character is really really well written. You'll think of them long after you stop playing. So many possibilities, so many things to do to see to read to explore... You'll want to start a second playthrough as soon as you finish your first (I know I did).If you like narrative games and aren't afraid of reading, this is a must play. One of those rare games that you will not forget. My GOTY for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: it's a really beautiful game that i think does a really great job of tackling adolescence and how people become themselves and coming to grapple with the circumstances they were born into. i get shades of The Dispossessed when i'm playing it and i think the game does a good job of exploring a lot of the interesting ethical questions of colonization.one of the tempting conclusions in a lot of science fiction is to assume that colonizing planets without people is kind of a freebie and isn't worth further interrogation, even when the environment might threaten our survival, but Exocolonist neatly cuts that knot by representing several characters who don't place humans at the top of a natural hierarchy. it's even easier to do that when humans are the newcomers! the first generation of a colony, with their reasons for being there, have to determine what it means to live their principles and to what extent those principles should balance with survival or prosperity.the characters have real preferences and the game is largely respective of their agency, the lengths you have to go to change what other people want can make you feel downright sociopathic but it's refreshing to feel like other characters want a relationship to be on their terms as well.i think the game does ask a lot of the player, the first playthrough strongly implies that you should probably do a few more and has more than a few punches to the gut, but once you know your way around you can start finding a lot of interesting corners in the story. after a couple of playthroughs, there's an option to skip text you've already seen, and i'd suggest enabling that.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: Would definitely recommend this game to anyone. The story lines are very diverse and well written, it seems like the devs put thought in every single thing. I love the fact that previous runs influence your gameplay, that you can skip the card game and previously read dialogue (very nice when you want to play multiple times to unlock all the endings), that there are so many different possibilities and that the characters are all very lovable and different. I've played more runs than I can count and I'm still curious to see what else I can do. This game honestly has a very special place in my heart. I love the art style as well, it's just a great game overall in my opinion. I don't even have a favorite character right now, I adore them all.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough, this game rocks. I'd call it a visual Novel with RPG elements, and it does both of those pretty well. The characters are endearing and well written, the sci-fi is grounded and cool, the art is amazing and varied. The game also provides a well-argued and interesting statement on the nature of post-capitalist societies, how they might work, their flaws, etc. Considering the amount of content that I missed, I can guess there's probably at least 7 or 8 more playthroughs of stuff to do, as well. Super excited. Also it has a gender slider and you can customize your pronouns. Nomi best enby.

_childDocuments_.review: Back when the game first released, I decided to pick it up on a whim based on jiving with the vibes of the visuals and soundtrack. Less than a week later I'd played 35 hours and could confidently say that yeah: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist (2022) had my attention for sure. This game has wonderfully strong writing, great characters, card game mechanics, AND time travel? Oh you got me. You got me GOOD. I've restarted the game several times because SUDDENLY a character whose presence I couldn't possibly continue to live without DIES and I'd wasted my min-maxing stats life on being a hard man of science and action when all I wanted to do was hang with my friends at the supply depot and I could NOT continue like this. "I can save you!" I declare, sobbing at the screen. "I can save everyone!" Well, everyone except maybe for Vace. I mean. No one really likes you, sugar. You're kind of a ♥♥♥♥♥. Nemmie: I'm watching you. Tammy, Rex, Nomi-Nomi: you have done nothing wrong ever and I believe in you.But yeah, for a game that was not on my radar AT ALL until like. The very month the game got released? This game is FANTASTIC. Please do give it a go if you can. For some reason, I get similar vibes to Disco Elysium and its game-ification of narrative, only with poker(ish) cards instead of dice rolls. I've completed the game once with what is arguably the golden ending, so now I'm playing the game with a slightly more RELAXED focus and seeing all the wonderful interactions I missed out on because I was too busy trying to max out all my stats (which I almost did! 11 out of 12 stats!) Did you know there's the Secret Funtime Club where all your friends get together and form a Scooby Gang what investigates various mysteries around the settlement or just hang out and design club uniforms? I certainly didn't! I had somehow??? Missed all this wonderfulness??? During my initial playthrough?????mayhaps that is actually part of the message running through the game's narrative that's being reinforced in the gameplay mechanics: that if you spend too much time on calculating the value of time vs output efficiency, then you'll be missing out a lot on life that way. MAYHAPS
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: "I was a teenage Exocolonist" is an absolutly gorgeous lifesim about growing up in an new and unexplored environment and how your deeds and friendships or lack thereof shape the future of the new founded colony and the people living in it.It is beautifully written and realy pulls on your heartstrings. It has not only huge replayability, but this replayability is actually part of the games concept. I wont spoiler you more, you have to see for yourself. If I wouldn't already own it because I'm one of the lucky beta-testers I would buy it all over again. Oh, and I still hope for the chance to buy a plushy of my little cute'ulhu.So for everyone, I just recommend to try it. I can tell you there is a lot of game in this. I'm currently at about 80h and still haven't seen all of it (although probably most of it). If you are into branching stories and a diverse cast of characters, and dont mind but actually enjoy feeling with the characters during their times of strife and joy, then buy it and experience what it's like to be as a person who can say "I was a teenage Exocolonist"!About the game mechanic: You have a set amount of month per season/year that you can spent either exploring the wilderness or in the colony to train or work etc., which will increase not only one or more of your various skills, but give you new insights about what happens and new cards to use in the card puzzles.The card puzzles work by drawing a random set of cards from your deck and then trying to reach a specific value to succeed in the test. So deckbuilding is as important if you wanna succeed as card placement is. Losing a skill doesn't neccesarily mean you get the worse experience or story, since through errors you can also learn new things helping you in the future.Therefor while I realy enjoyed the card game of this game, I wouldn't pick a specific choice only to get a specific card, but because it's what I as the character would do in the situation, and throughout multiple playthroughs you can pretend being different versions of the character therefor learning new things over and over and over again.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: The game comes out feeling unnatural when story events keep repeating periodically with no fault, and when all my "choices" are based of an artificial bar that is leveled up by playing a card game, and when characters keep saying the same unimaginative dialogue and all of their personality is based of a single trait like "sportive but dumb" "Intelligent but callous" or "shy and my sister hates me". The characters don't feel like people, they feel more like ideologies. If you asked ChatGPT to write a character based of a few adjectives , this is what you would get. It is a shame because on the outside the game is neatly packaged with a unique but modern artstyle that is frankly good-looking, and is very inclusive opening the door to being able to connect to an audience that not always is represented. Unfortunetly this isn't sufficient and the game comes out as being shallow because of its unnatural design and robot-like characters.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. There are a few minor typos but the plot is so well written you'll be too involved in the story to care. One complaint that I do have is that I wish poly-amorous relationships could be toggled (like in the case of Rex). I love Rex's character and design but I'm monogamous, the thought of being involved in poly/open relationships make me uncomfortable which adds a but of a dilemma being that the other characters I am interested in also involve poly relationships.
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: This game is part time management, part visual novel, part deckbuilder roguelite, and part dating sim. The art and character designs are gorgeous, and the music is great as well. The replay value is good so far, with 29 total endings, though some of them are repetitive (i.e. the same ending, just with a different occupation your character gets at the end). The story is fantastic, especially the first time through. I'm three runs in, and I'm already planning which characters I'll befriend and which jobs I'll do in my next life. The card game is fun, though you get the hang of it pretty quickly. I appreciate the ability to turn it off whenever you want as well. I also appreciate the separate appearance and pronoun sliders, as well as the ability to romance whoever regardless of your gender. There's plenty of great representation as well, with lots of same-sex couples and even some poly and non-traditional relationships. There is some more subtextual rep, but I'll let people decide those for themselves. Overall, I think this game is more than worth its full price, though i got during the winter sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I Was a Teenage Excolonist is a amazing game it changed my life for the better!let's start with the art IT IS gorgeous like seriously amazing some of the best art in a game ever. the gameplay is on a weaker note then the art but is pretty fun for what it is.the story one of THE BEST i have ever played it kept me entangled for 4 playthroughs.the stat rising is meh at best, but this is one of the greatest games of all time!truly a 10/10 i could recommend to anyone!
_childDocuments_.name: I Was a Teenage Exocolonist

_childDocuments_.review: I never really write reviews, but this game deserves every last bit of praise. The storyline is absolutely fantastic, and the characters are so well thought out, from their personality/appearance to how they react to choices being made. It's beyond impressive how much thought and effort went into this game.I did a quick play through and i did get a pretty sad ending (my whole game play was pretty emotional and made me tear up a LOT), but that just draws me in and makes me want to discover more outcomes. It was really interesting seeing the outcomes of every choice, and it wasn't a hard game to get used to or pick up either. I actually quite enjoyed the card game they had paired with each event.I enjoyed how inclusive this game was as well. Including the option of deciding pronouns/ how masculine or feminine you'd be was an amazing choice on the developers. The only wish is that I hope one day they can implement more options for how the main character looks or even add the option to have a customizable avatar. I understand it would be a lot, but maybe in a future game that could be an option too. Loved this and can't wait to play again!

_childDocuments_.review: It was an interesting game with a strong story and interesting science fiction elements. The characters are mostly interesting and they do develop as characters over the course of their lifetimes. All of this is reflected in the art and I thought that was a nice touch. The card game is interesting at first, but it can become tedious after awhile. Some of the explorer maps have mini-events that respawn every year so there is some repetition with regards to the exploration aspect of the game, but they become easy to avoid and knowing that things don't change that much outside of the colony walls helps with deciding what to do as the in-game time progresses. Overall, top tier game that is worth its price and more. I got about 16 hours out of one play through so the game is worth the price.

name: Dragon Marked For Death
detailed_description: Dragon Marked For Death is a side-scrolling 2D action RPG that can played solo or with up to four players in online multiplayer. You play as the survivors of the Dragonblood Clan who set out to take revenge on the Kingdom of Medius, who destroyed their home and captured the Dragonblood Oracle, Amica. To obtain the power they need to enact their revenge, they forge a pact with the Astral Dragon Atruum. Use your newly acquired powers to take on quests from villagers and raise your status in the kingdom. How you perform in these quests can have a direct effect on the game's final outcome. Quests aren't all about defeating enemies, though. You'll guard a ship's passengers from monsters, search for hidden treasure, rescue a princess from a castle under siege, and a lot more! Choose from four playable characters from the start (Empress, Warrior, Shinobi, Witch) and two characters that are unlocked once certain in-game conditions are met (Oracle, Bandit) to defeat your enemies, gain experience, and level up. You'll receive points as you level up that can increase your attack power, defense, agility, and other parameters. Customize your character in a way that best suits your individual playstyle! Team up with up to four players from all over the world in online co-op multiplayer action. By strategizing and working together with your party, you'll be able to achieve even greater results and reap even better rewards! Get ready to experience the unique, dark fantasy world of the Dragonblood Clan in this intense 2D action-RPG!

_childDocuments_.review: is an action RPG that was originally released on the Switch at the start of 2019 and now it’s on Steam with DLC characters included. Even though it has a lot of emphasis on playing co-op, the community seems to be lacking which makes finding a party to join difficult. This title shines the most when you’re playing co-op, but solo still provides a satisfying and addictive experience though clearly inferior to co-op.• The core mechanics work extremely well with one another• Post game caters to hardcore fans that love to grind for loot• Levels are crafted with all characters in mind• Six different characters to choose from, different weapons to wield and unique abilities• Addictive and satisfying combat• Higher level quests gives bosses more complicated attacks to dodge• Each character takes about 15 - 18 hours to complete the story with• Everything is hindered by the lack of community forcing you to play solo• Game was designed with co-op in mind instead of playing solo• Completing the game solo is can be challenging at times• Casual players won’t get as much time out of this game compared to players who love to grind for lootThe writing in this game is detailed enough to keep you hooked, though I would’ve hoped for more lore and backstory of each character considering it’s an RPG. Each quest that you take on has a small story that gives you a reason to help out and justifies why you’re here instead of just giving you a quest with no explanation. There wasn’t anything mind-blowing about the main story, but it was decent enough to keep you progressing to see what would happen.Upon starting the game you’ll be given a choice between 4 different characters to choose from (six in total but two of them are locked), each with their own unique fighting style, abilities and stats. All of the standard classes are here tank (Warrior), mage (Witch), warrior (Empress) and the rogue (Shinboi), each have their own passive abilities to help them navigate areas that others can’t access. For example, the rogue can double jump and wall jump, the warrior has like a grappling hook to swing from places, the tank can push blocks and smash rocks and the mage can create a temporary platform for herself. Each character feels significantly different from one another, you can really feel the weight of the tank compared to the rogue who has a lot more maneuverability and freedom. This further encourages multiple playthroughs if you wanted to complete the game with all the characters, though don’t hold your hopes for finding multiplayer matches to join very often…One of the main features that  highlights is online co-op, admittedly there isn’t anything wrong with how it’s presented, it’s more the fact that barely anyone is playing online at the moment. You’ll be lucky to find a game in your region, and even if you set it to global, sometimes you won’t find a single party to join. The main issue is that the game was designed to play co-op so when you’re forced to play singleplayer, it slows down your progression and forces you to grind if your struggling. It hinders the game a lot more than you might think since some characters are designed to play co-op and suffer more than others when playing singleplayer.This doesn’t imply in any way that the levels were badly designed, each one was crafted to ensure that each of the characters maneuver abilities could be used in every level. This could give you access to a different area or give you more freedom when fighting a boss to swing around the place or whatnot. There was a surprising amount of variety in the biomes that you explore and made the game feel a lot more varied with breaking up the quests in different locations.It’s no surprise that  is a pure grind-fest, it has all the mechanics in place to try and encourage you to grind. The quests that you complete can be replayed on higher difficulties to yield better loot rewards and higher amounts of gold and XP. Higher difficulties don’t just increase the health and attack of bosses and enemies, but actually give them different attacks that are harder to avoid. This might’ve been more appealing to me if I was able to join a group of people who wanted to grind, again this mechanic for me was hindered due to the fact that the community just isn’t big enough to find parties to join reliably. It wouldn’t surprise me if some people are put off by the game entirely because of the multiplayer aspect being inactive.However, what kept me coming back to this game was the combat mechanics. Every character has their own basic attacks depending on what weapons they can wield, along with special dragon attacks that each character has. These special moves cost Dragon Points that you obtain by attack enemies so you’ll always be using them, you don’t have to conserve these moves for bosses only. It’s extremely addictive to combo moves together for high damage output against the tougher bosses that you’ll come across.Post-game however, caters to the more hardcore fans of the genre. After completing the game with any character you’ll unlock a tower quest where each floor you clear the enemies get tougher and the rewards get better the higher you go. If the sound of senselessly grinding doesn’t fill you with excitement then you can always play through the game again with a different character on the same profile. All your gold and equipment that you have collected will transfer to each character as long as you stay on the same profile.The soundtrack throughout this game is fantastic, perfectly capturing the atmosphere of your quest and the environments that you find yourself exploring. Bosses have more intense and faster music that contrasts well with the smooth and calm nature of the music as you explore the surrounding area. The sound feedback when you hit an enemy with your dragon attack is extremely satisfying to listen to as it sounds a lot more impactful and harsher than your standard weapon. Though the one thing that slightly annoys me is the sounds that your character makes every time they jump, attack, take damage etc. It gets annoying after a while and there’s no way to turn it off or adjust it, which is a basic feature that seems to have been overlooked.The art style never dipped in quality and manages to stay consistent throughout the course of the game. Specific quests will take you to different biomes in the world where you’ll see a surprising amount of variation and detail to keep the game fresh for as long as possible. The sprite work and animations for the characters specifically are very smooth especially when you’re using two or three attacks in a combo and transitioning between them.The lack of online might be enough to turn people away from this title, however, despite playing singleplayer for the most of the game I still enjoyed it. Players who love to grind will get a lot more time out of this title compared to the more casual players. The combat is satisfying and addictive, the soundtrack is a joy to listen to and the visuals are fantastic. I’d still recommend this title to either audience, though I’d suggest waiting for a sale especially if you’re a casual player.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a little less than an hour on the PC version of DMFD, however, I have over 100 hours on the Nintendo Switch version. I have played and beaten the game with 4 out of 6 characters, not including the 2 new ones (the Oracle and the Bandit, and have beaten all Quests with my preferred character (the Witch). I have nearly beaten the game with the Oracle, and have played much multiplayer in the 3.0.0 update with the Witch. With that in mind...Dragon: Marked for Death is an Action Platformer with RPG elements such as Levels, Experience, Stats, and Loot such as Equipment and Accessories. You play as your chosen Class and choose your mission, attempting to accomplish whatever goal the mission has laid out. Sometimes that is an escort mission, sometimes it is to kill a Boss or Bosses, sometimes it is to get a certain item or to a certain location. Each class also can change its chosen Contract/Element, acting like a sub-class, which grants new abilities and stat changes. All classes have certain consistent powers such as their Dragon Boost ability, which is the equivalent of a temporary Super Form for each class. The classes each play very differently to one another:The Empress plays like a DPS class with few movement options. She has really good damage potential, and players must learn to skillfully dodge attacks in order to use her effectively. She also has a hook claw that she may use to climb on certain ceilings to help in platforming. Overall she is fast and fun, but requires a good deal of skill to avoid dying a lot.The Warrior plays like a Tank class. He is slow, but a heavy hitter. His damage is great, and has good defensive skills, such as his stunning charge (which staggers enemies, preventing attack), and his Shield which blocks all incoming attacks while providing a very minor health restoration effect. He moves slow, and can't jump high, but his charge allows him to knock over certain walls in Quests, creating a shortcut for the entire party. Additionally, if you prefer speedier attacks, using a Longsword instead of an Axe/Hammer makes the warrior attack a little faster, at the cost of damage.The Shinobi has incredible mobility and range, the most of any class. His damage ranges from low to average, depending on how his build and Contract, but his multiple jumps and flying kick make him the easiest to platform and avoid damage with. His weapons are Ranged Shuriken and a "Melee" Kunai Knife. I say "Melee" in airquotes, because his dragon skill allows him to hit a target with melee attacks at a far range. The most fun character for platforming, and good damage.The Witch seems to be outwardly the most complex character, being a Magic user with variable range and damage. She may suit many purposes, and her attacks are performed through Incantations, that is, inputting a series of button commands to create a spell. (Ex: AAAA makes a level 1 wind spell, and BYXAB makes a level 1 healing spell). She has attacks of up to 5 element types, that being Neutral, Wind, Fire, Ice, and Thunder. She also has a healing spell. Each of these spells can be augmented with many other commands, such as Condense (which makes the spell a Multi-Hit attack, hitting multiple times, OR makes Healing magic an AoE effect), Homing (which makes the magic seek out targets, including healing), and Power Up (which increases the damage of Neutral, Wind, Fire, Ice, and Thunder Magic. It also makes healing magic restore more HP. Additionally, the Witch has access to utilities, such as her Owl Familiar, which may stun weak enemies for a time. Shine makes her temporarily glow in the dark, making it so you do not have to zoom in to see in dark areas. Levitate is a very useful spell that gives her a platform to more easily avoid damage. This spell WILL save your life. She was also recently given 2 new spells, a Cure Ailment spell which removes Status Effects, and a Status Boost. Status Boost temporarily increases one of your stats, but can only be accessed with the Focus weapon type. The Witch has 2 types of weapon, a Tome and a Focus. This augments a few things, but most importantly is how her Healing magic functions. This is all a LOT to take in, but in all of my hours playing DMFD, she is one of the most rewarding characters to learn. Her damage is usually fantastic, if you use the proper element, and her spells' utility and range cannot be beaten. Her platform makes dodging enemy attacks just a bit easier, which makes all the difference. She can be any role in a party, and should not be overlooked.The Oracle has good Mobility and does acceptable damage. She acts as a mixed attacker, using a combination of spells and melee damage. I went for a Melee build, but her magic damage should not be underestimated. She has an incredible array of spells for Utility, but only 1 spell for damage. The damage spell Element is dependent on which Element/Contract your Oracle has chosen. It does good damage, but if the enemy is strong against your element, you must instead rely on Melee Attacks. Her utility magic is rather impressive, including the Witch's very own Power Up, Homing, and Cure Ailment spells. Additionally, she boasts Mirage, which creates another blade to significantly boost damage output in Melee as long as the spell is maintained, Feather, which grants a second jump, Protection, which prevents instant death, Quick, which greatly increases movement speed, and Armor, which prevents knockback on her. Overall, she requires a good deal of micromanagement, but is nonetheless a fun, if tedious, experience. I liked her, but I will be sticking with Witch for the time being.The Bandit I have the least experience with, so take what I say here with a very large grain of salt. He has a very diverse toolset, based in the usage of items called Relics. He can steal Relics from enemies using certain attacks, which are consumable items that allow him usage of one of many different attacks. These range from a very damaging explosion, to an extra jump that bellows damaging wind below him, or a water attack akin to FLUDD from Super Mario Sunshine, that damages and allows hovering over medium sized gaps. There are other attacks, but I will not go into them. They all seemed quite useful for their respective purposes. The micromanagement from needing to recollect Relics was a tad tedious, but it can be made less so depending on how you choose to build your Bandit. Overall, I felt his damage was okay, and his mobility was great. He's also a twink so he's got that going for him.Each of these characters will gain levels throughout the game, allowing them to boost one of several statsEvery 5 levels, all of your Class's stats will boost by 1, and every level, you will be able to boost 1 stat by 1. No matter which Class, every level has felt like an important choice. The decision to allocate between Piety's utility, Vitality's survivability, and the respective Class's preferred damage stat was never one I took lightly, as the difference between your health and the steadily increasing damage inflicted on your enemies was always one I took acute note of. One would do well to strike a balance between their own survival, their damage output, and the usefulness of Piety and Luck. One drawback that I do agree with is that no class truly evolves as they level up. I've seen complaints that the enemies' tells are too easy to read, but at higher levels they gain new attacks, and their attacks become more difficult to dodge, making going for higher level quests a very rewarding experience. The music is Inti Creates' first full orchestra soundtrack, and it was used to great effect. The music makes for an excellent backing track. I may not keep every song on my phone to listen to, but the game would not be the same without them. The locations are relatively standard fare for fantasy, but between Toru Nakayama and Makoto Yabe's breathtaking artwork, who cares? Every location looks drop dead gorgeous.
