_childDocuments_.review: So I put fair amount of time to make an opinion( lvl 78-79) of the current state of the game ( also did one beta weekend ). I do like the game alot but there is a big list of things that needs to be addressed .- Optimization : I got ryzen 5800x , rx strix 6900 xt , 32 gb ram at 3600 mhz , playing on 21:9 3440 x 1440  , 160 hz  - im gettin horrible fps  from 80 to 5 fps , hosting  a game 40-45 fps ,with dips during storms  t o 20-30 , i lower some the  settings but im not gonna run it like potato just to get  more fps - Alot of people cannot simply run the game so because its poorly optimized and very demanding- Bugs  - Constant  graphic flickering  you have to constantly play with FOV , items disappearing , exotic ore not returning to orbit , bugged ores in caves / plants / rocks / oxi deposits, animals spawning out of nowhere , etc .  I had several exotic weapons  and modules not returning to orbit or disappearing .- Game mechanics and economy - So the idea of  missions and all buildings   are temporary is fine , but has to match the economy . I just finished pay day with a friend I did several hours of the mission solo but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ took us  total 24 hrs game time to complete , one mission pretty much took all my weekend . And for what 240 exotic and 400 regular currency ... This is when I got to a point and decided the grind is not rewarding . I love grindy games I've played tons heck I think just on Warframe I got 4000 hrs , not even going to list the aRPGS , and other survival games I did on other platforms . The game needs to be more rewarding . Current balance may be OK , for current items but in the long run I dont see a reason to keep grinding . I see people already  have most items but they run same missions which are the quickest and more reward which at the end seems even more boring for me .I like to mix it up also my friends are getting bored to . The gold ore needs bigger increase so is the titanium . We need to be able to reach end tier faster and not grind from  whole weekend just to get there and finish the mission under 10 min . Heck I didnt even enjoy building since I need to be stingy on building mats  and resources because otherwise i have to spend another few hours to get more ore from a cave that is 20 min away running back and forward since everythign else in the vicinity is mined . Cave need to have the ore deposit respawning or some balance need too be made .  ( shout out to the interactive  icarus map that went out at least I can see types of caves and sizes )Missions objectives : Unless  you youtube or google ,  most of the time you wouldnt know what to do or expect for missions objectives  . You may travel to a location just to learn you need tons of stuff or different things you bring and you ll have to come back or have to build something you didnt expect. Carrying something on your back while sacrificing a  small leather back pack doesnt make much sense to me but that's just me . Game should have clear and precise mission objectives and not go to this location then its something to build that is not around you .Clear waste of time , i dont know what was the idea behind it but i assume its to make you stay longer in the game its tedious more than challenging . The realism of the game sometimes makes sense but as it does sometimes the game is very illogical , my fav examples are  boulders remaining in the air when you dig underneath ,ITS MAGIC . Dying from thirst while raining .Air bladder and water bladder made from the same material but one leaks liquid meanwhile the other doesnt leak air. Animals have perma oxite buff and teleporting talents . Valheim economy is pretty  damn good , take an example , yes the buildings there remain but if you go by ICARUS route of temp missions you need to balance the  economy .-RESPEC: talent points , thje famous respec issue  that most of us wants to be added asap and yet  wasnt even a feature to begin with . I may be wrong but I'm pretty sure I wasnt warn what I chose as talents are permanent nor that I wont get more after lvl 40 ... I do understand the logic of the  DEVs not to have all trees unlocked other wise the game will be boring but ... seriously . I cant tell whats good or not unless I try it . I started with SOLO tree since most my friends didnt buy the game , than i had 3 that gave it a go ... Now I'm stuck with  a SOLO talent tree that is worthless unless I'm alone .And if god forbids someone joins as I'm  transporting ORE , i have to go scream at them or kick them since all the sudden my solo skills are gone and im over my weight limit . RESPEC is a must feature and should be cheap to aquire not some  big exotic currency amount and needs to be done soon rather  later , and first one should be free .Workshop : I will be short on this one  ,most of the items are worthless or not worth grinding for [] . Some seemed overpriced for what they do as well . Im curious to see how the devs will take this further because it ll determine if its  worth  of farming and if they fix the disappearing issue or items not returning to orbit . Customization : Virtually none so skip for now since the game is in progress .The game clearly feels like mix of alpha and beta at the moment . No way this is a full release ,it  should be tag as early access and have in the description that the game is unstable and not fully optimized and to expect  poor game experience at times .  This would solve alot of the negative reviews as well or people being cheated out of their money . Conclusion : I dont regret of buying the game , i love survival games and this one has huge potential . Devs seem really active and responding  for now .  Do I expect to be more polished and  stable and  progress done ? Yes ( for now ), it is  in  very early stage . Is it worth of buying the game  in current state ? I would say wait, unless you are willing to go through some ups and downs .  and you have really good pc and hosting the games . Solo worth it  or playable. Yes but it ll be extremely grindy and long missions for little reward at the end . It's a good game to listen or watch podcasts but once you get used to the mechanics . You would be thrown into ICARUS  without any basic tutorials or help and it may be a bit frustrating . This is longest constructive feedback/review I wrote for a game on steam and its been 18 years since  I joined Steam . So I do care about the game but not in the current state . I burned out from last mission and  going to take a break until patches or improvements . Buy it on your own risk  :)

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: I, literally, stopped playing this game because of it's stupidity in application. Instead of using sprinklers to water crops, you have to use ultra-expensive things like hydroponic crop plots. Scope attachments (at this point) don't even have scopes. And there are various other things that annoy me but you, literally, have to invest DAYS (real time) to get where this game really starts to work right and then, at that point, you have to go to the other side of the map because you've mined the necessary resources away.THe bugs are INSANE and people, who play with me, lose their experience when going back to the station and i let them all go before me because the game cuts people out if the host goes first. I'm just TIRED of it.This game is not a fresh concept, it's an old concept with a slightly different twist. It's survival with air you (the entire world around you can breathe it) can't breathe. No zombies, just you against nature with a really pointless element....you can't breathe the air. Oh you can drink the water, eat all the plant and animal life...but you can't breath the air.The animals are, literally, stupid and i mean stupid for "animals". They will stand there and let a predator kill them even when standing inside a safety area. And where are the "true" fences to keep the Moas in?The space suit is a STUPID mechanic in this game.It is, literally, "man vs wild".I honestly feel like the "space suit" / non-breathable air was a wasted mechanic in the game. I would remove it because it both, gets in the way and makes no sense compared to the other things you can do naturally.This game is cloud saved so anyone can come in and play the game while another player is gone. However, if you "end" the mission early (and leave the other players behind) they all don't get their share of experience so, don't do that. Whoever "hosts" the mission should be the last person to leave the planet.The extreme weather is REALLY impressive and a major factor you have to deal with. Also, if you're hosting a game, be sure to leave LAST and make sure all other players have made it back to the space station first.There are a few cons like the map has "cracks" in it where timber falls into the ground and you lose it sometimes and not all the game mechanics are worked out (May 2022, and things may change in time) so don't let that sway you, it's still a good game.Like in a zombie game, stealth and head-shots count...remember that.There is one thing i find INCREDIBLY stupid about this game, the penalty if you even fall unconscious.Actually, there are probably a lot of coders (with survival games) that might really hate this project because it makes a bunch of them useless, it has everything they have but it far less complicated than some survival games mechanics-wise. Finally, it gets to be a tireless grind and you get tired of this game pretty easily after a couple of weeks.Note: I do not allow comments because this is a "review". A review with comments is no longer a review, but a conversation hence comments defeat the purpose of you telling how "you" perceive the game and not others attempting to question your point of view. A personal review should remain that person's take and no one else's, that's why they have forums....do it there.A word about the coding of this game: I've got games that are more graphically intense than this game and this game "drags" my computer so it's not coded well. When you can compare games that require more power and have better graphics doing well, the hardware isn't the issue.That being said, a true "Gamer" never let's another gamer sway them, what you like or perceive might be totally different from what another likes and there's nothing wrong with that. Play YOUR way.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is a session-based PvE survival crafting game for up to eight co-op players. You play as a prospector, sent to the planet Icarus to mine for valuable resources. Each session has a time limit, and you must return to your orbital station before your oxygen runs out.Icarus is a beautiful game, with stunning visuals and a vast, procedurally generated world to explore. The survival mechanics are challenging but fair, and there's a lot of depth to the crafting system. There are also a variety of faction missions to complete, which add an extra layer of complexity and challenge.One of the things I really like about Icarus is the sense of progression. Each session, you'll earn new resources and blueprints, which will allow you to build better gear and structures. This makes you feel like you're constantly making progress, even if you don't always succeed in your missions.Icarus is also a lot of fun to play with friends. The co-op experience is really well-done, and it's great to work together to build bases, complete missions, and survive the harsh environment.Overall, I'm really enjoying Icarus. It's a challenging and rewarding survival crafting game with a lot of depth. I highly recommend it to fans of the genre.Here are some of the pros of Icarus:Beautiful visualsVast, procedurally generated worldChallenging but fair survival mechanicsDeep crafting systemVariety of faction missionsSense of progressionGreat co-op experienceHere are some of the cons of Icarus:Can be buggy at timesSome balance issuesSteep learning curveOverall, Icarus is a great survival crafting game with a lot to offer. If you're looking for a challenging and rewarding experience, I highly recommend it.I had Google Bard write all that, but anyway, it's a cracking game.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - some missions are literally impossible to finish. There's too many system critical bugs that makes completing missions impossible. Drop points don't spawn, collection points don't spawn, drop points turn invisible, etc. There's also no way I've found to fix these bugs. I've tried returning to main menu, using unstuck, restarting the game, restarting my computer, nothing.What hurts even more is that so many missions take more than an hour to complete. Not that long ago I did a mission that required me to collect a lot of metals to drop off in 3 separate locations, all of which were pretty far from one another. The first pod spawned, no problem, finished the first pod, the second pod didn't spawn. By the time I reached the second spawn I was 1.5 hours into the mission. Hour and a half, gone. Tried fixing it (restart game/computer, etc), nothing. Had to abandon the mission.On top of all of this, missions being impossible to complete happens so often, I'm talking about like 30-50% of the time, which is insane for a 'complete' game. degradation requires clients restart the game every day or 2 to recover FPS.- Major P2P host performance issues, better to run a dedicated on same machine as a client.- Supply stockpile missions _childDocuments_.review: This isn't your usual survival game -- you go on missions, and the environment gets wiped between each mission. Your character keeps their progression, so you'll go through the early stages faster over time. It's intended for co-op play, but is playable solo -- but your character will never be the master of all trades. It's PvE, with the world's weather, highly aggressive wildlife, and basic needs (food, water, shelter, breathable air) forming your opposition. This is a game for the patient; the first mission completes almost immediately, but you're better off spending more time on it to level up and develop skills. For future missions, again take your time and PREPARE for the tasks/final fights/whatever.I *highly* recommend watching some let's plays or livestreams before you jump into this. It will help you understand what's going on and vastly improve your odds of survival.

The game really tries to push prospectors around the map but, too often it's in a very tedious and unfun way.Luckily, there has been some great changes over the past couple years. A lot of it was driven by demand from players. Especially the big change from real-time missions to game-time. And doubly so for the persistent open-world. The building system is pretty smooth and has had plenty of additions to make the game much more interesting, especially in the persistent open-world mode.If you're a hardcore fan of RPG survival builders, I'd say it's definitely worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is a great game with immense potential, and I’ve spent 60 hours enjoying it. However, despite having a good time, there are numerous minor quality-of-life issues that are quite obvious, but I’ll get to those later. So why am I giving it a negative review despite everything? Because I really want the developers to address these issues. The main one that killed my experience is performance. The game's optimization is terrible. Even on the lowest settings, I can get 100 FPS initially, but after a while, it drops to 40-50 FPS. On top of that, there are constant stutters and hitches when traveling through the open world, especially when exploring caves. After 60 hours, my patience wore thin. Optimization should be the developers' top priority.Another issue is the lack of small, obvious features. For instance, why can’t we bind Quick Stack to Storage? There’s a bind for Loot All but not for Quick Stack. Why is there no hotkey for repairing items, forcing us to use the context menu instead? Why can’t we craft items with a shortcut, like right-clicking, instead of selecting the item and then clicking craft? Why aren’t there binds to give commands to tamed animals? And why can we only split item stacks in half instead of taking a specified amount? These small things add up and become very annoying. It's disappointing that the developers release weekly updates but haven't added such simple features yet.The third issue is the building system. I spent most of my time constructing a decent-looking base, and I have to say, the building system in this game is terrible compared to others I’ve encountered, like Valheim, Satisfactory, or Enshrouded. Icarus’s building system is the worst I’ve come across. If you want to build a creative base, be prepared for hours of frustration. The current system is only good for constructing quick, blocky structures.Aside from these issues, the game is great and has huge potential. But in its current state, there are a lot of problems. I understand now why people are frustrated when the developers release new paid DLCs with more unoptimized content.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe it is me...Broken on launch. Co-op game with broken co-op. Had numerous problems not only connecting with friends, but then getting stuck in mission and unable to close out when playing in a friends server. They are fixing these issues and I am sure that will all be worked out soon enough. However, it does not resolve some fundamental game design issues that I am failing to understand. I will add this - I am not an avid Survival genre fan. Valheim was the first one I really enjoyed so perhaps I'm not the target audience here. This game is utterly boring. It is beautiful to look at and a graphical treat. But it entirely lacks purpose for the crafting/building component. Drop to the planet, craft/build shelter, tools, weapons. When the mission is over, go back to the space station (you never see), and return to the planet for the next mission and all your stuff is gone. No shelter. Wiped clean. At first I thought this was a biproduct of jumping between co-op 'attempts' above, and then I learned last night it is baked into the design. This is baffling to me. I have a base of ops...without being able to consistently build/upgrade this base of ops from mission to mission. Why am I even doing it in the first place? Why am I wasting time/energy on building and upgrading my skill tree, or trying to get better materials? Why do I need to advance beyond a basic wood shelter to complete 'redundant' missions? Last session I was shocked when I dropped into a friends session to play with them, only to find they skipped building a shelter in the first place and just ran around completing the mission objectives. Perhaps I/we are not far enough into the game to answer these questions, but after reading another review from someone further along, they had the same questions with 10x the hours into the game than I do.The beauty of a game setting/graphics cannot carry a game by itself. This is why indie games with 1980's graphics continue to upset large studios spending millions to develop pretty baubles. A game needs to have fun, and/or rewarding play (or flat out insidiously addictive 'loot box') at it's foundation or it is not worth playing. Icarus is lacking purpose other than the rather boring missions. Repeat the same mission you just did, but this time we'll 'insta-spawn' a tougher animal for you to fight. Ninja-bears, ninja-wolves, ninja-cougars, that suddenly appear out of nowhere when you drop your survey machine. Makes no sense other than trying to jump scare the player, or a lazy way to make a game more challenging. In a survival game based so much around 'realistic' play/crafting/science, Icarus lacks realism when it comes to any reason to build, or how/why the creatures in the game respond to you being there doing your thing in the first place.There is great potential here in Icarus, and I was really looking forward to this game from the moment I heard about it. I just don't think it is the game for me. Perhaps it will improve with time, but I'm having trouble seeing that happen without major fundamental changes to how the game operates at it's core. Again, this is only my perspective and perhaps I just do not understand the vision.This may be at the root of my experience - when I first learned of Icarus, I thought the concept was - 'terraforming went bad, you are stuck on the space station and the only way to escape back  to 'earth' is to do drops and mine materials to build components for the space station or a ship back home. Storms ravaging Icarus and limited O2, etc keep you heading back to the station rather than staying on the planet all the time.'This is not at all what I am seeing with the game and consequently maybe my expectations were misplaced. Good luck on your drops.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll break this up into an introduction, a pro, and a con, section for ease of consumption.IntroductionsAs a player, I have experience with a lot of the survival franchise as well as building/management sim genre. Titles of note would be Rust and Valheim as they relate closest to this title. Bottom line summary i could provide for Icarus is that it is meant to be unforgiving and at times daunting to survive, but does so in the oddest of ways which can sometimes be frustrating.Pros  Visually this game has a lot going for it. Its rich, textured, layered, and offers a lot of visual attractiveness. Coupled along with this is in depth and at times complicated crafting/building trees to which the opportunity to excel is catered to the player.   This game also offers a REAL weather system within it that does actual damage to you, your buildings, and your environment, which other titles do not offer. This weather can include mild rain showers to catastrophic lightning storms and damaging winds. Lightning to hit your home and set it on fire, and winds can blow apart of your wood building components. Weather also occurs in the other biomes (to which there are effectively 3 in this game) and each carry with it risks to themselves to be mitigated.  This game also offers a resource management system which impacts both your crafting, your repairing capability of crafted items, and your very survival. Not only do you have to manage your inventory of food whether its hunted or gathered, but you also have to manage the core 3 life essences to also survive; Oxygen, Water, and Hunger. Access and ability to have or maintain Oxygen and Water are core resource management components which will alter your ability to explore for more time, or even survive if a weather event strikes while you are away from shelter.Cons  While the wildlife to hunt is vast, the predatory wildlife is limited and honestly not very thought out. This environment is "earth like" and in fact the whole world is basically Earth except for 1-2 animals. In the Forest biome, in particular, you encounter wolves, boars, and bears, as "predatory" animals. While the wolves and boars are easily managed with your introductory tier weapons and gearing, Bears are the exception. Bears will find you and attack you from long ranges, in a charging fashion. You'll often hear of this from other players and refer to them as "heat seeking bears" or "intercontinental ballistic bears", as their conal visibility can often clip through rock walls and other. Bears, themselves, are armored tanks of pain and their "level" number to them does not truly reflect the threat they pose. Even a level 2 bear can shred you in 3 hits, with cloth armor on. Encounter a level 30+ bear, without having fur armor in Tier 2 unlocked, and its a death sentence most of the time as they can 2 hit you. Bear can teleport up mountains to get to you, and nearly instantly climb obstacles to reach you, like spider-bears. then there is a HP they carry. your basic bear will have at LEAST 800 HP on board, with 30+ level bears being closer to 1500 HP. Meaning unless you crit every hit with your stone weapons, they will break before you take the bear down. Same will go for Bone weapons like a spear. This only gets worse in the snow biome with Polar Bears, as often you'll find that they have 2000HP or more. Meaning the only effective survival of bears is generally to avoid them, which at times is impossible.  I spent a long paragraph on the bears because in honestly that is the ONLY real threat in this game once you leave tutorial. The game, otherwise, is quite sparse on what it offers. The story is non existent, and many of the prospect missions can be done without ever actually establishing a large built "base". The premise of being a space explorer gets lost quickly when you land and are faced with building what is essentially a Stone Age hovel and tools each time as your builds are gone once you finish a prospect. You cannot carry back with you advanced tools such as iron or steel axes, and are forced to start again each prospect. While there is a currency system as a reward, most are not worth unlocked as within an hour of landing you can build better. Bottom line  Its a hardcore survival sim which gets old quick and tedious even faster. While the building options are nice, because there lacks quite a bit of content to make your alien world alien, it may as well be called a Rockie Mountain Simulator with a Space-X suit on. While it has potential to grow into a great title, right now it falls a bit flat on achieving what it sought out to do.  I do recommend this game for survival fans, but understand its shelf life is probably locked to 40-60 hours before you put the title up for another.

_childDocuments_.review: I love challenging games, I really do. I'm particularly a sucker for the open world survival craft category. It's almost an "auto purchase" for me, and it takes a lot for me to really recommend people against even just trying one, but the payoff versus sacrifice balance that is stubbornly insisted by Icarus' gameplay quickly reveals itself to be severely lacking in reward.It's almost fascinating to me, at this point, to try and guess as to what drove the business-level decisions that directed Icarus' development. There's no in-app purchases. There's no financial incentive for them to punish the player. Typically games that make heavy use of a "permadeath" feature include some kind of long-term payoff that remains, despite the short term loss. In this game, I would have expected that to be the characters you create.Sure, you've got to get in and out in a certain amount of time. Sure, in some cases, that might include you having to permanently delete any work you've done on building a settlement in a world over a period of, in some cases, between 2 weeks and a month. Sure, that amount of time is calculated in _real life hours_, not actual game time, so you better make damn sure you're not starting a new mission right before you go on a vacation or suddenly get swamped at work.If leveling characters in this game wasn't such an immense grind, it wouldn't be so bad... buttttt it is. It's just not fun. I'm still playing the damn game, but I simultaneously hate it, and I feel like it would be a much better game if one of these aspects was not present, and that's just frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: Icarus is an odd, nonintuitive game that seems to hope players will give up and ask for a refund within the first 2 hours. It is an adequate survival simulation, severely mangled by fundamentally flawed concepts and failed innovations. I am going to overall not recommend it for the general gaming audience, but I will make a very restrictive recommendation for a specific demographic: Buy it only if it is !!! deeply !!! discounted on sale and you are a seasoned survival game enthusiast who either 1) is willing to grope and grind trying to figure out the (often) baffling way it works, or 2) is willing to have other players explain how it works, spoiling the challenge but leaving the grind.I chose route 1 after seriously debating whether I should simply refund. There were a lot of turnoffs soon after installing. The geriatric actors spewing game lore in video clips was weird. The unskippable opening computer art school demo reel was weird. The character models were not just weird, but the ugliest I have ever seen. By the time the gruff, Ol' West grizzled voice over started giving the least helpful tutorial advice in history, I was wondering if everything I had seen so far was 4 different concepts from a pitch meeting that asked the lead developer, "Which one of these disparate approaches best represents the theme and style of our future game?" To which the response was, "Yes."The concept that even the most basic first steps require unlocking techs without knowing what they will do is flawed. Choosing the wrong techs can hobble you before you get the basics, as can poorly timed first spawns leaving you at the mercy of creatures or the elements. The concept that early missions keep returning you to exactly the same regenerated map made the game seem laughably small and amateurish. Everything screamed - this game has not been thought out and is still in alpha.The literal game changer for me was switching to open world. Persistence brought meaning that regurgitated mission worlds did not. The switch was enough for me to keep the game and get a couple of weeks entertainment before the later game flaws became apparent. The primary being grind as technology scales. Many multiples of time and resources will be required to get negligible gains such as a +7% output bonus, so that keeping old tech is frequently easier and more efficient.I think the spirit killer for me though was when I finally looked up something about how the game works. I had a simple question for Google. Is there a way for trees to grow back? The answer was no. I had many small bases as I wandered further and further from my starting point, but looked forward to returning to my home base. I had deliberately tried leaving the environment there untouched to be more picturesque, but constant storms blowing and burning down all the forests around me left the landscape barren. The idea that this had happened simply because the storms occur where you are there to observe them was depressing. Persistence was never what they had in mind. With this decision, I think the developers are telling you - if you won't play this game the way we want you to, we're going to burn it all down.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT since the launch of New Frontiers:Devs have now released the promised content at £25 extra, they want your help as they're not a AAA developer and want people to leave good reviews.  This is why my review has changed from good to bad.  The original game STILL isn't full optimised or fixed and has incredibly stupid missions like trying to fix a house, whilst fighting off bear cubs (This makes no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense, just like a lot of the random animal spawns in the game).Well done, devs; in your pursuit of getting good reviews and appealing to your audience for good feedback, you've done the opposite and pushed those who supported you from the start away and I doubt very much that new players will want to spend money on such a poorly monetised scam of a project.And everyone said how much promise this game had at the start!!!  Which of your devs has their head furthest up their backsides that they couldn't see this coming?LOOK at the cons in my original review when I did recommend the game!!========================Just to start off, I thought I would mention previous reviews and say that I completely understand the frustration of others, but I do not believe the game is in such a bad condition that it warrants a negative review.Sure, the game has elements missing that were shown in the trailers and the game doesn't feel it's in a releasable condition, when looking at certain areas.  Also, the optimisation is quite the problem; players shouldn't have to research settings just to get the game to look acceptable and I still haven't been able to get rid of some of the horrible graphic glitches.CONS:In terms of the negative, you have the optimisation issues and missing features, as well as some mechanics that are baffling-ly unrealistic when compared with other areas, where realism has been a focal part of its design.  I can confirm that the whole 'getting pneumonia from a cave, when you can breathe underwater' is a bit baffling and also that your stone base can withstand massive storms, yet a wolf can bite it apart in little to no time, is also a headscratcher. DON'T unlock chairs, unless you want them for their aesthetics.. presently, you can't sit on them and watch the weather, like I wanted to.There is quite the limited character creation.Rocks and ores can clip through the map and other static objects, making it impossible to finish mining them.Nearly all the enemies in this game are just Earth animals and not alien, such as the cave worm.The farming in this game is very unsatisfying; it seems a simple premise but is quite confusing and it can cause you to lose a lot of crops.  I collected a fair whack of vegetables and thought I would separate them into different plots and they'd do their thing, with me checking every now and again, but then you check and they say 'no seed' even though it's full of vegetables in the input slot, whereas others appear exactly the same and do say they have a seed.  Then you just end up losing the hundreds of vegetables you put in there in the first place.  You may as well just go around collecting veg for the supply mission, because I'm sure I've picked up far more than the required amount, just in trying to grow them in plots.  I think it needs some more thought or an overhaul.There's something really weird going on with the storage in this game; most people use crafting stations to keep items, because the actual craftable crates hold far less.  The ice box only holds 12 items, meaning you have to make quite a lot of them to keep items for the aforementioned supply missions.One thing I do not like about the previous 2 points is that you end up having lots of plots and lots of fridges, which not only takes up a lot of space, but feels unsatisfying an unrealistic; this easily breaks immersion.PROS:With the positives, the assets and world look great and the talent tree and crafting tree are extensive and bountiful with interesting options.  The music is great; it reminds me a bit of Satisfactory.The options of game modes/missions has been complained about, especially with the permadeath feature, but I think a lot of people are being unrealistic and harsh about it.  There is a sandbox mode, where you can take your time, there are missions that last 30 days, where there isn't an objective, other than just to explore and there are simple, relaxing missions that take 2 weeks, where you can spend time on your base, exploring etc. and you don't need to rush about.  You can have multiple characters, so you can spec their blueprints differently and use them for different missions and the permadeath feature feels more like you have expendable, recyclable characters that you take risks with, when completing more dangerous missions.  I disagree that this is a bad thing, as if you did the same as any other game, it would just be a bogstandard survival game, like any other.A lot of the mechanics, their animations and sounds are really satisfying; especially when you crit and one shot an enemy and you get a slow-mo cutscene of them being killed, ala Fallout 4.The weather events are amazing and immersive and can be fun to sit .. ahem .. stand and watch.TENTATIVE:There are some things other players complain about that are warranted and further balancing is probably a good idea.  The weather events, as good as they are, do tend to happen quite a lot and a lot of them are wild storms that will probably batter your base, if you have less than stone parts.  The issue with this, is a lot of the time, you are racing against the clock for getting back to your base before dark and can end up hiding in a rock for 15mins and cause you to lose valuable time, or need food, water or oxygen in a pinch, which can scupper plans and irritate you, to the point you feel like all you're doing is waiting about, re-organising your plans.  There are also flash storms that turn nasty quite quickly and don't give you enough time to make a shelter.  Whilst I really like the weather system, it can be the most disruptive element to playing through a session.  If you are away from your base, trying to get to an objective which is quite far away and a storm comes, you're torn between trying to get back and repair your base or whether to carry on.  This feature can be quite punishing.Even though I did mention the enemies in this game being normal Earth animals, there is the suggestion these are placed there by humans and genetically modified, which somewhat explains that, so perhaps some lore is missing that would go further to explaining this.Concluding, whilst the game is priced like a discounted, released game, I think it is probably a fair reflection of what you can get from this game, depending on your playstyle and expectations.  The game feels like it is not finished and more of an early access game, HOWEVER, the amount of work that has gone into this game and its different facets is plentiful and would be far far far more than what you would expect from an early access game.  It's just unfortunate that releasing an unpolished, unfinished game can have people shouting 'SCAM' from the rooftops.  Yes, it isn't finished but what it has to offer and its potential is probably worth the £24 price tag it currently has.If you like a chilled world, base building, crafting, hunting and exploring, this game is a must.  You just have to be quite patient with the mechanics and developers, for the time being.

_childDocuments_.review: Addendum - After 1 year of development and me getting a new graphics card I can recommend this as an innovative and enjoyable Sci-Fi survival game that let's you play in multiple different ways - each with their pluses and minuses. If you enjoy the genre I think it has something to offer and I've had well more than my money's worth in enjoyment from the game.---Original review below---I really want to like this game - but it's an early access title being marketed as a full release. It's grindy - which is okay for a survival game, but there are many design decisions that don't make sense and have a negative impact on quality of life. The biggest of these is you have to start completely from scratch on each mission - nothing survives from your previous drops so you have you tech up which can take 3-5 hours solo for Tier 3 and 5-8 hours Tier 4 which you need for multiple missions. This is a core part of the game's identity (which is fine, makes it unique) but the tech tree seems optimized for permanent bases rather than this wipe-after-each-drop mission approach (based on the time to tech up). The talent and tech trees are very hit or miss with large swaths of them being completely useless with no reason to take them (I'm looking at you Thatch building tree), talents not working as intended. The meta-progression revolves around buying tools you can take with you each drop but these offer very small improvements and are often not worth the meta-currency you earn on the missions. There are expensive items that are worse than cheaper items, and many items that make no sense to buy (high tech coal? you can mine it in 30 seconds if you know where to look, high tech campfire? I can make one in less than a minute after drop).The graphics are extremely demanding and unless you have a recent GPU you will need to run it at low settings and put up with potato graphics.Overall, the game is fun to play most of the time, however it is at an early access level of development so due to it's billing as a "full release" I cannot endorse it in its current state.Pros:Nice graphics if you can run itNovel concept - session survivalCool loreCons:Poor balancingConfusing game mechanics that don't make senseNo incentive to craft Tier 4 tech because it will all get wipedEdit/Update: Given the pace of updates and the quality of the updates I'm very optimistic about the future of the game - if you're on the fence about buying check back in 1-2 months. My hope is that the game will reach a full release level of balancing and content in the next 2-3 months at which time I'll happily endorse it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to recommend this game as it stands today, based on the way I play it. To date I have played exclusively solo and in offline - and solo play is unnecessarily brutal. Here's a fairly unordered list of my personal frustrations:- My primary frustration is that this game has an incredible amount of grind baked into its basic gameplay loop. The game has a sprawling tech tree that's significantly larger than any other survival game that I have played, yet everything in it is locked off behind levelling. Each level you go up gives you three unlock points and levelling up is fairly slow. It takes *ages* to level up to even basic stone age equipment. Hunting seems the fastest and least boring way to level up so prepare for some serious animal genocide.- With a new character, it's virtually impossible to not spend the first few nights forcibly awake and in complete darkness. You cannot sleep without a bedroll and a bedroll requires quite a lot of materials, including fur. You have to kill several animals to have enough fur to be able to build one - oh and of course once you have, the bedroll must be in shelter and next to a lit fire with fuel. None of this is explained when you first play and I spent 3 or 4 nights this same way, I bet that a lot of people end up refunding the game in this period. It is possible to cheese shelter by finding a large enough rock and making a tiny cave, but the game engine does cope well if you do this.- Other survival games let you build static light sources that don't require fuel. Not this game. Night time in Icarus is DARK, you can't equip a torch and a tool at the same time so unless you cheese your gamma setting then night time is effectively unplayable. You need to be able to sleep through the night.- If you die - which in this game means being downed and not revived by another player within a time limit - then all your gear drops at your death location and you lose all XP for your current level. Of course in solo there is no revival, so every death is a huge loss, especially if you're miles from your spawn point (bedroll).- Random death happens in this game a lot. There are a ton of wolves roaming around, the game will throw random weather events that can seriously weaken you and make you even more susceptible to wolves and bears. Bears are difficult to deal with if one gets the jump on you.- There is a level cap that effectively means you can't unlock everything, I presume to force some sort of specialisation. This makes some sense for multiplayer, but for solo players this is insane and there's no respec. All those points I wasted in thatched housing are lost.- Wooden structures in this game are incredibly weak to fire and having an entire base burn to the ground in minutes - even during torrential rain - is a common occurrence. On one occasion I had a random bear attack me at my shack. With the bear smashing away at the wall, one of his swipes somehow managed to start a fire from my fire pit, putting me in the position of having to choose between fighting the bear or the fire. By the time the bear was dead, much of my hut was on fire and I died trying to put it out. The game then forces you to wait 30s to respawn AND drops you some distance away with absolutely nothing, so by the time I got back there was nothing left. Don't even get me started on thatched housing.- Stone buildings are far more resistant to both fire and the elements. However, they require iron nails and that's far more laborious to obtain. Nails require ingots and an anvil, the anvil requires an absurd number of ingots (20), ingots require ore and a forge and the forge must be in shelter... so you need to build a wooden hut first. Not to mention that ore only occurs in caves and they are always full of respawning blue worms that fire gooey blobs.- Building a stone structure is a major undertaking for a solo player, which make this games core gameplay feature all the more baffling - every 'session' completely resets the world and forces you to rebuild from scratch. Grind and repetition are not just gameplay machanics, they *are* the game.The only real progression in this game comes through the various unlocks - the tech tree, the perk system and the 'space points' awarded on mission completion that allow you to research and then buy tools to bring on a drop. The progression within any particular session that comes through crafting your way up to better equipment is all transitory, lost as soon as you leave... which is a shame as it's the most rewarding.This game could be amazing if it would let you take on all the missions one by one without having to leave the planet. I understand that the developers wanted to make a game that's fundamentally different to other survival games like The Forest or Subnautica, but they've done so by making an arbitrary and inexplicable change to the gameplay, whilst leaving most of the rest of the trappings intact. The 'Space Points' sticking plaster is not enough of a remedy, at least let the Player unlock something that allows them to leapfrog the early repetition and move straight to better equipment. In my hypothetical version of the game, you could only allow the player to cash in space points when they chose to leave and any return could leave them miles from their base. I wish this would be allowed for offline play, especially since offline and online characters are completely separated.All of this is a real shame, because the basic survival mechanics in this game are great. Chopping trees, hunting wildlife, the illnesses and remedies, the weather system, the fire mechanics, the extensive tech tree, the excellent and realistic graphics and the hand crafted map all form the basis of a truly great survival game. Unfortunately it all been ruined for me by a major design decision and a few minor ones that have fundamentally ruined the experience. I had fun on my 20-odd hours in the game and it's great value at it's current price... but I'm stopping playing for now and I'm recommending friends don't buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: First, disclosure: I played most of the beta weekends and have been looking forward to this game for a long while. I think the majority of the negative reviews are because the game is not necessarily un-optimized, but because you shouldn't have to dig through and manually figure out your graphics settings so you can get >30 fps with non-potato graphics. People who find a new game are going to want to load up, adjust settings to low/medium/high/etc and then have a streamlined experience (and this just doesn't exist at the moment). I think this is where they screwed up; those of us that played the beta weekends or are super into the game concept are going to tweak the settings to get a good experience, and there is a lot of material out there on how to get there with "ok" computers. I think they missed this crucial step during dev/testing so that the game automatically loaded with lower settings (but good frames) and then could be scaled up by the user as they became more familiar with it. There are still some bugs here and there, and the rigging/animation is not great, but the core game is fantastic. Should they have released as early access? Probably. Is it worth $30 and a bit of troubleshooting? Absolutely.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit 3:I still can't recommend the game. It wants to be fun, and aspects off the game are fun, but overall, it's just so poorly thought out and nothing is cohesive or makes sense. Why do you get pneumonia in a cave when you're wearing a space suit with an oxygen supply? Why do we eat plants that use air we can't? Why are the local fauna exactly like earth's and can breathe the air and we can't? Why can't a wolf walk up a rock? (Bad AI). Here's hoping in another year some of this may be fixed. Performance has definitely gotten worse since launch though, moving backwards there! Edit 2:I've been watching the updates, and they are on update 22 as of this edit. They are actively working on making the game less fun and I am really starting to believe that the developers don't actually play games like most people if this is their version of fun or making their game more fun. All that has been done is bug fixes, a few QOL changes and sadly make the game more grindy for no reason. At this point, I don't foresee ever wanting to come back to Icarus with their current design decisions and direction. Edit:Coming back to Icarus, I can't recommend the game anymore. Game just isn't enjoyable as a mostly solo player who occasionally may have people to play with. Give it a year at least before you touch it and maybe it will be a more enjoyable cohesive experience that just isn't "difficult" for no reason.  Original:I played through the beta and now launch. Launch has been pretty smooth. They've done a few tweaks since it launched causing a little downtime, but I'd rather they work on servers and keeping them healthy sooner rather than later. The game is really pretty. RTX and DLSS if you've got the hardware and it's just beautiful. If you don't have a higher end machine, the game runs pretty well on moderate setting and RTX OFF. People need to be realistic about their hardware judging from some of the reviews I've read.The survival aspects of the game are very well balanced, and you progress early on at a decent pace. The balance does feel like it's better playing in a group, and having a group mentality when it comes to spending your blueprint and talent points. Chop trees for 20 minutes and you're level 5 on the first training map and you're good to go from there. Everything is pretty self explanatory. Hunt for meat, put meat in some type of fire, eat meat. Drink dirty water, potentially get sick, clean water is good (rain catcher). Mine stuff, smelt stuff, make better stuff, go to harder areas, so on and so forth.The environmental survival is pretty brutal. If you watch the short movie they did on the backstory on YouTube (it's about 20 minute action and really well done), it talks about the brutal storms on Icarus and how destructive they are. They really did a nice job of making the players feel just how powerful the storms on Icarus are. The game is session based, so you aren't meant to build something fancy and this is your forever home. You're going to Icarus for a mission, so you're building to survive. Don't get comfortable. Your stuff will be destroyed. Get in, get your mission done, and get out! There are areas to "free" build, but I haven't explored that aspect yet as they are new with the launch. I will update once I get to put my hands on it for a while. I think Icarus has a very promising future, and the devs seem very dedicated to supporting the game going forward and listening to feedback. This is a great start and I can't wait to see where it goes from here. I'm confident they will continue to get better optimization as time goes, balance changes, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a love-hate relationship with Icarus. In addition to the ~55 hours displayed here, I also have 40-50 hours from the beta version. It has been a journey. At times it was fun and at times I was so frustrated that I nearly quit the game forever.All in all, I do enjoy Icarus, especially now that a lot of the time pressure has been removed by changing the mission timer to only count down if you’re actually playing. It is not a perfect game and can get boring and grindy if you spend too much time in the same biome/on one mission. But I think it’s a good game to play every now and then to get my survival fix or if I’m feeling in the mood for mindless grinding while listening to a podcast/video/stream.Currently, Icarus is getting new updates every week or so. This can be both good and bad.I appreciate that the devs are actively listening to feedback and seeking to improve the game. The reason I nearly quit Icarus was the way the mission timer used to work. Previously, you were unable to stop the timer from counting down even if the game wasn’t running. It would count down in real time and punish you for having a life outside of Icarus. This has since been addressed in an update. Now, the timer only counts down if you’re actually playing. What a relief!Updates keep the game interesting and give you new things to look forward to. But this also means you never know what state the game will be in next time you play. I haven’t played in a little over a month and there have been 6 updates since. Almost every time I play, I have to adjust to new changes (after waiting for the game to update). Once I feel like I’ve figured out the best/most efficient way to do something, it might change at any point in the future and make my strategies obsolete.Sometimes it feels like the release deadline was too ambitious and that most these changes were meant to take place before the full release, but are only being worked on now.I like survival games. I like games where you run across the map and discover new things with every area you pass through. Icarus sure makes you run a lot. But the planet doesn’t have much to offer once you’ve seen all 3 biomes. There is no variation in flora within a biome, no interesting structures from past civilizations to explore, nothing. Just the same landscape wherever you go. It looks impressive in the beginning, very idyllic and screenshot-worthy. But it gets boring after 50+ hours. The world feels pretty empty.Part of the problem is that planet Icarus is too earth-like. It is not our Earth (?) but it feels almost identical. A huge missed opportunity. Icarus could have been a creative and distinctly alien planet like the one in Subnautica. This would have made running across the map a lot more interesting. Or the game could have been a dystopian vision of what our Earth might turn into. But it is neither. Icarus is essentially just Earth with a few more natural disasters and some (only some!) foreign life forms.I really wish there was more of a story to the game. We don’t learn much about Icarus or the main character and are left with more questions than answers. What happened to Icarus? Why is it so earth-like? Who is this exploitative company that is sending me to recover “exotics” yet won’t even grant me proper equipment for my trips?A lot of things don’t make sense if you think about them too hard… E.g., if every mission takes place in roughly the same area, why are none of my own structures still there? I still have the same knowledge and skills so story-wise I am the same person and I have been on Icarus before!I’ve seen other reviews mention how grindy Icarus can get and this kind of goes hand in hand with the boring landscape. Maybe I’m in the minority but I actually don’t mind the grindiness. Mindless grinding can be fun. I think it feels rewarding to work towards the goal of crafting a new item by grinding for materials. It really comes down to your preferences.A minor detail but I had to mention it. It’s just so fun and easy to snipe animals with a bow. It never gets old and I love doing it. I’m not sure if those stealth multipliers even do much but it’s very satisfying.The session-based approach is interesting. When I play survival games, starting anew is more fun to me than late-game stuff. A game designed around starting over is an idea worth exploring. The extreme weather is also a fun twist. It adds tension and increases the feeling of temporariness.The building mechanics are alright. The structures themselves look a bit basic but placing them is easy and not nearly as frustrating as in The Forest, which has the worst building mechanics I have ever encountered in a survival game so I’m using it as an anti-benchmark.Icarus isn’t really the game for living out your architectural dreams though. The extreme weather conditions will damage weaker structures and since regular missions end with you leaving the area after your time runs out, you will not be able to keep your homes forever. It makes you wonder how much effort you should even put into building something nice. You can also build in Outposts, which do not have a timer and less extreme weather, but there’s little else to do in them and I assume resources are limited because they take place on a much smaller map.Tech and talent points are frustrating especially if you play alone. You can’t unlock all skills or perks with one character. The intention is that players make multiple specialized characters. But I don’t like that. I don’t like games with specialized character builds in general. I would much rather have one character that will eventually learn everything.Tech and especially talent points are limited. Talent points are hard/costly to revert and tech points cannot be redistributed at all. Not all talents or items are particularly useful either. Experimenting and discovering new skills or items feels heavily disincentivized. If you’re an overthinker like me, you’re gonna end up not spending your points on anything because you’re too scared of making the wrong decision and regretting it.

The Game is fun and lots of things to explore and do. the Missions are due to the Timer Intressting and the open world mode (which doesnt have a timer) is pretty fun and chill. Some things are done exactly how you sometimes wish it from many other games, in some things its a bit lacking. for example your lightsource doesnt require you to take it in your hand and can just be toggled on or off, a feature i wish many more survival games had. On the other hand though, "crafting from chests" which i think should be at least a option, just like in enshrouded, is sadly missing. luckly it doesnt take long until your main crafting is done at stations, which have their own inventory.i havent encounterd many bugs, but it sometimes feels like a early access in some aspects, luckly not many. the Combat is cool but also very simple, it doesnt take long until nothing is really a threat to you, which makes the game focus early on the crafting system. which is also shown by the amount of grind you have, from simple resources to the exotics and what you can buy with that aswell by the loads and loads of crafting stations and tools.the pretty big Techtree is simple and does what it should, nothing special but very helpful. what is super nice though, is when you play alone, you get also "solo" skill points and a new tab is available to you, which has many more skills to help you in your singleplayer adventure. you can carry your Character from world to world you make and if you play for example with someone else and go back to your singleplayer, your solo techtree is still intact. the system with the ship that takes you to the lobby, is a bit weird. basicly you make a world and when you start it, you can choose different starter things you can buy with exotics, which arent really needed, but super helpful. even doe i recommend buying at least the better suits with this purely ingame currency.sadly there is no way to pause the game, even in singleplayer. i recommend getting the "universal pause button" from github. ICARUS is a session-based PvE survival game for up to eight co-op players.

Endure a savage alien wilderness on Icarus, humanity's greatest mistake. Survive its brutal environment as you explore, harvest, craft and hunt while seeking your fortune.

From their orbital station, prospectors drop to the planet surface for limited time sessions, where they learn to endure the alien environment, complete faction missions and search for valuable exotic materials. Those that survive return to orbit as seasoned veterans, converting their exotics into advanced technology, and taking on ever more challenging drops with newfound knowledge. Those that get left behind... are lost forever.

name: Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception
detailed_description: When I awoke, there was snow⸺ Navigate the unforgiving wilderness of a turbulent new world! For almost two decades, this series of tactics-RPG visual novels has been beloved by Japanese fans for its spectacular music, art, characters, and story. Now it finally returns to its origins on PC. This sequel to Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen , first released more than a decade after the original game, is a great place to jump in to the series! _childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception and Mask of Truth are two halves of the same story and can't really be broken up. Thus, I will be reviewing them as a whole.This is my favorite VN of all time. The story, characters, sound, art, world, and gameplay all come together to make something magical and I think a lot of other people- even those new to the genre- will be able to enjoy it as well so I’m just going to gush about it and hope that convinces you to try it.Overall, the story will take you about 80 hours to get through on your first go. It seems like a lot, but that time is used very effectively. The characters are organically built up and the way I got attached to them over time is something I’ve only really felt the likes of in the original Mass Effect trilogy. The world gets very fleshed out with both ancient secrets and more mundane details that make it a very rich, interesting place to be. The story takes its time setting up big scenes so they hit like a truck and then paces itself with more lighthearted moments like wannabe Robin Hood pitching gold bars through people’s windows or giving a catgirl a suggestive backrub or getting drunk and stupid with your bros. Then it’s back to political maneuvering, destiny, war-crimes, mecha Godzilla battles, and suffering.The 2D artwork is absolutely gorgeous. The style is distinctive, the artists actually know anatomy, the sprawling landscapes make the world come alive, and the coloring is superb. The 3D sections were designed to run on the Vita so they’re chunky, but they don’t really distract. The screenshots can tell you more about this than words can, so I’ll move on.I still listen to the soundtrack on Spotify on a regular basis. Not every track is fully orchestrated, but even the parts where they didn’t splurge on the production values have excellent compositions that pull you further into the mood. When Utawarerumono pulls out all the stops, it won’t lose to any other video game OST and the way those songs are placed elevate the already good scenes into another world. It almost feels mean at some places. Like, I’m already an emotional basket case, why do you have to rob me of any semblance of dignity I have left by putting that on? On top of that, you have great voice acting for every line in the game. My only complaint about the audio is that one track, Sadame, is underused for how good it is.Utawarerumono has tactics gameplay sections but they’re by no means the main attraction since they only make up 10-20% of the playtime. They’re not going to dethrone tactics giants like Disgaea, but that’s not their job. Their job is to compliment the story, bring you into the action, and break up long sections of reading. For that purpose, they do quite well. If you’re a tactics veteran, there’s enough depth and polish to keep you entertained to the end. If you’re a tactics noob, there’s a turn rewind feature that will make sure you get through just fine. For major encounters, the gameplay is integrated surprisingly well with the story, and the final bosses of each part are made with a lot of care and extra touches so they don’t lag behind how bonkers the story is going.Mask of Deception has to focus a lot on world building and setup for story to come and doesn’t quite hit its stride, so it’s “only” great. Good news is, that it gets even better. There is also a bit of a hump in the middle where there’s a long slice-of-life section that drags a bit, even if each individual part is well done. However, you’re well rewarded for getting past it and it’s a minor inconvenience compared to the worst parts of other great games.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I have a love-hate relationship with this game. After the plot reaches its climax, the story is really exciting, and people can't wait to know the ending. However, the foreshadowing and daily life of this work in the early stage are a bit too long, and it is easy for most players to lose interest in the game in advance. The combination of traditional Japanese RPG and visual novel is a cool decision for players who have never been exposed to such games before, but the content of the game cannot be said to be perfect. The main storyline of this work took me about 20 hours. As a supplement and improvement to the details of the plot, Dream Arena also extends the RPG battle part of the game, suitable for those players who like SLG.The music and character design are both wonderful. This game is suitable for players who want to try a classic Japanese RPG game or a visual novel of fantasy world. However, the shortcomings of this work and the problem of the player group are destined to be difficult for this game and series of works to expand the audience.

_childDocuments_.review: Having heard great things about Utawarerumono, it was obvious that I was going to play it at some point. The only issue I personally had here is that I’m not really fond of playing on a handheld, although it offers a lot more mobility than a PC does. Lucky for me, Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception and Utawarerumono: Mask of Truth got a PC release after the PS Vita version launched back then in 2017. It was a surprise for me as well when the games got announced, along with the first game Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen. You see, Mask of Deception is a sequel to the first entry and takes place in the same world, although supposedly it’s possible to start with the, technically, second game, as long as Mask of Truth is played after it since it’s the grand finale and continues the second entry.Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception works with amnesia and thus, our protagonist suddenly wakes up without any prior memories. On top of that, it’s quite cold as he finds himself in a snowscape, but that’s not all, the world overall is unfamiliar and new to him. Suddenly, he gets attacked by a monster he never saw before. While trying to escape, a mysterious girl is appearing who saves his life, although there is something strange about her as she owns animal ears and a tail but seems human otherwise. Having found him, she feels responsible for him as he probably won’t be able to survive all alone. When she introduces herself as Kuon, she learns about his amnesia and decides on his name, Haku.The first thing that comes to my mind when I recall what I heard about Utawaremono would be heavily story-driven. Although I enjoyed its story and reveals a lot, which I never saw coming at all, most of the game tends to be rather light-hearted and full of slice-of-life scenes. The player will get through a lot of typical Japanese comedic scenes, just like in an average anime. Sometimes I found the scenes where Haku gets beaten up by several girls quite amusing and other times I found it was a little bit over the top but I suppose it was meant to be this way during picking up a lot of the harem anime premise. Whilst I didn’t expect this game to include that many slice-of-life scenes, it offers fan-service scenes as well in a, once again, comedic style.Yet Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception containing a lot of light-hearted scenes isn’t a bad thing at all, but it greatly contributed to the character development. You see, this entry is supposed to be a build-up for Mask of Truth, so it makes sense that the prior game functions as an introduction where it mostly gives their players a better understanding of their personalities. To be honest, I ended up sympathizing with each character and even when the game turns enemies into allies, I could still easily accept them due to their lovely personalities. Admittedly, I’ve always been a fan of several friends sticking together even during hardships, which is definitely the case here. It’s just wonderful when I saw the cast constantly helping out each other and never betraying each other.Visual novel elements aren’t the only thing available here but the player goes through different kinds of battles as well to spice the story up. After all, when gameplay gets added, it makes the game a lot more interesting. In Mask of Deception, the battles are only a very minor part and the player will find themselves mostly reading. The few fighting sequences that are spread through the game are implemented really well into the story and always fit the current happenings. Overall, they work like a turn-based RPG, although the goal isn’t always to defeat the enemies. Battle-wise, there are different preset combos of attacks, which contain several combos that you can unlock with level-ups. After the first time beating a stage, the members get a lot of XP, although it’s harder when you want to grind outside of the story.Luckily, when the player achieves a game-over, Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception is generous enough to give the option of either restarting the battle or rewind to your desired point. Sometimes, when the fighting scenes included follow up battles besides the first one, restarting brings you back to the very first battle, which turned out pretty annoying since the first one is always easily beatable, but since fallen allies remain dead for the follow-up fight when they’re tied together, it makes sense that the player finds themselves back to square one. Additionally, I liked the idea of the combo chains although they’re predetermined as the player has to actively press a key to trigger them, whilst I still have no clue how to trigger later attacks, there is also the option of just using the auto-chain feature where the game perfectly triggers all attacks.Graphic-wise, Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception works with two different styles. One of them is the typical presentation of a visual novel with a gorgeous art style and CGs. The game works with subtle animations here and there that greatly helped with the immersion during thrilling fighting, where you’re not having a battle per se but only read about it, and comedic scenes. Other than that, the game switches to 3D visuals that are even more animated and was a refreshing change. The player can already tell when a fight might very likely come up and I found this style very charming as it reminds me of the older JRPGs I’ve used to play.Whilst I was first confused about Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception containing that many slice-of-life scenes, I found it was essential for the build-up. The player doesn’t know what is happening at first, as they get thrown into this unknown world and are first getting familiar with the characters before the story gets revealed in any way, but that made the story only better for me due to me being already utterly attached to each of them. The fighting parts became more and more engaging to me until the last arc was very suspenseful and I ended up rooting for the cast. The battles offered a lot of refreshing change as well so the player doesn’t only have to read but can interact with the game as well, although most of the time, they will still find themselves reading a visual novel. That being said, Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception is a game with a great story, once you get past the long light-hearted introduction, with engaging battles, that made me especially curious about how Mask of Truth will turn out.

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception is a VN/J-RPG about an amnesiac man named Haku and a woman named Kuon that go on a journey together with various characters. I'm not going to talk about every single thing that happened in the story, nor will I recant it. I'm just going to say what I think made the story great. The game begins with Haku waking up in a strange tent with no memories (he even forgets his name), with a woman who has been tending to him while he slept. I usually dislike amnesia stories - I find many of them annoying, because usually something stupid happens, like the amnesiac character hits their head on a brick and gets all of their lost memories back. Or they see and/or hear something they had heard/seen before they lost their memories, and that somehow causes them to regain all of the memories they lost. But that doesn't happen in this story. Haku's amnesia is used as a tool for us, the player, to experience the strange world around him anew, which allows us to gain exposition we otherwise wouldn't have if, say, Haku didn't lose his memories and already had experience with that world.The woman who had been taking caring of Haku while he was asleep is Kuon, the headstrong animal-human hybrid girl. I'm not exactly sure  animal, but it doesn't really matter. Kuon and Haku's dynamic was very enjoyable. Haku's carefree, lazy, and brash personality clashes with Kuon's responsible, determined, and hardworking personality, which creates some enjoyable moments of comic relief. Some might ship them, but their relationship is more like a brother-sister one, Haku being the younger sibling.There are  of characters in this game that all have a significant part in the story. While I do think some got much more attention than others (*cough* Nekone *cough cough*), the game does a pretty good job of juggling everyone. It doesn't feel like the characters are crammed in all at once ― they gradually take their place within the story at times that make sense, meaning they don't feel forced. It was impressive.I was surprised to see the amount of slice-of-life moments/subplots, but they actually weren't a drag on the overall plot-line ― they helped me feel closer to the characters, while making me believe the characters actually got to know each other in a way that made the ending have its impact.The combat in Utawarerumono is fun. It uses a grid-based playing field with a turn-based system, where enemies and characters are splayed across the map. The frequency of a character's turn depends on their SPD (speed), which can be increased along with other attributes by using BP. I like that the combat is sort of like a game of chess ― you move your pawns around the board in a strategic way, so you find openings to attack, while avoiding being attacked by enemies. In some stages, you really have to try to think ahead, because a move you made 10 turns ago can affect the outcome of the current turn. It does feel kind of bogus because that takes nearly a level of insight fortunetellers have, but it's certainly possible to plan ahead in some instances. Another cool thing are the action chains. These are a set of attacks performed by a specific character, and if timed correctly, can land critical hits on an enemy. What I liked was each character's action chain is different, even characters that shared the same "class" (there aren't distinct classes in this game, but there are characters that have similar abilities).However, compared to the amount of VN in this game, the combat parts aren't much (with the exception of post-game dream arena). I would say it's about 75% VN and 25% combat, so people who would strongly prefer a game that prioritizes gameplay over story, I suggest passing on this game.The English translation is perfect. I don't recall ever seeing a grammar mistake, misspelling, or misuse of a word. Also, the UI is smooth, fits with the theme of the game, uncluttered, and isn't distracting at all.I loved the glossary. It was a unique feature I'd never seen in a VN before this one, and I really appreciated it being there. Being able to read extensive knowledge on the people, animals, location, and culture about the in-game world was very helpful. It wasn't a crutch, and it isn't needed due to the story not giving enough exposition ―it's there for players who might want to read up more about the world the story built.The art is purely phenomenal. The line-art is crisp, the coloring and shading makes it pop, and brings the world to life alongside the writing. At some points, I just stared at the screen because the art was so beautiful. It's the reason I have so many screenshots of this game. Amazing game that has beautiful art and music, and has great writing and characters. It's understandable if you'd rather wait until it's on sale, but it's completely worth full-price for 65-70+ hours of gameplay. It's apparent a lot of meticulous care went into this game. The music, art, writing, and voice-acting come together to create an awesome experience. This game ruined VNs for me, because this one raised the bar.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all this is part one of the Utawarerumono duology, which is the sequel to the original Utawarerumono. I highly recommend watching the anime for the original Utawarerumono (the 2006). While it is not entirely necessary to enjoy part 1, it will really help understand the world and some of the events that occur. Also Part 2 will have a bunch of moments that will be difficult to understand without watching it. Furthermore, DO NOT TOUCH THE ITSUWARI NO KAMEN ANIME I REPEAT DO NOT TOUCH IT WITH A 30 FOOT POOL, it takes away many plot points and overall is not very well done and will leave you very confused so I repeat DO NOT TOUCH IT. In the case you have though, its okay you can still read this, as mentioned before, many big plot points were left out of the anime, and many scenes in general were not in the anime, so reading the visual novel is still a wonderful experience. Also I highly recommend avoiding using youtube to listen to any of the soundtracks in the show, many of the CGs they use for backgrounds can be big plot spoilers so until your done the entire series I recommend avoiding youtubing anything related to this series.Anyways enough warnings time to start gushing about this series.The Utawarerumono has official taken the spot of my favorite series of all times. Everything about this series is fantastic as heck and I cannot even begin to express how much I love this series. Part 1 is a great intro to the duology as we enter a world filled with many mysteries surrounding it while at the same time being introduced to one of my favorite casts of characters out there. Everyone is super loveable and they only grow to be more loveable as the story progresses. This part has plenty of slice of life moments that I personally enjoyed a bunch but even if your not the biggest fan of slice of life, if it is something you can at least tolerate, it is a important build up for the more serious moments of the story. The strategy section of the game is pretty meh but its tolerable and only like 1% of the actual game and is something that can be easily breezed though. There is so much I want to talk about this story, the characters and everything about it but I want to avoid as many spoilers as possible so ill just say this I rate this game 10000000000/10 it is so good and If it’s a journey you decide to undertake, it is a journey you wont regret going on. Also Kuon is best girl <3
