_childDocuments_.review: When Fallout 76 was first announced, the waves of excitement could be felt across the gaming community. An online iteration of the beloved Fallout series promised to bring players together in the post-apocalyptic wastelands of West Virginia, a setting ripe for exploration, adventure, and untold stories. Upon its initial release, however, the game faced a barrage of criticism for numerous issues, ranging from technical glitches to a perceived lack of content. Fast forward to today, and Fallout 76 has undergone a transformation so profound, it stands as a testament to the dedication and resilience of both its developers at Bethesda Game Studios and its passionate player base. This review delves into the remarkable journey of Fallout 76, exploring how it evolved into a rich and captivating experience that both honors and expands upon the cherished Fallout legacy.Graphics and Atmosphere: The world of Appalachia in Fallout 76 is breathtaking. The graphical enhancements since launch have transformed the environment into a vibrant, post-apocalyptic landscape that beckons exploration. The attention to detail in the irradiated beauty of West Virginia is unparalleled, from the haunting glow of the Cranberry Bog to the rugged charm of the Savage Divide. Night cycles bring a whole new dimension to the game, with a dynamic weather system that can shift from tranquil post-rain mornings to ominous, fog-laden evenings, truly encapsulating the game's atmospheric depth.Gameplay and Multiplayer Dynamics: Fallout 76’s gameplay has evolved significantly. The introduction of NPCs with the Wastelanders update breathed life into Appalachia, offering players engaging stories and quests that feel both personal and impactful. The decision to introduce human characters and factions added layers of depth to the narrative, providing players with choices that resonate with the game's world and their place within it.The multiplayer aspect of Fallout 76 is where the game truly shines. Teaming up with friends or strangers to tackle events, quests, or the challenging nuke zones fosters a sense of camaraderie and shared purpose. The addition of public teams allows for easier grouping and social interaction, making the vast world of Appalachia feel a bit more connected and alive.Content and Longevity: Bethesda has shown an unwavering commitment to expanding Fallout 76, rolling out substantial updates and seasonal content that keep the game fresh and engaging. From the introduction of new quests and events to the ongoing expansions that add new regions and enemies, there's always something new to discover. The game's seasonal approach, with its unique rewards and challenges, encourages players to engage with the world and each other in dynamic ways, ensuring that the adventure in Appalachia never grows stale.Community and Support: Perhaps the most astounding aspect of Fallout 76’s journey is the community that has rallied around it. A vibrant, supportive, and creative group of players has emerged, embodying the spirit of rebuilding that the game itself champions. Bethesda’s support, through continuous updates, open communication, and responsiveness to feedback, has fostered a strong relationship with the player base. The developers have not only fixed past issues but also implemented new features based on community input, showcasing a commendable example of how player feedback can shape a game’s evolution.Final Verdict: Fallout 76 has overcome its rocky beginnings to establish itself as a deeply engaging, continuously evolving, and genuinely fun multiplayer RPG experience. With its beautiful open world, rich storytelling, dynamic multiplayer interactions, and unwavering support from developers, it stands as a shining example of how perseverance and community engagement can turn the tides of fate. Whether you’re a long-time fan of the series or a newcomer curious to explore the wastelands of West Virginia, Fallout 76 offers an adventure like no other, proving that even in the aftermath of fallout, new beginnings can flourish.

_childDocuments_.review: So I've put enough hours into the game to see both the good and the bad. The good if you have someone to play with and join and talk to. Since the in game chat system is either voice or emotes. And you can communicate outside the game it's great. But if you want to run solo it's just as good although a bit lonely the wasteland is vast and if you're not event hoping you won't see anyone for hours. The community is great, due to the in game currency system it is hard to unload junk gear due to limitations on how much you can sell to a merchant. But if you have the time the camp system is a game in and of itself really enjoyed tearing down and rebuilding just for fun to see if you can make something within the budget limit.... Now onto the negatives. The PvP system can be fun, but there are no training wheels that prevent the few bad apples from taking advantage of someone just trying it out to see if they enjoy it. For example one of the key selling points for this game is the workshop system. Take it over free resources to use just for its set-up not to mention resources from the shop itself. Good Idea... HOWEVER. Anyone can initiate PvP to try to claim the shop. Which can be fun to get into a back and forth with another player while running about the place. Good way to see if your defenses are up to par. The bad part is the people who have become predators when it comes to the workshop PvP zone that swoop in as soon as the see someone claim an unowned Workshop regardless on if they want to claim it. Just to Kill whom ever they find defending it, regardless of their level. I.E> lvl 24 claims workshop lvl 354 starts PvP and kills thew owner of the shop in about 3 seconds. PvP over. Kinda one sided and not really fixable in the long run. But you know how the saying goes, even among-st the ghouls there's always a few bad apples. but there are a lot of feral s in this one. *Shrug*

The NPC interactions are also kinda all over the place, and it's really hard to get into an immersion. Rebuilding civilization, but then also... a treasure hunt? I'm just trying to figure out what the hell is going on.If the gameplay wasn't disorienting enough, the constant instability of the game doesn't help. There was a constant flicker of light in scenes that was borderline nausea-inducing (I disabled Freesync on my video card to get it to stop but c'mon...). The always-online aspects too: my connection to the server dropped out about 5-10 times while I'm playing, and each time I leave I ended up restarted to either back in the Vault, or 15 minutes away from where I left off. Overall I'm pretty disappointed. I thought I'd give it a chance since it was free this weekend, and I've been a huge Fallout fan since 3 so I really wanted to give this the benefit of the doubt.... but no, this game is hot garbage. _childDocuments_.review: Whether or not you're going to like this game is going to largely depend on your point of view. Let me explain...I'll start by saying the game isn't "awful." It's playable. Sometimes It's even fun. So is 52 Pick Up.Pros: The world looks to be small enough you can explore it all pretty quickly. Mobs seem to level in tandem with the player, so there aren't really any "no go" or "OP" zones. In true Fall Out fashion, the game is just tongue in cheek enough to offset the grim atmosphere of the world you are playing in.Now the Cons: First, it's actually not all that much fun. Now, grant you, that's going to be a personal opinion for every single player, but in my case, the game is just kind of...there. You walk. You shoot. You listen to holotapes. You walk some more. It's not really "fun" but it's not really "work" either. It's just...something to do?Secondly, it's a multi-player game. Which means that while the best of humanity will be on display, so with the worst. Sure, there are players who will happily give you weapons, gear, and resources. There are also players who will happily follow you around shooting you in the back of the head till you either die, fight back, or they get tired of it. To their credit, the devs have taken some very solid steps to mitigate this problem; between that and the ghost town servers it's not much of an issue...but it is still there.The glitches/bugs. This game has been out WAY too long to be this unstable. There are times it won't respond to critically important key commands (like opening your PIPBoy so you can drink, eat, or equip something new when a weapon breaks mid combat).While I love the over-all aesthetics of the IP, the actual graphics leave a bit to be desired in my opinion. I've played games that look and feel better, run smoother, and are nowhere near as choppy, while demanding a lot less from my rig than this one does. Now granted, there is a LOT more to a game than just graphics, but when you add in the other cons, this one isn't helping the games case.The world isn't just small - it's arguably TOO small. You almost feel like towns are just on the other side of the next tree. For myself, it really disrupts the immersion into the world.Remember when I said mobs seem to level in tandem with the player? Well, honestly the real world effect of that is that your levels don't really mean anything anymore. They go from a mark of power and dominance you have earned, to hurdles you must reach just so can use level dependent weapons and gear. Not new gear, mind you. Oh no. For a large part, it's the exact same gear you are already using, just with a higher level requirement. Which, if we're being honest, means the more you level, the more you....sorta stay pretty much the same? You do get some new toys as far as looks or weight carried, but that's about it.Lastly, and most heinously in my opinion, repair kits cost real world currency. Forget about a favorite weapon, or preferred set of armor. Wear, tear, and the trails of war will soon leave you with broken toys that can pretty much only be repaired by purchasing repair kits with in game currency...which is primarily "earned" by actually BUYING it with real world money.In the end, if you are really feeling that Fall Out itch, I'd have to recommend actually playing Fall Out 4. Heck, even 3 is still fun.  ...but if you really want to hit the wasteland with a pal (other than Dogmeat), this IS pretty much your only choice. And, mind you, it isn't "terrible." It just isn't good.

_childDocuments_.review: Fallout 76's resolution will downgrade itself to a terrible one if you alt tab out of a loading screen, and tab back in before the game has loaded up. Make sure you hear the short whir, wait a few seconds and then tab back into the game or wait until you hear ingame world sounds.By no means is Fallout 76 a bad game. I liked it even before Wastelanders. But with each and every 'season' that comes out, I'm starting to think this game just isn't as good.After you get all the endgame gear and quests, the game becomes nothing more than an incessant daily grind of the weekly and daily challenges.Daily ops encourage you to team up and do it every day for some rewards. Usually you won't even get these good rewards, mostly duplicate items that are just terrible.They've added so many of these features that there's tons of people who log in every day and just do them. They farm gold, daily ops, plans and even items by serverhopping and HOPING for an item or random event to spawn.Plans are a very dumb feature, cool items are either unobtainable or locked behind big ingame prices, but at least they're not buyable with atoms.The atomic shop is cool and all, but atom gain is incredibly slow and the shop ALWAYS seems to have all the cool stuff added to it. The cool stuff goes in the atomic shop, the bland stuff goes in the basegame unlockable as plans.All this starts to resemble a time-gated mobile game. Log in every day for rewards...Oh yeah, the game is still badly optimized and I have to play on low settings to get acceptable FPS. Barring that, I also have had, since the day I bought this game, delays of 0.1 or 0.2 seconds [!] when attacking any sort of mob. I can shoot them, but it takes a bit for the mob to register that they've been hit... unlike a singleplayer game, where it's instantly registered.The quests are also menial and are simple fetch quests most of the time, doing their best to prolong the quest as much as possible. All this is very boring. Quests also tend to hold your hand and literally precisely tell you where to go. Most evident in the BOS questline that ends with Steel Reign.Why were items locked behind plans? I absolutely hate this feature and it's one of my biggest gripes with the game. At least in Fallout 4, you could use console to give yourself perks and items if you really needed them. But not now! Grind them all. Trade some guns you can't even get anymore for plans for some random melee weapon.They also nerfed bloodied builds, which is a build based around being a glass cannon. I was a bloodied melee user until they decided to nerf it and now I'm even more powerless against everything. I tried switching my build to guns, but it only was a waste of my perk points. Even a level 90 with a tesla rifle is better damage wise now.I am so used to bloodied melee that I just can't make the transition and I don't know how.Camp building is somewhat improved, but it pales in comparison to even a vanilla Fallout 4. There's a camp budget which is dumb, because now I can't decorate my camp as good as I could in Fallout 4. You see, in Fallout 4 you got over this with console commands.It was fun for a couple of hundred levels. The endgame is a total grind and bore. Add to that the constant lag that I couldn't get rid of. Sometimes bearable, sometimes not.Multiplayer Fallout is not a flawed idea; I wanted it before Fallout 76 was even announced. But not in this form; ditch the old, terrible engine and make a new one.Fallout 76 is worth it. But for 40 dollars? No. It's more a 20 dollar experience, probably less.Something in me wants to say that the game was worth full price even before Wastelanders. That's how much I liked this game before it.It's mediocre, but it's a damn shame that this is the road they are going down, terrible monetization, that albeit only cosmetic, is barely ever worth buying, or is worth buying but costs too much to be attainable by casual play. Fallout 76 encourages addictive playing like it's a casino, with the Fasnacht and cookout event showing that. Event runs every hour, and you do it hoping for a good mask drop.Further encouraging this are daily limits for scrap and caps from vendors.Pros:-Multiplayer fallout.-Excellent lore and backstories for even the most dead of locations.-Expanded legendary effects compared to Fallout 4. Items can have 2 or 3 legendary effects.-Mutations.-Has Enclave in it, but in a limited form.Cons:-New cool stuff they add, atom shop or not, will usually be timegated and hard to get after the gate is gone.-Encourages addictive playing. See cap/scrip limits and daily ops. You have to grind events for any of the better rewards.-There's even a limit to how much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ treasury notes you can exchange gold for per real day, that's genuinely ridiculous... and treasury notes are only attainable by doing ingame events or quests.-Omnipresent server lag. There has been delay in picking items up for as long as I can remember. Enemy HP will always bounce down, back up, and then down to the HP you hit them for if you are not using melee.-Alt tabbing in a loading screen will reduce your resolution. When I was writing these pros and cons, the game decided to crash my entire computer upon alt tab.-Camp budget. In Fallout 4 you could ignore this entirely with console commands. Not in this game, though... as a settlement builder who bypassed this limit with console commands, it's annoying that I have to keep track of all the tiny objects I place.-Fallout first. Absolutely horrible and disgusting as it fixes problems like no private worlds and helps with junk management... if you subscribe to it. Why have stash limits at all?-Nuclear Winter. Prime example of what the battle royale genre was in 2019, every game had it but then all of those battle royale modes were left to die after its popularity ran out.-Atom shop has the coolest stuff. Encourages you to buy atoms even more.-Lackluster updates... who wanted Fallout Worlds? -The new Pitt DLC is extremely meh. It's there, but that's all its good for, being there. If they focused on making Fallout 76 more like Fallout 76, instead of a fortnite battlepass every month or two (to induce artificial grind and playtime and make up for lack of ideas), maybe the game'd be more worth it.I've played Fallout 76 for so long that I had to use the Bethesdanet launcher to play it. I was hyped at the prospect of a multiplayer Fallout, as I had wished for just that when Fallout 4 mesmerized me.While I did buy the game half a year after release, I still had tons of fun playing it, and I can say with confidence that the amount of bugs Fallout 76 has at any given time has been thoroughly overblown. Most of the bugs I encountered were very much so only cosmetic, and I do not recall any quest-or game breaking bugs save for the monitor bug and omnipresent lag. But then again, this is the only game I've owned that crashes 4 times after bootup and at the same time freezes my entire computer...Fallout 76 has a dumb monetization model and updates that are lacking in every regard.Arguably  the game's charm was at it's finest when you were out on your own without any NPCs. Now, the game is more of an MMO that wants to emulate the older Fallout games, but fails as the new quests hold your hand the entire way and have little depth, fun or replayability included.In conclusion: the game is stale and its' updates are barely more than either new items to grind daily or just lazily made battlepasses. The dev teams' efforts are focused on the wrong things to keep the game remotely playable for older players, leading the game to become another generic post-apocalyptic  looter/shooter with precisely  to work for, or any proper goal.And oh yeah, I've also gotten harassed for playing the damn game.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I have received it for free because of having bought it at full price on a different platform. My Fallout 76 experience cost me €60, which felt like a good investment.Total playing time on other platforms: ~150 hours, on top of Steam.This game used to be a mixed bag, but, after lots of effort and updates from the developer, it eventually became a great buy.Story: 5/5. Can't say a lot about Wastelanders, but the original one is a masterpiece. Using environmental storytelling to this degree is something I've rarely seen, coming close to what you experience in Dark Souls - albeit in a slightly different tone.RPG: 4/5. There's no intricate skill system, and the base game won't allow for significant deviations from the path laid out in front of you. However, the player camps and perk tree allow for a lot of freedom in player-to-player role-playing, which balances the whole thing nicely.Graphics: 4/5. Appalachia is stunning. Your video card will hate you for it, but that's that. Characters leave a bit to be desired, but I guess that's what the engine can do.Replayability: 5/5. I find something new almost every time I start the game. Having recently started a new character, almost all of what I'm doing is fresh in a way or another. Totally replayable.Adventure: 4/5. You get to . You get to experience fear, excitement, wonder and frustration, all because of the stuff that you stumble upon randomly during your adventures.TL;DR: Bought it for €60 a year and a half ago. Do the same or wait for a sale, but definitely play this somehow.

_childDocuments_.review: Fallout 76, despite it’s terrible bug infested launch and quite infamously negative reputation both online and amongst the playerbase for a plethora of reasons, 76 has recently had somewhat of a revival due to continued support from the developers addressing game breaking issues and bugs while also releasing free content updates increasing the longevity of the game continuously.I was unfortunate enough to purchase Fallout 76 when it was released and endured my fair share of game breaking bugs, infinite loading screens and continuous broadcasting from other players in proximity voice having apocalyptically loud domestic arguments but alongside the typically frequent mentioning of it’s technical faults, 76 at release was quite an empty game, there wasn’t really much to do that did not seem repetitive, the challenges were quite repetitious and unimaginative [Kill 30 scorched] there was a noticeable lack of N.P.Cs that weren’t robots due to giant mutant bat disease which lead to this apparent empty world which was quite ironic considering this was the first online multiplayer Fallout game…But there could be other reasons for that.Also don’t even get me started on the initial pricing for cosmetic items and decorative objects within the Atomstore at launch….I returned to Fallout 76 what seemed like decades later, tempted by the notion of owning a free copy on Steam to celebrate the release of its free expansion and when I began playing again I was quite surprised to see a large amount of improvement.Most of the gamebreaking bugs, crashes and infinite loading issues that plagued me were gone, leaving but a small minority of infrequent crashes when travelling to certain instances, but no longer did I observes hordes of roaming T-posing fire-arm wielding Scorched or creatures half consumed by terrain, instead there were people, both N.P.Cs and PlayersPublic Teams had become a thing with players being able to opt into groups of other players getting rewarded for taking part in events and being given stat or XP bonuses that increased over time spent in group.Player C.A.M.Ps (Houses/buildings, to the layman) had access to player vendors where they could sell their weapons, plans, recipes etc with very little restriction alongside the ability to find your own crashed Astronaut who will gladly nag you to death about their headaches and never leave the house just like a real companion would.In stark contrast to when I first started playing Fallout 76 I found myself actually enjoying going on quests for my allies and seeing the changes to Wasteland, both in actual locations like Foundation becoming a settlement for settlers and new creatures lurking around like the Sheepsquatch.As it stands Fallout 76 has dramatically improved since its infamous launch, added free expansions, cosmetics and seasonal updates and has become a game that I’m not ashamed to recommend, albeit on a sale ofcourse, don’t go in expecting a revolutionary Fallout Game with high expectations nor a standard run of the mill title in the series rather a different more action RPG feel in an open world.With all things considered, if Bethesda continues to support the game with hotfixes, additional free and cosmetic content, the seasonal expansions and more allies/quests I see no reason why the game would not flourish.

The "One Wasteland" update in my option seems to change the pace and grind of the game. No longer was it like other titles of a nice rinse then repeat cycle of; Explorer, collect  then profit or redeem. Now the game feels like I fight most of my game play time in just sourcing ammunition for the next adventure just to waste it all on a rad roach or a few ghouls. Before one wasteland which was to -balance- the game for multiple people playing together at different levels, I felt like I was playing any other 3D Fallout title. The game now just seems like it's job more than a world to lose yourself. The feelings like the only thing to speed up gaining it is using a slow method of exchanging a set amount of an ammo type for another through a terminal. Ammo is hardly anywhere to begin with now even with perk cards to increase chances and vendors never seem to have much on hand. You can always buy it from players, if you got the caps, if they even have it or if the stay online long enough to get to them. You can buy it from some no-life on ebay and get banned.

_childDocuments_.review: The most positive thought in the context of Fallout 76 is that we should be glad, because Bethesda produces computer games and not, for example, software for respirators.Just imagine that vision of some parallel universe, where what I just said is a reality and everyday life, especially when we consider it's 2020 right now. We should all put our hands together in a prayer (you too atheists!), because in the end our lives are not in danger, only mental side of our health is somehow exposed, but in this case solution is simple - just don't buy Fallout 76, no matter how big discount is, no matter how much Todd Howard is waving at you, smiling, telling you that "it just works" and you should try it on your own. No, you shouldn't, because this whole thing is simply not working. I avoided Fallout 76 for a long time after it was first released, and I started playing it when it was launched on Steam. I got baited by positive reviews pretending game is now fixed, and it's safe to buy it. No, it's not and never will, because engine used to make this Fallout is simply too broken and too old to handle multiplayer game.There's a large pool of bugs and glitches, and Bethesda is pretending that they're fixing them, but in reality every single fix is bringing back old bugs. It's always the same scheme -> something is not working -> after two months (or even more) they apply fix (which break something else) -> week later new update break it to previous state for another two months -> then they release another fix... this circle never ends. You stuck in dialogue with NPC and can't progress your daily quest? Your turrets attack your own structures? Your perk/mutation is not working? Game is perma-freezing on loading screens and you have to restart it every 30 minutes? You lost progress because servers stability is a joke? Welcome in Fallout 76, where in endgame you will face bug every two minutes! I could make a very long list of bugs and other problems players face, but it would be just too long and it's hard to guess which bugs are active now, because like I said previously - Bethesda mastered bugs rotation in this game.Optimization in this game is just like everything else - how it work (when it work) is depending on various circumstances and changes every patch they apply. If you just made new character, and you run trough early game in 60fps, then in endgame you will have 30fps with regular stutters. It is like this, because amount of items you carry and store in stash directly affects your framerate, and to be honest I've never seen something that much broken in any other game. Fallout 76 in a nutshell. But let's talk about something positive this game has to offer, and in this case first thing coming to my mind, is community this game has. People are friendly and very helpful, they will explain everything you want to know, no matter how long it will take. They will craft gear for you, give you materials, help with quests, build structures you can't build on your own yet. But there is a dark shadow hiding behind all those friendly faces. I am talking about small group (but very loud) of players, fanatics, trolls and sect-like minority. To understand what I am talking about, you can just browse Steam forums of Fallout 76 for 5 minutes and you'll see it on your own. Why I am mentioning them? I am doing this only because Bethesda is doing nothing about problem, they are allowed to keep offending and attacking people who dared (how dare they?!?!) to criticize Bethesda. They'll keep striking on you and reporting your posts, and you might end up warned/banned for speaking your opinion in mannered way. Yes, Bethesda has their own "freedom of speech" standards, and it's very close to what you can face in People's Republic of China.Imagine you can build various items in your camp, and then you can use them to get buffs for your character. Great idea, right? In theory, yes, but you have to use each item for 40-50 seconds to recieve specific buff, so if you want to get all of them you waste 5 (!!!) minutes of your time, and one hour later you have to repeat whole process. Everytime you want to craft/repair/build you have to manualy change your perks loadout, which takes a lot of your time, and when you're done you have to manualy switch to your main build. Bethesda promised to implement perk loadouts system months ago, but it's not just about that. The thing is, that whole perk system lack any logic and common sense, because perks should be splitted into two categories - active and passive, and crafting ones should not steal slots. When you want to buff yourself using items from your inventory, you have to scroll trough whole menu to find them one by one. Every few quests/events, you have to do general cleaning of your inventory, because game keep throwing useless (and heavy) stuff at you as "reward". Every single system this game has is unintuitive, frustrating and not rewarding, and every simple thing you want to do takes ages to complete. At first it seems interesting, because you discover new places while hiking, do various quests, and simply enjoy it. But this phase ends pretty fast when you hit midgame, where grind begins and you realize how many limits this game has. In order to reach endgame you have to grind, everyday. How much you can store is limited, how big you camp can be is also limited, daily quests, daily currency gain, everything is made in a way to make sure you'll play game everyday to reach your daily cap, and make just a slight or no progress at all. Everything from events on map to daily quests is repetitive and boring.Game is designed in a way, where player feel hounded and forced to play everyday in order to reach daily limits, and if someone play everyday, that mean there's higher chance he will spend real cash to get additional stuff or to buy premium. Fallout 76 preys on basic human instincts, the desire to show off, being noticed, generaly speaking - need to be "cool" in other people eyes. Everything in this Fallout is built like a wall surrounding all these behaviours and feelings. They might tell you, that you don't need all that stuff, but believe me, you want it. That's how human brain works. Atomic shop is a masterpiece when it comes to psychological manipulation, fake feeling of items availability being "limited" by time, so you have to buy them before they're gone, discounts lasting for limited time, great deals for premium owners. Atomic shop, seasons, game mechanics, boring daily/weekly challenges, everything this game offers in the end has just one common goal - to make sure you're attached enough to play everyday, so at some point you might start thinking, that it wont be a crime if you spend additional money to make your in-game life easier and more colorful. I understand servers do not run on fresh air and companies want to earn money, and there's nothing wrong with that. But this is paid game, not some F2P title for android. It's also impostant to mention, that every new feature (like the newest thing available in game - shelters) is hiding 90% of new content and fun behind a paywall. Bethesda is literaly moving border to see how far they can go, and how much they can earn before this $ fountain dries up. In the end it's up to you what you'll do with your money, just think twice before you give them to Bethesda.

_childDocuments_.review: I never touched this game,  but I did follow the outrage when it released.  Playing this game now, 4 years after launch having paid 5 bucks for it , yeah I kind of get the outrage.  I would have been pissed off if I paid full price for this live service MTX driven game. Having come in 4 years later, having bought this game for next to nothing seems to do wonders for the game though. I am enjoying it. It is definitely a time sink. There are some QoL functionalities hidden behind a subscription. Infinite storage space being the main one.  Since you are scrapping all the time not having it is already becoming a pain for me on modest levels. For now I have enough space for my important stuff, but having to constantly manage my stash is a pain,  and it is a real scummy move to put that behind a paywall. Gameplay and visuals are much like Fallout 4, only a tiny bit yankier. It's perfect;ly servicable, but you definitely will notice that you are playing an online version of fallout. Oh and alot of the bugs that have plagued Bethesda games since Oblivion. are still there. Damn Bethesda is lazy.  If you take it for what it is, though and you can claim this game for free or a couple of bucks, it is quite fun if you are in the Fallout mood. It really does help if you like the pack rat, scrapping and building aspects of  Fallout 4, because the gunplay is as bad as it is in that game. It's a shame Bethesda ever charged money for this. But if you can get it cheap, it's worth a look.

I've installed it and hopped on.My take on the game:  - Honestly, progression since Beta and 2020-21 has become way easier, levels are easier to get and same with scavenging, which is quite nice to see, you could also just start off as a level 20 character and go on from there, the story is still not anywhere my expectations originally with the game, however it is still enjoyable. - I would recommend that you play with a friend group, if you don't have any friends to play this game with, don't worry as the game features public teams in public servers which you can join and team up with other fallout players to help you with progression. Solo is always a way you could go about the game, however it is just easier to level up your character and progress if playing with a team. - Honestly, the story seems more to me like fetching quests, there isn't really anything to captivate you into the story and really emerge you in it. - If you're looking for a multiplayer Fallout RPG Game, then yes. it is worth it, if you're looking more into a story game, I recommend you buy fallout 4 if you would like newer gen graphics or go for older games such as Fallout New Vegas or Fallout 3, both being some good story-telling games.I checked the box if you received the product for free in 2021 as a mistake, can't revert it anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start? If you're a Fo3,NV,4 player expecting the same experience you're better off playing FO4 with mods. FO76 is a psuedo MMOSRPG with a subscription service that is almost mandatory because the junk stash limit is sad, even as a 1st member I can't keep all of my weapons armor and ammo and run a vendor (when they work half the time) this should have NEVER been implemented into a crafting game. The daily grind is also beginning to take it's toll as well, demanding I log every day to hit scrip bullion and cap limits or else I'm behind is annoying and unwarranted. MAKE THEM WEEKLY! This is coming from a fan of your game I love MMOs and the grind but the grind also needs to be fun not a daily routine like going to work. Let me grind my ass off for 20hrs straight and hit that weekly cap and sleep for a day. As for pay2win in the Atom Shop: This isn't entirely true. Yes there are definitely items in the shop that improve QoL, You can earn atoms via daily missions and a huge list of world missions in less than a week to buy the scrap bots and a buttload of repair and scrap kits. I know this because I blew my atoms on a power armor skin then grinded out missions for a week and bought my communist protectron, When you hit endgame however, Atom shop repair kits aren't very interesting anymore and it's all about farming those improved kits from the Scorchbeast Queen(If you don't have the repair perks, Oh man I gotta bone to pick there!) You can easily repair your stuff for the cheap cheap. Finally for my biggest personal gripe with this game is the perk card setup. It is not fun nor immersive when I have to slot cards everytime I want to craft, forage, or shoot at something. For the love of god and all that is holy remove skill based perks from using slots or at least make those perks consume 1 slot where you can level up the skill by doing those actions like any other MMO with a crafting system on the market! As much as I am personally enjoying this game (I must be a masochist) I can't give it the thumbs up until QoL picks up in this game, limiting how much a player can carry is one thing, but limiting how much stuff they can store away for future use is ludicrous, It's also too time consuming stopping to slot perk cards to do pretty much anything in this game, and it's so rage rage inducing when you don't have a crafting card equipped, especially when you spend a ton of scrip on legendary modules and you didn't have super duper equipped when crafting those new legendary weapons.

_childDocuments_.review: Played more than my level indicates, altaholic. Pros: * Community. Reddit, Steam, I'm sure there are other forums but in general most of the community is pretty friendly. To the point of might aggressively chase you down to give you free things. Ask for help and you shall get it. * SCORE can be completed for free. * Seasonal events are relatively easy if repetitive and drop some interesting plans and other things; there have been more events added to limited duration events that will cycle back over time.* Updates are still ongoing for the game. New NPCs have been added mid to late last year. * Plenty of story. Even pre-wastelanders and NPC return there are a lot of holotapes, notes and other things to stumble across that gave story and storyline to follow. Pre-wastelanders was slightly more depressing as all the breadcrumbs in story and notes ended with 'and then everyone died to giant angry mutated bats' / psychotic AI.* Easy gameplay though your most challenging levels will be 25-50 in most cases. Generally players of all levels are welcome at the various events (Outside of Earl which is more end game and some players may be a bit upset if a low level shows to Earl as that is more limited on instance with that boss). The three nuke bosses being the exception to the 'easy' gameplay. - Community is usually willing to give direction on how to get ammo/resources to help with difficult levels etc.* Pacifist exists. There is no forced / surprise PvP. A player can fully avoid all forms of PvP (except trap camps) by turning Pacifist on and not claiming workshops (though a player can safely pass through a workshop area if not contesting it, owning or being in party with the individual owning a workshop).* In game event timers are predictable for when an event will show although it is random which of the events will spawn.* Recent update where when joining most major events the loading screen tells the objectives of an event. Just in case it isn't fully clear.* Push to talk for mic is an option, as is the option of muting players if needed.* Camp you can personalize with collecting plans: Build budget is limited but there are a lot of very creative camps that keep within the limit. Everything from camps focused on resource and food production to ones that are social spots around. The middle ground: * SCORE recently started to have a handful of things locked behind FO1st on the score boards recently; while the FO1st locked items use to be consumables recently it has shifted to cosmetics as well. * Bethesda does bring back most of the SCORE items into the atom shop over time so you can purchase with atoms. * Most if not all of the Atom/FO1st items are convenience. * If picky you can get much of the 'pay to pretty' items from the store over time. Very little of what is in the store is true 'pay to win'. It's pay to pretty and pay to convenience outside of FO1st which is Pay to Hoard. * Bethesda stated they will be rebalancing weapons 'soon'. ( Some 'legacy' weapons that were over the top are being removed today and some legacies that were fine/were underpowered (melee stalkers) will be gone. )* FO1st players can get their own private server with friends so they can avoid other players fully if not wanting to deal with them and wanting to just farm resources on a workshop etc. * Modding is not supported but can be done. Everything from changing the world to have winter snow to changing shaders to restore the darker look to some areas to mods that enable text chat and further load out saves.* Bank space is limited* Currency cap is 40k / Scrip cap is 5k - 300 per day / Gold bullion cap is 400 per day (Never hit the actual bullion cap, not sure that there is one). Bag and currency management is a thing, it's useful to get to know the community and use reddit to trade higher value items later in game, and it is always worth double checking the cosmetic item drops you get for their value. Some high value items can drop from relatively low level events.* Bag management. Usually not too bad but early on you will want to pay attention to it and what you're stashing/selling. The 1.2k stash limit creeps up quickly and items in stash will show weight based on your perks, not what it is actually taking up in stash so can be deceptive.CONs:* A few of the 'convenience / resource items are locked behind atoms. These are 'to get items you would farm otherwise faster' but still locked.* Only charging station for Fusion cores & for exchanging ammo to get different kinds are locked behind atoms or a $ purchase (which yes, atoms can be earned, be frugal with those)* Graphics lighting. For PC we can mod the game using reshade to bring back the deeper shadows in some areas but a few months ago Bethesda did a patch to add lighting sources to things that really degraded the graphics. Some areas that were relatively dark now glow in the dark. * Regarding NPCs, some old corpses / 'new' corpses in certain areas seem out of place given the people resettling the area. Certain things were swept aside so they no longer existed and some of the ones in early level areas and the like that are decaying but not skeletons are now very much out of place if viewed with the idea of the settlers returning and how long/recent it is suppose to be since the scorched destroyed everything with the first wave of settlers.* PvP battle royale mode with Nuclear Winter was removed from game making some old cosmetic items fully unobtainable. Servers with no 'passive' mode were removed fully so all PvP is only on servers with Pacifist options to fully avoid PvP. * No text chat for the deaf. Text chat has been requested since near launch.* Took almost 4 years to finally look at the weapon rebalance with the 'legacy' weapons which caused more drama than it was worth in the community.* Camp limits for the personal housing are sometimes too limiting. The build menu/mode was more or less carried over from FO4.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game, I bought it in preorder back in the day, and since I remember there was no NPC, just empty world with notes and clues to quests and history, overall nothing to do, so I quit. Probably not so long ago, they merged Bethesda store with Steam so I decided to give it a try again and now they do have NPCs, it's like Fallout 4, but online. However, there are zero interactions with other people, this definitely is not an MMO, but rather a "chill COOP" that you play with your girlfriend or something, there is nothing difficult to do, no ladder, no challenge, no PvP (there is but you won't enjoy it), no PvE either, even the hardest enemies in the game are just brute force, there are no tactics, just pump damage into it until it dies, whatever it is. You just enjoy the Fallout lore till you are not bored with it, they keep adding new stuff so for someone who does like Fallout 4 playstyle, and especially the lore, this is a great game. On high level (means 50+) you just keep min/maxing your gear, there is a lot of RNG and a lot of additional systems you can abuse with perk and gear, this is fun, but again why would you bother, there is no reward for you when you do it, you just kill enemies faster little, by little. The crafting system is sometimes confusing and a lot of RNG is involved, so what people do is simply afk and farming events just to be able to min/max a bit more. So I do recommend playing it, if you like Fallout, but don't expect an MMO from it.

_childDocuments_.review: Bethesda Launcher playtime: 1440 hoursSteam Playtime: 35 hours, as of time of writing.TLDR of this post is: Buy a copy of Fallout: New Vegas and use the multiplayer mod. At least that way there's more than a few hours of story.I want to talk for a moment about getting involved in a live service game which is not particularly live or service-like, but that has decent gameplay. I began playing this during the open beta. At first it was very exciting. Finally - a Fallout game I can play with my friends. I really wanted to like it. *They* really wanted to like it. The problem is, it's running on an engine that can't handle even last gen tech advances. Like reflections.Still, that wasn't a huge problem. My friends and I play a fair number of older games with nostalgic graphics systems. And bugs. Like, holy crap - coming down on AAA studios right now for being buggy is like obsessing that water is wet. Also, in some respects, it's undeserved. It's nearly impossible to get multiplayer mechanics that don't have some issues even a couple years after launch. In the case of this game, a lot of that boils down to a drop table that makes Path of Exile look generous, and a community committed to finding an executing exploits because they have no realistic chance of getting some drops.Another serious problem there was years of unprotected netcode. The first Fasnacht, for example, had people summoning mask-splosions because the mask drops were way too stingy. Imagine a sudden rain storm, but of masks. To the point where the second Fasnacht developed a team of nuke speedrunners who kept the area radioactive. At the time, this triggered a small critter spawn bug, making the event not completeable. Even now, their netcode is not particularly protected.It's not really the bugs that are the issue as I said earlier, though. And I want to really nail this in - *even upstart games like Valheim have network problems at first*. You simply can't test for every hairbrained, serious exploiter out there. Defense has always been a reactive game. It would be *nice* if, however, they could avoid restoring bugs they had previously quashed. You know, just once. Are the vending machines working this week, or are they exploitable again? For those reading this intent on purchase, vending machines are how you'll make some money or finally get plans from content that isn't providing them. If people are afraid to use them because people can steal from them, getting some things (thanks again, drop table) is impossible without literal months of grinding. Simple math: A 0.01% drop chance (yes, many things are or were that low) means you may have to play as many as 10,000 matches to get that object. The real averages people were hitting on some of these things were literally over 2000 matches - some of which were once a day missions. When Bullion came out, it worked out to 2 months of straight play time just to get the complete plans for a single armor set.On the Live services front, the Atom Shop is lying. They indicate there are no pay to win features, but the unlimited junk stash and a number of machines, buffing items, etc in the shop change the game so substantially that they became the basis for an ingame economy. 1st did the same thing, in case someone wants to quibble. The ability to build a private server means there is no chance of competing with other players for rare resources, and being able to return to public and trade those resources gave players a serious advantage in arming and equipping themselves. Gating significant features that allow significant ingame advantage behind a paywall *is* pay to win. It's odd that they don't understand that.On the economy front, you will be grinding for literal years to get enough of anything anyone trades in - because let me tell you, it's not currency. Their currency cap is radically too low to pay for items it took people a year to find. Most currencies are not tradeable. So you'll be trading in Flux (a rare crafting component) in the order of hundreds or thousands, or ammo in the order of tens to hundreds of thousands. Ultimately, the CAMP system was impossible to place close enough to your friends to really build anything interesting, so it didn't work for my friends. I was - even am - the only remaining holdout. Once in a while I pop in to see where things are. I won't pay for 1st again - not because it lacks features, but because it gives me an unfair advantage. If you're looking for a fun time-waster with limited content, this game works fantastic. If you want the things Bethesda was known for - good story, hilarious rather than frustrating bugs, fun mods, and a pseudo-survival feel, this one misses the mark.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the worst games I have ever played. The graphics are great. The user interface is a complete failure. Bethesda has assigned multiple function to each key, because this is really a console game. What does R do? It un-hides your weapon, or it reloads your weapon, or it loots all neighboring corpses with R R <Space>. If you hit E too long, you exit your power armor in the midst of a giant boss fight. Do you like dying? You will love this game! Get used to pressing a key, not a mouse control, and nothing will happen! Press 3 or 4 times to get a heal, it is random. I have an n-key rollover keyboard, this is not a hardware issue. You tell the game to turn on your power armor headlamp by holding tab. It turns off 100 times a day because Bethesda can't save this preference. You cannot do anything in Power Armor, so you have to exit it to craft. This involves a 5 second animation that you cannot avoid. Why could John Carmack figure out programming in the 1990s with terrible hardware while Bethesda have no idea how to make a button press work? If you buy this product on a PC, enjoy your suffering.

Wastelanders was a step in the right direction and I'm happy I decided to step back into it because getting to continue exploring the world of Fallout in a new and interesting location is something I find greatly enjoyable. I originally purchased this game on release, played for an hour, got disconnected ten times in said hour, then never touched the game again and since my  login is linked to Steam thanks to Fallout 4 and Skyrim I was given the Steam addition for free and I have had no connectivity issues since. Like I already said, there's still a lot of work to be done to 76 but it is in a MUCH better place than before and I am very hopeful for its future.Happy wastelanding, fellow vault dwellers!

_childDocuments_.review: Fallout 76 is an abusive relationship masquerading as a video game. It begs for your attention, gives you trivial trinkets to lure you in, and just when you spend money on it, something outside your control changes; things break, months of effort are undermined, and you find yourself left wondering what you ever saw in it to begin with. Then, a little time passes, you think it must not have been that bad, there were fun times, and you find yourself reinstalling to log in once more, just to check in, see if anything got fixed or changed… but no. Even when they say they've changed, a little bit of time together reveals they really haven't changed at all.This is the only Fallout 3 or 4 style experience available that has multiplayer. That's the only reason anyone would buy or play this. Of its merits, this is a game from a billion dollar company that is fundamentally flawed and has been repeatedly broken by various updates over time. There's a black market for trading 'legacy' weapons and duplicated items and power armors (I don't care what you do, just stating it exists). Quests are still buggy and broken, along with NPC dialogues. Events like Mischief Night (the Halloween one) just disappear and get replaced with the way more boring 'Spooky Scorched' (itself a retread of their Holiday/Winter Event), while others like Fasnacht are buggy and broken even after multiple years of hiatus and reworked returns.I avoided playing this game at the time it was originally out; before then, there were only robot vendors in the game at train stations, and the game had a heavy pvp focus, so I didn't have a lot of interest (despite other options like a Survival mode and the late-not-as-great-as-people-said-but-still-fun Nuclear Winter). I picked it up when it came to Steam with the release of the Settlers dlc expansion, and the idea I had was, despite the negativity I heard surrounding the game, if they were going to keep trying to add things and fix it up, I might have to give it a look.It's been over 1,000 hours. Help me. For the most part, what I found was an expectedly buggy but surprisingly fun series of quests loosely related to established Fallout things with other people occasionally trying to kill me. While I didn't always engage with the action combat, I did spend a lot of my time building different bases across the wasteland, with mixed results. While the combat is sort of taken from FO4 and rejiggered to be 'live', the building is ripped straight from that game and then has a bunch of strange limits imposed upon it, generally ending up in worse results. Look, I understand I can clip items together, and I know some people exploit camp budget to achieve their ultimate fantasy house - I don't care, neither of us should have to. The building system needs some serious attention, and while those of us who really enjoyed that part of FO4 will be busy (especially with Shelters now, in addition to the lackluster Worlds) those who don't engage with that content are really playing only half the game.The result is a hybrid game that wants to provide a lot of things, but doesn't do any of them very well. Those who have played previous Bethesda games (Elder Scrolls in particular) will recognize some of the bugs and find ways around them or just ignore them - the games are fun anyway. Even in stacking those against this one, this is the buggier of the bunch. The multiplayer and additional stresses really just push this engine to its limit, and lag in all its forms, with enemies teleporting and players sliding around or stuck in various animations, abound on live servers - especially in the bigger fights like  where the majority of the server's players group up to take down one big bad and lots of little adds. It's crazy and chaotic fun, but as something that drops items mandatory to progression (by which I mean, to advance your power you should participate in these events) it's hard to look at and say it’s a selling point. And this is the endgame.What else? Well SCOREBOARD bugs almost every season, and apparently a lot of people willing to pay $130 to skip it entirely and get all the things on Day One. Play how you want, but have you looked at the items on the Scoreboard as far as rewards? 5+ player icons? Scrip? Lunchboxes? Skins for guns, some camp objects, and the newer 'lite' player allies maybe be objectively worth it for some, but with lackluster rewards often so prevalent, it's definitely hard to see how this is justified ATOP the almost necessary Fallout 1st ($12.99/mo) for a scrap box not beholden to a weight limit (the same trick they took from Elder Scrolls Online and their Crafting Mats bag). Just as often, the FO1st member rewards from the Scoreboard are regularly pretty bad, and while many of the best items come late in the award path, these later few seasons have had pretty bad rewards for the final rank besides. (Um, your current event is Vault stuff - it's a lot of yellow paint and uh… Responder's building kit? Not a Vault Tec one?)Shooting aliens is a ton of fun, and a great, heavy pressure event - but also punishing for solo players and the under-leveled, so be warned if that's you. Give the rest of these events a few tweaks and this level of effort, and you might have something to bring more people back to the daily loop.

_childDocuments_.review: What makes Fallout 76 good is precisely what you'd expect. Generally speaking, it's more of what people generally liked about Fallout 4, that is, if what you liked was the settlement building mechanics, and the loot and shoot gameplay. Sprinkle on to that some light co-op and MMO elements, and that is basically Fallout 76. It's, honestly, fairly solid and inoffensive at it's surface.The problem, and why people hate on this game so much, is simple and straight forward. This is neither what fans of the series wanted, and nor does it make any attempt to respect the series as whole or why the series is just so popular. From being an unfixable bug-riddled mess at launch, to basically demanding you cough up cash to enjoy the game to the fullest extent. While they managed to put a lot of the good parts of Fallout into an MMO, they've distilled the worst parts of MMOs into this game, poisoning the well that is Fallout 76. Not unless it is sold for very dirt cheap. I got it as a part of Humble Bundle, and that's the sort of way you should get it too. For free, or as a part of some bundle containing some other, far better, game.To really dig into the core of why Fallout 76 is bad, and why fans of the franchise and Beth RPGs in general hate it so much, we really need to talk about what fans  from Fallout 76 when people found out about it. To get the obvious out of the way, the Bethesda and Fallout fanbase wanted, and continues to want, a multiplayer Fallout. That is obvious and without a doubt, as evident by the sheer success of Fallout 76 and Elder Scrolls Online in spite of fanbased backlash. Similarly one could look towards the like of Skyrim Together or TES3MP for examples of the sheer lengths people are willing to go to get a multiplayer Beth RPG experience.Fans were ecstatic to get to finally explore the world of Fallout together with one another. Finally get a chance to not have a companion, but to have their actual friend there beside them experiencing the world with them. To actually show off their cool stuff they got to their friends in-game, instead of just displaying it as some vanity project. Getting able to struggle together instead of alone, or even just screw around with friends. It's been seemingly a pipe dream, but now made real.And even more excited were people to finally show off their cool creations in-game using the Fallout 4 settlement system. And to hear you could place that settlement anywhere? Well, fans were really pumped for this. Finally something truly exciting again from Bethesda. A true revolution to the Beth RPG.Then it launched. Well, launched is a strong word. I'll not be going over the launch fiasco nonsense or the massive assortment of bugs as they're largely resolved and done deals. I'll be beating this dead horse enough, no need to wail on the truly decomposed bits. That aside, this was  what fans wanted. No. It was like going to a ramen shop, sitting down, and being given instant noodles without the salt packet, then told that the noodles and hot water is $40 but the salt packet is another $20.Fallout 76 feels more like an MMO wearing a fallout skin suit. Nearly every aspect feels like an MMO; and that's because a large portion of it is designed for the MMO portion of the game first, and the Fallout portion of the game second. This is, simply, not good. At first you'd think weapons degrading seems very much like a New Vegas sort of thing to do, except unlike New Vegas, weapons can't be combined to repair them, you need to disassemble them then use their components to repair your stuff...or you could use a repair kit which is typically purchased from the atom shop. At first you might be excited to see the vast plethora of weapon and armor variety, as well as the plethora of building components. Then you realize that weapon mod and crafting blueprints must be obtained through scrapping guns, and that a lot of the stuff is better purchased, again through the Atom store.Are you seeing the pattern here? Everything goes back to extracting money from you or making things take more time. This is an MMO, not a Fallout game. It's just wearing a Fallout skin suit. And nowhere is this more obvious than when it comes to Fallout 1st. Bethesda has, in their infinite wisdom, decided to sell the capacity to make private servers, but has still made it largely impossible to mod on those servers, to say nothing of the fact that selling the capacity to turn this into the simply co-op game that players wanted instead of the MMO that it is.See, a large part of why people love these Beth RPGs so much is because modding allows these games to completely transform into insanely more complex, indepth, and believable worlds. But Bethesda has entirely prevented any such development from occuring with 76. They've decided they'd sooner kill any good will they had then provide a possibility that people just enjoy the game without spending ridiculous amounts of cash.With that, Bethesda has made it clear that Fallout 76 will have no redemption arc. The one possible way was through private servers and modding, but that's gone. It's a squander opportunity. And that's what Fallout 76 is in general, and feels like in general. A plethora of squandered opportunities. From having a huge variety of equipment and customization, to being able to enjoy a Beth RPG with friends. It could have been amazing. Now it's a zombie of a game like ESO that only survives because it's the closest thing people will ever get to Fallout with friends for a long...long time.

_childDocuments_.review: The good: - Great social experience. Player camps are fun, public events are easy and rewarding. - REAL player growth. High level players are hilariously OP and have ridiculous amounts of materials. I find this fun. - Great community compared to other online games. I've seen people give away tons of resources and gear to newbies just because they can. - The environment is beautiful, especially the mountains of the Savage Divide. - Gameplay is incredibly free-form. Initially I found it too hard, but there are so many different ways of generating resources and perks, you’ll be fine once you get used to the various gameplay systems. The bad: - Human faces look odd… - Performance is rough, often dropping from 120 fps to 30 depending on where you are in the map. - Monetization is manipulative. It’s not necessary, as high-level players can still play with ease, but quality of life improvements like the scrap-box being paid only is bad. If the gameplay can be improved, then let it be improved for everyone. Monetization that holds back the quality of the gameplay is bad. - Game stability is iffy, and I have crashed in the middle of CO-OP missions.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, not a bad game. I played it entirely solo and got a decent 50 hours out of it doing most of the main quest arcs and a couple of the major side quest arcs. The survival elements are fun without being annoying, the base building is still fun, and the speech skill checks (and skill checks in general) are vastly improved from Fallout 4. The map is well designed and fun to explore. The photo mode is bomb as ♥♥♥♥, and I love that the photos you take become your loading screen images, encouraged me to spend time taking artsy photos of the Wasteland lol. My criticisms are as follows: the vanilla main quest is pretty disappointing. Mostly just fetch quests and listening to audio logs. Wasn't excruciating because I broke it up with the more interesting side content to keep me going, but pretty lame regardless. The weapons are tied to a specific level and can't be upgraded, you simply have to pick up a new weapon as soon as you outgrow the old one. On the one hand, new cool weapons are easy to come by, but on the other hand, I don't like that it essentially forces you to move on from ones you like. There is really no endgame outside of base building, or if there is, it's not explained at all. The process of getting nukes is also highly annoying and badly explained, and they're really not worth the payoff. _childDocuments_.review: Allow me to paint a picture for you.You and your husband/wife/grandma/whoever just finished watching the Fallout TV show. "Wow!" you say. "I really enjoyed that television show from Amazon^tm Studios! I sure would love a video game experience we could share in the same universe!"Your husband/wife/grandma/whoever nods and you look into it and woah now, Fallout 76 the MMO version of Fallout is on a free weekend to coincide with the TV show!You download the almost 100gb on each of your PCs and hop right in, and your first mission is to listen to an audio log, fun!Then, you go out into the world and start doing what you do in every MMO, questing. You get to a certain quest with your partner that requires you to place a camp and a sign, go to a radio tower, and then return to your camp. You each have to do these tasks individually, which is fine to a degree. Its your camp so it makes sense you have to do it solo. Then you reach a mission where you have to clear out a mine. You as the party leader enter the mine and your partner follows you in. You clear out the entire mine of scorched ghoul-like creachers shooting at you, and you make your way all the way to the bottom saving the NPC (npcs weren't added until 2 years after this games initial launch btw) that you were told to save. Upon exiting the mines, your partner goes, "Huh, the quest didn't update for me". Confused you have them stream to Discord and see that it, indeed, did not update for them. Thinking maybe it was just a fluke you both go to turn it in and at that point realize that you have encountered possibly one of the most egregious MMO design "choices" I have ever seen. For a game built around being a multiplayer experience to be had with friends, Bethesda has decided that quest progression being shared is not essential, but a *luxury* to be paid for with a subscription fee to Fallout 1st. They invented the problem and are graciously selling you the solution. This is the kind of MTX that people complaining about Dragon's Dogma 2 would be livid about if they could read.There's a million other technical issues with the game, it has so many problems that I encountered in my 4 hours of play that its not worth detailing here but Joseph Anderson has a great video called "The 1001 Bugs of Fallout 76" if you want to see some of the issues in action. The servers are marginally better than they were in that video but the game is largely unchanged aside from the addition of NPCs and some very, very minor QOL from what I've researched. The game is very much still in a broken state and Bethesda seems to have done practically nothing in terms of preparation for the influx of players that comes along with a free weekend following the insanely popular TV show. Oh, thats a lie actually. They're adding a UI update to Fallout 4 almost 10 years late that no one asked for that's gonna break everyones mods and is delaying the release of the game sized Mod called Fallout London :) Great job Bethesda. Eat ♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Still very buggy, though I havent encountered anything progress halting or game-breaking. Microtransactions are NOT pay to win, despite what people say (except scrap box, definitely can be considered an unfair advantage). Game itself is very fun, with my favorite map from the series and lots of unique locations. Story isn't anything special, but the voice acting makes it more than bearable. Overall, a solid game if you can look past the bugs, and I recommend it to fans of the series willing to look past these cons.     So, I bought the game on Bethesda a few days before Wastelanders released, as I wanted to experience the game in its original state to see how much of a difference Wastelanders would make. First few hours were incredibly boring, and I almost regretted buying it. However, I pushed through and started to see how the game could be enjoyable. I enjoyed putting together stories through the holotapes I'd come across, and felt a strong sense of progress through leveling and starting to find more powerful weapons. However, like many of the complaints around the launch, the world felt lonely.     Wastelanders drops. I'm around level 25, with a good chunk of story completed, and immediately start the Wastelanders story. Right off the bat, the dialogue system felt better than ever, with view & DoF shifts, good voice acting, and likable characters. Skill checks & Fallout 3/NV dialogue menu return, which was a big relief. I play through the story, making steady progress and enjoying myself as I go. There were a few quests I hated (looking at you, Hornwright HQ), but aside from those it felt great. By the time I finished the story, I was level 50 with a solid setup.     Thats fine and all, but what about the world itself? With Wastelanders, many locations were revamped to include raiders, settlers, and other human factions. Some of these small locations are now my favorite to visit, as they really feel lived in, with their own small stories. There are now random encounters, many of which put a big smile on my face. Whether its two robots stuck in a conversation loop, settlers who need help fighting off local fauna, or wandering storytellers with tales of cryptids, they all felt unique and fitting of the world.     Next, the gameplay loop. The endgame is VERY grindy, and in a way many wont like. The new currency is capped at 200 a day, with many of the best plans costing over a thousand. I didn't get very invested in this grind, though, and still managed to get another 60+ hours out of the game. I loved walking around the world and trying to find every new location I could, finding spots to farm legendary weapons, helping new players with events, and slowly shifting my build from sneaky sniper to huge unarmed damage. While there is a clear meta for builds, you can very easily get by in the hardest areas using whatever build you want, as long as you pay some sort of attention to your damage output. Overall, the endgame is mainly focused on getting good legendary rolls, unlocking new blueprints for weapons, and perfecting/changing your build.     I see many complaints about the game that are either incredibly biased, misinformed, or straight up false information. On the "P2W" front, the only non cosmetic purchases are scrap kits, which allow you to store whatever scrap you have remotely (which is not worth it in the slightest), and repair kits, to repair on the go. However, there are repair benches scattered EVERYWHERE. You can barely go 30 minutes without finding AT LEAST one bench, and if thats not enough, there are free repair kits that are BETTER than the paid ones, which you get simply by killing an endgame boss, which many high level players grind. The only remotely P2W aspect comes from fallout 1st, of which complaints are completely valid. Unlimited scrap storage allows you to hold many more legendary drops, consumables, etc, which is a pretty sizable advantage. However, none of this allows you to get better gear, stats, or character progression than free players.     Rounding out this stupid long review that's probably a waste of time, is it worth the price? If you're on the fence, I suggest waiting for a sale. If you're a big fan and have seen gameplay that REALLY interests you, then I say go ahead and pay what you want. This game gripped me harder than almost any other game for nearly 3 weeks straight, which is unheard of for me (i usually only play a game for a couple weeks tops before getting burnt out and swapping games). I personally don't care about Bethesda's lying about the impossibility of features, only to add them later, as it has 0 effect on my enjoyment of the game, however I understand why many look down on it and refuse to purchase the game because of it.anyways any negative reviews are nitpicking and biased, i win, bye bye

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR; They managed to make this game even more boring than Fallout 4!After playing this a couple evenings (around 6 hours) in total, I have no desire to go back. Movement and shooting is subpar to almost every other FPS/TPS game out there. And RPG aspects are also severely lacking: even the beginning of the game (where you actually expect some great content to hook you up) has only boring fetch quests where your decisions mean nothing. And it gets only worse from that point: the more quests you get, the more you realize that they tell no interesting stories and only make you running from point A to point B.Exploration is also extremely luckluster. Yes, the map is huge, yes, there are many landmarks and buildings to explore, but all of that is completely unrewarding since the game has almost neither loot nor interesting environment storytelling outside of the areas you visit via quests, and as I said above, even quests are extremely boring.And I am not even talking about the technical aspect which is extremely bad for a game released several years ago. I have 12900k, 32 GB RAM, Samsung 980 EVO Pro and 3080Ti, and Fallout 76 manages to stutter all the time! I don't care if that's poorly done streaming or unoptimized memory allocation, but this is simply unacceptable for a game that looks so much worse than modern ones yet fails to deliver stable 60 fps.P.S. The game is in the Humble Choice until March 7th, go grab it and be disappointed as well.
