_childDocuments_.review: This first entry in the Utawarerumono series is a very good visual novel with very light tactics gameplay that brings a unique-feeling world to the table. However, it also shows it's age with some themes that would nowadays be considered cliche. The series as a whole does get better and better, so this is a good starting point.Pros:+Worldbuilding heaven. This visual novel portrays both epic-scale kingdom politics and intimate character stories with a lot of care; easy to invest in this world+Likable characters and character development+Fantastic character designs and background art. The whole Ainu vibe feels rustic and unique+Fully voiced, anime-quality voice acting+Great soundtrackCons:-The fan service is very 2002, which may make some people uncomfortable-Story has occasional tonal cliches and awkward pacing moments-The tactics combat is rather clumsy compared to other tactical RPGs on the market. Unwieldy at times, with some unnecessary mechanicsOverall, this visual novel is worth checking out on it's own merit! I also strongly believe the next two games in this series make significant improvements in the story/character/gameplay departments, elevating my opinion of this first game by a decent amount. So if you enjoy Prelude to the Fallen, you will almost certainly enjoy the rest of the trilogy.

_childDocuments_.review: Prelude to the fallen is a remaster of the original utawarerumono title intended to coinside with the release of the final two entries over a decade after the games intial release, with renewed gameplay and lack of pornography (making the story more palitable imo). The game is a slow burn begining as a slice of life in a small village and culminating into a continent spaning epic, a rags to riches tale of ultimate preportions. Most of the story is told through dialouge which makes the game very free flowing avoiding alot of the pitfalls of visual novel writing, where authors feel the need to continuously overexplain themselves. The story could easily be told as a series of epic fantasy novels, given the amount of craftmenship given to the story's lore, character building and world from the very first scene. Even if every story beat isnt masterful, utawarerumono's world is constantly expanding and beckoning the players imagination. The mix between slice of life content and srgp combat works surprisingly well, with an understanding of tone through each section of the story (the execution of an entire village is never followed up with a comedic scene). The main critisism i have for the game is some pretty poor characterisation for alot of minor antagonist that stand out among a well realised cast. The combat is also very easy, should be played in hard unless you have never played a game before. I am gay for HakuowoFinal rating 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen is the first game in the Utawarerumono trilogy and it's a remake/remaster of the original VN from 2002. The trilogy is an absolute masterpiece: it's one of the best stories ever told in videogames and it rightfully deserves its spot among the most highly rated VNs ever created together with like likes of Muv-Luv and STEINS;GATE. Utawarerumono also contains an SRPG component, but 80-90% of the game is story, and the gameplay is well integrated into the story and is generally used as part of the storytelling. That said, the gameplay elements are enjoyable on their own merit. Just keep in mind that gameplay is something that improved significantly with each game, peaking in the third part in the series, Mask of Truth.Prelude to the Fallen is the weakest entry in the trilogy, but don't let that discourage you from picking it up. It's still a really good game and it's clear that a lot of care and love was put into each element that makes it up. The characters are very endearing and the worldbuilding, while a bit slow at the start, is fantastic. Since you follow the perspective of Hakuowlo, who can't remember anything about himself or why there's a mask mysteriously fused to his face, the first several hours is just him getting used to his new life. However,  it's not all just slice-of-life fun. It takes a while for him to properly start remembering things about his past, but there are several little hints here and there that there's more to him than meets the eye. Despite his lack of memories, he knows things that are common sense to him while to everyone else they might as well be magic, and he's also the only character with no animal-like features. It's a very entertaining experience to watch the game slowly build up its mythos an the mysteries surrounding it. By the end of Prelude to the Fallen you'll have some answers, but not all of them. This game does a good job of setting the stage of the next two while still being fun on its own.Another strong point I would like to highlight is the music and the art. The music in particular is very memorable and it's always very well timed. Any time there's a powerful and emotional scene, you can count on there being a matching soundtrack that enhances the experience. For the visual part, the aesthetic is very pleasing and it definitely looks sharper and cleaner compared to the original VN. The major cultures in this world seem to be based on the real world Ainu culture, and the visuals depict this very well. If this is not something that you're familiar with then you're in for a very unique experience. A worry that some people have is that the game is in 720p 30 fps. Being a Visual Novel, graphic fidelity is not a major point of interest and it's not a focus of the game. Despite this, in my opinion the game actually looks pretty good an I don't think that running at 30 fps detracts from the experience at all, which honestly surprised me a bit since it's standard for modern games to run at 60+ fps. My expectation was that the 3D section (which is to say, the combat and some specific parts of the story) would be choppy but this isn't the case at all. The visuals are smooth and fluid, and they work perfectly fine.The SRPG part of the game is arguably the weakest part of this installment. I still enjoyed them plenty, and it created the base for the combat in the next two games, but once you pick up Mask of Deception you'll quickly be able to tell just how much the gameplay improves. The basis for the majority of the game systems and mechanics are definitely in this game, but the level of polish is much greater in Mask of Deception, and specially in Mask of Truth. To name my main complaints with it:> The equipment system is a bit clunky. Most equips either have vague effects or just aren't very good, and it's also confusing that several of them are exclusive to 1 unit but don't list who the user is. The consumables aren't great either because when you start it's not clear how many of them you will get in a playthrough and what their best use case is. By the end of the game you realize that consumables are quite plentiful but also not very useful. In theory they should be pretty valuable because Eruruu is the only healer you get, but 99% of the times she's is all you need and she's surprisingly not that hard to defend and keep alive. Items will be the most useful in the first few maps because of the game's weird difficulty curve (more on that later) and because you have 2 or 3 maps with isolated characters that Eruruu can't reach in a timely manner (plus some maps where Eruruu is unavailable but that's not very frequent). Incidentally, the devs very clearly took a lesson from this: Mask of Deception and Mask of Truth do away with this system entirely. In those games, all equips are universal, non-consumable and have clear use cases (as well as several strategic uses that add depth to the game in a way that the Prelude to the Fallen equips can't). > The difficulty is very front-loaded. In the early maps your units are much more frail and Eruruu can't always reach them in time to heal damage. Ostensibly the game gets harder again later, but it's very easy to trivialize the difficulty without even trying because of how some game mechanics work. The Bonus Point system is very easy to abuse. After completing any map, the participating units gain points that they can use to improve one of their base stats. The cost varies by stat and character. For example, Hakuowlo is very balanced, while for a character like Oboro improving his attack stat is dirt cheap at the cost of improving his defense stat being expensive. The cost of improving a stat never changes (in the sequels it increases every time you improve a stat), so the game very blatantly tells you to minmax. The most obvious result of this is that your damage dealers will probably be doing several magnitudes of overkill damage by the endgame, which makes the game not very hard even on hard difficulty.If you're itching for a challenge though, you'll definitely find that in the other two games. The systems are more balanced, the story maps are slightly harder, and their post-game maps range from decently challenging to completely brutal. More importantly though, Prelude to the Fallen DOES feature a single challenge post-game map. Be warned, however, that it's locked behind obtaining every item in the game. This isn't a problem for most items (they're all either gained by story progression or can be farmed after ending the game), but there are 2 that are permanently missable. Look up a spoiler-free guide if you're interested in unlocking the map.> Lastly, the zeal mechanic, while interesting, is much better in the sequels. This game has a few skills that scale off your current zeal, you don't lose it if you don't use it (sans getting hit with certain status effects that drain it), and it carries over from one map to the other, so there's no strategic depth to it: the obvious play is to hold on to your zeal forever unless you absolutely need the damage from the Final Strike. The overzeal mechanic from the sequels + zeal restarting every map is significantly better.This game is the beginning of an epic tale where you slowly discover how the world before you came to be. It's full of emotional moments of friendship, love and loyalty, and by the end of it you'll be left wanting to know how the story continues. To avid VN readers, this is an absolute must read. To gamers in general, I think this is an amazing first VN to read. It's easier to get into than something like Muv-Luv (and I say that as a big fan of that game). While it also has its big payoff in the form of the third game, both Prelude to the Fallen and Mask of Deception are very enjoyable on their own right. I can guarantee you that you'll quickly grow to love the characters, the story, and the world that they exist in.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone having already played the 2002 version of Utawarerumono this Remake was really enjoyable and nostalgic experience. The gameplay was improved: you don’t need to spend tremendous amount of BP to get more chain attack and final strike, allow gridding stats, extra story arc and Eruruu can do more than just healing and running away, training section to improve skill and farm items. Compare to the old version the gameplay was definitely better but I hate the fact that they heavily nerf some fights which was nightmare in the old version and become a piece of cake in this one, I remember that at the last battle of the old version when I only had one single unit left to solo the Boss and that was my most exciting and terrifying experience in this series. In my opinion, Character sprite of the Remake was not good also, the new sprite in the BP Allocation was really GOOD but they just used former sprite and brighten them which was disappointing, I really like the former sprite with gray and dark colors and that was the charm of an aged game. But the Remake just brighten them, at the result making them lose the charm of an early 2000s game and not as appealing as modern character sprite like its sequel as the same time (the Remake was produced after Mask of Truth). Overall, I still love it Utawarerumono was my very first SRPG/Visual Novel and a great opening for the Trilogy, reading this title is a must if you wish to have the best Utawarerumono experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen, long long ago when the anime for this first came out, it was one of the first anime I've ever watched. Ever since then I've been a massive fan of it. Every few years I would watch it and to this day I've watched the series 3 times. For my fourth time experiencing this series i was finally given an oppurtunity to experience it in its visual novel format and boy i will say it is still as fantastic of a story as always. The plot is intense with plenty of moments that will keep you at the edge of your seat and plenty that will make you bawl your eyes out. The humor is hilarious, plenty of times i found myself laughing my ass off and its cast is one of the most loveable bunch ever that you will only come to love more and more as you delve deeper into the story. One weakness of this visual novel that i will note though is that for people who are not fans of turn based strategy, there are alot of those segments in this game, far more then its successors which i personally did not like. Nonetheless though, Highly recommend still. For those who may not have much time or dont want to deal with the turn based segments the anime is a great substitute as well although a plot points may be missed but the major ones are all mostly covered. No matter which medium you choose though, this is a story you HAVE to experience!

_childDocuments_.review: I recently played through the entire trilogy, so this short review is meant for all three games. I really enjoyed the story, this series had me laughing, crying and everything in between. There are few parts where the slice of life fluff overstays it's welcome (especially in MoD), they are well written scenes but I swear at some points I could have fallen asleep. Of course there is a bunch of fan-service here and there, but nothing too distasteful. Where this series shines is creating a really interesting world and populating it with an amazing cast of characters. The villains in the Prelude are pretty weak though, with most of their dialogue consisting of maniac laughter.Don't play these games for gameplay. The battle system is good enough and mostly works to punctuate the story sections. It does get better in MoD and MoT where you get multiple different moves for each character, but overall the battle system is not that deep in any of the games.In short:+Great story, loved the characters and how they grow over time+Good music+Very lore-rich world-Locked at 720p and 30fps, but it's 90% VN anyway so it's not that big of a deal-Long sections of slice of life fluffGet these games on sale if you're interested, the full price might be a bit too much.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've played in a long time, but it's one that requires a lot of patience.The first 5-6 hours is the most dull, boring thing I've ever had to play through. LOTS of VN sections with little to no story development or notable events, and almost no gameplay. Then, around 5 hours in something happens (you'll know it when you see it) and the games story just takes off.Once it gets going the game is fantastic. The story is one of the best I've seen in a video game in a very, very long time. It's deep, complex and emotional, and will leave you guessing until the very end. Although the pacing can be a bit off sometimes. It also might leave you with a few questions at the end, but keep in mind this is only the first game of a trilogy. The voice acting is some of the best I've ever heard and it really adds to the intense, emotional nature of the game. The OST is really nice too.The gameplay is fun and flashy, very similar to FF tactics, but with Fire Emblem-esque attack animations, but it's also very easy. Even on hard mode you'll probably never fail a stage, and one shot bosses in a single attack. The game is still fun despite being as easy as it is, but it would have been nice to have a third difficulty that better scales enemies and bosses with your character levels.The only bad thing I have to say about the game (aside from the slow start), is that the PC port isn't the best. It's hard capped at 30 FPS, and hard capped at 720p internal resolution. Normally this would be enough for me to give it a thumbs down, but considering most of the game is a VN and the other bit is a top down tactical RPG, it really isn't a big deal.Overall, I'd recommend the game. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Fun game, would recommend, I will get the sequels. Surprisingly fun game play and an enjoyable story, though not as great a story as the reviews I've read here make it out to be. Long Version:First, the story, since that is the meat of the game, and also what people rave about. The game is very much a visual novel with tactical combat elements included, rather than being the other way around. The story is engaging, there are enough hooks to keep you interested even during the slower areas, things hinting to the player that a larger game is afoot and your (forgotten) past is almost certainly important to these at first seemingly unrelated events. (The primary character has amnesia, partially for story, partially to let you ask world building questions that any normal in-universe person would know, but that we the player are obviously clueless about.) I will say that for the most part I really enjoyed the story, there were a surprising number of moments that really got to me, where I was right there with characters, feeling their moments of happiness or pain, victory or defeat, anger and sorrow. It is for these reasons and the general story arc itself, which kept my interest, that I will pick up and play the next two games in the near future. However, at this point, having not played the other two games (and I've been given to understand its a legitimately interconnected epic of some sort), I DO NOT SEE, the amazing story that everyone who has played all the games is raving about. The story was fun, many of the characters were likeable and as previously mentioned, there were numerous moments that really drew me in, however, there were A LOT of weird, mildly uncomfortable moments throughout the game, for seemingly no reason, along with a handful of plot lines that are left glaringly unaddressed by the game's end. Which stick out considering some of said events were made out to be a big deal, but were left unresolved. For the unfinished plot points, I'm taking it on faith for the time being, that they will be resolved, fleshed out, or somehow otherwise dealt with over the course of the next two games. If in the coming months, I finish the trilogy and they're still unresolved, I will make note of it here, and vice versa. [EDIT: I have finished the trilogy, all the plot points mentioned above involve individual character arcs, or world building questions that aren't central to the story. None of them are answered, but it honestly doesn't detract from the narrative of the trilogy at all.]But even if those plot lines are resolved, there's still the matter of numerous incredibly uncomfortable interactions between the cast. Some of this is due to only occasionally found stilted dialogue during the game, which, considering the quality of the overall writing for most of the game, I would assume has to be the result of either different writers, or just as likely, translation issues. (I don't speak/read Japanese, so I played this game in English.) But there are a lot of just weird moments between the main character and the women of the cast (and it's not always the protagonist making it uncomfortable). I should note that some of these are clearly intentional and played for laughs or as set up for later events. But not nearly all of them, and they stuck out as unpleasant moments, partially because they seem so weird and otherwise out of place. On a related, but personal preference note, I have never, in my life, in any game, movie, TV show, book or any other kind of media, encountered so many characters that have, on multiple occasions, some variation of a, "Sorry, what were you going to say?" "Oh, n-nothing, never mind." interaction. I feel like I'd be low-balling it to say either the protagonist or someone you're talking to will say some variation of that phrase at least twenty times over the course of the game, and after awhile it started driving me nuts! (One character gets a pass, you'll know why when you beat the game, but just one!). This is entirely a personal thing, but it really, really started to annoy me by the end of the game. Regarding the game play. After watching the trailers, looking at screenshots and reading reviews, both here and elsewhere, (I'm a bit of penny pusher, I don't like spending money on games unless I'm reasonably sure I'll enjoy them, so I often research as much as I can without spoiling the story for myself.) I ultimately picked up the game with interest in it despite my initial opinions about the game play. I can be a bit of a graphic snob, and the tactical elements didn't LOOK that interesting, so I set the game to the minimum difficulty and headed out. I was quickly and pleasantly surprised to find that the combat was actually really fun to play. Not fun enough to turn up the difficulty and make it really challenging, since I really was here mostly for the story, but it was an enjoyable diversion most of the time, rather than an awful slog that I just wanted to get over with like I initially believed it would be. The combat is simple, but with enough nuance to allow you some fun tactical choices, while rewarding intelligent play, but not overly punishing foolish choices. I've heard it said that the combat in this game feels a bit tacked on, with combat feeling more baked into the next two games, so if more hardcore combat is more your speed, presumably the combat systems get more in depth, just as the story gets more in depth, the deeper in the series you go, or so I've been led to believe.Overall, I enjoyed this game, I was pleasantly surprised by how fun the combat system was, engaging without being boring or grueling. I enjoyed the story, it was set in a fun world and there are always questions about what's coming next and who you really are and why all these things keep happening. There are a lot of (to me) important or interesting questions left unanswered or for us to guess at, but the primary story elements are all tied up fairly neatly and presumably will be further fleshed out in the sequels. I look forward to playing the next two games in the future. Also, because I know for some people it matters, the game actually only took me about 40-45 hours to complete, it's just that I got called away from my computer for a few hours at a time, several times, while playing this game. Hope this helps, and thanks for braving this wall of text!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game on a whim because it was on sale and I saw that there was some tactical rpg gameplay and some cute art. I liked the majority of the character designs and mostly enjoyed the characters attached to those designs.The gameplay, however, was another matter. Even on hard difficulty and without extra grinding - I did play the optional training maps for completion to get their rewards - I accidentally became overpowered and none of the maps were challenging. The maps really didn't require any planning or strategy from me and I kinda just mindlessly steamrolled everything all the way through till the end. I honestly feel that my experience would have been improved if they removed all the gameplay and it was a pure text VN.The story is another frustration of mine. In general I'm not a fan of the amnesia trope, and this game is guilty of one my least favorite ways of handling it: introducing a character that has all the answers but drops zero clues about it until the end where they just bombard you with all the information. You can also really tell that the original version of the game was an eroge with the way certain relationships develop.I don't know if I'll be picking the rest of the series, considering my current feelings on this game as an overall package. I'll admit that I found the world and characters interesting enough that despite my above complaints, I can't help but want to see what the sequels have in store.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those times I really wish there was a Neutral rating.The combat is enjoyable and the art style attractive. One thing to keep in mind: Unlike most other tactical RPGs, killing the enemy does *NOT* get the killing character the most points. Instead, battle XP appears to be a formula of level comparisons, followed by amount of damage. Took me a couple battles to break out of the habit learned from other games in the genre.However, the visual novel part of the game is... mediocre. In particular, the first couple hours are tediously paced, purely setup. The characters are piles of slice-of-life/romance anime clichés. The political and philosophical elements, and the world-building are interesting parts, but they can't fully save the obnoxious cookie-cutter, predictable dialogue of the slice-of-life/harem romance moments.Also important to note: this is a linear story. There are no choices to be made. You play it, and you're done with Part I (this is the first game in a trilogy). Considering how heavily a lot of the visual novel portion borrows from harem anime, that's a disappointment. Especially since Obvious Main Girl is someone I find annoying because she has to check off the Trait Boxes of Archetype, rather than feeling organically like a true character.The tactical combat, while fun, is also not challenging. If one of your characters gets knocked out (there's no permadeath in this game), you planned poorly. But unlike other easy tactical strategy games (I'm looking at you, FE:3H), the characters and progression are balanced enough that you can't just organically build someone who can solo the map.Is it worth the $30 full price point? Absolutely not. Is it worth the $9 sale point? Maybe. I'm still undecided on that.The fact I'm undecided at 85% off pretty much answers my lean, I guess. Neutral-Tilting Negative, so it's a Not Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen is the first game in a series of 3 visual novels which depicts a generation of heroes prior to the ones from Mask of Deception and Mask of Truth. It is a combination between a visual novel and a strategy turn based combat game and it lasts from 30 to 35 hours without any idling. Personally, this series is quite a rare find, since I am not usually a fan of visual novels, yet I spent 120 hours reading the whole thing without any real breaks except unavoidable stuff like sleep or chores. I guarantee that a lot of people that enjoy anime, yet don't like reading manga or visual novels will enjoy Utawarerumono regardless of their preferences. I forced a friend that I family share to play them and he loved the series just as much as I did. starts with Hakuowlo, an injured masked man that lost his memories, waking up in a village of friendly people treating his wounds. Those people shortly became his family and Hakuowlo did his part to keep the village on its feet over the threats that kept escalating. It is written in such a way that those challenges they have to face don't feel looped or repetitive unlike big animes such as Naruto or Fairy Tail, there is no "power of friendship" that magically change the flow of fights and, even if it involves some bits of unrealistic illogical evil, the point of view of some antagonists does make sense most of the time. It is a beautiful story that left me a bit sad and jealous over the protagonist's luck to meet such wonderful people.  is a remaster from the original pieces drawn in 2002, when anime was sharper and the shading was rougher, but this does not mean it is bad looking, just look at this:It does have the vibes of old anime, but it is more like a different artstyle rather than inferior quality. I have screenshot every single artwork from the utawarerumono series because I like them so much.Outside the VN interface, in the RPG side of the game, the graphics are not very modern. It involves chibi low-poly characters covered in small sized textures ps2 or ps vita like. I did not personally mind that and don't think it would be a good reason to miss on this game, but it could've been better.   is a mix between the classic Utawarerumono from 2002 and the other 2 ones, but it can be set to classic-only as well. It is calming and emotional, the notes mixed with the voice acting creating a great auditory experience. Moonlit Flower is my favorite one and it luckily appears in all of the 3 visual novels.The gameplay, except for pressing the advance button a million times, involves turn based strategy as stated at the beginning of the review. There are 2 difficulty modes and the normal one is easy enough not to frustrate anyone nor bore you to death. It involves controlling Hakuowlo and the characters that become allies along the story. The remastered version does not include the adult content that existed in the official release from 2002 since the developers decided to widen their target audience. There are no patches, this game is family friendly.Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen (and its 2 sequels), despite being quite pricy, are worthy visual novels that can be enjoyed by everyone, even people that are not into visual novels. Piece of art involving marvelous writing, visuals and sound.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game because I liked Mask of Deception (the 2nd game out of 3) a lot, but, on its own, as a starting point, this game isn't very good. It's  faithful of a recreation of older versions of this 2002 game (it's based on the 2006 ps2 remake). That includes the problems with the pacing and the combat system. Watch the anime adaptation instead; it's much shorter, in terms of the number of hours you're investing, and it actually does some scenes  than this VN. On top of that, all the parts involving fights are handled better in the show.The SRPG combat mechanics are much simpler, and less interesting, than in the sequels. The timed critical hit system is less rewarding so there's less reason to care about it, and the interplay between the skills the characters learn is far lower. Almost all the abilities are boring passive effects that don't do much (including on the paid DLC guest characters from the other games!). There are zero ways (well, almost zero; the DLC character Atuy is an exception) to get extra turns (eg. Zeal filling up or certain skills in Mask of Deception), and even worse, the basic attack chains have almost no interesting effects. In the sequels, basic attack chains can apply certain debuffs or even hit in various AoE patterns. Here, there are no inherent debuffs on attacks in a chain, and most non-team attacks just hit one tile. There's a lot less strategic depth here.My review is still positive just because this is the beginning of a really cool story. The whole series has really cool underlying secrets. They can't even be called plot twists—it's more like a deep rabbit hole.The presentation is great, too. The drawn backgrounds are vibrant, and the character designs are memorable and endearing. The voice acting across all three games is top notch, but this is more true in the sequels. Still, in Prelude to the Fallen, the characters are pretty unique and fun, and they mostly don't fall into boring archetypes.The music is excellent, but a lot of it comes from the sequels.I don't recommend buying the DLC characters. A couple of them are exceptionally good because of strong abilities, good movement range, good stat growths, and (for some) great attack range, but they aren't at all necessary (the exceptionally good DLC characters are Nosuri, Atuy, Sasara, Anju, and Mikazuchi). Even on hard mode, this game isn't challenging, except in the optional, hard-to-unlock postgame extra fight that requires you to unlock all items. Plus, a very notable weakness of the DLC characters is that they can't engage in "Co-op attacks" with other units. Only units from this game's story can do that, and co-op attacks are really powerful, with good status effects, the ability to hit multiple enemies, and great range.

There is also a common trope that is exceptionally overused, and that is that many of the female characters are lusting over the main character but are naive to what sex is. It's obnoxious. That is my primary complaint with this game and if am made aware that future games are no better, I'll just spare myself the embarrassment. The combat is not very deep and is practically mediocre in its complexity and difficulty, but the combat is also not the reason one plays this game. I will leave this with an overall positive review, I hope I don't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game of a trilogy of visual novel strategy RPG hybrids. They tell a continuous, cumulative story.They play order is:Prelude to the fallenMask of deceptionMask of truthYou can skip free to prelude to the fallen to start with mask of deception, because that game changes the cast and takes place many years later, giving it some distance from the original that allows newcomers to enjoy it while still leaving room for callbacks for people that played the first one.However, you couldn’t skip mask of deception and go straight to mask of truth, because the two games take place one right after the other as a part one and part two scenario to the same story.I would recommend skipping the first game. The other two games do have callbacks to it, especially the third one, that won’t have as much of an impact if you didn’t play the first one, but these games are not short, and the first game is not great. All of the necessary story information Presented within the first game will be explained in the second and third game. The main reason to play the first game would be if you really like visual novels strategy RPG’s and fantasy/science fiction settings.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't play this first. There are two other games in this series that were released before this for good reason. This game is technically a remake of the "earliest", but not a good game by today's standards. They didn't make it before the other 2 games for good reasons. Wouldn't really call it a remake either, as it's essentially the same as the actual remake the original got on ps2. Yes, ps2. 2006. So it wasn't exactly much work. But whatsoever.-The writing is very questionable. Flat characters, every villain is mad and throwaway, funny scenes in the middle of bloodshed interchanging with overly serious stuff that's hard to to care about.  On top of that, at the end the game basically throws everything away for reasons, which makes you wonder why it was there to begin with.-The gameplay isn't offensive for the most part, but also not very fun. Status Ailments like to annoy, and this game had the single worst srpg map I've ever seen. A map where (on highest speed) you had to choose "wait" for all your 11 characters for 10 minutes or so, nothing else. Don't know how that actually makes it into a commercial game.-The music is okay, but some of the voices aren't. Notably the protagonist's gets annoying. You CAN mute the protagonist exclusively, but that's a weird thing in itself as well.-The game doesn't like you to actually read fast, which, given the quality, can be quite annoying. Sound effects full stopping text advancing until they are over (and you will hear them A LOT, like slurping, tea pouring..), or several seconds long transitions everywhere. Reading the story can get quickly frustrating.If you enjoyed the other 2 games, this could be interesting for science. Honestly though? Expect nothing. Because there's nothing to be found here. The original was made with a low budget during times where people got very experimental with this medium in Japan. And yes, this is incredibly experimental, if you would've played the original version in 2002. But like many of its brethren from that time, the popularity came from them being fresh, doing new things, and not being actually well done and polished. (they didn't even have the budget to buy a reference book for stuff they were doing, and had to borrow stuff from the library repeatedly... tells you something). To reach that part of the game, you need to beat roughly 70-80% of it. Is it worth it today? For most people I don't think so.

_childDocuments_.review: A great story with excellent characters, only held back by some average gameplay and some potential pacing issues.+Story is great, really goes places, very good ending+Well-written and likeable characters the vast majority of the time+Flashy combat finishers look cool+Some absolutely top-tier voice acting, some lines or scenes have extremely memorable delivery+Great artwork+/-Some potential pacing issues, depending on personal taste. This story is heavy on slow-paced character interactions and world-building early on, then transitions to having longer unbroken serious story sequences with occasional breaks of more relaxed scenes, before finally just becoming heavy story sequence after sequence with no breaks or chance to access the base menu.-I thought some of the story moments suffered from the presentation, some scenes rather than just being written and voiced use the 3D battle models and attack animations as part of the story and at times this looked goofy to me, I think just text and voice acting might have been better for certain scenes.-The battles are WAAAAY too easy. I played on normal mode and I think there is a hard mode so some of this is on me but I didn't realise how easy it'd be. No risk of losing, almost no tactical thought required, for the entire game. I think this additionally hurts some of the storytelling; it takes me out of it if a fierce boss goes down in a couple attacks, or a cool enemy powers up and enters a second phase.... only to then die in a SINGLE hit (this happened to me)It took me a long time to get through this game due to both the pacing and the lack of difficulty making the combat not engage me. However, overall the story/characters are the focus and those are mostly excellent, I look forward to playing the sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: Remake of the original Utawarerumono, which is a considerably famous game among visual novel fans   A hybrid visual novel/strategy RPG, it is clearly a story-first game, and has a decent plot and an entertaining and likable cast of characters who are really the stars of the show here. While you will spend a decent amount of time battling, at least on Normal difficulty, there's never a reason to grind (though you can do so if you wish for some reason), and getting through the story stages is very easy    I'd say it's mostly not a particularly strong game by itself, but instead adds valuable background to the story of the next two games that will help you enjoy the story of those games to the maximum. While this may seem odd since this was originally a standalone game with no sequels, I feel that is how this game works best today in the presence of the "Mask of" games. So buy it if you plan to play the entire trilogy (or have already played the other two). Either this or Mask of Deception will work as a decent starting point to the series, but definitely do not touch Mask of Truth first. Personally recommend starting with Prelude over Deception     And as another very helpful reviewer has said, do not touch the DLC characters if you care about story and  have not played the other two games

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fantastic. Easily a 7/10 experience. There's a few things that drag it down though. Also, before I get too far, don't even bother looking at or touching the DLC characters. They are spoilers for the later games. They are very much there for people who have previously played the games before this remake came out.First of all, the game is very much a VN first and tactical RPG second. The battles very much feel like an after thought to make it more interesting. The battles are still really fun and interesting but just don't expect a ton of depth. This could be a plus or a negative to some. The game also requires a bit of grinding at times, which can feel like a drag, but the system they have for it is decent enough if you're used to grinding in tactical RPGs. Secondly, the story is fantastic. Is it kind of generic at times? Yeah a little bit but that's part of the fun. Just know that the story only continuously gets more and more interesting as it goes on. There are *a lot* of filler scenes though and some of the filler scenes just felt totally unnecessary at time or just very out of place. The out of place ones are edits from when the game was originally an eroge and for some reason, despite adding nothing to the story, they're still there and just feel completely random. However, as long as you're willing to power through them I promise you the story pays off. Third and finally, the art and sound are fantastic(sometimes). The original art is a bit dated, sure. But it still holds up and I think it's quite beautiful plus the newer re-designs are top tier. The music is on point and the sound design is uhh...interesting. Like many other VNs the sound effects used in game are super repetitive. As a fan of VNs, and someone not usually triggered by sounds, at times the over usage of certain sound effects drove me insane. It was so bad that I had to rush through scenes because I could not stand another moment of hearing said sound. Thankfully they were only in filler scenes so there really was not much lost.The game definitely has it's upsides and downsides but overall i'd say it was a good, maybe even great, game!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Worth going through despite my mixed feelings, just for the sake of setting up the world and some of the recurring characters for the next 2 games, Mask of Deception and Mask of Truth.When I started the Utawarerumono series with this entry and finished the game, I wasn't exactly impressed a whole lot. And now, after playing all 3 games, I'd say that this one is by far the weakest both in terms of story and in terms of gameplay as in both aspects it shows its age.At first I genuinely loved the story and getting introduced to the world throughout the first ~20 % of the game. But at a certain point, the pacing kinda takes a hit as the plot very quickly settles into a loop of quite formulaic mini-arcs varying in quality separated by tons and tons of pretty average, never ending SoL scenes. This continues until the final arc. What actually made me invested again a bit was the ending which I think was handled very well compared to the slog of the middle part of the plot. It even surprised me a little how it managed to make me care about some of the characters at the very end despite feeling exhausted from the pacing and despite the fact that many of the characters felt rather one-note.The gameplay is fine if you don't expect much considering this is primarily a VN. It has some interesting ideas but some of the mechanics (like damage based on positioning) and level design/layout made me feel like I was encouraged to use the same tactic and formation over and over. Which essentially meant creating chokepoints with tanks supported by a healer behind them while obliterating anything that got close with archers in the rear. Nothing in the game really challenged me to the point where I had to change this strategy considerably.While all of this may sound kinda negative and I even felt a bit "meh" after finishing this first entry of the series, I can confidently say that it is still very much worth it to go through this one just for the setup alone. And to be honest, finishing the next 2 games even made me retroactively appreciate this one a bit more, as they provide some relatively satisfying conclusions to some of the characters from this first game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fine visual novel and a very average strategy game. The strategy game play is very standard stuff for the genre. _childDocuments_.review: I've loved this game for years. I played older releases using patchers and the like in order to get it in English. _childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Overall just a great story with strong characters. They all have a lot of time to develop and all get a lot of screen time which really helps you grow attached to them. I find it quite rare for a game to have pretty much every character be likeable and interesting, but this game shines in that regard. I only found a couple of the antagonists to be quite weak but one of them was just because they were comically evil which just isn't interesting in the slightest. Pretty consistently great all the way through in the story department, with many standout moments and with great music to accompany them. Towards the end, the twists got really interesting and I loved how they were presented. Very memorable story to me, even though most of it was slice of life it was all very entertaining and developed the characters well. My only real downside with this game is that the progression between story sections didn't feel very cohesive at times, it felt like it just randomly skips time without really conveying it to the player.The combat isn't all that great but I did find it satisfying getting everyone's chains maxed out and maxing their damage. Basically everyone becomes a monster if you just level attack, especially the ranged characters. You will pretty much one shot everything.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad I played this series. It's really slow even among slow games but it's worth it. Mask of Deception had me laughing the whole time while Mask of Truth made me cry a lot, and Prelude to the Fallen did both.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: This strange word, Utawarerumono, translates roughly to English as "Those of whom legends are sung".The Utawarerumono trilogy provides powerful evidence to support the claim that creative fictional works published as computer software can attain the emotional and psychological complexity and depth associated with literature, the theater, or cinema. These are characters whom you come to know well, who stay with you long after completing the story. In short, they are genuinely memorable. Importantly, this is not because of reliance on cheap jabs designed to provoke a reflexive emotional response, but because of the depth of characterization the authors have achieved through time-honored methods, through patient, careful development and compelling narrative and dialog. Unusually, the series also uses the technique of internally-voiced thoughts, in effect, verbal thought balloons, spoken by the voice actors amidst live interaction occurring in the story. The emotional intensity and depth are also the result of the sheer length of the arcs the authors have developed across three titles, each of substantial length individually. We've all seen what's possible in an hour or two of screenplay. Imagine what's possible in a narrative work involving a couple of hundred hours of reader involvement!Appearing to be set in something resembling the Middle Ages in rural Japan, they plot explodes out of this presumptive setting, revealing itself to be a work of an entirely different genre. This is powerful stuff. Characters evolve over time. They develop. Some die. We are never spared from the impact of events, and nor, by the time they occur, would we wish to be. We come to care about these characters. As in life, things are not monochromatic. There's delightful humor, genuine warmth, real outrage, understandable anger, and sometimes, terrible shame over appalling secrets, all in aid of advancing a deep narrative tale, a legend, worthy of the name. Highly recommended! Well worth your time! Deeply engaging, never a chore to work through, always interesting, sometimes profound, consistently surprising. Utawarerumono is a unique, standard-setting demonstration of what can be achieved with this new story-telling medium by excellent writers, artists, voice actors, and musicians.

_childDocuments_.review: This one...really hurts.  Okay.  So, U:PTTF is not a bad game.  The story is more or less very similar to the original anime version, and it's a good story.  I would recommend it fine on that level.  I really, really wanted to see them redo the original arc in the modern art style, but...the polishing-up of the old art looked better than I'd hoped.  It's not bad.Where I run into difficulties here in recommending the story more widely is that...that's basically all this game did for me.  I was hoping that the game would expand on some of the things that were missing in the transition between this and U:MoD/MoT, like Fumirul, or giving an explanation for Kuon.  Both of these things, it sort of touched on, but then skimmed over very quickly, and did not actually complete the story connections.  Those plot threads felt half-baked and poorly connected, and I was really disappointed to see that the ending was more or less 100% the same as the anime, with nothing (or very little) expanded or added.  It's still a good story, but I wanted a little more to make the whole series cohesive.And then we reach combat.  It fundamentally shifts a few things from MoD/MoT, adding elements like facing and changing the 'quicktime' system, for lack of a better term, from being a critical hit system to adding zeal.  It's *fine.*  I like the facing element, actually, and I find the lack of it noticeable as I go back to replay MoD.  I think I prefer the critical hit system, though.The part that I really didn't like is that a lot of the combat felt...asinine.  It felt like they worked on the story elements, then realized at the last minute they needed to have combat levels too, and jammed stuff in so that they could say it was done.  Several missions were entirely "hit this one thing/these ten identical things for half an hour until they eventually die".  One mission literally had you just running over to a corner and waiting for fifteen minutes.  It felt like filler, and I never felt that way with the later games.  I also...maybe I was doing something horribly, horribly wrong xD but the spellcasters in this game never became useful in the slightest, and maxed out at piddling damage compared to the rest of everyone.TLDR: I love the Utawarerumono series, I love the story.  If you're more of a visual novel type than an anime type, then I think you can play through this absolutely fine and have a rewarding experience.  You'll just have to be patient through some lackluster tactical levels.  But, if you don't have a particular attachment to the visual novel experience, then I think...at this point, if I was advising a friend who was trying to get started in the series, I would recommend they watch the anime and skip this game.  And that's kind of where I'm at with this game as a whole.  It's not *bad*, but to me, it doesn't bring anything extra to the table, and it can be a bit of a bear to get through sometimes.

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen is a pretty good game if you're into the visual novel genre and perhaps a good way to get into it if you haven't tried out the genre. There's a good mix of drama, humor, action, cuteness, and you probably will spend a small majority of the game going through the visual novel part. The story is linear so nothing to worry about in terms of saving and reloading to get the ending you want.It has a mix of turn-based tile/tactics/rpg battles thrown into the general text/music storytelling. Battles can be a little challenging but I think the average gamer can figure how to win the battles without thinking too hard. Replaying battles and playing training stages to get EXP, stat points, and items can be a tedious grind but not too bad in the first playthrough (there is a new game + if you want to replay the game after you beat it).First learned about the story watching the anime quite a few years ago, and enjoyed the way it was told and the world it presented alongside the characters. Discovered it was based on a visual novel and that got me to try it out. Compared to the anime adaptation, the original visual novel spends more time developing the characters so you get to know them better and the story. It doesn't just force you along and skip the small day to day interactions that make characters come to life like 23 minute episodes of anime do to try and wrap up story within however many episodes.As someone fluent in Japanese I would say the translations are alright but not the best. But the shortcomings with the translation isn't anything that would present a fatal problem to the story and being able to enjoy the game. Haven't had any crashes while playing the game but did experience some when browsing the bonus material (music, cg, etc.) after clearing the game. If you want to play the game in any of the supported languages, be sure you choose wisely, because the game files are basically re-downloaded again for that language. I have not tested whether or not the save files are compatible but switching the language setting had to be performed in the library (right click and go to properties and choose language), and is not done in-game.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: I did not expect this story to be so emotionally stirring. The moment you gain something, something else is shortly taken away. The artstyle and setting of a feudal japan-esque world is profoundly charming and lovely. Both music and voice acting are top notch. The characters are all truly vibrant in their own way, which may be why getting invested in those characters can end up becoming a double-edged sword for the reader.I almost wish this story would have followed a more traditional VN "route" design. The characters are all lovely, so much so that you almost want to dedicate yourself to each of them individually. The gameplay was honestly nothing special, and could have been left out without really harming the final product, but it was certainly not bad either, and did not detract from the experience at all.Personal bias aside, this was a wonderful first installment to a fascinating world.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Having been introduced to the Utawarerumono series through the anime, I finally get to experience the more detailed story through this game.story 7/10:The prelude is an interesting story, which started great with a mysterious masked person who has amnesia who tries to adapt to a world where strength is right and rises to power as a leader of a country for the people through resourcefulness, strategical brilliance, and camaraderie. This part of the story is like reading a well-paced book.Also all the people other than the protagonist have partial animal parts on them like animal ears and tails, but honestly, that part is pretty much flavor text and fan service.Then came the second part of the story ... which is some sort of sci-fi introduced at breakneck speed ...The pacing went haywire when the story  moved towards its conclusion, but since it's very spoiler-ish to talk about what happens, I'll just complain about things going too fast and crazy and made the finale not nearly as impactful as the chronological successors: mask of deception and truth.The game still presents a good story, but just not on the level of mask of deception and truth.gameplay 7/10:The meat of gameplay is in the tactical rpg element, where you prepare and field your group of companions on a tiled battlefield, as you deal with enemies in turn-based combat.The system is almost the same as the predecessors, but with characters of the prelude story, so it's still a good tactical turn based system that isn't too in-depth.The combat is engaging as you can watch your character perform ridiculously showy string of whoop-ass moveset on the enemies while trying to click on quick-timed mouse event in order to maximize the amount of zeal (Energy or adrenaline) gained through combat, which allows you to perform even more special attacks later.However, in this game, combat is too easy,  This is because the enemies do not become that much stronger as the game progresses, but your characters do become godly. In terms of escalation, your enemies progress in a boring way: they just have better stats. They rarely pull out any interesting new tricks on you ... as a matter of fact, end game enemies are just glorified meat-shields. At a certain point, you come across long and intimating boss introductions after which Oboro (one of your companion) pulls off his ridiculous special combo on the boss and ends up swiftly dispatching the said boss in a single action despite having disadvantageous elemental affinity ...Thus, we have an interesting tactical turn based system that lacks challenge ...Anyway, it's a good enough visual novel with ok gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Given the all age version was first released in 2006, I found the game is still enjoyable. Coming from the anime, I would say if you enjoy the anime, you would probably like the game. The plot is 90% similar to that of the anime with a little more details not given in the anime. You would recognize many of the same dialogues from the anime.I got it for around $20 USD when it was on sale and feel $20-30 would be a reasonable price range to get the game.Pros:- Excellent voice acting- Nice 2D graphics- Quite an amount of play time (took me 47 hrs to complete everything)- Battles are quite fun- Great soundtracks (in fact I went from soundtracks -> anime -> game)- Content rich (feels like the developers put in an effort to make it good)Cons:- 3D graphics is showing its age (still playable tho)- Gives you too many items when you can only equip 1 item + 2 consumables, should have made it 2+2- Kind of slow if you are not used to visual novel (which I am not)Overall, I would give the game a 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: More of a visual novel with a strategy game for intermissions, this is a very enjoyable game and lead me to grab the other two games in the trilogy (which were strangely released before this). The strategy game is turn-based with RPG elements so characters gain levels and you have control over how to build characters. This has the advantage that if you are poor at strategy games then you can repeat levels you have already finished to build up your characters but do not need to do so. As the story segments are very long, I found myself grinding between battles when I started getting tired of the story segment.The story is interesting and does a good job of building up the characters though the story segments make up the bulk of the playing time and tend to be a bit too long for me (though, you can do what I did and replay levels).  Most of the characters do make guest appearances in the sequels, but are mostly contained to this story. Playing this game before the other two games will prevent spoilers and will make the sequels a bit more enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Prelude to the fallen is the first entry in the Utawarerumono Visual Novel Trilogy, and follows a protagonist named Hakuowlo who was found unconcious in the woods with no recollections of his memories. This is one of the best visual novel around because of the music, characters, and story. As the story goes Hakuowlo's memories slowly comes back and made significant to the story. The characters are all very enjoyable and unique there is no way anyone could hate on any of them. Although this Visual Novel is listed as 30+ hours long, i can safely say that its atleast 40+ hours long so keep that in mind. All the time spent on this VN is a time well spent Very Reccomended and the sequels in this trilogy only gets better and better
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: I didnt played the old version of the game but i did watch the anime years ago, i remembered 2/3 of the game except the very last part of the story which is the most important. It took me 55 hours to have all the achievementsPositives :-A lot of different and enjoyable characters, mostly females, with differents personalities and backstory-Good story, univers and atmosphere : its a mix of drama, slice of life, war and fantasy in a sort of medieval japan. The last quarter of the game is very good storywise.-The OST variety : 100 musics in total from the trilogy games. It was not repetitive at all and some of the tracks are very good.-They keep the artworks of the old game but with better resolution/colors. They're pretty good, sad there isnt more of them.Negatives :-Difficulty is not existent even on hard mode, so the last third of the game was borring during the gameplay, im glad that the story and the characters are very good enough to keep me playing this game. The only map with a bit of difficulty is the bonus one. -Pacing between gameplay and VN is a bit off. Most of the time it's like this : hours of VN non stop, 4-5 battles then VN again etc...-The game is locked at 30fps, its kinda fine since the game is motly a VN with a bit of basic SRPG but come on its 2021...
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 amazing story the game play is kinda meh but the game is mostly light novel anyway which as the first time playing a light novel i came into it very skeptical but i found myself being told a very human down to earth story and i started looking forwards to the evening i could wind down sit down and just listen to a good narrative and take everything in at my own pace.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono is a visual novel with a gripping plot, charming characters, and a world that I've found myself really immersed in. The tactical rpg battles while a bit basic compared to some contemporary tactical rpgs, is still fun and mixes it up a bit with unique battle win conditions, rather than simply route the enemy. I have probably played less than half the game so far, but I highly recommend the game to any anime/VN/tacticalrpg fans
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Utawarerumono is a VN/SRPG hybrid game, that is really well crafted in almost every regard, I have yet to play the sequels but if they hold up to this quality, and hell i've heard they're even better. Then i'm gonna be in for a massive treat. This game made me happy, it made me sad, it made me angry, it made me happy again, then tore my heart out and told me to DEAL WITH IT. It made me cry and I rarely cry at games. The SRPG combat is surprisingly great despite the VN focus, and fights don't take 5 hours to get to like say oldschool Sakura Wars. The characters are wonderful, I was pulled into this damn world and it won't let go. I'm stuck for life.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Figured I'd leave a first-impression review because it's on sale. I'm not actually 4 hours in, more like 2.5 hours and 1.5 hours idling in the background.I got all three titles in the bundle even though I usually don't pay this much for games because I figured that if I was going to be disappointed, I was going to be disappointed on an epic scale, damn it.So far it's a really nice visual novel! Artwork is nice. Sound is nice. Translation is really polished. I'm enjoying learning more about the world. This feels similar to Senren Banka, so far, but that's probably just because it's a common story with common archetypes. Nevertheless, I like this sort of thing, so it's up my alley.One thing that I don't like so far is the lack of choice in the VN portions. You can choose which location to go to next, but you're going to all of them anyway, so it's really not much of a choice.I've only been in one battle so far so I can't say whether this is like the Holy Grail of FFT. I'm guessing not and that the SRPG parts are more tacked-on, but it might increase in depth as I go on.Anywhoozle, I'm going to keep playing/reading, which is nice because there was every possibility that this could have completely tanked for me in the first hour or two. So, if you're on the fence, you've got this positive first-impression review plus a ton of other reviews from people who have played a bit more. Happy gaming!Edit: After playing this for about 20 hours, it has pretty much lost its charm for me. I'm not saying that it's a bad story, it's just too slow-paced to keep me interested and the characters are decent but not memorable like, say, the characters of Disco Elysium, or Planescape: Torment, or Final Fantasy 7. I guess what I'm trying to say that it's average, perfectly serviceable writing, but there's so much average, perfectly serviceable writing. And the combat isn't like FFT or even as much fun as some of the indie tactics games here like Fell Seal: Arbeiter's Mark. So there's a lot of average combat.And, most disheartening of all, there are no choices in the VN. It's kinetic. Completely on rails.So I'm going to cut my playthrough short for now, but keep my positive recommendation, because it's not a bad game. I can see its appeal. For me though, it's just not a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game.Maybe a bit too easy, even on the HARD difficulty, but totally worth playing for the plot.It's beautiful, nostalgic, complex, sad, romantic and a million other things. It's a really well-crafted plot.The only downside of the plot is that it is a bit slow to take flight, being filled with events with no real meaning. But do not be discouraged, play it until the end and you will certainly feel rewarded.
_childDocuments_.name: Utawarerumono: Prelude to the Fallen

_childDocuments_.review: Prelude to the Fallen follows the story of a young man with no memories who awakens in a strange world, and is taken in by a tribe of kindhearted villagers. He is raised as one of their own, eventually receiving the name "Hakuowlo." When neighboring nations begin to encroach on his village, Hakuoro rises up against the tyrannical invaders, setting off on an unforgettable journey that lives on in the songs of legend.

name: Chorus
detailed_description: Take control of Nara, once the Circle’s deadliest warrior, now their most wanted fugitive, on a quest to destroy the dark cult that created her. Unlock devastating weapons and mind-bending abilities in a true evolution of the space-combat shooter. Along with Forsaken, her sentient starfighter, explore ancient temples, engage in exhilarating zero-g combat, and venture beyond our waking reality. A JOURNEY OF REDEMPTION Lead Nara, an ace pilot facing her haunted past, and Forsaken, her sentient ship. Their quest for redemption will take them across the galaxy and beyond the boundaries of reality, as they fight to unite resistance forces against the Circle and their leader, the Great Prophet, at all costs. VENTURE BEYOND THE VOID Enter a dark new universe, teeming with mystery and rife with conflict. Explore epic locations such as sprawling space stations and strange planes of existence beyond our own. Engage in exhilarating zero-g dogfights from epic cosmic vistas to tight crystalline corridors. Chorus balances the scale and spectacle of space exploration with frenetic, fast-paced action. ONE PILOT, ONE SHIP, ONE LIVING WEAPON Attain powerful and distinct weapons and combat upgrades. Master your ship’s unique drift mechanic and deadly mind-bending abilities, including extra-sensory perception, teleportation and telekinesis, to overcome massive hordes of enemies and take down titanic battleships. Chain your powers together to become the ultimate living weapon. FEATURES A compelling single-player experience Play as dual protagonists Nara and her sentient AI companion and starfighter, Forsaken, on a personal journey of redemption Experience fast-paced, frenetic action that evolves the spirit of classic space shooters Fight to unite resistance forces against the Circle and their ominous leader, the Great Prophet Face down hordes of enemy starfighters, titanic battleships and unknown Void entities Reclaim, upgrade and wield devastating weapons and abilities in zero-g dogfights Explore a dark new sci-fi universe, teeming with mystery and conflict Enjoy gorgeous next gen sci-fi visuals in 4K, from cosmic vistas to sprawling space stations

_childDocuments_.review: 🔵Space based 3rd person combat game with excellent story + background mechanics.🔵Soundtrack is magnificent (Hollywood standard).🔵Progressive story led gameplay.🔵I could not get past the controls; needs HOTAS & an advanced flight model.✔️Looks fantastic✔️Audio is fantastic✔️Soundtrack is Really fantastic.✔️Voice acting fluctuates but is Mostly decent or better.✔️Environments are spectacular.✔️Upgrades, loadouts and ship variety are decent.✔️Emotionally fuelled story keeps you pushing forwards.❌No HOTAS Support.❌Flight Model is clunky and restrictive (No Yaw and no Reverse).❌Tracking enemies and objectives can become confusing.❌No Multiplayer Co-Op❌No first person cockpit view.❌1660ti @4K stutters in combat.⭐Soundtrack + Game Audio + Graphics💡HOTAS SUpport💡Advanced Flight Model for more advanced players looking for more realism.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game play is nicely bug free, and the graphics solid i can not recommend this game.  The AI ships have a habit so zipping out of view and then suddenly vanish, and reappear behind you shooting you from behind.  The AI ships also reacts instantly to your mouse movement, instead of a slight delay after you fire.  The lack of an assisted aim tool made fights more tedious then fun.  Even when you used the hunt ability to get behind ships they would instantly shield in behind.  The first boss fight after entering the void turn out to be uncompleteable even on easy difficulty. _childDocuments_.review: A solid, straightforward space shooter with an uplifting, if imperfectly delivered message. _childDocuments_.review: - 3rd person only space shooter (you're in a ship 100% of the time)- You stay in the same ship for 90% of the game, no changing ships as you like, and no cosmetics to the ship.- Heavy story emphasis: I was surprised at how engaging it was actually- Abilities, basically magic make the combat very fast and fun when you get used to it. - 100% achievements require a bit of extra effort, but I 100% it at 20 hours.Don't sleep on this one, it's an unexpected treat.
