_childDocuments_.review: I overall enjoyed Chorus, but just barely. I am a sucker for space shooters - grew up with X-Wing: Alliance and its ilk - and the combat gets my thumb up. It's exciting, tough without being impossible, and spiced up by the unusual addition of your pilot having essentially magic powers that she can use to even the odds even when vastly outnumbered. The game also must have taken a cue from Star Wars (and Return of the Jedi in particular) because it's chock full of high speed runs in narrow twisty tunnels and capital ships that you need to take down by flying inside and destroying their power reactor. I love that stuff, to those are the pros.The cons are that this game could have been perfect if it had added some kind of rogue-like endless battle mode with increasingly hard hordes of enemies, and instead all it has is a story mode, which wouldn't even be such a big deal if the story wasn't so... ugh. Every voice actor sounds like they're constantly on the verge of an emotional breakdown as they deliver this ponderous tale of a woman who committed a pretty big war crime and has since defected from the cult she used to fight for to help those resisting it. And the tale is delivered via "memories", which are essentially in-game unskippable interactive cutscenes, which you have to go through again, and again, and again, for the whole damn campaign as well as most side quests. The story to me was just uninteresting, and its extremely dour tone also made it dull.The game looks and sounds really cool; the various systems are all very distinct and provide a variety of unusual space environments. Really, the forced narrative was the only negative for me. Still, this is definitely worth a sale price if you like space fighting games (and feel confident about tackling one that has a bit more teeth to it).
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: If you like arcade, fast-paced dogfight like Everspace 2 this game is for you. This game work so well with just mouse and keyboard. Don't pay attention to the sexist review like: why main is a female pilot, etc... If you expect a realistic combat, no this game not for you. If you want to chill by traveling through universe or discovering planets or be a merchant scamming NPCs with your crazy price, no this game is not for you. If you play this game prepare to fight everywhere you go. Final word if you like this game, buy it to support the DEVs.
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty cool short-and-sweet spaceship game about essentially a sith lord turning to the light and saving the world through having loads of grandiose dogfights made all the more epic and unique due to the inclusion of force powers! While I felt like the game was a little unfocused with some unnecessary open-world elements that drag the pacing down, I'd still consider it a big recommendation for people that are tired of the usual space dogfights and want some more spice added to them!PROS*Very dramatic and compelling story about redemption that's short and sweet, being able to get a complete experience in about 12-15 hours: fun to watch the main characters grow*Great combat design that's much more interesting than your typical endless circling and firing missiles you see in other space dogfighting games: a very diverse cast of enemies forces you to use everything in your toolset from your weapons to your force powers like drifting, teleporting, lightning, dodging and more to win*Incredibly epic scenarios and setpieces like crippling capital chips from the outside before flying into them to blow out their cores, trench runs, tunnel chases, as well as crazy boss battles against gigantic eldritch colossiCONS*Certain aspects of the story feel underdeveloped: some characters become your allies with very little resistance, some plot points that you think would come up later are dropped, culminates in your typical 'balance' and 'believe in yourself' philosophy 101 cliches*While the game has some incredible highs for its combat scenarios, these can be few and far-between the many easy-peasy scenarios that come up alongside just tedious flying around to get to the next objective: my patience grew thin at some points*Underdeveloped systems like ship customization, upgrades, side-quests and collectibles feel very token, like the game was originally going to be a big open-world but then they scrapped it half-way but still left it in: would much prefer a more straight-forward well-paced adventure than this game which lets a lot of superfluous fluff get in the way
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Full of fun space dog-fights set in the beautiful backdrop of a terribly tedious universe. Recommended, if on sale.The good:Flying around looks and feels great. While very simple in its control scheme, everything about traversal and combat feels exciting and weighty. The (very small) collection of ship weapons and powers, while limited in variation or originality, are fun to use. The game performs wonderfully, and has plenty of individually beautiful moments. The BadBY ALL THAT IS HOLY THE STORY-LINE IS TEDIOUS. The (beautiful) setting is very limited in scope. There are only a few maps which you will need to trudge back and forth to over, and over, and over, and over again. You will revisit the same handful of locations and characters for the same few quest types. It feels a bit like the entire game is just one long tutorial sequence for flying your ship that an edgy teen stapled a story to at the last minute. The story and quests are not fun. They aren't motivating. They should not be the reason you buy this game. You should buy this game to have a few fun hours of pulling awesome space acrobatics and blasting pirates to dust with magic space-wizard powers.
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, i can't reccomend Chorus.The Base is all there. Its somewhat solidly built and the gameplay loop is okay - But everything about it screams "B-GAME".The game is "OK" but you will repeatedly get reminded that it, like nearly every game nowadays, is unfinished or at least badly playtested. Granted, its not as bad as most other titles on the market.Major complaints:- The AOE, oh, the AOE damage effect. I refuse to believe that the developers played their game and thought. "yes, this is fine." It not only distorts your screen so intensely that you can barely see what you are doing, it also makes your vision nearly black and white - when all damage telegraphs, your charge beam visual que and enemy hit zones are colour coded. I CAN'T understand how this gets trough playtesting. This single screen effect got me killed collectively about 25 times on the same 2 occasions where you Can. Not. See. what you are supposed to to.-The objective markers are very small, fade out (??) and appear only 5-10 seconds after a conversation has ended you so just idle in space not knowing where you have to fly next until it appears.- Difficulty spikes MASSIVELY with me having to switch difficulty to medium on the first big boss due to there seemingly not being enough time to burst him down until his global DOT kills you. Feels like it was not playtested.- Same can be said against normal enemies where some that are clearly introduced as hard enemies can be killed within 1-2 seconds flat with your powers, while the normal, base enemy fighter, remains dangerous into lategame. Others feel like crazy bullet sponges.- Capital ships are so laughably easy to kill that a fight gets considerably easier if one spawns in.- The charge attack is what kills you 80% of the time, since the timing window for dodge is small and the visual que is very, very bad. If you fly up the camera blocks most of the visual que as well. Great design.- Starting with midgame, nearly 50% of enemy ships have said broken charge beam attack. There is also another enemy that has an attack that uses the same visual effect for its attack minus the visual que, making you spend your dodge sometimes just to be killed by the real charge beam.- A lot of the fights that randomly spike in difficulty that you fail over and over again, you suddenly win even though you did not change your tactics whatsoever, leaving you with the feeling that its just RNG if you get charge beam attacked in a bad moment and die due to that. Some even being over in 2 minutes when before you spent double that and half the enemies where still alive when you died.- It's normal that your allies do nothing in games, but in this game the trope is pushed to the max with your enemies ignoring them 100% of the time except on certain "protect" missions and you killing 100% of enemy ships. There is also almost no radio chatter so you even "feel" alone even in big fights.- Ship upgrade system is there just so the game can say it has one. - 90% of side missions feel like heavy runtime padding. All this can be patched out. And with some basic issues fixed, i feel like this game is definitely fun. Right now you get your fun tainted again and again by the issues mentioned above.
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Great gameplay with weak story. _childDocuments_.review: A fun space shooter with engaging combat and solid visuals. I was not expecting much from this game. I never heard about it until I saw it on the discovery queue and it piqued my interest. At $40 full price, it is a nice surprise. The combat is the main dish, it is frequent and enjoyable. _childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Chorus is an arcade space shooter with a focus on its narrative. It has an open world you can explore and traverse, but it's no Freelancer. Trading is nonexistent. The game gives you one ship, three weapon types with several variants as well as up to four "rites" - spells, basically - to play with. Being a space shooter, pressing and holding a button allows you to maintain your momentum as you spin around to shoot enemies behind you. The focus clearly is on flying, shooting and using this game's flavor of space magic, and the game does those things really quite well in my opinion. It is adept at making you feel good about the maneuvers you pull off.The narrative's presentation focuses heavily on the main character to the point of her being practically the only animated human being. It is evident that a significant proportion of the game's budget was put into her, similar to how the portrayal of Senua in Hellblade was a major focus of that game. Both games share a distinctly double-AA feeling. Chorus' characterization of Nara does not reach the same level of quality, unfortunately, but it does offer the main character a sidekick she can bounce off of.I liked my time with the game. Combat was highly enjoyable, exploration and traversal of the open maps was fun. The narrative is a bit esoteric for my taste, but that does not detract from this being a good game. My, as of the time of me writing this, 17 hours in the game amount to me finishing the story and doing practically all side content. I have no desire to replay it anytime soon, but I don't regret paying full price for the time I got out of it. It certainly is refreshing to finish an open world game without having to spend several dozens of hours. Discounted, I'd consider it a hidden gem. If you're on the fence about the game, try the demo.
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: First of all -- I do not agree with the hatred this game gathers. Now to the story and actual review.When I was on my early teens I picked a game from sale basket among few others. The game casket read as "Freelancer". Yeap you might already know where I am going here. Freelancer is the game which was groundbreaking in every layer when it came out and even when it's been two decades people still remember and refer it in almost every single time when some new action-spaceflight sim has been released.So did I got the successor for the legendary game? No, but I got Chorus!! The game is just incredible cinematic piece, with great protagonist Nara who evolves throughout the story as a pilot but also as a character. You also meet numerous side characters among companion Forsa who fights with you throughout the game. After tiny linear tutorial the current system is freely to be explored and there is numerous side quests, which are not achieved on space stations but by exploring the environment. Making money as merchant or miner is not an option in this, but several quality side quests compensate that in my opinion. Chorus is strictly battle based, but dogfights are always great fun! There is also many random encounters with different factions to make money, which you use to upgrade your shield defenses and weaponry. There is 3 types of weaponry and while there might not be so much variation the Chorus has another feature in its arsenal.Nara gets access into the Rites, magical abilities to deal with enemies and further you proceed the more of them you get. Nara also collects experience with rites and weapons and this should courage you to try different tactics to deal with enemies for all bonuses are significant and by adapting and learning you are able to do much cool stuff especially in the second half of the game.Speaking of the end game the ending was a true example how to conclude the story! The final minutes the game turned to be a bullet hell in a good way, but what did take the cake was the few last cutscenes - my skin legit went goosebumps and emotions kicked in! I had my expectations low for some games fail to give that final blow, but Chorus scored and for the good!After 18 long hours of flying and shootings I grant that Chorus can be a little bit repetitive and there is few aspects that are left simple. The playing with magics might not be everyone's cup of tea either, especially if one waits more factual setting. However I liked it and fell in love with it!Meet me... in Chorus.
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Chorus is a blast mechanically.  Lovely visual presentation.  Runs smooth as butter.Zipping and zooming and shooting and gliding and diving and skidding and turning feels fluid and intuitive!The combat feels great. Changing up the weapons and special attacks strategically per enemy encounter also feels natural and is a ton of fun.  There are occasional difficulty spikes, usually only with Boss encounters, which I found obtrusive.  I didn't enjoy a few of the "boss" battles.The story is serviceable, but nothing to write home about.  My main complaint is with the main character.  I didn't like her at all.  Bad writing and voice acting.I had a ton of fun with this title and recommend it to anyone that wants a decent "palette cleanser" of a game between the big AAA titles.  Shame about the Story, Characters and voice acting.
_childDocuments_.name: Chorus

_childDocuments_.review: Space shooters have become quite rare these days and when you see one that is able to catch your attention and guide you through its mysterious and fascinating narrative, you can only try to do your best to highlight its positive aspects. In Chorus you won’t find a space simulator, but a fantastic story-driven space opera.The protagonist, Nara, is an elder space pilot who was once part of a cult known as the Circle, which dominates the galaxy with its supreme power. Tormented by her past, she is now fighting the Great Prophet of the cult in search for redemption. This journey will lead her on a mission to free Forsaken, a sentient and powerful ship that she abandoned soon after leaving the Circle.As you explore many beautiful open environments, you will fight hordes of space pirates, cultist ships and alien forms that are threatening the galaxy. The quality of the lore is exceptional and you really feel like being part of a dangerous, yet believable, universe. Unfortunately, there isn’t a codex explaining everything in detail, but you can get a lot of info from residual memories and (long) dialogues with numerous NPCs.Visually, the game reminded me of  for often showing red twisted geometries and surreal moments. Just like Jesse Faden before (or Senua from ), Nara constantly speaks to herself and you can always hear her thoughts being whispered during dialogues, which greatly enhances her fears, doubts and motivations. Nara and Forsa are obviously the main stars of the game and their relationship is what keeps the narrative always interesting. There are also many other secondary characters, but they don’t have enough screen time to stand out on their own. Except for a few, the supporting NPCs are easily forgettable.That said, the game does an impressive job at keeping the focus on the plot. Even when you are doing one of the many side missions, you are always reminded of the ongoing main events. Initially, you can even find some optional missions that allow you to take a few interesting moral choices; sadly they are soon replaced with more linear ones filled with generic tasks such as escorting allies, rescuing civilians, retrieving cargos, freeing outposts etc. which are still kept acceptable thanks to the great focus on storytelling. You can’t win battles alone and Forsaken will not only be your friend, but your deadly spaceship. You will encounter many types of enemies and each one needs to be dealt by using a different tactic. The combat in Chorus is always quick and spectacular thanks to smooth manoeuvrability and the implementation of Rites. Through them, Nara can learn new abilities like drifting, teleporting behind enemies or boosting at the speed of light; abilities that are extremely important not only during combat, but also for completing a few puzzles and trials. Progressing through the story will give you access to more rites and upgrades, expanding the range of combat possibilities and making you feel in complete control of your spaceship. While there are only three type of weapons you can use (laser, gatling gun and missiles), you can find or buy different types of ammo and mods that affect their stats and aesthetic. Combining weapons and rites is fun and always encouraged as it is the only way to increase your level of mastery.Graphically the game looks quite good with some pretty weapons effects and explosions. The map is open and you can move freely where you want, with new different areas unlocking as you progress with the story. Looking back at it now though, I can’t recall any particular location. There are definitely some breathtaking visuals, but I feel like this galaxy was too static and missing iconic locations while some (like the Resistance HQ) could have been done better. Maybe there were also some budget limitations during the development, because you can see that Nara is the only character appearing during the well animated cutscenes when she is often confronting herself or other faceless models.Sound design and voice acting are brilliant, while the main soundtrack by Pedro Macedo Camacho (featuring Úyanga Bold) is one of the best I ever heard in a videogame and it perfectly fits the sci-fi theme while being tribal and evocative.Chorus brings attention back to epic narrative in space shooters and it does that without forgetting about the importance of gameplay, which is always fun and spectacular. It took me around 20 hours to complete the main story and all secondary missions at standard mode, but you can expect more if you increase the difficulty, although the game doesn’t offer any special reward for that (like better loot or a rare achievement). The challenge in standard mode is still guaranteed, with a few spikes during some more intense moments and boss fights. For some reason you can’t save during main story missions, which means that, before quitting the game thinking it auto-saved, it’s best to check the time of the last save or you might lose some progress.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game!  Takes a bit of time to warm up to, but the powers you get for your ship soon turn the combat into a dream.  Most fights tended towards being slightly too easy, but nothing ever felt tedious.  The final boss battle is a banger and well balanced - I felt like I was on the edge of failure right at the end.  The levels are simply gorgeous as well, which helped to immerse me in the world.  It seems there was a clear effort to make the game similar in style to open-world games like Witcher III, but then replacing people with space ships (for example, entire space ships are direct stand-ins for individual people in most instances).  Mechanically, this means the game has been designed for a lot of wandering, talks, and exploration to find quests.  I think they almost pulled it off, but it possibly would have been better as a linear campaign to keep the energy level up.The story does require you to make some inferences and fill in the blanks.  It's not the best, but it's fine.  The whole idea of an space cult is fantastic, and they strive for the golden mantra of "show, don't tell."  That being said, it could have been improved by more context in certain scenes.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember playing Star Fox 64 when it came out and having an absolute blast? Pick this game up and experience that joy all over again, 24 years later. You can even do the aileron roll (what the game incorrectly called a "barrel roll"). Remember watching Knight Rider? Or, seen the movie Stealth? Pick this game up so you can pilot a ship with an attitude. Want to drift a spaceship by transforming it into a "Drift Machine"? Pick this game up so you can do just that.Combat is engaging, graphics are beyond stunning, the little details are well done, the controls are fluid and tight as a drum, the story is fun and engaging, and the open world is so much fun to explore and find hidden items and quests.HOWEVER, where there is good, there is also bad. Several things that come to mind that you'll possibly find annoying would be the constant whispering inner dialogue that goes on. For the first hour or two, you won't think it's that bad, but give it time and it'll start to get on your nerves. It also doesn't come across as natural at times and feels disjointed versus plausible. (Supposedly, the developer actually responded to this complaint in a discussion thread and their response resembled that of a teenager texting; didn't bother capitalizing where they should've and failed to use punctuation correctly. This may not seem like a big deal to some, but to others how they respond can give you one impression or another. Personally, if I was a developer of a pretty good game and wanted to be perceived as someone who takes it seriously and professionally, I wouldn't use the writing skills of a middle-schooler. I mean, c'mon, it doesn't require a lot of effort to write a coherent sentence.)Another issue with the game would be how some missions might not make it so easy to see where you're supposed to go next or what to do. This is rare but one glaring example would be the mission where you have to escape The Guilt: you have to escape it and around the second or third time running away from it you're forced to a red barrier but there is no real hint as what to do. I got stuck/killed every time for the first 6 times I replayed it, only finally getting past the red barrier. Problem is that I had no idea what I did to do so; I was just randomly mashing buttons and trying to go in all sorts of directions while The Guilt was slowly killing me.And, the last thing I can think of is that the traveling long distances (even with "hyper-drive" engaged) can get tedious and boring, especially if you have to do it back and forth with no real form of fast-travel. There IS fast-travel but it's to whatever Space Jump portal you've come in on.All in all, even though it has some issues, which every game has, it's still a fun game to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Considering this is a somewhat Woke game, cobbling some odd things together and with some obvious creative deficiencies it has potential. As hostile as Woke is to people such as myself I'm not so objectionable to it when it's their own games and in this case I'm not certain to what degree it's intended. It's obviously for a female audience in one shape or form and is melding two disparity styles.What it's trying to do, well it's either not entirely possible or usually quite niche. Feminist theory just isn't based on reality which means that it tends to mischaracterise things that don't work as things that should work. If you're conversely doing something such as making a product for females who like something like fast cars that's always going to be a narrow primary audience. This game almost does fairly well in spite of that in that it had the potential to still appeal somewhat to a more general audience. You can get away with a lot so long as the gameplay is there and a few other of the basics are intact. You can put up with a few things not being to your liking but then there is sometimes just too much.This is where the game falls short, on the other areas. I could still enjoy the game just not taking the story line, bad acting, cliche, cheesiness and cringe too seriously nor heeding it much attention. Perhaps gaining some entertainment from laughing at it. There are various UX/QoL issues and bugs (it's hard to tell) to the point that it fails to pass muster. It always irritates me when I see this in gaming. It just takes one person to do one play through to pick up on most of this stuff.There are quite a few issues with bad timing. The decision to use a ground based plane mechanic for a space game is frustrating. Then there is picking up rites remnants and either due to a bug (perhaps opening the menu at the same time) or due to a lack of it telling you everything you've got there's no obvious bonus from it. Having no separate markers for scan and things like loot is extremely irritating. Then you have things such as you save a civilian, you finish and there is chatter which would indicate the conclusion of the encounter but as you leave it fails the mission. At least some of these things are quite easy to fix. It gives the impression of rushing it to wrap things up in the end. I have noticed another toxic tendency to over simplify in product design these days. Perhaps this contributes to some of the issues. I'm not sure.Either way this lack of proper polish is really too much for me. It's compounded by an apparent lack of information where it's needed. I would suggest releasing some basic documentation in future at least, perhaps putting up information on a standard wiki or something, there are a few out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I really liked the story and the character it borrows heavily from hellblade in its presentation (which i'm not a fan of)  I liked the story of the main character but the whispering narrative seems one dimensional, however the lead voice female voice actor is excellent. Presentation is big budget for a AA game it has impressive art and character design as well. The open world aspect is half baked and it lacks the  economic depth of a traditional sandbox space game which was in the developers roots with games like galaxy on fire. The loot feels randomized and the constant pop up of random quests is annoying and not interesting enough for you to want to go out of your way to explore. The lack of an fov option in game is critically missing as the game can get u nauseatingly dizzy. The fov can not be changed easily like in an ini file,  and  it requires and unreal cheat code engine instead (not recommended). The developer puts ability gimics like teleport and drift to try to help alleviate but it only makes the movement less fluid and more jarring. The constant ghost flashbacks where she visualizes what happened is pretty low budget and kind of generic feels like filler. Although the main story and cutscenes were great this game fails to have satisfying combat as fluid as like a star fox. The developers bit off more than it could chew in choosing to be open world. It doesn't succeed as a star fox rip off, and can't really compete with the depth of a game like x4 foundations. I'm all for a hybrid of the those 2 games, but the choices in its rpg lite mechanics were too limited and one dimensional gameplay style.  Gameplay was jarring and nauseating, upgrade paths were boring. Lack of freedom in different ship selections and abilities made me get bored after about 5 hours despite the great female lead of the main campaign's dark protagonist. Overall I would have like a more sandbox open style game with different ways to play and progress like space pirate, miner, trader, etc. I would like a sequel with a dark anti-hero in a way and thought it was a really cool idea.  I played with mouse and keyboard which controlled suprisingly ok but the lack of not being able to rebind your keybindings was a huge negative. Not bad, but too shallow to keep me interested. Overall 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: For those that enjoy EverSpace 2, then Chorus can also be recommended.Chorus has a high focus on the story and especially for the pilot you play as, Nara, who is a unique combat pilot. Nara works in the outer fringes of space as a scavenger for a home full of regular working people. Early on you will learn that Nara was part of a fanatical group called "The Circle", which swept across many systems to purge anyone not part of The Circle. Nara was considered the strongest pilot they had, but ultimately she started to reconsider her choice and actions when opening a rift that destroy an entire world. She decides to leave The Circle behind and escape far away to avoid all the mess they create. As you can imagine eventually some years later The Circle arrives in the system she considers her home and instead of running she decides to fight for her home and end The Circle. However to do so she must unite with an old friend......which leads us to the game play. Nara flies around in a regular fighter, which allow for decent speed and firepower. You can "mod" your ship with various modules that grant bonus to weapons, speed, Rites and so on. Weapons come in 3 types which are used during game play to counter enemies depending on their "resistances".Nara will replace the fighter with a unique ship called Forsaken, which has a sentient AI she's bound with. This bond with Forsaken allows Nara to do some rather impressive moves and makes everything much more responsive and explosive. The first part unlocked is being able to "Drift". It's best explained as moving in a direction, enable Drift and you keep moving in said direction, while you can also turn your ship at the same time. This basically means you move forward, while also able to turn the ship around and shoot at enemies following you.As Nara moves on in her quest to wipe out The Circle, she will re-visit her past and unlock Rites. These are special skills tied to Forsaken and makes you very lethal. For example you have the ability to teleport directly behind ships to start shooting at them, or strike them with lightning similar to an EMP effect. Rite of the Star is even more impressive that allows Nara and Forsaken to turn into a "shooting star" demolishing everything in that path.Besides the story, then Chorus has the main focus on combat mechanics. The game does offer some exploration, but it's very limited. The game is perhaps a bit short, but extremely enjoyable due to the conflict Nara shows and combat against enemy ships, including capital ships.The game ran extremely smooth, the environment was very well made and most things had good "oomph" soundwise. Slight disappointment was the sound on the autocannons :P

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever played Crimson Skies on the original Xbox (there's a PC version of Crimson Skies, too, but that's a different game to the Xbox version), you'll know what to expect from this gameplay wise. This pretty much Crimson Skies in space. Open areas that have main missions and side missions and plenty of talking and fighting. Of course the story in this is much darker, more desperate, and weirder, and not always in a good way. And speaking of story, that's probably the weakest aspect of this game. You don't get much background of anything to make sense of what is actually going on. You are a former cult member who want's to get rid of the cult that she now despises.The gameplay is the best part. This is purely a "3rd person" arcade space shooter. You don't have lateral or vertical thrusters, there's no cockpit view. What you do have is this evade move, afterburners and "drifting". And of course all the useful powers you get during the game (which aren't explained why you have them in the first place, or why you, and some others, can use them). You get some intense fights and eventually feel really good when you can zip around smash all opposition when you mastered your ship controls and your powers.The main character and the ship AI is also pretty well done, and their dynamic is nice to follow. Voice actors are good and they deliver their lines well. But, yet again, many times you left wondering did you miss something because the game doesn't bother to much explain anything. Some kind of codex would, at the very least, be a welcome addition to have some background on things.Graphically this is really good looking game and has some really nice aesthetics. Runs well, too.Overall it's a pretty solid game and I really hope they can do more with this universe in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat in this game is fun, but pretty much everything else is a slog and drags it down. I am desperately trying to enjoy it, and I may still try to finish out the story, but I've seen enough at this point to give it a negative recommendation even though I hope to finish it.Pros:Really fun combat, you have a bunch of powers to control the battlefield, your ship is really maneuverable and can pull some great moves, and it's really fun ripping capital ships apart from the inside out.Cons:- Story is absolute trash, the main character is annoying- Game likes to pull focus from you with popups that you need to hold a button down to close, which I found pretty disruptive especially after the first few- No way to skip the slow and uninteresting dialogue, too much of the game is just sitting in your ship motionless waiting for 4-5 minutes for everyone to stop talking so you can move on.- Sound mixing is weird, I had to turn music and sound effects to 50% to be able to hear voice over everything else being overwhelming- It's your standard open world game that doesn't need to be open world. The maps take a long time to traverse and there's really nothing there worth doing. There's a bunch of side content, half of which glitches out and doesn't give you rewards or resets progress, and the rewards you do get didn't seem meaningful to be worth doing.    - This could basically be called "fetch quest: the game".     - A bunch of side quests involve you having to chase someone and keep them within a certain distance to you. However, their ships are faster than you, you can only match speeds by holding down your afterburner, so I hope your finger won't get tired holding down left shift for 4-5 minutes at a time.- It's really hard to figure out what you're supposed to do in some fights. I just finished a mission where I flew around for a good 4-5 minutes being unable to figure out the thing I was supposed to shoot at. Target's won't automatically show up on your HUD, you need to spam your "sense" ability to see them, and then they disappear (in my opinion) in way too short of a time, so you find yourself mashing e over, and over, and over, pretty much the entire game. And nothing is really distinguished so you can't really distinguished between ships, turrets, pickups, and components to destroy unless you fly over to them and hope you have line of sight.Long story short, this would have been a far superior game if they just had a few big set pieces you automatically moved between, eliminated the sense button and just let you see all the HUD info you need at all times without busywork, and let you have fun being an unstoppable space fighter ripping apart everything you ran into.  I could handle the bad story if you keep me in the action, but there's way too much downtime. It's a 15-20 hour mediocre game that could have been a 6 hour phenomenal gameEdit:I finally had enough and uninstalled after a boss fight where it took 4 reloads just for its weak point to even be rendered on the screen to be able to shoot at. I really wanted to enjoy this, and obviously a lot of people really liked this game based on its overall ratings, but the combination of endless frustrations, jank, and bugs was too much for me. This is one of the few purchases I really regret making.

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshingly fast-paced space shooter with surprising story depth and combat mechanics. First hour or so can be quite bland and slow in terms of story direction and battles. But the game gradually builds upon it's immersive aspects and really starts to shine after a couple of hours. Visually this game is stunning and great fun!Found the story rich and interesting, although a little slow to understand at the beginning. Chorus offers epic space battles (especially when using the drift ability) and rites (powers) you obtain on your travels to evolve your ship. The game has a large open world offering freedom to roam solar systems, explore, gather and engage in side quests and frantic space battles. Good damage/collision markers when in combat. Combat is extremely fun, frantic and challenging at times with various hostile types, making you approach each battle differently. Flight controls feel smooth and easy to control after a bit of time spent flying around. Feels good on both controller/keyboard and mouse. Only downside no thrust ability to shaft left/right or vertically, however, drift ability does compensate for this minor missing mechanic. The best part of this game is the quirky side quests as well as the large and frantic fights in the main story quests. Once combat and abilities have been mastered. In my opinion, Chorus becomes a top tier space shooter that can provide tonnes of enjoyment from flying around in your ship; too blowing up hostiles with a laser, cannon or missile launcher :D.  Would defiantly recommend this game. But only on sale though, as I feel the games full price is a bit steep considering the lack of replay value and lack of end-game content. I give it a 8.5/10 due to its limited replay value. However, it does offer a permadeath mode which is unique and an enjoyable challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Space Combat Game with an interesting story.If you are an ace pilot this game will most likely be too easy for you.For all others:Flying your "ship" feels really immersive, with multiple options for gliding, using speed and mystical powers to defeat your enemies, who in turn also have a different set of powers and abilities, starting from the usual shield/weapon/armor combinations to abilities to slow you down or decrease your ability to maneuver.Using your surroundings to your advantage comes quite intuitive due to the maneuverability of the "ship".Also when not fighting, just moving between asteroids, through space stations and cities is just fun and does not punish every mistake immediately.Upgrading "ship" and player mostly depends on the player using their abilities. Yes, it is possible to also buy upgrades but those gotten from just using powers, weapons and moves are much more rewarding.The storyline is nice, though very linear and you have to be in the mood for the characters baseline.There are a few noteworthy sidequests which will be pointed out on the map and a lot of random encounters which you can also skip if you've had enough of them.

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite game of the year!ConceptThis game takes a very cool approach at a flight game. The concept here is "ship-to-pilot integration," except the pilot has something equivalent to The Force, and like the force, can be used for destructive purposes, or to defend the innocent. The pilot then forms a psychic bond with their ship, as a sort of extension of themselves and you happen to play as the "most gifted" of this lot of pilots.My take on the conceptThe only thing here is I would have taken a more alien/ organic approach for the ship...at least in texture and even if preserving the overall shape of the ship, to make it look a little less "hardware" and slightly more "living ship..." and better portray this symbiotic relationship. Kind of like Thargoid in Elite. In doing this, you could do away with any notion of cockpit and just have the pilot integrate their mind with the ship, to see as the ship would, instead of doing the Knight Rider approach and just having a talking ship.GraphicsGraphics are pretty good with an excellent art style as well, but it doesn't quite wow me quite as much as Everspace 1 does...which is probably this game's next closest competition and which still looks beautiful running on my Xbox One X today. GameplayNow, this is the bread butter.  At first I didn't care for the gameplay, on account of not having lateral or vertical controls and no rolling...but then I unlocked my first two rites, which are basically your abilities, it got hella fun and you begin to see the gameplay direction. Sure, I would still probably prefer to have full lateral and vertical controls but the gameplay but it still has a nice flow and rhythm to it, as is. Many people on the net will swear by mouse/ keyboard...I firmly disagree. I spent 2.5 hours on mouse and keyboard and found the key movements a bit too fumbley for how quick you are moving. Gamepad is the shiz in this game. This game was designed for gamepad. You're just changing directions so quickly and frequently that, on keyboard, you're mashing down keys too fast to always be doing it perfectly and I often felt that, as a result, you can end up off of the WASD keys and onto more of a ESDF pattern, leaving you wondering why you can roll right, or you end up reaching for the boost too quickly, in a time of urgent (defensive) need, and end up pressing Caps Lock or CTRL instead and getting blown up. You don't tend to press the keys this fast for a first person shooter, so I felt gamepad to be organic and natural...at least as long as you're one of those that holds the gamepad so that your index fingers are over the shoulder buttons and your middle fingers are on the triggers, that way you have full coverage of all buttons without letting off on any critical ones. You can even adjust your aim assist in the event that you're not good on gamepad.My only disappointments:1. No first person/ cockpit view (I would love to see this ship from the inside).2. Major lack of ship customization options - I feel like Forsaken should be able to be modded into any configuration, shape and size since he's sort of a living ship. I would have lvoed to have seen Forsaken be based on some sort of nanite tech that can be reconfigured, remolded and aesthetics complete changed, in addition to more colors. 3. Lack of DLC content/ game modes. So, I feel that once I beat the story and side-quests there will be no more combat, as the maps seem to lack random spawning open-world  enemy, as everything is virtually quest driven.4. No auto or manual rolling, or lateral/ vertical controls - A flight stick version of this game would have been much welcomed. You can still execute rites with full axis controls and real time strafing.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Everspace 2 but the focus is entirely on combat and some traversal challenges. So it's basically Everspace 1 but without the roguelike experience.Also you only get 1 ship for most of the game but if you like sharp angled designs it's arguably way better looking than all the procedurally generated ones in Everspace 2. Every weapon upgrade has its own unique behavior and isn't simply generated with new stats so you can get back into the action and proceed to the next objective without any need for grind or feeling like you need to use a weapon you might not like because it has the highest dps. Like Everspace, there are different weapons to handle different hitpoint types (hull, shield, armor) but you are always appropriately equipped with all 3 as they are introduced to the player. There is very little need for inventory management and you spend much more time playing the game instead.Control wise it's a different flavor in that you're controlling a jet fighter that has the benefit of being able to slow to a halt and it has Project Wingman's Angle of Attack Limiter except you have infinite duration and no cooldown on its usage. Whereas Everspace allows you to freely strafe left and right here you can only shuffle left and right when stationary or aileron roll when moving.Rites or what's more easily understood as spells can be cast from your slowly regenerating mp pool adds a level of strategy and aggression not found in Everspace or other dogfighting arcade games. You can get the immediate advantage on the fly or disable enemies with a press of a button which makes you feel like an anime ace pilot when used in combination with drifting and other combat options.The story is very much like an anime plot with all the weird and wild plot twists in addition to the over convoluted character backgrounds for the main characters. Some people will complain about the whispering internal monologue but I consider it an artistic license. Everything is voice acted which is a major plus and there are a surprising number of voice lines considering the price tag of the game. Scenerio wise, the game makes a great effort to make every main and side quest a little different and there isn't anything that feels exactly the same. You're often collecting memories and dogfighting but the sequences are never the same which is enough to keep the game interesting. The game is also running extremely well. I can maintain 120-144 fps on a GTX 108, the load times are minimal, and I have not run into any bugs or crashes. I'm honestly very impressed considering the state of gaming today. Outside of the pre-order skins bonus, no microtransactions or external contrivances. Just download, install, then play like the good ole days.I haven't reached the ending yet but I'm already hoping for a spiritual successor that improves on the gameplay and gives us even more interesting and varied things to do as well as more boss encounters. I would appreciate somewhat smaller maps or maps with a denser number of quests as traveling from destination to destination can sometimes take a few minutes of waiting for your ship to move there.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: Chorus is... an okay game. If you like space fighter sims with fun combat and pretty visuals, grab it, but only if it's on sale.Longer version:Chorus is one of these games where I really wish Steam had a "meh" option instead of the binary yes/no. I give it a total rating of 6/10. The things it really gets right are the music, the looks, and the combat, which is crisp, fast-paced, visually spectacular, and comes with all sorts of awesome quasi-magical abilities. It's a bit like controlling some overpowered Jedi flying a sentient space fighter with an attitude. Everything else about the game falls somewhere between average and bad. A particular example of the latter is the story that, while probably not bad in and of itself in the hands of a capable writer, is disjointed, confused, terribly paced, and generally feels like it's mashed together from a dozen other scifi franchises that did it better. I should probably get my eyes checked one of these days to make sure that all the eye rolling I've done over the past days didn't leave lasting damage.The protagonist is your typical bad guy defector trying to atone for past sins, but the worst of these sins is the murder of an entire planet with billions of inhabitants. There's no coming back from such an act no matter what you do, which to me made the whole point moot from the start. To stick with the Star Wars comparisons, it's basically why Darth Vader could be redeemed, but the Emperor was utterly beyond saving. You're playing as the Emperor in this case. It could've been pulled off by having Nara sacrifice herself in the final battle, but instead she survives and is cheered by everyone, her past deeds forgotten as if they never happened. What a great aesop for a story. Who greenlights such crap?If you can stomach or ignore the story and everything tied to it, feel free to give Chorus a try when it's on sale (10-15€ tops). It offers about 20 hours of solid space fighter action entertainment if you do everything there is to do, which is more content than many similar games today offer, so there's that. I don't regret my purchase. What I do regret is that the devs wasted so much potential of what could've been an awesome game.

_childDocuments_.review: Chorvs is an impressive debut, featuring some exciting space action, decent visuals, and a story that has some promise. Unfortunately, it's let down by some questionable choices about the art design, controls, and gameplay. This game really could've been exceptional but for each good element being balanced out with an equally terrible one. It's games like these why Steam needs a middle rating rather than a thumbs up or down. Take the story for example you take on the role of Nara a former fighter ace who flees a repressive cult after she destroys an entire planet. She abandons her wingmates and her sentient ship and retreats to the outer reaches of space to eke out a living as a scavenger. She has to jump back into the fray when the cult finds her again. So far, so good. Only the story isn't' told in any meaningful way, it's just front-loaded exposition. We're just simply told everything that happened with little to no visuals to give it any impact. Even Nara obliterating a planet is scarcely seen. It's such a stupid decision to deliver a sparse story in this way. Now the graphics. The space stations and some of the incidental backgrounds are lovely to look at and it's clear that a lot of effort has gone into the detailing of them but the lack of variety in the ships and that their designs don't have any originality is a real shame. There's a lot of wasted effort here. The gangs all have snake names and fly ships with yellow spikes on them, the resistance flies generic grey boxes with some flashing lights in some areas, the faceless fly boring looking crystal things and the cult fly red and black boxes with shiny yellow cockpits. Even the main ship you play as has no real finesse to its design. It's just designed to look fast. Plus, the level of model re-use is noticeable. There's one side-mission that has you track down a faceless ship that's 200 years old and pre-dates the cult and it ends up looking exactly like your ship. Gameplay is where Chorvs stands out. The vast majority of the space battles are magnificent. The controls are responsive and slick, the game moves at a nice pace even with maxed-out settings and the weapons have a nice satisfying feel to them when you're blasting enemy fighters out of the sky. The dogfights are all tense and very exciting and have a genuine rush to them. But even here, where most of the development focus is, there are a lot of poor choices. There's a heavy reliance on enemies who need VERY specific attacks to add challenge rather than providing anything original. You'll have your fighters, which are cannon-fodder. Shielded fighters, which are slightly more annoying cannon-fodder, and the heavy's which usually always have some form of incredibly specific invincibility which needs to be gotten around. The key case study in poor design choices is the enemies with a charged shot attack.  A charged shot is a ludicrously long-range laser attack that a lot of enemies (and almost all bosses) have, that locks on and ALWAYS hits regardless of how fast you're going. The only way to avoid it is to roll the instant before it hits. Essentially, it's a near instant-kill quick time event in the middle of a space battle and it's the most annoying and dumbest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing I've seen in a space combat game. The inclusion of this stupid attack means you can't have free rolling controls because it wouldn't work. So, in Chorvs, when you press left or right, your ship just does a full barrel-roll. The problem is that you can't always trigger a roll, there's a few seconds delay after you roll and the charge takes a few seconds to hit after you're locked on. So, when you've got the charged laser on you, you're stuck and can't dodge anything until the shot hits because if you roll, you won't be able to do it again. This attack also relies on you being able to see the laser change that signals when you should roll, so you can't have a cockpit perspective, like literally every other space/flying game around. This one ♥♥♥♥♥♥ attack design has forced the removal of two of the big staples of the genre. Seriously, whoever thought up this, needs to lose their job.  This lack of thought in the design even extends to the bosses. One boss you face is a corrupted cult elder in the same type of ship as yours. However, her ship seems to have twice as many weapons as yours and nearly ten times more armour. She can deploy mines, EMP nets, homing missiles and she has a charge shot alongside the usual complement of weapons plus the ability to redirect a lot of your physic attacks back at you. It's ludicrous.  In the end, Chorvs is a game with so much potential but is let down by a litany of seriously poor design choices. The main pros are a decent story, superb sound design, and combat that approaches Ace Combat levels of sheer excellence. Its faults lie in poor story pacing, lack of variety in the ship models, and some truly awful gameplay design. Try the demo to see first and try to nab it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The past decade has blessed us with a glorious resurgence of space games. However, not all of them have been good and some have even been pretty awful. With so many now available and their diverse spectrum of quality, it’s easy to have one fly under the radar. Chorus is one such game.Abbreviated Review: Despite being a notable part of the story and a word repeated no less than 50 times in the dialogue, Chorus is not a particularly alluring name for a game. It also doesn’t help that it has a V instead of a U in the name which made me wonder was “chorvs” meant before playing. However, that possibly poor choice aside, Chorus doesn’t do a great deal to differentiate itself visually from its contemporaries either.It can be challenging in this modern era of space games to look all that different when space has a pretty distinct feel. With so many games achieving a mostly-realistic design, usually more stylistic or even cartoonish looks stand out more. Chorus’s one notable distinction is that most of the areas you visit are squeezed into a moderately narrow slice of 3D space that includes a ton of physical structures giving it a lot of texture. The first map is in a densely packed asteroid field and, despite its incredible fields of brown, it does have a certain level of appeal. Yet, when you advance into new regions, you get massive orbiting cities, icy fields of frozen rocks, and areas with large central landmarks to add some spice to the otherwise fairly standard look.That bit of spice is only part of what makes it disappointing that this game didn’t get as much fanfare as it deserved though. The story elements make a notable departure from the normally loose introductions many open-world space games deliver. Rather than just being a ‘nobody’ caught up in some big event, you’re a former powerful warrior of a cult that commits a genocidal act and decides to abandon that life. You leave behind your powerful ship and extreme psychic capabilities in favor of middle-of-nowhere life. The only thing that brings you back into the chaos is that cult’s continued spread and its now (more) deranged leader. However, the most unique and interesting part of this game is the combat.The combat of Chorus is frantic, vicious, and best of all, satisfying. With pacing through the rest of the game fairly slow, every fight is a welcome experience. I even found that I had done so many of the side quests that randomly spawn as you’re flying around the universe that I unlocked an achievement for it rarer than the one for finishing the actual game. The action feels almost as if it would be the space combat equivalent of what you’d encounter in a Platinum Games title like Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising. Something where spectacle is as much a part of the fun as the victory. The only thing it’s missing is a letter grade rating system.Chorus achieves this by mixing a blend of a rock-paper-scissors weapon system with the use of a growing arsenal of powerful psychic abilities. While you can upgrade to different varieties of weapons, you’re always going to have available lasers, missiles, and Gatling guns. These serve to effectively take out shields, armor, and ship hulls respectively. With this design, you may be facing three or four different types of enemies attacking at the same time all possessing varying levels of shields or armor (or neither).Once the game has eased you into the concept of using and swapping these weapons dynamically, it starts to introduce the powers. At first, you gain the ability to teleport behind a targeted enemy – instantly giving you the advantage. Later, you gain a sort of “shock” ability that can temporarily stun enemies and strip their shields. There’s even one that allows you to charge through swarms of weaker enemies ripping them apart. While all of these are incredibly useful and effective, they are also necessary since your ship isn’t that much stronger than anyone else’s. Getting caught in crossfire or maneuvering poorly for just a bit of time – even on medium difficulty – can result in a quick death.Chorus has plenty of appeal, but it is slightly overshadowed by some of the quirks of the design. The first is that, despite having a decent voice acting crew, plenty of characters, and a competent story, it doesn’t deliver the impact that it should. Part of that is that so much of it, including nearly all of the characters outside of the protagonist and the ship’s AI, are rarely represented in anything but a small picture with a glitchy filter over it. There are moments where people lose loved ones, sacrifice themselves, or are subjected to terrible events that are conveyed wonderfully in audio, but are just a floating ship and a static image visually. When the rest of the game is high-intensity action conveyed wonderfully through audio and visuals, this feels weird. When you do encounter full cutscenes, they are much easier to appreciate and absorb – though the animations do feel a little stiff.That limited medium through which the story is told makes it a little more difficult to follow than it should be – especially with several characters and faction references. It comes together toward the end in a satisfying way, but the journey can be rough. Honestly though, if the balance between story and combat included a bit more combat, I probably wouldn’t have noticed. While I did do my fair share of fighting, it felt like outside of a few key moments, I’d finish off enemies just when I was getting in the groove.With these quirks, the odd name, and a price that seems a bit high for a new franchise in this genre, it’s not surprising that not many people were talking about Chorus. However, the quality is there and, even though there isn’t the polish of a AAA game, it’s something to check out if you’re looking for a space sim where the focus is on dynamic and exciting combat. The story and mild RPG elements are a nice addition, but this is probably the first time in a while that I’d like an extra mode dedicated just to fighting. Maybe one with weekly challenges or something. As long as I can turn off the in-combat chatter where you and your ship AI keep finishing each other’s sentences…

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of promise, speaks to me on a few levels, has a lot of potential and would have been amazing as an indie game.  I think the publishers expected some sort of blockbuster and there's just no way it would ever reach those heights.  I need to be honest, I did not like writing that previous sentence, but I don't write out of malice.I'll get to some of those more nuanced points but I'm going to amuse myself in describing the game first.  It's much too late to expect this is going to influence sales, but I just like writing, so I hope you like reading.As a game, it controls much like Freelancer (or Echelon, if you might remember that) does:  Third person, move the mouse pointer, and your ship turns towards your mouse.  Keep the mouse in that position and the ship keeps turning that way, with a priority on pitch and yaw.  So it's very shootery, and flying is abstracted.  The ship yaws very readily.  If "yaw" doesn't mean a thing to you, the ship just turns, and you don't do any fancified rolling to get the ship to move.So combat in the game--and that's the point here--is a lot of "put cursor on bad guy and click the mouse."  Except they've made everything very, very fast, so it's a very action-filled experience.  Unlike most scifi space games, you're flying near a lot of large obstacles a lot, which adds a whole lot more spice to the combat.  Don't hit things, shoot the guys, try to avoid being shot.And in a way, it's hard.  Your ship isn't a whole lot tougher than theirs.  The difference is only that your ship regenerates shields quickly, so to be successful in combat, you need to find stragglers and pick them off, or otherwise dash in, get your licks in, and dash out quickly before you're pummelled too hard, and then stay away 'til your shields are back on.Later (and they do foreshadow it pretty early) your character develops all kinds of magic/psychic powers that help in combat, but you still can't go toe-to-toe with most any enemy, and you're still playing dodgems while your shields come back online.  "Magitech" is a genre that's underserved, if you ask me.  (Don't talk to me about Star Wars, this isn't the time for it.)It does some things other games in this genre haven't done:  big interior spaces to fly through, asteroid fields with rocks that are properly sized (multiple km across), speeds that seem more likely in space (a couple thousand km/hr).  It's a pretty game, for what it is.  You sometimes fly *through* enemy ships to attack their interior spaces.  It's not deeply realized, but it's very fun. I just would have liked a stupidly huge ship to fly through, a battleship or a carrier or something.Sometimes, your character gets into spontaneous conversations with various, relevant NPCs, which is kind of a nice touch.  It breaks up longer flights with a bit of background.Downsides:  The game suffers for playtesting.  I don't mean it's buggy, it's worked great that way.  I mean some encounters and scenarios are just punishingly rough.  The single race is frustrating for reasons that would take six paragraphs to explain and resolve.  Flying quickly down curved tunnels can be punishing, and several times you're required to do that.  Several boss encounters are punitive, to say the least. One of them even involves high-speed flights down narrow tunnels strewn with obstacles and poor visibility.  I was... frustrated, but I saw it through.The plot... well, it's ambitious, but I wonder if it wasn't originally more elaborate and then pared way down, perhaps too aggressively.  I don't hate it, by any means, but some NPC shows up out of the blue (especially Circle-related folk) and the plot is waist-deep in plot by the second sentence.  Getting into all the introductions and explanations would take time from the shooting, I'll grant you, but there's lots of opportunities to dripfeed that information.  As a whole, it does feel like it's trying to convey a 400-page novel of Important Story, but summarizing whole chapters with a sentence or two.There's one thing really chafing me.  The ship you fly in most of the game has its own personality.  Both your character and the ship talk in combat, a lot, and at some point (not really a spoiler) they become more of a team.  So they start merging their usual catchphrases together.  There's just awkward little pauses in there, it doesn't feel natural.  I'm kind of big on audio, so this might not bother you as much as it does me.  I have ideas how to fix that too, but let's consider hiring me first.Anyway, I wound up getting the game deeply discounted.  For the price I paid, I should have just shut up and said, "Yeah, good game, maybe I underpaid a bit."  And it kind of is a good game, except there's guaranteed to be some part of it that will frustrate.  But the frustrations aren't so great that I won't finish it, cussing out certain encounters as I go.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, the ship to ship combat in this game is fantastic. The story does its job, though it can be hard to associate or really care about many of the characters. The side quests are forgettable but thankfully short. The map makes navigation somewhat difficult at first, and mission tracking can be frustrating. Many side missions are started, and stopped, by physical proximity alone, which is odd and can be confusing.Despite its flaws, this title delivers on its core promise. Some of the dog fights are downright exhilarating and make you feel like a total bad ass as you zip about, firing thrusters, launching missiles and blasting enemies into oblivion. If you can power through the slower sections and handle the new-age pseudo-religious dogma story, you'll enjoy this one.

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10 overall, spaceship combat is fun but lacking in enemy variety and mid-late gear end up oneshotting most ships. _childDocuments_.review: How to best describe this game? Probably if Freelancer and Ace Combat had a baby. _childDocuments_.review: A great space action shooter with a story and character development. The action and fighting is fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I find it necessary do dispel the idea that this is some woke garbage. I too am quite fed up with the diversity and inclusion rhetoric around media(e.g. 50/50 men and women, having protagonists with as many oppression points on the intersectionality scale, etc.).However, Nara does not seem to me to be some sort of token emo lesbian. She is kind of cringe at times, but I blame that on the script or the budget, as it's still cringe if you replace her with a dude. Other than her haircut, which would make sense for a military woman to have, her only specifically male feature is her leadership, which I accept, because women make great leaders sometimes. She appears quite vulnerable and distressed in a girly fashion throughout the game, and gets support from her male voice AI powered ship, Forsaken, so she's not really the stereotypical "strong independent woman".With that out of the way, I want to review the actual game:WARNING-Small spoilers may be aheadSTORY: 5/10-Not exactly original. The protagonist betrays the evil forces and ends up fighting against them.-Serviceable cast of characters, though they do not stand out particularly well-Many Sci-fi cliches, like the bad interdimensional aliens being manifestations of human emotions, the protagonist fighting her own inner demons, the protagonist defeating the big bad with the power of self-acceptance AND the power of friendship=I would not recommend this game for the story, but it's not bad per se, just average. Don't dwell on it, enjoy the gameplayCOMBAT: 8/10-This is where the game shines brightest-Note that this is a dog fighter game, you cannot strafe, but you get a drift mechanic early on, which makes the combat a lot more fluid-The controls are well adjusted and the fights feel bombastic and dynamic-Your arsenal can be quite basic if you do not do some side content, but special guns and parts can be earned-Some enemies are quite annoying, like the Faceless Swarms, but most of them feel well balanced-The big ship battles are quite cool, as you get to destroy ships piece by piece before exposing their core, Star Wars style=Generally great, with some annoying enemies and perhaps the lack of strafe might put some people offEXPLORATION/OPEN WORLD: 6/10-There are plenty of side mission, though they are mostly simple and repetitive-There are a few good side missions, like one where you help pirates in a coup against their corrupt queen-Open world loot is rewarding enough to make it worth it. I think you might have trouble with the end-game if you do not complete most of the side missions on Very HardGRAPHICS: 9/10-This game is gorgeous in every sense you can think of.-The landscape is a colourful and varied rendition of the cosmos. It's unrealistic but it's pretty-Models look unique enough and the UI doesn't get in your way-The only relatively small issue is that some models do not get rendered in HD in time occasionally, allowing lower poly versions to be seen. It's quite rare, though=A stunning looking gameSOUND DESIGN: 8/10-Blockbuster movie soundtrack, which is just average, not necessarily bad-Where the sound design shines is combat, though. Each enemy and their respective attacks and abilities have distinct sounds. I didn't even notice this until after I finished the game.-Your guns sound quite satisfyingOPTIMIZATION: 10/10-For how great this game looks, I am surprised they managed to make this run so smoothly-I have had only one frame drop in my entire playthrough, and that was before starting the final boss-For reference, I have the following PC configuration: Ryzen 5 3600X, Radeon RX 590 Nitro+ Special Edition, 16 GB of RAM and the game has been run on an M.1 SSD-I have been running the game with all settings set to maximum=Probably works on every potato that has at least PCIEFINAL SCORE: 7.5/10Conclusion: Despite me not liking Nara too much and the story being average at best, the game is worth buying at a sale for the smooth and satisfying combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Story was ♥♥♥♥. Controls were ♥♥♥♥. Characters and their development were ♥♥♥♥. Field of view made the game feel horrible. And the HUD icons made it so hard to identify friend from foes. One good thing about it: The last boss battle did give me a bit of nostalgia when it comes to Lylat Wars (Star Fox 64). Oh, and did I mention that the background and walls are red as well during boss fights?Save your money and buy a proper game that actually does things better. If you want proper dogfights, go for Project Wingman or Ace Combat 7: Skies UnknownI wanted to complete the game to give it a proper and fair review. Because who knows, it might get better.However, There were even some VERY weird scenes where it seemed like the story was written as if the interaction was supposed to be between people standing in front of each other, and sitting/flying in ships. And And the side mission order was weird as well. There were several times in the first map where I unlocked a side mission by "accident" that was supposed to have a mission before that. Like  before the mission telling me to ", pretty much messing up the order.AND THE ENDLESS WHINING! I swear, this main character is such a whiny little turd.All she does is whine. They really tried to cram Senua from Hellblade (in a very horrible way), Commander Sheppard from Mass Effect (but without a proper heroes journey), and a space dogfight without properly maintaining momentum of a space ship. _childDocuments_.review: This is a classic tale of Red Queen. You get booster. They get shield.You get drift. They get snipers.You get rockets. They bring more heavy gunship with very strong shield. You get teleport. They bring flyers with right angle turn and numbers have increased.You get emp. They bring heavy ship with invincible shield.You get more weapon set that has a special abilities. They now bring dreadnought. You get ultimate dash attack that one shots almost every small flyers in the path.They now bring carriers that spawns more ships so that you will drain your mana if not dealt with. You get another ultimate that one shots most ships but now its time for the final battle. It only ends when you clear the game. And because there is no such meaningful amour upgrade, you will act aggressive. But do not worry if you die. Unless you are an sadist who enabled permadeath, checkpoint is so frequent that you will pick up from where you lost.

_childDocuments_.review: In brief: this is excellent, if you've any interest in the genre or premise, it will not disappoint.This game is one of the best action flight games I've played in my life. It flows incredibly smoothly, it rewards learning its systems and mechanics with a great feeling of power, it doesn't waste your time, and it has probably one of the best-executed climactic battles I've played in the genre. The side content is for the most part either snappy enough that more filler-type missions don't bother, or executed to a similar level of polish and attention to detail to the mainline missions. There are some light RPG mechanics but they don't feel essential or overly hindering: I experimented with pretty much every weapon and item I found, and almost everything seems to have some kind of niche to be appreciated. The story and setting are competently executed and have some creative ideas, even if it's nothing mind-blowing, and it must be restated that the climax is simply sublime for this manner of game. Which is not to say it doesn't have some issues worth noting. It was clearly not made on a AAA budget, so while the game is visually stunning on an environmental level, it is clear where corners needed to be cut, mostly in recycling basic enemy designs and in the cutscenes having a severely limited asset pool, admittedly justified by mostly being internal character conflicts. Despite this, Chorus does an excellent job of not placing too much focus on these problems, which leaves you free to enjoy the game for what it is. I got a solid 15 hours of time through my playthrough, engaging with all the side content I found, and it never felt like it had run out of ideas or had overstayed its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: As of this writing, I feel like this is a criminally underrated gem. Works very well with Thrustmaster T.Flight HOTAS 4 flight stick. Story based arcade-y space sim with some really clever little tricks. Slow to start but after the tutorial, you'll find yourself boosting away from an enemy, drifting to whirl around and fire lasers behind you, draining their shield, *teleporting* behind them, and finishing them off with your Gatling. Story is unique for the game type and setting so far, and genuinely looking forward to finding out what's going on in this universe.Editing to add: Its noted in a lot of other reviews that the MC whispers a lot. It seems like its supposed to be "edgy" but with a character who you only see talking in cut-scenes, the whispering quickly and efficiently delineates between what the MC is thinking and what she's actually saying to other characters while in-ship.

_childDocuments_.review: What drew me into this game was the voice acting and the cut scenes. Incredible quality on both parts and really sets the environment. Combat gets really really fun after the first hour or so, and I can see how it's only going to get better. My only issue so far is the pickups and the friendly/enemy ships. With the pickups I don't know why they are these magical things that just go into my ship. I would have liked it if they where like tractor beamed into a cargo hold on the ship. The other issue with ships is that the game feels like the Cars movies, with ships being a person, not a ship with people in it. They have prison cells for ships. Not for the people, but for the ships. That really broke any type of immersion when I feel like I am talking to a ship, and not a person flying a ship. But those aren't really huge issues, just things that I feel like in future games could be improved on to fix the immersion.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is fun, the world is nice, and I REALLY wanted to like this game but the combat goes from tedious to frustrating.  Lowering the difficulty only made the combat feel worse, not better.Zero atmosphere and microgravity?  What's that?  Your ship flies like it's in an atmosphere, so the side to side movement is either a massive roll or a barely noticeable bump and you have to keep tapping the key to keep moving laterally.  You can't jank side to side like the enemy ships.  No backwards movement, either, so lots of looping around if you pass something.You can at least stop all forward momentum, though.Pretty soon you get some big laser cannons that will, even though they are clearly gimbal mounted, will only give the slightest of aim assist, most of the time.  Occasionally it will seem to snap to a target, but more often than not I seem to be shaving the eyelashes off of a target as I watch my huge laser bolts miss by a hair.Despite a few cutscenes showing a first person view from the ship, you CANNOT leave chase camera, so your view is CONSTANTLY being blocked by your ship.Using a controller is frustrating because you are forced to steer with the right stick and control your speed with your left stick and that CANNOT be changed.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's so much fun. The drifting and teleportation mechanics make for incredibly fun dogfights. I love the open world nature of it. I enjoy the story. I hope more people end up sing for chorus.Edit 1:I finished the game today. I'm surprised how long it took me to beat it. 22-ish hrs over the course of several months, but I sort of burst through +75% of it in the last 2 months. At first, I absolutely loved the combat, then they debuffed you and it was really meh, then the story was meh as well, everyone in the game was depressing, challenge was harder than I needed for the time, then I started getting better equipment, parts of the story got progressively better as people start believing in you, and it finally sank in that "hey, I love this game." It could have been better. Do not ask me how. I can see why Chorus got the initial reviews it got, but still think they are undeserving. I think if more critics played more then they would have gotten to the heart of the game. It feels like Witcher 3 in a way where side quests feel good to complete because they feel meaningful. The ending was very campy, but it had a point to it. It feels like a trade off in a game where you get god mode for the last 30 seconds of a game, but the game may feel boring if it lasted longer. It could last a little longer than 3.6e-4 of the my total play time :3I hope more people discover Chorus, and have fun with it.
