_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely holds its own against Spelunky 2 and Hades and plenty of other brilliant roguelites released this year, and that's about all you need to know.But, I really enjoy this game, so alright. I'll write a couple more words of praise.Going Under has great combat. I played BOTW on an emulator for a bit. I really disliked how weapons would break so fast. It's kinda similar here. But I love it here. I think it's a case of there never being a shortage of weapons around and the game being based on small rooms rather than one big, explorable area. Also not having to deal with inventory management. That's probably the biggest factor. But yeah, here keeping an eye on how intact your weapons are adds to the fun and hectic feeling of the combat rather than it feeling like a chore as it did to me in BOTW. Also, the whole using random furniture to attack people thing? Reminds me of Indiana Jones and the Emperor's Tomb, and any game that manages to remind me of that one is gonna earn my love right away. Just saying.Going Under has a great visual style. It manages to parody (or maybe just pay homage?) to corporate graphic design and illustration trends, and it feels absolutely spot-on, while also outshining the vast majority of art you see used for those kinds of purposes. Just brilliant character designs and visual gags. I also enjoy that some of the abilities change your player model.Going Under has a great narrative structure. It's kinda similar to Hades, actually. There isn't any chatter when you pick up upgrades or any abilities to give gifts to characters (that I know of at this point), but just like in Hades, death never feels annoying because returning to the hub area and getting to chat with your coworkers is fun.Going Under also (so far) seems like it's a breath of fresh air in the roguelike genre in that it seems... okay with you getting to see most of what's on offer pretty quickly and not requiring literal hundreds of hours to be beaten. I might be talking outta my butt (and I might edit this part of the review in the future). In my current playtime, I've manage to arrive at what seems to be a final boss fight, maybe? I haven't beaten it, and based on the achievements, I assume there are probably more challenges ahead, but yeah. So far it felt a lot more forgiving than many other games in the genre, while still being challenging and interesting. If you're usually the type to swear off roguelikes, consider giving this one a shot anyway.I think that's about it. Look, just buy this. It's great and the devs have a fantastic sense of humor.

_childDocuments_.review: A swell little roguelite. It's no Hades, but it's neat and competent enough to grab and keep one's attention.It's very tongue-in-cheek, and it's also very, uh, zeitgeisty. This may not sit well with some, I imagine, but personally I'm enjoying the game's style and writing just fine.Metaprogression feels surprisingly mild, so while the game does provide certain ways to permanently improve your character, they aren't numerous, and they have to be earned. Going Under is meant to be challenging, something that's directly stated when you're starting a new game, but a customizable assist mode is available (can be tinkered with whenever).Combat revolves around weapons having durability, meaning you are always looking for not just better equipment, but equipment in general. I'm generally not a fan of such systems, but what Going Under has going for it doesn't feel awfully restrictive to me. It helps that there are plenty of respectable "midrange" weapons, while junk can always be utilized as throwable weaponry.Overall, a perfectly solid game that's easy to enjoy and appreciate.

_childDocuments_.review: This is very much a thumbs in the middle review, very slightly tilting upward.Going Under is a cutely presented and occasionally amusing office spoof. It shines in its presentation and entertaining character interactions. The wide variety of thematically-appropriate weapons, some with quite clever twists (eg a ream of paper which becomes smaller and reduces in damage with each hit), make for interesting variety. There are a good range of skills, some which make for different strategies.Unfortunately, the gameplay is weak. Combat is too hectic, especially in more difficult stages, for such floaty controls and inconsistent mechanics (particularly in respect of cancelling enemy attacks). The invulnerability window after getting hit is just too short for a game where you can wind up surrounded by enemies in a cramped and visually busy environment - it's too easy to lose a huge chunk of health in a few seconds. While these problems can be glossed over in the early portion of the game, as it's not especially challenging, they are overwhelming in the second half when the difficulty spikes. They are compounded by the limited return for runs.Much as I enjoyed aspects of the game, it got too frustrating by the end. I slightly recommend it just because it's a bit different and was fun for a few hours, but with a strong caveat that it quickly wears thin.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm seemingly halfway through, I am absolutely in love with this game. The humour is perfect for me, it's topical for modern day twenty somethings. The music is stellar, I love what they've done putting so many twists on the corpo tunes, and the ART, oh my god, the ART! Art is often the last thing I'm focused on in games, when you put the 3 core facets in front of me (gameplay, art, sound). The first thing about this game that drew me in was the reclamation of the corpo artstyle, and how much amazing personality they give that style. The character designs are super endearing, monsters are varied and clever, and animations are perfect for each personality. It's hard for me to fully explain, but the way this game feels is so comfortable. There are a few games in history where I just feel comfortable in their hub worlds, namely Super Mario Sunshine, A Hat in Time, Splatoon 1, and now, Going Under joins that small group of games where I just feel at home. Everything about it, from the stage design of the hub world, to the music, the decorations, the level of detail inside and outside, and the population of these characters... I'm totally enchanted in a way I can't describe. I'm not quite done and I anticipate many more great hours with this game, and I want to give a full proper review later. As it stands, though, this is already a game I wish I grabbed on launch, at full price, had I known aggrocrab was so talented. This game makes me want to pick up game development. I'm a composer, but this makes me want to learn how to 3d model, how to animate, how to code. Everything about this game makes me wanna learn how to make something this cool. Thanks aggrocrab, hope to meet you guys at PAX one day :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a weak thumbs up. It is with great hesitancy that I give this game a thumbs up. I both appreciate and despise that the combat system is like Zelda: Breath of the Wild (BOTW). The fact that weapons have finite durability is actually quite fun. It's a great feeling pummeling some enemies with a hockey stick, having the stick break, and then having to dive roll into a battle fan to continue pummeling the enemies. In this sense, I really enjoy the frantic nature of the combat. However, since the combat feels like BOTW, it feels like a worse version of a combat system that I'm well-versed in. The game simultaneously feels both tight and slippery in its controls. The game does not usually expect precise dodging (in the cases of e.g. boss fights and individual enemy attacks), but it does start throwing you into situations where it is near impossible to avoid damage without the access to precision dodging. In later levels, the enemies will swarm you in such a way that avoiding damage (due to the enemies newfound super armor) comes down to hoping that there is not too much debris in the way of rolling into a safer location. Also, the roll is inconsistent. Sometimes it does what is expected, other times it randomly gets caught on the hurtbox of an enemy or some debris.I really wanted to love this game, but it just feels worse to play than the other action roguelikes that I own. The art is great, the tongue-in-cheek dialogue is charming, and the concept of the combat  are all strong points. However, the game fails to deliver in the game feel of its combat, which is the focus of most of your time while playing.Buy the game if it's cheap, but don't expect to put it on the same shelf as Slay the Spire, Enter the Gungeon, Spelunky, or any of the other great roguelikes on the market.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: C-Rogue-likes are an incredibly crowded genre, especially in the indie scene. Making any indie game stand out is difficult but all the more so when you have to compete in such an overpopulated arena. When I saw such positive buzz online about the game and its developer, I put it on my radar. Unfortunately, being in such a crowded field means there are plenty of comparisons and Going Under cannot compete with any of the heavy-hitters of the genre.   Visually the game’s a mixed bag. The genuinely wonderful 2D character art stands in sharp contrast to the 3D visuals of the majority of the game. Models aren’t just simple but they feel like they lack polish. In combat sections, it becomes easy to ignore so let’s do just that. To be completely fair, this game was made by a small team and this was their first game as a studio so problems with visual fidelity can mostly be set aside.  Unfortunately, the visuals aren’t the only aspect lacking. The gameplay feels tired. By the end of the game, I had to force myself to keep playing just so I could say I have finished it and could fairly give my thoughts on it. Dungeons have random layouts, as is standard with rogue-likes. They don’t matter. At all. Because of how levels are structured, random room order doesn’t make a difference since you will be required to visit every room which isn’t a shop. The layout of each floor might as well be a straight line for all the difference it makes. Each dungeon also has a very limited number of room layouts and since you need to see so many per run, it becomes tedious quite quickly. Further compounding the issue, to beat the game each dungeon has to be cleared twice (with one being on hard mode). The hard-mode dungeons have changes in aesthetics but they feel almost entirely the same.  Monotony is sort of a theme in this game. Weapons might have a different number or coat of paint but all fall into just 4 major types. Since weapons also break frequently, you will always find yourself with a loadout with nothing but that dungeon’s basic 4 or 5 damage item. Even the upgrades lack any noticeable punch. Most change things so slightly they might not even be there. One of the game’s best upgrades makes the more powerful 2-handed weapons swing like 1-handed which provides a noticeable power boost but makes the game’s weapons feel even more homogenized.  The game’s humor around hustle and grind culture and the toxic aspects of the American workplace works well enough. Nothing too crazy but the characters did constantly provide entertainment to the point I was disappointed when they ran out of things to say before I finished the game.  I hope you fine more enjoyment from this title than I did. I tried my best to enjoy myself but I just didn’t have much fun. If you are thinking this might be for you, I’d only recommend it to fans of action rogue-like games who have burned through the big names  like Hades, Enter the Gungeon, and The Binding of Isaac.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a diamond in the rough. Modern, at times hilariously dystopian, and with a strong emphasis on never giving up, it's a roguelike that will surprise and charm you with every twist and turn. It's colourful and sweet and I really enjoyed it. Potential spoilers ahead as I pick this game apart;You play as Jacqueline, a fresh college graduate eager to take her first (unpaid) step into the world of corporate advertising! Unfortunately, she doesn't get very far before being asked to deal with the goblins - sorry, Joblins - in the basement.If that gives you any idea of what this game is like, good. It stays like that. The whole way through. This game will absolutely challenge you to your limits and keep you on your toes, but treats failing as a natural step, and just like any good roguelike, you're making progress with every run on the dungeons. The controls are good, and while I will be the first to admit I was not great at this game, it has solid enough controls that they fall very close to that sweet spot of 'easy to learn, hard to master'. Speaking of dungeons - the theming. Wow. Just WOW. The creativity, especially with the characters and setting, were incredible. The story is not quite at that level, but it doesn't need to be. It's strong enough to carry these characters and the setting, and that's enough for me. My favourite was Winkydink, but Joblin and Styxcoin were equally strong. I spent about 20 hours on my completed file, and I unlocked almost all the skills available to the player in that time, as well as finishing all the internships the characters give you. I didn't touch Impostor Mode or Overtime Mode - the extra content provided by the Working From Home Update - but if you're looking for a challenge after the main story, that's where you'll find it. TLDR - Great game, not quite as polished as the triple-A developers yet but they definitely made a winner with their first game. Going Under is fun, sarcastic, and genuine, and I really enjoyed playing it. If you like Roguelikes at all, you'll really like the fresh perspective that Going Under has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: With at least 10 hours of gameplay to complete in my experience, Going Under offers up plenty of content and inherent replay value by random generation, and the constant desire for one more run. Honestly, it’s one of my favourite games to release this year. As someone who has been playing Risk of Rain 2 non-stop as of late, but has been looking for something a little different to scratch that itch, I’ve finally found a new game to invest in.The gameplay alone is solid enough to be worthwhile, but what really makes the title shine is the story, characters, and writing. Even some twists and turns you may not expect, both in lore and gameplay, as time goes on. If I had any complaints, it’d simply be wanting more dungeons. The game isn’t lacking in content, it’s just so good that I’m left wanting more regardless. Of course, the future is full of possibilities, so maybe down the line we’ll see more to come.Either way, I highly recommend this game, to anyone who loves rogue-lites and hates tech-bro culture.And even if the genre isn’t normally your thing, the easy-to-pick-up, challenging-to-master style of gameplay in Going Under may offer an excellent launchpad into the genre. And, topping it all off, a customizable assist mode is available to those who want to play but would otherwise be barred by the game’s difficulty. A very welcome feature I hope to see in more and more games going forward! Game good, please support these devs.

_childDocuments_.review: This game nails its setting, its characters and its plot. The music is fitting, and the progression is unique. However, the gameplay itself is Not That Good, for reasons ill get way in depth over, but its not a complete deal breaker. The controls of this game work when the game is easy. Unfortunately, towards the second half of the game, it starts asking more of the player than the controls can provide, and the game goes from easy to bullsh*t. This mainly stems from the fact that every action is non cancellable. Started an attack animation and noticed an enemy starting theirs? Too bad, nothing you can do about it (this is on top of most of the weapons having long wind up animations). Again, this is fine when the game is easy, as enemy numbers and aggression are low. But as soon as those go up, it starts to feel like youre a dark souls 2 character being dropped into bloodborne.The lock on mechanic is also basically useless most of the time. Its main role is to help with lining up targets for thrown objects and thrusting attacks. Neither of these attacks are worth using. The throwing action feels especially weak, as you are not throwing AT them, you are throwing TOWARD them, with a predefined arc, meaning even when locking on you can are either too far away or too close, as it travels in an arc over their heads There are a wide selection of weapons in this game, most of them being unique to each area, with many different animation sets. Unfortunately, only about 3 per area are actually any good. If a weapon does not have an sweeping attack, ie, thrusting weapons, its not worth picking up, as on top of having no crowd control, it wont have increased damage to compensate.This is extremely frustrating in the second half of the game, as on top of getting more enemies, with more health, with higher aggression, the game gives you less good weapons. Many times you will find yourself walking into a room, seeing 7 enemies and a bunch of cardboard boxes, pencils and junk items. And on top of that, theres weapon durability, meaning on the rare chance you DO find a weapon you actually want to use, it lasts exactly half an encounter.The durability in this game feels like its balanced around the first iteration of the areas. The enemies arent too tanky and theres enough weapons lying around that you would want to use that it makes the game fun. Youre constantly cycling through weapons, its chaotic and fun. Unfortunately that second act happens, and it turns to frantic and frustrating. As mentioned, In the second act, the weapon pool gets scaled to favour the crappier side, with weapons that have the same durability against more enemies that have become more tankier. Its frustrating to be halfway through a fight, finding yourself with all the weapons you started with broken, and left running around the room praying that theres something that isnt a thrusting weapon or a junk item. In short, the accessibility/assist options could have helped to fix this, with options to change player health, enemy damage, invincibility frames and durability. Unfortunately, it can feel like a putting a cast over a light graze.I opted to turn on the durability assist, as i was getting too frustrated with the system. I could have stuck it out, i already beat one of the three areas without it, but i wasnt having any fun doing so. Unfortunately , instead of being a slider, it was a toggle, and it jacked up the durability way too far for me. So now the durability went from frustrating and frantic to nonexistent and braindead. For an assist menu that opens up with "everyone has fun in their own way", its quite odd that im not able to tailor the experience been not enough and too much Minor things that i either took issue with or think that adding them could make the game better, in no particular order - There needs to be some sort of outline or indicator for the player for when they are behind or under something, as it is extremely easy to get lost in the frame - One of rays perks needed to be "pin 2 skills", it just makes too much sense to not have that - While holding a blank card, highlight enemies that we have not yet added to the rolodex. - Let us pick up the card if we miss an enemy, its super annoying to have it disappear into nothingness- Let us toggle something so that the only perks that show up in the level are ones we have yet to endorse, not a fan of having that be left up to chance - The marv fight is not good. This is a boss that feels like the only reason why you would ever use the lock on mechanic, and yet the lock on goes away every time he teleports, please let the lock on stick onto him - Why would you make it so that the floating objects in on the way to the marv fight block you, its lame - The styxcoin event never feels long enough- some of the mentor challenges just dont show up half the time. there was multiple times where i went through a dungeon and the the game forgot to spawn the mission room, unsure if intentional- please give swamp a higher chance of stealing the game console, having to rely on the rng sucked- weapons take durability damage when hit, but hitting weapons is the only way to get them off a high shelf. this is lame- the fists suck to use, even with the power up. on top of having no damage they dont even stun the enemy. i know youre supposed to pick up stuff, but come on Keep in mind tho, that despite how negative this review was, i still mostly recommend giving it a go

_childDocuments_.review: A modern office drama combined with a simple yet fun roguelike, Going Under lets you live the life of a college graduate desperately trying to get an unpaid internship in the hopes of someday having a paying position with health insurance. It all starts off with having to clear some goblins out of the basement, then you have to crush the hopes and dreams of cryptominers and horny people. Things get kicked up a notch when your company gets bought out by Not-Amazon. The cast of characters are all varied in personality and make the journey all that much more enjoyable.Albeit a little buggy (I've mostly had some camera issues that were solved with alt tabbing out and in), the game is well worth the price tag for the laughs and hours of gameplay. For an extra challenge, an optional dungeon rush mode unlocks about halfway through. If you like jokes about work (not to be confused with workplace humor), have ever dreamed about bashing a coworker's head in with their keyboard, or just enjoy quirky roguelikes, I highly recommend giving this a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: I've worked in startups before and the writing, humor, and satire here is really charming and at times, kind of insightfully poignant. Its also chock full of tech world easter eggs and I think people working in that industry will appreciate the inside jokes.The gameplay is pretty stimulating, forcing you to equip and re-equip items on the fly and switch between weapons in different combat scenarios. Weapons break easily but practically everything in the office environment can be used as a weapon and it can be kind of fun just going around wrecking everythingWhen it comes to criticism I'd say that the gameplay can be a little shallow. The game experience itself is over pretty fast and I found myself using the same weapons and strategies after a while. Towards the end I started getting to a point where I would no longer get flavor text between runs. I also wouldn't mind seeing these characters interact with each other in a daily standup every so often. The writing is the best part of this game so I wish there was just more of itOne last thing I will say is that for some reason, I can't shake a certain melancholic feeling at certain scenes. This game ended up being pretty prophetic in terms of how technology would negatively affect our lives in the future. I don't see this as a downside of the game itself, but maybe just some food for thought on how the obsession with new technology isn't always a positive and a reminder for us to foster connection with real humans rather than robots, AI, and apps

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a wonderfully delightful action roguelike with addicting gameplay and lovely artwork and witty dialogue.I'm really not a fan of roguelikes so just the fact that I play this game says a lot about the game. The game is great fun and the witty dialogue and conversations are actually enjoyable to read. I think that says twice as much considering I really don't like reading or anything visual novel like but I enjoy the conversations the characters have in this game. The dialogue NEVER (at least if I can recall) repeat, like you can't talk to the same NPC and have them spit out the same text again, each time they have a dialogue above their head there's always a delightful/comedic conversation presented.Something random to point out but the game feels really polished! I don't have any particular examples it just feels right in every way.Some minor critiques that stick out immediately that could be a turn-off:- The in-game artwork is honestly quite ugly in comparison to the artwork, more specifically the characters look kind of dumb in their 3d form, but in the 2d artwork visual novelesque the characters are all quite attractive and the art is great. Not all of the 3d elements are bad, the map and the decorations are fine it's just the 3d models of the characters look kind've ugly.- Apparently there's not THAT much content in the game. I'm about 6 hours in and I've finished 2 of the dungeons out of the 3 (I think there's more than 3 technically but apparently they're just repeats with variability here and there), but the each dungeons do have great replayability, I've played the first dungeon maybe like 20 times already. Going Under is a great game with fun gameplay, pretty artwork, and entertaining dialogue. While the game has a few flaws (some which are subjective), ultimately if the idea of smacking enemies with various weapons and abilities sounds fun to you, then I would give it a recommendation. Is it worth $20? Errr... yeah it is but only if you're a fan of this genre and style... I'm really not a fan of roguelikes but I got this game for about $10 and I'm having a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: Protip: Don't be afraid to turn on assist mode. I was nervous to, thinking it might break my save and disable achievements or something. (It's hard to find any information on it, but if you just...just click it once, it explains everything.) Anyway, Going Under drew me in with its art style and writing when it first came out -- and Aggro Crab seem like legitimately cool developers based on how they dealt with trolls and dorky gamergate kids. It's a good game, but I was left disappointed by the gameplay.I enjoyed the first fourth of the game or so -- before you get to the True Founder dungeons. It was repetitive to a degree, but it didn't wear out its welcome quite yet. After you beat that chunk, however, the difficulty spikes through the roof. (Note: You'll find lots of complaints about this online, it turns out. The good news is a recent update lets you go back to replay the easier levels if you need to grind without stressing out.) It doesn't, unfortunately, spike in such a way as to reflect clever souls-like design principles, but rather because the combat is a bit clunky, the hit boxes questionable, some enemies are just not balanced well at all. A lot of the second and third acts of the game rely on RNG more than anything, which I found *so boring*, and led to my time being inflated by just hours upon hours of grinding the same dungeons over and over, leveling up mentors, &c. It doesn't help that all the dungeons are recycled with added difficulty, so you're only left with three total dungeons overall -- one of which (Styxcoin) I felt was notably worse in design than the other two.The final battles are full of so much screen shaking and endless hordes of enemies it was impossible to tell what the heck was going on and I was left dodgerolling and hoping for the best. This was the point I gave up and turned on assist mode; I wish I turned it on much earlier.Most grinding is to level up skills (of which there is a literal plethora) and your mentorship relationships, which provide extra bonuses. The high number of skills keeps things interesting, though a hefty chunk of them are not helpful. Only Swomp's mentorship is, imho, worth pursuing. (It's also the biggest pain in the butt, RNG-reliant to max out.) Three of the five are borderline worthless, and I am kicking myself a bit for wasting the time it took to max them out.I think this game really shines most in the aesthetic and the script. Having worked in and with the tech industry, the perspective and jabs on that culture and its obsession with buzzwords is just too on-point and clever not to admire. Who hasn't stood by muttering no, don't, stop, you don't know what you're asking for, while air-headed managers fall prey to the latest business fad like work culture mindfulness or slapping neural networks on frickin' everything? The digs at the frequent misuse and misunderstanding of machine learning and AI particularly killed me; they were too accurate. Sigh. The script was fantastic, it's just too bad the gameplay was such a chore long before I hit the ending, making this *barely* get a recommend from me. Definitely into it enough to follow Aggro Crab in the future, tho.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under quickly became one of my favorite games. The gameplay, art, and writing all weaves together nicely around a unique setting based on a hellish job market inspired by present-day, making it oddly relatable despite all the absurdity happening. The gameplay has you constantly adapting to your surroundings, as all the furniture and appliances in the room are weapons to take and break. The combat features many lil' quirks and interactions that make the improvised office fights more fun and chaotic.The aesthetic is simple and colorful, and generally makes something nice and charming out of an otherwise sterile corporate artstyle. The animations are lively and full of personality that add to the game's flavor. There are innumerable visual gags and thematically appropriate puns hidden in plain sight, and the character interactions got me looking forward to all the dialogues that'd pop up in-between runs. The plot is also more than I expected for this kind of game.The main caveat is that the camera takes a bit getting used to for this 3D dungeon crawler, but that becomes second nature relatively quickly. Overall, this game is definitely worth the investment.

Hades showed the world how to do an isometric, dodgy action roguelite with heaps of charm and compared to Zagreus, maneuvering our heroine in Going Under feels like wrestling a three-wheeled shopping cart.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under has a great soundtrack with satisfying and challenging gameplay. If you grew up on the internet or around tech in the 2010s, then you'll probably enjoy the jokes and writing in this game.The game is about 10-30 hours long depending on if you want to unlock all the skills or just play through the story. There are 4-8 dungeons + some high difficulty post game content to complete and there are assist options if you get stuck on the hard parts. The combat system can be compared with Breath of The Wild, but more hectic and with a lot of dodging. Abundantly available, easily broken weapons cause you to use a variety of fighting styles depending on the weapons available. The quests from your mentors flesh out the character personalities and draw attention to some of the little details that you may miss when playing the game normally.Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who wants a short-ish action game that has some good challenges to it and some relatable dark humor about startups and the working world.also, happy birthday nick

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent little rogue-lite with great satire and not serious gameplay.Pros:Combat feels good and dodge rolling is very responsive.Using throwable junk is an interesting combat system that adds to the weapons breakage formula.Runs are not long at all, with most being 20-30 minsSatire is great. If you are familiar with startup culture and silicon valley tech companies you'll enjoy it.Game is a good length.Mentor abilities are interesting and add a lot of replayabilityCons:Due to the physics based gameplay, items and enemies will sometimes knock you down and keep hitting you. It's entirely possible to lose a run just from being hitstunned into a corner.Mentor quests are a great idea but they fall flat when they require specific dungeons. I beat the first dungeon on my first try which meant I had to keep going back in for many many quests.The difficulty also felt wildly inconsistent. I beat the first 3 dungeons all within 3 attempts (2 on my first try!) and 2 of the second set within 3 attempts. And then one took me like 12 tries.There are too many skills for the length of the game. You would need to grind to unlock them all. I unlocked 66/99 in my run and that was after buying them every time I could. Why would I want to grind for skills post game?End of floor fights felt... pointless? There are no bosses aside from the final one in each dungeon so why bother making a special arena room.Probably the most damning thing about the game is that the first 3 dungeons are recycled to form the second 3. To be fair, they are ramped up in difficulty and have unique bosses, rooms and enemies. One of the game's strongest points is it's theming though and you have to redo 3 levels with the same theme as last time.The game's second to last dungeon has around 8 rooms filled with the same 2 enemy types that are massively tanky. If you fail the boss you have to do this over. The rooms and enemies never change.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, well written, and funny game with a great soundtrack. It's all very thematically coherent and full of sharp wit. If you work with any sort of IT or tech you'll probably have your own version of most of the characters in your office. So why can't I recommend it? Because after playing the game for 12 hours and making some ten attempts at the last boss the game clearly started going easy on me, skipping half the fights phases to allow me to finish. That is the opposite of satisfying, it feels like I've ran a marathon and someone spat in my face at the finish line. It also tarnished my whole experience, how can I be sure I ever actually got better at the game and it didn't just secretly lower enemy hp or remove mechanics without me knowing? Not to mention the camera is absolute arse at times.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played my fair share of soulslikes, but I don't think I've played one so unique and so creative as "Going Under". It is also a beat 'em up, a dungeon crawler and a roguelite, all while being visually arresting, funny and satirical about today's companies. It's a game that evokes different ideas and succeeds at them all, without ever feeling aimless.This game is so many things... where do I even begin with? For starters, I would say this game isn't much of a RPG; it's a roguelite first and foremost. Death means starting over again, but it gives you the opportunity to buy perks and improve your chances at each run. Still, there are no character stats, no leveling up. This doesn't disqualify the game as a soulslike, due to its lock-on mechanic and dodging. I will admit I didn't make much use of the lock-on, since my approach to combat was much more based on getting closer to my enemies and then button smash rather than the more tactical combat from "Dark Souls". But by God, I dodged a lot in this game, which is a central characteristic from the games by FromSoftware. In combat, multiple enemies will come at you at once, so dodging and moving are key for combat.As you crawl into dungeons, the game really shows its beat 'em up colours. Almost everything around you is a weapon, and can be used against your enemies. You can only carry three weapons at anytime, but some larger objects can only be used when they're at your hands, meaning you can't store them. Some weapons may come with buffed attack speed, damage or critical hit chance. Weapons naturally are of limited use and eventually break; there will be times when environments around you will be scarce of weapons, but so often one will be hanging in a wall nearby. Also, if you have no weapon at hands, dodging at an object will automatically make your character take it, which may have been a way from developers to avoid having your character be unarmed in a fight, but I would constantly grab useless items. Yes: they're here too.Dungeons in this game are randomly generated, meaning that a run will never be precisely like another. However, they'll always be divided in different floors, and as you move to a floor, you can't go back. Once you get to a room with enemies, you can only leave it by disposing them all; some rooms have these optional battles that, if you accept them and perform well, can grant you nice items. There'll also be specific rooms with shops, printers and perks. In shops, you trade the money you made for weapons, perks and health: pretty basic stuff. Printers - and this is when things get interesting - give you this blank paper that does massive damage, can only be used once, and that can convert enemies (even bosses) into cards, which go to your card collection. My problem with these printers, however, is that you can only take one paper from one of them, meaning that if you waste it, you're screwed.Perks are these buffs that grant you some extra power for that run only. Once you use that perk enough, you'll unlock it and be able to start a run with that power. But that's not all: it gets complicated. Before that, you need to buy these perks at the hub area, so they'll be available to be found in dungeons. And there's a different currency for that, called "cubits", which can also be found in dungeons. Whereas you can't take regular money with you back to the hub area (since it can only be used in dungeons anyway), cubits are used to buy these perks in the overworld, as well as card paper. Some are game changers, and when combined, can pretty much guarantee you a successful run. Still on the matter of perks, you'll also find at dungeons rooms with this vampire-like character offering a negative perk: it will affect you for some battles before dissipating, but you'll gain access to three items of interest, so it's up to you to judge if it's a worthy sacrifice.From time to time, you'll come across secret rooms that are not in your HUD map, and they may contain powerful weapons. There'll always be a boss at the end of your run, and once you defeat them for the first time and take their prizes, your basic health capacity increases permanently.Then there are the mentors. God, I love them as a mechanic and as characters. The mentors will give you side quests, which are really these Rebellion-like challenges in which you're requested to dispose of enemies in specific ways, or do runs without buffs, or not get hurt for so long. At some points, mentors may ask you to eliminate enemies that will appear at dungeons in special rooms. But the absolute worse is when they ask you to buy them things in the shops: it may look simple, but these items will be specific to one shop at a specific floor only, and once you move on, even when you get the necessary cash, you can't buy it. For that, you need to make use of tricks that, fortunately, you can pull off. As you complete such tasks, mentors will grant you interesting advantages, such as shoplifting, or starting the run with a food box.And then there are the apps, which can grant you momentary buffs such as high speed, health recovery, invincibility and so on. If you have a certain mentor selected, apps will be replaced by soda cans, and the difference is that while apps are powers for you, cans generate these blasts that affect nearby enemies in different ways, and I personally preferred doing runs with soda cans. The high variety of weapons, perks, apps, soda cans and mentors allows players to try different playstyles and techniques, so if you feel like you have already found your style, it doesn't hurt to leave your comfort zone and try something different - maybe you'll find something that suits you even better.There are three dungeons in the game, plus two special levels. I can't reveal anything more without spoiling, but suffice to say, there will be a moment when you go through them again, but with different, harder enemies. Dungeons have these little nuances that differentiate them from each other, but they play more or less the same. One of them even has its own currency, just to make matters more complicated! In the end, "Going Under" is not extensive, but more of a game in which you play the same levels in different ways. And no: it doesn't get tiresome.This is very much a game for completionists. Everything about it feels like it was designed for players to keep coming back for all the side quests, perks, cards and achievements. It's a game that, with its very addicting combat, feels so compelling to play that you want more from it. It indeed got the "Work From Home" update, which added a new challenge, but unfortunatley it's incredibly repetitive and grindy, and a major sore point. The game also features what it refers to as an "assist mode", which is to say it gives players options to customise the game's difficulty. So here's a HUGE difference between it and the works from Hidetaka Miyazaki.Last but certainly not least, the presentation, and its biting satire of modern corporatism. The characters, the visuals, everything is evocative of today's companies. Dialogues - which are presented as text messages - are delightful and don't at all feel like tanking the flow of the game. The characters are all stereotypes who seem straight from "Silicon Valley", and they're so enjoyable that I connected with them and their little dramas - I wish I could romance Jackie with Swomp, seriously. In fact, the whole thing looks like it could be a colaboration between Paul Verhoeven, J.G. Quintel and Alex HirschIn the end, "Going Under" is a bright, funny and addicting game from all the involved. It feels like a passion project though and through, and the future for Aggro Crab is bright if this was their debut.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a damn shame 'Going Under' went under a lot of people's radar — to the point where the devs are pulling the plug on future development — because what's here is really, *really* good. It's a world I would be more than happy to pay and see more of.Make no mistake, what is here is a fleshed out experience well worth the asking price. While combat is engaging and choices are plentiful, where 'Going Under' truly shines is in its sharp writing, unique aesthetic, and absolutely banging soundtrack. The game is really quite brilliant, and I'm bummed we won't be seeing more anytime soon.Buy the game. Groove to the soundtrack. And maybe look at some of their merch if you become a fan. These devs certainly deserve the love.

_childDocuments_.review: A pleasant surprise, and a damn good time considering how much I normally despise this style of dungeon crawler. Going Under has a lot of good stuff going for it. The art style is unique and colorful, the combat is very hectic and requires a lot of improvisation thanks to a BOTW style weapon system, and pretty much every skill results in a significant game play change. It's not as in-depth as something like Binding of Issac or Enter the Gungeon, but the 3 worlds and relatively low amount of items in comparison to those games didn't get boring at all during the game's relatively short campaign. It's much more of a bite-sized rogue lite, which is perhaps one of the reasons I enjoyed it so much. Progression in Going Under is rapid as hell, often resulting in multiple unlocks from each run. The game is very happy to dish out currency for unlockables as well, which makes each run actually feel worthwhile. The only area where Going Under hits some speedbumps is with the Mentor unlocks, which are essentially character abilities that get unlocked through specific mission objectives. The only problem is that these objectives rely on some pretty hefty RNG a lot of the time, and will have you confused as to how to proceed. You will be lucky if you have more than one mentor fully leveled up by the time the credits roll, which is a shame because a lot of the abilities seem like a lot of fun.Going Under has all the workings of a great rogue-lite and then some. The combat is punchy and satisfying, (most) enemies are balanced, and the boss fights are a ton of fun to complete. The game avoids a lot of frustration that I feel from other rogue lites by having runs last usually a max of 15 minutes, and progression that would normally 10 hours in other games here takes 2. It does cheapen the thrill of the unlocks occasionally, but you also have a much more tightly packaged and designed game that feels rewarding to play and is addicting as all hell. I can't remember the last time I completed a game in 2 days, let alone one so far outside of my comfort zone.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is an amazing game with an unique and charming art style, engaging gameplay, well written characters and an interesting story. I've wanted this game for a while, so when I saw it on sale, I had to buy it. I wasn't expecting more than a dungeon crawler with a funny premise, but it hooked me quick. The gameplay is very fun and full of action, it can be challenging, but never in a demotivating way. The many mechanics makes it about strategy too, not just pure skill. Combining and deciding on skills, apps/cans in your inventory and finding a perfect match is amazing. The art style reminds me of that art from giant corporations, and that really fits in the context of the game. The characters are well written and this game had me laugh out loud many many times, the humor is great all around and specifically around the corporate style of the game it's right on the money. As someone studying IT and very privacy conscious, Kara had me laughing a lot, and <spoiler, you know what i mean if you played it> was amazing.I was not expecting a story at all, but it ended up being interesting and fitting the game really well. I really recommend playing this game, it's great!

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a fun roguelite about being an unpaid intern in the corporate world of start-ups. There are 3 dungeons in the game, which seems like not that much at first, but they do change and become more difficult as you progress through the story. The game itself is 3D and the combat relies on picking up random weapons with varying durability off of the ground as well as throwing junk and dodge rolling to avoid damage. The controls are rather intuitive. Using a controller is heavily suggested.As far as I've played the game there doesn't seem to be this crazy amount of cool synergies between items as there are in games like Enter the Gungeon and Binding of Isaac. I am still only 3 hours into the game, but I already feel confident in recommending this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Dungeon Crawler!At first glance this game didn’t look like much from the steam page, but I was pleasantly surprised once playing.The plot is modern and different from any other theme I’ve seen in this genre. It’s very hip heh…The characters have a fun stereotypical design, and the dialogues are easily digestible. I wouldn’t say dialogues had anything special about them other than it fit the theme of what they were going for with each character really well. Still, something I appreciated when playing.I loved the music in this game being something like a mix between lo-fi and futuristic chillwave I guess?? Either way, it has a very nice soundtrack to have on while fighting your way through these dungeons and talking to people. I usually play these games and watch something on the side, but the music kept me engaged and vibin.The combat is probably where the game is good but not as good as other dungeon crawlers I’ve played. Personally, like combat that feels like you are hitting your enemies and I did not get that feeling when playing this. However, the weapons felt very creative in relation to what dungeon you were in and had good variability to them.At first, I thought the game was a bit too easy but as with many other DCs, it got harder when progressing. I would recommend it for both casual and experienced players.	The visuals are stunning making me want to eat my monitor. Everything is very bouncy and marshmallowey. The locations had fun details that fit the stereotypes I think they were going for, and NPCs fits their theme making me think that developers put a lot of thought into it.All and all I would say for those looking for a satisfying and fun dungeon crawler with great visuals and an intriguing story, this is the one for you!

_childDocuments_.review: The best way I can explain this game it's a fun roguelite and it is not meant to be taken seriously. I have played games of the same genre which are more punishing and stressful therefore was on a lookout for something different. I came across this gem, while on the surface the game might seem shallow and even lacking but actually a lot of stuff is hidden for you to explore. The game has its own level of difficulty it is fairly challenging and like any roguelite it is meant to be played again till you get it right so death is inevitable but the game is far from frustrating. On top of that the combination of different perks and debuffs in the game and weapon choices, there's a good amount of them, they are as I said before fun to explore and experiment with. The levels are procedurally generated that means you get a different layout of the map with obstacles placed at random can give you a strategic advantage in some rooms except for boss floors those are pretty much the same or at least what I have observed so far. But still I feel it's not going to be everyone's cup of tea but if you dig the art, the vibes and the silliness of the story which is hilarious I definitely recommend to try it. Although my advice is that make sure you talk to all the characters before you start in the beginning they will give you objectives that will help you unlock some cool stuff I had to find the hard way don't just go straight to the dungeon. i can definitely see myself returning to this game maybe in a long while after beating it overall a really fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to enjoy this game, I like the art style and the music is for the most part great. But the combat is some of the worst I've ever played in a Rougelite, none of the weapons feel particularly creative and they break too fast for you to get a feel for the more rare ones. Pretty much all the perks are meh besides the ones that offer a straight up damage increase. The active items, called apps in this game, aren't very well explained. There are three or four of them that I have no idea what they do even after using them a couple times. The one's that are straight forward enough to understand are just whatever, excluding the shop discount. The game itself isn't very difficult, the enemies and even the bosses have very basic attacks that are at least well telegraphed. The only reason you wouldn't glide through the game in an hour or two is the weapon degradation, which only makes the game tedious. You'll burn through a whole weapon per room unless you luck out with a durability modifier and even then it'll only last an extra room on top of that. Bosses on the other hand will deplete all three of your weapons in like 30 to 40 seconds, unless you hoard a rare weapon until the fight in which case it makes the boss trivial.The game also has no faith in your ability so you have to repeatedly back track to previous dungeons to complete "Mentor" relationships. Which are just tedious challenges that unlock passive effects. The effects are alright, some definitely better than others. But unless you want the minimal amount of additional story the mentors offer you can pretty much get away with only doing one. Speaking of story, it's also kind of whatever, you're an intern that has to dungeon crawl to get these artifacts for your obviously evil boss and that's pretty much it. All the characters are fairly shallow with one or two quirky traits, which is disappointing because the character design is so unique and fun.Can't really recommend, I got it heavily discounted through humble bundle and even then I'm disappointed with it.

_childDocuments_.review: 07.08.2021.Game #170You know what I hate? Getting an internship job at a new company and from day one someone telling me to kill monsters under the company floor. That really sucks. I mean, come on! I applied for the marketing department and they are telling me to go downstairs, grab whatever I could find, and whack monsters until there aren’t any left? What am I supposed to whack them with? Laptops, potted plants, fake swords? That’s basically Going Under and the above description pretty much describes the game, except for the part where I say that I hate it, because I love this game.In this game you go into randomly generated dungeons where you fight monsters, collect power ups, different weapons and eventually beat a boss at the end. It’s very similar to most rouge-likes such as The Binding of Isaac  or Enter the Gungeon  but not as deep. The biggest difference here is that you do everything from a third person view and have full control of your camera wherever you go. While we’ve seen a lot of whacky rogue-likes with wacky weapons, I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game where you use almost all office supplies for combat. Mugs, pencils, potted plants, protractors, mining picks (for bitcoin mining, obviously), laptops, you name it.Each dungeon is making fun of a certain company culture and each dungeon feels a little different than the last. In one dungeon for example, you fight against bitcoin miners and in another against job trolls. It’s both funny and endearing. Most importantly, the game is fun.From what I described above, you’d think that combat would be chaotic. While it can get a bit messy with too many enemies I almost never had a situation where I didn’t feel in control. Moving and using weapons is very responsive and very simple. While you may be tempted to grab the biggest thing in the room and whack enemies with it, many weapons break easily so you are forced to swap between them quite often. Not as frustrating as Zelda: Breath of the Wild but it still makes you think twice before picking a weapon for the next room. Also, each weapon has weight and physics. It’s take twice as much to swing a heavy weapon than a small pencil. Each weapon can also be thrown at enemies which is a great strategy when a weapon is about to break. You can also dodge roll, which works really well.You can also use fire to burn enemies, power ups to make some encounters easier, buy things from the dungeon shops… I mean, for a joke game like this, this is a very deep rouge-like.From the presentation, I thought this was going to be a walk in the park, but no. This game can be really hard, just like any good rogue-like. It took me quite a few runs to reach the end of my first dungeon but it never felt like the game wanted to screw me over. Sure, the game can be hard at times but it’s one of those cases where, the more you play the more you learn.  I adore the way Going Under looks. It’s so colorful. I’m a sucker for games with bright colors and this just makes me hopeful for the future. Why do all games nowadays have to be dark and gloomy? Why don’t we have more silly games that make fun of startup companies? Combine this with a simple yet catchy theme with each dungeon and you’ve got yourself a rouge-like that’s really eye-catching. As of writing this, I haven’t really played this game too much but I know that I’ll be back for more. Yeah, sometimes I really need a quick run of a dungeon and I think Going Under is going to do just nicely. I’m looking forward to seeing more of its parody on modern companies.Next game: A Golden Wake

It's still fairly emotionally flat (at least in the first 3 hours).- This setting has already been mined pretty hard as a parody target and the punches don't quite land, If you've been tapped into the world enough to get the jokes, you're not going to get any new thoughts (or new jokes, really) about tech business culture.- The imitation of generic tech graphic design tropes is very clever in places. (There are other places where it doesn't commit to the bit enough IMO - like the overall art style, which takes a stab at stock art vector-people that's muddled by the lighting and animation choices and set dressing.)- The protagonist would be more memorable if she were either more blank or more filled in - she occupies a weird middle space where her personality and goals are too specific for your imagination to give her your hopes and dreams, but not specific enough to understand and care about her hopes and dreams. _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could leave a mixed review, but I'd rather give this game a thumbs up than a thumbs down because of the things that it does right.The characters, art style and dialogue are very good, its a successful parody that at no point feels preachy or bitter, it pokes good fun of corporate culture through the dialogue and art style.My main issue comes from the second half of the game, where the difficulty just gets cranked up way too high and the combat doesn't support that.Most weapons you use don't give you enough time to dodge, coupled with the problem that some enemies don't flinch even when you are using heavy weapons that take way too long to swing and can be interrupted mid-swing along with the fact that weapons can break. It makes for good chaotic gameplay on the first half, but when the difficulty gets increased cracks start showing, I was excited for harder dungeons until I found myself unarmed multiple times because I wouldn't have enough weapons to deal with all enemies (being unarmed is the same as giving up, as your character does 1 damage per punch).Sometimes I'd start a run, have nothing to grab on the first room, get put into combat and have to deal with 5 enemies unarmed, which is pretty much impossible.Luckily the game remedies that by having an assist option that gives you more i-frames on your dodge, increases your health and weapon durability and makes the enemies less spongy, it feels cheap but I'll take that over unfairness I guess.This game really didn't have to be a roguelike, I'm guessing the developers were scared of it being too short and people feeling like it wasn't worth their money, but I would be completely fine with a shorter experience that didn't annoy me, I'll take a finely balanced game over something randomized any day.Overall the story is good enough to bother dealing with the second half of the game, its still very charming in its presentation and execution of story and characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a third-person roguelite developed by Aggro Crab, and their first game at that. Roguelites have become a bit of an oversaturated market over the past few years, but I think Going Under definitely sets itself apart from the crowd.Interestingly enough, the fundamental gameplay was probably my least favorite part of Going Under. Not to say that it's bad. Keep in mind this is coming from someone with a ton of experience in roguelites, so I'm comparing Going Under to the best of the genre in terms of pure gameplay (i.e Dead Cells, Hades).The basic gameplay is pretty simple. You pick up weapons you find in the dungeon and use them to fight a wide range of enemies. There's a durability system, meaning your weapons break after enough use. Thankfully, you can store up to 3 at a time. I'm not a fan of durability systems in games but I think it works very well in a roguelite. It forces you to use weapons you might normally not use, which helps add variety to runs as well as getting good with all sorts of weapons. There's a targeting system to focus on a specific enemy, which is super useful. It's very similar to Z-targeting from the 3D Zelda games. You can also throw weapons at enemies, which I didn't find particularly useful most of the time, but is a nice option anyway. While I wasn't huge on the basic gameplay, the systems present within the game are all fantastic.The skills in Going Under aren't as fun as some other roguelites. Don't expect to find some completely broken combination that will let you easily steamroll the game ala Isaac. They are, however, still fun and provide the player with a good deal of choice. Each floor has a guaranteed skill room, which has 2 skills. You choose 1. This gives the player some degree of choice as to how they want to play their run. Even after completing the game, I still haven't unlocked all of the skills, so there's definitely a good variety present. Once you use a skill enough, you can endorse it, which means you can start a run with that skill already learned. This is really great in my opinion, removing some of the luck from a run and allowing the player to start the run on their terms. Big fan of this, wish more roguelites did stuff like it.All the characters in the game (barr Marv and Avie) have a mentorship you can progress through. Basically, you talk to them, get missions, and complete them to progress through the mentorship. There are 4 levels to each mentorship, and each level has a unique perk that gives you an advantage. I love how each mentorship is strongly tied to the character (i.e Ray is hugely irresponsible and gives you the Company Card, etc.). Just like the endorsement system, this gives the player a lot of control over how they play each individual run. It can be very fun to try them all out as each mentorship is distinct.Going Under features multiple, short dungeons to choose from as you progress through the game. There are 3 main dungeons, and each has 4 floors, with the final floor containing the boss of the dungeon. They each have a unique theme (as they're each based around a fictional company) with different enemies, events, shopkeepers and bosses. The dungeons you explore are very linear. There isn't any real exploration to do on each floor of the dungeon you're going through. The most I've found after around 12 hours in the game were some hidden rooms and a few branching paths. This linearity isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it's something to take note of. It makes each run decently quick, but can definitely impact the replayability. Thankfully, in the most recent major update, the devs added Impostor Mode, which lets you go through all of the dungeons at once, much more like a conventional roguelite. Definitely a good choice to add.The story and characters are what made me really love Going Under. They're genuinely fantastic. The basic premise is that you, Jackie Fiasco, are an intern at Fizzle, a subsidiary of Cubicle (which is basically Amazon). Unfortunately, you're forced to go through a bunch of dungeons instead of marketing work. Thanks Marv. I'll leave the rest for you to find out!The characters are all a lot of fun. You really understand each character and we're they're coming from. Fern's genuine love of his work. Tappi's frustration with her inability to reign in Ray. Kara's hatred of her job and indifference to the fate of the company. Swomps.... swomp-ness. Ray's privileged and carefree nature. Marv's indifference to your situation. The character writing is something to commend. Every conversation in the game is pretty great. One of the reasons I like the mentorship system so much is because you learn more about each character and their personality as you progress through their tasks. Going Under is super, super satirical. A lot of dialogue focuses on satirising working in the modern day, and particularly startups. The game is pretty much a metaphor for working as an intern at a startup. Except instead of doing menial unrelated jobs in the workplace, you're going through dungeons and murdering monsters. It's made super  clear that Ray and Marv aren't paying attention to what the people working in Fizzle actually want. Tappi is constantly frustrated at Ray refusing to stay on budget. Marv often makes promises to the team (especially Jackie) that he clearly never intended to fulfill. A lot of the game's satire is focused on how poorly workers are treated in modern day corporate spaces. One of Ray's missions is literally to bust a Joblin union. The team essentially gets replaced by Avie, a super-advanced AI. Ray and Marv's refusal to pay attention to their team makes it clear that Fizzle is doomed to fail. It's clear that everyone (barr Swomp, I guess?) is overworked and underappreciated.Jackie is a great protagonist to deliver a lot of laughs. She often plays the straight man, and it's very easy to relate to her struggles. She's just someone fresh out of college looking to get a start in the corporate workplace. Her conversations with Marv are all funny, but a bit sad. Jackie just wants to get some real experience, dammit!That being said, I would be remissed if I talked about the humor of the game without mentioning Swomp. Every line Swomp says is f*cking hilarious. Maybe my sense of humor is just really dumb, but he's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ funny. He talks in all lowercase, uses crappy grammar (i.e saying "ur") and is just a super carefree, chill dude. His missions are so, so funny. Just completely stupid sh*t, like running over a car with a car, or buying a dank gaming rig (actual words used in game). He often refers to Jackie as "beb".I seriously recommend completing his mentorship, because his business card is probably the funniest thing in the game.Going Under is really unique and fun visually. I love the polygonal artstyle, and how bright everything is. Each dungeon has unique theming and colour palettes, and each enemy looks distinct. The character design is fantastic, you can pretty much understand the basics of each character from their vignettes in conversation. The enemies all look unique and separate from each other. The design of Fizzle office is pretty much an ideal hub world. All great stuff.The music is genuinely splendid. Love, love, love it. Whatever tone the game is going for, the music complements it brilliantly. The mundane but slightly upbeat tune that plays in the Fizzle office. The unique themes of each dungeon (especially Joblin, can't get that track out of my head). The epic boss battle songs. It's all so, so great.If you read through this whole thing, congrats. I wrote it all and I could barely do it.  I hope this review convinced you of the merits of Going Under.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a top-down roguelite dungeon-crawler set in a fantasy city called Neo-Cascadia. As Jackie, a newly-graduated intern, fortunately receives the marketing job offer at the famous beverage company Fizzle. However, the "job" does not seem to be what she expects: weird marketing plans, irrelevant budget usage, and worst of all, dungeon-crawling?! Battling joblins, skeletons, and demons is definitely far from marketing. Players will help Jackie conquer different dungeons of failed companies, as well as unmasked the beautiful facade of Cubicle. This is the roguelite game I've played that hits home. It's satiric approach of corporate greed, underappreciated employees and misplaced intern mock the reality of our society. A consistent and coherent story seasoned with tons of mockup names of real-life company and business phrases really makes the game charming and joyful. I highly recommend everyone trying Going Under out. The focus on story makes up for lack of variety in terms of room spawn, and the fast pace and short runs are great feature for people looking to experience the beauty of roguelite.A combination of Deadrising and Breath of The Wild is the accurate summary of Going Under's weapon system. Everything you see in the office/dungeon is a potential weapon for your survival, and there are tons of items to weaponized: from typical furniture to office appliances; from classic swords and hammers to that body pillow which is too embarrassing to show. Beware! These "weapons" break easily, so make sure to have something you can bash the mobs with nearby. Besides interesting weapon system, the game also introduces various perks as Kiosks, which can shape your combat style. Helping yeet things faster and more accurate, or disguise yourself so you can avoid combat, you name it. My favorite so far, is baby Jackie with beef-up arms and a spinning saw blade around her waist. How terrifying to see a tiny person running full speed at you, swinging a moai like a piece of plastic.The npcs in Going Under is a perfect replication of a typical company: an overlooking entrepreneur, encouraging but manipulative manager, a depressed accountant, an engineer who hates her job as an engineer, a weird scientist, and an out-of-loop guy. These npcs feels alive with their special interaction with Jackie the clueless intern, though most of the time complaining. They also offer different tiers of side quests you can complete during the run. While most of them are simple tasks, some have leave me interesting memories. Like Kara tier 2 quest: walking Eclaire through B3. The leash actually binds your movement. As a result, you need to time your dodge well and make the best of your maneuvers. This side quest adds a lair of difficulty in this rather easy roguelite game.This game is oozing satire from head to toe. The opening cutscene is a mockup tech demo concept video. The overall art style is Alegria Motion but wackier. The dungeons in nothing short of fun. The Joblins are contractors and freelancers that help promote caffeine; The Styxcoin is the embodiment of the digital-mining cryptocurrency - they literally put "mining" and "crypto-" into this dungeons theme; The Winkydink is straightforward ridiculing those dating apps all over the place, including emojis sexually-spamming through the character. And you cannot miss this. Remember that guy who brags about his Lamborghini and "knowledge", he is in this game too, as a vampire!While I do say that the focus on the story makes up for lack of room variation, this is still a glaring issue in terms of roguelite games. Even though I consider Going Under to be a short roguelite game exploration-wise, I still think the room spawn become easily repetitive after 3 to 5 runs. To be fair, the devs do design three challenges unique to each dungeon, but there are still more rooms to be desire. After all, the funny joke and satire can only go so far. I suggest adding some kind of racing challenge: the room is full of environmental hazards, and the player needs to go through it either to progress or obtain a super strong item. Basically, adding more "high risk, high reward" situation to spice up the run.

_childDocuments_.review: Good:-Visual appealing ranging from it's colorful and fluid art style-Has a funny sense of humor with its writing, terminologies, and references-Friendly rogue-like with a balance of intrinsic and extrinsic progression-Lots of weapons and power-ups that encourages experimentation with different play styles-Combat is fun, fast-pace, and challengingBad:-RNG can greatly affect runs (especially on imposter mode)-Descriptions for some skills are unclear due to its comedic writing-Character dialogue might be a turn-off since some text are paragraphs longFor me, I would say the strongest points of this game are its art style and combat. The alegria art style suits this game since it revolves around advertising and business. It's an art style used by most modern tech companies since vibrant colors and fluid shapes are visually appealing. Ironically, it's one of the reasons I bought this game. The combat has a lot of depth as there are many weapons and power-ups that can be acquired which can encourage experimentation with different play styles. This game has a good balance of extrinsic and intrinsic progression. Players are able to increase their max HP and gain new skills to use in future runs. However, intrinsic skill such as adapting to RNG, dodging attacks, and patience is also needed to do well in Going Under since the game gets more challenging and chaotic overtime. A few main issues I have are the RNG and the descriptions of the skills. RNG can greatly affect runs especially on imposter mode where you can't start with a mentor or starting skill. Some runs can be good while others can feel unfair. As for the skill descriptions, some are confusing to understand due to the game trying to be comedic and witty. The least the devs could've done was be more detailed on what certain skills do. But despite my complaints, I think Going Under is a very fun game.
