_childDocuments_.review: You know what's worse than playing a bad game? Playing a game that starts being awesome and then suddenly changes mid-way, turning into something that you do not enjoy anymore and leaves you bewildered as to why such a change was necessary.Going Under is one of those games. A game that starts very well, managing to use its narrative features to gloss over its shortcomings and reel the players in, but fails to keep itself going and starts focusing on the wrong things as well.Going Under is an enjoyable critique of current work culture dressed up as a game. The game's events happen in a world very similar to ours, with mega corporations that grow with each passing day, taking smaller companies and startups as their own and then doing whatever the hell they want with them. You start the game in the shoes of an unpaid intern named Jackie, who is assigned to an already struggling startup to do marketing, and gets entangled in a whole lot of stuff instead.It's actually amazing how well this game handles work-related topics in our current world. The whole story and all of the dialogues are cleverly written commentaries of various topics such as corporate greed, workplace culture, startups, artificial intelligence and even overuse of the technology. In fact, some of the story events literally depict what we have seen happening around us and in bigger corporations in recent years.And the game delivers these commentaries through clever jokes, well-done references and easter eggs, fine humor and a cast of likeable & colorful characters, with occasional drama to make you really feel what the main character's co-workers are going through. All of the characters you will see in this game have distinct personalities and mannerisms, to the point you can't help but constantly get reminded of real people who are currently working at a corporation or running it. Hell, some of these characters and what they told me even reminded me of people who are around me and are not even working a corporate job.When it comes to easter eggs, Going Under has one of the best instances of hiding them or giving subtle nods. The game literally puts the easter eggs in front of your face but unless you are paying attention, you won't be able to identify them. And the things the game references with its easter eggs are wild, from other video games to actual people and even viral internet things that you would never expect seeing them in a game like this.And the game needed such well-done narrative presentation, as the gameplay does not have any charms of its own to encourage players to carry on.Despite what people are saying on this game's store page, I firmly believe Going Under is not a rogue-lite. This game is a beat'em up at its core, with rogue-lite elements sprinkled in to inject some variety to the gameplay. And honestly, they're not enough.The meat of the gameplay consists of arriving at a dungeon and going through multiple rooms that are randomly put together by the game, each either containing enemies to fight, showing a specific optional task to do or offering you to pick up potentially helpful powerups and skills in forms of special rooms and shops. Your goal is to get to the ending room and fight a final wave of enemies for the first three floors of the dungeon, and then face the boss and beat them on the 4th floor. But you won't have access to weapons from the get-go; You have to pick up items that are scattered around the room and use them as weapons, and them maybe switch them with the actual weapons the enemies drop; either to get a better weapon or switch your currently damaged weapon before it breaks mid-combat.However, contrary to what you might think, the combat is not fun. Despite the game offering the mentorship system (unlocking passive skills in exchange for mission completion), curses (temporary debuffs in exchange for items) and a boatload of skills to unlock, the combat is still very underdeveloped and the novelty of the whole thing quickly wears off. Because what you do through all of the available dungeons is literally the same thing and the optional missions sometimes are more infuriating & time-consuming rather than being challenging. That's why the narrative presentation is so strong. The game simply uses the story and the witty commentary to make you want to carry on with the gameplay.The game does this for the first 4-6 hours, at which point you will finally feel the gameplay fatigue kicking in, with the story being unable to stop it. By this point in time, you have reached the mid-point of the game, awaiting the second half of the adventure to begin. But while you expect the game to reveal its next big thing and add something new to the gameplay, it just does something completely different, dramatically decreasing the value of the game in the process.The second half of Going Under features one of the most severe quality nosedives I have ever seen in a video game. And I do not mean it has ♥♥♥♥ quality. The game just starts focusing on doing the opposite of what it was already doing, completely forgetting how it kept the experience going for so long.Upon starting the second half of the game, you'll see a series of dramatic story events and then the quality of the game sharply drops afterwards. At this moment, the game completely stops being fun; because it changes its focus from what works for it to what doesn't work. If the first half of the game focused on carrying the gameplay through narrative, the second half tries to carry the narrative through gameplay by removing all of the story and dialogues, and locking them behind gameplay progression. There won't be any optional conversations with the NPCs or story cutscenes until the very end. If you want to see more of the story, you have to beat all of the dungeons again and reach the final boss. And that is without mentioning the difficulty spike you'll be facing.In the second half of the game, you will be forced to run through harder versions of all of the past dungeons and bosses in order to access more story content and reach the ending. In each encounter, the game will throw more enemies at you with significantly increased health and more armor points, turning them into literal damage sponges. Meanwhile, you'll be using the very same set of abilities that you've been using since the start of the game. This makes the game unnecessarily hard and in the case of the second dungeon, even unfair & poorly designed. And that's where everything falls apart, because as I mentioned before, the gameplay gets incredibly stale after a while and it's the narrative and commentary that drives the players forward in the first half of the game. So, by switching the driving factor and not adding anything of value to it, the game completely loses its appeal.And even if you power through and try to finish the game with all of the gameplay issues and frequent bugs (like curses becoming permanent, item descriptions getting messed up, optional missions becoming unbeatable, and more) your reward is a disappointing final boss and a lackluster ending, with the story being completely unable to salvage them. By this point I was completely burnt out and didn't even bother with the optional game mode the game offers you. Because honestly... I didn't want more of the same gameplay I was playing until that point.Starts great as a charming & enjoyable game with clever commentary on corporations and work culture, then the quality sharply nosedives upon getting to the second half, changing the game for the worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow.This is by far the best rougelike I've ever played by a lightyear. Most rougelikes are just cheap and quickly made video games to give someone a lot of mileage from a moderate bank of assets via remixing and challenging progressive gameplay.This, on the other hand. Is ART.It has a fun and cute artstyle, the world and characters are bursting with charm, the amazingly deep-rooted understanding of pop-culture of 3 generations is so one-of-a-kind here. Every single aspect of game development is nailed here.The themes and underlying message of this game are so on point it hurts. And it's just so well-handled.And the finale just slaps so hard. It's rare to see a game stick a landing so hard.But onto gameplay.This one of the most accessible rougelike I know of. I didn't see the options till after I beat the game but wow, it's cool that even a more casual audience can enjoy the story!It's also refreshing to play a game in this genre where learning, patience, and skill are rewarded and can carry you without needing the luck of a "good run". Usually devs make cheap or unfair enemies/levels to further pad out the genre, not here.The loop is fun, the curses are more fair than they should be IMO, and the mentor missions really mix up how you play some dungeons. The progression of skills and mentorship are very rewarding and satisfying. The second half of the game is pretty brutal, but never gets to the point of frustrating.I beat this game feeling inspired and happy. And if I could I would give the entire dev team a standing ovation for this incredible game. If you like action games and rougelikes, you owe it to yourself to play this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under? More like Going Underrated! - A vibrant, colourful aesthetic. - Amusing dialogue often full of corporate humour, pop culture references, or general silliness which, quite frankly, is right up my alley. - Charming, loveable NPC colleagues each with their own personalities. - A large variety of melee and ranged weapons to use against your enemies, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Each weapon also has a 'charge' attack that behaves differently, e.g. small swords perform an AoE spin vs a sledgehammer which does a slow, high-damage overhead attack vs a spear doing a leap attack, etc. - Roughly 100 or so perks to collect with various synergies. You can also select one to begin with once you have found it a few times during gameplay which is nice. - Various limited-use consumables to collect with varying effects, e.g. an 'app' that repairs and randomly buffs your equipped weapon, or cans of soft drink that cast elemental novas that apply status effects to enemies. - Occasional secret rooms with special weapons and enemies. - Various risk and reward mechanics to keep you on your toes, e.g. take a debuff for X rooms, but get a few perks/weapons as compensation or kill an optional wave of enemies for a chance at a box containing strong items, etc. - A great soundtrack that fits the areas. - A 'mentoring' system where you can complete challenges to gain passive improvements and can select between the different groups of improvements, e.g. one mentor focuses on improving apps, another on item boxes and money, etc. - An optional 'assist' system where you can enable certain crutches if you find the game too hard, e.g. more health, more item durability, etc. I think this is a nice feature for the more casual audience. - Completing the rolodex (beastiary) can be rather challenging. You can only add an entry if you last-hit an opponent with a special blank card item. You can usually only get 1-2 of these per run and they are a one use item, so it can take some time to obtain this if you don't time things right/miss/die before you are able to use it. Pro tip: make sure you have the 'focus' key pressed when using the card! If you intend to get all the achievements, then this shouldn't be too much trouble as you will have completed enough runs to get this by the end. - Changing your weapons is a core part of the game. They only have a limited durability and will break after extended use, forcing the player to find new ones which keeps things fresh. I can see some players might find this to be annoying. On an attack where a weapon would break however, the attack will deal double damage which I find surprisingly satisfying. - Certain items bounce around to an annoying degree, e.g. if you open a crate and a jobwich (healing item) pops out, you usually have to spend time chasing after it as it bounces around the room. - Particular room/enemy combinations can be quite difficult to deal with initially, e.g. fast/AoE monsters in a small room. This becomes easier to deal with as you get familiar with the game however. - Enemy corpses sometimes wig out and fly around the room.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a satirical dungeon crawler that takes you on a journey through the dark and twisted world of failed tech startups. With its unique concept, sharp humour and engaging gameplay, this game is sure to keep you entertained. But be warned, the procedurally generated dungeons, rogue-lite elements, and button-mashing combat might not be for everyone. The game's concept of using failed tech startups as dungeons is both original and thought-provoking. Players take on the role of an unpaid intern, Jackie Fiasco, who must explore these procedurally generated dungeons to defeat the monsters that have taken over. The game is set in a dystopian version of Seattle, where the startup culture has gone too far and has resulted in the creation of monstrous dungeons. You will encounter a variety of comedic characters and situations throughout the game, and the humour is often self-referential and satirical. The game pokes fun at the tech industry in an entertaining and thought-provoking way. It's like the developers have been reading my twitter feed.The art style is like playing in a cartoon world filled with vibrant colours and unique design elements. You'll feel like you're in a dream, a very weird dream. The game's dungeons are procedurally generated, meaning each playthrough is different, like a choose your own adventure book but with more monsters and fewer illustrations.The gameplay of Going Under is based on a combination of action and RPG elements. Players can use a variety of weapons and abilities to fight monsters, and they can also collect money and other items that can be used to upgrade their character. The game also includes a rogue-lite element, where players will have to restart the game after death, but some progress will be carried over, which provides a lot of replayability and encourages players to explore and experiment with different playstyles. It's like a real-life unpaid internship, but with less coffee runs and more monsters. And don't worry, you'll respawn and be able to keep some items and abilities, just like in real life.In conclusion, Going Under is an excellent game that is sure to provide hours of entertainment for players of all ages. The game's unique concept, humorous writing, and colourful art style make it stand out from other dungeon-crawler games. The game's procedural generation, rogue-lite elements, and replayability make it a game that is worth playing multiple times. Overall, Going Under is a game that I recommend, especially towards the younger generation. However, this is byfar the least enjoyable rougelike i have played out from Dead Cells, Risk of Rain 1 and 2

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a really fun action-rpg I'd describe as something like 2D Zelda meets Enter The Gungeon, with a dash of Breath of the Wild. It benefits from a really fun, simple approach to combat, based on using and discarding breakable weapons throughout procedural dungeons. The weapon breaking system works better here than in BOTW, as the dungeons are full of all kinds of junk and weapons to beat up your enemies with, and the chaos of breaking weapons and scrounging up new ones on the fly adds to the combat. Macrogame progression-- that is, getting stronger over the course of runs-- is handled via  acquiring and mastering skills, and advancing mentorships with the cast. Each mentor has different perks and requires you to complete quests in the various dungeons to level them up. This allows you to tailor your runs to your playstyle.If you enjoy a good action-roguelike, this one is quite lovely.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for June 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 6th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.This is a Dungeon Crawler slash Roguelite with a corporate environment theme.  You play a young intern who is hired to work in the marketing department, but ends up going into the basement to slay monsters, in your Amazon-inspired office.  Going Under had me laughing quite a bit, perhaps that’s because I’ve spent too much time in Corporate America or I recognize what most of these scenes and characters are supposed to be.  I don’t know if this will translate to everyone, but I still got a lot of chuckles out of this game.The gameplay is as solid as the writing.  This is a typical rogue-lite but focuses on a Breath of the Wild style durability system, but in the case of a rogue-lite where you’re constantly moving rooms and locations, that is a pretty solid system, and it keeps players from favoring a specific item.  Each dungeon also has a different selection of tools, so there’s no one strategy to win the game. Pick this up if you like Roguelites, clever writing, or like this art style.  There’s something funny about knocking an enemy out of a car to drive it around yourself, or fighting goons who use moving dollies to smack you around.  Maybe it’s just me, but I couldn’t get enough of this game. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic little roguelike that combines an action RPG with the kleptomania of party balls in Smash Bros, and carries with it some hilariously witty and absolutely  writing about Silicon Valley and Seattle startup culture.The challenge level is set to be challenging but not insanely so, around the level of Hades or Hand of Fate 2, without making it insurmountable due to level- or collection-gated progression. Successful first runs are possible (albeit very difficult), the control scheme is very tight and fluid, enemy attacks are heavily telegraphed, and failure is generally caused by a war of attrition that feels fair instead of from cheap or unexplained mechanics.That said, the game does stumble in a few places (and not just from slipping on spilled coffee in the middle of a run). Items occasionally (but rarely) clip through other objects or the floor, certain text boxes do not line up with their effects in Impostor mode (the more roguelike of roguelike mode), and there are cases where the AI simply cannot deal with certain mechanics and stand there to take a beating. In particular, I was able to stunlock a significant story boss by using a single ability to deal damage while dodge rolling, and their otherwise brilliant AI script could not handle it and stood there doing nothing (please fix this!). Other similar broken interactions between items and abilities exist (albeit very rarely), though they felt appropriately niche and amusing when I exploited or succumbed to them.But frankly, these are forgivable in an otherwise fantastic game from a small development team, and while they're notable, they feel like nitpicks against how much fun I had playing this. As this is their first game, I'm looking forward to seeing what Aggro Crab does next.

_childDocuments_.review: So. After 13 long hours (or what some might call a long work day), I've finally beaten Going Under. Was it worth it?Absolutely.This is a charming and funny game for anyone who enjoys roguelikes. Take on corporate Neo-America as an unpaid intern doing near-slave labor. But, you know, slaying monsters and clearing dungeons instead of endlessly fetching coffee and making copies. If you take the time to pay attention, this game will NOT stop poking fun at the corporate workplace, mindset, lifestyle, and so on. If you've ever worked corporate, you won't stop laughing. And hell, even if you haven't, you'll laugh up a storm! I know I did!The difficulty is just right, which is hard for a roguelike. There's some luck involved, for sure, but once you learn key skills like resource management, effective dodging, battle tactics, and careful skill selection, you'll work your way up to being unstoppable. I personally enjoy the mentor and key skill mechanic, as it allows you to prepare for a dungeon crawl with your own strategy. It also rewards you, even if you don't clear the dungeon on that go. The only time I had an issue with difficulty was in the final boss. Without spoiling it...it's not the best programmed section. I often had to endure weapons falling through the floor, or off the stage at times. And it occasionally doesn't play fair, as it's VERY easy to get combo hit to death if you get unlucky. The combo hit issue is present throughout the game, but it became a lot harder at the final boss. But if you're ever struggling, you can always turn on assist mode. But I never found myself needing to use it, even with the final boss.It's also gorgeous. Poking fun at the corporate artstyle is a great choice, especially since they flavor it to make it interesting. Every dungeon has its own general color theme, too, which helps things feel fresh and alive. I never found myself getting bored on my repeated tries to clear a boss.My only real downside that I have yet to mention is the card mechanic. While you can go out of your way to use a blank card on an enemy to get their business card, which unlocks a profile...there's honestly not much reason to do it outside of completion. I wish it provided some form of bonus, though I understand the game wouldn't want to go overboard.Overall, a fantastic game. Would not complain about seeing a sequel of some form. Even if the place is going under, there's a lot to go back to.

_childDocuments_.review: I figured I'd be a bit more indepth than I usually am with steam reviews because I have a lot to say about the game.So first off, the game is fun and I do enjoy it. The combat is simple but fun if a tad janky at times, the enemies are all easy to understand and have good tells for their attacks, and there's a very simple joy in beating a goblin over the head with a cactus rather than something more practical like a sword. There's four dungeons in total from what I've seen, with three floors and a fourth boss floor for the first three and... I'll get to the fourth dungeon, but it's real bad.Visually the game is very pleasing, with some great character designs for both the main characters and the dungeon inhabitants. There's some amazing visual comedy on display here as well, which more than makes up for the game's lack of any real comedy in its writing.Yeah, I won't sugercoat it; the humor in this game is not great. There's a severe overreliance on memes and forced attempts at being quirky that can get rather annoying due to the game trying extremely hard to be 'relatable'. It's basically "How do you do fellow kids" in video game form. Which sucks because when the game isn't trying to be funny, it manages to have some genuinely heartfelt and meaningful moments. This isn't to say the jokes never land, some of them are well executed, but memes are not punchlines and the game's writing won't age particularly well as a result.Also worth mentioning is that the music is good; special mention goes to the Styxcoin boss theme, it's a bop.Now, about that fourth dungeon. It uh... it's basically just a series of rooms where you fight enemies from across the game rather than a new dungeon with new mechanics and enemies, which would have been infinitely more preferable. Maybe there's a fifth one in the second half.Which... did you really have to take the Ghouls N Ghosts route and make the second half a harder rehash of the first half? Something tells me I'm not gonna enjoy it.The game is still good and fun though and I do reccommend it; I just think it could do with a bit more work in some crucial areas.3.75/5

_childDocuments_.review: A biting satire of workplace culture and a just plain fun and well made game with loads of charm and personality, as well as replayabilty. I'm on my third playthrough between this and the Switch version, and I could see myself putting many more hours into this game, especially with updates coming. You want a good roguelike AND a good story too? This game's got you covered. Just play it, it'll be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick disclaimer: although steam says i only played for 4 hours i actually played for 13,I just don't have internet all the time. Going Under has been one of the biggest gambles ive made buying a game. i first saw this game on twitter and was hooked on the concept as a whole but when i played the demo for the first time i really didnt like the combat, i couldnt get a hang of the controls and i was really unsure if i should buy the game. Fortunately i did end up buying it and this game is absolutely amazing. I think i had to just get used to the combat format but after the first 15 minutes of play i was loving every second after. Going under is a fun rouge like beat em up with a engaging world, story and combat with wonderful music, characters and dialogue. essentially everything is fun and packs a punch.I'm going to be hyper vague and brief about the story because this story and the humour cant be spoiled. essentially you play as an unpaid intern at a company in a future where capitalist endeavour has spiralled out of control causing all sorts of mayhem. if you haven't guessed the game is always taking a jab at current views on all aspects of work and business and it shows it off so well you never feel like its a serious critique even when it definitely is. combat is the main aspect of the game, and it shines all the time. Before when i said i didn't enjoy the demo i think it was because i wasnt expecting the enemies to be so difficult for a demo. Dont get me wrong, each enemy goes down in a few hits but when you first start the game you can feel overwhelmed with the variety of things you can use as weapons (essentially everything), overwhelmed by the fairly smart AI that can stunlock you and surround you with no mercy, overwhelmed at the buffs that are super under explained and overwhelmed by how unprepared you are for the game. it will take a  run or two to understand the mechanics and a few more to really begin mastering each of the three very unique dungeons. After a while youll know which dungeon you like best, which buffs are the best for your play style and how to tackle each enemy with ease.  its a wild ride and i never wanted to get off. the other aspects of the game are just as good, music is smooth, fun and playful and will never be a distraction or forgettable,  just perfect. characters are really fun to interact with and completing their quests are rewarding and achievable. and Aggro Crab as a whole are cool as hell top props for making such a sick game.in the end i would 100% recomend this amazing game no matter what.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, which Going Under intern tripped and fell headlong into the "publish" button only one week removed from Hades? That's almost "Suikoden 2 releasing right before and immediately getting steamrolled by Final Fantasy VIII in North America" levels of unfortunate timing.Although Going Under is not quite the Suikoden 2 to Hades' FFVIII, it sure is a delightful little game. The dungeon crawlin' action starts off rough and -- after you've gotten used to the dodge timing, weapon types, and the various perks and boons -- honestly peaks at a middle-of-the-road "acceptably goofy." However, the writing is extremely sharp and funny right off the bat. Genuinely some of the funniest, silliest (and, on frequent occasion, most incisive) writing I've seen in a video game in a while. Paired with the charm of the world and the (mostly non-punishing, which is a plus to someone like me who sucks at 'legit' roguelikes) one-more-run-based structure, it all adds up to a highly worthwhile package.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like the Dead Rising series, but the brutal difficulty, the constant time pressure on quests, and above all the bleak humour of the zombie apocalypse turned me off.  What I liked most about Dead Rising was the idea that you would be constantly salvaging weapons from your surroundings and using them to defeat the enemies around you.  Even if you prepare yourself with a full inventory, eventually your weapons break or run out of ammo and you need to find more.This game does that, but with the Hades-esque room-by-room progression through a dungeon.  Each run is more bite-size than Hades, which is different (not better or worse).  Getting new skills each run and either maximizing their use or (more frequently with me) being pleasantly surprised when one triggers to my benefit, learning to fight enemies and dodge their attack patterns, figuring out which weapons are good and how each weapon swings or shoots, all feel good.  Well, mostly -- I still have fights where enemies will attack faster than I expect, and suddenly a single room feels impossible to get through without losing half my health because I'm being shot at from three different angles, but those are few and far enough between that they primarily add a sense of danger and spice to runs in general.  There's a feeling of skill, moreover.  Attacks take time and you can't cancel them out with a dodge, particularly attacks with heavy weapons.  You can't just button mash -- you have to read enemy body language and consciously queue up only as many attacks as you think you'll land.  It feels rewarding to get into this flow.I was prepared to dislike, or just tolerate, the writing of this game for two reasons.  First, because a game about Living Under Late Capitalism, even as a satire, strikes me conceptually as depressing rather than funny.  (I am admittedly a sensitive soul.)  Secondly, because I got here through playing the (edited to correct:) Veewo / Team 17 game Neon Abyss, a 2D shooter roguelite, and while I find that game fun to play, the writing is hacky, overly referential, and not really important to the game anyway.  I wasn't sure what Aggro Crab might bring to the table that was different.In that sense, I was pleasantly surprised.  Meeting your co-workers in this game, and getting to know the distinct voice of each, is rewarding.  After each run, much like in Hades but in a less complex way (it's hard to avoid the comparison here), you return to the hubworld (Fizzle Beverages' office) and are given the opportunity to check in with your co-workers and supervisors, as well as add new skills to the pool that will appear in the dungeon.  Each co-worker feels like a well-defined character, even with the cartoony, slightly caricatured tone that Going Under takes: Marv is the archetypal middle manager, smoothing over but not resolving problems.  Tappi the accountant has surprising nuance in her cheerful appearance hiding her inner conflict, and Swomp feels like a very real slice of easy-going minimum-wage nihilism.  Even Jackie, the main character, has a likeable personality (my feeling is that it's tough to make a protagonist feel both heroic and interesting).  My greatest complaint is that, after what feels like too short a time, you run out of conversations to have with anyone in the game.  They become idle-animation models, nothing more -- no more conversations to have.  Then again, when your greatest complaint is "the writing ends after a while," that says something about its quality while it was there.I like the story, which I've just completed, beginning to end.  Good news, though: Once you finish the story, there's another mode to keep you engaged in achieving more without just repeating things you've already done!  (The developers compare this to Hades' escalating scale of difficulty through the Heat system.  Look, it's an influential game.)  I like the gameplay quite a bit, so I appreciate there being more to discover as opposed to just 100%-ing the list of skills, business cards, and so on.If you like roguelites, chaotic but controllable combat, the joy of discovering something new and often silly in the next room, and like your games colourful and vibrant, Going Under should do it for you.  (And if you aren't sure, well, there's a demo!)

_childDocuments_.review: I have something to tell you all that is very important. A game that isn't turn-based is NOT a roguelike. A roguelike is a game that PLAYS LIKE ROGUE. If it has Rogue-inspired elements, like permadeaths, randomized dungeons, etc, but doesn't play like Rogue, then it is a roguelite (note the 't'). This distinction is important. Please do not ignore it....Also, yeah, the game's pretty neat.

_childDocuments_.review: Very conditional recommendation from me, I wish there was a "mixed" option for reviews. I like the presentation of Going Under, and believe it is the best aspect of the game. The art style, writing, and music are all truly excellent. However, the more you play it, the more frustrating it becomes. It's already a pretty difficult game with weapon durability (which I loathe), an extremely short hit invulnerability time (you absolutely will get locked somewhere and get hit multiple times, the base dodge roll is also really bad), and a pitifully low starting HP pool. But the worst part is the endgame, where you have nothing left to unlock, are forced to replay harder versions of the same dungeons, and then playing the game feels like a chore instead of fun. Some people will be able to look past this, and see the greatness of the game, but I do think the designers could have done certain aspects better. Here's hoping their next game, "Another Crab's Treasure," will use the lessons they learned from this.7/10, it's (mostly) good.

_childDocuments_.review: Funny, well-written characters and a cartoony atmosphere with unique weapons and game mechanics have very quickly made this one of my favorite roguelike games. Going Under is definitely much more welcoming to players who haven't experienced roguelike gameplay, too. Although a lot of the items aren't fully explained (or explained at all), the combat gives you plenty of room and time to experiment and figure things out. Playing this game doesn't feel like a grind, and it doesn't feel defeating when you fail to beat a dungeon. The story progresses regardless of your success and implements your experience into the dialogue, making it feel like every defeat is understandable and somewhat expected. There are so many little things that have made me chuckle or smile in this game, and without a doubt I've only scratched the surface. The dialogue is often hilarious and the concepts they poke fun at are super relatable to anyone who's been in a low-level job. Overall a great game with a great atmosphere and I'm excited to work my way through the other start-ups!

_childDocuments_.review: Use your sick days,  is a great 3D rogue-lite and satire of contemporary work culture that’ll keep you locked-in for hours at a time. You play as Jackie, an unpaid intern who’s told to go into the literal depths of failed start-ups to kill monsters (employees) and claim their magical business items.There are three separate dungeons to attempt, each with their own themes, enemies, and boss encounters. Like any rogue-like, each run will have you encounter different randomly-generated floors—of which there are 3, plus a boss floor, for any dungeon—helping to keep each run fresh.The combat in  is simple on its surface, but allows for a fair bit of fun when you start layering on skills you obtain and different weapons you pick up on a run. Almost every object in the game can be picked up by the player, and this isn’t limited to conventional weapons. You can pick up pencils, reams of paper, staplers (which you can use as staple ), as well as swords, bones, maces, pickaxes, and lots more. Each object falls into one of a few weapon types. Longer weapons, like brooms and spears, have a long narrow reach, pencils and other similarly shaped weapons stab short and fast like daggers, and larger weapons like the mace or dolley can dish out heavy, slower swings.You can also  anything you pick up, and you better believe each of these categories have different throw mechanics too.Now, it might conjure up uncomfortable memories of , but all of these weapons can break, and that’s a good thing. Whereas ’s weapon-breaking paired poorly with long treks with the wilderness and a persistent inventory, ’s weapon-breaking feels so right. Weapons in this game break , so you’ll have to be constantly picking up new ones littered throughout the level, changing up how you approach any given encounter. They of course break all of the time while you’re fighting, so get ready for a lot of frantically looking for something to wack the dolley-wielding goblin before they wack you.Death will force you to reattempt the dungeon you were in from the beginning, and it’s in this hub world that you’ll be experiencing much of the story, which I enjoyed a great deal. It takes constant jabs at capitalistic work culture, which is funny and kind of sad at the same time. Each character has unique noises to accompany their dialogue, a la  or , and simple but expressive 2D drawings to go with it. In fact, the whole visual style of the game is minimalist, an obvious parallel to many corporate logos and branding. The player character Jackie is basically just some sausage limbs attached to some circles. It’s appropriate thematically and a joy to look at.I’m a huge fan of the soundtrack, with the 2nd Joblin theme and the Joblin Boss theme being my favorites. They’re upbeat and catchy, and I find myself bobbing my head a bit to the beat while I’m in that dungeon.A small thing I take issue with is the inability to rebind your controller inputs. I would’ve liked to switch the button I had dodge on, but it wasn’t too hard to get over, only taking a short readjustment period every time I booted the game up.Aggro Crab has done an excellent job with their debut game. It’s wonderfully made, and I can’t wait to see what’s next. The only big mistake they made was releasing it a little over a week after , the gold-standard for rogue-likes.I highly recommend it, especially if you’re a fan of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of my favourite games of all time.I've explored some rouge-likes before, and Going Under has a fresh take on it by surrounding the game in a pretty immersive narrative about the struggles of start-up culture. The 3ish different dungeons, the characters, the dialog, and the story made me wanna continue every time.The game is designed to be a bit hard, you go through a couple of randomly generated dungeons until you reach the boss floor. You pick up almost anything you see lying around and hack and slash monsters until they break. The way having weapons is designed makes your gameplay different, dynamic, and fluid. Your item management is what's engaging, not necessarily what weapon combos you have.The more strategical part of the game is having skills. You can pick up skills twice every floor: one in a shop and a choice between two in a room. This allows for some zany strategy that scales well as you go later on in the game. The RNG of skills is my biggest gripe however, since some skills just kind of suck loool.When I finished the game, it was really fulfilling, I was able to see how the characters you fell in love with wrap up their story of being in a crappy start-up. I felt like the time I invested really paid off. And the dialog you have with your enemies was really good commentary on the culture too haha. After the Work From Home update came,  that's where I really grinded. With the game play I mentioned before, you can really test your micromanagement of items and your character while strategizing what skills you choose or not choose.tl;dr Pros- fun rouge-like with a fulfilling narrative- micromanagment of weapons usage and skill strategies is very engaging- funny, witty, colourful world and characters- post-story grind of Imposter mode if that's more your thingCons- there are some bugs that i had to restart the game but since it's a rouge-like it wasnt the worst thing to happen- a little too rng when you get meh vs really good skills

_childDocuments_.review: I have finally finished the main game (haven't beaten Impostor mode, nor have I finished the Rolodex. But I'm close!), so I feel comfortable doing a thorough review.Pros:+ Great story and writing, enjoyable characters, and very entertaining jokes.+ A pitch-perfect satire of startup culture, mega corporations, and the hell of being an intern.+ Very wide assortment of weapons, enemies, skills, and tasks to achieve.+ Terrific soundtrack!+ Great initial gameplay loop---I really felt hooked on it after only a couple dungeon runs.Cons:- Only 3 main dungeons, so you'll be seeing a lot of the same enemies and weapons, despite there being a good variety to begin with. Without spoiling, there is a point in the game where you return to the dungeons to find some stronger, different enemies, but for the most part they're variations on ones you've seen before.- The combat system is pretty basic---everything has good weight and animation, but you really see a variety of 4 weapon types.- Sometimes hit detection feels iffy, especially during chaotic moments onscreen.- Generally, did not use certain mentors because they didn't seem to provide a good enough bonus.- To the above point, I think the game encourages adopting your own playstyle and sticking to it, to its detriment. I would experiment sometimes with different mentor/skill combos, but I never found them to be as effective as what I usually did.Conclusion:This game is worth playing for the story and writing alone, but it also boasts a fleshed out (and challenging!) roguelike system with very addictive dungeon crawling loops. Though it may get a bit repetitive, especially as enemies are concerned, I spent a good 23 hours trying to get as many skills, mentors, and business cards as I can---and I intend to keep going after this! I'm excited to check out Aggro Crab's next game and I look forward to seeing what they do in the future!!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a wonderful little dungeon crawling hack n' slash. The core gameplay loop has you going through 4 levels of a dungeon on a single life, with randomized room layouts, enemies, weapons, and powerups. The combat is a lot floatier than your third person action game fair, but actually is very satisfying with charge attacks and an invincible dodge roll. Adapting to the random weapons you're provided, or even pick up mid combat, makes everything have a chaotic energy that's supremely enjoyable. But the star of the show is the story and aesthetics here. The setting of failed startups as dungeons is very amusing, and the social commentary is light enough to not be preachy while still getting its point across. I found most of the characters funny and endearing as well. Definitely pick this one up!
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: If you love roguelites then Going Under is a must. It is amazing in every way: great music and art style, endearing characters, and fun gameplay. I greatly appreciate the assistance options available as well. You can adjust the game in different ways to match your experience and/or abilities. My only issue would be the sudden increase in difficulty after a certain story event, but it wasn’t too daunting as to be annoying.Going Under is incredible and wonderful, but it’s unfortunately overshadowed by Supergiant's Hades. Hades deserves praise of course, but so does Going Under. Perhaps it’s just unfortunate timing. This is Aggro Crab’s first game and it’s a banger! So I’m excited to see what they have in store, both in game updates/additions and their future games. Devs, you have all my love and support, keep up the good work!

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked rather fun at first, but upon actually playing it, it quickly becomes clear that it is not designed AT ALL for any degree of difficulty. Enemy attack wind ups are often comically short, the dodge is unreliable, and you are constantly breaking the only good weapons you can find.Rather or not you can clear a dungeon often relies on getting great rng on the first floor or two of the run, which is quite rare seeing as a large quantity of the available perks you are offered are complete and utter garbage and occasionally lack helpful descriptions.Many of the perks you can unlock between runs from the shop are said complete and utter garbage, but you *have* to clear out the shop for the next set of items to appear, so you're encouraged to bite the bullet and buy junk you never want to see in your run or be stuck with an incredibly small pool (which arguably makes the game easier, seeing as you could get the run-saving lifesteal perk more often.)It was alright in the first half, became unbearable in the second half when they tried to make the game difficult.I'm a bit late on this review, having last played the game months ago, but the game hasn't received any balance changes or combat polish since, so I'd say it still stands.I could write on and on about my negative experience with the game, but others have already done that quite well, I just wanted to write a big note about the between-run shop because no other review has.

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't laughed this much playing a video game in awhile. My career is in programming and tech so this game was exactly my cup of tea in satire and jokes. Also I always love me a good roguelike. Unlike most roguelikes, this one isn't as frustratingly challenging and I got the true ending in 12 hours. Some people might dislike the short runtime, but I thought it was nice to play a roguelike that didn't require me to play a super perfect run just for the chance to get one shot by a random enemy. However, there is a mode that you can unlock that will provide you with that challenge if you wish. Overall, I loved the characters and all the fun jokes in the descriptions and the dialogue. _childDocuments_.review: The characters and story here are really fantastic and charming, even while dealing with the hell of "innovative" startup culture. The gameplay has a great arcade-type feel, which is a bit different from other very precise rougelites. It's super satisfying destroying enemies with their own office supplies. I haven't found too many areas challenging and failed runs aren't much of a setback; it's more about making lots of stuff go smash.Also, if you've ever worked at a place like this the game is extremely cathartic. It's like it was made from my subconscious rage during every meeting. While the game is great fun on it's own it really is a solid artistic critique of Silicon Valley stupidity and its accompanying unfair treatment of workers.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS IS A MUST-PLAY FOR PLAYERS THAT HAVE STARTUP OR TECH COMPANY EXPERIENCES.As a rogue-lite, this game is neat, but as a tech-startup parody, it is absolutely fantastic! The jokes are well-written and the reference are on-point. You will see everything that is right and wrong about tech company culture in this game:☑ You will see companies/products such as Amazon, Soylent, Uber, Tinder, Bitcoin, etc.☑ You will see cultural comments on corporate sexual harassment, overtime yet underpaid workers, AI and personal privacy breach, etc. ☑ You will see familiar startup/tech concepts in item, skills, dialogue such as hustling, vesting, disruptive, low-hanging fruit, SaaS, "mOVe FaSt anD bReaK tHiNgS", exit-strategy, etc. The whole game is written using that tech-startup lingo.☑ You will literally see yourself, your colleague, your boss in this game.6/10 as a rogue-lite, 10/10 as a tech-start up parody. This video game equivalence to the TV show Silicone Valley will be well worth your time if you can recognize its myriad references and jokes.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite roguelites, easily. Going Under has extremely creative design, both artistically and game-wise. The soundtrack has plenty of earworms, and it all keeps you coming back for more, which fortunately the game offers plenty of. I'm just about finished with the game at 27 hours as a slower player (there's plenty of challenge to be found here), but there's still a lot more to do that will surely keep me playing even after completion. Any fan of roguelites and soulslike action will see much to enjoy here, especially so if you appreciate the pop-culture humor littered all over the place.
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under was quite a refreshing experience for me. It is an interesting twist to the rogue-like genre with tons of personality and charm.First off, let's start with the obvious: the artsyle is amazing. I love how they used a 'graphic design' approach to everything (UIs, companies' logos and visual identity, character design...), and then made it 3D, achieving a high degree of designery flavour that gives the game a lot of charm. The tech company vibes are on point and definitely give Going Under a distinctive flavour among other recent indie game releases. The music and sound design also fit that friendly-looking corporate theme completing the startup-esque experience quite accurately.As for how the game deals with its story and message, you should not expect a deep narrative with lots of social commentary or lore. Going Under does throw in some criticism and satire to the modern entrepreneur environment, but it is done in a humorous, lightweight manner. It does throw a punch here and there with some dialogue lines from time to time, but it always tries to do it in a not-so-serious way.Gameplay-wise I must say I had a ton of fun playing through it, and I'm sure I will keep playing a bit more. The controls are buttery smooth, the combat is fluid and very straight-forward (though rather deep if you take your time to learn all of its potential) and the Tasks give you constant new challenges and twists to how you approach the dungeons helping them stay fresh for quite a decent amount of time. And speaking of tasks, you should definitely take your time pursuing them in the first half of the game, otherwise the second half will become a very steep difficulty spike for you. It has an interesting approach to managing dungeons, progression and content by mixing everything up and adding in some new things, but if you are still in a very early state for your character and power-ups you will suffer a lot. Fortunately Going Under comes with some very cool accessibility options for you to tweak in case you just want to have simple fun at some point.I just hope they keep adding content via DLCs in the future, because that could increase the game's playtime quite a lot. They already have all the ingredients in place, so I'll be keeping an eye on future developer's updates.Totally recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: It is rare to find a piece of satire about the modern world that manages to be both honest and heartwarming, and Going Under hits those notes perfectly. It is a game that wants to talk about the dangers of corporate congolmeration and the silliness of startup culture, but also has genuine empathy for those who try to work with and around it. The writing is witty and charming, the art style is a delight, and the visual puns are off the CHAIN.Not only that, but the gameplay itself is cool as heck. The combination of "almost everything is equippable" and "everything equippable is yeetable" means that you end up interacting with the zany dungeons a lot more manually and making the flow of combat unique and intersting. Also this is the only game I've found that produces the sensation of running about in a panic hurling office supplies and coffe mugs at goblins.TL:DR Charming, funny, timely satire with engaging dungeoncrawlery. _childDocuments_.review: Ok, so i really dig the art style here.Game has meaningful progression systems both during runs and between runs.You can unlock more skills, you can select one to bring with you to the dungeon if you used it enough.Also these can alter you gameplay style quite a bit, it's not just mindless stat boosts or whatever.BUT, and that's a big but, game feels sooo randomized at times and not in a good way.Like it's supposed to be tough, and most of the times it is, but i frequently encounter moments when it is like too tough or too easy due to random things just happening and not due to my choices or errors.For example, i had a couple of tries at Marv after you clear first three dungeons and he yeeted my ass all the way back to Fizzle just because at the point when i got to him i had like 0.5-2 hearts left. And then on the 3rd try RNG god decided that it will just give me all the most comfortable and hard-hitting weapons, all the best skills, spawn easiest enemies almost exclusively, and i also happened to gather enough money to enter the final fight with like 5+ hearts.On the other hand, after the "Going Under" event, game is consistenly whooping my ass by spawning 2 or sometimes 3 of these armored trolls that tend to spin 75% of the fight, and NOT spawning enough good (long reach, fast attacks) weapons or skills to deal with them.So yeah, balance is definitely a bit of an issue here. _childDocuments_.review: A neon drenched sugar coated cartoon comedy rogue like with a heart of rainbow.According to the store page tags, this is an action roguelike dungeon crawler beat 'em up.  I'd say that's a fairly accurate description.  We play heroic intern Jackie Fiasco, and it is her job to descend into the subterranean levels deep beneath her new office to confront and defeat the nasties that dwell there.  This involves travelling into "dungeons" beating up lots of crazy characters, and slowly unlocking new perks and skills which can then be utilised in subsequent runs.The story is filled with humour, existentialism and some socio-political commentary.  It is a pastiche of our crazy consumerist times, told through the eyes of a downtrodden and mildly jaded young woman, just starting out on her career path.  A protagonist that most of us will be able to identify and sympathise with.  We've all had those days where we feel like work is hell, and that we are just little cogs working for the giant corporate machine; selling our souls for a pittance.  What better catharsis than smacking up some jerk manager in a garish dungeon?!A hyper stylised, brightly coloured aesthetic makes this eye catching and fun to look at.  The screen literally fizzes and pops, and there is never a dull lull.  The character designs for both the protagonists and the antagonists are quirky, but cohesive and really help to build a world that makes contextual sense.  Level design is clever and succinct.  You can tell everything you need to know about a dungeon within a couple of rooms.  The overall art direction is absolutely outstanding.  Company logos are clever, the co workers are diverse, levels are varied, even the menus and title screen are all designed so that any individual element will be instantly recognisable as belonging to the game.  I'm sure it's a kind of irony that there is such perfect brand synergy on display here.The sound design is equally good.  Combat sounds are just perfect.  Enemies signpost attacks with vocal cues.  Things explode nicely and impacts are sufficiently weighty.  Each character has a specific sound when they speak (no needless full vocal tracks here) and it's amazing how such simple effects can really capture the essence of a character.  Special mention must go to King Felix's original soundtrack.  The music is a blend of styles, but there's an overall vapourwave, electro chill vibe that I really enjoy.  It's also the first instance I ever remember of a soundtrack making me laugh.  There is one specific track which plays in the Winkydink (think Tinder for demons) offices which is just so raunchy as to be hilarious.  Standing ovation for that alone.Gameplay follows the standard format for these games.  Go to dungeon.  Defeat many enemies over a number of floors.  Gain skills from combat and from shops.  Face off against boss.  Defeat boss and get McGuffin.  Return to hub world.  Purchase more skills with loot from dungeons.  Next time you visit dungeon, these new skills will appear at random.  It's a tried and tested format, but the combat is pretty tight for such a goofy looking game.  And don't be fooled by the cartoony looks, this game is challenging.  My first run didn't last very long.  Still, as you unlock more skills, you begin to stand a slightly better chance.  Once a skill has been used enough times, it becomes endorsed and can be activated before a run.  However, only one endorsed skill can be activated prior to a run.  More will be available on the run, but they are random.  It is rare that you will feel overpowered.Another aspect is that each of your co-workers will set you tasks to fulfil on dungeon runs.  Kill so many of enemy x, get object y, discover thing z etc.  Complete enough of these tasks and your colleagues will become your mentors.  Selecting a mentor unlocks permanent perks such as a packed lunch, or better items in the shops.Boss battles are fun and again have great design.  They can be pretty tense and especially the last few battles are particularly tough.  I think I finished with one tiny sliver of health left, but boy did that victory feel well deserved.  My victory was Jackie's victory and vice versa.  Art imitates life on this one.If you do pick it up, definitely try to complete it.  I played for nearly 22 hours, but had I played in a couple of longer haul sessions, it may not have lasted as long.  As is often the case in this style of game, the longer you play, the more you enter into the flow state.  Time away from the game will result in a steep fresh challenge on return.  This is no bad thing.  It never feels unfair, and your skilled play is justly rewarded.What a delightful time I had with this one.  Sure the beats are all pretty familiar, but it's just packaged so well that it is much stronger than the sum of it's parts.  I highly recommend to fans of the genre, and to those who like a little poignant humour that pokes fun at the society we Western devils have come to rely on.Fizzy.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a parody game throwing shade on the entire Silicon Valley startup culture where you, as a brand new (unpaid) intern, are assigned to smash your way through remnants of other failed startups, defeat the ghosts of workers past, dismiss the zombie CEO (i.e. beat him up) and acquire their secret sauce (read: intellectual property) so your current employer, Fizzle (a nutritional/sports drink company) can use it. If that sounds too complicated... it's a 2.5D smash-em-up where you fight various enemies on screen, clear each room, and keep clearing levels until you defeat the end boss... I mean zombie CEO. The graphics are low-poly and stylized the fighting physics are good, some tactics are called for, and add some extra between mission interaction (with your co-workers) with the same sense of parody and you have a parody game. While you can fight with your fists alone, you really should pick up weapons ASAP, as well as pick up any object in the room and even throw them as improvised weapons, from computer keyboard to ban-hammer, from mugs and office crossbow, there are plenty of weapons available. Even the giant red stapler.  You can sometimes take on bonus jobs, which gives you a special reward box. Beating the end boss also gains you a reward box. As you wander through the "dungeon", you will find occasional cafes (where you can buy items, skills, or heal, and you only have X number of hearts). You can also come across storage rooms where you can pick one of two skills to improve your resume. But the obvious objective is to beat your way down to the boss, and beat him. That will trigger an evaluation (which also triggers if you fell during your quest). Between forays into the dungeon, you talk to your coworkers, who may give you extra requests while in the dungeon, which if you complete, unlocks him or her as your "mentor" with bonuses. Using the skills will lead to an endorsement, which levels up the skill as well. You can also install some apps which enables finding more bonus items The game definitely is not easy, so much so you can turn on "Assist" mode to make the game easier by giving you advantages, as well a penalize your enemies. And the game *is* hard. So if you just want to enjoy the humor feel free to turn on the Assist (or should it be "intern assistance program"?)The opponents are not that hard, but the bosses can be challenging. Fortunately, their attacks are well telegraphed. So if you just pay attention and dodge in time they are quite survivable. All in all, if you understand startup culture and the humor here, the beat-em-up is just a bonus.

_childDocuments_.review: Executed with spirit but sadly not with an equal amount of competence.Going Under is one of the best-written games I've played in a while, it's extremely charming on all layers, from enemy designs to dialogue to music, and you'll very quickly *want* to like it unless you're some sort of heartless ghoul.This is why it's a sad fact that the actual game under the charming exterior just isn't good enough to consistently like. The issues are a combination of minor things that pile on to make the tougher end-game areas unfun, but they're two-fold:Firstly, poor information. A lot of power-ups just don't concisely explain what they do when picked up and used. If there's someone who can figure out the effects of every can of Fizzle and every App without visiting a wiki, I'll eat my own shoes. Hell, even some of the perks are kind of vague about their effects. I also still have no idea how the dating challenges work.Secondly, the visuals that give the game a lot of charm are kind of poorly served by the gameplay purposes they're put to. The big blocky designs don't work well with cramped arenas and tons of effects(both active and graphical) that make it hard to tell exactly what's going on half the time. For the kind of gameplay intended, either a simpler style with less flair or larger arenas with more space for the chosen style would've done a lot to make it more easy to parse at a glance.Lastly, poor random generation. About half the game's perks, weapons and mentor effects are either useless or clearly very vastly outclassed by others, so you are very much at the mercy of whether the game designs to spawn a room composed of 90% trap tiles(walls AND floor) and a dozen armored enemies which you have to defeat with a folding chair, or a room containing several high-powered weapons, no traps and a single enemy.In short, I really like what Aggro Crab does in terms of writing and presentation, but unless they take some serious lessons in *gameplay* design, I'll pass on their future games unless they're dating sims or turn-based.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game more. It has a fun style to it, and the dialogue is witty without being over-the top. I like the setting, and when I found a succulent plant I could pick up labelled 'Potted Succ' I felt I was guaranteed to have at least a slightly good time.The actual act of playing this game, however, is very obtuse, and the controls feel weirdly clunky in a way I can't quite articulate. Certainly the 'pick up weapons that break after a while' is a hit or miss gimmick, and it fell on the 'miss' side for me... every time I found a cool weapon I wanted to use, it was gone within a room or two, leaving me feeling empty-handed and helpless. Even the act of hitting enemies felt unsatisfying, like they weren't responding to my hits at all, and the dash has minimal i-frames with a lengthy recovery period. I wish I had more good things to say about this game, but the third time I came back to it I got thrown into a giant unskippable chunk of dialogue. Then I was reminded that I've been getting meta currency the game still hasn't told me how to spend. Every time I die, I think to myself "yeah, I guess, but I'm not really sure what I could have done differently". It just doesn't feel satisfying to control or play. Possibly there is a really great game underneath here, but all the style and personality in the world can't make up for bad gamefeel. In this day and age I find it is sometimes the case that giant parts of a game will change wholesale after enough feedback from consumers, but I wouldn't recommend holding my breath for that. For now, if the idea of clunky core mechanics and the weapon switch gimmick don't sound fun to you, I would recommend avoiding this despite its lovely writing and art.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the satirical sense of humor in this game!  If you love this kind of humor, buy this game and play it!The rogue-lite elements are done well in this game.  I love the how the system of skills and mentors work.  If you pick up a particular skill enough times, you can have it as a "pinned skill" and choose to start with it at the beginning of each new  run.  Mentors provide you support in one form or another to provide you perks such as "free" items at shops.  Each mentor can be leveled up to provide even more perks.Dungeons are randomly spawned with different layouts and items to go in it.  The available dungeons in this game are uniquely themed and distinct.  Most of the items in the dungeon can be used as weapons.  It's fun to be able to use items in an office-themed environment to beat up monsters in this game.I don't think the combat is perfect.  It's fine during the first half of the game when there isn't many monsters spawning but when the second half of the game begins, the difficulty spikes way up.  I feel like this is because of how cluttered some the dungeon rooms can be when they're generated and the amount of monsters that are spawned.  When you're in a small/cluttered space with tons of monsters, it just feels unfair because you can't dodge or get away from all the incoming attacks.I can still recommend this game even with what I've mentioned in the previous paragraph.  The graphics, colors, rogue-lite elements and humor all come together to make an entertaining experience.  Edit: Update with "The Big Run" is out, it's got replay value now.

It took me about 15 hours to complete the main story and the mentor missions. There are some really difficult challenges on the side if you really want to spend a lot longer.Going Under is pleasingly very light on mechanics I'd call grindy. The skill endorsement mechanic is the only thing I could really point to, and that's shallow on purpose (it only takes 2 to 4 runs to finish a skill, and there's limited payoff since you can only have one skill endorsed at a time anyway.)

_childDocuments_.review: To keep it short and sweet:Going Under is a rogue like/lite game that uses a humorous and unexpected environment to put a fresh twist on the genre. It's easy to jump in and out of the game at your leisure for longer or shorter sessions. Difficulty is well scaled between the earlier and later parts of the game.As a whole, I have no trouble recommending this game at even the normal price tag. _childDocuments_.review: Can you believe they turned being an unpaid marketing intern into a fun game? Me neither. There's not much marketing to do here though, the game sells itself!Anyways, the game, yeah - it's a roguelite, you go trough randomized dungeon and beat up enemies and collect random upgrades. This one is action-centric like many other topdown roguelites - apart from bashing enemies you get to dodge their attacks a lot. Another important bit is that you have a limited inventory and everything breaks fast. While there are some "proper" weapons including extremely rare and powerful ones, there's a big focus on using improv weapons like staplers, furniture, and eggplant emojis. Yeah. There's means to power up weapons, extend their longlastingness, etc, but you have to prepare for the fact none of them will last. Also there are bossfights and progression of unlocks, but that's staple roguelite stuff. I think gameplay is fine and fun but better highlight is story and setting - something you would never expect from a roguelite is that it's a satire. Of startup culture. It doesn't say absolutely nothing new, but it's all wrapped in a good comedy and ties with the gameplay which is quite an accomplishment! It is amazing how hard this satire aspect permeates the game - like the game's art style is like a 3D rendition of that art style startups and major companies love, with goofy misshapen people of all sorts, all flat and simple. Except while the particular style is usually considered pretty soulless, there's plenty of heart put in this game's renditions. The sound is on point too.One major criticism I have is that the game's second half after you complete three dungeons and beat a major boss is rather disappointing - you retread the dungeons again, but with a major increase in difficulty and some few additions. Personally at that point, if you struggle or feel bored of retreading (makes sense, it's a roguelite), I recommend going to main menu and cranking Assist Mode to the max because the proper finale after retread is very much worth your time if you appreciated the story and character bits of the game. Nonetheless the part between fourth boss and finale is genuinely the weakest part of the game that feels too hard and adds too little.I dunno who exactly to recommend it to, like exact audience - too much grinding for narrative-centric players and kinda lacking in depth and content for roguelite fans - but I guess it's a really good roguelite for people who find most roguelites too long and unmotivating, while still appreciating the premise?

I had a bug that made some of the content impossible to complete, but seeking out the Discord gave me a solution that fixed the bug.That's one of the game's 2 problems. There's a few bugs, most of them are small and kinda funny. Only one (permanent curses) was large and negative enough to impact the game.The other problem is that without the assist turned up, weapons break too fast. BotW pulled off breaking weapons by giving you huge pockets, ranged weapons, shields, and a way to freeze enemies if you needed a breather. This game gives you 3 weapon slots, plus your pathetic fists as a backup if you can't find a weapon. It's more frustrating than challenging.The game has many positive aspects too. The dialogue is hilarious and very well-written, the characters are likable and interesting, the weapon variety is great, combat is not too simple and not too complex, and the atmosphere of job culture is nailed perfectly. _childDocuments_.review: I saw a Let's Play of this game and was instantly curious. The humor was right up my alley and I liked the art style. Three hours later, and this might be the best $20 I've spent on Steam in a long time! Rouge-Like dungeon crawlers are typically not my style. But the humor was enough to keep me playing. They've managed to capture the look and feel of Corporate America right down to witty satire. Maybe it's because I'm also in Marketing, but this game hit on all the right notes for me.Instead of being frustrated when I died, I immediately went to talk to coworkers and did it all again. Each try felt like a new day at the office. It's quite brilliant how they've managed to capture the theme perfectly in the gameplay and aesthetic. Not only is the gameplay loop addicting, you'll unlock more dungeons as you progress.There's a nice balance of quests and progression in the story to make each death rewarding when you return to the office. Combat is easy to pick up as well and weapons are littered throughout dungeons. A mechanic I hate in Zelda BOTW (weapons breaking) actually works perfectly in this game. With there being so many weapons in a single room, you never feel like you are at a loss when it happens or scrambling to find a new one. This game surprised me a lot. But in the best way possible. _childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a love letter to our soulless, lifeless and contradictory experience of corporate life. It's also a roguelike with great writing, cool art style and a messy combat.If you've ever worked in an office or startup, the setting and characters of Going Under will certainly feel familiar to you. Surprisingly this game has a lot of cool dialogue between various characters, that feel over the top and funny. The game makes fun of so many stereotypes and corporate lingo and there are even scenes where the personality of these characters clash, just like in real life. The artstyle mimics the popular design of many-many startups and creates a cohesive and unique visual identity. It's incredibly well done.The game has multiple dungeons and offers a really active combat experience. Your weapons degrade over time so finding and picking up new ones or improvising something else is essential. This elevates the combat a lot, since I never felt like I found a meta weapon and the game was always pushing me to try new things. There is a wide array of passive abilities you can unlock, most are not that impressive on their own, but once you have a large number of these you can become almost unstoppable. The combat is honestly really fun and chaotic and even if you get hit it's not the end of world, since you can buy back health every once a while. There is a surprisingly large number of weapons and other items you can use, some come with special abilities too. The enemies are varied, but their attack pattern is quite simplistic. You have to look for their telegraph and dodge accordingly or rush them down and stun lock them. This is were the first issue emerges, sometimes enemy telegraphs only last a few frames and are impossible to react to. In late game areas, the game just increases the enemy count, which would be fine, except the environments are quite small and cramped with detail, meaning it's really hard to make out what exactly is happening when you have 2 allies and multiple enemies of various sizes trying to attack you. The player character gets lost in the visual clutter too often.The combat becomes too chaotic and too hard understand, and enemies can hit through each other potentially hitting you multiple times before you can even react to the first hit. I think the devs probably realized this, since one late game section takes place in a much bigger area and crowd control works really well there.Going Under has a lot of content, but just like with every roguelike, at some point it will feel like work, (which is funnily enough the exact thing the game criticizes) and that's the point I lose all my motivation.  In this game that moment arrived quite late, so that's pretty great.I would recommend Going Under not just for its unique combat, but for it's story and general aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot going for it. The story is exceptional, the characters are fun, the roguelike elements stay fresh for a long time, you have lots of customization, lots of different ways to play, great sound design, it's all wonderful.The gameplay is just one step short of amazing though. It also has a lot going for it! The boss designs are interesting and are very interesting. There are a good amount of different enemies across the various biomes you'll run into. But there's an essential clunkiness to the combat that makes things much harder. Your attacks have a pretty hefy windup with most weapons, and while enemies do telegraph their attacks well, the density of enemies in rooms and the long follow-up animations most weapons have, locking you out of dodge-rolling, makes it very easy to take a lot of damage if you don't play very very safe.Now I've played through the game and beaten it, but I will say that this essential clunkyness did add some frustration. It's a game that makes you want to wade into combat and skillfully weave through enemies, like say, Hades, which it takes a lot of good notes from in style, but because of how unwieldly it is to fight, you really can't do that. Your dodge roll is too short and long-cooldown, while getting stopped by enemies, and your attacks are far too slow.Still, overall, a very fun game. Would recommend if you're a fan of other top-down action roguelike (or roguelite, if you insist), type games.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★Going Under is a game that sold me on its charm and kept me with its depth and its story. A surprisingly short experience with comparable replay value to games other games in its same genre. Going Under takes a similar approach to Hades, where your reward for playing the game isn’t strictly getting more powerful each run but instead leans heavily into developing relationships with your coworkers and moving forward a very engaging and poignant story. I found myself shocked with how impactful the contents of this game were with how short the narrative experience was. Going Under also exists in an incredibly unique design space, its visuals are unique and eye catching, but its design problem “what if there was a dungeon crawler where you play as an intern, set in the body of failed tech start ups, set dressed in a corporate Alegria art style” is something that I have never seen before, nor knew I wanted. Going Under’s Alegria charm doesn’t just stop at its premise though, between the “smart” weapons that track enemies, the incredibly creative puns/concepts behind each of its dungeons, having your coworkers “mentor” you to give you passives on each run, and the hilarious variety in its enemy/weapon/“app” this game was in all ways surprising and fresh. I find the rogue-like genre space to be completely over saturated with fantasy/sci-fi design, and this game was a refreshingly ballsy move away from it.Going Under is a must have experience from an upcoming studio that took an incredibly new and fresh take on a genre that has become over saturated with sameness.
