_childDocuments_.review: Despite the protestations of far too many game studios recently trying to deny this, it turns out that video games can be really good at political and social commentary. What makes this even more fascinating is that there doesn’t even seem to be a limit to the ways that this can be achieved; we can have gritty shooters like Spec Ops: The Line expressing the horrors of war, and that can rub shoulders with something like Flower; a beautiful exploration game that explores the idea of environmentalism. Yet, despite knowing this, Going Under’s mix of styles still came as somewhat as a surprise to me - a comedic roguelike that both comments on and parodies the sheer absurdities surrounding internships and the start-up world. Um, ok? It’s probably best to take a step back at this point and explain a little more of what’s going on here; You play as a marketing intern in the hottest new drinks company, Fizzle. Yet, like many internships in the real world, it soon transpires that you won’t be doing much of what’s listed in the job description. Instead, you’re tasked with killing the monsters crawling up from the dungeons of the failed start ups that have preceded you – such as a cryptocurreny company full of (literal) skeleton miners. All the while you also have to assist your co-workers, including the ambitious yet clueless company owner, a boss who forces everyone around him to work harder while doing very little themselves, and many other stereotypes anyone who has ever found themselves in a similar job situation will immediately recognise.  Even with explanation I admit it’s a strange concept, and you may be thinking at this point that Going Under is being rather on the nose with its criticism about such industries. And… Well, you’d be right. But even though it may be trying to make a point, it does it in such a light hearted and jovial way it’s nigh on impossible not to be charmed by it all. There are just so many superb little jokes or jabs dotted throughout the experience - for instance, buy things you can’t afford, and your debt takes the form of a literal ball and chain, slowing you down. In another example, leaving your controls alone sees the main character toss everything aside and start lazing around on their phone in a matter of seconds. There’s even a brilliant nod to a classic YouTube advertisement many will remember, where it’s not the Lamborghini in the garage the owner is proud of, it’s his vast wealth of knaaawwwledge on the bookshelves behind him. The constant good-natured teasing and sly observations are honestly perhaps the greatest part of the game, and they’re certainly things that never failed to bring a smile to my face.  All the charm in the world, however, means nothing unless there’s a decent dose of gameplay backing things up. In Going Under this takes the form of running through randomly generated dungeons, grabbing whatever lies around the place to pulverise the monsters that are determined to make your career a short one. These weapons range from the expected, such as swords and maces, to the odd, like body pillows and potted plants. Couple this up with a healthy selection of skills from the ever-growing unlock pool, a large chunk of dodging and weaving through attacks, and the obligatory challenging boss fight - all pretty much staples of the genre. It’s entertaining stuff, for the most part – there's a certain glee to be taken from trashing up each room, tossing things in frenzy at your foes. Yet while the core appeal never truly falters, sadly there’s a ton of little issues all over the place which cause the overall gameplay mechanics to truly stumble in their paces.For example; you have the ability to change your attacks and lock on to foes, but both of these slow you down a considerable amount. As it turns out, this is a big no-no in a world where enemy attacks are rapid and constant, and movement is a key skill in not being overwhelmed. Therefore you soon realise your effective repertoire when it comes to seeking success is essentially whittled down to running and slashing. Skills suffer a similar fate – some are effective in every situation and others have extremely limited implementation, so many will never see much use unless you have no other option but to take them. Even weapons are blighted by the same plight – you’ll soon realise most are garbage or simply too slow to use (without the right skills, at least), so you soon learn to avoid these and as a result endlessly pick up the same stuff. Weapon degradation and destruction does help to mitigate this final point, but there were very few situations where I found myself left with a massive shortage of good gear. And yeah, I get it – there’s always the ability to self-impose challenge upon yourself, and exploration should always be encouraged. It’s just a shame large chunks of what's on offer here don’t really have a practical use beyond that, and instead seem to be sidelined as mere curios. Another problem comes from the game’s erratic difficulty. It never gets truly insane or soul crushing (I completed the story in a little under ten hours, which if anything is short for a roguelike) but it does feel like it jumps all over the place. The first half of the game, for instance, is straightforward once you’re used to the mechanics. Hit the second half, however, and suddenly the challenge level shoots way up, with any sort of success requiring a good deal of focus. These jumps in difficulty even affect individual rooms, where one can have a single lowly minion to easily turn into paste in a wide open area, only for the next to have exceedingly powerful enemies cramped into a small space. There’s also the recently added imposter mode, which I’ve only dabbled in, but seems to require insane amounts of precision to succeed in – and that’s before that mode’s exclusive difficulty modifiers kick in. Experiences may vary - you may struggle and others may storm through – but it never feels like a truly streamlined appearance. Such cracks in the quality extend to the last thing that needs to be touched upon, and that’s the visual style. Glancing at a single screenshot is all you need to spot the game’s unique flair, and it’s certainly used well to create a world that’s extremely fun and engaging to be part of. Two issues come part and parcel with this, though. The first, I admit, is a miniscule one; all the text initially is presented with an odd blurred and distorted effect surrounding it, which to me was so incredibly off-putting it actually made me feel oddly unwell. Thankfully this is only a minor annoyance, as there’s an option in the settings to turn this off - and I highly recommend you do so. The second issue, however, is a far bigger problem. You see, the bright colour palette and sheer plethora of visual effects that start filling the screen when a fight really gets going are good enough to look at in a vacuum, but couple that with combat that often requires your close attention and it often becomes difficult to tell what’s happening. It can only take one major visual distraction to whittle off a major chunk of your health, and for that to happen due to something that feels out of your control is incredibly disheartening. It’s the one thing that let little spikes of anger seep their way into my general enjoyment of the game, and that’s a real shame.Overall, though, Going Under may not like the polish or substance that really makes it stand out as a must play, but by no means does this make it a complete write off. There’s a lot here to enjoy and appreciate, and let’s be honest - any game that lets you smash computer monitors over a zombie’s head must have something going for it. It’s worth playing (although there’s a small part of me that would suggest perhaps waiting for a sale before doing so), and certainly not one that deserves to be thrown on the scrapheap.

_childDocuments_.review: for more reviews like this.I'm very conflicted about this game because I want to love it, I really do. The art style, the music, the whole theme of it. It's all unique and very nicely well done. There's so many little details such as the lofi music mode in your room, the little nods to corporate business structure, and the parodies that each of the 3 dungeons are themed after. The aesthetic of this game if fantastic. They really did nail every aspect of it. Unfortunately the developers failed on the most important part of an action game. THE COMBAT IS A MESS. Your dodges leave you vulnerable and the way the rooms and dungeons are set up, there's explosives, and traps, and hazards filling every room on top of 4-5 enemies and you simply do not have the necessary space or dodging abilities to properly avoid damage. There's also virtually no hit invincibility period so if you get cornered, your run's done. The dungeons are simply not laid out properly for the movement options the game gives you. It's a shame because this game could have been truly fantastic but there's just so many games that have combat systems that work so much better that it's hard to recommend this game over those.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. It's a pretty well done roguelike with very active/hectic combat and a lot of fun upgrades to unlock. The coolest part is definetly that the upgrades change your character's visuals in a similar vein to Binding of Isaac (though a lot less grotesque). The art is neat, the models are cute and the music is good and unique (In my experience, at least). There are some things that pull it down though. 92% of the time everything works perfectly, but the game does not handle unforeseen circumstances well at all (such as: perk-linked companions perma-dying in certain scenarios, allies breaking bosses by attacking mid-cutscene...), which can lead to frustrating moments. Impostor mode also has a tendency to get a bit confused when you buy the same mentor twice in a row. None of these are deal-breakers, but they did dampen the experience whenever they appeared.If I were to score this game, I'd give it a 4/5. It's good fun, and the plot surprised me in good ways. Worth picking up if you want a 3D roguelike with a bit more color than it's peers.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sat here at 1:30 AM forcing myself to stop playing this game and go to bed. It's got its hooks in me, and I can't help but be endlessly amused by the meta-textual significance of that feeling. The game is a satire of the addictive, self-destructive nature of the modern social/media/technology landscape, and it has that woven so deeply within its DNA that the actual visceral experience of playing it evokes the same complex cocktail of emotions brought on by engaging with said landscape.It's obvious in the visual presentation: a clear parody of the minimal, block colour Alegria style that is the current trend in social media graphics. But where those illustrations are flat, uninspired, and often lifeless, Going Under manages to inject the style with vibrancy, personality, and charm. And there's a subtle but profound attention to detail in the design here: for instance, particle effects are depicted as bubbles and sparkles, which fits naturally with the business your character works under. The logo of The Cubicle - the mega-conglomerate to whom your employer is a subsidiary - is innocent enough, but gently suggests an eye, gazing out, watching every move.The game is FULL of this sort of thing, from the most overt jokes (an enemy designed much like Mario's Chain Chomp, simply called "Block Chain"), to the subtler (a sign on the wall of the 'Fizzle' - soft drink/meal replacement company - headquarters: "make your dreams fizzle!"), to the subtler still (commentary on cryptocurrency, the gig economy, online "swipe" dating, the crunch crisis, dude-bro venture capitalists, Tai Lopez in his garage, the list goes on), this is a truly complete, encompassing parody piece. And I love it so much for that.And if it was just that, that would be fantastic. But it's also a weighty, chunky third person action game, that is satisfying in that tactile "feel it in your bones" kind of way. And it's tough too, in a way that makes me ache to explore the game's systems and master it all. It implements a full contingent of tried and tested rogue-like mechanics: perks, active items, weapon cycling, "curses", bosses, shopfronts, meta-run upgrades, etc. And it does all of this solidly, but in many of these iterates dramatically on convention. I love the Breath of the Wild style weapon breaking system; in fact, I think it works better in this game than in that. I think that the small scale, fast paced combat effectively distils that mechanic into its purest form, eliminating its downsides and strengthening its upsides.And, as stated before, the artistic presentation of all of these elements isn't just a "media corporation" sheen. The references, terminology and themes are all up-to-date and relevant, and are not just skin-deep. And I find myself, as with other games that make these kinds of points (check out the game Deep Rock Galactic if you want more like this), amused and somewhat disquieted by how the game's progression systems are a kind of pastiche of real-life "gamified" applications, which I suppose brings it all full circle. It's apparent to me that this is an intentional part of the point here, and I find it disquieting because I can feel myself buying into it. The numbers crawling up, the arbitrary progress points, the artifice of upwards mobility, all of it satisfying the reward centre of my brain, just as it does when real-life corporations use the same tricks. And so I buy into it, just as I and everyone on some level buy into the hyper-capitalist ultra-consumerist world that we live in. And that's a hard lump to swallow completely, but this game draws these kinds of complex, introspective conclusions because it evokes complex and introspective emotions. Even the weapon breaking mechanic can be read as a comment on the consumptive, destructive results of the culture we live in.At the time of writing this, I've only played the game for 3.9 hours. But I do believe this game is something really special. It manages to do what only the greatest games do: use a holistic combination of gameplay, mechanics, feedback, visuals, writing, and tone to achieve ludonarrative cohesion and deliver a reflective commentary on pertinent themes with breadth and depth.If any of that sounds like a good time to you, buy this game now.Thanks for reading

_childDocuments_.review: A charming, delightful, and surprisingly deep game - both in mechanics, and writing.I expected a short, silly adventure - but fell in love with the varied gameplay, inspired design, drool-inducing graphics, and bombastic fights. As a lover of souls-games, I was not anticipating I would be impressed or so fully engaged by simple controls and silly physics - but there is a shocking amount of creativity and skill required to push your way through the game's disparate challenges. Learning the intricacies of the 'elemental' weapons actually felt intriguing and useful - not just a silly gimmick or graphical flourish.As for the theme-ing, never have I seen such a delicate and well executed balance between cynical satire, and sincere comedy. The eye-rolling lambast of modern work is cutting, but never becomes grating or depressing, and characters that appear as flat-jokes will later reveal nuance and charm. The game is (thankfully) light on cutscenes and dialogue, so every line feels well placed and intentional.A masterful work - far more fun than I expected, lasting far longer than I would have thought, and worth far more than what they are charging. Easy reccomend!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I wanted to like more than I did. The art style and writing stuck out to me in footage, and they're honestly the best aspects of Going Under. The characters and environments have a colorful, simplistic look which pairs well with the narrative about the dysfunctional workings of big corporations. Dialogue in the game is consistently funny; interacting with your goofy co-workers makes returning to the main hub a fun break between runs. Unfortunately, Going Under really just doesn't deliver on the roguelike side of things. While combat seems enjoyable at first, it's dragged down by a lot of small issues that really add up. In general, your character's movement is sluggish and clashes with the frantic, crowded scenarios that the game throws you into. It feels like the game wants you to play aggressively, constantly breaking items and maneuvering around enemies, but you often find the most success from playing cautiously. Because health items are shockingly scarce, taking minor instances of damage can be incredibly punishing over the span of a run. The game's difficulty isn't helped by how little room there is for synergy building and resource management. Many items have borderline useless effects that clog your runs with bloat. They may not be very exciting, but having more flat stat buffs would really benefit the game; anything to make you feel like you're actually getting stronger. Without digging too far into balancing, there are far too many moments that make you think "Why was this designed this way? Doesn't this seem like a useless addition? Couldn't this have been fixed with a small numerical change?"Going Under is a perfectly functional game, but it's ultimately more enjoyable to watch than it is to play. I think the developers are capable of making something really great, but their efforts here unfortunately fell short. I believe the most enjoyable way of experiencing this game is turning on the assist options so you can speed through the main story and get the most out of great visual and audio presentation.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★ stars"Going Under" is an unexpected gem that completely took me by surprise. Recommended by a sibling, I dove in without any prior research and emerged with a newfound appreciation for dungeon crawlers and roguelike games. The game breathes new life into the genre, offering a fresh, innovative take that kept me captivated.What sets "Going Under" apart is its exceptional storyline, which masterfully blends humor with a poignant critique of corporate America. Its randomly generated dungeons ensure that each run feels new and challenging, pushing players to their limits while also encouraging them to keep trying. The variety of weapons is a highlight, turning everyday office items into tools of dungeon exploration.The difficulty is well-balanced; challenging enough to be engaging without being frustrating. Additionally, the inclusion of NPC co-workers who provide assistance adds a layer of depth and strategy, making each attempt unique."Going Under" excels in creating tense, edge-of-your-seat gameplay, where success feels rewarding and each run is a roll of the dice with the RNG gods. Whether purchased at full price or found on sale, this game is a must-own for fans of dungeon crawlers and roguelikes alike. _childDocuments_.review: I like Aggro Crab as a company and hate to give this a negative review, but I have to be honest and say that the gameplay in this game just isn't up to the standards set by other roguelikes. It's slow, clumsy, not especially responsive nor even the slightest bit satisfying. There's very little weight to the attacks, weapons break in literal seconds (at least early on) and the fun factor just isn't there. And, while this is more of a personal preference, the character models in-game are EXTREMELY off-putting. They remind me of those creepy little mascots Kroger grocery stores have taken to using, with their tiny, perfectly round heads and featureless, tubular appendages, and I absolutely hate everything about them. What makes all of this so disappointing is that I adore the atmosphere of this game and everything attached to it. I love the character art and design (basically everything about them except their actual models during gameplay), I love the music and the overall art direction with its bright colors and cheeky references, and I love the very idea of battling corporate hoards through the ruins of failed tech start-ups. The story actually seemed like it had potential to keep me interested, at least for a while, and the sound design while not perfect or mind-blowing, was more than good enough for what Aggro Crab was trying to accomplish. It's a wonderful idea overall, but the execution of the gameplay is the most important part, and it's where the game blatantly falls on its face. I plan on keeping an eye on this studio in the future regardless, and while this game may not be for me, I think others will certainly find enough enjoyment in Going Under to keep them coming back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best games so far this decade for this price point. Game currently has some crashing issues and camera flickering bug but those have been announced by the devs as known issues being fixed, once those have been fixed the game is easily a contender for game of the year. Overall extremely well-polished game that has the best balance of difficulty for a single player that keeps you playing even after finishing the game to challenge yourself to get even better. I don't usually bother with single player games for the simple fact of it being a matter of 1 playthrough of ~10 hours (sometimes less or more) and it's repetitive onward, the exception is this game has a much more generous price than it should (imo), while offering every run to be completely different from the other by a fair margin. It's also not a bad game for those who are fans of speedrunning, although rng would be a factor it's still a well balanced game that the differences of good-bad rng will still give you some competent weapons as long as you manage them effectively. _childDocuments_.review: A really fun rouge-like that has a fun art style, fun combat, and some pretty good writing that although can sometimes be a little cringy, is a lot of the times pretty funny and isn't that overbearing with its commentary on the toxic working conditions of tech companies.It's soundtrack is also incredibly good and fits the silly aesthetic of the game.The game has it's flaws with the absence of a warning for a big difficulty spike that occurs after defeating a certain boss, a throwing mechanic that is usually a waste of your time, and a dodge roll that is a little underwhelming. When you do hit the difficulty spike though I feel the game gets way better and becomes a lot more challenging and makes you think more about some skills that I though at first were pretty useless but proved to be very helpful with the ramped difficulty (Example: one skill has a chance to charm the last enemy left in a room, which when enemies are pretty weak in the easier mode they are underwhelming wit their damage output. Once there are a lot more difficult enemies though, you can strategize to kill off the easier enemies first to leave you with a chance of charming a pretty helpful and powerful enemy while also now not having to fight that strong enemy anymore). The difficulty spike also changes the dungeons in so many ways and it made the game a lot more fresh and fun to play!Despite those problems however, I think this game's variety and game loop is very enjoyable and makes it a worthwhile purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: A cute and funny action game where you play an intern at a startup that has to clear out the dungeons of other failed startups underneath her company. Combat plays out room by room like the original Legend of Zelda or Binding of Isaac, and you equip yourself with the office junk and weapons when you can find them. However, the core gameplay loop of going through a dungeon run, getting incremental upgrades of your abilities, and repeating is one that I'm just worn out on. I also found the maps cluttered, with the junk constantly getting the way of movement and making it difficult to maneuver in fights. If you like this Hades-esque genre of games and are not sick of them yet you'll probably like it, but it's not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a cute little roguelike with a great unique style that for some reason hasn't popped off like other roguelikes.Going Under is as standard as standard can be with the roguelike formula. Enter dungeons, find varying items and weapons to defeat increasingly stronger enemies until you reach the boss. Thats all very standard in the genre, but where Going Under differs is in its very unique style. This game looks, plays, and sounds fantastic, with this hipster indie company office vibe you'd find in something like GTA5 as a side mission. You start each time at the office, where you can talk to and accept side objectives from the cast of pretty damn funny characters, aswell as spend currency on unlocking new perks and items to find in your next dive in the one of several dungeons.The combat is essentially a beat'em up with dead rising style weapons, If you see it, its most likely a weapon. Chairs, plants, keyboards, spears, swords, pencils, the list goes on and on. The game actually feels alot like Zelda Breath of the wild with its weapon durability and ragdolling enemies, even the first enemies you fight are goblins. One issue i had however, is the combat isnt the best in general, rolling doesn't give you many I-frames and its very easy to be stun locked on the larger enemy's attacks, and the combat just doesnt have the same feeling of mastering it like Hades or Enter the gungeon do for examples. Its not bad combat, just lacking.Going Under is in desperate need of getting its name out they're, its a solid game with alot of potential, but is very easily overshadowed by larger names like Hades. $20 is very fair, and more content is on the way, buy it now to support the devs or wait for a sale if your hesitant.

_childDocuments_.review: There's only one real nongameplay or story issue i have with the game thus far, when i boot it up and talk to an npc. the game lags for the first conversation.Other then that and the difficulty spikes. the game is fun, for sure.Let's start with the basics. Roguelikes have bad difficulty curves, usually, this one is still not perfect, as there's a few spikes that make sense storywise, but still aren't as fun to deal with inside gameplay. The gameplay is very basic in theory, so it's easy to learn it. But it's difficult in the same way a sport is difficult. The few fundamentals you have to rely on (dodging, weapon management, health management, positioning, hazard/gimmick adaptability) become fleshed out in the best way. Let's just talk about one, and then you can imagine the others.Dodging enemies is a basic thing, but because environments change from room to room, and because you're dismantling the room (cover objects- like tables, hazard objects- like red video game containers), the game becomes less repetition and more decisionmaking. This becomes more complex as you gain abilities that use room props as weapons, cover gets destroyed, enemies with projectiles are introduced, then spawned in groups, bosses generate enemies that are also forcing you to dodge in certain ways.All of these things, they fluidly interact with the basic dodge roll you are given. The few but unique and satisfying upgrades you can find within runs do not BREAK the mechanic or fundamental. They only give the mechanic more wiggle room, and more player choice gets added to the decisionmaking.A roll upgrade may give your rolls a status effect, you can hit enemies and set them on fire with it, making you roll INTO the enemies. The fundamentals of this game all are like this, very basic to understand, very hard to separate, but most importantly, never complex enough to overwhelm the player with rube goldberg number status chains.this is because the writing is supposed to, and is definitely first for why you should play the game.The best way to represent the writing in a roguelike is through respawning and interacting with the story each loop. At least. that's what it seems like recently developers are doing.The approach isn't perfect for a long narrative, or a highly complex game of thrones style plot, but it works for narratives about repeating themes. Like for hades, futility, willpower, meaningless struggle, and how drama and lessons come from failure and success.In Going Under, the tone and comedy tells itself via repetition, how the insanity of tech startup culture becomes more obvious, the more you understand the personalities of people who exist within that culture.The worst boss isn't a bad boss because he's making one decision that hurts employees, it's the mindset that drives everyone up a wall. It's so much more funny to see the consistently horrible decisions, BECAUSE he is telling you about his grind, and his idea guys, and why beating up union workers is cool. The comedy comes from the absurdity being consistency.It's so on the nose, and so brutal, because it uses repetition. Artistically. I LOVE the vision and the tone.The art style, the absurdist, nihilist sarcasm, the killer soundtrack, the writing, the game design is all there.The only issue i have IS the difficulty spikes being so jarring. _childDocuments_.review: Going Under has an interesting opener, as a breakable weapons, dungeon exploring, beat em up. However while the general tone and humour is spot on, the game mechanics themselves lead to disaster as time goes on.For one thing the actual combat, it's fast paced and frenetic, but certain features lead themselves to making the experience feel tilted against you. The dodge action being the worst offender. The dodge is easy to manage while you have open room and can focus on a target, but when clutter starts inevitably building up and more enemies start attacking it ends up being a rather large detriment. It doesn't go past enemies or objects meaning you often end up stuck on terrain and it has an alarming rate of sending you no distance on the side dodge, since it follows the camera, so enemies can quickly get you during the non invulnerable frame. Picking up items automatically during the dodge may seem useful, until you accidentally pick up something on fire, or something about to explode. Lastly you can't cancel attacks with a dodge, so unless you play extremely conservatively it won't be able to be used when you actually need it.Hit stun is also a problem in that with so many enemies you might feel like trying to hit and run would be useful, except enemies enrage after being hit enough times becoming immune and certain enemies never get stunned outside of electric damage. It means when you get swarmed there's basically few outlets to run and this comes up more frequently in the imposter mode, where healing is scarce and you're denied end of act skills and beginning boons. It's also frustrating when hit stun applies to you, especially when knocked down as the mercy invincibility is just short enough to stand you up to get knocked down again.Finally some skill combinations can doom you down the line because of poor implementation, the slow down on dodge seems fun until you realise it just means when you encounter a boss it just stacks all its attacks into an impossible frenzy (Looking at you Hu$tleBone$), larger strength and size also means larger hitbox, and setting things on fire is great until they get up close and personal and set you on fire too.The camera and item pick up distinction also starts getting aggravating as time goes on. The camera has a view of things from a tilted down perspective, but when objects start blocking the view or you're backed into a corner it is incredibly difficult to actually see what's going on. Then because items inevitably break, you might need to grab another, but if there's a lot of items around (and trust me, it gets messy later) then you'll often end up unable to pick up the one you actually need in the heat of battle. Pick up and make do is fine on occasion, but when it comes down to a 50/50 between a plant pot and the weapon I need to kill something I far too often end up with the plant pot because it is just bigger.Finally there's too many run ending bugs, the three most common I keep encountering are as follows:1. Curses don't expire - Can happen randomly during a run and it makes it so much harder than it needs to be. Pretty much dooms an imposter run too. Worst offenders are the debt and first person curses for this.2. Camera spin after leaving first person - This one means you can't see as the camera spins wildly out of control, it's run ending and nauseating to boot.3. Locked in one direction - With the way weapon mechanics work you aren't always going to be guaranteed an item that works well no matter which way you swing it. Also locks dodges down to a 4 way path.There are others but they come up far less frequently.Basically I would sum it up as follows:It's fun for a while, finishing the story is enough to walk away with an ok experience.If you are getting it, get it on sale, and don't feel pressured to do any more than the base experience or you may just end up frustrated with the total package.

_childDocuments_.review: Some games are made with so much heart that it shines into every aspect of its design. This is one such game. If you live in Silicon Valley or any such tech bubble, you owe it to yourself to play this game because the humor is on-point. (Heck, even if you don't, there's a lot of humor one can unpack simply from being online or having worked in an office before.) That's not just the jokes, but everything: The enemies, the abilities, the concepts behind the dungeons, and the slapstick nature of it all.It all comes together and fits the atmosphere of the corporate workplace, namely in how it replicates the upbeat oppressiveness of new-age capitalism. Other details that add to this atmosphere include the art style, the bumping soundtrack, the specialized loading screens for each dungeon, the dialog system resembling messenger. It's so cohesively, consistently good. I could get lost in it and I'm sure I've forgotten some things too.The game-play itself is kind of am odd mix. You can see the user tags for that, but honestly, I'd describe it as most similar to a roguelite "Breath of the Wild" with constantly throwing and breaking weapons, but it fitting the experience much more with your limited space and surroundings. It's fast, frenetic, and chaotic, leading often to getting mobbed in small rooms. There's a sharp difficulty spike partway through the game as well, so if it seems too easy at first, that might be because it sort of is. They take the training wheels off later. Though I also feel obliged to mention, the game is a bit short with only three primary dungeons. Eh, it can't be helped with how small the team was on this game.If it seems like even remotely your type of thing, I encourage you to give it a try. Heck, there's even a free demo, and a good one at that! You won't get the same density of humor from the demo, but trust me, it's there. It's incredible to me that a small studio is able to produce a game of this quality. On their first try, too!To borrow a term from the game itself, in a sense, this whole thing seems like it was "an object made of pure despair" for the state of corporate capitalism. But they've really done well in making it into something so cool and I'm glad I got to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an outstanding game for so many reasons. The gameplay is fun, surprisingly deep, the characters are full of personality, the soundtrack is absolutely amazing and catchy (one of the few I've actually listened to outside of the game). I hope the devs will one day add more content in the future.Hopefully if there's enough support then they can add extra levels (there are currently 3 dungeon types, each with a unique theme and aesthetic). It's hilarious how many ways they've managed to lean into the start up theme, whether it's item names, enemy types, etc.There's a great attention to detail and depth they added in a number of ways. One of my favorite discoveries is a perk you can get which allows you to purchase items that you normally can't afford. If you do this, however, you are burdened with debt for the amount that you couldn't pay for. This comes in the form of a ball and chain that attaches to you and slows you down. The higher the debt, the bigger the ball = the slower you move, but this shrinks as you defeat combat encounters. This is already more depth than many games would offer, but you can also use that ball and chain as a weapon (albeit slow).Another example is a dungeon that is a failed cryptocurrency startup. Instead of spending money normally like in the other dungeons, you can (and in some cases must) convert your cash to cryptocurrency to purchase items. Just one of the many creative details included in the game.If you enjoy the roguelike genre at all, absolutely check this game out. And encourage the devs to revisit it and add more content!

_childDocuments_.review: I just wrapped up Going Under (as in, saw the credits, I still have a mode to investigate) and I might be inclined to say I enjoyed it more than Hades overall. Hmm. A few things I love about it:The theme isn’t just a wrapper; it bleeds into pretty much every aspect of the game, from its structure and concepts, to its enemies, weapons and skills (even the ‘Working From Home’ update is a genius marriage of our current real-life predicament, an in-game scenario and the new mode itself). The writing is very sharp and witty, Aggro Crab-stabbing at capitalism, the tech industry, consumerism, corporate culture, automation, exploitative labour and various other related topics, all with some serious flare, creativity, humour and heart. How it balances all that tonally is very impressive. I thought Atomicrops’ puns and wordplay were good but Going Under’s is nuts.The gameplay loop isn’t as immediate or addictive as Hades, but that’s fine because, damn, Hades was dangerous. The combat is loose and has more in common with Zelda’s L/Z-targeting and Power Stone’s room-wrecking chaos. Weapons break frequently so you’re constantly having to improvise and grab what you can, thrashing and throwing stuff as you go. It can be absolute carnage, but in the best way.The big thing for me is the structure and length of Going Under. Each failed tech startup is its own distinctively themed dungeon, with unique enemies, weapons and bosses, and they each take around 30 minutes to complete. As you hit different milestones, the story develops and escalates, new skills get added to the pool, the dungeons and bosses change, all while you’ve got the different mentor objectives to juggle and complete. All these layers keep things interesting and the big finale/showdown is the cherry on top--it's so good!It took me about 25 hours to do my first run on Hades and another 25 or so to roll the credits. I’d be lying if I said it maintained its momentum throughout that time. Your last run isn’t wildly different to your first run. Hades was one of my games of the year but I was honestly glad to finally wrap it up.It’s taken me 25 hours to roll the credits on Going Under (your mileage may vary) and I’ve had such a great time from start to finish. There’s variety and plenty of surprises here so I didn’t burn out. I actually finished wanting more, which is the best feeling to end a game with. There’s an ‘Imposter Mode’ which is a gauntlet of sorts so I’m keen to try that out now. ‘Imposter’ as in ‘imposter syndrome’ and you access it via the mirror in your tiny company flat. It’s a very clever game.The presentation is impeccable too, skewering the popular 'Corporate Memphis' aesthetic perfectly. It’s chunky, bright and bold and the graphic design pops and transitions beautifully. The soundtrack is also fantastic.Edit: there's a generous demo for this that's well worth checking out if you're unsure.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my god, I absolutely ADORED this game.Wouldn't have even discovered it if not for finding the soundtrack on Spotify (the music is stellar btw, go support the composer feasley if you want), and I'm so glad I didn't miss it in the flood of roguelites this year.The art style is charmingly simplistic with expressive character portraits, the gameplay is fun regardless of your skill level, and the story was genuinely engaging instead of being fluff around the edges. Oh, and there's enough puns to feed a minimum wage worker for years.The tasty lil' snippets of dialogue and character interactions show that the creators were clearly run through the rougher parts of the industry, so all the more respect to them for being able to make something positive and enjoyable out of it.Two things before you buy though, because they might bother some of the game's more hardcore prospective audience:1: Be prepared for a few bugs, maybe even ones that'll end a run. Most of the game's performance was 10/10 and I saw very few recurring bugs, but sometimes you'll get a run where every bug rears its ugly head at once until the geometry itself is out to get you. I got stuck in focus mode a few times while unable to attack, one run ended with me being flung through the ceiling while driving a car and slowly losing 5 hearts until I fell back into the map, and one attempt at the final boss turned me into a statue who couldn't make inputs or take damage.2: Impostor Mode is HARD. If you're an achievement grinder, be prepared to sink some serious time into the increasing difficulty tiers, as well as abandoning more reckless playstyles in favor of delicate ones. The best comparison is Risk of Rain 2's Eclipse modes, where you have increasingly detrimental debuffs slapped onto you over the course of a much longer dungeon crawl. Not quite Tainted Lazarus levels of pain (if ya know, I feel for ya), but you'll have quite the challenge to chew on nonetheless.To be clear, neither of those reasons should scare you away from the game, especially since a small dev team can't possibly do flawless stress tests on every aspect of their creation. I still 100% recommend it, and thank you to everyone who worked on it! Looking forward to see what you do in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: If you aren't someone who's worked at a startup or in a corporate environment, Going Under is a competent and colorful roguelite, that may seem to make a few odd decisions.If you *have* worked in a larger corporation or at a startup (I've done both), this game becomes something special. Everything about the game shines when you see how they've taken aspects of modern white collar work culture and adapted to every part of the game. For intance:- The character art is based on simplified, inoffensive HR-inspired cartoon human shapes- The skills you get during a run are all based on phrases and personality traits you may have heard in an office environment, but adapted to in-game mechanics- The different environments representing failed startups are well-realized satire of familiar startups and businesses that actually exist, with the additional twist of working in a sort of 'monster' enemy type in each one that is unique- The other characters that can act as your mentor feel like fairly standard office personality archetypes: the jaded software developer, the overly-passionate creative, the anxiety-ridden accountant, and the platitude-filled shallow dudebro CEO as examples.- Some of the dialogue in the game gave me flashbacks to real interactions I've had; subtle gas-lighting about performance, not doing the job you were hired for, seeing someone above you say or do something you can't wrap your head around but know you have to accept to not rock the boat...it was actually surreal at times playing this game.- weapons in levels feeling like they are based on either great puns or cringy startup office toys.The game starts off pretty easy but ramps up in difficulty after you get a few wins. Luckily your 'coworkers' can be assigned as mentors and you can do quests for them to get more benefits (like starting levels with allies, more item drops, special shops, etc). Gameplay is fast and frantic, as weapons break quickly and most rooms have quite a few enemies along with a lot of office furniture.I still can't believe how relevant this game is. I know it's design inspirations may limit who finds it compelling, but if you are familiar with the tech work grind and enjoy roguelites in general, please give this game a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: Going Under

_childDocuments_.review: This game is simply amazing. Very simple mechanics, smart jokes and lots of references to real world struggles.If you have any experience with startup culture, you won't stop laughing at every single dialog. _childDocuments_.review: I didn't like this game (reasons below), BUT if you are a massive fan of the roguelike genre and need something new, I could see it being worth to pick this up just to experience its more unique mechanics.For a more casual fan like me though, I really felt like the combat started to feel clunky after the mid-game difficulty spike. The enemy spam, tightly packed rooms, and fast character movement seem to indicate that the devs want you to be aggressive and fast paced, but its quite easy for enemies to chip away at your health. So you have to be overly defensive, which imo just doesn't really work well either, especially after the difficulty spike.Since you have to manage your camera its not uncommon for projectiles or enemies to come flying at you from off screen before you can react. Enemies move telegraphing is also pretty hard to read when they are all crowded up and you have to manage your camera - on top of explosions and other effects that obscure your vision.I honestly didn't feel like there were many interesting stand out skills either. So most of my runs ended up feeling very similar because unlike a game like Binding of Isaac where you have like 8+ floors, you only have 3 floors + a boss floor here, so not many chances to get super crazy item effect combos. Especially since in hard mode health drops when completing rooms is extremely rare. I've gone through whole dungeons without getting a single one regularly, this means unless you play perfectly you have to spend your money on health instead of upgrades when you go to the shop.The ability to get buffs through leveling up your mentors was pretty cool, and the endorse mechanic (which lets you start your run with a skill of your choice if you use said skill enough) was as well. But ultimately I just got frustrated with this game and didn't want to finish it.For more detail, consider checking out my full video on it!

_childDocuments_.review: A well made short and sweet roguelike that leaves you wishing for more, and delivers like a monkeys paw.The controls are simple and the camera doesn't get in your way whatsoever which is a surprise considering how busy every room is. There is so many different items to unlock that it took over twice the length of the game to get them. Certain combinations let you do different builds and depending on what you got the last few levels are going to be really easy or really hard. Enemies have fair "tells" and ways to dodge their attacks, and bosses are difficult but fair, it gets harder as you progress, the same enemies get upgraded and no longer can be stunned. Curses are handled much better than other roguelikes, they aren't run-ending like other games like Binding Of Isaac, they are a temporary challenge with rewards should you survive. The best part about this game is that you can recover from a bad run easily, and there are multiple paths to take for fighting and retaining HP. You have apps that can summon more weapons, give you health, have every object in a room attack your enemies. The store, you can steal from and get discounts on. Fizzle drinks that do who knows what. You can base an entire run around any of these not all inclusive ways of getting upgrades, health, and surviving, or you can combine or switch between them depending on what you get. There is a LOT of perkbuilding here and tons of fun combos that can help you and hurt you.The story is cute and relatable as someone who has worked in a corporate environment before, they got the personality types down to a T. The art direction is fantastic for each of the 3 worlds you explore, it's consistent and clever, as long as you dont look too closely. It starts off as an obvious parody of the corporate art style but kind of forgets about that and throws in whatever's colorful and cel shaded. The music is surprisingly good as well, it changes between rooms slightly and remixes the track when you've reached the harder difficulty. The art direction, and naming scheme of items and places are extremely clever, make for interesting enemies, and items and bring a groan at the wordplay.The weapons are cleverly designed and you are forced to use everything in your environment to hit people with due to the durability mechanic. You have to learn the fighting style of each weapon and not get married to a select few since they'll be gone in 2-3 fights. Better or upgraded weapons add something for you to be on the look out for and using sparingly when needed, there is quite a bit of resource management involved.This game is fair, and mostly balanced towards the player if anything, but there are two enemies that are NOT fair, because you cannot dodge their attacks. The upgraded chain chomp, and the hands. Both have attacks that cannot be interrupted and they almost constantly attack. The chain chomp has virtually no way to avoid taking at least 1 damage from. This is really only an issue in the challenge mode which is already broken though.This is one of the few games I have seen with a zig-zag shaped learning curve. It took me around 40 hours to beat the main game and I ended up getting what I thought was reasonably good at it. After trying the challenge mode, I realized not only was I not good at the game, but the challenge mode was broken. The challenge mode is broken because all curses never lift. The first person curse IS a run killer because it never lifts. This is a glitch that people have posted about in the forums and has been ignored. I couldn't get past it because of the glitch because taking curses really did help you a lot so much they weren't really a risk to take since they lifted in 3-5 rooms. After a long time of struggling I finally learned to beat the FIRST LEVEL of the challenge mode without curses, and the second, and finally the third had a new challenge involving curses which fixed the glitch for the harder levels thankfully. I hadn't felt that frustration in a long time, the game took off the baby gloves and I had to relearn everything that the main story taught me, the game hadn't gotten harder it had just required more endurance. While it wasn't intentional by the developer it was interesting to experience a huge skill wall.A challenging colorful game with deep gameplay mechanics and tons of build opportunities. Just be weary of the challenge mode. PLEASE FIX THE CHALLENGE MODE!I finally 100% this game after 135 hours. I actually went back and played the base game after completing the challenge mode and it's trivially easy now that all the chains are gone. I didn't love the RNG grinding especially after seeing that better weapons were more common in the regular mode, I felt like I had overcome an insurmountable task beating it. The game itself was against me, sometimes glitching out and forcing me to end a run. I beat it. Looking back on it I think the reason I kept coming back to this game in the challenge mode was that each new compounding "rule" presented, changed the way I had to think about the game, it became almost a puzzle game with things like order of room clearing, whether or not to even pick up a powerup and in which order, and finding some really specific mechanics to give me every edge over the game. I enjoyed having to scramble to win under increasingly menacing game mechanics. The game itself is not really meant to be played at some of the higher difficulties because there are some mechanics that are just plain unfair, like: There's about a 30% chance that hitting the enemy in the middle of its attack will not cancel the attack. It's hard to rely on anything to your advantage, mimicking the corporate environment. Maybe hard work does pay off? ;)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super fun. I like Tappi a whole lot, but Fern and Kara are closely tied for second place (also Kara's dog is a cutiepie and you CAN pet him!). The storyline is really interesting and it is part of what helped me steamroll through this game in like three hours straight when I first got it. The art style is also gorgeous and vivid. _childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty fun for an indie roguelite, a genre that I'm not on the best of terms with.The combat is decently varied if a bit button-mashy, and the breath of the wild-esque weapon breakage is at least unique even if I'm still not sure if I like or hate it.The story is a less-than-subtle critique of hyper-corporatism and the struggle of the young jobseeker, and the graphics emulating that ugly, disgusting artstyle they all use is a very nice touch.Unlike most roguelites, a run only consists of a few levels in one world rather than needing to go through the entire game every death, which makes it perfect for short gameplay sessions.I'm not a fan of the character questlines that rely on luck to complete, and the difficulty spike with the second set of worlds is a bit on the  high side, not to mention that some perks don't have any description of what they actually do. But all in all the experience is an enjoyable one, even if it isn't groundbreaking or mindblowing.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a gift from my colleague and fellow intellect, Occamsnailfile, whose opinions I sometimes seek and always respect.  She was right.  Get this game.  It stands in stark contrast to anything else I've been playing over the last few weeks, and I've wielded a foam thumbs up to beat up anybody who disagrees with my opinion.  Don't try me, it does huge damage.Anyway, threats aside, this is a roguelike.   It follows the tropes of roguelikes quite closely.  You will assail a randomly-generated dungeon, you will likely die a lot,  You will gain character skills, and you will learn how the game works over time, and you will get better.This one brings a bit of whimsy and light-hearted humour to the genre.  The art style is striking, the game is kind of silly, and the humour is subtle and sly.    (Seriously, I laughed like an idiot at "low-hanging fruit".  That's class.)Some of my friends don't like roguelikes, and I get it, it can be frustrating to bounce off the same content repeatedly.  But this one keeps it short and punchy; my longest run was only 20 minutes, but my average run time is much shorter, and there's all kinds of between-mission interactions setting the tone of the world.It's a charming game.  And, as the respected intellect Occamsnailfile notes, the difficulty can be adjusted if you grow weary of smashing your face against a roguelike wall and want to just get through the game.That said, as of this writing, I've beaten two dungeons as of this review.  I know there's much more to it after that, but it feels surmountable, as opposed to Heroes of Hammerwatch which just felt like a mountainous slog.So anyway, get this if you need quick shots of action gaming.  It's brunch-sized gaming; long enough to feel substantial, short enough you can do other things with your day.

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under - A Vibrant, Dungeon Crawling Delight - In Going Under you play as Jacqueline, an unpaid intern at a start up success called Fizzle, a company that manufactures soft drinks which are also a meal replacement because let's be real who has time to eat these days, it's all about convenience! Upon joining the company you quickly discover that the depths of your building, accessed via a series of slides, are filled with bizarre creatures living in the remains of previous failed tech start up companies who all need to be dealt with swiftly and efficiently. So before you're even able to settle in to your brand new job in the marketing department you're tasked with seeking out the boss at the end of each of these dungeons and putting an end to them in a timely manner. Thus begins your journey into Going Under, head down into the failed tech start ups, battle your way through the sprawling dungeon using whatever you can get your hands on to survive and attempt to overthrow the maniacal boss who waits at the end. Simple.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if I can recommend this game.Depth wise the game runs its core gimmick dry in a few hours. The dungeons are boring and lose their charm after the third or forth time being in them. The combat isn't compelling enough to keep me interested, there isn't enough ways perks and items synergize with eachother to justify continued playthroughs. Of all the mentors only like two of them have interesting potentials for builds.It really pains me to give this game a negative review, it started out *so* strong and it does genuinely have a lot to say and a really funny sense of humour. But I just can't be bothered to sit here and work through runs of this game over and over when there isn't anything here to work with.The wink wink nudge nudge humor of the game stops being funny when the dungeons stop making sense and just become weird and gimmicky. The apps are barely useful and there isn't enough of them, the perks are more often then not completely useless and theres no real way to cleverly synergize fun builds for a run. You are following the dreaded issue that plagues a lot of roguelikes which is that you're just kind of hoping the RNG rolls the way you need and gives you a run that doesn't suck balls.Combat just becomes a frustrating floaty mess, constantly getting stuck on geometry trying to side hop is not interesting, and as interesting a gimmick it is to have anything you pick up be a weapon, in reality like a handful of the stuff you can pick up in a dungeon can actually be useful. The rest of the stuff is liable to get you killed if you try use it.Overall its a disappointing experience, this game had me so hard in the first few hours but its quickly become a chore to even play the thing. I just don't care enough to see what else the game has to offer and given how much praise the game is getting its very unlikely we're gonna see the combat and dungeon overhauls the game really needs to live up to the potential it has.

_childDocuments_.review: Unpaid internship in the form of a dungeon crawling roguelite, where every level is a different abandoned office/business.Lot's of charm in this one, your basic gameplay flow is trying to get to the bottoms of each of the new offices you unlock - and defeating their boss. Your weps are.. improvised! See a stapler? Pick it up and start shooting staples. See a laptop? Now it's a melee wep!You can throw weps, too - they have statuses( liek shock, freeze, burn, etc ) some are ranged weps ( like water guns, or a fire extinguisher ) and you can hold 3 weps at any time ( weps also have durability, so they will often break, forcing you to scramble for a new wep in the heat of combat, sometimes ) in addition to weps, you also have phone apps - which basically serve as a consumable item - some shock enemies, some put you in a rainbow car of death, some heal, some give you shop discounts - there's a bunch of em. in addition to those additions, you have co-workers that offer you missions in the offices, and once you complete them - you can take that co-worker as a mentor, which offers you benefits in the runs. Do more missions, level them up, get better perks from your mentors. in addition to the addition of the additions, you have all your various perks ( stuf you expect in any roguelite ) liek makign your melee stronger, adding a chance to infclit status, super sizing all your weps, etc ) and the more you use them, the more experienc you earn for them - once you complete the bar, you can " pin " the perk, which allows you to start with it. I'm loving the game so far, the runs are fast, colorful - nd every new office has a theme, all the weps change and the enemies change, and there's gimmicks, too.the first office you enter, JOblin - is your un of the mill entry level in a roguelite = it's just gonna show you the ropes.the 2nd one is a cryptomining office, and you fight literal miners, complete with minecarts, and lil missions to harvest as much crytpocoin as you can ( called Styx here ) The writing is siblime, the characters all have plenty of charm to them ( and the squiggle vision animaiton for them in portraits is petty cute. ) I'm not sure if there's more than 3 offices atm - but I'm afraid that's all there is. Not to say the game is light on content, I just wanted to see how far and wacky the devs got with the new levels. one level is for a dating app, and you literally can use a bodypillow as a wep.It's got a good sense of humour to it, might not be the most hardcore roguelite out there, but it's a fun romp.TL;DR - fun style, charming writing mixed with a roguelite that uses a dead rising style combat system.absolutely reccomend.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game with a unique theme. Haven't played a satirical game in a while, if at all! It is easily the most unique theme I’ve seen among rogue-like games, and brings attention to American corporate & startup culture with some pretty good humour and awesome characters. Even the art style has that corporate non-opinionated look, though they make it work in interesting ways and it hasn’t really grated on me. Also the music ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slaps, I love it so much! It’s in line with the different “dungeons” you visit, and I honestly vibe to them outside the game at times.Fizzle Beverages where Jacqueline, the MC, is assigned as a marketing intern is a newly acquired subsidiary of Cubicle, which is basically Amazon in 30-40 years.  You get to visit defunct subsidiaries such as an overworked contracting company, a “handsy” dating app, and a hype-fueled ♥♥♥♥-coin firm.The characters are really fun to listen to. You have the jaded programmer, the improooover / self-help CEO, the distraught accountant, the dreaming creative, the overbearing project manager, and the chill dude. Of course, these characters are archetypes, but their interactions really make the game shine, whether in getting at least a little attached to them, or revealing the dynamics of the workplace in the conflicts that keep unfolding between them as the plot progresses. You also get to do tasks for them in the dungeons, which adds some longevity to the game. You get to do tasks for these characters, such as “Go steal from the pizza party,” “Go bust the union forming in Joblin,” “Go find the golden cucumber in WinkyDink” etc. etc. These are fun, they are in line with the characters that give these tasks, and they fill up mentorships which lets you take a bunch of unique skills from a character to spice up your dungeon runs. The tasks, since they have you revisit the dungeons, also pair well with the Rolodex feature which has you finding a special card weapon to use it on enemies and get their business cards to fill up your bestiary / rolodex. I got pretty caught up in this Rolodex collection challenge and kept repeating content since the dungeons were pretty fun, the skills I kept gaining as I went on were interesting, and there was the occasional secret room. Also they have some humorous descriptions at times. The procedural content and the variety between runs was not really top of the line, but I kept coming back because the dungeons were unique between themselves. Each one has completely different types challenge rooms, enemy types, themes, and even currencies! Joblin is more standard, Winkydink introduces charm mechanics, and Styxcoin is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chaotic and has a speculative cryptocurrency investment system. They introduce different weapons and even mechanics too, with WinkyDink heavy on fire & frost for example. The mentorships you gain and the fact that you can pin up to one endorsed skill (use the skill a couple times to take it with you at the start) as you go into a dungeon also lets you control your experience a bit and spices up the runs further, while also adding long term progression. The real progression is in unlocking more and more powerful skills which you can then find in the dungeons though.The combat is... alright. It really starts to shine in the late game after the ending, but I’ll get to that. As far as the base game goes, your weapons break quite fast, you can throw stuff, you have a dodge roll (but no stamina so its not a souls-like! :P), a shop, etc. etc. So far so good. What breaks up the fairly standard combat here and takes it to something more fun is the skills, mentorships that give rest rooms, apps, status effect inducing beverages, as well as the curses you can take on, the different weapons you can find etc. It’s not perfect by any means, and some enemy animations have odd wind-ups, the rooms are sometimes cramped and you get hit multiple times without being able to do much, etc etc. but by no means is it unfair. The fairness does come from most rooms and especially bosses in the early  game being easy though, so yeah... Some enemy types  are quite lethal at least, and combined with the occasional deathly room, the game keeps being challenging, especially when the difficulty ramps up in the later mid and post-late game. The game literally has a sword named “The Cornercutter.” I love this game. I think especially when it came out, it really lacked the variety and long-term progression a game like this needs to keep people coming back though. The Working From Home update has tried to fix that, and I started playing the game after that update, which introduced the rolodex that kept me engaged, a bunch of new skills, and the Impostor Mode. I have talked quite a bit about the “base” game which I imagine has been a lot of people’s experience with Going Under. This game used to be a 10-15 hour long, solid, imaginitive, if a bit combat-wise stale journey, but this new update has tried to carry the game to a whole new level. The reason why I engaged with the Rolodex grind was because of the new skills, secret rooms, weapons etc. that I kept finding, a lot of which came with the update.In the late game, especially in my Impostor Mode runs, I suddenly found myself being able to do creative combos as I picked up skills & weapons. There is the commonly found combo of upscaling a rare weapon, since upscaling also resets the durability, making it possible to use it for a long time and making the weapon stupid big. There is also the interesting combo of having a slime ally when you get hit spawn, or any charm ability, paired with the skill that has your allies lose HP instead of you. There is the ability that increases fire damage, as well as the one that charms enemies on fire, paired with the skill that lets you put enemies on fire by focusing on them occasionally or the one that ignites your thrown items. There is the skill that gives you 2x more money but makes you lose it faster, paired with the skill that has you hit for more the more money you have (I think it scales up to 2 times). There is other combos too, some I have found, and probably quite a few I haven’t. Of course you pick up a bunch of different skills in a run, so often you can complement these combos you create with different skills. Quite a few are helpful all the time, especially the ones that give a minion or shock enemies occasionally, increase survivability etc. etc.The game seems to have gotten a bunch of these great skills with the Working From Home update which brought in the late game Impostor Mode, the Rolodex grind (good kind of grind for me though), secrets, more curses etc, and I assume even some of the really rare weapons I came across like once or twice in 40 hours. So the game has these build variety inducing things largely after the “base” game finishes, and we get into the 10-15+ hour mark which I assume how long it took for people to finish the game. Unless you are like me, fell in love with the theme, and proceeded to grind the Rolodex entries in dungeons you already completed before finishing the game :PUnfortunately the game suffers from a host of bugs at this point of longevity. I encountered none in the base game, but the Impostor Mode and the new skills are so heavily littered with them that I started to  come across a game breaking bug once every 2-3 runs.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with some bugs that still need buffing. I played through the entire story over the course of 2 days and had a great time. I spent the rest of my time trying to beat the challenge mode 'imposter mode' and had a huge bug. Without spoiling anything, I got to the challenge boss who then glitched when it reached half health making the game unbeatable. I couldn't damage it and it couldn't damage me but we just kept going. Normally not a problem, if not for the fact that the most difficult dungeons in the game precede this boss so it left a bad taste in my mouth on an otherwise impeccable game. In fact, this game is so good that my only concern the entire rest of the time I was playing it was 'oh man I hope there's more content here.' The visuals, music, and gameplay all feel great and create a cohesive world that successfully parodies startup culture.  Personally, I'd highly recommend this game with an 8 out of 10. Everything that's on the table really comes across as a labor of love, and the game places a high emphasis on quality over quantity. The 2 points are being taken off because:1. The bug I mentioned really pulled me out of the experience. That was the most drastic example, but there were others (for example companions spawning into walls in another critical boss fight making them irrelevant.2. I said quality over quantity and I meant it. For a Rogue-lite there isn't a ton of replayability beyond the really solid base experience. The item catalog is small and items don't synergize in interesting ways. There are maybe 6 separate worlds that get recycled. In spite of those points this is still a fantastic game to start off anyone's 2021 and there are moments that will have you bellowing with laughter at your screen. The question is, once your hooked how are you going to feel 10 hours later when you hit that wall?

_childDocuments_.review: Going Under is a rogue-lite dungeon crawler where you can use almost every object in the game as a weapon. Beating up a bunch of monsters with a laptop or a fire extinguisher is so much fun, and because each object only lasts a few hits you need to switch weapon regularly. Another great idea are the mentors: by completing specific tasks for them they give you unique perks. You can also install "apps" that temporary give you benefits, and like most rogue-lite's you'll find random skills that you need to unlock by killing enemies.While I had a few hours of fun with this game, I've retired after beating all 3 dungeon types. After that, you are required to beat all 3 dungeons again but with stronger enemies and different bosses. The unique rooms in every dungeon are already very limited, so it felt like playing a game you just finished again from the beginning on higher difficulty level to me. What I played was definitely worth it tho.

_childDocuments_.review: People would benefit from more games like this. This game starts off with Jackie, a newly hired intern at Fizzle a company that was recently acquired by a huge corporation named Cubicle. Yes, this is an adventure based on life working on the corporate ladder. Jackie applied for marketing at Fizzle but is instructed to instead perform clean-up duty by defeating all the monsters! This story is refreshing! Yet, in its way, it can be very relatable. The story has you growing closer to the characters around you as you get to know them at work. The fact that the characters embody the craziness of an actual workplace is itself very impressive and fun. I won't spoil too much but I will say that the monsters are perfectly themed and designed. These characters...have character...and that is great to see!The atmosphere of the game is simple but colorful. It very much looks like an Indie game that does its best for what it has. I think the creators pulled it off very well even though it could be described as "cellphone game graphics". Like many other Indie developers, the characters are best expressed during conversations with visual art avatars rather than the avatars you see during gameplay. Each character does come alive and become more like actual co-workers the more often you speak with them. Plus the environments of the dungeons are hilarious and perfectly fit for the themes of the enemies.Ironically, I would say the gameplay in itself is the weakest standpoint in this game. That is not to say that the gameplay is bad, it is fun to hit your enemies with a tennis racket or computer monitor, but rather that it is very simple and has been done many times before. So the gameplay is simple, but is ironically tricky, making you likely to add "assists" to your profile to finish the game. It's great that you can modify the difficulty, and I would recommend it so you don't get burnt out on replaying the dungeons. I say this because I don't want people to quit this game mid-play through! The end is worth experiencing!Overall, the gameplay itself isn't what makes this game stand out but rather the unique storytelling and characters. This game would be a perfect gift for someone who just got a new job or promotion! People would benefit from more games like this.Score: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Set within Neo-Cascadia, Going Under sees you working for a carbonated drink brand called Fizzle, owned by shipping giants Cubicle. You play as Jackie, an unpaid marketing intern arriving for her first day and within minutes of getting there, monsters appear within Fizzle’s building. Adapting to this unexpected situation quite swiftly, Jackie is pressured into defeating more baddies by her manager, Marv, leading us to an unwinnable first dungeon before being introduced to her new co-workers: Swomp, Kara, Fern, Tappi and Fizzle’s CEO, Ray. It becomes clear this wasn’t the internship she was previously advertised, and soon enough, she gets co-opted into further fights.At the heart of any satire is a political message, and behind this colourful visual presentation, Going Under communicates its own message with consistency. Parodying Amazon via Cubicle, it tackles mind-numbing corporate culture, capitalism’s worst excesses and a jaded workforce forced to participate in a broken system. It treads into other subjects with less focus, including modern-day privacy concerns and the trading of civil liberties for convenience. This is all backed by a strong sense of humour – though it's an admittedly niche one as it sometimes relies on memes, one example being how the exit screen states “Noo don’t leave, you’re so productive haha”. Those who enjoy these jokes will love it but that humour soon becomes dated.Within Going Under, failed start-ups don’t disappear; they get banished to the underworld, cursed to remain there for all eternity as wandering monsters. It’s a harsh punishment for failure and these ruined companies become your foes. There are three procedurally generated dungeons in total, so no two playthroughs are ever the same, and each start-up spans across four floors, comprising of gig economy recruiters, cryptocurrency and dating app employees. Waiting at the end of each dungeon is the respective CEO, bringing a literal definition to "boss" fights. Whether you’ve chosen traditional weaponry like a Warhammer to office supplies including the humble stapler, anything you find can be used as a weapon in this game.Combat is simple, giving a basic attack whose strength varies depending on your selected weapon and a dodge roll for defence. Attacks can be charged for greater damage, too, also letting you throw items about, but each weapon has limited durability, so you must regularly switch things up. Skills can also be gathered throughout each dungeon run and these add buffs such as increased health, proficiency in two-handed weapons or dropping bombs when dodging. They don’t stick with you upon leaving, but using them gains experience and if Jackie becomes proficient in them, she can enter dungeons with one skill already equipped. Upon gaining a smartphone, apps can be randomly found, and these have their own perks like ordering in new weapons, creating a dummy Jackie to fool enemies, and more.It’s easy to learn and by mixing together skills and apps, combat holds a surprising level of depth, helped by a good variety of enemies so it never feels repetitive. The only downside is throwing items, which can prove rather cumbersome in terms of aiming – but that’s honestly quite minor. Once defeated, enemies drop money (plus the occasional sandwich) and each floor holds an underground shop to purchase items from, providing boosts like food for health refills, extra heart containers or new skills. You can also earn Cubits, a separate currency that sticks with you once you leave a dungeon and that can buy further skills back in the office.Dungeons are quite challenging, so take what help you can get and you’ll need to make good use of that dodge roll to survive. There aren’t difficulty levels, but if you find yourself struggling, Going Under includes assist options which grant extra lives, higher weapon durability, lower enemy health and more, making it a more accessible experience. Optional challenges also emerge once per floor, tasking you with missions like “Defeat the enemies quickly” or “Mine Styxcoin”. Your performance is ranked out of five stars, rewarding you with various item crates that depend on your score. The "Hauntrepreneur" offers his own challenges too; it doesn't cost coins but makes life harder in exchange for skills, such as causing enemies to explode upon their defeat.Outside of Marv, each Fizzle employee becomes Jackie’s mentor, making for quite a clash in personalities; they ask her to carry out various tasks inside dungeons. Usually, these are simple requests like “defeat X amount of enemies with a particular weapon”, but some offer special challenges, including crashing a demon pizza party and walking Kara’s dog. Upon completion, your colleague relationship levels-up and that offers increasingly beneficial perks, such as Ray’s company credit card or monster allies to assist you. Only one co-worker can be selected at a time though, so choose carefully. This essentially amounts to side missions and not only does it bring some good character development, it adds a level of replayability which means that the game remains interesting.Going Under makes for an excellent debut from Aggro Crab. Though the humour won’t be to everyone’s taste, it brings us a corporate satire which hits closer to home than most, and by doing so consistently, never feels ham-fisted in its execution. This isn’t the longest experience you can find on Switch – taking around 10 hours to fully complete including side tasks – but it provides an entertaining story, and one that’s filled with great combat and high replayability. Keeping you hooked until the end, this dungeon crawler comes with a modest recommendation.
