_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is the very definition of a hidden gem, and I'm so glad that Steam recommended it to me even though I had played few text-intensive games such as this one before. Deep story with well-written dialogue and complex characters, expansive lore with a journal that records your findings, multiple route options where your choices actually have consequences, impressive isometric pixel art and classic RPG elements such as jobs, gear and battles, all set in an universe where nature actively fights back against anyone trying to destroy it, locking humanity in a permanent medieval era. The music wraps up this game in a neat little bow, as I feel like it represents the very nature of Roadwarden itself: grim and melancholic, yet hauntingly beautiful and oddly comforting. It's a must-buy for anyone who enjoys a "choose your own adventure" game, especially if you're a fan of the dark fantasy genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: So... I haven't "finished" this game--insofar as one can finish a game with so many possible endings. I did complete one run, and got quite a bad ending! This was because I simply ran out of time (I played on normal difficulty), which I sort of expected, because there's quite a lot of content and you do have to plan out your travels a bit for a 100% run. That is what I was attempting on my second playthrough, before life got in the way. By the time I had time to return to it, it was long enough that I felt I really ought to start from the beginning. I still plan to, but this is really the kind of game you want to dedicate some good time to digging into, which I just haven't had yet.I did enjoy every hour I played it though, which is why I look forward to returning to it eventually.You won't like this game if you don't like reading, or if you're impatient. You need to take your time exploring the options available to you and unraveling the story, which is quite compelling!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I spent two full days playing it until I finished it. Exploring the peninsula, and getting to know it's people was a really fantastic and inmersive feeling. It has that same vibe that Citizen Sleeper has, the idea of being just one small person in a world way bigger than you. Surrounded by extremely different people, with different problems and different ways to live. It's just one of those games where I can pause at any moment and listen to the music while i sink into the world and feel myself sharing a life with the friends I made along the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice, choose your own adventure - visual novelesque rpg, of sorts. Sets a fantastic mood with its writing, but also with the music by Nick Roder and Dan Caine.Not a very long game, the time it takes to complete it depends entirely on how fast you read, for me i'd say one playthrough took maybe 7 hours. Roadwarden does offer some replayability though, as you probably will not find a good end on your first foray, and there are secrets to find that you might have time to completely figure out.Well worth your time, if you are into this sort of thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: If you are put off by the graphics and the fact that it's mostly text, I understand. But give it a chance, you will NOT be let down. The writing is rich, pleasant to read, emotional, and original. You "feel" like you are there! The game systems are not too complex, in a good way. They serve their purpose perfectly.The feeling of accomplishment when you reach the end is quite unique.9.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Not much actions per se, but an intriguing and engaging story.  Hard to disengage from it.  I'll return to update review after more hours, but I'm enjoying it so far.  So, I've now completed a play through.  The earliest computer games I played were text based, so this game was somewhat nostalgic to me.  BUT, this game's tags did not note that it proselytized LGBTQ+.  If you're into that, it'll be an added attraction.  But if you're not into it, then it's a distraction from the story.  If developers want to cater to that audience - then it should be a mod, not the default setting.  Also, I recommended the game at first, but with the LGBTQ+ stuff, I no longer feel comfortable recommending it.  I actually feel neutral, but once you do a thumbs up, you can not go back to neutral, you can only do a thumbs down.

_childDocuments_.review: MidIt's a sorry state of gaming that something this... mid can be so well loved. The art style is cohesively bland and completely forgettable. There's zero animation as well, if that matters to you.Some of the word puzzles are good and some go full bizzaro logic for no reason. The worldbuilding is a decent mix of normal fantasy staples and new stuff, but almost all the new stuff is pretty forgettable. The emerging story is... okay? It's not very subtle about it's representation. I've played for about 4 hours and I've met at least 4 homosexual characters with more being expressly mentioned, am trying to find a lost trans person, and even played matchmaker for a woman who wanted more kids but was lesbian (??). Bear in mind that's out of roughly 30 named characters so far. It's like one in five people on the peninsula are some flavor of the rainbow. If that bothers you, stay away from this title. Combat is not very mechanical, it's more about tactics and positioning. That said, I've scummed a few encounters and the internal logic is all over the place. Narrative-wise you're warned to avoid risk, but in some really tough-seeming encounters the best option is to sprint in screaming and swinging your axe like a madman. Other times it seems like an easy fight but you get dunked on unless you run away. The religion system is weird and doesn't really make a ton of sense to me. There's all these factions, but they share a holy symbol, but they don't get along, but there aren't holy wars.... I have no clue what's going on with it honestly. It's even a tracked stat on your character sheet but I've yet to see it matter in a choice.The economy takes a lot of management to come out on top. That said, if you use the fish cages and don't care about being dirty (it really doesn't seem to matter too much) and make sure you sleep somewhere with a free option, you can amass money without toooo much difficulty.  Idk fam. Maybe my expectations were too high. Just feels really mid. I'll try to update this when/if I finish it

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent writing, excellent worldbuilding. The choices you make along the way hold significant weight, and it is more than possible to fail if you aren't applying the knowledge you have on hand.  Very immersive and enjoyable, I devoured this game in basically a single sitting.  My only regret is that I couldn't condition my Roadwarden into more of a battle maniac. _childDocuments_.review: Okay so this game is super interesting for what it is. Ultimately, it's a text adventure. However, it's one with really well done pixel art, and a really bleak and well done atmosphere in my opinion.Combat: Non-existing for the most part. You make educated choices based on your knowledge (Or lack thereof) of your foe. There's some RNG aspects there I think, but I am not 100% sure how much is RNG and how much is "you just picked wrong, idiot."Story: In my opinion it's pretty incredible, it's a very down to earth game. You end up feeling like you really are interacting with people who have lived among dangerous monsters most of their lives. They are harsh, untrustworthy and skeptical, and it's one of those games where it felt like earning trust/reputation was an actual challenge, not something you can just pay your way through.  There is a LOT to this game, and it's a LOT of reading as is any text adventure can be. There's secrets to be found almost everywhere. Overall though, the game is pretty damn hard. It takes a lot of planning, some math, and some logic to work your way through this dark fantasy world. It's grim, and it gives off those GOT vibes of feeling small in a much larger world often. It isn't the longest game in the world, I beat it at about 18 hours using the scholar character, but I dabbled with the warrior and mage, each class did feel balanced and able to excel in some social interactions due to their chosen skill set, and it made other conversations much more difficult. Now one thing I *Really* like in a game is player agency. This game gives it to you in spades for the most part. I will be honest here and say I played the game on the longest time frame, and honestly I have no idea the amount of min-maxxing needed to complete the game on the shortest time setting. There is just SO much to find and do. You'd have to do some Stardew Valley level time management if you want to get far. You need to consider your provisions, your travel time, your rest, armor status, and more. All of these things factor into your choices in battles and in other scenarios that test your characters abilities both mentally and physically.I am absolutely in love with the world that the Dev created here. I'm a huge fan of low/dark fantasy where magic is there, but it's not some over prominent overpowered ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's grounded and it makes sense. I played this game on steam deck. It wasn't the smoothest experience, but I was able to play the entire game on steam deck, and given what the Dev states in their updates, they've put work into it as well, so kudos to them there, I doubt they thought they'd need to make a controller config for a text adventure. Definitely extra points for being adaptable. Overall, I can't recommend this game enough if you like to think and figure out actually hard puzzles, or you enjoy text adventures or just simply a fantasy addict. It's very unique and one of a kind in a lot of ways and honestly one of my GOTY's. The price is good if not generous as well, given the amount of work that had to have been put into this in terms of making everything this game throws at you work in such a cohesive way. 100% Recommend if you are into this game from the screenshots etc. Good on the Dev for being responsive and squashing bugs too.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A short charming choose-your-own-adventure story where you roleplay as a roadwarden, which generally consists of patrolling around a circular loop of a rural peninsula to keep the roads safe, and running errands for various people from nearby settlements, along with the more specific task of finding your missing predecessor, and securing cooperative deals with the local settlements for your big city employers.The game involves a lot of reading, which is perfectly fine as the writing is enjoyable, and functional – gathering information is important for directions to points of interest, interactions with people/creatures you’ve yet have to meet. It also has fallout/fallout 2 style epilogues to show your impact upon the world at the end, which is nice. Not all choices are impactful, quite a lot of them are flavorful, but still enjoyable as it allows you to express who you are and sculpt the world according to your tastesGameplay consists of picking one of the provided text options, and occasionally typing out something specific to do – it’s a choose-your-own-adventure story.You pick one out of three classes early in the game, each with unique equipment, skillset, and situational options/dialogue choices There’s a bit of resource management involving managing food supplies to keep your stomach full, managing your health/vitality, keeping your light armor intact, and keeping your appearances presentable. There’s also some light inventory management involving your tools and equipment.There is an adjustable time limit when you start the game, but the middle settings provide you more than enough time to finish everything to do on the first blind playthrough, unless you are wasting a lot of time or really bad at time management.The save/load system is very handy and conveniently implemented, with enough compulsive saves you have a lot of freedom to experiment in explorations and encounters, without worrying about ruining a run and needing to restart.

_childDocuments_.review: extremely delightful, and a game where the world really is shaped by your choices. if you like to Read your games you'll love it. was genuinely invested in everything, and it was a fun mix of playstyles. my advice is to keep the 40 day time limit so that some paths are left unexplored. i played as a scholar and it definitely helps to be able to read stuff lmao. 5/5! will be thinking about for a long time i suspect
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing storybook game! Dive into a unique fantasy world whose engaging and nuanced characters encourage you to learn more about the world through dialogue and moral choices. You have to balance limited resources, money, favors and even personal appearance while travelling the roads of the land. Choose to fight and kill monsters, spare their lives to reduce their reprisals or even go hunting for loot in the unforgiving woods. All in all an amazing game that I enjoyed thoroughly. The story puts you in the place of a Roadwarden trying to bring about a new age to the countryside through the sponsoring and protection from "the big city" to the south. Pursue mysteries, help locals, be a violent jerk or a sensitive friend of the forest. If you like reading, fantasy, choice based rpgs, pixel art and some choice music you will love this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal text-based game, with an amazingly written story filled with interesting characters, locations, customs, in a unique and very immersive world.The player has a lot of freedom on how to approach various situations, and will be required to make strict usage of his resources and time.I dont agree with other reviewers about the 40 day limit being too short or restrictive, I managed a first playthrough with all quests that I could find done, and with a few days remaining. In any case, the game gives you the option to scrap the time limit altogether.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very very good, might be the best low-fantasy media I ever engaged with. You do fight unleaded and kill monsters but 70% of the time the best course of action is running away and the absolutely most important thing you do in this game is gossip. No joke, you can finish the game with flying colors without killing almost anything but if you don't gossip like your life depend on it you're going to die I ♥♥♥♥ you not. The comparison to Disco Elysium is apt. One word of warning though - the open-ended-enter-words puzzles don't really work in wild or the ruins, just try some things until you are pretty sure you got the gist of it and google the solution. Absolutely do not do it with the open-ended-enter-words GOSSIP puzzles though, because it's the best part of the game. Finding some sweet sweet leverage on the bandits or the location of some secret place by asking the right person just feels like magic.

_childDocuments_.review: What to say about this game? The world, the lore, the choices you face and their consequences, the freedom to tackle problems in a variety of ways and express your personality through your character, all of it is so well done and so incredibly captivating. My first playthrough took 15 hours, although I plan to play again with a different class. The class you pick, and the choices you make about your character do have an impact on your experience. FWIW, I thought that playing as a mage was a good choice for a first time character. The magic is helpful (especially healing) and although you don't start with great weapons, it's not difficult to purchase better gear once the game starts.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is one of those games which I like to call "games I like to read". Do you like reading?Specifically, do you like reading prose that is very detailed and well-researched? Prose that, unlike most visual novels, isn't just composed of dialogues and monologues, but provides many interesting worldbuilding details through means of a narrator? Do you want it to immerse you in a quite down to earth, believable fantasy world that's a mix of historical facts and fiction? Or rather a small excerpt of it - a peninsula in Dragonwoods, some of it rustic, populated by common folk rather than kings and nobles, most of it an untamed wilderness. It is a harsh place, yet strangely tranquil, its mood rather sombre but not cynical, its characters human, flawed, yet many of them decent people just trying to carve their path through life to the best of their abilities. It is rarely clear which of those paths is the right one.That's what you'll find in Roadwarden.Dragonwoods is a solace if you find the incessantly bombastic narratives of 'a Powerful Honorable Badass Chosen One single-handedly saving the (hapless) world from Ultimate Destruction at the hands of Absolute Evil' exhausting. If you want to focus on smaller, more grounded and intimate slice-of-life stories for a change. To play a tiny part in a much larger world. Where you take pleasure in small everyday things, like a meal shared, a friendship forged, work completed.But perhaps what you'd like even more is venturing into the unknown, the joy of discovery, observing as your map gradually fills up with places that become more and more familiar? Perhaps you dream of taming the wilderness, getting rid of beasts (violently - or through trickery), clearing up the paths, filling it up with traps to catch fish to sell or eat? Perhaps you like helping people while earning some coin in the process - to purchase better equipment or for your friend back home? Perhaps you want to see people get to trust you more and more? Maybe what you want to do is carve out your own little place in this new, hostile world? That's a crucial element of the Roadwarden experience as well.But how does it play, you ask?Well, do you like computer role-playing games? Do you cherish the freedom of doing things in whichever order you like, an order that subtly influences how the interconnected events play out? And if you ever played old-school isometric cRPGs like Fallout - perhaps you fondly remember the way they ended, how the game summarised the future of the places and lives you encountered on your adventure, the future strongly influenced by your actions during the playthrough? But at the same time... perhaps you are getting tired of complicated combat systems constantly interrupting the flow of the story and, worse, creating a ludonarrative dissonance where your noble sympathetic hero is at the same time a bloodthirsty, and somehow invincible, mass murderer with a body count in the thousands? Perhaps you are annoyed by time wasted on repetitive animations, most notably of walking, and wish more and more for the immediacy of "I click it and it happens"? And all the grind, oh, the grind...And maybe you find some solace in the visual novel genre for your story-centric needs but are starting to find their experience a bit too passive? Maybe you wish they had more interactivity, after all? Perhaps you asked yourself: what if they experimented with so-called *RPG systems* a bit? Like simple but impactful inventory and resource management? And dice rolls maybe? We all hate RNJesus, yet we miss Him so when He's gone...Roadwarden is an answer to all those wishes. Even more than that, it innovates.Speaking of resource management, for example, are you a bit bored of the concept of "health + stamina + mana"? Have you wondered if the game could keep track of something else? Maybe... how clean you are? Or the quality of the clothes you're wearing? Yes, Roadwarden does make you challenge the stereotype of a "dirty smelly dumb peasant".Also, are you unafraid of the fact that you can't do everything and instead cherish that your choices make for a unique playthrough that will be markedly different from your next one? More specifically, does the notion of a progression of in-game time* fill you with dread, or do you rather see it as a world-building tool, as an incentive to strategise and carefully plan your in-game days and, again, something that will make one playthrough different from another?Indeed, Roadwarden is maybe the first time I felt that day-night cycle is not just a gimmick. A roadwarden's life is bound by the rhythm of seasons just like anyone's, peasant's or king's. By the time you finish the game you'll be older - your character too. The weather will be colder, days shorter. You will have to say your goodbyes.Lastly - we all know the good old trick of "choose one option our of four", but are you open to less conventional means of interaction - such as puzzling out what word to type? Yes, having to come up with a word in your head, not be given one by the game. I found it quite refreshing, myself. Though it might be an issue if you're not confident about your English vocabulary. But don't worry, it's not too hard, the game's quite reasonable in its demands and always offers other means of progress. It only comes up in a few places.Finally, the presentation. Does the idea of sepia-toned pixel art that depicts only places but leaves people to your imagination appeal to you? Do you find that when the image is revealed gradually with each step of exploration it stimulates your explorer's curiosity? Would a combination of melancholic guitar music and the sound effects of nature be exactly what you need to immerse yourself in that world?It is all "yes" for me, and the OST should be a fine addition to my bandcamp collection. For autumn walks. After some time passes - I have the tunes drilled into my head by now.Have all these questions helped you decide if Roadwarden could be for you a bit? Myself, I will forever remember the Dragonwoods' peninsula as a place I've visited, got to know intimately, make my home, for a little while. Where I've befriended, or antagonised, various people, like Iason, Foggy, Eudocia, Dalit or Thyrsus. As much as it mostly happened in my imagination, there remains a reality to that. And that's the thing I say about all the best stories.----------------*Although there is a time limit on normal difficulty and up, there's also a non-limited difficulty option too, but to me the time mechanic was an essential component of the game's unique character. Without it, it wouldn't have been the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Commits the classic adventure game blunder of requiring a B.S. in Moon Logic to figure out some quests -Dolmen wants you to type 'trapdoor' instead of 'hidden door', 'fake door', 'hidden passage', 'secret passage', 'secret door', or even 'keyhole'. -A spear is needed to make a quest less dangerous. You can recklessly fight a mob across the map, and if you "win" you get a spear (why would you do that? The game repeatedly drives home the point that unnecessary risks can be lethal and you don't know what you're going to get until you've already done it), or lie to someone to get it in time for the quest (you have no knowledge that you'd get a spear that way, and the game implies that your reputation is important, thereby discouraging lying)Uses Pokemon "open world" design, where it looks open, but most of the paths except for the pre-determined one are either hard locked (come back later when the shiggus diggus leaves) or soft locked behind requirements so expensive that it makes zero sense for the player (doing a dangerous encounter exhausts you to the point you have to rest a few days before you can venture forth again, or you spend all of your money on something not worthwhile.)The general time limit on the game is incredibly stupid. It encourages the player to "solve" the game instead of experiencing the open world naturally.That being said, there are quite a few likable characters (nobody trusting you initially gets tedious), the world is decently fleshed out and presents a novel scenario, although if I squint really hard I can see this game being The Witcher fanfic (roadwardens are treated an awful lot like Geralt in Witcher 3). But once you see the man behind the curtain, typically if you die and savescum and play around with different choices, the game falls apart.Overall, I wouldn't recommend to most people, especially not those on the fence about adventure-choice gamesAs an aside, what's up with all of these RPG games with glowing overwhelmingly positive reviews being a mixed bag of turds and truffles? I swear it's getting worse.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent text-based RPG, with only a few negatives and a bunch of positives.The Good:* Excellent storytelling, characters generally felt believable and motivations make sense for the setting.* Deep lore without being too difficult to navigate** Rewards careful reading of notes/journal information without being too painful if you overlook something* Forgiving save system that gives you enough save slots to reduce tedium and trial-and-error, and allows you to save (almost?) everywhere and at any time.* Items and skills are interesting and varied. Most items have at least one obvious use and a handful of secret/less obvious uses.* Descriptions and tooltips are interesting and often entertaining (particularly those relating to minimal/maximal traits and statuses)The Neutral:* Some interactions with characters and the environment are non-obvious, primarily those relating to acquiring trust.** On the one hand this makes sense since several characters are hostile towards you from the start, and don't give you a step-by-step for earning their trust.** On the other, many areas offer rather straightforward descriptions of what is missing/required to proceed, which usually includes a description of exactly 'how' the missing thing may be obtained.* Some items are prohibitively expensive (even on casual) when exploring the areas they would be most useful in.** This makes sense since it encourages prioritizing goals instead of wandering around aimlessly, however the actions/quests needed to obtain discounts are often those that would have benefited directly from having the item in the first place.The Annoying:* * Some missions require a sizable amount of backtracking and running around, which can feel annoying when the destination is the place you were just at.Overall 9.5/10: An excellent game that makes me wish this were just part 1 of a series.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: It feels more like a choose your own adventure book than a game, but it's well made and the writing is smart and enjoyable. On the game design side, there are three different classes to choose from and your character's goal as a Roadwarden. The classes all have different strengths and allow you to make different choices for solving problems, finding treasure, and adventuring in general while you go through the story. (Ex. a scholar might build a bomb to blow up a door, but a warrior will rely on their strength to bash the door open.) I'm about 7 hours in and have yet to complete my first run. If you like to read books, this game should appeal to you. I struggle sometimes to remember everything I'm actually doing in the game, which can also be a problem when you come back to it after some time away - especially if you decide to lie to people since they will remember lies you tell to them. I'm not sure if it's in the game, but I have yet to find a place to replay old conversations I've had. This would be helpful for remembering things that I'd done a few days before. Anyway, this is getting dangerously close to a book rather than a review. It's good, check it out.

I bought this on a whim and just wanted to see what it was like before bed but now I'm addicted to heroi-- this mysterious setting full of rising dread and rich characters. Actual forest sounds created impressive immersion for both me in my grimdark ranger fantasy and my cat son IRL as he remains on the lookout for egregiously nonexistent bird prey. 10/10 might actually finish a game this year

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a text-based RPG where developers decided to focus on the depth and originality of their story more than anything else. It paid off as it is one of the most engaging world-building made in quite some time. At the crossroads of a  book and a novel, Roadwarden is an excellent game at a great price tag.In Roadwarden, you are the new… Roadwarden, as soon as you arrive on the , you can see this gloomy, wild and dangerous world that will make your mission difficult. The City’s merchant guild is sending you to open trade routes; you will also need to explore the world, try to soothe it as best as you can, tame the wild monsters, and why not figure out what happened to the previous Roadwarden while you are at it.The gameplay revolves around large blocks of text and some contextual elements that will help you throughout your decision-making process. From the get-go, you will see that everything revolves around the writing, including the art design of pixel graphics accompanying each piece of text to engrave an image of the world in your mind. Extra panels will remind you who the characters are, the places you visited, the quests you have or even a bestiary. Roadwarden makes sure all the context you have discovered so far is in your archives and easily accessible.Throughout the exciting dialogues you will have; Roadwarden is letting you dream of this world, of your character, and you can easily replay the actions in your head due to the excellent quality of the writing. You will wonder what would have happened if you had handled this situation differently, said something different, or taken a different approach. As such, you can replay the game to experience it fully. With three different difficulty levels, Roadwarden can be either forgiving or pretty challenging; you will decide this for yourself.Something that stood out is the freedom offered to you; the way you will conduct yourself is your own, and while the game lets you pick between three starting classes, your background story is yours to make, and so are your actions. Each decision will allow the plot to evolve and remind you that your choices matter.Patrol the roads, protect towns, fight monsters, explore dark caverns, take bribes, negotiate, and accumulate wealth. Please do whatever you feel like; it is up to you. Of course, your health, nourishment levels and armour quality are essential for you to balance as they will provide bonuses or negatively impact you on your journey.Sadly, I experienced tiny bugs such as my mouse cursor highlighting the text I didn’t pick or some text lagging to appear and having me skip it by mistake. Nothing game-breaking, but assuming it would have happened at a different time, it could have been highly punishing and frustrating. Though needless to say, the pros far outweigh the cons.Usually, my experience with text-based RPG is with mixed feelings; games featuring heavy writing often fail to make you dream the world or let your mind wander. Roadwarden doesn’t have that issue. As you play and follow the story, you will have no problems visualizing all the action in your mind and at your own pace. We also need to credit the music; while discreet, it perfectly fits the game and ambience.In the end, I had a fantastic time playing Roadwarden, and it is one of the most engaging world-building made in quite some time. At the crossroads of a  book and a novel, Roadwarden is an excellent game at a great price tag. If you liked this review, you can check my curating page for other games you may like.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden : By Triple F"Roadwarden," developed by Moral Anxiety Studio, is a text-based RPG that offers a unique blend of interactive storytelling, exploration, and choice-driven gameplay. Released in 2022, the game combines elements of classic RPGs with a visual novel style, placing players in the role of a Roadwarden, an itinerant protector, messenger, and occasional mercenary tasked with patrolling a desolate, isolated peninsula. Unlike many modern RPGs, "Roadwarden" relies primarily on its narrative depth and atmospheric writing rather than flashy graphics or action-heavy combat. The result is an experience that feels both personal and expansive, where every decision, encounter, and discovery impacts the player’s journey through a world filled with intrigue, danger, and lore.At its core, "Roadwarden" is a deeply immersive narrative experience, emphasizing storytelling and player choice as players explore the peninsula and its varied inhabitants. The game’s text-based nature allows for rich, detailed descriptions of the environments, people, and creatures encountered along the way, encouraging players to imagine the world in their own way. The player’s role as a Roadwarden allows them to interact with diverse communities, settle disputes, and uncover the secrets of the peninsula. The branching story paths give the player agency over how they want to approach their role, whether it’s as a compassionate protector, a calculating mercenary, or something in between. This sense of autonomy makes each playthrough feel unique, with choices that influence relationships, alliances, and the very fate of settlements across the peninsula.One of the most striking elements of "Roadwarden" is its focus on survival and resource management, which is carefully woven into the game’s narrative and mechanics. As players venture through the peninsula, they must contend with the harsh realities of being a Roadwarden, such as keeping track of food, money, and supplies while navigating dangerous territories. Decisions are often impacted by these limitations, creating a realistic tension where players must balance helping others with their own survival. The peninsula is unforgiving, with dangers like hostile creatures, unpredictable weather, and treacherous roads. This resource-based challenge adds a level of realism to the player’s journey, reinforcing the idea that being a Roadwarden is a physically and mentally taxing role that requires strategic planning and forethought.The dialogue and choice system in "Roadwarden" is exceptionally nuanced, with conversations that adapt based on the player’s previous choices, skills, and reputation. Interactions are more than just dialogue trees; they’re gateways to the player’s own interpretation of what it means to be a Roadwarden. NPCs have their own agendas and moral complexities, and players can approach situations with a range of tones and choices, from empathy to intimidation. Additionally, skills and character traits chosen at the start of the game, such as knowledge of herbalism or combat experience, unlock unique dialogue options, further influencing how the story unfolds. These choices don’t just impact the current conversation; they often have long-term consequences that can ripple through the rest of the journey, lending weight to every decision.Exploration is another core aspect of "Roadwarden," as players traverse through forests, mountains, and villages, each with its own lore, secrets, and quests. The peninsula is a diverse landscape filled with points of interest, from abandoned ruins and haunted woods to bustling villages and hidden shrines. Unlike many RPGs, "Roadwarden" doesn't rely on a map filled with waypoints; instead, players must learn to navigate based on their knowledge and intuition. Discovering new locations and uncovering the mysteries of the land feels rewarding, as each area holds history, hidden resources, or a chance to impact the lives of the inhabitants. The game encourages slow, deliberate exploration, where players absorb the world’s atmosphere and gather information that can shape future decisions.Visual and sound design are minimalist yet effective, using pixel art and atmospheric soundscapes that complement the game’s text-heavy style. While the visuals are simple, they’re crafted with care, using detailed illustrations to represent various scenes and encounters. The pixel art conveys the desolate beauty of the peninsula, reinforcing the sense of isolation and danger. The sound design is equally understated but impactful, with ambient sounds of rustling trees, distant wildlife, and eerie silences that enhance the immersive quality of the game. This minimalist approach allows players to focus on the narrative while providing just enough visual and auditory cues to create a vivid mental picture of the world they’re exploring."Roadwarden" also shines in its approach to world-building and lore, drawing players into a well-thought-out fantasy world that feels both mysterious and grounded. The peninsula is a land filled with ancient ruins, remnants of lost civilizations, and a complex political landscape. As players progress, they uncover details about the different factions, religions, and communities, each with its own beliefs, customs, and conflicts. The game doesn’t force-feed exposition; instead, players learn about the world naturally through conversations, environmental cues, and the choices they make. This organic approach to storytelling allows players to feel like true explorers, piecing together the history and culture of the peninsula at their own pace.In conclusion, "Roadwarden" is a masterfully crafted narrative RPG that succeeds through its immersive storytelling, complex choice mechanics, and richly detailed world. While it may not appeal to those looking for fast-paced action or cutting-edge graphics, the game offers a profound and atmospheric journey that rewards patience and curiosity. By combining a strong narrative with realistic survival elements and nuanced character interactions, "Roadwarden" creates an experience that feels both intimate and expansive, drawing players into the life of a Roadwarden navigating a land rife with mystery and peril. It’s a unique addition to the RPG genre, and for fans of interactive storytelling and exploration, it’s a journey worth taking.

_childDocuments_.review: Narrative is heavily saturated with feminist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at every corner. Grammar sucks. Punctuation sucks. Game loads way too slowly, and even the mouse itself lags. On this pixelated game where everything follows a script, the mouse itself ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lags. _childDocuments_.review: Could not recommend this game enough. I fell in love with the story and got very invested into the beauty this game has to offer in its art style and soundtrack. When it comes to gameplay: you can expect a lot of text based combat that's dependent upon your starting class and equipment you packed along the way with you. A well written conversation mechanic that not only makes you learn as much as you can before speaking to characters, but also makes you consider what you say and even if you should reveal some of the things you learn on your journey to people who have a vested interest in them for their own benefit (and sometimes even to another person's detriment). And the occasional quick random encounter that keeps you on your feet coupled with longer, more in-depth encounters that you can prepare for as in-depth or as balls-to-the-wall as you so wish :DIf text based adventures are your cup of tea, play the demo and see what I'm talking about. If you despise reading and wish for God to blind you for the curse of being able to string words together, hit that green button to play the demo and give it a try, it's something new and might still catch your interest with it's medieval fantasy world!Just finished my first ever playthrough and I can say for certain this is one of my all time favorite games now. I'll probably return back to this game in the future to give this game a second run as another class and maybe do it as a roguelike run where I won't savescum as often just to see what happens :PThank you for reading this word salad, give the demo a chance for an hour or so to see how you like it, and may the Wright guide your journey in peace and prosperity traveler!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: The smallest choices have the strangest impacts. Roadwarden is an incredible visual novel. I just can't say more than that, because that's the soul of it. Anything else would be inadequate. It takes an interesting look at community, tribalism, colonialism, the effects of economic domination and systems of reliance.... but mostly it's about being a roadwarden. And that's mostly about not getting killed and eaten! Among other things! Your personal agency is literally unmatched. Your choices are more far reaching than you think, and little action is wasted for an inquisitive mind. If you like puzzles, politics, earning peoples' trust, uncovering secrets, and weighing your safety against exploring just ONE MORE dark tile on the map... you'll like this game. I LOVE this game. A couple of minor annoyances/ quirks:The 'save' menu is separate from the quicksave/quickloads visible from your main UI screen. That's a function of it being made in ren'py, so it's not exactly unexpected. It's just easy to miss during the course of regular play. If you want to take advantage of multiple save slots for exploring branching narratives (and you can save at literally ANY point of dialogue), hit escape and go to save. I would recommend NOT save scumming as much as possible for your first playthrough. The writing is hilarious, poignant, and unexpected. Just trust it and see where your actions take you. But yeah. Save files. They exist. Second, the muted colors can be a bit hard on the eyes. I wish this game had some alternative color schemes for reading, since there is a LOT of it, but it's beautiful and matches the artwork, giving everything a very "legends and myths" type feeling. Something about those sepia tones just make you think of a story, told so many times over with the details changing.. There are two font options, one a pixel font and the other a serif, though I found both a little hard to read at some points. You can get a good look at your options from the game trailer though, so you won't be surprised. Finally, you can make notes!!! IN GAME!!! And you will use it!! Or else!!! Type- er- write! Your thoughts into your journal for easy reference later, when you're trying to remember that person who so-and-so told you about... er.. at that place.. uhh...Listen. Just trust me. You're gonna need it.10/10 Penicillin shmenicillin. We don't need that, we've got healing potions!

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic game. I've never been one for fantasy or the text RPG genera but I decided to give this one a shot and wow did it not disapoint.  You enter a stressful and hostile world with danger lurking every turn. The people of the land distrustful of strangers and weary of change. Now you as  the character get to carve your mark, befriend people, spy, carve your way through the heart of the forest.  All while learning the lore from the mainland and our dark little corner of the world.  I'd highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys a good book and wants to play something with choice and conciquense.

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a fascinating game. It is dripping with atmosphere and has an incredible soundtrack. Before this I hadn't played a game that so thoroughly assessed my ability to read, comprehend, and recall information. I made choices in this game that added up to real consequences that had potentially devastating outcomes. I played on the normal difficulty with no modifications and felt challenged. Even if you play on the easiest difficulty with every advantage you'll get sucked into the story and start counting every coin and ration with fervent care. Do yourself the favor, buy the game, turn off the lights, put some headphones on and lose yourself in the woods.From a friend who watched me play through the whole game: The story is incredible. Every decision you make matters and has a profound effect.

_childDocuments_.review: Wanted to like this, but when it takes three paragraphs to describe each one of multiple useless nooks and crannies in an empty, uninteresting location it really makes me wish I was playing Disco Elysium instead so that I would at least find those three paragraphs enjoyable to read.It also doesn't take long to become skeptical of the game's claims of RPG and "choices matter" style gameplay. These systems feel shallow right from the start, and reading through some of the negative reviews from people with longer playtime it seems to be an issue throughout the game that ends up making the whole thing feel more like a tedious choose-your-own-adventure book rather than a game. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't manage to stick with text-based games for very long, but this this game plays a unique magic trick that had me deeply engaged with the story the whole way through. Even though the game is -on an extremely basic level- almost exclusively pointless descriptions in text form and tedious micromanagement, all of it feels so meaningful to me personally. So *real*.'The game never stops inviting you to reflect on the mechanics of the world and the happenings within it. You get to decide whether you see your mount (and by extension animals in general) as a dear friend or a barely-tamed monster. After travelling with it for a while, you are asked to consider what color it is. Whatever you choose, you will be provided with some history and superstition related to that breed of horse. This prevents you from abstracting away the experience of riding horse into pressing the 'I want to go here'-button. One night, you are prompted to share your thoughts about what you think the moon is. (A creature? A rock in space? An eye?) By forcing you to have an opinion about the world, you are made to feel like a part of it in a way I haven't seen done before.I can greatly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys getting absolutely lost in even the most minute details of a fantasy world, to anyone who enjoys piecing together a world's history and internal politics, and to anyone who enjoys a game that requires you to take notes - but kindly takes those notes for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A smart choose-your-own adventure with excellent writing and atmosphere, flexibility for fleshing out your own character and backstory, plenty of choices that matter in the short and long term, many interesting characters and factions to navigate, and a great moody soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: Hi, if you've seen some of my other reviews you might be puzzled by this choice. Let me reassure you that this is worth every penny. Let me say stuff about the art direction/music first; it is unique, and I mean that with sincerity. It's got a clear goal of what the developer was trying to convey both visually but auditory as well. The music is top notch. I'm very happy to hear the developer's final update post included information to listen to it and credit the authors. The art while simple is comfy and while paints a picture also allows you to interpret or imagine it in a sense. The cozy hearth in the inn near the start vs the ruins you could sort of fix up. All dusty and covered in bugs. Not to mention what may come at night.The game operates on the simple text based adventure system I wish we had more of. This game is not just a throwback but a re-imagining of that genre. It has a plethora of options out the gate in different scenarios depending on your character background or skills or even kit. That bottle you didn't buy? Well because if you had it and some base alchemy knowledge you could make some useful potions. That fishing basket? You just got yourself a meal free of charge or some extra coin for no work or risk.The premise of the story is also full of moral consequences and physical consequences. Will you save the random man in the forest who's injured or ride along? Would you help the old lady and her sons at the lake? Will you clear out the goblins in a nearby ruin or leave them as they are too much for now? Perhaps you wish to seek a new faith or destroy that of other's in a crusade of a sense?After all you are here to report on the progress of the Island in 40 days (game has awesome tweaking feature; can set to 999 days). The status of settlements, their woes and fortunes, your own experiences as well. It has natives and they have their own faith like anyone else.I truly recommend you this game. It's simple yet makes you think, hard but in a fun way, interesting and cozy. Please make sure to review it as it really helps these solo devs/small teams. Good luck Warden.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I did pretty good on my first playthrough and survived to the end! You have 40 days to pull all of the loose threads you can find in the peninsula. This is a real role-playing game where you play as a Roadwarden, which is not quite a ranger or an adventurer but something in between. It's text-based but the writing and music did a perfect job in helping me build the scenes in my head. I couldn't help but imagine myself defending myself from giant cats in the dense woods with my wand and an axe.The game is oddly similar to a long vacation to a foreign country. On your first trip you're a tourist, but you become a better traveller as you learn more about its people, places, and things to do. I'm already thinking about what things I'd do better on my second trip back! That's really all there is to this game. I  recommend you buy this game especially if it's your first text-based RPG (like it was for me)!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A game that reminds me why I love fantasy writing and text-based games. Roadwarden is exceptionally well written and responsive to your decisions. Playing it carries the same feeling as a friend DMing a homebrew tabletop game they made specifically for you. The music is also shockingly amazing. I found myself playing the main road track in my head while working.Sodal is the best steed a roadwarden could ask for.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: The storytelling and world-building in this game is really well done. I'm at 17.5 hours in at the time of this review. Roadwarden uses a bunch of fun mechanics to drive the core-plot while allowing the player plenty of room to explore and get to know the world. I was hooked within the first 30 minutes of playing. This whole game , so if that doesn't sound enjoyable, this game might not be for you. The game uses passage-of-time, and a variety of health/status meters that you've got to maintain, but it's pretty easy to do so. If you enjoyed Disco Elysium, there's a good chance you'd like this game too. If you're unsure, give the demo a try first, but I'd wholeheartedly recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game has incredible depth to it... I am blown away by the sheer amount of writing that must've went into it.  It's full of interesting secrets and requires a bit of planning and strategy to be successful.  At the start of the game, you're given a 40 day time-limit to try and accomplish your goals of exploring the peninsula (with hopes of establishing it as a colony for your home city). The difficulty lies in making good choices, choosing who you ally yourself with, managing your time on foot as you travel, and taking calculated risks.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a good book. Once you finish it, you feel jealous for the people who has yet to beat it. I mean it.Extraordinarily creative set up, amazing story and storytelling, harsh but great mechanics. It's an indie game, so it doesn't last like its Red Dead 2, it is relatively short. But in the condensed of its campaign resides its beauty. You are working against the clock in the game.Truly, one of the best indie games, and one of the best rpgs i have ever played. My compliments to the chef.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game about time & resource management, morality, difficult choices, and novel experiences. I'm also amused and impressed by how differently the stories and gameplay prioritization changes between the classes, despite there only being negligible differences between the three. Overall I think if you like reading, you should give it a shot.My only critiques however:Inconsistencies in how Gale Rock's (A town) interactions are compared to every other town. It uses the 90's / early 2000's type text exploration system, where you put in keywords to look for things, as opposed to pretty much everywhere else where you see all of your available options. - Not saying it's a bad way to explore, just inconsistent with everything else. Where most places besides the dolmen it's just for information gathering / lore.I wish the skip tutorial option was a box you could select for the preset difficulty modes.TL:DR - GIVE ME MORE
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I write this review because I really do believe that this game deserves way more exposure. Roadwarden is the definition of a hidden gem. A heavily narrative driven game, the atmosphere created by its amazing writing and a great soundtrack is extremely captivating. Decisions matter, build up, and intersect each other in so many ways. Additional plus that there's three classes you can play as that add unique choices and systems to the game which adds to its replayability. If the store page remotely interests you, try the demo out! Sold me completely. Strong 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: In Roadwarden, you play a traveler hired by a big city to wander the "wild" peninsula outside of the cities, where beasts roam free and small settlements are few. As you wander these roads, you can choose what do do, make a fortune, help out villages in need, help form connections in the peninsula with the city. Just keep in mind, not everyone feels the same about Roadwardens...Roadwarden features:-Quests, lots of them-Loads of endings which change based on every little thing you do-Different religions to pick from, or none at all-Zombies-Lots and lots of text-Ethical and moral dilemmas a plenty -3 classes to pick fromPros:-Top notch worldbuilding, making you really care about every character, settlement, and story you come across-An amazing soundtrack that makes you feel fully immersed in travelling the roads -A pretty carved out economy and money system-Easy to pick up, no quick time events at all and infinite saves in case you want to undo a choice. -You can learn about the beasts of the game and fight them more effectively with the knowledge you haveCons:-The game is essentially a text adventure with pictures, so if you don't like reading a LOT then this might not be for you-Pretty basic class system with few mechanics-Somewhat unengaging combat, though not frequent
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Deep narrative game with a *lot* of meaningful decisions to make along the way, and only very few of them are clearly good/bad but instead generally have a lot of nuance. A surprising amount of content and things to find/explore as well, and despite my time with the game (~12 hours) apparently I still didn't find everything.I'd recommend it to anyone that enjoys games that let you roleplay characters the way you want them to, enjoy worlds where humans act with their own motivations but no one is really evil, and people who enjoy fantasy worlds where 'monsters' are just animals.Also, I recommend playing this on the easiest difficulty if you enjoy immersing yourself in fantasy worlds. There's still plenty of things you can screw up, but you have a lot more time to explore and just enjoy the world - which since world building is such a big part of why this game is cool actually makes me feel like I 'won out' by making that choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful text-based adventure paired with lovely pixel graphics in a fantastic frontier setting, where the monsters and wiilderness retaliates against too rapid human expansion.I would write a lengthy review but since this is so story-heavy, the only thing I want to say is that the writing is superb. If you want a game with a story you can immerse yourself in, this is perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I'm quite disappointed with the lack of character portraits. The writing is fine and does a good job describing who you're talking to, but the lack of any art other than item icons and areas is really noticeable. I guess I'd say this game lacks flair. It's very choose your own adventure book like. More book than game.I feel I'd really enjoy this game if there was more art to go along with the story. Your imagination is pulling damn near all the weight.Good game, not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Just an outstanding piece of work. A narrative/text-driven adventure that's fascinating, imaginative, and mysterious, with a beautiful soundtrack to boot. I love the title screen theme and find myself using the OST as background music for writing. The world-building is pretty stellar too. Looking forward to diving into the rest of the game and seeing what it has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: "Goblins? On  road?" It's more likely than you think.Roadwarden was a game that piqued my interest a couple years back and stayed on my wish-list for a very long time. That is, until my interest was piqued once again due to me playing some more text-based RPGs and let me say, this game delivers and I can see why this game is Overwhelmingly Positive.The immersion is very well done along with the world building, however I will say that at certain points characters including the player will sometimes say things as if they just happened and not expand on it. It's not that big of a deal to be honest, just felt a little off only a couple times. Speaking of characters, almost all the various people you meet are pretty unique in their own ways. Another thing to note is that when this game gives you multiple choices when getting attacked, responses, or talking it doesn't feel like it's forcing you to act a certain way or the other. I had little to no glitches while playing, it ran well.So long story short; it has good world-building, characters, lots of choices when deciding crucial moments, and is pretty much a good time.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A charming text based RPG with some illustrations. There's a lot here and a dynamic and shifting world that will surprise and delight you. It really nails a theme that I really love in game recently but have found hard to express, which is the feeling that your efforts are making the world of the game a little better, bit by bit. It's clearly a rather low budget affair, but there's a lot to love here.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game! I've played through the game twice at this point, as an alchemist and a mage. The story for this game is incredible, interactive, and pays attention to smaller things which you may have done and forgotten about, and at the end everything ties back together very nicely. The art and music are amazing as well. 10/10 would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: The writing broke my immersion very quickly. Everybody is basically a modern person for some reason stuck in a medieval world of swords, magic and scarcity. So sorry, but it's not how the real world and real people work. After reading the dialogs for almost 2 hours, my suspension of disbelief just gave out.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my first two playthroughs. In one, I played as a somewhat religious warrior who helped the peninsula but didn't fulfill some of my duties. In the other, I became a scholar turned hero, and embodied a successful roadwarden.Initially, I was concerned that the 40-day standard time limit is too short to ♥♥♥♥ around and find out, and that it would limit my exploration, but once I understood the game mechanics from my first playthrough, this wasn't an issue.If there were to be a sequel, I would suggest some minor improvements and additions, such as romance options, character portraits (retain this art style), and timed events. Overall, Roadwarden is a near-perfect game.Update: On my third playthrough as a scumbag wizard.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This is it, finally - a combination of the best of a novel and a game! And I only had to search for years! Something about Choice Of games always bugged me, maybe because they felt formulaic and young adult, like an editor was checking boxes on relationships, family issues, magic (always magic) and character growth. Those are all in Roadwarden, but here they feel natural, revealed by investigation and social interaction. Many fantasy novels read worse. This is the perfect mix of maturity and adventure, and it offers wonderful little tools to affect a melancholy-but-hopeful world. And all it requires is patience.Oh and pick a good name for your horse. It's a good horse.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Oddly specific audience I am reaching out to here, if reading books is tiring for you for whatever reason, but reading big strings of text in things like video games, comic books, or fanfiction is relaxing, boy howdy do I have the game for you. In all honesty, this game is a lot of text, but the dialogue is so interesting and steeped in that good almost hard to find in new stuff, truly classic fantasy genre aspect. And it has a lot of qualities unique to the game to balance it out! One of my all time favorite games, I find myself wanting to replay it over a long stretch of time again and really take my time with it. If you want to find an odd cozy comfort with an easy to identify with and understand fantasy setting, and do some good ol fashioned text rpg type gameplay, you will adore roadwarden.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: If you're even remotely considering buying this and wondering if its the game for you, it is.  It's exactly what you think it is.  Buy it right now.People have blown millions trying to make RPGs that are a tenth as engaging as this.  The music, the systems, the world... it's all fantastic.  The game is almost entirely text driven, but at the same time it's sparing and evokes a world rather than drowning the player in exposition.  The world and the characters in it just come alive in ways that again, far more expensive games utterly fail to pull off.I haven't been as interested in exploring since I played Subnautica, and I haven't been as intrigued by the mysteries in a game since I played Obra Dinn.  This is that good.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing text-based RPG. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical - a fully text driven game? So old school! _childDocuments_.review: Appearances are deceiving! Roadwarden is a charming RPG with themes of medieval politics and survival. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the Demo extensively, going through each of the three Class options and exploring what I could within the Demo's time limit of a few in-game Days. I had a lot of fun exploring the different options each Class brought to the game.Now that the full game has released, I decided to pick the Scribe Class, as it appeared fairly useful in the Demo. There are three difficulty settings, the easiest of which completely eliminates the full game's time limit of 40 in-game days. The hardest difficulty cuts this to 30. The UI is gorgeous, and the text can either be displayed as an old-school pixel font or a more elegant modern font. Everything is pretty intuitive, and it won't take more than a minute to navigate the entirety of the menus. The Journal option is SUPER in-depth, and a must for referencing names and places to NPCs. The ambient guitar music needs mentioning: it's not very repetitive, and it's actually quite soothing. You'll be hearing a lot of it, but with different tunes--occasionally some drums for battle, or bells/chimes for more pensive areas. It's a Choose Your Own Adventure game, with a lot of modern Quality of Life features (quick save/quick load, a fantastic repository of knowledge a few clicks away, an enormous Glossary for any lore-based terms, etc). I was told that this game has about 30 hours of gameplay, and I can believe it--especially if you play as the other two Classes, and the mechanics between the Mage, Scribe, and Fighter all vary greatly. I definitely recommend Roadwarden, especially for $10.EDIT: With some extra time to think about it, I wanted to add some things:There are some sections of the game where you will need to type out an answer to a prompt (I alluded to this feature at the end of my third paragraph). For example, you can ask an innkeeper for some gossip on characters you've met, or you may be in a strange room and the game will ask you to name what you look at. For the former, you can reference your Journal and look at Character names and type them into the prompt. For the latter, you'll need to use some detective skills and describe where in the room you'd like to look. It isn't always so simple: you can mention names to the innkeeper that aren't in your Journal yet that you only heard in passing, for example. The prompts want specific answers, but are relatively forgiving (a funny example is when a character asked me if I knew where they were from, and I had misspelled the name of their village... They corrected me, but said I was "close enough." I thought that was clever). In addition, I overlooked a key aspect of the game: the graphics themselves. It's all pixel art--a lot of greens, browns, yellows, greys... But the detail of the art is stunning. Coupled with the text, you can tell exactly what's going on in the landscape you see before you. It's also incredibly satisfying to reveal parts of the otherwise black map. There's a true sense of exploration here--neither you nor your character have any clue what you have gotten yourselves into, and it's nice to have some evidence of your progress after a particularly grueling day. There are also plenty of shortcuts you can create or discover, which will make your travels much more efficient: very important, if you're playing the normal or hard difficulty. This is kind of fun, so I'll come back to this when I keep finding important things to note. Still loving it! Try the demo!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is an incredibly well-done text-based adventure that keeps you engaged both in the story and in the choices you make. Choices really do matter in this game: the way you talk, the paths you take, the things you do...all of it shapes your character and your surroundings. I found myself emotionally invested in the characters and the endings I was giving them. I did my first run as a scholar (I like learning lore) and am so happy I made that choice!This game is pretty replayable, but you may find yourself skipping through the text of things you've already read before. Good news though! There's different ways to interact with folks, which allows for you to see new sides of characters in later runs. If you play in character, that will help too! I love how this game encourages you to make up lore about your own character, their values and religion, and their environment - which all appear on your character sheet as you "share" that information with others. I really, really enjoyed that. It allowed for me to better create my own character's story as well as uncover the story of the npcs. I found that forty days was just about perfect for me and my missions. Due to the lack of an easily visible day counter, though, you can easily waste a few days travelling around...I'd probably be better about managing my time if there was one. I wish there was an easy way to check how many days you've been there (other than the dreams telling you that you're at the halfway point or only have five days left). I strongly recommend folks play this, especially if they love other text-based games or if they enjoy games where the choices are vital to the story. I'll certainly be playing this game again!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Well written RPG text adventure. I really like the world, texts are not too long and interesting. Enjoyed characters that can be found, and feel there is a potential for replayability due to three different classes for the main player.The only disadvantage I see is that the way the game is done really promotes save spamming, which is hard to avoid as a player.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid game, with a few caveats. After having completed Roadwarden on its middle "standard" difficulty, I'd highly recommend playing on easy/casual. Standard doesn't change much except add a 40 day time limit to your game, something I personally hated.Easy recommend if you're okay with reading a lot. Pixel art is gorgeous and goes great with the presentation, soundtrack is great though the limited track selection did start to grate towards the end of my playthrough. Very interesting world built entirely through dialogue in a way that feels natural.Really my only complaint is the time limit. It sucks, and I ran into it hard at the end of my playthrough, rushing through the last couple quests I wanted to complete and running out of time anyway. Time pressure in the game is otherwise almost non-existent and the time limit feels tacked on to add some kind of urgency to a game that is otherwise pretty relaxed. This feels strongly like a game that wants you to take your time and really dig into it, and the time limit feels so completely at odds with the rest of the game that I have to wonder why it was included. It genuinely feels like it ruined my playthrough and retroactively soured a lot of my time with the game, and if I'd had the option to turn it off in the final stretch I would have done so without a second thought.Despite this really long rant about what a pain the time limit is, I strongly recommend Roadwarden. Despite selling itself as a dark fantasy game it neatly dodges many of dark fantasy's pitfalls, presenting a world that, while harsh and unforgiving, has bright spots of humanity that are a real joy to explore and interact with.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Masterfully written. The world is full of characters and the setting is so rich and the music makes the experience truly immersive. The amount of content that's been crafted so well is truly impressive, and I can recommend this to anyone at this price point. The text is more engrossing than most novels I've read, and I look forward to what the developers make in the future. My only complaint is the lack of nighttime art for the environments, because the static ones used for villages do get old, and some more variety and change to make it truly feel lived in would go a long way.Overall, this is a fantastic experience and one of my favorite text based adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the writing was overly verbose and difficult to tell what is important what isn't.Also difficult to gauge how much of a problem something could become or what the outcome might be of a certain situation.Combat isn't interesting. You might end up dying in one hit, you might end up losing nothing at all. For exaple: you charge at a bunch of goblins, kill one .... And then run away? I'm feeling fairly confident but apparently my character isn't. Then there's the why-part. Why am I doing this? You get to choose your own goal to some extent but it didn't quite motivate me to move on. You run into certain situations along the way which automatically turn into quests. Why? I guess it's because you're a roadwarden and you feel a need to stick your nose in everyone's business but why should I care?

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely have enjoyed playing this game. Its perfect for those who like a more story driven option.  I'm not much of an achievement hunter, but trying to uncover all the possible outcomes of the game is what keeps me playing. If there was any criticism, I do wish that there was greater variation in the character interactions or choices. It feels like 90% of the game is the same each playthough no matter the character or class meaning you need to perform the same interactions with the same NPC and conversations are repetitive. Good if you want to complete the challenge modes and speed run the game, I guess.  After 2 rounds, I'm already 75%+/- complete so after another 2 there won't be much replay ability. Despite that, I would like to keep my eye out for future games from this developer. I would love to play something similar again, maybe with some different class abilities and something along the lines of "randomly generated" towns within the map. Say there are 15 'faux towns' with NPC's and each time you start a save it takes a random sampling of 4-5 of those created towns. It would certainly add to interest and longevity if you could look forward to meeting different people, having different tasks, different interactions between villages, and different conversations every time you played.  A LOT more programming, I know; it would be a monster of a game, but it seems there's a lot of positive feedback around games like these and I think with added variation you could really bump up that price quite a bit and people would willingly pay it.

_childDocuments_.review: Text, environmental images, dice rolls, and music make for a fun role-playing game. Resources, stats, and time management influenced a lot of my decisions more than anything else. Would recommend for the engaging experience.
