_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is not a game, it's an e-book that's been dumped on Steam masquerading as a game.  As a visual/interactive novel, this doesn't feature any notable gameplay, it's just a lot of clicking through badly written dialogue that would never have been accepted or published in print, which poses the question, "How did something this badly written end up on Steam?".  When someone hoping to become an author is unable to get published in print, they spend $100 and dump their high school fan-fiction onto Steam, under the guise of a game.  This e-book was slapped together with the godawfully bad RenPy Visual Novel/E-Book construction kit, so just like no professional writing took place here, no professional game development took place either, it's just a product of filling out templates in the construction kit.This E-book features Choose-Your-Own-Adventure elements where you make some decisions that don't do anything to change the fact this is just an E-Book.  Nobody finished reading a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book and said "Boy, what a great game I just played!".   Because E-books aren't games.  And neither is this.In fairness the developer did spend a bit more time with Ren'Py than your typical asset flipper fanfic writer does, as you get a few more of Ren'Pys very shallow pool of functionality available like a couple of meaningless stats and a meaningless inventory system (that could have just been tracked internally with the Ren'Py CYOA stuff going on), so at best one might be kind and compare this to a Steve Jackson Fighting Fantasy book, but then that would be insulting to Steve Jackson, he was successful. Visual novels/e-books are tedious at best... imagine the best novel you ever read, be that Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy or 2001: A Space Odyssey or Twilight (if you have terrible taste in literature), but then translate that to a format where the words dribble out and you have to click your mouse every time you wanted to read the next sentence, instead of just turning the pages. You'd think it was garbage.Now imagine that experience, but with much worse writing (because if these guys could write professionally, they'd be published authors and this would be on shelves in bookstores, and they wouldn't have to pay Valve $100 to self-publish this on Steam), and you have your average Steam e-book.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the E-book is extremely low as a result.While there are options to change the resolution for the E-Book, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the E-Book, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for readers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Roadwarden has the ridiculous price of $11 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games (real games, not E-books).  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given you can get better quality books and comics for free online or from public libraries, or from bookstores for a fraction of the price of this "game".  Steam isn't a comic book store, neither is it Netflix, it's for games.  Your gaming rig is not a Kindle.  It's impossible for me to recommend things to PC gamers that aren't really games.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is my new gold-standard for RPGs. The combination of having to juggle multiple resources (food, money, health, and even personal hygiene for social encounters) and getting to choose a personal background and goal to pursue while playing "main story" of the game are two things that really elevate Roadwarden to being one of the best games I've played in a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, with deep emphasis on forming and understanding relationships between various groups of thought. I liked how the interactions weren't solely "he says this, she says that" but also describing discrete movements such as "showed palms facing up, stormy eyes, scowl, walked heavily, voice cracks, kept hands hidden behind back, etc.". Roadwarden does an amazing job of describing the world around you, from how the people are, to what the environment looks and feels like. My play through lasted ~41hrs and i was able to complete and experience all interactions in the game while playing under the difficulty setting of normal (40 day limit). In the end I had about 15 days to spare before closing my journey. Your choices in the game matter greatly; from your choice to how you respond to people, to what your personal thoughts are, and especially to how you administrate your time and make the most of the day. The game is all about reading and interpreting situations based on what you read, as such, if you enjoy reading this game is highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I am so obsessed with this game. The art is beautiful and the storytelling is so immersive. The sound design really gets you into the scene. The writing is incredible. One of my fav interactive fiction/choices matter games!!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only ~3 hours in so far but am having a fantastic time with Roadwarden.The music, ambient sounds and descriptions paint a fantastic mental image of the areas the character goes through and it really feels like the next step up from the Choose Your Own Adventure books I grew up on!Other than a couple of _tiny_ grammatical errors, I have nothing negative to say about Roadwarden at all. If you think you'd be interested in a text-based adventure I don't think you can do any better than this!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A great, atmospheric and grounded RPG, mostly about travelling between ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ villages where no one trusts you, in a solid low fantasy setting.People you meet have very real and (in a good way) boring needs and wants.The world is small enough where you're never unsure WHO to talk to and it's all about HOW to get them to talk - but also big enough that 20 hours in there are multiple places I didn't get to explore fully or at all.If you like what you see on the store page preview images, you will not be disappointed.Most of the time the simplicity leaves the perfect amount of room to the imagination while keeping you on track.Though, I do disagree with some of the other reviews when it comes to replayability.Even though you do sign up for a lot of reading when you buy this game, its a lot of reading and small enough map, where you would re-read 80% at least.The only 'negative' that comes to mind is that the world has a lot of strange creatures in it, and the game has images of the surroundings and such already. The choice to not include pictures of the creatures is a slight disappointment.A great adventure and well worth the full price of 11€.4/5

_childDocuments_.review: Tldr--Fantastic game if you like reading, not so much if you don't. Great attention to detail, its as easy or hard as you want it to be, you are basically Aragorn with an axe. Oh and it makes you feel like a detective. Worth every penny.Great game, especially for the price. It plays like an interactive fantasy novel. You are a Roadwarden--basically a ranger hired by the merchant guilds of the larger cities to keep the roads and wilds safe for travel. You are sent to a very inhospitable place where humans are absolutely not the top of the food chain and are tasked with gathering information about the peninsula, negotiating potential trade deals between the locals and the merchant guild, and finding out what happened to your predecessor.The harder difficulties have a time limit. You need to get everything done within 30-40 in-game days so you need to be smart about the routes you take, the trades you make, and the risks you gamble on. They can actually be a little stressful at times, but in a way that's fair and manageable. At the time of this writing I am about a quarter of the way through my 40 day playthrough and while resources were scarce at first, I am finally at a point where I am getting my feet under me after having explored most of the peninsula and unlocked the map.The easiest difficulty has no time limit so you can just focus on the story, so this game can be enjoyed by a wide variety of players.I will say that in the very beginning, you are faced with a choice that you literally can't refuse. You come across your first camp and the game asks if you want to check it out or avoid it in case it is a trap, but the option to avoid it leads to the game telling you that you can't. At first, I took this as a negative and thought I was being railroaded. However, as time went on I learned that even when you can't do exactly what you want, all options reveal at least some information about the world. Even when you are denied, the game will use that dialogue to expand on the game's universe with more flavor text. Once I realized that, it took the sting out of the illusion of choice. It is just another vehicle for the player to learn about the extra fluff in the world. That being said, there actually is quite a bit of choice. In fact, its an impressive amount considering the game's price point. The attention to detail is great and this game truly does rely on your problem solving skills. There's plenty of detective work to be done and the game rewards you for being extra thorough.All in all, I recommend this game to anyone who likes reading and fantasy novels, or if you like resource management games in the vein of Oregon trail.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure if I would enjoy this sort of game. While I sadly don't, this was certainly the right game to try for this. The writing is excellent, the mechanics simple enough to interact well with whatever scenario the writer comes up with and the limited visuals reminds me greatly of reading fantasy books. Many things are never shown, like the omnipresent "beasts" but you can imagine them all to well from the vivid descriptions. The entire game is very stylish and feels wellmade. The introduction is pretty good as well, I didn't feel lost most of the time. Even the replay value seems rather good with three very distinct classes that so far had quite alot of unique interactions and stuff. The only faults I could point to, is that some interactions/ places can flow confusingly and timed quests being really really obnoxious. "Hey, we go hunting in like 9 days, be sure to be here then." Like what? I guess it's fine, you can traverse the entire map in like a day, but still, this is annoying.For me this really doesn't work as a video game as i often feel powerless, unable to plan ahead or "play better" in the moment, while simultaneously giving me far too much freedom and control to be engaging as a story, but I suppose that is simply a personal incompatibility with the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, perhaps the best I have ever experienced. _childDocuments_.review: An absolute gem of the game. Having finished my second play through (of at least 3 or 4 more to come) I can say that I have enjoyed the experience this game provides quite a significant amount more than most Triple-A titles released within the last 5 years minimum. (EXTREMELY light spoilers ahead for gameplay effects)The experience this game provides puts you directly into the mind and soul of an adventurer who has the odds stacked against them, yet prevails. Travel the lands, encountering nightmarish scenarios that batter and bruise you, and send you limping back to the nearest tavern or town, aching for a brew and some place just to be able to lay your weary head for a night. Your encounters only provide you with experience and skills that you can use in your next encounter with all of the secret bonuses you get to rolls as you play the game that come and feel very natural for the kind of person your character is.You also are able to gain tangible knowledge that not only affect secret chance-based rolls in the background, but open up entirely new scenarios between yourself and the creatures that prowl the mysterious Peninsula, as well as the people who inhabit it. Talk to the locals, figure out secrets and knowledge only certain people have, unravel mysteries and intrigue, slay/drive off the creatures who inhabit the land, or attempt to make your peace and subdue them through nonviolence; however you want your character to act you usually have that option.Roadwarden is a game meant to be played on the normal difficulty, which is under a time limit that will take, on average, 5-10 hours to complete. There *IS* a story-mode where the time limit is a non-factor and encounters are easier, but that takes away from the experience that is Roadwarden. Some people find the time limit to be too stressful or a detriment to the experience, but the reality is that the world and area that Roadwarden is set in are exactly that: Almost insurmountably stressful and dangerous. However, as you travel and make decisions, your choices have a tangible impact on the world around you, significantly reducing that stress and danger through one method, or another. Travel times between well known places decrease as you solve problems plaguing the land and make allies, traveling during certain weather conditions either benefit or harm your chances at certain actions or traveling, but you can reduce the impact that random events have on the world through your own actions.The game is not without flaw, of course, but they are so few and far between that they won't bother most people. To give an example, there are certain areas where you have to type out when looking for specific things or people, and searching for relevant information can be somewhat difficult or not entirely accurate, but if you spend the time to think critically, you should be able to figure it out. Another example being that solutions to a few certain problems are *quite* vague, but as long as you're open to exploring and leaving almost no stone unturned, you should figure them out eventually, and if need be, come back on your next play through with that knowledge already in hand and bust out these problems with little issue. These problems, as stated, don't come up often and don't detract from the overall excellent experience.Overall, Roadwarden lends itself well to avid readers and explorers. You will stumble, you will fail, but you will learn to prosper. Roadwarden lends itself, as well, to something important for a game so short: Replayability. Your first play through, you will likely mess up. You may not even get what could be considered a "Good Ending." As you learn from your first play through, however, if you're anything like me, you will become determined to change the outcome. You will play through again, and possibly more than a few more times, using your previous knowledge on how to handle problems and interact with the people of the North to quicken your goals and unravel more and more of the mystery that surrounds the entire peninsula.Verdict: 93/100
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Some may say the text-based RPG genre is dead. Some would be wrong. Roadwarden is proof that, with a compelling story, immersive world, and endless choices, even a genre as old as the classic text-based adventure can be compelling. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very good little game that desperately needs another coat of polish. The core mechanics are quite good, the storytelling is mostly excellent, and the scope is pretty much perfect. I enjoyed my time with it, and I do recommend it. However. The translation/localization has many errors, some large enough to completely derail a scene or confuse what's actually going on. Sometimes it's not even a translation issue, just a piece of the description being completely left out. The game mechanics are also poorly explained, and I found myself getting screwed over in the beginning because of the lack of transparency. I was also quite saddened overall by the depressing tone of the story. You can do some good and make some friends, bu the game has sooo many more opportunities to be selfish or destructive. And casting a shadow over everything is the fact that you're working for a colonial hegemony that would like nothing more than to spread its rule over this rural land that you're now responsible for. Added to the number of rude, mean, cruel, and sometimes evil NPCs that populate the game, it does become hard to feel good about your overall impact. All that said, when the prose, characterizations, and storytelling isn't being hampered by lack of polish it is very absorbing. The characters are all distinct and fully fleshed, and the peninsula has a life all of its own. The world, monsters, religions, accents - so many things bring it to life. Put that on top of some very solid mechanics (once you understand them) and overall I am glad I played the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: When this game initially came out, I was playing it the most compared to any other game at the time.It's similar to a choice matter game, and the reason why I say "similar" is due to some actions - at least when I was playing - did not seem to have any meaningful impact or influence. I enjoyed the narrative driven aspect and seems to pull me in to the story better, compared some triple A games. The music is also fitting of the setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that I know I will never find again, and I hate that. Everything is done with the maximum attention to detail, creativity, story, atmosphere, the list goes on. Think of whatever you want in a game, story, and journey and be ready to be impressed. I'm so glad that there are people out there willing and able to put their all into what will be labeled a niche experience because I can't imagine whats being missed by everyone who hasn't taken their first step as a Roadwarden!
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: "We have nae to give and do ne wish to trade with outsiders."Roadwarden presents itself rather straightforwardly. You are a roadwarden, a person hired to manage roads in an isolated peninsula, a stranger to the people who inhabit it and as such, are very often rebuked by the townspeople when you barge into their homes and begin asking questions. You will not have the trust of people you speak to initially and it takes time, work and much conversation for people to open up to you. The game also lets you starkly know that you will return back to the city of Hovlavan within 40 days and use your time carefully. However, there is a great deal to explore, many past events and relationships to discover and the fate of the peninsula to decide. The game is engaging and doesn't hold your hand, forcing you to choose what you wish to accomplish within 40 days. It constantly remind you that you are only an outsider and you won't have your way in a grand fashion as you have with many other RPG games, and are just the messenger before the flood gates open. There are a few complaints I have; Old Pagos and the white marshes really felt underwhelming in terms of the interactions you can have and the number of villagers present to interact with. There are some other choices which could have been fleshed out far more, namely .  However, overall, this game is a gem and I recommend it for people who enjoy text based adventures relying on imagination. I do hope for a DLC to expand on the peninsula or even a second game where the player can play a more centred role and interact far more deeply with characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: It's a Choose Your Own Adventure game bordering on visual novel with well integrated, but small RPG elements and very good writing.✔ addictive atmosphere - I  the roadwarden and I feel like I lost something precious after finishing my adventure✔ writing - both worldbuilding and the multifaceted characters living in it✔ economy - it never feels like you are so rich that currency becomes worthless✔ story/writing itself is often the reward for overcoming challenges, it's realistic and worth it❔ most of you time is spent reading descriptions and dialogues, occasionally making decisions and travelling to new/known locations. That's the "game" and I personally loved it, but your mileage may vary❔ there is not much real rpg-like progression, it's mostly about what equipment and knowledge you carry❔ the pictures add a lot to the writing, but it's a shame they are generally top-down maps or landscapes and never show the characters you encounter❔ I feel like there is some political influence that the writing is pushing in the created world when it comes to gender roles. A lot of it could be explained by , which exists and permeates everything in this world, but definitely not everything. And the game doesn't try to justify any of it, you just have to accept that despite all differences between the villages and their inhabitants they are on the same page regarding this and it's not even worth mentioning. It's not handed badly, definitely not ham-fisted, but could have been better. Exploring possible societies from other worlds is great, but there should be reasons for  could have made them so different✘ the world is smaller than I expected. You can split the game into two halves - first is mostly about discovery, when your map is blank and second about solving as many of the issues/quests you obtained. It's a very rough split, but the first part definitely had more  in it. That's not to say that the second part was bad mind you✘ the game mostly avoids it, but there were some cases where I wanted to use something I had in an encounter, but it was not accounted for by the creatorsIt's the best game of this type I have ever had the pleasure to experience. Play it if you feel like reading something with choice/management gameplay on top. If you don't want to read then stay away - screenshots are very honest.

_childDocuments_.review: i really, really love this game.like a lot of people i'm sure, i was nearly put off this game because of the large walls of text and the game looking like a slow crawl. but after playing it, i had fallen in love with it. i've recommended this game to a handful of my friends already, even though i hadn't even "beaten it."i think this game is probably better if you know a little bit going into it (i had gone in entirely blind), but i don't think that's necessarily a bad thing. this game can be a challenge, but it's meant to be - the life of a roadwarden, in its own description, is not easy. as with everyone else's suggestions, i would definitely recommend starting without a time limit. i just would also take it with a small grain of salt, because i've been having a lot of fun playing with the limit on even if i don't necessarily know what i'm doing still.this game envelopes and swallows me, i can get lost between the words so easily and it's beautiful to me. i love the writing style and i really enjoy the exploration and uncovering of things (including things i already knew). the setting is entirely wonderful, i love opening this game and being greeted with the soft music and whatever ambiance i had left on my save. it immediately draws me in when i click continue or new game.it wasn't my first text adventure, but it was the first one i fell in love with.

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice game. Slow however still exciting. Simple yet rich. I'm a fairly seasoned reader and the writing is not at all unbecoming, but rather impressive although its modesty. Lately I've leaned towards less intensive games, making the gaming experince a more restful one, and this game suits that need really well.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like you will either be enraptured by this game or drop it as soon as you realize what exactly it is. Its reading, a whole ton of reading, weighing options, more reading, time management, reading, item gathering, managing relationships, and its all wrapped in even more reading.I love this game, and how its story allows you to go about your day as you see fit with so much freedom for a text adventure game. The start of the game is rather unfriendly as you don't have many resources and many people do not enjoy outsiders, but give it some time and you will be able to make your own way in the treacherous lands laid before you.I struggle to have anything truly negative to say about the game outside of a few instances where I felt there were not enough varied dialogue, and I feel like sometimes there are just too many questions to ask, and quite a few scenarios where not asking a question can block you of from something almost completely unrelated, so ask as many questions as you can, for the most part.Apparently the game has quite a few grammatical errors, but I didn't notice them till my friend pointed them out, and it didn't detract from my experience at all, and the weirdly written speech of the accents improved it.This game is definitely a Niche, but I'm so glad I stumbled upon it. Highly recommended to people who can stand the massive walls of text.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sad, funny, and achingly beautiful at times. It doesn't hold your hand, and it expects you to closely consider how you see and understand what you're reading. I love it. I understand that it may not be for everyone; the premise of a text based game in this day and age places it very much in a niche, but it has good music and excellent writing.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: never played any text-based games until this point, so I was sure this was a game i would skip over. it was on sale, and i wanted a single-player game to play. this game has far exceeded my expectations. the more you play, the more interested you get into the lore and the complex interpersonal relationships between the villages in the peninsula. would recommend to any and everyone. easy to understand and easy to dive into
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

An incredible care put into the scope and stakes of a low fantasy setting such that you always feel like one small traveler, while still conveying the larger scale motions of the world as a whole and making the things you participate in mean something to that whole.Also i really like when people in the game are astonished by seeing a horse for the first time. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A very good text adventure with pleasantly tight resource management to prop it up: mistakes are not unforgiving but not free of consequences as well.Character creation choices affect your playthrough in a meaningful way, the way you interact with other npcs matter and time limit that restricts your entire adventure helps with pacing a lot.If you're not afraid of reading text and like a good adventure, you are unlikely to be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good text-heavy adventure game. Not really an RPG in the traditional sense, as the progression is more about inventory management than stats. Really nice UI/UX, relaxing music, good writing. Took about 7 hours for my first playthrough. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: What a perfect game. The type that gives you the tools to chart your own path. Essentially a story book game with great music and good art. Amazing script and dialogue that allows you to visualise events clearly. Likeable characters that you feel attached to and want to help. Awesome conflicts and encounters with an amazing main story line and side quests that make you feel proud after completing them. I didn't expect to find interest in such a game but Roadwarden really drew me in. Loved it. Asterion you bastard, you were a hard one to find.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting misteries. Great roleplay without relying on cheap "hats" for your PC. First playthrough will be relatively short if you're playing one of the timed dificulties, but it incentivices replayablility.Overall a great take on text-based adventures that understand how to be more than white text on a black background.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is missing a lot of lore necessary to make the world believable. For example, the characters presented are not plausible within a primitive society stuck in a constant battle for survival. Historically (in the real world) males fight and dominate hierarchical power structures. For some reason the author flips this truth upside down but does not give any story explaining why so many females are in combat and at the top of the power ladder. To be believable, either the rules of this world must be greatly different or important historical facts are missing. Your main character doesn't even notice this oddity even though your character comes from a more civilized part of the world. Unfortunately this breaks immersion throughout the story. There are other flaws, but that example is repeated the most often.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: The game is incredibly fun, and extremely addicting. It's mostly story based, but it does have a sweet and simple gameplay loop that keeps you moving through it. That being a moving around between settlements and ruins to heal, repair, eat, and sleep. My only real complaint is that I wish there was more content. A sequel or DLC could do this game nicely.The story and setting is also extremely solid, along with being unique from most fantasy settings. You can very easily take this whole setting and turn it into a unique DND campaign. (Any DMs, take note)
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is a gamified Choose Your Own Adventure book, tarred and feathered with sepia and pixels. The old school aesthetic combined with RPG system mechanics lured me in, then I got hooked by the low fantasy worldbuilding that's beautifully complimented with weighty roleplaying consequences. You're placed in the boots of a freshly trained, and soon to be overworked, civil servant on horseback armed with an axe and a customer service oriented focus. The primary objective is to uncover why contact was lost with the previous Roadwarden, who was assigned to patrol a peninsula at the unmapped edges of the kingdom's frontier.Class choice significantly changes your available approaches to problem solving, and a 'personal quest' of sorts is selected to provide another narrative angle with its own benefits and pitfalls. There's 40 days on the clock to accomplish your goals before the region locks down for the winter, so avoid becoming like the bodied players in the negative reviews and manage your time wisely whilst roaming the untamed wilds. Don't hyper focus on a single region, act like the militant postal service you're equipped to be and macromanage your neighborhood route. Engage in local politics, accept Jesus Christ into your heart, condone necromancy, consider the social ramifications that misdemeanor and felony aren't in this fantasy lexicon yet, then die violently because a bunch of flesh eating gibbons induced a full body stroke with magical screams. Spoiling any of the characters or plot points would be a great injustice, but know that this meat's dripping with flavor. Just as a note-- using a fighter with no guides, I finished up everything my heart desired with a whole week remaining, and my play was definitely not super optimal 100% of the time.Definitely try to make the most out of your first go-- it might be because I'm not the typical visual novel player, but for me, this is one of those titles that can only truly be experienced once since prior game knowledge invalidates much of the mystery and intrigue. My only real complaint, and I'm gonna be really vague to not spoil anything, is that there are some potential forced sequences where the player may be given the impression that a particular plot point can only be resolved a certain way, however, the game's epilogue does allow the player autonomy to choose a different outcome as long as the proper conditions are met. There could have been a better way for the game's systems to account for a player's potential shifting motives but, ultimately, it isn't a huge deal. Just put some faith in the system.By the way, game is woke AF and would be on that Steam woke content blacklist if its moderators could read.

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes me back to when I first go into mythical stories like Lord of the Rings. To see a written tale as more than just words, but a world, is truly something difficult to accomplish. Yet, Roadwarden is able to crates a world that feels lived in, but also drags you into it, and more than makes you feel as if you've been part of it for years. All of this is thanks to the outstanding writing and care that has gone into this project. Yes, there is going to be a lot of reading in this game, and I can understand if that can turn some people away, but at least for me, Roadwarden proved it more than capable of keeping me reading for hours and hours without a hint of boredom. Of course, there's also the RPG elements that are simple, yet are perfect for what this game is. Another thing I have to mention is the game play loop, which is so well tuned, that despite being, at it's heart, a bunch of sides quests. They all fit together perfectly and keep you more than busy. Not once was I left with nothing to do or felt the quests were boring.But hey, and even if you're still hesitant of buying this game after I just spilled my heart out for it, wait for it to go on sale. 11 bucks is already a steal for this masterpiece, but you can't say no to 8.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Scratched a retro itch I didn't know I had.It's a very pleasant adventure game-♥♥♥-visual novel with a lot of replayability if you go into it blind, due to a number of different decisions (which do, in fact, matter) to make and people to please (or displease).This isn't a crapsack world, but it's not a happy high fantasy one, either. The woods are dangerous and  growing more so by the day. Tightly knit villages are doing everything they can to survive, and the Roadwarden can aid them, or try and steer them from a questionable path.The casual attitude toward queerness and gender was really refreshing for a world that comes off as pre-medieval, with a pseudo-Christian church slowly absorbing Pagan communities.I love the pixel art but it almost makes me wish the soundtrack were equally retro. The relaxing acoustic guitar occasionally got repetitive but was atmospheric and pleasant enough that I wouldn't call it an issue.Highly recommend for visual novel readers and fans of very retro PC gaming.

At the time, the game was so new and the ost hadn't been released yet other than very barebones recordings of the opening menu theme, which was still amazing to find. Now, I can enjoy all the music. Either way, the memory brought me back to the store page. I realise I never left a review, and I wish I had at the time when my thoughts were fresher, but I have this: the game left a huge impression on me. _childDocuments_.review: VERY engrossing game. It's like being able to dive directly into a good fantasy novel, but instead of the story laid out before you, you get to help shape it. I already completed a playthrough, but I know I missed so much. I played on the intermediate difficulty first, but I want to do a non-timed playthrough for story purposes. Each choice you make leads to so many different outcomes, both immediately and at the end of the game. Choose one dialogue option, and you'll wind up getting praised. Choose another, and you'll wind up getting beaten, tied to your horse while you're unconscious, and sent out into the wilderness. There is no good vs evil, and how you interpret things actually matters since you're helping shape the narrative. Does that make your interpretation factual? Not necessarily, but isn't that life itself? Truth and goodness are often in the eye of the beholder.

_childDocuments_.review: absolutely fantastic. has great writing, and a truly impressive atmosphere considering how few tools the developers gave themselves to work with. it really shows how much difference a static image and music can make in fostering a deeper connection to a world than a book might, or at least in making that connection more efficiently. by the way, that's what this game is: a book, accompanied with some static scenes, music, stat & inventory mgmt, and most importantly, player interactivity (specifically you can not only make decisions in dialogue but also navigate your roadwarden throughout the game's world).the best parts of this game for me were uncovering the various secrets the world holds (i won't say any more), really feeling like i existed in the game's world, and being able to slowly peel back layers of history in the settlements and of characters.for me, this game is either second place or tied for first with elden ring for goty 2022. also overall better than pentiment and citizen sleeper in my opinion, and i liked those games a lot. i only played a little bit of norco, so i can't judge it against that.

_childDocuments_.review: Received as a gift from a friend.Good game. Well written and designed. Pays dividends to be attentive to details.Very text heavy, so be prepared to be fully immersed and devote time solely to it. However, I found myself getting over the volume of text once I really got into it. I was also surprised by how slowly invested I was getting into the world of Roadwarden too! By the end of the game, I was kind of left feeling wanting for just a bit more, but I think the length of the game is very satisfying.The beginning was a bit difficult but once you start clearing some quests, you'll get a lot of money that will smooth the experience and make it less stressful.Only criticism I have is that while it's great that the game rewards you for listening and being attentive to dialogue and other bits of information, it is also frustrating that you're relying on remembering that bit of info. A lot of the information can be synthesised which is great, but after you've had a long day and are jumping back into the game after a day or 2 away from it, having to remember something isn't what I want to do to unwind.Definitely recommend if you're into RPGs and are okay with those that are text-heavy.

_childDocuments_.review: You've heard of walking simulators, now get ready for a reading simulator!If this game was a book, I would have finished it in one sitting, or as close to one sitting as possible. As it was, I finished it in like 15 hours spread across three sessions, one of which stretched well into the wee hours of the morning. At some point I would love to replay it and focus more on a different part of the North than I was inclined to on my first playthrough.The world is beautiful, imaginative, the characters are extremely real, and the writing is very good. It has a realistic/gritty fantasy feeling without being too depressing (well... I'm sure it's possible to make decisions that lead the world to an extremely depressing state... but it's not consistently depressing). The portrayals are thoughtful and sometimes endearing, sometimes exciting, sometimes philosophically provocative.Really awesome tabletop RPG + novel + choose-your-own-adventure book type feeling. I don't read novels super well these days, but I used to love reading fantasy novels as a kid, and it was easy for me to focus on the narration.Would love love love to see more content from these creators.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, where to begin? First off, I'd like to say that this game was absolutely spectacular. I purchased it and sat down to play until the first good stopping point, to get a feel for the game. But the beautiful music, incredibly detailed pixel-art scenes and gripping story drew me in, and before I knew it I'd been playing for 11 hours and had beaten the entire game, though I am sure I missed many secrets and quests, and I know for a fact I missed several characters in one of the towns. And thus, I will definitely be embarking on another playthrough with another one of the three classes. The story is really intriguing, and the way details were presented made me hunger for more, searching constantly for more information from each character, exhausting every dialogue option. There are moral dilemmas presented at various point in the game, and while I attempted to play all sides during my first playthrough, in the future I will definitely be choosing a more specific and concrete "character" next time. It takes place entirely in text, so be aware that enjoying this game will require concentration, especially as there are countless names, places, and quests presented to you, and the game's journal and archive system doesn't have all the details. But, if you are on the fence, definitely consider picking this game up.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A treat scratching my itch for something between a really good book and a game. More freedom to explore a story than a book, but without sacrificing the narrative due to gameplay limitation. The game is quite simple, and is more or less an interactive novel, sprinkled in tidbits of resource management and decision-making, at time it can be vague, but with some effort taking notes and immerse yourself in the game world ( which is incredibly easy and fun, considering how well the worldbuilding is presented ) it can be easy to work through. The people in the world felt real, with their own struggles and drives, creating a magical story through the player's own imagination and the writer's masterful choices of words.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Been playing the first few hours of the game, I think this is an excellent deal for roughly $10 for anyone who's into CYOA games. Each class has their own advantages (Which can be used to essentially eliminate poor choices or avoid having to roll a dice), I do highly recommend people new to these kinds of games play the Fighter first because he will have the easier time with the combat encounters at first and those are the most immediate things that can ruin your run. However my brief time with a Mage play-through has been interesting just to see how differently you can play the character with his additional resource of Pneuma (Mana in this universe).The world seems well fleshed out, though be ready to read as the journal is full of information which fills out as you play and engage in dialogue to get more information on subjects, history, individuals, groups, and wildlife. But I love the "frontier-fantasy" setting that they created for this.While not absolutely needed, it might be helpful for you to keep some of your own notes alongside this just for quicker reference, but this is mostly just to save a few button clicks. This is because some conversations will ask you for prompts to type in exactly what you're looking for, and particularly for character names they may not always be in your journal.Dialogue choices do matter, as how you talk to a person can determine how readily they are to share information with you alongside your actions, your religion (if you have any) can also play a role, and there are various options to approach people (and certain subjects will make certain people more icy).The pixel art is well made and gives good imagery to scenes with how much detail they put into it.Overall, I love the frontier-fantasy setting they created here, and barring a the occasional spelling error in descriptions the writing is very well done. Definitely recommend for any classic RPG fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally leave reviews, but this game I felt was truly outstanding. Its a nice sweet text-based adventure where you are a roadwarden, a person hired to travel around an area because the roads are often too dangerous for people to do it on their own. It did an excellent job of describing the world, in both its unfamiliarity and harshness. Your actions have consequences, and it is so satisfying to see that your work as a roadwarden actually is making a difference.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down my favourite text-based RPG. I'm amazed at how much this game managed to do with so little elements. The expansive, non linear narrative and the sense of danger and hardship made this game one I won't forget. I found it had a good rhythm and pace, despite being a relatively slow game.Well worth full price, it'd be a steal at a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun illustrated text based rpg. Exploring the peninsula feels exciting and dangerous, and dealing with the various factions WHILE uncovering the mysteries of the peninsula and its people is a blast. I loved all the interesting characters so much. Each person feels complex and historied. I think Dalit at the Pelt is my favorite cause she's badass AND funny. Its not an easy game, but also it doesn't punish too severely for your mistakes. As an out an proud save-scummer if the story isn't going my way, I usually fix it, but the "mistakes" I made felt so real and interesting that I never did. I'll probably go through a second time to see what I missed but yeah, the game is a blast and I honestly can't wait for a sequel or a even another game in the same setting (with the same mechanics). Overall 10/10, definitely play through this if you like TTRPGs or story-based adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: An experience halfway between reading a novel and playing a computer RPG. I have little experience with such games, but really enjoyed it. Most importantly, the characters are memorable, your choices consequential.But many key tradeoffs are handled well, too. A good balance is struck between concise descriptions and providing enough of a sense of immersion in the world. The default time limit is also well chosen, giving you enough leeway that you don't feel rushed for most of the game, but closing the story before you can explore all the narrative threads fully (which would endanger immersion).One little nugget I particularly appreciated were the sleep sequences, in which your decisions are not about what to do, but what and how you recall about your past life.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great visual "Chose your own adventure" book. The game mostly consists of text and when combat arrives, a little bit of luck and dice rolling (behind the scenes). The story telling is where this game obviously shines and has a few routes to take your character RP wise. This game was a breath of fresh air in a wave of stagnant games.Edit: Still enjoying the game, the visuals and storytelling hold up through out the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the text adventure genre has needed some sort of upgrade for a long time. I grew up playing games like this, but without anything to significantly shake up the formula over a long time, the genre started to become stale.Roadwarden feels like a breath of fresh air for the genre, and I cannot be more grateful that I discovered this gem of a game. Although replay value is somewhat limited, the depth of the game itself is astounding. I've not felt more immersed in any game in what feels like forever. The writing is verbose and descriptive, every character is distinct and believable, and there's a lovely air of mystery I wasn't expecting for something of this genre.I recommend this game to almost anyone and encourage people who usually skip all dialogue to give this one a shot. You may be surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Highly satisfying text-heavy adventure story with RPG-lite elements.Excellent characterisation and world-building, although at times the text could be quite dense. With some minor glitches, the story felt satisfying and coherent. Thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough. Would suit someone happy to do a lot of reading; perhaps less so players looking for quick payoffs.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a magnificent piece of writing, and captures a sense of adventure and discovery I haven't felt since I was a young child reading every fantasy book I could get my grubby little hands on at the library, while carrying an unforgiving melancholy that resonates deeply with me as an adult. The picture Roadwarden paints is a harsh one, full of danger and catastrophic mistakes with steep consequences. The people of it's world are a wary, hardscrabble lot with well-deserved suspicion of some foreign agent coming in asking questions and doing a duty no-one really asked for, and the lands you find yourself exploring will gladly kill you and anyone else foolish enough to venture in unprepared, but if you stick it out and learn to survive it's dangers, and give people reasons to trust you, you will find an incredibly vibrant and believable world. The characters are complex and feel very human, and each settlement has a distinct culture, with it's own history, values, dialect, and goals. There are countless different leads on countless different problems to pursue, and most quests can be resolved in multiple ways, with multiple results, and while some people might find the 40 day time limit on standard difficulty polarizing, I think it really enhanced the experience. There simply isn't enough time to figure everything out and resolve every problem, and while this can lead to some very harsh outcomes, it makes the things you *did* take the time to dig into feel that much more significant and real. (Just like real-world roadwork, the final boss is ultimately the deadline.)Across the board, this game is very tightly woven. Nothing feels like an afterthought, and progressing in one area of the story frequently and organically leads to new options and revelations about other parts of the story. Each settlement's history and goals are tied up in everyone else's, and even seemingly minor characters often wind up being tied into a whole bunch of other story threads. The worldbuilding is also very deliberate, and very well-researched, taking heavy inspiration from medieval Europe in a way that manages to feel fresh and grounded rather than cliche, with a really wonderful amount of attention paid to everyday life in the middle ages, whilst putting a fresh spin on classic fantasy monsters and carefully considering how their existence would realistically impact daily life. It also provides the opportunity for you to define the history and culture of the region your character comes from in a very organic way when characters in the game ask what your home is like, which I think is a brilliant choice for a game where the player character comes from a set location and exists in a fixed profession/role.10/10, would improve the lives of those I touch in small ways and acquire a found family to the detriment of the world because I am a mere mortal with finite time and non-negotiable obligations that prevent me from saving the world from massive, complicated, systemic problems again.

_childDocuments_.review: Simply incredible. After Golden Treasure and Citizen Sleeper, I was sure there's no way that 2022 would have another great text adventure ready for me. But Roadwarden is not only great, it is amazing. I will preach it's grandeur with the zeal of a priest, I swear in Wright's name.Dense worldbuilding, a huge cast of varied and detailed characters, incredible freedom of choice not only in dialogue but even in combat, I can barely stop gushing.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: A great text-based RPG that rewards you for exploring thoroughly, thinking critically, and writing down notes. Playing it feels like reading a Forgotten Realms fantasy novel, except you are the one deciding how the story will unfold, because you control the protagonist.In terms of gameplay it's similar to text-based RPGs and point-and-click adventure games from the 1980s and 1990s, but with better visuals. In terms of content it kinda reminds me of Planescape Torment crossed with Fallout 1 -- there's more conversation than combat, the game has a time limit, and when the game is over you get to see what happens to each of the settlements you discovered based on your actions throughout the game. I left the game running a few times so my hours on record are inflated but there's easily 30+ hours of content in this game if you take the time to resolve every quest and explore every location. I loved the game so much I binged it over 4 days, and would definitely recommend it to others.However one consideration I will call out is that less than 13% of players have the achievement for finishing the game -- presumably because many don't have the patience to play/read through so many hours of text -- however if you enjoy reading and you've made it this far in my review I'm confident you'll love Roadwarden. For only $11, why not?

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those "I'm recommending it for fans of text adventures...but..." reviews. Fortunately so far, the worldbuilding and charcters are all interesting and I like the mechanics- they remind me of the Lone Wolf books I read as a kid. My one complaint is the Steam deck support is lacking in the controls section. And if youre reading it, wouldnt it be better to be able to read it on the Steam deck like youre holding a book?Review-I'm old enough to remember the days of Infocom and Magnetic Scrolls and all the other graphical and non graphical text adventures out there. Its really is a lost art - text based adventures are impossible to find nowadays as most people just dont seem interested in reading. And, I'm one of those people who doesnt own a TV or watch movies - I only read and play video games. I love reading, and I read the way people watch media -if I'm relaxing and not gaming I'm reading. I love Roadwarden so far. The only thing I wish is that the Steam Deck support was better - it works, sort of, as the controls are very finicky using the touch screen and controller mouse. It would work better if the pointer wasnt so slim and the "hitbox" for the text options were better. I dont want to sit at my gaming PC and read. I want to curl up with my Steam deck like its a book. And I cant. Which is the only thing thats prevented me from playing this game as much as I want to. I either get annoyed sitting in my gaming chair reading on my giant monitor, or I get annoyed at the finicky Steam deck controls and wander off to read an actual book or play different games. So Devs - this is my one complaint. I love text adventures but can you tweak the controls so its easier to use on Steam Deck?

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished the game, and now I sit empty and sad, and don't know what to do.This speaks to the strength of the art, no doubt. But you know how you feel sad that a great story ended, and want to go back, and immediately start a new playthrough? It's not like this for me with Roadwarden. I'm sort of glad it ended... but also would want to have a chance spend just a little more time in the game to uncover all of its mysteries.There is a timer in the game. A final countdown for the entire game. It's a default mode. You could also choose to turn it off when you start. I should have done it. In the end, I didn't have time to finish a couple of main quests.But it was okay. I reached the ending. And I've done a lot. Actually, you could finish the game right after the start. Roadwarden gives the player a lot of freedom. Everything in the game is optional. I think, I had wrong expectations. Maybe, overhyped a bit. The game was compared to Citizen Sleeper and Dysco Elysium, two of my favourite games. Roadwarden does have many things in common with them - it's a narrative emotional RPG with no combat. Just choices.It was good, but just a bit unaligned with my tastes. Just a bit too much exploration at the start (yeah, I'm one of those rare gamers who love RPGs but do not like exploration). Just a bit too hard for me to read text (English is my second language, but I'm quite proficient with it. But not enough for Roadwarden, it seems). A bit too distant of a view. A bit too few ways to develop relationships with some of the characters I would like to do so. Roadwarden is human. It does no shy from portraing generational trauma, religious intolerance, alienation and mistrust. Also, kindness and warmth, friendship and loyalty. It's mysteries are vast, and well-presented. Places feel dictinct, and their denizems are varied.It has some interesting game design elements: you have to manage stats, such as being clean and well-fed, which reflect both in narrative and the way you can overcome encounters. You can choose a way you talk, from threatening to pitiful which affects how others percieve you. You can have many currencies besides actual money - it's not like many of those you meet will have any use of coins in the wilderness.The main progression is tied to gaining trust. You gain trust of a character, they agree to give you more information or to provide some service.Where the game stands out for me is in two different areas.One, small human moments. At one time a tough character asks you of a permission to ride your horse — something they have never done before. Another time, when you have gained the trust of another character, and they let you stay at their home at night, when you wake up, you can choose where to sit. I know it doesn't sound like much, but such small touches let you express yourself in the game, and have people react to that expression. These are quiet and very well written moments.Two, big mysteries. Something happened 10 years ago. What was it? You see ripples affecting the entire game map, and you feel very good when the dots start connecting.Overall, I'm glad I played Roadwarden. I'm a bit sad that it's not 100% for me, and I'm a bit more sad that I didn't answer all the questions I wanted, and I don't feel like I'll play the game again, at least soon.Still, an adventure worthy of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Well written game.  Took me something like 80ish in-game days on casual to explore everything and finish all quests and the game.  Died once.Even though I did extremely well tactically and followed the plotlines pretty well (probably found the majority of clues before even having to use the blunt sledgehammer type tools in the storyline to crack them open), strategically as far as the character's overall goals in the region the story writers had extremely subtle philosophical points they were able to get across without coming out and saying it (they did at the very end in the summary).  There was only one of the typical leftist BS LGBT ideology type descriptions in the game ("not a man even though he was born with a prick") - yeah, when people BS me I pretty much ignore them - if it was possible to rescue those hunters by fast response I certainly didn't bother.  Yes, there are aspects of reality that are just blunt.  For instance, take a word like "gender" which already has a definitive meaning (even if it's a retarded one in language that adds no value whatsoever) and assigning it to a completely incorrect idea of being able to change something which we have absolutely no way to change and which every cell already has biological code to accomplish)...yeah, stop being idiotic.  You're only going to hurt yourself and your mental state by forcing yourself to flip a truth state and keep track of it.  The very few people who simply have an extra chromosome are an absolute minority of you.Oh, by the way, if you want more LGBT stuff, just go to the northeast-most town in the loop or do the matchmaking quests (they aren't worth the pay but are counted overall toward your points which determine whether you succeed at setting up the political or power structures for your employers late game - you could probably substitute something else instead and ignore the worthless fantasies of those npcs).In any case, I enjoyed the game.  You aren't an over-the-top hero, you're not going to go beat entire villages, your job is simply staying alive in most cases, and if you can do that, you'll be able to get back to where you were as far as health or armor.  I don't know really how people play on harder modes and actually get done with the final objectives as when I played on casual I could only reliably stay alive by taking my time to regenerate health over days.  Probably you'd remember what you learned over multiple character deaths / games.It's interesting to me that you find these kinds of narratives of humanity needing to stay at subsistence levels to survive long term usually existing ideologically next to propagation of LGBT for everybody.  Hmm, wonder why that is.  Granted, if you don't have growth or don't have enough ways to grow then your kids probably aren't going to live as well as you.  I'd think the solution for that would be more education, not flipping truth tables.  Make tons more engineers, and not necessarily the LGBT kind either, more like the ones who can get their hands dirty.  Humanity has to develop all the tech to get off this rock before we have the inevitable species-killing dice-roll events, and a bunch of defeatist ideology will NOT help us in that.  /end rant(yes, I can recognize value in a game and time spent writing well even though portions of that are absolutely aggravating because they're against any kind of common sense)

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best videogame narrative I have seen in recent memory. First of all, I would strongly advise against turning off the time limit; on normal difficulty it isn't even particularly strict, and what's more, it is an important part of the game's core concept. This isn't a sycophantic RPG like Skyrim designed around ingratiating the player and allowing them meander around doing everything to reach a perfect outcome. The developers didn't put in so many different endings because they wanted you to ignore half of them and only go for perfect results. Removing the time limit completely eradicates any sense of narrative urgency, so I would recommend playing with the timer enabled.The game gives you the freedom to do as little or as much as you want, and ignoring whole questlines is entirely accommodated by the narrative and ending structure of the game. On a subsequent playthrough I ignored 90% of them and just headed out immediately on day 15 with my retirement fund to live a life of comfort.The writing goes incredibly hard. The plot and characters are nuanced, and the prose is beautiful and empathetic. Quests are flexible and have numerous outcomes. Your actions (and inaction) have consequences. Do the best (or worst) you can within the time allowed.I got this game in the humble bundle but it is easily worth the asking price and more.

_childDocuments_.review: Really something special. A resource-based, story-and-choice-driven RPG similar to Disco Elysium, Fallen London, Citizen Sleeper, or (without the ship combat) Sunless Sea or Sunless Skies. You have 40 days as the new Roadwarden (like a more responsible witcher) in a frontier area to scope it out on behalf of a colonizing merchant guild, help out people, find what happened to your predecessor, ally with various factions against one another or your employers - the web of decisions and possible story threads to pick at is bewildering, and you won't have time (unless you are a strict min/maxer) to do it all. So your playthrough feels very personal. Haven't felt this great about a story-and-choice-driven RPG since Citizen Sleeper. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt, it's an insanely immersive adventure, and all the little graphical elements almost make you forget that this is a text game - with events vividly appearing in your mind. I can still see my character standing there, shirtless, boots half immersed in the swamp waters, axe in hand, facing some kind of mountain lion; bleeding, dirty, but determined. And yet, Roadwarden suffers from a pretty major issue which holds it back greatly: there's a time limit, and it's rather tight. I hold this somewhat unpopular opinion that time limits aren't bad per se - they can add a lot of tension and additional strategic layer in which you need to consider your options very carefully; but they need to be well communicated and reasonable. Here, the limit is well communicated, but I don't think it's reasonable at all.To keep it short: I played the game with the foreknowledge that the time limit is tight, tried my best to minimise pointless travel, always acted with intent, was mindful of my resources and chose my goals carefully. And even with all that the ending I got wasn't one I'd call good; I simply didn't have the time, or even visible means, to complete a pretty crucial quest.Now, you could say, what's the problem? Just replay the game, go straight for the important goals, choose your options better, etc. And to that I say: no. And that's for a very simple reason. (the game allows you to replay it, that's not what I meant)Think about it. For all the clamouring about replayability, whenever people talk about their most potent experiences with a game, they usually say "when I first saw X..." or "it blew my mind when I realised that Y". It's simply not the same when you're doing it again, it can even feel like you're being dishonest, since you - the player - have knowledge that the player character doesn't. This argument might feel nonsensical in the age of wikis, roguelikes and social media, but there still are many, many games that are straightforward stories - and Roadwarden is one of them.And what a story it is. It really manages to suck you in; your dialogue choices matter, your decisions affect the world around you. Your resources are limited, and so is your power. You need to maintain your health and hunger, but also the state of your armour and even your hygiene. Wash yourself in the river, maybe brush your teeth if you bought a teeth cleaning set, or perhaps pay for a bath in the village? But it's so expensive. Anyway, you need to wash off the blood on your face, and your clothes are torn from getting through the thicket, better visit the tailor.The worldbuilding manages to avoid being your generic fantasy with some cool twists, such as the fact that human bodies just kind of rise on their own after death, as if everybody had a dormant zombie virus from birth. Horses are a rarity, and your equine companion is often seen as a curiosity by almost everybody; the previous roadwarden used a big lizard as a mount instead. Also, you often get asked about otherwise unseen parts of the world, and whatever you answer will be treated as true for the rest of the playthrough, that's pretty cool.But what's really golden about this whole game is that it really feels like an adventure through an unknown territory. The closest thing I'd compare it to is a pen-and-paper RPG session, where you truly feel like anything can happen, and everything is so viscerally real. The quality of the writing is excellent, too; it has this rare quality that comes from being written by a non-native English speaker who managed to attain the mastery of the language the hard way (the writer is Polish).There's a lot more to say about Roadwarden, but I think I've said enough. The time limit is a grievous wound on an otherwise impeccable experience; luckily, you can select easy mode which disables it - and I suggest you do just that, pride be damned. Or simply be prepared to play more than once. Either way; if you don't mind reading in games, I can easily say that Roadwarden is very much worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically a young adult-level CYOA book with tons of illustration, dice rolls that don't get over-used, and sensibly succinct prose.You are a roadwarden, a job that spends as much time in the saddle as it does in danger. Although keeping roads clear is part of your work description, you're really little more than a lawfully-sponsored adventurer: You're to explore the paths of a wild peninsula and build a rapport with its isolated villages to make them malleable to the suggestion of foreign commerce. You have 40 days to gather a report and make vital connections for the investments of the merchant guild that hired you. How you spend your time is your own discretion, but it should always be advancing your goals in some way. There's always things that need doing, and it's up to you to adequately prioritize them.There are choices both banal and important, with equally polarized consequences. Items and equipment to collect, some of which offer utilities to make your travels less weary and others that have no readily apparent usage, and encounters to face with varying degrees of assurance. Do you use your meager savings to invest in a paper lantern for help with dark and dangerous places, or treat yourself to a teeth-cleaning kit that will help you make better impressions of trustworthiness on people? Do you sell an old bronze axe head you found for some quick and pivotal wealth, or keep it while looking for a handle so you can turn it into a new weapon? Engaged with a saurian beast, do you prefer to keep an eye on its tail in case it whips at you, or do you pay attention to its maw to be sure it won't bite you? Decisions aplenty across all kinds of interactions. Some correct, some incorrect, some pointless either way, and some based on chance.Ultimately however, a playthrough won't be difficult. It's very easily save-scummed and meta-gamed, especially going through it subsequently. But if you go blindly with the flow, through good and bad, the narrative will immerse you in ways that haven't existed since the MUDs of yore. The characters you share drinks with, the questions you ask each other, and the struggles your journey drags you through will feel like more than just text on a screen.It takes all the engrossment of a good book and applies it to an interactive medium. And for practically  the price of a decent paperback book? It's hard not to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I simply loved this game. _childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best RPG I played in 2024 so far, and I'd say it should be on any top list of RPGs for people to play (as long as they are willing to read).Let me tell you what brought me over in totality:You are a Roadwarden sent to an untamed land where your duty is to help out distant villages and to keep the roads safe while you are also You can choose if you're a warrior, scholar or mage (and maybe something else I forget)You have to explore the whole place with basically zero knowledge, and you have to get the local scoop from the people you meetYou can infer a lot of extra information by just paying attentionBut one of the best features is that sometimes you don't get a text choice you instead get a text prompt option, like in old DOS games. Like "What are you looking for?" and then you type what you want to see. It's not always there, only in specific scenes.The thing that made me recommend it, is that in one of the settlements you get a chance to use this text prompt it asks you "Who do you wish to look for?" and I basically exhausted all the usual options, like leader, smith, merchant, church etc.So I'm thinking, what else can I even ask and i look at my Appearance stat (your cleanliness + clothes):I'm dirty as ♥♥♥♥, so i need some cleaning to be presentable to the people of the land. So I type in"maid" (because I forgot how you call a bathmaid)This ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game put me on a sidequest to become a matchmaker for villagers because of that promptas two villagers (one of them a *maid*) are looking for a spouse.
_childDocuments_.name: Roadwarden

_childDocuments_.review: Roadwarden is amazing game. It's very slow, but in a good way. Deeply atmospheric and well written.After completing it today in 19 hours. I got few suggestions for the Developer and (heavy spoilers) Why I didnt like it.So first suggestion: Since there is many places and characters, it's sometimes a bit hard to follow who everyone is. Pillars of eternity 2 had a system where highlighted names could be hovered over and had a little information box to remind you. I wish you could add something similar.Second suggestion: The "find a correct word" puzzles were fun, but sometimes extremely hard if you don't find certain right word. I would often understand what the Developer was trying to hint at, but just could not find the right command. You could maybe give a bit more hints, or make the right command a bit broader. It's not fun if you have to google what your supposed to write, after it takes too long to figure it out.Alright spoilers time:I would really hope to see a sequel in the future. There is couple of rough things that could be still polished with the story and couple of mechanics, but that should be fairly easy to fix. I could swap my review to recommended when the endgame is a bit better addressed.TLDR; Great game, but story and mechanics could still use a bit polish.

_childDocuments_.review: I had no idea what I was getting into when I picked this up, but I'm so glad I did. I feel quite attached to this fictional piece of land.Great writing and world building. Gaining the trust of the characters you meet is difficult, and I kept having to weigh how a decision I made with one person or tribe would affect my relationship with another. No Skyrim style "do everything in one playthrough" questing here; your choices  close some doors and open some others.
