_childDocuments_.review: Great spiritual successor to franchises like Caesar, Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom, Pharaoh, and other iso-city management games. You have everything you expect from a game that looks and feels a lot like Caesar: production chains, managing the needs of the different classes of citizens, and trade, all while having to do so on maps that offer challenges when it comes to irrigation and available space. The caravan system makes managing all of this really easy and intuitive as well. It's still in early access so improvements are on the way. I think some fine tuning in the economy (it's very easy to get into death spirals when one resources starts to run low). I also think the caravan system can benefit from a "assign caravans to routes" rather than a custom route for each one. There are quite a few instances where you have to run multiple lines through a town to make sure everyone has access to the goods that they need. 8/10, great game to scratch that Caesar itch but you don't want to play in Rome again.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: To save anyone else from the same disappointment I had: This is _NOT_ a city builder game. It's a collection of 12 structured campaign missions. I only played three of them before requesting a refund but they essentially provide you with a checklist of buildings to place, you place them at the start then fast forward time until the mission completes. The maps are also very, very tiny.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Check out my .Nebuchadnezzar is an exceptionally polished and fun game to play, and moves the subgenre of the Impressions city builders from pure city builders to logistics planning and simulation. While it only has a single campaign and no sandbox mode, it offers a lot in terms of gameplay, especially if you find that period of history interesting.The only drawbacks I had were some uninspired campaign missions that were essentially reach x number of y, and that trade was a nuisance in that other cities would regularly demand items for no reward other than preventing a loss of reputation.Other than that, I can highly recommend this game, as it is clearly built by inspired devs and the game is essentially bug-free, a rarity in this market.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Rise of the Middle kingdom is still my favorite. It feels really good to have a perfect flow of goods. I think this is a good #2 on that subject (better in my opinion than the Caesar games and all other known franchises of 25 years ago). Well worth the play if you miss playing those kind of games. Not sure what newcomers to this genre will think of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, relaxing logistics game. Its absolutely worth buying IF that is all you are looking for. Its not much of a city builder, there is no combat system, and the main way you could lose is if you run out of money, which can be easily generated once you set up your first trade with another city. The logistics part is a lot of fun though, and it steadily ramps up over the campaign.Also, there is no replayability value, as you only get to play with the ~12 campaign missions, with no random map generation so if you want more out of it, then maybe you can wait for some workshop content.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely best city-builder available right now, I don't remember when it was the last time I enjoyed any game so much. It probably won't appeal to everyone, but for any fan of a peaceful city builder and deep management - a must. Great mechanics, great attention to details, great visuals and audio design, great balance, great gameplay overall.The game is not perfect and I hope devs will add some useful features and cool scenarios. But until then - thank you very much for bringing the genre to life. Looking forward to your next project.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: You can look down on Nebuchadnezzar as stripping out some of the features from the old impressions games or you can focus on what this addition to the genre does well. - More than twice the resources as Caesar 3 (35 in total)- Almost three times as many resource chains as Caesar 3 where you turn one thing into another- A succinct 30 hour campaign that doesn't drag on past its welcome- Three different types of citizens to manage and upgrade with different needs- A reworked walker system for more player control- A customizable monument system for those with a better artistic sense- And a modern setup for newer computers where you wont have to mess with .ini files or mods to get it running.- All for less than one third the price of the old impressions games when they first came out? I loved the short time I put into the game for what it is instead of criticizing nebuchadnezzar for things it isn't trying to do, and that's an experience I would recommend for any long time fan of the city building genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: There are some good things about this game and I will explain why I don't recommend it. Graphics are fine. I dont expect anything more so it satisfies. But at the same time it is not important because graphic is not something important in this type of genre. Building temple is a good idea and I really liked it. Caravensarais are nice. Tutorial is quite nice. It is fun and explaining everything pretty clear.However, I cant think of anything else which makes this game different. Still, this is still not a big problem. The big problem is that the map is extremely, extremely small. Maybe it gets larger later on but I finished the tutorial and stuck in the 6th mission. It is not hard by the way. It is totally doable with what is given in the map. But it is painful. Not like dark souls. I felt like an accountant who just waits for the shift to be over. Agriculture is painful. There is no place for farming (which make sense). But what doesn't make sense is that when I build 2 grain farms almost one fourth of my map becomes unusable. Why? Really why? Why the map is that small? I said the idea of building a temple is good. It is... However, just a temple takes a huuuuuuuge amount of space. Again it makes sense when we think that temples are huge. Sure! But why the map is that small? Why there is only and only 1 place I can build a dock? (There is 1 more in the 6 mission. But you cant use that dock if you build there beacuse you cant put a warehouse.)Ah yess.. Warehouses. Again why are they so small and so big? Why they can take only 36 goods? If you put 20 fishes and 16 breads, you cant put anything more. But these warehouses are big too. They take a huge space as well. So if you try to be a bit generous and put 1 more warehouse then you supposed to then everything gets difficult. One other thing is that your city can collapse in a matter of seconds. For example I forgot to change the maximum number of bread a warehouse can take. So, no one could put milk in it. Therefore, everyone in the city left. Just like that in couple of seconds. So there was no one to work in the fisheries. Because of that all the people in villas left as well. At the end I had  only 2-3 hundred people while I had almost 3000 people 30 seconds ago. To be honest fixing these things and then constantly checking if everything is fine is painful not fun.I was excited for this game but it is not really up to my expectations. If you "need" to play a city builder game sure give it a try. It is not expensive. But frankly, I believe this game could be a huge deal if we were at 2001. However we are not.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I was hungry for a builder but what I found was a puzzle game.I think the game design on this one is super flawed, to the point where this feels more punishing than it should be. it's disgustingly hard even on easy, particularly about income. annoying popup messages, UI and clunky infratructure handling. There is some beautiful art in there to be sure and from an aesthetics view, it is getting Pharaoh vibes, but it unfortunately feels like worse than those games even though they came out 20 years ago.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Huge letdown for me.I expected a relaxing city building game that gives me the old Pharao vibes. This certainly isn't it.1. There is no "free play"-mode where you can build your own city freely but only missions with a predefined goal. Once you reach the goal, mission is over. You can continue to play but you never unlock more buildings. What the actual ****. Who creates a city building game with no free play mode??? I don't know that's like creating a shooter and not adding any weapons it feels like the most common-sense thing to do doesn't it?!2. The game  limits your creativity because it doesn't give you enough space to build. Maps in general are terribly small for no apparent reason, but whats even worse, maps are intentionally build in a way to 'challenge' you. For example there is no terraforming (why?) and then they add mountains that can't be removed to limit you from building water channels and other structures. You don#t get a 'map' you get get a maze of unbuildable terrain and you kind of have to figure out the correct way to place all your buildings. Terrible design decision, makes it feel like some sort of puzzle game.3. Buildings have a rediculously low range/working area. It's a real chore to set up production chains, again, as I said before it feels like a puzzle game. Did I mention they give you a laughable amount of fertile land?4. You have to  set paths for  trader that sells a good at  market in your city . WAT. Who came up with that idea?! I will now refund this game, it's certainly not worth 20€. Go play 20 year old Paraoh instead, seriosly I play city building games a lot an this isn't anywhere near the top 20. So angry right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, having enjoyed Ceasar 3 and the entire impression serries.But where the game had fun, this game has you looking at graphs a lot more and just... Not having fun. I spent most of the time fighting with the production menu and waiting to see when it would accurately reflect my base game then I did designing a fun city or enjoying myself, and didn't get far passed the tutorial due to spending the whole time on "E" high speed mode just waiting for ♥♥♥♥ to happen.Not to mention the most annoying crap like needing to individually shut down industry if a worker shortage happens and having to manually assign over workers to certain things - which is fine when you have like 6 industries but boring when you have 100. The game is far more of a hassle then it is an enjoyment.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Have literally been waiting YEARS for this game to come out and it does not disappoint. It's close enough to the old Pharaoh to be recognizable but with improvements to game play which are great. The few times I came across something that didn't seem to work I managed to figure out what I was doing wrong.  I can't wait to see how it develops. More Please!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: For a brand new game, this has an exceptional level of polish.  It has been a very reminiscant day, reminding me of the likes of Pharaoh and Ceaser, but with the gameplay perfected, and the whole game modernised.  I thoroughly look forward to more and will watch the developers with great interest.  Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: *** I got a preview copy of the game but bought a key immediately after release to really support the devs***If you played older Impression games, this is the ultimate modern game for you. It isn't the same - let's clear that right out of the gate. Also - ancient mesopotamia? What a great setting!The game is much more logistics oriented and you need to make sure everything runs smoothly and effectively. You don't need to place police, firemen etc. - you need to make sure your markets are sufficently supplied, your walkers are walking efficent routes, your workforce is in the right places...Trading is pretty much the same, nicely done, good interface - overall very nicely done!Missions are interesting, map design is superb - you always need most of the map, so you have to plan accordingly and there isn't much place for mistakes... That's even better than most missions in older games.There is no military but I can't see it as a bad thing overall...Should I say something in the end, it would be that if you like city building, ancient Mesopotamia and wish to support a group of fine, hard working devs - this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: It's good for the price, and quite similar to old classics like Caesar 3 and Pharoah.All the mechanics you'd expect from a game like this are mostly in it, such as overlays for desirability. An improvement is custom routing for street-walkers.It can be hard, I had to reset mission 3 about 3 times due to running out of money. You can only make money through trade so far and only get that laterSpace is a premium for I guess balance as it mentions space being "the most valuable thing" so you feel boxxed in to a degree. You might have a jagged coastline in a mission so only 1 space for a dockThe game's supply chain system is its biggest weak point. The caravan system (of getting goods long distance between warehouses) is confusing and I had to fiddle with buttons for a long while and observe to actually get a successful transfer of goodsA few bugs, that do impact gameplay so far, such as irrigation ditches that wont extend fertility In the Akkad mission (southern shore). Also possibly a bug or I'm not getting the system but one where bazaar merchants will claim "No resources" despite a full warehouse right next to themNote all that is in the game so far is the singleplayer campaign. There is a scenarios option but no scenarios with the game shipped. I wonder if there is a scenario editor or map maker with the game as that is what the scenario system hints at?
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The game is nice, I liked it very much, but seems repetitive and the only real difficulty is the map size. You play a campaign mission a couple hours to realize that you ran out of space because you didnt planed your city and resources 4 hours ahead, and thats just in normal difficulty. If devs wants to be unforgiving with the map size, then they need to add, at the very least, a plan feature, like in oxygen not included, where you can lay your grand design beforehand.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Everything that makes impressions games' city builders great with a focus on logistics. Distribution of goods is defined by the player. The balancing act of keeping your houses topped off and using resources for trade and buildings is challenging when you must expand to take care of other objectives. The game is as complete package as can be without it being fully open source: modding and scenario editing are available and extensive.The negatives are that the sanitation and safety aspects are a little out of your control and wonders are less impressive but i've yet to complete the campaign. Easily one of the best bangs for your buck if you like historical city builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: oooofffff. What a HUGE disappointment this game is. Graphics are not that good, but much worse is the gameplay. I love games like Caesar 3 and 4 for example, but the gameplay of this game does not make sense, at all. I expected much more. The tutorials are very very hard to follow, the actions you have to perform do not make sense at all GUI is very user unfriendly. So my conclusion is: Mesopotamian city building, great idea, extremely poorly executed. I asked for a refund. Simply not even fun to play. It looks like a completely failed attempt to rebuild caesar 4 in Mesoptamia.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This is an ambitious and good-looking historical city builder that has obviously been shown a lot of love by the devs, and should be fun to play, but isn't. The risk mechanic ruins this game for me, over and above the unusually demanding level of micromanagement required. All the overlays and statisics are opaque  and bare bones, but the risk overlays in particular are incomprehensible in relation to what is going on, and tell you nothing. Police, fire and healers walk all over the map without any way for you to control them or direct them, regardless of where the buildings are placed, unless you spam service buildings everywhere. I am a veteran player of all the Impressions city builders, and was really looking forward to this game. It still is playable, and even enjoyable at times, but the flaws make it very frustrating. Instead of the addictive gameplay one expects, you very soon tire of literally putting out fires, not to mention quelling riots and strikes that seem to respond to nothing the player does to mitigate them. I would give this three out of five stars, solely because of the risk dynamic.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me of  Caesar and Pharaoh.   Needs some tweaking on how to identify placement of clay pits and other water based industries and maybe so routing work for caravans but so far it is pretty good.  I am just now about to build a monument for the first time so will revisit review after a few more hours of game play.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game, even though it is still in its starting phase it brings back a great feeling. The music is beautiful and I spend almost more time reading and researching about the detailed historic explanations before the missions than actually in the game - and not because it is too quick, but because it is very interesting.There is great potential and even though there is a bit limited content at the moment I don't regret a single penny spent on this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun city builder, I like the setting choice, the art design, and the music is pretty nice. The city building mechanics are pretty much a more streamlined version of Zeus, walkers can be directed through routes meaning that roads aren't cluttered by roadblocks, production buildings can store a minimal amount of goods and directly send them to markets which slightly lowers the amount of storehouse spam in the game. Mechanics that could be completely ignored in Zeus like invasions and unrest were cut out. The player is given a lot more room to worry about the more interesting parts of logistics and I appreciate that. The amount of content in the game is limited, but optimising logistics is pretty great if that's what you're into.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I love Pharaoh and Cesar and got this game on day 1 thinking it was not early access but it is early access there will need to be a fair few updates and patches. For example the Campaign is more a tutorial and there is no sandbox mode or scenarios yet. The tutorial or in game guide does not fully explain how to work the custom monument feature. I don't find the layout for checking your resource balances intuitive. It is a bit of a boring table with a few numbers. If you spend long enough looking at it you will understand it but not fun or interesting. The game is a bit OTT on efficiency (maybe it needs balancing better). I love efficient layouts and stuff but the game does it a bit too much for me and it sucks the fun/freedom out of it. For example, a new system where every farm or industry can only deliver goods to storage yards 4 or so, tiles away is too limiting. I would love the range to be a more just to give a little flexibility and fun when building. The irrigation wells can only fill a few tiles of irrigation ditch so you end up spamming wells and using the bare minimum/most efficient irrigation ditch layout. I would say worst of all the maps are crazy small and you end up building right to the map edge where it becomes a pain to see what you have built without rotating all the time because something is covering the buildings in the corners and edges. In fact the maps are so small you cant build a city without focusing on efficiency only.Plus there are a few bugs i am getting only with this game for example it always loads on my secondary monitor so i have to unplug the secondary, load the game then plug it back it. Easy work around but a pain. Also if I rotate the map alot the game crashesI will keep it and see if it gets better. Im
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: this game could be the very perfect throwback it deserves to be, but the systems are very. cumbersome. You must set up trade routes for every single good through buildings, calculate everything, buildings have specific ranges. It's basicaly Anno but you do not have the magical warehouses. The system of waypoints for markets is also simply impossible to understand. These two are the absolute basis for city builders and this little unpolished gem sadly doesnt cut it for me
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Zeus, Emperor, Pharao, and even Lethis. This game, while having its differences, has the same atmosphere. I feel like a child again. Thank you for creating this amazing game of one of the civilizations that was missing.PS: Perhapps you could look to the Americas in the future? I long for growing crops in them Inca mountain farms.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played the first 4 missions. As a fan of the Zeus + Poseidon series I'm really enjoying this so far.I'll update my review once I accumulate more hours of play.Quick Notes (Work in Progress):Pros:Something I appreciate is a comprehensive and digestible tutorial.This game does a good job of teaching you the mechanics without boring you with endless walls of text.Cons:It keeps starting in my secondary monitor on a multiple monitor setup. **** This was patched today, there is now a settingI REALLY wish you could zoom in just one or two more levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Aww, it's really too bad ;( I was hoping for a new Caesar itch-scratcher with this one...The awesome stuff:1) The music2) The beautiful artwork in the loading screensThat's about it for the first hour, and that's not good enough. What I'm missing:1) No free rotation (there's just 4 compass directions and boring isometric view).2) Zooming. Even though the tutorial says you can zoom, none of the zoom options do anything, I just stay in satellite orbit view, and the land and city just looks light brown with no details.3) Good looking graphics... This looks kind of like early SimCity's, but in higher res because 4K. I get that this is not a multi million $$$$ investment or anything, but it's just not pulling me in enough.A minor gripe: the tutorial text is way too verbose. Like, entire unnecessary sentences. If there's a button "end tutorial", there doesn't also need to be a long-winded sentence informing the player that they can, if they so choose, finalize the tutorial by finding the button for ending the tutorial. (See what I mean? :) )So yeah... This does not scratch any itches, in fact it creates more itches. Maybe I'm hoping for too much here, but I would really like a city builder that doesn't make me want to replay 20 year old city builders like Caesar 4, that had more and better functionality and much, MUCH more charm-factor in the UI, graphics and voices (even though that was not a great game).Too bad, Seeing the review ratio I had really hoped for more... Maybe it's actually a great city builder game in terms of city mechanics, but as (to me) this feels more like a sandbox engine demo, it doesn't pull me in to the point where I quickly start to enjoy that gameplay. Not like all the old games did anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: One of those games you'd love to love, but it just has too many flaws. First of all it shouldn't be hard to release game in 2021 without having minor updates which adds walls or fires. Second of all it also shouldn't be hard to have fluent controls in this type of game in 2021. I understand these mechanics that would smooth the gameplay were harder to implement 20+ years ago, but now there shouldn't be excuses. Camera is awful and maps too small. Often you have to build farms or whatever to spots you can barely see. Third of all the atmosphere is lame. It doesn't feel like you're operating city. It feels like all houses are in separate universes. I didn't want a literal copy of Emperor or Pharaoh or something. I wanted a well made economy strategy city builder in the spirit of those games. And even Emperor had more things when it was released. This is not a bad game really but I wouldn't buy it again if I knew better.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. Enough remaining of Pharoh to be familiar but different enough to stand on it's own. Obviously there are some things that I would have changed in the design (Increase irrigation pump function am I right?) but there is nothing serious to knock. If you are a fan of the 2d city designer, this is well worth the get!
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: So, is it Pharaoh in Babylonia? Yes.Is there a certain lifelessness in your towns due to the absence of walkers, like the Steam reviews are saying? Yes, they're right. I don't think that walkers need to fulfill any function necessarily like they did in Pharaoh, the game works a bit differently in that respect which is not bad because the Pharaoh system definitely had issues (looking at you, market seller that randomly stops going left for 1 year and lets the houses on the left side of the market degrade into huts), but it would be really nice to see the people walk around, even if just for decorative purposes. I hope they'll add that eventually.Still worth it? Sure. I mean, it's Pharaoh in Babylonia, is there any other "Pharaoh in Babylonia" game that you can compare it too? No, so go and get it. Worth every €.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely great game, silky smooth logical intuitive practical interface, with all numbers quantities clearly stated. If you're missing something you can tell why immediately. Love the graphics, clean and gorgeous. An absolute must for anyone remotely interested in a city builder, and a great intro to the genre if you've never played.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this out of nostalgia as I enjoyed some of the games this is inspired by in my youth.Ultimately I couldn't get into it, mainly due to way to much micromanagement - probably this was also the case in it's predecessors, so perhaps it's not a fair judgement, still, I don't think I'll be picking this up again.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun to play although it has many frustrating aspects.  I do wish the Steam scoring system had more granularity - if it did I would give it 4 out of 5 in part due to its clunky trading system. It is a classic city builder.  One major drawback is the size and shape of the maps but if you like building cities and managing resources then this is a game for you
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game that gives me the vibes of Sierra classics like the Pharaoh and Caesar series.  My only complaint is that it often takes a very long time to boot up which makes it hard to enjoy when I have a limited time to play (thus, the reason for my low play time, I had to move on for now but I'll come back to it)
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar offers the classic isometric, resource-management game, which we got to know from Pharaoh and Ceaser. Much of the gameplay is similar, but it's simplicity (in essence) makes it very good and it keeps it entertaining. The way the campaign is done, allows the player to continue learning new things in a progressive way. The campaing offers two types of victory (military or presitge), giving more flexibility for the player. The combat is a bit mediocore, but I guess that was never the main focus of this game. I really like the statistical overview the game shows you, allowing you to optimize the production chains  of your cities  vs. the consumption of your civilians. I can't tell if the old games had this before, but for me makes a huge difference in how to organize your city. The manual distribution of your goods (via caravans) can be (a bit) laboursome, but It will also allow you to optimize your producion chains even more. I really like this puzzle. The 3 difficulty options are very nice; it will allow you to make the campaign more challenging if you want to.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Opinion: 6.5/10 This game has some potential. It's somewhat like Anno 2000 BC would be. I found the management of supply chains tiresome, as others have mentioned, stockpiles have practically no range so half of your city is a matrix of stockpile buildings and overall ... felt a little lackluster (I felt like "Why am I playing this and not Anno 1800" ).It's not a bad game, it's just not exceptional either. (Tough I have to commend the tutorial, it was quite nice to have one that is not overly restricting and actually quite helpful )If you are a sucker for the era and art design, then go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly fails to learn any of the lessons of two decades of city building games that came after Pharoah and earlier games of the same genre. Lacks the modern sensibilities of games like 'Grand Ages Rome,' or even 'Sumerians.'I realize this 'failure to learn,' is actually an artistic choice, I just don't think it is a good one.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. It has huge potential. But first things first. I'm a huge fan of Sierra's Pharoh and I'm confident this game will be a worthy successor.This game has no bugs I couldn't find any in 55h of gaming. This is incredible since the whole game was written by one developer supported by 2 game designer, art and music designer (5 people in total).First missions are easy but the further you go it gets harder. The balance of the game is really good, and it is always possible to recover from city collapse (although tons of clicking will be required to close production and later to reopen it). Not many things can wreck your great city, the city won't burn, you won't be robbed by unemployed citizens, there is no military mechanics etc. but given the games price and it's quality it still provides a lot of entertainment and I'm pretty sure developers will extend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: this game could be the very perfect throwback it deserves to be, but the systems are very. cumbersome. You must set up trade routes for every single good through buildings, calculate everything, buildings have specific ranges. It's basicaly Anno but you do not have the magical warehouses. The system of waypoints for markets is also simply impossible to understand. These two are the absolute basis for city builders and this little unpolished gem sadly doesnt cut it for me
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I want it to be as good as Pharaoh or Cesar 3, but it is not.Though it feels much the same it is way to boring in the long run, but fun the first 5-10 hours.Every missions is the same, but you have to play for a bit longer each time. There is no variation on the needs or goods required for the population, other then a new one each mission. So every time you start by doing the exact same and wait until you can get the new one. Once gained, you expand your town with the new one, build a bit more of what you have and wait until complete.Yeah. You had to wait a long time for the pyramids or the phinx to be completed in Pharao, but here the "wonder" is build 3 hours before the mission ends. Even after 10 missions its the same building. Only visual changes.- Where is the diversity in needs and buildings? - Where is the challange? - Why do you allways have access to the same lists recourses and the same list has to be traded?NOT WORTH THE MONEY
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: The game imposes a reduced space for the construction of buildings.Okay, but we should be able to move the buildings with their configurations (merchandise AND! transport).When you do it manually (even with pausing), you lose!The population leaves (the time for the AI to update, etc.) and it is the decline!Pity.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Charming game that takes you back to the Impressions-games era. There aren't disasters like fires or buildings collapsing but that doesn't mean the game is easy - caravans, storage, production and irrigation are key to making sure citizens are fully stocked up with all the necessary goods. Oh, and the soundtrack is pretty amazing too.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like games likes Caesar 3? Then you will like this. There are a few differences but in general, it's the same style. You will see some people complain about challenge. It has less "challenge" because it isn't actively trying to ♥♥♥♥ you over like the old games did. Feels a great modern update the old genre we all really like!Solid quality of the game. Had a few issues because I bought it within minutes of release. That was sorted with 15-20min.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I am rather disappointed with this game.  I was a great fan of Isometric city builders like Pharaoh and Caesar.  There are many other reviews that detail faults.  I shall add a couple more: There is no zoom available ( despite the game saying there is ), so you can't get in close to buildings and see what is going on.   People rush around like demented zombies even on the slowest game speed.  Games like Pharaoh were much more relaxed.  Clicking on people ( if you can get your cursor to catch them ) does nothing.  No sound or information.  I just get the impression this is very early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: So far (4 hours) I am not really enjoying this game.  It requires a great deal of micro management,  and it's not very intuitive.  The structures do evolve - which is nice - but the look of the buildings is very similar,  so not as rewarding as it was in say,  Caesar II etc.    I have yet to figure out how to edit the maps,  so even in sandbox mode,  you can't add water or set things up in a creative way.  I find it tedious and more work than fun.... :(
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Caesar and Pharaoh. I didn't love Nebuchadnezzar. It follows in the footsteps of its predecessors, but I would expect better visual appearance and playability from a modern game. Now it feels awkward and amateurish. The resolution and animations are poor The historical context provided is enlightening, but it is presented in a dry and unimmersive manner. There are plenty of other city builders that are way more appealing and fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: the Sargon DLC needs workfirst. the barracks do not tell you which class of recruits are needed or their cost for a full regiment2- the military supply posts have way too limited a range, 3.  the 2nd mission is beyond understanding as to why there is only a maximum import total at the start of 40 wood given the sheer amount of high end population that must be maintained in order to even begin to field the military needed for the more difficult targets.4. the fieid of battle display is clearly a work in progress but its rather annoying  how we can have the overwhelming advantage in numbers and somehow still lose. . further the officer quarters does not let you choose which reginents they are in charge of.perhaps im missing something.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Swell little city builder. Excellent art and music set the tone for a relaxed and fun atmosphere. Fairly easy to learn, the UI is good enough to get by without overloading you with unnecessary information. While the gameplay loop is relatively simple at first glance, managing a multitude of different resources quickly spirals into an addictive cycle of planning and expansion. My only complaint is the priority for Haulers' AI is sometimes a bit wonky, leading to situations where they fail to function properly. Overall though, would absolutely recommend as a nice relaxing way to fill an evening.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Setting up constructions is ALOT LONGER than in caesar or pharaoh because you have to set every single trader's path.It was a great idea to let player custom the paths but it's completely killing the rhytm.Played 10 hours and never opened it again, was expecting alot more.A default path should be automatically defined when you build a market or a well...
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I could barely play this game. So many bugs. One of them is for some reason this game takes like 15 mins to start and load on my 2 year old PC that blows these requirements out of the water.Edit: Over a year later and the game loading times are still garbage. It takes 20+ mins to actually start playing the game. And it's an interesting and fun game when I can play it but these load times are absolutely atrocious.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Maps are too small. The size of the map + the cheap look graphics made this game feel like a mobile game. definitely not worth the current price, a pity because the game is fun and has potential, the campaign is fun, it's raising the complexity in a good way through the missions. I feel is very unlikely that those two aspects to be fixed, that s why I dont recommend it.They are clever selling this game without a demo version. if I had played a demo, I definitely was not gonna bought the full version.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: Great, very much like old Impressions Games / Sierra historical city builder games (Pharaoh, Caesar, Zeus etc.) but not exactly like them, it is more like some a modern restart, if you enjoyed the overall mood, art style, overall polish, city building / production gameplay, music of these games then Nebuchadnezzar is for you. It is fairly similar to the old Sierra games with some things of its own like monument building which allow a bit more customization than before and some game mechanisms like you can add/remove different type of workers in building, the game also rely heavily on fixing production issues and transport / import / export / optimization of supply chain / roads. It is refreshing to see yet another game like this in a different time period, the time period is well chosen. The UX could be better i guess but it also has some quick shortcut that make it ok.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: A spiritual successor to Impressions Game's city building series, which included: Caesar, Pharaoh, Zeus: Master of Olympus and Emperor: Rise of the Middle Kingdom.I recommend it to anyone who loved the isometric city building series like I did back in the 90's.I nominated this for the'Sit Back & Relax' award, 2021.
_childDocuments_.name: Nebuchadnezzar

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing under the strong impression of my first gaming addiction: Pharaoh, from 1999. At that time I was about 12 years old and was looking for the game. Contrary to what many would think, however, it is not just a childhood memory; I still play this classic from time to time.That was also the reason I bought Nebuchadnezzar. It exuded that pharaoh flair in the trailers. Now you can think what you like about the games of that time, but they have aged gracefully. _childDocuments_.review: When I've fondly remembered the old Sierra city-builder games over the last 15 years, wishing they made them like they used to, this is the game I imagined.First off, it just  great. It manages to combine the nostalgia of  and  with the extra breathing space of modern UI, controls, and menu design. It's clear that the art has been done with a lot of love and attention to detail. The music is professional, atmospheric, and varied enough that it doesn't feel repetitive after several hours of play. The ambient sound design is almost perfectly immersive (I did catch one market crier hawking his wares in English, but I can forgive that - it's not like there are many sound libraries of people speaking ancient Sumerian). It's also great to see ancient Mesopotamia get some love, and downright cool to design your own temple or palace complex, even if the monument interface could do with some quality-of-life improvements.My biggest gripe: I feel like it could have been made clearer that this isn't yet a feature-complete game. As of writing (19th Feb 2021), the only playable mode is a campaign, so there's no sandbox mode (although the devs have just announced it will be in an upcoming update, and there's an everything-unlocked scenario mod in the Workshop that does the job for now). Scenario mode is available, but there are no dev-made scenarios yet, only what you can find on the Workshop.That said, the campaign is fun to play through, with a well-thought-out tutorial that strikes a decent balance between holding your hand and getting out of your way. The pacing might be a tad slow for some - at times I felt impatient to get to the higher-tier buildings and industries - but I never stopped enjoying myself. Even if you don't have all the toys yet, it's still damn satisfying when you get things humming along just right, industries well-balanced and all your Mesopotamish citizens happy with your rule.Praise Marduk!

_childDocuments_.review: I’m a huge fan of the classic city builders (Caesar III is a personal fav of mine), so Nebuchadnezzar was definitely something I had to check out.This is not a full-blown strategy game with warfare, diplomacy, and the like. Rather, it’s more of a straight city builder with a heavy emphasis on building and expanding, one developed by a two-man team at that. Despite that though, there is a surprising amount of depth here, both in the building and management elements. Having now played the game for over a dozen hours, I’ve grown to enjoy this little indie city builder.If it wasn’t already obvious, Nebuchadnezzar goes for that same isometric viewpoint that the classics did, albeit with the ability to rotate. The graphics follow suit and are generally low-res across the board (which becomes very apparent when you zoom all the way in). Granted, this is likely by design and it never felt off-putting. The music is comparable, nothing too great there – but not bad.As this is a 2021 release, Nebuchadnezzar also brings some modern upgrades. Most notable would be its support of higher resolutions up to ultrawide 4K. My only problem there is that the UI cannot be freely scaled. There is an option to enable a 4K UI, but nothing if you just want to adjust it a little bit – the game could really use a UI scale slider. The entire experience is also capped at 60 fps, which was a bit disappointing to see, but at least it was a stable 60 fps.Most of my time was spent in the campaign mode, which itself is made up of a bunch of loosely connected scenarios. The goals usually involved reaching a certain population, prestige, or smaller stuff like having a set number of a certain building. There is a nice learning curve in that you’re only introduced to a few new goods and buildings with each scenario, giving you time to get acquainted with them before repeating the process with the next.By the end of the game there is a ton of stuff to juggle, including multiple social classes that can only work specific jobs, a dozen or so different buildings needed to craft certain goods, and an involved house upgrade mechanic that will have you setting up a ton of different worker paths in order to get goods where they need to go. As I said before – there’s a surprising amount of complexity here. Despite this, it doesn’t go overboard and the core loop is very satisfying once you get the hang of things.It has a similar feel to something like Factorio or Satisfactory, where you spend all this time setting up harvesting and manufacturing of one good, just for that to open up paths for you do to the same with even more goods. It never gets old seeing this small village become this massive web of buildings, farms, and workers travelling all over.As there is no warfare, crime, or disasters of any sort, the challenge is instead shifted to how well you can optimize and make effective use of the space provided. You can just slap down some buildings, connect them together, and call it a day, but there’s a lot of fun to be had in coming up with the most efficient farm layouts, the shortest possible pathing for distributing goods, and the most profitable trades with other cities. This just so happens to be my favorite thing to do in city builders, so I felt right at home here in Nebuchadnezzar.I believe the biggest flaw people are going to find with the game comes in the form of its lasting appeal. Once you’ve completed the campaign and scenarios, there really isn’t much in the way of replay value. At least, not from the base game itself. I say that because there is a mod manager and, with time, I could easily see the game becoming more robust through all the different stuff people add to it.There’s also the issue of quality of life – and let’s just say that Nebuchadnezzar has some room to improve there. Being able to copy-paste routes across different merchants would be my most-wanted feature, but it would also be nice to be able to delete bridges over canals without actually deleting the canal along with it. Minor stuff for sure, but improvements to be made nonetheless.As a fan of classic city-builders like Caesar and Pharaoh, there’s a lot to like here. There’s the polished and satisfying core game loop, the heavy emphasis on building and expansion, and even the more unique stuff like the house upgrade system. Sure, it’s not a challenging game and could still use some quality of life improvements, but it’s a fun experience overall and impressive given that it comes from just two people. If you’re a fan of such city builders, it’s worth a look.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

Roads? Yes all there. Distance? Who knows? Go blunder a bit. It's a fun learning experience for your unproven as yet to be beloved product. And if they don't want to read your mind? Screw them.It just goes on from here. There is not enough player feedback. That's the entire problem.I paid $16 US for a peek into what should be my favorite genre for 30 years. But I'm not impressed. Heck Settlers in the 1980s understood this. Pick your reason: arrogant developers, or underfunded developers who don't understand market buy in... means they can go off and do wonderful things.What I saw instead was just another well intended "let's do everything game" that flounders because it doesn't do much of anything, does not appeal to the casual player to build up product market share, arrogantly assumes what is not obvious into the minds of the developer means the players is stupid or unwilling to create an ecosystem to cover for the developers' false assumptions.Recommendations? _childDocuments_.review: I was apprehensive to play the game at release due to an apparent lack of depth, having said that, Nebuchadnezzar has been greatly enhanced since then.Nebuchadnezzar seeks to emulate the old Sierra games, mainly drawing inspiration from Pharaoh and Caesar (3), and does a  good job of combining the intricacies of each title. That's not to say Nebuchadnezzar is simply the "best of Sierra Studios" though. While the game is quite similar to the aforementioned titles, it manages to carve out it's own identity in the genre by simplifying certain aspects (or even outright omitting them), while simultaneously expanding upon others. While I did claim some mechanics are "simplified", its more accurate to say that they're deceptively simplified in order to place emphasis on others. For example, the distance between housing and any sort of work is irrelevant. Peasants can live and work in total opposite corners of the map with no issue. In part due to the house/work relationship, road placement becomes less crucial as you no longer need to formulate the perfect path for jobs. That being said, the placement of buildings and roads still matters greatly once you understand what the main aspect of Nebuchadnezzar is: logistics. Sure, it might not matter where a wheat farm and house are located, but what does matter is how, or rather, where you're going to store that wheat in relation to the farm. After you've stored the wheat, it's turned into bread. But where do the bakeries go? Where is bread stored? Where does it get transported (if needed) so it can then get distributed to your citizens. Oh, and after that, where do you place the markets in order to distribute the food, how many merchants do you use, and what path(s) do you give each one? The process continues with over 2 dozen different resources alongside a multitude of services (religion, healthcare, crime, etc.) all feeding into one another. Nebuchadnezzar doesn't actually place so much emphasis on building a city, but rather building and maintaining an ever-growing distribution chain where your goal is to maximize efficiency, and minimize any points of failure.And as far omittals, the only noteworthy example is the total lack of any militaristic features. However, that's actually being added in the forthcoming update. Speaking of, updates (both major and minor) have been coming at a steady pace ever since release.  Its a good game, but as it stands, I don't think Nebuchadnezzar is quite the same caliber as the games it seeks to imitate. But with the quality and frequency of updates so far, it has the potential to not only reach those heights, but even eclipse them.

_childDocuments_.review: From the detailed background information about the different cultures in ancient Mesopotamia, one might think 'finally an ancient city simulation game which gets history right'. Short answer: Not so much. As a seasoned ACOUP reader, the first thing one notices is how peaceful the cities of the game generally are. From my understanding of history, cities were administrative centers used to extract resources from the surrounding countryside by violence or threats of violence. So the first thing one would assume a city to have would be soldiers. As there are likely to be other would-be extractors around, the second thing one would assume a city to have are defensive structures, at least a palisade wall around the granary. Instead, external threats are absent, and the eventual city guard mostly deals with the occasional criminal and certainly does not seem to collect taxes from farmers at spearpoint. Agriculture is only slightly less ridiculous. Okay, the irrigation system idea is neat. However, irrigation pumps only cost a fixed amount and then run forever, for free. The practical limits on irrigation are the amount of straight sections of the river/lake coasts (which are also needed for fishing and harbors) where pumps can be build. Land comes functionally in just three flavors: inaccessible, grassland (irrigated or naturally wet) and desert. For both pastures and horticulture, you need grassland. This seems totally ahistorical to me: wheat is obviously a much better way to use good land, while pastoralism is important because it allows the utilization of marginal land. Fun fact: if there is a single thing one might think to be in abundant supply in Mesopotamia (which includes modern Iraq), it would be desert land. In the game however, while waterfront real estate is probably the most limited resource, overall accessible space is often also rather limited. I would have assumed that the vast majority of people are subsistence farmers from whom a tiny amount of surplus is extracted to feed the city folks. Instead, it is very possible to have most of the lower class unemployed without anyone starving. On the other hand, the populations appetite for ceramics is truly insatiable. For every three people working the fields, bakeries and goat farms, expect two working clay into pots. I guess that eventually the Greeks will discover that you can actually reuse pots instead of using new ones all the time. There are no mills. Both the bakeries and the kilns operate without fuel, powered by sunlight, magma or power of will.The overall economy is weird. From the start, it is currency-based. You pay your employees fixed wages, slavery doesn't exist. Anyone living in houses with suitable amenities pays taxes, irregardless of employment. How do the unemployed make money? Unknown. Prostitution, freelance software programming, synthesizing gold from thin air. In the first few levels, the housing level is limited, so you will probably only make a surplus by trading with other cities, which are willing to overpay for your ceramics. Non-wage labor, which I would have assumed to make up the bulk of labor (e.g. subsistence farming, in-house cloth production) is completely absent. Buildings are made out of two materials. The gigantic monuments are made out of bricks, every other building is made out of money. Most of the game is actually about managing logistics. While employees can teleport from their homes to their place of work, transporting goods by haulers is subject to strict union regulations based on the maximum norm of the vector difference of the position of the two buildings in question, regardless of the actual walking distance. To transport goods further, you need warehouses which can be connected by caravans. The placement of some industry buildings is reasonably governed by land use considerations. For other industry buildings, transport efficiency can be improved if a hauler can directly move goods (e.g. grain) from a producer (farm) to a consumer (bakery) instead of the producer->warehouse=>warehouse->consumer chain which involves two haulers and one caravan. Any goods in warehouses are also directly available to fulfill requests of other cities. In my head canon, this is because some Rimworld escapees crash-landed in Mesopotamia and taught the Sumerians how to construct orbital trade beacons. Every citizen of ancient Mesopotamia has an Amazon Prime membership and thus is unwilling to walk (or teleport) to wells (did I mention that Sumerian well drilling tech is superb: you can build a well miles from any wetlands, and it will just work) or markets to fetch daily life goods. Instead, markets are basically delivery centers employing people who will delivery the goods directly to their customers. These are also unionized and the maximum distance between their waypoints and the delivery center is limited. However, if the shortest road connecting two waypoints takes them out of that area, they will happily provide houses along the road with goods as well. Also, distance does not matter because they do not actually haul goods from the delivery center to the houses, but instead carry a portable consumer good teleportation unit to teleport the goods from the markets directly to the doorstep. Giving these unfavorable contracts, it is little wonder that they refuse to carry more than one type of consumer good at a time. Copper working is a thing in the game -- we are not in the stone age any more, after all. Of course, the only use of copper is to sate the upper classes hunger for copper  jewellery -- basically the NFTs of ancient Sumer. Never mind that by 2000 BCE, they ought to have long discovered bronze and used it for both tools and weapons.Just beyond the border of the map, countless ageless gender-fluid people of all classes camp in the desert, waiting to move into your city should they find suitable conditions. And that is where they will return quietly when the conditions of life take a turn for the worse: "Maggy, no priest has visited us in a year. Pack your stuff, we are moving out into the desert again." The parts of the game that are not directly logistics are mostly related to keeping a sufficient workforce supplied. Personally, I think that too much detail is lost when you go from simulating individual citizens (e.g. Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, Tropico), which have home, job, skills, philosophy, politics, relatives and so on to aggregate statistics only: "You have 1224 peon level jobs. Your city has 986 peon class citizens. 248 peon-level jobs are unoccupied." Unlike Sim City, Nebuchadnezzar does not even have the excuse that they have to many citizens to simulate, as the amount of people is artificially inflated anyhow: A residential building might house 70 people, while a bakery might employ 75 (in convenient groups of 25) -- not to shabby for a preindustrial civilization. Just divide by ~25, make the bakery have three employees and the house have three (working-age) citizens, and you can suddenly give them actual identities. There are some educational games in which the game mechanics are actually tied to the setting. Kerbal is definitely one for teaching spaceflight 101. If ACOUP is to believed, the Paradox games are rather good for teaching history. Nebuchadnezzar will teach you whatever you read in the info boxes (which seems plausible to me as a layperson), plus the fact that irrigation is kind of a big deal. If you enjoy logistics/planning heavy games, but can't be bothered to get into Factorio, Nebuchadnezzar might be okay for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I hope Nebuchadnezzar gets more love in the form of content; what you get today, as a "feature complete" game is a resource management puzzle rather than a city builder.  Each scenario map pits you with a challenging layout of unbuildable terrain, jagged rivers and little overall map size for fertile tile growth.  It's your task to build some housing blocks that can receive the necessary goods from your production chains, in the little available space provided to you; money comes only in the form of trade with other cities (and you can only sell/buy specified goods each map; so if you're overproducing milk? Too bad).And, well, that's the game in a nutshell.  It's fun, but it's not really fair to compare to Caesar, Zeus or Pharaoh; these games had additional layers (many!) of complexity.  You would hire prefects for theft protection, well water carriers to fight fires, you would require medicines and have health care, you would set up taxing agents for tax income from your plebs, colosseums and other entertainment buildings for joy, etc.  None of that is here in Nebuchadnezzar.  You simply provide goods to your citizens, and that's that.If you're looking for a Caesar, Zeus or Pharaoh style game in modern times, you're probably looking for Anno or Path of Progress.  Nebuchadnezzar is not a bad game by any means and I recommend it, Nebuchadnezzar simply took a different path but leads you to believe it's a Sierra game of old, when it's not.  It is a resource management puzzle game, and for that, it's at least a very good one.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is an ancient-style city builder similar to a couple of other older city builders like Pharaoh, where you attempt to build up an ancient Mesopotamian city and meet certain requirements to finish scenarios.The problem is that the tutorial mode is very broken. The first mission asks you to stockpile bread and wheat, which are part of the same supply chain: wheat gets harvested and turned into bread. It does this by having you build a wheat field (which plants and harvests wheat once a year) and then build two bakeries (which turn wheat into bread and operate 24/7/365 unless told specifically not to). Once you do this, the game goes "Oh, it's fine, just let the simulation run and it'll eventually complete on its own."The problem is that the scenario will never actually complete if you do that, because the bakeries will grab all the wheat and start cranking out bread and you'll never reach a point where you have enough wheat stockpiled. In my case, I managed to just turn the bakeries off and finished that part of the tutorial that way... even though the game never actually told me how you do that.A lot of the problem is that the game does the Paradox thing where it has a wiki and provides you links to the wiki for everything.. which is bad game design. Wikis do not excuse a bad tutorial. Then I get to the second scenario, which involves making bread and milk and then distributing them through a market to the residential areas. The goal is to get the residential areas to level up by giving them enough bread and milk via the market. Again, I ran into a problem: the game goes "Just let the sim run and all the houses will eventually level up, and then the tutorial will end."Unfortunately, that's not true either. The actual scenario goal is to reach a certain population and have a certain number of leveled-up houses.. which never happened for me. I let the sim run at 12x speed for like ten minutes and nothing. I'm not even sure it's possible to reach that population level with the houses the game starts you with. The second tutorial was just.. bad. I couldn't get past it no matter how many farms and houses I had - I tripled the number of houses and had four farms doing nothing but making wheat and another four doing nothing but making milk and still couldn't get the goal to complete. There's also a lot of very questionable mechanics that are extremely janky, if not bugged. As an example, wheat farms need to have fields manually placed around them, but also need a road connection directly to the farm building. If you place fields all around it, you can block the road from connecting and then have to manually demolish the fields to put a road in. What I don't quite understand is why I'd ever want a farm with less than maximum fields (since as far as I can tell, fields don't cost anything) or why the farm building doesn't have a road automatically attached to it so that you can't render the entire thing useless by surrounding it completely with fields.. or better, have a road connecting to the fields themselves count as a road connection.Overall, I'd say avoid this until they fix it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar is reminiscent of Pharaoh, while adding some much needed improvements. I loved Pharaoh; however, I would always become frustrated being unable to truly control the walkers' pathways--in Nebuchadnezzar you are allowed to do just that which makes for easier management and distribution. The game itself is beautiful and the music is wonderful (except for the song with a piano--don't quite remember that instrument being found in Ancient Mesopotamia). The developers definitely wanted to make the game more challenging: the maps are small and require strategic planning and forethought to build your city. As another reviewer put it, though, this might be challenging but it limits the player's creative expression and doesn't allow for major expansion or very large cities. If there is one thing I could request it would be to see the gods and goddesses walking around the city like in Zeus, Poseidon, and Emperor, but possibly the developers wanted to keep more in line with Pharaoh.

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed this game way more than I expected! I remember that initially on launch there were some rough reviews, but it's great to see that developers kept adding to the game and it seems like they've managed to create the definitive Impressions Games-style city builder.The tutorials could've been a bit expanded, I've been confused by a couple of mechanics. But after checking two 10 minute videos on youtube I got the hang of things.I love the economical and logistical tightrope you need to walk in order to grow and expand your city, with challenges (like trading, diseases, fire, gods) being thrown at you. I wish more city builders were as reactive to your choices as this game.Warfare is another recent addition to the game. I was a little intimidated by starting a campaign with warfare goals. It didn't have a dedicated tutorial, but it was quite easy to figure out. It's definitely not what you expect it to be, however it is an interesting additional system on top of other things that you need to manage when building your city. It's not mandatory to the game, you can turn warfare off it you want, but it's adds an interesting challenge to the mix. I've yet to go in-depth with it, but first impressions are pretty positive.Either way it's a great game! Great job devs for sticking to your vision and listening to the community where it was appropriate.Update: After finishing the final mission, I can say that I've loved it! The educational part of it was also amazing and fun to read, especially the one after the final mission. I would say that warfare missions are way harder than regular ones. But if you learn to optimize your city (there are some great Steam guides) you'll manage just fine.The difficulty scales gradually throughout campagin, with the later levels being the most challenging, and it was very satisfying to complete those, even though it took me up to 2 days to work through them.

_childDocuments_.review: Nebuchadnezzar really should be called nebu-chad-nezzar :)A wonderful game and a worthy tribute to the classic we all love (I assume that's why you're here)A short breakdown to the similarities and differences to pharaoh:Overall, the resemblance is obvious: A city-building game set in an ancient era. Many of the game's core mechanics come straight from pharaoh: You build a city, tend to its citizens and build up an economy that provides stability in this symbiotic circle of people, economy and state. The campaign introduces you mission by mission to the mechanics of the game, starting with a small village that's self-sufficient but is very simple in functionality and variety of goods. You then get introduced to irrigation, the gods, monuments, trading, diplomacy, warfare... all the stuff we know from pharaoh. Where nebuchadnezzar shines though, are a lot of welcome, nicely made improvements:______________________________________________________________PathfindingPharaohs horrendous flaw was that of its horrible AI. You had to structure your roads in a particular way to make sure that providers would walk the path where they would do their service, and not have the bazaar lady running around in an industrial zone, while your poor citizens would starve to death. What nebuchadnezzar did is provide an easy way to set actual routes for providers. Each provider building comes with haulers, who grab resources from nearby warehouses. Furthermore, each building has a number of slots which can be filled with eighter providers or haulers. You can also choose which provider distributes which wares, resulting in high customisability, but also a higher learning curve in finding the best setup for your supply chain.Other service providers such as firemen or healers simply head out and check buildings by sorts of in-built logic you have no control over. There is some attention required from time to time, as your growing city will require more and more service providers to keep risks in check, but so far, when something happened, it was really my fault for not paying attention, instead of a flaw in the game's pathfinding mechanics. ______________________________________________________________The godsUnlike in Pharaoh, deities are not the resentful pricks who condemn your city to pain and suffering unless you have built 3 temples, a monument, 10 shrines and keep providing a sacrifice to them once per year sodom and gommorah would be proud of. In Nebuchadnezzar, 10 years may pass and you haven't bothered building any religious facilities whatsoever, which is when you will get the notification that your main deity is a bit sad that you haven't called in a while, and therefore your clay miners reduce their productivity by 4%. Festivals are also not something you have to be bothered all the time, which is quite the relief when you just need to skip time until certain conditions are met. Once a festival is planned, it starts immediately (which is also observable in your city),  and you cannot hold another one (meaning you don't have to worry about it) for quite a while. An honourable mention is also that you may customise your festivals: The goods to be consumed, a bigger variety defining the size of the festival, and addressing it to up to 3 deities simultaneously. ______________________________________________________________MonumentsA huge funbrake in Pharaoh was for me the mind-numbing long times it took to build monuments. While they are still a somewhat resource-demanding and basically time-consuming issue in Nebuchadnezzar, you can quicken the process by throwing more resources per minute at it, and since that is also a price to pay, it doesn't take away from the satisfaction.The system to build your own monument is lovely. There are certain conditions you must meet, to not cheat your victory by building a shack and calling it a temple, and if that isn't your pair of shoes, you can still pick a premade blueprint.______________________________________________________________Economy and balancingThe overall feel of the game is more demanding than Pharaoh, but that is also the fun in it. The new possibilities with routes, logistics and distribution make building your city an engaging and incredibly satisfying experience. There is a whole new learning curve to be tackled in this game, and I had so many moments where I found new ways to make my economic  systems even better. Managing your city will be a constant challenge: In order to generate money, you will have to start trading with other cities, which means less resources for the population. ______________________________________________________________Trading and diplomacyWhile trading is pretty much the same as in Pharaoh, they have refined it with some nice little additions, as well as adding diplomatic functions. Whereas your kingdom rating would raise in Pharaoh for completing requests, you now tend relationships with each individual city. As you become friends, you also can demand favours from them and send gifts to improve relationships. On the world map, you also see the military strength of each city, and eventually, you want to declare war on them.____________________________________________________________WarfareWhereas in Pharaoh you've built an army for more or less defensive or diplomatic reasons, Nebuchadnezzar allows you to send your troops out and conquer other cities. While you do not actually control captured cities yourself (they will send tributes in form of wares), it still adds another strategic layer to the game. Combat is depicted in a rather barebones tactical map, where you move your troops in fixed fields forward or sideways. It's obviously not total war CA level of combat, but it's certainly a lot more engaging than what Pharaoh did, not to mention Pharaoh: A new era.______________________________________________________________PresentationThis game is a work of art. The map, the animations, artworks and UI all work together marvellously in pulling you into this wonderful world of old. The music is beautifully composed and of a flawless quality, and hits the tone of the game deadeye. Buildings are clustered with visual detail, and pretty much everything is animated that needs to be: Industrial buildings show the workers doing their job (IF they do so), barracks are gradually filled with soldiers, markets change their colours to represent the goods they distribute. The plazas and gardens we know from Pharaoh make a return. And here's one little critique: While I love how you can design your plazas yourself by not only handpicking from a broad variety of designs but by also setting colour schemes, it is a chore to place whole districts that way, piece by piece, unless you use one design solely. Unfortunately, it is the same with gardens: There is no option to just pull a square and have it filled randomly, it's either one design on the whole place, or handpicking field by field. A style editor and distributor would have been lovely.Another point of critique may be the voiceovers: I doubt the mesopotamians spoke with such a stark british accent. But honestly, as far as I know, Nepos Games is a small studio with just one game released, and when compared with the rest of the game's presentation, this really is not even worth the mention.______________________________________________________________Famous last wordsAs you might have noticed if you have read this whole review, I am genuinely stunned by this game. It is one of those miracles in the indie gaming industry, the standard only a few meet. If you liked Pharaoh, get this game. It is a brilliant, highly polished gem, and belongs in the masterclass of modern gaming development. If you are displeased by the current gaming industry, get this game. It is a love letter to quality in graphics, difficulty balancing, and player experience, and quite frankly to gamers :)
