_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty mixed game that is way too repetitive for its own good.The protagonist of the game is Mordred. After killing King Arthur, the latter cursed the land and now everyone in Avalon is either running around as a brigand or an undead. Mordred is brought back by the Lady of the Lake to kill the variety of evil monsters King Arthur's soul has been twisted into. Along the way, Mordred recruits a variety of characters from Arthurian legend to help him while rebuilding Camelot.The gameplay of this game can be summed up in one word: SLOG. You select a team of knights to go on a mission. The missions are largely redundant; you go to a crypt or some burnt out ruin, fight a handful of encounters, open up a few chests to acquire gold or gear, and complete the mission. Your characters have armor (which wears down over time) that mitigates damage, but your characters have two health resources: hit points and vitality. Hit points are replenished to their maximum after each mission, but lost vitality does not regenerate unless you put the respective character in Camelot's infirmary to heal over time. Mordred's Round Table can have up to a dozen active members at a time, but there are 30 different characters that you can recruit over the game's progression. Some characters, like the Black Knight and Queen Boudicca, are absolute powerhouses, while others like Sir Ywain and Sir Damas are pretty worthless. The encounters in this game are tedious and redundant, especially at the beginning, where you fight undead. Tons and tons and tons of undead. To make it worse, the undead in this game have an effect where they will reanimate themselves after 3 turns if their remains are not destroyed, adding to the tedium of this game. Every objective is the same - grind down the enemy's vitality to 0. "Here's a bunch of bad guys, kill them to advance" is virtually every victory condition for almost every mission, main and side, in this game.The environment and terrain for these combat encounters do not help either, as they are completely static, always taken place on a flat surface that may or may not have a few pillars of cover at most. The crypts and ruins you are sometimes required to delve into look as if the assets were copypasted - corridor, chamber, corridor, chamber. The outside environments are a consistent mixture of gray and brown with swampy, fog-filled bogs. Between these boring missions you return to Camelot, where you click through boring "base management" and boring lordly decisions. Camelot's management screen looks like it was made in a very early build of the game and the developers decided not to change or improve it. You will be treated to ugly fonts etched on ugly windows, of which there are many. Equipment management is abysmal, as nearly every icon shares the same sword or cuirass icon. You have to actually highlight the item with your cursor to see what class it corellates to and how it will change stats - and by change stats, I mean it's yet another game where it's a matter of "Green numbers = good". Mordred is also required to make decisions on the realm, and what he chooses will affect his morality chart, which ranges from Christian and Pagan on the X axis, and Rightful and Tyrant on the Y axis. These determine which heroes you can eventually recruit, in addition to seemingly trivial bonuses, but after a while you will stop bothering to read these moral dilemmas and just pick the option to boost the morality you want. Sometimes this will irritate various heroes in your arsenal (i.e. building a church may anger your Pagan-following heroes) and if their "loyalty" gets low they will take penalties in combat, but that's it. They don't defect, they don't express their outrage at your leadership. In fact, the interactions with your vassals and followers is virtually nonexistent. Your hear the thumping of your armor as you run to-and-fro on a mission's map, and one of your party members may make a quip about Avalon's state of affairs, which is only followed by more awkward silence. It's a lack of interaction that adds on to an egregiously dreary setting.This game is, unfortunately, one of those games that people seem to power through just to see the ending because it becomes repetitive and unenjoyable. This game is long - probably too long. With the way the game's leveling progression pans out, you are essentially required to do every side mission - partially due to leveling up your main squad, partially to progress your other knights' training at Camelot in-between missions, and partially due to recruiting certain heroes that are flat out superior.Overall, I would give this game a 5/10. For every good aspect this game has, it's overshadowed by two negative aspects. But if you're interested in playing it, wait until it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing turn based strategy game. I've yet to come across a game in this genre that is this polished. I'm not finished so i'm unsure about what the replayability looks like but this game certainly is better than the XCOM series...and it's from an indie studio.XCOM is really mostly all I can compare it to but here it is:- No hit rating probability BS where you can miss a 99% shot like in XCOM (extremely frustrating).- Relevant to the above, they have total health split between HP and vitality where HP replenishes after each combat automatically while when HPis depleted you take vitality damage which DOES requires further 'resting'. This is a nice alternative giving that all attacks will hit outside of dodge probability.- Armor is far more meaningful in this game which does add to the two mentioned above- Far more items and gear to kit out your soldiers- More in depth skill trees to tailor your play- Being able to see the line of sight of each unit on squares before moving to them- Having additional side objectives within main mission and side quest that are not a copy/paste of just a few options- No time based mission BS (I like to play very methodically so I dislike being rushed)- You are able to free roam in between encounters in every missions trying to find treasures and perhaps side objectives- There are no randomly generated soldiers as all are predetermined with name and class. This is a negative for some but for me a positive as it gave greater meaning to each person which also extends to special missions and interactions they have in certain missions and side quests.Just my thoughts.

_childDocuments_.review: Have been completely hooked on this game since I first started playing it.The dark theme, and alternate story line are actually very well done. Graphics match the theme - it is dark. Voice acting is also really well done.Thoroughly enjoy the turn-based combat, but it scales pretty quickly, so you definitely need to invest in skills for your knights that help deal with crowds/multiple enemies.  You also need long-range knights who can take out their archers/mages - otherwise you are going to hit a wall really quickly.The Action Point system takes a bit to adjust to - although if you have played something like Divinity you will pick it up qucikly.The armour/HP/vitality system actually works pretty well, and means you need to think through your actions and how to position your characters rather than just charging headlong into a hack and slash. The backstab mechanic is a bit frustrating but once you know how it works you need to be aware of that in positioning your front line.Mobility is key. Each campaign mission has an objective, and once you finish that you can move on. This sometimes means you can make a straight trade of XP/gold/items from sub-quests or side missions vs just completing the main objective. Given rest points are limited in each map, and vitaility, injuries are things you cant deal with during a campaign (must be at Camelot) it definitely adds a challenging dimension and means you do need to think through whether you really take that fight or not (on harder difficulties).The ability to customise your knights and their abilities is good. It does feel a little "sameish" between knights of the same type (e.g. all champions seem to have very similar skills - maybe just in a different order, or start with different ones when you pick them up), but there is a really good variety of knights available as you progress which makes this less of an issue. The way combat works you really do need to have your knights focus their skills into certain paths rather than be generalists, and that means they dont all end up the same. (which is great).The morality system also means that different knights are available based on the decisions you make, and the further you move down one path the less you can utilise knights of an opposing persuasion - means you have to make choices - but "them is the breaks".The equipment/relics you pick up as you go have some variety - but I am finding that is perhaps the least interesting aspect  in terms of the variety of things you find.Out of the box, if you are not familiar with this sort of game you are going to struggle. There really isn't a lot of tutorial/guidance and no real hints on what buildings to focus on for Camelot or skills to develop for you knights. I would therefore highly recommend a couple of YouTube videos to get you up to speed - Slandered Gaming and FextraLife are two channels that will help you out with some of the game basics. I would also suggest a newbie cranks the difficulty down to "Story" initially so you can get a handle on the way combat mechanics and other things work before cranking the dial back up.Overall a very good game worth the investment.

_childDocuments_.review: I am hesitant to not recommend this game, because there's a lot to like, but here's what I don't:- Recruiting knights really is the driving force behind the game, and it's fun, but after they stop showing up, the game loses steam fast. Also, once you add them to your party they become a generic grunt with little to no further development beyond skills in battle. If there was some sort of dialogue system, maybe events to build camaraderie, something, anything more than just a portrait with a handful of voice lines... - Why on earth are knights that you dismiss gone forever? It makes NO sense! The whole point of the story is rebuilding a kingdom to save the freaking world from certain doom- You don't think they would prioritize that over literally everything else?  So what? Put them in the garrison or send them out to help others. Anything is more plausible than permanent banishment... I know it was done for replay value and to force hard choices, but it's just that: forced. You can spend half the game getting your morality to a point just for a recruit, then say sorry pack your bags and don't come back I already have two vanguards and don't need another. It's not a good mechanic and I will stand by that.- The battles got repetitious sooner than I had hoped, mainly because the environments you fight in are almost always just flat rooms and clearings with some scattered obstacles. It's very rare for there to be any kind of elevation or hazards in play. So if you are a veteran of games like Xcom, Divinity or Solasta, you will find it lacking.- This game isn't very well optimized, especially for older systems (my GPU is four years old, shame on me), and there are persistent bugs like floors disappearing if you tweak the wrong setting to try and  improve FPS, which is mostly a fruitless endeavor. There's this baked in motion blur and grainy volumetric fog that make everything muddy and icky, though maybe that was the point.I really like the character designs, music and morality system, but I put over 50 hours into this game and even though I am near the end of the story, I don't know if I'm going back in.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big Xcom fan, Divinity: Original Sin, the list goes on. I liked this game at the beginning. But it's so repetitive and the issues just keep creeping in. I think it has good potential and if there is a second game to improve on what this one is lacking I'd say it'd be a gem.First, the bloody crashes. No matter what I still get really annoying crashes mid fight and we're talking system crash, not just the game.Almost 40 hours in and every fight is the same since enemies don't require special tactics. It's a chore to be in a fight you've done a hundred times.The writing is not great. The dialogues are quite uninspired. Also, it's 2023 for gods sake, but this game is one big sausage party, there is plenty of women in the lore so that was a choice to not use them, one example of many: you could easily switch who's saving who in the Tristan mission, .The Dark Souls aesthetic is nice but it gets a bit dull after a while. The surroundings become boring because everything is muddy gray and you see it from afar. Which is a shame since the separate details are well done, why don't you work your camera? Like when you meet the blind Pict father, zoom the camera on the son, it would change the whole encounter. I've spent the first couple of hours looking at everything up close but you can't be doing that the whole time.What I would love to see is utilizing your characters more. I didn't like Mordred all that much, I'd prefer making my own knight. Being able to take a look at the knights and customize them like basically any other modern turn based game of this size. I had zero connection to them because of it, if someone died I wasn't devastated like in other games.Tip: If you're using Irish, at least make the voice actor read it how it's supposed to be pronounced.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not like this game the first time I played it.  I figured I'd give it another shot.  I still don't like it but now I'm just past the refund window.  Ugh.The writing is bad, especially the dialogue.  The acting is also bad.  The 3D design of the environments is lazy.  For instance, walls become partially transparent when the toons are inside, as they should.  However, this shows that the walls are hollow:  you can see the back sides of the quilts that are supposed to define the solid.  Maybe it's because I'm an engineer but this REALLY pisses me off.  Non-solid parts are a no-go.  You could just make the whole wall disappear or make the objects solid.The rest of the setting is this drab boring gray which clashes with the cartoonish interpretation of arthurian legend.  More on the interpretation:  it just does not work in my opinion.  I expected something semi-realistic.  Some magic, sure but mostly gross muddy people with sticks and swords.  This is all demons and zombies.  The armor design is also very diablo-esque.  Why spoil arthurian stuff with this generic RPG crap?Otherwise, it's a competent enough tactical game.  But there are many competent enough tactical games and generally the setting makes sense and the writing isn't terrible.

_childDocuments_.review: Some other reviewer summed it up nicely - this game deserves a neutral rating, but as there is no such thing available, I will go with negative. It ticks all the boxes for a player like me - party based, turn based, you have unique skill trees for the heroes and the skills are mostly nice and combine well, you can upgrade your base, upgrade weapons and armor, there is a morality system with two scales giving different bonuses, there is loyalty scale on your companions as well. So on paper the game looks great.But in reality the playthrough still felt repetitive and uninspiring. In almost all encounters, you get similar map with several chests and several groups of enemies. Their skills and defences do not differ that much once you have played several missions so very soon each mission feels like the previous ones. There is very little outside of battle so if I have to sum up the game, it is something like that - buy/upgrade/heal in the castle, pass an unispired copy paste mini event (either click a button to send a companion to do a job or just pick the right choice based on your morality), go to the next boring repetitive mission (and then repeat). Although there is morality, the game does not push you to make any tough choices, you just pick a type based on the bonuses that it gives you and stick with it (I even stopped reading at some point and just clicked the button that matched my morality choice).Honestly, the only reason why I managed to finish the main story is because I was listening to audio books on the background.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually play squad based tactical games (Ex. XCOM) that utilize firearms. I hesitate to play similar games where the combat is primarily melee because, in my opinion, they lack combat depth (height advantage, cover destruction, etc.). However, King Arthur: Knight's Tale (KAKT) is an exception and rivals similar games in the genre, such as Expeditions: Rome. Good:- Combat mechanics- VFX- SFXAbove Average:- Graphics- Voice ActingAverage:- Strategy Layer (Base management, overworld events, etc.)- Map VarietyPoor:- Performance on some maps - Inventory Management designPersonal Gripe:- Difficulty settings: Early in the game, enemy group size increases from about 8 to about 10-17. You will still encounter about 4-5 groups of enemies per mission. On normal, enemies deal low damage and your knights will easily survive as long as you are not careless. On hard, enemies receive a substantial damage and health boost (about double damage and 1.75x health). Knights with high armor values and who are oriented towards the attacking enemy (you do not receive increased damage if oriented towards an enemy) will still lose a large amount of health and armor. The enemy damage and health boosts, along with the large amount of enemies present, leaves no room for play mistakes. A few play mistakes, which would usually cost a knight some health or armor loss on normal, will cause your knight to be severely injured or killed on hard. I expect to be punished for play mistakes but the difficulty gap between normal and hard is too significant. I would recommend that the developers lessen the enemies' health and damage boosts or lessen the amount of enemies present. KAKT is good game for the price and one of the few games in the genre that excels in multiple aspects. With a little improvement, KAKT could become a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews, but I have never played a game like this. On one hand it has +great atmosphere+cool setting+good music+interesting classes with varietyOn the other hand, -many voice actors sound like they have no idea what they are doing-the conversations are often absurd-there are many bugs (mostly graphic)-random FPS drops-the balancing is unbelievably ♥♥♥♥:I was Playing a SIDE mission and absolutely no problem. Killing each camp, barely taken any damage. Final encounter (again: SIDE mission) a huge beast, so many armor symbols I cannot count it, massive HP, summons a bunch of other giants which stun, aoe etc., even has a potion that heals HP AND armor! Srsly who made the balancing in this game? Or did you just hit “randomize all”? It seems in general that towards the end of the game you fight large groups with 2-3 stun+ 2-3 blind + 2-3 other CCs vs your 4 char team. Meaning you are CC’d and can just watch how they mutilate you. No, kiting and dodging is not a thing.This was the end for me, due to this game breaking reason: You have often a choice of 1-3 side missions and 1 mainQ. The mainQ requires a higher level so you basically have to do all side missions. You have no other way to train your chars (except the training ground which also takes 1-3 missions for one level up). So, you are forced to do missions to improve your chars this or the other way. This is the game breaking problem: you have basically no idea what awaits you in the mission. Once inside, you can't leave, only reset the mission. You also cannot change difficulty, equipment or chars. Meaning you are TRAPPED IN THE MISSION. Which ultimately means, you might end up in a mission which you cannot finish because the balancing is ♥♥♥♥ and this ends the game for you. Absolutely ridiculous.Oh, and you can only bring 2 potions/scrolls so you cannot save yourself with bought items as well.I am 40h+ deep in the game but cannot continue. Kinda salty I cannot refund this. It is a game that you might end up not being able to finish.Better get Divinity or Baldur’s Gate.

_childDocuments_.review: It's...OK. I'll recommend it for tactical RPG enthusiasts, and enthusiasts only. It's not a bad game - it's generally well made, and has all your bells and whistles, you know; kingdom management, morality chart, the works - and I found the take on Arthurian lore unique. But...I quickly found myself getting bored and not really looking forward to the next battles in each map. They just became so tedious, because the core gameplay is very limited and conservative in scope. The game wants to be tactical, but I found it more or less a very straightforward RPG-ish experience, and the gameplay to more of just hack and slash rather than taking into account positioning, turns, environmental factors. Yeah, these elements exist, but they make a very small impact on the overall game experience. Like many games in these crossover genres they open up later on, but I found myself not really caring for the core gameplay. Hell, Final Fantasy Tactics offers a more varied and rewarding experience and this was a game made over 20 years ago. Like, come on guys. Is this all there is to the gameplay? A few interesting class skills? Focus down enemies one by one? A few meaningful abilities on each unit? Snore. Perhaps I'm spoiled by Expeditions Rome's gameplay (which offers a superior tactical experience tbh). I found myself sighing to myself and complaining... "not another zombie level", or "not another brigand level." Additionally, I found the art design to rather drab; greys, browns, and blacks. Must we copy the color schemes of boring modern movies too? In real life, Medieval settings were actually much more colorful than what is portrayed in modern media. The writing is also bad, with some real cringy dialogue choices. Overall I would only recommend this to hardcore tactical RPG fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Totally no.The story is completely bland starting by putting you in the shoes of a hatred knight and then telling you that you need to retake a throne for the greater good (so wasn't I supposed to be a bad guy?). Then you just keep meeting random so called knights who all seem to hate you but will nonetheless join your cause just because.... well because.Do you get any interest in any of them? Nope they are just there to act as random controlled characters. I could not care less for the loss of any of them if it was not for the obvious fact that at some point I'll run out of new troops. All of them are suppose to have a background and story, but it's just a blunt paragraph of text on their bio. Or some ideioti story during a side mission. Even RPGs that make you control nameless toons or robots make a much better job at giving you an interest in them.Running around the combat zone map is not much better, you are in free roam until you trigger an fight, but that feels like a total waste of time, just to maybe find some random loot and healing areas. There is no thrill, no real reason to explore (besides the loot) and with not map or view of the area you went through, it gets a chore after 2 encounters.Again there is a story in each map, but the dialog are so stupid and ridiculously written it would feel better if they could all just shut-up.The world map doesn't save anything, it's just a pair of areas where you just click to build stuff (think Heroes of Might and magic cities) and a second area where you click on available missions. There is no animation, no life sense and the missions even appear at seemingly random places on the landmarks even increasing the sense that the story isn't actually one but just a big pile of garbage text between mildly interesting combats.Would have refunded if I didn't get past the timer before realizing all this.

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, that's right, despite the title, in this game you take on the role of the anti-hero Sir Mordred! A very refreshing twist on Arthurian legend. Even more so when you factor in this is dark fantasy, so undead, magic and all manner of beasties come in to play.I found it great to approach this new tale from an unusual angle. Mordred is exactly the weapons grade bellend you want him to be. A towering defender full of one liners, snappy comebacks and scathing putdowns.A presence so terrifying, that even the members of the court and table of Camelot quietly accept his contempt as he gathers them under his command.The game itself plays out in series of missions, that are essentially skirmishes with a goal or parameters that must be met to achieve victory. These missions push along the story as well as providing the necessary XP and loot to progress and build out Mordred and your party.While loot and XP are gained as you combat and explore the mission locations, neither can be applied to party members until the mission is over and you are preparing for the next. This "intermission" is also a chance to apply your morality points. A kind of Paragon system based on decisions you make out in the game world. These place you somewhere between Tyrant and Rightful for your actions and Christian and Old gods for your allegiance. Points spent here can be used to unlock modifiers, abilities, buffs and followers. (for example: if you level Righteous to 13 you unlock the Pious Prick Lancelot)Progression is really well designed, more like an RPG or MMO's set of skills, abilities and modifiers with extensive and varied customization. Loot is likewise diverse and spread among the now obligatory common, uncommon, rare, legendary tiers; some locked to specific classes. Tooltips are, for the most part, clear and helpful and with a little bit of planning it's relatively easy and extremely satisfying to build out a character that synergizes skills with equipment loadout. This synergy can be further explored between party members and there is a certain Divinity feel during combat when this is exploited.Combat in Knight's Tale feels more Xcom like than Divinity though however and there is always the risk or permanent injury or death for your party members. I did find myself genuinely invested in my party's welfare. The well scripted back and forth and excellent voice acting had a big part to play in this I'm sure.The combat is everything you'd expect from a tactical RPG, AP, abilities, situational positioning etc. etc. A tutorial you have played a hundred times no doubt. But while Knight's Tales doesn't really do anything new in this respect, it does it very well. Combat moves along at a good pace, abilities are well thought out, easy to use and the area of battle is easy to navigate and clear to interpret.Knights Tale builds atmosphere really well. While it doesn't have the most jaw dropping aesthetics, it does a good job in painting a picture of dark despair and foreboding, a muted colour palette of monotone and grays remind you that this is no Bugsnax adventure, this is "Serious Business". Environments have been built by using photoscanned environments and complemented by high-quality mocap animation, then rendered inside a modern PBR engine utilizing DirectX 12 to support strong, atmospheric effects.Audio is again top notch, as I already mentioned the voice acting is on point. Particularly with fantasy games, its very easy to go HAM over the top or conversely fall short and seem like shy nerd mumblings. Here however the voices, dialogue and conversations are all very well created and add immeasurably to the over atmosphere and immersion. Sound effects add weight and gravitas to actions and abilities; while the background music is the sweeping choral ooohs and aaaahs you would expect from a game with this title.All in all this is an excellent title and very enjoyable even in Early Access. I'm someone who has never really quite clicked with the tactical turn based genre, but I do love an RPG. Knight's Tale takes aspects of other fantasy genres to make itself accessible and enjoyable to a broader range of players and that's a great achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: + grim atmosphere+ quality combat system + a choice of different ways of developing the group's based on morals and beliefs+ relatively many types of enemies- progress brings only a little new to gameplay- weapons and equipment with random stats available in shops and lootThe move King Arthur surprisingly lets us play as his nemesis Mordred, who is revived by the Lady of the Lake to save Avalon from King Arthur tainted existence. Depending on whether he leans towards good or evil and the old faith or Christianity, Mordred gains different companions on his way, who have similar parameters. And then it depends on the player to match a group of compatible heroes, because if their loyalty to Mordred is the highest, then they have the best qualities. Fights take place on pre-generated maps of individual missions with mostly 4 of heroes, the possibilities of healing or repairing damaged armor are relatively limited within the mission, and damage to vitality can lead to permanent injuries or death. There are 5 basic hero classes, but their development trees are implemented slightly differently within each character.Each character can be improved with equipment, using consumable items or permanent improvements through special challenges.Combat is high-quality, built on the AP system, contains various combos and synergies, and the range of enemies is just as wide.The atmosphere is dark, the graphics and the sound underline it.Difficulty is optional, I personally chose normal in combination with roguelite (one save), when the game was relatively easy.It's a bit frustrating that the number of hireable characters is higher than the castle's capacity, and therefore not all available characters can be hired and player have to choose whom dismiss for good, when he choose someone else.Overall, I consider the game to be a very successful in turn based genre this year, but I enjoyed Chaos Gate: Demonhunters a little bit more.

_childDocuments_.review: King Arthur: Knight's Tale is an engaging and entertaining RPG that immerses players in the legendary world of King Arthur and his knights. The game features a deep and complex narrative that explores the political and personal struggles of the characters, as well as a challenging turn-based combat system that requires strategic planning and decision making. The graphics and sound design are top-notch, and the voice acting is superb. The game also offers a high degree of replayability, as players can make different choices and decisions that will affect the outcome of the story. Overall, King Arthur: Knight's Tale is a must-play for fans of RPGs and the Arthurian legend.

_childDocuments_.review: After 40 hours in, I have had no critical crashes or bugs.  I can say that the game is fairly resource-hungry, as many others have pointed out.For those who like the Arthurian legends, the developers did a tremendous job of putting a grimdark spin on many of the legends!  The storytelling in the side quests and main quest are interesting to me from that perspective, and it was a fun game. The combat/management is similar to xcom. As a plus (in my opinion) there is no researching technologies like Xcom, but instead, your decisions in quests impact your morality/faith, which in turn leads to unlocking new buffs/unique knights etc.  I like this system.The game also feels very long in terms of content, so I feel that it is good entertainment:cost ratio. Looking forward to future iterations of the game and polish.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy the King Arthur theme in all genres, books, games, films including all the lore so buying games like this will always  happen. I think it is only fair to be honest straight from the outset, it is a very short early access game which is quite expensive for the content you will receive so you should only consider this if you are looking to support the Devs or like me as I mentioned previously this is something that really interests me so supporting the Devs in completing this game is worth my investment. The game plays with exploration opened in a liner world with combat entering in to a X-Com esque environment. There is thoughtful tactics which brings tension during each battle. The RPG element is enjoyable and you can see even with this limited amount of content that every action will have a consequence. _childDocuments_.review: This game is reaaally good, especially if you love the Arthurian legend and knights in shiny armour. The story is a bit dark but good, the characters are very good, graphics are excellent (I love those shiny armours and the 3D-models are very detailed and realistic). _childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game but it's way too long for the type of combat it has, let me explain.Being a turned based combat your team takes it's turn then the enemy team does. The problem appears when you get 5+ encounters per mission with 10-15 enemies it will burn you down and get sick of the combat just like me. There are barely any good upgrades. Most of the skills are bad and don't help you that much. The armors and weapons are a joke and the trinkets are worthless aside from 3-4 relics that give you extra powers (teleport, life steal, heal).I really hate the companion mechanic where you have a maximum amount of characters permitted and in order to get more active ones you have to dismiss the ones you already have.The story expects you to know every damned character in the arthurian mythology and what battles happened. I know just what was presented on the Merlin tv show from 2008I resisted this tiresome combat up until midway through act 3 and it's enough for me considering i'm getting at least 10+ enemies per encounter with 4-5 encounters per map.It's an ok game but not at the current price tag of 45 euros. Maybe when it's around 20 it might be a good time to pick it up. I rate it at around a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Good turn based strategy.For first few hours may be boring, unless you have got a squad and start managing items.Game is good and interesting, even though it quite unbalanced:- some skills are much more useful than others- you are depending on dropped items- some classes are stronger that others (also depends from dropped items)- round table makes no sence (with its 2 laws and 2 decrees)- poison / bleeding / freezing / burning (for archers) sucks.Game doesn't force you to shuffle active team. Most of time you can take top team. And game often punish you if you don't do so, because of difficulty spikes (played on top difficulty). Sometimes on mission, they are throwinge eg. 5 strong enemies at once, that you can barely win with wounds, and healing after. Next time, there are 1-2 of same stong enemies, that barely scratch you. Maybe that is related to items you have got as well, but after Artur shard 3, i barely had people to go on mission.Overlayy, i like the style, dialogs, atmosphere, difficult parts of game, and some tough fights that i had.In the end, Mordred became killing tank, with boosting damage to 100 from hit, that is also over satisfying :)

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this when it was a Kickstarter because it looked cool and showed great promise. Fast forward through early access and full release and it still looks cool, but that’s about it. It is very ambitious but tries to do way too much and doesn’t deliver.Let’s talk about story, battle mechanics, and game mechanics.The story is promising. It takes place after the canonical legends end and something has gone horribly wrong and it's up to us to fix. The trouble is, it's a poorly told story and quickly falls apart. Luckily it’s linear, but the end result is that you feel shoehorned through the devs’ ramblings rather than invited on a quest. Most of your plot development takes place during missions where the dialogue goes from ok to incomprehensible. (I'm honestly shocked at the poor grammatical quality of the English script, poor narrative quality aside.) Dialogue choices don’t really add much and the only impactful choices you get are either required “let’s go!” type responses that are needed to move you through a dungeon or “do I side with Character A or Character B” and add one to my court instead of the other.Worse, characters are more caricatures. Because this story takes places after the end of the Arthurian saga, once more or less everyone is dead, literally every player in Arthuriana is available and the devs bring them all along for the ride. The problem is that they also play a lot of inside baseball and swamp the player in characters who get little development. This is a high bar for players and bad storytelling, but also means the folks we interact with have the depth of a daytime soap opera cast, veering towards tyrannical Christian’s and virtuous pagans in a way that becomes predictable and off putting. None of my characters have died yet, but if they did I wouldn’t mourn them, I’d just replace them with another jaunty knight with more or less the same skill set and a similarly poorly communicated backstory and significance. Then, we'd just happily bumble through the next missions as they make non sequitur comments that don't really add anything to the experience. The mind-numbingly linear nature of the story, the poor plot development, and the flat characters give me little reason to finish this game, let alone replay it.On to the battle system! Ah, the battles. There is a delightful array of skills and the classes are fairly well developed to fit traditional RPG roles with a unique flair.  There’s also something satisfying about hacking down wave after wave…after wave after wave…after….wave…of the same types of enemies map after map after similar map. As you might guess from the description, it becomes boring and unsatisfying quickly. Each mission is effectively a skirmish and feels like a one-off since the narrative development of the game is lacking. I’m not totally sure why I’m in a (bog / crypt / wasteland) again, but if I run around enough I’ll meet some (bandits / skeletons / barbarians) sooner or later and if I kill enough of them then the mission will end. The maps themselves are beautiful, as is the character art, but it doesn’t make up for the fact that every battle after you encounter a new type of enemy feels like a repeat of the last one. There’s an attempt on some missions to add in named characters as mini-bosses or dungeon bosses but, again, when the world building is lacking at the macro level, I struggle as a player to get hyped up to take on Sir Named-Skeleton IV, who was prideful in life, alongside all his mates when it’s just another skeleton fight. It’s gotten to the point where I dread the battles, not because they’re difficult, but because they are so repetitious, boring, and shallow. It's just a grind.Ok, let’s talk broader game mechanics, specifically: base building, item acquisition, and companion management.The base building mechanics are fine, though often a bit clunky and neither revolutionary nor particularly impressive. The bonuses some companions can give to different buildings is a nice plus, but it’s a minor bonus. Resource acquisition is totally based on mission outcomes save for the occasional world event, so you may be rolling in gold that you can trade for building points at unfavorable rates, or you can wait it out to build that addition to the Round Table until you finally get a mission that rewards you in build points. There's no real rhyme or reason, the game just trundles on and you make the best worst choice you can without ever having sufficient resources. This is fine because the bonuses offered by different buildings are nice, but they don’t feel particularly significant - there's nothing I felt I had to have beyond the basics.Item acquisition is random, as is the way that things show up in the shops. This means that you just work with what you get and if you don’t get anything better for a particular companion over the next 5 to 10 missions, well, that’s the luck of it. While uninspiring and making things feel stagnant, I didn’t find this hampered my progress much since damage and defense progression feels pretty flat. It might benefit from a tier of unique weapons that have to be reassembled like “the Excalibur” so that there’s something predictable for folks to work towards. Instead, I feel swamped in bland junk with low resale value.Finally, the knights of the round table. I've commented a bit on them already in relation to their character development, but let's talk about party management. You find these folks all over - some from story quests, some from optional quests, some from unlockable quests based on your moral decision making. With few exceptions, this all feels arbitrary and comes down to the poor world building. The devs decided who be available when and it just feels capricious and annoying, or it would if they had character and weren't just a series of interchangeable class archetypes.Once you acquire a character for your court, there is little to no relationship development. There may be a little dialogue during missions or they can do a little quest of there own, but you don’t have dialogue with them in a meaningful way, you don’t get to know them. Once they join your court, they’re just sort of there. To suck more of the joy out of things, you’re also limited on space, so after a while you’ve got to start kicking knights out or letting them die if there are particular knights you want to have. There's no real reason for this I can see beyond the devs wanting to force a choice on players.This brings us to the loyalty system. Loyalty, and the bonuses you get from it, is more or less determined by the moral choices you make. These hit at a macro level rather than an individual level, meaning in the late game you’re shoehorned into what characters you can use most effectively based on the alignment you choose. If you’re a pagan, all your Christians will hate you. If you’re a tyrant, all your just folks will hate you. If you get someone who’s a tyrannical Christian, well, it’s a wash, which is fine as mechanics go but makes no sense from a narrative point of view. This also means neutral heroes just sort of persist, never getting penalties but also never getting bonuses. Luckily, the bonuses and penalties you get aren't very significant so your characters liking or not liking you feels more of a cosmetic choice than a game changer.In sum, the battle mechanics and graphics are stellar, but that is worth little when the cost is paid in lackluster world-building, poor narrative, and shallow characters. Make me emotionally invest in the characters, make the loyalty system worthwhile and sensible, clean up the script, give things proper context and then I'd be more than happy to give this beautiful game more time. Til then, it's just a flat, boring grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good. It has it's issues, but it's early access. Grammar, a few collision issues, had a few save issues. But the only one that really bothers me is what I'm encountering lately - framerate issues. I'm on a very capable setup (no, I'm not flex my "specs" bro) and I'm having issues about 9 hours in. We'll see if that improves.Otherwise, it really is like XCOM medieval version. There are no misses or dodges and I really like that. Shielded units can block, of course. Inventory management and base upgrades is simplistic. I'm playing on Hard difficulty and that's a decent challenge. I tried starting on the ironman-type setting and it was brutal. I wouldn't recommend that on a first try as some enemies literally explode and it's game over. The game doesn't tell you that either lol, you just get blown up and you learn. I've been enjoying the game, but it's definitely clunky and it's possible Devs will have that all resolved upon release. I appreciate they are not rushing the release, either. I'd say it's currently 7/10 with FAR more potential if they can polish it up a bit.

There is more to do, to build and find. E.g.: The Cursed Wood mission about sir Yavin was really nice and the atmosphere was creepy, mysterious and melancholic. _childDocuments_.review: I do like this game a lot  Others have described it so i just comment some of the issues raised by others. The game is quite difficult  ( I think it is but I'm an average player I think/hope) . However there are many difficulty levels from a walk in the park to ridiculously difficult for a pensioner like me.  There are also some   difficulty spikes but they can be overcome by resetting the difficulty level for any scenario whilst in Camelot . Cheesy perhaps but no one else need know.1. I completely agree with the poster who complained that party members can't share potions. Each character can only have 2, Apparently there is an upgrade that can allow a char. to have a 3rd but I've never  been able to get that. This means that I  have to use hit point recovery points only and a very occasional armour repair potion but I rely on camp fires to mend armour.  Shame as there are many types of potion and single-use are in practice unavailable. There ar some potions/scrolls that can be used pre-mission and last for the mission and there are useful - and rare2 Some quests require/forbid a particular char. from participating. That's OK but it can be a pain because you rarely have more than 4 or 5 decent knights for the scenario. There is training for other knights in your rota, but in reality that does  not enable them  keep up3. Side quests don't always require sending out a knight, but the result seems to be   a bit hit and miss. Success seems to be dependant on the lavel/abilties of the knight sent out, but  I have no way of knowing. Success can sometimes bring in useful benefits but often they only benefit the knight who was sent  because he/she wasn't useful for main quests.4. My sanity has been saved  by  checking out you-tube gudes for all aspects . I've found Maxallos betst though there were nade in 2022 so may be slightly out of date in some respects,5. I do like the high-camp absurd armour etc and the voice acting is excellent - rather than the  uninspired  quality heard in many other games6. The worst part for me is 1 of the missions (level 4 I think) in which saves are disabled. It is difficult for me to be able to play  the whole mission in 1 session. The lack of saves is an unnecessary and disrespectful of my time especially as I get quite a few CTDs  when playing: though that may just be on my PC as  I haven't read other complaints about crashing.All in all though an excellent game which  is very goood value for money and could and should easily be made even better with a few tweaks.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: satisfying, dark, medieval X-ComMessage for devs: Take good care of the story. Focus on atmosphere (see Darkest Dungeon 1) and heavy-duty story, take some inspiration from Dark Souls 1 if needed. Great work, looking forward for more.Pros: - Surprisingly addicting x-com like with a great twist on the legend. - The dark setting adds to the experience, with very nice music that reflects the Pagan and Old Druidic Ways- Good customization for heroes for both skills and items- Good customization for the kingdom (i.e. build orders, construction, etc)- Nice RPG options for Pagan Vs Christianity, and Benevolent Ruler Vs Tyrant which adds depthPros:- Could get "grindly" later on, and unless you have a good story to support this grind as a foundation it might become stale- Dialogue seems uninspired - especially YOUR own options to interact with characters, often times seems.... silly and childish, you might ask yourself internally: "oh wow, this...doesnt seem like smth Mordred would say at all..."- I would appreciate some recognition for higher level difficulties, maybe even a stupid achievement or something, or perhaps even one single dialogue line, anything really, ANY recognition for playing in harder diffs plus roguelite, anything at all- Takes time until you get to unlock the "good stuff" in the talent tree, plus you cant diverge from ONE single path, otherwise you fight your own progress in the talent tree.Overall yes quite good, would buy a decent DLC and follow-up.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a top notch Turn Based Strategy game with elements of Darkest Dungeon, Xcom, and believe it or not, RPG like exploration. If Xcom, Divine Divinity 2 or Darkest Dungeon are your thing, buy this game; don't wait for a sale, because I hope the Developers make enough profit to make a bigger sequel. This game reminds me very much of the original Xcom remake, in that it has great core systems, but is lacking in scope and budget; a sequel could be something along the lines of Xcom2. The combat system is very similar to Xcom, but with a greater emphasis on attacking, planning mid battle ( Xcom lets you setup encounters, with positioning and attacks, this game does not, which takes a bit getting used to) , staying on the offense is key here in most battles. Maximizing your damage and setting up your damage dealers with buffs is a priority. There is a base building aspect and an over world map, but it resembles Darkest Dungeon more than Xcom. Lastly, I think the system in the game that seemed to have the least time and effort put in, could easily be the most interesting, if it was expanded upon in a sequel, the exploration and real time control while in a map. You can navigate the maps with a WASD control scheme, and although the environments do not stand out ( the environmental graphics are passable but nothing great) there are glimpses of good map design, that have secrets, lighting torches to open doors etc., and many hidden areas with extra rewards and side quests, like a traditional RPG. Overall, I still consider XCom2 the mark to meet in this genre of game, that being said, if XCom2 =-100, I give King Arthur: Knight's Tale an 85. It is worth anyone's time that is interested in this genre of game: it adds and borrows a few things from adjacent genres to great effect. The game ran great for me with only one crash in 50 hours; also, the lack of Mod support and cosmetic changes or visual upgrades for your characters are glaring omissions.Positives: A great Xcom like game- good voice acting- music- sound effects- animations- I had one crash to desktop in a 50 hour campaign- the game runs great with HIgh FPS ( due to simple environments and lack of destructibility)Some Negatives: The environments are lacking in detail and can be a bit Janky (hit boxes) in areas- lacking enemy variety- no cosmetic upgrades or changes for your characters. This is a huge thing for me, especially in regards to replayability. None of the items or armor you equip effect your appearance, so your characters look the same from the beginning to the end of the game.- No Mod support

_childDocuments_.review: Rock solid game for those who like this genre.  Pros:  - Resource management is straightforward, makes sense, doesn't get cluttered and stays balanced.  Your money decisions are not going to be easy.-  ambiance and music are on the button.  Dialogue is interesting and quests are loaded with winks to those who know their Arthurian lore.  - Combat mechanics are clean and AI knows what's up.- Alignment system rewards you without being intrusive- Graphics hold up, portraits also very good, UI is clean.- Progression system has some building options and some of the classes actually require a learning curve to use.Cons:- Kinda wish there was a little more granularity in the difficulty modes. _childDocuments_.review: A fantasy xcom, what's not to like?You start with a couple of knights and you unlock more as you progress trough the story. The knights you unlock and some missions depend on the choices you make, although most of the missions and the mains ones are allways the same.As your progress, your knights level up and unlock new skills and you get better gear. The missions are real time until combat starts. Then it's turn based and you and the enemies have action points to move, attack and use skills. Depending of the knights there are several different strategies and it's very rewarding to discover tactics that allow your knights to kill a lot of enemies without giving them chance to strike back. It's not super deep, but the combats are tactical enough and fun. Although you unlock several knight, you can only take 4 for each mission. I played the campaign twice, to unlock the 2 morality and religion knights, and in both cases I ended up using mostly 4 to 6 knights on each, that were my favorites. The others were just there.The graphics are nice but not mind blowing. The sounds and music are also nice.Regarding the achievements, they are simple and not very hard to get them all. If you do a roguelite and evil morality campaign you can unlock them all in one go plus and online game (don't have to win). I did 2 campaigns and  it was fun. Doing all side missions took me about 50 hours for each campaign.Now lets wait for a DLC with more missions perhaps.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very well-designed strategy based RPG. This category definitely needs more resources. Recommended for all S-RPG lovers. The game itself is a combination of exploring, simulation, and turn-based strategy moves. Well-told stories. The difficulty levels are quite different from one another. Yet, even the hardest level is not too bad. So take some time, think about your moves, and plan your resources well.Now the negatives:The map exploration kinda just got thrown out of the window post ACT II. Little to No surprise at all. Four-member squad seems too small. There are only few types of enemies, which makes the game a little redundant post ACT II. Same with the classes, only a few different classes available. Even if you want to use different characters, usually you cannot do that since many of them are not even close to the level that the quests are requesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it.  The story really worked here. Familiar characters seen through a new angle.At first glance there are only 6 characters, but most characters have a unique feature about them and a few are very different than their base class. For example, there are 3 or 4 flavors of Arcanist; this keeps variety high.  I found all builds were at least somewhat viable and even more interesting there were characters I loved in act 1 and 2 and stopped using in act 3 and vice versa; that kept it fresh.  Their contribution to the strategy layer made for some tough decision making and that is one pillar of making a game with RPG elements.The AI was competent most of the time; they would attempt to flank and generally avoid walking into overwatch.  The only glaring mistake I saw as when the AI swarmed an invulnerable character.  The varieties of enemies were ok.  You’ll definitely see them again and again; part of that is there are a lot of missions.  Challenge could use some tweaking, at least in one instance.  I had one character mission that party wiped me multiple times before I made adjustments and got through with multiple injuries but the other missions before and after that I breezed through; they were rated the same level.  Other than that, and 1 other non-plot mission, the balance was consistent. If you like turn based tactical that isn’t in the cover shooter style pick this up.  Note, Marksman can also do cover shoot but that isn’t the entire game principal like some others in this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: To put it simply: this is a sort of XCOM with swords and magic, and (at least for me) with a more engaging story. If you like this kind of tactical games, this game won't disappoint you.The pros:- great gameplay, combat and story- 6 different classes (and enough options/abilities to make different builds of each class)- amazing design (dark medieval fantasy)- good voice acting- interesting morality/faith system, encouraging replayabilityThe cons:- the limit of only 12 heroes with no ability to swap them between reserve and active, you either keep them active, or dismiss them for good (*)- the endgame (after campaign) ramps the difficulty up several levels (!), might not be for everyone(*) Although the fact that you cannot try all the heroes in one gameplay encourages to play the game again, especially for the ones locked at certain moral/faith level, it is frustrating to not being able to swap them at least for a trial mission. An option to swap active heroes for other in the reserve (with some kind of cool-down mechanic, damaging their loyalty or something else to limit its use) would improve this game.(!) For the main campaign you can choose the difficulty, but after the campaign, when you start the endgame and its many missions (which is 100% cool that they added it), although it would seem that you're still playing on the same difficulty, you encounter enemies with much more health and/or higher number of them at once, for the balefire mission, it gets ridiculous. That may be great for those seeking tougher challenges (but hey, you already have the difficulty setting...), but for more "casual" players, it turns each mission into a long bothersome and cumbersome task, IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: To whom I would recommend this game:- if you love turn-based tactical combat. Then this game will absorb you- if you like or don't mind a very dark and cruel fantasy storyTo whom I would NOT recommend this game:- if you expect an immersive RPG - if you dont like cruel storiesPros:- lots of recruitable heroes that allow you to create different fighting teams for every mission - a lot of side missions and a seperately playable endgame mode- well designed and adjustable difficutlty levels (though if you have experience with tactical combat and you'd like to think a bit more about your combats I recommend you to play on "hard" difficutlty. I played on "normal" and did not lose a single hero and only had to reload once in the entire campaign.)- my absolute highlights of this game are two: 1. Heroes can get minor and major injuries, which might seriously affect their fighting power. And they need to be treated for that to cure them. I also very much like the split of your health bar into HP and Vitality-Points.  2. You have a base (Camelot) which you can improve over time in the matter that seems the most helpful to you. Cons:- if you play all the side missions you will see the same kind of adversaries over and over again. :/- the very fact that you CANNOT OPEN YOUR HEROES' EQUIPMENT PROFIL DURING MISSIONS is super frustrating, absolutely annoying and simply not understandable !!! Do the devs expect me to memorize all the buffs and debuffs of my equipment? - comparing items is a nightmare !! A lot of items look the same, the description window jumps around and heros do have individual item bags but all share one. What is more, the item headline sums up situational damage output and presents it as overal damage output: e.g. "this sword does +7 more damage than the one you have equipped" but the +7 might come from damage bonuses against only certain type of foes or be otherwise situational and so the help is basically misleading !- the mission design is very flat. You cant walk two meters without coming across YET ANOTHER pile of human carcasses or heaps of human skulls or bones, or walls of human skulls. This very quickly has the reverse effect of the intended: before the first mission is over you are already numb to it. It then only serves as a reminder that you walk through a very cruel world and everyone aim (including yours) seems to be to eradicate the world from evey living being.- last but not least, and I know I could say that about almost all fanatasy stories in video games: the story is kinda garbage imao ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Mission difficulty is wildly random; some missions give enemies map wide buffs and spawn every encounter as an ambush with 15+ enemies behind your party and others a boringly easy with 5-8 enemies per fight in front of you visible before you engage.The alignment system seems very interesting but is terribly skewed in character distribution, almost all of 2 of the classes (sage and arcanist) are one alignment, and one alignment had 7 heroes while another boasts 11.There are still also several bugs and balance issues present in the game. Some character skills and passives do not stack or work in brokenly powerful ways. Your projected damage is not modified by the weakness debuff, but is modified but positive buffs, so you have to be very careful and count every modifier in some fights or you might leave a corpse at 1 hp (despite your minimum damage promising to destroy it) letting it return to full life and armor and take its turn.Edit: The new checks put in place for the vanguard class are a very good step forward but the lack of mission rebalancing shows very little foresight on the developers behalf. Once they adjust the missions now that theyve removed most players crutch, I'll come back and give it another try.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'm giving this a negative review. I don't think you should buy it right now. TLDR; 7/10 it's a buggy unbalanced game, but if you can deal with that it's fun. It feels like it's still in early access, which is very disappointing for a full release. Not as bad as Cyberpunk's release, but they could have done a lot better since it was in early access for quite a while.That said, I do believe it will be worth your money in a month or two because it was released in a rather buggy state. I have crashed 4 times in 33 hours, soft locked twice, lost a save twice (in fact my first campaign was lost because it seemed to have never made a save file in the first place), and encountered many graphical bugs including glitches, frame rate drops, and texture problems.Audio is a solid 8/10, one note footstep balancing is awful, very loud or squelchy all the time when moving about.Voice acting is hit or miss, some actors were clearly very enthusiastic, others kind of just phoned it in. The Black Knight is as hilarious as it is bad, strongly recommend recruiting him for the amusement, but I can't take him seriously which I thought was the tone of the game.Gameplay 9/10, the concept is solid, the gameplay is there and it is full of replayability. Characters have different skills at different points, even unique skills that others can't obtain or not until extremely late game. You will have opportunities to collect many knights to hone your roster, however currently you cannot dismiss a prospective knight that you're not interested in accepting to your table without first accepting him onto your table then banishing him. 'There's a lot of equipment, and resource management feels fair, if quite tight, if you like buying gear from the merchant, you will be short on cash when events come up because this game is quite frugal. I expected it to open up later and be a bit more generous, but it doesn't, you can mitigate it however by using certain knights in certain positions to increase your gains and rewards.Combat is fun, challenging some of the time, occasionally frustrating, and it is clear some missions are in dire need of a balance pass. It seems some of the Knight or Lady recruitment missions can be exceptionally punishing, though often your party of four is somewhat aided by the presence of a temporary fifth member on those missions, even so they are among the most difficult missions. Combat is turn based, with you almost always having the initiative, I can count on one hand the times I was ambushed in 33 hours of gameplay. You execute your entire teams actions then wait through the enemy's entire turn, you can speed this up in game. Actions, spells, attacks, and movement all cost AP, very similar to Divinity Original Sin, though this game seems to be more generous with AP regeneration. At one point one of my champions had an axe that teleported him to another nearby enemy after he killed one, with enough AP regeneration on kills he was able to telegank entire rooms, very satisfying if not very fair. There are classes, defender (tank), champion (melee 2hand dps), vanguard (dual wield rogue type with sneak attack bonuses and traps), marksman (bow class with poison and fire), sage (Buffer-blaster mage), and arcanist (Blaster-buffer mage). I found class balance to be a little strange, there is an achievement for using 4 marksmen in a single party, but it feels really really bad as a composition, MMs don't feel like they do enough damage unless you have a pile of max damage overwatch bows and let them walk into your fire. I found my best successes were tank, and three big melee beatsticks, though the vanguards damage output is not to be underestimated. When you start getting mages later they can hyper your dps classes and often do more damage through their buffs than their spells.I should note I have not tried the multiplayer aspect, though it is there, I won't make any conjecture on it except I have a feeling it may resemble XCOM multiplayer which is a wild cluster at the best of times.Graphically 5/10, this game is doing nothing to push envelopes, which should mean they have all their graphical stuff worked out. However as mentioned before it drops frame rates constantly, the graphic options are quite limited currently with very little indication of what is being changed. As for color palettes, I hope you like grey and green, because 75% of this game is that color, its a dark palette for a dark tone to match the developer's vision of the game. One other graphical issue is there is something uncannily off about the Lady of the Lake in the cut scenes, something is wrong with her proportions and the way she talks, at points I thought she was going full mouth of Sauron, very creepy.Story 7/10 It's fun, lots to read, and most of it is voice acted, quests follow a formula of go into an area, meet someone, resolve their problems occasionally in non violent ways, but often violently, you can definitely play a villain or a hero and experience two sides of a coin with some repercussions for it and a morality gauge with unlocks for playing into those roles. There are a handful of times when it gets hamfisted and the evil is almost cartoonish, but by the same measure the good can be as well. Christianity and Paganism play large parts in this game as well, but they don't try to do it offensively, but there is a constant presence and many of your knights fall on one side or the other and will show their loyalty for siding with them.Overall 7/10 game, it has bugs, it has problems, but at the time of writing this review devs had released a hotfix patch, which funny enough had typos and duplicate entries in the patch notes. It's still a fun game, but feels like it was rushed out of early access and therefore still feels like an early access game, that's not really acceptable and you should wait until the game is ready before purchasing.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR 5/10. Not a bad game by any means, just "meh".-----------------------------So, lets' starts with the basics.GRAPHICS & ARTSTYLE: 3/10One word: boring. The developers went for the "paint everything bleak grey" artstyle, I'm assuming to give a grim-dark-depressing vibe of the world. Unfortunately, it failts completely. You wander from one grey zone into another grey zone with grey houses, grey graveyards, grey people, grey castles that are impossible to distinguish from one another. As for the quality of the graphics - they are right in the middle of the road. Not bad, but hardly enough to warrant a single "this looks good!" from you.STORY & LORE: 5/10.I do like the setting, but again it is not very well implemented. You are playing as sir Mordred, one of the more evil knights of the Round Table, and encounter various knights on your journeys. Well first of all, while the knight quests (getting the companions) are interesting, there is zero interaction afterwards. They stay in your party and there is not much more to it. What's even more weird is running through the world, when one of the knights in your party says something like "Sir Mordred, I wonder if you have really changed?". You would expect a snarky remark from Mordred or at least something - but no, nothing happens.I also have to add that SIr Mordred is meant to be quite an evil character, from his appearance to his dialogue and voicelines. But the game allows you to roleplay him in a few ways. This breaks the immersion quite a bit, because some decisions - especially the RIGHTFUL ones (more on that in the alighnment section) completely contradict Sir Mordred's nature and are something he would never say or do.The quests are also pretty meh. Most of them are either "kill everyone" or "find 5 of something" and give you a simple reward at the end. In other words, pretty unremarkable.MORALITY & AlIGHNMENT: 5/10It was supposed to be a fun system where you can make different choices that affect your morality (rightful vs tyrant) and religion (old faith vs christian). The problem is that the best bonuses and characters are locked behind going deep into either direction, and staying neutral is the worst outcome. So instead it becomes a "I need good old faith buffs, so I will have to make all the old faith choices" situation.COMBAT: 6/10If you've played something like Divinity Original Sin you will be very familiar with this type of combat. This game does it pretty well. There are however a few things I didn't like:1) The difficulty usually comes not from the enemies but froms swarming you with 20 or even 30 enemies at a time, which I didn't find very fun.2) In the beginning, the characters have too few skills to be fun. Most of them have a basic attack and one other skill, which doesn't give too much variety to combat3) The battles get repetitive very fast. It's usually using the same tactics again and again while trying not to get swarmedVOICE ACTING: 8/10Really well done, I enjoyed most of the characters, and Sir Mordred sounded really goodMUSIC: 3/10There was something playing. I have no memory of it.ICING ON THE CAKEThe Game is still 120GB(!!!) in size. Yup, you heard it right, it's of the same size as Dragon Age 1, Dragon Age 2, Dragon Age Inquisition and Divinity Original Sin combined.Overall, I found it to be a pretty average game. It's definitely not a bad game. But when compared to Pathfinder, Dragon Age, Divinity: Original Sin or even XCOM, it pales in comparison.

The armour you and your heroes are wearing is just so. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. beautiful. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game for two reasons:1) I like to fund Indies as, they are often as good or better than, the big titles at twice the price.  2) I know of Neocore Games from the similar VanHelsing game which, I thought they did a good job-with.- I agree with one of the community who commented on the lack of content (2 main story quests, 7 side quests) leading to a refund.  NeoCore walks a fine line in asking the community for full support contribution vs. expectation for reasonable content.- I'm not refunding as, I found the story and content to be compelling enough to finish the game as it stands and look forward to the developer bulking up quickly on existing content.I liked: - The story, music (a little repetitive), assignment of tokens representing armor, weapons, rings and artifacts.- Upgrade-able castle buildings, nothing new but, a definite must-have for this type of game.- No crashes at 21 hours of play time, decent graphics (at least I had no issues with an MSI G73).I didn't like:- The full (Indie) price of the game vs. minimal content (more of a demo than a full in-development game).  I'm inclined to let this slide as, I'm familiar with NeocoreGames and believe they will earn the trust placed in them.- No mapped keys for essential buttons used all the time during combat (Overwatch, Reserve, End Turn) making combat way too "clicky."  Probably simple oversight but, hope NC addresses it.- Very simple-looking mini-map (and main map) stands out as underwhelming, relative decently-present graphics in the battle area.  More importantly, it lacks independent orientation relative to the group's current facing (i.e. mini-map should rotate with the group for better bearing on group's position relative to the terrain).Summary:Good start to a game by a known good developer but, manage your investment expectations, definitely a demo at this point.  The game is currently one evening's worth of gameplay at best.  If you need 40 hours or better of game play, maybe wait a few weeks.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game for anyone who's a fan of tactical/turn based grid gameplay or into King Arthur/Camelot lorePros:+Combat is fun and fair. I'm playing on "Moderate" difficulty (between Normal and Hard), and the game sits at a very nice sweet spot difficulty wise+Some people won't care for it, but I like the unique characters and their stories+EVERYTHING is voice acted, and voice acted well+Game runs smoothly, no crashes+There's a "just one more mission" sort of vibe the game gives off because of the aboveNeutral:-A lot of people are bothered by the 12 hero limit. Hasn't bugged me at all to this point-The Camelot/base building idea is cool, but needs to be more fleshed out to shine. Think a very basic version of base building in Darkest Dungeon-The world map looks cool and thematic, but all you're doing is choosing missions from it. There's room for some more neat stuff here.-Classes tend to be same-y with a couple skill variations here and there. This could have been better, but isn't horrible (meaning one Vanguard class feels very similar to another Vanguard class unit)Negatives:-A lot of QOL things need to be added i.e. range indicators for ranged units when they haven't moved.-The level design is very same-y. Grimdark color palettes, no verticality-Level objectives are always the same: kill everything you see. Some variety would have been nice.-I'm maybe 15-20 hours in thus far (AFK time and all), and I'm seeing a lot of the same enemies. So far, there have been 2 enemy "factions" introduced (Lost and Pict)-No aesthetic changes when putting on new armor/weapons (this is a bummer)All in all, I'm enjoying this and will continue playing it. However, you should know the primary draw for me has been the combat simply because of the nice level of difficulty and good mix of strategy and tactics. This may not be for everyone because of some of the stuff above.

_childDocuments_.review: It´s good to be bad.. or the tale from other side of the round table..After the final battle between King Arthur and his arch nemesis Mordred the story ends.. normally - with Arthurs death. "King Arthur: Knights Tale" just begins and with it a quite different view on especially Mordred and the Knights of the round table. Since he has to save Avalon from destruction, by killing Arthur again!To do this you follow the story of what exactly happened with the Lady of the Lake, Arthur and forbidden rituals. All this while building up a new and improved Round table, made up of dark versions of the original Lords and Ladies. To do this, you can choose from five classes (Defender - Champion - Vanguard - Archer and Magicians). All of these have their own character (which gives some nice rpg elements from time to time) and also a bit different skill trees, which offers diversion in the strategy department.You will need a good setup in the over 50 chapters (including side quests), while hunting Arthur and fighting all kind of enemies of the realm. While your group of four characters runs in kind of Diablo-like levels, which range from castle cellar to Fey lands but always keep their dark/grim atmosphere, you fight in turn based combats. While a good Defender as tank is nearly a must in my opinion, you can build your party as you like and as fits your style. Due the wide variety in skill sets/weapon and items as well as special perks, the possibilites are nearly without limit. During the missions you also should repair your camelot, so you can heal your fighters, send them on training and get better equipment.The battles themself mostly throw you against an superior number of enemies, which are also working adequatly in the AI department (e.g. the archers use cover, front warriors like to attack the flank and especially your weaker characters). So you always need a good and fitting group, to prevail. Also keeping an eye on the strenghts and weaknesses is key to victory.Last but not least there are also quite some dilemmas for you as ruler to solve. Most of these will change your alignment, which goes from Old Faith versus Christian and Lawful versus Evil. Depending on these scales you can recruit some extra fighters and get bonus to your rule. While this makes it even more interesting to try at least a second playthrough, it makes you ignore the actual content of the decisions  most of the time and just further your alignment.Despite this and some levels, where it is not really easy to keep an overview of where to go (despite a quite useful map), are these already the main drawbacks of an otherwise very well done strategic game, with much charme. Maybe the fixed number of twelve Knights (and that you cannot just set one on the bench - if you fire a guy he´s gone for good) is also a bit annoying, but it also makes you think harder, whom you actually take on.Conclusio: I like the bad guys most of the time, so this games story was ideal for me. Besides that i very much liked that they gave most of the people some character, with even a bit of interaction from time to time. So i can fully recommend this Jagged Alliance in the Arthurian Universe for every strategy fan.Point Score: 9/10
