_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR It has great potential but still lacks content comparatively to its predecessorBefore I begin full disclosure, I had over 2,000 hours on Crusader Kings 2 (CK2). This will definitely skew my feelings on this game.Graphics: this is a vast improvement over CK2, I was initially concerned with seeing barony level holdings and the 3D portraits but after some getting used to the graphics at large are a vast improvement over CK2 including everything from characters, windows, the map, and more. Could use more flavor and character.Overall 9/10Audio: I am by no means no expert on game audio, with over 600 hours the music does loop but I would say the tracks are solid. could use more region based music like CK2 and more tracks at large.Overall 7/10Gameplay: Gameplay ranges from the more pragmatic side, (diplomacy, warfare, economics) to the role-play side (Events, decisions, activities, ETC)Warfare is much more satisfying in CK3 than previous games, the knight system and min maxxing accolades, knight effectiveness, retinues and commanders is very satisfying and allows many different strategies. I would say this is a vast overhaul to CK2.Diplomacy is also much more interesting with the introduction of the lifestyle system, this is about the same as CK2 though overall considering that it functions mostly the same as CK2.Economics is where I believe that the game could use some improvements, I miss merchant republics and the laws system which allowed for more management as a king or higher with vassals. the introduction of development and the new various holding upgrades is nice but its missing much of CK2's critical developments. Also clans, nomads, feudals, and tribals all feel the same, much more flavor is needed on this front which I think developers are moving towards.Roleplay is both much more and much less satisfying at the same time in CK3. The stress system is a great addition, providing more incentive towards playing like your character. There are significantly less decisions and events comparatively to CK2 and i miss the absurdity (and that it could be enabled and disabled in the menu). Activities, royal court and struggles help alot but its still missing much flavor. I hope they continue to add more depth and events and consider adding back some more fantastical elements. Secret societies are dearly missed as well. The culture and religion system are fantastic and would greatly benefit from the aforementioned suggestions. I also hope that they re-implement diseases and the black death to help mitigate the super high late game development and purge alot of characters to help with lag. Overall as of time of writing, 6.5/10UI and other technical stuff: Overall the UI is aesthetically pleasing but is a bit scattered. It was hard to find menus and they are scattered with every update. I feel this is mitigated with hours in the game so I will not hold it too harshly. Performance in CK3 is much better than its predecessor as well, it still lags in the late game much like any paradox game but its much better than the old game.Overall 8/10I hope they continue to develop the game and show it love, In a few years it will vastly outclass CK2 but that will take dedication and hard work from the studio.Final rating as of time of writing: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: The Crusader Kings franchise is quite popular in the strategy community, and for good reason. The second game saw support for over a decade, which meant that the game has managed to develop itself into something that is wholly unique. Many grand strategy games cast you as a faceless leader of a nation, with much of the gameplay centered around expanding your borders and making sure you don't end up on the business end of a far larger empire's greed. CK3 has all of this in spades, but what truly sets it apart from many of its contemporaries is the characters that take center stage in nearly every facet of the gameplay. No longer are you playing the concept of government. Instead, you play as the head of your bloodline, tasked with making sure your dynasty survives the middle ages. This means you'll be the head of your very own eugenics program where you carefully breed yourself (and your offspring) with other families in order to get the best traits, alliances, and prestige. The many random events, as well as a heavy focus on RPG elements that allow for some immersive emergent gameplay. Take part in the Viking raids on England. Unify Africa. Conquer Rome. Murder the pope. Marry your pestilence-ridden daughter to your liege so he dies of some easily preventable disease so you can use the ensuing power vacuum to get yourself a few of his titles. Turn Jerusalem Norse. This game is absolutely brilliant even at 1.0, with a host of systems to keep you entertained for longer than almost any other game, provided you can stomach the learning curve. Luckily, CK3 has a way better tutorial than CK2 ever had. If you liked 2 or would like a strategy game that is more about people and less about borders, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: From what I've played so far, I enjoy CK3. It already feels more streamlined and somehow more complex than CK2 - with a lot of things you remember and enjoy from its predecessor, with little additions / improvements on it. You still feel like a medieval ruler trying to claw your way to prominence in a harsh and unforgiving world. It takes a bit of time to understand all the different parts of running a duchy or kingdom, but that's a part of what makes the game so much fun. I played through the tutorial ruler and the rules breakdown helped a lot in understanding all the little things you have to pay attention to.That being said, I usually don't write reviews for games that are technically still in development. Lots of planned content for this game hasn't been released yet, and to my understanding much of that content will have a sharp impact on how you play game, including what choices your ruler has to make, and what obstacles they will face (it's not just cosmetic art changes, more starting rulers, or additional timelines). I prefer reviewing games that have added all the elements they intended for their game; right now it feels like I'm critiquing ingredients in a sandwich. I like what they have on it so far...but will future additions make it even better, or will they spoil the whole? I will say CK2 left me with high expectations, so I'm hopeful the additions will make the game better and better.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has played and loved other rts games like Civilization and Age of Wonders, I had heard about CK3 for a while and decided to give it a go.Let me tell you, if you want to enjoy this game, understand that it is very different from the afore mentioned games. You can bang out a Civ game in 5/6 hours and call it a day, but Crusader Kings 3? After playing for 5 or 6 hours, I felt like I was making no progress, which is when I took to YouTube to try and find out what I was doing wrong, there I learned the truth. Think of it like a DND campaign you play for a couple hours every week and slowly make progress towards. In addition to that, there is no real "win conditions." There is a hard end date of 1453 in the game, but there are no specific win conditions, just whatever YOU want you legacy to be. Over the course of your campaign, you are in charge of deciding what you want your goals to be. Learning that this is a game that you can take slow over the course of a couple weeks has really changed my perspective and helped me enjoy it a lot more. I think CK3 provides a really unique gameplay experience and would definitely recommend trying it if it looks like something you'd be interested in, but maybe wait until the game is on sale.PS. This game takes ages to load. I have a gaming laptop from 2019 (which yes, is kind of old) but the game takes about 20 minutes to load up for me, so don't freak out if after a couple minutes the game is still loading :)

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Answer? CK3 is an absolutely amazing game and if you like roleplay, strategy, and history you should grab it.Longer Answer? I spent about 60ish hours playing the original Crusader Kings. Then I spent well over 2k hours playing Crusader Kings 2. I bought every DLC and some of the cosmetic packs for CK2. I absolutely adored that game. BUT CK2 was quite hard to get into. The UI was clunky, the information you needed to play hidden, and it just had an extremely steep learning curve.  I should know, a few of my tutorial videos on CK2 are still watched today, and after CK2 became free to play I got a lot of people commenting on videos or coming into my stream asking how to do things. Why? Because it just wasn't easy to understand anything and the tutorial was a hot mess.CK3 is an entirely different story. The UI is EXTREMELY far from clunky (though it does need a few tweaks, as I've said in a recent video, but they're all fairly minor). There are amazing tooltips inside of tooltips, making the knowledge needed to play the game very easy to access. There's also a great gamepedia in the game for quick access to information.Now, that's all about learning the game. But what about playing it?The entire CK experience is so much richer. The character events are much more detailed, and the responses you can pick are just so much more meaningful and entertaining. The 3D portraits add a lot of life to the game, making you genuinely care about the characters. The new Way of Life trees bring a lot of things to the surface that were hidden before. The combat is quite streamlined, as is building your army to suit your needs.  The fact that you can convert to any religion at any time, or change your religion as long as you have the piety is quite brilliant.  The new Dynasty system really makes the fact this game is built around playing a family, not a nation, so much more visible.Basically, the developers of CK3 took everything that worked in CK2 and made it better. And then they took everything that didn't work and either made it work, or entirely tossed it out for the release. I know many of us are hoping for the return of Merchant Republics and Nomads in the future. But, you have to admit, those governments had some severe issues and limitations in CK2. So, my hope is that if/when they come to CK3 they'll be just as marvelous as the governments currently in the game.Full disclosure, my game key was given to me by Paradox Interactive, but my words and opinions are my own.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best empire builder games I've ever played.  It's a tough one to learn, though.  If you've never played it before, there's really two ways to "git gud" at this game.  The first is similar to trying to knock down a brick wall with your forehead.  To do this, simply start up the game, pick somebody to play, and give 'er a go.  You'll lose that game.  You'll lose the next game.  And the next game.  And the next (see a pattern?), but after a handful of frustrating experiences the wall will start to crack and you'll figure it out.  If you chose this strategy it's best to have the stubborn trait, or a very hard head (sadtrombone.mpeg).  The second way, and definitely, totally, 100% the way I did it is to go on the internet, read some FAQs, watch some tutorial videos, and learn a thing or two from people that have put hundreds of hours into the game.  I mean, you're still gonna lose the first few games you try, but you'll save yourself a good 50 hours of frustrating game play and all it will cost you is about 50 hours of boring YouTube videos.  Jokes aside, the game is excellent.  The creators did their research and set up the map and peoples as best as you could ask.  If the title didn't tip you off, the game does focus mostly on "The West", but they did add the option to play a multitude of peoples all over Europe, Northern Africa, Central Asia, and India.  You can create your own character, religion, culture, and empire, or play one from history.  You can be a savage raider, noble monarch, pious priest, scurrilous rogue, or any number of other words I learned in college.  The game does let you play multiplayer, so if you have friends that also like homework simulators then you can nerd out over this game together.  Bit of advice though - record your voice chat session with your buddies so that you have things like, "*Sigh* I just had to kill my spouse AGAIN!." or "Why do I have a baby in prison?" on record for later.  My head hurts from all this thinking, so I'm gonna wrap this up.  It's a lot of fun and it's great way to play pretend history, but the learning curve is steep.  Gets my full support though, for whatever that isn't worth.

_childDocuments_.review: While early on it lacked the depth CK2 accumulated through the sheer number of DLCs and mods the second game received, CK3 is a phenomenal blend of strategy and personal intrigue. I love how the game uses stress to encourage you to play the way your character's personality would indicate, while still allowing you to act out of character - struggling against your nature to do what's best for your dynasty/realm. Because of this, I think this game may be worth a shot even if you're not traditionally a fan of grand strategy. If you're a fan of political intrigue, there could be enough here to keep you engaged. My brother is not a fan of strategy at all, but as a Game of Thrones fan, he was able to sink hours into this game.While I haven't kept up with the DLC and updates, the new free additions that have come along with the new DLC have looked great. I think legitimacy does a good job of rewarding lawful play styles and adds some fun emergent gameplay - no more marrying random beautiful peasants. Plagues look like they have potential to bring mortality rates up to be more in line with what one would expect historically. I've heard people say that these mechanics need balancing but I can't comment on this as I've not spent much time with them yet.Overall: I recommend this to fans of strategy games and more broadly to fans of political intrigue.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III, is an improvement on the predecessor CK2 in almost all aspects. It comes with most of the content that the CK2 DLC added already built-in. However, some of the more super-natural features are not currently included. Modding –There is already an active modding community allowing you to tailor your game to improve your experience or just to mess around with some silly features.DLC – I am hoping that the future DLC will work in the same way of CK2. During the development of CK2 a free content patch was always added for all players and hopefully this is continued going forward. Difficulty –As with the last game you can change the difficulty settings to suit your skill level, but I feel that CK3 is much easier to learn for new players than CK2 it clearly shows why you can or cannot do certain actions.New features –The skill tree system for characters makes the game much more interesting as you really need to focus on character development to get the most out of their reign. Whilst they benefit from different trees depending on their childhood development.Renown, the new dynasty renown system makes it benefital to have a powerful family instead of just killing of all the members who may oppose you, meaning you can benefit from the potential risk, allowing you to balance out the pros and cons. Using renown, you can get bonuses for all members of your household which makes a big difference in the long run.Piety & Prestige, this used to mean very little other than other characters opinions but now they have a much bigger impact on what you are able to do, only a famous king can declare for major wars without reason. Stress system – This system means that you must make decisions based on the characters traits otherwise you will cause them stress which can in turn lead to them ending their own life. So, you can no-longer just make the same choices each-time without negative effects.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings 3's biggest achievement is making Crusader Kings 2 virtually unbearable to return to. For all its flaws, it's a good shell for Paradox to continue developing and adding content to. That is, provided you have the patience to wait a decade for the most complete version.Patch 1.5 (Royal Court) is a major improvement to the game. The culture rework, court positions, artefacts and languages are really nice additions. If you already like what CK3 is, you'll enjoy CK3 more.Patch 1.6 (Fate of Iberia) fixed many database issues, added some new cultures and religions along with new 3D map art that are gorgeous. I hope we see more of in the future.Patch 1.7 (Friends and Foes) improved the AI and made the game more fun to play competitively. It also cleared up some bugs and longstanding issues that needed fixing. CK3 is a stabler experience and the memory system adds a lot of value to the roleplaying experience. It's very nice to see that they add event art into the base-game now, especially art that wasn't part of the theme.While patch 1.8 was a sleeper with some art, patch 1.9 (Tours and Tournaments) proved necessary for a better experience. With the location of the character mattering changes how this game works fundamentally and the only flaw is that it made character teleportation when it does not use the travelling system more apparent, which needs to be fixed eventually. The reworked activity system is like day and night to the old. I often find myself slowing down and enjoying the activities more, and I hope more decisions and events are converted to this system in the future. The era system with progressively unlocked fashion is a huge deal for the gameplay experience and makes it feel fresh. The 1.9 cycles of patches also fixed many fan issues and complaints, marking 1.9.1 the patch that brought sanity to seduction in the CK series, somewhat. CK3 feels like in a good place.Patch 1.10 (Wards & Wardens) was not particularly signifact. Hostages is at best a novelty and at worst an annoying popup.Patch 1.11 (Legacy of Persia) sure did gave us a reason to play clan governments and made it feel special as opposed to the feudal gameplay. I like the changes to database changes to Persia and the wider region.Patch 1.12 (Legends of the Dead) got a lot of good stuff. I enjoy the diseases well enough and the free art is great as always. Legitimacy steals the show and brings a lot of needed challenge to the game, even though it soon fizzles out as you get powerful and you can almost ignore it. _childDocuments_.review: Be warned: The AI will completely break if you enter a war with too many belligerents.The AI Does not know how to merge armies. This means every time you defeat an army, and they are routed with 1 or 2 people, they will go and meet up with another army to join them on the same tile but they will not merge. It is common to see 20+ armies stacked on one another, only to realize they are made up of 100 units each, with multiples from the same kingdom or duchy.To make matters worse, the AI does not know how to move at the same time, and there is no option to 'attach' your army to another allied army. That means the AI will send their units in, 100 at a time, into your cluster of 20,000. By the time you defeat their 100, the next army of 100 is ready to join them. They march single file into whatever deathball waits for them on the other side. This is not a glitch, it is simply AI behavior, and has been consistent throughout my multiple playthroughs.Theres some more stuff. I once watched the AI stand outside of Byzantion, sieging it with 1400 units. The problem is that it needed 1800 units for any progress to be made. The AI had two stacks of 4,000 units standing to the side, not helping the siege. I think its because the AI doesnt want to stack on a province if the province doesnt have enough supplies to support them. The result is that the AI has a schizophrenic meltdown, and does dumb stuff like siege a city for 3 years even though they lack the manpower to achieve any progress.Another side effect of the supply system on the AI is that they will stop sieging a settlement if their supply runs out. This messes with their brains, since some cities can hold out for years at a time. So, the AI will start sieging a city, get it down to its last legs, and then 1 week before the siege completes the AI just bails because it realizes it doesnt have supplies. It walks away, grabs some supplies, and then goes back to the same city. Rinse and repeat for 5 years. Anyways, thats how I conquered Wallachia when I was outnumbered 40,000 to 20,000.The AI makes large wars nearly unplayable.The nonsensical decision-making of the AI is so painfully obvious that I can only conclude that Paradox was fully aware of these critical failures and decided to release anyways. This is a game literally called Crusader Kings, and I have yet to have a single functional crusade.Anyways, I never played CK2 but from what I gather, CK3 got dumbed down. So thats disappointing as well. I would definitely wait for patches / mods before purchasing this.

_childDocuments_.review: It'll be another DLC heavy game, it lacks replayability and real depth or, pretty much anything that CK2 had.Its an entirely new dev team so I'm not surprised they don't know what Crusader Kings is, or how to create a Crusader Kings game, But they definitely had the opportunity to at least implement something like a ruler designer from the start, and the fact that they haven't done....This is literally like hollowing out and massively, massively simplifying CK2, and removing all the DLC and all the different levels of intricacies. Its fun for a few hours and initially it looks and feels great, but the more games you play, and the more you hop about and checkout how different mechanics and nations work, you can quite easily begin to realise how bare bones this is. - Though this could be obviously because I've played a lot of CK I guess... and all this provides is a, "modernized" and "low key" politicalized version of the game, without any content provided by DLC, or any content that could save this game from its seriously bad lack of depth or, any real content.More than confident we're going to be seeing content that should have been in the base game, released as DLC priced higher than the game itself should be.I won't be refunding, and I still intend to play, but I have found the game to be as I expected. (I made, some.....Predictions.. whilst discussing the dev diaries with friends awhile back) It did somewhat initially beat my expectations but, after awhile, that, NEW SHINY THING vibe settles down and you can see it for what it is. Minor political correctness influences, and a vanilla platform for DLC content to be built on. Not to mention, without having the ability to create your own character, your own dynasty. Do stuff that really feels like your own story... It just inevitably loses any semblance of replayability. It just isn't there, and I honestly felt bored after I'd learn all the new ways they've done the same old things. Though, Again it does still just, simply, LACK most of everything CK2 has. Its just, newer and I love the new Man At Arms regiments lol.The only major new systems are essentially just there to impair your ability to conquer new land from what I've seen. They had every chance to improve things, including peace conferences, but decided that of everything they could have brought from CK2, it'd be the lacking peace choices? lol.As per CK2's old style of warry things-(at least early game, late game you should be able to access culture research that can unlock the right to declare war for multiple titles...fun..)- you often find yourself at war for a single county. Repeatedly. Its like having to take limited numbers of nibbles out of a sandwich over the course of 24 hours. Its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoyingly limiting lol.It of course makes everything even more of a ballache if you lose some your land after your first character passes away, which happens quickly in most cases as most characters you play as are middle aged.With inheritance, it directly screws you over until you get to the late medieval age, because you have no way to stop your land from being split constantly and massively often, depending how many sons you have, though you can try to disinherit some as a counter to that, if you choose to dump hundreds in prestige at a time for each son. (EDIT: A counter to this would be rushing to an Emperor/King Title. That way your heir gets the major title, and everything beneath it gets split between X heirs. Just, be careful. Make sure you don't hold multiple same rank titles when they're your highest rank. e.g. destroy some kingdoms/duchies if your not gonna make it to the next major title in time.)Its honestly like someone who played CK2 for a few hours and watched videos of the memes tried to create a copycat "RP heavy game", then they just casually nerfed people's ability to carry out war with the county control system and integration systems.Then they just casually pilfer graphics from Sims 3 and Civ V, force them to have a baby and applied that to the game. Then they dumped in a couple new systems to stop anyone being able to gain too much land too quickly so they avoid anyone getting too big too quickly, I guess?- It would make sense.That way obviously, it prevents you from noticing the general lack of content the game has outside of just, murder-war-murder-war-seduce his wife-murder-war.Replaying too often - Which I suppose happens when you can complete goals you set out for yourself quickly because of how, for the most part just overly simple a game is - Just ends up leaving you feeling less and less motivated. Its literally just the same ♥♥♥♥ each time, there isn't any individuality or uniqueness to any one run. I think give it say 10 - 20 playthroughs if that. Would figure its around that the average person would probably just, be done. Bored. All that.Other than maybe some rare events or the fact that you could maybe use different perk trees, there's just nothing to it. It just lacks, everything CK2 has, and it looks uglier, doesn't understand the setting it sets itself in at all, and clearly lacked historical expert advise during development. Meh, very meh. Though, hey, I called it, the devblogs made it clear how bad this game was going to be, alongside the stuff they would say during interviews and things. And they did the exact same stuff they did when hiding the lacking content of Imperator Rome, so. Is what it is.4/10(Edit: Gave it a quick look through, made some changes. Hopefully its not too boring to read. I appreciate the attention it's gained. Bare in mind all this comes from a very frustrated, very passionate CK fan. They had all the funding and the time in the world to create a great successor to CK2 and they utterly failed to do so. Its more than blatant DLC is probably pre planned for this game. Its honestly disgusting.)

U spend money to construct buildinds and improve ur economy or troops. Warfare - this is a hard one - its again comparable, but as in buildings segment, its missing something. To win u need to either siege whole enemy country, win battles, or capture their ruler/heir. The game combines grand strategy with detailed character management, making each decision impactful and engaging.Rich Historical Setting: The game’s rich historical setting, spanning centuries of medieval history, is meticulously detailed. The intricate gameplay and the need for long-term planning may not be suitable for players looking for quick, casual sessions.Occasional Bugs: Although the game is generally well-polished, there can be occasional bugs and performance issues. The developers are actively addressing these, but they can still affect the gameplay experience.Recommendation: I highly recommend Crusader Kings III to fans of grand strategy and historical games. Its deep strategy mechanics, rich historical setting, and intricate character systems offer a deeply engaging and rewarding experience. While the steep learning curve and time commitment might be daunting for some, those who invest the time to learn the game will find it incredibly satisfying. _childDocuments_.review: having put 300 hours into the game, it's time for a review.after putting in so much time with crusader kings II, I eagerly awaited the release of this game, like many others.I'd say the first 100-150 hours was a pure joy after crusader kings II, the new looks and the new bells & whistles are sensational for sure.there are admittedly many of the same problems in this game as there were in the previous one. historical errors abound. there's nothing particularly special about increasing your rank and gaining titles. becoming king or emperor is easily done and basically all that happens is you can do a few more things and have higher rank vassals. I thought it was great that towards the end of ckII they added the "coronation ceremony" and I hoped it would be expanded upon but it seems to have just been done away with. you don't really get any additional respect or boons or benefits to becoming king or emperor, there's nothing mystical or majestic about it in terms of events or mechanics even though sovereigns as such would have been seen to have been imbued with these things historically. at each new accession I've experienced immediate factions for liberty, independence, putting someone else on the throne. this just didn't happen that much, especially towards a dynasty that had possessed the title(s) for hundreds of years. I suppose I'm not quite sure how to put it, but there's just no "oomph" to becoming king or emperor.it would be great if there was more options, for example, starting as just a baron or a mayor, even a bishop, and having the ability to become king or emperor from such a start. even an option to start as just a courtier with no land but the ability to get on a lord's council and 1 day purchase (or get a "hook" for) a lordship from him would add more depth.I love how they have evolved the character portraits. they look great for the most part, though some still do look kind of troll-like even if they have 1 of the traits that grants attraction. I'd also love to see more accessory and head-wear options, along with being able to change a character's color pattern, if, for example, you don't want your character stuck with green garment patterns their entire life. the byzantine emperor should also have access to imperial purple garments. the byzantine emperors were famous for their imperial purple robes, where are they?primogeniture succession is time locked to the year 1200, and even then still takes time to "research," despite primogeniture succession being a "thing" long, long before that. the house and dynasty mechanics leave a lot to be desired. dynasty legacies are too expensive. you should be able to change/customize the coat of arms. also dynasty members creating cadet houses needs to be toned down. pretty much as soon as they get a title they create a cadet house. your infant children/grandchildren will at times go on trans-continental adventures. (????)tyranny penalties from revoking all titles from a heretic/rebel. (????)warfare is still the same siege & whack-a-mole. you're basically cheating yourself out of more customers at this point, since many players who enjoy total war-style games would love to play crusader kings but are turned off by the fact that you don't actually see your armies or control movements or see the battle. it's called crusader kings, where's the blood and gore and glory?for some odd reason the ability to choose many different start dates was taken away, and although it was said you could play on beyond 1453 this time around, you cannot do so if you want to get achievements. so...there is a major lack of achievements as of the writing of this review, only 56 and some of them do not make sense/are not fun to get/have terrible imagery. the "kings to the seventh generation" artwork doesn't even show a king but a queen, and the starting character for this achievement (count eudes/aka odo of france) is not even the ancestor of the king who this prophecy was for, which was hugh capet. hugh capet's grandfather was odo's brother robert. I can't help but wonder if paradox even utilizes historians or even takes the time to read historical texts. it is absolutely ridiculous that to get the (terrible artwork) achievement "norman yoke," you are required to convert all of england to "english" culture. who at paradox believes that the norman conquest promptly resulted in a native population of millions of anglo-saxons and scandinavians suddenly coming together in common culture with their foreign rulers? and within william the conqueror's lifetime no less?vassal titles get inherited out of the realm despite crown authority laws and despite the fact that this did not happen historically.heresies are excessive and pretty annoying.the player is penalized for holding "too many" duchy titles and counties, despite kings and emperors personally holding many such titles in history.I'm glad that they did fix the disputed heritage event, which is incredibly frustrating, although I do find my soulmate wife of 20+ years at times having the "strumpet" modifier or becoming adulterous, so perhaps this still needs some looking into.going on crusade and creating a crusader kingdom is essentially pointless outside of the gold and prestige rewards, since the AI usually loses the crusader state within 15 years or so. unless you, the player, constantly babysit the crusader kingdom and feed them an endless stream of gold, they're gonna go under. doing this or even sending gifts in general becomes tedious since you can have 150,000 gold and only be able to send 153 in gifts at a time.I've also come to find that in the last 150, even 200 years or so of a game, it becomes very empty and boring. there's not really any point to warfare by then unless you're just interested in adding on more territory to your realm. you make more gold than you'll ever spend, and at least for me I end up just funding other character's wars while waiting to go on a hunt or take a mystical communion every 5 years. you run out of buildings that you can build, which doesn't make sense. you're basically just sending gifts to vassals to get them to leave you alone and educating kids. there aren't any late game events or mechanics going on, at least not any that I actually noticed or that posed any sort of threat or challenge.that being said, and to keep this somewhat short, basically, if you've never played a crusader kings game before, then this game will be an absolute blast, especially the 1st 100 hours or so you put into it.if you have played crusader kings before, don't come into this expecting a lot. it is a somewhat different game from ckII and there's going to be pleasant surprises and fairly bitter disappointments.it has only been a month & a half since release, but the game is in desperate need of some DLC to add more content throughout the game, especially mid-to-late game. the game is also in desperate need of a historical mode. it quickly becomes bizarro world and at least for me its very hollow like that after 100 or 200 years. I can't speak for everyone but I have no doubt that there are others like myself who would like to play out their game in a more historically accurate setting.in my original review for crusader kings II I said there were a thousand thrills to be had. there aren't that many this time around but it's a great start and I'll probably come back to the game after some DLC comes out.as an aside, I do have to say that 1 of the paradox moderators here on steam acted arbitrarily and unfairly towards me and this individual has not only tainted the game for me but has also made an enemy for life. I will never forgive nor forget how that moderator has treated me.

_childDocuments_.review: Often when you see a sequel to a popular, expanded upon game, you would expect it to release with less content than the previous entry. Crusader Kings III defies this expectation - by taking all of the best features from its previous entry and its expansions, and adding it all to the base game from the start, you get the same amount of content as you're used to as well as a whole bunch of new, exciting features.Everything from lifestyles, to the Indian sub-continent, to customizable religions, randomized starts, and many more features have been carried over. In addition, changes to how traits work makes your characters come alive. Your Just ruler can no longer arbitrarily imprison their rivals without penalty; if they do, they may risk a mental breakdown from going against their sense of justice.On the user experience side, everything seems to be an improvement as well. The UI is easy to navigate, contains plenty of tooltips and explanations for what the different actions, traits, and terms mean. And if you're in doubt, there's a massive encyclopedia right at your fingertips to help you out.This is one of the few times I'll gladly and heartily recommend a Paradox Interactive game on its launch day.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III vastly improves on almost every aspect from the previous title with aspects like AI improvements, scenarios, and player choice being the most improved. The technical staff and art team do a superb job at bringing together multiple aspects like culture, faith, and dynasty which can very easily be missed. Want to play a viking raider or a cash cow steward and really immerse yourself in that time period? This game has layers of intelligently built systems that will only enhance that immersion with random events like disease and family relations and drama to throw a wrench in your dynasty plans. Without many flaws, bugs, glitches, or any underdevelopment, this game is continues to push the boundary for this series with constant updates and an awesome community of modders and influencers. Even aspects of first/third person scenarios are being implemented and further developed which really shows the future the title has. The main gameplay loop is very satisfying and additional fun can be had by simply rising another Dynasty to fame or experimenting with faith and culture dynasty relations. _childDocuments_.review: After 642 hours I guess I should post a "review".I went from CK2 into Ck3, I played CK2 with all DLC's so I guess you could call me somewhat of a fan yet I remained skeptic when CK3 was released as results from the past don't give any guarantees for the future.Paradox and their Crusader Kings team did not disappoint me however! Base game was already good and with the DLC put out so far the game-play only became better and a lot more fun, which makes me believe it will only become better and better in the future.As a player of CK2 I understood a lot of the basics that was in CK3, it made the learning curve a lot less steep but I can understand that new players could struggle to learn all of the mechanics that work in this game.As I am a history enthusiast, this game obviously has a lot of draw to me.The big learning curve is something which can be a deterrent to people interested in this game but to those I would say: take some time to watch YT let's plays or YT tutorials, this is how I learned the basics of CK2 when I bought it and combined with playing, trial and error, recognizing the errors you made and learning from them you get a grasp of the game. When I moved on to CK3 I already had most of the basic mechanics and game-play in my system.This game is for those who love grand-strategy, RPG, history and games that are difficult to learn and even harder to master.The "drawbacks" of this game are the steep learning curve and fairly high price.For me this game is a "casual game" because I have had over a 1000k hours in the current and previous game (CK2 & CK3) but be assured for new players this is not the case.When getting into the CK games and loving it, it costs you dearly because it will keep you busy for lots of hours as well as having you spending hundreds of Euros (or whatever currency you use) as the games is frequently updated through DLC's that add features and lots of game playing changes.So in short (TLDR) if you love history, grand-strategy, complex game-play and are committed to learning the game, then this game is for you!Be on the look-out for sales on Steam or Paradox Plaza if you are not sure or even try out the free version of CK2 over here on steam! _childDocuments_.review: I need to stress beforehand that this is a paradox game. So, keep in mind: expensive dlc for the "complete" experience.  With that out of the way, the review. After 1 583 hours, I can safely say this game is pretty good. Not perfect, but let's start with the positives. I never played any other game from the CK franchise before this one, so my first time playing this game was extremely hard and overwhelming. In the best of ways. The gameplay loop, although simple at first, gets more and more complex. I learned that playing with my own rules and run wild is the most fun this game ever gets. So highly reccomend you do that, try different traits on the ruler creator. Try them all at once! Want a challange or to complety rule the world with ease? it's all possible. Also, this game actually can teach you some history and geography. Now, if you have ever heard or played a CK game, you know what you are getting into. You'll stare at maps for hours. The events and activities you can do (especially with the DLC ones) can somewhat give you something different, but let's be honest. You'll stare at a map. It also requires a good setup to run properly. Specially when you advance, the game can get laggy if your pc can't handle too much. I have to say this again here: this game is heavy on DLC, pricy DLC. You can get it at a discounted price after a while, but the newer ones will come at a heafty price. Are they worth it? It depends on what you want out of the game. The DLC so far it's been okay. some hits and some misses. But I have to say, Tours&Tournaments is a must have. Lastly, and definetly not least, the modding community. This is the best thing about CK3 in my opinion. Modders make this game go to its full potencial. _childDocuments_.review: I'll recommend this for now, but I need to explain some disappointments, relative to the 2nd one (of which I have logged 1,300 hours or so, in Steam and beyond).First, I am recommending it because I love Paradox as a development team and have faith they will improve this game as they improved CK2 over the years.  I have always, happily, paid for the expansions and am happy to fund their company.Some of my initial experience has been a bit disappointing.  Combat has been stripped down to a bare-bones version; if you have better knights (commanders from CK2) and a better strength of your army (basically, from 1-5), you have advantage, and will do more damage.  There are some idiosynchracies, like horse regiments (retinues) doing more damage in open plains, and archers doing more damage in hills, but this has lost the ability to put specific generals with specific regiments (horse commanders taking the horses, etc.) and made it more simple.  Less planning goes into combat and troops move around the map much faster.  Also, any amount of troops can just turn into boats when they get to the water, so "landlocked" nations can send huge amounts of troops across the ocean with no sweat.  It has diminished the strategy of sea warfare.Another very strange and bizarre feature is that you set a rally point for your troops and, when you raise them, they all appear at the point.  You can control all of Europe and set your rally point to Russia and raise your troops; all of the troops from Western Europe will instantly appear at the rally point, and not have to travel across the map.  Then, when that is done and you dismiss your troops, you can move your rally point to Spain and raise them again and they are all instantly in Spain.  It removes the time and planning it takes to move raised levies to locations and dumbs down combat planning.People only have three traits, instead of the open ended trait line from CK2, and there are fewer sins and virtues.  And I can't play as a republic (Venice was my favorite game in CK2).  This feels very basic and streamlined; like you get more troops, more alliances, and steamroll.  There doesn't seem to be much fear of rebellion or fracturing.I'll give it more time, and it's not really worth comparing it to CK2, because it's a different game.  It doesn't have societies or artifacts yet.  Still, if you liked CK2, I would advise getting it and supporting Paradox because I imagine they will add good expansion content.I normally don't review games until many, many hours in but I find myself wanting to play CK2 while I'm playing this for some reason.

_childDocuments_.review: I am 32 years old.My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings II player with over 500 hours played.UI AND AUDIOCK3 has no event log, and important combat messages flash up fast in very small fonts even on the slowest game speed. The UI is very hard to navigate. I appreciate this appears in two places, but it is not obvious enough when the game is paused. It is impossible to monitor events for important characters as we could in CK2--pinning them does not have the same effect.It's hard to click on what you need. The tooltip modes are all difficult to use. Useful information screens are buried or gone. The colour palette is ugly and everyone is wearing shades of brown. All the 3D models did was put most characters' eyes in shadow, making them seem much less relatable. Holy war music is extremely loud compared to other audio.ARMIESArmy movement cannot be cancelled reliably--when attempting to cancel, sometimes the unit does stop moving and other times it insists on going to the target and coming back. The new hostile armies mechanic (armies of other rulers being hostile when at war with the same target) is surprising, dangerous, and doesn't seem realistic.LEDGERThe CK2 ledger is gone, making it difficult to tell which holdings are producing the most/least gold and levies. This has greatly reduced the player's ability to make comparisons and make informed lifestyle choices for the ruler.CHARACTER SEARCHCertain search criteria are available on some character search screens and not others. It's difficult or impossible to look at character details while some windows are open. Many windows are not movable.POSITIVESMore people are playing than ever before.The soundtrack is good.The paintings that appear when starting the game are pretty.OVERALLThis feels really unfinished. The thing that made CK2 great for me was the game informed the player about the consequences of their actions at every stage, and allowed the player to have enough information to make plans. In CK3 it's very hard to get information at the level of detail needed, especially with the immovable windows, and with detailed calculations just gone from the UI.I have heard from newer players that CK3 is easier to get into, but I've found it much more difficult myself because there are unexpected consequences, illogical results especially with armies and wars, missing screens, and the fonts and other important UI elements can be brutally tiny.

_childDocuments_.review: -- I started to write a reply to someones negative comment and it turned into a full fledge review and decided to just put it as my own review so at times I will be ranting, enjoy. -- As I read through some of these negative comments I find people want to assume that this game is "incomplete" or "empty". As I play through the game I haven't randomly thought "they need to add more to this or CK2 did this better" What paradox have done is create a well polished game with a lot of the ideas from CK2 and also a lot of new ideas. I don't see any malicious intent here. If I were you I would play the game and make up your own mind.Some things they could improve on (I have not played through to end year and experienced everything so some of these could already be implemented and I have not experienced it yet):- Character Creator - I have heard they are releasing this for free but I could be mistaken.- More cultural clothing, hair styles and cultural images for Eastern and African countries. (Temple and town image artwork.) Just to make the experience different from western cultures.  - Ability to restrict clothing to what tier and culture your character is. It is weird you can put a Byzantium crown on my Indian lord.- Game balancing - some empires tend to steam role the map with little to no internal issues or breaks. - Artifact/Item system. I did get a horse but I didn't know where I could find it. Didn't get much of a chance it died shortly after ;-/ RIP horse Odin.- More decisions - this will come with time there is enough but I think they could put in more to make it more interesting. Maybe make these decisions change due to culture.- Secret Societies - This was an interesting DLC. My character became a witch and I really didn't know how to continue from there. Maybe some sort of structure or more thorough event chain (This maybe already implemented and I didn't get to that point yet.)- Naval Warfare and navy in general - They need to expand on this. I have not seen anything. Your armies just go straight onto a boat I never build any or anything. I do like how smooth this is especially if you are on a island but this is a grand strategy you should have to at least build them. Navy battle implementation would be good.Thing they did right:- Roleplay Elements: Paradox have worked out why a lot of people really enjoy this game. It is the complex roleplay elements that this game brings to the table. So they have greatly improved on this element. I can't wait how they move forward with this.)- General mechanics and UI: Some people hate the UI I like it, I had to get used to it from CK2 but it is a lot easier to understand and if you don't know what something is they have added tool tips you can hover over and the game continually suggests thing you can do or you have missed. The mechanics how the game runs is a lot smoother. moving armies around,adding them on boats was an ordeal so I'm glad that automatically happens.     - Different playable Cultures: When CK2 came out you were very restricted on who you could play when it came to different cultures. CK3 is very different you can play anyone you want and they have put effort into their religious and cultural beliefs. I had a quick game of some African woman who dominated their society and were pretty much warrior amazon women.- Expanded map - CK3's map is a lot larger than CK2. Hopefully they continue to expand it more so we can play Mongolian, Japanese and Chinese cultures.- Realm development - I was always frustrated in CK2 because it was so hard to build anything or develop my land and country. They fixed it. There is so much more but I think you need to find out for yourselves. I have only touched the tip of this game so I am no expert and what I like you may not but it is good and I don't usually write this much so...I feel if Paradox just put out their games and not continually supported and improved their games over 7 years people wouldn't be complaining about this. It is only that they do release DLC and continue support and develop their game that they get slack for it.I would suggest maybe look at what they have improved upon from CK2 because it is blatantly obvious that they have put a lot of thought and love into this game and it plays a lot better and the roleplay elements gets me intrigued in what they can do with the new game mechanics and setup.So, all up it is the mindset of people. If this game was bad or empty, I would be right along with you but it isn’t, so I'm confused why some people are complaining. This is the finished product; paradox is a company that continuously develops their games but to do that it costs money and over time the DLC builds up. People might go no they are doing it to make money and yes you are right they release DLC to make money they also make the game better (or worse depending on the DLC)

_childDocuments_.review: - New UI design was poorly implemented and thought out. Changing from the pattern of every other Paradox game to something new that isn't any better is pointless.- Hiding most of your pop-ups in a single button is also not helpful. Wait, 16 notifications here? Since when?!- Too much useless information in many of the pop ups and tooltips that overlap and block other items. UI just too cluttered.+ Interesting implementation that expands the detail of character interaction. CK2 really just was a war game with a sideshow of characters and dynasties. Now you absolutely are involved in character interactions. Possibly to the point of micromanaging that takes away from the overall speed of the game. Depends on your own opinion.++ Beautiful world map, seamless transition as you zoom in and out. Wonderfully designed character avatars with genetic inheritance of appearance and changes over time based on traits. Just great.- Frustrating map system. Click a Duke vassal and your map mode changes. Try to click off? Nope, that's his title. Gotta hit Escape.- Pop up tips at the top? Well, click that and see that you've got actually closer to 50 messages, not 17. Right click to dismiss? Kidding, only for a little while. Oh, wanna get rid of this intrusive window in the middle of your game screen? Hit the X or hit Esc. You can't just click off it.- Event pop ups. Guess what? Sometimes they pause your game, sometimes they don't. --- Trying to fight a cohesive war with coordinated army movements across multiple provinces? Better hope you don't get into a battle and need to quickly move that force immediately after because the game deselects your army after a battle. Why? Who knows. - Form HRE was broken initially, now it seems INCREDIBLY easy to form and perhaps is an issue for some, such as myself. No control over electors, I would like to see electors as a title that can be given or retracted.- Form Danelaw. Can't unform Danelaw.- Form Archduchy of Austria. Form Archduchy of EVERY title you possess from b to k- Help a friend win a claim on title X. Friend becomes your vassal, rather than independent and holding that title. Did they really win the title, or did you just annex France?- Saxon elective monarchy. Don't lose your kingship because your game will end. Why? Because the game registers your duchy and counties as worthless. Your son/daughter inherit them as they should, but your game ends anyway because your primary title was lost. Game-breaking bug. Honestly, this game is beautiful but the execution is pathetic. Most of it takes away from the actual playing of the game. Who thought these massive windows with so much wasted space would be a good idea?

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of paradox games, in particular the CK series. >2000 hours played in CK1, >4000 hours played in CK2. I've only played 6 hours of CK3 thus far, I'll write another review when I'm post 100h. EDIT: I've played another 100h of CK3. The TL;DR is this: I keep returning to CK2 over CK3. I'll add the rest of my update review below the original.Visuals: Contrasted with CK2 the graphics are actually a step backward. It's like replacing a renaissance painting with a DC comic, sure it's newer... but it feels cheap and tacky. The majority of the map filters look like a child's water colours, with the terrain view resembling M:TW2 after a graphics card malfunction. Gameplay: My experience so far is that despite CK3 having been out for >1 year it's still full of bugs and a severe lack of polish. Here's several examples:- No easy viewing of vassal limit (I was not actually able to find out where the limit is listed and how to calc in CK3, just received a message that I was about to exceed it)- A couple of CTD errors.- No warning when attempting to hand out counties that one of them was actually a bishopric. Found that out when my son-in-law ceased to be an in-law and the resulting grandchild lost legitimacy and became a bastard.- Weird changes to de jure vassals on peace acceptance (pressed claim for a kingdom, after I won, all the de jure duke-level vassals became vassals of another neighbouring realm wheras said duke's de jure count-level vassals became my vassals.Music: It's there.These are all highlights of why I would not recommend CK3 to other players to purchase. This is not to say there are no positives to the game, but I would suggest to anyone new to paradox games that they pick up CK2 instead - it's free-to-play and a superior game in all ways (at present).Edit: Thus far, I think what has impressed me least with CK3 is that the whole game boils down to a series of progress bars. Want to change culture in a province? Click start and watch the bar progress for a couple of years. Ditto religion. Ditto researching tech. How about seducing your vassal's wife (or your liege's). Same thing. Click start and wait for 12 months. Every character can and will succeed in 1 scheme at a time.So far as conquest and military goes, the men-at-arms system is rubbish. I'm not talking about the rock-paper-scissors, that's fine. I'm talking about how emperors and dukes are close to parity in troop numbers.Everyone gets one regiment base plus one per rank. Count gets 2, Duke 3, King 4, Emperor 5. Plus additional regiments per tech and some specific holdings. This means that by the time you're in the high middle ages, A duke with his 3 county duchy will have 8 or 9 regiments of men-at-arms and an Emperor with 200 counties will have 10-11 regiments. MAA are what win battles. Levies fall in a heap. Because of this, the seduction focus is the best military way of life. Have a 100 kids = have 100 alliances. Even an ally count can muster ~1/3 as many elite troops as can the Byzantine Empire.The system needs a complete overhaul. I would suggest borrowing from CK2 and the Europa Universalis series. EU-style slider bar between Feudal Levies and Professional Army that requires tech/culture advancement to unlock. At the Feudal end it works like CK2 tribals - call your vassals to war - and at the Professional end it works like CK2 Retinues / EU4 armies, ie you have manpower and a standing army.I have just picked up the Viking flavour pack. I'll explore that content and update again ~200 hours. For anyone wondering why I am continuing to play if I don't recommend: I like paradox games. I'm still playing CK2 10x as much as CK3. I'd like CK3 to succeed. I really want to like it. At the moment though, CK3 feels like it should still be in beta.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming into CK3 as a longtime CK2 and EUIV player, I was slightly concerned about the content and playability of CK3. After all, CK2 in its initial stage was very limited, and it was through the course of very many DLCs that fleshed out CK2 to what it is today. CK3, being brand new, and (rightfully) with no expansions, felt like it would be in danger of being a pale imitation of its predecessor. However, now with over 40 hours in CK3, I can safely say this game lives up to everything that CK2 brought to the field and more! The UI is much, much more intuitive and new player-friendly. Furthermore, content that was added over a long period of time through expansions/DLCs like India and Tibet are in the game right off the bat and immediately playable! There are also many new, welcome mechanics, at least for people like me who like to roleplay their dynastic legacies or 'jump ship' so as to speak. Let me explain!To start myself off in CK3, I decided to go with an old favourite, the Magyars. Leading the fore as Almos, I led the Magyars to migrate into the Carpathian Basin, snatching it from Bulgaria. Following this, I attempted to conquer enough lands to reform the Taltoist faith, but combined pressure from the Carolingian Kingdoms and the Byzantine Empire led to the death of Almos and poured cold water over my dreams of reformed Taltoism. As Almos's son, Arpad, I turned Catholic, and used 'holy war' as an excuse to conquer all my heathen neighbours despite being pagan just years ago. With Hungary formed and its borders secure, Arpad finally passes on. As the 3rd-generation King Szonuk, I noticed Bavaria was no longer in the hands of the Karlings, thereby breaking their tripartite alliance. I bide my time, building prestige, formed alliances with West Francia and the Byzantine Empire, and proceeded to invade and conquer Bavaria, creating the Austro-Hungarian Empire centuries before its supposed to exist. As Szonuk dies and my 4th-generation Arpad II takes the throne, I notice I am, in fact, able to claim the West Francian throne for my mother. So I invade my former allies without further ado and put dear mum on the throne. As my mother passes on and the throne of West Francia comes to my greedy little hands, the Austro-Hungarian Empire has surpassed even Charlemagne, and stretches from France to Hungary. My son, Szonuk II, through careful eugenics, is a genius, and my grandson, Arpad III, a HERCULEAN genius! Nothing can stand in our way now!But wait. A killer roams the castle. I am shocked and horrified to discover my herculean genius grandson dead. Dead before he even has a chance to fulfil his glorious legacy. I vow to find the killer myself. Clearly, it must be a Karling loyalist, or maybe even a Byzantine spy trying to undermine my power. As I investigate, I get ever closer to the truth... and then receive a letter, from none other than the killer! The killer says they have been living under my nose this whole time, and that the truth will only bring me pain. I push on nonetheless... I must know the truth! And when I confront the killer... its...... My son, Szonuk II! Why?! How?! it's your own son! My grandson! I am aggrieved. I disinherit him and put him in jail immediately. My successor changes to one of my other, more virtuous, less kinslayer-inclined sons. As I ponder what to do with my insane genius kinslayer of a son, the Pope's messenger arrives. A crusade, he declares, is to be launched into Jerusalem. Being the pious Emperor that I am, I of course, agree. To my surprise, my son qualifies as a beneficiary of the crusade, due to being disinherited. Hm. So be it. I free him from jail, force my son to be in the frontlines as a knight, and send him off to lead the imperial armies and hopefully die a virtuous death despite living as a sinner. The crusade against the Abbasids goes swimmingly. Too swimmingly. In a twist of fate, my sinful son becomes monarch of the holiest kingdom, Jerusalem itself. Well. So be it. He'll probably die defending the holy city once the Abbasids recover and launch their counter-assault. I have no inclination to help him. So, I click past the notifications, and...... I accidentally click "I wonder what kind of King he'll be?" And now all of a sudden I'm the kinslaying villain disinherited by the Emperor, and sent to be king of a forsaken holy kingdom that i have no chance of holding. With a single demesne, with all my vassals and everybody in my family hating me because I'm a kinslaying nutjob. FFFFF-Just as I consider ragequitting, I figure... Hang on, this might be the most interesting character to roleplay as yet. A kinslaying, lunatic-genius exiled from home and sent to die fighting for the cross to atone for himself. So I lean into it. I become the most insanely fanatical holy king ever. My first order of business is to imprison and revoke the titles of all my vassals from the contributing houses of the crusade. Now my demesne is full and my coffers are slowly filling up. Then, I befriend the Byzantine Emperor, bribing him with huge amounts of gold, most of it given to me by the Pope despite my lunacy due to my renowned piety (thank you, Your Holiness!) and swaying him with my evil charisma. I see that he has three sons. I marry my daughter (thank god I didn't kill YOU too) to the youngest matrilineally. Now we have an alliance. With the aid of the Byzantines I survive in the land of the infidels, and slowly expand by absorbing the smaller Islamic emirates around me, never lifting a finger and simply burning prestige to let the Byzantines do their thing and wipe out my enemies. Following this, I systematically kill off the very helpful Emperor's older sons. The first murder goes unnoticed. The second, unfortunately, is traced back to me. The Byzantine Emperor is very understandably heartbroken and furious with me. So I assassinate him too. Now my son-in-law is Byzantine Emperor, and he hates me for killing off basically his entire direct family. Sure, understandable. I check my daughter and see she already has two sons born to our house. Cackling madly all the way and out of my mind with stress, I commit suicide. Now I am my daughter. Over the years, I watch as my husband drinks himself to death, leaving the Byzantine Empire to my oldest son, who I groom into another herculean genius. By the time I pass on and play as my son, the Herculean Genius, Hungarian Catholic, Byzantine Emperor and King of Jerusalem Szonuk III, I look to the west and see our ancestral legacy, instead of imploding like I thought, has remained intact, and blossomed towards England and Scandinavia as well. As I look at the sea of Arpadys covering the map, I vaguely realize I've recreated the Western and Eastern Roman Empires. What can I say except 10/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: Over the past two years or so, I've been enjoying my ongoing exploration of 4X and grand strategy titles. Paradox, being the legends that they are, make a good majority of the titles out there. For all the grief they get (sometimes rightfully so), these guys really do amaze me in that they have so many different franchises that have unique twists on the 4X/grand strategy genres.  for traditional grand strategy.  for a space 4X spin on grand strategy.  for economic simulators.  for World War 2 wargames. And then, you have arguably their most complex and well-known franchise: . I'm an RPG fan, much more than I'm into grand strategy, so it's probably no surprise that I tend to gravitate toward the  games more than any of their other franchises (though  is probably my favorite PDX title to date). CK2 was a great game but unless you got the DLCs, the base game felt rather limited and there were just too many to collect them without doing the subscription. Enter .One of the most noticeable aspects about CK3 is that this game really is a modern iteration on everything that CK2 had, at least for the most part. A lot of functionality that was only added with DLCs to CK2 is just in the vanilla experience. For example, CK2 required the "Way of Life" DLC to truly allow the player to roleplay their characters but CK3 enables life paths/goals, greater interaction with other characters and so forth, no DLCs needed.However, it's not just a reskinned version of CK2 with most of the DLCs. It also adds  UI and map improvements, such as animated character avatars, more streamlined menus for managing your kingdom, a more in-depth way of knowing character traits and where you stand with other characters and so forth. It's also a particularly beautiful map, making it feel less like paper on a table and more like a bird's eye of Europe.Not only this, though, CK3 includes gameplay improvements as well. Interaction events with other characters feel a lot more like a choose-your-own-adventure sort of experience. Random occurrences like tournaments or hunting trips truly feel spontaneous. This, more than any other CK game, truly does allow the player to live out their fantasies of being royalty and running a family.Because the  series is a blend of grand strategy and RPG, one of the best parts of this franchise is that you get to choose how your characters play. For example, you could have one king act like a cruel tyrant but their successor might be played as a benevolent leader. What's interesting is that this series tracks the way other characters feel about your characters. This has an impact on your children and other family members as well, meaning that sometimes the heir has a severe problem with trying to get vassals under control simply because their parent ticked everyone off. The way characters feel about your player character drastically impacts and changes your gameplay experience overall, making every single playthrough feel immersive and truly unique.This also means that the CK games can sometimes be a great political simulator as well. You have to really pay attention to your vassals and neighboring kingdoms. You have to make concessions and ensure that you keep the most powerful people happy... because you certainly can't keep  happy. It's this never-ending balancing act because your real goal with this game is to create a strong dynasty, not just by blood but through marriages and alliances with other kingdoms, as well as your vassals. also seems to be taking a much-appreciated approach to its post-launch content. In the past, Paradox has received hate because of the sheer number of DLCs they add after launch. In many cases, this content feels more like cut content being added back in, rather than a proper extension to the core gameplay. Thankfully, after , they seem to have toned this back and gone with a more traditional approach to expansion content. CK3 is no exception. While some of the DLCs are less important than others, the main DLCs here are more like proper expansions. A great example of this is the "Royal Court" DLC, which extends your roleplaying and political maneuvering into a more tangible realm (kingdom pun intended). It adds deeper RPG mechanics that truly do make you feel like a king, even moreso than the base game already did.Should you buy ? The answer depends entirely on what you're looking for. If you're wanting a more traditional grand strategy game centering around resource management, trade and military might, then you might be better off looking into  or the  series. If you prefer exploration and 4X types of games,  is your game. However, if you really enjoy roleplaying AND grand strategy, then I'd  recommend buying this game! The vanilla experience is solid enough but I'd definitely go for one of the DLC packages because they don't feel like content being re-added to a crippled base game.If you've ever had a fantasy of being royalty and if you enjoy roleplaying and grand strategy gameplay, your time has come. Claim your throne and live the royal life you always dreamed of!

_childDocuments_.review: War, schemes, intrigue and medieval role-playing. What sets the Crusader Kings franchise apart form other historical (grand) strategy games, is it delves into something different than those; a character driven political landscape. The goal is simple, you play as a ruler, from a lowly chieftain the grandest of emperors, but you don't play as the 'nation'. Everything you do is tied to your character and all characters around you. The goal? Create a dynasty that stands the test of time, or fade into nothing. Play as you want, pursue your own goals and accomplish them as you see fit, but if your dynasty fades into nothing, the game ends. What makes this a great historical game, is that it allows the players to immerse themselves into the medieval minds of old that most other historical games can't.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings 3 is an incredibly engaging and immersive game that has kept me entertained for hours on end. The level of detail and depth in the gameplay is simply amazing, from the intricate character interactions to the vast map and the numerous cultures and religions.One of the things that I particularly enjoy about CK3 is the sheer amount of options available to the player. Whether you want to play as a powerful emperor, a humble count, or a scheming spymaster, the game allows you to follow your own path and make your own decisions. The possibilities are truly endless.I also appreciate the attention to historical accuracy and the ability to shape the course of history. It's amazing to see how the world changes over time as you play, and to see your own dynasty grow and prosper (or fall into ruin).The visuals and soundtrack are also top-notch, adding to the immersive experience. And with regular updates and expansions, there's always something new to discover in this rich and dynamic game.Overall, I highly recommend Crusader Kings 3 to anyone who enjoys strategy games and is looking for a deep and engaging experience. It's definitely one of my all-time favorites.

What kind of game is it if you don't actually make any decisions anymore and don't think at all, but just choose what suits the character's characteristics? That is far too passive for me, I might as well watch TV. At least I have found something that increases the level of difficulty. Stay historically accurate: don't mess around with religion and culture, limit your options and partially ignore them. You do that in role playing too, but here I think you should adapt the chosen restrictions to the chosen culture. My tip for a challenge that, in my opinion, should be rewarded with a steam achievement, which is not the case: Start with an Armenian ruler with the apostolic faith and try to survive without changing religion. That then creates a unique gaming experience that the game would not otherwise offer, and you can also see what an achievement it was for the real Armenians to remain apostolic while surrounded by Muslim powers. You have to actively seek out challenges in the game and impose additional rules on yourself so that it can remain interesting. And well, there is also very little flavor, the path from count to world ruler works the same regardless of which region you start in, unless you set yourself restrictions. And not everyone can play historically like me without help, I studied history. It would be great if there were predefined scenarios. There are some of them, but they are a) often not challenging and b) only included in DLCs that you have to buy separately.Another possibility to make the game challenging, that always works: restrict your domain to 1 or 2. But to puzzle and play with your domain is fun you would miss then.What Paradox should definitely do is nerf the buildings. Their bonuses are just too high, that's why I recommend to limit your domain. But that also means, that the balancing in this game is just awful. My bonuses stack up so much that i can wipe out armies that are twenty times bigger than mine without having any losses. Hah, sometimes I not only had no losses, but even kind of minus losses and at the end of the battle I had more fighters than before the battle. Paradox is sometimes paradoxical.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there, fellow rulers! Ever fancied running your own medieval dynasty? Dreamed of being a benevolent king or maybe a cunning, backstabbing queen? But oh boy, the rabbit hole goes deep. One moment, I'm hosting grand feasts, making allies and living the good life. The next, I'm dealing with rebellious vassals, plotting against me because I, uh, might've accidentally imprisoned their favorite jester. Oops.And the family drama? Forget about it! Between arranging marriages, ensuring my heir isn't plotting against me, and dealing with Uncle Bob's constant desire to start crusades, it's a full-time job. Who knew ruling a kingdom would be this hectic?But the real beauty of CK3? The stories. Every decision, every alliance, every betrayal crafts a unique tale that you'll be dying to share. It's a game of strategy, wit, and sometimes just pure, hilarious chaos.In conclusion, if you're after a game that's a blend of strategy, storytelling, and medieval shenanigans, Crusader Kings III is your ticket to the throne. Just watch your back; medieval politics is a tricky business. (Because in CK3, we go big or go home.) Aspiring monarchs, strategy buffs, and anyone who enjoys a good medieval drama.If this review gave you a chuckle, smash that like button!
