_childDocuments_.review: The first things that's obvious is that the game is absolutely BEAUTIFUL. The music, the world, the campaign map, the characters and the UI. Being a professional UI developer in real life I can truly take in fully the level of detail and beauty in this new UI. Some of the snappy animations could probably be toned down but it's a feast for the eyes.Now my first experience with the game was a Duke, with a small bit of land and actually lost the game 2-3 times before I settled on the play through I'm on. I was being destroyed and punished for my aggressive behaviour, for my lack of care for planning my military excursions and feeling the wrath of rebellions and outside raiders. At this point I was upset, I took a break from the game and came back later that night........oh boy what a difference does actually taking part in the Crusader Kings mindset and playing with real strategy. When you start to plan out and really get stuck in, the challenge of playing a Duke on CK3 is so much fun. I managed to survive the early years by changing my strategy, swearing fealty to a large power. I was betrayed several times, but I was still standing.The most amazing part is, the connection you build with the characters in this world. The pacing of the game is slowed down to the point where the people you hate, you actually begin to like. To the people you like you start to realise, they don't really have your back. I've had my realm split in two by rebellion permenantly and watched a powerful kingdom blossom from that. I've watched my family take over neighbouring kingdoms and their young children take power but would not me bully them around and instead defeated me in combat....though instead of punishing me, they extended an olive branch and become GREAT allies after humilating me and we've fought many great campaigns together.I have a mutual respect for my enemies and more importantly, I feel, I'm immersed and I'm loving every moment of this game. The most amazing thing is, the lands you end up conquering you take on the vassals of those you've defeated and you can either integrate or remove them. Integrating allows to make some powerful allies that you normally wouldn't have in your court and become great councillors/generals etc.The combat is strategic and your army composition matters. The skills trees are a delight to play and make character progression meaningfulThis in my opinion is one of the few games in the last 10-20 years that has lived up to the hype and made you excited to come back and play.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to get into Crusader Kings II when it first came out.  It seemed like there was an interesting game in there, but it was locked behind an overwhelming and confusing interface with arcane terms you had to look up to try to decipher.Crusader Kings III is a VAST improvement.  I've played one campaign to completion (in this case, completion being the ending of my house's holdings after 300 years of slow prosperity and 50 years of terrible mismanagement and hostile neighbors) and have started 3 others to try out various mechanics.  I'm very impressed by how intuitive the interface is, given the complexity of the game behind it.  Each screen presents you with only what is relevant to that window, with tooltips very clearly marked for any term you may want to know more about.  Moreover, you can go into tooltips within tooltips, and they all collapse back out very neatly when you're done with them.  It's not perfect, and there are still things that are a bit confusing until you play around and learn by trial and error.  But it's easy enough to just get into a campaign and react to things how you think a ruler might in those situations and watch things unfold more or less how you'd expect.The most important thing to know when considering this game is that you'll likely have a lot more fun if you don't constantly min/max stats and try to "win" it.  The tutorial even points out that "winning" (painting the map your color) is certainly a potential goal, but that it's not the only way you're intended to play.  The game goes out of its way to try to give you interesting dilemmas via the Stress system.  Bad things happen in your ruler's personal life?  They get stressed.  They act against their nature?  They get stressed.  They act with their nature and/or good things happen to them?  They lose stress.  But sometimes the things that are best for your house are what stresses your ruler the most.  It creates an interesting tension and encourages you to role play each leader of the dynasty through the years.Battles are rather simple affairs.  The animations are very plain.  And once war is declared it's mostly about army positioning, finding terrain advantage, and coordinating with allies.  Honestly, that last one is my biggest con.  I really wish I could tell my allies "stop following me.  Go siege that castle - I'll use my larger army to keep the enemy army from reaching you."  But overall, battles serve their purpose.  Like many Paradox games, the outcome of a war is often a foregone conclusion by the time it's declared.  That's not a bad thing.  It encourages thinking ahead instead of relying on battle AI that can't stand up to a clever player.Overall, this is a very good game for grand strategy gamers who enjoy a bit of role playing in the much more traditional sense, and a bad fit for those looking for grand graphical spectacle or intricate battle tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: "Crusader Kings 3" is less a game and more a simulation of realpolitik, intrigue, and the brutal machinations of dynasties vying for dominance. It is a world where titles are not given—they are taken, through cunning, manipulation, and force. In that, I find much to admire.The complexity of managing a kingdom is staggering, from handling vassals with their own agendas to ensuring your bloodline continues through strategic marriages. A wise ruler knows that family can be both a weapon and a liability. One must never rely too heavily on any one person, and the game captures this truth well. Treachery, of course, is an ever-present threat, but also a tool. Betrayal must be anticipated, sometimes cultivated, and only a fool is surprised when it comes.The mechanics of Crusader Kings 3 are labyrinthine, but such is the nature of ruling. In real life, power is not handed to you in neat, simple terms; it must be deciphered, torn from the hands of others, and wielded with cold calculation. The game rewards patience, foresight, and the ability to strike at the right moment. It understands that the sharpest sword in politics is timing, and like a Lannister always paying his debts, the repercussions of every action come back in time.War is not always the answer, but when it is, it must be swift and decisive. Yet, it is the intrigue—the webs spun behind closed doors—that define this game. In "Crusader Kings 3," much like in Westeros, battles are often won long before they are fought, through schemes, spies, and whispered words in the dark. It is the art of control without appearing to control, the soft power behind the iron fist.However, I must admit, not every aspect of the game feels as polished as it should. The interface is often clunky, and while the depth is admirable, one occasionally wonders whether some of these intricacies serve to enhance the experience or to obfuscate it. But, much like dealing with an unruly council, it is a frustration to be borne with stoic patience.In the end, "Crusader Kings 3" is not a game for those who seek immediate gratification. It is a game for those who, like me, understand that true power lies in the long game—one where every decision has ripple effects for generations. The game doesn’t just let you rule; it forces you to think like a ruler. And in that, it succeeds. Rating: 9/10. Because even a perfect plan must occasionally adjust for the whims of fate.

_childDocuments_.review: This would be closer to a neutral review rather than a negative one. However, I still would not recommend it to anyone who played Crusader Kings II. Now, that is out of the way, let me also deal with another point. I did not vote this down because it lacks the sheer content of Crusader Kings II. It is perfectly fair to compare this game to it's predecessor upon release because I am taking into consideration how the game will evolve from here.  So, what is wrong with Crusader Kings III? It is a sequel but feels more like an off brand copy of the second game. It has less content, less traits, less schemes, and over all less to do than Crusader Kings II upon release. Regardless of rank or title, every game plays exactly the same but things are much easier. You can get the titles you want faster than Crusader Kings II, alliances are more obvious and who will join what wars is pretty easy to weigh before hand. Crusader Kings III, is an attempt to make lightning strike again in the same place, but this is the third try and nothing interesting of note happens. Perhaps, the development cycle of Crusader Kings II just went on way too long and nothing they put out would really feel innovative.                                                                                                                                                         Keeping all that in mind, this is not a bad game. If you found Crusader Kings II interesting but too complicated or time consuming this might work well for you. The game goes out of the way to hold the players hand and show them how to play. It is very safe, generic and certain to be a financial success. I just do not like it. The events in court are lacklustre. Rather than a chain of events, where you as a child, miraculously survive several assassination attempts only to have your regent burst into your room with a sword screaming "Just die already!" Instead, we get new innovative story lines like, there are not enough servants in the court so your heir is going around with a dirty diaper. Now, perhaps I just have not found the really amusing events yet but it seems mundane drudgery of the Middle Ages is the fare here. Not wild, unique, schemes by crazy characters fit for a soap opera.                                                                                                                 So, since the role-play aspect is pretty bland, as a player you tend to focus on politics, dynasty building and ultimately striving to establish that empire. Should be pretty easy right? Like I said, Crusader Kings III easier than Crusader Kings II. Well, obviously the developers realized they had dumbed things down a bit too much and that is where "Confederate Partition" comes in. What is that you may ask? If you played Crusader Kings II, and do not recognize it, that makes sense because it did not exist in the last game. Basically, the default succession in the game magically creates any eligible kingdom titles out of your lands upon your death and divides it up among your heirs. You cannot change this succession type, it is the default. So, upon each succession unless you create an empire title, your realm will shatter and implode, every single time. Remember what I said of the repetitive and bland nature of the game? This is where the developers doubled down on that idea. Since the game lacks any of the interesting events and mischief you and your vassals could get into from the earlier game, they had to give players some sort of challenge. Their answer is shoehorning a particular type of succession that actually did not exist for much of Europe in this time period. Your realm implodes every time upon death. no message, no listed reason it just happens. I suppose this is supposed to give the player a sense the game is dynamic and evolving. In reality, your kingdom has been torn apart by an arbitrary limit imposed by the developers to give the illusion of organic game play but in the most boring, contrived and repetitive way possible. Eventually, I figured out a the way to avoid this is just rush for an empire title every time but by then, I just did not care any more. The actual game play is just too boring to make this tedium worth it.                                                                                                                                                 In conclusion Crusader Kings III is safe, easy, it gets the point across. In the example of your heir with a dirty diaper, it makes a clear point: you lack servants but to be honest, this discovery is not really interesting. You can wait ten years for Paradox to bust the game under a burden of content, or you can just go to Crusader Kings II, buy it on sale and save yourself a lot of money and wasted time.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, where do we even start with the grand tapestry that is CK3? Imagine a game where you can become the medieval ruler of your dreams, and by dreams, I mean those weird ones where you're not sure if you're wearing pants and somehow your neighbor's cat is there advising you on state matters. This game, my friends, is the quintessential blend of strategy, intrigue, and the sort of family drama that would make even the most seasoned soap opera writers go, "Hmm, maybe that's a bit much."First off, let's talk strategy. If by strategy, you mean marrying off your children to secure alliances, only to have those alliances crumble because your son decided he'd rather be a poetry-writing monk than a king. Or perhaps you fancy yourself a master tactician, raising vast armies to conquer your foes, only to have your plans foiled by your own court jester who suddenly pushes you out a palace window. Yes, strategy in CK3 is like playing chess, if the pieces had their own wills and occasionally banged their siblings.And the fluff! Oh, the glorious, wonderful fluff. This is where CK3 truly shines. It's a game where you can start as the King of England and end up as the Emperor of a new Roman Empire headquartered in Damascus, because, why not? The game's depth allows you to explore every facet of medieval life, from the divine right of kings to the divine comedy of trying to manage a realm when your subjects are more interested in gossiping about which noble is sleeping with whom than in paying their taxes.The family dynamics are where the real game is at. Forget about the Holy Land; the real crusade is trying to keep your dynasty from imploding because your third cousin twice removed has a claim to your throne and has decided that now's the perfect time to press it, during an outbreak of smallpox, no less. The game beautifully simulates the intricate relationships of medieval nobility, where you're never quite sure if your brother is your staunchest ally or is plotting to poison your wine because you got the bigger slice of the kingdom from daddy.In conclusion, CK3 is not just a game; it's a lifestyle. It's a masterclass in chaos theory, a tribute to the complexity of human relationships, and a reminder that no matter how grand our plans, they can always be undone by a lustful courtier with a penchant for intrigue. You can play the same start 500 times and get different outcomes each time. Sure, your Guy the XXIV will always be a 400-pound pox-addled beautiful genius, but the way he got there will be different each time. It's the best strategy game ever made, not because of its strategic depth, but because it understands that the real game of thrones is played not on the battlefield, but in the hearts and minds of our pixelated subjects. So, raise your banners, sharpen your wits, and maybe keep an eye on the cat in your dreams advising you. In CK3, anything is possible.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend Crusader Kings III, but there are some issues.It's the greatest game out there when it comes to skullduggery and intrigue. Get in touch with your inner Machiavelli or worse. Everyone playing this game has insane stories how they crushed their enemies, subdued rebellious barons and guided their dynasty to ascendancy.The tactical and strategic part of the game is rather weak. Wars go on forever, because enemy armies lose a battle and retreat. Only to come back a few days later, fully reinforced... It's almost impossible to corner an enemy because they retreat to the sea and land in your rear. Naval battles have been cancelled from the game. The biggest army always wins. There's no tactical dimension to this game besides the stats of your commander. When it comes to greater battles (20-30K) it only needs the opposing army to outnumber you by a thousand men and you will be defeated. Despite being called Crusader Kings, it's almost impossible to achieve the objective of a crusade. The defending AI is always far superior to the coalition of crusaders. As there is no cooperation between the western armies, the 30K strong defending army can always destroy them piecemeal.The makers of the game seem to think that medieval Europe was a multicultural and diverse place. So now and then you get visitors from all over the world. Medieval Europe was not exactly tolerant of other religions. It destroys the atmosphere of the game when Mongols, Moors and Africans suddenly show up as courtiers in France and England.But that's the age we live in, I guess...

_childDocuments_.review: I like the in-depth political aspect of the game. For me it was a complete change I'm used to military focused RTS like Rome Total War. I'll say biasely, that I wish we had more control over the military conflicts because I know I can win a lot of the battles that are fought, but that might be way too much for the game. So for those reading its a great game just understand this is more focused on politics, utilizing policy and economy to grow your "kingdom" and warfare you must have a jus ad bellum... unlike RTW you cant just roll over your enemies. Which makes you have to play by somewhat of societal rules, which is a cool aspect. However, I love the intrigue aspect of the game it allows you to really build informal alliances that help you accomplish your objectives. Only downfall, but I dont want them to change this, is that when your character dies all of your hard work essentially goes down the drain. Which is cool because nations in real life often collapse after a great leader. Short review: Great game, new type of RTS for me, and time consuming. Only con is its heavily focused on Europe, and DLCs dont really include much of the Middle East or Africa. I'm ready for a game like this that allows gameplay in the Middle East, Asia, Africa and Europe... Which im sure would be massive.

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy heir to the throne! CK2 is probably my favorite game of all time, so CK3 had some pretty big shoes to fill. Thankfully, as a base game, I think CK3 does it job perfectly. Visually, the game looks beautiful. It runs extremely well at all speeds, even in the late game. A lot of the systems are simplified, while still maintaining the depth of game play, so it is easier for new players to start, without sacrificing the replayability for experienced players. My only possible complaint (which is more an issue of the genre and Paradox as company) is that many features in CK2 have been removed, which is understandable considering they were added with years of post-launch development, but I must admit the expectation of years of dlc is more daunting than exciting, as I dont wish to get fleeced again for features and flavor that take the majority of the map from being a slightly altered copy of Western Europe, to a historically accurate depiction of its medieval political and cultural layout. I am eager to see how the next few years of development expand this promising start, for better or worse.

_childDocuments_.review: After 107 hours played, from 867 to 1453, I think it´s a good sequel and the skeleton of a good successor of ck2.        I think it´s a bit easier to enter for a newbie in this game, the mechanics feel similar for those veterans of ck2, the ui seems to be at some point more intuitive and in others seems to lack deep ( like, there is no diplomacy mode ).         While i want to keep it short, in summary i recommend it and i´m hyped waiting for the expansions, i´m gonna say:     - The game is more serious than the ck2. I miss the surreality of the inmortal games, glitterhoof, the societies , inmortality events, the spawn of the devil, etc... Doing the large campaign, i noticed that there is a point where is a bit dull. While ck2 manage to keep the full attention with a cascade of events of any kind, here you almost are in a loop of Reign, successor, keep at bay the rebels and so on.       - Until the early years of 1200, the game is really hard because that is the point where you can unlock primogeniture and ultimogeniture. After that it feels snowballing the map.    - Something is going on with the ia armies going forever at seashore to the sea to avoid you or wasting money deciding that is the short path. They abuse it.       - Commoners rebel too much. You crash one rebellion the next one of the same people is knocking at your door after you manage it.    - The mechanic of fervor is a bit unbalanced. Converting a county to your faith is really a monumental effort. I don´t know about other religions, the catholic event sinful bishop spawn too much often and winning a holy war shouldn´t decrease your fervor to the point it does, in my opinion.          - The hook mechanic is really great.         - The faith creation is awesome.         - The lifestyle trees are super. It really matters what you pick. There are some combinations that should be revisited by the developers because they are too much powerful.     - While the battles lost the flank generals, is still important in a different way to have a proper general and some men at arms. Supply matters.There is something else i don´t understand. For example, if you have your domains in a place and you want to raise the armies in the farest place of your empire, it seems to take the same time to raise them as if they were in your domains.     There is always someone sneaking at your door and be careful with the carpets....     I hope this is useful.

_childDocuments_.review: For disclosure, I have never met a middle ages game I liked.  Just not a fan of the time period in history, in Total War I would only play as the Romans (Byzantium).  The trouble is, of the games I have played (the total war series among others) the games focused on petty kingdoms conducting petty wars and building simple buildings with simple stats resulting in little cookie-cutter bonuses to provide a little assistance in your petty wars with petty kingdoms.  THIS IS NOT THAT.  CK III political system rich, alive, and full texture and is a game within the game all on its own.  Its battle system unsurprisingly feels much like EU IV (my favorite RTS to date though this is running a very close second) which admittedly has much to learn from Total War (TW) (and their engine).  Paradox seems to invest their time outside of the personally lead battles with individual unit control of TW. Instead, they invest their time building a world that is so feature-rich you feel as your nation's leader.  Perhaps that is more realistic when you as king or queen send your armies to battle you are not there or away where it's safe so it would auto-resolve so to speak.  The only downside is even out of the box so to speak, there are so many features sometimes navigating to find them is a chore.  While it is nowhere near as frustrating as EU IV, it is something the devs should worry about as more content is added.As a convert from the TW world one thing they do a better job of and I was hoping paradox would do more of was economic specialization.  When an entire region, state (group of provinces) are owned, specialization of the natural resources of that area should be allowed to provide bigger bonuses.  Or in areas that lack natural resources some other form of specialization.  The building mechanics of EU IV and CK III are the big part that leaves me scratching my head as a miss.  It seemed EU IV was moving that way a little with its latest patch allowing some additional building types but still no option for a cohesive national economy.

_childDocuments_.review: is a great game, one of my favourites. It took me a while for it to click with me the first time, as my introduction to Paradox had been through the  series. But as the years went by, I enjoyed CKII more and more. It was just as I was really beginning to appreciate CKII's genius that CKIII was announced.  is, at this point in time, a broad and beautiful slate upon which any number of novel roleplaying experiences can be lived out. The expansions to CKII's Way of Life system were a great decision. The perk trees makes the game feel much more like a roleplaying game, where you determine what your character's specialties are, rather than RNG dealing them out to you. You have a bit more control over that side of your character. The game's roleplaying scenarios and pop up events are deeper and more satisfying than ever before, at least from what I've seen. You can romance, seduce and befriend pretty much anyone, and rivals form factions against you to depose you (as bloody usual). You get gold a lot faster in this game, which means the game has a slightly faster, or at least more "interesting" pace - you get the sensation that more things are happening than they might have been at CKII, at least to begin with. However, my experience with the game has left me feeling slightly... empty. In spite of all of CKIII's improvements - and boy, I just can't go on enough about the roleplaying elements being vastly improved - CKIII feels gutted. I played two hour stints as three characters to get a formative experience for the game - once in good old Ireland, once as an Indian king, and my favourite experience so far as Duke Otto in 867. CKIII seems to have shed strategic depth in favour of roleplaying depth. Maybe this is simply a result of the new UI being big and flashy in favour of CKII's more utilitarian design, which I've come to regard as a work of UI genius. This makes for a much shinier game to look at in the trailers or to watch other people play, but an inferior game to actually navigate yourself. The information is squashed away into small boxes while character portraits (now 3D models, which I've found are slightly hit and miss, though I do enjoy watching the hair slowly change colour as you age and other nice details like that) are placed front row and center. CKIII appears to have gone the route of making the game more understandable for an RPG person (such as myself), but sadly has sacrificed some of the strategic depth of the game (which disappoints the strategy fanatic in me), making the game feel less like a Grand Strategy game and more like a Grand Roleplaying game.  CKIII aims for different targets than CKII, and hits pretty much everything it was going for. CKIII wanted to be easier to get into, easier to connect with characters, easier to play a role, and prettier to look at. And it succeeds at all of this. The map is simply gorgeous, but there are barely any map modes any more. They removed navies as an option instead of having naval battles. The politicking and scheming now feels done for roleplaying purposes rather than strategic purposes, as the game is rewarding you for much different things. It rewards you for playing your character, rather than strategically trying to manuever your way through webs of lies. And it's down to how you want your  experience to feel. Do you like the boundless depth and complex menus and decisions to make? Do you like a slightly lesser roleplaying experience in favour of more opportunities to make exactly the kind of world you like? CKII with DLC attached probably still has you covered if a lack of complexity and strategic depth at this stage worries you, and the new roleplaying opportunities haven't convinced you. However, if you've never ever played a  game before out of fear that CKII would buck you off like some wild horse, CKIII is a great roleplaying experience that encourages you to feel like your ruler, rather than as a nation that has a human face only 75% of the time. Paradox have released a great game with cool new features I'm looking forward to trying, like founding a new religion. If you adopt the game early as I have, I thoroughly recommend actually playing as a Catholic/Christian nation - i.e. an actual Crusader King - because at the moment the deepest experience seems to be there. I'll try Muslim and Viking rulers next and come back to change this review if their experience (and future playtime) showcases depth I haven't yet had a chance to see.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing game that will have you feeling like a ruler in no time.  Perfecting your rule of the realm is where the beauty of this game lays.  So many options on how to rule, so many challenges on the claim of your realm or attempts to steal it from underneath you.  Decisions made by your starting character that are still relevant, and some times even more prominent, during your grandson's rule!  And the sheer amount of content is this game is mind blowing!  Do you want to paint the map with your dynasty's color?  Do it!  Do you want to puppet the world by having a ton of children and sending them out to slowly rise to power while you just watch from your mayor house?  Do it!  Want to make the world a true melting pot of culture where everyone can grow to accept each other?  Yep, Do IT!I have over 700 hours in this game at the time of this review and I just found a major decision line to Dismantle the Papacy and replace it with worship of my Sun God!  I was aiming to create the Persian Empire but my goal may have just shifted!  It is great to play a game for so long and still be rewarded for your game play with new content!  Not a concept from in any games today and even a slight surprise for Paradox Interactive.The game runs very well with minor hiccups sparsely seen in you play through.  One being a person's face not rendering but the eyes and mouth still do!  And funny yet horrifying sight that goes away with a reload or sometimes just closing the panel the character was on!  But that's one of the biggest bugs right now.  Anything major that comes up is squash pretty quickly.  It seems like this game has become the gem of Paradox for the time being.  Thus it is receiving the best updates and DLCs out of the current generation of Paradox games.  Meaning the gaming experience is just getting better with age.  Wonderful.Graphically gorgeous!  Pretty much full customization of everything from your character's appearance to your dynasty's banner, right down to how your soldiers look!  The assets are intricate and your character's appearance develops as result of the events in their lives!  Maimed on the battlefield, your character will need a shiny metallic mask to cover that up!  Life is really hard and your character finds solace in drink, watch their cheeks flush, eyes become soggy, and the way they move in their portrait as they drink their life away.  And the map is just beautiful as a game mat to look at while you make the world yours!I can't say enough great things about this game!  In fact, I stopped in the middle of a play through to drop this review because I was so happy with the content I found.  Time to see if the Caliph will help me permanently remove Catholicism from the world!Nope!  Looks like I am back to praise this game even more.  A few minutes after posting this review, my Caliph (Empire if our culture was based from Anglo-Saxons) and Liege died of old age.  I clicked on his character to see who my new liege would be and found out what this character do with their life.  What I found out is that his father, uncle, and two brothers were all the Caliph prior to their deaths.  This particular character just happened to have a great amount of attribute points in Intrigue which meant he was a sneaky boi!  So I decided to see how his family of Caliphs died.  Turns out three of them were murdered and one died in their sleep!  Meaning this sneaky boi killed his way to the top!  Then I noticed his nickname - "Child Killer".  Pretty Intense but this man executed an entire family of the neighboring ruler who tried to take his lands!  All these actions taken during my one life as the starting character!  What a narrative for a character the AI controlled!

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III is a fantastic addition to the series and the genre. It engrosses you and really makes you feel like a medieval ruler. Every choice has consequences, and every war has stakes. Your experience playing CK3 will be unique — no one will have exactly the same story to tell when a game is over.In my very first game, I started as an independent count between Sweden and Denmark. I ended centuries later as the Emperor of Greater Jerusalem, controlling Sweden, Ireland, random duchies in eastern Europe, and a huge swath of the Middle East. I had dozens of rulers in my family tree, and I remembered many of them and their accomplishments as I looked over the line of succession.In my second game, I started as a Norse invader in England. I ended 30 years in, when the Catholics effortlessly conquered all my lands in a crusade. My ruler was forgotten to history, but the story remains in my mind. I can learn from his mistakes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first recension I write with one of paradox´ games as topic. I use CK3 as an example for what in my opinion has gone wrong with paradox´development and sales politics in the last years. The game itself is okay - not worth the price regarding complexity and final polish, but okay to be bought on a sale - if you don´t compare it to it´s predecessor and if you don´t have paid lots of money for this predecessor and its DLCs :Let me mention first that the first Paradox game I bought was Europa Universalis - when it originally came out decades ago. Since then I bought and played all their grand strategy games (EU,HoI, Victoria, CK, Stellaris). Up to the  first titles with a "2" in the name, I really enjoyed their products: Well developed, finished titles; complex and reliable gameplay which similarily was fun; and (but this of course is my personal taste and shall not influence this review) scripted historical events, which steered the course of the game, confronted me with foreseeable challenges and at the same time refreshed and expanded my knowledge base regarding history. Excellent Mods like VIP, Kaiserreich and ?AGCEEP? (I´m not sure I remember the name correctly) multiplied the fun and immersion.Then - starting with Victoria 2 and CK 2, but even more with the "3s" and Stellaris - they began their DLC-based development and sales strategy. And here I start my review, using the example of CK 3:1. There are two predecessors to this game - CK 1 and 2. 2 was a major upgrade of 1 even in form of  the base game; it got many DLCs and developed. CK3 startet with better graphics, but regulated complexity down, leaving out major content included in my version of CK2 + several DLCs.If I buy the next game of the same brand - and have already invested xxx € into CK2 + DLCs - why, the hell, should I want to play a simplified, graphically polished new version of the same game and AGAIN pay xxx € for DLCs which over months and years may lead to the in-game-complexity I already reached playing the predecessor? Why should I AGAIN pay for adding the nordic lords to the game? Why should I pay relevant sums for almost cosmetical DLCs, only entering some new skins for units? Why should I pay a price equivalent to full-scale-titles for Dlcs mediocre in size and quality?2. The next point of my criticism is that the DLCs and Patches which are offered over years (CK2, Stellaris,EU4, HOI4) often do two things: They break savegames and alter key mechanics.Regarding the first, for a working guy like me who invests time into one playthrough over months, sometimes over years in his scarce free time, this is not only a moderate nuisance: It´s stolen lifetime!For the second, it makes me feeling unfamiliar with a game I last may have played months ago and which I liked in its state at that time. So, every time I get back to Stellaris or EU, even if I don´t buy DLCs because I don´t like the changes they do, I have to learn the game mechanics anew - often in form of a newly started playthrough because of the savegame incompatibilities. Referring to Stellaris, often I didn´t like the changes - the more minimalistic data screens for populations/ planets for example or the new penalties for population and empire growth which seriously harness empire building. Of course, CK 3 isn´t at that point in it´s development already, but the signs aren´t tuning me confident. For example, the "free" artifact updates accompanying the "Affairs of the Court" - DLCs publication feel shallow and loveless for me - they are no fun. If I want to enter more variety and deepness to this single feature, I would have to pay 30 € for a DLC - thank you, PARADOX!3. And the last thing is PARADOX´ sales politics by which I as an adult of moderate intellective capacity feel mocked at: Every few weeks there are "sales" in which base games are offered at discount prices to get customers lured to the good stuff (I bought this game at such a sale). The prices of the relevant DLCs, on the other hand, never get beneath 50% of the standard prices - even if the games are on the market for YEARS. I definitely won´t pay 30 or 40 € for the typical Paradox DLC (in this case: "Affairs of the court") - but even with 10 to 20 € the typical Paradox DLC in my opinion is seriously overpriced. This is even more true when you look at the sheer number of DLCs for the older main Paradox games. To complete your collections you would have to invest insane amounts in one single game which often is on the market for years.I have collected quite a steam library in the last two decades. I have played and followed many games over the course of the years. And I have found no other publisher which had its fanbase pay so ridiculous amounts for updates camouflaged as DLCs. Some examples how to do things better:Firaxis/ Civilization: DLCs are big additions to the base games. Some time after the publication of the game, Collections including ALL major DLCs are offered on sales with a relevant discount, leading to a fair price.Bethesda/ Skyrim + Fallout: Relevant DLCs of varying quality. You can add them separately and leave out what you don´t like, because they don´t depend on each other.Total War: Many Dlcs which are costly and similarly disappointing as the ones offered by Paradox. The prices also don´t get below a fixed discount for years. BUT: Those DLCs don´t alter the core game mechanics. And there is fair mod support, so I can refuse to pay for the DLCs, get a fairly complex and finished base game and alter it by extensive mods, like the ones published by RADIOUS.Not to mention the many developers and publishers who still offer finished and (more or less - sad but true) polished, complex base games which are only perfected by patches and DLCs. There is a relevant number of them - and they don´t seem to vanish from the free market because they don´t spam mediocre DLCs step by step leading to a full-scale-game over years or don´t allow in-game-purchases. To finish this review in a constructive way: I would suggest to the paradox developers to reactivate their old core competences: Offering big scale complex strategy games for a niche fanbase - which some years ago made Paradox unique. Please offer your core games with a new number only when you have to offer a surplus value in comparison to the predecessor which exceeds polishing the graphics. You did well with getting from EU to EU2 or HOI to HOI 2 - get back to your roots.Take a higher price for those bigger base games - because as far as I experience it following forums and the modding community, we, your niche clientel,aren´t 14 to 16 years old and lack money. For a well designed Victoria 3 which get´s back to the complexity and historicity of the first part of the series (the second one was - well - mhew!) I would without hesitation pay today´s standard AAA-game-price of 60 €. Be economically succesfull and make us pay a fair price for your work - you deserve it. But, please:  Stop that greedy and dull DLC - based sales policy - it makes veteran hardcore fans and customers like me loose confidence in you. And don´t argue against me with the game pass - there are reasons not every one likes ♥♥♥-solutions like that.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradox did an absolutely bang-up job with this one - one of their most welcomed releases. I think RPS got it right by saying that CK3 feels like a pure distillation of the best things about CK2, purifying the overall experience and concentrating it. They made the game much more approachable to a newcomer, and yet preserved all the complex interactions that kept all the veterans fans around. They got rid of the more idiosyncratic features from CK2, like having to consolidate your tiny armies from all over your realm, or two few shipbuilding provinces with a limited navy that can only ferry your massive army over in small batches, or the annoying pandemics that would prompt you to build hospitals all around your borders. The game is streamlined exactly where it needed to be, without dumbing down the features surrounding it. All in all, I'd say this game is well deserving of its score on Metacritic.Like with any distillation, you're going to lose some of the core from CK2 - which in this case I think that's fine, this game was built from the ground up, and Paradox has years to add back in the DLC and patches that made CK2 brilliantly nuanced and intricate. This game is a great vanilla experience on its own, and I enjoy it much more than vanilla CK2 - I don't see much reason to go back to the old game. Plus, this will serve as a strong foundation for the 50 or so content packs that Paradox will undoubtedly release to nickel and dime you, too.There's some valid points in the more scathing reviews on Steam and Metacritic, like certain streamlining choices, debates on the amount of cut content, and UI reorginization ... but IMO most of the negs are just salty about either Paradox's business model or the apparently bad Russian localization. There's one Metacritic user review that uses the word "cuck" about six times, so that's worth a laugh or two if you've got 10 minutes to spare.

_childDocuments_.review: So before you read the rest just note this was in the new game glow. 30+ hrs for a game like this isn't much. Really 90 isn't either, but it's how long it's taken me to get to 90 that affects my overall review. If you liked what CK 2 had become by the end, please don't buy this game thinking it's a straight improvement or progression from that. I thought maybe I'd enjoy some of the community mods in the mean time while waiting for updates and DLC, but the games limits are what they are and the mods are therefore limited by them. Give this game a few years to ramp up or catch it on sale for 50% or up. Otherwise it'll just sit in your Library while you go back to CK 2 for a more complete game. If that doesn't matter much to you or you are as addicted to CK games as I am then the rest of the review is for you.**EDIT ABOVE**Okay. So I'll admit it. I have a problem. I'm addicted to CK games. It's not healthy, but hey this about the game not me.Pros:-It's a new CK game.-Graphically pleasing.-Console commands available.-Neat new mechanics.-Dynasty matters.-Expanded religion mechanics.Cons:-Some features in CK 2 are absent from CK 3.-AI Ally swarm tactics and no ability to coordinate.-Tech locked based on culture seemingly regardless of conquest.So, I really enjoy the new map and the levels of viewing. Little confusing sometimes, but once you figure out what level you need be at to see certain information then it's no big deal. I heard rumors of no console commands or it being locked out. This isn't true. I enjoy creating Super Emperor Chad sometimes and just wrecking house. I enjoy being able to have some clue as to the effectiveness of my councilors and the display of how long until and event triggers is right up my alley. Also, in some if not all cases, if your councilor dies their replacement picks up where they left of. Your dynasty gains renown that can be used to unlock benefits for your House as a whole. Also, you can use renown to "Disinherit" and "Denounce" house members if you are the head of the house. Nice external control mechanics for errant family members. Not to mention the ability to steal titles from family. The expanded religion mechanics are A+++. Easy to view rule sets for all available religions. Ability to eventually found a custom religion or heresy. Very spicy.Cannot play a Republic. I assume so they can charge us for an expansion pack for that feature. No 'Ruler Creator', though I hear they should be rolling that out as a patch or free DLC?? So those were really the main ones for me. Okay so when you call in your allies to a war you get one of two responses. "I'm going to raise my armies and just sit here." or "HEY GUYS I JUST SMOKED A BUNCH OF FUNNY SHROOMS AND I'M FREAKING OUT! I'M GOING OVER HERE. NO WAIT, I WANT TO GO THERE. CRAP THERE IS SOMEONE GOING THERE. SCREW IT I'M GOING BACK OVER HERE. WAIT IS THAT A DRAGON. SCREW THIS MAN YOU DIDN'T SAY ANYTHING ABOUT DRAGONS!" My last complaint about tech I can see what they were doing. I just don't like it. I don't think in an alt-history sim there should be such tightly locked tech restrictions. I mean if I'm a tribe and I take over a fully functioning Feudal county with a city and castle I think I might benefit from the tech that exists. Also, over time their culture would slowly start to melt into the rulers culture. Not only that, you should be able to assign your Steward or Chancellor to actively seek out advancements in culture from a subjugated culture.TL;DRI love it. I would recommend it. I have nit pick issues that will probably be addressed or not because I'm not the only person who plays the game. If you aren't a die hard. I would highly suggest putting it on the wish list and waiting for the first 4 or 5 DLCs to launch and then when Steam Summer sale comes around, buying them up for about 50% - 75% of what I'm probably going to pay.

_childDocuments_.review: I put in hundreds and hundreds of hours of CK2, and I have a feeling I will for CK3 as well, with some caveats.Let me start with things that I think need to be said: First off, I genuinely think the way religion works right now is kinda borked and needs a redo. The fact that your more likely to have heretical thought when you win more holy wars to me is just bizarre and I don't know what the devs were thinking about that. Even they seem to know it was a mistake as they've scrambled and fixed it in certain ways in basically every patch, but I really think they need to just cut and remake it from scratch in order to un♥♥♥♥ it.Related: moving from tribalism to fuedalism has also been touched on in basically every patch, and good, because on launch it was busted even more then religion. Another mechanic that I think they just need to have a big rethink on.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out of the way, why did I give this a positive? Simple: They very clearly are focusing most of their efforts on this game being the game where you play as a character, and whose stories come from that fact first and foremost. The stress mechanic, where you gain more stress up to and eventually including potentially dying from over stress for going against your characters wishes, regardless of if said wishes would benefit or harm the kingdom at that very moment, shows a willingness to purposefully scold power/metagame players that want to ignore the stories they are creating, and IMO (as I'm not one of those) great! Keep it up! Storytelling should be the name of the game here in CK, and the more they put towards increasing the awesome water cooler moments of this game the more into it I'll be.That, combined with an already pretty vibrant modding scene (up to and including two mods that explicitly fix the two big complaints I had at the top of this, kudos to you all), and I have a feeling CK will remain my favorite Paradox franchise, and CK3 my new favorite entry within it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, let me cut a few words about Seljuk and Turkic successions and how they can be represented more accurately in the game;First let me talk history, and then game mechanics suggestions;In the Seljuks, it didn't matter who the eldest brother is or who is named as heir. All princes have the equal right for the title of sultan or any other title. When a ruler dies, it's usually chaos and free for all between the princes. The prince who is favored by the previous sultan was usually given a beylik (similar to county) that is very close to the seat of the sultan. Whether this prince is the eldest or not is not important. So upon the sultan's death, it is expected he arrives the capital first and claims his sultanate. This was also the case in early periods of the Ottomans.Now to game mechanics;The Partition is fairly ok in early and mid middle ages for Seljuks and Turkic dynasties. But a twist is needed. The game forces you to continue playing as the eldest son and makes him the heir. Instead, the player may be allowed to change the heir to any adult prince to represent that this particular prince is favored by the sultan and is sent to a close distance beylik to either govern it directly or learn governorship and train himself there. Of course, if this prince and new sultan is not a popular figure, not favored by other emirs and beys and princes etc, the game's usual mechanics of factions may emerge to dethrone him and instead install a more popular prince. The Partition also makes sure that other princes go to some other beyliks and grow strong there, always remaining a threat to the sultan. During late middle ages, Primogeniture should not be available to Seljuks or there should be very strong opposition towards it, maybe calling all princes (except the heir) and vassals except the allies of the character to a civil war immediately if Primogeniture is activated.Now one more thing; this is an infamous chapter of Ottoman history and it is maybe not good for the era of this game but the killing of brothers can also be brought in during the late middle ages. Maybe a new succession type named Elimination can be enabled instead of Primogeniture. If this is enabled, when a new sultan takes the throne, he is presented with an option to eliminate his brothers who are in his court. (Those outside his court can't be touched.) He can choose to eliminate or not separately for each brother. When he chooses to eliminate, the system determines based on his intrigue and the other prince's intrigue if the elimination is successful or not. If not, the prince leaves the court and escapes, going to some other random court. Also, this decision should put considerable stress and very cruel traits for the character.Thanks for reading, enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: The strength of this game lies in the stories you tell. You should not worry too much about playing things optimally or savescum against setbacks. Clawing your way back is when you're having the most fun. You make your own goals in this game and your tool to achieve them is your current ruler. Sometimes you have to adapt your goals to your rules strengths and weaknesses. Sometimes all you can do is ensure the succession is safe. In my first playthrough of this game, I tried to win. I ended up conquering 95% of the known world and my dynasty ruled over all. While the journey there was fun, the last hundred years or so of the game was quite boring. World domination just ain't all it's cracked up to be.As more DLC's are released, the game just becomes richer with content and things to do. I look forward to this game growing further.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short review from a Paradox fan who tried to get into CK2 but bounced off it hard, not because I didn't like the game but because I didn't have a bloody clue what was going on. And the UI was hard to navigate or to work with. Now that I'm a bit more familiar with the new game, I can say that part of the reason for the bounce was because I thought this game was going to be a lot like EU4 but set in the medieval age. That was completely and totally wrong. This is a role play grand stratgey game and is unique.There is a good tutorial for this game which walks you through the absolute basics. It is not going to teach you everything, just what you need to know and if you choose to go on with the tutorial after it formally finishes, the game will give you advice about other topics as they crop up. If you expect the tutorial to teach you everything, you will be disppointed. It will teach you everything you NEED to know but not everything you WANT to know. That comes from playing the game itself.It is going to require a lot of work on my part to learn to play this game but the gameplay is more than good enough to make me want to learn it and to enjoy learning it.  A bit of time in the game will also help you to understand what is going on in the Youtube videos you might watch. I would recommend watching a short one about managing the UI and the settings at the start of the game. And returning to re-read the developer's diaries is also more revealing. Now you KNOW what provincial development is and so it all makes much more sense.Culture, innovations and development are particularly handled in a very interesting way in this game. Unlike many other games where you choose a tech to research and wait until the research bar fills up, this one is very different. Depending on your start, you may not be able to influence your cultural fascination and even if you are, it is still slow compared to ther strategy games, especially civ.There are also quite a number of different buildings you can build in your holdings which give you very small benefits at first but they accrue over time. And bear in mind, this is a very long game, especially if you  choose the early start. The buildings available depend on the terrain, the type of baronial holding (City, Castle or Temple) as well as being unlocked by tech/culture. Same with your options for choosing men-at-arms.Otherwise, it's a game of vassal management, war and intrigue. Of them all, war is the easiest to manage and perhaps the least fun while managing your vassals and your family and scheming is a pretty substantial part of the fun. If war is what you are after, the war aspect is not particularly brilliant but the scheming, oh-my-God! This is about as good as it can get.There's a lot more to this game than I've just described. It's a big, complicated game and it will need a lot of time and work on my part to learn all the systems. So that's about it for now but let me finish by pointing out that it's not all sweetness and light. The AI has a pretty annoying tendency to embark its armies and siege your capital at the moment. Apart from viking raiders and a few other cultures, it was march your army here and back again in this period and not get on a boat and head for the enemy's capital. But if you are alert to this, you'll soon find ways to deal with it. I expect AI behaviour during war will get some attention sooner or later.

_childDocuments_.review: Endless Gameplay Choices Matter Strategy/RTS Worth the full priceSo I bought this game wanting something similar to the old fashioned RTS games that I grew up with (such as Ages of Empires and Rise of Nations: Extended Edition, but with a more updated flare. I made a really good choice apparently. CK3 gives you the ability to customize and make your own ruler, forge alliances through marriages, gain land through conquest or inheritance, secretly assassinate your enemies, and carry on elicit affairs. CK3 gives you all the strategy of an RTS game with a heavy emphasis on diplomatic matters. You're no longer just a nameless, faceless ruler that directs their people with the click of a button. You  must now contend with the intrigue of court, deal with heirs fighting for your throne, and still manage to defend yourself from invaders. This game is worth the full price, although I would say the DLC should be bought on sale. This game will provide you endless hours of gameplay. Also, I would like to recommend the steam workshop mode LOTR: REALMS IN EXILE if you want to play in a more fantasy type of setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly the best RPG story generator I've ever played. I could give an example, but almost anything is possible (in the context of medieval feudal lords). And I haven't even scratched the surface of what can be done. Paradox is renowned (and sometimes vilified, unfairly in my opinion) for their DLC policy. For those who don't know they release about 15 DLCs for each of their games (over the course of a decade), which means the total cost of the game can be pretty extreme. But even if you don't buy all the DLC each one adds new things to the base game, so by purchasing the base CK3 you'll get free improvements for the next 10 years. Anyway: Even without all the DLC we know is coming CK3 feels like a whole and complete game, even if there never was any DLC I'd be super happy with this purchase. I'll be even happier when we get China, Republics, and whatever other DLCs are coming. In short: this is a fantastic game, if you are a fan of PDS - buy it! If you are fan of medieval grand strategy - buy it! A fan of roleplaying medieval rulers? Buy it!

_childDocuments_.review: CKIII is quite the game. Its as complex as any Paradox game, but ultimately falls short of delivering a really good experience without spending quite a bit of money on expansions. Maybe its because I've spent such a long time playing CKII (over 1000 hours on steam) but I can't but feel that CKIII, while a needed reset due to the bloat of expansion in CKII, ends up becoming basically, a mandatory expensive upgrade from the prior game. And of course, upon release it was missing features and felt quite ... boring and limited. Now, its been a few years, i've bought a bunch of expansions, and while I'm having fun, I do have to admit it was expensive. I got my money's worth, hundreds of hours of fun, but really, it makes me feel a bit bad about it. CKIII is still an amazing medieval sim. Building your dynasty and conquering Europe, or Western and Southern Asia, or maybe parts of Africa, is plenty of fun. The game has some robust systems for things like culture, combat, religion, and of course, succession. The basics of the game are all there: build your dynasty through careful marriage and intermarriage with other nobles. Claim counties, duchies, even kingdoms and go to war to press your claim. Amass power and prestige, wealth and influence, and turn your backwater county into the envy of the known world. But yeah, it really feels like several of the expansions, namely the Royal Court and Tours and Tournaments, adds so much to the game that make it feel like a more fulfilling and complete experience. Maybe if I didn't have 1000 hours in CKII I wouldn't feel like that though, and that's why I'm giving this game a Thumbs Up. Oh, and the 245 hours and counting probably helps.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice game but it has too many DLCs which mostly consist only in pop-ups, events and cosmetics. The game loves interrupting you with nonsense events or petty squabbles of your vassals in key moments like when you enter a war and have to move troops (timing is everything sometimes). Many times your options to keep order are absurdly few. Activities take for far too long and are absurdly overpriced (your kingdom consists of one county, your income is 1,5/month and a pilgrimage, feast or tour can cost 200+ gold and doesn't give any significant benefit). When you finally get to save some gold there's always some sucker event that makes you lose it all or get absurd amounts of stress, legitimacy loss or that kind of punishment, and you can't even grab the sucker and make him/her disappear like any serious medieval guy with an army would historically. It's the only game in which you being an emperor any lowborn sucker plays you and it takes 12+ months to get rid of him. You make your nephew a witch and later a court event makes you denounce him or get stress?? What kind of nonsense is that?? Come on. That kind of nonsense is untouched while they try to sell you 20 DLCs that don't bring anything substantial into the game. I enjoy this game but I can't recommend it as it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Instead of spending my holiday reading or trying some writing or researching career decisions or trying to get into better shape I instead fell in love with crusader kings 3.It happened slowly on the third day. I realized what it was all about. Crusader Kings is all about living, just living. You live your life, you marry, you expand your territory a little bit and then you die and start again. I started small and am now working my way to the control of a small peninsula. My first king died having fathered 15 kids and his heir was living well and life was good when a sudden series of scandal's drove my kingdom reputation into the garbage but I had a son and the kingdom continues on!I love it the slow burn of strategic marriages forged alliances and schemes to be hatched are great. Yes like tic toc, snapchat and discord I had to watch many youtube video's to figure out how it all works. But when I did boy-o-boy does it make for a good time!It's a hard game to nail down. The goal is just to live a life and then live your heirs lives until the end of the game. That end can be many things. A lack of an heir, an "accident" or a massive country routing you and taking you prisoner then rotting in jail mostly with out and heir. I would recommend this for anyone who loves monotony and court intrigue and subjugating friends and family.

_childDocuments_.review: some cons:I'll be blunt, this is a skeleton of a game with a nice layer of paint over it. Everyone and everywhere you play is the same except for religion and one of 3 three government types: feudal, tribal or clan. And they all work kind of the same as well unlike ck2. There are no region specific events, only lifestyle events that you will get bored of really quickly. You can practically teleport armies across the map with no cost. broken and completly destroys the need for embarkment funds. Battles have been tweaked, but now, you can't win impossible battles anymore by carefully selecting commander traits and units... It degenerates the entire game into a numbers game.Seduction is the bane at the moment... everyone does it and just gets tiresome.You can't change your personality over time (not even at the cost of some extreme stress) which i personally find boring.Vikings are being vikings and introduce bordergore everywhere with their exclaves. I mean, who doesn't want some icelandic norse people in Egypt?For some reason, crusader states become sunni/norse/... after a generationunreformed faiths should have a way to lose fervor and should have more difficulty to convert counties.some pros: prestige and piety are a currency, sometimes they are hard to get, but overall a good additionMercs make sense and make contracts for some yearsPerk tree is nice if sometimes not overpowered at certain pointsNew decisions are nice, but lack anything to follow up on. Just a button that does stuff without any flavor (for example witch coven).Eugenics are fun and the visual representation looks greatTraits make sense and can make it interestingconclusion:Suffers from cut content that is being made for DLCs really hard at the moment. I predict flavor packs (event packs??) and "new" government types that might bring some life into the game.Don't be mistaken, early game is usually a blast, but mid and end game have no real challenge anymore (except imploding, but the new system makes that really easy to avoid)Can't really recommend it at this moment, wait and see how they will hanle DLCs an make up your mind then is my advice.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings III is a solid game! In my opinion, the graphics are far and away the best feature of the game. CK3 improved the franchise in a lot of ways, like the graphics, optimization (for the most part), and generally making things balanced. CK2 is still a superior game, however. CK3's DLCs, freedom, gameplay and diplomacy system is inferior.The DLCs are worthless, IMO. The first DLC was Paradox turning a new leaf with a cheap DLC that didn't have a lot of content, but was still worthful for the Norse players. Then - Fate of Iberia. What a disappointing buy. I had some hope with the relatively cheaper DLC but Fate of Iberia didn't add much to the game besides some flavor from Iberia, which is the bare minimum. A lot of players don't play in Iberia as well. After the Royal Court DLC flopped, I think this game was a lost cause. Paradox has mostly forgotten the game and DLCs are sparse. The in-game content is still barebones, almost 3 years after release.The gameplay hasn't improved at all, the combat/war system in-game is ridiculously easy. It was never ominous to begin with, but I understood and even beat literally anyone I could within 30 minutes of gameplay. At least it doesn't take 100+ hours to understand every corner of the combat system like HOI4.Overall, I think CK3 is still an enjoyable game. Maybe not worth the full price, but CK3 is a solid buy on sale. I would give the game a 6.75/10. I do recommend it on sale for under $40 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: The Crusader Kings series has always been about playing the hand you're dealt. Not even the most well-laid plan survives contact with reality. It's not Starcraft, it's not Civilization. The CK games have never been games that were about minmaxing or optimizing strats' - and while CK2 retained some of that DNA from Europa Universalis, CK3 has become its own beast.This is a story generator and a role-playing game. CK3 encourages putting yourself into your character's head and acting accordingly. This is helped by a smoother UI, a generally improved AI and absolutely gorgeous graphics and sound design. If you are looking for a strategic challenge as a player, this is not the game you're looking for. If you want to see your *character* struggle with what life throws at them, it absolutely is.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, it will strike you as a game with an immense depth and allowing for numerous strategic and tactical approaches. However, after having played more than a 100 hours and having tested several approaches, I came to the conclusion that, in reality, the game leans heavily (too heavily) on "RNG". I'd say that 60% or more of what happens in the game is the result of "random" events that are aimed at making the game more challenging for you. If you are doing great, you'll notice that more and more unfortunate events will start popping up, and when you are doing bad, the game will throw you a bone or two. The most striking example of this, is the whole plot to kill virtually all your sons. This was most notable when I was playing as ruler of Desmond and married more than 1 wife.  In the 10 test games I ran, 9 of them had a plot where I would lose all sons except one (clearly indicating that one of the wives was scheming to maneuver her son into a 'heir' position. It didn't matter what traits the wives had. This plot would kick in, even with the most trusting, temperate of wives. The game simply forces it no matter what you do. That, to me, is simply a sign of a poor AI. By the way, when I did some test runs as Desmond and only limited myself to one wife, the plot where my sons would get assassinated never happened but, ironically enough, in 4 of out 5 test runs, I would lose 1-2 sons to "unfortunate" events like Gout, Hunting Accident, and, oh yeah, they are prone to die in the very first battle. The game has more of these ill-chosen plots "just to add to the story line" or to pretend that everything is a lot more sophisticated than it really is.  The most notorious one must be the "Twins".  Feel free to Google this one. It appears that twins come hand-in-hand with scheming and murder plots. Heck, in some cases I have heard that almost entire dynasties were killed off because one of the twins felt jealous.  I must admit, I only dealt with twin kids in one of my game and, yes, it did lead to a murder scheme by one of the two, but I can't personally say that twins are 100% messed up (in game, that is). But then again, it has been reported numerous times by other players. All in all, it is a very cheap way to create plots and story lines, while in the mean time, kind of, ridiculing the effort and skill that the player brings to the table. So, frankly, in my opinion, the AI is horrific.The first couple of playthroughs, you'll be amazed by the story lines until you realize that it is all very shallow and you run into the same story lines virtually any successive game you play.

_childDocuments_.review: In the fashion of a fellow reviewer, I will separate this into two sections; one for new players and the other for experienced CKII players.For new players, if you feel like you like the game go for it and enjoy it, try to figure it out and don't let the bias of experienced players discourage you from playing it.For experienced CKII players, this new installment is a bloody mess, I speak as a normal player with 800+ hours and ironman gang member, it just has a lot of issues that seem to make the game pretty much unplayeable and I will address them individually:- The succession laws make you have no real incentive to expand;Why? You may ask, the issue here is that as soon as you create equal titles to your own, these will become independent as soon as you die and there seems to be no actual way of changing to hereditary rule until your culture discovers it, which seems to be locked in at least 100 years of research, making it pretty much as boring game to begin with.- The start dates are stale;Both the 867 a.D and 1066 a.D make it for an extremely boring game where you either already start with a sizeable domain or you're some massive blob giving no actual interesting character to start from a humble position, unless of course you like to play as a vassal and like plotting, to which I say I'm not a fan of this approach.- The combat system is pretty broken:Basically no matter how better your commander is, there's always a dice roll that decides things, so you might as well no longer care about getting good marshalship because in the end you will be in the hands of luck, which also reminds me that you can no longer get good counciliors by inviting people to court, because that too is now broken. - Children can turn queer at any given point when growing up without any warning or any notification popping up;You may be screwed without knowing it, should've seen it coming, bigot.I'm dissappointed; hopefully it can get fixed so it becomes playable, if not, there's always CKII (:

This means that for almost 400 years, every time you die, if you pumped out a lot of kids, your titles will all be divided till your heir is left with just a county (+ duchy + kingdom + empire titles if your are one of those things).However, I think that is how the game is supposed to be played where early game everyone is setback with the horror of many children making the game much more challenging while late game rewards what you've accomplished earlier with this. Also, this actually goes in line with the fact that you, as the liege, must have the strongest powerhouse in your realm in order to... keep you vassals in order, and that is where dread comes into play!Thanks Paradox! _childDocuments_.review: This game is surprisingly good. They have done what i always thought was missing from their previous games:Made you actually see and feel like you're dealing with PEOPLE, not stats.Yes, you're still of course dealing with stats, but you now feel much more involved. For example actually seeing and choosing your bride to be actually makes getting married seem worthwhile. You're not just marrying for her lineage and how that will help you in alliances, but, for some, you also care how she looks. Ok sometimes she's beautiful, but has the kind of character that makes you back away very slowly... But then you just find the right one, she has the right standing, right stats- and actually looks attractive! Let's hope she isn't already spoken for!Then you see her join you as a simple wife, but over time she grows,  helps you out in the Court and you actually start to notice her and appreciate her  more.Then she has a child and you watch that child grow and have to decide how you're gonna prepare him for life... It really makes you quite invested in having a family.And they all have their little quirks and problems.And that's inbetween the whole Empire-building stuff you have to do!Also the game was not as hard to get into, it sort of gradually gave me hints explaining stuff on the way.I used to always say that the problem with games like this is it's just a spreadsheet. I don't mind the spreadsheet, but there's ALWAYS the people-side of it you have to deal with as a leader- or commander and I wanted to see that too. People would reply dumb stuff like, "This is a strategy game, not the sims!" Completely not getting it.Well now CK3 is geting where it should be: You're a King, governing a Kingdom and having to deal with foes, and especially friends who get in your way. And your friends can be worse than the enemy if you don't handle them right and can see them animated a bit in realistic detail.Also as an artist myself, I find the artwork and art modelling of the people is excellent with subtle animation that makes them look very real with multiple faces from harsh to demure. Well done, artist and modeller.Thankfully you have realistic historical options before you begin, although, there are still some 21-st century 'pc'ness shovelled in there, and as an amateur historian, it can make me cringe a little.Criticisms and why the downvote?The rip off pricing. I'm pretty disgusted with it and so I cannot accept that. I will not allow this greed to rip me off of my hard-earned cash, especially not now when life is becoming very, very hard. Sorry, but a message must be sent, I've had enough of tolerating this kind of thing from games and Paradox.I'll wait for a super-sale in 5 years.So sad, they were so close, but greed got in the way.

_childDocuments_.review: So, first of all, it's a beautiful game. Great, intuitive UI, a worthy predecessor overall. What makes this a deal-breaker, in my opinion is the combat system and how the limited the aid the AI allies are. In CK2, it was great: you could assign AI allies to specific counties, attach them to your own armies to supplement your forces, etc. Here, the AI does what the AI wants. There is no ability to actually supplement your forces with the AI aid. Furthermore, I like the Men-at-Arms and commander/knight idea. It's fantastic...but, you can't decide what flank you want specific troops on like you could in CK2. Makes everything completely random. _childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings was a Paradox title that I never thought I would like. Oh boy, was I wrong. In this game, it's about YOUR DYNASTY, not the whole nation you choose comparing to Europa Universalis IV. You make a royal family and rule for hundreds of years. This can get interesting depending on the person. You can role-play and get super-involved with what's going on between everyone, to memeing and having a GigaChad with max stats that may or may not be involved with Habsburg-like ideals. It's about the characters that you make and interact with along the way. Every character has their ambitions int the game.In one of my games a few hundred years in, my dynasty started to split due to disagreements and separation between family members in the family tree, to the point that my current king's cousin, plotted her entire life to dethrone me and put her on top. We even had max relations; She faked it all! It got to the point that it was imminent that her plots would put her on top... Assassinations after assassinations, to meddling with the government. There was also another interaction where a lady joined my court and she really liked me. It got the the point that she confessed, but I declined because I was loyal to my spouse. After this, her traits and interactions got sketchy and unstable. One point, she quit her position in the kingdom and I forced her to come back (because she had good stats for her role). Her health and got deteriorated and then, I found out that she was plotting an assassination on my spouse. Total bruh moment.Anyways, the game is tons of fun and is definitely worth a buy.
