_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE 2/16/21: I still cannot recommend Crusader Kings 3 in its current state. If you can look past Crusader King 2's dated graphics and somewhat laggy late-game, it is much more fleshed out and complete, and is free-to-play (though much more enjoyable I think, with all DLC except Sunset invasion, which I do not have but have been warned to steer clear of). It does have a much higher learning curve than CK-3, which personally I find rewarding. Now the 6-month post-release rant:My main concern with the state of the game at this point, is more from a customer-relations standpoint with Paradox, The communication about development specific to the game has significantly stalled, so it seems. Much of the community was waiting for a release of today's Dev Diary with hopes that it would contain exposure of content and fixes that have been addressed, and hopefully soon to be released, as it has been almost 3 months since the last patch.Instead, the much-anticipated news we received in this Dev Diary was more like a company memo which announced staff changes, which, I'm not sure if I should be glad or worried about. I worry that major staffing changes at this point might indicate some internal strife in the development team that they would rather not be made public, but that is only suspicion on my part, and with such a gross lack of communication, suspicion is all I have. I will admit that I am not the best at verbalizing these concerns regarding public relations on their official Paradox forums without my frustration coming through, so I have to be rather restrained, but I have noticed that unless you absolutely suck-up to the developers, you run a risk of being censored. This is akin to filing a complaint with the auto-maintenance shop manager that the vehicle you brought in for an oil-change seemingly hasn't been touched in 3 months, and if you demand an explanation, you get kicked out the auto-shop. I understand that it always looks bad to have a complaining customer in the public lobby, but at the end of the day, it is my car on the lift, and my $50 game in the library, and the situation could be forgivable if there was some evidence of progress being made. (This is not something specific to Paradox or CK3, but an overall reflection of the insufferable leniency that gaming customers give game developers, especially long-established ones, which they likely wouldn't bestow on other businesses.)--------------------------------------Original Review:Missing a lot of depth. Tough to give this one a down vote as I do find certain aspects of the game enjoyable, but as a veteran of Crusader Kings 2 I often find myself asking "why can't I do this?" or "Man I wish we could still do . . . ", and ultimately I think that's what led me to my conclusion. A lot of elements from its predecessor have been simplified (or as many are putting it, 'dumbed down'). I think where the developers went wrong was taking out features from the series that rookie players found too difficult to deal with, but ultimately saved avid players a lot of headache.

_childDocuments_.review: A game of the inherently unpopular strategy genre made to appeal to the broader audience by drastically decreasing difficulty. While even the previous game, CK2, wasn't really all that difficult once you got your head around how the mechanics work, the difficulity bar has been lowered even further.So, lets start with the BAD:-  So, most of your interactions with your vassals are based on how much they like or dislike you, on a scale of -100 to +100, with them being generally compliant at higher opinion and rebellious and nasty at lower one. The problem is, the game has A LOT of easily stackable, passive,  opinion boosts, so even when you play your game normally, most of your vassals will absolutely adore your character. -  So, as in CK2, your character has 5 primary stats: diplomacy, military, stewardship, intrigue and learning. In theory, focusing on a particular stat opens up new ways of playing the game, with different stats being good for different situations. To further emphasize that, CK3 has an addition of perk trees, 3 different trees connected to every character stat (so 15 in total) so you can further customize your character. Sounds cool, except it is not: There is one stat to rule them all, useful in, basically, every situation, and this is Stewardship, which gives you both more money from your holdings AND increases your holding limit, so having high stewardship means having both more money, and more troops, since you will have more holdings, and more coins to actually improve your holdings. Now, that could've been somewhat offset if the perk trees for Stewardship were underwhelming, but it also has some of the best perk trees in the game, giving you even more holdings, massive opinion boosts with your vassals, less vassals joining factions (feeding unto the fact your amount of holdings and therefore, amount of troops is already higher, since the character focuses stewardship), vassals providing even more cash and levies... It just make it the best idea to focus on Stewardship in 9 situations out of 10.-  Men at arms made the professional core of your army, made of specialised units, like skirmishers, heavy infantry, light cavalry, etc., with specific counters attached to each, so Light Cavalry will counter Archers, while Archers counter Skirmishers, Skirmishers countering Heavy Infantry, and so on. Again, very cool in theory, but is broken by the fact, that you can increase the power of your Men At Arms using buildings, with a few unit types getting much, much more power increases than the rest (Hello, Archers and Light Cavalry!), allowing you to make absolute annihilators of all living things if you focus your building strategy on them, completely breaking the troop-type balancing.Also, feeds onto the aforementioned power of the Stewardship stat, as more personal holdings means more slots to build Men-at Arms-improving buildings in. Remember CK2, where your retinues were raised in the provinces they were bound to, and you had to merge them together manually, while allowing you to intercept pieces of the AI retinue before they merge? Making you group your holdings close together, so you won't spend ages while gathering your troops? Worry no longer, as your entire army will now appear as a single large blob in a province you designate as a rally point, nearly instantly. And that point can be changed freely, as many times as you like, no cooldown. Have a rebellion? Get a rally point in a nearby province and crush it in a few seconds! Got a random province on Ceylon as a king of France and want to invade India for further gains? No need to spend money on ships and logistics, get a rally point there and raise your entire army in India, cost-free! Needless to say, it trivialises a rather large part of warfare. Now, bad AI is a constant problem of Paradox games, but nowhere it gets more apparent as in Crusader Kings 3: Your artificial opponents are absolute dimwits at managing its own vassals. None of the lesser vassals in a large AI realm will ever stay in their de-jure borders, the balance of power between the AI vassals and the AI liege will be terribly off most of the time, with the top ruler often owning 1-2-3 holdings directly, while their powerful vassals having 7-8. When you fight a war with another independent realm, you mostly fight the top ruler's own levies, complemented by a rather small percentage of his vassals' levies (usually around 10-12%). This often makes smaller realms, where a top ruler holds most of the holdings directly, stronger than large realms with large numbers of strong vassals. So it generally equals to player being able to fight AI realms up to 3-4-5 times his size, since the AI is terrible at managing its titles and seemingly large realms having small-ish armies most of the time. Not to add the constant rebellions and civil wars that the AI experiances, while the player and can usually evade them quite easily.Not everything is bad in this game though, it has some good moments too, so...The GOOD: While the new interface looks very confusing for a CK2 veteran at start, it is actually quite clean, providing all of the relevant stats without going into menus inside menus inside menus... The map is gorgeous as well, with you being able to see how your realm is split between vassals in a single click, very convenient. As i said in a previous point, the map is gorgeous and convenient. The province depthis improved as well when compared to the previous title, with every province now actually having subprovinces which actually are possible barony-type holdings, so you can now actually tell a province's worth at a glance, without opening any additional menus. Religions now have discerning features, named Tenets, with each religion having 3 of those. Some religions allow ritual suicide for your old ruler without inducing opinion penalties, some, like Zoroastrianism, give opinion boosts for marrying close kin, some give you piety when you sacrifice prisoners... There is quite a few different tenets with a lot of possible combinations. Every religion now also has a special list of character traits, which are considered virtuous by its adherents, with each virtue increases your piety gain and gives an opinion boost... which somewhat feeds into a "opinion stacking" problem though. There are also lists of sinful traits, but, just like in CK2, those can be generally avoided quite easily. Now, each character trait, besides its usual set of stat bonuses, also has a list of actions that your character will consider stressful or relaxing. So a Shy character will gain stress for socially interacting with other people, a Greedy one will get stressed when sending gifts, and so on. Reaching high levels of stress is dangerous, as it often gives negative traits (so-called coping mechanisms) and take a toll on character's life expectancy, so high stress should generally be avoided. It opens up an entire new way of roleplaying inside the game, as the game kinda forces you to behave according to your character's traits, as when you don't, your character gets stressed. Those look pretty good and change with your character's traits and actions. Thats cool, nuff said.Now, there are certainly some good moments abouth the game with definite improvements over the previous iteration, but i honestly feel that quite a bit of the game-making systems made a huge step backwards. You might like the game as a newcomer to Paradox Grand Strategy or if you're just there to roleplay, but as a long-time Paradox and strategy game fan, i feel immensely disappointed, even if i really wanted (and still want) to like this game.Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a long review. The tl;dr is that the game grossly misrepresents history and stereotypes people, mainly non-Europeans and especially subsaharan Africans. These issues are pretty unlikely to get fixed. I recommend people to go get CK2 instead.I was excited to try out this game. I played for hours on end after purchasing it on sale only a few days ago. There were all sorts of cool things added. I wanted to love this game. Sure, it feels like a lot of things are missing, but - knowing that there will be expansion packs and updates - that didn't bother me too much.But the more I messed around with the game, the more wrong things seemed, and in ways that are unlikely to ever be changed by more expansion packs, heavy modding or updates. In their rush to promote a game with shiny new customisation and 3D character models, they have made a game that's less historically accurate than their preceding titles and worse at representing non-Europeans. While simplification has made a very hard game much easier, something I appreciate, it has subtracted so much else.The varied government types of CK2 have been replaced with "Clan", "Tribal" and "Feudal" - with all Christian Europeans being Feudal and everyone else being the other two. As if clans didn't play a large role in European Christian cultures in the Medieval Ages (Gaelic, South Slavic and Albanian cultures come to mind) or as if clan and tribe weren't synonymous terms. It feels we've gone from well researched, culturally specific government systems for Islamic regimes to racial stereotyping.I also see outside of Europe and the Arab world widespread conflation of drastically different cultures and languages, using outdated linguistic classification and geographic lumping that masks cultural differences. For instance, in the game we have a "Gur" culture in West Africa - based off the obsolete "Gur language family" that is no longer accepted in linguistics. The main branch of this obsolete family, once called "Central Gur", is called today the Mabia language family. It has 70+ different languages, many of them mutually unintelligible, but the game ignores this tremendous variety. Yet it was seen as very important to distinguish Catalan from Occitan when these are largely mutually intelligible languages whose main basis of division between each other is the boundary between Spain and France. The Gascon dialect for Occitan, for instance, is about equally divergent from both the rest of Occitan and Catalan but is usually not considered separate from Occitan to the same degree as Catalan and is unrepresented in the game. So we have hairsplitting based on entirely political divisions in Europe, and lumping in Africa based on entirely linguistic divisions (and very broad ones at that). Back to the "Gur", they belong to the Upper Guinean Highlands cultural group in the game. This group also includes the culturally extremely different and linguistically very distantly related Malinke (if related at all, Mande's relation with Atlantic-Congo is extremely doubtful). Meanwhile the most famous and widely spoken Mabia language, Mossi (the Mossi people are currently around 50% of Burkina Faso's population) is "Sahelian". Yes, northern Burkina Faso where the first evidence of Mossi kingdoms are is in the Sahel - but there is absolutely no credibility in saying that the rest of the Mabia speaking-peoples (who also mainly live in Burkina Fasso) have less in common with the Mossi than they have with the Malinke! Additionally, the Sahel is just a broad stretch of similar biomes on the southern border of the Sahara stretching from southern Mauritania all the way into Eritrea; hardly an actual zone of common cultures. I see this again and again with other cultures in the game, mainly but not only in Africa. Contrast this with how much painstaking research went into making sure every Indo-European ethnicity in Europe is as accurate as possible. I feel it would have been less offensive to just not include subsaharan Africa at all than to so thoroughly butcher things up.Of course, cultures can easily be fixed with mods and updates. It is possible that someone will mod a richer government system, although I doubt it. Additionally, each additional expansion will likely make the governments more entrenched and harder to mod without breaking the game. And none of that will solve the real root issue: the developers seem to care so much about improving gameplay experience that they have completely abdicated their responsibility to sensitively and accurately portray history. Even the titular crusades have changed - no longer does the game automatically wait until the First Crusade to launch the First Crusade. (I actually like that feature personally but I think making it default will confuse people.) An accurate, in depth portrayal of history is what attracted me and many others to this franchise in the first place. The Paradox brand association with accuracy and realism is so strong that many people learn about history through Paradox games. I am not a highly competent and skilled player. I love the idea of having an easier, more accessible version and am not faulting the developers for making one. But no amount of accessibility is worth pushing half-assed representation as the reality of history, and that’s what the game does. If this were the first title of a new series, I would be okay with this. But this is an established series that not only I expect better from but I have already seen better from.I really hope this is not the general direction Paradox plans to go with in their other history games. In the meantime, I'm going to stick with modded CK2.

_childDocuments_.review: This is tough, I recommend the game as it is a solid game, I’ve played it and thoroughly enjoyed most of my time doing so. There are many changes/advances from Ck2 a lean into RP elements and a strong foundation I am sure future patches and DLC will enrich and build upon if you enjoyed Ck2 or really any previous Paradox game you’ll enjoy Ck3. However, no one wins if I just kiss ass, in saying that I was a little disappointed, the game can quickly become repetitive, once you’ve gotten your footing it’s rather easy to become a powerhouse and dominate, while the game’s early succession mechanics seem to be an intentional roadblock it is easy to skip around until you can change laws. The game lacks the feeling of governance as there isn’t much for you to do as a ruler, there are limited interactions between characters in your court and realm and most or triggered events like feasts or based on random timed events like what to do with cattle, very on the surface basic stuff. Part of me thinks it scratches the surface now so it can be developed more in future DLC. Fighting is also ‘meh’ mostly just hope and pray, would’ve been cool and a massive step up to see some sort of Total war battle mechanics in some fashion or to at least have the option. Factions and council remain an annoyance, I find I’m punishing myself more often than not with council, as I’m placing the strongest vassals on the council who tend to have poor traits but only doing so to keep them on side, but it isn’t enough because I have more powerful vassals then positions on council. There should be a “influence in realm” or something mechanic and keeping their opinion of you high enough might maintain their support and prevent them from plotting against you. Overall, I think CK3 has some solid groundwork, but also far to go. Knowing paradox, I’m sure there are many patches and DLC to come so if you’re umming and arghing perhaps hold off until its seen a few more updates. However, in true fashion for a paradox game there are a number of mods and total conversions already in the works which are exciting and will only increase playtime and look to smash the previous set stands for mods by previous titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Crusader Kings 3 adds a level of depth to grand strategy that I never knew I was missing. In most other games, I control a country through fairly top-down, uncontested means. My actions seem to embody the zeitgeist of whatever nation I control. However, in CK3, I commit actions as one person, head of a dynasty, trying desperately to satisfy the interests of other members of my house, my vassals, and foreign powers. Uniting a duchy, kingdom, or empire are all unique struggles of their own, not to mention holding them together to stand the test of time. My control is not total; it's a delicate balancing game of appeasing many different actors. Now that I've gotten a taste for this style of management in grand strategy, I find myself missing it in the other games that I play. I give it my highest recommendations despite my inevitable death drowning in a tidal wave of Paradox DLC, with a total MSRP of $372. I'll figure it out once I get there.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I like a lot of things about this game. The developers did a good job of making "an heir" to CK2. Most notably, players were afraid that "we'll pay again for the same DLCs that we've already paid for in CK2", but this is mostly not the case. They have been building on existing concepts from DLCs (i.e. dynamic religion) and introduced them in the base game. Overall, the game is very enjoyable. However, I want to focus on the drawbacks in this review, so that the review is more useful.Compared to CK2, the conquest has been made very streamlined. The new Claim throne, Buy claim and Forced vassalization Casuses Belli, that can be made available (with some investment) for any character, ensure that you can take pretty much anything you want in a single war. So, the experience is much closer to something like Total War games, maybe with a bit more planning involved.For the same reason, the whole "marriage game" becomes kind of redundant. You can, of course, marry your heir to the emperor's heir, then wait until their children (of your dynasty) inherit the empire. But, this scheme takes two generations, and can easily be disrupted by assassination or even a bad case of flu. Now, you can also just claim and conquer the empire (Buy claim works unless you're also an emperor). Which path to choose... Hmmmm...Another problem is the army mobilization system. In CK2, you needed to raise the levies in your holdings, then explicitly bring them to where they're needed. This led to a number of interesting situations, where you could beat a larger army before it gathers, or needed to avoid losing war before your army comes. In CK3, you just make a rally point anywhere in your realm and wait, like, 3 months, then do a decisive battle or something.This, along with some other tweaks, makes the game... too simple. Remember how in CK2, restoring the Roman Empire felt like an achievement, and was a focus of the entire playthrough? In CK3, I did it yesterday as an afterthought in my playthrough where I roleplay "crazy mountain people".Overall, while I like features like dynamic culture and religion very much, the game lost a lot of depth compared to it's predecessor. A playthrough or two are definitely worth it, but after that you've learned the game, have a solution for every situation, and there's just nothing interesting left to do.Maybe DLCs will improve the situation, but I don't hope for radical change, because the devs seem to prefer simplification over depth. If you want depth - play CK2 (or Victoria 2, by the way).P.S. Developers, if you read this, you're welcome to comment on it, I'm interested in what you think.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game, but, to be honest, it's quite a soft recommendation. Crusader Kings 2 is my most played game. I spent countless hours having fun in it. I've already spent over 120 hours playing this one, and I've had fun. Compared to CK2, I find this game much more playable. I'm not sure I'd say it's easier, but it's certainly a smoother playing experience. The objectives your character should be aiming for are much more obvious, and it's a lot easier to do things like fabricating claims. I think the game is very playable, and quite arcadey, in this respect.Unfortunately, I also think this game lacks a LOT of the things that made CK2 great. Granted, many of those things came in the form of DLC, but still, I don't think this game improves on anything enough to be worth buying if you own and love CK2.I suppose my review boils down to this:I do recommend this game. It is a lot of fun and you can whittle away the hours playing it quite nicely. However, when compared to CK2, it lacks a LOT of content, a LOT of depth, and it's missing the spark that CK2 has. CK3 adds 3d character models to replace CK2's portraits, but these models seem lifeless. Where a portrait in CK2 was a glimpse into what a deep character would have looked like, CK3's models feel like caricatures. The art is nice, but they pull silly poses, and all the characters in CK3 are predictable and boring. Everyone feels the same. Or, rather, it feels like there is three or four characters perpetuated over and over again. Because of this, when you play CK3 you will play roughly 3-6 characters before realising you're repeating yourself, and the game very quickly loses any charm it had.Every mechanic in this game is like a shallow but pretty version of a system in CK2.I wholeheartedly recommend this game to someone who is quite a casual gamer, who wants something smoother, easier to get in to, and with less depth. If you want a deeper experience, then I recommend CK2 instead. The characters in CK2 feel living, and because of that, the world feels living. You never know what is going to happen. It's like a simulation of a medieval world. This game is like a bundle of relatively fun minigames. It's fun, but it's missing the heart and soul that made CK2 so good.

_childDocuments_.review: OK this is a game where you control a medieval noble family trying to make the most of your realm.  You make decisions about religion, culture, military, economic development, going on pilgrimages, arranging marriages, hiring spies and assassins, etc. It's part role playing game, where you make decisions from specific characters' points of view, and part strategy. Based on that, I am interested. There are some great things about it, and one or two not great things. but I recommend it. The idea of playing through the middle ages not just from a Civilization point of view but really from the point of view of one royal family with high stakes battles, a variety of quirks and a whole story ... is great. I really liked the characters within the family in Total War: Rome and this has built on that and made it more  involved. The family development system is flawed but still cool. I like the "lifestyles" concept with the learning trees. Finally, the art is cool. The game looks good (the music is ok not great). Paradox tries to make the technology and military dynamic realistic. I think there are improvement opportunities on the military side but the more I play the more I like it.

In CKIII, playing a viking jarl in bum♥♥♥♥ nowhere, Scandinavia feels the exact same as playing as a christian king, and both feel the same as playing a muslim sultan in the Middle East, a raj in India, and a Khan in the steppes. I'd be okay with less flavor than CKII, because that game got eight(?) years worth of content, but the state of the game is simply unacceptable.In a few years, after more patches are released, this game might actually be worth playing, but until then I can't recommend this game at all. Sadly, those patches will be locked behind hundreds of dollars worth of DLC. I already paid sixty dollars for this game and paying more for this game to -potentially- become good is quite frankly a scam. _childDocuments_.review: I know what you're asking yourself. You're reading the reviews, and you just don't know if it's worth buying CK3 when you already have CK2. Everyone's saying it's different, but not many mention how. I will do my best to answer that question by telling you the pros and cons of CK3 compared to CK2PROS:+ a WILDLY superior way-of-life system+ a much stronger / more consequential family and dynasty structure+ technology progress is controlled by how much territory your culture as a whole controls, not just your owned territory+ you are able to take a more direct role in all of your assassination plots.+ councilor tasks like "fabricate claim" no longer have a percent chance to succeed based on their skills. Instead, the task is guaranteed to succeed, but it will take much, MUCH longer if their skills suck+ you don't need to buy any DLC to play as muslims or indians, every leader is available to choose.+ most characters have dirty little secrets. If you learn what they are, you can blackmail them into doing anything you want, like permanently pay more taxes, or adopt a specific inheritance law, or revoke one of their titles, etc.+ penalties and bonuses for relationships fade with time over many years, not all at once after X amount of years.+ playing as a tyrant is viable in CK3. there's a 'dread' mechanic that tells you if your subjects are afraid of you or not. If they are, then it doesn't matter how much they hate you, they won't dare do anything to oppose you.+ your dynasty unlocks unique bonuses as the game goes on; forging a legendary bloodline is a process, not an event.- factions pose absolutely no threat in CK3. Just fight them to a white peace, then you can freely imprison their members and strip them of their land. Same for defensive wars: a white peace is your best friend in this game- Plagues aren't a thing. you can still get sick, but you will never have to deal with a plague- Secret societies aren't a thing. no devil worshipers, no warrior lodges, nothing.- There are 3 and only 3 kinds of government: Fuedal, Clan, and Tribal.

_childDocuments_.review: After spending around 50 hours into the game in the first week of it's release there are some ups and downs I'd like to address. I also like to mention I have many hours (1300ish) in ck2 so I'll be drawing a lot of similarities to CK2 and CK3. Lets begin!Pros: Ck3 is beautiful, easier to read and is still a lot of fun. The interface is a major overhaul from Ck2 and the tutorial in CK3 is probably one of the best tutorials I've seen Paradox push out in a long time but still manages to miss on some important points in game-play to which I'll go over in the cons. War is more interesting with more layers of depth to really make you ponder more about what your troop composition is like to make the most of your soldiers in times of war. Speaking of war, from my experience I'd say it is easier to declare war in ck3 than it was in ck2 until ck2 added the jade dragon dlc that lets you just unjustly declare war on thing around you. Sure, a claim is still better because if you just went up and conquer things, your counties aren't going to like you being in offensive wars all the time. Characters seem more real than Ck2 as far as their decisions go and how they go about in the world but there are some AI goofery at times.CONS: Ck3, even though it has made strides in certain areas that Ck2 lacked in, at the end of the day it comes up short on a lot of content compared to Ck2. No more duels, no more orders to join (holy, cults, warrior lodges etc), no more secret cults to spread before you adopt the true faith, no more shattered realms start, and no ruler designer. None of that. I'm sure they'll add some of those things in future DLC's but that's also an issue I'd like to call the "Bethesda Syndrome" where a reputable game company develops a really bare-bones game an let the community make it more entertaining or shove a bunch of DLC in the face of the customer to bought this for $50 (or $75) to pay more for what the company considers "extra content". Not to mention the tutorial, albeit better than most of Paradox's attempts of providing a tutorial, just only barely covers the basics of how to play so, if you want to learn more about the game beyond just the basic's then you're gonna need to visit the Wiki or Youtube to get schooled, which to me is a very big deterrent from getting players into the game. They expect to buy a title, play it, be taught reasonably well enough to do good and keep playing. Not take a 2 hour break to read a wiki about how to gain as much prestige as possible to do basic things to get ahead that you could've done for free in CK2. With that being said, I can safely say that I still recommend CK3 as it's own game but not for $50. I'd say it's worth more like $30 dollars as it is now.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is genuinely annoying to play. The AI couldn't tie their shoe laces together if they tried. You have basically doomed your Kingdom otherwise you'll have to force them to take vows, kill your own sons (what's wrong with you Paradox?), make them marry matrellinially or ensure they never get any land (by killing them obviously).This game tries to get you to make a dynasty, then forces you to kill everyone close to you so you can actually have SOME control of the outcome once your player character passes away. _childDocuments_.review: When a sequel to a game is worse in every way but visual it is not a good sequel. When a sequel to a game is released it should use the previous game as a building block on which to improve. CK3 does not do this, even closing in on 3 years after launch. CK2 remains the more complete game (with all DLC) in every way but visual. The DLC from a previous game such as the CK series should be included (at least for the most part) on launch of the sequel. CK3 is a slap in the face to fans of the game series when previous features and changes are removed from the base game only to be sold to you again later. It is a greedy practice that Paradox games are well known for. If I had to suggest either CK3 or CK2 to anyone currently given the price difference, I would recommend CK2 easily because for the same price you can have most of the impactfull DLCs and there is (in my opinion) a much better mod base from which to customize your experience. I love these games, so it's sad to say that CK3 is an utter disappoint, it was on launch and it remains so almost 3 years later with minimal quality of life changes from its predecessor and less content, flavor, and fun for the player. If you are thinking about getting it, do not bother for at least another 3 years at this rate get CK2 and the DLC with the money you would spend instead.

_childDocuments_.review: 2023 update: This is the best Paradox game and quite possibly one of the best strategy games ever made. For anybody not familiar, of all Pdx games, the Crusader Kings series comes the closest to truly simulating the whims of the interpersonal relationships of the ruling social elite, as opposed to an abstract monolithic "country" entity. Characters (people!) live their own lives and you interact with them as you play the head of your dynasty, resulting in a very RPG-esque addition to the grand strategy genre.- The simulation is a perfect trade off between detail and manageability.- The user interface and character graphics look and handle better than in any previous Pdx title.- The map looks very good and on par with Imperator: Rome (boils down to taste).- The army AI is good enough to enjoy the game although it will screw up a lot, but I do think on balance it's the least derpy of the Pdx titles thanks to supportive game design.Note that I don't own a single DLC and I don't feel like I'm missing anything. Yeah, the pricing is what it is, but like me you don't have to buy it until a sufficiently good sale comes around.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; As someone who is new to grand strategy, I can confidently recommend CK3 to other players who are also uninitiated to the genre, if the medieval setting and series reputation for dynamic storytelling is a draw. While intimating at first glance, the games tutorial is good, but short. Be prepared to invest several hours coming to grips with the game and it's many systems before the game really takes off.Crusader Kings III is blast— after you get over the learning curve. The Crusader Kings series has a well known reputation for being an interesting mash of role playing, dynasty building, and emergent story telling. This has always sounded compelling to me, but as someone who was completely new to grand strategy games, these types of games have always felt daunting and somewhat impenetrable to me. With the first big expansion (Royal Court) dropping soon, I decided to take the plunge before the game gains more complexity. If that is your experience, than this review was specifically written with you in mind.CK3 requires a certain level of commitment upfront to learning the game before it really gets good. The game is at it's best when you understand what your options are and you feel like you're driving the narrative where you want it to go. The first few hours are a slow, but necessary. The game holds your hand and does it's best to ease you into things with a competent tutorial. You'll learn how to navigate the UI, about important actions and decisions you can make, and key concepts like claims, vassalage and hierarchy, succession, etc. Use the games keyword tool tip system liberally to get more information about these topics.The tutorial is kind of short and while giving an overview on how to get going, it does not try to address the many potential situations that obstacles that you will find yourself faced with. You deal with them as they come up. I made a lot of mistakes the first few games I played. You will ask questions like: "Why am I always broke?", "What is a good method to managing the number of vassals I have?", "Who are good candidates to make vassals?", "How do I minimize losing titles in succession?", "What do I do with all of my other children who are not heirs?", and so on. You will have these kinds of questions at first. There is no shame in checking youtube or using google when you feel stuck. If you can push through, after a few games these types of decisions will get easier and you can focus on playing your ruler how you want.In conclusion, while the game is dense at first, I've found that it has been manageable with a little patience. My enjoyment has increased dramatically after playing and failing a few times. The systems will start to take a back seat and you're left with in narrative sandbox with loads of interesting decisions to make every step of the way, which is where CK3 really shines.

_childDocuments_.review: * In general, the roleplay system has been improved dramatically from CK2. The Lifestyles are awesome, Stress is a very good way to encourage the player to roleplay your given traits without removing agency from the player. * The trait system has been thoroughly revamped and improved. All traits have now negative and positive effect which makes it way more fun.* A lot of the mechanics from CK2 (and it's innumerable DLC's) have made it over to CK3 which makes CK3 a very deep strategy game from the very beginning. * The religion system is very well thought out and dynamic, although currently Heresies seem to be too prevalent. * The playable map is huge and you are able to play as almost everyone which gives the game huge replay value. * The game runs great and it's generally stable. * Huge modding potential. * By far the worst aspect of CK3 is the combat/warfare system. It's basically a simplified version of the warfare system of CK2. Just like in CK2 warfare always comes down to who has more troops ,there are basically no ways to win by using strategy if you are outnumbered (outside of hiring Mercenaries or "Men at Arms" who are not balanced at all)   - Sieges take WAY too short a time  (especially if you siege units)  - there are no ways to give commands for your allies  - you always have to Benny Hill style chase your enemies which is extremely frustrating  - Scattered Retreat is ahistorical and artificially lengthens every war and makes huge battles feel meaningless  - no peace treaty system like in EU4* The soundtrack is just .... meh. I'm a big fan of Andreas Waldetoft music but in CK3 the score is rather underwhelming. Thankfully you can get the CK2 music on the Workshop.* The only thing that CK3 is really missing from CK2 is the dynamic plague system. In CK3 the plagues feel random and not very impactful at all. * The UI is sometimes not very clear and convoluted. For instance, it's very difficult to see what counties you hold as a king.- The game is just too easy. The AI isn't able to keep up with the player and once you have a kingdom title you are almost unstoppable. You also tend te live for a long time. * There seem to be a lot of mechanics that make the game artificially grindy like the Piety/Prestige resource or the fact that you can't press all your  claims at once.

_childDocuments_.review: [up to date impressions as of Apr 2021 (Northern Lords update)]This game distills a lot of what made Crusader Kings II great, and focuses on it to magnificent effect.Where its predecessor was still fundamentally a grand strategy game with role-playing elements, Crusader Kings III is much more of a true role-playing/grand strategy hybrid, with a slight focus on role-playing, where the strategy elements serve to reinforce and inform the RPG part of the game, rather than the other way round.The star of this game is undoubtedly the stress mechanic, where you gain stress every time you act contrary to your character's traits, and vice versa. It's a wonderfully elegant and powerful way to encourage role-playing, and incidentally fixes one of CK2's biggest problems, which is that you could always play a certain way no matter what your character's personality was like. The other cornerstone mechanic, secrets and hooks, generates a web of interpersonal intrigue and obligation that adds a lot of texture on top of the feudal and dynastic structure.I do have a couple of gripes with the game, chiefly surrounding event variety and war AI, but these are more like minor, easily overlooked quibbles rather than dealbreakers, because the core design is so robust.More generally there are a lot of little refinements to the UI and general balance that need to be ported over from CK2, but as it stands it's already a masterpiece. Every part of the game brims with deliberate design intent that fits together into such a beautifully cohesive, endlessly fascinating whole. Every game is a grand generational soap opera, with protagonists and antagonists cycling in and out. Arcs conclude with satisfying denouements, or the ageing and death of the main players, to be then replaced by a new generation, and a new melodrama.This is, without a doubt, the best game Paradox has ever put out.

name: Aragami 2
detailed_description: You are one of the last elite warriors of your kin, the Aragami. Victims of a supernatural affliction which corrodes the body and devours the mind, the Aragami control Shadow Essence - a mystical power which grants the ability to control the shadows. With this power the Aragami carry out their tasks and quests - assignments made all along the valley to ensure the subsistence of the village and to free the Aragami enslaved by the invader armies. PLAY IN SINGLE MODE OR IN CO-OP WITH YOUR FRIENDS Discover a full campaign and join the assassin squad up to 3 players in co-op. ENGAGE IN FAST-PACED STEALTH ACTIONS Manage covers and powers with agility. Take down your enemies with stealth kills and non-lethal takedowns. ENTER INTO COMBAT AS A TACTICAL DECISION Become the master of a skill based combat with high risk and high reward. BUILD YOUR SHADOW ASSASSIN Craft your weapons and armors and upgrade your elite warrior with a wide variety of abilities and shadow powers. PROTECT THE RASHOMON VALLEY Save your people and defeat the curse before it ends with you and discover how the Aragami became a legend.

_childDocuments_.review: When this game is on its usual sale, it is honestly worth the pick-up. The game has a main hub where you customise and upgrade your character's abilities and you go to a mission board to accept missions (all of which advance the main story). I like the different ways you can take a mission (do you avoid a pack of guys and take a specific route to the objective, do you assassinate/knock out certain groups, do you just pull your sword out and fight?) and the new difficulty system lets you ramp the difficulty up if you're finding it too easy. TLDR - Pros:Easy to pick up and playMissions make you think about how you want to play out a strategyUpgrading abilities gives you a way to complement your playstyle (I loved the long-distance shadow kill which also clears away the body upon death, it's so handy!)Cons:Story is mehThere are five or six main maps/biomes (I believe?); the 50-odd missions all take place on various maps within these biomes and it can get a bit repetitive towards the late gameCustomisation could be a bit more fleshed out, but it is satisfying to earn the best looking gear and colour dyes from in-game progression and collectible-hunting (so refreshing to earn in-game rather than have the microtransaction option!)

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game after I finished the first part. Now that I'm done, I'm almost sad that it's over.Of course, I've heard about the problems and bugs and read about them in the reviews. Either I was very lucky with my gaming experience or some people exaggerate a bit because the second part is different from the first.While I played alone, I didn't have any problems at all. I was able to complete all levels and tasks. That's why I have a suspicion that some problems are related to the multiplayer. However, not many problems occurred there either. The biggest problem would be that you go into a level and you can't use your abilities, so you can't take out the enemies. However, this problem could be fixed by restarting the level/game. Of course, this isn't ideal, but it doesn't make the game unplayable or unenjoyable.In general, I would recommend Aragami 2 in multiplayer. It's significantly more fun and the levels are easier. The story was good and interesting. The differences from the first part are clearly noticeable, but I don't think they are bad changes. The games aren't directly connected, so I think the change is pretty cool. I was happy to experience something new. Of course, you have to get used to it, but personally I like the gameplay in this part more. The gameplay feels free and flexible and I just enjoy it.I can only recommend the game and when the bugs in the multiplayer are gone, I would also recommend the game at full price. If you are unsure, you can buy it in the sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Definitely a huge improvement over the first game. Unlike the first one, the special abilities you unlock are available to use without going to a specific area on the map in the first game. Replay Value: I could see myself playing this again in the future, but as if now, seeing no option for a new game plus, it gets a little boring after collecting everything I needed. There are 48 levels with 48 perks. The game starts to get easier as you achieve more useful perks but I also noticed that you can change the difficulty for missions, so I kinda lost my motivation to continue playing the game. There are collectibles as well but I don't see myself collecting all of them. Maybe back in the day when I had more time to kill.  The sword combat is okay. It's not too hard to understand but it becomes boring after you could only do so much with left click and right click to parry. It will take a while before I can enjoy this game again.The missions do seem repetitive because some missions are on the same map but you start off in a different area. Some of the missions made me feel like I was playing Assassin's Creed. I love the stealth, though. I'm also glad they added cool combat mechanics in to this with the sword fighting.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2~~~~~~~~~After the immense success of the first Aragami game, Aragami 2 aims to bank on the critically-acclaimed experience of the first title and take it to new levels. Aragami 2’s story takes place about a century or so after the first game’s timeline. This time around you are going against the Akatsuchi Empire, a fierce invading force that aims to take over the land of The Aragami clan, known as Kurotsuba.Plot: You play as the Aragami ninja, who after a selfless heroic battle against the Akatsuchi Empire, gets pinned down and cursed by the enemy and barely manages to escape the clutches of the Akatsuchi Empire. He finds a safe haven in a nearby village ruled by a peace-loving clan. After battling the curse he manages to control it and as one of the few Aragami capable of using Shadow Essence to their advantage, it is up to you to fight off the Akatsuchi Empire.Free your people and defend this new village that you call home.Gameplay: Aragami 2 in short is a linear, story-driven game with mission-based format where you take up contracts for eliminations, information gathering, stealing items of interest, and rescue ops.You take the control of Aragami, a ninja who uses Shadow Essence to his advantage. After each successful interaction with villagers and clan elders, you are provided with missions and contracts.Each of these missions/contracts takes place in the Rashomon Valley over and over again within a limited number of locations with minor changes to the locations' layouts. It was a constant battle between the ultra-linear story structure and repetitive mission locations, versus the genuinely fun stealth gameplay. In the end, the gameplay managed to keep me occupied for a good amount of time.As mentioned, you get to play the same types of mission over and over again with minor storyboard changes and different map layouts within the same locations, constantly backstabbing the same rusty old enemy AI. The only saving grace, Combat: Aragami 2 just drops you off at your starting positions and gives you full control over the playable area.And my god this system is so good, there are literally no restrictions; you can do whatever you want as long as you get the job done. You can go full jungle fight scene Rambo, no F…s given. A brutal mixture of a nimble ninja sneaking past his enemies to Rambo, backstabbing 3 enemies in a row and running away while the rest of the enemy goons come after you.This time around you get some consumable/throwable items in the game to enhance your combat effectiveness and get creative with items such as the Shuriken, Amnesia Needles, Potions, smoke screens, and more. Throw in some experience-based supernatural abilities to unlock, and you’ve got yourself an ultimate shadow-dashing, high jumping, wall-climbing killing machine. Sadly, everything is not perfect here, and three major downsides bring down this awesome combat section – 1. Parry: Yeah the parry doesn’t work as intended. Drains stamina too fast leaving me defenseless, damaged, and dead. 2. Enemy AI: Just horrible, in every single mission certain enemies will randomly start walking in the wrong direction, randomly ignore a buddy being killed in front of him, randomly start throwing fireballs without detection and so much more. 3. Auto-locking- My god this feature is a load of hot trash! Whose idea was it to put auto-locking in a stealth game? And for what purpose? Every time I died, I swear to God it was caused by this faulty auto-lock system.I killed an enemy and was detected. Okay cool, as I’m trying to run away from the enemy, this stupid system auto-locks on him and slows me down, causing an animation chain reaction where I lose all defenses. World design: Aragami 2 is supposed to take place 100 years after the first one, but visually and artistically both look the same to me. This time around the maps are much bigger, giving the players a big leg to stretch their muscles. The map layouts across each mission were really good, although I wished they had implemented more unique locations rather than changing up the map layouts for each mission. Visually there’s a lot left to be desired as well. Expected a bit more charm and sparkle. Music and sound effects: What Aragami 2 really gets right is its background music. It’s really good and very relaxing, suitable for a stealth game for sure. I demand more of such music in the upcoming updates and DLCs. The same goes for the sound effects; very good sync with the combat and parkour throughout the game, especially the blasting spray of blood coming out of the enemies as I stabbed them repeatedly; that was nice. Positive: + Linear story + Fun stealth gameplay + No holds barred, just get the job done+ Mission rating system without a leaderboard! + Strong, balanced tree of abilities + Balanced and useful throwable/consumable items+ Decent amount of character customization + CO-OP PvE support Negatives: - Minor animations issues - One-way mirror map layout wall, with holes- Problematic Auto-lock feature - Dumb and rusty enemy AI - Repetitive missions - Story structure could’ve been improvedNo holds barred Stealth action; just get the job done! Anything goes in the fight against the Akatsuchi Empire. 7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: is a game that improves on various gameplay elements of its predecessor, but sacrifices its tone, charm and unique nature in the process. The enjoyable teleportation mechanic has been replaced with one that offers less freedom, the clear sense of progression was ditched in favour of repetitive filler, and the focused narrative has become a wider and far less concise affair.  Judged as an independent game and not against the virtues of its predecessor,  is a decent game at best, and an absolute drag at worst.Beyond the tutorial, our story starts with the Aragami, our protagonist, being killed and thus discovering that he can respawn.  When he does, he finds himself in Kakurega Village, a place populated by other Aragami who immediately start giving him jobs to do.  Being an entity seemingly lacking independent thought or desire, our protagonist then proceeds to perform every theft, assassination and scouting mission asked of him without question. The motivation for all of this is that, apparently, the Aragami suffer a curse that grants them their abilities, but slowly consumes their minds.  If you're a fan of the first  title, you've probably noticed that everything I just said clashes with the entire plot of said game.  It seems that  is not so much a sequel as a re-imagining, and the protagonist's appearance and the general theme of his abilities are the only meaningful connections between the two.  This would not necessarily be a bad thing if the new story were grander and more fleshed out, but it was not to be.The first game featured a relatively simple and narrow plot in which the Aragami was a shadow spirit called to assist his summoner by defeating her enemies and enabling her rescue from the forces of the light.  With that, we had a simple light vs. dark theme facilitating and being reinforced by gameplay mechanics. This story was not an especially deep one, but it provided a clear setting and a simple premise that saw players continually progress through new areas with a clear goal in sight, encountering and overcoming new obstacles along the way.  Such a sense of progression or theme is completely absent in , dropped in favour of something larger but with little depth.  Kakurega Village acts as a hub for the player to return to between missions, and offers limited services such as a vendor for the game's new consumable items, including health potions.  The main function of the village, however, is to house the NPCs that continually give the player missions.  The nature of said missions is the game's biggest problem by far.  To begin with, players move between several areas, completing simple objectives such as assassinating a target or stealing an item. These objectives are broadly the same as those featured in the first  title and are quite enjoyable the first time.  You may be tempted to take your time, plotting your path and making use of your stealth abilities and the host of new combat items such as stun grenades and poisoned needles.However, if you found yourself in this same place again, heading for the same building as last time but for a  different objective, would you want to put so much dedication into it again?  What about the third time?  What about the fifth?  Content is endlessly reused, with very little challenge or variety added in the process.  Some new enemies appear, but this changes nothing about how you'll play the game, and I rarely felt it necessary to use the majority of my abilities or items.  New locations do appear now and again, but you'll always end up coming back to the same old places from the start of the game – places that often look very similar, to boot.  The objectives you'll be taking on in these places hardly change, either.  This constant revisiting of old content slows the story's progression to a crawl, and it's painfully obvious when a plot point exists solely to make the player do more of it. At over eight hours into the game, I found myself in the same place, doing more or less the same thing that I was doing at one hour into the game, and with no noteworthy challenge or mechanics to make it different.  It was at this point that I decided I was done with the game, and to write this review.  I normally like to finish the games that I review, but moments of interest are so few and far between that I am simply too bored to continue.Something that bothered me when playing the first game was the Aragami's inability to scale low walls or climb ledges.  addresses this by adding not only ledge-grabbing and climbing, but a double-jump and mid-air dash as well.  When combined with the reworked teleportation ability that allows one to instantly move to a nearby ledge, it's possible to traverse terrain at significant speed – something that quickly becomes very useful when ploughing through the filler content.If one doesn't feel like avoiding enemies, the game does have a combat system, though it is more likely to cause the player's death than an enemy's.  This is not because the combat itself is particularly difficult, but because the game tries to force players into combat mode when an enemy attacks, snapping the camera to the enemy and severely inhibiting the player's movement.  Combine this with the enemies' ability to seemingly teleport to and strike a player who is attempting to flee, and there's cause for much frustration.  If one does stick to a stealthy approach, however, the gameplay is solid. Running the game on its max settings, I got a consistent 60fps with no drops.  Bugs were minimal, with just a few minor issues that did not impact gameplay in any meaningful way.  I did, however, discover some baffling design decisions; namely a complete lack of keybind options or a pause function – even for singleplayer.While  graphics are a technical step-up from the first game, they still look rather dated and no longer have a stylised flair to mask the fact.  Though this game does have some nice-looking areas, I think the original looks better.  Smaller visual elements such as animations, meanwhile, have been improved and generally look quite good.Upon arriving in Kakurega Village, one may notice a beautiful track playing in the background; it's the highlight of the game's soundtrack, which is of high quality and lovely to listen to, for a while.  Unfortunately, its tracks seem to be few in number, and they quickly get old.  The rest of the game's sound effects are of decent quality, and there's little to complain about on that front. While  would not qualify as a worthy sequel to its beloved predecessor, it would pass as a decent and relatively enjoyable stealth game if it were not burdened with a weak story and unnecessary filler that drags the experience down into the mud.  If played in co-op and/or in short stints, the game is serviceable, but it meanders far too much to hold my interest.  This makes me sad.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE this game, it's scratching the same movement game itch that popped up after I played Ultrakill, and while it may not be as fast paced, the movement is freeing in comparison to a lot of games in the stealth game genre, and utilizing the movement it provides you with give *me* the same feeling of catharsis. I'm not sure however if I can recommend it at full price, at least unless you're almost certain this is up your alley. It's something that I feel like appeals to my very niche requirement for a movement based stealth game with medals/ranks tied to whether you either don't kill *anyone* or kill *everyone.* *I* find this very engaging, and I plan to play it far longer than the 12-13 hours I've played it so far, but I planned to pass it up for the $35 price tag and while *I* may feel like that's a decent pricepoint for what *I* can get out of it, I don't think it's worth it to the average gamer. Grab it on sale, it's absolutely worth it for like 15-25 bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is quite a bit of a change from the first one, at first I didn't enjoy the change and was as annoyed as some of the others who wanted just more of the first game. Warping to shadows was removed and replaced to warping to ledges, waiting in shadows to recover your ability is gone and replaced with constant stamina recovery, combat is now a thing instead of being 1 hit, the list goes on. However after playing several levels I got use to the new mechanics and found it somewhat refreshing. Sure it wouldn't force me to restart the level after being discovered and getting hit by the enemy, but I could still restart the mission myself if I wanted a more of a challenging pure stealth run. You're not exactly forced to use the direct combat that they introduced (except for some specific mission objectives). There are bugs at launch but the developer is very actively addressing them as they are brought up and discovered. If you enjoyed the first game and you are open to learn new mechanics instead of having a carbon copy, it is a fun game especially with a friend. The bugs at release can be frustrating at times but they can also provide some hilarious moments, like when an enemy asserts his dominance over you with a T-Pose launching fireballs from his crotch (The Dev has already addressed this bug).

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami is an excellent game to this day, but its sequel feels like the team over at Lince Works wanted to give us the world by implementing more modern experience and money systems, more free-flowing movement, a whole new combat system, massively improved and personalized customization, consumables and build-making, tons of collectibles... wildly ambitious for a small team. And on all of these fronts, Lince Works actually pulled it off and delivered these features.My issue with Aragami 2 is that so many games have these features already, but the Aragami series had its own unique things going for it that I loved so much, which are now just husks of their former selves. Shadows are now meaningless compared to the almighty power of being two feet above your enemy, money grinding for items you have to buy isn't nearly as satisfying to get as it used to be when you obtained a no-kill medal in every single level and earned your new outfit, and most egregious of all?I say this with all the love in my heart I can summon: this game is not finished. Bugs occur constantly, the polish is not present, time and budget was poorly allocated. I could've lived without grinding for gold, wandering around looking for collectibles, or having weird and ineffective methods to completing the missions like consumables and combat if it meant we didn't constantly have to restart because all the enemies turned immortal and started T-posing at us again, or if gameplay wasn't balanced in such a way that you could get free undetected aerial kills on literally any enemy just by jumping.TL;DRThis is a good stealth game for the price. It's just not Aragami.

_childDocuments_.review: You can clearly tell that Aragami 2 tried to improve the formula of Aragami, but lost itself in the process.Animations are less stiff (mostly) and character has much more mobility with dashes, jumps and double jumps. Also, hand-to-hand combat is also an option if an enemy spots and detects you. You can even survive 1v2 with correctly executed parry and blocks. All skills have their own separate cooldowns, which enables some good combos if you get to use them in quick succession. But this alone didn't bring the game and series to another level. Storytelling is worse than it was in Aragami. And even in the first game it was sub-par at best. You do missions, talk with the same several characters between the missions and that's it. Chapters end abruptly. Rinse and repeat.There are a lot of missions in this game. Like 51 or so. After 10 or so the game becomes excruciatingly repetitive and boring. Most missions have very simple objectives like - collect 3 things of something. Talk to an NPC and find him an item or two. Or just bring an unconscious npc to the map portal. All these objectives get very repetitive the longer you play. There are 10 areas in this game and some missions take place in the same area 4 or 5 times. replaying the same areas just with a bit different objectives and a bit different enemy placement is far from being fun. At first I tried to kill all/most enemies, but I soon realized that I'm just wasting my time and I began to speedrun the objectives and sneak around most enemies. This way I could finish levels in 10-15 minutes instead of 30-40.Skill progression is slow and skill unlocking is way to grindy. In the first game you could unlock most/best skills early on if you were collecting (not so) hidden scrolls. While in this one you have to play for a very long time just to get to more interesting and powerful skills.. If you aren't playing on the hard difficulty - you'll unlock more powerful skills way after the mid-game (you get like half a level from a mission completion if you play on normal difficulty). Which is a shame in my opinion. This is probably the biggest reason why this game gets so repetitive only after a few hours.There are a lot of bugs too. If you carry a corpse and try to put it somewhere in the corner - you get teleported into an open area where like 4 enemies can see you (insta-death). Sometimes your character can sink through terrain into the void. There are a lot of animation bugs too.Aragami 2 should have had much better and more interesting objectives, more interesting enemies and better skills progression. Sadly, I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not nearly done with the game, but at this rate, I'm excited to delve further into it. Don't let the mixed reviews scare you off, this is still a lovely game. The main critique that I (and many others) have is that this second game loses some of its "Light against Shadow" concept by making it more similar to a normal ninja game, but personally, I don't mind it much. The story is still interesting, it still goes into a theme of a supernatural ninja, and you are still being rewarded for playing stealthy over becoming a blood-lusting killer. The stealthier you play, the higher your Rank (S being the highest for a level), so the easier you will unlock abilities. For me, the game still holds the charm of feeling like "the big bad boogeyman that strikes from the dark" that the first one had, but improves on it even more by giving your Aragami a chance of combat when being spotted. You aren't simply struck down anymore, you can fight back against a small enemy group, and the ability to use items you can unlock through collectibles for your own benefit is quite enjoyable too. And the amount of customization possible makes your character truly "yours", unlike the first game, where there was only about 4 clothes, here you have many more outfits to unlock, mix and use for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is a great stealth game, however I would strongly recommend playing it on classic mode only as the shadow mechanics are much more like the first game and make for a much better stealth experience. The story is pretty uncompelling and there's a lot of recycled areas, granted with enough changes in each that you'll need to rethink your strategy a bit. The biggest problem with Aragami 2 though is that too many resources were invested into the combat when the game really doesn't need it. The first Aragami feels like more of a pure stealth experience, but the added mobility, more reliable shadow leaping to ledges, a better range of tools and abilities, and being able to move bodies are all very welcome changes in Aragami 2. My hope is that the developers will combine the best stealth elements of the first two games and bring them into Aragami 3.

_childDocuments_.review: A really great stealth game. Nothing more satisfying than observing your enemies movements, sticking to the shadows and striking at the most opportune moment to knock out all your foes in an area without being seen or heard. You can choose complete stealth, complete fighting, or a mix. Similarly, the way you approach missions can be done from multiple angles. The maps sort of have a relatively open feel to them, with each location being able to be approached from different directions. So there is a good feeling of control over the way you do each mission. Did feel a little bit long, but the gameplay was so enjoyable that I didn't mind too much. This story was simple, which actually worked in this game's favour and I enjoyed it. The game only had a couple of issues. First of all, you can't manually save, so if you mess up during a mission and get spotted (and you're going for complete stealth runs) you have to start the whole mission over again. More complex missions can take anywhere from 30-50 minutes, so messing up at the late stage of a mission was very frustrating. Second, in rare cases, the button prompts for performing actions on enemies wouldn't appear. Aside from that, there were only some very minor animation bugs. Overall, this was a fantastic stealth game. It's a shame to see the dev team has disbanded, but I wish them all the best in their future endeavours.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the really great bones of a phenomenal game, but lacks so much polish in almost every department. Some abilities are broken entirely, combat is a mess when it's even visually functional, and the content comprises of 10 hours of filler. Areas repeat, which is not the worst thing in the world, but the barriers to these areas are arbitrary. Enemies are redundant and repetitive, and each mission/task/quest gets repeated 3-6 times in each area (10 total).  This was not a terrible experience, but it definitely hurts to see what could have been. Art direction and unlockable aesthetic content ends up feeling very similar. "tools" you can purchase have no real reason to exist, they are never needed. Runes are never worth their value. This game does provide a unique multiplayer experience, but rather than making you feel as though your "aragami" is unique or that its a cornerstone of play, it rests on more people doing the same thing. This feels like early access pushed out as complete.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a stealth game that tries to be metal gear, splinter cell, and ghost of tsushima but manages to fail at all of them all at once.Pros:- Its a stealth game, hide in bushes, assassinate while trying not to get caught. If that's your cup of tea this game is for you- Stealth is manageable and your character is rather mobile for a stealth game making him feel like a shadow spirit walking in and out with little a whisper- Designs and art are rather charming and not bad to look at- Customisation is there and not bad- Multiplayer is also there and can be quite fun with good friendsCons:- While this is a stealth game it felt like it was a game about speed running your way through every level as even on higher difficulty I was literally finishing levels in sometimes five minutes or less.- Enemy AI is trash, often glitching and spotting you from 100km away or not spotting you at all, or simply glitching in a state of awareness and permanently being stuck looking in a corner screaming about someone being dead.- Speaking of which there is no downside to killing versus knocking out apart from knocking out take longer which for this game was just painful. + there is very little downside to simply running around slashing anyone in your way as blood doesn't trigger enemies and it's way more convenient.- Level maps are repeated which is fine, however some maps were used up to 4-5 times and with little variation beyond more enemies that seemed to be dropped like someone was blindfolded in garry's mod with their left click taped down.- Item's are rather useless and I rarely if ever used them as they bring very small benefit beyond healing and emergency smoke grenades once and a while.- Not only can levels be completed rather quickly, but there are apparently 51 of them! which would be fine if they were there own zone with well thought out dynamic to get around. But considering this is the fifth time I am in the mine to collect/assassinate/destroy/meet a contact/ or destroy a couple boxes became quite boring after the first 20 times I had to do it, and especially tedious when they are used as padding between the main story missions.- Speaking of the story is complex and makes little to no sense, it seems there is lore here but even other people who played the previous game say the lore in THIS GAME doesn't make any sense. In addition very little is explained as to what or who people are or why any of the story is transpiring.- The HUB area which while pretty was another form of padding making me run up to a temple to get a small bit of dialogue, a pat on the shoulder from the leader before I am sent back to the bulletin board for another mission. It's also good to note this is mostly to hang out with your friends and buy items however my friends and I started trying to speed run these sections as they became absolutely monotonous very quickly.- Single player is present however many times during the game I felt that certain areas were meant to be tackled as a team and not to waste anymore time I simply did my best to sprint through them- In addition while the game says "Skill based combat" think some of the new assassin creed games but infinitely worse as players can only handle around 1 -2 enemies at a time not because of skill or speed, but because enemies have an absolutely absurd stamina bar that the game doesn't really provide skill to counter and main attacks only take slivers while they take large chunks out of yours. But wait I hear you say, "Isn't this a stealth game?" why yes it is, and while that would be appropriate for a pure stealth game unfortunately they added a mission completion bar based on how many fights you got in like splinter cell.- while there is a skill tree I barely if ever bought skills as 90% I didn't use beyond the passives, upgraded whisper, and the multi kill- Personal pet peeve, but considering your charging 40$ for this and you are repeating several levels, bugs, the story is incomprehensible, and there isn't that much content seriously put's a damper on recommending friends to purchase this game.So to conclude is Aragami 2 a bad game, no. for certain people or a good group of friends it can be a passable experience however considering all the issues it would need a few things before I could recommend this to anyone.- Shrink the campaign, if you need 20 missions to tell the story then make it 20 and make them good instead of adding 30+ filler episodes especially when the filler is all on the same maps with slightly different objectives. (they can be added, but keep them optional to get xp or items instead of slowing the entire story to a crawl)- Overhaul your combat system to where it is passable (ie add more combat based abilities or tweaking combat to handle more enemies) or don't have it at all with it there mostly for escaping and creating distance.- And make the lore understandable, I didn't play the first game and if I can't even figure out why my character is in this fight beyond ThAT GUy bAd then it needs some work.

_childDocuments_.review: I had hoped this would have been an amazing game like the first one but was very wrong, the story in here feels confusing and overall this game feels more like a new company bought the rights to the old. In the first game it was about stealth and focus heavy on that with a mix of abilities where as this game feels more like dark souls were you can be stealthy if you like but not required. The first one had a comic book feel overall with visuals while the second game feels a completely different way. Sadly this game took a turn for the worse, the story feels very weird, the visuals looks overall worse than the first one, the first game the devs made felt very unique and amazing while this one feels more like they trying to either A) copy someone else game or B) just trying to implement too many things and barley focus on any of them. If the devs ever create a third game i hope they go back to the roots of this game and make it as amazing as their first game was cause their second is just overall trash even feels worse with controller.

_childDocuments_.review: Man what happened, this is just not Aragami. It's a series of small open worlds with random quests and gameplay totally separate from the story, a story which is told through janky cutscenes with awful volume mixing. None of the interesting stealth action gameplay of the original, just the same sort of gameplay you'd expect from a wii shovelware game. I have never seen a sequel go so far in the wrong direction before. If you liked Aragami, leave it at that, don't try this.

_childDocuments_.review: Love it like Aragami 1.It is a different game though, it is more like Sekiro now... Well, for me thats an ugrade! This time there are all kinds of cosmetics to purchase via ingame progress.There is NO World Builder this time, so you wont get random fanmade maps, thats a big Fail, especially that made the first game really enjoyable.I encountered no gamebreaking bugs, just a bit of heat on my GPU.

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like a college project. Or as if developers run out of funds and had to quickly shove the project out of the door.Holes in terrain.Holes in assets.Missing mechanics and items.A bit clunky controls.Enemies with 270 degree field of vision.You can fight enemies, but if there are two or more of them - you die, since you need to auto-lock and parry in time just to kill a regular guard.No actual choice whatsoever as far as the story is considered, just like in the first issue of the title.I like this game, but the frustration is just too much, have to say "No".

_childDocuments_.review: This game is overall a very solid game.Its story, though not linked to the first game, is not bad.The gameplay is a massive improvement, in my opinion. It feels much smoother and more satisfying to jump around and you can get much further now. Fighting is not necessary but a nice gesture. (Parrying is just so satifying)Enemies are mor attentive in this game, which is very nice. BUT there are little problems.This concerns solely multiplayer though.Sometimes it is difficult to join or let someone join your/his session.The delay is in combat horrible as you don't see the stamina bar lower or parrying being much more difficult.Sometimes you can't assassinate/knock out anyone and using support items have no effects on the target and models multiplying so you can't decern them.Lastly, you are more likely to encounter bugs/glitches if you are not the host.All in all, this game is perfect if you play it solo, but this game needs fixes if people want to play with friends.
