_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a sequel to Aragami 1, look elsewhere.While Aragami 1 was all about shadows, the main movement-related shadow mechanics have been removed in Aragami 2: teleporting is limited to ledges only unless the player chooses the Classic difficulty. Neither teleporting to the ceiling/walls (shadow surfaces) nor creating shadows is possible.However, movement in general feels more "free" because sprint speed seems faster and the player can jump. There is also "Shadow Leap" which helps to cover long distances (with the included risk of being glitched underground).Aragami 2 offers hand-to-hand combat with parrying, but it feels very clumsy and buggy and is best avoided completely whenever possible (which is most of the game, outside of maybe 1-2 missions).I found the length of the game (51 missions) way too long and the gameplay repeating. Most missions include finding something or someone, and there are no markers until the player gets very close, so most of the time is spent wandering around and wondering where in the ♥♥♥♥ the objective.The story seems to happen in a completely different universe and I did not notice any references outside of there being a Legacy Armor set. I cannot compare the story to that of Aragami 1, because frankly, I don't remember ♥♥♥♥ about the first one - though the main (only) female character was better in the first game.There are also a few albeit frequent bugs where vaulting over an obstacle sometimes results in the player falling through the map. Teleporting (while running?) also sometimes teleports the player backward, out of bounds, with no way back to the mission area, forcing a restart.In summary, do not expect a sequel to Aragami 1 and just treat it as a standalone game. It is a bit long, somewhat buggy, and the combat sucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: significant step back from the 1st aragami game in terms of story, gameplay and progression.just play the 1st game, which is well worth your time and money. additional notes: missions only take place across a handful of maps, the terrain gets repetitive fast. later missions are incredibly buggy, to the point of borderline unplayable in that you cannot interact with most enemies except through select actions.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a really nice yet simple feel to it.The mechanics work well, graphically it's simple yet has all the detail you need.I'm only just a few missions in yet the story seems well integrated and simple to keep up with, and the characters and customisation are again simple but very fitting.The controller support is full and fantastic, my only gripe would be the pointer select rather than a simple up/down/left/right navigation in menu's.I truly think it's a nice edition to the ninja genre and well worth a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the game can be a pretty fun and fast paced stealth sim but less than halfway through the missions all bleed together due to an underwhelming map pool and boringly repetitive troop placements. The story is bland, mostly because it only exists in the hub world and you don't really *feel* the impact your missions have.Most egregiously the game is a buggy mess. The amount of times I've had to restart a mission because I've gotten stuck inside the terrain, been seen because I clipped through an object or, my personal favorite, been unable to kill a quest target because they "died" but didn't die (don't take warp strike. If your kill is in any way interrupted it'll put whoever you targeted in permanent stasis. I'll admit that the cause of this bug is user error, but it shouldn't exist regardless)And honestly, I despise this game as a followup to Aragami because it feels absolutely nothing like the first game. Unique HUD that was on your character in the first game is completely gone, and so is the ability to teleport via shadows (sorta. Technically you can take it as an alternate game difficulty but it's a buggy mess since the game wasn't designed with shadows in mind)I genuinely want to love this game. It has a lot of heart, and it starts off strong but... The longer I play, the more I just want to play the first game again. It's sad.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely beautiful. I was a huge fan of the original Aragami, so i was very pleased to see updated movement and parkour added! The customization options really add in the extra flare that I love when making my character as well. So much to work for and show off once you get it all unlocked. One of my favorite additions to the game is combat once youre  discovered. You can now Parry as well as dodge and attack in standard sword fights. Its very satisfying when you win a tough fight against some of the stronger units, and the game even allows you to build against stealth and more towards a dedicated fighter! Its all very satisfying and is an absolute cherry on top when you hear the soundtrack. This game will always be a hidden gem for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game from a friend of mine who is super into stealth games in general, and I wasn't super interested until she mentioned there was multiplayer so I was like you know what? Let's give it a try, and boy was it worth it.This game deserves so much more attention, definitely one of the better stealth games out there. While the multiplayer can be buggy, it didn't take away from the experience in the slightest. However, I do have two problems with this game.#1: The abilities feel a bit unbalanced. For example; there is one ability you can get that pretty much allows you to roll directly in front of enemies and not be spotted (There is no cooldown for rolling, just stamina).#2: This game needs much more content. All in all this game would have taken about 6-10 hours if we were not going for 100% completion.That being said, this game is still very worth it and I fully recommend it to anyone looking for a solid stealth game.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Having great fun with this. Major Tenchu vibes. Few little quirks now and then but overall absolutley loving the experience. If you liked Tenchu, get this one. Multiplayer is also a great touch.First one's story is a bit better and is a better 1 player experience as there's a few more tools to play with. But love the fact I can go through levels with a friend and have my own crack team of ninja, very fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Didn't play it very long, until now, but I LOVE it! It's such a good game and more than I was hoping for. The graphics are beautiful and even a bad PC can run this game very good. There are so many good new features and you can play it for so long before it will get boring! I can fully recommend this nice Ninja-Action[-Stealth]-Game!
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: My feelings regarding this game are a little complicated. I beat the first game just a night before starting this one and really enjoyed it, the stealth gameplay of it and absolutely having to be sneaky really appealed to me, and as did the art and setting. This game is not that game, but that doesn't mean it's bad, just different. This game is closer in style to Assassin's Creed or Shadow of Mordor than Aragami or Tenchu. It is super fun, Aragami is tense and methodical, this game is fast and punchy. Where it does stumble and fail however is the repetition, there are 51 missions in the game, and only a small handful of maps. Worst of all many of those missions are the definition of filler and should have been optional, but missions that boil down to (find 6 sacks of food) are somehow a main quest, and are the majority of them. Listen, if you want fun stealth gameplay that awards being sneaky, a fast and great parkour/traversal system, great artstyle, and a lot of content and can handle some repetition this is a worthy investment as there is a lot of content, but towards the end of this game it did feel like a chore for me. In the end I would recommend it, but with those important caveats above.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game has received a lot of hate regarding how the gameplay is nothing like the original Aragami, so the devs being as awesome as they are made a classic mode that makes the game as close to the original game as possible. on the mission board before you start a mission you can change between normal and classic mode.I wasn't going to make a review until i beat the game but when this update came out I knew I had to make one, this game is a great sequel with evolved gameplay, better level design, better movement, more collectibles, and more skills then Aragami 1, although it can get repetitive at times with playing the same 10 missions with different objectives over and over again. I 100% recommend this game to anyone who are interested in ninja games and that goes for aragami 1 as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR BUY the 1st game NOT this one. (IMO)Nothing like the 1st game. I understand this is a separate title and all that but the 1st game was great.This games combat feels clunky and the movement (for me) feels jarring.The lock on feature is extremely bad and I'd rather play without it (something like fighting unlocked in dark souls).I've also found when exploring the "hub" location that the terrain has gaps in it allowing you to see through it in places.Even when doing the 1st proper mission with the new leap system I found myself unable to teleport as I would've liked to and all these issues alongside the teleportation removal and the terrible combat with its lock on system make this game terrible compared to the 1st.

_childDocuments_.review: even after adding classic mode it still doesn't feel like Aragami. You can't leap to wall shadows. Half the time what looks  like  a shadow cannot be leapt to and what looks to be well lit CAN be leapt to. yet more clumsy, half baked development from Lince. all in all, still disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly disappointed.To me, there were two main things that truly made the first Aragami game so interesting and enjoyable: - The ability to easily create shadows and teleport between shadows, which offered an incredible amount of freedom and flow.- The cape that the Aragami wore, bearing the symbol of your equipped power and displaying any changes in your shadow essence.Scrapped are both of these great features, instead replaced by a restrictive movement set, a basic stamina bar, and a frankly drab-looking character. This is not to mention the numerous other things I've taken hassle with; finicky controls, boring combat, lacklustre abilities, a new contradictory and bland story... Perhaps I'd have fewer qualms were this a standalone title, however calling it "Aragami 2" is frankly taking the piss and is an utter disgrace to the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: THIS GAME IS PERFECT!I enjoyed the concept of Aragami1 but Aragami2 is everything I wanted in a game such as this. Coming from a background of dark stealth games: Tenchu, Dishonored, Shinobido, Sekiro; Aragami2 is now a solid part of this severely underrepresented theme.Pros: Fluid combat, movement and stealth systems. The shadow dashing feels very natural and weighty, and comes across as a well implemented blink/ grapplehook mechanic you'd find in Dishonored or Sekiro.The stealth kills have a decent variation to them depending on how you approach it. You don't have to kill but I'd rather.The ranking system feels fair and has good variation based on how you prefer to play.Level design: there are multiple ways in which you can approach the mission, there's a lot of freedom in this game. It feels really good.Sound design is nice, it glides well with the locations and dynamic moments so it all comes together as naturally as a film would.Combat: Some people say it's clunky but I'd argue that it's on par with Sekiro in terms of fun and flexibility. So far, after playing a few missions and entering into combat a few times the parry system feels great. Just time your block right and knock them off balance until their stamina is depleted so you can perform a fatality (or finishing blow).cons:Optimisation. Somehow despite the low res textures there's still some chunkyness happening on my pretty high end system. It's ok though it doesn't detract from the game itself so much.Bugs: Don't carry a body and then attempt to vault a fence.Limbs: Enemy limbs seem to stay intact :(Blood: Needs more ridiculous blood spray, the spatter itself is fine, there's so much of it and it's hilarious. Much like Tenchu 1 really. It's amusing and feels good :)

_childDocuments_.review: Minor bugs nothing game breaking. But the gameplay is great! Hilarious if you want to have a relaxed time playing multiplayer with friends. Or it can be a very intense parkour stealth game. Those two types don't usually go together in my experience but this game does it really well. 9/10 have finished the whole game. Sad the devs are having to disband ;-;

_childDocuments_.review: Steam really needs a neutral option for recommending games.  I played through this game co-op with a friend of mine and overall I would say we had a good time and the game was worth but, but my god I can't ignore the various bugs that just insisted on screwing up our experience.  As a stealth game it performs alright, nothing revolutionary but not bad.The main problems come from two big issues.  The first is the bugs that cause the game to just randomly not perform correctly, and i'm not even talking the desync between host / co-op partner.  Sometimes you use abilities and they just fail.  Throw your sword at a guy and teleport to him to execute him instantly? nah instead you just did an uncontrollable regular swipe and now he and everyone in range sees you and is pissed.  Trying to distract a guard with your whisper ability? sometimes it just goes on cooldown and nothing else.  Turn invisible to get in close to a guy and give him the stabbing? Invisibility just decides it isn't working today.   The fact that the skills can so regularly break is frustrating at best, and actively killed our play some nights simply because we got too fed up with a given stage.  Then there are the items.  You gather a pitiful flow of money through the game which can be used primarily on cosmetics and dyes for your outfit, but also for modifiers runes and consumable equipments (throwing knives, damage amps, healing items)  But they are all worthless.  The rune effects are lackluster at best.  Attack boosts when fully stacked won't give you a breakpoint to even kill an enemy one swing faster, and defense is pointless thanks to stun locking by some later mob.  The only rune effects that 'do' anything are essentially stamina recharge so you can run around more.  The consumable equipment is even worse, costing exorbitant prices per usage.  To kill an enemy at range requires a kunai, of which you can only hold 3, and they cost 200 gold per.  Problem is even at late game most stages are only worth around 600-800 gold.  So you can blow your payment for the mission to kill 3 people.  In stages with upwards of 60-70 enemies.  Or you can buy things like portals to warp back to town quicker at the end of the mission.  That will run you 900 gold to buy, keeping in mind you won't even make that much.  For this game to really earn a recommend, it desperately needs the bugs to be fixed, nearly 3 months on and this is just not acceptable.  Second, for the sake of the game just being at all satisfying or fun, the consumable items need a serious look at.  If I spent a boatload of money but the items were restocked every stage and I could screw around with em? sure that could be fun.  If the items were dirt cheap and using them was just a minor fee, I could accept it.  But the idea that you blow nearly 2 stages worth of funds to accomplish nothing? That is just a bad joke.  It's a shame really, I pushed a friend of mine to get this game because of how much I enjoyed the first Aragami and the fact that this game was so.... frustrating more often than fun is just really not a good feel for the game.  It wasn't out right offensively bad, so I wouldn't say folks who like stealth games should not get it, but if you aren't explicitly a fan of the style of game, I would never recommend this to most of my friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of very good ideas but bad execution. I really liked the first game and was hyped tfor the second but it sadly didn't deliver the anticipated fun. Being able to fight is cool but the controls feel uninuitive, especially online taking damage is sometimes buggy and the focus of the game shiofts weirdly. THere are no checkpoints in the levels and you only have two trioes, meaning you have to repeat the entire long level somewhat often making it more tedious than challanging. The addition of fall damage doesn't make sense, the new movement options are cool, but taking away the shadow jumpo and other old ones is clearly a mistake and the new controls also feel unintiutive as you arte sometimes really just searching your keyboard for the right button. But most of all there are no animations for stealth kills making them way less satisfying. Espacially the air kills just look buggy af because they only use the normal on ground kill animation and teleport you into it.Long story short: Great ideas, bad execution. If this was the first game than I'd say they improved a lot comparing it to the actual first game, but this feels like a downgrad. It's still somewhat enjoyable and I'll probably finish it, but I wouldn't recommend it

_childDocuments_.review: Keep in mind that I've played this game on xbox game pass. However, the game was removed today. I saw the 50% sale, and I picked the game up on steam. When I played the game pass version, I loved it. The game borrows HEAVILY from Assassin's Creed. But I don't see a problem with it. It's an indie company taking what they love about a certain game, and putting a fun spin on it in their own game. Every movement mechanic makes sense and I love just bouncing around in the hub world. Aragami 1 is a game that I love, but I believe that it's to slow to really make me feel like a badass. But Aragami 2 on the other hand, oh man. You just feel like a sneaky ninja taking down enemies while you shadow leap around the place. I also love the combat in this game, Aragami 1 didn't have a combat system and Assassin's Creed combat is just spamming mouse 1 until someone attacks you and you counter-attack to kill them instantly. Aragami 2 has a good combat system because it's really difficult to fight multiple enemies at once, but you will win most duels without a single hit. It doesn't overstay it's welcome but it feels so damn good to use.So, my verdict?The game is good. Would I pay 40$ for it? Not really. However, if this game is on sale, it belongs in your library. ESPECIALLY if you like stealth games and Assassin's Creed games.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished the game as of yet, but from what I've seen so far, I can recommend the game.I was a huge Shinobido and Tenchu fan and this game feels like the closest we've got to that on PC at the moment.You have a HUB where you come back after every mission and upgrade your character and purchase different items, then you go back to the board to accept a new mission. _childDocuments_.review: Right, now that I've completed the game, I can update my review. In short - the game is a VAST downgrade from the previous installment. In long terms? Here's a list.FIRST THE PROS (cuz its short af)-CO-OP play-more sneaky beaky gameplay-the skill tree is quite interesting and especially helpful for the stealth side of the game. Some skills are a tad too powerful, but that's related more so your skills-some of the maps are well-designed and aesthetically pleasing-the new enemy class variety is a strong upgrade from the previous game-the apparel you unlock at the shop bears a cool design, most notably the Oni setNOW COME THE CONS-the AI is very terribly designed. They will sometimes just detect you from across the map (and I mean that literally. It happened on multiple occasions), detect bodies hidden in grass, pathfind THROUGH walls, sometimes they hear from far away while other times you can perform a knock out mere meters away and they won't even turn their head-the aforementioned skill tree has some useless additions, too! The combat skills shouldn't exist - this is a game focused on stealth. Why can we have a melee brawl and survive it like it was nothing? - and some of those combat skills are pretty mediocre at best-your utility arsenal (kunais, grenades, etc.) is mostly irrelevant. Realistically speaking, the only weapons you need to remember bringing in are the sonic and smoke grenades, and needles. The rest is either combat-oriented (and again - the first game was all about stealth. Why ignore that fact in this game?), or just there to collect dust-and while on the topic of the shop. The essences you randomly get have such little impact on the game, you might as well remove them. Hell, some just straight up make you weaker-you are forced to dash at the beginning of every sprint, which is a damn big problem if you don't have a specific skill unlocked. One dash and you're 30% depleted on your stamina. Now take in account that shadow leaps and mid-air dashes all consume a hefty chunk of stamina, and you'll quickly realise how slow the game isin the first half-the parkour is SUPER buggy, especially on later levels. Last few hours of my play time consisted of my enemies fazing through walls, me fazing through walls, or bodies I had thrown fazing through walls. And if you're not fazing, then the simple movement mechanics like dash jumping causing you to grab onto the ledge instead of simply flying over (or the much more common 'forced into a cover lean instead of just walking around the corner), will irritate you throughout the whole game. Some objects also can't be teleported to/climbed on top of/jumped over because of their T H I C C collision boxes-speaking of the environment - most of the maps are very lackluster in their design. For such an expensive game I was expecting a damn golden gem, not... whatever we got. Seriously, the forest map should not exist, nor should the very big city-the first game was all about sticking to the shadows and night time raids, this game is all about broad daylight assassinations and enemies ignoring the menacing shadow figure right above their heads. Why the hell was such a massive and illogical change necessary?-the standard enemy class (the one that is littered everywhere) is laughably deaf and/or blind, so that's pretty lame. On the other hand, however, you have the resurrected undead enemies! Undead will hear and spot you from much further off, and the ninja class basically has wall hacks. Too bad their pathfinding is the worst in the entire game-now, I'm not saying the story of the first game was some god-sent blessing from the heaven's - beautiful, poetic, engaging, yadi yada - but this basically doesn't have a story. It's all told you line dialogue you WILL skip through, the occasional cutscene is somehow worse quality than the first (just my opinion. you can have yours, while I have mine), and the general progression of the missions is just "Huh?"-the last mission. Not just some nitty gritty detail, but I mean the mission as a whole. The map is somewhat poorly designed and buggy, the AI bugs out and doesn't move when resurrected, the fight cutscene was so horrible in more ways than one, and just that the 'fight' itself feels frustrating or boring-hidden achievements. Yep, this game has 'em. And that's not a bad thing in of itself, more so that EVERY achievement but the "Complete chapter X" is hidden. Quite annoyingOverall, terrible game for such a steep price tag. Linceworks, ya'll made an amazing first game, then butchered this game so hard, the studio shut down. Rip

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted Aragami 2 to be Aragami 1 gameplay wise, I didn't get that and I feel like this game is worth $15 or less not $35.I missed the shadow teleport mechanics constantly.I hate the hud, I want the No-Hud from the first where it tells you what you need to know on your little cape.The in-game currency is stupid, and the gold sacks you can find in missions are not needed.I beat the game with over 12,000 gold, only ever really buying the healing items and smoke bombs.Not enough armors to feel the want to buy them or just have them.A good chunk of bugs like flying when climbing a wall while picking up a body, camera issues, losing camera movement completely sometimes, at some point I crashed idk why.The game feels like Fetch-quest central. and when you do get an assassination quest, the targets are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nobodies, generic ass NPCs.and when evil guy is revealed the "New" NPCs you have to take care of are just reskins of the generic ones, and they don't give two flying ♥♥♥♥♥ about a dead body. So the game kinda gets easier when that happens.The enemy AI is completely stupid, they see a dead ally, run up to it and say well ♥♥♥♥. Then act like nothing happened.I got annoyed having to go back to the hub world just to run to some ♥♥♥♥ so that ♥♥♥♥ can tell me to go back to the quest board and accept a mission and go through the portal. Game is about 10 hours long or so and at the 6 hour mark I was so bored with the missions I started just running through them to get it over with.The 2nd to last mission was a little different with you holding a button to interact with a rock.... and you do that 7 times and kill 4 Necromancers.The last mission was a lame boss fight (and the only boss fight). what a let down.I will never play this game ever again unless a friend gets it and we ♥♥♥♥ around in coop.DEVELOPERS!You failed at making another Aragami game!But please don't let this prevent you from creating another one, or making extreme changes to this one.Hell i'd take a DLC if you made the gameplay mechanics similar to Aragami 1 inside it.I loved Aragami 1, not for the story, but for the fun and different gameplay mechanics you had implemented.

_childDocuments_.review: The actual mechanics work okay, but the quest and game design made me and my friend want to die. I played the entire thing co-op with a friend, and the amount of times we would burst out laughing over the fact they are throwing another 4 fetch quests on us was absurd. Not even creatively named, surely you can think of something better than "Help the People I", "Help the People II", and "Help the People III". These missions came after the supposed death of a major character I should mention. Could've named it something like "In their Memory" or "For ____". All of these repetitive missions also go on in the same 8 maps, which are used over and over againAlso, there are no objective markers for the items you need to collect until you get within urinating distance of them, and with maps as huge as they are, each level turned into a huuuuge scavenger hunt. We player through one most of the way and died, took us about 10 minutes. Second time around it only took us about 2 because we didn't have to scour every building for the last bag of riceWhat they probably should have done is cut the missions to 20, and then give you extra rewards for doing certain things in each level. _childDocuments_.name: Aragami 2

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is basically built on the concept of quantity before quality, it's a long game, yes, but you will feel like you've seen everything within the first 10 hours.Now how should I begin? Aragami 2 is definetly nothing close to Aragami 1. I preferred Aragami 1 in almost every aspect to be real with you. Aragami 2 throws away established lore of this universe, but is in its core still a stealth game. The aesthetic is still the same, but everything else has been changed, even though some things didn't have to be deleted. I think the story is far worse in this one, the combat is very clunky, the game is unpolished, rushed and too long.Aragami 1's unique design of putting the UI on the character is missing, its very cool looking stealth kills are mostly sped up or missing, but it doesn't feel as cool, because the Aragami just teleports its sword back into the sword holder thingy. They got rid of the teleporting and instead of encouraging active exploration you end up having a level system that you wont be able to finish 'til the end of the game. Cosmetics and color settings are nice tho.Aragami 2 is semi-open world, meaning that it isn't as linear as Aragami 1. Most parts of the map have multiple districts, which is why you won't be able to see them combined later. This semi-open world isn't memorable, most of the time you know where you are when you're in the level. Furthermore, this semi-open world comes with the flaw that they're forced to reuse the map again and again and again. The game is 51 missions long and at some point you dont see anything new. It's just supply mission after supply mission and I prefer Aragami 1's linear approach, each chapter had a different level with multiple parts to it.The worst parts of this semi-open world is the removal of checkpoints. You get 2 lives. Aragami 1 had checkpoints with no lives. There's a good chance that you try to finish a mission and then suddenly there's a boss, so you end up dying and have to redo the COMPLETE mission. This is terribly frustrating, especially when you consider that nowadays lives are considered old game design. How come Aragami 1 has a more modern approach than Aragami 2?The fighting system is a joke. I expected it. It's just parry a few times and then you get a few hits until the enemy dies. Now don't get me wrong, implementing a fighting system is a nice idea! Sadly, this fighting system only works against 1-2 enemies. You easily get overwhelmed and end up realizing that it isn't worth to fight in this game, it just drags everything down. Swinging your sword and instant kills are on the same button too, so if an enemy is suddenly out of reach you might end up attacking nothing and the enemy spots you. Enemy variety only gets fixed in the late game btw.The story basically ♥♥♥♥♥ on established facts and rules of the Aragami universe. The Nisshoku are mentioned once and never again. I don't think you need to make a direct continuation, but disregarding everything we know about Aragami and then mentioning a clan from Aragami 1 is confusing and makes no sense. The characters in this game are nothing more than just a bunch of 3D models with no soul. The game always mentions that a war is going on and that your characters are helping you, but everything happens off-screen. Rarely are they truly useful and not some words in a textbox. Out of 51 missions maybe 12 of them are story related, most of the time you just collect stuff, the leader says "good job" and the next supply mission starts. You never grow attached to the characters, even though the game tries to, but I can't remember most names. The villains showed up at the 15 hour mark, but never are they a real threat. I cant remember most names, everything seems so unnecessary. I cant grow attached to characters if there is a story mission every 4 hours. I don't feel like im a part of anything. I also want to mention that the 2 only characters who show their faces have no face animation. They talk without any movement and don't even express emotions. How can I take this seriously, especially after Aragami Nightfall that had the SAME problem? Are you just lazy, Lince?Aragami 2's biggest flaw (the quantity) is also noticable when it comes to abilities and items. You have 10 different items and 30 variations of them. You have around 20 abilities and 3/4 are passive abilities that automatically happen and are simple boosted stats. I never changed my approach because the game offers you only around 10 interesting items you might end up having fun with. Even Aragami 1 was better in terms of abilities, I dont want the game to do everything for me as I watch. Let me double kill and choose my target instead of automatically choosing one for me!The only thing I like about this game is the movement, it's way faster than Aragami 1 and doing parkour is fun if there wasn't a stamina mechanic.To sum it up:Aragami 2 is not even worthy to be called a proper Aragami game. _childDocuments_.review: If the header sounded like I was stuttering then yes I was. Let me explain.Aragami 2 is a janky, enjoyable mess of a stealth game that leaves me wanting more.  As someone who absolutely hated the artstyle and presentation of the first  game, I found myself at home with Aragami 2's pseudo Japanese style. It reminded me of Ninja games from the past like Tenchu or Shinobido. Levels are detailed and big enough to have a freedom of approach but things start to look a bit messy when seen from upclose. Low resolution textures, small gaps in the environment and white neon glow on your character are jarring to look at. Nevertheless it was a big improvement over the prequel. Aragami 2 leans towards Tenchu style gameplay while retaining some of its abilities from the previous game. To some people this might be a turn off. To me it was a welcomed change as the gameplay has become faster more fluid and exponentially fun. Darting through the sky and dropping on unsuspected victims never gets old. Using interesting abilities each with its own cooldown drastically improved my stealth gameplay to the point of killing dozens of guards in matters of seconds. You can chain assasinate two targets at once then using mesmerazing shadow power  stun guards who come and try to investigate and lastly finishing with a smoke bomb or a dragon consumption ability... to pretend that you were never there. Stealth gameplay in Aragami 2 is on serious steroids and I love it. However every light source must cast a shadow. As such Aragamis 2 melee combat is a janky mess that simply doesn't feel good. It reminds me of Sekiro, especially on later levels where enemies have more HP and getting their stamina bar to zero, just to get a chance at hitting them, is a chore.  Occasionally button prompts for assasination stop working and missing jumps just to fall through textures is not that fun. Luckily it doesn't happen that often and its nothing that a few patches can't fix in the long term. Story of Aragami 2 is told through various characters that will offer you missions. To put it in simple terms, you have to save  Aragami village from certain villans and find out the origin of Aragami. It lacks the presentation and style of games like Tenchu but for an Indie studio they've done a good job here.If you do decide to play CO OP then be ready to get your games ruined by some impatient randomers. I recommend getting a two player session, since the lag is not that noticeable and some levels weren't really balanced for many ninjas in mind.All in all Aragami 2 is a good stealth game that is dragged down by a janky combat, occasional bugs and repetitive missions. I am happy to recommend the game for anyone who likes Tenchu series or just stealth games in general. Just don't go in with high expectations. 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game  because I wanted to play a co op stealth game with my partner. I played the first game and thought the story was fairly interesting, but what I enjoy more is the setting and characters. Although it's an entirely different style of game play from Aragami 1, I have really enjoyed this game so far. It has its bugs and glitches, and some errors have lead to a bit of downtime, but the developer seems to be working on them as they get reported and they are doing their best. While it's not as complex as some of the AAA stealth games, it feels like a throwback to games like Tenchu and especially with a partner, there are plenty of ways to defeat enemies using a combination of the right timing and tools and sometimes just luck. Frankly, some of the things possible are just cool, and chaining kills together is really fun. The movement feels really fun too, especially at later levels when you regenerate stamina faster. Character customisation is pretty decent, and mixing and matching armour types and dyes can lead to some unique looks, even with only male bodies. The costumes have a lot of character and I especially enjoy the way things glow in the shadows. Let's hope they add some female armours and perhaps some more diverse locations in future updates and DLC. That would be all that's missing for me at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: UPD: The game added the second "gamemode" which made the game play much like the first one. It helped a ton and now it feels more playable and true to the original. Although the size of the location makes it much harder and unkillable enemies are still annoying, it is a massive improvement. Soma controlls still feel clunky though, but it might just be my inexperienceAfter spending 5 hours in the game, I had a certain negative impression, which you can read further. And, although the game itself is not bad, its main disadvantages, for me personally, outweigh the pros.Let's start with the pros. The graphics really got better, the game became more pleasant to watch. Having the ability to hang on ledges is just as nice. Different types of missions add variability to the game, which also pleasantly surprised. The system with the purchase of skins, that is, cosmetic equipment through in-game resources is pleasant, but not for me, although I see some advantages in it, for example, the selection of my own "look" in the game. Functional equipment (runes and consumable items) is new, and so far they look interesting, but there is also a big question about their use, which I will touch on below. The starting location is very nice and gives you the opportunity to just jump and practice the controls. Plus the interactivity with the NPC complements it. It's nice to see that the mission is given 2 chances, perhaps the biggest plus of the game at the moment, and the presence of HP allows you to make more mistakes. Having improved skills allows you to greatly customize the gameplay, which is also a big plus.As for the cons. The plot, so far, seemed weak to me compared to the main game, but this may change, so this can not be considered as a point. Where the main problems turned out to be is in controlls. For the first 5 hours of the game, Shift and Shadow Jump (f) are simply shortened compared to the first game. If in the first part the player had the opportunity to really jump across the entire map, on the edge of shadows, then in the second game you are limited to a short shift and ledges, windows, etc. (which takes away from the feeling of a shadow ninja. And although I didn't get to the later upgrades, I suspect that the ability to jump in the shadows of objects will not appear, and even if it does, the beginning of the game is very upsetting without it). In addition, bouncing off the wall sometimes does not work, or the controls are not intuitive. Often, hanging on the windows, instead of jumping away, I jumped inside the building. Later I realized how to "jump away" correctly, but it is extremely inconvenient on the keyboard and mouse. Stealth kills (executes), due to the fact that the combat system was added, were also cut off and now it is possible to kill from stealth only if there is a red circle around the target, which does not work on the principle of the proximity of the enemy to the character, but because of the camera angle (at least that was the impression)?? Murders from around the corner especially suffer from this problem, since the character sometimes just "peeled off" from the wall or could not "stick" to it, which was also very annoying. Bags of money were spawned in locations that could not be reached without being noticed, at least without some skills. The wheel of abilities and items are on the same button, which is why you often use the wrong thing (it would be better to either separate them, or give the opportunity to take only one type of items on a mission and record it on one button). And the items themselves seem very expensive to me (especially when they are used 90% by accident), although perhaps I have not gone far enough and the problem with the prices of items will be corrected. Also, some of the protrusions are simply not working, although they look like they are.In general, as I have already said, the game is not bad, but the control problems that I have encountered in the game at the moment are very frustrating. The most terrible moment was when I had to move the stunned target to the portal, I went down to the bottom of the map by accident and it turned out that I had to throw the target over a hole in the map (there was water there). Slightly wrong angle - my target fell into the water and the entire run (40 minutes without detection with all the murders) was reset)) After that, I closed the game and walked away from it for a few hours. In the stealth-action genre, controls are very important, and in this game it upset me a little, plus the "vibe" itself, the feeling of the game is very different from what I imagined and expected from the original Aragami. The main mechanics of the game were simply removed from the game. Therefore, as a fan of the first game and to the same people as me, who loved the first part and are thinking wether to buy it or not - I suggest you don't, you will probably be disappointed. Fans of the Assassins Creed series will like it more.

_childDocuments_.review: Aragami 2 is a better looking but far-worse sequel to a truly classic stealth game marred by and bogged down in confusing design decisions. And that kinda sucks. I want to preface what I'm about to say by saying that  It was a wonderful stealth game. Playing through the campaign with my friend was great. The levels were wonderful puzzles where stealth was the key, the abilities were interesting and impactful, and the enemies felt powerful. Points where they are deserved, Aragami 2 improves on a lot of my complaints from the first game, and I'm still enjoying the experience. The game looks wonderful, has a lot more detailed environments and characters and reuses assets less often. The story is easier to follow where the first game could get a little tangled. And of course, the animations. Aragami 1 looked kinda awkward, but the animations filled their role. The Sequel has some excellent animation. And the added movement options feel wonderful to use. We even get true cover options and tall grass to hide in. But that's where it stops. We ran into issues from minute 1. As soon as my friend and I finished the tutorial, we tried and failed to connect, he had some issues between his network an the servers that prevented him from accessing the game. After an hour of him fumbling around while i jumped around the ninja village, we posted in the dev discord and gave up on it for the night until we could fix it. while he was trying to figure that out, I found a half dozen or so places where i could fall through the geometry of the world—one of which resulted in a soft lock. Another idiosyncrasy caused me to repeatedly vault over a rock until i released the sprint key at which point you'd fall into the water and respawn. I also found a way to get passed this boundary and while it's funny to run under water for a bit, the rest of the bugs in this game aren't as silly. Two days after, we were able to get it working. His network blocks any connection to Russia for reasons and disabling that allowed him to connect. Which is weird. What could possibly needed to route from Russia when we're US east? regardless, we get to play. Aragami 2 is just not as compelling as Aragami 1. A large part of this comes down to worse level desgin; the guard placement and paths feel a little too easy to work past, and there are seemingly a lot of paths that aren't really even guarded. This is exasperated by the fact that maps get reused, blocking off some areas and changing up guard locations depending on the mission. We played through the first level on normal and the second on classic and stuck with classic. The shadow system has been gutted and it's kinda sad. No longer are we phasing through gates and levels are often much brighter which messes with the mood. Light is no longer dangerous, so that's one less tool in the level designer's toolbox. The other major issue is the combat.Honestly, I think the default left mouse sums up the change from 1 that I think could have ruined the game for me In Aragami 1, the left mouse button lets you create shadow the targeted location that could be used to hide in, teleport to, or use for abilities. In Aragami 2, the left mouse button is the attack button. This difference colors the entire game.If you didn't play one. Every single guard could 1 hit you at range by throwing a fast-moving blade of light from their sword at you. It honestly feels like they tracked you longer and farther in that game as well. They were . It was very much a stay hidden or die game, which made you feel like a badass every time you got the stealth kill. Even bosses which required multiple hits were still about finding your way in to hit them from stealth and then getting away again. Essentially, there wasn't combat. In 2, you can just fight them if you like. Thankfully it's not as obnoxious as assassin's creed's "parry, kill, repeat" style of combat. facing your enemy head on is still not good plan, but getting discovered is basically a non factor. You can mostly just run away because most of them have to hit you with their sword, while a handful use fireballs that are less accurate and slower moving than . The only times I was really in danger were if the guard i whispered decided to hop the wall i was hiding behind instead of walking around it or i accidentally got the attention of the sorcerers and the fireball hit me threw it and this completely robbed the tense feeling that 1 did so well. Another big difference is how the abilities are limited. Aragami 1 used a charge system while 2 uses a recharge timer. If you have ever played a game focused around stealth and tense slow movement, you know which makes more sense.If you play on classic, it's closer to what 1 was, but the guards are still easy to just run away from even if they do usually one hit you (I survived managed to survive a direct hit fireball with a sliver of health for some reason during one mission). That said, playing this mode doesn't bring back the full mechanics from 1, and I miss shadow summoning.The thing that actually ruined the game for me was a bug. I actually didn't see any of the weird boundary or fall through bugs in the levels, which was nice. This bug we—well, at least  ran into came after unlocking a second action through items or active skills. only I, being the second player, ran into this bug, but it ruins a large portion of the game. If i had multiple powers and items—which is available as early as level 2 or maybe 3—I could only use one of them. I'm still not totally sure on the effect. i noticed it first after unlocking the blacksmith and single use items. I discovered I could only use the vitality potion and could no longer access whisper, the first power. I also had the shuriken that I couldn't use. I originally thought it might have just been an item bug and ignored it because the items ended up being pretty unnecessary anyways. I used a single potion after accidentally falling off a high point. But unlocking the invisibility made it clear when i tried to whisper and turned invisible. To clarify, I could still select the other abilities, but attempting to activate them changed my power to whichever one was taking precedence and using that instead if applicable, so i could only have access to 1 ability.All The Small Things

_childDocuments_.review: Look, it's a 6/10; if you can live with the incredibly infuriating game-breaking bugs there's fun to be had. If they repair the serious issues, it'll be an 8-9/10. The game isn't complex enough to have a lot of moving parts so the things that have gone wrong are seriously fundamental to what you're doing.The game has a ton of glitches and bugs that are incredibly punishing in the stealth/never-get-caught genre. It's about 80-90% of the way to a polished, finished game, and if they fix the single most imporant bug (I'm not holding my breath; seems to be a fundamental part of the game) it'll actually be fun. How they took a step back from Aragami 1 (or even 1990s Playstation 1 games it's based on) I can't understand.The good: Animations are a little better. Leaping around into shadows and ledges like a ninja is still tons of fun. Multiplayer assassins is great fun. Skill progression is more dynamic and integrated into playing the game.The bad: Hoo boy.1, When you sneak up behind an enemy or near enough to one on a ledge, *most* of the time you get an instant stealth kill reticle which lets you execute your enemy. Some enemies just wont trigger, in which case they'll see you and set off an alarm (or stab you in the head *and* set off an alarm). This is essentially game-breaking as no matter how well you play, probably 1-3 times per mission enemies just wont die instantly no matter how well you play. As this is ***THE FUNDAMENTAL MECHANIC UPON WHICH THE ENTIRE GAME IS BUILT***, screwing this one up is unforgivable. Examples: you're hanging off a ledge, you lure an enemy over, you can't kill him and he alerts. You're hiding by a wall, an enemy walks by, the reticle doesn't trigger, and you wildly slash your sword initiating combat. Etc.2. Hidden bodies of enemies will sometimes just be visible through walls or grass to patrolling guards. Enemy alert AI seems buggy in this way. Congrats, you just went down a rank because some enemy saw his dead bro through 200 feet of cliff face.3. Some enemies that are meant to be lured by your essential/core skill "Whisper" wont respond to it. Guards of a certain type aren't supposed to respond to it, but patrolling guards are meant to and some are just missing the code to react correctly.4. Carrying a body and triggering the "leap over barrier" animation triggers an infinite, wall-breaking airborn floating glitch that is hard to break out of and often means a forced level reset. I'm terrified of low walls because of this. I have seen the void (and once rolled through an entire castle only to land in a pack of very angry fire guards).5. There is, for exactly no reason, a multi-second delay between murdering an enemy and picking the enemy's body up. After you kill an enemy the "E" prompt pops up to pick it up... you then have to wait about 1.5-2.5 seconds before hitting "E" does anything. Badly coded, quality-of-life issue.6. Stealth range (vision cones, sound range) is never well explained.7. Fall damage. What. In a ninja platformer there's fall damage for some reason.The reason I'm not confident these issues will be resolved is that they seem really close to the essential, root coding of the game and I doubt there are easy fixes here. In a genre where you're generally going for a perfect score, having seriously problematic issues like bug 1 above diminishes the fun by a good 50%.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the first installment, I'm puzzled by the sharp criticism surrounding this game. While the controls have shifted away from the original, resembling more of ninja stealth classics like the Tenchu series, it seems tailor-made to appeal to fans. Simultaneously, it retains elements from the first Aragami, resulting in a faster and more dynamic gameplay experience.You can play this game using both a controller or a keyboard, accommodating various player preferences. Additionally, the inclusion of the Classic Mode specifically caters to fans of Aragami 1, offering a mode closely resembling the first game's control scheme across all levels.However, the absence of a level editor, a feature present in the first game, is a noticeable drawback. Overall, it's regrettable that the studio faced financial troubles, as I would have loved to see further iterations of the Aragami series.Rating: Despite the changes in controls and the absence of a level editor, Aragami 2 offers an engaging experience that blends elements from its predecessor while introducing new dynamics. _childDocuments_.review: This is probably an unpopular opinion for the fans of the first game, but I very much enjoyed the change of pace in this sequel. The movement feels more natural, quick and fluid, and the new mechanics and powers are very satisfying to use. The AI has improved a bit as well, although still pretty dumb, but that doesn't ruin the experience at all. The story has been decent so far, but I might update this review once I get to the end of the game. If you're looking for something like the original game, this is  it. In the first game, stealth was absolute key in order to complete the levels, but in this one you have more freedom to create different playstyles. You can go full berserk (or "oni", if you will) and just engage in melee combat with every enemy you find (which I wouldn't recommend, but I'll get back to this later), be a pacifist and not kill any enemies, be an agile ghost that can complete the level without even touching a single enemy etc. The progression through the ability tree (where you can unlock new "shadow powers" and "passive abilities") is quite slow compared to the first game, since you level up slowly and only get  ability point per level up to spend on the ability tree, with every shadow power costing 2 points and every passive ability costing 1 point, but all of that is probably because Aragami 2 is much lengthier and the progression has to make up for that.The melee combat is just awful, with unresponsive controls, glitchy animations and just a general overload when facing more than one enemy at once, since the targetting system doesn't work like the industry standard and you have to press it too many times for it to target the enemy you want.The stealth system has seen a major upgrade from the original game, adding many new enjoyable possibilities. I don't really have anything to say about it, it's just great!This might be a bit biased since I already loved the art style and graphics from the first game, but the graphics have definitely improved a lot. The game looks beautiful! The lighting looks pretty and realistic, the shadows look great and work great for stealth gameplay. The textures and the visual effects look stunning as well.The animations during gameplay are fluid and satisfying to see. Although there are a few bugs here and there, they don't impact too much on the experience. I do have a major complaint about animations during non-cutscene dialogues, though: they look pretty bad, I think the developers could have polished the facial animations and such a lot more.Nothing extraordinary, but they bring you a nice and classic Japanese vibe. Generally enjoyable, with high quality audio.I don't regret preordering the game, since I've had a fun experience so far. I've seen people who refunded it due to it not being at all like the first Aragami, gameplay-wise, so bear that in mind before buying it if you're a fan of the original. For me, this game is a great choice if you're looking for something in the stealth genre, it certainly delivers that. If I had to give the game a score, it would be . Not excellent, not extraordinary, but a great, fun and enjoyable experience. Forgot to mention that, on launch, the game lacks rebindable keys, which is stupid, to say the least, since that should be industry standard by now. I forgive the developers, though, since they've taken notice to this issue and have announced a beta branch with this feature that's coming very soon.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the sloppiest most unpolished messes I have ever played. The game is full of bugs, actually hindering you from trying to do the stealth route. I played in coop the entire time and the amount of resets we had to do because of bugs or inconsistencies (like ranged enemies being onehit-able with Shurikens but then in another attempt surviving two Shurikens before getting into a downed state on the ground (but still alive)) is incredible. That's right, health bars are a thing now, combined with stamina bars for you and enemies so you can parry hits to get an opening for an insta-kill hit. Don't get me wrong, the combat system is fun (if it works), but after having thoroughly enjoyed the first game, a sequel seemed very promising to me. Also, seeing the Ninja, Stealth and Assassin tags kind of made me think I would get a game primarily designed with these ideas in mind yet it feels like the actual blade to blade combat was what they intended to be the key aspect/selling point of the game.When I complained about the bugs online, the community told me to "Just live with it, they have been there since launch" which shows an inability to fix these bugs or maybe it's indifference. However, unlike Sly, wherein the 2nd game largely built upon the first in all aspects, including the stealth mechanics, while drastically overhauling many of the core systems of the first game, Aragami 2 does not. If anything, it goes backwards in stealth while giving the player more direct combat capabilities. While it's a fun game, save for a few bugs, it is definitely not an Aragami sequel and your expectations going in should be as such. If the first Argami game was a stealth game, Aragami 2 feels more like an Action-RPG with better than average stealth mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: It is generally expected that a sequel has some resemblance to the game that came before it, and even make some improvements. Aragami 2 fails on at least one of those objectives. It is so far removed from the original, it might as well have been a reboot, though as best as I can tell, it was not. Regardless, getting into the meat and potatoes of this review, the  feels very generic compared to the original, as they completely butchered everything that made Aragami unique. Though the amount of  is vastly improved over the original. Meanwhile, the  is halfway decent, but it fails to make up for the remainder of the price tag.For a game where you play as, what can best be described as a shadow ninja, shadows don't really play a huge part in this. That is the single biggest criticism to be made of this game. Whereas shadows played such an integral part to the core gameplay of the original so much so that one of the earliest ability you got in the original, was the ability to make shadows, now shadows are so insignificant. Shadows play the exact same role that they do in every stealth game, that being that you can hide a little bit better in the shadows, but even that minor effect is taken away by the addition of tall grass which hides you better, and is in abundance on every stage. Furthermore, whereas in the original you had to regain shadow essence by sticking to the shadows, in the sequel it seems as though shadow essence is just a part of you. Your abilities no longer draw from any kind of pool of essence, they just go on cool down when you use them.The A.I. is relatively stupid as well, they might as well be saying "Must've been the wind" they give up searching for the player relatively fast. On one occasion I was spotted by a ranged enemy and he threw a fireball in the complete opposite direction of where he last saw me. The variety of enemies basically amounts to some enemies being stationary, and some having patrol paths. Furthermore, one of the A.I. behaviors that seems to have been removed in the sequel, is guards alerting other guards when they see a body, or the player. If there's some type of alarm system nearby, they will try to alert others. But in the original game, if a guard saw a body, he would just yell out to the other guards.The addition of a combat system, while being new, it's completely unnecessary and goes against the very idea of this being a stealth game. Why the developers felt a need to include a combat system in the sequel is unknown to me. I can't imagine who would buy this game wanting to explore the combat system.The one positive thing I can say about the gameplay, is that you have a lot of freedom of movement, You definitely feel like a ninja playing this game. For $10 that might be a sufficient experience. But for $30, I need more added to the gameplay.The one major improvement that was made over the original was the amount of game there is to play here. I completed the game in roughly 20 hours, whereas the original base game can be completed in 7 hours, with DLC included it goes up to 10 hours. Furthermore, the missions you find yourself going on are quite varied compared to the original. One mission you might be tasked with assassinating a target, another you might be gathering supplies or intel. And there are some missions where you're rescuing or kidnapping someone. This amount of content is definitely a vast improvement over the original.Here is another aspect where the sequel underperforms compared to the original. Overall, looking back on it, the story isn't that bad, but it fails to keep your interest as you're playing. I feel that one part of it is the amount of characters you're being introduced to as you play. Whereas in the original you had just 1 character you were in contact with, and the story was being explained through both her and flashbacks, in the sequel there's at least 3 main characters, and you don't really form an attachment with any of them.Beyond that, the sequel often conflicts with what you learn about Aragami in the orignal. For instance, an Aragami, being made of shadows, it disintegrates in the sunlight. Hence why in the original the story takes place all in 1 night. But in the sequel, there's multiple missions which take place in broad daylight. You almost begin to wonder why this game is a sequel to Aragami when it doesn't seem to follow any of the previously established rules for what an Aragami is.While the content is there, the gameplay just isn't. The only reason you might play Aragami 2 is to feel like a ninja. But beyond that there's so many other games within the stealth genre that are more unique in their gameplay. It's just hard to justify spending $30 on Aragami 2. You don't get much value from the story, the unique gameplay of the original didn't carry over, the one saving grace is the variety and amount of missions.  But that isn't enough to justify the price.Overall I would give this game a 5/10, if it went on sale for $20, I maybe could see that value being justified, but nowhere near $30.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a far cry different from the first, that is for certain. The branching perk selections are a nice step up from the original, especially because the abilities are unlocked through combat proficiency (whereas in the original you had to find hidden scrolls to unlock skill points that could be spent on abilities and upgrades). It's also nice that there are multiple profiles now; that way I can experiment with different perk trees and progress through the game at my own pace while maintaining a co-op profile geared more toward shared utilities that help us as a group, and have a single-player profile with abilities that only help myself. It could be from playing Aragami on the hardest difficulty prior to my play-through of this, but it seems that the difficulty for Aragami 2 is significantly lower. The controls for this are much more intuitive (you can jump around finally - yay!), and the combat mechanics are a breath of fresh-air from the first. In the original you physically couldn't duel any of the enemies because you're basically a shadow demon and all the enemy NPCs wield light magic; in this one, you can get a second chance to redeem yourself if an enemy discovers you: one good-ol'-fashioned sword fight where you can block their attacks, parry their blows with well-timed counters, and mash M1 until their health goes down. At first I was honestly a little bit disappointed with the combat because it is so different from the first (and all-too familiar from other games...), but overall it's not too far off from the first. I took the original as more of a strategic elimination puzzle; like chess meets Assassin's Creed. You had to be careful and plan out your eliminations in the original: wait for the patrolling guards to get into position for you to spring your ambush; there's a lot of that in this one, but it's mostly a matter of waiting in a patch of tall grass, or behind a fence; in the original I loved being able to watch from around a corner, teleport to a shadow behind the guard to take him out, and then teleport to another shadow. Biggest drawback right now I would say is the co-op; there are legitimately game-breaking bugs for online play that make the game not only un-fun but an exercise in futility: if you restart a mission, there's a high chance that player 2 will not be able to see stealth indicators on enemies and see which ones are spotting them or if they are about to be spotted; same with using shadow abilities that normally leave a status effect on NPCs as well as an indicator of how long that status will last. Additionally, the actions for assassination kills don't always appear on enemies after restarting the game; co-op players could walk right up to an enemy and count coup with them, but there is no prompt for assassinating them, so clicking the M1 button will just slash at them, which will always lead to the player being discovered. The only way around that is to stun the enemies with a one-time-use utility or a shadow power with a long cooldown - even though player 1 has no such issues.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is janky. It's got some weird animation glitches, occasional graphical hiccups and it's not the most visually impressive game out there, and every now and then the control scheme can fail you if you're not 100% precise in your movements.It's also the most fun I've ever had with a co-op stealth game. While it may not have the polish or reputation of Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, it has the same thrilling joy of coordinated, ghostly slaughter. When playing alongside a friend, with whom you're on the same wavelength, utilizing your skills and abilities in tandem, there's few games I've played as rewarding as Aragami 2.It's worth noting that it's a pretty significant departure from the gameplay and story of the original. Mechanically it's much more high-mobility, and instead of encouraging more deliberate, stealthy approaches favors a more high risk-high reward approach. Additionally, unlike the first game where you're almost certainly instantly dead if spotted at all, Aragami 2 gives you the tools to actually stand your ground and fight, allowing you to kill your way out of a mistake rather than returning to the previous checkpoint. Still, you're much deadlier when attacking from the shadows, and it's easy to get overwhelmed once spotted as enemies will call for help, so there's still plenty of incentive to play smart rather than simply playing aggressively.If, like me, you've been searching for a spiritual successor to Chaos Theory, it's finally here. Easily the best gaming purchase I've made in quite some time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me confused as to what year this was. It's obviously brand new, but the game design is straight out of the early 00s. The enemy AI is laughable, as are their patrol routines. They walk in two lines, patrol in a square, or stand in a single place without moving. They have no peripheral vision and are insanely stupid. It's almost like going up against the Chuck E Cheez band. They get around this by covering the levels in dozens and dozens of enemies, but this game is still extremely easy no matter what. Unless you try to fight things, at least. The combat is horrible. The game automatically locks on to the first enemy to attack you, which makes crowd control and getting away clunky as hell. The camera also shakes like crazy when swords clash. It's just purely awful. You're supposed to lower your enemy's stamina like Sekiro, but it feels like the lowest-rent knockoff imaginable. The missions themselves are all basically copy-pasted to death. There are 11 maps and you'll either be eavesdropping on enemies, stealing things, or killing enemies. There are 51 missions and most of them feel interchangeable. Only a few are actual story missions. The game is reasonably fun for the first 30 minutes or so, but I started getting sick of it quickly. It feels so insanely padded for no good reason. It's purely a quantity over quality thing. On top of that, the game's mechanics are unreliable. Assassinations don't work reliably unless you patiently wait for the prompt to appear. If you're trying to speedrun, you'll end up simply slashing at foes and alerting them to your presence instead of assassinating them. It's a crapshoot as to what happens when you actually aim for speed. The movement is solid and I really like the air dash, but the inputs for all sorts of things just don't feel all that great, as if there's a disconnect between you and the character.The game will also randomly decide you're not crouching anymore, so prepare to get spotted when your Aragami starts standing up for no reason. You can unlock skills and many are useful. Reducing stamina cost and adding invisibility upon dashing basically breaks the game, so you can just dash your way through missions without even being careful. One ability is supposed to assassinate a second enemy when you assassinate someone, but I could almost never get it to work. This is a really disappointing game with a lot of dated, unreliable mechanics that often don't work as they should.

_childDocuments_.review: In short:A sequel only in name, if you are coming into this game expecting more gameplay like the first you'll be left extremely disappointed, even the iconic freeform teleporting and creating of shadows is not in this sequel.What is there instead is a much faster and more open feeling sandbox that is an absolute blast to burst through due to the sheer amount of options available to you at any time. If I had to choose between the two I'd most definitely prefer the sequelGood:- Looks, sounds and feels great- The movement system is extremely open, especially compared to the first game, allowing you to (sometimes literally) soar throughout the entire map- Customization allows you to really adjust depending on how you want to play, almost all skills provide new options in one way or anotherMeh:- A ton of missions involve going to already explored maps but with a different objective, minor tweaks to enemy placement and new small pieces of the map opened up, expect to see the same maps a lot.- On the easy side of stealth games, especially when reaching the higher levels and opening up more abilities- AI can be questionable at times, especially in their yellow "aware but not quite alerted" state- Minor bugs such as the FPS limiter not properly working when set to 60FPS and mouse sensitivity glitching out after conversations (note: opening the ability wheel fixes this)Bad:- Performance on certain maps can tank, nothing unplayable but there are certainly dips on some of the bigger maps- No key rebinding (apparently being worked on but, atleast at the time of writing, not ingame)- The story is (atleast imo) meh and most missions more feel like side missions in any other game- Currently on launch face to face combat is near-unplayable when playing as a client in someone else's game due to extreme desync, stealth has no issues with this though and feels great-

_childDocuments_.review: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is a 2019 action-adventure game developed by FromSoftware. It was released in Japan by FromSoftware and internationally by Activision for the PlayStation 4, Windows and Xbox One in March 2019 and for Stadia in October 2020.Sekiro follows a shinobi known as Wolf, who attempts to take revenge on a samurai clan that imprisoned him and kidnapped his lord. The gameplay is focused on stealth, exploration, and combat, with a particular emphasis on boss battles. It takes place in a fictionalized Japan during the Sengoku period and makes strong references to Buddhist mythology and philosophy. Lead director Hidetaka Miyazaki wanted to create a new intellectual property (IP) that marked a departure from their Dark Souls series, looking at games such as Tenchu for inspiration.Sekiro received acclaim from critics, who praised its gameplay and setting and compared it favorably to FromSoftware's past work, although opinions on its difficulty were mixed. It won several year-end awards, including the Game Award for Game of the Year, and has sold over ten million units as of September 2023.During the late Sengoku period, the Ashina clan, led by Kensei Isshin Ashina, seizes a land rich in divine favor, including a foreign deity dubbed the Divine Dragon which can grant immortality through a bloodline dubbed the "Dragon's Heritage" and through the Rejuvenating waters and its mukade-infested Sediment. During this time, a nameless orphan is adopted by the wandering shinobi Owl, who names the boy "Wolf" and trains him in his ways. As Wolf grows up, Owl entrusts him with safeguarding the young lord Kuro, the last of the Dragon's Heritage line.Two decades later, the now-elderly Isshin is on his deathbed and the weakened Ashina is besieged by the forces of the Interior Ministry to finish the unification of Japan. Desperate to save his clan, Isshin's adoptive grandson, Genichiro, seeks Kuro to use his blood to create an immortal army. Disagreeing with his grandson's methods, Isshin has his private physician, Emma, warn Wolf so the two can flee. However, Genichiro confronts them and defeats Wolf in a duel, severing his left arm and capturing Kuro. Wolf is saved by a man called the Sculptor, who gifts him a prosthetic arm. To rescue Kuro, Wolf assaults Ashina Castle, where he meets Isshin and is given a new name: "Sekiro". Optionally, Sekiro can revisit his past; three years ago, Kuro's home was raided by bandits led by the shinobi Lady Butterfly, leading to Owl's apparent death. While Sekiro defeated Lady Butterfly, he was fatally stabbed by an unknown assailant and only survived after Kuro shared his blood with him.Sekiro again duels Genichiro and defeats him this time. However, he survives due to having used the Sediment to gain corrupted immortality and escapes. Afterward, Kuro refuses to flee and instead wants Sekiro to perform the Immortal Severance ritual on him, which would result in his death and eliminate the Dragon's Heritage. Sekiro reluctantly agrees and sets out to collect the necessary materials for the ritual, including a weapon that can kill immortals known as the Mortal Blade from the Divine Child, the last survivor of experiments with the Rejuvenating Waters. After collecting most of the ritual elements, Sekiro is confronted by Owl, who faked his death in pursuit of the Dragon's Heritage and revealed to be the one who stabbed him three years ago. If Sekiro renounces his loyalty to Kuro on Owl's orders, he fights and kills first Emma and then Isshin while Owl kills Genichiro. However, Sekiro then becomes corrupted by bloodlust and kills Owl as well while Kuro watches in horror, leading to the "Shura" ending.If Sekiro refuses, he kills Owl in combat and enters the divine realm to recover the final ingredient for the ritual from the Divine Dragon itself. Upon returning to the mortal realm, Sekiro discovers that Isshin has passed away while Ashina is under attack by the Ministry. Fighting through the chaos, Sekiro eventually finds Kuro under attack by Genichiro, who has retrieved another Mortal Blade. Upon defeat, Genichiro sacrifices himself in a ritual that revives Isshin in his prime so he might restore Ashina, a wish that his grandfather attempts to honor despite disagreeing with it. After killing Isshin, depending on the items gathered, three endings are available:- In the "Immortal Severance" ending, Sekiro performs the ritual as instructed, killing Kuro and making himself mortal again. Afterward, like the Sculptor before him, Sekiro spends his remaining days carving Buddha statues while keeping his prosthetic to pass on to someone else one day.- In the "Purification" ending, Sekiro performs an alternate ritual worked out with Emma's aid which has Sekiro sacrificing himself while freeing Kuro of the Dragon's Heritage. Afterward, Kuro prays at Sekiro's grave with Emma before departing these lands.- In the "Return" ending, Sekiro collaborates with the Divine Child to make her a vessel for the Divine Dragon's power. After defeating Isshin, Sekiro takes the dying Kuro to the Divine Child, who absorbs him into herself. The Divine Child and Sekiro then leave on a journey to return the Dragon's Heritage to its home in the West.Development of Sekiro began in late 2015 following the completion of Bloodborne's downloadable content, The Old Hunters. It was directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, who had previously worked on the Dark Souls series and Bloodborne. Sekiro draws inspiration from the Tenchu series of stealth-action games developed by Acquire and published by FromSoftware. The team initially considered developing the game as a sequel to Tenchu; however, it quickly outgrew the concept. Miyazaki intended the combat changes to capture the feel of "swords clashing", with fighters trying to create an opening to deliver the fatal strike. He and the team also created the game to be an entirely single-player experience, as they believed multiplayer to have limitations they wanted to avoid. Despite the game taking place during the Sengoku period of real-world Japanese history, no historical people or locations are featured in the game.The game was revealed via a teaser trailer at the Game Awards 2017 in December, showing the tagline "Shadows Die Twice". The game's full title was revealed to be Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice during Microsoft's press conference at E3 2018. The game was published by Activision worldwide, with FromSoftware self-publishing it in Japan and Cube Game publishing in the Asia-Pacific region. Sekiro's soundtrack was composed by Yuka Kitamura, with some contributions from Noriyuki Asakura. The game was released for PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One on 22 March 2019. A collectors edition was also released the same day and included a steelbook case, a figurine of the protagonist, an art book, a physical map of the game's world, a download code for the soundtrack, and in-game coin replicas. A port for Stadia was released in late 2020. On 31 October 2020, a free update was released that added new content to the game, such as new cosmetics for Wolf and a boss rush game mode.The word "sekirō" (隻狼) is a contraction of "sekiwan no ōkami" (隻腕の狼), which translates as "one-armed wolf." The subtitle "Shadows Die Twice" was initially meant to be used as a slogan for the teaser trailer until Activision requested it be kept for the final name.
