_childDocuments_.review: Everything is be 95% spoiler free other than mentions of some names.Overall it's pretty much your ace attorney experience with new characters, so if you've been playing ace attorney, it's gonna be a very familiar gameplay. This game is definitely more for Ace Attorney fans, but still playable for new players.Score: 8.5/10Gameplay mechanics:- Introduction to pursuing other witness' testimony felt slightly fresh although in the end it's very clear on what you have to do except maybe once on chapter 1.5. However I do feel like due to the tendency of player to immediately pursue another witness, they could have just made it that we could get clues when we actually decide to NOT pursue the other witness.- Judicial Assessment is another new thing in Ace Attorney Series. At first I was quite scared that if I actually pressed on certain testimony, I would actually get a quick guilty verdict for the defendants, but in the end it's just the same thing as Cross Examination, just toward the jury.- Sholmes Deduction Spectacular... or something. A mini-game for investigation, just like Pearl's magatama or Edgeworth's game with connecting clues. However I do feel like... having to listen to Sholmes (stupid) deductions and have it repeated again when we correct it feels even more.... tiring.- Personally I like the trials more than the investigations, but at the very least the game gives you hints if you haven't finished looking for everything yet (Thanks to Susato or Iris). But of course, there's no mention of what the clue is or what you need to present to the person.- The game is very forgiving when you do mistakes. 5 chances, refreshed after every trial part. Unlike some parts in normal Ace Attorney series, you get a life bar and it will be depleted each time you do something wrong, however there are times when the game would do major or critical damage if you would do something wrong in the normal game. Although you can just save and load the game, I feel that it made your decision to really be accurate and you must not miss at all. GAA doesn't have that at all and you're free to make mistakes if you want to and I kind of... feel that it's a bit of a miss.Character (Art, Character, Voice)- It has always been something with Ace Attorney character designs where the defense will always have wide eyes and the prosecutors having sharp eyes. I guess they're always trying to give the same 'Bright Eyed, Phoenix Wright'-like defense lawyer as protagonist. But then again given by the surname Naruhodo, the protagonist is literally the ancestor of Phoenix Wright, japanese wise. But also all prosecutors in ace attorney have always been hot, one way or another.- Maybe it's just me missing Detective Gumshoe but there's not many big and bulky character except 1.2 and  2.5. However they do have diversity of character designs, mostly from the witnesses.- Name changes still happen for english adaptations (aside from the obvious Herlock) but does not do much for the game experience (other than the obvious sholmes)- I'm only playing with English voice so I'm not sure how it sounds in Japanese, but I do feel like the 'Objection' part, at least doesn't leave as much impression as the old Ace Attorney games where Phoenix would just literally scream the word. Van Zieks' 'Objection', though does suit him very well but that might be me being biased. Judging from the videos I've seen on YouTube, they probably sound better (Especially with van Zieks being voiced by Tsuda Kenjiro)- Character breakdown after they do something wrong, especially the culprit's final breakdown after they've been exposed has always been something that most players are looking for, however perhaps due to the usage of 3D models, they're very limited on what they can do along with the expressions compared to their previous games with character sprites and animations all drawn by hand. Although the best Culrpit breakdowns do happen in 1.1 and 2.5, for me personally.- They try to put different British accents in the game so it is quite good for the diversity, although it might be a bit of a problem for those who might not understand them or even uses English as their second language.- If it's not obvious, I love Lord van Zieks, thank you very much.Sound and Music- Perhaps due to trying to match with the Britain's music back in the 19th century, the music feels quite lackluster compared to the previous games with more.. upbeat and perhaps retro sounding (which is considered modern compared to the ones in GAA)- There's no option to adjust the volume of music, voice, and sound effect. Only on or off. I wish there's a liberty for the player to adjust them to taste- They do keep the same sound effects from their older games like the shocking sound when someone says Objections or Hold It, the twinkling sound when someone realizes something, the sound when someone is shocked, and even the judge's gravel sound. It makes it even more nostalgic with the familiarityStory (No spoiler, just opinions):- The game is split into two parts. I personally find the second part to be better as things start to be in place.- Personally the best case which makes things fall into place so well is still 2.2 where I have no trouble in fitting the pieces together. It also has a good ending for not only the defendant, but also the culprit, I suppose.- Just like your usual Ace Attorney game, there will be times when you feel really stuck and you're not sure which exactly evidence to present even when I know which part of the testimony to pick. For me it was 2.3 right near the end, and 2.5 somewhere in the middle which was where I had to consult to a guide.- A lot of part of the story during the investigation really made me feel bored not gonna lie. I had everything on auto (except 2.4 and 2.5) but I guess it's because it's an unvoiced visual novel other than a few scenes and things like 'OBJECTION'Others:- I love van Zieks so much. He's actually much smarter than most prosecutors I've encountered in previous Ace Attorney games. I love his design and I sympathize him.- WTF, Herlock and No ♥♥♥♥, Herlock.-  Always. And I mean ALWAYS show your defence lawyer badge to everyone during investigation. For funsies. You might not know what you'll get (spoiler: a certain steam achievement)- I wish Wagahai would make more appearance in the game. But I guess she's replaced by the appearance of Toby in part 2 as she loses her significance to the story.- As usual, the game has one route only. Me personally I would be van Zieks' side because dude definitely needs a friend like wtf- 'YES!' is so weird. I don't know why they put it in the game, mostly in 1.1. But I suppose Naruhodo was still a greenhorn.- They actually put some inside jokes for Ace Attorney fans as easter eggs. I find them endearing.TL;DR. Your usual Ace Attorney game with new characters. Not my most favorite Ace Attorney game, but enjoyable nevertheless. Van Zieks I can be your brother yes.Score: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: "Suspended disbelief, never heard of it...."Overview: A beautiful and fun story game if you're chronically bored (and possibly masochistic), and you enjoy sitting through 30 minute stints of bizarre dialogue before you're allowed to present the clue you figured out 5 minutes into the current section of the story...  "Suspended disbelief, never heard of it...."[Long form review bellow, quick checklist at the very bottom of the review]I first came across this game years ago while browsing for highly rated community games. With 94% positive reviews, I added it to my wishlist, however the high price at the time kept me from pulling the trigger. I had seen some sales come and go that almost tempted me to jump in, but it wasn't until yesterday Steam finally got me! :-DBackground---- I am not familiar with the franchise, so I came into this game a complete newbie. I have played many story based, visual novel type games, and I've enjoyed everyone I've played so far. I also am a big fan of mystery/puzzle games. I cut my teeth on classic Adventure games like Kings Quest, The Secret of Monkey Island and Discworld. Based on what little I knew about Ace Attorney, the glowing reviews, and my past history, I started the game.The Game---- You're treated to a beautiful animated cut scene introducing you to the world you'll be occupying for the next 5-6 hours as you navigate your first case. The intro is captivating, and I applaud the writers choice of introducing the game mechanics in a Japanese courtroom during the fall of Sokaku, the Japanese period of isolation from the Western world at large.As the concept of western legal proceedings was new to the Japanese people during this time, the sets the perfect pretext for character dialogue to explain game mechanics, and how trials work, without ruining the immersion of the story. In my opinion, an early indication of any truly great game is how intuitively you are introduced to the world and the mechanics. With that said, while the story flowed well initially, several mechanics were awkwardly shoehorned into conversations over the next few hours of game play. These new mechanics often felt forced and out of place.I found often I would realize I have discovered something relevant to progressing the story, but I was unable to do anything with that until 30 minutes later a new game mechanic would be introduced that would finally allow you to act on the item you figured out a lot sooner. I soon found I had been "trained" to view all new information as part of a formula, I just needed to wait until the game presented me with the question I needed to plug in my answer.The result of this is you begin to loose the story. I found myself no longer caring about the dialogue, the characters, or anything else that was happening. I knew the next thing the game was going to ask me to progress, my job now became hitting the space bar as fast as I could until the prompt finally came up for me to enter my newly discovered information. Unfortunately, that usually involves sitting through 20-30 minutes of often repetitive dialogue before you can proceed. This ultimately becomes the fatal flaw with Ace Attorney, at some point the story becomes the gatekeeper preventing you from moving to the next step. A great novel game ensures text/dialogue is always nourishing you, building tension, compelling you to root for the protagonist, misdirecting you for future surprises, and most importantly of all, a great novel game must excel at suspending your disbelief.Suspended disbelief is crucial to every story ever told. You've probably experienced how jarring it is to suddenly realize the movie you've been completely engrossed with for the past hour suddenly makes zero sense. I remember watching Star Wars: The Force Awakens when it came out in 2015, and specifically, the exact moment when Rey, who picked up a light saber for the first time about 6 minutes ago, defeated Kylo Ren in a light saber battle..... Kylo Ren, who had been trained as a Jedi his whole life... defeated by someone who just picked it up..... WTF?! I remember thinking "this makes absolutely zero sense at all...." I mean, Luke, who at least had some training with Yoda, lost his freaking hand when he battled Darth Vader, and yet here comes Rey who magically stomps all over the super villan in about 8 seconds on her first attempt.... it makes no sense at all.Not the magical mind control powers, the Faster-Than-Light spaceships, or any other of the totally ridiculous things that occurred for the first two hours of that movie.... nope..... just her sudden proficiency with a light saber..... Which goes to show how absolutely crucial the suspension of disbelief truly is to a great story. When done well, you are pulled deep into the narrative world the author has created for you to enjoy. No matter how magical or bizarre, you accept whatever is laid at your feet and become a citizen of the universe that is presented to you without questions.During the first case, the plot holes in the mystery, the formulaic dialog progression, and the forced game mechanics all combine to ruin the suspension of disbelief, and make you all to aware that you're not interacting with a great story, you're simply playing a game and mashing a space bar to get to the next step. In the end, Ace Attorney feels much more like the man behind the curtain than the Wizard of Oz, which I found very disappointing given how long I have waited to play this game and all the glowing reviews.If I was able to refund a game 5 hours in I would have with this one. With that said, since it's mine now, I'll probably try another story to see if they are able to pull me in.❤ Audience ❤ ---Casual Gamer☼ Graphics ☼ ---Beautiful♬ Music ♬ ---Good☠ Difficulty ☠ ---Easy to Average§ Bugs § ---Very Minor☯ Story ☯ ---Decent but multiple plot holes ruin the immersion ⚔ Gameplay ⚔ ---Frustratingly long$ Price / Quality $ ---Buy on sale or pass, many other great story games out there!

_childDocuments_.review: After many years of waiting, we finally have The Great Ace Attorney available officially in English. I honestly thought we’d never see the day, but I am definitely not complaining now that they’re finally here!The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a collection of two games: The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures and The Great Ace Attorney: Resolve. These two games are spin-offs of the main Ace Attorney series and take place in the Meiji era (late 1800s to early 1900s) rather than the near-future. The two were first released on the 3DS in 2015 and 2017 and were never released outside of Japan. As such, this is the first time we are seeing them officially in English in any form.These games are basically full-blown visual novels with some light gameplay additions thrown in. The vast majority of your time will be spent simply reading text, but the gameplay elements that are here are pretty cool – letting you take part in investigations, presenting evidence in court, pressing witnesses for information, and generally just being able to move around and interact with the game world.The Great Ace Attorney takes this gameplay up a notch compared to the original games. The same core “investigate for evidence, find contradictions, present evidence” system is all there, but now you have a jury to worry about and you’ll need to swing their opninions in your favor by pitting their own words against each other. It’s like a regular cross-examination, but with an additional layer and it was pretty cool in practice.In general though, the gameplay here is still not too complex, but a nice step up from what I was used to with the main games and it gives the story that touch of interaction that it needs to keep you involved.The first case is a bit slow to get going, but once it does, it really hooked me. In fact, that was pretty much every case after that point. They each follow that same steady rise in pacing as they go on and get more and more complex. What you think happened at first is never quite right and the twists and such are both ridiculous, yet feel right at home in this series and some of them really caught me off guard with how well executed they were.The third case in particular takes a very interesting turn towards the end that is quite unlike any other case across the entire series. It exemplifies all that I like about these games: pacing that rises and falls naturally with each development, characters that actually have... character, and mysteries that are somehow 10x more complicated than they look. Each case is a journey in itself and I’m happy that these two games were able to maintain that same level of quality from the main series.The games also manage to have all of these serious cases and crimes to solve, but never lose that lighthearted feeling. There’s the ridiculous character quirks, the dumb one-liners, and I really love how this series is able to make references to itself even when its not necessary. I laughed out loud when I found out who the first prosecutor was – because of course they had to make him the same as the one from the main series but bill him as an ancestor.It’s the little touches like this that really give the series its unique feel and I know some may say this makes it hard to take seriously, but the story can get serious when it wants – it just knows when to do so and can actually manage that balance there.You can expect around 60-80 hours for the two games combined. The second game is longer than the first, but they’re both fairly meaty visual novels and are comparable in length to the recent Ace Attorney Trilogy release despite that one containing three games instead of just two.The collection is hard locked to 30 fps but does support higher resolutions. I played them on both 1440p and 4K and the 3D models and such look great and I didn’t have any technical issues there. Control-wise, the collection plays fine on both controller and keyboard and mouse – the latter of which is rebindable.Simply put, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is the best visual novel release of the year. It takes all of the series’ strengths, throws it into a new and interesting setting, and delivers an Ace Attorney experience quite unlike any other. On-point writing, excellent comedic balance, gameplay that is actually interesting – it’s got pretty much everything and is an easy recommendation for fans or even newcomers to the series.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: This duology manages to strike a great gust of fresh air into the franchise, elevating the series to even greater heights than the original trilogy managed to achieve all that time ago.  The extra focus given to developing grounded, believable character relationships shines especially brightly here, leaving you feeling far more attached to the narrative and cast as a whole; it undoubtedly makes every well-earned revelation even more impactful than you'd expect from the series so far. I think the series could be a great entry point for new fans, too. Don't feel like you have to play all the other games to give these two a try: you can easily approach these as if they're a soft 'reboot' of Ace Attorney as a whole. Something, truthfully, the mainline games have been crying out for for some time. I'll be looking forward to a third game, if it ever arrives!

_childDocuments_.review: An Ace Attorney collection truly worthy of its name. Certainly the closest the series has come to matching the quality of the original trilogy. It has all the components for a great Ace Attorney game: It's got an interesting plot with an overarching mystery over the course of the duologyIt's got great characters who are always likeable and entertaining (making Sherlock Holmes a comedic relief character was a bold choice)It's got good puzzles, with no solutions that are absurd reaches (something the rest of the series is a tad infamous for)There are only a few things I criticise the game for. One for the amount of repetitive and unnecessary dialogue, which is never more prevalent than in the Dance of Deduction sequences. It really slows the game down, especially since the dance of deductions are so easy.Another is the fact that while the mysteries are interesting, it seems that the writers struggled to fit the discoveries in the courtroom format. This leads to witnesses and jurors sometimes saying completely irrelevant things to keep the plot progressing forward.

_childDocuments_.review: The Ace Attorney series has been around since 2001, We've seen the story of Phoenix Wright, Maya Fey, Mile Edgeworth, Apollo Justice and the many characters that span throughout all the games. But now we get a look into the story of Ryunosuke Naruhodo, an ancestor to Phoenix Wright who starts his career as a defense attorney in England during the 19th century.The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles contains two games, The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures, and The Great Ace Attorney 2: Resolve. Both were first released for the 3DS back in 2015 and 2017, now finally getting a official localization with a few name changes due to certain characters from existing media being in both these games.To keep this review from having any spoilers I'll keep it as brief as possible.Story: 10/10, both games easily have one of the best stories in the whole AA franchise, with the second game being my all time favorite (For a long time it was Investigations 2)Music: 9/10, these games have some banger tracks that are catchy as hellArt: 9/10, character designs really stand out and are pretty interesting, backgrounds are really detailed and look so goodCharacters: 10/10, what these games do that past games don't is that they make every character interesting and likable, whenever it's the main group, the antagonists, hell even the side characters, their all just so fun to watchIn conclusion, to anyone who likes the Ace Attorney series these games are a must play, and are definitely the best in the series.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this now, I just finished the last case of The Great Ace Attorney : Resolve and decided to write a short review now just out of sheer love for this game.Now to get the obvious out of the way, my recorded playtime is way too low to have possibly gotten through the entirety of both of the games. _childDocuments_.review: The eight Harry Potter movies total over 19 hours. The six extended versions of the Hobbit and Lord of the Rings movies all together are 20 hours. All eleven Star Wars movies put together are 25 hours.So this first "Great Ace Attorney" game has no right to clock in at 30 hours (according to  it somehow took me 39 hours - maybe I left it paused for a while?).Don't get me wrong; there are five cases here, and some of them are rather good. (I personally liked cases 1, 3, and 5, but felt that 2 and 4 were disappointing wastes of time.) The problem is that they are . So very much text to wade through; the characters have leisurely side-conversations at length about every little thing. Yes, I know this is so that the player might not notice that small facts mentioned here and there might become important in a case later, but still. For a completely linear game where all you can do is get through all the text from start to finish, I could have spent my time better than by sitting here for 30+ hours watching Sholmes being daffy, Iris being precocious, and Susato being guarded. Time and time again I thought I was finally on the way to seeing a case wrap up, but no; there would be a curveball thrown, Naruhodo would again find himself on the verge of losing, and the entire case would be run through again from a slightly different point-of-view.I've played several of the Ace Attorney games and have really enjoyed them; my favorite parts are the courtroom scenes where I get to analyze statements, compare them with evidence, and find contradictions in them. So I was disappointed that so much of this game occurs outside a courtroom. (I think episode 2 doesn't even have a courtroom in it at all.) There are plenty of places where a plot point is visible hours before the characters start mentioning it in dialogue, and that's always frustrating. It also has a few leaps of logic that don't really make sense, and a few places where to make progress you need to present a non-obvious item at a non-obvious point during witness questioning, so having a walkthrough to refer to is a must. says that Great Ace Attorney 2 is even longer than this one by four hours, so even though it'll doubtlessly bring answers to the questions left open in the first game, there really are more fun things to do with my time.I miss the days when an Ace Attorney game took around 20 hours. I think that's a much more reasonable length: all of the turnabout without all of the fluff.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow!  This game is amazing.  Extremely funny.  Keeps surprising me.  Totally off-the-wall storytelling with lovable characters. _childDocuments_.review: Few games bring me more joy than a new Ace Attorney game, so a recommendation is obvious.  There's a lot going on with this game that's different than the usual fare.  It's a prequel series to start with, taking place a hundred years before the other games, and takes place in London.  Also, Capcom dropped the ball immensely by not localizing the games when they first came out.  In slight compensation for years of neglect, you get both games for the price of one, which is 10 cases and 70+ hours of content.  The PC release is also appreciated.The stories are pretty good as always.The gameplay is the usual fare with very minor additions.The graphics are a clear tangible improvement from previous games.  Despite losing a step when they transitioned to 3D a couple games back, characters and animations look really good this time around.The music is wonderful as always.That's not to say everything is perfect.  There's probably more flaws in this pair of games than any of the others in the series.The games are far more tightly coupled than any other games in the series before.  The other games follow a pretty rigid formula - case 1 is a tutorial, case 3 has nothing to do with any of the others, and case 2 and 4 combine for a big finale in case 5.  These games almost ignore the formula and you might as well consider them just one big game.  Case 5 in the first game ends not with everything wrapped up but with loose ends everywhere.  Had these games came out separately years apart I would have been rather disappointed with the first half, but fortunately you can just jump straight onwards into the second game now.But as a result of the game being essentially 10 cases, there is a ton of reuse through the game.  The same characters and locations and music come back over and over, which can be a little fatiguing.  Even Edgeworth Investigations got a different full complete soundtrack in both of those games, but the soundtrack is shared here so even the best music can get old when you hear it again and again in every trial and investigation.The new gameplay gimmick sections are kind of weak also.  The deduction sections with "Herlock Sholmes" are far too obvious and often go on too long.  The jury system in trials is extremely weak.  The summation examinations are thematically rote and predictable, instead of being a last gasp to turn things around they become expected and annoying when the idiot jurors swallow the clearly flawed arguments.  And you'll notice most of the jurors rarely speak again afterwards for the rest of the case so their presence barely matters.I also really wish the ability to skip text was on for the entire game by default, so you could accelerate the rate at which you read through the game's avalanche of dialogue.These weaknesses don't matter in the grand scheme of things.  They detract only slightly from the huge enjoyment you will get throughout.

_childDocuments_.review: Up-Up-Update: oh f**k it, despite it's flaws the story is great, and I've come to love these characters. 10/10.Up-Update: the climax of trial 5 is so bad, it's a disgrace. As some point a familiar character delivers a piece of evidence left behind by another familiar character, and the initial excitement for this development rapidly goes down the drain as you realize how badly the story falls apart from there. Spoilers:The crux is the real killer couldn't have seen what happened behind the door because the peephole didn't exist until Susanto created it with Iris' invention. The problem is, during the animation for the discovery of that crime scene, which we are led to believe to be as true as can be, Susanto was pre-occupied with helping Shomles who was injured, and Naruhodo was able to see the crime scene through the peephole that was already there. The game literally shows Susanto not making the peephole but then pulled that out of its butt and to claim "oh actually it definitely happened."Think I'm nitpicking? When the judge give you one chance to prove Graydon is the real villain, the right choice is apparently to prevent Iris' catdoor maker. I can only assume the logic is that the device can make peepholes, so the peephole wasn't there earlier, but THERE'S LITERALLY A PHOTOGRAPH IN THE COURT RECORDS SHOWING THE DOOR WITHOUT PEEOPHOLES! Having a catdoor maker doesn't mean it was used to make the peephole, but the photo is concrete evidence of the peephole having been made after the crime, so the game's preferred evidence is actually not logical. When asked how we know the peephole was really made with iris' device, she just claims "the peephole's size is exactly the same as my device", when at no point in the investigation progress did anyone notice that, no one even took a measurement of the peephole, or the device, but how she magically knows the exact dimensions.What a shame, the story was so intriguing up to now, and it crashed and burned into a dumpster fire of just sloppy game design and messy storytelling. I love Ace Attorney, so I've been giving this game a thumbs up till now, but the climax of the finale is so disappointingly bad it has to be thumbs down now.Update: the end of the first trial in Britain has completely turned around my opinions of the game. I'm fascinated by how the story will progress and applaud the writers for such an interesting cliff hanger.My original thoughts: THE FIRST CASE IS A F**CKING DRAG. It's filler after filler of dialogue, literally, what I just sat through:Judge: "What exactly is this [evidence] telling us this?"Player: "... Everything, Your Excellency."Prosecutor: "Everything?!" (shock emoji)Player: "Yes, I believe that these [evidence] in the [evidence] here..."(Pause)Player: "... amount to conclusive evidence in this case..."(Pause)Player: "Evidence that will prove beyond any doubt who [did the crime]!"Witness: "Shut up!"(Pause)Witness: "Conclusive evidence? How many times have I heard that today?"(Pause)Witness: "You wouldn't-"SHUT THE F**K UP! ALL OF YOU STFU!Phoenix Wright's first case was also easy, but it moved fast, that whole trial took 30 mins tops and gave you all the basics of how the game is played. I'm 2 hours into the first case of this game and my space key is halfway in hell from how much I'm spamming it trying to skip the UNSKIPPABLE FILLER DIALOGUE!Maybe it's designed for newcomers to the AA franchise, but unless a ton of nematodes are picking up the series for the first time, it's easy to the point of insulting. Normally if I feel dumb playing an AA game it's because I'm stuck on a hard puzzle, here I'm feeling stupid by proxy because all the characters wouldn't know 2+2=4 if you don't write it up on a whiteboard and shoved their faces into it.Giving it a thumbs up only because I'm such a big AA fan I want Capcom to keep making these games, and I'm curious about the lore, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the first level is a masterclass of sh*t game design. Whoever is responsible is found GUILTY and hereby sentenced to replaying the third case from every AA game repeatedly for a year!

_childDocuments_.review: A great take on the AA games, The Great Ace Attorney follows the same trial formula with some new twists. It breaks up the investigation and trial sections neatly, adding a breath of fresh air, along with some nice quality of life improvements. It follows a fun cast of characters who keep things entertaining-- including the legendary Herlock Sholmes!From Japan to England, rookie defense lawyer Ryunosuke Naruhodo's cases range from simple to anything but. You'll have a great time yelling OBJECTION! and enjoying the old fashioned English dialects from the colourful characters you'll attempt to wrangle into submission. Fans of the original AA games will have a blast revisiting the courtroom, while new players will get to start entirely fresh with new characters, sleek play concepts, wonderful art, a developing storyline, and a beautiful soundtrack.If you're looking for a game without much gameplay required, then Great Ace Attorney is a wonderful way to chill out and play with little spoons needed. I enjoyed it a lot!

_childDocuments_.review: A must have game for the Ace Attorney enthusiast. _childDocuments_.review: I’ve played every English-translated game in the Ace Attorney series (including spin-offs) except Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice, so maybe my word won’t have the same bearing as another Ace Attorney fan’s would. But I will say that I think The Great Ace Attorney is one of the best games in the series, if not the best.Maybe my memory fails me since it quite literally has been more than a decade since I’ve played most of the other games, but I’ve never felt any game in the series has a story that’s so intricately and carefully woven as this one. Loose ends I thought they could never neatly tie were mostly covered by the end of the series; I was especially impressed by how flawlessly the second game flowed after the first. I had expected the second game to either have a storyline that was completely divorced from the first one, or for it to feel like an afterthought. It felt like neither of these things; it felt like it was planned from the very beginning to be a two-game series, and I mean that in the best way possible. It never felt rushed or like it was just putting filler in; it knew it’s pacing well and stuck with it for an absolutely wonderful finale.I would remark more on the wonderful balance between ridiculous comedy and tense drama that the dialogue has, but that’s honestly just a mainstay of the Ace Attorney series rather than a specifically GAA thing. The writers of this series present a masterclass of visual novel writing; they know when to pull punches, and they know when to hit hard. And boy did they use it for this game.The (relatively, for an Ace Attorney game) small cast of characters had such strong personalities and were endearing. I really cared for a lot of them, and I even felt a lot of sympathy for a lot of the ‘criminals’ in the end. Everyone felt like a fully conceived character with motives and aspirations, and I really understood where they came from, even when I didn’t agree with them or their actions.The music is phenomenal. Not only because of how it sounds because hey, it does sound great, but because of how it was used. I can’t say much on this because I don’t want to spoil anything, but there were several times a leitmotif began playing when I didn’t expect it to or there was an emotionally tense moment in the story, and it made me absolutely lose my mind. You can tell the composer paid very close attention to the script and worked with the writers, and it just… really made my experience.I was glad to see the classic mechanics were still being used. It’s always nice to have the familiar trial and investigation sequences to get back into the series. I was fascinated by the fact that the first GAA game didn’t necessarily follow the usual sequence, though. The sequence I usually expect is that the first episode is purely the trial, then the subsequent episodes are investigation-trial-investigation-trial. They revert back to that in the second GAA game, but it was refreshing that the first GAA didn’t follow the formula.It made me laugh that the jury system was brought back, it just brings wonderful flavour to the games. Sholmes’ Dance of Deductions were a nice addition to the investigation sequences, but they did drive me a little insane towards the middle of the game because you kind of have to sit there internally screaming while listening to how Sholmes is wrong at first, and THEN you have to sit through it AGAIN to correct it. I’d say eventually they were worth it to see the last Dance of Deduction, but I did wish there was a way to expedite it a little.I could go on a lot more about what I loved about this game, but I’m so scared of spoiling it for people. Most of the fun of these games is getting to the bottom of the mystery after all.  I am definitely extremely biased, but I think that the Ace Attorney games are the king of visual novel/puzzle games, and The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a must play addition to the series. Also, ultimately, while I’ll miss the cast, I hope they never make another GAA game. It’s a perfect package already.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay I like the game so far, it has some cool new features to the old games, and as usual the story is compelling and the characters likeable.I'm on the first case, but what I really don't like is that in the first case, while the other games weren't always steeped in realism, it at least remained grounded. In the first case we have people lying on the stand, and proven incorrect, which should have their testimony discarded but they just ignore it. Then even more shockingly, a "witness" takes a piece of evidence and destroys it in while on the stand and basically says, "HAHAHA now you will never know cause I destroyed it" which should be an obvious sentence of guilt, but they just ignore that too.I hope this gets better or I will be changing my recommendation of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Phew. This game is a bit of a drag, I won't lie. Compared to other games in the same franchise, it's pretty slow. There are some interesting things pulled from history here and there, but the game is way more dialogue than actual "game" where you get to connect the thoughts. There is like 30 minutes of core dialogue until you get to actually interact and gather actually pertinent information. I find myself putting this game on auto and doing chores before making another decision that will take a bulk of time to say nothing.The opening act was interesting, but the nonsense to entertain quickly fell off by episode 2. And yes, I also wanted to nap in the middle of these games. Good lord, sitting through the full deductions just to turn the camera 15 degrees and click something an inch away is a bit groan inducing. I only recommend this game if you're not an overthinker and like watching silly displays. Even then, I feel the older Ace Attorney games are a bit more to the point for that. I'll let this slide this time only because I think they're trying to experiment with more content in their games since departing the DS days.

_childDocuments_.review: During the six months that passed since I first completed the Chronicles, and the inclusive two months since I returned to get the rest of the achievements, I have gotten around to completing the rest of the Ace Attorney series, from the Investigations duology, to the sequel trilogy, and finally, the Professor Layton crossover.While there were games from that list that I greatly enjoyed (notably Spirit of Justice and the Layton crossover), the Great Ace Attorney Chronicles remains as what I personally consider to be the peak of the Ace Attorney games. Lovable and memorable characters, charming music, great usage of the 3D visuals, and a beautifully written overarching story. While I do admit that the first game fell a little to the mundane side (both story and pacing wise), the second game takes those problems and manages to not only polish them up, but somehow manage to bring back underdeveloped plot points and wrap them up in a natural and enjoyable way. Returning characters either keep their charm from the first game, or become even better somehow, and seemingly one-off characters are brought back in a way that makes them some of the most memorable of the cast. It's no wonder then that people comment on how the first game exists to provide the necessary bases to make the second game as good as it is.Overall, a fantastic experience, and a delightful duology. To any Ace Attorney fan contemplating on whether to give the Great Ace Attorney Chronicles a try, it'll be a definite recommendation from me. Maybe you'll like it, maybe you won't, but if you've enjoyed the original trilogy (which I do recommend you play beforehand), chances are that you'll enjoy the Chronicles just as much, or maybe even more.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney is a very special game from Capcom. This is, one of the greatest games Capcom ever made, a game that has a deep history to it, and a rough history. A title that for many years was trapped in Japan on the 3DS, unable to release anywhere else in the world, and for many, it being on this Steam page is a dream come true.Let me take you back, to 2012. Capcom is deep in development of the ambitious crossover with Level 5: Professor Layton vs Ace Attorney. Two DS mystery game icons join forces on a grand adventure filled with mystery, with the gameplay combined of both series. At the time, Ace Attorney had stagnated. Gameplay was the same, stories weren't that interesting, and there hadn't been a mainline entry in years. Development of PLvAA was a rocky road with many ideas scrapped, as not only were they on a tight deadline, but also planning to try new things Ace Attorney never tried before. This crossover was Ace Attorney's first game in the third dimension, so in light of this Capcom felt it was time to do more. More presentation, voice acting, more animations, more detail. Ace Attorney in the past relied on reusing assets a lot and using as little resources as necessary in order to create their compelling narratives. It worked wonders for the original trilogy, but it was clear that after so many games, they needed to shake things up, and my god did it pay off. Despite the rough development, the crossover was a success, and really innovated the Ace Attorney games for the better.However because of how long development took on PLvAA, Capcom needed a new mainline Ace Attorney game. Problem was, Shu Takumi, the series' main architect, was too busy with PLvAA, so the spinoff team had to make the new mainline game, Dual Destinies, themselves, given a blank slate to tell the story they wanted. Dual Destinies (as well as the following game Spirit of Justice) were amazing Ace Attorneys, however the innovations brought in PLvAA did not make the cut. Not that this is a bad thing, but what PLvAA did just felt...more, and really made the games even more fun.Enter the Great Ace Attorney in 2015. Shu Takumi has a grand idea: A new Ace Attorney storyline set years in the past the late years of the 19th Century starring fledgling Japanese lawyer Ryunosuke as he is sent to study law in the Empire of Japan's new ally Great Britain. Along the way teams up with the legendary great detective himself, Sherlock Holmes, a name I think you already know, and unravels mystery after mystery with Holmes both around London and in the courtroom defending many interesting characters.So what happened? Two things: The first, The Great Ace Attorney was not a success initially. Originally, gamers in Japan hated the new direction, and sales struggled. Not only that, but the game could not release internationally due to one character: Sherlock Holmes. The Conan Doyle Estate are ruthless copyright trolls, who despite the character being public domain, is still covered in legal red tape, and no matter what negotiations Capcom tried, the Doyle estate wouldn't budge.Given time and a sequel two years later, Japanese gamers realized just how great (pun intended) this masterpiece really is, and now both games rival even the original trilogy. But how? Because of new gameplay from PLvAA refined in this game: Multiple witnesses, extra presentation, the new Jury Examinations, and most importantly: Memorable characters, stories, and drama. The Great Ace Attorney lives up to it's name.One piece of gameplay was improved tremendously: Investigations. In the past investigating in Ace Attorney was a chore. You have to point and click everything and it was not fun, engaging, and rarely memorable as everyone just wanted to get it over with so they could get back to the more fun court sections. The Great Ace Attorney fixed this with one character: Sherlock. How? The bulk of investigating has been greatly condensed into investigating with Sherlock Holmes, and performing his "great deductions" in which you will deduct characters and crime scenes with him, and they're amazing. Converting investigation time to Sherlock Time was genius and actually make you invested in investigating.For years, this game was impossible to get internationally. Most people had to hack their 3DSs and run pirated copies of the Great Ace Attorney using fan translations, and while the translations did a good job, they were far from perfect. And honestly, this wasn't the best way to experience this masterpiece. Fortunes changed last year, as Capcom decided "screw it" and went the Arsene Lupin route of changing Sherlock Holmes' name to "Herlock Sholmes." Surprisingly this copyright dodging move actually made things even better. Sherlock now feels like he fits into the Ace Attorney universe. Combine that with the upscaling of the graphics, and both games in one massive package that will last you over 50 hours, and we have the perfect storm for a breakthrough masterpiece.So all this is to say: for the love of all that is holy, BUY IT! JUST BUY THIS ABSOLUTELY AMAZING MASTERPIECE I WAITED 7 YEARS TO FINALLY COME TO THE WEST!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of the Ace Attorney series and TGAA Chronicles really left me satisfied and yearning for more. I appreciated the new characters, all of them: Ryuunosuke is one of my fav protagonists in this series, I loved Susato, I simply ADORE Barok and professor Mikotoba and this version of Sherlock is really amusing (I appreciated how they balanced his apparent sillyness with his more serious moments).My only objection (LOL) is that you can't play TGAA and TGAA2 separately. The two games are two separate acts of a single drama. The first three cases of the first game feels like a sort of introduction to the complex world of TGAA, a sort of "ucrony" set at the start of the 20th century with a touch of steampunk. I really, really appreciated how the game highlighted the problem of racism and xenophobia in Victorian Great Britain towards Japanese people. That said, I found the last two cases of the first game and the cases of the second game more compelling, but I still dearly love this game and the way it ended - even if the jury system left me a bit cold from time to time.Recommended if you're an AA fan but also if you're a novice and want to try the titles of this awesome series!

_childDocuments_.review: REALLY BAD pacing issues. Each game is about 40 hours long—twice as long as older entries. This could have been one game.As a longtime fan, I still like the writing and the characters. The filler and needless length is egregious, though. Two of the mechanics—deduction corrections and the jury system—are trivially easy and unnecessary. It's mostly the meandering filler writing, though, that makes these games so long.In earlier entries, you'd feel smart when, in a witness testimony, you could spot the contradiction or the statement to press right away. These two games almost always make you press every statement to reveal new statements before you can glean anything. It's especially bad in the first game; it doesn't feel like you use your brain at all. Just press every statement and the answer is spoonfed to you.Early on, the main prosecutor of this series lacks presence. He barely interjects (and during the bad new jury system mechanic, the prosecution is flat out forbidden from saying anything—pretty obviously making it filler junk), and says a lot of the same stuff (does he have to act surprised every time the defense calls for a summation examination?). Over and over again he'll talk a lot of trash just to, seconds later, say "no way!!!!!!! you've pulled it off again???" like the same thing didn't happen 7 other times in the past hour. And then the case ends in his defeat and he still acts like he schooled you.Still, it's an Ace Attorney game written by Shu Takumi, so it has a lot of charm and a great overarching plot. It's just annoying that it falls victim to the padded nature of a lot of modern Japanese games, stretching their stories out with soulless filler.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game, but it could've been better. It should've been much shorter, but the music and spritework were so beautifully done that I couldn't mind the lengthiness that much. If you played Rise from the Ashes in the original trilogy, that is the vibe you get playing GAA, but with less standing in front of Detective Gumshoe and presenting every piece of evidence in your inventory three times. Too long, but interesting and heartwarming.Susato was the blandest assistant in the series, and the game could've been so much better if she was shown to be a flawed character or even just a character with quirks. Nah, she just physically harms other people and it's presented as being cute and funny. She was more a collection of plot devices than a human being, and the only unique thing about her is that she's an assistant who isn't an orphan. She was better in game 2 case 1, but any flaws she was given in that case were immediately taken away for the rest of the game. If I could wave a magic wand and change one thing about the game, it would be to make Susato a better foil character for Ryu.Oh, and Hosonaga should've been invited to the Forensic Science forum. But I only have these complaints because the game was so close to being phenomenal.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a solid entry to the Ace Attorney series. TGAA: Resolve (2nd game in the Chronicles) has to be up there in my top 3 favorite AA games. Not only are the characters all likeable, but this duology also possesses hands-down one of my favorite prosecutors in the series, Barok van Zieks (tied for first place with Klavier for me). I don't have any gripes with the main characters, besides me not liking Naruhudo's "Objection!" line, but that isn't a huge issue. The rest of the cast overshadows that small nit-pick. There wasn't a single case I just outright hated or got bored with too like I usually find with every other Ace Attorney game (and this game is two in one so double the chances for that to have happened). If you're worried about playtime, it took me around 80 to 85 hours to beat these two, and I'd say I played at an average pace. And of course the soundtrack is amazing. Nothing short of expectations there. Overall, I feel this duology is worth it, even at full price, and I would recommend it to both Ace Attorney newcomers and veterans alike.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles Adventure and Resolve.  The period setting in London was an interesting idea and the soundtrack was fantastic and one of the best in the Ace Attorney series.  However, these games have pacing issues that made finishing them more difficult than other Ace Attorney games.  Still the last cases of Resolve are good enough that I recommend these games.  Here are my thoughts on each case:The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles: AdventureCase 1 - It's the worst example of dialogue padding.  Tutorial cases tend to be on the weak side, and though the overall plot to this one was ok (especially in light of Resolve), the glacial pace of the story made me want to fall asleep and I thought about not continuing because of this.Case 2 - This one has some funny characters but the plot was pretty stupid and I'd rank it low on the Ace Attorney case tier list.  There also isn't a lot to investigate even though the case was pure investigation.  It is sort of a tutorial level for Herlock Sholmes' minigame but they could have come up with something better. Case 3 - This is where the game really picks up.  It's a great case with good characters that ends in an impactful way. Case 4 - This case is hit or miss for people, but I personally liked it.  The Garridebs are amusing and the defendant is both adorable and annoying.Case 5 - Wow, this case so very long.  Fortunately, it was interesting enough to keep me going but the dialogue padding was a problem at times.  The ending was decent but I wouldn't rank it up there with other final cases.  The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles: ResolveCase 1 - This is another tutorial case but it goes along at a much faster pace than the one in Adventures.  Resolve overall has better cases and pacing, but some of the cases tie to Adventures so you need to play the first one. Overall, this case is about average.Case 2 - A character from the first game gets put on trial again.  This one had a more straightforward plot than the one from the first case but it was also a bit too predictable.Case 3 - This is the longest case in the game, but it has a lot of cool set pieces and interesting characters.  It's one of the better cases.Case 4 & 5 -  The fourth case is more of a setup for the fifth case so it's difficult to evaluate these separately.  Both cases are my favorites for Adventures and Resolve because they tie so many loose ends from the games so well.  I predicted some of the surprises but not all of them, and the ending was very satisfying.   Overall, I'd say there is enough to like that The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles should please a fan of the series, but newcomers should check out the original Trilogy first because those games will offer a better experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles (TGAAC) is an amazing two-part journey of murder mysteries and courtroom encounters with some of the best characters & musical soundtrack in the Ace Attorney franchise. It was a pleasure to finally get to play this game localized, and I dare say it might be my favorite overall Ace Attorney story even though it is a spin-off from the mainline games.Visual novel, point-and-click investigations, murder mysteryTGAAC, like the mainline Ace Attorney games, largely (for most cases but not all) takes place in two halves: one half being about story exposition with sections of gathering evidence/talking to witnesses, and the other half being the courtroom battles where you take the defense attorney bench and pursue the truth in order to prove that your client is not guilty of the crime they are being charged with. Of course, in the courtroom it is your job to debunk witness statements & claims made by the prosecution by presenting evidence that contradicts their statements and in doing so, it is up to you to figure out who is actually responsible. New gameplay elements that were not present in the previous mainline Ace Attorney series come in the form of summation examinations and the Dance of Deduction. The summation examination occurs in court where you need to convince the new jury to change their stance away from guilty, and the Dance of Deduction is where you need to "fix" Herlock Sholmes's brilliant deductions by observing the environment and replacing some of his keywords with ones that make more sense. TGAAC was originally a 3DS/Mobile game so it retains much of the 3DS-era Ace Attorney games appearances, but with options like upscaled resolution and anti-aliasing available on PC. In fact, the 3D animations are very well done as many of the characters have a variety of idle poses/animations that they smoothly run through. TGAAC is set in late 19th century Japan & Great Britain and follows the story of Ryunosuke Naruhodo, an ancestor of the mainline Ace Attorney series's protagonist, Phoenix Wright. Without spoiling anything, Ryunosuke finds himself traveling from Japan to Britain on a study tour with an assigned judicial assistant, Susato Mikotaba, as a means to better immerse himself in the legal system of the most powerful nation in the world at the time. On this study tour, the pair of foreigners encounter many eccentric characters that they often befriend/defend in court. The story is told in a total of ten cases throughout the two games within, and as opposed to the story of the mainline series in the past, every case in TGAAC is largely interwoven with each other to form an overarching plot. •The localisation is excellent; I only encountered one singular (obvious) typo in the entire game (not counting the instances of choppy text to symbolize various European accents). •The game doesn't stray away from addressing issues of xenophobia felt in the game's time period by deliberately including various British negative preconceptions about the Japanese. In a time of political tension where countries were beginning to open up and form alliances, it only made sense to keep such tension intact in the dialogue of the game.•TGAAC introduces some of my new favorite Ace Attorney characters. Many characters tend to stick around for more than one case which gives them ample time to develop, and a lot of the character development is just amazing. Watching the protagonist, Ryunosuke, grow from being unsure of his ideals to being a resolute defense attorney is quite inspiring over the course of his adventure. •The overall story payoff by the end of TGAA2 beautifully ties up the ends of all the interwoven cases together into one singular narrative. A lot of anticipation is built up after every individual case as new mysteries keep popping up and becoming forcibly unexplained by the characters. In the finale, everything comes out and you finally understand why something happened previously and why that event was so significant to so many characters. •The music is phenomenal and rivals, or dare I say bests, the soundtracks of the other Ace Attorney games. The upbeat character leitmotifs are very cheerful and the downtrodden, melancholy reverberations of sad memories feel very foreboding and uncomfortable. I find myself listening to them on repeat in my free time because of how catchy they are. •There is a "story mode" option available to new players who just want to experience the story without being prompted to input "correct" responses. This option lets the game play out as a movie where every correct option is chosen for them (so it is also useful when you get stuck on one problem for a long time).•The game's voiced audio moments can be toggled between English and Japanese.•The game comes with DLC in the form of viewable key/concept art, various unreleased music tracks, supplemental unrelated story chronicles, and more. Most of the DLC comes with developer comments too and it was fun to read the designers' thoughts about scrapped ideas and concepts that didn't make it to the game's release.•Like most Ace Attorney games, there is a toss up between amazing, mind-blowing cases and mundane, slow-burn cases. The great cases make you persist towards the end to find out what happened, and the alright cases are the ones where you figured out what happened already and want the game to acknowledge your intelligence already.•Also like most Ace Attorney games, you might find yourself in the position where you think you are presenting the right evidence, but in fact you need to be presenting the other one of the same nature that the game is assigned to recognize as the actual "answer" to the question being posed. (Not particularly a weakness but more of a statement):•Sherlock Holmes was renamed Herlock Sholmes in order to avoid legal disputes in the English localisation. I see some people trash on the game just because of this, and in my opinion that is such a dumb reason to have for refusing to play a game.9.5/10TGAAC is now one of my favorite, if not my favorite, Ace Attorney games even though it is a spin-off. I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing around in a late-Victorian London setting and interacting with many memorable & charming characters. I liked the long story payoff, the music is phenomenal, and overall, this 65 hour adventure was a pleasure to behold. I would fully recommend this game to be played.

_childDocuments_.review: To go against the grain, I wanted to list a few reasons as to why you wouldn't want to play this game. Full disclaimer, I think the game is amazing (see my hour count), but perhaps for those who wanted to get some no spoiler cons (assuming you want a comparison to the original Phoenix Wright Trilogy):- Some of the accents can be difficult to understand in written form (especially if English is a second language). There are important story elements that can be missed if you don't know how to parse a English Cockney, German, Italian, or Irish accent and one character talked like Shakespeare, etc...,- The game is easier than the Phoenix Wright Trilogy in my opinion during the court portion of the game in terms of deduction.- Investigating is also more linear and easier than in Phoenix Wright - although it's probably more fun with the addition of deductions (it's also harder to get stuck looking for that last clue)- The game is somewhat anti-British in its portrayal of some of the colonial English people (but I didn't mind)That being said, the story just comes together so well in the end, the characters are all so fleshed out and established with complex motivations, and the ending had me shed a tear. I thought the backdrop of the 1900s wouldn't work well but the developers do a good job incorporating into the story (e.g. how to conduct a murder trial without finger print tech). It's also a very long story - 80 hours to finish both games if you play at a normal pace without distractions.In terms of game mechanics, the new additions to the standard find evidence and present it AA formula are also a good change of pace. This includes jury trials, multiple witness on the stand, examining evidence for new clues. All-in-all get it if you liked AA or even have a fleeting interest in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: This review only covers the first game as its the only one I've played so far.As a fan of the original Ace Attorney Trilogy, nothing could’ve piqued my interest more than the setting change to a Victorian era courtroom and all the miniscule setting changes that would entail such as the lack of better forensic technology. I see this as allowing them to have more freedom in the cases they can write as more simpler events can’t just be hand waived with just searching a single aspect like blood DNA or fingerprint. Storywise this entry is definitely a visible upgrade from the original trilogy, granted I can’t say much compared to the Apollo Justice games as I haven’t played those. Each case feels incredibly significant to not only the characters involved but also Naruhodo’s development as a lawyer in a foreign nation. With each chapter, there’s a sense of progress in the main character’s understanding but also how well realized the world is in which Naruhodo feels a stranger to yet acclimatize. This culminates with every courtroom battle feeling tense but also hype when he eventually gains his victory, with him being an underdog making it all the more rewarding when he does bring the truth to the court.The gameplay remains largely the same with previous iterations in being mostly a visual novel with some interactivity when investigating and choosing options in the courtroom. There’s some added features to it which makes it more suitable for the era it's in but nothing substantial enough I would point out here. What’s worth noting though is the puzzle element in this game feels the most forgiving in previous games as although not obvious, they also never make it too apparent as to what is the key in solving a particular scenario which I appreciated a lot. This level of difficulty really lets me fully engage with the story while being challenged, yet never overwhelmed to the point of ruining my immersion which I feel these sorts of visual novel mysteries tend to struggle in balancing.My biggest highlight for this game has to be its presentation. They just completely nail the 19th century London aesthetic creating this drab yet lived world where a couple of Nipponese ambassadors would feel unwelcome. The brownish color palette is just perfect in encapsulating the melancholic vibe of this fictional London’s unforgiving atmosphere perfect in the winter season this game is set in. Couple this with the elegant soundtrack which captures the British class culture, creating an enamoring experience where I’m just fully immersed in the setting of the world as Ryunosuke Naruhodo.The Great Ace Attorney Adventures is an amazing entry to the classic Ace Attorney series, and works well even as an entry point as there really isn’t much background you need to know to get into this game. It takes its time in getting you invested with its world and characters while also providing a dramatic narrative with twists and turns as you navigate a mystery with its intuitive system in both investigating and the trial. There isn’t much negative to say about this game besides the fact if you’re not into this genre. 8.5/10, that cliffhanger ending makes me grateful the re-release comes with both games.

_childDocuments_.review: I will keep the spoilers minimal, as I think games like these are the best enjoyed when going in blind. If puzzle solving aspect doesn't interest you, then there is always the journalist mode that can be selected in the options menu.Adventures:The biggest weakness of Adventures is the way that the story is unnecessary stretched and presented as hopeless situations, even though any person with common sense would quickly come to a certain conclusion without having to take all the flak head-on. It becomes even more blatantly obvious on case 4 and 5, when the jurors are incompetent. As part of the jury system, the jurors are allowed to decide the fate of the defendant through their whims. As part of the mechanic, you get to convince them to overturn their verdict, but the testimony the jurors give most of the time are either blatantly racism or has nothing to do with the case on hand. There is improvement in the story writing in case 5, but the odds are unnecessarily stacked against you. The situation is always unfair and anyone who is new to the AA series will find this to be a big turnoff.Resolve:From Resolve on, the concept of science plays a much bigger role and the complexity of each case changes to reflect on the evidence being more modern. The jury is as incompetent as always in case 2, but when they pronounce guilty, at least the reason this time is somewhat more reasonable. However, case 3 shows a dramatic change in quality of the jurors, because the jurors in case 3 (among them a scientist, a magician and a police officer) are actually capable of helping our protagonist out. And most importantly, they dont have the itchy trigger finger other jurors seems to have and are willing to reason with our protagonist.Overall:I really hated how the Adventurers was narrated, but all of the shortcomings were fixed in Resolve. I have not finished Resolve yet, but I strongly recommend this game. You will have to suffer through the first five chapters of Adventurers, but once you've finally gotten over it, you will appreciate the fine story telling that is provided in Resolve.

_childDocuments_.review: If you really like the Ace Attorney series and want something more story focused and less gimmicky, this game is for you.While it lacks the gameplay "flourish" and variety of ways to investigate/interrogate of other games like Psyche Locks/Emotion Reading, it has a few hiccups in pace and conveyance on certain parts (re-inspect your items often, even if you think you know the evidence is good, the game will refuse to progress until you've done all checks and item updates!) and the two games are just one game cut in two parts, with some of the chapters are really just 2 chapters in one, so you have 8 actual chapters instead of 10...The story more than makes up for it, and has its own little quirks of its own. The story is in my opinion one of the best ones in the entire series, the characters are as varied and quirky as usual, the music is good as well.I can definitely recommend this to someone that likes Ace Attorney as a whole, though do not expect much from the "gimmicks" of this game, but instead turn yourself towards the characters and the story it offers, because it will not disappoint in that way.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finally completed  I can say this is probably my new favorite Ace Attorney game. I know it's actually two games from 3DS that only got a Japanese release in 2015 and 2017, but they were meant to be played together. The story was written as a whole by series creator Shu Takumi, who wasn't working on the mainline games anymore. It did take me about six months to complete as I took breaks between cases to not get burned out and to better absorb the story. The tone of the game is much more grounded than other Ace Attorney games. No longer set in the nebulously defined land which fans call "Japanifornia" but primarily in London *around* 1900, but don't bother looking for a definitive year that aligns with real people and events.The Japanese protagonists have to deal with quite a bit of xenophobia from the people of London who would already see them as untrustworthy, especially in a court of law. However that doesn't mean the game isn't funny or without ridiculous characters. There are many ridiculous witnesses and jury members, and of course, Herlock Sholmes. His character is already hard to describe, but he will also create inventions that mirror our current technology that put him pretty far into steampunk fantasy. Ryunosuke feels more competent than Phoenix, relying less on bluffing and more on eliminating the impossible. He's earnest but still fun with his interactions with Sholmes. I do wish his voice actor gave a stronger "Objection!" Assistant Susato is pretty calm, knowledgeable, sweet but serious, but is a total fangirl for Sholmes. Meanwhile the primary antagonistic prosecutor feels smarter when it comes to standard law practices when compared to those we've seen in the past. All of the other main characters were very enjoyable. If I didn't care for character initially, I had grown to like them by the end with their complex motivations and moral shades of gray. Most 'one-off' characters were good as well, but there were a few annoying ones too. The music is phenomenal with many songs that stick with you long after you stop playing, orchestral sounding pieces with lots of stringed instruments, accordions, and harpsichords. There isn't much else to say besides me just gushing about each song individually. The overall story is great with several shocking moments. There are are some moments that were less shocking and were more expected. I suppose that balances out but some of the unsurprising moments reminded me of events in the original trilogy. For the individual cases, most I couldn't stop once starting. The first two cases did feel a little slow, like I had figured out things out ahead of the story, and the first case took about 4 to complete. And there was one case that kinda annoyed me with its crime and characters, but the rest are some of the best cases in franchise. All of the cases are pretty long, but it's not a problem for the good ones. The game has many quality of life features that make it hard to go back to previous entries: reviewing recently mentioned text, seeing at-a-glance how many parts a witness testimony has and which part you're currently viewing, and an auto-play toggle to automatically advance dialog after short moment so you don't have to press a button to advance to the next text box. The game also has a 'story mode' setting where the game plays itself for you to watch, solving puzzles for you. I never used it to try it (it disables achievements.) I hope future games have full voice acting. Also many characters have their dialect written into their text, so I had to read some lines aloud to understand what they were saying. I can see this being more difficult for non-native English speakers, so an option for plain text would be cool to see. Graphically the game looks great. The backgrounds and character designs are fantastic, no complaints here. While the other Ace Attorney 3DS games kinda made me miss the 2D sprites, this game is how I want to see the series look going forward. Characters are able to interact and look at each and into the background. The camera pans and sweeps add a lot of flair to the scenes they're used. The game is locked at 30fps and looks fine, but if you have it on Steam, you can install a mod to increase it to 60fps and the character animations look so silky smooth. I highly recommend this game for fans of the previous game, or ones who thought the prior games were too silly, or newbies who have been interested in these silly visual novel games and want to see the best they have to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Good games with extremely wonky pacing and a terrible PC port.First off, some housekeeping!Should you want to play this game, do yourself a favour and get the file from this guide an absolute legend has provided us: It fixes the embarassingly glaring resolution issues the game still has, heavily improves performance and ups the framerate to a buttery smooth 60 FPS, which in turn also makes the game's text flow much more smoothly - it genuinely makes a huge difference.The fact that Capcom just left the game in this state is frankly shameful, considering how easy these fixes are to implement.Also, do yourself yet another favour and avoid the community content tab for this game like the plague - that section is absolutely overflowing with spoilers, which is a bit of a problem when the game actually features a couple very good plot twists.Now, as for the games themselves - a lot of people in the Ace Attorney fandom consider this duology the pinnacle of the series. While I certainly do agree that it does a lot right - the setting is actually meaningful to the plot and develops alongside the story, the overarching plot is interwoven throughout the entirety of the games, the characters themselves develop in a far more nuanced way - the one place where the game suffers is unfortunately one that can make or break the experience. These games absolutely LOVE to reiterate points that were already well established in prior scenes over and over and over and over again, all for the sake of adding character interactions. This ends up utterly destroying any semblance of pacing in the early game and apparently remains an issue all the way through to the second case of the second game. Hell, the first game's tutorial cases (yes, there are two of them this time) can take anywhere from 3 to 4 hours each to clear, while the fourth case in that game has to be one of the most annoying, even sort of insulting things I've ever read - spousal abuse sure is funny so long as it's a man that gets hurt, huh?The third case is fine though, for what that's worth!That... does not make for an enjoyable experience if you're not already a hardened, remarkably patient VN fan. This is one of those cases where a neutral rating would honestly be welcome - hopefully the rest of the game will turn me around on the experience.Will update after finishing the collection.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: The two games are basically one single game, with complete unity of plot, and as such it must be the most ambitious entry in the Ace Attorney series. The coherence of the plot over the two games is really impressive, with some questions introduced at the start which are only solved at the end. Starting from scratch with new characters allows them to integrate character development and relationships into the plot really well. I liked all the main characters (I found Soseki a bit over the top, but not too bad). The relationship between the two main characters is more developed than in other Ace Attorney games and the way their affection for each other grows while trying to figure out a foreign country gives the game a really sweet atmosphere. Herlock Sholmes is very funny, and mostly the game avoids the risk of making him OP by making him erratic, depressive, forgetful, and overconfident (I think they do fall into the trap a bit at the end, but it doesn't do too much harm). The trials and investigations are almost all interesting (I found Chapter 4 of the first game, particularly the investigation, the weakest and unnecessarily drawn out). The investigation and trial mechanisms work pretty well (it is, somehow, possible to miss reactions from other witnesses in the cross-examinations), and there aren't many points where the inference they expect you to make turns out to be a bit groan inducing. Overall, I really liked it, and I'd love it if they were to make a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I am no lawyer myself, but this game was a rollercoaster of fun. The world and character designs are flashy and cool, and the narrative is really hilarious. I pressed Q everytime to hear a new dialogue, and inspected every corner i could to see what Ryunoske and Susato would comment next. My favorite character in the entire series is Herlock Sholmes, shocker no shocker for a Sherlock fan, and I think he was cleverly written in this adaption. If you are someone who enjoys novel games, and want something light-hearted, fun, and interesting in terms of problem solving/crime investigation, then you'll enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: okay, as a fan of ace attorney and one who played all of them except SoJ (sorry, i will get to eventually, Dual destinies left me kinda unsatisfied)I genuinely believe The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles IS THE BEST game (or games if you count them as two separate games) IN THE ENTIRE FRANCHISE. The atmosphere and story are interesting, the game knows how to make you see something a certain way, and then flip it upside down and surprise you. The game IS very talkative, and that means the game HAS A ♥♥♥♥ TON OF DIALOGUE TO READ, AND I MEAN A ♥♥♥♥ TON, it is still filled with humor and heartwarming moments, and i never felt as though it was just trying to fill up play time.I do admit that the first game of Chronicles is slow, like incredibly slow, and the insane amount of dialogue does not help the case (hah) . The second game does  shines through and gets you to finally experience and enjoy a bit more of every single step in your journey of becoming a defense lawyer. I had multiple times where i audibly went "WHAT" as the game surprised and intrigued me where i wouldn't believe, the over-arching plot the game has is rich, each case you get a little bit of the big puzzling mystery that is looming over the entire game and it is incredibly rewarding to get to each new point where you find out yourself, as Ryuunosuke Naruhodo, what event occurred in Great Britain in which you were thrown into out of mere coincidence as a foreigner who is  also not welcomed very nicely. Chronicles consists of 2 games, each one is around 30 hours, making it 60 hours as a whole, same amount of time as the original trilogy. I see it as one huge game with 10 chapters as both are connected with one over-arching plot, as the first game barely has a satisfying ending as a whole if i'm being honest.TIP: ENABLE TEXT-SKIP IN THE MENU TO MAKE THE GAME DIALOGUE GO FASTER, YOU CAN CLICK SPACE AND NOT WAIT FOR IT TO SLOWLY APPEAR ON SCREEN AS THE ANIMATION IS SUPER ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SLOW.
