_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem, and a complete improvement over the original AA trilogy in every way. This game is, unlike that trilogy, firmly based in its historical setting in all ways. Racism, taxation, international politics, relationships and conspiracies are all key elements of every case and it feels incredibly real and immersive unlike the original series which seemed unwilling (at least in localized versions) to even acknowledge it was set in Japan. The fact that this also set in the Victorian era helps lend credibility to some of the more out there and previously non-nonsensical elements of the original trilogy. Many technologies we have today simply did not exist, and the game takes advantage of this. As a game on its own, GAAC offers an incredibly tightly wound and complex narrative that ends in a very satisfying way. Some cases definitely felt out of place in the moment, but all of the pieces eventually fall into place. The characters are also very charming, including Herlock Sholmes who brings so much to the table in both the story and gameplay. The two games together are also surprisingly long, taking me 60 hours to complete both. It did drag at times, for the most part the game has a great momentum filled with shocking twists and genuinely funny moments.I highly recommend this collection, and I desperately hope that we get a Great Ace Attorney 3 someday.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Oh wow, what a ride!I had only played the original Ace Attorney trilogy before, so I got to The Great Ace Attorney without having experienced the other installments and spin-offs. Even so, I never felt Chronicles was just more of the same, instead it really felt as a step forward with a fair share of new features that expand and refine the original formula.Since at the end of the day we are playing a series of narrative adventures, let's get straight to the most important aspect of this package: its plot and characters. It contains the usual twists and exaggerations that are commonplace in the first games, and they are masterfully handled here. The plot (the specific of each case and the overarching one that spans both games) are very well written and superbly laid out, I never felt that any scene was lacking nor had any loose end stitched like a patch. Each case is well crafted and never loses the sense of discovery or progression, and there were few times (although they do exist) when I felt it was obvious what was going to happen. Fortunately everything is properly closed and explained by the end, avoiding the inclusion of a cheap cliffhanger to squeeze new installments out of it. This is a universe with many possibilities and Great Ace Attorney still has a long way to go, but the creators do not force the ending to give rise to artificial sequels, and that is something that honors them and I am very grateful for.As for the characters, there is a great variety of them and they are all properly fleshed out. The secondary characters have a lot of charisma and their personalities are well defined, with special care put to the use of accents, dialects and other paraphernalia that contributes to make them a more colorful bunch. This is accompanied by sensational visual designs and a perfect animation work, picking up the 'minimal animation' style of the original trilogy and translating it to 3D in a quite successfully, with fantastic results.The group of main characters has a nice balance to it. On the one hand, we have the set of protagonists who are direct heirs to the Phoenix-Maya-Edgeworth trio in the original. In that sense, they are similar characters in terms of approach and personality, but they still feel different and some of them (I will not tell which one so as not to spoil the surprise to anyone) have a deep additional development in the last third of the collection. On the other hand, the remaining main characters breath new air into the formula that expands beyond themselves.I'm talking, of course, about the world-famous Herlock Sholmes, who is a more experienced and resourceful counterpoint to the lawyer-to-be protagonist, while also acting as an occasional comic relief. With Sholmes comes the first (and super fun) new feature of Great Ace Attorney: the Logic and Reasoning Spectacular events. They are a series of scenes that act as a breaking point in the exploration process' pace and consist of a kind of "dances" between the famous detective and our protagonist, where mysteries and contradictions in the crime scenes must be solved, sometimes with the presence of those involved using our observation skills to assemble together the puzzle of the event in question. These scenes are a blast and I always felt like I wanted more, the animation and sound work in them is out of this world and every time I reached one my heart started pounding with excitement. Great gameplay design here.The innovations do not end there, however, and the already classic trials have undergone an important facelift. This time, one additional "party" is included in the judicial process: the people's jury. In each trial we will have to convince not only the investigating judge but also the members of the jury of our position, sometimes using their own arguments against them and pitting them against each other to achieve our purpose. It involves an additional degree of reasoning in the trials that makes them more varied and deep. Besides, now there may be more than two witnesses testifying and being cross-examined simultaneously, so we will have to focus not only on their testimony but also on the reactions of the other people on the stand in real time. It does not have a great difficulty and it's almost impossible to fail when a reaction takes place, but again it contributes to breath additional variety and depth into the original formula.As for the remaining features, this game achieves excellence in all of them. Visually it is, for me, the most polished of all the entries I've played, with a great deal of work done in environments, effects and, especially, characters. As I have already mentioned before, I am in love with their extravagant designs and animations, full of expressivity and personality even in their simplest instances.Likewise, audio is quite amazing in this pack. The series' spirit is still there, keeping the old sound identity in menus and actions with SFX that are recognizable by any fan of the franchise, and in terms of soundtrack, this is arguably the best installment in the series. The themes have an immense quality, both the reimagined classic themes (few) and the new ones (specially all those related to Herlock Sholmes, really memorable compositions).All things considered, this was a memorable experience for me, one that I've enjoyed every second of and I'm already missing. If you are into narrative games, there are few better representatives than this one, and if you are an Ace Attorney fan then this is a must stop.

_childDocuments_.review: I ultimately really enjoyed this game, but I would highly recommend playing it in chunks. This is a VERY long game and the length can get tedious at times. There are also, from the very first case onwards, TONS of dangling plot threads that quite literally don't get sewn up until the very end. I will say, that every single thread does get wrapped up in a very emotionally and satisfying bow, but considering the length, just let the mysteries wash over you because it's going to take a long time for all of them to get resolved.Each Ace Attorney game seems to have a new courtroom mechanic, and this one includes two: the jury system and also the fact that more than one person takes the stand at a time very frequently. I enjoyed the jury system as it added a lot of personality and flavor the court proceedings, but it did get a bit predictable. At some point in every trial (often twice) the jury will decide that they've made up their mind on a guilty verdict and you've got to pit them against each other in order to change their mind. While I enjoyed it generally, I feel like these moments would have had greater impact if used more sparingly. The fact that more than one person can testify was an interesting idea in concept, but I sort of hated the execution. That's primarily because the game has a wonderful "auto-play" feature where you don't have to keep pressing the space bar or mouse to continue the text. This was awesome. I could sit back, sip my tea and just read along the screen until it came time to make a decision. But the way multiple testimonies work is that in the midst of a conversation with one person, another person on the witness stand will make some change of expression, and you have to catch it and pursue this other person in order to get the new bit of information or elaboration, which essentially means that when more than one person testifies (which is probably about two thirds of the time) you can't use the auto-play feature when pressing witness statements. Also, there's absolutely no deductive ability at all. It's just a way of stringing along already very long trials.I know that all that said, it might sound like I don't recommend the game, but I DEFINITELY do. The cases were typically convoluted and wonderfully complex, just how I like 'em. But by FAR the best parts of the game are the three main protagonists: Ryunosuke, Susato, and of course Herlock Sholmes.Ryunosuke and Susato are both so incredibly winsome and earnest. In a 19th century Britain teeming with jaded, cynical, and often bitter characters (though delightfully eccentric as always) Ryunosuke and Susato are constant breaths of fresh air, and the fact that they have each other's absolute decency to lean on did an amazing job of offsetting even the darkest moments. I think I prefer them to even Phoenix and Maya. I think they both have more personality, frankly, and their situation (fish out of water) and their earnest resolve made them much more easy to identify with and root for. I ended the game loving them both very much and seeing their friendship (and more....????) blossom throughout the series was my second favorite part of the game.My first being, of course, the inimitable Herlock Sholmes. We haven't had a character like Sholmes in an Ace Attorney game that I can think of and he is a DELIGHT. I actually remember being pretty put off by him during his first appearance, and I will say his mini-game during investigation sections, while interesting are VERY unchallenging. But his humor and personality grows steadily throughout the series. I found myself laughing more at this game than I have in any other than I can remember in a long time, and I'd say 85% of that was Sholmes. He is fantastic. Bumbling, often hysterically wrong, conceited, but at the same time always a source of boundless enthusiasm, joy, and unexpected wisdom. He's a singularly charismatic character, whose fun and mystery only grows with each case. I don't think I've enjoyed a video game character so much since I played Disco Elysium. A brilliantly unorthodox take on "The Great Detective" and it makes me want to retcon every iteration of Sherlock Holmes ever and make them the adventures of Herlock Sholmes instead.So all in all, highly recommend the game, but don't expect to binge it. I think I binged the first game but then after starting the second one, it got too overwhelming and I had to take a break. Just go at each case leisurely if you can. It's a lot to get through, but they really nail the conclusion and the characters grow very much throughout the course of the two games.Also: the prosecutor Von Zeiks is insane. He dresses like a Transylvanian count, is constantly crushing wine glasses and bottles, and occasionally hoists his leg up on the banister like drag queen doing a seductive stretch. He's definitely enough to give the Edgeworth shippers a run for their money.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game is AfootThere have been very few games I have recommend at full price, this is one of them.Before you say anything, yes, £31.99 is 110% worth it.If someone were to ask, "what is an example of absolutely brilliant story telling" this is one of the first things that would pop to mind. The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is 2021's, localised bundle of the 2015, "The Great Ace Attorney: Adventures" (Dai Gyakuten Saiban: Naruhodou Ryuunosuke no Bouken) and the 2017, "The Great Ace Attorney 2: Resolve" (Dai Gyakuten Saiban 2: Naruhodou Ryuunosuke no Kakugo)After years of fans begging Capcom to bring the Japan exclusive Ace Attorney prequels to the west, we finally received them, and they are glorious, not only does TGAA improve on major problems that have plagued the Ace Attorney franchise for years, but also serve as a new story, following Ryunosuke Naruhodo, the ancestor of Phoenix Wright (Ryūichi Naruhodō in Japan), the lovable and more competent than Maya, Judicial Assistant, Susato Mikotoba, along with Sher- sorry, Herlock Sholmes, and his adopted daughter Iris. _childDocuments_.review: 6/10I can barely recommend this game, and that makes me really sad. While having two games in one finally come to the west and proving to be faithful entries in the Ace Attorney-series, I am confident in saying that among all  these are the ones I enjoyed the least. I can barely say that I enjoyed them at all. Let us get into why.The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a compilation of two games, previously only available in Japan. The games center around Phoenix Wrights ancestor Ryunosuke and his journey towards becoming a great defence lawyer in Great Brittain. On his journey he meets colorful characters, solve (mostly) murder-cases and uncover plots on a national level, sometimes with the help of his friend Herlock Sholmes (Actually Sherlock Holmes in the Japanese version, funny enough). In the game there are ten chapters, each with it's own (moslty) murder-case (apart from the last chapter in the second game. There are some bonus-scenes as well, totaling about an hour of extra dialogue. Those are mostly fan-service as there is no gameplay, jsut clicking through dialogue. The game consists of reading, pointing out clues while investigating crime-scenes, solving crimes through interrogations in court and doing a lot of deduction. Now to these entries are the "dances of deduction" that you perform alongside Herlock Sholmes, in which he tries to solve cases thorugh perpostrous ideas and you correcting him towards the truth, a fun mechanic, compared to certain "mini-games" in earlier entries (I do not miss psyche-locks). Otherwise it plays like earlier entries in the series.Start by noting that it took me 77 hours to finish these two games. That is a lot of game for your buck, but as these games are mostly clicking through dialogue, the "game" mostly consists of reading. In order for that to be a good experience, you need to have writing that justifies that much reading. Sadly, this is not the case. As many reviewers point out, the pacing is terribly slow. Points that could be made in a sentence is stretched out over an entire paragraph, characters talk around the point constantly and gags are repeated over and over and over again in absurdum. Almost 40 hours for five cases gives us in rality seven hours per case. Seven hours is a long time, especially when you at an early point in the case have it all figured out and just need to click through the long dialougue for the characters in the game to draw the same conclusions as you do. A subjective opinion of mine is that I do not feel as if the characters generally are as interesting as they are in earlier entries (with a few exceptions), and that some of the main characters are borderline annoying most of the time. Also, since most characters are brittish, the writers try to accentuate their accents through them using a more phonetic language at times, making reading what they say kind of hard. Sometimes you really need to read through their dialogue multiple times to understand what they are trying to convey. It is more immersive, but as the main thing about this game is reading and there is so much text to read, it sometimes becomes annoying. I could summarize this critique as the game not beeing wacky enough to be funny and not serious and well-written enough to be as enticing as many of the "darker" cases of earlier entries are. The game is set in the late 19th century but that is not identity enough for it to feel as spectacular as I had wanted.That said, the game is otherwise fine. It looks great, it sounds great and the gameplay is the same that we all know and love. It is just that the content itself is so lackluster and LONG that is so frustrating, giving it a lower score.+ Great graphics+ Great soundtrack+ A faithful entry to a great series- Way longer and slower than it needs to be- Not enough dark OR wacky charactersI would say that this entry CAN be skipped, as it is a prequel, of sorts. Fans should play it if they really want to but be prepared for a long and slow experience. The feeling it left me with was more "finally, it is over" than "Wow, I can't believe it is over".

_childDocuments_.review: How is anyone getting through this? Everyone takes 16 times longer to say anything than they should. Every character wastes so much time on quirks that aren't interesting or amusing, talking about plot points that go nowhere, talking about plot points that will go somewhere in what the writers probably thought was foreshadowing but was actually just needlessly drawn out filler, or they just talk about nothing. The protagonist is almost as useless as Apollo was in his first case, except this lasts for two whole games. The assistant is bland, though is at least preferable to the parts where an adult is accompanied by a 10 year old girl. I don't know the pedo laws over in Japan, judging by most anime they seem to have none at all, but over here we're not into that. This game does seem to have two unique gimmicks... one which wastes time during investigation, and one which seems like a good idea but mostly just makes every juror into an idiot who doesn't understand the stakes of a murder trial. The only good thing about this game that Trials and Tribulations badly needed was telling you where to go during Investigation. Everything else makes me wish I stopped played these games after Dual Destinies, which was much better than this and had more interesting gimmicks and characters. This is obviously just a poorly written excuse for a game made by someone who just discovered Sherlock Holmes books and wanted to include a character based on that. The inconsistent British accents of every character make it clear that they didn't care about anything besides that.In conclusion, here's an example of how most of the dialogue should have been written vs how it was written:_______________________________Prosecutor Dracula: What evidence do you have for your claim?Protagonist Useless: This - (Shows evidence)but instead we get:_______________________________Prosecutor Dracula: What evidence do you have for your claim?Judge CopyPaste: Yes, show us your evidence!Assistant Bland: Protagonist, this is the time to show the evidence!Protagonist Useless: (I need to think carefully about the evidence...)Assistant Bland: I am responding to what is supposed to be a thought because the translators didn't realize that words in parenthesis were not actually said out loud.Protagonist Useless: I am about to present the evidence that supports my claim!Prosecutor Dracula: What?!Jury Moron 1: !Jury Moron 2: It can't be...!Jury Moron 3: My preconceived notions are being challenged??Jury Moron 4: I bet I'm secretly the culprit all along, how convenient that I am a member of the jury.Jury Moron 5: I have nothing to add and will take a full 10 seconds to state that.Jury Moron 6: What?Protagonist Useless: The evidence...Prosecutor Dracula: Racist insult. I throw my glass backwards.Protagonist Useless: ...which I am about to present...Judge CopyPaste: Gasp! My hair animation will play for the 400th time!Protagonist Useless: ...is this, which would have saved a lot of people 6 hours of pointless dialogue if I had the option to present it earlier.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not gonna act like I didn't have fun with this game. I'm glad it got localized, the music is great, the overarching storylines are good, the graphics are good. It's more Ace Attorney for the fans who have already played all the other Ace Attorney games, and that's really the only demographic I would recommend this game to. If you want to get into the series, play the Phoenix Wright trilogy. If you played the trilogy and want more, play Apollo Justice or Miles Edgeworth Investigations.Because DEAR GOD this game is a slogfest. this game is stacks on stacks on stacks of overly explained yet entirely simple mysteries and extraneous dialogue that isn't funny enough to justify the absolute time sink of a single sentence at the slowest text scrolling speed known to man. Why bother writing two mysteries when you can write one that takes twice as long because all the characters stop at every opportunity to say "There's a mystery! "How did you not notice the mystery?" "What mystery?" "How could there be a mystery?" "Oh, we sure have to solve this mystery!"Like, the core element of Ace Attorney is the cross examination of testimony, so you'd think with such a long game you'd have lots of opportunities to press witnesses and find contradictions, right? But if you actually count the number of individual testimonies, you get maybe like... eight in a case. A trilogy case would give you twice as much, meaning more puzzles to solve, more lies to uncover, and just more exciting moments. It's not quality over quantity here, either; you're really just supposed to press every statement until some evidence or a statement gets updated, and then you know that you have to use whatever got updated, taking away half the puzzle. It's even easier when they give you a big exclamation point because a different witness wants to say something. Questioning the jury about voting guilty is similarly easy and goes just as slow, but it's a good mechanic and fits right in.The investigations... are very, very long. Investigation segments in any Ace Attorney game tend to be the less exciting half in exchange for the necessary buildup of mysteries and evidence, but the investigating in this game railroads you harder than ever. Go here, ask everything, look at something, repeat. You're not solving any puzzles besides the occasional "Dance of Deduction" (Great segment. Could go a little faster).And it's not like I hate the characters, either. They're all expressive, funny, and interesting. But the best characters in the world don't mean anything when I'm just waiting for a plot that refuses to move forward at a reasonable pace. If the writers trimmed out some lines to make the game less repetitious and gave an option to double the text speed, especially on first playthroughs where you can't skip ANY new dialogue, I'd still have some issues, but I wouldn't be giving this thumbs down. Great Ace Attorney is a 70 hour game that should be a 45 hour game at maximum, and if this review seems needlessly elaboratory on that point then I've given you a good idea of what you're in for.

_childDocuments_.review: I must say, this is by far the best Ace Attorney games by far, it almost saddens me that every other Ace Attorney pales in comparison. The story was the best told and executed out of all the games, previous games have attempted and over-arching plot from case to case but this game not only did it the best, but also managed it over not one but two games. The way they set up things in the first game to be brought up in the second was done masterfully. The actual story contents-wise is not only my favorite out of all the Ace Attorney games, its up there with many of the greatest visual novels. The soundtrack to this game was straight fire, the best in the series, I literally have listened to both games soundtracks on Spotify from start to finish multiple times. The characters were the most like-able out of all the games, not just the main characters but I even found myself enjoying the side characters presence, even the bad guys. I won't deny that there were times I got stuck during the cases and had trouble figuring out what to do, and there was one instance during the final case that I resorted to looking up which evidence I needed to present during a cross-examination, but that's par for the course for an Ace Attorney game, and even though I didn't use it, there's a story mode option that automatically goes through the story so you can basically just watch the game without having to figure out the puzzles. Unlike typical Ace Attorney games, I felt that I enjoyed every single case in both games, even the one I considered the worse, the first case, wasn't as bad as cases in other games, I just think it was much longer than necessary and I hope it doesn't turn off newcomers from continuing because every case after that is so much better. Basically, I think this is one of the best visual novels I've ever played, I think it IS the best Ace Attorney I've ever played, I'm very glad they localized this finally so its more accessible, I hope it sells exceedingly well so Capcom will make more Ace Attorney games of this caliber. Its a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ 10/10, perfect game, if this was any other game I'd be upset that I'll have to play it again to get all the off the path achievements but I'll gladly do it for this masterpiece :)

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to preface this with the fact that i have not previously played the Phoenix wright series however i have seen an edited play-through of the first 3 games, that being said:This game/games was amazing. The story was phenomenal with each case being an interesting tale with twists at every turn, sometimes you had some cliche parts which fit in quite well and sometimes you had some stuff were you are like "eh, that could have been done better", but there was not a single part of this that i would consider bad. Obviously the cases are unrealistic with many many coincidences propelling the story forward but this is a main staple of all detective games as there isn't much to get around that and still have the case be intriguing, but i found it dosn't hinder the story at all and adds to the experience. The story follows a case by case story-line each expanding on the tale of Runo (the shortened name of the main character), showing the young lawyer's journey from nothing to greatness with a very intricate subplot that spans both games in the series and ends in an epic 2 part finale. Each of the main characters has a deep personality that has you grow attached no matter how annoying they were to start (looking at you Sholmes) and every case features a cast of wacky sub characters to help spice up the court proceedings. One thing i think people will like is the lack of magical happenings that featured in the Phoenix wright series, as much of that was used to bail-out the player in a end all scenario and its much better written in this game. The evidence and cross-examinations i found to be quite well put in without super obvious guidance but some good hints here and there, but sometimes its not clear at all what you need to choose so you just filter through the evidence list until you eventually choose the right thing. One thing that really hinders this game is if you leave a case mid-way; Cases often take 3-4 hours and everything is procedural, so if you stop playing and forget what exactly happened or how a piece of evidence relates to something past you can get stuck reloading till it just happens to be correct. One thing i really enjoyed about the evidence was the ability to view most of it in a 3d space and poke at it for clues and details, sometimes even opening things up or combining 2 pieces of evidence.The music in the game is fantastic, constantly setting the tone and allowing the player to truly put themselves in the shoes of Runo. My personal favorite theme is Iris's as it perfectly fits her character. One thing that really threw me off however was the occasional voice acting, as I played the game i built up unique voices for each character in my head and every once in a while (like every 2-3 cases) you would get a voice acted segment and while its the characters definitive voice, i feel its sparse use really clashes; The interjections in court however were fine in my opinion (Runo's did feel a little lack-luster at times) and it did add to the characters and the court experience.Overall i give this game a 10/10 but do be warned about its length, i'm fast reader and it took me ~30-35 hours to finish (though reading fast isn't a big impact because the game limits text speed  when you first read it which i understand its to properly pace and set things up but was annoying)

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I feel like I should write something about this game. Ace Attorney is probably my favorite game series and this was an entry I was excited for. I finally finished it last night, and I have to say it is quite spectacular.There is some challenge to totally leaving the cast that your players know so well behind and constructing a brand new one, in a different time period no less, and this game succeeds on this front. The characters are marvelous and even the ones specific to one case are very strong and memorable.This game benefits in a very similar way to the way Miles Edgeworth's spin-off games Ace Attorney Investigations does, in that the first game, while good, builds toward the second game's conclusion. The final three cases in the second game of this duology, Resolve, is one of the finest sequences of the Ace Attorney franchise. The story of the two games is well laid out and the conclusion is beautiful.I think this one improves on the mechanics of the previous games in the series; the earlier games falter with me a bit with very long, boring and cryptic investigation phases where as they are a bit streamlined here will still being an interesting phase to meet new characters and learn new information about the case. The cross-examination of multiple witnesses from the Layton crossover is an excellent mainstay here and other new mechanics like the Dance of Deduction and Summation Examination are really great too.Sometimes the game feels a bit long, but that isn't necessarily a complaint for me. Some people are likely going to feel its length but I don't think its much of a problem at all.Anyway, this is a really fantastic pair of games and I can only hope that we see more access to more games in the Ace Attorney franchise on modern consoles and PC such as Apollo Justice, Investigations 1 and 2 and the 3DS-only games. I would also hope more Ace Attorney games are in the works at Capcom.If you like Ace Attorney, buy this game. If you are interested in getting into Ace Attorney, this is just as good a place to start as the original Phoenix Wright trilogy, in my opinion.And remember: pursue the truth, no matter how painful it may be.

_childDocuments_.review: A Great Departure Signaling A Much-Anticipated Return to Form~!A lovingly crafted return to a much-missed series, The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is as much a treat for the eyes and ears as it is for the mind. Fully embracing its turn-of-the-20th-century Japanese setting, the game introduces its (as always) well-written and oddball characters, from our hesitant legal savant protagonist Ryunosuke to the painfully pathetic Auchi. Aside from a spoilerific segment first introduced in the second case, the game utilizes mechanics adopted across previous games and interweaves them with newer mechanics to create a smooth, enjoyable experience. Two cases in, and there's very little to complain about, so if you're a die-hard fan of Phoenix Wright, give it a try!Pros: Fresh world, fresh characters, and background conflict that's interesting and easy to understand. Music and visuals are on point, and gameplay is frustration-free and fun.Cons: Unless you own a Switch, you're not getting a physical copy of this. Oh, and one of the characters is a bit annoying, but I'm sure that'll sort itself out soon (it's a game about murder mysteries and raison d'etres. It'll fix itself one way or another, through death or character growth... or both).

_childDocuments_.review: Although I've played the other games in the series, Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is a good entrypoint into the series with a new protagonist and a good first case to cut your teeth on learning how the game works. As always there is plenty of levity and humor; the horrible puns and over the top animations temper the often dark and gritty nature of the mysteries.The cases themselves are nicely inter-related with one another and form an interesting overarching narrative with plenty of twists and turns and reveals that make each individual case a satisfying mini arc unto itself. The music has some great leitmotif from the originals that gets played with to give new themes to the individual cast and situations, and I found it all to be pretty good.There are definitely a few small qualms I had with the game, but not enough to keep me from recommending it. Firstly, this game suffers from the same issues as all the others in the series where you'll need to complete a checklist of things before the story can move on, and often what you missed is very obscure especially in the later cases. This means you'll either need a walkthrough, or to spend your time meticulously mousing over every inch of every location and presenting every piece of evidence to every person you can talk to during investigation segments until you find the one thing you were missing. During cases, especially the first half of the game it's pretty easy to figure out the clues and where the game wants you to go - to the point where a few times I'd figured out the twist long before the characters - and other times I had no idea at all what I was supposed to do and had to look up a solution which made no sense even after it was explained. In several instances, I had selected the proper item but hadn't examined it thoroughly enough for the game to accept it yet, so it marked it as incorrect. My advice for new players is to simply play until you get stuck, and if you get more than one game over look up the answer instead of trying to brute force your way through it; doing it the hard way by presenting every piece of evidence on every statement isn't "earning" it since you don't know why it's the correct thing anyways, so looking it up is just saving you time and aggravation.My other major gripe is with the text. You can't increase the speed at which text displays the first time you see it, so if you're a fast reader it can feel agonizingly slow, and although the dialog can be charming at times the script is really over-written. I honestly feel like most of the exchanges could have been significantly shortened without losing anything information or characterization-wise.All in all, a great entry in the series and a solid game overall. 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: When first I started The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles, I was frustrated by the pacing, presentation of characters, and lack of brevity to every conversation. However, my opinion on just about everything did a complete 180 after I simply changed how I viewed the game. I approached the game from the lens of someone who has been playing Ace Attorney for years, and for better or worse, it is a series with a somewhat predictable formula. I had grown comfortable with that formula, but I only now realize, after being shown just how much that formula can be shaken up, just how stale it had become.Great Ace Attorney feels like a breath of fresh air to the Ace Attorney series. The orchestral and somber musical score is perfectly suited to the period, and every theme feels masterfully tailored to the situations they play in. By comparison, the 3DS titles we did initially got, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice, feel almost slapdash and I am only upset we didn't get these games sooner.I genuinely feel that Great Ace Attorney should be the bar moving forward, having shaken up the storytelling formula kept so firmly in place by Ace Attorneys famous 3 day trial system, and that the mechanics introduced, the jury system and Dance of Deduction, should certainly make a return. The Dance of Deduction especially is worthy of praise, as it managed to do something I had never expected of an Ace Attorney: it made the investigation phases genuinely interesting.Overall, grand game, wonderful soundtrack, memorable characters, and a well-told, if sometimes overly verbose, story that often had me laughing and sometimes crying. I am filled with new hope for the Ace Attorney franchise and hope that Mr. Shu Takumi can continue to deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney is, at the very least, on par with the original trilogy- I can guarantee that much. But when I was playing it, particularly GAA2, it occurred to me that these games, when considered as one, contiguous story, and two parts of a larger game, might actually be my favorite in the entire series.The original trilogy is incredible, no doubt about it- an enticing combination of solid characters, engaging mysteries, humor, and slowly unraveling overarching stories. Then, when I played Apollo Justice, the fourth game in the series, I thought I'd be in for more of that. Many people overlook AA4, but I really enjoyed it. AA5 and 6 didn't quite live up to my hopes. Solid games, of course, with some excellent moments, and overall quite enjoyable, but they miss the mark in a few areas, namely the writing. One particular thing that irked me was that the switch to 3D models over 2D sprites was wasted, and the classic expressiveness of Ace Attorney characters seemed to be lost.The Great Ace Attorney lives up to the promises made by the original trilogy. The writing, is, thankfully, much improved- Shu Takumi, series creator, back in the director's chair-, and unlike the second trilogy of the main series, GAA is not afraid of telling an overarching story. Crucially, it takes the same approach that AA1-3 took to its characters, where many, if not most, appear in multiple cases, allowing the world to feel vastly more connected, and creating much more affinity for the characters that appear. GAA also uses the added dimension of the 3D models to its advantage; characters look like they belong in 3D, instead of being odd, frequently uncanny translations of existing characters. The mere fact that this game allows multiple characters to appear in the same frame at once sounds minute, but brings significant improvements to the flow of dialogue and storytelling.Gameplay is mostly unchanged, with typical investigation sequences and courtroom battles, but two new mechanics make everything feel just varied enough when compared to the original. Unlike the Mood Matrix (which had its moments) and Divination Seance (which was terrible except for the literal last one in the game) of AA5 and AA6, these mechanics feel naturally integrated and match the story. The introduction of a jury addresses a common logical complaint about the Ace Attorney series- the lack of a jury in all but one case in the main series-, but having to persuade jurors in what are essentially special cross-examinations brings a new layer to the courtroom battles. In investigations, you now take part in the Dance of Deduction with Herlock Sholmes (that's not a typo), which utilize the 3D space and provide a fun break from the typical talk-investigate-move loop of investigations.The setting is one I absolutely loved; a heavily stylized Victorian London with minor steampunk elements, and an opening set in Japan. It doesn't provide any profound commentary on the period, nor would I expect it to. The game leverages its setting to create charming characters and enjoyable environments to sleuth through, frequently using the time period in its humor and often its mysteries (for example, while in the main series, fingerprints are bound to appear in almost every case, they are not yet accepted as evidence at the time of GAA).There's not a single character in either game I hated (by which I mean, a character the developers did not intend for me to hate, because there are plenty of those), and some of them have risen to be my favorites in the series. Ryunosuke also (potentially unpopular opinion) has a more defined character arc than Phoenix ever had, and Susato is one of few times where they've succeeded in giving you a companion as enjoyable as Maya Fey (Trucy Wright and Ema Skye being the others, but the series completely forgets about Trucy, and Ema is relegated to Gumshoe's replacement). Van Zieks is a strong prosecutor, perhaps not quite the series' best, but still in the upper half. The best character, of course, is Herlock Sholmes, who steals every scene he appears in, and is, at all times, entirely entertaining.I won't speak too much on the overarching narrative and the individual mysteries for spoiler reasons, but I would argue that there is no 'bad' case in GAA, and all are at the least, very good. The average quality of the cases in both game is alongside or above the original trilogy (and I'd lean towards the latter), and a very well-rounded, varied package. I didn't find too many logical inconsistencies (though I also don't spend my time nitpicking at every detail like some, so go figure) in the cases. The overarching mystery slowly unravels, but I will admit that in retrospect, the first game definitely takes a lot of its time to set up GAA2. Despite this, GAA tells its own story and still manages to exist by itself, even with the heavy connection and build-up to its sequel. To fully appreciate them, though, you must play both.I would strongly recommend The Great Ace Attorney, whether you enjoy the main series or otherwise. You can enjoy GAA without playing any of the others. Play it if you love mystery/detective stories and visual novels of this style. If you want more Ace Attorney and haven't played GAA, you really can't go wrong here, and I strongly encourage anyone with similar feelings towards AA4-6 to myself to play GAA, as it's probably what you're looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: I owned the Ace Attorney trilogy, Ace Attorney Apollo Justice, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice games on the 3DS.  I've never loved any of them enough to include them on a list of all-time favorite video games, but I've liked them well enough to buy and play them when they've been on sale.This is the first time I've played any of the games in this franchise on PC.  One thing I've always disliked about this series is that you aren't given the option to set the text display speed, nor are you allowed to click through the dialog windows at your own pace.  I was hoping that by now, having made their way to PC, that those things might finally be an option.  But no.  I still have to sit waiting for text to crawl across the frames at its own pre-set speed to read it, and wait until it's finished doing that before I can click through to the next sentence.  Nor is there any option to skip ahead (although if the game has in fact shown you some dialog before, it will remember that and allow you to move through the text faster on subsequent playback by holding down the button).  This leads me to conclude that not being given the option to do otherwise is a deliberate choice on the part of the developers in order to artificially pad/stretch out the game's length.  Which is really tedious, especially when you know what the characters are getting at but they haven't gotten to the point yet.This is a marginal thumbs down because the rest of the things about the game range from adequate to enjoyable.  As of right now I'm almost halfway through the game (I believe), but I'm close to being fed up with this aggravating UI feature.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played all the Ace Attorney games officially available in english: The original trilogy via DS emulator, Apollo Justice, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice on the 3DS, and Ace Attorney Investigations 1 also on a DS emulator. When TGAA was announced to have no plans of localization I was sad, but having it finally available now on PC makes it no less of a wonderful experience. Of this writing I have just finished TGAAC, the first half of the stories included in the steam release.What I find fascinating is how intricately crafted TGAA is, even when compared to its former games. All the games have 5 cases, and often the cases are isolated from each other, with some cases being completely unrelated to the overarching theme. TGAA has dense and layered stories both within each chapter, and that builds off previous chapters, the finale being the most notable example. Previous titles often had long and confusing investigation sections that were less interesting that the courtroom battles, TGAA condenses investigations and also adds a new mechanic that allows for looking for and deducing contradictions outside of the courtroom setting. All the games primarily deal with 'finding contradictions'. Other games had mechanics that used supernatural elements like the psyche locks, the mood matrix, and the divination seances. TGAA supplants the 'finding contradictions' gameplay by including multiple characters on the witness stand, as well as the jury. While I've enjoyed all the gameplay in the series, having mechanics less reliant on supernatural things and being more grounded on reason and arguments made it even more enjoyable for me. Going backwards in time for the setting allowed for some interesting changes. The other games almost all have Phoenix Wright, Maya, Apollo, Athena, or Miles Edgeworth. Breaking off from the established setting allows for a lot of new things to be done narratively. I understand why it must have been seen as a challenge to localize this game for a western audience. The themes of cultures and societal roles plays a large part in this specific story. There are a few unexplored questions at the end of the first game that I imagine are answered in the second, I imagine that the two games are ideally meant to be experienced together, much like how the original trilogy ended up being.Character designs and animations are excellent, music is excellent, story is amazing. The puzzles are not difficult - there is often much buildup and anticipation before the game requires input by the player, which hints at what needs to be chosen, and input is not required often. What is enjoyable about the series is the deliberately nuanced unraveling of a finely crafted scenario. It has taken me a long time to read this far, but I'm looking forward to reading the second half of Chronicles.I will make the Empire of Britain and the Empire of Japan my enemy to protect Gina.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of this series since around 2015... so, basically around when DGS was released. Also, being that these are in an entirely new setting, they need to introduce it fully, which regrettably takes some time.- Yes, animations can be long. But personally, it adds a lot of charm to the game! I really love the expressiveness of everyone and wish they animated like this more frequently.- Some evidence choices are weird. _childDocuments_.review: This game may not be flawless, but it IS a masterpiece. Parts of game feel slow, and there is A LOT of dialogue to get through, but if you're patient and enjoy the mixture of humor, period fitting flavor text, and a ton of information that later connects to other parts of the story, I think you'll enjoy it. I was very skeptical of the game being 3D, considering that the only other Ace Attorney games I have played are the original trilogy. While I do miss some of the charm and visual gags of the 2D format, this game pulls off 3D well, and has such nice characters to look at. Seriously though, the music is something else. It took some getting used to and at first seemed like a downgrade from the brain-crack that is the music from the original Ace Attorney trilogy, but this music is incredible in its own right. Just about every song is bursting with a ****load of instruments, actions, emotion, and fits the ~1900 setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Played great on the Steam Deck. If the anime cutscenes don't play right (for example, looking like a rainbow test pattern) try switching your Proton version for the game. _childDocuments_.review: You know when you're reading a manga or watching an anime, and there are those moments when characters just keep saying what is happening and what's going on with the plot? Like during a fight scene, Goku will think "I need to use the spirit bomb I learned from King Kai, but I may not have the energy to do so, and I may not be able to hold off Android 88 while doing so." And then we'll cut to sideline characters explaining the same thing, then to King Kai on his planet saying the same thing and so on and so forth. This game has that peculiar over-explaining, where you'll see something like the judge saying "Ryunosuke, if you interrupt at the wrong time, you will be penalized." And then Ryunosuke will think "If I interrupt at the wrong time, I will be penalized." and then the person next to Ryunosuke will tell him that if he interrupts at the wrong time, he will be penalized.In the first case, I knew what evidence I should be presenting, but I kept having to wade impatiently  through endless dialogue just to get to the point where I could start interacting with the court experience. It's really poorly-paced.I never played past the first Appolo game in the main series (and I played the first Edgeworth game), but part of what made AA games appealing was the pacing. Characters' animations were snappy while the text speed seemed to speed up and slow down to match characters' excitement. GAAC is just so much more verbose and sleepy.I wanted to like this game, but I can't. I agree with most of the negative reviews that this game's script could be cut in half without any real loss. Every character just babbles on and on, explaining minor detail while the text crawls by at a snail's pace.

_childDocuments_.review: Going to regard this duology as one game, and not as "TGAA1/TGAA2". It's only fitting, where, for all of us Ace Attorney fans, we're used to story threads usually being introduced in the first 2 chapters and all loose ends being tied up at the last chapter (the exception to this rule being Trials and Tribulations, turning AA1/AA2, 2 standalone titles into part of a trilogy, with the strong prequel storytelling.Anyway. Viewed separately, TGAA1 was honestly slightly boring and - dare I say - even slightly painful to play through at times. Mind, not because it was 'bad'. I believe this was a very deliberate storytelling direction taken by the designers. They obviously envisaged TGAA Chronicles as a duology (even more so than they viewed the first 3 AA games as a trilogy) and not as titles that would satisfy an avid AA enthusiast such as myself. As such, TGAA1 focused more on introducing mysteries/plot elements that promise a huge payoff... but not by the fifth chapter. Heck, it felt like TGAA1, as a whole, was just an "appetizer", for us to get used to Meiji Era "Phoenix Wright", and for Naruhodo Ryunosuke to get accustomed to living in London.But man oh man, when TGAA2 came along.... The kids' gloves were off. Hype and excitement just kept building for me starting from the third case, and it was an amazing ride all to the final second. Personally, I feel that if the Ace Attorney franchise were to wrap up and sent off by this prequel duology - considering that Phoenix Wright, Apollo Justice, Athena Cykes story and character arcs in the present have ostensibly been wrapped up - I'd have no complaints. None AT ALL. TGAA1: 7/10TGAA2: 9.5/10TGAA viewed as a duology: 11/10 (My favorite Ace Attorney game, even when compared to AA1 to AA6)

_childDocuments_.review: Once again a great adventure game in the Ace Attorney series. Although the formula hasn't changed that much, you want to keep on playing because of all the strange characters, the various plot twists and the court room interrogations. However, if you were not a fan of the previous titles, you will not going to enjoy this either.The graphics are 3D, but retain that nice cartoon look and feel. You can play with Japanese sound/speech if you want, but subtitles are in English. The PC port is solid with some minor issues. You cannot control the various sound volumes; you only select on/off. Also mouse support is with fixed buttons which is annoying for me being left-handed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: As a devotee of the original trilogy, I remember being anxious that I wouldn't come to like Apollo Justice as a sit-in for the role that Phoenix played. I was pleasantly surprised as I found myself longing more and more for Apollo cases by the end of that trilogy.I felt the same feelings here with Ryu and his journey. Phoenix's ancestor. Over a century in the past. How could this game even remotely exhibit the same energy that Phoenix and Apollo gave. Once again, I'm happy to say, I was pleasantly surprised.The Ace Attorney games have been able to weave a narrative and interesting gameplay mechanics in a way so smooth, that even when it can seem repetitive, they still find a way to keep me engaged. Shame on me for ever doubting that Capcom would dish out another hit on this franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: the drama is so good (which is great for a story driven series like ace attorney, i wont get into spoilers) but i want to point out the quality of the animations, the detailed artworks, and the animated parts. this game is more than a visual novel sometimes and i love it! plus, the music is awesome! its not without problems, with historical context and problematic undertones but i will admit one of my major gripes with the game, the "casual" racism van zieks shows (although he is not the only one...) is fully adressed in the second half of the game, resolve. this behaviour is persistently condemned which is good, but it is also grating that its so present sometimes, so be warned.on another note, the game is long!! like the first case takes 5 hours of gameplay, that is absurd for literally the first case of any ace attorney game. it took me 92hrs to get through the main story of both games! that is a LOT of content!in any case, i'd recommend the game, it is very much an ace attorney story and a good one to boot in my opinion, so if you want to dive into that, don't hesistate to! be warned that the historical context leads to some awful behaviour (luckily not from the MCs).

_childDocuments_.review: The first game has a slow start but once this duology gets going it never stops and it is absolutely glorious! Absolutely love Ryunosuke he is great and there are so many insanely unique, funny and well written characters in this game. The entire main cast that keeps returning is super likeable there wasn't a single moment where I was frustrated or cringing because of a character. Every single trial in the second game is fire. The ending should have been extended a bit imo but its still great. Susato crushes Maya and takes her place as easily the best judicial assistant in my eyes, also one of the best female characters in gaming to be very honest. All the designs also look very good while also being very fitting to the era. The character animations are also stellar they easily nailed the 3D anime look which is incredibly hard to do. I wish they did a bit more with Sherlock and showed him do some badass detective work but its obvious they didnt do that because they didnt want him to overshadow Ryunosuke. I immensely loved almost every bit of these two games and I wholeheartedly recommend this 9.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Played until the end of the fourth case and I can already say this is by far my favorite ace attorney! (Maybe some nostalgia factor is at play here, obscuring the equally slow pace of older titles)So yeah, this game is awesome, and the music is great too! _childDocuments_.review: Great game from a great series.Very interesting story and all episodes are connected/related to each other in a very unexpected way. Utill the very end you have no idea "who did it" and how everything will pan out.As original game came out in Japan there are many references to Japaneese culture. One will learn a lot of new things. Be prepared to meet a lot of new words and google them.Character are unique and all the hidden references are fun to detect. I really liked design of most of them. Some of them are brilliant!Music is very good. You never get tired of it and it really helps to create the atmosphere. One thing that was really dissapointed is English voice acting. During the Sholmes cinematics voicing is brilliant but during the anime-part and during the cutscenes it's just terrible. Japaneese voicing is really good as well.Puzzles/cases in general are rather logical and you are able to figure them out. There were only 2 moments during my whole almost 100h of playing when i felt being stuck. One moment was when I missed one clue to move forward. That one was probably on me. But second one happened during the trial and there was NO WAY one would remember one very specific detail  in order to be able to present it. AI is not very helpful either to point you in the right direction. If they just updated the text of the clue - that would make all the difference. So that one was on the developer. Overall, I think difficulty wise this game is not very hard. But you need to had patience to visit all the places and uncover all the clues. Comparing to the old games I really liked the structure and ballance of the game. It feels more logical.I can highly recommend it to anyone who played previous games or completely new to the series.I really hope that Capcom will release those felt doll charms. I would love to own them.I wish I could play this game on my Nintendo DSi....P.S. If you have DLC - spend some time and explore it! There is a ton of material there that will reveal a lot of very interesting and new details about the game, characters and game design in general.

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow, defying all possibility, this duology is even better than the Phoenix Wright trilogy by a million miles. These games perfect absolutely everything about the Ace Attorney franchise, from the gameplay never outstaying it's welcome, the phenomenal soundtrack that is genuinely in my top 5 favorite osts ever and most importantly, the thorough and deep characters and narrative. I don't think there was a single trial in these that was a miss. Even if you never play any other Ace Attorney game, please play this one. Definitely Shu Takumi's magnum opus. 11/10

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the length and seemingly slow pacing stop you. The second of two installments is one of the best games I've ever played and one of the best hunks of juicy fiction I've ever experienced. Characters are top-notch. Crimes are complex but darkly plausible. Court action keeps you on your toes. It picks up pace as it goes, and the downtime builds immersion and emotional investment up until the banger of an ending. As Ace Attorney games go, this could be the series' magnum opus.This is the last Ace Attorney game my family and I have finished together, and now we cry.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I haven’t had the chance to play too many  games, the only one (or, rather, three) I finished was the . I really enjoyed it, so I was very happy when this new collection came out on PC earlier this year.I, for one, liked the idea of moving the plot to the steampunk version of Victorian-era Britain and Japan, but at first, I wasn’t sure how to feel about the whole new set of characters. After a few hours of gameplay, I admit that I grew closer to most of them, and Ryunosuke and Susato proved to be a fun pair of protagonists, but not as much as Phoenix and Maya, at least in my opinion. Sholmes, however, was always hilarious!That said, I can’t complain about any other aspects of the game. There’s more than 70-80 hours of content here, and that’s without all the extras. The cases are sometimes surprisingly challenging, the extremely well crafted, overarching storyline puts many political thrillers to shame, the 3D graphics look gorgeous (for a visual novel, of course), and there are even a few tiny changes and improvements in the gameplay here and there.If you’re a fan of the franchise or adventure games in general, then you should definitely grab this two-game package. I hope Capcom will release more instalments on PC – I’d surely have no  to that!

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: yep it's goodI have played through Phoenix Wright collection, and compared to that, this one fixes a bunch of things that bothered me (, lack of things that can happen in a court), adds a couple of cute mechanics to spice up the gameplay. Even though they still are pretty simple, I did enjoy them when they popped up.These games are a bit more grounded, the cast has lost some of it's craziness, which I did miss, but as a benefit - there's a much larger set of characters that can't be summed up in 1 sentence and have actual depth, so this might be seen as a plus or a minus, depending on what you prefer.It's important to note that with similar playthrough time to the Phoenix wright trilogy, this game has 10-ish cases, whereas the original trilogy had 14 (if you count tutorial ones). This means two things:1. Mysteries are more developed and not as obvious. I enjoyed discovering what really happened much more than before.2. Sometimes, the plot really drags on and stops moving. If you plan to binge all of it, lots of information dumps will be repeated again and again - this was present in previous titles also, but here I think there's more of it, because clues within the case get repeated together with overarching plot points again and again. Because of that, the game really benefits from making significant breaks in between cases, otherwise you might feel exhausted at the end, as I did.Other things that I think would really improve the experience - but I'm sure there's good reason they aren't there:1. More voice acting!2. More animated segments! I think there were none in the second game, and it was a bummerAlso huge kudos to the addition of the autoplay, I hope it's also in the Apollo Justice port.To sum up, I do think this is an improvement over Phoenix Wright trilogy, and worth playing if you liked it, or if you are a newcomer and this would be the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: Will update review later for 2nd game.I'm an Ace Attorney fan who has been parched for games since 2016. Very excited to play this, was not disappointed. I would only note that Ace Attorney originated on the small screen (the NDS) and moved on to mobile. For several reasons, I don't think the big screen of a PC fits the experience. If you can get this game elsewhere or play on a rather small screen (like a Handheld Switch), I think it will be better. The text is purposefully large for smaller devices, and it just doesn't have the same charm on big screens.This game made me laugh out loud a few times, which Ace Attorney games have rarely managed to do. I liked the characters a lot, the whole idea of setting the franchise one or two centuries back in time to 'reinvent' it. Its setting of crossing Meiji era Japan and 20th c. England is rather unique, perhaps even innovative. A point of criticism: it might feel like not a lot has happened in a case, and that might be because of the setting! One of the plot points is that science isn't all that advanced, so there's usually less evidence and more testimony. This is understandable, but it can make cases drag out. Though I've played thirty hours of the first game, it still felt 'short', and it might be because 'not much happened'. The last case of the game suffers from this greatly: probably an hour before the end, you already know what happened, but you just have to keep on proving it. This is the case in other games too, but I feel like it usually is ~20-30 minutes max?As a final note, unlike previous Ace Attorney titles, this one is obviously written as a prequel -- there's at least four unanswered major plot questions at the end, one of which is set up in the first case. Which means to say, you can't really just play the first game and be done with it! I expect at least another 30 hours from the second game.I just finished the second game (76 hrs of playtime, though sometimes I left the game running). I played the game on and off, and I enjoyed the cases. I could anticipate some of the plot twists, but I admit that (especially in the final case) the game caught me off guard! The end, unlike the first game, drags out a lot. There is a big dump of revelations at the end, and the writers want to dedicate enough time to each one; but this could have been handled better, I think. The reveals could have been fed to the player little by little, throughout the game, instead of all at once near the end. Also, in retrospect, the first case in this game really feels like a filler; even though the game otherwise is really masterful at tying in almost every single detail you've seen throughout this entry and its prequel.I prefer the first game only because this one felt like it overstayed its welcome, but maybe that's always been the case with Ace Attorney? The first game had higher highs, too (but not lower lows). In any case, you should play both of them if you want the full story. Though there are some cases I would skip if you only wanted the overarching plot (e.g. first two cases of the second game).

_childDocuments_.review: Edit, after finishing the second game (I've still got a few lines of dialogue left to read, but the case is finished.)This isn't really two different games the way that, say, Dual Destinies and Spirit of Justice are two different games. It's really better to look at it as one whole game.And this one game picks up considerably in its second half. Even the "first" case is very pretty and decently tough—no mere tutorial.The Famous Detective's deductions never get much harder, but they do get a lot more fun. Some of them even gave me chills.The writing improves in the second half, all around. I think even the jokes got funnier.Overall, the game's improvement is significant, and I'm glad I stuck with it. I feel I got my money's worth. I can now recommend it.My previous thoughts will remain below.---I love Ace Attorney, but this game is annoying so far.I'm on the 4th case in the first game. I won't give any story spoilers but I will give minor to moderate "gameplay spoilers". I'm sure you all know this game is set in the late 1800s so I won't spend time on those details.My main complaint so far is with the writing/pacing. There's serious "show don't tell" problems. It seems like in the OG Ace Attorney games there would just be a few short words loaded with meaning, and a pixelly facial expression, and you'd bring your own feelings about that to the situation. There wasn't 5000 words explaining how Nick feels so bad about what happened yesterday, how death is terrible and court is super important, repeated over and over, and how as a result he's scared about what's going to happen today. Like, the game trusted you to just get it, and you did. This game is telling me what I'm supposed to feel, A LOT, and it's really messing with my enjoyment.Related to this and also impacting the emotional response, I'm getting accused of stuff for no reason other than that the prosecutor is just generally being adversarial. Like if you look above in the preview screenshots here on Steam, there's one where the guy is saying, "that is what is termed a baseless accusation." Well, in context, it's not baseless at all, you actually went to a lot of trouble to establish a basis, and you're also not even making an accusation, not directly at least, so neither part of what this guy is accusing you of doing wrong makes any sense. So that's one. Well, any game can make one mistake right? Well that exact same kind of thing has just happened again at another point in the game and it's what made me annoyed enough to write this review. Because twice is a systemic problem with the writing. I know it's way too hipster to "like their old stuff better" but all the old prosecutors were better. Even Franziska, while she was ridiculous with the whip, she was pretty serious in court otherwise and what she said would actually make sense. Like I could actually suspend disbelief well enough to believe she was a prodigy. And she's my least favorite OG prosecutor. Seriously even, like, Prosecutor Gavin felt like a worthy foe to cross swords with. This guy is overreacting to everything. I do really like the whole Dracula thing he's got going on though.Don't tell me it's a translation problem with this prosecutor just saying random crap, I paid money for this official localization. Oh, speaking of which, there are still all the standard Phoenix Wright typos but at this point I'm used to that from these games. HOWEVER, beyond that, I noticed in the current case, that there's something on the GROUND, (outdoors, in the snow) but the game has now twice referred to that thing as being "on the floor". That is a weird mistranslation or something and while I'm used to typos in Ace Attorney I'm not used to stuff like "ground" and "floor" getting mixed up.My other big complaint is that the game is too easy. MAYBE the game will get harder later, if so and if you can update reviews on Steam, I will do so. But so far, it is really easy, and it's not just because "oh you already played 8 phoenix wright games now you're too good at them."Do you remember in Apollo Justice when you had to use the bracelet to examine people. Do you remember how hard that one newspaper dude's tell was to find? Well there's a couple unique mechanics in this game that could have been amazing, and they're both similar to the AJ bracelet, in that you observe people. (One mechanic is during trial, one is during investigation). But they took all the difficulty out by having pop-up effects (like, you will visually see a question mark or exclamation point appear on screen) along with sound effects, or the person's demeanor will just violently change in an unmissable way, so that there's no subtlety or difficulty with the observation. It takes all the tension out. On the investigation version of this mechanic, it also suffers from a serious lack of red herrings. So it's about as hard as sesame street "one of these things is not like the others..." Feels like I'm just clicking the equivalent of a blinking, shiny red X marks the spot...The hardest questions to answer so far have actually turned out to be questions where it didn't matter what I answered because the story was going to continue the same either way.Don't tell me the 3DS Phoenix Wright games were also this easy, Dual Destinies had some serious tension by the third case and even Spirit of Justice had its moments.Another thing I want to complain about is the jury system. Yes there's a jury in these trials but so far they have added nothing good. The jury members are some of the flattest possible characters and they aren't even lovable anime stereotypes. They switch from GUILTY to INNOCENT on a dime, being a bunch of emotional dumb morons, and it is dissolving my suspension of disbelief like an acid bath while infuriating me at the same time. The presence of the jury does not change the basic Phoenix Wright trial gameplay, except that whenever they have one of their little "GUILTY GUILTY GUILTY" hissy fits you have to do a new mechanic where you show how they're contradicting each other. If you played Danganronpa V3, it's a little like the debate scrum... If the debate scrum took 10 minutes and just stated the obvious. It's not that fun and it feels like padding.Now I've aired my grievances I'll say some nice things.I really like the Famous Detective. I wish he was a bit smarter, it feels weird to correct such a Famous Detective. But that's an okay compromise if it allows a cool new mechanic, I just wish the mechanic wasn't dead easy like I said above. I like the Famous Detective's Roommate though I haven't seen very much of her yet.I like how some of the cases (trying not to say anything that would be a spoiler here) have an ambiguous resolution. I don't remember having ambiguous cases before in Ace Attorney so it's cool to see it here.I start a new Ace Attorney game with faith in the game at 100%. My faith in this game took a few hits over the first couple cases but I'm like "okay the first few cases are allowed to be easy, Steel Samurai was the first good case in the original and that was case 3". But the constant fanfiction style blah blah blah, the padding, the taking 10 minutes to cover an obvious objection, the stupid prosecutor and stupid jury, all of it is having a steady eroding effect. Right now I'm at like 50% faith, meaning I think there's about a 50% chance this game will pull out some really good stuff like I've come to expect from Ace Attorney by the end. That's all I want. As for the second game in the package I'm still at 70-80% faith, since I haven't played it yet so maybe it's way better and skips the hand holding.IDK like I said I will update this later if that's a thing you can do. I want to be able to recommend it, at least to fans of Ace Attorney, but I can't yet. Maybe by the end I will change my mind.

_childDocuments_.review: The Phoenix games only came out as good as they did because of hardware limitations.Lift, those and the word count jumps by 90% but still conveys the same amount of information.The cast is extremely dry this time around, the few wacky characters that are present can't properly bounce off anything because of that, resulting in them just being annoying.The new jury system is a interesting idea, but it never reaches the same impact it had when it was first introduced when it seemed like a dynamic system. The jury exam is sadly linear and will always happen at the same time, a criticism of the system would usually be that it detracts from the Prosecution (the rival character), but since he is so boring this time around, the jury is quite welcome.The trials are interconnected in this one, leading to some great late game cases, what is not great is that the setup cases often feel unsatisfying or unresolved because they have to build up the final.I just don't believe in investing so much time until a game gets good.Too much of what made Ace Attorney so enjoyable is just not present in this title.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey, im on the 4. case of the first game now and I think I can give a sorta good opinion on the game so far? The first trial was really good from my perspective, the second one of the other hand was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chore. _childDocuments_.review: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles is not only a return to form for the series, it is in my opinion the best game(s) in the franchise!A story so carefully planned throughout 10 cases, each being of great importance to the plot, and with a such a charming colourful cast of characters, it is truly a marvel to play though it.The investigation parts of the game has never been paced as well as here, also adding a new very fun minigame in the great Herlock Sholmes's Logic and Reasoning Spectacular absolutely stealing the show!The same goes for the court proceedings, now featuring a jury and multiple witnesses at once presenting their testimonies, making the game feel truly unique.The witnesses themselves have never been less annoying as well, in fact the whole cast of characters from more to less important ones have never been funnier and more charming. I applaud the phenomenal character and story writing that manages to beat the best entries in the Phoenix Wright's timeline, just as well as the new mechanics that reinvent the game a bit and make it feel fresh again!
_childDocuments_.name: The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Although the setting is no longer in modern Japan/USA, the heart, humor, and suspense is still on point for the Ace Attorney series. Generally a good entry point for newcomers due to tangential references to the original Ace Attorney franchise and updated graphics, Ace Attorney Chronicles is a good starting point for those who were always on the fence with Ace Attorney.

_childDocuments_.review: By no means perfect, definitely has its share of strange contradictions that barely make sense with the relevant evidence that the series is known for, but the Story Mode letting you skip those parts without trial & error / looking things up makes it a lot more tolerable. (no game, a person slumped over after being shot is NOT a contradiction with their death being immediate. wtf you thinking)A few of the cases felt a bit underwhelming, and the final testimony of case 3 of the 2nd game was hella rushed just to sloppily cram in one last plot twist that wasn't really necessary.However, of all the Ace Attorney games, this one does by far the best job at telling a coherent story. Plot elements from the start of the first game are still relevant in the end of the 2nd, cases tie together very smoothly without feeling forced, and every character and subplot is given time to shine throughout the 50 hour story.
