_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most unique games I've ever played. Probably the first game where you actually make deductions based on evidence like an actual detective and can use evidence to come to your own conclusions way before your character does. The visual style is such a mishmash but somehow it just works. The music is a fantastic blend of synthwave and smooth jazz. The worldbuilding is beyond anything I've seen in games and is the most original setting for a game I've ever had the pleasure of playing. The pixel hunting aspect can get a bit tiresome but, for the most part, actual clues and evidence is usually in obvious places and extras aren't all that necessary but you'd be advised to at least have enough to get certain collectibles and gather testimonies from a particular character though it's enough if you keep a buffer of 15 gems all the time. _childDocuments_.review: This game was a pretty big disappointment for me. Surprisingly so after playing and loving similar games like all 3 Danganronpa games, Outer Wilds, and multiple visual novels. It was like a mashup of a different genres and gameplay mechanics that I like but Paradise Killer falls flat.To keep this short here's a list of why this game went from a 9/10 in the first 10 hours to a 6/10 after 100%ing this game in the last 10 hours.Janky air mobility. After getting some movement upgrade's it gets better but this problem never goes awayFinite currency. Something that was always worrying was that you can over spend money on fast travel and soft lock yourself out of key evidence that require money to get.Amount of useless collectables. At first it's interesting to read all the descriptions of relics you get but half of them dont matter to the story at all and 90% are not needed for the final trial.And the biggest disappointment: The Final Trial. After collecting everything, finding all secret areas, maxing hangout time for all character, exhausting all dialogue options, I went into the final trial waiting to stick it to these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. However the trial plays out like a check list. Your character just says I have this evidence, the judge does it's calculation , if you got at least 60% of the evidence the person is guilty, NEXT! Besides the first of the 7 cases no one really reacts at all for being charged guilty besides 2-3 lines of dialogue. Worse yet if you decide to kill a friend like Lydia, Lady Love Dies has absolutely NO reaction, no remorse, not even a line of dialogue before killing her.On top of all of that the ending never changes, you could find everyone guilty or all innocent and the ending will play out the exact same.I really do feel like this could have been an indie masterpiece, and I do recommend it, but lack of time or talent in the game's mechanics and narrative resolution leaves me disappointed because I know there's a great game under all these problems.Plus the music slaps.

_childDocuments_.review: Facts or truth, are 2 different things. Remember it, because in case of this game it’s one of the first lesson and it’s most important tip.To avoid spoiling too much of the plot and the world. We’re part of mysterious Syndicate – organization of “pious devouts” that tries to resurrect gods, whose gave them powers and partial immortality in exchange for endless loyalty and worship.Paradise (titulary island and secondary “hero” of this story) is endlessly reworked ideal island, hidden in pocket dimension; which serves as a Syndicate base of operation. Why "endlessly reworked" and how ironic island name is, I won't spoil.Plot is brilliantly presented and it’s hard to tear away from it. Entire story is driven by detective game of interrogating remaining members of Syndicate, and comparing their versions to other testimonies and evidence found on island.Keep in mind, that everyone has a motive, everyone has believable alibi, everyone had reasons to commit this crime, everyone shifts blames on another, everyone is willing to throw someone else under the proverbial bus. Isn’t it surprising, that only innocent in the story with clearly aligned morals is Shinji? Demon by race and tourist by profession.All characters are well written, overstylized and hyperbolized, with clearly defined personalities. As someone else noted in another review – this game feels like Danganronpa.Art style is vaporwave mixed with 80’s stylistics and designs; while architecture style clearly hints postmodernism influences, mixed with Egyptian and Sumerian temple style.✅😐Art style - you'll love it or hate it, nothing in-between. Neutral, because it really depends on personal preference.❌

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable one time experience. _childDocuments_.review: --The game looks beautiful. The setting is a virtual simulation which looks like a tropical, upscale Tokyo. --The dialogue is fun, especially for the demon characters. The mysteries are not bad.--The tone is wildly dark. The government ruling over the island openly and regularly kidnaps and murders thousands of slaves to collect blood sacrifices to bring back ancient alien gods. There is no way to fight the mass-murder or slavery in any way or bring its perpetrators to justice. The only crimes you DO get to solve are crimes against the leaders running the mass murder system. You're not an actual investigator, you're a Peter Strezok fixer. --Gameplay design is stunningly unfriendly. No auto-save is savage. Money is critically limited, and *finite*, there's only so many crystals to pick up around the map, but costs are NOT finite, every time you want to use the fast-travel system costs money. So expect to slog your way up like 10 super-tall-ass apartments collecting $1 at a time because there is no other way to pay for stuff. Being broke all the time absolutely sucked. Peter Strezok doesn't pick up $1 at a time. --The map system is complete garbage. It's like walking from New York to New Jersey and you somehow end up in California with no idea how you got there, how to reach your intended destination, or how the hell they screwed up a map that badly. The same guy who took out the autosave, no doubt. --The upgrade system is super-non-intuitive. All of the mobility upgrades are trapped behind $5 footbaths in a game where $5 is a lot and there's no indication the footbath matters. Each footbath gives you a superpower like a double-jump or dash jump that make moving around MUCH more livable. If you don't blindly spend $5 on the footbaths you are in for a whirlwind of hurt.--The execution on the trial is lacking. In a classic mystery game like Ace Attorney, the first part of the game will be you collecting evidence and then in the trial the game challenges you to piece together the evidence to show you understand the case and can see through the culprit's lies. In this game, if you have all the evidence, your character will just read it out and then the person will be found guilty, with no choices or deductions or mental work on the part of the player. This felt very rushed.

_childDocuments_.review: I will start off by saying I do not normally write review, but this game has compelled me to do so.I would wholeheartedly recommend Paradise Killers. You can tell from playing the passion and thought that has been put into the game. It may not be as highly polished as AAA title, but the developers have used what they have available to the highest standard. The attention to detail is phenomenal, and the game oozes style. It is a very stylish game, and it wears that on its sleeve. This style even wanders into the absurd, and this is what makes it for me. Being a fan of detective games, this is one of the best examples of that genre. This game very much drops you into the mystery and leaves you as the "investigation freak" to explore, and unravel the mystery on your own, which is very enjoyable. This is more than anything else a game of exploration. The exploration is made even better by the setting it takes place in. I will just end by saying that that if you are a fan of detective games then get this, of course its not for everyone, but honesty I enjoyed every minute of it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're not the type of person that enjoys heavy detective games or RPGs, keep reading, I'm one of those people. Paradise Killer did a great job of captivating me from the get-go. I'm not the type of person that was interested in games like Danganronpa, and I've always disliked RPGs, but Paradise Killer falls in it's own little spot that is awesome. Open world exploration, in conjunction with some tough puzzles, a bit of social engineering, and interpreting what you're given makes this game what it is. I really love the atmosphere (not for everyone), and the killer soundtrack. I thought that lots of mechanics were just flat out cool, like finding secrets and music tapes. Some mechanics are a bit annoying, like picking up currency shows a splash screen every time. This isn't a big deal, but one of the slight annoyances that contribute to this game feeling a bit slow. I was a bit skeptical about the 'open world' claims about this game, and boy was I surprised. Instead of being a linear story with one concise solution, you construct your own solution which I absolutely love. It is really fun to mentally connect two conflicting pieces of information and extrapolate any sort of suspicion on your own based on that (without the game's help!). Personally, I loved the atmosphere and soundtrack, which may not be for everyone but is well done in my opinion. The story is very deep, I lost it a few times but could generally keep track of what was going on. It did take a lot of attention, and gets really existential and flat out won't make sense sometimes. But, to be honest, I was still there just to enjoy being in the world rather than worry about the gods' higher powers or whatever. Of course, I'm still paying attention to the story, but you can certainly tone down your direct attention to the story and still have a blast. All the tid-bits you can collect and certain small side stories are cool as hell. If you enjoy exploring, doing your own thing, and appreciating video game atmosphere, Paradise Killer is awesome and I personally highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I never review but this game was great.Completed in one sitting to my satisfaction, i believe i collected all the evidence and the journey was thrilling the whole way through. Never played a game in this genre before but have had a brilliant ride. _childDocuments_.review: [NO SPOILERS] (And YES, I do compare this heavily to Danganronpa in my review)Coming from someone who loved the Danganronpa franchine, I gotta admit I am a bit dissapointed with Paradise Killer.The game is obviously attributed to the works of the Danganronpa franchise as the two share a uncanny amount of similarities. Yet, I can't help but feel like they somehow placed a strong focus on the most boring elements from Danganronpa - and at the same time but a lack of focus on the elements that made Danganronpa a good franchise. To elaborate on this, I feel like the investigation parts of the Danganronpa games are what holds the games back the most. Walking in the halls is clunky, and all you do is click "INTERACT" with anything that lights up when you approach it. While it is interesting to slowly start building your take on the crime based on this, I feel like Paradise Killer just streches this to 11. The island is way to big, and you spend the majority of your time just walking from A to B. Yes, there is a fast travel feature but it costs money and honestly takes forever to finish because they show this fancy taxi animation whenever you use it. Additionally, all the amount of crazy ♥♥♥♥ that happens is just a tad bit too excessive (and that's coming from the Danganronpa fan). When the game decides to introduce new plot-points and laws of the universe we are in at the ending segment of the game, it feels kind of annoying to have all your pre-thought notions out the window. As for where I felt the game under-delivered compared to Danganronpa is within the conclusion of the story. For the sake of keeping this spoiler-free I won't mention any specifics. But I kinda got the feeling this system was left half-finished. At the point where you are accusing suspects for crime X, there is no option to select multiple suspects and it feels like the game just instantly "knows" you meant to select the ones you did. Which feels kinda underwhelming because it sort of puts things in a "it'll be alright no matter what you pick". All of these accusations were also (mostly) only consisting of you (the player), the judge and the accused, which I found really lacking in terms of writing. Surely it would've been more natural for all the testimonies to speak for themselves instead of a prompt shown on screen that "character Y testified to this earlier". This also brings me into the manner of which this accusation was done. All you do is click through all your gathered intel, which is sorted out for you. There is almost zero choices to make here, zero ways you present your evidence, zero ways in which you argue your claims and zero ways the defendant tries to disprove your claims. Which completely breaks the entire "gotcha!" moment the game builds up to with the whole trial imitating a TV show! :((TL;DRIdk, maybe I'm just being harsh on Paradise Killer because I expected more out of a game with such stellar reviews. But in my opinion, you should definitively play Danganronpa > Paradise Killer. Unless the anime aesthetic of the game is a absolute no-go for you and you're more into LGBT characters, then that's fair - this is a good game; I just had higher hopes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lengthy, open-world detective mystery. You explore the beautiful island as an investigator, searching for clues about a mass murder. The truth and the facts are yours to decide. Conspiracies are everywhere.The  island is beautiful and varied. Nothing is spoon-fed to you, everything is up to you to discover. There's upgrades and abilities to get and it's up to you to discover how to get them. In the current day of tutorials being overbearing and forced, I greatly enjoyed that this game trusts you to explore and learn at your own pace. The lore of how we ended up in our current situation is interesting. The characters are eccentric. The music is jazzy and upbeat. The game struck me as an indie passion project.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone because I can't work out who it is for.It's not a detective game. There is nothing to solve. The critical path will force you to the conclusion by just following instructions.It's not a great visual novel. It belongs to the "throwing constant nonsense with no context at the reader" school of worldbuilding and you quickly tune it all out as you got through the game.Ultimately the most enjoyment I got out of the game was hoovering up the collectibles at the end and even that is kind of a pain. The fast travel system requires a currency and the menu's are slow. "Detective vision" has to be constantly refreshed and the movement system often behaves just a little short of what you expected.Game was clearly made with a lot of effort and it has a banging soundtrack (available on Spotify) but it's a sort of hollow experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly addictive game. It is an open world investigation game. You are free to explore the island for clues and question suspects in any order you choose. _childDocuments_.review: Quick disclaimer, this review might have some light spoilers:This game drew me in so hard. The crazy lore and worldbuilding, the murder mystery, The stylish aesthetic and amazing art, the groovy as hell music, and the big open world ripe for investigating. The world is the perfect size too, not too big to be frustrating to get around, but also not too small and cramped. I do with there was a better or faster way to get around, or free fast travel, but it wasn't a huge issue. I would like to say the mystery that you're investigating in this game is extremely well crafted with a lot of crazy twists, but never seeming too out there or like it's stretching for twists. Talking to everyone and building up the real story piece by piece is such a delight. Don't look for much in terms of fast paced gameplay, if you're here for something like LA Noire then turn back. this game is pretty much a visual novel with walking mechanics and an open world. Though the collectathon-ish aspect adds to it's appeal for me at least. It makes it more than just a VN. There are two gripes that I have with this game, amazing as it is. There's only one ending sequence. With all the evidence you can twist it in any way to convict, prosecute, and execute literally any character; you will never be told if your accusations are 100% correct or not. This in itself is not a bad thing. It is actually very poetic and a great design choice. The truth is what you make it, that seems to be the whole theme of this game: find YOUR truth. The issue is that no matter who you end up executing, the ending will always be the same no matter what. No different dialogue, no special conversations, no extra after credit scenes, no easter eggs or secrets.  It just feels so unsatisfying. Not only that, but (Spoilers incoming, skip to next bracket) the whole game alludes to everyone being unsatisfied with the islands and how they work. Some want to end them all together and just move on. There are many choices in which you can agree or disagree with these sentiments, calling the syndicate corrupt or evil and saying their ways must end. There is no wrap up to these dangling strings set up. You can't choose to leave the islands in the end, you can't choose to help free Henry, and you can't choose to help change syndicate ways. Hell even the judge agrees that the way of governing is bad. It is another thread that just feels unsatisfying. (End of spoilers read from here). My second gripe is how anticlimactic the final trial is. If you are expecting something exiting like (and forgive me for even inciting this) Danganronpa, with a trial that has actual gameplay mechanics, think again. This game only has one final trial and it is more along the lines of a Pheonix Wright game. Which isn't bad in any way, I did actually enjoy the trial, it was fun and exciting piecing things together, and the fact that you can twist the evidence any way you want is really awesome. However I played around 16 of investigation with this trial being teased and held over my head, I was expecting a bit more. It was really short and a little disappointing in the moment. But again, I did still enjoy it a lot. To sum it up, this is an amazing game, and an amazing work of written fiction. I really hope for some kind of sequel or spinoff, and I look forward to whatever the devs work on next. the small gripes I had didn't ruin the experience and they are no reason to avoid it.  I give this a solid 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw Paradise Killer, I instantly went “nope” and moved on. I mean, it looked like a weak attempt to mix the currently still popular 80s aesthetic with Suda51 and Danganronpa that had all of the flair, but no substance. Yet, as time went by I’ve heard more and more good things about the title and eventually decided to give it a go myself. While my original assumptions weren’t entirely disproven, Paradise Killer turned out to be a really enjoyable game.Paradise Killer is an open world investigation adventure game with elements of a visual novel and, possibly most uniquely, fully unrestricted first person traversal controls. You can walk whenever you like, crouch, jump, even unlock additional traversal options at specific points. And you can explore the island you will find yourself on any way you see fit. It’s not exactly unheard of, since the story exploration games/walking sims started similarly and the revival of first person perspective adventure games with horror themed titles of Frictional Games all played similarly, but it’s still quite unique just how completely unrestrained you are in this game. Given that the island is also full optional items (some of which can be helpful for the investigation), it’s very unusual to see the game just be totally fine with the player abusing the jumping physics or weird geometry inconsistencies and, in fact, almost expecting many people to do that.While that might not be a defining characteristic of the game, it certainly shows how open the title is. There’s a setup – a mass murder, – and a certain expectation at the start that people would at least look at the crime scene first. But you may choose to just go in a different direction and explore as you want, finding more potential leads or even new cases as you explore and talk to the weird inhabitants of this bizarre and effed up world. Suda51 comparisons are unavoidable and the developers are wearing their influences as a badge. And they do try to take this weird vaporwave meets Old Gods rule the world dystopia feel different from what you usually get from Suda51. Resulting in a universe that makes more sense, feels more consistent and doesn’t flippantly invent some crap just because it was fun. Which might be disappointing to some (not that there isn’t any “punk spirit” in the game), but I found at least interesting. And while I personally didn’t love the a e s t h e t i c or even the catchy soundtrack all that much (as it’s more “plain” and far less “quirky” than something Masafumi Takada would do), I’m sure lots of people would love this far more than I did.Now, if you want this game specifically for an investigation part, you might be slightly disappointed, as lots of it requires you to also want to explore and “hang out” with characters, and also because there are no real “bad choices” you can make up until the trials start. You can find a bunch of evidence, talk to a person and ask them about literally everything with no consequence whatsoever, you can’t say a “wrong” thing or play your cards too early here. I didn’t find that disappointing, but, as a result, it did make all of the talks work far more like just clicking through stuff to get it over with, rather than thinking about what you talk about with whom and when. Additionally, given the size of the island, you might sometimes get in the situation where you remember seeing a place you need to go to with an item you just found, but the game doesn’t keep any information on that. It actually does track pretty much everything and any, say, computer you found that you “hack” with a simple minigame, will be tracked and shown in your AR mode. And it will smartly sort all of the evidence items for you in the computer interface. Yet if it’s just a spot on the ground which you saw several hours ago and can’t remember where it was now that you can interact with it – can’t help you there.I suppose, the main strength of the game, in how nicely it flows and how open it is, is also it’s downside. Even during the final part of the game (which you can initiate whenever you feel ready) – the trials, – you usually only have to select the person you consider guilty, the rest will play itself based on the evidence you have uncovered. No need to explain yourself, no need to point out the specifics, no need to word replies carefully or not choose some options. Just select a person and go through all topics, just like with the dialogues. If you don’t have enough evidence to support the claim, it won’t fly, if you do it will, as simple as that. The game does focus on the concept that “a fact isn’t the truth”, which comes into play when you consider if you actually wish to condemn someone who is clearly involved, or let it slide and remain outside the truth of the matter. And it’s a nice concept. Yet, I can’t say that it would make you truly pause and think before acting, more likely you will have made up your mind far before it comes to making the choice.Still, I really enjoyed exploring the island, learning more about the terrible world of this game and investigating the cases. They’re nicely written and voiced and the game isn’t all style with no substance. But I can’t say that it engaged me as much as the investigative parts of, say, 999 or Danganronpa which it clearly borrows from. It’s a really nice game that’s worth checking out – it might be just the thing for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A uniquely aesthetic detective game with an open world twist, where no one (and everyone) can be guilty as long as you can mount a case against them. Brilliant music, pleasant art, surprisingly deep worldbuilding presented mostly in an organic manner, and a mystery convoluted enough to have you piece the parts of the grand conspiracy on your own (and then, more than a day after you put it away, still consider what you might have missed).

_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty unique mix of Visual Novel, Platformer and Open World in an even more original universe. Each time you think you have figured it out you get a new lead that may make you doubt everything and rethink. It remind me a bit of Danganronpa with how extravagant and stylished the characters are and how every character feels like the culprit.The world is very very well built, if you see it you can go there. I never felt like I was not supposed to be somewhere. If you are bad at platforming, you'll still be able to go everywhere you need for the investigation. If you are good, it feel pretty rewarding to reach a roof with no stairs then jump somewhere else and you can "sequence break" ( It's open world, there is technically no sequence beside a few areas needing an upgrade to open. ) your way to some later leads before the previous that would lead you there.The open world is also very detailed and full of details, the only places without anything would not have anything like a beach far from the town or roofs with no way to access normally. The different sectors are small enough and different enough that you won't feel like you're walking in the same place all the time.The leads you get and the small number of characters you can interact with mean you won't ever get lost or overwhelmed, you'll always have something to check out if you don't feel like exploring by yourself. The many fast travel points combined with how well put together the island is mean you can quickly get where you need without turning it into a walking simulator. Most of the game I walked everywhere because I would always find new collectibles until the last hour or so when I had everything and used the Fast Travel a lot.The only thing I like less was how easy the game is, the game pretty much do the detective work for you by getting the clues and talking with the characters. Starlight, your super computer, is too good and take care of the leads for you and you are left without much doubt.I'm very looking forward to their next game and I recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably not as politically meaningful (and definitely not as open-ended) as Disco Elysium, and not as cleverly contrapted as Return of the Obra Dinn - but still, those are personal favorites of mine and arguably among Paradise Killer's closest peers in these regards. This one's politics are definitely a lot less silly than they appear to be at first - on the contrary, the allegories seem to me to hold up pretty well, with the general population being used as cannon fodder by elites that care only about their own well-being, ideological disputes and power plays (with the military having to pick their side), their indifference to everything else playfully disguised as sun-bathed cosmic horror (and it actually works, somewhat surprisingly so). Also, the complete freedom given in how to proceed with the investigation (who do you talk to, what do you discuss, what do you look for, how thoroughly you do so, who do you accuse in the end, for what and based on which evidence etc.), while a little overwhelming at first, becomes tremendously engaging as things go and leads to a surprisingly complex endgame: piecing everything together right before the final series of trials was both intellectually challenging and very rewarding, while the ending felt right in its ambivalence.Oh, and of course, the game's presentation (visuals, music) and sense of style are both top-notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The characters are fun, the mystery is clever and pulls no cheap tricks, the exploration is engaging, even if slow at times. It's the first game in a long time that has delivered the kind of wonderfully bewildering experience I used to get from Suda51's early games. It's far from a Suda51 ripoff, but the influences from Flower, Sun, and Rain and Killer7 are obvious. The trial and epilogue sections are unfortunately under developed, with the former feeling more like a victory lap than an effort to prove my theories, and the latter feeling like it didn't have enough writing in it to justify.

_childDocuments_.review: A story based first person collectaton with useless collectables mixed in with suda51 and anime references. What it boils down to is basically running around the place collecting stuff since you can't really tell apart what significance the items have once you get them (there are very important ones inbetween) and backtracking between people, shaking them for more answers to which they usually go "yeah i don't know, and if i knew, i wouldn't tell you" there is very little deduction going on, and even in the end you basically present every evidence as if "yeah here you go" as the crime solves itself. It's alright, but not a spectacular game, its shortcomings come from the horrible gameplay design (yes i've 100% this game and collectables are completely useless) and it's a shame since it's not badly written.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably best described as a non-linear, Danganronpa-esque open world walking sim with some collectables thrown in, all played to the backdrop of some great music that truly ties it all together.There's a certain type of zen feeling as you're gradually exploring the island, finding collectables & clues, all the while peeling back the mysteries of the island/game world.I have some nitpicks - the consumable blood gems being used for fast travel can get a little annoying towards the end if you run low on them, but there are some permanent buffs you can acquire to make finding collectables & traversal much easier, so it balances itself out for the most part. The trials all taking place at the finale of the game also gives the ending an abrupt sort of feeling, especially given the trials themselves are mostly open & shut cases provided you've gathered enough evidence; there's no real opportunity for any of the defendants to throw a wrench in your prosecutorial case against them, which is a shame given how lengthy and back-and forth Danganronpa/Ace Attorney's trials tend to be, you can't help but think the conclusion here would be a bit more epic if there were more of a showdown.Overall, though; a lot better than I thought it would turn out, it's a really nice palate cleanser between other games if you fancy trying something different.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A truly wonderful hidden gem of a game. The setting, characters, and murder mystery are all extremely unique. I have never experienced a fictional universe like the one presented by Paradise Killer. Although extremely bizarre and psychedelic, it has its own internally consistent rules and lore that makes the setting work, no matter how outlandish everything might seem. Everything that is presented to you is so absurd yet so genuine and unironic, that slowly the absurd becomes the plausible. Then the plausible becomes the mundane. Yes, this is a game that managed to make a vaporwave-inspired metaphysical universe with immortal beings with names like "Kiwami Eyes" or "Crimson Acid" existing in a pocket dimension kidnapping and enslaving humans like cattle to farm their psychic energy to resurrect a bunch of genocidal gods seem reasonable and mundane. Trust me, that's not even a tenth of the picture. But this game sells itself as a murder mystery. How's the mystery then? The mystery is wonderfully complex, and the investigative gameplay is one of the most organic that I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. The key difference between this game and most other detective games is the fact that it has a free-roaming 3D sandbox, like Danganronpa or LA Noire but with much more verticality and higher density of ♥♥♥♥ to find. Exploration really is the name of the game here, as the things you find in the environment are usually 10x more revealing than whatever these shady ass characters are feeding you. Facts and evidence are presented to you in completely random order, or more specifically, in the order than you stumble upon them in the sandbox. And believe me, every single second, you will stumble into some sort of clue merely by exploring this jam-packed sandbox that the developers have so lovingly crafted. They really put in the effort to fill this place with secrets and answers, and I have had multiple instances where I've wandered off into an obscure corner of the map just to see if the devs have put an easter egg in there or something, only to discover that there is a massive clue to solving the mystery hidden right there in the corner. Along with Danganronpa, Phoenix Wright, or the Zero Escape games, this game is the patron saint of those "OH ♥♥♥♥" moments where you realize something you thought was true was actually wrong all along. TLDR: The world is surreal and unique, the characters are colorful and fun, the mystery is complex with intertwining plot threads, character motivations, and political intrigue, and the investigative gameplay is extremely immersive and rewarding. Get this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: 'That's human nature: we need mysteries.''But a mystery can make you insane!''That's the knife edge we all walk.'Paradise Killer is a weird game to recommend. It's not without its flaws and even more importantly, its strange setting, deliberately awkward graphics and simple gameplay will be a turn off for some. In essence it's a simple whodunnit in the form of a graphic novel meets walking simulator. Interactivity is limited to exploring the environment and collecting items, which in turn will create new dialog options with the characters. Then start the ending at any time you think you have found enough 'evidence'.Where the game shines in my opinion is the lore and quite original world combined with a vibrant 90s 'Active Worlds' aesthetic and a jazzy synth soundtrack. It's as if HP Lovecraft wrote one of his stories of terrible unimaginable Elder Gods while snorting cocaine in an 80s Miami. The game drops you in the thick of it, and the earlier hours of the game it's all quite baffling. But continue playing and things become clearer, and vastly more mundane and therefore also somewhat less interesting. Basically the game is slightly too long, even though it can be finished in about 15 hours. The writing is pretty good, but the goofy design of the game gets kind of in the way if the story it tries to tell. Still, I enjoyed my time on Paradise Island 24 and hope to explore more of this world. But hopefully with slightly better graphics, since after one game of neon colors and 2D sprites I think this gimmick has now run its course.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Just beat the game and honestly I'm kinda torn about it.The game is mainly divided into two modes of gameplay - Island exploration and dialogue.The island exploration is interesting at first and has a certain old school charm but quickly becomes clunky and tedious. The puzzles are repetitive as all hell with only a couple of interesting ones here and there.The dialog and story are very engaging, the world created here is out of the ordinary to say the least and the characters are fun. The more you learn about the mystery the more you become engaged in it and want to solve it fully.So I guess if like me, you don't mind walking around a whole lot and picking up mostly useless knickknacks to get to a good story, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: There isn't anything quite like early japanese mystery visual novels. It's not the high detail pixelated streets of japan, but the feel is just as cool. A fairly short game, a combination of collectathon and a 3D visual novel mystery, Paradise Killer is a great excuse for listening to too much city pop again. You can spend the time to solve the mystery completely or just botch the entire thing in ten minutes. My only criticism is that I wish it were longer. It is not nearly as detailed a mystery as I would like, especially the ending, which plays itself a bit too much. Ultimately for the length of the game I can't complain. I hope there will be more like this to come. There is nothing quite like solving a galactic murder scheme while city pop is blasting on the city speaker system, and the only god we summoned is laughing at how incompetent we are.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: was recommended this by a friend, picked it up on sale and gave it a try and wow i really like it, a lot more than i was expecting to! vaporwave admittedly is not my top choice of aesthetic but for some reason the vibes in this game really did a number on me, i love existing in the world, not to mention the really good music and characters. really enjoyed putting together all the evidence, and appreciated that the player is left to interpret it for themselves, leaving the explanation only for the end-game trial section. even as i was doing the trials i was still deliberating over the evidence, trying to decide who really dun it! and it was rewarding to see that my investigating and hunches led to a (mostly correct) verdict. i am rambling enough so i will leave it here for now, PLAY NOW IF YOU LIKE DETECTIVE GAMES!
