_childDocuments_.review: My review on Paradise Killer went from negative to positive. With helpful devs that are on the lookout for bugs, it's been a really nice breath of fresh air. I've downloaded Paradise Killer on switch, and I'm not planning on refunding the one I got on steam, so that my friends can try it out.The game has been quite the unique experience! Playing it on switch was even better, as I got to passively play it on the side. From what I've been gathering, this is a game about "finding your own truth"- this means that you present the evidence, and those facts will become the truth, shaping a new story. It was plainly amazing to play this game. I've managed to make Henry Division not guilty, and I was damn proud!The game was amazing, but few things were a little meh, on my own stance:- The game is so focused on "your own truth" that there's no realistic consequences/ending to who were guilty. After the trial is done, you're allowed to execute/exile people on your own accordance, which does... nothing much? At least, I haven't found anything like that. There seems to be little after-trial content, making it seem like my decisions are kind of irrelevant.- Game's got so many typos! It's wonk. And even if we ignore the spelling mistake, there's an astonishingly high amount of lacking commas, which, uh, well. The game's meant to be writing in a sort of poetic way, with all these odd, alien terms that are a big hard to grasp, but seems to tend a lot toward the "casual" writing style. Things like "No worries LD." instead of "No worries, LD." were majorly popping off everywhere. It's not something big that ruins the game, but I can say it made a few sentence feel weird to read; especially in the trial part.- This is way more personal opinion, but playing as the bad guys doesn't feel right. As I said, I managed to find Henry innocent of all crimes... but what was the point? He's going to die, anyway. He's a Citizen. People like Lydia had very little implication with the murder itself, and in the truth I found, was mildly manipulated/deceived, but was still executed over a milder punishment. I love the idea of this game, I absolutely adore the theme of it, but playing as tyrant cult leaders that abduct people doesn't exactly feel good.All in all, Paradise Killer was a very good game, and I know I'll be playing it more to find more truths.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic game! Let me start by saying that I am a huge fan of the Danganronpa games and the Phoenix Wright series, so I was quite interested in playing this indie detective game, and I am very glad I did! Paradise Killer is essentially a murder mystery with you as the lead detective trying to find out who killed the council of this strange 80's fusion island. The island itself, wow, I think is one of the most creatively unique game worlds I have ever seen. The story itself was also brilliant!To the comments that this game is a little pixel-huntey I would disagree, with the caveat that there are some secrets on the island that I think are perhaps a little too well hidden, but a quick google can often help you sort it out. Overall, a very warm recommendation from me. Spent about 9 hours in this fantastic unique world, and I enjoyed every minute of it. Hell I even kept hand written notes on the case as the game progressed, not because the game required me to, but because it was so fun building up notes on who did what and why.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as I know there isn't another game that has this mix of gameplay, story and style. There's something so enjoyable about having an open world to explore and trying and find secrets. Every character is strange but interesting and the mysteries they're holding onto and the wider investigation kept me interested throughout my entire experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Early on in this game I saw something behind a fence and I did some precarious parkouring to get to it. I made it and felt bad, assuming I had skipped some progression elements and cheated the game of its natural flow. Then an hour later I found a double jump powerup and realized this game was a lot more than what I thought it was. This is a great game to just experience. It's not really full of high level puzzles or all that much logical deduction. If you talk to everyone and find the collectables the case will solve itself. But this is one of those games where the journey is better than the destination. The world of Paradise Island Sequence 24 is coated in this lovecraftian vaporwave aesthetic that is as interesting as it is messed up. You're investigating the murder of a group of terrible people, with a group of suspects who are equally as terrible. The actual facts are less important than the truth you aim to prove. Don't come into this expecting Professor Layton puzzles or Danganronpa style logical leaps like the infamous "seesaw effect" moment. This game is simple, yet complicated in its delivery. If it sounds even remotely interesting to you, I say you should give breathing life back into Paradise a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets a big thumbs from me 👍 I really enjoyed the cast of characters, the "sound-bites" during dialog, and the blending of Visual Novel and 3D open-world exploration. Without giving anything away, some of the evidence near the end is a little too easy to miss. I also really like that the truth is what you want to make of it! Well worth playing!!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I've said it before but the hallmark of a great game, or a very good one at any rate, is whether or not you're compelled to play it until the very end. Paradise Killer is an expertly constructed murder-mystery detective story from a first person perspective that takes place on an ancient island that goes through cycles of regeneration, i.e., births & deaths. You play as Lady Love Dies, a lead investigator for the Syndicate who's been brought out of exile to solve the crime to end all crimes, lol. This game is extremely well made and runs perfectly. The island is a lot of fun to explore and the plot keeps you guessing up towards the very end. The soundtrack is very nice as well. The trial at the very end is a stellar experience that doesn't disappoint. There's not much to complain about here. But if I could point to something, it would be that perhaps the game starts to drag a bit towards the end. During the last 2 or 3 hours I must have gone back and forth between Carmelina Silence and Witness to the End at least 20 times to gather info...it just got a tad bit tedious towards the end of the game but as I mentioned, the final trial was a LOT of fun. This game could be anywhere from 15 to 20 hours long on average so there's a lot to solve here. I suppose I'd give Paradise Killer a solid 8.5 out of ten. It's a well made game that's very definitely worth playing through. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Pros:-Unique and interesting characters in a fantastical world that feels alive-A real banger of a soundtrack. No joke.-Vaporwave as all heck-Incredible world sound design and voice talent-Personality brimming in every nook and cranny of this game. I can tell this was a real labor of love.Cons:-Kinda drags on a little long for my taste (You can essentially go to endgame at any time, but I wanted to see as much as possible and that made for a 6-7 hour long runtime that should've really only been like 4-5 hours)-Can't pet the dog-There's a lot of text. A lot. It makes it easier on you by tracking anything of note in your case files, but towards the end I was just mainly slamming through every textwall and checking notes afterwards.-Barry "Epoch" Topping doesn't get enough credit for the OST. Give him some love, people.-Seriously, it's an amazing soundtrack and I hadn't even heard about it until now.

_childDocuments_.review: This game stands out for its unique, and stylish world and character designs. Beneath that however lies a solid detective game with interesting characters, stories and clues aplenty.  From start to finish I was gripped by the need to discover the truths for all the strange events that happened. The way the ending was done is amazing. _childDocuments_.review: I'd strongly recommend Paradise Killer to people who can find the appeal in the following: If you can appreciate all of these things, you'll find an experience I've never seen the likes of before: a blood-soaked mystery on a sun-drenched island created to resurrect unknowable cosmic beings with the sacrifice of the innocent. _childDocuments_.review: Excellent "open world" investigation game in a slightly under-served niche. I found the exploration and mystery solving highly satisfying, *almost* as enjoyable as Return of the Obra Dinn and Outer Wilds. Even though I like the basics of the theme (alien gods, immortality, etc.), to me it feels there's a lot of "weird for the sake of weird" in it.In particular, this ends up making the early portions of the game seem a bit aimless, but as soon as you start revealing aspects of the mystery (motives, alibis, and so on) the experience and the theme really click into place. Highly recommended if exploration, discovery, and mystery are your jam.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer offers an intriguing blend of open-world exploration, vaporwave aesthetics, and murder mystery investigation. Set in a surreal world filled with immortal council members, gods, and bizarre characters, it hooks you with its eccentric yet deeply engaging narrative universe and the promise of uncovering the truth behind a mass murder. However, while the game boasts a unique charm, it stumbles in several key areas.Visually, Paradise Killer excels in creating a retro-futuristic world, but the actual gameplay environments feel sparse and, at times, repetitive. Despite strong world-building, the execution feels rough around the edges. The overused assets, 2D art awkwardly integrated into a 3D space, and repetitive textures create a disjointed experience. Combined with the constant collection of meaningless "relics," it’s difficult to recommend the game to players who prioritize gameplay over story.That said, the soundtrack is a standout, blending upbeat electronic tracks with soothing synthwave melodies that perfectly complement the game’s dreamlike atmosphere.Character interactions are plentiful, and each suspect offers a distinct perspective that enriches the immersive world you're thrown into. The pacing of the mystery is masterfully handled, with the investigation consistently pushing you toward new leads and revelations. I rarely found myself wondering, "What now?" as each piece of evidence led naturally to the next, driving me deeper into the mystery until the final judgment.Overall, Paradise Killer is a fascinating experiment, but one that doesn’t quite live up to its potential. It’s worth experiencing for its style, atmosphere, and incredible story, but be prepared for a rough gameplay experience. Despite the lackluster 3D visuals and the tedious collecting, the core creative aspects—story, characters, and world—manage to shine through.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty cool and novel game.I really like the way how it's essentially an open-ended investigation game where you can come across any number of evidence and testimonies in wildly varying orders, not to mention how all the information you gather begins to slowly but surely piece together into a coherent murder plot. The characters are all colorful and full of personality, their designs are awesome and the way you have to bounce around them as you collect more information is a pretty cool feature. Not to mention how you can just end the game by going on trail whenever you want with whatever evidence you have in handy.There are some problems with that approach though. First and foremost, the whole island the game takes place in is fairly big, and walking through it can be boring, annoying and sometimes even frustrating. The physics behind the thing and the weird way terrain works can make you miss jumps and fall way off your destination, for example. Also, the game sorta balances the way you progress through its sandbox behind a collectathon mechanic. While most collectibles outside of hidden key-evidence are just lore-expanding flavor text, there is a currency called Blood Crystals that is incredibly useful throughout the whole game (you even have to pay for fast travel), and these are scattered throughout the whole island, effectivelly forcing you to go out of your way to find them, which can pad out the experience significantly. You may be heading somewhere, but then you find a blood crystal just over there, and on your way to pick that up you find another one nearby, and then there's another collectible right there, but you miss your jump and land somewhere else, etc. While it sometimes leads to you finding some cool stuff/evidence off the beaten path, it can get pretty annoying, and I only imagine how much hair completionists will be tearing out from their scalps trying to collect all the hundreds of trinkets. I also didn't care much for its puzzles, which are mostly rather simple, time-consuming affairs, like aligning bridges through buttons to form a path, or that Starlight minigame.The setting is pretty creative, completely bonkers fare (the character's names alone can tell you that), and while it does have loads of charm, it's a also a bit TOO convoluted for my tastes. I mean, essentially anything can happen in this world, and yet the whole thing is so detailed on its own dream-like logic that it can get a bit overwhelming.All in all, this is definetly a great experience, and one hell of a stroke of genius from the developers. I hope we got more stuff like this from them in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: THE GREATEST DETECTIVE GAME ON STEAMParadise killer sees you, the chief investigator for a syndicate of cultists who worship dead alien gods bent on the destruction of humanity, return from your 3 million day exile to solve the murder of your leading council on a vaporwave island pocket dimension. Sounds simple right? Despite this BIZARRE premise, this game has great presentation, great investigation gameplay, and great game design that actually allows for you to feel like Sherlock rather than Watson.Uniquely for this genre, this is an open world game. The island that you are on is pretty small, but fairly dense. You wont soon run out of places to check for potential clues. This also allows you to investigate crimescenes and suspects on your own initiative, and follow up whatever leads you deem important without being told what to do, where to go, who to suspect, or what to investigate. This leads to a much more authentic "detective" experience.Another unique thing about this game is how it handles the ending. You can end the game at any time by calling for a trial once you think you have enough evidence to solve the crime. That's not all however, you can accuse anybody, and can get them convicted if you have enough evidence. This means that you can not only convict the wrong person without knowing it, you can purposely frame someone if you play things right. Why would the game let you do this? Well, it actually asks a bit of a moral question from you at the end. What is the difference between the facts and the truth? What is the difference between being guilty and deserving punishment? Does justice matter when you and your cultist friends are ultimately the bad guys?This game is well worth the money and time I put into it, and had me staying awake at night trying to wrap my head around the elaborate crime and potential suspects. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A great open world visual novel-esque game with an absolute banger soundtrack by Epoch. The game does a really great job at capturing the loneliness of an empty paradise and the few characters you do meet are well characterised. There are a lot of collectables too but the power-ups you receive make getting all of these easy. Only downside of the game, in my opinion, is the final piece of the puzzle for the true mystery; it's very convenient and ties things up a bit too neatly to just come out of nowhere. Regardless, highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of fun exploring the island and uncovering all the evidence. Only wish the island had been a little easier to get around on. Even the fast-travel mechanic was a bit cumbersome.The story you're investigating is remarkably intricate and there's quite a lot of evidence and testimony to discover. And during the trial, as nobody seems truly innocent, there are some tough choices to make. Truth be told, I wanted to ensure that this horrible civilisation would not continue.The weakest part of the game in my opinion was after the trial and speaking to those who remained. A more extensive epilogue for those characters would have been nice.On the whole, I'd say this is unlike any other game I've ever played and that alone would be enough to recommend it. But more than that, I had fun and was intrigued.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a fantastic mystery + puzzle game about figuring out the hidden truth behind the murder in *paradise. Comparably similar to the Danganronpa series, which I really enjoyed playing in. In which being the similar investigation and trial phase.Though the Danganronpa series is often referenced in most other reviews, this game further adds in a few gameplay mechanics which allowed me to immerse myself deeper. Such as it being open world,  and limited fast travel to minimise the boredom of constantly moving back and forth between areas.There are an insane amount of collectables in this game that can potentially keep the player engaged for HOURS to even clear out a single area.All the characters and ‘items’ in the game are 2D sprites which are highlighted clearly. The buildings and terrain looks surprisingly beautiful traversing around truly deserving of being called *paradise!There are lots and lots of symbolic references regarding gods and demons, however since I am not really familiar with that topic, I wouldn’t talk much about it here.Extremely fun to unravel! Finding out what has happened to paradise inhabitants and exposing a little bit of the lore behind the island itself was really fun. But close to the end, the story suddenly felt a little rushed and ended off really anticlimactically.As I have been rushing along the investigation part and not collected much of the collectables and only went through the judgement trial once, I believe that the average completion time should be longer than what is shown on my total hours played. It is definitely worth the $13 I have spent on it! If you really enjoy mystery and/or the Danganronpa series, this game is definitely worth playing even if it is $20!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a fun mystery game, this might not be for you. Paradise Killer is a lot of things. It has an intense style and insane world-building. But something it lacked for me was a compelling mystery.I often found exploring this game and gathering clues quite tedious. There's something to be said for the fact that you have to piece together motives for murder in a world where you're also trying to understand the basic operation of society. But, ultimately, I found those motives quite boring and so mundane for such a fantastical setting.The most interesting aspect, the characters and their relationships with the protagonist and each other, felt quite on-rails with no real room for the player to affect the story. The development of these characters and the game's mystery is stopped abruptly when it's time to go to the judge with your evidence. If you've collected all the clues, which is not hard to do - just time-consuming, it becomes a simple matter of laying down accusations and scrolling through soooo much dialogue recapping everything you've already learned. Then you shoot a bunch of people and the game is over.If you're into vaporwave and games that look intentionally kinda bad, or even just wild lore about an alternate earth history with demonic gods and cross-European wars, you might enjoy this. If you're looking for a satisfying, complex mystery game, this one might not be for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Completely enrapturing title. Wandering around the open-world while I had no idea what the ♥♥♥♥ was going on is one of my favourite gaming memories of the past few years. I have some stylistic quibbles (the writer clearly hates commas) but this is a very, very well-written game. The characters are distinct and engaging. The history of the world you're in is fascinating. The central mystery is legitimately well-constructed: hard to figure out in advance, doesn't feel cheap in retrospect.

_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I would have preferred the game concentrated on the narrative, investigation, and character interaction parts rather than having open world collect-athon. collect Blood Crystals, gems, find all the Jackal guys, random items, collect evidence. unlock fast travel. collect soda cans. collect relationships with everyone. do side quests. Its too much. Even with the provided cheat/hint system (which is slow to activate) revealing locations of every single collectible, It's just too much to bother with. I also found it difficult to follow the trail of the case. There is big info dumps and long conversations I couldn't really follow. It's helpful all information gathered has summarized notes in-game, but there's so much information I still found it confusing and not an enjoyable way of interacting with information or characters.As an exploration game, this is a decent. There's plenty of things to find and places to explore. The surreal 80's/90's retro-wave aesthetic is quirky and fun. There is some fun banter and bizarre sense of humor if you can bother to get through the conversations. As a detective game, I don't find it very satisfying. The comparison between Ace Attorney and Paradise Killer is unreasonable. There is no character development, emotional moments, or satisfying "ah ha" conclusions. It did scratch the klepto-itch till i got bored. DNF

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of detective games, I really wanted to like Paradise Killer. There's all kinds of promise in the system (OMG, a detective game with a proper timeline of events related to the crime!). But in the end it just did not work for me on any level. _childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Loved playing this game. I'm a player that prizes exploration and uncovering story. While not game mechanic heavy at all, nor filled with physical puzzles to figure out, trying to get to the bottom of Paradise Killer's story had me enthralled without effort for the three-ish days I spent playing it in spurts. Definitely one to play if you like visual novels, walking sims, exploration, trying to uncover every little bit of story, or are a collection person that wants a night on impossible task of finding every single hidden lore object.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what an absolutely stellar experience. This game is like Phoenix Wright meets Danganronpa, but open world. It is so much fun. I had a great time unraveling the mystery and discovering the lore. THE LORE. The lore is incredibly fascinating and learning about the world that Kaizen has created was so much fun. I've seen a few complaints about how the game doesn't really tell you where to go or what to do, but I loved that aspect. It allowed me to really dig into the world and discover what it had to offer.My only real complaints about the game are regarding the map and travelling around it. The map only shows you what 'zone' you're in, but you don't know which way you're facing so it can be a challenge to navigate, especially early on. Additionally, the game's Fast Travel system costs currency each time you use it, which I found frustrating and therefore I only used it when I absolutely had no other choice (As there is one area you cannot access without using Fast Travel).Despite that one gripe though, I have nothing else truly negative to say about this game. There were a few small things I think could have been executed differently, like the Trial at the end, but I'm not mad about it. This was a fantastic, fun, sometimes horrifying, but always intriguing experience. Absolutely get this game if you're on the fence. Between its brilliant sense of style, the AMAZING soundtrack, the fascinating story, and the entertaining characters, this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. I truly hope Kaizen releases a sequel because I can't wait to return to Perfect 25 and the world of Paradise Killer.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer could be thought of as an evolution of the Ace Attorney/Danganronpa formula, but I think that undersells how it inverts the investigation/trial dynamic and focuses on a single, massively interconnected mystery. This changes the genre from a thriller, where the gameplay is to guess what the next twist will be using knowledge of genre conventions, to a mystery, where the gameplay is building a mental re-creation of the crime from evidence to determine who did it. This philosophy is embodied in the writing as well, which understands that the player is a detective and thus should be able to piece together the world from context clues instead of having everything painfully spelled out. And the world and characters that these clues illustrate is both fantastic and bizarre but at the same time uncomfortably similar to our own.It's not perfect. Item scavenging can be tedious, the hacking minigame is trivial (though this is infinitely preferable to a bad hacking minigame), and the open world means the pacing sometimes fails. But apart from one or two questionable details the mystery itself and the mechanics for solving it are solid and will leave you satisfied for solving it.And on top of that, the soundtrack alone is worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts off interesting, then it nosedives with the pacing and lack of a clear "mission path" so it feels overwhelming a bit, especially if you don't get the upgrades quickly.Then it becomes really good to the point I collected everything in the game. The later part of the game also feels very annoying to play since you will have to run from one character to another to progress the story, and they all stay in the same place, so that means you will know these routes by heart. After talking to a character they will reveal some info about a case and you will then run to people that said info was about. Felt like an errand boy.Still the music is good, the art is nice but the voice acting is annoying so i turned that off and immedeately the game was a lot better... except when jumping. Does the main character always have to moan when landing from like 1m height? It really is uncomfordable at times while running and jumping.I really couldn't be bothered to read all of the dialogue, just the gist of it and I wanted to see the ending of the story.The main issue is that your character automatically summarises the story because you just collected all the info you needed. There is no way to make a mistake other than deliberately doing it or by not doing any digging or talking and just starting the final sequence.The fun part is the end where you can talk to the characters after the trial and even kill or exile them. In the end it is an alright platformer/item collector but not a detective story. It turns into a light novel with vaporwave vibes,  item collection and some platforming.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game, it's a shame it's so underrated!!! I had to go through many steam queue games to find this one.Lots of Danganronpa vibes, but it's by no means the same game. Just because you like Danganronpa doesn't necessarily mean you'll like Paradise Killer, but I think if you do then it's definitely worth a try.You only have one trial. The whole game is you gathering evidence for that trial. You don't really end up putting the pieces together yourself - the computer kind of does that for you if you find all of the evidence, logging and sorting it into where it belongs.I think Paradise Killer has a fantastic world and the thing it does best is immersing you into it. I became invested in many of the characters and couldn't put it down until I completed it. It's the type of world that I won't be able to forget and feels super nostalgic.The game looks great for what it is - it seems to have been made on a small to medium budget and kind of has a lo-fi feel where things aren't super high fidelity, but are still beautiful. (My boyfriend says that the game looks like it was made in source lol.) I loved the colors they use and their choices in aesthetic and art direction - everything fits together so well. And the music is great.There are some issues of course. Some large areas do feel kind of empty except for collectibles. And some things just feel kind of wack - I don't know, it might just be me, but there was a fair amount of platforming required for collectibles, and while the game gives you the tools to do it, the movement just doesn't feel super tight. I ended up getting stuck in some areas, but luckily there's a Respawn button in your options menu if this happens.I don't think the game is for everyone - since there's only one trial, I wish that the actions you choose at that trial have an impact on the ending - but I suppose that's kind of one of the messages the game tries to give you anyway, that in this world, things don't really matter. Regardless, I think that the game definitely makes up for these shortcomings with its environment ambiance, interesting world, great soundtrack, etc. It's a game and world worth experiencing, and I really hope this studio makes more games like this, so I fully recommend (:
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Quite good indie game with unusual design, enjoyable music and lots of reading. _childDocuments_.review: If Steam would allow me to give a "meh" rating, this would be one of these cases.The game has quite a bit of going for it, including the art style, world building and general premise of the game. _childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of fun with Paradise Killer even though I am not super big on story heavy games. However, there definitely are pros and cons to this game.First of all, the art style is gorgeous. I love the colors; just how funky everything is. There are quite a few things you can collect which is right down my alley as well. You certainly have to pay attention and keep your wits about you to figure out whodunnit. There is an investigation going on that you need to solve and the way the game trickles information down on you is very smart. You really have to invest time to come to a conclusion, there is no super obvious solution that you arrive at after 15 minutes of playing. The character designs are pretty dope too and simply what characters exist was fascinating to me.On the con side, things get repetitive. As I said, you will be talking to everybody again and again and again until you squeezed every last bit of information out of them. I know that this is to some degree simply how story-based games work, but there was a point where I was just running back and forth between the same characters talking to everybody in turn. There were not other elements that made things more intriguing, to be honest. It’s also the walking about that gets somewhat annoying. The map can be a bit confusing and navigating it or at least certain parts of it is irritating at best. I probably wouldn’t have minded the back and forth so much if this had been a tad less laborious, to be honest.However, criticism aside, the game was intriguing enough for me to want to collect everything. I certainly would have finished things a lot earlier if I hadn’t been hell-bent of snagging every little collectible. While some were fairly easy to locate, others definitely were more grindy to get. But hey, that is a me problem, not everyone decides to do that.Long story short, overall, I enjoyed playing this game. It felt very different from everything else I’ve played, starting with the art style. Well, while I liked playing this, it’s definitely not something I would see myself installing again to replay it. So, keep that in mind when making a purchasing decision here. Other than that, if you like investigative story games, this one is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is an open world detective adventure game with the most insane cast of characters you can imagine. The closest comparison I can make is the Phoenix Wright series, but even then it's only a close approximation as I don't think I've ever played anything like it.The 80s Japan vaporware aesthetic combined with some superb music and a well thought out mystery has definitely made it a memorable experience that I don't think I'll soon forget and the soundtrack will be a part of my playlist for a very long time. Would totally recommend to anyone who likes a good mystery and I hope to see more games from the studio.There are only two "negatives" I can think about:- The voice acting, it's bad, like really really bad. You get voice quips from characters during dialogue that sound like they were recorded in a bathroom and don't match the dialogue at all.An example would be the text saying "I don't think so" and the VO being "WHAT THE HELL?!".Not a word for word example but you'll know what I am talking about.Thankfully there is an option to disable the voice quips, so not a problem really.- Some of the character art is quite sloppy, some frames can look good, but others are just deformed. Crimson is a prime example of this, her upper body just looks horrific in some frames, hopefully this will get cleaned up in the next game.Overall the game has been solid and I think is a must have for any fans of the genre, whatever genre that was.

_childDocuments_.review: For people who adore the Zero Escape / Nonary Game series, AI: Somnium Files, Pheonix Wright, and Danganronpa series and looking for something like them this is NOT for you.The world is interesting and the characters are OK, but I felt no attachment to either. The world is littered with collectibles which are supposed to serve as tidbits of interesting lore but instead just waste your time. The game is littered with animations all of which serve little purpose but to waste your time. Every single collectible you pick up - including the game's generic currency - displays a full-screen flash-card + audio queue that needs to be manually closed out of. Every single time you 'fast' travel, you have to go to a telephone, wait for a loading screen to get into the vehicle, THEN choose a location to teleport to. Finally the 'detective' piece - what I believed should be the most important part of the game is simply a collectathon as well with the most anticlimactic payoff I've seen. Throughout the game you literally go into your menu and go through a checklist of items to figure out until the list is no longer there, running back and forth and back and forth and back and forth between the suspects as you go. As you collect the evidence you piece together a 'truth'.The trial, which after ~7 hours of running around in circles for clues consists of no cross-examination, accusation, back and forth. No catching people in a lie, contradiction, or detective work needed. Just another checklist with a bunch of dialogue. Now I'm not saying every game needs to be Danganronpa, but I mean there is no payoff at all. I was holding out and genuinely excited for the trial, and it was entirely flaccid. Endings are critical for me in games and this one left a bad taste in my mouth. It's open ended, which is fine, and you design your own truth - but there's only 1-2 real answers, and the game basically tells you who to choose as well. The immortal demi-gods of the world practically roll over once you provide your checklist that you ran around collecting. The entire end felt lackluster, unimpactful, tacky and most of all unsatisfying - and in my opinion is the most important part of these types of games.

_childDocuments_.review: Tough balance here, but a no from me, ultimately.On the one hand I applaud the novelty of the aesthetic how cohesively it's delivered through all the elements of the game - the UI, the music, the art, the lore: You really feel like the island is a real place and is the tip of a much bigger world.But in terms of a gameplay experience the fusion of open-world collect-a-thon and detective game gets stale very quickly. The premise feels very open, but in practice the world is very empty, and progression actually involves asking specific things to characters in a set order and finding set objects. So you mostly just track forwards and backwards across the same space. A smaller world with more in it, combined with more open detective options would have turned this into an excellent experience.

These are minor problems that don't diminish the quality of the game and if you enjoy murder mysteries in the slightest, pick this one up.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely enthralling! _childDocuments_.review: Easily one of my favourite games. If something gets me to go after every single collectible despite not even having an achievement for it (sad), I must have really liked it.It's very unique in its style and identity unlike other vapor wave-inspired things that often rely on the aesthetic so much that it all becomes generic. This is definitely not the case here: the vapor wave is the icing on the cake; the writing and design has you quite immersed in the universe, and actually paying attention to little tidbits of lore that you can find. Its sense of humour is lovely as well. Characters are varied and might cause intense dislike and hatred in the player, to sympathy and adoration.I'm not generally a big fan of investigation games a la Ace Attorney et all, but this game is different in that your role of investigating is a lot more direct and within your control, not least of which because it happens in a 3D world rather than classic 2D and point-and-click games. The quirks of the art design throughout are quite nice, and the sound design does great to enhance it (there is a part of the world I hated going into because the sound design was so great it made me shudder when I had to go there).I might be on the minority when it comes to this last one, but I also felt that the game (and especially the ending) brought up interesting questions to me about what justice (and a judiciary and criminal justice system) actually even is and represents; but the game is not concerned with answering any of those questions, rather it gives the player a lovely lore to munch into and take it however or as far as they want to take it.I'd love if there was more variance to the potential endings - after spending so much time with all the characters, and considering the different options you can take at the end, more detailed differences when you do those would be great, but ultimately the journey was so good for me that that lack of variance at the end couldn't sully it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game! It's a great example of the detective genre. It existed in this strange space where it combines  esoteric and surreal world-building with a Phoenix Wright style investigation with colourful and interesting characters populating the world. There were a few things that really stood out to me about the game after I completed it- The judgement that I made in the game really made me sit with the the decisions and the investigation that I had taken part in.  The MC's catchphrase is 'truth and facts are not the same' although it is quite annoy after awhile to hear the same voiceover phrases spoken again and again, this is something that really sticks out, especially in a detective game. Depending on what your own opinions are ideas about the case are, the trial portion of the game will change, offering you a different POV of who is guilty and who isn't. _childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful game, with a beautiful soundtrack, and definitely worth a play.  It unrolls more like a free roam visual novel than a traditional investigation game like Phoenix Wright - it won't require a lot of lateral thinking to piece together evidence into a narrative.The world-building is truly alien and will require you to keep your eyes and ears OPEN.  Everything has kind of an odd Full Sentence Name that can throw you a bit, and since it's free roam, there's little effort taken to structure the lore in a way that would make it easier to digest.  IMO, this is the part that's the "real" investigation challenge for the player, as the lore will quite likely influence how you choose to perform the investigation.For gameplay reference, I finished the game with all collectibles and full exploration in 12 hours.  You could likely finish it in as few as 4 if you are just trying to complete the investigation and do nothing else.This is a must-play for fans of investigation games, lore freaks, and vaporwave.

_childDocuments_.review: Heeeesitant recommend. If you go for it, do so on sale.Psychedelic vaporwave walking simulator with good tunes, vibing and collectibles first, investigation second. I completed almost everything, didn't bother getting every collectible. Reason why I got most of them, is explained in negatives.+ Pretty uniquely themed+ Looks good+ Rather good music (saves the game)+ Funny, at times+ Lore building, while in a nonsensical setting, is consistent* The only minigame is passable, nothing crazy bad/good* Investigation struck me as amateurish/nonsensical, which partly makes sense considering the theming, but in the end it did not deliver for me personally- More or less entire game is combo of fetch quest or walking around collecting items, with occasional dialogue- Movement upgrades exist, but are hidden in the world and there's no tell where, I missed one of them untill I looked it up after beating the game. On the plus side, you don't need them to achieve an ending at least. They also trivialize certain things like locked gates in some places, since you can skip the "puzzle" of finding the button to press to open it- Permanently missable items (though I THINK they don't mess with the endings)- Weird design choices at times, where player's time gets wasted for the sake of being "artsy", example being...- ...fast travel costs non-renewable resource, if you spend too much you might not be able to get stuff you care about. At least it's unlikely this will happen, I believe you can fast travel about 50-ish times total before getting punished. Not that you'd have a way of knowing that- Very unclear, I believe deliberately, what gives clues/progress, it could be certain dialogue, it could be collecting things untill you have X, could be fetch quest 6... you never know, which is why I ended up collecting almost everything- Lite puzzles in the game world while walking are kinda bad, but at least they don't take a lot of timeI didn't really feel like I was investigating as much as I was collecting random items everywhere, though once I was mostly done with that, I was able to focus a bit more on trying to follow the plot accurately. Although I'm pretty sure you could wait untill the final trial and then just go from there with a couple of save scums at worst, even if you didn't pay much attention.Overall I occasionally enjoyed it, enough to finish it, but that was thanks to the good tunes. I wouldn't suggest going for it unless on sale and you have a clear idea of the type of game that it is... which is "art first, game second".
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: There are a few things to like about Paradise Killer: the open yet compact world, the unexpectedly interesting movement, and the unique and well realized setting.Other than those specifics, I don't think the game delivers. The central mystery is inelegant, crowded with perpendicular motives. The writing swerves between twee and overbearingly philosophical, and is undermined by constant mistakes in grammar and punctuation. The voice acting is mediocre and repetitive to the point of breaking immersion. The aesthetic has that classic vaporwave problem: it's ugly — but with a wink! — which doesn't stop it from still just being ugly. Nothing wrong with the character designs, though the portraits themselves lag behind those of many freeware VNs. The puzzles are either trial-and-error affairs or fetch quests in disguise.Ultimately, the trial sequence is a summary of previous information that asks little of you in the way of deduction. The game wraps up abruptly, without acknowledging the player's choices almost at all. I can appreciate what was attempted here, but unless you suspect you're squarely in the target demo, I wouldn't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible synthesis of aesthetics (Unity Default and Vaporwave) and genres (First Person exploration, Detective and Visual Novel). I'm still early but am already enthralled by its central mystery and compelling intertwined characters. Also the OST slaps. _childDocuments_.review: Imagine if Agatha Christie wrote a crossover of Warhammer 40k and Stargate, used the characters from Danganronpa, and set the whole thing in the Miami of Miami Vice. Because that's basically what Paradise Killer is. It's also an incredibly ambitious who-done-it where there's few clear answers and the truth is left up for you to shape based on the facts that you find. And it's set in an absolutely vivid world.The island itself, both in design and story, is the game's strongest aspect. It's an absolutely insane mish-mash of vaporwave visuals and music and colors over a "paradise" fueled by slave labor for corporate entities and bloody mass slaughter in Sumerian temples to satiate the appetites of horrors from beyond the stars. It's massive Brutalist buildings lording over cramped Japanese shantytowns, with colorful corporate mascots and posters advertising idol contests next to blood soaked altars and the ever present fear of demonic corruption. You're given no backstory or understanding of the mythology before you're dropped into the world and left to piece it together through conversation and finding relics and doodads. As every worldbuilding brick dropped into place and I saw just how horrendous and colorful the world I was in, the more engrossed I was in the island and its history and people. Gameplay wise, it doesn't deviate too much from detective visual novel standards, but with a heavier emphasis on exploration and hunting for secrets. You talk to people, find info or hear something that contradicts their statements, talk again, etc etc. There's a bit of a relationship system to the game, akin to visual novels, but it's light and doesn't consist of much more than clicking the special dialog option when it's available. It doesn't seem to lead to any special routes or anything. You can max out your relationship with every character, learn a little about them, and get a special flavor item that tells you more about them or the island. The mystery plot and trial aspect will draw a lot of comparisons to Danganronpa (such as the one that I did) and while it definitely does take some inspiration from there, the truth is much more malleable in this game. As characters remind you constantly, "facts" and "truth" are not the same thing and it is up to the investigator to stitch together a narrative out of the facts presented and I think this is the game's second strongest aspect: by developing your relationships to characters, you are actually allowed to (attempt) to present your case in a way that lets a guilty party you're fond of go free or pin one or more crimes on a character you don't like that much. Instead of a strict linear story, much of the evidence discovered in the game points to more than one suspect and you can choose to ignore (or build a case on) weaker, tenuous, or circumstantial pieces of evidence to push the story in the way that you want. That absolutely fascinated me and felt like my character was an active participant in the politicking, the conspiracies, and the backstabbing that was prevalent in the rest of the cast. (That said, as a caveat, if you're the sort that needs a concrete, developer-created "good" or "right" or "true" ending, this game might disappoint you as there isn't one. There seems to be a series of immutable facts about the events that led to the crimes, but the exact perpetrators and their level of involvement is up to your discretion and if you feel that might leave you unsatisfied in the story, this might not be the game for you. I personally find player-shaped narratives and stories told through the player-character's biases to be a huge reason why I become so engrossed in games like this and is part of the reason I recommend this game so highly, so this is definitely a Your Mileage May Vary sort of game.)The game's two strengths are a bit weighed down by a few weaknesses: the island is huge and largely very colorful with lots to explore, but the map is not useful at all except as a general guide to where major landmarks are. A fast travel system exists, but it costs some of the game's (admittedly plentiful) currency to use, and some areas of the world feel underdeveloped and under utilized compared to others. The ambitious goal of letting you shape your own narrative of events leaves a few characters underdeveloped compared to others and one or two pieces of evidence that don't seem to fit into any of the possible explanations for the crimes. The trials themselves lack the excitement of Danganronpa's mini-games and in one occasion, I presented a piece of evidence that led to the conviction of a character I wanted to spare because the option to pick it was vaguely described. There were also a few minor issues here and there, like UI elements not disappearing when they should or misspelled words, but none of these issues - major or minor - detract from the overall depth and enjoyment to be had with this game. It's easily one of my favorite game worlds already and totally worth a play if you're at all interested in mystery games, colorful and strange worlds, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up narratives.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty neat murder mystery game. Definitely takes a lot of inspiration from Danganronpa and Suda 51/Grasshopper Manufacture's games (especially Danganronpa 2 and Flower, Sun, and Rain). Soundtrack's great and does a good job of selling the tropical island vibe the game is going for. Was pretty surprised at how interesting the setting actually is. Hopefully the developers do more with it in future projects. The first person platforming can be rather frustrating at times, and having fast travel be tied to a finite resource was a rather weird design choice. The actual trial itself was a little underwhelming as well since aside from hand picking the suspect yourself, all that really happens is that you just go through the list of evidence you have against them. _childDocuments_.review: Paradise killer is one of those special games where you can relax, explore to your hearts content and try and solve a mass murder on an island of deranged imortals. _childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a murder mystery exploration/collectathon and sort of a visual novel where you are released from your 3 million year exile to solve the biggest crime that happened on paradise islands. You are dropped on an open world island that you can explore at your own pace. The mysteries unveil as you talk to characters and find clues.The story is very well written, all the characters  have unique and charming personalities. The ending was a bit unsatisfying but i think the journey you took to get there is what makes it great.The island is really beautiful. You will learn every part of the island and admire the aesthetic it offers.The soundtracks are phenomenal and worth a listen outside of the game.The gameplay is just a medium that helps tell the story in Paradise Killer so don't go in expecting an intriguing gameplay. What you should expect from Paradise Killer is an atmospheric walking simulator with a huge focus on story. Because of that, i think this game might not be for everyone but for the ones that are interested in what i said, i can gladly tell that Paradise killer offers a completely unique and unforgettable experience you will only experience once in a lifetime.

_childDocuments_.review: In my reviewe I will focus on the aspects that stood out the most, namely the art, soundtrack, and characters, as well as less than pleasant experience with the platforming and exploration elements.Paradise Killer presents a fascinating visual experience with its stunning art style. The vibrant colors and unique character designs create an immersive world that is both captivating and intriguing. The game's aesthetic is undoubtedly one of its strongest points, as it sets the tone for the unconventional narrative that unfolds throughout the gameplay.The soundtrack is equally impressive, featuring a diverse collection of vaporware tracks that perfectly complement the game's atmosphere. From upbeat tunes that evoke a sense of exploration and adventure to more somber melodies that capture the darker themes of the story, the soundtrack enhances the overall experience immensely.The story is complex and engaging, with many twists and turns that kept me enthralled until the very end. The characters are well-written and fleshed out, with their own motivations and secrets that are slowly revealed as you progress.However, as someone who did not enjoy the platforming and exploration aspects of the game, I found these elements to be very tedious. The open-world exploration can feel overwhelming at times, and the platforming sections are frustrating. That said, the captivating art, immersive soundtrack, and memorable characters make it worth pushing through these less enjoyable aspects to fully appreciate the game's unique charm.In conclusion, Paradise Killer is a uniquely captivating experience that excels in its art style, soundtrack, and character development. While the platforming and exploration aspects almost made me quit, the game's strengths pulled me in, and I appreciated a rich narrative experience and a unique, immersive world.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A game absolutely oozing personality. Beautiful art style, fantastic sound track, and a bewitching island to run riot in. The characters you encounter are fun and interesting in their own ways. Conversing with them, getting to know them and teasing out little admissions is highly enjoyable thanks to some wonderful writing and characterisation. However the star of the show is Lady Love Dies. A wonderful, spunky and utterly charming protagonist. It's an eighties-retro-lovercraftian-detective game, what else is there to say? It's really good!

_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Look. Paradise Killer is not a good game. Paradise Killer is, however, a fantastic world with an interesting story to tell, and I'm not convinced that there's a better way to tell it. Mechanically speaking, the investigation isn't as thorough or as interesting as that of Ace Attorney or even Professor Layton, but the meta-narrative of the difference between facts and truth and between judgment and justice make it all worthwhile. I've found myself thinking about this game long after I'd finished playing, and that's a testament to its strength. For a first-time game developer, I'm blown away by Kaizen's  product as writing is typically a secondary concern (and also the hardest thing to get spot-on!). I'm definitely going to buy whatever they make next, and I'd recommend you do the same.TL;DR Paradise Killer is, more than anything else, something different. It may not be for you, but I heartily recommend giving it a try if only to see how weird things can get.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic first-person exploration game, combined with a murder mystery visual novel.A lot of people have compared this game to Danganronpa.  While it's true that the art style, music, and themes are clearly inspired by that, if you go in expecting Danganronpa, you will be disappointed.  This is not a game where you yourself solve the mystery, or have meaningful choices that affect the outcome.  Instead, it's more like a book that you can walk around in and choose which order the events occur in.However, if you enjoy intricate murder mysteries with lots of twists, schemes, and interesting characters -- and if you enjoy the parts of Skyrim or Fallout 4 where you scour every corner of every room, digging through trash to find hidden pointless rewards -- then this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. The crime-solving aspect is I guess technically open-ended in that the game will allow you to screw it up and see the end credits and technically never confirms who is or is not a culprit, but if you chase down every lead and pick up every collectible you will arrive at a pretty clear understanding of the case in a fairly straightforward manner.The environment is I think helped more by the worldbuilding than the "open world" format. It's kinda vaporwave Bloodborne and maybe strays occasionally into "lore for lore's sake" but serves to keep things unsettling.As for the map, it's a cool tropical island that's fun to explore but I'd say it's more like a very large puzzle room than an "open world". There's nothing dynamic, and the only thing to unlock is fast travel waypoints. In terms of scale it just starts to rub up against that annoying sensation that everything is slightly too small to be believable. It's not Death Stranding's "walk across the US in an hour" levels of cramped, but they tell you there's 3,000 civilians living in like a handful of apartment buildings and only like a third of the Syndicate have an identifiable "home". I do appreciate the attention to detail of putting farms, a power plant with poles and lines running around the island, a convenience store, etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A great time. A city pop infused investigation adventure set against the backdrop of a mad neon wonderland populated by demons, gods, and the people who do their will. But despite the insanity of the setting, one truth remains - there has been a murder, and someone (or someones) are responsible. It's up to Lady Love Dies to find the truth with her trusty laptop and a lot of jumping. If you dig the aesthetics of Suda 51 / Grasshopper Manufacture games you'll find this game to be a loving homage. Give it a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: A unique and really fun investigation game. It forces you to use your brain to solve puzzles but is also casual enough to play in a relaxing fashion. Really liked the original world and how insane everything really is. Its a fantastic backdrop for a mystery. Well done. I played through it all and got the investigation solved in 22 hours. I like how the game allows you to explore in whatever fashion and order you choose to, in a manner most games don't. I will remember this one for awhile and will definitely play a sequel when it happens.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Well, that was  The setting was very creative and interesting, the character art was really cool, and the music was jazzy and neat, but the investigation was just a dozen hours worth of running around doing parkour to pick up worthless trinkets, the writing felt a little noticeably amateurish (sometimes through pointless pretentiousness) to me at times, the trial was basically just clicking through a checklist to get dialog where you reveal all the things you learned during parkour, and the ending was just "And then the protagonist  because it was her job. Life goes on. End of game" which felt pretty unsatisfying to me. The best part was the weird little anarchy-loving demon you keep finding throughout the game. He and the protagonist have some great Phoenix-Wright-and-Maya-Fey-type banter, and I kinda wish the game had been less nonlinear in large part because it would have given the devs an opportunity to better integrate him into the plot rather than just having you do parkour to pick up random interactions with him like they're trinkets (also because when I play a game about solving mysteries I normally don't want the longest most engaging part of the gameplay to consist of doing parkour to pick up trinkets)

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is an open world murder mystery game with an extraordinary amount of freedom. The game's world and setting are both original and sublime. The game also contains some first-person platforming if you want to collect all the collectables.Personally, I liked the story and exploring the area, but it took a bit of time to get into the world of the game. However, when the game pulled you in, it didn't let go until the end. Even after the game, the different choices and theories kept running through my mind.The game is by no means perfect, but the exceptional world and game mechanics make up for a lot. I can recommend the game to those who like visual novel style games and who can tolerate exploring the game area from the first person.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: An astonishing game.Has the exploration of Elder Scrolls or modern Fallout, combined with one of the most imaginative and best-written worlds I have experienced in 30 years of gaming.It's like your favourite sci-fi book was spliced with an anime and an Elder Scrolls game, set to an amazing electronic soundtrack.Highly, highly recommend for people who enjoy the language of games (exploration, rewards for platforming skills and exploring hidden places, collectibles) but also the language of storytelling and imagination. I will buy a sequel on Day One.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: This was a game that caught my eye at Summer Games Fest, and I decided to give it a try as a it seemed like just the kind of low-energy game I could manage to play after my work day (as I'm often just too tired for anything that requires too much precision button pressing)And, boy, was it a good decision.Paradise Killer is a great game. Its not something I'd ever really played before, but theres a lot to enjoy here. The murder mystery is well crafted, truly gripping and is immensely satisfying when it all finally starts clicking into place. I don't want to admit how long I spent going over this case while I was trying to fall asleep. My total playtime clocked in at 14 hours, so you could easily get through it in a single  dedicated day, but I was playing in smaller sessions of 2-3 hours. So... lots of time to think the facts over before I finally went to Trial. The world of Paradise Killer is... bonkers. Utterly bonkers. But I adore it. The game (and the murder mystery) is made so much stronger for its worldbuilding, lore and history. I was not really expecting space gods and demons, but i am 100% down for every bit of it. Its integral to the core of the murder plot, and found there wasn't much in the way of worldbuilding that wasn't, in some way, relevant to the main plot. I also appreciated how much there was to explore and find in the open world. I've become very fed up of games whose maps are "open world" only to increase the amount of time it takes to go from a to b, instead of actually giving you something to . Paradise Killer, as a detective game, actively wants you to go everywhere and look at everything.I don't want to potentially spoil too much here, but justGame goodGive it a chance
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Paradise Killer is a well written visual novel that breathes fresh life into Danganronpa-sytled games.I loved the open-world aspect and the choice to start the endgame trials anytime during my playthrough. The story was enjoyable, soundtrack is phenomenal, and the characters and motivations all made sense.The endgame trial is my low point of the game. It became a process of spamming the advance button to move along text for ~20 minutes, as the game reads along the evidence I have collected against my accused.  I was expecting an experience similar to Phoenix Wright, where the player uses clues at the right moments to build a case. Because of this, my experience felt more akin to a collectibles game rather than a deductive-reasoning game. I would recommend this if you like visual novels or wanted a game with exploration and tons of collectibles, well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Good but can be great. I think what this game needs is an extra mode in which you, the player, take your own notes and/or select the evidence yourself. As it stands, the game takes all of the notes for you so you don't really have to pay all that much attention to the dialogue amidst all the lore and exposition dumps. Initially, I thought the game would be too overwhelming being an open-world game but I don't think it is. Gathering clues and doing some of the puzzles can feel rewarding given how much of it is based on exploring with no objective markers to speak of, but that aspect is fun and absorbing enough. The ability to call your investigation to a halt and to initiate the trial whenever you want is a really great idea but I wish there were less rail-guards in the design. I loved finding new clues in the dialogue and calling people out for their lies and contradictions only for the game to have done most of the heavy-lifting for me so that elation I experienced soon turned into mild disappointment. During the trials, you're not expected to link clues, testimony and evidence for yourself. These things are treated as collectibles in the game-world. The more you have, the stronger the case you can make. You still need to read the clues and such carefully in order to make accusations you believe will lead to convicting the people, which is great but also more puzzling why they didn't go further. It seems like a golden opportunity presented itself but was compromised. I admire the game for letting you miss them if you're not observant but I wish it went the extra step of letting the player not applying or linking them correctly when it matters most. Still, I do recommend the game, especially to people who really like the Ace Attorney games. The game's aesthetics, characters, and the world itself is a lot of fun and the soundtrack is superb. There is a lot of fun to be had exploring, following up on clues in your journal, and making sense of what information you've gathered from the suspects.
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: Very immersive - quite confusing at first but things do eventually clear up and I'm glad I stuck with it (on my second or third try admittedly). A number of mysteries that can be solved many ways - meaning either with complete or incomplete information - it's up to you when to finish the investigation and who to accuse. Scores of nooks and crannies, parkour exploring and tidbits galore to find scattered across this bizarre island world. I only wish it had Achievements so I could easily figure out how many crystals and relics I missed!
_childDocuments_.name: Paradise Killer

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game more to help with the metrics of the site. I know it's a rotten tomatoes style, percentage of positive review type thing, but "Overwhelmingly Positive" has certain connotations that can lead people to be very disappointed with this game. One of those people was myself. In truth, I find this a more middling game that has some impressive strengths along with some unfortunately large flaws.Paradise Killer is a hyper stylized murder mystery game that takes place in an original alternate universe dominated by cosmic gods and demons. To start off with some positives, the island on which the game takes place is very visually interesting and populated by a killer... by a wonderful soundtrack. Really, the soundtrack alone is so good that it helped get over a LOT of this game's shortcomings. That said, the island is far too big for the amount of exploration that is encouraged. This is further compounded by how limited your traversal is in the beginning of the game. Additionally, the island has some confusing geometry in the name of admittedly interesting design. Trying to navigate to specific locations can lead to frequently becoming lost or falling to areas where you have to restart.These transportation annoyances should be lessened by the fact that the game has a fast travel system, right? Wrong. In an over indulgence of flavor and attempted detail, the system can feel to be more of a slog than just travelling. If you want to access fast travel, you will first have to activate a telephone to act as a fast travel spot. Sure, this is a proven way to keep people limited to places they've been before. I would argue that it is pointless in this game, as there are only two or three telephones in areas that would require unlocking a path first. Allowing the player to simply travel to a number of beacons with a few requiring activation would have cut down on the needless busywork the game uses to stretch out the play time.  Furthermore, the fast travel system is one of the slowest I have encountered. Once you have paid the fee and selected fast travel, you don't get to just zip over to the other location. Instead, you get a crash scene as the transition loads, and then you are riding in a car with another character. She asks you where you want to go, another (quick)  load screen, and then you're there. I'll be lenient and say this whole process takes about 15 seconds. Now, this may not seem like a lot, however it causes the prospect of simply walking to where you need to go to be much more appealing unless the location is on the opposite side of the island. The fact that you have to pay to use it as well makes it even worse, which leads me to another point.Blood gems, the currency of the island, are both too plentiful and largely useless. How can there be too much money, you ask? When there is a several second "item get!" screen each time you find one, and you'll be finding them all over the place. Usually only ever single blood gems on their own, unless you are able to finish one of the scant side quests to earn, *gasp* TWO blood gems. Despite their abundance, to the point of finding them getting the same disappointed energy as unwrapping underwear for Christmas, there is a hard limit on the number in the game, which makes them paradoxically feel too valuable to use on non-limited transactions, i.e. fast travel. While they are largely useless, there are a few instances where you NEED them in unknown quantities in order to find information about the game. Starlight (your laptop) generally require some amount of blood gems to unlock, there is a character who requires blood gems for testimony, and there are shrines that require blood gems to activate. While, in the end, you probably only need about 20 in order to unlock every bit of game affecting content, you don't know that until the very end so you will constantly have the RPG problem of "I can't use this now, I might need it later!"Now, if somehow you have read to this point, you might be thinking that I'm spending a lot of time complaining about what are, at best, tertiary systems. Surely these are just nitpicks if that is what you're complaining about. However, that is the experience of Paradise Killer, constant painful thorns in your sides. You're right, though, I could overlook these if the rest of the game slammed it out of the park like Mark McGuire on a day with some extra potent 'juice." Sadly, the most egregious of Paradise Killer's faults is its writing.Any game that says 'Nani the Hell' deserves scorn.The main crux of Paradise Killer's game play is investigating a mass murder. This is primarily done by means of dialog with the various characters of the island. The problem is that 90% of these characters are absolutely  vile, and, . In a game where the whole point is unraveling the mystery and trying to piece together a crime, I found myself dreading talking to people, especially if I knew that they'd have a lot to say. Everyone is very one note and easy to grasp within the first few lines of talking to them. There are no surprises that will make you second guess your first impression; that's just how they are. There is no subtlety, no depth to any motives, and no complexity to any of their ♥♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ personalities. That said, some can be nice to talk to and there are a few instances where you interact with people you are supposed to be friends with and you actually feel like the characters are friends.This game has far, far too many "I'm fourteen and this is deep" moments. The main character's catchphrase is "facts and truth are not the same" and the game wants to make this a theme. However, it does nothing to establish what it means by this, just waving it around like "if you don't understand, that just means you're not smart enough to." At the very end, it started to feel like it was meaning that by 'truth' it meant a forced perception of reality a la 1984's 2+2=5. However, our investigative main character has made no indication at all of wanting to do anything but to find the pure reality of what happened. If, say, the character had either a goal of framing the story in a particular way or had a history of distorting facts to create outcomes she desired, then that could have been worked in as a character moment, but that is not the case. There is no character arc in the game at all, in fact. The only difference in the characters by the end of the game is that several of them are dead. I guess you are also free to participate in you murderous cult as well rather than watch from the sidelines, so hurray?Finally, there's the mystery itself. Now, I'd be lying if I said that it was a total flop. There is some intrigue to be had here and the revelation moments did feel nice. That said, said revelation moments where a bit -too- packed compared to other parts of the game where it could feel like you were just spinning your wheels. My main complaint here is the resolution. Not necessarily the answer to the mystery, which was fine, but in the game treated itself as if it was not as decisively solved as it had been in the trial. My guess is that, since you can start the trial at any time, they wrote with the assumption that you didn't scour everything before starting? Possible, but it still made the game feel like it thought it was much deeper than it was. Which, to be fair, the writing regularly does. Now I have rambled a lot, so I will end here. Sure, I could go into how the EXECUTION OF JUSTICE was a bit bungled, how the puzzles were worthless, or how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pretty the game could look at times, but I'm out of space. In the end, the game is one of glaring flaws that is held together by some very intense style work. To fix it, I'd give Paradise Killer a C.
