_childDocuments_.review: Came for the interesting gameplay, stayed for the fantastic writing and narrative.What makes this a good game is that you have to buy oxygen and fuel refills periodically from your employer, but if you pat attention and are strategic about it, you can find those refills inside the ships, and use them instead and make better use of resources that way.What makes this a great game is that that tension between getting the refills from the company versus finding them in the ship is written into the game narrative and is used to reinforce the story of a company using you as indentured labor to colonize the solar system.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: So, the game is more or less in open beta, it's a bit of a resource hog, but in its own way, the salvaging of the ships in zero-g is a bit...zen.  Almost meditative.Of course, this is a game full of reactors, coolant and fuel tanks, so one shouldn't get TOO zen out there.  She's a puzzle game, and one wrong move can sometimes have you reduced to vapor and having a big mess of shards to clean up when you're resurrected.  Come for the relaxing blues music and salvaging among the stars, stay for the surprisingly deep world-building and the puzzle of "how do I salvage THIS one without being atomized...and get paid as much as possible doing it?"
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR.: grab it on sale, it's a solid timewaster!It's definitely not for everyone. If you enjoy timewaster games (like power wash sim) with the slighterst hint of puzzle elements, that let you watch something on the second screen  in peace or just think about stuff while doing something with your hands, this is a perfect game. As the title says, you break up ships in a space salvage yard orbiting above Earth. There is progression by upgrades to get, salvage goals to reach, and in the late game you do have to use your brain a tiny little bit sometimes to avoid a reactor meltdown or fuel tanks blowing up. You can adjust the difficulty by turning off oxygen consumption and shift time limits, or go full hardcore with a single life even. The choice is there, which is very welcome in this type of game.The gameplay is mostly solid, you do have to pay attention though to your laser clipping into stuff and accidentally blowing stuff up, and also the physics can be unintuitive, sometimes outright the opposite of what you would expect. Thankfully it's weirdness is consistent so once you figure it out, it's gonna be part of the fun.The biggest annoyance with this game is the "story". It supposedly has one, although it's so lame and meaningless that having to wait through the unskippable voice messages will provide you with nothing but frustration. Thankfully they are short enough and rare enough. You can find other items that add to the world building but I just couldn't care after a while. I was there to cut stuff up, swing stuff with my gravity gun into the huge chambers of flames, and just generally turn my brain off while listening to something on my second screen.Graphics are good enough for this type of game, sound design is okay, and the music pretty solid, although repetitive.Overall I do recommend this game if you like this genre, it's a proper experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Very satisfying physics!! Even though most of the ships in each class are the same at the moment, its a lot of fun to try new ways of taking them apart to either make the most off the salvage or try to get the whole thing done as fast as possible. still some bugs and improvements to be made but nothing game breaking. For an early access this game is amazing all around and i cant wait to see how it progresses.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: A nice timewaster with an unnecessary garbage woke story.The game loop is fun and relaxing. The problem with it is that it gets quite boring around the middle of the story - it's quite repetitive. Menial, really. So it's a nice thing to relax to while listening to a podcast on the side or something.The problem with the game as a whole is, after you learn all the tricks of the game and it becomes this reflexive tax-paying thing, the only thing keeping you playing is either the feeling of the zen experience cutting the ships up (that would be the BETTER part) or playing through the whole story to the end (the CRAPPY part). I mean the story is ripe with new age unionizing communist/marxist ideas, woke characters (budget Karine Jean-Pierre woke ufckster) and a storyline that's just as everyday menial as the gameplay. soo.....Play it for the work experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun sim game with a lightweight storyline but the core mechanics and fun come from the work you're doing to cut these ships apart. Each one is a unique 3D puzzle to figure out how to most efficiently, effectively, and safely salvage the craft. After you hit about 80% - the ships do become repetitive but there are things about each that change and are unique about them - but eventually you get to know them and they become old friends. The voice acting is... ok. It gets the story along, but this ain't no AAA game with deep pockets for professional talent. All in all, it's a blast. I'm thoroughly enjoying this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Chill game on Free Shift, with no time limits, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to drag it out past it's welcome.Could have done without the extremely ham-fisted "Capitalism Bad!" narrative.Makes me wish I could vote, "Buyer Beware," or "Meh," instead of good or bad.Get it on sale if you're weird like me and like doing mundane tasks in sci-fi/fantasy.Also, they need to put in the ability to skip the awful dialogue, and just let me salvage in peace.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful puzzle game, where instead of putting the pieces together, you pull them off the ships in many different ways. There is lots of diverse mechanics that make it interesting and somewhat challenging. Story was kinda meh and I feel like they really fumbled it by not introducing coop mode with guilds where each person could pick a specialization. The development has been completed, so don't expect any new content. Highly recommended tho.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Thought this game was a lot of fun, could chill out and pull the ships apart.Could benefit from a few new classes of ship, but was relatively varied. _childDocuments_.review: I have a rule for Early Access games: The game must be in a state where I don't need updates. If the devs abandoned this game tomorrow, I would be content with it, because the game is already there. It's relatively repetitive, but it is very satisfying.I have two favorite pieces: movement, and progression. The movement is simple: true zero gravity motion. Some late game ships get rather large, and I have found myself coming out of a ship only to have to look around and reorient myself as to which way is "up," because the motion is completely relative to your position. There is a bit of "air resistance" that prevents things from floating off infinitely, but the zero g motion is very real.The second, progression, is even better. Because it is a mix of getting new tools and learning new tricks with what you have. You learn how to split a bulkhead just right with a det charge, how to grab 2-3 things while moving and sling them to the appropriate places, the right order to disengage fuel lines to keep the ship from explodingg, and when to evacuate a ship because it's about to explode and dying is expensive.Honestly, just those two pieces, combined with variation in the ship designs, results in a game that can be played and enjoyed as-is, with nothing else required, but the game is still getting updates!In short: play the game. Even if it becomes abandonware tomorrow, it is still a great game as-is, but the devs are still working on it, meaning it is getting even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Slow-paced and relaxing.  That was my feeling from four hours into the game and onward, at least - before that point, when I was still figuring out how to do it well, it went explosive and stressful fairly regularly.  It's also somewhat tedious and repetitive - but hey, so is Sudoku.  "Tedious" is a genre, not a complaint.  You mostly move around with standard spacesuit thruster controls... the good kind where you can freely turn on every axis, and you unlock better movement and better tools as you go.You get slightly-randomized ships, and as many 15-minute blocks of time as you want to take them apart, by cutting or vaporizing bits of them off and then grappling or tethering those bits into furnaces.  Generally you have to duck out to refill your oxygen once during that time.  You want to avoid explosively decompressing the ship, nicking a fuel line and blowing stuff up, electrocuting or whacking yourself by pulling computer consoles off the wall too hard, or all of those things at once.  As you proceed, you go from small thirty-minute ships to bigger hour-long things, but you can rush to complete only the objectives you care about, or go as slowly as you want.In theory, you're trying to pay off a billion-credit loan, and you've got big expenses each shift (because it's an exploitative frontier company, played mostly straight).  That pushes you to rush your assignments and extract value as fast as you can, but I think that's a mistake.  Money has literally no gameplay impact.  If you want to spend a whole shift just checking out a new ship and planning your approach, losing money in the process, that's great.  If you're offended by the idea of spending five, ten, fifteen minutes just floating around a ship and planning out your approach... well maybe this game isn't right for you.The state of early access at the end of 2020: It doesn't save ship progress when you quit out, so if you can't play for a half hour or more at a time, wait until that feature is finally implemented.  There's enough ship types that I'm not bored, but it is still fundamentally limited, so yeah it's repetitive.  The way I play it, repetitive is fine; it's a relaxing time-waster.  Physics are overall very good, but there's some occasional glitches with the larger ships; you'll have to be tolerant that those sometimes blow up unexpectedly right now, or have objectives that don't complete right; It hasn't put me off, but if big glitches utterly infuriate you, hard pass.  Updates are of the "every few months" variety, and they are still experimenting with some of the features.  Everything that's currently in is extremely playable, but it's clearly lacking endgame content.Weaver, your handler over the radio, has a really cute drawl.  He makes my heart go pitter-patter.  <3

If you just loved the aesthetic of Homeworld and Deserts of Kharak, this is for you.If you like your science fiction blue-collar, hard-nosed with calloused hands, this is for you. If the powerlessness of being a tiny cog in a huge machine and the power of tearing apart huge machines with dangerous yet awesome machine tools are your jam, you need this. _childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a fantastic game about dismantling obselete and derelict spaceships. At its core, the game is about reading the architecture of a ship and how to dismantle it. It does this extremely well, even for early access alpha. There are full-priced games that release in far worse states than this. I am mainly writing this review to clarify for people afraid of having timers in this game: do not be afraid of this game. I started afraid at first, but I think this is because the game isn't great at communicating what's at stake in terms of the timer components.There are two timed components to any shift, your O2 meter, and your shift timer. O2 ticks down over the course of the shift, but can often be found inside ships you are working to top you off, and is easy and extremely cheap to refill at the Jack, which is like your base. If you are paying attention you will never run out of O2, it's just a way to get you to get out of the hull and come back with perhaps a new approach to the job.The shift timer is basically setting a 15 minute cap on your demolition, but all that actually means is you are paying an amount that can be decreased with time upgrades for a shift on the job. You can keep working on a job for multiple shifts. All you need to do is think in terms of efficiency, "how can I tear this ship apart cleanly, and quickly" is the name of the game. The only thing the timers ultimately penalize you with is debt, which is just a big red number that is more of a joke than anything. Upgrade currency is completely separate from this number, and you will always be able to finish a job even if it takes multiple shifts. The largest ships at Tier 6 take me a minimum of 3 shifts to knock out most of the work orders. Those ships are a lot of work!So if you see the timed component and turn off immediately, don't. It's not bad at all and has helped me learn how to get a job done quickly and cleanly, just like Lynx would want.

_childDocuments_.review: There are many games out there about building things. Whether its cities, vehicles, or structures, you can always put things together. There are even more games that have you destroying things intentionally or as a byproduct of combat. However, Hardspace: Shipbreaker is one of the first I’ve seen that has you meticulously taking things apart to save as many pieces as possible.Abbreviated Review: Shipbreaking is a real job that has workers descending upon retired ships to strip them of all useful or valuable parts before they’re fully destroyed. When a ship goes beyond its lifespan, it can cost more to repair or retrofit it than it does to build a new one from the ground up. Pulling the best parts out of these ships has been a worthwhile venture for as long as boats have been on the water.Hardspace: Shipbreaker takes this role into orbit. Yet, this time instead of a team of breakers swarming over the task, you’re a lone soul in a spacesuit with a couple of useful tools. Just like in the terrestrial version, the goal is to pull/cut/explode off as many valuable pieces of the spaceship as possible and put them in the correct area. Doing this will add to your end-of-shift payout as well as fulfill the various tasks on your work order – the goals for each ship.The breaking area, which I’m probably going to improperly refer to as a dry dock, has three types of salvaging repositories around it. Below you is a large flat barge, which is where you’re supposed to toss every fully functional part you find. Things like furniture, computers, engines, and even the valuable reactor. The second facility is the Processor where you send items that are made of the most valuable to be broken down. The final destination for everything else is the Furnace where metals are scrapped and melted down for the smallest payout.To facilitate this meticulous destructive process, you’re given two tools for the job. The tether gun allows you to grab specific items and pull them free from their mounts. It also can produce tethers that magically connect items and pull them toward each other. This is what you’ll use to get pretty most things from their location on the ship to their required processing area once cut free.Your other tool, the cutter, also has two modes. The first mode is a precision laser (Stinger) that heats and melts parts. You can use this in tight spaces without any fear of collateral damage. However, it will heat the tool and takes much longer than the “Splitsaw” mode at cutting through weak points. What you risk with the split saw is the potential for cuts that go beyond your intended range and damage other parts. Virtually every error I made in my time playing involved the Splitsaw in some way.These tools, as well as much of the rest of your gear, have several upgrades. The cutter can gain the ability to take more heat or cut further from you (which can be far more dangerous). The tether gun gets more pulling force and can hold more tethers. Even the scanning tool, with its somewhat limited use, has upgrades to allow it to have more modes and function further in your view. Upgrades to your suit give you more oxygen, movement capability, resistance to damage, and generally make the hurdles Hardspace: Shipbreaker puts in front of you a little easier to overcome.Hardspace: Shipbreaker is fun in a strange zen-like way. Methodically tearing up ships is far more fulfilling than blowing them up as you would in other games. Sure, you can accidentally blow them up, but that’s usually a bad thing (though doing it right can be effective). The seemingly insurmountable billion-dollar debt you start in and slowly chip away at a few million at a time adds another strangely rewarding feeling to the process. Trying to make as much money in every shift forces ingenuity in your efforts even when you don’t realize it.Yet the limitation of the shifts can be a bit of a problem. In early ships, you can knock out most everything in the 15-minute time limit. For larger ships, you’re revisiting three or four times just to fulfill the work orders. Finding efficient methods to cut ships apart can only go so far to resolve this, so it just feels like a chore reloading every 15 minutes. Couple that with crazy physics bugs (don’t try to pick up a fuse) and items being pulled into the wrong processing area and some big issues need to be resolved. On top of that, the UI isn’t particularly friendly and on PC currently has static keybinds that aren’t consistent across the menus.Despite those issues, the allure of zero-g space ship salvage drew me in. I’ve always loved salvaging in games so this was a must-play for me. It delivered most of what I expected and some things I didn’t even consider. Hopefully, the developers can work out the bugs and figure out a middle ground on the timer (which I do think is necessary in some form). I’d recommend this in its current form mostly for crazy sci-fi salvage-loving nerds like me.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Only recommend if you can get it on saleObjective Gameplay: 8/10Controls: 6/10Physics: 5/10Story 2/10Art 7/10While I enjoyed this game and will continue to play it, there are some elements to it that were not properly communicated in the descriptions and marketing that probably would have stopped me from buying it. Overall I'm having fun, but due to steams all or nothing review style, I have to give this a not recommended at full price.Gameplay:As a simulator, gameplay mechanics should make up the majority of its value. Story is a bonus but simulation games are, at their core, about replicating a situation in detail for the player. Overall, Hardspace: Shipbreaker has solid core gameplay    Objectives: The core gameplay is pretty fun for a simulator, I’d give it an 8/10. Basically, you just tear apart a ship using a set of upgradable tools and sort the pieces into three categories (which are clearly labeled on each piece). It was very satisfying taking apart large ships methodically, coming up with plans for depressurizing compartments safely, or removing reactors before they melt down. In the career mode the progression feels good, the jobs become more complex as you go, but they retain elements of the simpler ships so every increase in difficulty felt like an upgrade to gameplay rather than leaving something fun behind for something slightly more fun. One con I would point out is that there are resources like O2 and thruster fuel that are basically pointless mechanics. To buy more costs so little it might as well be nothing and the place you buy is right next to the work area. Really all it does is interrupt your fun every couple of minutes with a blaring alarm, adding 0 difficulty to the game. My assumption is it's for realism, but it's just too low stakes to provide anything but 15 seconds of “well I guess I have to drop what I’m doing and fly over here for a second”.    Controls: The controls are ok, I’d give them a 6/10. You are in a 0G environment so you need three axis movement which can be a pain. The thrusters can be sluggish even with upgrades and reorienting yourself or navigating complex paths can be a chore. However you don’t really need rapid movements most of the time so this was not a major obstacle to enjoying the game and sometimes the stress of maneuvering added tension to the gameplay. I did really enjoy slingshotting around with the grappling tool, that was fun especially when I got the hang of it. I played with both controller and KBM, I personally would recommend controller but KBM is totally usable if that’s your preference.    Physics/Engine: The physics in this game could be pretty frustrating and probably my biggest gameplay complaint. I would give them a 4/10 or 5/10. For example to sort the pieces you need to move them into zones, there are two that are directly side by side where you put the largest pieces. The zones pull things automatically when they get close, but the pull zones overlap so with the largest pieces they can get stuck between the two zones and they are a HUGE pain to get off. This game also has a time limit on each shift so you waste a bunch of time trying to unstick bits. Another common issue is you pull off a piece from the ship and it flings back and hits you like a rubber band which sends you flying into space. If you’re still holding the piece that momentum is transferred and hits you again, rinse and repeat. Story:    I’m just going to be blunt, the story is bad, and it's a huge downer 2/10. You’re basically a space debt slave working for the most cringe heavy handed dystopian corporation. If you work a long day at a real corporation and want to come home and relax, this is not the game. Now that alone isn’t really the problem. The problem is that this is a simulator game, and when the story scenes start (and there are A LOT) it locks you into the homebase and you can’t do anything. You can’t start your shift, can’t upgrade your tools, can’t skip, just gotta sit through some heavy handed social commentary written by a teenager. The characters are all one-dimensional cliches. You’ve got the grizzled father figure, the nervous goodboy with a hard homelife, the tough-as-nails lady with a soft spot, and the most overplayed, crusty crab, greedy middle manager type.  Also the characters are just annoying oversharers. If you work in an office you know that one guy, and they are all that guy. The bad story isn't a big deal since it's a simulator, but forcing the player to sit through a bunch of unskippable dialogue made those scenes go from story to gameplay, and when all you want to do is dismantle some ships it feels incredibly out of place and just huge drag.Art:     Nothing groundbreaking, but the designs are thematically consistent and interesting. I honestly didn’t think about it too much but it has a 1979 Alien feel to it which worked well I would say. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: An exceptionally addictive combination of first person games and puzzle games, Shipbreaker tasks you with overcoming a monumental debt by cutting apart spaceships. While earlier ships are straightforward and without danger, over time the difficulty ramps up, throwing more and more types of hazards at you. The story and atmosphere emulates the ideas of 1900s Company Towns and their problem of debt slavery, with a twist; since you're very likely to kill yourself at least once, you can be cloned (for a price!), with the genetic material that the company has ownership over. The level of care that you take is up to you; you can choose to measure twice, cut once, or you can choose to measure never, cut lots, and hope you can think quickly enough to avoid catastrophe!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I love the game. There is something very relaxing and therapeutic about breaking a ship apart into it's components. The game also does a fantastic job of making the ships feel real with interlocking systems and steps you need to take to safely disassemble a ship. My main complaint is story. The story itself isn't bad, but the way is implemented seems to do more to hamper the gameplay than anything else. The basic premise is that you work for a megacorp that has buried you in a mountain of debt and you have to work your debt off. Each ship part has a dollar amount so the more parts you salvage, the more money you make. You also have to purchase oxygen, fuel, and repair kits for your equipment.The problem is that the amount of debt you are buried in is insane. I am talking over $100 BILLION. Meanwhile, most ships you take apart will net you $20-40 MILLION at most. There is no way you are going to pay off the debt without putting hundreds of hours into a single playthrough. The game knows this and getting the debt canceled is a main part of the story.The problem is that this debt mechanic makes the dollar amount tied to each ship component almost meaningless. There is no point in keeping track of how much you spend on fuel or repair kits because no amount of money you make has any impact on the gameplay. You will often find yourself caring more about upgrade points than money, IN A GAME ABOUT MAKING MONEY.Still, the rest of the game is fantastic. I truly hope the game gets a sequel that uses the money you make for some kind of meta progression.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: This is a gem that hopefully will get even more mileage once they add more ships to break down.Pros:The gameplay is straightforward enough to pick up pretty quick.The challenge is trying to accomplish goals within the shift limit (you will need multiple shifts for the larger ships to accomplish all work orders).The music isn't intrusive but gives a good vibeCons:Only 2 types of ships right now. This really limits mileage once you figure out a fast method for dealing with them. The fps will chug hard if you go nuts with the splitter to cut up chunks. Each one of those little itty bitty bits has to be tracked and that is probably the reason. However sometimes this is necessary when a big piece gets stuff on the mouth of the furnace. You can be precise because you can't get close or you will get eaten.Tips for new players:1. o2 should and tethers are good early upgrades.2. Devise a strategy for breaking the ship down.3. The less you have to move yourself while doing tasks the quicker you will be.4. Braking while grappling is a good habit to get into.5. The valuable stuff is going to the barge. Dont sweat furnace stuff unless it is in your way.6. Listen carefully.... when you place look at the weight as you target stuff. You can quickly tell if something is broke off when the weight drops. This can be really helpful when cutting so you dont have to swap back to grappler. 7. Tethering the reactor straight to the barge is a good idea. 8. The quickest way to die is explosions. The second quickest is a hard hit to the face. You break the helmet and lose air along with the initial hp dmg. 9. If you go back to the master jack for air or tethers make sure to get the other as well if its more than a little down. Also that is a place to buy repair kits. Buy them regularly. Topped off equipment works better so you get more done during a shift.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is pretty tough to review. On the other hand, I find it quite chill and relaxing, especially when turning off the time limitation and oxygen drain - as it's just a nuisance to go fill the oxygen tanks often and really doesn't add anything to the game loop - On the other hand, it almost feels like actual manual labor but you're not getting paid. You may have to be unemployed in real life or somehow twisted in the brain to enjoy this game. I think the best part is the quite realistic newtonian physics, meaning when you accelerate to a direction, there's nothing to stop you if you don't counter the inertia. There is inertial dampening on roll motion, however. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: at the bottom this is a bit of long review. I'm an Early Access buyer and the end result was disappointing.To explain the disappointment I need to explain what I thought I was buying. When I bought the game there was a general premise. You were a ship breaker, in a salvage yard in the relatively near future. The game play loop was that you had to take apart space ships in various states of disrepair with different tools. You had to think ahead, plan how the disassembly would go for maximum profit, and, of course, not blow up and die. Essentially the game was a 3D puzzle with a equipment upgrade grind. Overall the world was fun with a simple goal, you were 1 billion dollars in debt with the mega corporation, Lynx, that run the facility. Sounds bad but after your first few ships you're making multi million dollar days. So you can pay it off after 90 or so game rounds. Lynx was tongue in cheek evil to explain game mechanics, IE making you buy extra oxygen, or pay for repairs to your equipment, or paying for clones if you die, etc. There was even a bit of an in game world building where you were finding data disks that brought up the history and recent developments of the in game world. There was even hints of an AI rebellion brewing out beyond Jupiter.When I got the game there was two ship classes and two variants of each and there was promise of a lot more.  With a lot more tools to discover and new hazards to be added to figure out. There was even talk of having a ship creator mode so you could upload to the workshop and have player made ships to take apart.That's what was suppose to happen.What really happened was that there seemed to be a change mid stream where it wasn't about the game anymore. It wasn't about the ships or the puzzles. It was about "The Message". The Dev's, for whatever reason, decided that there needed to be a more structured story, even though no one asked for it. From that point on additional content seemed to slow to a crawl. They added two additional ship classes an additional variant to each class, and an extra hazard was added but that is far from the initial goals of the game. This is over the course of two plus yearsIf you're wondering what "The Message" was it came down to a grade school rendition of unions good, corporations bad, rise up, fight the power. You are drafted into a proto union, (you literally have no choice), to fight the now cartoonishly, mustache twirling, evil Lynx. I mean, OK, Sure, Fine, Whatever, but it is so heavy handed, it's like taking a two by four to the face and then having a cinder block dropped on you just to make the point. To top it off, and why I'm so salty about this, you are completely railroaded into the story. I mean it's so bad that you are literally tied down to the train car and forced on rails to the end. You have no say, no agency. You can not influence or affect the story in any way. The story isn't even about you, you are a minor side character to the main character. I mean there are games with silent characters that follow a story script, Link, Master Chief, Doom Guy, etc. where you don't talk or barely talk but people are reacting to what you do, what you put into motion. Here? Here you're completely removed from the action, the choices. What you do doesn't matter. The hilarious thing is that the Dev's are just as authoritarian and heavy handed in forcing you to hear "The Message", completely disregarding around a year of people telling the they didn't like it, introducing such 1 and 2 dimensional characters, with grade school level understanding of business, that they actually make Lynx seem like a reasonable organization half the time despite how they act in game. There are times where you go, "Well, Lynx does have a point".Last thing. Don't take my hours played as a sign of the game I finished in about 8-10 hrs. They restarted progress multiple times during development and you have to grind to get to the new content. Plus I did try to clear my debt in one play through. On top of that, I think they made the game easier. And because you can now 'win' the game, a lot of the drive to go so long and clear the debt is now gone.So TLDR: The game has good game play, graphics, and music, but the Dev's decided to get preachy and focus on a "Message" instead of game play and content. There is between half to a third of what ship classes was originally scoped, there is no planned ship creator, no planned workshop addition, and the challenge of the game seems to have been watered down. If you can get the game for what I did $10-15 it's worth it if you can deal with the 'story' but avoid if it's not on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: To talk about Hardspace: Shipbreaker, you have to understand that there are two things going on simultaneously.The first, is the game itself. The actual gameplay of taking apart ships, sorting them into their various components, and turning them in for profit. This part is good. It's a pleasant experience, and the time in EA has made it relatively polished for how much physics is going on (there's still some wonkiness, but that's going to happen with any physics game). I don't have too much to say, but that's praise. It feels good, it's fun, it's a good experience all around. Second, we have the story. The story is basically a visual novel, and is presented as other characters expositing at you in one of four ways: Before/after the shift, in e-mails, or over comms during the shift. If you don't particularly want to listen to the exposition, sorry you have to listen to the before and after shift messages. I didn't find a way to skip them. At least the comms during a shift can be mostly tuned out while you actually play the game. The plot itself is okay. Evil megacorporation is bad, unions are good. Some of the human moments are touching and sweet, some of them are really boring because it's stopping you from playing the game.So, the story's ok, and the game's good. But there's one big problem: They don't match. They don't fit together. Most of the story revolves around corporate and managerial malfeasance. However, this malfeasance (almost) never touches the player. You're faced with "extortionate fees" of over 500,000 credits per day. Of course, you can make over 10,000,000 (ten million!) credits per day. So these extortionate fees are... maybe 5-10%? That's less than people pay in real-world taxes! But you don't get that money, it's just paying off a debt, of course. A debt of about 1.2 billion credits. So at a pace of ten million credits per day, it would take around 120 game days (or approximately 30 real-world hours) to pay your debt. If we compare this to real world student loans... um... find me someone who paid off their student loans in 120 days. I'll wait. The training (tutorial) provided to the player is more than adequate, even though we're told that other characters weren't getting sufficient training. Other characters struggle with faulty equipment, but everything provided to the player runs perfectly fine. The game gets harder at progressive points, which are laid out perfectly clearly ahead of time under "certification progress." But when you hit those points, the story acts as though you're being forced to progress. All of this creates a feeling of ludonarrative dissonance -- the unpleasant feeling when the narrative doesn't match the feelings evoked by gameplay. It's far harder to buy into the story and believe that times are tough when you're making money hand over fist.However, all this said, I still recommend the game. The core game is absolutely fun, and the feeling of progression is well-tuned. It's just a darn shame that the narrative is so divorced from the actual game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a game all about salvaging as much as you can, from now defunct spacecraft.The lovely thing about the game is the freedom you have with your tools and canvas, as well as the relaxing atmosphere.You've got a cutter, which allows you to either use a focused beam to destroy connections between walls, freeing them up.Or you can switch to its alternative mode, which is a Dead Space-esque plasma cutter with either a vertical or horizontal line. You can use this to cut literally anywhere you want on soft metals. This means you can be as efficient or inefficient as possible, ranging from cutting one beautiful big square off a wall, or dicing it up into hundreds of pieces.Some metals are too strong for your cutter, which is where you'll need to get into the ship through other means, and then dislodge the bolts holding the wall in place. It's actually a lot of fun figuring out how to approach each ship. The ideal way would be to go through the airlock. If you activate it properly, this will depressurise the ship, and allow you to enter safely. If you fail to do this, and instead, say, cut a hole right into the ship, it will depressurise violently, and launch you alongside any cargo on the inside. This is bad because, first, you can die from a savage impact against a wall in your station. Or two, you damage goods that you could have salvaged, which puts a dent in your income (which I'll go further into later).Once you've gotten in successfully, and dislodged walls, you have a few options.The first would be to use your energy grabber, which allows you to manipulate objects from a distance, provided they are light enough. You throw them into the right container (furnace, processor, barge), and get a reward.If they're too heavy though, you'll find that grabbing them with your tool will pull you towards them instead.This is where tethers come in. They're super fun tools that allow you to attach objects to each other. Depending on the angles, and weight of them, you might have to put multiple tethers, which allows for some fun playing around with physics.Once 15 minutes have passed, your shift is over, and you return to your home in space. This is where you can use your earned tokens to purchase upgrades for your gear. This includes increased range, faster thrusters, increase oxygen timers, etc.Most of them are just number increases, nothing super interesting.Once you're done, you pick your next ship to work on (or continue the one you were using before), and start your next day.  That's the main loop!The game is so incredibly relaxing, despite some of the dangerous encounters you can get into. The music is some chill country guitar, and floating around feels peaceful. You can actually reach out with your hands to grab onto walls to stop yourself from floating around, and can even crawl around if you alternate your hands.The game becomes more intricate when you want to maximise your money earnings. You'll want to pick apart as many pieces as possible. For example, instead of throwing the whole back of the ship into the processor, because the majority of it requires that, you will instead go in, pull off some lamps, chairs, throw them into the barge, then get some beams and put them in the furnace, and THEN put the rest in the processor. You start to feel like you are really mastering the job.My problem with the game lies here though: The forced limitations get in the way. The 15 minute shift timer is not that fun, and just forces you to rush towards the end of your shift. On top of that, your tethers and oxygen are limited, and need refilling often. It's not a huge deal, because you can fly over to the outside of your home and refill on that stuff quickly, but it breaks the flow, and forces you to be conservative in an unfun way. I would be all for limiting how many tethers can be active at once, but the system implemented just impeded the fun for me. You can upgrade all of this stuff to allow you to carry more, but it just felt tedious until that point. It's not a dealbreaker, but it does force you to take 30 second breaks every now and again when you might not necessarily want to.There is fortunately a freeplay mode where you can pick a ship and do exactly the same thing, minus all the limitations, but the only issue there is you lack the feeling of overall progression in the career mode.Speaking of Career mode, the story is that you work for Lynx. Trying to work off your 1 Billion dollar debt! Unfortunately for you, they also charge you for renting all your tools, accomodation, and even add interest on top of that. It's actually a subtle, but silly little world that the game is based in. You can also find some lore based tapes and such, for those interested in that.Overall, I love the game. I think there are issues with it in its current state, like not properly explaining some mechanics, and being rough around the edges sometimes, but in the end its a lot of fun disassembling stuff, and I recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun solo experience where you take apart old spaceships. Good graphics, immersion, and sound design.Warning that content and support for this game seems to have stopped cold after its full release. Once you finish the short story mode, all there is to do is keep taking apart the same ships.The story is interesting, but pretty cookie-cutter and entirely linear. Most of the story focuses on your role as an expendable worker in an anti-union corporation. There are sometimes corrupted/alien AI infecting the ships, but that plot goes nowhere and is just another style of hazard in the ships.Once you are familiar with the small variety of ships, it's sort of a relaxing way to zone out and feel like you're accomplishing something.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, early access is starting to end and while the game was ambitious and has solid mechanics, it seems that it was maybe a bit too ambitious for the studio to handle. _childDocuments_.review: So, while this game is still quite under development (and it's received several updates even in the short while I've been playing it - each adding a bit of spice to what is already a fun formula - it's remarkably entertaining. And that's kind of odd, as it's a simulation of a job I wouldn't really find much fun in real life on Earth.Floating around in space, I find myself thinking hard about which parts to cut and which to leave intact, what to use my valuable tethers on and what to use my grapple (and some valuable time) on instead. The game is surprisingly strategic and loves to kick your butt if you manage to get careless with your cutter. A hint about the grapple: don't use the charged push function unless you're really sure the part you're pushing is no longer attached to the ship. Hitting the station at high speed hurts.The only flaw I can see so far - and I do hope that just needs a bit of polish - is that the game sometimes still crashes on me, and usually when I'm almost done tearing up a Gecko. I'll have stripped the thing down to its frame, put all the valuable stuff on the barge, and then poof, the game crashes and I don't get any of the benefits of my hour of work.Two thumbs up to the developers for the sense of humor and the well designed gameplay. Keeping an eye on this game to see what comes up.

Which it did at least once every 30 minutes.You will even lose progress if you end your work day, return to your habitat, cash in your salvage and then exit to the main menu and close the game. The next time you log in you will be back in the previous work day with an unsalvaged ship and no money banked.There are so many ways to lose progress in the current build.This is exacerbated by the fact that the game doesn't do a great job at explaining what you need to do. My only deaths were from putting things in the wrong place and the company shutting my life down. Great, so you didn't tell me where to put this antenna I guess I'll try to blue light bay? Dead. Ok, the furnace to melt it down? Dead .... um.... Oh, there's a green net over there, is that it? Now do that with a reactor that it takes 30 minutes to pry out of a hull where you'll have to start from scratch if it blows up or you put it in the wrong place?It's frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is one of those games you will either love or hate. It's not going to appeal to everyone, and that's OK.If the idea of breaking up spaceships is your idea of fun, then it has you covered. The story feels a bit hamfisted in and some of the dialogue is... not great, but reduce it to reducing ships and your work-related debt and there's plenty of hours of entertainment to be had here. (90% of my playtime is on-deck play)Campaign is a good 30+ hours, depending on your shipbreaking ability.A good chill out game for those who like to kick back and play at their own pace.Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: A rare example of a game that was incredible on release in Early Access and subsequently got worse with every update. The reason for this is a complete misunderstanding as to what made the game great.Out of the gate, you had a brief 2 minute prologue in your awful, cramped, noisy apartment, and reading a tablet with a couple text blurbs that describe how gross and awful the in-game world is. This was a fantastic opening and communicated everything that was needed to be said about the world. You were then thrust into a very satisfying and chill gameplay loop where you break apart ships, with no NPC chatter, making for a very relaxing experience.Then, with each subsequent update, rather than focusing on the incredible core gameplay loop and adding more ships, they focused on story. You have NPCs chattering in your ear constantly with poorly written dialogue. You have to watch unskippable cutscenes between missions. You have a story that really isn't good or interesting or say anything new. Corporations are bad. All they needed to do was add more ships for you to break apart, as the game is called "Shipbreaker". Instead they invested in a really mediocre story, rather than the core gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: The UI is confusing to me:1. There's a clear pixel style, but in many places UI elements and the font are rendered blurry/scaled up (at 1440p). IMO, if there's pixel aesthetics, it should be rendered crisp. When you play with subs, the font is different. Not sure why.2. During the tutorial the UI felt very overwhelming. I got stuck two times:- The game told me to cut something, but it just didn't work. I needed to return to the game a 2nd time to figure out I was just slightly out of range for the cutter. Overwhelming: There's so much stuff on the HUD, I didn't detect a visual clue for this.- Later in the tutorial the game told me to dispose of some large side chunks. So I did what I learned just a mission earlier, but the objects just turned red (forbidden? disabled???) in the disposal zone. My guess is that I had to do something different, but the game didn't use clear language.(These two points might be clear to other users and maybe I didn't pay enough attention. I played with subs, so maybe I missed visual pointers while reading the text)I think this game in the current state can be very interesting to many people, but I personally didn't enjoy it. I disliked that you cannot move the head freely, but instead there's a drag (I understand why (spaaace), but to me it feels too restrictive and I know that this core concept won't ever get changed). I really loathed that you have to play with debt, that just felt really bad. Finally, the southern American radio buddy didn't work for me at all. Similar to the debt, I just cannot stand when people got a negative "Hinterwälder" attitude. It's fun for some minor NPC questgiver, but as my boss?? Pass. In my opinion these are truly weird choices for a game that's meant to be Zen.The developers seem to be quite open minded, so it pains me to leave a negative review. I wish Steam would have a less harsh "not quite" rating for early access games.Edit: I loved the game start with the forms and signup. That one puts you right into the proper mood.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at the bottomEdit: With the release of the first patch, additional resolutions are now supported, so I have changed my review to a recommended review as of June 25th, 2020.So, what about the game itself? It's fun! It's sort of like Viscera Cleanup Detail meets Space Engineers. If you like either one of those games or both of them you should have fun with Hardspace. Cutting up the ships and depositing salvage is satisfying, there appear to be quite a few upgrades to the existing equipment and what I've gotten to use has been satisfying, intuitive and fun. The movement feels great and the game does utilize the zero-g environment well. The movement and equipment are easy to pickup but there's room within the mechanics to creatively problem solve, which is great! The soundtrack is great if you're a fan of any kind of Space Western soundtracks. In fact, in terms of immersion, the game is outstanding right from the moment you boot it up. Hardspace really wants you to get into your character and your role early on. Everything from the UI to the music seeks to immerse you straight away. The game is pretty, although texture quality doesn't hold up when you're smashing your face into the wall of a ship (and you will, a lot). The game also features full gamepad support which, in a game with 6 Degrees of Freedom, is a pretty big must have, personally.TL;DRPros+ Cutting up ships is fun and creatively challenging.+ Equipment is easy to pickup but complex enough to be creative + Movement is fun, satisfying and not too hard once you get used to it+The soundtrack is awesome+The game is very immersive right from the moment you boot it up+ Full Gamepad support+Additional Resolutions now supported in 21:9 aspect ratioCons:-Textures are a little muddy close up-The game is a little content light at the moment, but I suspect that will change over time.-I have had several crashes in my 14-15 hours of gameplayConsider staying away if you have a higher resolution than 1920x1080 and you don't want to play in windowed mode

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun grind! It's not a linear game that holds the player's hand all the time. You choose the ship and the game presents you with a few items to salvage for experience and upgrades, but beyond that you can recycle whatever you want, in any order, and in any way you want for money. You can be careful and dismantle everything down to the smallest detail, or you can just go crazy and start cutting structures to salvage only the most valuable items like reactors and leave behind what isn't profitable.The microgravity movement is part of the game's challenge because there are many degrees of freedom compared to walking on the ground, but after a while it became natural for me and I was flying around at high speeds. Sometimes things go wrong, I collide at high speed and damage my helmet, get sucked into the furnace, I make mistakes when cutting and the fuel tank catches fire, or the nuclear reactor takes a hit and leak radiation. It's all part of the fun of the game.Currently, there are only 3 classes of ships in the game, but they have a lot of variety and in my 20 hours of gameplay, none of them were identical. Despite being in early access, it feels like a complete game and I didn't feel like anything was missing. I only experienced one crash and one audio bug.The negative point is the size of the shipyard, which is very cramped, and the game doesn't save the progress of the ship being dismantled when you leave. I was a bit disappointed with the short turn time (15 minutes), but it's an incentive for the player not to waste time being meticulous.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game and I think it's solid. Creative concept and execution. I'm not going to blather about all the good things cause there's a bunch of reviews that probably hit all of that. Just has a few flaws/issues that's I'll highlight here.1) While there's a crew to try and make the game feel less isolating, I found I ultimately didn't care about any of them merely because they talk at you rather than to you. Would have been nice if you could interact with them so you felt like you were more a part of the crew.2) There's not much left in the late game. If you want to reach level 30, you'll find yourself repeating all the same ships because there's nothing new. That part gets kinda dull. Now that's in some ways that does capture the vibe of what this job would look like but it would be nice if there was another ship or two that would appear late game to get more variety.3) I kinda wish there was more to do in the HAB? Again it feels on vibe with sleep work eat repeat. But it would have been neat to have like one "fun" diversion there.Fun experience and highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Release version review:Happy to say that they have fine-tuned many of issues I was previously having and have added story elements to the game, the game now runs smoothly and is feature complete.After playing again for tens of hours its become clear that Hardspace Shipbreaker is actually a horror game and it seriously nails the experience of working for a company that wants you dead in the name of more obscene bottom lines. Sometimes you don't even get the tools you need to properly salvage a ship and you get berated by corporate for not achieving the impossible. Once more I highly recommend the game for those with a decent PC as it is a wonderful experience and you can really get a feel for the world you are playing in.Early Access review:A bit light on content and it could use some optimization.The physics are fantastic and the game has great atmosphere.Sometimes your tool will smash an object straight into the wall you're pulling it off from causing an explosion or other damage to the object.The game would probably benefit from a bit more story like there being an underground militant union forming to overthrow LYNX or something like that.For an Early Access game I would say it's fairly solid thus far.

_childDocuments_.review: "Hi I'm Mal Reynolds... No relation to Captain Malcolm Reynolds. (But I have to admit the sound track to this game is relaxing and sounding like it came straight from the TV series Firefly.)I'm a relatively new cutter here at Lynx. Pushing near 15 hours experience.I have to say this job may seem a bit boring in the sense that it looks repetitive. But it's not. Every day, every ship, every job. Is different. Today like always I start by safely decompressing the ship then cutting the floor from under the reactor. As I cut the last support, before I could blink. WHOOSH!!! I'm sucked into space! (I forgot to actually final the input sequence to decompress the ship.) Nearly sent my knees into my shoulders, if it wasn't for the fact I upgraded my thrusters the shift before. They were the only thing that stopped me smashing into the barge below. I blame the management for putting so much pressure on us to get the job done. (We could do with a longer shift time. It's quite a challenge to finish your work order in one shift. 20-25 mins maybe.) Anyway if you like something different, something relaxing, (but still keeps you on your toes.) Then this is the game for you. Good luck out there. Think twice... And cut once. Mal out!!"

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - I like the game enough that I've gotten into the top ten on the leaderboards both times.  I have some minor changes I'd like to see but so far so good.The narrative is heavy handed but the game play itself is fun.  Although the new .4 progression takes a lot longer I've made it into the top 10 on the leaderboards both times.  One suggestion I would make is don't take all of the range upgrades on your cutting tools.  It's too easy to hit something explosive if they can reach way out there.  A long range grapple is essential though.  I feel like the difficulty is slowly being reduced over time when it doesn't need to be.  Also there is a distinct lack of a SAFE way to deal with a ship that has no working air regulators.  I think we need either a consumable or an ability to safely vent pressurized ships.

_childDocuments_.review: This game scratches an itch for me. I love the mechanics gradually becoming at the same time more difficult and easier with upgrade. I love the fact that you can choose game modes that aren't only making the game artificially longer nor gate-keeping the achievements. I love the fact that mistakes are not so punishing, while still being an incentive to do better. I love the story, how despite being about a not-so-distant future, there are many different hints that it is a critic of nowadays companies. My main issue about the story was that I felt so close to the character that at a certain point in time, I really felt oppressed by what was happening. It might also be a little too optimistic for me, but that's really a personal opinion.The only mechanic I missed was the capacity to hold on to a surface while cutting. As of now, if you hold on to a surface, whenever you cut, you have to press the button again to stick to the wall again. I stupidly died many times by pressing the wrong button just after doing a "controlled" depressurization...But that's really far fetched. Thank you Blackbird Interactive, it was a real treat!

_childDocuments_.review: The core of this game is very good. Taking apart spaceships is satisfying, and they have nailed a lot of key gameplay factors like weightiness, the 'feel' of the tools, and the core setup of sizes and distances. They got so much so right at the start.They have since let themselves down in a few apparently small, but cumulatively obnoxious ways.The dialog is poorly written and - that most egregious of gameplay sins - UNSKIPPABLE. When you should be taking apart ships, you're instead stuck there twiddling your thumbs as line after bland line of poor voice acting is read out, or stuck in your Hab waiting for someone to read out the subtitles for you. And speaking of the Hab - your room between shifts, although it's actually quite a nice apartment with a beautiful view (which doesn't fit the game's narrative) - what an absolute mess. You lunge from desk to desk with lurch after sickening lurch, instead of having free movement. The menus are inexplicably spread out across the room. It's badly designed and badly implemented. It's obvious what has happened, of course. The devs spent time and money on developing the Hab, and even though it actively makes the game worse... well, they can't just remove it and go back to the far-superior simple menu system, because they spent time and money on it! So we, the players, are made to suffer pointlessly.There's also the matter of the economy/debt. What could have been an interesting, balanced drive to work the numbers and pay off your debt is instead largely meaningless. There's no nuance - they've just whacked a big number of "debt" on you at the start of the game, and that's pretty much it. And again, it doesn't quite fit with the game narrative, because if you crunch the numbers, you'll be able to pay off your debt after about six months, and then start making massive profits and be an in-game millionaire - which is completely at odds with the "worker grunt" motif in the "story",These failures add up, and it's a shame that the devs have undermined such excellent core gameplay in this way (EDiT: I just want to say this again - they really nailed the gameplay. It feels like a job, but it never feels like a chore. It can be so satisfying to swing around in zero-G and fling a section of hull directly into its receptacle. Also just want to say that I'm playing on a pad, and while one or two controls seem like odd choices at the start, it doesn't take long for everything to click. You're almost never fighting the controls, which is great to see in a game like this.). However, the last year of development suggests not an exciting future for this game, but instead a downward spiral.At this point, with the recent price rise and failure to fix simple issues over the last year or two, I'm recommending against buying the game.But I hope I'm wrong, that the devs start to work smarter, and that I can see some positive progress that allow me to recommend this game in future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that somehow end up becoming mind numbingly boring to the point where you nearly stop breathing because of the lack of brain power required to play it. Ship variety is limited so you will find yourself breaking apart every available ship in no time. You have small scouting vessels, small research vessel, slightly larger scouting/research vessel, medium merchant ship, large merchant ship, large fuel transport ship and large cargo ship with some different flavors of design spread to 3 or 4 different in-game companies that only get referenced as ships they had once owned. The lack of loose tolerance on micro amount of scrap is absurd. It is nearly impossible to 100% a ship since the tools you use can permanently remove material from existence such as with some panels on interior ship structures that are connected to iron frames that must be separated or else you incur a penalty for incorrectly sorting these frames with the panels still attached. Sometimes you can come across incorrectly labeled panels that say they can go into the processor but will incur a penalty if you do and others that they go into the smelter but incur the same penalty if done so. No update has been put out to rectify or give options to players on any of this and it is unlikely there will ever be one.

_childDocuments_.review: The setting was more realistic than I would have liked, but the story was good and the gameplay was solid. It did a great job of making me careful about how I approached each new ship to make sure I was getting the most value from them while having the least number of "accidents." And there were plenty of ways to mess up.I do wish there was just a tiny bit more depth or breadth to this game. There aren't a lot of ship designs and a number of them are just bigger or reconfigured versions of others. The different ship systems had some promise as they required multiple steps, precision, or skillful maneuvering to dismantle, but they never got very complicated. You also only have 3 tools to dismantle the ships, so not a lot of player decisions there either especially when the cutter only really worked on specific parts of the ships.Overall it is a very relaxing game about taking apart ships in space and does a great job at that.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect too much when I saw this on sale for the summer.  I picked it up out of curiosity and a bit of trepidation regarding early access games.  What I found out is after 60 hours later, it's come to be one of my go-to games after a long day at work.  A blend of chill with the right mix of complexity, and skill required of you to be successful without the chaos of flanking gunfire or the like.  The data caches provide some idea to the world you're in, but otherwise, you're on your own floating in orbit over Earth leaving it to you to figure out how best to dismantle freighting spaceships and other peace-time vehicles.  The tutorial is enough to get you started but leaves it to you to figure out how best to proceed.  Your game, your terms, your demise.  And, watch out for the black hole of the furnace...it'll suck you in.

_childDocuments_.review: HS:SB is an amazing, relaxing experience. _childDocuments_.review: Why. Why in the world is this game as addicting as it is? You're just a wrecker. Ripping apart space ships right? Right. I am eagerly awaiting the next major update that expands the story, let alone updates that add more ships to tear apart. So far there's a limited number of ships to wreck, yet each has their own challenges. And even though some may be the same Mackrel class transport, their power cells, fuel cells or other hazards can be different or arranged in different patterns. Maybe it's pressurized? Maybe evil AI is causing trouble? There's so many different ways to tackle every ship breakdown. Do you go carefully? trying to get every last buck out of your salvage? Decompressing chambers, opening doors with control panels and such. Or go for some "Rapid Disassembly" AKA, blow it up with explosives. Cause that is an option. Just... watch out, flying debris can damage your suit, causing oxygen leaks, cracking your visor or kicking you onto another radio station.If you enjoy games where attention to detail is important then by all means try this game. If you don't like taking your time and would rather rush stuff? maybe this game isn't for you. It's about patience, taking your time and trying not to make your already substantial debt any worse. Admittedly progression can be a LITTLE slow, but this is also affected by what kind of ship you're breaking and whether or not you're using all your tools. I neglected using tethers for the longest time and now that I'm using them my salvaging speed has increased substantially. (though even doing this progression seems slow, and needs improvement or fine tuning. Though at least the DEV's are more concerned with adding more gameplay and FINISHING the game rather then balancing it at every update prior to the full launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let people complaining about the timer trick you; this game is actually quite chill. You can very comfortably take multiple shifts on the same ship and still make a profit. The timer isn't there to penalize you so much as encourage you to think on how to take ships apart quickly, methodically, and safely.Once you get good, you can take apart anything smaller than the biggest ships in one shift (if you're just going for work order objectives and not full completion). The biggest shifts are MEANT to be done over multiple ships, and it's really satisfying to watch these enormous ships get smaller and smaller as you cut them apart for everything valuable. It's like watching a big project come together; you're not expected to do it in one go, and it's immensely pleasing to watch it progress bit by bit.I'm looking forwards to how it develops. There are a couple bugs, notably objects sometimes go ballistic when you pull them off wherever they're mounted, which is a major issue when those objects are fuel tanks, and some crashes. But even as is, I give it a hearty recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is loads of fun. Physics based disassembly of spaceships - whats not to love? I miss the original pitch of "more, bigger ships and yards" which was sadly cut. I hope to one day see a 1.1 or 1.2 release with that met, or perhaps even as an affordable DLC option. The story feels like a distraction from the gameplay, although it is nice theming, and the RPG-elements feel pretty grindy, but you get past that.♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ aside, its a very zen game. Listen to music, ponder how best to get the most salvage value time efficiently, make a plan and get it done. Adapt on the fly as you need to. Success is not the key to happiness. _childDocuments_.review: Incredibly challenging and rewarding space ship dismantling simulator.You play as a debt-riddled astronaut breaking apart ships during 15 minute shifts. During a shift you have a work order that consists of objectives such as collecting electronics equipment, metal parts or reclaiming the dreaded reactor core. You do this with the use of two tools: a laser cutter and a grapple lasso (think gravity gun). You float in zero gravity using a jetpack, flying around the ship in free 6 degree of motion. Fulfill work orders and do extra work for more cash. Upgrade gear and rinse repeat.What makes the process interesting is the Newtonian gravity and the sheer physics at play. To optimize you want to work quickly but taking a ship apart carefully takes time. Slowly you start learning each ship class's intricacies and optimal workflow. For example you might cut off the floor off a passenger vessel, granting direct access to the furniture within, allowing you to simply push the seats and boxes downwards towards the reclamation barge. Or you may use the tether tool to connect multiple objects together to create a linked chain of hull panels to lead them all in one go to the nanocarbon reclaimer.The career mode has excellent pacing. However if you want to just break apart ships without concerns for resources or time limits, there's a freeplay option as well. It's great for learning the ship structure on your own time.The game supports both keyboard+mouse and controller input but I felt that controller is the best way to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game pretty early on in EA, before they added the story, the hab, or most of the ships.  I played it for a few updates, but the new ships took too long to come out, so I stopped playing, but was following it so I could try again when 1.0 came out.  I picked the game up again at the beginning of this month because I was in a mood to really just satisfyingly break down a massive ship and hope I didn't explode.  What I got when I returned was an honestly subpar and hamfisted story with unskippable cutscenes and only 2 more "brands" of ship with a few variations each.  I played for a while, then put it down once I saw 1.0 was actually coming out the same month I picked it back up again along with a progression reset.  I honestly wish I hadn't come back now.The story would have been a forgettable mess if I could skip it or have it just play in the background while I was doing the thing I came here to do, but I couldn't.  I had watched most of act 1 and a decent chunk of act 2 before I went back to waiting for 1.0, so when I started over, again, I felt like I alt+tab'd for roughly 1/3 of my whole playtime while waiting for the story to get around to letting me play the dang game.  The final kick in the pants is the ending, so...spoiler I guess?  Another issue I have is that they either cut a lot of "data drive" content or made it significantly less accessible than it was when I first bought the game.  They were stories about the ships you're breaking down and little snippets of the world outside your station and was handled very well, so I'm very disappointed that it looks like those were traded out for the terrible mess described above.In terms of gameplay, it was basically what I remembered and what I wanted from the beginning.  The only issue for me was a lot of the instability in the ships wasn't fixed.  And I suppose that they also changed the ships so that it's basically impossible to 100% a ship now because you *have* to destroy value parts (not cut points) to actually get some of the super valuable components now.  Also, I have no idea why, but they completely messed with the pressurization of my favorite ship brand (Gecko) in 1.0 to the point where, as far as I could tell, it was impossible to actually depressurize the ship in a logical way.  The breaking of ships is basically the only reason I will ever come back to this game, because it is an extremely satisfying loop.It seems like the developers really wanted you to get their story super quick with the 1.0 release, because I got through the entire thing in like 5-10 hours, where to get to the end of the story pre-1.0, it took me like 10-15.  Though it was a bit padded with grinding, it actually gave me time between BS story to actually play the game and enter a zen state where I could focus on breaking my ships down.  This time I was constantly broken out of the state so badly that I mostly quit the game to take a break every 1-2 ships so I could do something interesting without waiting for story I didn't care about at all to finish.This game was so close to a game I would play over and over again for years.  And then they shoved a story down my throat and I'm not sure I'm ever going to turn the game on again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a solid thumbs up in terms of the Primary Gameplay Loop (PGI). The story of this game is why I'm writing this review. It's not good. BUT, there are parts of the story that demonstrate how this could be better. The rest of the review contains various levels of spoilers.Example: I just experienced a post-game dialogue where the team lead communicated family and money concerns to the other team members over comms. They had a very brief interaction with some small encouragement at the end before the team lead acknowledged the commentary, thanked them, and suggested they get back to work. The above section is what the majority of the story probably should have been. I like unions, I'm happy to see the pro union approach, but "ham-fisted" sums up the delivery of this story with a depressingly nice bow. The characters are very obvious templates: the leader, the rebel, the newbie (not us), the veteran, etc. And that's not bad! That's actually a great way to get people into the flow. So what does hardspace do next? Well, it brings in an intentionally insufferable admin as the low level antagonist, along with an elusive and slightly more subtly insufferable company head which, by the way, has some unflattering art drawn that just very blatantly tries to make them look nefarious. Why is this a problem? Well, it doesn't have to be. But there's a political edge to this game, and if you want to take that route then you have to be careful. The game's depictions of the antagonists are so blunt it felt like their target audience were children. I felt like I was having this show to me as if I were 5. That can have backlash effects for one, but it's also just bad writing.Let's go back to my first example about the team talk. This is what I want to contrast. The game went for a fast climax rather than a slow burn, and I think that contradicts the style of the game. This is a relaxing slow burn kind of game, but the story feels way too fast paced for that. Things ramp up quickly until someone almost dies and then the story just ends and  That's it. I like the post game because it shows an realistic examples of what happens with unions. There's still crap to deal with, and people keep living their lives. And I wish the main game had been like this too. How about this. Instead of bringing in Hal, why not just focus on building a really sold cast? Don't even show the CEO lady. Just show us the characters, their struggles, why they're here, the problems they face, and work to get us invested. Then, the company puts in new initiatives that make strings tighter and room for error narrower. Keep pushing the requirements while docking the pay. Keep the characters talking, struggling, and growing closer. Everything, pushing and pushing, until someone says they've had enough. Then drama ensues. I like the minor twist with the newbie being a traitor, although it was moved past pretty quickly. I think you can still keep that in. Maybe only bring Hal in on the final act to act as catalyst for the climax instead of that "oh btw per your contract we own you now" catalyst. That was god awful. That's about it for now. Story is already here to stay I suspect, but I hope their next game is even better. The team has great potential. If you've read this far, give the game a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a puzzle game. A genius puzzle game disguised as a ship disassembly/debt management simulator. Nothing beats the rush of looking at the engine/thruster/reactor you've got to pull out, working out the how of it in your head, and then saying 'screw it', bum-rushing and botching the job, only to pull it off by the skin of your teeth. It's a strange endorphin rush you can't put into words.Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a zen-out game. A beautiful masterpiece of corporate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and tedious micro-tasks that has you meticulously picking apart a ship piece by piece; carefully lining up your shot into the Processor or Barge, and letting that bad boy fly with a satisfying 'pathunk'. It allows you to play at your own pace - spending hours pulling apart the same ship for maximum profit; or up the difficulty  to force you to prioritize how to best use your allotted shift time.Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a game. A great game... an underrated gem that has gone from perfectly executed but rough initial concept, to a pristinely polished gem that will give me - and I'm certain others as well - hours of play time. Multitudes of ships, multitudes of fun, multitudes of danger... and enough Spares to go around. I would solidly say this game is worth it at full price, but if you can find it on discount cheaper all the better.Don't sleep on this. You're missing out if you do.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: What I like about this game is that I don't need to be a genius to play it. I don't need to spend hours learning the mechanics. I don't need to search for tutorial videos on Youtube. I don't need to handle a hundred buttons at once, and I don't need lightning reflexes to get the job done.What I don't like (currently) is that every 10th or so gasoline or coolant tank goes completely crazy, flipping all over the place and destroying half the ship. If it's a bug, then I hope it gets fixed. If it's a feature, then I hope there will be an option to disable it.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Still way too buggy to play the Hardcore mode. And in *most* modes, if a bug kills you, you can just respawn and get right back to it with very little downside.
