_childDocuments_.review: An interesting and chilled out game that really makes you feel like a blue collar Joe grafting away in orbit.There's a good mix of skill and puzzle solving, and personally I find you can pick up and continue this game when ever you want a nice change from other games you're playing.I don't think there's anymore development of this game going on at the moment, which is fine as it works as is, but personally I'd like to see VR implementation, that'd be cool
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: !!!Spoiler Alert!!!this is your spoiler alert, you've been warned.Played the game when it first came out. loved everything about it; the music, the setting, the atmosphere, everything felt great and immersive. Gameplay felt great, with the right tough of puzzle solving, navigation and money management. I took pride in the fact that my assignments were completed with caution, surgical precision ZERO deaths. There were a few close calls but i could safely say in the context of the plot, i was the original shipbreaker that Lynx hired on and not a spare clone...Then an update came out that added in a new bit of information after the intro that showed your transfer from earth to the Space port you'd be working at...They added an "on-boarding" video to better immerse the player into this environment of "yes, this is a valid job in the year 3129 (or whatever)". then after that they kill your character to extract the bio material needed to clone you... so right out the gate, you're a clone...This might not seem like a big deal to others but it kinda disconnected me from the character's well-being and left a bitter taste in my mouth. I won't get into details of ethics and crap and how this is supposed demonstrate the dystopian Future filled with corrupt companies, but this really bothered me on an existential level and disconnected me from caring at all about my progress in the game and whether i did my job flawlessly or not.and don't get me started on the "anti-corporation/union uprising" story that's literally forced into your lap now. All i wanted was a game where i break apart ships and now have to worry about whether or not i'm the real me or whether some co-worker i don't care about who's trying to get me into trouble with the company i'm working with because they're corrupt. And no, the answer to this problem isn't "free play" because there's no sense of progression or accomplishment other than "you done did good". Adding in a "legacy mode" would be beneficial to the game as it would allow player who liked the pre-release gameplay to enjoy that rather than be forced to sit though this story's bs. Gameplay is still fun. Just personally wish the devs didn't add that extra crap in...

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot I like about this game, but the progression systems feel extremely unrewarding, and really make no sense to me. Most of the upgrades feel like they don't really add anything to the game, and there aren't enough interesting tools in this game to unlock to really make it feel like you're getting anywhere with it. The only real upgrade you feel in this game is the oxygen. Your tools never get any more interesting. They just increase in usable distance and durability. Really? That's it? In a fully deconstructable environment we only get the same linear upgrades to usable distance? I bought this game in early access on the premise that there would be more added to the gameplay beyond more ships, but this is the same game I played a couple of years back. Nothing has really been added that makes the actual process of taking ships apart more fun. Grav boots, mini thrusters, remote hacking tools (for the small amount of interactibles), more heavy duty cutters, or even a thermite launcher or something that lets you hit the weak points of a structure with less tedium. For how cool the actual setting is; it's so severely underutilized.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: So good. I honestly cannot recommend this game enough, you gotta try it. Story's decent, albeit unskippable and long winded at points, kept me interested and pulled in even though I just really wanted to salvage. Final conclusion to the story is phenomenal and makes me feel all warm and fuzzy.It's about 20 hours for one playthrough, probably a bit longer on your first though since you'll likely blow up a few ships getting the hang of it. The progression is absolutely amazing and kept me wanting to get salvage goals for new upgrades and I LOVE how this game rewards patience and being careful. It's like a physics puzzle game at times trying to get everything safe to salvage and it feels so good being methodical and getting mini me stickers every ship (still never bother with the lights, just leave em on, same with wires).Just such a cozy game that just makes you want to relax and work off some debt the old fashioned way. It's just a grindless grind full of comforting but upbeat music and forced labor! What more could a man need?!

_childDocuments_.review: Pull apart decomissioned space ships for salvage in order to repay your crippling debt to Earth's ruling giga-corporation!Choose a ship to be delivered to your assigned orbital salvage bay and get to work. Fly around with your jetpack in zero-g, six-degrees-of-freedom style. Open up the ship, find and cut the attachments between the various pieces, and grapple-gun the bits into the Processor, Furnace, or Barge as appropriate. You face ever more structurally and mechanically complex ships as you qualify for higher ranks. Deal with fuel/coolant pipes which can rupture, electrical equipment that arcs when damaged, and of course there's always explosive decompression! Try to keep everything intact as possible to maximize value.And of course, time is money. Each shift you work, you're being docked interest, rent for your living quarters and gear, and you gotta pay for all the thruster fuel, oxygen, and the other supplies you need to get the job done.Anyway as bleak as the backstory is, the game is very fun and addictive. Learning and improving your efficiency gives the same type of satisfaction as Viscera Cleanup Detail. If you like that sort of manual-labor-simulator like I do, then you'll like this one too.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game; I played through early access, just completed the campaign of the completed game, and I will play more. _childDocuments_.review: The most fun you can have as a debt slave laborer in a cyberpunk dystopia.  There's no neon aesthetic because you're on an industrial space station as a captive labor force so there's no one to advertise to.  Instead you've got a great sorta Homeworld looking visual style that also kinda reminds me of the anime Planetes.  The story is a pretty interesting one about trying to better your circumstances when you're all but legally enslaved by a corporation who can clone and replace you at their discretion, but the gameplay is probably the biggest draw.  You fly around your salvage bay with full 3D movement in Zero G.  Basically a space sim, but you're just an astronaut salvaging ships.  You can cut holes in basically anything with the right tools, but cutting the ships are of course full of valuable and potentially dangerous components that cutting into could destroy, so you need to learn the layouts and hazards of every model and adapt on the fly.  Things can so sideways with just a moment's carelessness... but taking too long can result in you not generating enough profit to cover your expenses, which of course you're entirely responsible for covering under your contract with Lynx Corporation.  It's hard to describe the gameplay without just showing footage.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:  I'm leaving this as thumbs up, but I do want to say that I am pretty disappointed with the 1.0 release.  When this game first appeared in early access I was absolutely enamored with the gameplay loop, the setting, the music, everything that it had to offer was exactly up my alley and it made me super excited for it's development.  What I was most excited about was the addition of more gameplay content, more ships and tools, game modes, etc.  Here we are a couple years later at 1.0 and what do we have?  A couple more ships, one new tool (explosive charges), one additional game mode (R.A.C.E), a more interactive HAB, and... a plot.  Essentially a fully voiced visual novel that plays while you break ships.  You don't even really interact with it, it's just... there.   I would have been excited to have weaver giving me historical info on each of the ships that I was taking apart, where they've been and why they're being broken down.  Instead we get Weaver and some other people talking about unions and the exploitative nature of corporations and how to make the world a better place.  Don't get me wrong, these are important concepts that need to be talked about, but I really feel like they could have accomplished this without beating us over the head with it.  I also wished they would have spent their time and money on expanding the core gameplay and left out most of the voice acting, and have the story telling done in more subtle ways, easter eggs for the player to find.  I still love this game and I hope they continue to create content for it in the form of new ships to break down and new ways to do so, and I would be happy to pay for that in DLC form.  Unfortunately, since their focus is turning to consoles, I doubt this will ever happen. As it is right now, I would say it's still worth a buy, but only when/if they put it on sale.ORIGINAL REVIEW:Alright Cutter, listen up.  You see that number up there?  That great big red one with the minus sign in front and all those zeroes at the end of it? A lot of people will tell you that it's your "debt" or "how much you owe" to Lynx, and that you signed your life away the day that you agreed to become a shipbreaker.  But you know what?  Those folks ain't never been cutters, and probably never will be.  They won't ever get to experience the joy that is slicing an aluminum panel in twain, or that funny tickling sensation of waking up in a new clone job because you forgot to check for the fuel line behind that aluminum panel.  They'll never feel elated like when you send a 10kg chunk of nanocarbon into the processor, nor will they get to feel that special kind of sadness when your chunk of nanocarbon somehow misses the processor and winds up in the furnace. Or like that one time, when you pulled all the panels off of that class 2 reactor, grabbed it with your grapple gun and chucked it off towards the barge, only to watch it bounce off the side and off into space before that lovely purple explosion... actually, let's not talk about that.  My point, Cutter, is that the great big number that people say is bad really ain't so bad at all.  Heck, it's the whole reason that you get to experience all of these things every day.  Maybe show a little gratitude to Lynx for that great big number.  Think of it as all the time you get to spend cutting up these ships and living the best life there is out here.  I'll see you tomorrow, Cutter.  Oh, and try to remember to use the darned maintenance key before you start pulling the thrusters. We'll have less pieces to clean up that way. Weaver out.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay itself is GREAT. It's super relaxing to take all kinds of spaceship apart in your own way, sort them out and clean your dock. The atmosphere is fantastic: relaxing music, great view, colorful and detailed. There's a few options to make the game more laid-back (no oxygen usage, no shift timer) and through it's development the gameplay improved by fixing bugs (although some persistent ones can still ruin your experience, like decompression) and adding variations of a total of 4 ships. The future appeared bright with so many options to add: new ships, different tools, various ways of handling problems, you name it. Until...Devs threw all their promising progress out the window in favor of the narrative. Does "black lesbian fighting oppressive corporate capitalism through a socialist organization" sound like any recent cultural phenomenon to you? That's what the game is about now.Because of this change, the entire purpose of the game changed. No longer are you the "blue-collar spaceship salvager", instead you are an npc to someone else's story, literally grinding the same 4 ships over and over to progress a boring and predictable narrative. There's no opting out of it. No skipping dialogue. Break ship, get level, hear story, repeat. There's no incentive anymore. And I tried. Maybe it would get better (yes, sunken cost fallacy). But it's all so predictable. Oppression by greedy megacorp, workers rise up, revolution, good times for everyone. Doesn't matter what you do, just follow along."Just play free-play mode"... Is as weak-sauce an argument as saying "use mods" when potentially good games are bad because of dev choices. People were sold a different game, they changed it and I would not buy it in it's current form because it's lacking in content.Oh and don't get your hopes up for new content. Devs have literally posted that adding new content is "too hard" and they'd rather focus on porting to XBOX and PS5. Check out the flaming pile of dung that is the Community Discussion FAQ. No workshop, mods, new content or co-op. Just reasons why they coulda-shoulda-woulda but didn't.Do not buy. Massive disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though it's in early access, this game already has a high degree of polish on its core mechanics. the people over at Blackbird Interactive have done an incredible job on the core mechanics, and are hard at work developing the story to go along with those mechanics.Even without a finished story, however, it provides an excellent gameplay experience. Id totally recommend this game to someone looking for something to sit back and relax with between study breaks, or just looking to kill a little time. play a couple of shifts, watch the debt counter go down, maybe learn something about how to strip a ship faster, and apply it on your next shift. this is a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game awhile and not watching any videos or tutorials, I can say it was pretty new user friendly.  Especially for being an early release.  I highly recommend this game to people that like chill, low anxiety games. I would build a new PC to play this game in 4k. My new favorite game. 11/10Technical Jargon:     The graphics are beautiful. This is such a chill game, sometimes I just float around, and set off ship wide chain reactions for S&G.  I play on a RX 590 8g O.C.  I get 60 FPS in 1080p, 45 in 1440.  This game will use all 8g of video mem.  It is GPU intensive.  That being said, this game is not a destruction\sandbox game. If you purposely create catastrophic events, you will see large FPS drops.  The new UI updates for >1080p look good. Gameplay:    I am currently Rank 7, Ship tier 5.  Seriously though, after playing a few rounds, I was already pulling in 1.3 mill a day.  The "timer" is nothing more than a day clock.  When the day ends, you go back to the HAB, and have the choice of continuing on that ship, or starting a new one.  Daily fees come in at under 500k, and you have the option to buy equipment as you go, reducing your daily costs.  I like how the ship systems are networked, and you have to figure out a system of disabling each without causing too much damage.  I'm looking forward to more ship systems, and difficulty.  My max haul so far is 5.1m.  Ten times the daily fees. I have already worked off over 50m of my debt. I'm ready for Stations.Negatives:     My only slight issue is the amount of tethers I waste from parts rotating too much and breaking line of sight.

_childDocuments_.review: Game runs very well for an early access title, only had 1 crash in 34 hours so far.  Starts off easy enough but as you progress through the levels the ship dismantling becomes reasonably more challenging.  My only gripe is when you're being delicate about plucking a fuel or coolant tank from the ship and for no good reason it instantly decides to travel at mach 10 into the hull exploding everything around it.  Recommend starting a mission with detaching these so if it all goes wrong you can start over.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Breaking ships is fun, it's satisfying, and the progression doesn't feel grindy.  This game really is enjoyable, and it's a game for people who like to chase progression and achievement, where they can tune out the world and focus on a job, and even relax.  There's catharsis to it.Cons: The new storyline the devs introduced late into development seems to have taken away too much of the time and focus of what the game seems to have been originally envisioned to be back when I bought it in EA.Before the storyline was introduced, progression was more grindy, but not overly so.  Each of the 30 certificate ranks mattered, and you would work hard to unlock them to get access to much-needed upgrades. Now, you reach about certification level 18, and that's it. There's nothing more to look forward to. No new ships, no new variants, nothing.  Just another 10 or so certification ranks that give you nothing.But they have stickers now!  That's something!The world building was done through abandoned data drives full of mission logs, personal messages, and historical recordings, left by the people who once called home the ship you're tearing apart for salvage.There used to be a decent amount of puzzle-solving involved with more complicated ships, requiring specific buttons to be pushed and keys to be turned in specific orders to safely salvage a ship.  Much of it is still there, but it's been dumbed down and simplified.The game also has the bones and the structure to essentially add onto it endlessly, with new ship types and variants, new world-building events that introduce new challenges and hazards (e.g. like the "ghost ships"), new puzzles and challenges to overcome as we become a more and more skilled and experienced shipbreaker.But unfortunately the devs have already said that the game, for them, is done.  It's finished.  They said they have no plans for more content, and no more building on top of the foundation they've created.Which is a shame, since the game in it's current state, with the certification system now almost too easy, with the new storyline that seems to railroad you quickly to a conclusion in a game where part of the experience was that there really was no real end, and a progression system where you have everything unlocked and have seen all there is to see 2/3 of the way through - it leaves the game feeling hollow and a shell of what it could have been.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a core set of mechanics to play from. Very simple to understand and master. The same goes with the objective of the game. Very simple, always the same. However the fun is in that you can go about doing the job however you want. Yes you're always cutting a ship apart, but there are different sizes, different hazards, and endless ways to cut a ship up. Just mindless fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Oh yeah.  This one gets into your head and gets you feeling - in a good way - like a working stiff working a hard job in a weird place and it makes it satisfying when things work and frustrating when they don't and magical when you work out how to do things in just the right way to get them sorted properly.  Well worth the money.I could suggest a few UI tweaks - let the conversations play out in the shipyard rather than forcing you to listen to them back in the cabin where you can't DO anything for a start - but, really, even with the UI as-is it's a lovely game and great fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: I do not like this game. It's physics ♥♥♥♥ up any time I try to do much, it flat out doesn't tell you how to decompress compartments without atmospheric regulators, and has killed me over and over again for doing what it said. Or because the physics screwed up and I touched a wall that was moving at a single meter per second and the universe decided I needed to have my organs spread across the star system.I was looking for a calm casual gaming experience, and instead I'm met with broken physics and just flat out stupid engineering designs. Who the ♥♥♥♥ makes a thruster that has to be set on fire to be shut off? Like, I get that it's supposed to be forced adversity on the player's part, but it's a stupid design and is so unintuitive because up TO that point, the game make sure there is a safe way for everything, that I had to look up how to do the thruster because SETTING IT ON ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ FIRE DELIBERATELY was not what I was expecting the game to... Well, expect.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) - If you enjoy a bit of a puzzle mixed in with your simulator type games, I think you'll enjoy it!The tutorial mission gives you the basics, but not everything.  There's a sense of accomplishment when you figure out something for yourself, or find an easier way to crack a ship open.  I don't want to give you any hints save one...  Really look at what you're doing at any given point...scanner, ship environment, how things fit together...REALLY LOOK at things.  I can say that on day 5, I was still finding things that I didn't know existed.  It's not as casually put together as it appears.  A lot of thought went into the ships and how you take it apart.  There's also more than one way to get it done.  Pros:  -A sense of mass.  When you move objects, you really feel like you're moving some heavy stuff around-Some subtle dark humor in there.  Take time to read the warnings and other things you find-Logical progression of difficulty on the ship designs, even if the exteriors seem somewhat limited at the moment-15 minute sessions (You'll see this under the Cons too, but I'll explain there)-You feel pretty awesome ripping these ships apartCons:-Not all of the things are explained.  Quick path to victory, slower path to mastery-Some glitches with the Barge collection.  Avoid high-speed deposits (you'll get it later)-15 minute timer ( I promised and explanation, and here it comes..)15 minute timer...That's how long your shift is.  Each shift costs you money, so you'll want to target enough salvage to pay for your shift AND make a profit.  The frustrating bit is that you can be right in the middle of a complicated extraction and have time run out.  On the plus side, you get to pick up where you left off next shift.  It's gonna cost you another fee though.   Some have really had a bad time of this, but I think it adds a bit of prioritization to it.  You have to think about what you're doing, in what order, and adds a bit of complexity to being profitable.  All in all, I've had a great time with this so far and I've put in just over 90 hours at the time of this review.  Go for it, you probably haven't played anything like it.

_childDocuments_.review: This games has one serious problem with it, a lack of new content.Otherwise it's a good game. If I wanted to feel like I was in an ACTUAL dystopian future setting where I made money only to never see any progress going anywhere with my efforts, then this is the game that does it right.It's a real shame too, since I think with a lot more ships, interesting gadgets, different space disassembly plants to go, and more it would be a lot less boring and redundant. I mean, that's kinda apart of the point, but this is more akin to mowing your lawn than it is anything else. Some love to, others hate to, but at least you can get outside and enjoy the smell of a fresh cut lawn after your done. Here, we have nothing.There is no reward that's decent, worthwhile, nothing of value. And even if that was apart of the gameplay loop, the problem is the ships we deal with are just the same old ones we have already for the last 50 breakdowns. We need more, there HAS to be more in space other than just these dopey things floating around! RIGHT!So ya, if you enjoy mowing your lawn, but not smelling it after your done, this is the game for you. Enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Even right out of the gate in early access, this game has definite potential, and there's already enough content for some satisfying game time for the price.It's a lot of fun identifying cut-points and how the ship is put together, and forming a strategy to take it apart as quickly as possible. Time is money, after all.I hope the devs seriously explore the co-op potential of the game, because I can already see that being a lot of fun. There's so many little things can be cut, pulled off, salvaged, that there's plenty of work that could be divvied up between 2-3 people. In fact, I think having something like 4 player co-op for much larger ships could be fantastic.Cons? I think there's too many 'bars' to keep in check. You only have about 15 minutes per work shift, and you have to manage oxygen, jetpack fuel, tethers, AND health. I suggest either drop the fuel or the oxygen, because having to worry about both on top of everything else and the overall time limit is a bit much. Sure, you can sometimes find oxygen or fuel canisters inside ships to save you time, but it isn't guaranteed.

_childDocuments_.review: I refunded the game.It was a hard choice, because I really like the idea. I had about 30-45fps at the start (which I was happy with), but as soon as I got a full ship in the tutorial I was down to 15fps (on a pc that runs fallout4 all on ultimate at steady 60fps). I really enjoyed the little gameplay I had time for in the refund period, but I felt huge pressure to assess how the game ran before time was up, and the game seemed to be fighting me on that one. Having to sit through cut-scenes and actually start the tutorial and go through initial steps before I could even access the options screen - that's not good. In the limited time available to make a choice, I need to get straight in to it.The download size is small (less than 2GB iirc) so it doesn't have huge textures, and yet "texture size" is the only real graphics option. This doesn't make sense guys: I don't think there are many people who have less than 2GB video memory, and you're game isn't all texture, so I don't think that option is helping anyone (it certainly made no difference to my fps). If I could have turned off some of the other things, maybe I would have found a level I was happy with. _childDocuments_.review: Is this game fun.........OMG its addictive and I love it, yea its early access and when I started playing there was only 2 ships but its since been updated to have multiple ships from small passenger/cargo ships to medium sized and large passenger/freighters and it also includes an exploration vessel. Small ships are pretty straight forward in terms of stripping out the power core and engines then unzipping the hull plates from the ships frame to larger more complex ships which takes a bit of time to strip systems away from the explosive core in order to get to it and 'salvage' it before an explosion. Its set in an orbital breakers yard and your the agent assigned to dismantle the ship which goes towards paying off and astronomically large dept. Because its an orbital installation it means your in zero G, so that means you get all the mind boggling fun and dizziness inducing disorientation that comes with it when your not keeping track of which way up you are.The only thing I'd like to see is large to massive sized ships where the internal gravity is still functioning and you have to disable systems in order to start demolition.I you love space games, Home world style graphics/art and a back water style sound track, you will love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be equal parts relaxing or stressful, depending on your settings (e.g.: you can disable oxygen drain and time limit). _childDocuments_.review: Firstly, as I have to dip in and out of games I tend not to play online multiplayer titles. Hardspace Shipbreaker is perfect for bite-size play or long binge. The shifts are 15 minutes long so nice for allowing you to choose your play length.The game play itself is excellent for an early access. Many people have commented how surprisingly engaging deconstructing a spaceship is. Who would have thought un-building something cold be so addictive?! Having to consider the random state of systems like fuel and compartment pressurisation adds a nice amount of challenge and allows you to develop your own best practice procedures. Some missteps can cause injury, equipment damage and of course your swift demise.There are many ways to go about taking these tubs apart. The shopping list of parts you're given each shift by your thoughtful employer mixes things up even more.Hopefully in future updates, saving between shifts when you are still working the same ship will be possible. Currently exiting the game clears your bay, forcing you to complete a ship breakdown before exiting.Earning your upgrades and a steady progression through more complex ship builds provides a nice sense of achievement and allows a steady learning curve. The free-play option is nice for exploring your tools and the ships in your own time and without worrying about oxygen and other supplies.This is already a great game and as far as I know quite unique. It's well worth a try if the images, video and other reviews interest you.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Truth be told, this game is early access at its worse. With one update a year, for a game 2 years in "development", to have this lacking amount of content, shows that the game is more of a side project more than anything.While there's over a dozen ships to salvage, they're all the same layout of 4 classes of ships. Once you have a vague idea of how each ship class can be broken down, you'll just be going through the motions rather than actually feeling like you're solving a puzzle. That is, assuming, a well known glitch doesn't vaporize your ship within seconds of starting. A rare occurrence, but an infuriating one nonetheless.As for the story, you get dragged into a character's antics without any say on the matter and everyone suffers for it. Politics aside, the character in question is meant to feel friendly and sympathetic, but comes off more naive to the point of annoyance. The other characters even call her out on provoking the villain of the story. Speaking of which...As for Lynx Corp, it's gone from a faceless, ever present entity that can get a few chuckles from how phoned in its corporate attitude is, to a Saturday morning cartoon villain, complete with a sneering CEO and dramatic music for effect. tl;dr: story feels thrown out there just to say it has a story. 2 years for this half baked plot isn't worth the wait.If you can get it on sale, try it. be warned, it'll get stale pretty fast. There is no endgame to strive towards and after this long, it may not be worth the wait.

_childDocuments_.review: I grudgingly recommend this game, solely due to the fact that its central premise - breaking apart ships - remains fun. It's a strangely meditative, problem-solving game, that unfortunately falls far short of what it could have been. The game will throw you a story; ham-fisted, poorly told, and absolutely without any player interaction.  At the end, the impression that stuck with me, is of a game that was pushed out the door by a team that is already working on its next game. It's fine for what it is, but a shame for what it is not: A little bit more work could have produced a few more ships and variants, player records, a count of shifts working this salvage, a real tutorial, some sort of efficiency measure, something  to buy with all this money, salvaging in the earth's shade, maybe real customization for your pod/suit, some real choices when buying upgrades, and maybe some ability to interact with the story. Sadly, none of that is here

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game. For me, it has the potential to be "the one" game I always wanted to play because I love space-related games with a creative bone in them. Currently, I would say this game is exactly about 15 hours of playtime before you get a little bored with the content, although it is early access and issues with the game are not too major not to change them later in the development. So, the superb stuff is the aesthetic, the audio, the lore, and the physical size of the game (it is 3GB only!). I guess other people open up each topic more, but I don't really want to. Instead, I will leave my criticism.Although many complain about having a 15-minute timer for a single shift, I don't find it that much disturbing. It is there to push people into dismantling the ship for the most expensive things first and deciding if you want to come and scrap more later. You can go on a second, on a third shift, but you will lose about 500K each time. The choice is made by the player: I never went negative from a single shift, and towards the end-game, I don't do a one-time-only shift. Although, 15 minutes could be extended to 20 minutes, and the community might find this more acceptable. The amount of content in the game could be put on a scale from 0 to 10 as 6. There are plenty of ships, but they do get repetitive after you have figured out the go-to scheme. Currently, the game doesn't offer any hacking games, lose-or-lose-harder decisions, no passive or active hazzards inside a ship that the player hasn't created, and no really massive ships that are like a maze. I wish the game would have just more content right now, but I guess not.Speaking of content, there is a wide range of mechanics you can master inside the game! I really like hopping with the grappler, and I now use tethers quite differently from the beginning of the game. I enjoy the possibility to master the game, and this game definitely provides this feeling. But one of the reasons I won't suggest getting the game right now is bugs and optimization. The situation isn't that bad, and the game isn't fast-paced, meaning FPS drops are not impacting the game as much, but stuff can get better. Graphics are on-point, but I do feel like Unity Engine just dies a little from all the physics going on, especially while something is exploding. Yet the game still runs fine and looks quite amazing for 3 damn GigaBytes. To sum up,The game is very good and is enjoyable right now, but it needs the love and attention of the developers. Everything can be ironed-out with feedback from the community. I feel the game having all the possibilities in the world to be not only just better, but having a sea of additional content coming and coming (especially with mod support and with a strong community communication).Worth a buy, but maybe a little bit later. Definitely deserves a spot in a wishlist!

_childDocuments_.review: The main gameplay mechanics are a lot of fun, but can't recommend the game at the moment for two reasons:1) The performance is awful. On a Ryzen 5 2600, 16 GB RAM and a GeForce RTX 3060 it takes around 10 minutes to even get to the main menu, and several minutes on any consequent loading screen. In-game FPS fluctuates between 20-60 FPS which makes aiming quite annoying. There is some (non-configurable) mouse acceleration which is apparently tied to the FPS and as a result the aiming is unpredictable and all around the place.2) The hab UI is very poor, reminiscent of 90s FMV adventure games and not in any good way. _childDocuments_.review: Shipbreaker is one of the most satisfying, fascinating games I've ever played. It can be incredibly zen meticulously removing all the computers or furniture or whatever your current work order says. It can also be incredibly tense and exciting. There's enough challenge to force you to be careful while cutting the ship apart, and each piece of the ship requires a slightly different procedure. It's a unique, fun idea in a sea of copycat games. Almost a new genre of game. I'm excited to see new ships get made.The simulation is just complex enough to be really Fun*. If you cut into a pressurized room you can have explosive decompression. There are cut points protected by ceramic coating, but you can break it off by throwing something at it, which allows you to cut the cut point, but don't accidentally hit a coolant line (I blew myself up that way lol). If you cut into the wrong wall, you could hit a computer terminal which sparks and the sparks carry along something metal nearby and damage a fuel line which causes a small explosion that damages a coolant line which makes the reactor start to melt down. If a reactor is melting down you better hope that you've removed enough of the superstructure that you have a big enough hole to remove the reactor and get it onto the barge before it melts down and you get a big, colorful explosion. It can be infuriating to lose 15 minutes of progress and all that money, but my god the explosions in this game are good.There is, of course, a sandbox mode for people who don't want the stress of having to worry about the budget or the 15 minute shifts in Career mode. Meticulously take apart every piece of a ship with no time pressure, or find the fuel tanks and throw them at strategic points on the ship to your heart's content. Some of us want it to be a Game, with constraints and challenges, but it can also just be a Simulator that you interact with.I give it 10 out of 10 deadly sparking computers.*Fun as in it takes a lot of time to learn, but it feels worth it

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this review first by saying that this is a really good game, and given the Devs continue to fix it, I will be happy to change this review. However, in its current state, it is not something I can recommend to the person sifting through reviews trying to figure out if they'd like this game. Hard crashes come every two or three hours, without rhyme or reason. The same visual bug appears every time I resume a salvage operation, although it is fixed by doing a 360 rotation, oddly enough. While these are all minor inconveniences, the real issues lie in the gameplay itself. You can be in the process of stripping the outer hull off of a ship, and without even having one in sight, or nearby, you can randomly rupture a coolant pipe, resulting in a reactor meltdown before it's time to pull it out safely. Same things happen to fuel pipes, but you can mitigate this by using the utility keys in the reactor console. The same cannot be said for the coolant pipes, because coolant must be flowing to the reactor until you're ready to remove it. It's unfortunate because the random nature of this ruins the mechanic of being aware of what you're cutting and what's behind it. It feels like even though you're aware of the danger, you can still get punished randomly, with no mechanic to prevent this.Pressurization is another mess in this game. Without using an airlock, you can explosively decompress a ship if you don't depressurize it properly from inside. Just use the atmosphere regulator. Easy enough, right? Wrong. Every cabin has it's own unique pressure, and with no airlocks between interior cabins, there will always be rapid decompression when opening doors. So, even if you play the smart play, and void the largest interior, before opening the smaller ones, you still run the risk of a bag of chips whipping out of an airlock and killing you. This is of course, a much more merciful outcome than the random explosive decompression that occurs. And by explosive, I mean destroying the compartment in question, and more than likely the nearby compartments, yourself, and killing your desire to continue playing.Next up, something more personal annoyance based on design choices. If you're unaware to how the scrapping gameplay goes down, imagine the ship in the middle of the letter U. On either sides of the U, near the base, are the furnaces, and beside those, moving towards the open end, are the reprocessors. Both of these openings have a suction mechanic when nearby to help draw in the scraps. Basic metals go in the furnace, and carbon based products in the reprocessors. About 90% of a ships hull will go in the reprocessor, and about 90% of the interior structures (walls, floors) will go in the furnace. The problem arises when trying to move the outer portions of the outer hull past the furnace, and into the reprocessor. Even with 4 tethers pulling it as far away from the furnace, without running into the ship, removing the rear section of the outer hull is difficult as it can often get sucked into furnace. A smaller annoyance is the equipment durability. Repair kits can only be bought in mission, but equipment can only be repaired out of mission. So if you forget to buy repair kits, or you forget to repair your equipment, you're screwed until you can get in/out of a job to do what you need. With equipment durability offering nothing other than a broken cutter cutting slower, it's just an annoying mechanic that's not essential for gameplay.At the end of the day, these bugs aren't frequent, but they're often enough they can make enjoying the game difficult. I hope that sooner, rather than later, I have a reason to change this review, but at this time, there are design choices and bugs that need fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: It does what it says on the tin. If you're a fan of those "oddly satisfying" videos this game may well be for you!Some teething issues, but that's what early access is for. The game is very basic at the moment but it's not a plot driven game. You pick a ship and get 15 minutes per shift to break it down. You can use multiple shifts to do it, but each shift incurs a rental fee; not really much of a penalty. There's also a free play mode to skip that.Your cutter can only do softer metals, so you have to plan around the stronger stuff. There is an upgrade way down the tree to cut through anything, but getting to that point will take a while in career mode. The ships are also packed full of explosive or sparky stuff that you don't react well to, so be careful when cutting around tanks or pipes!As mentioned, there's a certain satisfaction when you pause for a moment and just see a skeletal structure after you've torn the panels off a ship and hurled them into the processor bins. The bigger ships are much trickier, but I find the little ones (mackerels) perfectly sized for jumping in and quickly stripping down in a shift for a quick gameplay fix. Hopefully the devs integrate all the feedback in the discussion area, but as-is the game's a great time sink.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Don't buy this even when it's out of EA. The devs have no clue what they are doing. They should have launched the game as complete when it went into EA. It was a much more fun game then and the few QL changes they made are the only good updates.This game is very pretty. The graphics alone are enough to make you drool. I have changed my view on this game otherwise sadly. I don't honestly think this game is worth anyones time. Countless issues pop up with every update, and the number of bugs they fix seem to only be really small stupid things like a minor visual glitch instead of game breaking bugs. I used to have quite a bit of fun with this game when it first came out, but now with all of the changes it's hardly the same game. The HUD when ship breaking is absolute trash. The old system had timers on your oxygen so you could actually time when you needed to go back to the hub and refill but now it's just some obscure bar with no good indication of fill level. Their story aspect is boring and stupid as well. But I can deal with the HUD being hard to read, that's fine. The real issue... what in the ♥♥♥♥ is the terminal UI change? Holy hell is it ugly as hell and super painful to even look at for more than a few seconds. Then, with the most recent update (Act II), they have now split up the terminal into several "interactable" spots around the hab. So cool, we can now move around a space in order to do stuff... that's cool, right? It's a glorified point and click interaction with long and weird camera shifts to get around the room, and it's not even a point and click, it's just click. It's not easy to use, and just makes it even harder to repair you gear, upgrade gear, check messages etc. . I really feel like this dev team has just said ♥♥♥♥ it to what worked in the past, we need to be new every update to keep attention and let me tell you, it's not keeping anyones attention.The new Javelin class ships are super cool to look at, but that's about it. There are so many problems with this new ship that it is just too hard to actually make use of them. If you want to disconnect the parts of the ship, you have to destroy other parts such as the air locks because the outer hull is solid rings instead of segmented panels like ALL of the other ships. The air locks get stuck between the outer hull parts that need to go to the processor, and the inner living spaces that need to go to the furnace. So say goodbye to using the airlocks and sending them into the barge. So many things are attached in unexpected ways, that you literally wont even see the attachment, because there isn't a physical one. The big fuel tanks in the middle of these new ships are connected via KSP's magic quantum struts that you can't see. You have to cut up areas of the ship that make no sense, just to get it loose from the rest of the ship that it isn't physically in contact with. No it's not just getting stuck, it is literally anchored to parts with out a physical anchor.  My other gripe is about the new demo charges. Why in the hell, do they have the power of an atomic bomb? Just place one of these tiny, 5inx5in pads on the ship, detonate, and send the ENTIRE ship flying into the damn furnace. I understand it's space and they should have a little push, but these things can literally fling the whole ship from one side of the bay to the other and ruin your salvaging. I personally didn't have a problem with the laser cutter chopping up the hull pieces. I was smart enough to not just willy nilly cut the ♥♥♥♥ out of a ship which I feel like is part of this games angle. Being smart with your cuts, so you don't destroy the ship but can salvage it. So making the laser ONLY a lvl 1 cut, and demanding the use of the det charges is horrible. I like the charges, they are very cool and I enjoy using them. But with the force they apply, it's worthless to me. I don't know if I will put much more time into this game now. If I have to be using these charges on the internal parts of ships... I wont play it more than a few more hours, if any at all. This game was so much fun before the det charges were added and they may just have single handedly ruined the game for me. This game is still very cool, and beautiful. I love the new Javelin because it looks really cool and who doesn't like new free content? But it's kind of unplayable for me. Maybe these are super specific issues that someone else has a solution to, but I have yet to find one. I have tried putting the det charges in opposing directions to fight the force of eachother to little success. Since they are sequential, and there (as far as I know) isn't a simultaneous detonation option, you can't fight the pushing they do. The ship will still be flung around. I'm one of those people that want to salvage everything, and forcing us into a corner where we HAVE to blow up something, or break tons of stuff just to get one other item isn't a fun thing. I have mastered all of the other ships. I can get 100% scrap all of the other ships with almost no loss of valuable material. I can even get the damn reactors out of the giant Geckos with out any kind of reactor issue and that's a chore. I'll leave this as recommended because I do like this game a lot and it is very pretty. But the new changes have ruined many of the things I liked so much about this game.New Update to game as of 5/7/2021:Doesn't look like any of the weird issues have been fixed, just more added. The game now crashes rather frequently on the first cut you do on a ship so that's nice. They have added a new 20 cert levels, removed the objectives for collecting certain things in the certs and work orders are non-existent. So what has this update done?1. Dumbed down the entire game. They removed the specifics in favor of a really generic percentage of ship salvaged (which doesn't actually show you a percentage).2. Dumbed down the HUD. There are no longer numbers for health, O2, or fuel, there's just some obscure bar that drains which is totally better than seeing an actual number on how much you have of those... The timer on your shift is now obscure and hard to notice at first and is kind of hard to actually read. 3. Added, from what I can tell at cert 8, 1 new type of ship.4. Spread out the progression to extend play time, aka, more grinding to get to the same spot as before.5. Increased the max debt while making it seemingly harder to money.6. Released about 4 campaign driven events (just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue that doesn't change anything about how you play).7. Introduced a bug where pieces of the ship will just not move no matter how many tethers are on it. 8. Changed the barge, furnace, and the processor to be turned off when you enter the yard every time. This sounds cool since you get to see the really cool barge start up sequence and giant puffs of blue/red smoke come out of the holes, but in reality it just causes tons of lag and weird issues. You have to wait about 15 seconds before the barge can be used so if you throw something down there, make sure you watch it and see that it doesn't hop back out.9. Screwed up the way the barge handles items it doesn't want. Say you put a reactor cap in the barge and it had a shield still on it, well, that shield is now one with the barge. Since the barge is now a volume box instead of just a snapping grid, things get stuck under the top level of it if it doesn't score them.

_childDocuments_.review: That was basically my original review, when I once recommended this game. Since then I've watched the devs focus on an unrealistic and controversial story instead of new ships, go through issues with a workplace abuse scandal from a 'woke/politically charged' member (who is now fired, iirc), change from a fully 2D menu to an interior 3D that's nice, but not release new ships, and be so dedicated to a specific look they needed to issue an emergency patch because a new visual look was hurting people's eyes... and not release new ships.You may be noticing a theme, but it's worse. But there is a fundamental flaw with your logic: you did, in fact, NOT listen to most of your customers in early access.More ships. That was what almost everyone wanted, and did not get. _childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong: this game seems like exactly the kind of thing I'd be into. I love simulators, and I love space games. For now, I'm marking this as "not recommended," and requesting the refund.My main issue with the game is that the tutorial was extremely confusing. I felt like I was dumped into the deep end of the pool and told to complete tasks without really being told how to do them. That's not how you want your first moments into a game like this to be. A new player shouldn't have to seek out YouTube videos, or forum posts, or guides just to figure out how to play your game. I spent half an hour trying to guess what I was supposed to do throughout several parts of the tutorial, and all it did was make me want to play the game less and less.For example, the tutorial tells you to pull two antennas off of a ship segment, and salvage them. I launched one of them into one of the areas labeled "furnace" on the side, as they were much more prominent than the "barge" label at the bottom of the HUD. Work order failed, restarting.Later, the game told me to use the line cutter to open up the ship segment. The window showing an image of how to do it was semi-transparent, and very hard to see while holding any tool in most lighting conditions. When trying to use the tool, it would keep fizzling out. I was only able to use it to cut thin slices off the sides of the container, which didn't seem to help.I finally get the container open and launch two packages into the barge. Okay, good. Next up they want me to get amounts of materials.. but I can't tell what items have those materials, or what I'm supposed to do once I figure them out. I launch one engine-looking piece into the "processing" window and get told it doesn't accept that. I launch another piece into the "furnace" window and get told that I wasted resources, and will have their cost added to my debt. I get that the line was meant to be funny, but all it did was make me feel like more of an idiot.It's also possible that I just had a really poor first impression. Maybe, when the game is finished and out of Early Access - and being sold at a significant discount - I'll give it another shot. Until then, let me just say this: anybody looking to buy and play this game needs to have the patience of a saint.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good, it's absolutely deranged. It's the most exciting and engaging non-linear puzzle solving game I've ever encountered. The controls and layout are a little uncomfortable at first, but it doesn't take very long before you feel completely comfortable floating through this game. The first time I found myself having to redefine "up" in order to orient myself, I found a part of my brain stimulated like never before. From the creative use of physics and tethers to increase your money from salvage to the snarky and frankly hilarious personality of the game, this is a must-try for anyone out there that's looking for a new puzzle game that will force you to look at things differently. This is truly a game where you find yourself learning what not to do by accidentally doing it...and blowing yourself up in the process usually. But I've never had so much fun failing before! Occasionally I find myself inciting chaos in the game just to see what will happen, and the explosion physics in zero g is endlessly satisfying. You want this game, you just don't know it yet.

_childDocuments_.review: this game brings you in far more than you think it would. but use a controller...if you are at all somewhat interested, give it a try, it surprised me with how much i liked it.its the type of game that i would recommend for kicking back, relaxing, putting on a podcast or some music in the background, and spending a few hours enjoying the experience. i tend to get fully drawn into the game, really immersed in it. the gameplay consists of cutting apart certain parts of the ships, and sorting everything into 1 of 3 areas to either be salvaged, melted, or scrapped. it sounds simple, and it is, but good design adds just the right amount of danger and required thought.the game has so much potential with future content and ships, any new design could be so different than the others, and i hope they branch out with more interesting ships that aren't as similar to those that exist now. the learning curve is smooth and most things are easy to understand after your first couple close calls with them.the pressure, gas, coolant, and energy systems add a need to really think about where you should prioritize scrapping first and it really makes the game work. the possibly lethal mistakes are easily avoided, and screwing up and having an unstable reactor blow up the whole ship don't really set you back any if you planned ahead at all.there is a surprising amount of atmosphere in the game, the logs you find can add another layer to that if you want. the only complaint i have is that the control scheme for mouse and keyboard isn't all too good. but thankfully plugging in a controller felt a million times better, it plays really well on any.

_childDocuments_.review: Contrary to the popular opinion, I love the backstory. It is very clearly an over-the-top, dystopian caricature of what might happen to humanity if corporations run the solar system unchecked. Gameplay loop is great and satisfying.To me it's non intrusive and adds a lot of purpose to the game. Right from the start, it is very clearly an over-the-top, dystopian caricature, and that's how I'm approaching it. I guess a lot of frustration in the reviews comes from the fact that the promised story had a different delivery. Luckily I wasn't around when that promise was made and it lets me enjoy it as intended. The lore makes sense for everything that's happening in the world, right down to even the very tools you're using.The gameplay loop, as everyone already said, is great. As you work on a ship, you can seamlessly switch between almost meditative, satisfying tasks and risky challenges - whatever you feel like doing at the moment. Working on a single ship is segmented into time-restricted shifts, which is a great opportunity to take a short/long break and refresh/reflect on your approach as to what to do next - works great for me.Overall, I'm surprised by how much I'm enjoying it. The small scale, seemingly simple concept of gameplay, is executed perfectly. The backstory and some side stuff complements it by giving it a personal touch but doesn't get in the way of the gist of the game. There's something special happening here.

_childDocuments_.review: Most (not all) of the glitches have been worked out. There's a new bug after 1.0 where the ship spawning code superimposes multiple parts on a desk. Otherwise, the gameplay scales well based on your adrenaline preference and time constraints, and the plot is motivating and impactful. Some frustrating mechanics: if some value hasn't been destroyed, and the berth is empty, where have those parts gone? If a compressor is exposed to a larger interior space due to e.g. door damage but that space is still sealed from the exterior, why do compressors arbitrarily disable instead of just "working slower"? Why is there no such thing as a pinhole leak in the ship, though it's entirely possible for there to be a pinhole leak in your helmet?The physics are a little eye-rolling sometimes (explosive decompression doesn't happen like that; objects in space drift to a halt; your own velocity decays to a coasting speed of at most 1m/s). But I can successfully choose to suspend my disbelief because overall these don't usually impinge on the fun. Despite its kinks it's still entirely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best "job simulator" games I've tried. The concept is pretty simple - you tear apart ships in space to scrap. The hook comes in upgrading your equipment, along with a solid story told out through conversations with your fellow scrappers over space walkie-talkies.I appreciate the ability to play the game without shifts, as that makes it a much more relaxing experience, which was exactly what I wanted out of this. I love puzzling out how to take a ship apart without doing too much damage, but it's a completely viable way to play just going in and wrecking the ships fast.The controls are spot-on, the space movement just right. The tools are all easy to figure out, while the game keeps you on a treadmill with plentiful upgrades.If I have one major complaint, it's the soundtrack, and it's largely one I level at the space game genre in general. The space truckin' thing was played out a long, long time ago. We get it. Firefly was great. Let's go for something new or different when it comes to space music.Apart from that, the game just needs more variation in its ships. You get some new ships to take apart as the game progresses but I'd still like to see more, especially since the core ideas for so many of these feel so similar. Fixed lights that you could move around to different angles while working would also be a cool and much needed fix for the somewhat problematic lighting from the helmet, but that's just an idea.Overall, a fantastic game, and highly recommended if you need a podcast/audiobook game or something to just Zen out to.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Super fun and chill game (though when you O2 runs lows it can make it a little stressful).  I really enjoy the challenge of mastering the controls in 3D (as well as trying to not fix myself in an up/down orientation).  The ships, while similar in format, are varied enough to keep it interesting.  Being able to see tangible proof of how you are improving is very rewarding.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, Hardspace: Shipbreaker is basically a physics puzzle game. Each ship type (and each variant of each type) is like a giant jigsaw puzzle that you have to take apart by cutting, pulling, and sometimes exploding the right pieces in a safe, but timely, order. Because of this, it's a great game for relaxing with music or a podcast in the background.But it's also a game that can go from 0 to 100 in an instant. One minute you're happily peeling away the outer hull of a ship, and the next, you're careening toward the furnace after a stray cutter shot violently decompresses the compartment you were in. Whether you like to play slow and safe or fast and reckless, Shipbreaker is fun and satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Deconstruction simulator with a store for buying upgraded gear and a series of increasingly complicated ships to deconstruct. Each ship is made of different parts that need to be thrown into different bins but individual working days are time limited and come with rent costs so there is a constant tradeoff between maximising value vs the time spent to gain that value. There is a story bringing it all together about a labour union seizing the means of production that is well done and some brief asides about what it means to be a clone. Would maybe have benefited from more ship types as every archetype is identical in structure even if the inside is randomly generated, so they all come apart the same in the end. Otherwise a solid game for relaxing to without too much to think about.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that can't get out of its own way and let you have fun. The main game mechanic has potential but every other feature is built around detracting from it. If you play with the survival elements you're constantly interrupted by tedious busy work, having to coast slowly back to a console to press the "don't die" button every few minutes; if you turn them off it all feels a bit easy and pointless.It's got an incongruous cowboy/frontier vibe, with the tutorial guy talking to you like you're his new rancher, and the music follows the same theme (which can thankfully be muted).The entire idea of putting you in massive debt at the start just sucks the fun out of earning anything, and the whole "lol aren't corporations evil???" brand of scifi humour was already exhausted when Outer Worlds did it and it certainly hasn't been revived here.There's a bunch of boring and unskippable dialogue - you can't even listen to it in the background while you do other stuff like look into equipment upgrades, the UI locks while the dialogue is playing. And for a game so built around physics, the physics are occasionally quite wonky.I wish I had stopped trying to find the fun before 2 hours were up so I could refund. It's a game that desperately needed some better high-level design work.

_childDocuments_.review: A first impression:It's surprisingly well-made for its development phase. Neat intro, music is incredibly fitting and relaxing and there's some good dialog. From the roadmap it seems the core gameplay is in position, with additional (comparatively minor) addons coming later on.It's already a good game in this stage. The tutorial starts you off with the basics of tools, the hazards of reactors and how to cycle airlocks. There's not much info on how to tackle certain problems, such as "I've removed the hardpoints for the ship, why is this panel not moving" or  "How do you detach the atmospherics console from the wall?"Other than that, gameplay is fairly straightforward, and your tools tell you to which salvage processor your parts should go.One of my favorite parts of this game is its soundtrack. It's a warm-sounding country soundtrack, with steelstring guitar, banjo and lots of reverb.It adds a lot to the relaxing nature of this game. It also fits the voice actor of Weaver, who teaches you the basics at the start of the game.I'm hoping this will eventually be released as a soundtrack since it's really good.That said, if your google-fu is decent enough, you can find some tools to rip the audio from the game yourself.Some notes from my first time playing this:The navigation took some time to get used to, as I'm more experienced with Space Engineers, where your jetpack suit has automatic dampeners. Instead, H:S has a manual dampener (Ctrl) which you need to press to stop moving. This also doesn't seem to work while grappling onto something, but that might be an upgrade later on.Having to press this key while also navigating around the ship is a little too much effort at certain points, an automatic version would be neat to have.Rotating your view by moving your mouse also has some drag to it, so you need to overshoot and move back to compensate for this. I'm hoping later upgrades minimize this, as precision movement isn't trivial. (I'm not saying it shouldn't be there at all, it's a realism-oriented simulator, after all!)One feature I'd also like to see is being able to control the length of the grappling beam. A mechanic like the Physics Gun in Garry's Mod would be nice, where you can move the object towards/away from you by scrolling the scroll wheel, like 'reeling in the fishing line'.If you deposit salvage in one of the processors, it tells you that salvage was accepted and credits have been added, but I haven't yet noticed how many credits you get (other than the screen at the end of your shift).Finally, the 15 minute timer adds quite some stress to an otherwise relaxing game. I'm hoping this can be changed to a user-set time limit, so you can work for longer (but you should also be reminded to take breaks to avoid an 8 hour shift :).Anyhow, for a first experience I had quite some fun. 9/10 would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game but the story mode is freaking awful. The game mechanics are really enjoyable and if you like powerwash simulator you should love this, the games progression system of buying upgrades goes at a great pace too but there are times when the characters ramble on for ages and you cant skip the dialogue, I get it the writer of this wanted to be an activist here you go heres a cookie you almost ruined a game with your garbage. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Hardspace: Shipbreaker is very much worth the money. Its mechanics aren't really innovative, but they are really well-tuned. Progression is quite engaging, it has amusing lore, and diverse ship designs make it a standout title in the genre.Long version - HS is an engaging twist on the disassembly genreIt offers a unique and immersive experience in the disassembly and cleanup genre, thanks to its fantastic 3D flight and maneuvering mechanics. Navigating in zero gravity while carefully dismantling ships adds an exhilarating layer of depth and challenge that keeps you on your toes.The onboarding process is smooth and well-paced, with ships becoming more complex gradually. This ensures that you never feel overwhelmed and can steadily build your skills as you progress through increasingly intricate vessels.The game's lore, while not incredibly deep, is highly amusing and a clever commentary on capitalism at its finest. It adds a humorous backdrop to your salvaging endeavors, enhancing the overall experience.What truly keeps you hooked is the variety of ships you encounter. Each new vessel presents fresh challenges and requires different strategies, keeping the gameplay engaging and dynamic for a long time. Going into ships of the same type multiple times allows you to figure out how to perform the dismantling faster every time.
_childDocuments_.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker

_childDocuments_.review: Very polished for Early Access.Unique and addictive gameplay loop, nice Firefly-esque setting. The 15 minute shifts break down the game into manageable chunks, though you can zone out and chill in free play if you don't want that timed / career progression experience.My only real critique so far is that the initial hour of the game is pretty rough around the edges. The game attempts to give you a tutorial, but isn't really clear that it's a tutorial, and it isn't real upfront that it's giving you unlimited time/health/oxygen that it will then severely limit later on. The tutorial bounces wildly between spoonfeeding you (press the roll for X seconds!) and expecting you to figure things out with no explanation (you're running out of oxygen with seconds to spare! go find and figure out how to interact with this kiosk that we've never mentioned to the player even once).Frustrations like these can turn a "wow this is cool" moment into a "this is stupid BS" moment for people playing the game for the first time. I almost ragequit twice in the first hour.Also, if you play with an Xbox controller, there's no way (at the moment) to remap buttons, so expect some very sore thumbs from constantly pressing down on the sticks to brake/roll. Remapping these to LB/RB would make much more sense to me.

_childDocuments_.review: With yes only 13 hours of playtime, I can disassemble a gecko in 3 shift if I make cuts on the fly. While maintaining good cuts not as much is wasted. Sometimes my first and second shifts are just making nice hull cut and removal of the floor to send down any technology/electrical or any other special cargo. Also during this time I am opening up the ship best I can so I can start this process. Once you figure out how to approach the ships and what layout you want to do, it can be very relaxing. As for now this is a good start for this game. I'm sure content will come. With I hope more complicated scenarios come with or maybe something with critical thinking.

_childDocuments_.review: It could be nice, but it's trying hard to be what it's not.This disrupts the gameplay and my enjoyment. You have to go refill O2 all the time, while in 1st levels it's not required, then you introduce this undesired mechanics. Do it from the beginning instead of showing us a better version of the game before.Then you get message from people and we don't really care about that when it's introduced.If there are people interactions, just introduce them right away and make it relevant to the the game. Not after 4 hours of play, "BTW there are other people talking to you in this game...Maybe they will serve some purpose later on, but for now you can keep not caring about it for the next few hours."At that point it's just a What/WhyTF moment.  This game is thorough in the obligation of dismantling everything and yet very shallow in the put this here and that there.  I believe this is where it falls flat.There's something very satisfying in dismantling things and finding stuff. Even though these mechanics are well realised in this game, I believe it would be better in another context. I think it would made a great exploring game where you try to find things for some purpose and use the tools to gain access. _childDocuments_.review: -- EDIT -- so apparently in the release version developers decided to make playing open shift more annoying. Now it actually asks you whether or not you want to enable oxygen drain every time you start the game. The game is basically being condescending to the player asking whether or not to remove a "hard" mechanic even though I already made this choice. I am not playing open shift because I want the game to be easy, you idiots. I am playing open shift because your game doesn't make sense in standard mode.---I really like this game. I didn't at first, before open shift was introduced, but with open shift it is a much better experience.I am not sure why developers have decided to bundle open shift with unlimited oxygen, but whatever, fortunately I can opt into one without opting into the other.Below is my take on open vs. timed shift. There are plenty of reviews describing the game, so I am not going to.-- SPOILERS BELOW --A lot of people complained about the "standard" 15 min per shift mode, but I think most of the complaints were for a wrong reason. By itself, the timed shift mode is a perfectly valid gameplay, like timed puzzle solving. It might not be my thing, but there are plenty of people out there who enjoy this type of game.The problem with timed shifts is that it breaks the narrative. The game goes to a great length to establish that you are a desperate, low level worker, basically indentured labor, working for a decidedly evil, slave driving, AI killing, terrible secrets hiding corporation. You are in deep-deep debt with them, they nickel and dime you for everything, the work environment is dangerous and unforgiving and they don't care, if you die they will just replace you.In this narrative, open shift makes sense. You work crazy hours and you "use the whole buffalo", you pull every cent of salvage out of that ship, so you can crawl your way out of this crap as fast as possible.But timed shifts don't make sense. All the talk about "using the whole buffalo" goes right out of the window. I just watched one of the best speedrunners and at the end they still had a large part of the ship still intact. And once you yank out more valuable components it becomes economically unfeasible to return to the same ship on the next shift. So it makes more sense as a regular player to yank out the reactor and maybe the thruster and move on to the next ship. So the same company that will charge you for every bit of oxygen and complain when you burn an aluminum panel worth maybe a few hundreds is perfectly fine with you discarding millions of credits worth of salvage just because your shift is over and it is not worth your while. This breaks the suspension of disbelief.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: It's a really lovely, fun game. Sprinkle some cool sci-fi lore on top, plus a tiny bit of creepiness at times (no spoilers!), and this game is definitely in my favorites. The game mechanics are very fun - the ship classes all have distinguished approaches and when something goes wrong, it really *goes wrong* - spectacularily. Voice acting is great, the characters feel authentic - however the story? Ehhh, pretty generic, and it kind of leaves you uninvolved? It's not a great selling point, really. Being just a grunt, keeping your head down to pay off a collossal "debt" to your corporation, chipping it off bit by bit steadily feels like it could be good enough of a story for this game. At some point, I'd really hope to see more ships and tools and diversity though.Overall, I'd give this game a solid 8.25/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Hardspace: Shipbreaker is a completely unique, brilliantly crafted experience that transcends the genres of simulation and science fiction by fusing them into something that no one would ever have thought they could want to play until they sat down to chop up their first Mackerel with a splitsaw. I've been wielding my multipurpose grapple tool since the early days of early access for Shipbreaker, and I've watched it evolve from an amusing and creative sandbox experience to a deeply immersive and satisfying gameplay loop, not to mention the surprisingly compelling and relevant narrative that now accompanies it. And after all of these hours, I'm finally in the midst of my first playthrough of the full campaign since release.This game is supremely underrated, and if you're even the least bit interested, I promise it will impress you. During early access, I remember enjoying it thoroughly, but being a bit worn out by repetitive ship layouts. Now, I feel like there are so many that it really will take me until I work off my 1.2 billion credit debt to master them all, from the long and narrow Atlas Scouts to the densely packed salvage Geckos. And even then, the competitive Cutter's Race mode could potentially keep me occupied until the end of time, trying to figure out how to creatively cut apart a vessel as fast as possible.The features on display are certainly worth noting, but perhaps the best part of the experience is the painstakingly crafted world in which the game sits. The realism is bolstered by the fine details that litter the interior of the various ships you cut apart, from the occasional poster (which you can now swipe to decorate your personal HAB) to the idly drifting data drives you can delve into for nuggets of gritty space lore. And all of this detail speaks to the love with which it has all been intimately fabricated. Because of this, it is easy to become fully immersed, and to cringe when you accidentally chop an air filter in half because you forgot to switch to your stinger instead of your splitsaw, or to feel your stomach clench when you realize you pulled out the power supply before disconnecting the thrusters, meaning you now have pipes of volatile fuel that will easily detonate if you so much as jostle them. But on the flipside, it is also what makes it tremendously satisfying when you learn that you can bash the fuel pipes with a cannister of coolant to freeze them up, making them safe to cut. That kind of lesson is something the game doesn't directly teach you (it might be found in an obscure data drive, but it's definitely not in a tutorial), so discovering it on your own or through online forums lends a sense of discovery and authenticity to the game that makes you feel like you are truly becoming a professional shipbreaker as you play. If, like me, you played this during the early days, boot it back up and give it a whirl. You will absolutely not regret it. If you've been considering it for a while, but are unsure if it deserves your time when your steam library is already full of games yet to be played (a problem which I attribute almost entirely to Humble Bundle), then consider no more. This game will blow you away with the force of a Class II Reactor meltdown.

_childDocuments_.review: In shipbreaker, you dismantle spaceships. There is little to no incentive to just spam a new ship, and rip out the 3-5 components worh > 200k, and repeat.
