_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because I absolutely loved the sailing element of Windwaker and watching the trailers for this game really brought back that itch. I've been playing for 8 hours and it really is scratching it. However, if you are expecting a game with an epic story and fluid combat like the Zelda titles, then this is not the game for you. If you enjoyed the sense of exploration and the sailing element of Windwaker, then this is definitely a game worth considering. I've been playing survival mode for 8 hours, and have been taking it slowly. Combing over islands and gradually upgrading my boat and learning what items are the most useful to keep on my person in the event that I die and need a restart and it has been very relaxing. The cell shaded graphics are wonderful to look at and the music really harmonises with the environment and the overall vibe of the game which makes just simply being in the game world an absolute pleasure. It's because of this that it has been really easy for me to overlook the bugs I have encountered.Some of the issues that I have encountered have been:- Animals being launched into the air when I killed them (3 or 4 times) which is annoying as you do lose any arrows you shot into them and the resources you were after.- Animals getting stuck on terrain making for easy kills which does detract a little from the immersion- Odd jerky boat movements when boarding and alighting from your boat on the beach which can be a pain if you have been crafting on your boat and have left items on the deck as these can be pushed into the sea where they are too deep to retrieve.The movement is not as polished as some titles released by bigger studios and the combat is not as fluid as a lot of people had hoped for (restricted to straight lunges with the spears and slings are very slow) but as with any game, once you get used to using the lock on and dodging it really isn't as bad as people are making it out to be and, as I said before, since I like the setting it is certainly not a deal breaker, far from it.TL:DRIf you want a fast paced action-adventure, do not buy this game, you will probably hate it.If you loved the sailing in Windwaker (even without control over the wind direction) and you like a slower paced exploration style game with some crafting thrown in, then at least give it a go, especially if it is on sale.It's a beautiful game. If you take your time with it, you will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to talk a bit about the negatives of this game before anything else. The transitional levels between the main over-worlds are a bit dull and felt too cumbersome to traverse in comparison to the majority of the game, but again, these are things I can live with. I adore this game to no end, even with its faults.This game is absolutely breathe taking, and surprisingly fluid. Windbound tries to be a lot of things, and while it may not succeed in some of them, it thrives in its atmosphere and sailing mechanics. As a kid, I loved playing Windwaker, and Windbound brings out a age old nostalgia that I had completely forgotten about until I had built my first boat, and set sail to the hauntingly beautiful music of Zander Hulme. If you have the time, please play this game, you won't regret it at all.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a game in here for someone, but not for me[I'm a big fan of gameplay of the nomadic survival type, itches that can be scratched by ATLAS, World's Adrift, No Man's Sky and the like. And, by all accounts, Windbound should scratch that itch, and combine it with another of my favourite genres, action combat.Unfortunately, there is a genre I also can't stand. Roguelikes.Despite it's presentation of breath of the Wild like graphics and cute fluffy animals, Windbound's gameplay is strongly bound up in the rogue-like formula. Dying even in casual mode sets you back to the start of the chapter and takes away almost everything you've earned. Dying in Survival difficulty is outright permadeath and the whole game starts over.This'd be less of a concern if it wasn't for the fact hostile wildlife can respawn practically on top of you without warning, and often dead animals will fly into the stratosphere, denying you their precious food and resources, without which your survival chances are greatly diminished and the odds of you ending up back at square one rise sharply.Meanwhile the gathering lacks a certain something that is difficult to pin down, and the combat can only really be described as 'there', while infinitely better than the mess that is the majority of survival titles like ARK, the 'action combat' elements feel ponderously slow and basic, with the dodge button having a noticeable delay to trigger. Outside of combat your character gets winded after a short doggy paddle or stiff jog up a flight of stairs, and has to eat like she has a wasting disease to avoid starving.I want to like this game, and maybe the devs will make adjustments to appeal to players like me. But as it stands, this game just isn't for me. It's a Don't starve style survival roguelike dressed up as Breath of the Wild

_childDocuments_.review: Upon starting a new game you’ll have the choice of two game difficulties, Survivalist and Storyteller. Survivalist are for those players who want the full Windbound experience. The game difficulty options include, only items in “Held” inventory slots are retained upon death, Return to Chapter One upon death and Standard combat difficulty. Storyteller difficulty is for those players who want to focus on the Windbound story. The settings for this difficulty include, Full inventory is retained upon death. Chapter Progress is retained upon death and combat difficulty is reduced. You can change the difficulty setting at any time from within the Gameplay options menu. There’s a storm raging on the open sea, the waves crashing against your raft as you try to stay afloat. You can see the dim lights fastened to the masts of other rafts as they ride the waves up and down. Suddenly a giant Nautilus appears, tentacles flaying about when it comes crashing down upon your raft casting you in to the rough sea. You slowly sink beneath the waves, when suddenly you appear on the surface. The storm and waves have gone, everything is calm as you stand upon the water. Before you is a bright swirling light in the centre of some stone ruins, arches which rise from out of the calm sea.  You make your way towards the light, walking through you find yourself washed up on a beach … The Lost Islands (Chapter One). You begin with a knife and there are some resources across the island to help you survive. However, you’re not going to be able to survive on the island for long. At the far side of the island there’s some ancient ruins, on what looks like an altar is an object with a blue crystal at one end. After picking the object up it transforms into the Oar of the Ancestors. A mysterious, ornate and ancient oar which occasionally trembles in your hands as though something resides in it.  Now that you have this mysterious oar, you’ll have to put it to use. This means you’ll have to build a boat so that you can move between the islands. With limited resources you’re not going to be building any speedboats or luxury cruise liners for now though you’re going have to with a canoe made of Thick Grass. You can find Thick Grass growing most places and can be cut down using your knife. Once you have enough grass head over to the shore and select canoe in the crafting options and you’ll craft your first means of transport in this mysterious place.  When you collect resources, they may unlock new items for you to craft. There are also some animals on the islands, some big and some cute n cuddly ones. However, all will provide some resources when you ring their bloody necks. Resources such as bone, silk thread, raw meat, skins, jaws and other wonderous creature parts. Sticks, wood, rocks, palm fronds, flowers, berries, fish, bamboo are just a few of the resources available for you to find and craft into new items.  On some of these islands stand these mysterious structures with blue crystals at the top. Climbing these structures to the top will reveal a Nautilus Key, three of these keys are required to unlock the exit to the current chapter. Once you collect a Nautilus key a blue beam of light heads upwards to the heavens. There is also another light which can be seen somewhere in the distance, this is the exit point once you have collected all three keys. After going through the exit, you find yourself in a large courtyard with five sides and a pathway leading out of the courtyard, The First Crossing. A mural starts to appear on one of the sides which depicts a story of worship to the Nautilus.  At the end of the pathway there’s your canoe, which you’ll use to paddle your way under the stars over rolling waves. Eventually you spot a small plot of land with the same bright swirling light you first seen in the storm. On the bit of land though are a couple of statues, here you can make an offering and have a blessing bestowed upon you. To make an offering you need Sea Shards, these can be found in blue jars once they’ve been smashed. You can also collect shards at any shrines you may come across on your journey. Once you’ve finished with your offering and blessing then head towards the light and you’ll then find yourself on Chapter Two. As you progress, you’ll encounter different creatures which will pose far more deadly than the cute n cuddly Bleenk. Luckily for you, you will be able to upgrade your grass canoe to a sturdier boat using bamboo and later wood. Adding sails will help you travel faster than paddling. However, it can be quite frustrating trying to keep the speed up if you don’t keep the wind in your sails. Also watch out for those reefs especially in a grass canoe, hiding in those reefs are Crobsters which will jump onboard and if left will destroy your boat. I did lose some items had stored on my boat from one of those little blighters the first time I came across them. In the options you’ll find settings for Display (Full Screen, Resolution, Refresh Rate, V-Sync, Field of View and Brightness). Quality (Shader Quality, Shadow Resolution, Soft Shadows, Antialiasing, Anisotropic Filtering, Textures, LOD Quality, SSAO, Bloom and Volumetrics). Sound (Master, Sound Effects, Background Music and Creature Music Volume Sliders). Gameplay (Mouse Sensitivity, Aim Sensitivity, Invert Aim Y-Axis, Show Contextual Controls, Tutorials, Difficulty, Outfit and Vibration). Language (English, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Russian, Polish and Chinese).  Positives + Great looking graphics + Enjoyable and relaxing game to play + Two game difficulties + Good music + Has achievements  Negatives - Sailing can be a bit frustrating - No cards currently Craft yourself a seaworthy boat, let the winds guide you as you explore and unlock the secrets of the Forbidden Islands in Windbound.  8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game gets more dislikes than it deserves:Lore wise it's very rich, and Gameplay wise I think this is honestly pretty good; much of its mechanics/gameplay caters to a good deal of people. The sailing and camping qualities are really quite relaxing, while the ship building options and crafting interface are fun to play around with. The combat- while not the greatest- is still enjoyable, and every chapter unlocks new beasts to fight and gear for your character. Players can select between several different difficulties/modes when starting their game, which includes an endless mode and a peaceful mode. The entire game has a good deal of replayability, as the levels are procedurally generated and hold different challenges and treasures each time you play. This game seems to get a bad rep, and I enjoyed this game more than I expected I would, from sailing to gathering to hunting: the game itself is solid and made with passion, and I'm glad I got it- If any of this piques your interest, I think it is worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little game which could be a lot neater with some fairly simple improvements. This is a case where a bit of judicial modding would definitely come in handy.Pros: Gorgeous art design, nice soundtrack. The water effects are really stunning, and lend a lot to this game's atmosphere and mechanics. Exploration's fun, and there's a decent amount of variety in the exploration. Cons: Can't rebind the keys, and especially in water navigation, the WASD binding becomes really tedious. There's also moments where the camera becomes locked, and cannot be mouse-turned, which makes WASD even more egregious.  The combat's clunky, again, because of the forced bindings.  Once you've built your first sail, you may find as I did that while paddling is slower, it's also much more reliable and less complicated. Beyond that, simple quality of life adjustments would be nice: length of days, stamina degradation (which is entirely too fast, and leaves you spending far too much time just hunting for food.) At times, basic and essential resources become entirely too scarce. (Can't build a fire without long grass... which is slow to respawn, for example.)  Overall, if you're patient with it's flaws, I feel it's worth a few bucks, and a few hours of your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Fair warning the sail mechanics are really tough but more importantly even in the easy mode the combat can be frustrating with possible deaths.  After 6 hours I barely grasped sailing, with constant crashing into islands and reefs even destroying my ship mid sea with no recourses to rebuild it. As for combat a lot of rage quits over dying since I still haven't been able to dodge properly once (as the game I think forces you to target something to dodge it I still havent been able to successfully dodge once hence my rage towards combat). And let me make this clear, dying sucks. When you die in this game you lose a ton of progress. On harder difficulty all but a handful of items are kept with story progress being lost. But even if you choose the easy mode all bags on your ship are lost and you reset your progress to the start of the act. Nothing hurts more than having farmed up a lot of stuff for hours trying to find that one item you need to make a better ship only to die to an enemy you've just seen for the first time and losing 30 slots of items. If there was creative mode I'm sure the game would lose its charm very quickly since there is very little you can do, all the gameplay comes from low resources and hard mechanics. There is a charm to the ship making but you are given so little resources that building a large ship would take a lot of effort. But even then the limitations are obvious, once you see a few parts you've seen them all and the combinations are not endless.I was curious about the barely minimum story however the frustration over the controls and the amount of progress lost really outshines everything. The main mission is boring and repetative; as every single time you find 3 islands with towers, climb them to unlock another island, then rinse and repeat 5 times I presume (I was on act 4 when I had  enough) The game is gorgeous to look at with beautiful sounds I'll give it that. Though perfect for casual gamers, or else it would have been if not for the difficult combat and lack of progress save, so who is this game for exactly? Hardcore survival gamers I suppose. So if you like dark souls but wished when you died going back to your corpse to regain lost items was for losers and you wanted everything you worked for to be lost everytime you encountred an enemy you couldn't figure before they killed you, then go right ahead, you have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: As an old school player, I enjoy difficulty. Survival games really entertain me and Windbound is one of my favorites right now. I don't mind losing the items everytime I die and restart the chapters because it's part of the adventure.The world is random generated, so you will never sail the same ocean twice, even when you back to chapter 1.Your sailboat is the focus of everything, since you are a castaway trying to get back to your family/tribe.I deeply enjoyed sail through the isles, face storms and fogs, fight the wind and explore. The sail system is "realistic", so if you enjoy this activity the fun in guaranteed.Kara is beautiful and her animations was clearly made with care. She carries everything with her and even the arrows have their spot and number acknowledged.The energy management was cleverly implemented and together with the inventory, offer a good challenge, since you can't carry everything until pass this barrier. For any survival game player, I believe this will be a fun "puzzle" to solve.There is a good amount of practical items to craft, from food, inventory and weapons, as parts for your sailboat, and not enough resources for everything. The animals respawn tho. Ah, the boat can be destroyed, so you need to repair it sometimes.I didn't encountered any bug, but sometimes the camera focus the wrong enemy and you need to release and click the button until the right one is selected (like in For Honor).The pace can be slow if you want, exploring, looking for food and resources, crafting everything possible in the chapter and then moving to the next, which will offer new challenges and more difficulty.I recommend Windbound for any survival player who enjoy a lonely adventure full of discoveries.

_childDocuments_.review: I admit, the game has a bunch of new updates from before.  The fights are a bit better than they were before, but I have an issue with the way you die.  I understand the there are different difficulties where you could change not losing all your progress when you die, but even in the casual difficulty you would have to start all over from the chapter you were in.  That means having to explore all the islands again, having to find the three key seashells to open the final door, or every little thing you have to do to get to the key seashells.  There are still the limitations to what you can build on your boat.  You can't build more than one item per platform.  I would have thought building a platform would allow you to build more per square, but the game won't allow you to build anymore than one per square.  The bag and chest don't make any sense.  How does a Heavy bag hold more than a Wooden Chest.  It would make sense if the chest allowed you to stack items more in it which would make more sense to craft a chest.  Now instead of items stacking to only 10, the chest allows them to stack to 20.  I would rather farm the materials to make the heavy bag and bag stand than waste materials making the chest.  4 out of 10.  Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been so invested keeping my boat afloat and movingSAILING People complain about the sailing here but I do not understand. So I had to constantly set my sails lower or higher depending on the circumstance to not fall over, so good. You cannot sail effectively on this game just holding one button. Pay attention to the wind and your boatSURVIVAL/BUILDINGThere are survival mechanics here, hunger and exhaustion, but why can't we sleeeeep??The hunger mechanic is good, I enjoyed managing my health,stamina and hunger, there are enough resources ot keep yourself healthy, but hoarding them is not optimal since they decay quite quickly, so I can see why there is no sleep, since it's more meant to be a moment to moment survival and not a long term planning survival like The Long Dark or something like that. _childDocuments_.review: It's not terrible. It is very nice atmosphere wise, and the movement and mechanics feel generally good. There is an issue with Steam Pre-Orders where nobody received their bonus DLC. The Windbound team has responded and is working on getting them distributed.Windbound does not hold your hand too much, you are left to discover most things by accident. I believe this is what the studio creating this had intended. It's supposed to be a gradual discovery of tools/weapons, game mechanics, and story/lore.The story and theme surrounding the game is intriguing and definitely makes you curious of how things are going to unfold for Kara. The combat I did find to be a bit clunky but not terrible. The sailing feels fairly good overall. Sometimes you run into issues with the game not registering that you have favorable winds. Quickly fixed by readjusting your sails away from and back to the position you think they should be in. Overall a small gripe.I do like the crafting system and how you slowly discover more and become more efficient with your objectives through it. The first zone took me an hour and a half - the second took me half that.In my current experience I would say the game is slightly overpriced - by about $10 CAD. If you can grab it for 25% off I'd say it would be worth it. I'm going to play through the rest of the game as I am enjoying it and am past the refund stage now. I'll update the review upon completion to give a more thorough understanding of what you are in for in Windbound.EDIT:Upon finishing the game (which took my roughly 9 hours, I visited each island on all the maps and took my time) I found I did enjoy the game but it has very little to offer in respect to replay value for me.  You have the opportunity to spend "Meta currency" at checkpoints in the game to customise your games with a buff (i.e. unbreakable spear) for further playthrough's. But other than that there was nothing besides the Steam Achievements.You are in for about a 9ish hour survival experience that is quite pleasant but fairly simple. There are some neat concepts in there and I do really like the base game - I however have found little to no drive to replay it and would love to see that implemented more in future updates.Currently I still support that the game is worth it at %25 off for survival game fans. _childDocuments_.review: So far it's very promising. The artstyle is beautiful, and my gaming laptop can run it with no issues at all. I've myself always enjoyed exploration and the game immediatly let's you go and explore whatever you please. The music is very relaxing, and fits the game extremely well. I'm looking forward to exploring more of this beautiful world.Positive+Beautiful game with a lovely artstyle+Amazing music+Player is free to do practically whatever they want from the start+Two difficulties to chose from, one that is for players who just want to relax and experience the story and one for players who want a challenge (in the more challenging difficulty the player loses every item not "held" and is returned to the start of the game if they die)Negative-The survival elements of the game are a bit tedious at times, as the player character is constantly hungry - this is not challenging really, but tedious-I've come across places where the camera turns automatically and I'm not allowed to turn it manually - although this is just a pet peeve of mine and not really a problem-I got motion sickness at first, but increased field of view to max and it disappeared. Worth noting is that I get motion sickness very easily-Combat is very basic, and to get the materials you need to do things you have to defeat enemiesAll in all, so far the game is very nice and interesting and I will make sure to play more! As I haven't played for that long I might get a different opinion later, but so far I really like it! There are some glaring issues, like the hunger bar needing a bit of a chill pill, and I'm pretty sure I'll get real tired of the combat later on. Hopefully the devs will change up some things (please nerf the hunger bar if you're reading this), and in the meantime I will leave this review as recommended as I'm enjoying myself with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I had high hopes for this game, the concept looked promising. The game as it stands left a lot to be desired. The promotional material for this game making it look like it had elements of Breath of the Wild, combined with Wind Waker, and survival weaved in. Had me going in with expectations.There are some high points, I really enjoyed the music, and the story(however brief and limited) was enjoyable.The survival aspect of the game can be a bit rough, food takes too long to cook, and spoils too fast.Combat feels very clunky at times, dodge/swing(hit boxes can be a bit off), ranged combat feels poorly designed.You can completely customize your ship to get around, building it to your specifications. However, materials are so limited, that you probably won't be able to build anything you truly want before the end of the game.(and if you happen to die in survival, you start from scratch with the exception of a few protected slots in your inventory).There are numerous bugs I encountered such as enemies falling through the map, or being launched into space upon death, or just not being lootable(very harsh given the survival element of the game). Wind also just getting bugged on rare occasions, leaving my ship stuck in the middle of the ocean no matter which way I turned(forcing me to reload).Overall the game just feels like it isn't finished, like an early access title. It needs more, and I hope the Devs give it more attention. I finished the survival mode in about 12 hours, and that is with taking my time, exploring as much as I could. Even hunting down and crafting items I didn't in any way need, whilst also expanding my ship.As the game stands, I really can't recommend it, especially not for the current price tag. Should also note, the Pre-Order bonus was never delivered to the folks who bought on Steam. Though it is a known issue, they didn't fix it before myself, and numerous others finished the game. So that's another disappointment to add to the list.Hopefully they add more modes/difficulty options, more variety to the island layouts, crafting options, enemies available. The list goes on.

_childDocuments_.review: Mid-rez 3d exploration/survival game.  You are the last of a seafaring people who went out for One Last Hunt and, for the most part, didn't survive.  You wash up on the shore of an island with some crafting skills and a knife.  Find food, gather resources and learn crafting skills to make tools, workstations and boats, so you can go explore other islands in the ocean.  Navigate winds and waves.  Hunt and cook and eat.  Craft stuff.  Rediscover your heritage.I want to like this game.  A lot of work went into it.  And it's pretty and innovative in certain ways.  People have praised the sailing mechanics, and the waves and wave motions are dynamic and interesting to navigate and even seasickness-inducing.  But there's so many odd little things I keep tripping over...You need to craft tools to get things done.  But rather than the usual variants of stone-on-stick hammer, pointy-stone-on-stick pick, sharpened-stone-on-stick axe and so on, your tools depend on animal horns, each tool needing a different animal's horn.  Don't find the animal, don't get the axe.  Can't kill the animal, don't get the shovel.  Unrealistic and it gets old.There's a map that shows where you've been, the path your boat has taken, the islands you've discovered and your current location.  But it doesn't show which way your boat is pointing, and you don't have a compass.  You're the daughter of a seafaring people and you have no clue which way your boat is pointing, except to go in what you think is a straight line and check the map to see what kind of path you cut.  Kinda makes it difficult to do the search sweeps you need to do in order to get sight of new islands to land on.Most of the time the camera angle is over-the-shoulder, but there's times, at certain particular locations, when it unexpectedly switches to isometric fixed-camera arrow-key navigation.  Hate that.  A lot.You can build multiple boats.  You can store things on boats.  But if you take one boat out for a sail and come back, the other boat disappears.  Along with the stuff you stored on it.  Including those spare animal horns you didn't want to carry around with you.Resources respawn in a very inconsistent way.  Grass and edible mushrooms seem to come back overnight.  Bamboo, which is notorious for spreading rapidly, sometimes doesn't respawn for days, if at all.  Same with sticks, needed to make fire, tools and other things, not to be found on the ground, but requiring being chopped down.  Unlike the trees, which need an axe to chop down.  Assuming you find the right animal to make the axe.There are levels, and things you need to do to progress to the next level.  Doing them results in a cutscene, which is the same each time you do the thing.  It's skippable, but it's just disappointing that your character makes the exact same noise of surprise and wonder each and every time.  Cuz you'll be doing it a lot.I wishlisted this game before it was released because I liked the trailer, and because a buddy of mine who windsurfs was very enthusiastic about the mechanics.  On release day the reviews talked about bugginess and repetitiveness.  Not really seeing the bugginess, so I guess a lot of that was worked out.  The repetitiveness is indeed there, inasmuch as you have to keep gathering food because the game implements hunger and food can decay in storage.  Also, you need to do a lot of sailing in order to find the islands, especially since some of them have hidden bonuses that are worth finding.  And then, once you've found all the secrets in your current island grouping, it's time to move on to the next island grouping.It makes me think of No Man's Sky.  At sea.All told, I'm glad I got it at the sale price of $10 rather than the store price of $30.  It lowers my expectations enough that I can find this game a passable switchoff from my $15-per-month MMO.  If you can get it for that price, give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Windbound is a game that is brimming with potential both in atmosphere and gameplay, and is a beautiful idea in that right. They make use of that potential atmospherically, offering up some incredibly stunning visuals and a great soundtrack that invoke a sense of hope. _childDocuments_.review: Update:Is this game a roguelite or not? 90% of the game I enjoy: the combat is fine, its got a large crafting list, procedural oceans, I love building my boat, art style, music, it's all there. But there is a MASSIVE red flag that the game desperately needs to warn you about.THE FINAL OCEAN portal is a boss battle, and a hard one at that. BRING SUPPLIES AND AMMO. I don't care if this is a spoiler, you'll thank me later. I went into that boss battle with absolutely zero expectation I'd have to fight some villain I was only now being introduced to at the very end of the game. After dying I was sent back to stage one. 13 hours of what feels like wasted grind.  This current system is immensely harsh of a punishment for something the game severely lacked to communicate to the player. I got the game on release, and back then if you died you were merely sent back to the beginning of the CURRENT stage you were on. Somewhere during the updates, they must've switched it to a roguelite structure as you now are sent to start over from the very first stage. Roguelites are meant to be short runs, 3 hours at the maximum. Due to the harsh conditions of survival in this game, where everything degrades, including food, you are forced to take your time. Add onto that is the sailing simulation which also pads your game time immensely.  A traversal mechanic that was supposed to be relaxing while still engaging the player, instead now feels like an insult to my time.  It took me 13 hours to reach what should've been the end of my first "run". And now I'm sent to the beginning, dumbstruck and absolutely devoid of desire to press on anymore. Again: This isn't a matter of "git gud" because the game failed to communicate the stakes at hand. The game had set the expectation that transitioning between each ocean was going to be the same set of activities. Then suddenly introduces a new threat in the final gate, without warning. I'm only leaving this review as a "Yes" because if you know what you're getting into on that final gateway and properly prepare, then you should be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Sailing, survival, exploration, crafting, story, Windbound has a lot going on. In fact, one could say that it maybe has too much going on. The question is though, is it able to combine all of these without losing that fun factor?So I’m gonna start with the game’s graphics, as that is something it does really well. It’s got that Breath of the Wild look going for it, with tons of bright colors on top of cel shading. There isn’t a lot of fine detail, but the studio has done a good job at really making the environments and the life on top of them pop. This is even evident in the water, which may not be Sea of Thieves-level quality but is still some of the best I’ve seen from a survival game like this. And it does this while running at 1440p 150+ fps, so it’s definitely an optimized game if anything. Then you got the atmospheric music to tie it all together, with the sailing theme in particular being my favorite.Now the gameplay is where the problems start appearing. I want to say that Windbound is just a survival game, but that’s not really the full picture. Sure, it is a survival game at its core, but it’s also an RPG, an adventure game, and even has some roguelike mechanics thrown in there. The problem being that it doesn’t really do any of these well. Despite the guise of being a survival game, your goal is actually to follow along this linear, cryptic storyline that has you sailing between islands, activating pillars, and then going through a portal to the next set of islands to repeat the same process.It’s already a pretty boring process, especially considering that there isn’t really anything thrown in there to shake things up. Of course, that’s if you exclude the survival mechanics, which feel like they were mostly incorporated to increase the length of the game rather than to add anything meaningful to the experience. While the goal may be to activate these pillars and progress along this story, you’ll have to make numerous stops along the way to find food, stock up on supplies, and ensure that your character doesn’t die of exhaustion.Yes, that’s core to what makes a survival game work, but when your character needs 5+ meals a day just to keep going, it does become a bit annoying. Food expires over time in your inventory, so it isn’t like you can just stock up on it, you have to constantly visit islands just to hunt for your next meal. And in order to get those meals, you’ll have to engage in the game’s awful combat mechanics. You would think that a survival game would put in a bit of effort there, but here in Windbound, the combat is pretty much just “attack” and “dodge”. Attacking is simple enough, but dodging can really feel clunky at times, and it often felt like I was getting hit by attacks that I should have easily been able to dodge in time. The finicky lock-on feature is definitely not helping either.What makes all of this even worse is that, if you do end up dying because of the clunky combat (or any reason for that matter), the game hits you with the roguelike classic of restarting the entire thing over again from the very beginning. And no, not just the beginning of the area you are in, but the very beginning of the entire game, losing your boat, story progress, and contents of your inventory in the process. Normally, in a good roguelike, there is some sort of progression here to make the next run easier, or at least make it feel at least somewhat different from the last run, but in Windbound that is simply not the case.I could go several hours and make some really good progress only to die because the game’s lock-on and dodge failed me and got me one-shot by a giant animal. I would then have to proceed and activate all the pillars again, collect a new set of supplies, and build an entirely new boat. Sure, I could change the difficulty to “storyteller” so I only have to restart at the beginning of the chapter I was in rather than the whole game, but I still lose my boat and any progress I made in that chapter, which could equate to hours. It’s like the game took these roguelike elements without realizing what makes those elements work.And on the topic of sailing, there are a few issues there as well. The sailing in general feels okay, but I found that most of the time I was sailing into the wind, which makes it really painful to get to the next island as you have to constantly tack in order to get any speed. What’s really odd is that you lose the ability to row your boat once you attach a sail, which would have been very helpful when traveling against the wind.So while Windbound may have some good ideas, the overall experience just isn’t worth it. It feels more like a mess of things thrown together without any of those things having the depth necessary in order to make a fun video game. The combat is barebones and clunky, the survival mechanics feel tacked-on, and the core game loop just isn’t satisfying. You activate a pillar, sail to another island, collect food, activate another pillar, and repeat this process over and over all while trying not to lose it all to some unfair death. I could see this maybe working as an Early Access title, but this is being sold as a full, finished product, and I cannot in good faith recommend it.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Generally speaking this game could be interesting. Graphically it certainly has enough to offer.Problem is the combat, it's stiff and unresponsive. I'll just mention one thing that'll serve as a good example to let you get a feel for what I mean:I'm fighting a small boar-looking thing. It's turning to me, while I'm already winding up my sling. As it begins charging towards me, I release the rock and it flies true and hits the thing in the head. Cool, that felt good. But the boar is still charging to me, so I hit A to dodge. Nothing's happening. I keep spamming the dodge button, but I'm sure not dodging, so I get hit by the boar and knocked over. After getting up, I test the dodge, and it works just fine. So, wtf?Turns out that throwing that rock locks you into a recovery animation that lasts way too long. Why? I dunno. That type of animation-locking hasn't been part of action combat for a while now, because the devs figured out it feels terrible. It's still used very selectively, after specific very big attacks or to give a weapon a specific identity (Monster Hunter: World is a great study in this), but Windbound does not handle it properly.Frankly I got turned off by this unresponsive combat immediately. I barely spent one hour playing the game. I don't feel like I can even approach a fight, because taking any action will get me locked in place as if I had been stunned, leading to my death.Until they add animation-canceling, I'm probably not gonna try again.That said, I do see the potential. If they can fix my biggest issue, the terrible animation-locking, then I'd continue playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Windbound is a very beautiful game and i strongly recommend to play it (with controller).Atmosphere, sailing physics, sounds, character- world- and menu-design and animation are fantastic.Crafting your catamaran and sailing into the sunrise using the precisely working sailing and ocean physics is highly enjoyable!The multiple possibilities and combinations in boat crafting are interesting and fun to try out.Why are there so many bad and bad-ish reviews then?We have developed the general idea that, if something doesn't work the we we've tried it... we solve that problem by trying it the same way, but harder! giving up after 5 to 10 repetitions, totally frustrated.If something doesn't work a certain way... what about trying a different way?This is a game about those different ways.In some points it is like the "Ancestors" game which i also liked much. You have to find out how ingame mechanics works.Anticritics:____________First, windbound is often said to be very unforgiving:If you think you can rush into the first wild boar and kill it with one stroke of your tiny start knife...yes, this survival game will not forgive this. Same as in any good soulslike.How about a amnually savegame before trying something that could turn out deadly?Unnerving constant need to find food? If you don't like that, don't buy the game. Instead of buying it and moaning afterwards.Read the description before buying the game.You don't go to a fish restaurant and complaining that there is no rumpsteak at the menu, do you?Many moans about no/far to few food:Yes, hunting the few quick and/or strong animals on islands will cost energy and resources or your life. This is a sea game. Ever looked for fish? Keeping an eye on fish from the start and there is no hunger any more!Small fish can be found around ANY island, even the tiny ones and will not try to kill you.Too few bag slots?Erm... what exactly did you expect? Ingame philosophy sais: nomads don't need more than they can carry.If you craft the first bag and boat basket at first opportunity (1st chapter, 2nd island) there is room enough.You still have to make desicions about what to take and what to leave and thats exactly whats the game is about.Dropped stuff will stay were it is so you can get it back later.Yes, its not zelda, where you can carry 20 weapons, some 100 bits n bobs, a whole dressroom and 40 meals at the same time.Too few resources?Exactly, and you have to deal with that. The game gives opportunities and yes, you have to find a workaround.That is called survival.Clunky fight mechanics?Not at all. Again, if you think you can kill whatever prey or enemy just by hack'n'slay, yes, you will die.Its simply not meant to be played like this. Use dodging! And be quick and careful as the game advises. Again, savegames are your friend.Enemies don't follow you on most rocks and not into water so you're save there and you can even attac from there.Weapons braking all time easily?Yes, but there are unbraking bonus weapons early and even such that don't need ammunition (witches broom!)If youre not a hardcore survival fighter, look for soul slivers and get that broom stick at level 2! With that thing all fighting becomes nearly too easy! Especially, if you combine it with fishing.No sailing against the wind?Sorry, ask any sailor: sailing against the wind simply IS not possible.This is not an unnerving bad game mechanic but precise sailing physics. You can sail cross-wise with tight sails quite easily.Boat "poffed" away out on the ocean and you drowned?Even the grass boat will not be destroyed by the first collision with a rock or riff. But maybe at the third hard collision.First, how about beeing careful?Second, the boat can be repared, even at sea. At a hard collision with a rock the boat will flicker red and will even show signs of destruction.Just check whether its needs repairs before hitting the next rock.Fiddling menus?Yes, handling the crafting and item menu can be bit fiddling at times but there are worse by far, even in games by big established game studios.__________________________________________________Did you give up the first time frustrated? Play it again. Why? You get your achievement bonus weapons of the first run from the start!And the levels/islands are kinda random/different with each new start.So if you got e.g. the unbrakeable bow at level 2 but did quit the game frustrated, give the game a second chance and start a new game overwriting the old savegame.You start with that bow, now everything starts much easier. Choose the broomstick at chapter 2,hold on to fishes and enjoy that wonderful game!

_childDocuments_.review: The 7 hours I've played at the time of writing this review was all in one sitting. This game is incredibly underrated and I'm shocked that so many people would complain about that combat system and difficulty of the game, to the point it has "mixed" reviews.Easily one of my new favorite singleplayer survival games. From what I've seen thus far, it deserves a seat alongside games like The Flame in the Flood EASILY.Pros:-Music is really nicely done and fits dynamically with environments and various enemies.-The movement system is phenomenal. Beautifully done IK bones and transitions for all sorts of traversal.-Physics are spot-on for the boat play, and it ties well into the movement system mentioned above.-The story and atmosphere are very well done and ties perfectly into the brutal yet beautiful gameplay (themes of life, death, and acceptance of a challenging but simple life)-Lovely details added all over the place. Every single item has thought put into it and how it fits with the world.-Superb pacing and progression.Cons:-It may be too brutal and difficult for some, but they have an "adventure" mode which removes the permadeath aspects from the game so it's really up to the player there-Any tiny thing that might be frustrating can be amplified by the unforgiving nature of the game. Maybe pass on this one if you're easily frustrated.-You are reset VERY far back if you die, which means in some cases you may die from your very first encounter with an enemy type because you don't yet know its move set. In my mind this is immersive but I can see how it could be upsetting or annoying to some.-Difficult to get enough inventory space for everything you need/want.Overall thoughts: This game rewards careful, methodical gameplay. You play at your enemies disadvantages and you NEVER step out of line to put yourself at a disadvantage. In my mind, this core concept of combat is one of the best things a survival game can achieve, and Windbound does this well.

_childDocuments_.review: Very hard to put not recommended but its just way to little of a game for what they are charging.Pros- A very good sailing/boat building sim. Wind direction, waves, dangers at sea are very similar to atlas and sea of thieves.-Graphics are polished and the game runs very well. Animals AI is well done with animals sometimes attacking and sometimes running away. Combat for the most part is designed well with you having to put thought into each fight or risk dying.-Very good sound track. Immersive cut scenes and some explorationCon's-Very short and not worth 30 dollars. The amount of content is laughable. Its build a boat/upgrade your boat and move to the next chapter. They added endless mode which is fine if it actually added something else to the game to do.-Survival mechanics are worse than games like subsistence. The second you are on a boat plan on going hungry and always having to look for food. This mechanic alone removes a lot of reason to explore vs move to the next chapter.-Other than island hope for towers to move the story further along there is little reason to actually explore a map zone. The only things to find so far are their currency to buy additional powers or find a treasure map to get a new power added. Then when you complete a chapter equip that new power etc. The islands change visually but thats the end of it. Its the same graphics with a new color palette and similar animals to hunt.-This game suffers an identity crisis. Does it want to be a survival game or does it want to be breath of the wild? It needs to commit to one of the two as its lite on both aspects. Shipbuilding, hunting, crafting basic gear, and eating is about all the survival mechanics in the game. While finding X tower is about all there is for a story. Its boring very quickly as you know what to expect each chapter over and over again.-Basic small patches to their game they advertise as free DLC's. This are very slim patches and the first thought in my mind is conditioning their playerbase to pay real money for slim future content. There so called free DLC's are literally an outfit and a few bug fixes with a few revamps. With the high price for what little content you get mixed with this you can easily tell this company only cares about money and not an actually game.If it was cheaper like 10 bucks it would be worth the money. In its current state mixed with their shady way of claiming small patches are actual DLC's this game is just not worth it. Its cute and a chill adventure/survival game but offers very little at all to do long term and all other games in each genre this game mimics is done way more polished and better overall.

_childDocuments_.review: WindBond has a good prmise, an interesting idea and a cool setting. The sound and the graphics are cool, buty for me there's two major throwback that made me put down the controller and see if I could have a refund. The first problem clearly reside in the lack of content. The islands arte way too similar to one an other, and you'll be doing the same thing over and over. Which is not a problem for me generrally : I love roguelike. But here it doesn't feel rewarding, because of the lack of content. The roguelike mechanics feel more shoehorned than a core mechanic of the game. The second is the delay in attacks and the bland machanics for combat. There's often a delay in the way the character reacts because of the animation, and it would be fine if you had other weapons to adapt you strategy or find something more fitting your playstyle; but there's 4 weapon,s and it's pretty much : 2 almost useless (knife and slingshot) , 1 very slowly animated (spear) and 1 overpowered (Bow). This game could have been awesome, and I love the idea behind it. But it just feels like a (very) early release.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really interested in this game when I first saw it. The Wind Waker feeling from the old days, the light touch from Breath of the Wild... It looked like a game that cribbed a lot of things and used them for itself. This is generally not a bad thing, because you don't have to reinvent the wheel. But it takes too many things that you can't use.I have now played 1 hour (30min online and what counts for the playing time) and I have no idea who I am, what I do, what my goal is and where I am. You get to know sequence snippets of story, which is told by text. There is no storytelling, no dialogues. It is simple building and survival. I don't expect games to take me by the hand - I really don't. But I don't expect nothing to happen either.The main character is hungry 24/7, of course it's a woman ;) Women are always hungry, but I never thought you could eat so much without being done. The music is wonderful but I simply miss the goal storywise. The fighting system is not original and when I am getting asked what makes this game so unique... I would say: "nothing"?It is a building system like in any other game, survival aspects like in any other game, just more annoying... it doesn't do anything new or original. Nothing stands out or makes Windbourne so great. After I've reached the 6th island which nearly looked the same i stopped playing. The same goals I had in chapter 1 - repeated itself in chapter 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Meh, kinda trashy.Graphics, music, the design of the main character are really nice.. that's about it.Combat system is wonky as hell.Resources are scarce. i know it's a survival game, but still... you have to travel between islands to be able to gather resources. Maybe cool in the beginning, gets extremely tedious and frustrating on the long run, especially since sailing is just not fun.Food gets rotten in like a minute or so.You die, you get thrown into the middle of the ocean and all your progress (whatever it really is.. lighting up some towers or what) gets erased.Ship can get destroyed in a blink of an eye. All the stuff you might have collected and put in the basket on it will vanish with it into oblivion.As soon as you put on the mast you can no longer raw, meaning no wind you stuck in one place. _childDocuments_.review: * Super clunky, 3rd person fighting is very bad* Stamina mechanic is awful, it's essentially non-existent* Why can't you row when you have a sail and just put the sail down?* Inventory too small to start, even with a bag added* Why does she have to brush her knees off every time she stands up from crafting. _childDocuments_.review: Really disappointed in the game.Refunding it. Claiming to be 40 hours worth of content in the game, where's the other 38?Check the achievements. I got the "Finish the game" achievement. Pros:The music and art design are just perfect.Cons:Everything else. This game is just a dearth of activity. Aside from building your catamaran there is nothing else to do in this game. The gameplay loop is to climb (jump) on 3 different 40 foot tall pillars on 5 levels. (3 pillars per level.) Then you go to a yellow pillar and push buttons so the stairway comes up from the ocean for you. You then sail through a tunnel and see a sea monster poke its head out of the water and look at you before going back down. The story (Spoilers) I thinkAs another review wrote, it's the typical indie ambiguous story where there was a civilization that worshiped beings that came from the sky and fell in the ocean, offering them gifts before receiving drinks that made them get extra abilities I guess or go mad. Eventually there was a war or the sea monsters felt they weren't being worshiped enough and destroyed the civilizations. The game ends with you bringing the sea monsters babies to it and as a reward the sea monster sends you back to your people but the babies are in the water too. Possibly repeating the cycle. Improvements I would like to see:Essentially my problem is that we can't build cabins on our boat. My hope was to be able to build a bedroom on my boat that I could sleep in while my boat sails the seas. Unfortunately all you get is the typical flat platform that coasts on the water. The game is very similar to Raft from 2 years ago, where sea critters just slowly bite away at your boat. You can build spikes & armor for your underside of the boat and it just fractionally makes your boat stronger. Just like sharks in Raft, lobsters in Windbound can eat wood. Overall:I don't like this game. I'm going to refund it, but I'm giving it a thumbs up because it's doing something different. It's a step in the direction of where I'd like to see games go. Building boats, sailing the seas. That was fun. It's just like most games that try something different, there isn't much meat on the bone. I plan to buy this game again someday when it is on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game. You quickly get introduced to the crafting aspect of the game, though I was only able to build one fire... I mean... the game would never let me build another one. I had a few weird moments when I saw an Elk looking creature jump off a cliff... but it got stuck on nothing and so it floated there, saw me, and then the combat music activated, but we just kept staring at each other. Or I actually think I'm just going to delete the game off my computer...The combat is the weakest part of the game... but then again... I thought I could just find level ground and then it'd let me... but no... everywhere was off limits.The art design is fine.The sound effects are good.I hated the music, though some reviews say that they enjoyed it. I just felt it was disjointed and weird.And most of the time, to progress in the game, you need to climb the same stupid tower that's been copied and pasted all over the map and you want to blow your brains out because you're wondering "why isn't this game fun?" and then you touch some stupid sea shell and then a bright light shines in the sky and then you repeat three times. _childDocuments_.review: I honestly think this game gets too much bashing and it needs some more love. Yes it is challenging and frustrating, but that just means it is not for everyone. I think the best way I can put it is: Type A: quick gratification, progression is gradual and satisfying. Once geared enough, you can walk right up to a boss and slap them silly without any fear. Type B: The game will give you a survival knife, a pep talk in the form of a cryptic riddle and drop you off in the woods. A year later no matter how hardened you are, you slack and you will get mauled by a mob you've killed many times. You must always be vigilant, always calculating. When you succeed, you feel like it was earned through blood, sweat and tears. Windbound is much more of a Type B type of game, though not as unforgiving as some other survival games out there. There are some tricks and you just have to play smart. I am not great at games and it took me a long time to get good enough to just not die. I think I was stuck on chapter 4 for like 3 streams in a row, but boy did it feel great to finally complete the game. Complicated mechanics and inventory management aside, the game also has a rather morbid storyline. If you take the time to read it you will see it sets quite a dark undertone. That, and probably the countless hours I spent trying not to be awful at the game, have definitely formed some fond memories of Windbound for me. Lastly I would like to say that the sound design and soundtracks are fantastic. It's not every day you hear throat singing in a game, but it fits so well.All in all a huge thumbs up from me. Tentatively recommended, as it is indeed a hit or miss depending on the person.
_childDocuments_.name: Windbound

_childDocuments_.review: This really is one of those games that has the potential to be so much better if it had a lot more polish in places it needs it to be. Everything about this game is so needlessly clunky and bad that I really wish it was better because I like the idea of improving your boat and going from island to island as you slowly progress. The combat takes some getting used to but it's so clunky and unwieldy that it just feels awful fighting anything. I hate that you can't simply upgrade certain things like your boat and its pieces. You're literally expected to build an entirely new boat when you reach the next tier and then you have to dismantle your previous boat to get the materials back. This is made especially annoying when you're trying to upgrade the storage on your boat but with a limited inventory on yourself that means either making another storage on land and moving everything there or just dismantling it and letting your items float around and then build the new one and juggle your inventory trying to put everything away again. Some sort of ability to move pieces or a way to replace them and dismantle them at the same time would make everything so much better, yet its not. Full price, probably not worth it, I've barely played much of it and it just isn't fun dealing with how janky everything about this game feels.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure: I played this game on Adventure difficulty.I enjoyed WIndbound. It's an easy-going, survival game with enough to keep you entertained for a little while. It is peaceful at times, but can also be tense and that adds a bit more flavour to the whole thing. I liked the narrative, it wasn't anything groundbreaking but it was enough to keep your attention and pique your curiosity. I think the game is a pretty decent length, it knows how much content it has on offer and doesn't overstay its welcome.I'm not too sure why so many people didn't enjoy this game. I couldn't find anything fatally flawed about the game, but perhaps I'm missing something here. I think if you tried on survival mode and found it too difficult or frustrating, playing on Adventure difficulty might be more enjoyable for you. Games are about having fun after all, and if you're not having fun, you're doing it wrong. There's no shame in dropping the difficult for more enjoyment overall, that's what the different settings are there for.All in all, I think if you go in with reasonable expectations and a little patience, you'll enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: So far - I love it.Don't buy into the complaints about combat. Its just that combat is not easy, and very much soulslike. When you lock, you have parry, dash and attack - and of course, stamina. When you attack ranged, there's no lock, you have to estimate the distance and shoot above the target to hit it.Enemies are a bit tanky, yes, but nothing that can't be overcome with tiniest bit of patience and grace.Plus - the difficult combat makes the survival that more rewarding.Plus - when you play a normal difficulty, if you die, you lose every item except your handheld inventory, and start back at first chapter (you retain your special abilities).The sailing is simple, but has enough agency to remain fun.If there's a gameplay complaint I have, its that by chapter two, islands feel fairly small and uninteresting, but I just started chapter 2 (after dying once).The other complaint is related to a very weird feeling of mouse input filtering: it seems like mouse velocity affects how much you scroll in a non-linear fashion. I suppose this is made to help you precisely aim your ranged weapons - but it just feels odd until you get used to it.IMO - very much worth the cash.Also, if you try it, and happen to like it - I strongly recommend trying Outward as well, which has similar formula but is more soulslike and more of an RPG than a survival title.
