_childDocuments_.review: Fairly challenging ( in very unfair ways ) enemies knock you back into pits, tons of death blocks ( instant death )enemies take a bunch of hits to kill, plenty of intentionally placed hazards designed to make you pull your hair out.UNike the original release, this one removes the randomly generated Nerd swears when you die, and it saves you a lot of time getting back into the action. I have nearly completed AVGN1 ( just gotta beat Fred ♥♥♥♥♥ ) But I did check out the sequel a little bit to see what to look forward too.the sequel is WAY huger than this game, you get some smaller levels, but there;s tons and tons of em. You also get new powerups, like a wall jumping move similar to Megaman XThere's also some more gimmick stages, like riding on a crossfire piece through parts of a level, it's pretty neat.I'd say this is worth the dosh, it's fairly priced, there's some new bits and bobs ( and a couple boss replacements ) Also some newer content after you beat first and second game ( you may also hav to collect all the NERD carts in each level ( which appears ot be new ) The Ghost Mansion level on the first game is pretty ruthless, I lost more live there than anywhere else, mostly due to how dark it is. And the boss was a pain as well.Ben having a blast dying over and over as I learn the stages - each time, getting slightly farther than before.there's 5 difiiculty settings ( I stuck with old school, feels appropriate ) and they basically change how many lives you have, and continues as well.Iirc, the hardest difficulty gives you 1 life, andno continues - truly old school.HIghly recommend this, and if anything else comes up while playing the sequel, and the newer content - I'll add it to the bottom.Quick break down for AVGN 2 and TowerMore levels, but smaller and more focused - 3 per area, plus a final boss level ( with NERD carts in each but boss ) The upgrade system should be explained better, as it makes most of the game a lot easier.  ( for example, in monster madness, there's an entire section where the pit is covered in hidden blocks you only get with the head scanner ) Bosses weren't too difficult ( aside of Tower ) Fred F's final boss was WAY easier to beat this time around, due to rng giving me to mecha jesus powerup attacks in a rowI think overall, AVGN1 is the better game, it encapsulates the old school feeling well, while AVGN 2 brings more modern implementaitons to the series ( and shorter levels means much easier to tread ) The tower bonus content is pretty much just an additional level for AVGN 2, so 3 more hard as balls levels + a final final boss ( which was very fun )The levels there iomplemented everything in the entire 1 + 2 , and I enjoyed that.I think AVGN 2 is a bit tougher to 100%,  but I think overall level design shines in favor of AVGN 1.AVGN 2 had me getting frustrated with each death ( especially in virtual insanity ) while AVGN 1 had me chompin at the bit to retry when I died. overall, I still recommend this remASStered pack.Two slight complaints the audio mixing seems to be done poorly here, and if you play over 144 FPS, you just invented a new difficulty mode - bc the game doesn't work as it should when you play above 60 fps. This includes ( but not limited to ) being thrown back further on hit, powerups dealing incorrect damage, and wall jump in AVGN2 not working properly. A slight mar on an otherwise fantastic game collection.Here's hoping we get to bring the NERD out of hell in AVGN in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the most mixed I have felt in awhile.This game is definitely based on those old NES games... even to their faults of poor design at times. (All perfects on all levels still pending)Out of the two, I recommend AVGN2 on Old School while I only suggest AVGN1 Old School if you're into those types of harder retro styled games. In general, AVGN2 is the better game here, and the new chapter they added has good levels as well (the addition of Bugs B- I mean 'The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rabbit' adds an additional AVGN element that was missing before).Try this game with caution.Good things:- Music is really good, whoever they got knew what they were doing for the OST of both games (Tower of Torment has some of the best tracks).- The main movement controls are pretty good, the lock-on button for aiming makes shooting easier to perform.- The level tilesets and backgrounds have some really nice pixel art to them, all of the new art in AVGN1 is such an upgrade.- Most of the boss fights are fairly fun once you learn how they work (Not a fan of the boss in Boo! Haunted House.)- Stages can be really fun to play due to their stage gimmicks and theming, AVGN2 has much more variety in stages.- Difficulty options as well as an Auto-Fire option help tame the difficulty or add to it depending what you're looking forIssues:Some of the mechanics are inconsistent which can cause frustration with the type of game this is.-Walljumping doesn't always grab onto a wall when trying to reach for one.- Walking on stairs while aiming messes with how you move on them.- Cape gliding sometimes doesn't work which can get you killed.- Some stage hazards have different timing depending on how you load them in.- Shooting next to the beams in the final level of AVGN1 causes you to get killed by it.- I also found a bug where I broke B.S Man's animation statesThe biggest issue is what they were going for and fully intentional with how they did it, however intention doesn't fully justify bad game design choices.The game has very poor enemy and hazard placement in a good amount of screens in the levels (Just because it's intentional doesn't justify it.) _childDocuments_.review: I've been watching some AVGN videos recently, including the 20 minute video released late November in 2020, that discussed the work that went into creating The Angry Video Game Nerd I & II Deluxe (AD). The video made it seem like this was a passion project, where more creativity was instilled into the process of blending both games into a definitive version. As another benefit, the developer learned from making other games, which would further tighten up the gameplay and level design. Surely this must have made a big impact on the final product. At least, that was the impression I got from the video, but how much of that was just hype or self-aggrandizing for the new release?Appropriately enough, AD plays similarly to NES era run and gun platformers, with the benefit of being able to play the stages in whatever order you wish. The first game has nine stages that end with boss fights, all built around a retro game theme, such as spooky monsters, and even more terrifying, Hell itself. In the second game, there are five small worlds, made up of three stages, followed by a separate boss fight. I believe what led to this change is that more stages allow for more versatility, as it's easier to build game mechanics that will be maintained throughout the level when it's smaller. For instance, with the second game, some stages are particularly short because it's an auto-scroll or chase level, whereas the first game's longer stages occasionally switched to a SHMUP section, before returning to normal again. When I played with my controller, AD seemed responsive and was reading my inputs correctly. One aspect I didn't like is that I have to rapidly mash 'X' to fire weapons instead of being able to hold the button down. There's a reason for that in the second game, but that could have been included with the first one. Otherwise, I find the controls work pretty well, as I didn't find the controls slippery or laggy.Some changes were made to the story, with most of them pertaining to the second game. All references to the AVGN movie were replaced with the antagonist from the first game, as Fred is trying to thwart a machine he made that's turning the real world into lousy games. Otherwise, both games follow the AVGN getting into antics with games going awry at the hands of his nemesis, Fred, before concluding with a fight against that rascally rabbit in the additional area made for the deluxe version. It's not Shakespeare or anything, but redirecting the 2nd game's story to fit a larger, more consistent narrative, was the right choice. Overall, I'd say that the game looks pretty good. The pixelated visuals provide plenty of detail due to good shading, with backgrounds supporting the atmosphere of each themed world. However, I found that this was undermined in certain parts of the 2nd game, as they'd be ruined by effects. For instance, the Cinemassacre inspired levels utilize a grainy effect on top of removing the color, which simply doesn't look good. The Nerd Gaiden levels and the autoscrolling Board James level put in so many visual elements, such as lightning bolts, enemy spam, and neon signs that it oversaturates the screen. Even for someone who likes bold colors, I find the color scheme of Alien 52 incredibly harsh. It's such a waste of otherwise quality visuals.The sound track for AD is solid, and I think many of them would qualify as chip tunes. Instead of using conventional instruments, the beats and music is built with sound effects. I notice a different emphasis between the 1st and 2nd games, as the 1st seemed a bit more constrained in its use of noises, so though they both sound pretty good, the 2nd one has more range. There were only a few songs amongst them all I didn't care for, which isn't uncommon for any musical composition. Similarly with the sound effects, a few could have been improved upon, but they otherwise do the job, and I wouldn't have much reason to complain.🌟 Theoretically, patches will be released so you can see more information on the overworld. For instance, which stages you missed secrets on.🌟 If you really liked the original games, at the very least, this is slightly better than they were.❌ The boss fights were really unbalanced, particularly in the 1st game. Some of them don't seem to behave consistently or have a defined pattern. For instance, Hyde would jump at random intervals and heights, and even tire out at different times instead of after a set number of moves. The green head initially follows an infinity symbol loop, but as you blast away the heads, its pattern disintegrates completely, and I couldn't find a way to dodge it consistently. ❌ Since the AVGN focuses on playing lousy games, I think some traps are made because it's supposed to be the jerk developer purposely screwing over the nerd. Including a few of these tongue-in-cheek cheap tricks fits the motif. However, I also think the crappy game mindset is used to justify lackluster design choices or oversights, “That was done on purpose. Probably?” 🔍 Many threats, including enemies, are made inert or much easier if you move forward incrementally. Instead of jumping all the way forward to kill an enemy, shoot it from a distance. I'd say this was intentional if it didn't completely neuter some encounters, and simply make them a waste of time. 🔍 Unless you have previous experience with these games, I'd suggest going for Normal difficulty on the first playthrough. That way you don't have to worry about restarting a level from the very beginning if you die too many times. 🔍 Due to the way the secrets are hidden in the game, it's probably easier if you just look up a guide in advance. It'd save a significant chunk of time.Frankly, I found myself disappointed by AD. It's clear that improvements were made to how the first game looks, and the rebalanced difficulty options helps make the game more accessible and less frustrating. Also, the ascent up the Tower of Torment is a nice inclusion to give the package deal more value, but with it ending on a cliffhanger, it seems more like a way to shoehorn in a connection to a concluding sequel. Since this was supposed to be an improvement on the original games for a definitive, all in one package, I can't help but think that other changes could have been made. Looking at AD, the price is the same as if you were to buy both original games at full price. Even if it were cheaper, I'd still find $10 steep for a game that can easily be finished in an afternoon. Like games of old, the playtime relies on difficulty and players intentionally challenging themselves with repeated attempts on harder difficulty settings, as there's not much content. Seeing as how level design and boss fights could have used more work and refinement, I don't see how this is a deluxe version of the AVGN games. There's enough quality here to say that they didn't just polish a turd, but I wouldn't recommend getting it either.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a fan of the Angry Video Game Nerd (or, "AVGN", for short) since I first saw his angry game reviews on YouTube during the summer of 2006. At the time, I was going through an extremely bad breakup and was feeling incredibly depressed and hopeless. However, upon watching AVGN's review of the original TMNT on NES (his first video I ever saw), I found myself laughing at the crude, vulgar humor. While it did not make me feel completely better, it at least cheered me up a little bit. In fact, it inspired me to check out his other game reviews and, to this day, I never get tired of watching them. Without a doubt, AVGN/James Rolfe is one of my favorite YouTubers of all time and his warped sense of humor never ceases to amuse me. For the longest time, I had seen footage of "Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures" and "Angry Video Game Nerd II: ASSimilation", but put myself off from playing them, myself. I am glad I finally decided to try them out! Admittedly, I never played the original versions of these games, so I decided to simply buy this Deluxe Edition. I was NOT disappointed!For only $10, you are getting TWO games for the price of ONE, and it is well worth it! Both titles consist of classic old-school 8-bit/16-bit sprite designs, catchy music, clever level designs, and challenging (but fair) game play. In addition, some of the levels also made me feel nostalgic for the days of when I would play Super Nintendo with my siblings or regular Nintendo over at a friend's house (The Castlevania-esque stage, humorously titled, "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥", comes to mind). Although I DID die multiple times, most of the time, it did not feel cheap or unfair. In fact, there were more than enough checkpoints to help me get by. Furthermore, I loved collecting all of the secrets in each stage (including the letters to spell 'NERD' and hidden playable characters that can be unlocked) and the bosses were very fun to fight. Of course, the humorous elements worked perfectly!While playing through the first installment, I could not help but laugh several times at the crude jokes, which truly captured the spirit of the AVGN show (the "Blizzard of Balls" stage especially had me cracking up). The dialogue (spoken by AVGN/James Rolfe and the enemies/bosses) was also utterly hilarious from start to finish! Truth be told, I needed a good laugh today and after completing the 'AVGN Adventures', I can now easily say that it most definitely did the trick! Now I need to go and play the sequel, 'ASSimilation'.Containing classic sprite designs, an addicting soundtrack, nicely constructed levels, and challenging (but fair) gameplay, this is, undoubtedly, one of the best platformers I have EVER played! If you are a longtime fan of AVGN (like me), do NOT hesitate. Get this collection NOW!EDIT: Played through all of AVGN II. I thought it was just as fun as the original! I truly do hope that there will someday be a third installment.

_childDocuments_.review: Game play is pretty much how it plays from the 2nd game throughout all 3 games, don't expect original AVGNA physics. It plays really good and responsive. Last Chapter is a pretty short addition to this remake, features some AVGN references as well and has new music remixed throughout the levels, it's really good. Easy mode this time is really easy. A lot of the death blocks you've known to despise are now spikes that simply damage you. The good thing is you can go through them too ;)The invincibility frames are drastically shorter this time, an odd decision as the same enemy / spikes can knock you back and while you're holding forward it'll damage you again, it can get frustrating at times. As far as calling it a remake, yes the original AVGNA game was redesigned to play and feel like the 2nd game, with some graphical changes. The 2nd game only has 1 level that was majorly changed, and some small details altered here and there, but it's pretty much the exact same game as the original. The 3rd Chapter adds 3 new platforming stages and a final boss battle, you can consider it an extra world for AVGN II as it uses the progress data from that game to know which upgrades you have collected.Overall, the price for this remake is worth it whether you owned or are new to the series.To anyone else, have you found the hidden path to get Mike without Guitar Guy yet ;) ?

WORSE than CrazyBus or Desert Bus! It is known as Hong Kong 97, and I've been getting requests for it up the ass. This is one title that we DEFINITELY didn't get on the Super Nintendo.​The Nerd: It was made by (he speaks in a false happy tone) HappySoft. HappySoft was most famous for making... (he speaks in a true serious tone) Hong Kong 97, their one and only "masterpiece". (scene switches to an animated scene of HappySoft, rising from a fiery pit, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out Hong Kong 97) On this one occasion, they rose from the depths of Hell, EXCRETED this unholy turd onto the Earth and then descended back to where they came! It's SO rare that to this day, not a single cartridge or physical copy has shown up at all! I can't even find a PICTURE of one! The Nerd is surprised.)​The Nerd: Nooooooooo! No way! (chuckles) How do you like THAT soundtrack? THAT won't get annoying at all! I've heard games with 5-second music loops before, but... not with LYRICS! There's options for three different languages. Strange, considering how the game didn't travel very far, at least not until the Internet got ahold of it. Alright, I'm picking English. (reading) "We will sell your original S-NES [sic] games, 1/3 of the gross profit will be yours. We welcome games of any kind." Oh, I bet. "So please send us your floppy." (chuckles) Hee-hee, send us your floppy. "Would you like to sell our products at your store? We are looking for dealers worldwide." Enough already! How desperate could they be to sell this game? And I guess still nobody bought it because nobody can find a physical copy! Then finally the title screen appears. (laughs) Jackie Chan?! Apparently, Jackie Chan is in the game! Who I doubt gave any consent to HappySoft, or was even AWARE of it. The image is stolen from the film Wheels on Meals. The game was released, uh, made, or at least copyrighted in 1995, but set in the future... of 1997.​The Nerd: "The year 1997 has arrived. A herd of..." (stops, sees the text saying "a herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥' ugly reds") This can't be real. No. NO! Somebody's pullin' my leg! A herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ugly reds?! Was "A herd of ugly reds" too weak? Did they really need the F-word to ♥♥♥♥♥♥' drive home the ♥♥♥♥♥♥' point?! This was before cursing in games was common. I remember how shocked I was when I first played Rambo on NES and saw the word "Hell." But here, they dropped the F-Bomb! THEY DID IT! A game made for the Super Famicom! (scene cuts to Mario flying past the Super Nintendo logo, with the word "♥♥♥♥" appearing on screen) It's the closest you'd ever get to a Super Nintendo game that says "♥♥♥♥"!(The 5-second loop of "I love Beijing Tiananmen" continues.)​The Nerd: And the music is still goin'. (blankly bobs his head side to side to the music before he continues reading) "A herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥' ugly reds. Period. Are rushing from the mainland. Crimes rates skyrocketed! Hong Kong is ruined! Therefore, the Hong Kong government called Bruce Lee's relative, Chin." Bruce Lee's relative. Just HAPPENS to be as skilled as Bruce Lee. Not a brother, a son, or even a cousin. Just some unspecified relative. Doesn't make any sense. Like, if you were related to... I don't know, Michael Jordan, would that mean that you're automatically good at basketball? OK, so Bruce Lee is in the background, the guy at the podium is Chris Patten, former governor of Hong Kong, and over there is Jackie Chan. Which one is "Chin"? (he keeps reading more) "For the massacre of the reds. Chin is a killer machine." That's Chin?! (laughs at the irony) Is Jackie Chan playing Bruce Lee's relative, Chin?! Ohhhh, Chin! What a name! Could it be any more common?! (groans and resumes reading) Ohhhh, "Wipe out all 1.2 billion of the red communists!" (laughing) Stop! I can't- I can't take anymore! I haven't even seen the game yet! Ohhhh-ho-ho-ho! Ohh! (laughing) Wipe out 1.2 billion people! (becomes serious again) And if I'm not mistaken, in 1995, that would have been the ENTIRE POPULATION OF CHINA! Bruce Lee's relative is SO powerful, he's the equivalent of a thousand nukes! He's gonna murder the entire population of China by breakin' their necks! Even when Bruce Lee would take down 20 people, it took him a little bit of time. But now comes Chin! You don't ♥♥♥♥ with Chin!​The Nerd: (reading) "However, in mainland China there was a secret project in progress! A project to de- tran- tran- (laughing) to transform the DECEASED Tong Shau Ping into an ultimate-" (laughs before finishing) It's killin' me! (sighs, and becomes serious again) So apparently, for the character of Tong Shau Ping, they used an ACTUAL IMAGE of a real Chinese leader, Deng Xiaoping! Couldn't they have at least had the courtesy to wait for him to die before transforming him into an ultimate weapon?! This is the most EPIC, ABSURD opening to any video game I've ever seen! However, on Jupiter's secret moon, a master plan is conceived to resurrect the astro-demonoid Dill Clyntin into a mecha-doomsday machine."​The Nerd: Now that I've digested all that, let's play the game. (The game begins, playing the 5-second loop of "I Love Beijing Tiananmen". Chin runs at the bottom of the screen shooting at enemies coming from the top. He gets hit and dies.) One hit, and the game's over. Why would I expect anything more? (A real surveillance image of a man lying motionless appears) NO... Oh, please. I hope that's not a real dead body. NO. This is almost as tedious as Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. The song never needs to reboot! It's quite impressive, actually! NOTHING can stop that loop! You'll be hearing that in your dreams!​The Nerd: So let's talk about what's happening here. Obviously, it's a 2D shooter. Nothing more to say. What ya see is what you get. Chin's only method of attack is throwing projectiles, because if you're related to Bruce Lee, that means you can shoot white balls. This guy's so good, he does it all with his back turned. _childDocuments_.review: While I'm a huge fan of AVGN, I'm not generally the type of person that gets a lot of joy out of a coat of paint that simply references something I like. For some reason there was a disconnect while playing this game, in that there were a ton of references to stuff I was familiar with, but none of it felt deep enough to actually connect with... more like pandering.To a certain degree this is probably inescapable when you're designing something based on an external IP, but it's a difficult feeling to shake that this game might not function on its own without the AVGN branding.For that reason I attempted to play these games mostly as pure platforming experiences, and to judge them based on their merits purely in that category.As a result, I feel like my ultimate verdict is to not recommend this package. The first game still holds up in a weird way, probably heavily benefiting from a secondary difficulty pass and extra modes. The second game, however, feels much more grating, and almost like it was designed to be difficult by someone or someones without a perfect understanding of what makes difficulty 'good'.An example of this is how cycle-based platforming works almost always in this game: you start at a save point and there is a set of obstacles in front of you that requires timing to navigate. The obstacles almost always start in the ON position, however, meaning that if there's one adjacent to your save point, and there almost always is, you will have to add an obligatory 3 second wait at the start of every single attempt you make from that savepoint.Because of the relative simplicity of the controls and mechanics, as well as the sometimes blatantly malicious level design, it was easy for me to compare this game to fangames of IWBTG and determine immediately there were things missing. An instant level or checkpoint button, for example, isn't in the default control mapping, so if you want to retry a checkpoint you'll have to kill yourself manually. You have the obligatory waiting periods, and the respawning is fast, but not instant, which adds up over time as well.When the platforming *isn't* cycle based it can be genuinely enjoyable in terms of the layout of the stages and enemy placement, but it also far more often devolves to mindless corridors of garbage mobs you're meant to blast or instant death auto-scrollers that suck time out with every failed attempt. The bosses are potentially interesting, but almost all of them have an incredibly small set of attacks, and there are random difficulty spikes in both games with one or two bosses having required waiting phases that make them take 4x as long as any other boss and also make them feel that much more frustrating.The third game added as a reward for beating the main two games is so short I feel it barely counts as content, and the extra boss that waits at the end is the worst in the entire game, involving long obligatory waiting periods and a vulnerability period that functions almost purely on how much beer you get via rng. It felt like there was legit nothing I could do to mitigate how random this boss's projectiles are, and when I finished the game I was much more relieved than happy or triumphant.My take is that as pure platformers, this game/pack of games has too many serious problems to be worth playing over something like Shovel Knight or Cyber Shadow or Gravity Circuit. All of those games are amazing examples of retro game design in action platformers, and the AVGN games are examples of purely regressive and clumsy design under the guise of retro. There is a difference between 'old' and 'retro', and also a difference between 'frustrating' and 'challenging', both distinctions which these games seem to struggle with.tl;dr: nyehhh, this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sucks! what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of ♥♥♥♥! nyehhhhh, what were they thinking? AAAASSSSSS♥♥♥♥ this game, watch it go

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10For what you get in this compilation, it is a very solid purchase. This game combines AVGN Adventures 1 and 2 and adds on a 15 minute long final area with more levels and challenges. I would strongly recommend buying this if you question which purchase to make.AVGN Adventures 1 & 2 are 2D action plattformers with a lot of focus on tight platforming and shooting. Lots of shooting. You play as The Angry Video Game Nerd, the famous character on YouTube. These games are naturally made for fans of the character and the media he appears in and a lot of references and gags lean in towards the fanbase. If you know nothing of the character or the media, I would recommend watching the show on YouTube first and see if the humor is your thing, otherwise the game might fly over your head. The gameplay is tight, with precise controls, adjustable difficulty and stages that are between 3-5 minutes long. If you only play to complete it, this entire bundle with last you about 3 hours maximum, but there are secrets to find and achievements to get. The soundtrack is nice and the presentation really nails the AVGN-universe. I had a good time playing this and I think it was well worth the price. Note that the gameplay is nothing fenomenal or groundbreaking, it is just a solid experience that lasts a few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent remaster of the first two games. The first game has been remade in the second game's engine (Unity) rather than the original (Clickteam Fusion), and it shows.The cameos from the original game have been replaced by "Future Nerds" who travel back in time to bring you weapons and upgrades from AVGN II. I feel like this change works well, and is a welcome addition. There was also a boss fight that got updated to reference a gag from another AVGN episode, though I won't spoil which one. The character sprites for the final boss have also been updated to reflect his depiction on the show.AVGN II seems to have had more changes than AVGN Adventures did. The aliens in the Area 51 stage now look different for some reason, as if it's trying to distance itself from the movie. I believe the boss sprites in that level were changed as well, but can't quite remember at the moment. The fight handled the same though. Some level names were also changed from the original AVGN II, and the story has been changed to remove the Nostalgia Critic and replace him with Fred.After you've finished both games, you unlock the Tower of Torment, a small set of new levels with a new final boss fight that's fairly amusing. This reminds me a lot of the Wily Tower from Mega Man: The Wily Wars.All in all, I feel this is a worthwhile update to the original games, with a few new surprises for those of us who have played through the original games.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game!! Sure it's difficult, but they changed it up enough to make it fun to play. I beat all 3 chapters in one sitting on the Nintendo Switch version.Pros:Cool Power-UpsInteresting Characters to switch between (in the first chapter)All the NERD Cartridges are easy to collect (in the first chapter).The Power Glove (in the second and third chapter) allows for a stronger, close-range attack and allows the Nerd to break through barriers.The Super Mecha Death Christ Power-Up really helps in the Final Tower in Chapter 2.You can choose how hard you want the game to be.You can control camera shaking and flashing lights.The F-Bombs are fun to throw.The level design changes made to the first 2 chapters really help even the most expert players.Cons:High difficulty (sometimes near impossible).I still can't find the BS Man in Chapter 1.You can't hold more than one item at a time (kegs, SMDC, etc.). I would be nice if you could switch between them.It's too easy to die if you're an absolute beginner.The Virtual Insanity level is the hardest of all the levels within any of the 3 chapters. I simply cannot perfect it.I can't find all the Nerd's armor. I'm still trying to find the Uber Scope and the Cape.Long story short: Play this game! It'll keep you entertained for hours on end.

_childDocuments_.review: This game WILL take you back to the past! Reawaken your old school platformer ptsd as you blast your way through some of, in my opinion of course, the best designed levels I've played since the great games of yesteryear.  The soundtrack is on par with the best of classic Mega Man tunes. The old school difficulty is definitely the way to play, keeping the tension high and at times bringing you to the point of rage quitting, until you finally get past the death block onslaught that's been tearing you to shreds. Or that boss you keep getting down to ALMOST zero health before being blasted into a fine pink mist. The payoff when you beat such a challenge feels amazing. I can recommend this game to anyone that want's to relive the fond memories of 8 and 16 bit action platformers, or anyone that enjoys a good challenge that never feels unfair. Not to mention the amount of references and jokes sure to please any fans of the Angry Video Game Nerd. Grab your Zapper, don your Power Glove, and blast your way through an absolutely fantastic gaming experience!

_childDocuments_.review: I originally bought the first game way back on the Nintendo Wii U and the difficulty was what I would consider to be very high but can be beaten in a weekend if you're used to castlevania and mega man for the NES. However, the updated the engine in this re-release and it completely changes the game (for the better). The first game has some quality of life changes in the difficulty options like changing some of the death blocks to spikes. You can land on them and take dmg, not die instantly, also easier to jump over imho. They also added a health regen item (beer keg) which was a nice touch. Second game was much of the same. I never got it when it originally came out so I cannot say what was updated. It appears, from where I have researched, that the first game got the most attention since it ran on a differnt engine and they wanted both on the same due to cost and convenience for developing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing this because I am a fan of the show. I am playing on easy. At first, that was really hard for me but then I got better but I'm still working on my first run though on easy so I can see everything.I never really played games like these very much because I was a computer gamer and we went from Duke Nukem the side-scroller to Wolfenstein 3-D pretty quickly, so, except for a brief stint of playing Donkey Kong Country on the Wii, I haven't really played a game like this.I would say the art is really good and engaging. The environments are fun. I only just finished the fourth environment in the first game which was a sort of homage to Doom,  think. It seemed to take place in Hell, at any rate. So each game, like all games there are power-ups and other things to do like collect the letters NERD, which I am familiar with from the first Duke Nukem game where you collected DUKE for an endgame bonus. I'm not sure if there is any bonus here except for the satisfaction of collecting all the letters. Maybe game content is opened later?You can also play as other characters when you find them. So far I have only found the guitar guy whose attack as  a musical wave which was needed to turn a gear that was out of the Nerd's range.There are also Easter eggs. I don't know how many but I found the pickle guy in the Hell level.The music is superb. I don't know if this is common for the types of games this game is parodying but it is just fun to listen to the music. It was especially good on the second environment which was called something like "Joy Town."This game does have a lot of toilet humor, which isn't my cup of tea, but the character is funny enough in spite of it, I cringe and move on.This game is for any adult who enjoys games and enjoys AVGN.

_childDocuments_.review: Contrary to what some say, you don't need to be a follower of the Angry Video Game Nerd on youtube. While, some of the jokes work better if you are a fan, this game is a homage to the 2D platformers that were criminally popular during the NES years. As a matter of fact, these games were so huge, that even the 16 bit era continued the development of more games in the genre. In addition, with all the nostalgia around, a lot of game developers have created "new old" games that follow the trend. This one being quite a decent one. This games work better for those who were around in those days, as you will recognize hundreds of nods to classic videogames. This "Deluxe" edition updates the graphics, soundtrack and some levels (plus a brand new unlockable game once you complete the first two) However, the most important update is playability. Some levels were nearly impossible in the older versions. Here, you have more balanced chances and even a difficulty setting. It's an excellent compilation. Make sure it's on your collection no matter how many ♥♥♥♥♥ you give about this heavily criticized youtuber.

I got through both remakes and the new tower added to the end. It's all just the perfect amount of hard to frustrate you sometimes, but never enough to want to give up. Every other screen, if there wasnt some new gross enemy, there was a quick hilarious reference to something the nerd has yelled about before. Solid game, great comical pacing, awesome challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid playing SNES I used to get so pissed with games that I threw my controllers at the wall.  I've never done it since but this game got me REALLY close to doing it again...That's not because it's a bad game but because it's a retro platformer made by people who clearly know what makes platformers great (and ♥♥♥♥♥♥).  It's everything that an old school platformer should be - you need quick thinking and quick reactions to beat the levels and you get a sense of achievement every time you nail a particularly tricky section.If you're a AVGN Nerd then the whole game is full of references to the show.  Some are subtle and some are blatant but you'll definitely get a kick out of them.  I can't remember the last time I laughed at a plaformer but when I saw Fred ♥♥♥♥♥ say "you were expecting maybe the Addams Family?" I LOLed at the screen.That's not to say the game is perfect.  There are some sections where I genuinly beleive that the game is more to do with luck than skill from the player. You just have to take a few hits and hope you have enough life left to get through. But then again sometimes you think the devs made a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decision and it turns out it was quite intentional.  An annoying autoscrolling level that is reference by the boss at the end of the stage about how annoying it is springs to mind.  Part of me thinks that this is maybe AVGN gettting revenge for being forced to play ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games for the last 10 years.But for anyone who grew up playing platformers like this it's an amazing throwback.  Big ass sprites, obnoxious music, garish colours, seizure inducing background animation, insane bosses... and the urge to throw your controller at the wall!9/10 Rotten Skunk ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: Not much to say, it's the great AVGN games we know and love! It's hard and sometimes it feels cheap but it's as if they were classic NES platformers but with the production standards of modern retrogames (as in the difficulty doesn't come from bad level design but from carefully calculated enemy and hazardous elements positioning). It looks and play amazingly but I do have some complaints about this game.It has a problem that I find very annoying with remasters: changing some aspects that makes the remaster somewhat different from its original counterpart. I'm talking about how all the cameos in the secret areas have been replaced by Future Nerd, which is amusing but I would've liked the option of playing with the original cameos. and there's also the fact that they replaced the Nostalgia Critic in AVGNA2 with Fred ♥♥♥♥♥, which I find disappointing. I feel like I'll have to finish the original to get the authentic experience.But overall, this is a fine game, worth getting if you have finished the previous ones some time ago and you feel like going back. I hope the ♥♥♥♥♥♥' Nerd gets more official videogames.

_childDocuments_.review: When i bought the original 2 AVGN games they were a shockingly great time...Excellent soundtrack, great gameplay mechanics, and awesome references to classic AVGN episodes. However the games, especially the first AVGN adventures game were not perfect, level designs were unforgiving at times and the dreaded instakill blocks were EVERYWHERE.This game smooths out all the issues i had with the original games making it the perfect AVGN fan game. name: The Making of Karateka
detailed_description: Prince of Persia creator Jordan Mechner was a college student when he created one of the biggest-selling games of 1984: Karateka. Now, in a new interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse, the story of how a teenager with an Apple II created one of the most groundbreaking, influential games of all time. THE ORIGIN STORY OF A LEGENDARY GAME CREATOR Discover how Karateka was made through an exhaustive archive of design documents, playable prototypes, and all-new video features. Like walking through a museum, you can explore the interactive timelines at your own pace. PLAY THE ACCLAIMED ORIGINALS Enjoy pixel-perfect versions of the original Karateka games and a variety of never-before-seen early prototypes, with rich quality-of-life features like save anywhere, rewind, chapter select, and director's commentary. TWO REMASTERED GAMES Karateka Remastered is an all-new version of the original game featuring cutting-room-floor content, commentary, achievements, and more. Deathbounce: Rebounded is a fast and frantic twin-stick shooter based on Jordan's unpublished prototype. A GROUNDBREAKING MASTERPIECE Discover how Karateka became one of the first games to include cinematic scenes, a moving original soundtrack, rotoscoped animation, and a Hollywood-style love story, influencing the decades of games that followed. THE GOLD MASTER SERIES New from Digital Eclipse (Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection, Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration), the Gold Master Series presents iconic games in an innovative 'interactive documentary' format, putting the shared history of games and their creators into one comprehensive package.

_childDocuments_.review: I've always thought more can be done with games as a medium, and this documentary game really highlights how much more can be done with some outside the box thinking. The execution of preserving the original game, telling its story, and making it comfortably playable on modern devices, with every single version they could find, is amazing. A game from almost 40 years ago, comfortable, and fun to this day, with the love and care that it (any many other games) deserve.This is a shining light of what game preservation needs to be going forward.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up: A really amazing documentary in interactive and playable format, containing multiple (prototype and final, with ports of Karateka as well) versions of Asteroids, Deathbounce, Karateka. The last two games also have reimagined versions, with Deathbounce being a real glowup. Thumbs sideways: One issue is that Karateka really is not a very fun game: a series of mirror matches with AI opponents and confusing hitboxes and hurtboxes, and you do have to learn how to cope with this in order to get anywhere.First conclusion: Thumbs up for the package, moreso than for the outdated game design... but this is museum piece, after all.Karateka Remastered thoughts: it's a much better version, EXCEPT for the panther fight. This gameplay is horribly unforgiving in terms of timing, taking the gate timing puzzle and just making it feel far worse to engage with successfully. HOW TO WIN - look up "The Making of Karateka Remastered Playthrough" on YT for the answer, and skip to 11:50.However, it's then redeemed somewhat by the improved bird fight in Level 3. The animation means that you can react with a kick correctly every time.The solution would simply be some kind of clue as to how to beat the panther, and fairer timing on getting through the gate without dying. I swear it doesn't work the same as the level 2 gate puzzle.Final conclusion: As a celebration of gaming, as a museum piece, as interactive history - amazing. As a series of fun games to play, not without issues. This is shown by how few people have the achievements for finishing the Karateka prototype / Apple II game / ports.Other thoughts: The initial Asteroids ripoff is considerably more fun to play than Deathbounce, and I can see why Deathbounce didn't lead to a published game. Just goes to show how it's not easy to design a 'simple' game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting and well-made interactive documentary about one of the most important titles of videogames' history, and the people who contributed to its creation and success, with also interviews with a few developers who were inspired and influenced by Mechner's masterpiece. There are also several games to play, including a few prototypes and complete versions, and two modern revisions of Karateka and Deathbounce, one of the very first games Mechner worked on before Karateka, but that was never published.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played Karateka as I was about 4 years too young for that at the time. But Prince of Persia sprung into my life on both my Amiga and on the PC's at my school. And I recall making animations in Deluxe Paint that mimicked what Mechner did in PoP. I loved that game.The distinct "flat" style was a particular thing I loved about it. And I also recall being incredibly disappointed with PoP2 which had a very odd and much more cartoonish style. I didn't like that game at all.But I've since learned of Karateka and appreciate what it did for computer games. And this interactive telling of the story is a perfect way to learn about the story behind it.I've seen the rotoscoping material many times online. But this pulls it all together.The menu system in the experience takes some getting used to. There's some odd horizontal vs vertical vs "click enter" stuff going on with the different selections. So I had to backtrack after a while as only then did I realize I could press enter to view more images under the same selection. But it's no biggie.Enjoyed it!
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic format, an interactive museum, and I'd like to see more games showcased like this.  I missed entirely Karateka along with a ton of early computer games when they came out so I really hope to see more like this.  Many more games should have their stories told and preserved, I absolutely recommend picking this up.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I love playing games while learning history of gaming simultaneously. If only all lessons at the school or college can be fun like this. :3If any of you are PC gamers since the psychedelic 80s era, then you surely knew or heard about Karateka (1984) and also Prince of Persia (1989). I played both and love it without knowing who is the creator and how he made those two famous games just by himself. Geniuses are so rare nowadays.This is a complete archives of everything related to Karateka, and you can play the very earliest version to the remake one but still got the classic vibe. But keep in mind that the Remake Version of Karateka which released on 2012 is sold separately, not in these archives.Overall, this is truly an interactive documentary for a remastered game. Thank you, Jordan Mechner. I truly respect and salute you!b(^_^)d
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Getting this out of the way first: the experience was not "structured" the way I thought it would be. I'll get more into this later but be aware that there is a fair amount of work on the player to "assemble" the experience here.I'm really enjoying what this groundbreaking release is: a combination of  a gaming documentary with actual gameplay to help create a whole new experience. This is a must-try for any retro game enthusiast whether you've heard of Karateka or not. I really, really hope to see more of these and a Nintendo or Sega one would be incredible.My only criticism is this felt a little half-baked/unpolished and could have benefited from a more "guided" experience - less input from the player in order to advance the content. They did a wonderful job with the documentary footage and the structure of the documentary in general (having you play the prototypes first and then watching the story behind them) but I hated getting booted back to the UI where I needed to navigate to the next section. It totally took me out of the experience and it made it diffcult to enjoy the experience with other people who wanted to watch too.I was going into this figuring the experience went like this:Video footage > player taken directly into a game while commentary continued > once player was ready to move on they'd press a button > right back into video footage > repeat till endInstead it was like:Navigate slightly confusing UI to start the experience > first video ends....booted back to UI > manually cycle through things but I wanted to get back to the movie > finally found the selection for back to the movie > back to the UI > now I'm playing a prototype thats awesome > ok where is the next part of the movie I dont want to look at photos just put them in the movie! > back to the movie finally > another game to play, cool > ugh more non-movie/non-game stuffI really just wanted them to take me through the movie and games without needing to return me to the navigation UI. This would've worked so much better as a Netflix "experience" like Bandersnatch.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Works flawlessly on the Steam Deck. Absolutely amazing experience that feels like you are playing a wonderful documentary. From the prototypes all the way to modern remaster the entire journey is unlike anything I’ve played before. Can’t wait to play the next game in Digital Eclipse’s Gold Master Series—which feels like it’s the “Criterion” of gaming!
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: In a perfect universe all games' histories would receive such a loving and thorough treatment. This is a combination of a special features disc on a deluxe 4K boutique Blu-ray, and a museum exhibition, and it's fun! Even the earliest, roughest prototypes (there are playable prototypes!) are fun. What better way to understand the history of such an important work of art than to experience its growth and changes directly? I hope to see many more like it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: I got to interview Karateka creator Jordan Mechner about this project for , and I'll slap a telling quote here:---"Karateka was really the culmination of a six-year timeframe," Mechner says. "From getting my first Apple II in 1978 as a freshman in high school, I made games, and each time I kind of hoped that it would get published. All of those 'almosts,' each raised the bar a little bit. All that time, the industry was evolving very fast as I was trying to evolve as a game developer. So Karateka really brought together everything I’d learned on the previous attempts—and it makes the most sense in the context of those earlier games."When pressed on this point, Mechner offers a rare tinge of regret: “Especially when I was a young developer, I would have loved to have an exhibit like [Making of Karateka] about any game I had played and liked! At age 16, 17, I was in the dark. Not just about the technical aspects, but also the human side of programming. How does it work? What’s your relationship like as an author with the publisher, with players, with other people? To see somebody else go through that, all the emotional ups and downs. The excitement, the disappointment, the blind alleys: I love that.”---As far as a "review," Making of Karateka is a fantastic opening salvo from the Gold Master Series, and I hope it's indicative of much more to come. If you've seen Atari 50, the setup is similar, only instead of telling the story of an entire company, this collection uses old documentation, recent interviews, *and* freshly unearthed prototypes of prior games to focus its lens on a single masterwork game, Karateka. The approach does a great job showing how Jordan Mechner started as a teenager making Asteroids clones, only to mature rapidly to make a game unlike anything else of its time. Context matters when approaching older games, and that's why I love Digital Eclipse's approach here.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Here you will find a list of problems about Digital Eclipse: Interactive documentary (same interface as the Atari 50) that brings a lot of information about the development of Karateka and other games by Jordan Mechner (creator of Karateka and Prince of Persia).List of "14" games:Karateka - Apple IIKarateka C64Karateka - Atari 8-bitKarateka RemasteredDeathbounce: ReboundedDeathbounce First PrototypeDeathbounce "Colored Balls" PrototypeDeathbounce "Little Man" PrototypeDeathbounce "Space Train" PrototypeKarateka Jordan's PrototypeKarateka Brøderbund Prototype 1Karateka Brøderbund Prototype 2Asteroid BlasterStar BlasterPositive points:Good emulation;Extras that are interesting to watch.Negative points: Karateka had several versions, both for computers from the 80s and video games, but it only includes the c64, Apple 2 and Atari 800 versions, because the devs say that these are the best versions. As someone who thinks the preservation of games is important, they could have included all versions of the game, and I still think there are several versions of Karateka that are not present in the collection, but it is better than the c64 version. Missing versions: Atari 7800, NES, MSX, NEC PC 9801, ZX Spectrum, Atari ST, IBM PC/DOS, Amstrad CPC, Game Boy. Ask anyone who bought the game if they wanted more versions (even if they weren't as good as the originals).BUGS: It happened a few times that I played Karateka c64 or Karateka Remastered, and the space image appeared when I ctrl-clicked.Once it happened that I couldn't play the c64 version, and I was forced to leave and enter the game.I played on the keyboard and could identify these bugs, but there are also controller bugs that some users are reporting in the community tab.Conclusion: I particularly enjoyed the collection, both the interactive documentary and the included games. It's worth the price, but I was very disappointed that not every game was included (and Digital Eclipse could have done that).6,5 (I wish there was a neutral review option.)The low score was because Digital Eclipse has a history of leaving several bugs and not correcting them, as is the case with SNK 40th ANNIVERSARY COLLECTION and Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The Making of Karateka is a master class in game preservation and is essentially a digital museum. It's amazing that Jordan Mechner held on to all of this material for 40 years and that we get to glimpse into how the games industry operated in it's infancy thanks to his efforts to preserve all of this material. Digital Eclipse did an amazing job with presentation from the interface down to the sound design. It feels great being able to flip through concept art, listen to Kirk Hamilton talk about the importance of Francis Mechner's influence on game composition, examine 3D mockups of game disks and box art, and play various iterations of both Deathbounce and Karateka. A wonderful and masterful work of video game preservation by Digital Eclipse and Jordan Mechner.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: This is amazing. It manages to squeeze a gripping narrative from the act of parsing old docs, it’s really good in telling its story, it lets you play with prototypes and put your hands on stuff that is usually not accessible, it contains well emulated classics and also adds two very good modern remakes, that let you play in a more welcoming way games from forty years ago. It’s full of great ideas and unexpected ways of deconstructing an old game. I hope they will make dozens of these, if only because it seems like it could be a very versatile approach, with very different ways of doing a similar thing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A masterclass in game preservation and history; The Making of Karateka is the type of preservation I wish I could see for many older games. Imagine if games like Wolfenstein or Doom had as high quality interactive art experiences like this? From getting the interviews, the documents, the art, uncovering lost content, and then topping it off with the best version of Karateka classic to play; it's a perfect preservationist piece.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A fascinating in-depth look at the making of a video game classic.I’ve known about Karateka for decades but never had the chance to play it.  As a young teen in the 1980s, I would watch with fascination as the demo ran at my local computer shop until I saved up enough money to buy my own copy for the Commodore 64, but, unfortunately, the third party disk drive my dad had bought was apparently only 99.99% compatible with Commodore’s own 1541 disk drive, and it seems Karateka was the only disc it wasn’t compatible with, and so, sadly, I had to return it for a refund.And now, four decades later with “The Making of Karateka”, I finally have the opportunity to not only play this piece of video game history, but to also learn about the history behind the history.  Developer Digital Eclipse has created one of the best documentary packages I’ve ever seen, with video interviews and archival footage, photographs, original concept art, design documents, correspondence, and, of course, the multiple versions of the games themselves, all combined into an interactive timeline that takes you on a journey from designer Jordan Mechner’s childhood and early fascination with computers, through several failed video game projects, to the making of the titular game, and, finally, a look at the genesis of the never developed sequel which eventually morphed into Prince of Persia (“But that's a story for another time…”).Along the way, you'll find a number of playable games that include Mechner’s earliest effort for the Apple II called Asteroid Blaster, a pixel perfect clone of Atari’s Asteroids, which turned out to be a little  perfect since the publisher who bought it was immediately slapped with a cease and desist from Atari!  Next is Mechner’s followup project, the absurdly titled Death Bounce which went through a number of iterations but was never finished to publisher Broderbund’s satisfaction, and as you play the various prototypes and multiple attempts at a finished game, you can’t help but agree with their decision.  Finally, there’s Karateka which is presented through several prototypes showcasing its evolving development, and three versions of the finished game for the Apple II, Commodore 64, and Atari 800 computers.  While Karateka was ported to many other systems, Digital Eclipse decided to focus on only the versions that Mechner was directly involved with.  The emulation here is perfect, and the games all look and play exactly like they did on original hardware.  To enhance the authenticity, the screen is bordered by the outlines of a bulky monitor and rendered with simulated scanlines and a slight barrel distortion to mimic the CRT displays of old, but this can be disabled in the settings if you find it objectionable.  There are also options to switch from the original one- and two-button control schemes to a six-button variation that is a bit easier to play, and you can lock the framerate for consistent performance, but I personally prefer to leave those settings off to enjoy these games as they originally were.As if that wasn’t enough, developer Digital Eclipse went above and beyond, creating two new games, a remaster of both Death Bounce and Karateka, to round out this collection.  Each remaster retains the old school charm of the originals with high fidelity pixel art, but they play with the speed and fluidity of a modern game.  Now Death Bounce might sound like an odd inclusion given Broderbund’s dissatisfaction with Mechner’s attempts to bring it to completion, but with this remaster, you can see that there was actually a really good idea there for a fun game even if Mechner was unable to realize it at the time, due, perhaps, to his inexperience and the limited hardware of the Apple II.  As for the Karateka remaster, it simply plays like a better looking, more fluid version of the original, and while it’s still great fun and has added value with developer commentary, a time trial mode, and achievements, I prefer the look and feel of the originals.  There's just something about those chunky sprites that I find endearing.It took me about five hours to get through this interactive documentary, and I enjoyed every moment of it learning a lot of things I didn't know before, such as a letter from Broderbund to Mechner that mentioned a special fast loader on the Commodore 64 disc that was likely the culprit that stopped me from playing the game all those decades ago!  And the games themselves naturally have tremendous replay value which makes “The Making of Karateka” well worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A really well-crafted piece of interactive media, that sets a very high bar for future video game "making of" projects. I had only vaguely heard of Karateka before, but nevertheless really enjoyed how this story was told. All the supporting documents, assets and (playable) prototypes are presented in a neat timeline, alongside the released games and remasters, with video interviews that tie it all together into a great story.If you have an interest in video game history, solo video game development, or game publishing in the 1980s, do yourself a favor and check this out!
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: As an old school gamer who grew up playing this game on the old Apple IIe after school.  This was a great trip down memory lane.  I absolutely loved everything from the original game, to the remastered version.The documentary is great to see the history behind the game.  If you love the history of the gaming industry, this is a must.  However, if you don't like the old school games and are into a lot of greatest, newest, eye candy .... this is not for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This release, like Atari 50 before it, is amazing. I'm so happy that Digital Eclipse has gone down this road of creating true retrospective re-releases. This is so much more than just a re-release of Karateka, one of the most important games of the Apple II era. _childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge Jordan Mechnerd, this game/documentary is incredible. Seeing the notes and playable games from an ambitious young game designer in the early 80s is endlessly interesting as a historical piece and in contrast to how the industry has changed since the innovative Kareteka. I would like to see this type of presentation on more of Mechner's work and other landmark games in general.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: My review video: This is the first entry in Digital Eclipse's new Gold Master Series, where they take a single game or series and do a deep dive on it, working in partnership with its creator. It's less a game and more an interactive documentary, with a timeline including video interviews, historical clips, high-res scans of art and development assets, among other things that detail not only how the game was made, but how it influenced the industry today. It's presented in a slick interface that's easy to navigate. You also have access to various different versions of Karateka, including prototypes of both this and some of Jordan Mechner's other earlier games, plus modern remakes of Karateka and Deathbounce made by Digital Eclipse that look and play great, complete with in-game goals and developer commentary.To most younger players, Karateka isn't a name that necessarily means anything, but it is formative and critical to many of the mechanics and trends that came in gaming after it, even to this day. Packages like this aren't for everyone and Digital Eclipse knows this, but if you have an interest in gaming and industry history, this is a great and importantly, interactive way to learn some cool things about a game that's heavily contributed to games that we know today. Even as someone who knew a lot of the history of this beforehand, I still very much enjoyed myself and highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: A remarkable achievement, and a must-play for anyone interested in game history or in the possibilities of interactive documentaries, for which this (hopefully) represents the new standard. To be fair, I don't imagine many other subjects would offer such a depth of primary sources to work from (multiple playable prototypes of a 40 year-old unpublished game? Really?). But here's hoping!Random stuff I learned:
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: If you are at all interested in early video game history or have enjoyed Karateka at some point, I highly recommend picking this up. It's a very rich multimedia documentary of sorts with most playable versions of Karateka as well as a variety of other early games Jordan Mechner developed during that time. It also contains a brand new Karateka and Deathbounce remaster by Digital Eclipse that is worth the price alone. Just a fantastic experience all around.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The Making of Karateka is a must-have for any fan of classic video games and anyone interested in the medium as an art form. This interactive documentary tells the story of the creation of one of the most influential games of all time, from its humble beginnings as a college project to its current cult status (and I was there when it was originally released).The documentary is packed with fascinating details, including never-before-seen concept art, interviews with the original developers, super-interesting official documents between Jordan and the publisher, and even playable prototypes of various games. It's a fascinating look at the creative process as a whole.They also added Deathbounce: Rebounded, a new game inspired by the original Deathbounce prototype. It's amazing what they've done to honor the original concept.Digital Eclipse's work exceeds all expectations that a retro game fan could have. The documentary is well done and informative, the interviews with the original developers are fascinating, and the playable prototypes are a great bonus. I did not expect it to be this good, this is something that should be preserved in a museum, this is the well documented history of the pioneers who contributed to create this multi-billion dollar industry. Thank you, Digital Eclipse.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: After this game and the equally excellent Atari50, Digital Ellipse has become the gold standard for presenting older games in their proper historical context, with the necessary background information that helps people understand why these games were so important to video game history.The information is provided via an interactive timeline that's intuitive to use and easy to follow and understand. Digital Eclipse has organized everything here in a way that naturally tells a story and properly puts the context needed around Karateka to understand its impact. I wasn't familiar with the game before playing this, and now I *get* it. The older, mostly unmodified games play ... pretty similarly to how you'd expect. Your mileage will vary on those, but it's at least nice to play through the stuff you've been reading/watching about. Having modern touches such as rewind is also nice. The new remastered games are excellent, and play as well as anything you'd buy on the market today. If you're at all interested in video game history and how this medium came to be what it is today, feel you owe it to yourself to play this game. Karateka may not ultimately be the most important game in the world, but packages like The Making of Karateka are a crucial way to bring back the context and background needed to understand how we got from Karateka to the games of today. Really hope this is the start of a long-running series by Digital Eclipse, but even if it's not, this is well worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone who played this game back in the day then I HIGHLY recommend this, also for those interested in game history. For anyone younger or haven't experienced older games such as Karateka then I would say pass on it. It will just feel archaic to you. Broght back so many memories for me and finally explained to me why that damn bird always killed me. (Apparently it's insta-kill if you had a pirated copy, which my parents had gotten this copy from a neighbor on our Commodore 64. Hope no-one comes and arrests them now 40 years later.)
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: The Making of Karateka is the flagship entry of Digital Eclipse's new Gold Masters Series, a line of interactive documentaries using the format of their previous release Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration and paring it down for smaller, more specific stories. As the title indicates, this one covers the development of Karateka, a mid-1980s action game that incorporated cinematic elements. It dives into the background of developer Jordan Mechner, including his previous releases and a canceled prototype for a commercial game, the process of porting the game to other platforms, and even how it led into his next game, Prince of Persia. It does so with large library of documentary featurettes, design documents, business letters, and marketing materials, and it even has a interactive demonstration of the game's animation process. Of course, it also includes multiple versions of Karateka itself, including a number of prototypes, multiple ports, and even a new remaster that tightens up the experience, as well as prototypes for the aforementioned canceled title Deathbounce. And all of this is arranged in a compelling chronology that's easy to follow and navigate.Karateka gets little in the way of fanfare nowadays, but The Making of Karateka makes a strong case for the game's place in the canon of video game history, as well as a strong case for future Gold Masters Series releases.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorites as a young teen and now I know the story behind it! Hot from the heels of Atari 50, Digital Eclipse has done it again with The Making of Karateka. Until now, I only played the Atari 8-Bit version - it was wonderful expierencing the Apple II & Commodore 64 versions as well as the prototypes. Remastered versions of pre-Karateka game, Deathbounce and of course, the remasterd Karateka our my faves and I can't stop playing them. The interviews and archival footage and photos make this package a must for retro fans.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent interactive documentary and a thorough preservation of a landmark title. Tons of fascinating photos, concept art, interviews and archive footage, what I like most are the old prototypes Jordan Mechner coded, now made available to play, plus a really cool remaster of Deathbounce, with modern twin stick shooter controls. And of course the crown jewel of the whole set, a terrific remaster of Karateka, with a lovely look, great attention and love spent on it, and it plays better than ever. I am excited to see what Digital Eclipse can do next with this Gold Master series, I would absolutely love a similarly comprehensive package for Prince of Persia 1&2.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: This is a medium-pushing work, and I'd call it a new standard were it not for the fact that Karateka is one of the most well-documented classic games, so it'd be unreasonable to expect this much of all video game documentaries. That said, this new documentary format is one I can get behind fully. The ability to explore all the scans and games at my own pace rather than be told about it in a linear movie format is something I've never experienced with a documentary before, and I want more of it. I highly anticipate the next game this studio covers, whatever that may be.My only real criticism would be that it relies heavily on screenshots for representing the ports of Karateka that are not included, which made me want to play them and mildly disappointed that I couldn't do so within this collection. The versions that are included are very solid though with great emulation and unexpectedly good screen options.
_childDocuments_.name: The Making of Karateka

_childDocuments_.review: Digital Eclipse’s Making of Karateka is a fantastic interactive documentary giving a Criterion Collection quality exploration of a game as well as persevering it to allow people to play it. The collection focuses on Jordan Mechner’s early years in game dev up until the release of Karateka and its ports. The collection is structured in chapters chronologically with each chapter being comprised of timelines that showcase a smorgasbord of information dealing with Mechner’s early works and Karateka. This information includes content such as concept art, magazine articles, interactive viewers that allow you to see how the animation process of Karateka was designed, and present day interviews with people like Mechner, some of the old Broderbund crew who worked on Karateka, and game devs inspired by the game such as Tom Hall and John Tobias. The way this all is structured is really engaging. The interviews dealing with Mechner’s early years are especially charming as he and his dad reminisce how the whole family inspired and worked to help Jordan make Karateka like how his dad dressed up in a karate gi and essentially did the motion capture for the Karateka MC and how he composed the whole soundtrack. Making of Karateka also does a splendid job preserving not only Karateka and two of its most popular ports, but it also has playable prototype builds. It also has previously unreleased games Mechner made before Karateka complete with earlier design builds as well, one of them being Death Bounce, an Asteroids inspired space shooter. There’s just so much clear love and care put in this collection’s creation and it’s truly splendid to see, especially because video game history and preservation isn’t considered as a serious undertaking compared to older artistic mediums such as literature and film. Video games, being the youngest of the mediums, was born in the age of mass corporatization where being a product that sells is considered to be far more important than being of piece of artistic media that should be celebrated. Films managed to emerge right before rampant commercialization happened so they were still able to be considered art that needed to be preserved, but games haven’t been as lucky and tend to just be considered expendable products, especially by major publishers. It’s just so heartening to see something like this exist. I do have one problem when it comes to this whole package though, I think Karateka is just a straight up bad game. Karateka may have been a technical marvel at the time, as the documentary materials extensively shows, but it has completely aged like milk and is just not a good game to actually play anymore, especially in the present when a vast plethora of games have surpassed it in all regards. It’s slow, clunky, and repetitive, combat is just mainly spamming kick and moving and back forth, the hitbox on the eagle is an absolute pain in the ass, and running is super awkward and can lead to enemies’ one-shotting you if you don’t get into combat stance fast enough. There’s no lives or continues so you just gotta slog through all those boring fights and unskippable cutscenes all over again. I’m admittedly not a big fan of 80’s games, but I can pick up games like Super Mario Bros., Tetris, or Galaga and have fun with them and respect their quality, plus they’re still quite accessible. Karateka is just miserable, to the point I’m surprised people even liked it at the time. Like it’s kinda sad to me the most fun I had with Jordan Mechner’s older games in this collection was his blatant ripoff of Asteroids he made in high school. Similar to my thoughts on Night Dive’s remaster of Rise of the Triad this year, I feel Digital Eclipse gave a gold star treatment polishing to a turd, an influential one, but a turd nonetheless. Digital Eclipse also did their own remasters of Karateka and Death Bounce, they’re more playable but they still don’t really salvage the games at all to me. The Karateka remaster does add the option of giving yourselves extra lives and it does play a little better but it adds the leopard that got the cut from the original game and that section is just awful. The Death Bounce remaster is okay, though I feel the Rover is just kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, though arcade space shooters ain’t really my forte.Overall Making of Karateka is a wonderful documentary and preservation package for a game that has unfortunately not stood the test of time at all. Regardless if you have any interest in video game history I whole-heartedly recommend it. Definitely looking forward to Digital Eclipse possibly making this an entire series and cover games that were influential and actually good, like Doom or Monkey Island. Man, I want a Doom one so bad…
