_childDocuments_.review: This is magnificent from start to finish.The ethos of the Gold Master Series complements the interdisciplinary design innovations that defined Karateka, which is likely the primary reason the making of this game is the showcase debut for this series.  Just as the game uses tropes from action/adventure stories, cinema generally, and martial arts movies in particular, the series uses existing formats and techniques--video interviews, design specs, process docs--with elements that are singular to gaming--interactivity, playable prototypes and remasters, analyses of game bugs and how bugs can turn into features and vice versa--to elevate what could have been a stale hagiographic making-of yarn into something genuinely intriguing and engaging that forefronts gaming's best, most definitive attributes.There are some things I didn't like, and would appreciate seeing improved as this series progresses.  First, there were a lot of personal, hand-written documents, which is great!  I think that you can't get a fuller, better source of the who, how, and why of a game than from the pen of the creator, but only if the hand-written material is clearly legible.  I understand the importance and the authenticity driving the use of these sources, and I don't suggest eliminating them; I recommend complementing them with a type-written transcription, so that you get the original documents in concert with text that is clearly legible.  The game does something similar to this already; multiple pages are quoted directly from Mechner's journals during the time he spent conceptualizing and realizing Karateka, and these are all typed transcriptions, not hand-written.  In cases where the handwriting quality of the author interferes with audience understanding--as here, for me--I'd like to see typed transcription complementing all of the handwritten sources, not just some isolated cases.The biggest criticism I have of this game specifically (and what I'd like most to see addressed as the series progresses), is that the making of Karateka wasn't acculturated enough, meaning that, beyond three game makers who were clearly enamored with and influenced by Karateka, attesting as they did in their interviews, what was the game's larger influence on gaming culture and pop culture, and how did contemporaneous culture influence the game as it was being made?  This is especially pertinent in Karateka's case, where explicit racism was used as a marketing tactic--the hero looks like Don Johnson just walked off the set of Miami Vice and into Medieval Japan, and the villain's primarily villainous quality is that he's Japanese, according to some character concept documents--to promote the game, echoing the methods and strategies of sibling media from that era like the Karate Kid.  The Digital Eclipse-developed remaster included in this game addresses this by making the player character and Mariko Japanese, although they saddle the PC with a truly embarrassing haircut as an apparent homage to the white savior of the original game.  A distillation of what I'd like to see in future titles in this series is this:  How did this game fit within the culture of the time it was made, and how did pop culture respond to the existence of this game?Overall, this is an excellent game, and an awesome exemplification of the techniques and artistry that make games great, as well as spotlighting the interesting and influential people who make those games.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a lucky little kid. I got to play all kinds of great computer games on my granddad's IBM compatible 286 and my mom's Commodore VIC-20, Commodore 64 and Atari 2600. Unfortunately for me, the only place I got to play Karateka was on DOS in EGA mode (not one of the 3 best versions). It still struck me as something amazing and has been in my brain ever since.The Making of Karateka is a fantastic product, and I loved hearing the story of Jordan and his father Francis. Everyone associated Jordan Mechner with Prince of Persia, but this truly is where it his career picked up steam. If you're at all interested in the history of video games, do yourself a favor and pick up a copy of this and savor every minute... and go get Atari 50 while you're at it haha

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic museum piece about a foundational game and what went into its creation  - including design documents, prototypes, and interviews with the creator and publisher.  A unique package that helped me understand why a game that is almost as old as I am captured the hearts and imagination of so many game developers, and why it deserves a place in history.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★Karateka, a classic that captivated a generation, has been masterfully reborn in its Steam version, 'Making of Karateka.' This game not only pays homage to the original but elevates it to new heights with its intricate storytelling and innovative gameplay mechanics.From the opening scene, you're drawn into a beautifully crafted world that blends nostalgia with cutting-edge graphics. The developers have done a phenomenal job of preserving the essence of the original while infusing it with modern elements that resonate with today’s gaming community.The combat system is a standout feature, striking a perfect balance between challenging and rewarding. It maintains the original's rhythm-based mechanics but enhances them with a variety of new moves and strategies, keeping the gameplay fresh and engaging.The narrative aspect of 'Making of Karateka' is another area where the game truly shines. The story is rich and immersive, with well-developed characters and a compelling plot that keeps you hooked from start to finish.The attention to detail in this game is remarkable. From the authentic sound effects to the culturally rich landscapes, every aspect has been crafted with care and respect for the source material. It’s evident that the developers are not only skilled but also passionate about this project.In conclusion, 'Making of Karateka' on Steam is a triumphant revival of a beloved classic. It offers a seamless blend of old and new, making it a must-play for both fans of the original and newcomers to the franchise. It’s a testament to how classic games can be reinvented for the modern era while respecting their roots. An absolute masterpiece and a jewel in the crown of Steam's game library

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed learning the history of a game I never even played before. I didn´t know how many things Karateka did first and how important it really was for Video Games as a whole. I also love that there are builds for games Jordan did before Karateka included in here. The Beta builds of Karateka itself a re a really nice touch too of course. I had a lot of fun with the several builds of Deathbounce and I think that Deathbounce: Rebounded really could, and should be, a available as a  stand-alone release for a few bucks.What I do find puzzling, and a bit disappointing really, is the fact that there are "only" 3 historical retail versions here. You get the Apple II, Commodore 64 and Atari 8-Bit versions in here. All other versions are either just mentioned, or at best showcased with a few screenshots. It kinda feels a bit incomplete by not having those other historical ports in here.Still very recommended to anyone interested in Video Game History.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first interactive documentary I've experienced, and it is amazing!The amount of effort Digital Eclipse put into documenting the making of the game, allowing us to play the classic games made by Jordan Mechner, and even allowing us to play the remakes of the original games was worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: (for whatever reason, my steam deck didn't sync up all of my playtime, which is higher than listed)As someone who loved Atari 50, I had to pick this up, despite not knowing anything about this game other than it being a precursor to the massive hit Prince of Persia, a franchise that continues on and off to this day. A great thing about Atari 50, which this continues, is that largely if I played Karateka in a vacuum I'd shrug and say "ok well that's kind of interesting for the time, so what?" This thoroughly makes you care about the game, explain why its so important, how it developed (including prototypes and a ditched previous game he was working on), and beyond that its just a nice sweet documentary about a very supportive dad allowing his son to follow his muse even though it was just murdering him academically. I'm now a Karateka fan! I get it! I'm also now just in the tank for whatever Digital Eclipse makes in this Gold Master Series. _childDocuments_.review: The faithful recreation of Karateka provided nostalgia as I replayed it just as it was originally on the Apple II. The collection includes several other versions, and prototypes as well. The presentation of the game, and the history around its creation was an excellent museumesque experience, and an wonderful example of video game preservation.Not only is Karateka included but also a few other games and protypes that Mechner created while a student at Yale. The developers of this title remade both Karakeka, and Deathbounce as with improved graphics, and some changes in design while preserving the identity of the originals.

_childDocuments_.review: Even leading up to its release, I wasn’t sure what exactly The Making of Karateka would turn out to be. A collection of games? A documentary with interviews? Some remasters or reinterpretations of the original titles? All of it, turns out. And it’s a fascinating compilation that, in a way, was possible due to how impactful and important Karateka was and because Jordan Mechner, its creator, detailed his experiences in a diary that was published as a book years ago.While I can’t say that Karateka had a huge impact on me directly, after all it was released before I was born, I still vividly remember encountering it in my childhood and being fascinated by it. I’m not sure if I had already experienced Prince of Persia by that point or not, a game that had a far greater influence on how I saw games, I still liked elegant simplicity of its design in both gameplay and storytelling. I also remembered how incredibly rude several traps and enemies were, which was unfortunately reflective of the game design school of the time. Though, I’ll still give Karateka that it, at least, had not too many cheap ways of killing you that you could not predict. Those that were there were very cruel, however.So it was very curious to see how exactly this game came to be and the experience of doing it through The Making of Karateka felt very novel. You get your interviews and videos, as one would expect from a documentary, and those are full of interesting facts and details. But also you get scans of documents, photographs and physical objects that you can rotate and read. And on top of that, and most interestingly, you get faithful recreations of different versions of two games. An unreleased title Deathbounce, that was developed right before switching to Karateka, and the main game itself. And by different versions I mean several prototype versions and games that were never released before, the retail versions of Karateka on Apple II, Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit and new remastered versions created specifically for this collections. You can just play the games from the game library, but the intended experience is going through the timeline of events that mix all of these mediums together into one coherent journey.Of course, the question is – how fun is it to play Karateka today in any of the available versions? Well… That’s a bit of a tough one. I would say – yes. Even if only for historic value. While the game might feel slow and even sluggish, even in the Remastered version, and some occasional traps are genuinely unfun, there’s still a lot of wonderful craft behind the title. And some of the ideas feel ingenious. The two stances, that would become even more important in Prince of Persia, have since defined entire genres, where you have different sets of controls depending on you’re attacking or exploring. The way your and enemy health regenerates during battle and between battles strikes a really curious balance between being patient but also being aggressive. Some of the cinematic techniques and general framing of the shots in the game still look fantastic. And while I question the desire to keep some of the jank of the original games and even add new one by restoring originally not implemented ideas, I also appreciate how original versions of the game allow some quality of life features and a rewind feature while the Remastered version allows you to have more than one life.It looks like Digital Eclipse is marketing this as a start of a collection of interactive documentaries and I can’t wait to see what other games will get a similar treatment. But starting with Karateka seemed like a very smart choice and I recommend checking The Making of Karateka to people who grew up playing this game at some point in their life and those, who love videogames but have never heard about this classic gem before.

_childDocuments_.review:
Prince of Persia creator Jordan Mechner was a college student when he created one of the biggest-selling games of 1984: Karateka. Now, in a new interactive documentary from Digital Eclipse, the story of how a teenager with an Apple II created one of the most groundbreaking, influential games of all time.

THE ORIGIN STORY OF A LEGENDARY GAME CREATOR

Discover how Karateka was made through an exhaustive archive of design documents, playable prototypes, and all-new video features. Like walking through a museum, you can explore the interactive timelines at your own pace.

PLAY THE ACCLAIMED ORIGINALS

Enjoy pixel-perfect versions of the original Karateka games and a variety of never-before-seen early prototypes, with rich quality-of-life features like save anywhere, rewind, chapter select, and director's commentary.

TWO REMASTERED GAMES

Karateka Remastered is an all-new version of the original game featuring cutting-room-floor content, commentary, achievements, and more. Deathbounce: Rebounded is a fast and frantic twin-stick shooter based on Jordan's unpublished prototype.

A GROUNDBREAKING MASTERPIECE

Discover how Karateka became one of the first games to include cinematic scenes, a moving original soundtrack, rotoscoped animation, and a Hollywood-style love story, influencing the decades of games that followed.
